result of a military coup. The political his-
tory of Ecuador is similar to that of other
Latin American countries, with democratic
governments, military rule, and nonmili-
tary dictatorships taking turns in power
throughout most of the twentieth century.
Land distribution in Ecuador is skewed in
favor of large estates, although not as se-
verely as in some other Latin American
countries. There are some moderate-sized
farms, but many of the poorer farmers have
very small plots of land, and many other
people who live off the land have never
been able to obtain formal title to it and are
labeled squatters.
According to a report produced in
2004 by Ecuador’s Ministry of Foreign
Affairs, the bulk of the country’s trade with
Africa takes place with Algeria, the Republic
of Congo, Madagascar, Egypt, Ghana,
Morocco, and South Africa. Ecuador has
also recently traded with Botswana, Côte
d’Ivoire, Guinea, Equatorial Guinea, the
Seychelles, Kenya, Libya, Malawi, Namibia,
Nigeria, and the Central African Republic.
From 1995 through 2002 the trade balance
was in favor of the African countries. The
balance shifted toward Ecuador in 2003
and 2004 due to increased exports by
Ecuador to Egypt, Ghana, Madagascar,
Equatorial Guinea, and South Africa and
to a gradual elimination over a span of
several years of liqueﬁed petroleum gas
imports from Algeria and Congo. The year
2004 saw reduced trade with Algeria,
Egypt, and Ghana but increased trade with
Congo, Madagascar, and South Africa.
Ecuador’s exports to African countries
include a wide variety of items, including
bananas, palm hearts, passion fruit, sardines,
tuna and other ﬁsh, coffee, roses, and
scopolamine, a drug used in nonprescription
sedatives. Ecuador’s imports from Africa
include liqueﬁed petroleum gas, hydrocar-
bons, butane, propane, laminated iron
products, wire, and acrylics.
There are also historical ties between
Ecuador and Africa resulting from the slave
trade, which brought Africans to Ecuador
and other Latin American countries during
and after Spanish colonial times. Although
the government does not track the country’s
population by ethnicity, scholars estimate
that from 5 to 13 percent of the population
is of African descent. The failure to
acknowledge openly racial differences while
persisting in racial discrimination results in
the economic and political invisibility of
people mostly of indigenous or African her-
itage. Most of the current black population
lives in Esmeraldas province, Imbabura
province, and Carchi province. Blacks con-
stitute the largest ethnic group in Esmeraldas,
a remote northwestern area where very little
infrastructure is provided by the state. Blacks
have lived in the northwestern part of the
country since the mid-1500s. During the
late 1500s, fortiﬁed villages called palenques
were built in that area by runaway slaves.
Communities of blacks and Chachi Indians
are still referred to by blacks as palenques.
In the late 1990s, blacks and Chachis
began to organize with the goal of demanding

EFIK
The Eﬁk people are an ethnic group, located
in present-day southeastern Nigeria, whose
origins go back to the fourteenth century;
they have lived in the Cross River region
since that time and have been involved in in-
ternational trade, including the transatlantic
slave trade, since the ﬁfteenth century. 
The Eﬁk migrated from the hinterland
to the coastal region to work as ﬁshermen.
During the migration, settlements were
formed among the Ibibio and Igbo people
inland. T welve Eﬁk clans migrated from
Ibom, an Igbo area, to the Ibibio area of
Uruan, where they ﬁrst became known as
the Eﬁk people. The name “Eﬁk” is said to
derive from the Ibibio word ﬁk(to oppress).
When the Eﬁk left Uruan, seven clans formed
the ﬁrst Eﬁk settlement at Ikpaene; they
moved to found Creek T own on the Cross
River several generations later. The Eﬁk
people were early inhabitants of the town
of Calabar, alongside the Qua and the Efut
peoples. Early Eﬁk ﬁshing communities
consisted of patriarchal family units based
around minor lineage segments of the clans.
Each family was headed by the etinyin, the
oldest male in the paternal line, and families
were grouped into obio (towns) based upon
clans. From the fifteenth century, the
transatlantic slave trade transformed Eﬁk
economic and social organization, and
“houses” ( ufok) emerged as important
social institutions. Houses were corporate
groups organized around a major lineage
segment, which traded independently with
the Europeans. Each house was headed by
an etubom, who was selected according to
skills in coordinating the canoe system of
transport and trade networks that brought
slaves and palm oil from inland areas.
Houses were grouped into obio (towns),
each headed by an obong (king). In the
nineteenth century, European shippers,
missionaries, and the British consul came
to inﬂuence the appointment of kings, with
the consul crowning King Archibong III as
the obong of Duke T own in 1878.
The ekpe (leopard) secret society ﬁrst
appeared among the Eﬁk in the seventeenth
century, and it became the highest authority
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 480 ---
404 E GYPT
of law and order. Eﬁk traders and kings,
and European traders as well, could join
the society for a fee. By the nineteenth cen-
tury, a small group of wealthy Eﬁk traders
had centralized political and economic
power through their control of trade and
the higher grades of ekpe. In the colonial
era, the Presbyterian mission and the
British consul coopted the authority of the
ekpe society to impose colonial edicts.
Holding high ekpe grades remains presti-
gious within Eﬁk society; members take
part in rituals associated with traditional
kingship, and their land and other property
are safeguarded by the society.
Centuries of international trade meant
that many Eﬁk people were literate, with
some proﬁcient in several European lan-
guages, when a Presbyterian mission reached
Calabar in 1846. The mission published an
Eﬁk translation of the Bible in 1868 and
an Eﬁk-English dictionary in 1888. The
indigenous cosmology encountered by the
mission continues to have importance in
contemporary Eﬁk society. Eﬁk cosmology
is centered around a supreme being, Abasi
Ibom. Ndem are intermediaries between
Abasi Ibom and the human world, and are
examples of the mami wata spirits found
along the West African coast. Each Eﬁk
town continues to be associated with a
Ndem, and the unity of all Eﬁk people is
represented by the tutelary deity, Ndem
Eﬁk.
The Eﬁk diaspora includes people liv-
ing in Europe, North America, Angola, and
Cuba and reflects the long history of
Calabar as an international port. In the
twentieth century, Eﬁk people have made
many important contributions to Nigerian
literature, music, and politics. The play-
wright James Ene Henshaw dramatized the
colonial era in This Is Our Chance (1956)
and A Man of Character (1956), while the
educator, Dr. Ekpo Amaku, was the author
of school texts and poetry. Adebayo Martins,
whose mother was Eﬁk, was a pioneer of
Afro-jazz in the 1950s and 1960s, predating
the music of Fela Anikulapo-Kuti. Margaret
Ekpo, from Creek T own, was a leading
trade unionist and politician during the last
decades of the colonial era and in the early
postcolonial era, and in 1961 she became
the ﬁrst woman member to be elected to
the Eastern Assembly.
Philippa Hall

EGYPT
Egypt is a republic of northeast Africa and
southwest Asia. It has played an important
role in shaping the concept of African
civilization’s origins in antiquity as well as
having an impact on international and
transatlantic politics.
Geography
Egypt, described by the Greek historian
Herodotus as the gift of the Nile, is ofﬁcially
known as the Arab Republic of Egypt. It
has the second largest economy in the Arab
Middle East. Its capital, Cairo (in Arabic,
al-Qahira, or the victorious), is the largest
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 481 ---
EGYPT 405
Arab, Middle Eastern, and African city.
Alexandria, Port Said (Egypt’s chief port),
Luxor, Aswan, and Assiut number among
its major cities. About a tenth of the total
area of the United States of America (nearly
400,000 square miles [over one million
square kilometers]), Egypt has a strategic
location in the extreme northeast corner of
Africa coupled with a small area of south-
west Asia called the Sinai Peninsula. It is
bordered by the Mediterranean Sea to the
north, Sudan to the south, the Red Sea and
Palestine on the east, and a desert border
shared with Libya on the west. Both the
Eastern (Arabian) Desert and Sinai Peninsula
have picturesque mountains (some of them
are more than 8,600 feet [over 2,600 meters]
above Red Sea level), and the Western
(Libyan) Desert enjoys several oases. In
1859 the French began constructing the
Suez Canal—a watercourse linking the
Mediterranean with the Red Sea. It has
since become the most used shipping canal
in the world.
The Mediterranean coast enjoys a mild
and rainy climate, while the rest of Egypt is
generally hot and dry. The Egyptian spring
brings a severe and dusty wind called the
Khamasin. The river Nile, 6,695 kilometers
long, ﬂows through Egypt from the south
to the north, splitting into branches and
creating a fan-shaped area, the Delta, before
meeting the Mediterranean Sea, irrigating
Egypt’s agricultural land. Hence, most of the
inhabitants are centered in and around the
Nile Valley and Delta, leaving two-thirds of
the Egyptian land, the Western and Eastern
deserts almost empty. The Nile has always
been the source of life for Egyptians; ancient
Egyptians showed their respect by worship-
ping it, while modern-day Egyptians still
refer to it as “the sea.” The construction of
the Aswan High Dam in the 1960s on Lake
Nasser, on the southern part of the Egyptian
Nile, helped contain the annual ﬂoods
caused by the African rainy seasons.
Papyrus, the water plant that was used
for making paper in ancient times, together
with the lotus ﬂower, are the symbols of
Egypt. However, palm trees, cypress,
sycamore, mango, lily, acacia, and many
other trees enrich Egyptian ﬂora. Egyptian
fauna is characterized by domestic camels,
gazelles, and hyenas as well as crocodiles,
hippopotamuses, and, although they are
becoming rare, ostriches; numerous kinds
of lizards and snakes, many of which are
poisonous; and hundreds of kinds of ﬁsh
and migratory and native birds.
History
While recorded American history is no older
than 500 years, Egyptian history dates back
to around 3000 BCE, when Egypt gave rise
to one of the world’s greatest and most
ancient civilizations. T oday, Egypt is one of
the most visited countries in the world,
mainly because of its historic past. The
Egyptian Delta witnessed the Kingdom of
Lower Egypt, whereas the Kingdom of
Upper Egypt prospered in the Nile Valley
over 5000 years ago. Around 3100 BCE
the ﬁrst pharaoh, Menes, united the two
kingdoms, making Memphis (very close to
the Cairo of today) their capital. Pharaonic
Egyptian history, which lasted about thirty
centuries, can be divided into three main
kingdoms, the Old, Middle, and New, and
thirty-one dynasties. The biblical story of
the Israelites, the Jewish Exodus, and the
prophet Joseph is said to have occurred
under King Amenemhat III (around 1662
BCE, the Middle Kingdom), who appointed
Joseph as his vizier.
For 200 years (ca. 525–332 BCE) Egypt
was under the grip of the then-greatest
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 482 ---
406 E GYPT
empire in the region, the Persian Empire,
whose rule ended when Alexander the
Great invaded Egypt. Upon his death in
323 BC, the local Ptolemaic dynasties ruled
Egypt until 54 BCE, when Julius Caesar
forcefully took over Alexandria, a city built
by Alexander and hence named after him.
The famous Egyptian queen, Cleopatra VII
(51–30 BCE), immortalized in Shakespeare’s
play, ruled Egypt under Caesar’s protection
after marrying him. On Caesar’s death,
Cleopatra made an alliance with Mark
Antony, who also married her. Upon their
suicide after being defeated by Octavian
(later known as Emperor Augustus), Egypt
lost its independence and became a Roman
province until 395 CE. During the reign of
Nero (the Roman emperor known for
burning Rome), St. Mark is said to have
brought Christianity to Egypt around
61 CE. Egyptian Christians are still known
as Copts.
For the 300 years after the Roman
Empire split, Egypt was ruled by the
Byzantine (the Eastern Roman) Empire.
From 640 CE on, Egypt became part of
the newly expanding Arab Islamic nation.
After ten centuries, however, the Ottomans
tightened their T urkish, though Islamic,
grip over Egypt for the next three centuries.
When Western Europe regained power over
the Ottomans in the eighteenth century,
Egypt fell to the French after an invasion in
1798 by Napoleon Bonaparte, who sought
to threaten British trade with East Asia.
Only three years later, upon Napoleon’s
defeat by the British, Egypt was ruled by
Muhammad ‘Ali Pasha (1805–1848), who
although originally Albanian, became a
viceroy to the Ottoman sultan Salim III
and his heir, Sultan Mahmud II. The T urkish
inﬂuence continued to be very strong in
Egypt under Ali’s successors (known as
Khedives, or Lords), who, although of
Ottoman origin, rebelled against the
authority of Istanbul. They were also very
enamored of the Europeans and, hence, the
process of westernization was intensiﬁed,
giving Egypt a more European touch. The
Khedives supplied Europe with Egyptian
cotton when American cotton failed to
reach Europe due to the U.S. Civil War in
the 1860s. While technically the Khedives
ruled Egypt, their extravagant way of living
forced them to seek British intervention to
help them control the country. The British,
who together with the French built the
Suez Canal (opened in 1869), continued to
consolidate their presence in Egypt. In 1882
the British took the Egyptian government
by military force.
Politics
T wentieth-century Egyptian politics is very
complex; however, the main occurrence, as
in many developing countries, was a rise of
nationalism that resulted in Egypt becoming
the independent republic it is today in June
1953. When T urkey sided with Germany
in World War I, Egypt formally became a
British Protectorate. The Nationalist
Revolution of Saad Zaghlul in 1919 ﬁnally
brought formal British rule to an end in
1922; Egypt, however, continued to be part
of the British Empire as British troops
remained and a puppet king, Fuad, was
installed. He ruled until his death in 1936,
leaving the throne to his son, King Faruq.
In World War II the British defeated the
Germans, who attempted to capture the Suez
Canal during that conﬂict. Egypt became a
founding member of the United Nations in
1945 and played an active role in establish-
ing the Arab League. The rise of various
political factions—liberals, nationalists,
and Islamists—in the twentieth century
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 483 ---
EGYPT 407
resulted in the Revolution of 1952. A mili-
tary coup by Gamal Abdel Nasser toppled
the monarchy.
Under Nasser, Egypt went through
large-scale changes: nationalization of the
Suez Canal; industrial and agricultural
reforms; guaranteed employment for all
college students; introduction of a social
security scheme; and the building of the
Aswan Dam, ﬁnanced by the Soviet Union.
In spite of close political and economic ties
with the Soviet Union, Nasser joined the
Non-Aligned Movement (an organization,
founded in April 1955, of mainly Asian
and African states that sought to distinguish
themselves from both the capitalist and
Communist camps). He ruled Egypt under
a one-party socialist system.
Nasser’s era was also characterized by
antagonistic relations with Israel, the newly
created state in Palestine, which invaded
Egypt in 1956. At the same time, both
Britain and France intervened in the Canal
Zone, capturing Port Said. International
and local pressures, however, forced the
Europeans out of Egypt. Nasser had a vision
of creating a uniﬁed Arab state, and in
1958 Egypt and Syria did establish what
would be a two-year union, called the
United Arab Republic, which made Nasser
a national hero to all Arabs.
Anwar Al-Sadat ruled Egypt after
Nasser died in 1970. Sadat gradually liber-
alized Egypt, both politically and econom-
ically. He allowed other political parties to
form, but they had to function under his
immediate control. Rather than Russian,
Sadat sought British and American goods
and arms. Improving relations with the
United States culminated in the signing
of the ﬁrst Arab-Israeli peace treaty (known
as the Camp David treaty) in 1979, which
led to Israel’s withdrawal from the Sinai
Peninsula. Many Arab countries broke off
diplomatic relations with Egypt as a result.
Hosni Mubarak has been the president
of Egypt since Sadat’s assassination in 1981
by Islamic extremists. Politically and eco-
nomically, Mubarak followed in the foot-
steps of his predecessor. Egypt’s relationship
with the United States became stronger
than ever before. He joined the U.S. military
forces in Iraq in 1991 and the “war on
terrorism” that began in 2001. Many
Egyptians see Mubarak as a traitor rather
than as a liberator. Although the “cold peace”
with Israel has held, Mubarark has also
tried to improve Egypt’s relationships with
other Arab countries. More recently, under
increasing pressure from the United States
and human rights activists, Egypt is under-
going changes toward greater democracy.
Culture
Egyptian culture is as hybrid as that of
Brazil. With an annual population growth
rate of 1.8 percent, Egypt has over 77 million
people, most of who are Arab Muslims.
Christian Copts make up about 6 percent of
the population. Both Islamic and Christian
festivities and holidays are observed. There
are other minorities: Berbers (who speak
Berber) in the Siwa oases in the Western
Desert; Bedouins (desert nomads who have
settled in villages); Nubians (who speak
northern African and Berber-related lan-
guages) in the south; and tiny minorities
of Greeks, Italians, and Armenians, who
speak Arabic as well as their own languages.
Written or classical Arabic is more or less
the same formal language used throughout
the Arab countries; however, spoken Egyptian
Arabic is better-known than any other
Arabic dialect thanks to the fact that Egyptian
ﬁlms and soap operas are shown on most
Arabic screens.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 484 ---
408 E GYPT
Like Egypt’s history and geography,
Egyptian culture has always been unique
and complex. The Pyramids still testify to
Egypt’s early miraculous architecture. Early
Egyptians also used our modern 365-day
calendar and their own hieroglyphic writing
almost 5,000 or 6,000 years ago. In the
nineteenth century, Egypt was the ﬁrst
country in the Middle East to become
westernized. Cairo became both the eco-
nomic and intellectual capital of the entire
Middle East. Writers, artists, and scientists
left other Arab countries such as Syria,
Lebanon, and Iraq (where the Ottoman
grip was much tighter) and settled in
Egypt, developing modern Arab journalism
and theater. A women’s rights movement
was also initiated in Egypt by such people
as Qassem Amin and Huda Shaarawi (both
Egyptian), Zainab Fawaz (Syrian), and
May Ziada (Lebanese) in Cairo.
Even today, three-ﬁfths of Egyptians
make their living from agriculture-related
work. For these people, life in the Nile Valley
and Delta is very challenging. Egypt still
has to import food to sustain its growing
population. City dwellers have a completely
different life from that in the villages. They
are more westernized in their lifestyles in
comparison to very basic lifestyle of the
fallahin (villagers). Although the Egyptian
government provides free education, the
illiteracy rate in Egypt is still 42 percent. As
in many other countries, unemployment is
a problem. Many Egyptians seek work
overseas, especially in the Gulf countries.
Egypt has a long tradition in the arts.
Modern Western artistic forms are fused
with local ancient traditions and folklore in
literature, music, moviemaking, and the ﬁne
arts. Cairo is known as the Hollywood of
Arabia, and Egyptian Naguib Mahfouz is
the only Arab writer to have won the Nobel
Prize in Literature, which he received in
1988. He was followed by Ahmad Zewail,
an Egyptian who won the same prize for
chemistry in 1999.
Like Brazil, Egypt is a soccer-loving
nation, but it is in music and dance that
Egypt has excelled. Egypt produced the
legendary singer Umm Kulthum, whose
death was mourned by millions of Arabs
in 1975. Sayed Darwish (1892–1923) and
Mohammad Abd el-Wahab (1907–1991),
two enormously gifted musicians, champi-
oned Arabic music with their innovative
styles combining Western and Egyptian
music.
For Muslims, Al-Azhar Mosque/
University is still one of the most respected
Islamic centers in the world. And even
though Egypt, especially under Nasser,
championed pan-Arabism (Arab national-
ism), Pharaonic history, preserved through
the pyramids, the buried treasures, and the
unique technique of mummification,
makes all Egyptians, regardless of their
religion, language, or ethnic origin, very
proud of being Egyptian. Egyptians are
known for their friendliness, love of music
and dance, and a special sense of humor.
Nawar Al-Hassan Golley

EGYPT,A MERICAN
MERCENARIES IN
An infusion of nineteenth-century America
into northeast Africa resulted from the
military policies of Egypt’s ruler, Khedive
Ismail (r. 1863–1879). Looking to improve
his army through the import of martial
talent, he recruited numerous European,
T urkish, and American mercenary ofﬁcers.
The Americans were an interesting group,
forming a significant community that
played a role in military, geographical, and
exploration history.
These men, and sometimes their fami-
lies as well, took long voyages to a land very
different from home. Why did they go?
Calling the American ﬂag “that hated em-
blem of cursed tyranny,” former Confederate
Henry Derrick succinctly explained his
motivation for moving to Egypt. More
common was the view of another southerner,
Samuel Lockett, who, like Derrick, was
barred from returning to duty in the U.S.
Army and could not ﬁnd work. “It is awful
to be poor,” he wrote. This opinion was
shared by northern counterparts like
William Dye and Charles Stone, who saw
no future in the rapidly demobilizing U.S.
Army of the late 1860s.
Ismail offered these men payment in
gold, at rates compatible with similar
American ranks. He also promised promo-
tion based on reorganizing his army,
exploring uncharted regions of the Sudan,
and the possibility of military glory as
Egypt tried its own version of imperialism.
This was a generous offer that attracted
over ﬁfty Americans between 1869 and
1882. Some lasted only a few months,
while one, Stone, served the duration. A mix
of Confederates and Yankees, they were often
less divided by North-South issues than by
their jockeying for power with Ismail’s
European and T urkish mercenaries.
Not especially successful in that struggle,
the Americans focused on empowering the
general staff. Stone, who was chief of staff,
sent many of his fellow countrymen to
explore the backlands of Egypt’s colonial
holdings in the Horn of Africa. This resulted
in signiﬁcant cartographical results, one of
the major accomplishments of the American
mercenaries. These efforts also convinced
Stone to add his voice to a chorus of advisers
pushing Ismail toward war with King
Yohannis IV (King John) of Ethiopia.
A war with Ethiopia began in 1875
and featured efforts by American represen-
tatives from the general staff to exert their
inﬂuence a year later at the battles at Gura,
present-day Eritrea, wherein the Egyptians
were defeated, ending their invasion of

EGYPTIAN SOLDIERS
IN MEXICO
“[T]heir skins are as black as tar and their
clothes as white as snow. Scrupulously neat
in person and dress, they are always ready
for dress parade.” Thus did William M.
Anderson describe the only regular African
troops sent to ﬁght in the New World.
Speaking in 1865, Anderson had just
observed the Bataillon Negre Egyptien in
Veracruz, Mexico, a most unusual compo-
nent of the French-directed multinational
force supporting Mexican Imperialists against
Benito Juarez and his Republicans.
An elite force, these “Egyptians” were
actually Sudanese, whose deployment to
Mexico rested partially on their renowned
ﬁghting skills. For much of the nineteenth
century, the Sudan was part of a greater
Egyptian Empire and provided signiﬁcant
numbers of long-serving infantrymen.
Additionally, Egypt’s ruler, Said Pasha 
(r. 1855–1863), fostered close relations with
France, whose emperor, Napoleon III,
agreed to pay all expenses of the Sudanese
force. Napoleon III held favorable views on
Egyptian soldiers based on their record in
the Crimean War and, equally important,
was inﬂuenced by then current medical
theory that considered Africans a better
choice than Europeans when ﬁghting in
tropical zones.
Vera Cruz, a vital port for Imperialist
supply lines, is located in the tropics. It
maintained a reputation as a place of
disease during the 1860s. Nearby swamps,
lagoons, and dank forests created a belt of
malaria, yellow fever, and other deadly
diseases. Spread by swarming mosquitoes,
virulent and unstoppable by medical sci-
ence, these diseases caused a high mortality
rate for troops stationed there. Indeed, the
local cemetery was sardonically referred to
as a “garden of acclimatization.”
Some men survived, and veterans of
previous encounters were reasonably
immune to repeat attacks. Thus, the latter
were viewed as especially valuable for
deployment around Vera Cruz. While troops
of this nature were not available in France,
Egypt had signiﬁcant numbers in her army.
Equatoria, the area from which many
Sudanese regiments obtained their man-
power, existed in an environment similar to
that of Vera Cruz.
Between 1863 and 1867 the Sudanese
helped guard the port, served as train
escorts, and participated in counter-guerilla
sweeps. In every case, the Sudanese were
active participants in the failed effort to
create a Mexican Empire. Their service was
exemplary, which only increased agitation
among Republican forces and their American
backers, who were especially bothered by

the employment of African troops in Mexico.

the President, Negroes, natives of Africa,
cannot rightfully be employed as soldiers in
any way to subvert established political

soldiers was cause for the poorest relations
between Egypt and America until the 1950s,

France, whose withdrawal in 1867 guaran-
teed that the Sudanese would quickly follow.
Returning home after a triumphal visit to
Paris, where every soldier obtained the Mex-
ican Campaign Medal from Napoleon III,
the Sudanese were spread among Egyptian
garrisons throughout the Sudan. These veter-
ans played important roles in the 1870s and
1880s. They often were noted by travelers for
their smart military bearing and the distinc-
tive colors of the ribbons attached to the
medals given them by the emperor of France.

EKWENSI,C YPRIAN ODIATU
DUAKA (1921–)
Cyprian Odiatu Duaka Ekwensi is one of
Nigeria’s most proliﬁc and versatile novelists,
short story writers, and children’s authors.
A pioneer in many ways, he is the father of
the Nigerian novel. An Igbo, he was born
in Minna, Niger State, on September 26,
1921; attended Government College and
the University College, Ibadan, in Yorubaland;
and trained as a forestry ofﬁcer before
studying at the Lagos School of Pharmacy
and the Chelsea School of Pharmacy,
London. He wrote hundreds of short stories,
dozens of novels, some twenty children’s
books, and four collections of folktales as
well as radio and television scripts. Most of
his works have been on school syllabi for
decades. His ﬁrst publications, When Love
Whispers and Ikolo the Wrestler and Other
Ibo T ales,both issued in 1947, were closely
associated with the rise of Onitsha market
literature. Committed to the production of
reading material for Nigerians, he later
spearheaded the transition from Onitsha
market to a mainstream audience with
People of the City(1954). Ekwensi’s most ac-
claimed novel, Jagua Nana(1961), was pub-
lished in the United States in 1969. That
same year, he visited the United States with
Chinua Achebe and Gabriel Okara, lectur-
ing at universities. His exposure to various
Nigerian cultures and his travel experiences
greatly inﬂuenced his writing. His works,
now translated into many languages, includ-
ing French and Arabic, reveal the impact of
the urbanization and inﬂuence of Western
values on the lives of ordinary citizens. He
presents the urban cultural mix and coexis-
tence of traditional and Western cultures as
the cornerstone of the country’s modern-
ization and gives women a signiﬁcant place
in the development of this mix.

ELLISON,R ALPH WALDO
(1914–1994)
An author of short stories and essays, Ralph
Waldo Ellison is best known for writing
one of the most inﬂuential and widely read
novels of the twentieth century, Invisible
Man (1952). Born in Oklahoma City,
Oklahoma, and raised by his mother,
Ellison studied music for three years at the
T uskegee Institute in Alabama before
moving to New York City to ﬁnd work in
music. There, Ellison met numerous writers,
began to publish, and by working for the
Federal Writers’ Project became acquainted
with a wide range of African American
experiences, histories, and folktales. By the
time Ellison entered the merchant marines,
serving from 1943 to 1945, he had over
sixty ﬁction and nonﬁction publications.
In 1952 Ellison published Invisible
Man, whose outstanding attributes include
its recapitulation of twentieth-century
African American history, its “jazz narrative
aesthetic” and incorporation of the black
oral tradition, its “existential” critique of
both “white” and “black” spheres of Amer-
ican society, its informed optimism, and its
literary sophistication. For many African
American intellectuals, however, some of
these characteristics of Invisible Man were
seen as, if not capitulations to “white” society,
then at least as distractions that dulled the
de rigeur radical politics of African American
literature.
From the 1950s until his death in
1994, Ellison worked on his second novel,
amassing some 2,000 pages of manuscript
that John Callahan edited into the novel
Juneteenth (1999), with more forthcoming.
In addition to two novels, Ellison published
ﬁve collections of short stories and essays,
Ralph Ellison, whose novel Invisible Man has become a
classic of modern American ﬁction, wrote compellingly
about African American experiences of racism in
contemporary American society. (National Archives)

taught at numerous universities, sat on
many boards and commissions, and won
multiple literary awards in both the United
States and Europe. Ellison’s particular im-
portance includes the individual’s struggle
to attain self-knowledge; the broad scope of
his work, which incorporates not only the

EMANCIPATION
PROCLAMATION
The Emancipation Proclamation is the
U.S. Civil War document, proclaimed in
1862, which declared that all slaves in areas
under rebellion against the Union would be
forever free. On September 22, 1862, almost
a year and a half after the beginning of the
Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln
announced his Emancipation Proclamation,
to become effective January 1, 1863.
Lincoln’s handling of emancipation had
been extremely cautious. While a longtime
critic of slavery, his primary goal in the
Civil War was the quick restoration of the
Union. Lincoln’s objective during the ﬁrst
year of the war was to maintain the Union
as it was, without directly threatening
southern institutions.
As the war continued with Union
victory seeming distant, Lincoln increasingly
turned toward emancipation as a means to
aid the war effort. During the summer of
1862, he discussed the idea with members
of his cabinet. With the Union victory at
Antietam in September, Lincoln presented
his Emancipation Proclamation to the
nation, and since Lincoln had no authority
under the Constitution to end slavery in
areas loyal to the Union, the Proclamation
was a military measure applying only to
Confederate-controlled territory.
Despite some criticism in the North
that the Proclamation did not free slaves in
Union territories, no border state seceded,
1864 engraving of the Proclamation of Emancipation
with an eagle and U.S. ﬂags over a portrait of
Abraham Lincoln and composite of seven scenes of
slavery. President Lincoln issued the Emancipation
Proclamation on January 1, 1863. (Library of
Congress)
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

414 E MECHETA,B UCHI
nor did any signiﬁcant number of Union
troops desert. Instead, Lincoln had dealt an
effective blow to the Confederate cause.
The Union war effort was now ofﬁcially di-
rected against slavery. European countries
no longer considered supporting the Con-
federacy. While the South of course did not
abide by the measure, Union armies liber-
ated thousands of slaves and began actively
recruiting freedmen into Union service.
Most importantly, the Proclamation initi-
ated the end of slavery across the nation by
helping pave the way for the Thirteenth
Amendment, which abolished slavery
shortly after the war.
Ian M. Spurgeon

EMECHETA,B UCHI (1944–) 
Buchi Emecheta is a London-based Nigerian
woman novelist writing in English. Born of
Igbo parents on July 21, 1944, in Lagos,
Nigeria, Florence Onyebuchi Emecheta,
living in London since 1962, is one of the
most inﬂuential African women writers.
Since 1972 she has published nineteen
novels, already translated into fourteen lan-
guages, plays for the BBC, poetry, essays, and
books for children. She draws her material
directly from her own life to document the
experience of Africans in the diaspora,
focusing upon the lives of the black immi-
grant women, and considers her experience
of immigration to Britain as a major inﬂu-
ence in her work. Her ﬁrst novel, In the
Ditch (1972), initially titled “Observations
of the London Poor” and planned as an
article for a magazine, was inspired by her
experiences in a north London slum. Her
writing, focused on exile, women, gender,
and crosscultural issues, presents black
women struggling to maintain their identity
and ﬁghting to win economic independence.
In 1982 she set up her own publishing
ﬁrm, Ogwugwu Afor, with her journalist
son to provide a platform and ﬁnancial
support for black artists.
The turning point in her life came
when she left Nigeria to join her husband
in the United Kingdom in February 1962.
Four years later she left him and started
writing while studying, ﬁrst for a bachelor
of science degree in sociology with the
University of London, which she received
in 1974, then for a masters degree in social
education at the University of London. Her
studies helped to provide her with analytic
tools she used to structure her observations
and ideas. After completing her formal
education, she pursued a dual career as
a writer and a social worker, served on
numerous public committees, and became
a respected voice on feminism and integra-
tionist issues.
In 1975 Second-Class Citizen (1974)
received the Daughter of Mark T wain
Award. In 1978 The Slave Girl (1977)
received the Sunrise Award and won the
New Statesman’s Jock Campbell Award for
Commonwealth Writers for its stand in the
feminist debate and its attempt to deﬁne
new understandings of African feminist
literary theory. In 1979 The Joys of
Motherhood (1979) was selected as Book of
the Month Club choice and won the Best
British Writer’s Award in 1980.
Emecheta’s style is rooted in her culture;
she describes herself as a storyteller and sees
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 491 ---

herself as oral communicator. Her homeland,
Nigeria, is the setting of several novels: The
Bride Price (1976), The Slave Girl (1977),
The Joys of Motherhood (1979), Destination
Biafra (1982), and Double Yoke(1982). The
Rape of Shavi (1983) is a parable about race

by American and British literary critics but
very little by African critics.

ENGLISH,A FRICAN
AMERICAN VERNACULAR
African American Vernacular English
(AAVE) is the everyday spoken speech of
African Americans, composed of grammat-
ical elements and linguistic structures that
contrast with the ofﬁcial standard. It is a
language referred to historically, with
numerous connotations, as Negro Dialect,
Substandard Negro English, Nonstandard
Negro English, Black English, Vernacular
Black English (VBE), Black English
Vernacular (BEV ), and Afro-American
English. It is currently referred to as African
American English (AAE), African American
Language (AAL), Black Talk, Ebonics, and
Spoken Soul. Such a variety of nomencla-
ture is indicative of the controversy sur-
rounding its history.
African American Vernacular English is
an ethnic variety of the language spoken in
the United States by many blacks whose
African ancestors were formally enslaved in
British North America and subsequently
the United States from the sixteenth
through the nineteenth centuries. The term
“vernacular” applies to the unmonitored,
everyday speech spoken in a local commu-
nity; it contains and is deﬁned by socially
stigmatized grammatical elements and
linguistic structures that contrast with 
the ofﬁcial standard. African American
Vernacular English differs in some way
from community to community, but shared
patterns of pronunciation, vocabulary, and
grammar identify it all as AAVE.
Beginning with the introductory works
of J. L. Dillard and William Labov in the
1960s, AAVE has been the focus of more
studies and more published work than has
any other ethnic or social variety of American
English. Since then, linguists such as Guy
Bailey, John Baugh, Salikoko Mufwene,
Geneva Smitherman, John Rickford, and
Walt Wolfram have generally focused on
four central questions: (1) Is AAVE a dialect
or is it just slang produced in an unsuccess-
ful attempt at standard American English?
(2) Did AAVE originate from remnants of
early American and British English or from
creole structures from West African lan-
guages? (3) Is AAVE converging with other
varieties of American English or becoming
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 492 ---
416 E NLIGHTENMENT PHILOSOPHY
more like them? (4) What inﬂuence does
AAVE have on education and culture?
The longest-standing explanation for
the origin of AAVE lies in the Anglicist
hypothesis, which argues that slavery wiped
out most, if not all, African linguistic and
cultural tradition and that the apparently
distinctive features of AAVE come from
English dialects spoken by British peasants
and indentured servants. Some scholars,
taking an Africanist stand, contend that the
African American vernacular bears the
vivid imprint of the African languages
spoken by slaves who came to this country
in waves from the seventeenth to the nine-
teenth centuries. For the Creolist hypothe-
sis, the central question is whether AAVE
was ever as different from Standard English
as the creole varieties spoken today in such
places as Jamaica, T rinidad, Guyana, and
Barbados or whether it was ever inﬂuenced
by them. Both the Creolists and Africanists
believe that, since the Gullah language of
coastal South Carolina and Georgia is a
conﬁrmed creole and since Africans settled
at these sites in great numbers before mov-
ing inland, the resulting AAVE must have
creole origins.
While it is certain that AAVE is chang-
ing, the question that arises is whether the
change is toward being more like main-
stream Anglo-American English or becom-
ing more distinctive from it. Some sociolin-
guists believe that when social relationships
between black Americans and white Amer-
icans improve, the two groups begin to
pick up features from one another, with
AAVE incorporating mainstream charac-
teristics in a process of convergence, but
that when social relationships between the
two groups degenerate, then AAVE speakers
choose grammatical and especially vocabulary
features that identify them as speciﬁcally be-
longing to an AAVE community. 
The Ebonics debates of the late 1990s
revived the 1960s deficit-or-difference
arguments that linguists thought had been
resolved. Proponents of the deﬁcit theory
maintained that not only was the vernacular
grammatically insufﬁcient to communicate
adequately, but also that its use inhibited
the effective thought and communication
processes of its speakers. Regional and so-
cial dialect studies proved these varieties to
have differences that were consistent with
language systems, and that social and eth-
nic dialects persist because they contain
means by which a community can main-
tain its cultural connections. The Oakland
school board resolution on Ebonics recog-
nized that the distinctive language of
African American children was a valid
linguistic system by which to educate and
communicate.
Mary Ziegler

Green, Lisa J. African American English:

English. Malden, MA: Blackwell Publishers,

ENLIGHTENMENT
PHILOSOPHY
By the “Enlightenment” is meant the
eighteenth-century international move-
ment in thought, characterized by a faith in
universal human rationality and a skeptical
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 493 ---
ENLIGHTENMENT PHILOSOPHY 417
attitude to traditional dogmas and ancient
authorities. A noteworthy feature of this
movement is the absence from it of any sus-
tained discourse of race. At the beginning
of the century Gottfried Leibniz was pre-
pared to dismiss the idea of race altogether.
By the century’s close, ﬁgures such as
Wilhelm von Humbolt interpreted the
Enlightenment task of perfecting humanity
and human society as crucially bound up
with, in his words, “establishing our com-
mon humanity—of striving . . . to treat all
mankind, without reference to religion,
nation or colour, as one fraternity, one great
community” (Malik, 1996, p. 48).
This is not to say that the idea of race
was altogether unknown in the period.
Rather, conceptions of race developed
piecemeal in the context of debates con-
cerning the relative signiﬁcance of social,
environmental, and biological factors in
accounting for human variation. Carolus
Linneaus distinguished ﬁve major “vari-
eties” of human being, holding that the
causes of human variation lay in cultural
and environmental factors such as “educa-
tion and situation” and “climate and art”
(Eze, 1997, p. 13). Georges Buffon has
been considered a key inﬂuence on nine-
teenth-century racial theory, but he too
considered human variation to be primarily
environmental in origin, a product of what
he said was “climate, food, mode of living,
epidemic diseases, and the mixture of
dissimilar individuals” (ibid., p. 13). Im-
manuel Kant wrote extensively on anthro-
pology, and his work exhibits debts to both
Buffon and Linneaus. In Kant’s terminol-
ogy, Linneaus’s ﬁve human varieties are
interpreted as “races.” That is to say, they
constitute a range of types generated
from a single original stem and capable of
engendering fertile hybrids, while each is
also capable of maintaining its distinctive-
ness over successive generations when
transplanted to an alien environment.
Kant’s conception of race is apparently
a response to the perceived inadequacy of
purely environmental explanations of
human variation and the absence of any
developed genetic theory. The lack of any
clearly articulated scientiﬁc consensus on
race left Jean-Jacques Rousseau, writing in
the middle of the century, able to effec-
tively ignore any implications for human
perfectibility that might have been thought
to follow from the observed fact of human
variation. Rousseau treats human variety
nonreductively and as essentially plastic in
the face of social, cultural, and environmen-
tal change. Nascent ideas of race only begin
to pose a real challenge to Enlightenment
A philosopher of the Enlightenment, David Hume’s
discussions of reason led him to brief, but often-cited
speculations on the nature and origins of race. (Library
of Congress)
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 494 ---
418 E NLIGHTENMENT PHILOSOPHY
ideals when human variation is understood
to have a ﬁxed biological basis. There is a
suggestion of such a view in David Hume’s
essay “Of National Characters.” Hume
voices the suspicion, in a footnote, that
blacks are “naturally inferior” to whites, im-
plying at the same time that the causes of
the alleged inferiority go beyond the envi-
ronmental: while “moral” (social, cultural)
factors sufﬁce, Hume argues, to account for
the variety of European national characters,
and while such physical factors as air and
climate might explain certain other ob-
served differences between races, it seems
necessary to invoke the idea of a natural
“original distinction” to explain the con-
stancy of black racial characteristics in the
face of changed social and geographical cir-
cumstances. Thus, Hume was led to doubt
whether blacks could ever rise above their
existing “slender accomplishments” in the
arts and sciences (Hume, 1985, p. 208).
Kant was apparently prepared to follow
Hume’s lead in this matter, regarding the
differences between whites and blacks as
“fundamental” and “as great in regard to
mental capacities as in colour” (Kant,
1960, p. 11). (Given his views on human-
ity’s common origin, however, it seems
unlikely that Kant would have accepted
everything that might be read into Hume’s
claims concerning an “original distinc-
tion.”) Much has been made of the fact that
eighteenth-century ideas of race, including
those of Kant, were grounded in a concep-
tion of nature as a “great Chain of Being”
(Gates, 1992, pp. 64–65). According to the
Chain of Being concept, nature exhibits a
hierarchical order of divine origin. How-
ever, this concept was distinct from both
medieval teleology and nineteenth-century
evolutionism. Unlike evolutionism, the
Chain of Being idea interprets the order of
nature as essentially ﬁxed. Unlike medieval
teleology, it does not place either humanity
or God straightforwardly at the apex of the
hierarchy, as the ﬁnal cause of the whole.
Consequently, the Chain of Being idea
remains open to surprisingly egalitarian
interpretations: every being has its proper
place in the chain, and to each belongs the
perfectibility characteristic of its kind.
While the various links in the chain are not
equal in dignity, the raison d’ être of each is
never to be found in its utility to another
(Lovejoy, 1936, pp. 188–189). In Goethe’s
words, “every animal is an end in itself”
(ibid., p. 189). Even sympathetic inter-
preters of Kant have described his views on
race as “deplorable” (Wood, 1999, p. 4).
But it is important to appreciate that he
firmly respected Rousseau’s distinction
between physical and political inequality.
For Kant, nothing follows from a human
individual’s physical or intellectual attri-
butes with regard to his or her ethical or
political entitlements. Kant’s moral theory,
as he famously wrote in Groundwork of the
Metaphysics of Morals, requires us to act so
as to treat ourselves and others “ never
merely as a means but always at the same
time as ends in themselves. ” Accordingly, he
emphatically condemns slavery, along with
other examples of the purely instrumental
treatment of human beings. Indeed, Kant’s
low estimation of the intellectual abilities
of some nonwhite groups enables him at
times to underscore his ethical universal-
ism. In his Metaphysics of Morals, while
simultaneously emphasizing the supposed
intellectual inferiority of various nonwhite
groups, Kant condemns European appro-
priations of their land and goods as ﬂa-
grantly unjust.
The task of disentangling Hume’s
ethical and political views from his views
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 495 ---
ENVIRONMENTALISM 419
on race is more difﬁcult. Hume, like Kant,
was opposed to slavery; and many of his
arguments anticipate those used later by
more vigorous opponents of the institu-
tion. However, combined with his views on
the natural inferiority of blacks, Hume’s
moral theory yields an unpleasantly prag-
matic approach to the ethics of slavery.
According to Hume, moral virtue is a mat-
ter of exhibiting qualities of character that
afford to a spectator “the pleasing sentiment
of approbation” (Hume, 1975, p. 289).
Such qualities usually involve beneﬁcence
or humanity and suggest a “tender sympa-
thy” for others and a “generous concern”
for the human species (ibid., p. 178). This,
however, leaves judgments of virtue highly
susceptible to cultural bias. Judgments
founded on what happen to strike mem-
bers of a dominant social group as useful
and agreeable qualities are apt in practice to
reinforce morally repugnant social inequal-
ities. Hume himself criticizes slavery
primarily on the grounds of its pernicious
effects on the slave-owning class—it is
corrupting of ordinary human relations
among the masters and is not economically
beneﬁcial. One might reasonably object
that these are very far from being the best
or most urgent reasons to oppose slavery,
and that ideals of justice and human equal-
ity ought to ﬁgure in any genuinely en-
lightened discussion of the topic.
Peter Lucas

ENVIRONMENTALISM
Environmentalism refers to the concern for
and attempt to reform policies relating to
the treatment of the natural world. After
decolonization in the 1950s, 1960s, and
1970s, American and African environmen-
talism merged under the auspice of
American-based developmental aid, univer-
sity research programs, and nongovern-
mental agencies. United Nations meetings
in 1992 and 2002 in Rio de Janeiro and
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 496 ---
420 E NVIRONMENTALISM
Johannesburg initiated signiﬁcant environ-
mental collaboration between the Americas
and Africa.
American and African environmental-
ism stem from the same origins: the British
Empire. The two movements diverged
from the 1880s to the 1970s due to the fact
that the British, French, and Portuguese
controlled large parts of Africa, curtailing
any political, cultural, and economic ties of
the Western Hemisphere nations with the
African continent. The postcolonial era,
however, has seen important points of col-
laboration between African and American
environmental movements and substantial
discussion of common interests around en-
vironmental degradation, global warming,
the loss of biodiversity, and urban pollution.
Environmentalism in Africa and North
America—at least regarding the implemen-
tation of large-scale environmental reforms
such as soil conservation programs, the
establishment of large forestry departments,
and the creation of large land reserves for
the protection of plants and animals—had
its antecedents in British India. British
Indian forestry, begun in the nineteenth
century, became the model of large-scale
state forestry for Canada, the United States,
and large parts of British Africa. South
Africa, the British East Africa Protectorate,
Nigeria, the Gold Coast, and Sierra Leone
all adopted forestry charters and created
forestry departments similar to those of
British India in the early 1900s. American
and Canadian forestry borrowed from
British Indian forestry laws, forestry
methods, and departmental structures.
From the 1910s to the 1960s, American
and African environmental movements
also diverged as American countries such as
Canada and the United States developed
their own traditions of forestry and
environmental protections that differed
from the British and French imperial
methods and models. During this period
the Americas and Africa were intellectually
separated on environmental issues, largely
because African leaders were focused on
ﬁghting for independence from British
rule. Once Africa nations gained their
independence from colonial rule in the
1950s, 1960s, and early 1970s, American
and African environmental policies could
once again inﬂuence each other.
As the British, French, and Portuguese
ruling elites left Africa during those
decades, the United States turned its eyes
toward the African continent. The U.S.
had a great degree of interest in African
political affairs, including its environmen-
tal policies, as American diplomats worried
that the Soviet Union’s inﬂuence might
sway some African states toward Commu-
nism or socialism, such as Zimbabwe in
1980. Half of American aid during the
1970s and 1980s went toward agricultural
and environmental reforms so as to allevi-
ate hunger and environmental degradations
resulting from deforestation, soil erosion,
and the extinction of native animals.
Canada, as well as the United States, created
numerous programs for African countries
that promoted the dispersion of forestry,
biological conservation, and agricultural
knowledge.
At the same time that the U.S. and
Canadian governments increased their aid
to Africa, a variety of nongovernmental
organizations began funding environmen-
tal projects thoughout the whole of Africa.
The collaboration of nongovernmental
agencies as well as the combined research
of scientists and humanists in Africa and
America allowed policy makers and philoso-
phers to see environmental degradation and
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 497 ---
EQUATORIALGUINEA 421
solutions in a new light. Environmental
philosophers began to look at environmen-
tal degradation, both in Africa and in the
Americas, as a process of hasty industrial-
ization brought on by the West. Instead of
American environmental solutions, largely
derived from scientists and policy makers,
environmental philosophers looked toward
traditional African lifestyles as a way to
increase agricultural sustainability and
environmental protection.
Alongside these intellectual develop-
ments were a variety of international agree-
ments created in the 1990s and early
twenty-ﬁrst century. The most important
developments in the 1990s stemmed from
international cooperation between various
American and African countries at United
Nations–coordinated meetings. The ﬁrst
important gathering, the United Nations
Conference on Environmental and
Development of 1992, also known as the
Earth Summit, met in Rio de Janeiro and
created a large number of goals and inter-
national regulations that attempted to curb
the loss of biological diversity, slow down
global warming, and protect the health
of people in such dangerous environments
as expanding third-world cities. T en years
later in Johannesburg, South Africa, the
2002 World Summit for Sustainable
Development reviewed the progress of
various Earth Summit regulations and
agreements and created more international
agreements on sustainable development.
African and American environmental
policy makers continue to create new
scientiﬁc and legal relationships, especially
through United Nations meetings. As
scientists respond to the possibility of global
warming, the astonishing loss of biological
diversity, and urban-related environmental
pollution, the partnership of Africa and the
Americas will continue to grow throughout
the twenty-ﬁrst century.
Brett Bennett

EQUATORIALGUINEA
The Republic of Equatorial Guinea, with a
population of about 523,000, was—along
with part of Morocco—a Spanish colonial
possession on the African mainland and
includes the island Fernando Póo. T oday,
the United States is the country’s second
largest trading partner, with oil anticipated
to be an important future export from the
African country.
The Portuguese arrived in 1472, and
after many disputes between Portugal and
Spain, the rights to the territory were given
to Spain in 1777 by the T reaty of San
Ildefonso, but the Spanish did not make
any efforts to colonize the territory. Instead
they invited the British to lease the island of
Fernando Póo (now Bioko, in Equatorial
Guinea), to be used as a base to stop slave
ships sailing from nearby Nigeria. In 1844
Spanish settlers arrived on Fernando Póo,
and eleven years later Spain appointed its
first governor. The first official U.S.
connections came in 1859, when Spain
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 498 ---
422 E QUATORIALGUINEA
authorized the U.S. government to estab-
lish a coal supply base at Playa Carboneras,
near Santa Isabel. T wenty-one years later
the Presbyterian Church in the United
States opened a mission in Río Muni, on
the mainland, which twelve years later was
also under Spanish control. This mission
continued until 1968. From 1930 until
1936, and again from 1960, the mission-
aries’ ecclesiastical district of Corsico (in
modern-day Equatorial Guinea) was con-
nected to the New Jersey synod. The
Protestant World Evangelization Crusade
from Fort Washington, Pennsylvania, was
also active in Spanish Guinea for many
years.
Spanish Guinea, as it was known ofﬁ-
cially, was proclaimed as a Spanish protec-
torate on January 9, 1885. On July 30,
1959, Spanish Guinea was divided back
into Fernando Póo and Río Muni (which
included Elobey and Corisco), and these
became two overseas provinces of Spain.
On October 12, 1968, the two were again
merged together to form the Republic of
Equatorial Guinea.
The first president of Equatorial
Guinea was Macías Nguema Biyoga,
who—five years after independence—
renamed Fernando Póo after himself.
During his rule, which ended in 1979,
widespread human rights abuses took
place, with reports of up to 50,000 people
killed. He was executed after a successful
coup d’état in 1979, in which his nephew,
T eodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasongo, took
over, and despite some attempts to improve
the international reputation of the country,
there are still allegations of political abuses
of power—although nothing on the same
scale as under Macías Nguema.
Since achieving independence,
Equatorial Guinea’s second largest trading
partner has been the United States, ﬁrst in
terms of the African nation’s imports and
third regarding its exports. Diplomatic
relations were established on November 21,
1968, six weeks after independence.
Equatorial Guinea’s ﬁrst ambassador to the
United Nations, S. Ibongo Iyanga, began—
on his arrival in the United States—
research for a thesis on international rela-
tions at Columbia University. It was never
completed, as he was assassinated six
months later. After that, diplomatic rela-
tions with the United States were strained,
the latter worried about a possible spillover
of the Biafran War. After the unsuccessful
coup Macías Nguema became extremely
critical of the United States, which he be-
lieved was behind the coup effort. He forced
out of the country the Protestant World
Evangelization Crusade, which had been
operating in Spanish Guinea since 1933.
In speeches and press releases, Macías
Nguema accused the United States of sup-
porting coup attempts against him, and the
U.S. embassy in Santa Isabel, then the cap-
ital, was closed by the U.S. in 1971, follow-
ing an incident in which a U.S. diplomat
A. J. Erdos, killed his colleague, D. J.
Leahy, the only other U.S personnel com-
posing the U.S. mission, with a pair of
scissors. Erdos was later charged when he
arrived back in the United States. In each of
the years 1971 and 1972, U.S. diplomatic
staff visited the country twice, but no U.S.
citizen lived there with the exception of
one working for the International Bank
for Reconstruction and Development. As
relations deteriorated, the U.S. embassy
in Cameroon became responsible for
Equatorial Guinea until March 15, 1976,
when diplomatic relations were suspended.
After the 1979 coup that removed Macías
Nguema from power, the U.S. government
reestablished formal diplomatic ties and the
USS Spiegel Grove paid a goodwill visit to
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 499 ---
EQUIANO,O LAUDAH 423
the country. Aid from the U.S. government
resumed, and the Peace Corps began func-
tioning in the country. With Biafra so
close, it was long thought there was oil in
Equatorial Guinea that could make the
country wealthy. Early oil prospecting by
Gulf Oil, Mobil Oil, and Chevron had
limited success, until large ﬁndings were
made in 2004.

EQUIANO,O LAUDAH
(1745?–1797)
Olaudah Equiano was a formerly enslaved
sailor, possibly of Igbo descent, whose
early slave narrative, The Interesting
Narrative of Olaudah Equiano (1789), is
frequently taught as both fact and ﬁction.
In his narrative Equiano tells of being
kidnapped from his Ibo family in Nigeria
and sold into slavery in 1755. T ransported
to the Caribbean and then Virginia,
Equiano was owned by a series of sailors
and merchants, one of whom renamed
him Gustavas Vassa. By engaging in trade
Equiano was able to secure enough capital
to purchase his freedom in 1766; he then
took to sea.
Olaudah Equiano, an ex-slave who purchased his own freedom, spoke out publicly against slavery and the slave
trade, becoming an important ﬁgure of the eighteenth-century British abolition movement. His widely published
autobiography was a major early work against slavery. (Library of Congress)
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 500 ---
424 E RITREA
Equiano traveled through the Arctic,
the Middle East, and the Mediterranean,
all of which he documented alongside his
search for salvation. Accompanying his
religious struggle was a political struggle
against slavery. In the 1780s Equiano
became active in the antislavery movement
in England and was prominent in a group
of black men, the Sons of Africa. In his
Interesting Narrative, an antislavery work,
he documented his biography as well as his
involvement in a number of enterprises,
including a plan to colonize Sierra Leone
with repatriated Africans.
In 1792 Equiano married an English-
woman, with whom he had two daughters.
He died ﬁve years later. In recent years
Equiano’s biography has become a subject
of some debate. The scholar Catherine
Obianuju Acholonu engaged in anthropo-
logical research to locate Equiano’s point of
origins, uncovering an oral narrative which
suggested that his family arranged for him
to be kidnapped to pay off debts. In con-
trast, Professor Vincent Carretta has uncov-
ered a baptismal certiﬁcate as well as a
Royal Navy muster roll, both of which give
Equiano’s place of birth as South Carolina.
Jennifer Harris

ERITREA
One of Africa’s newest countries, Eritrea
declared independence from Ethiopia on
May 24, 1993, after a thirty-year armed
struggle. It is one of the smallest African
nations, with a population of about 4.5 mil-
lion in an area about the size of the state of
Pennsylvania. Located in the Horn of
Africa, Eritrea is bounded on the south by
Ethiopia, on the northwest by Sudan, on
the southeast by Djibouti, and on the
northeast by the Red Sea. It also includes
the Dahlak Archipelago in the Red Sea. Its
capital city is Asmara, with a population
of half a million; the Red Sea ports of
Massawa and Assab are also important
cities. The name Eritrea was given by the
Italians, who colonized the area from 1889
until 1941, after the Roman name for the
Red Sea, Mare Erythraeum. While 80 per-
cent of the population is agricultural or
pastoral, only about 5 percent of the land is
arable; the rest is either too mountainous or
too arid for farming. Like Ethiopia, the
population is evenly divided between
Muslims and various Christian groups,
including Eritrean Orthodox (which sepa-
rated from Ethiopian Orthodox in 1993),
Roman Catholic, and Protestant. The
predominant ethnic groups are Tigrigna
(50 percent) and Tigre (40 percent), and
the major languages are Tigrigna, Tigre,
Arabic, and English.
History
Eritrea’s location on the Red Sea across
from the Arabian Peninsula has been a
major factor in its history. The Red Sea is
one of the busiest shipping lanes in the
world and has been an important avenue
for trade as far back as the ﬁrst millennium
BCE. Goods from the hinterland, such as
ivory, gold, and slaves, were transported to
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 501 ---
ERITREA 425
the Red Sea coast to be exchanged for
textiles, metals, and other manufactured
goods from the Middle East and the
Mediterranean. By the ﬁrst century CE, the
state of Axum controlled the seacoast and
what is now Eritrea; it dominated the re-
gion commercially and militarily until the
eighth century CE, when Muslim power
began to grow. Successors to Axum re-
tained control over much of what is now
Eritrea until it was occupied by the
Ottoman Empire in the sixteenth century.
The Ottomans were eventually driven back
to the coast, and the inland area remained
closely tied to Tigray in northern Ethiopia,
with which it had linguistic and cultural
afﬁnities. However, the coastal areas were
subsequently occupied by the Egyptians,
and while Ethiopia’s emperor Yohannes IV
was able to fend off further incursions by
the Egyptians in 1875, Ethiopia did not
regain its access to the coast until Eritrea
was federated with Ethiopia by the United
Nations in 1952.
The opening of the Suez Canal in
1869 made the Horn of Africa and the East
African coast more accessible to the
Mediterranean. It also made Europe’s pen-
etration and colonization of Africa much
easier. As early as 1869, Italy purchased the
Bay of Assab, though Egypt claimed the
coast at that time. Assab was not declared
an Italian colony until 1882, after Italy
had opened diplomatic relations with
Yohannes IV . Italy soon sought to expand
its holdings along the coast, occupied the
other main port of Massawa, and then
began moving inland toward the highlands.
Following the death of Yohannes in 1889,
the Italians, under Prime Minister
Francesco Crispi, signed the T reaty of
Wichale with his successor, Emperor
Menelik II, which effectively gave Italy
claim to part of northern Ethiopia. The
Italians began conﬁscating land for Italian
settlement, but the residents resisted;
Italian retaliation to the resistance culmi-
nated in their shocking defeat by Menelik’s
troops at the Battle of Adwa in 1896.
However, the Italians retained their colony
of Eritrea, as Menelik’s army lacked the
power to drive them completely out. The
new civilian governor of Eritrea, Fernando
Martini, who served from 1897 to 1907,
abandoned the plan to settle Italians in
Eritrea. Instead, he consolidated colonial
rule by striving for both stability within
Eritrea and good relations with Ethiopia.
Eritrean stability was particularly impor-
tant in light of the colony’s role in supply-
ing soldiers to support the Italian efforts to
consolidate their rule in Somalia and Libya.
Thus, what became the modern coun-
try of Eritrea was established by an Italian
military venture: it was the territory that
the Italians were able to seize and retain.
Eritrea remained an Italian colony until it
was taken by the British following Italy’s
declaration of war on Britain and France in
1941. In 1935 the Italians used Eritrea as a
staging ground for invading Ethiopia,
which they occupied for six years. At this
time, the Eritreans serving in the colonial
army comprised 40 percent of the entire
male labor force, and Italy returned to its
settler strategy for Eritrea as Italian laborers
and soldiers arrived and the colony was
converted into a commercial and industrial
center for the Italian East African Empire.
This project was short lived, as Italy was
defeated in World War II and its colonial
holdings were parceled out to the victors.
Britain took control of Eritrea and Ethiopia
and maintained them under separate
administrations. The future of Eritrea was
deliberated for several years by the Great
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 502 ---
426 E RITREA
Powers (Britain, France, the United States,
the Soviet Union, and China), who were
unable to agree on a solution. The Eritrean
population was divided between those who
wanted to unite with Ethiopia (mainly
highland Christians) and those who
wanted independence (mainly lowland
Muslims). Ethiopia sought to acquire
Eritrea in order to regain access to the sea,
claiming that Eritrea had been part of
Ethiopia prior to colonization. The United
Nations became involved in 1950, and the
United States pressed to have Eritrea
attached to Ethiopia but with an au-
tonomous government. There was consid-
erable American interest in a communica-
tions station in Eritrea that had been built
by the Italians and also concern that it
would fall into Soviet hands. The federal
solution seemed the one most likely to keep
Ethiopia’s favor while placating Eritrean
separatists.
The Ethiopian government proceeded
to impinge on Eritrean autonomy, impos-
ing Amharic as the language of instruction
in Eritrean schools; suppressing the
Eritrean ﬂag; and, in 1960, downgrading
the Eritrean government to an “administra-
tion.” Eritrea effectively became a province
of Ethiopia, losing its relative autonomy.
A group of exiles in Cairo formed the
Eritrean Liberation Front (ELF) and began
armed attacks within Eritrea in 1962. This
insurgency continued for nearly thirty
years. The Marxist-oriented Eritrean
Peoples Liberation Front (EPLF) eventually
supplanted the ELF as the main insurgent
group. In 1991, together with the Tigrean
Peoples Liberation Front (TPLF) in
Ethiopia, they overthrew the Marxist
regime that had taken control of Ethiopia
in a 1974 revolution. Once again, the fate
of Eritrea was up in the air. The TPLF and
EPLF had made an agreement that Eritrea
would become independent, but the EPLF
also agreed to postpone independence until
a 1993 referendum to give Ethiopia’s new
government a chance to stabilize. In the
meantime, the EPLF became the provi-
sional government of Eritrea, but Eritrea
lacked international recognition and the
means of acquiring foreign aid to help with
postwar reconstruction. Also, nearly 80
percent of the population was living on
emergency relief because of the war and re-
curring droughts that had devastated the
agricultural sector. Nevertheless, the provi-
sional government pushed ahead with its
own reconstruction plans until the 1993
referendum established an independent
Eritrea.
Eritrea T oday
The new government of Eritrea faced a
monumental task of reconstruction and de-
velopment following the war, in addition to
devising new state institutions and other
nation-building tasks. The old colonial
infrastructure had not been maintained by
the Ethiopian government after it acquired
Eritrea in 1952, and very little new had
been built since. Recurring droughts and a
lack of resources had left the agricultural
sector a shambles. The EPLF , led by Isaias
Afwerki, became the People’s Front for
Democracy and Justice (PFDJ) and contin-
ued as the dominant (and only legal) polit-
ical power through the designated transi-
tion period (1993–1997). A legislative
branch, the National Assembly, was estab-
lished in 1993, consisting solely of PFDJ
members. Isaias became president of the
transitional government, and a constitution
was drafted and ratiﬁed in 1997, though it
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 503 ---
ETHIOPIA 427
did not go into effect. The PFDJ inherited
the resources of the EPLF and became the
main investor in the postwar economy,
founding numerous “private” enterprises in
construction and other sectors. In fact, the
PFDJ, while remaining the only legal polit-
ical organization in the country, has tried to
promote itself as a mass movement distinct
from the state.
Everything seemed poised for Eritrea’s
smooth transition to a democratically
oriented independent nation. However, re-
lations with Ethiopia became increasingly
tense, and a border war began between the
two countries in 1998, following the Eritrean
invasion of the town of Badme, which had
been one of several disputed areas. Despite
a formal end to the war in December 2000,
the border remains disputed, and a physical
demarcation originally scheduled for 2003
has not taken place. Neither have Eritrean
elections. The border war became an excuse
for the transitional Eritrean government
to postpone elections indefinitely, and
the 1997 constitution remains unimple-
mented. In addition, the war with Ethiopia
has set back Eritrean reconstruction and
development considerably.
Jericho Burg
