ETHIOPIA
Ethiopia is one of two countries in sub-
Saharan Africa that was never colonized by
a European power. (The other is Liberia.)
Because of this, and its rich and well-
documented history, it became an impor-
tant inspiration for anticolonial move-
ments in Africa, Latin America, and the
Caribbean. More recently, from the mid-
1980s, Ethiopia has become famous for
drought and famine and, consequently, for
being a major recipient of international hu-
manitarian aid. The third most populous
country in Africa, with seventy million in-
habitants, Ethiopia is home to approxi-
mately eighty different ethnic groups; the
largest are Oromo, Amhara, Tigrigna,
Sidamo, and Somali. Nearly half of the
population is Muslim, while Ethiopian
Orthodox Christians still predominate in
the central and northern highlands.
Located in the Horn of Africa, Ethiopia is
bounded to the south by Kenya, to the west
and north by Sudan, to the southeast and
east by Somalia and Djibouti, and to the
northeast by Eritrea, which gained inde-
pendence from Ethiopia in 1991. Despite
being in the heart of this conﬂict-prone
region, Ethiopia has become a center of
important political and economic activity
on the continent. Its capital, Addis Ababa,
hosts the headquarters of the African
Union and the United Nations’ Economic
Commission for Africa, among other
important international organizations. Even
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 504 ---
428 E THIOPIA
so, and despite a long history of centralized
rule, Ethiopia remains a nation of small-
holder farmers and pastoralists, with 85 per-
cent of the population living in rural areas.
History
Accounts of Ethiopia’s long history often
begin with Lucy, the name given to a 3.2-
million-year-old female Australopithecus
afarensis skeleton found in the northeastern
Afar region in 1974. Called Dinkenesh by
Ethiopians (Amharic for “you are wonder-
ful”), a replica of Lucy’s skeleton is on view
at the National Museum in Addis Ababa.
Other human ancestral remains have been
found in Ethiopia, including Australopithecus
africanus, Homo habilis, and Homo erectus,
which eventually evolved into Homo sapiens,
or modern humans. Thus, the region
now called Ethiopia was a site of human
evolution, and much important fossil
evidence has been recovered there. Ethiopia
was also one of the early centers for the
domestication of plants and animals; by the
second or third millennium BCE, several
important crops had been domesticated,
including ﬁnger millet, teff (a staple grain
in the highlands), and ensete, the “false
banana” that is a staple in the lowlands.
The ox-drawn plow became an important
feature of rural life, and it continues to be
today.
During the ﬁrst millennium BCE, a
series of states formed in what is now
northern Ethiopia, participating in eco-
nomic and cultural exchange with southern
Arabia and the eastern Mediterranean
world via the Red Sea. The state of Axum
emerged as a regional commercial and mil-
itary power that came to dominate the
region in the first century BCE. The
Axumites learned about Christianity
through contact with the Roman Empire,
and the Ethiopian Orthodox Church,
which has its own patriarch, developed
from the inﬂuence of two Syrians in the
Axumite court in the beginning of the
fourth century CE. Axum continued to
dominate Red Sea trade until the rise of
Muslim power in the eighth century. After
this, the region of Ethiopia became more
isolated from the Mediterranean world and
lost its control over interior trade routes.
The center of the kingdom moved south
and eventually came under control of the
Zagwe dynasty, one of whom, King
Lalibela, commissioned the eleven rock-
hewn churches in his capital of Roha, now
called Lalibela. Dating to the early
thirteenth century CE, this remains one of
Ethiopia’s most famous historic sites. The
persistent Christian beliefs of the Zagwe
dynasty gave rise to the European legend of
Prester John, a Christian priest-king ruling
an exotic land who had kept Muslim
invaders at bay. The Zagwe dynasty eventu-
ally succumbed to the so-called Solomonic
dynasty, a line of kings that ﬁctitiously
traced their ancestry back to the biblical
King Solomon and the Queen of Saba
(or Sheba) in order to win support.
Modern Ethiopia:The
Nineteenth and T wentieth
Centuries
The traditional core of Ethiopian
Orthodox Christianity and centralized rule
through feudal lords can be traced back
many centuries. Modern Ethiopia was born
out of conﬂict between this traditional core
(geographically located in the northern
regions of Tigray and Amhara), Muslim
states to the east, and the Oromo people to
the south and southwest, as well as internal
conﬂicts between feudal lords. By the mid-
nineteenth century, the Ethiopian state had
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 505 ---
ETHIOPIA 429
expanded to the south into Oromo lands.
Under a succession of emperors begin-
ning with T ewodros II (r. 1855–1868),
Ethiopian territory reached its current
extent, but not without considerable
conﬂict and resistance. T ewodros, though
striving to modernize the Ethiopian state,
resorted to such violence that when he
went so far as to imprison the British con-
sul, a British-led force deposed him in
1868. T ewodros was eventually succeeded
in 1872 by Emperor Yohannes IV , who fol-
lowed a more cautious strategy of uniﬁca-
tion and fought off an Egyptian invasion in
1876. However, the most famous of the
nineteenth-century emperors, Menelik II
(r. 1889–1913), succeeded not only in
fending off an Italian invasion at the
famous Battle of Adwa in 1896, but also in
expanding Ethiopia to its modern bound-
aries and establishing the national capital at
Addis Ababa in 1892.
The defeat of the Italians at Adwa had
international reverberations for many
decades. It was a victory of Africans over
Europeans at a time when the rest of the
continent was falling under European
domination. This victory and continued
independence made Ethiopia a symbol of
hope for blacks not only in the rest of
Africa, but also in the Americas and the
Caribbean. However, Menelik was not able
to drive the Italians completely away, and
they established a colony, Eritrea, along the
Red Sea coast. Ethiopia remained indepen-
dent into the reign of Emperor Haile
Selassie (born Tafari Mekonnen), who suc-
ceeded Empress Zawditu, Menelik’s daugh-
ter, in 1930. The Italians occupied Ethiopia
brieﬂy from 1936, though Haile Selassie
sought exile in England to avoid defeat
by drawing in British involvement. The
Ethiopian army continued to ﬁght against
the Italians, who were driven out when
Haile Selassie returned with British assis-
tance following the Italian declaration of
war on the Allies in 1940. When the British
tried to incorporate Ethiopia into British
East Africa, Haile Selassie turned to the
Americans for support. Ethiopia thus re-
mained an independent nation, with
American military and technical assistance
through the 1950s and 1960s.
Haile Selassie’s success in maintaining
control of Ethiopia caused his international
image to attain messianic proportions,
even spawning the Rastafarian movement
(taken from Ras Tafari, the emperor’s former
title and name) among working-class
blacks in Jamaica. Haile Selassie gave the 
Rastafarians a land grant in the town of
Shashamane, inviting them and others of
African descent to live there; there are some
200 Rastafarians living in Shashamane
today. Despite his international popularity,
Haile Selassie’s increasingly autocratic rule
led to growing insurgency in Eritrea (which
the United Nations granted to Ethiopia fol-
lowing World War II) as well as swelling
opposition among diverse groups such as
peasants, intellectuals, and minority ethnic
groups. The shift of American interest from
Ethiopia to Egypt in the late 1960s, as well
as the increase in international oil prices in
1973 and a severe famine in 1973–1974,
all paved the way for a military-led Marxist
coup d’état on September 12, 1974.
Mengistu Haile Mariam, a major in the
Ethiopian army, led the coup and estab-
lished a provisional military government,
popularly called the Derg (Amharic for
“group of equals”).
The Derg ruled as a Marxist-Leninist
regime, engaging in massive nationalization
of both rural and urban land. However, the
regime faced a series of crises, including
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 506 ---
430 E THNICITY
renewed insurgency in Eritrea led by the
Eritrean Peoples Liberation Front (EPLF),
a liberation movement in Tigray (the
Tigrean Peoples Liberation Front, or
TPLF), invasion by Somalia in 1977, and a
major famine in 1984–1985. Following the
famine, the EPLF and TPLF entered into
an alliance and were able to defeat govern-
ment forces in a series of battles. Meles
Zenawi, chairman of the TPLF and a new
multiethnic organization, the Ethiopian
Peoples Revolutionary Democratic Front
(EPRDF), and Isaias Afwerki, the EPLF’s
general secretary, began planning for a
post-Derg Ethiopia and an independent
Eritrea with the United States. In 1991 the
combined movements surrounded Addis
Ababa and demanded Mengistu’s resigna-
tion. Mengistu ﬂed to Zimbabwe on May
21, 1991, and the EPRDF controlled most
of the country shortly after that, ceding
Eritrea to the EPLF . However, relations
with Eritrea became strained, and in 1998
a two-year border war broke out between
the two countries. The border has yet to be
formally demarcated, pending Ethiopian
acceptance of a 2002 delimitation pro-
posed by the independent Eritrea-Ethiopia
Boundary Commission.
Ethiopia T oday
The EPRDF established a transitional gov-
ernment with support from the United
States, with TPLF leader Meles Zenawi ap-
pointed president. In 1995 the House of
Peoples Representatives voted to adopt a
new constitution, establishing the Federal
Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, with
Meles as its prime minister. Through
elections in 2000 and 2005, the EPRDF
retained its dominance, with Meles still as
prime minister. Ethiopia’s political struc-
ture is that of an ethnic federation, with
nine ethnically based regions: Afar,
Amhara, Benishangul Gumuz, Gambela,
Harari, Oromiya, Somali, Tigray, and
Southern Nations, Nationalities, and
People’s Region. Each region has consider-
able autonomy, including the right to se-
cede. The federal government consists of an
executive branch (president, prime minis-
ter, and Council of Ministers), legislative
branch (the House of Federation and the
House of Peoples Representatives), and
judicial branch (the Federal Supreme
Court). The EPRDF retains a majority in
the legislature, but the Coalition for Unity
and Democracy gained support during the
2005 elections, and numerous smaller par-
ties are also active.

ETHNICITY
Ethnicity identiﬁes and classiﬁes people
into groups according to perceived cultural
similarities and differences of beliefs,
values, customs, histories, and any other
relevant views and practices that are subse-
quently passed on to future generations.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 507 ---
ETHNICITY 431
The historical presence and use of the idea
of ethnicity is important to understanding
both transatlantic colonial history and the
postcolonial world. The peoples of Africa
alone belong to more than one thousand
different ethnic groups. While the Greek
root ethnos refers to people, nation, or for-
eigners, the adjective “ethnic” denotes a
way of life, including shared cultural attri-
butes and customs. The term ethnic group
continues to denote minority groups out-
side of the dominant, institutionalized
national culture. “Nationalities” then, may
be seen as ethnic groups that either have, or
are attempting to acquire, sovereignty for
their own country. The complex contem-
porary interaction between ethnicity, racial
classiﬁcation, and nationalism is part of the
history of European and American expan-
sion. Ethnic differences were often used to
create colonial hierarchies. Ethnic groups
also emerged in resistance to colonialism.
In the postcolonial world of Africa and the
Americas, ethnic identity is both a source
of political cooperation for marginalized
peoples within nations; it is also the focus
on conﬂict in places where sharp disparities
in access to political power and economic
resources appear to exist along ethnic lines.
Commonly held cultural characteris-
tics encourage a sense of ethnic identity in
which members of an ethnic group deﬁne
themselves as “us,” while outsiders become
a derisive “them.” For example, the T ewa
Pueblo Indians assigned the ethnic group
name (or ethnonym) Navajo, meaning
“thieves,” to their Native American neigh-
bors in the southwest United States. The
Navajo, however, call themselves Diné,
meaning “the people,” a common practice
among many Native American and African
ethnic groups. Therefore, ethnicity is not
simply a concept used to help explain social
consensus; it also highlights differences
from others by creating boundaries that
represent the “social organization of cul-
tural difference”(Barth, 1998, p. 6).
Different deﬁnitions of the function of
ethnicity exist. Some explain ethnic group
afﬁliation as a rational choice based on in-
dividual and group interests. For example,
in nineteenth-century Rwanda, one could
move from being a subjugated Hutu to an
upper-class T utsi by accumulating wealth
and status. This characterization of ethnic-
ity as socially constructed, however, has
been criticized for failing to account for
long-term ethnic group stability, neglecting
the role of context on individual choices,
and downplaying enduring emotional at-
tachments to particular groups.
Some observe that ethnic identity can
be contextual and that people share ethnic
identities and discuss, negotiate, and mod-
ify them in everyday interactions poten-
tially leading to cultural change. For exam-
ple, in the western Darfur region of Sudan,
Fur agriculturalists also own cattle; how-
ever, they prefer to leave their livestock in
the care of the pastoralist Baggara. As their
investments in cattle increase, Fur some-
times choose to take up the pastoralist
lifestyle. They become marginal nomads
rather than remaining wealthy landowners
who risk losing their accumulated livestock
capital. Accordingly, writes Gunnar
Haaland, “Through the nomadization
process individuals are thus sloughed off
from Fur local communities and eventually
incorporated into Baggara communities”
(1998, p. 65).
Ethnicity and ethnic group labels also
provide important political distinctions.
Politicized movements of group solidarity
such as the Jola peoples’ Movement of
Democratic Forces of Casamance (MFDC)
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 508 ---
432 E THNICITY
in southern Senegal continue to assert their
uniqueness by referring to indicators of
ethnic authenticity such as language and
dress.
Ethnicity, then, often encompasses
politically charged identiﬁcation categories
based on political autonomy (the nation-
state), sociopolitical organization (e.g.,
tribe), and phenotypic biology (race).
When an ethnic group is believed to have a
biological basis, it is called a race. Race is
not signiﬁcant as a scientiﬁc concept; how-
ever, distinguishing people based on physi-
cal traits (e.g., skin color) remains a socially
acceptable practice in many countries. The
U.S. Census Bureau still classifies the
American population according such racial
categories as “white,” “black,” and “other.”
A homogeneous American nationality (i.e.,
the melting pot), then, is perhaps more of a
symbol rather than a reality. Ethnic con-
sciousness in the United States continues to
rebound, although deciding on ethnic
labels can be a difﬁcult exercise. Ethnic,
racial, and national classiﬁcations are often
problematic because they vary according to
the traits they represent. Hispanic, for ex-
ample, is an ethnic label lumping millions
of people from Spanish-speaking countries
together. The term Latino, on the other
hand, is a more geographic label, including
the Portuguese speakers of Brazil as well as
Spanish-speakers from Central and South
America and the Caribbean. Members of
these and many other ethnic groups often
switch between identifying themselves
based on their genesis, nationality, religion,
gender, or race, depending on need and
circumstances.
In the context of European colonial ex-
pansion beginning in the ﬁfteenth century,
ethnicity, along with race, became a rhetor-
ical tool used by the colonizers to promote
and solidify advantageous ideological and
geographic boundaries. The hierarchical
nature of eighteenth-century capitalism re-
inforced rigid state boundaries on a global
scale. States (or independent, centralized
political units) claimed legitimacy based on
their representation of distinct populations,
whether national, cultural, or ethnic. This
remains often the case today, even though,
due to migration, conquest, and colonial-
ism, ethnically homogeneous nation-states
make up less than one-fourth of the world’s
countries. For example, of the more than
ﬁfty countries in Africa, many have more
than twenty ethnic groups within their
borders. Nigeria alone has more than 350
different ethnic groups, all with their own
customs, languages, and traditions.
Colonialism has had a major role in
shaping how ethnic groups and identities
developed. Precolonial groups such as the
Khwe Khoe, Basarwa, and San peoples of
the Kalahari Desert often acquired newly
synthesized ethnicities based on attribu-
tions from political agents such as colonial
European officials and anthropologists,
who, for example, labeled all Kalahari
peoples under a single derogatory term, the
Bushmen. In addition, disparate peoples
lumped together and forced to coexist
often created ethnic identities to strengthen
their group’s cohesion, including the
linguistically similar Khoisan of southern
Africa. Reinforced by proximity, cultural
familiarity, and social pressure, members of
an ethnic group often procreate primarily
with members of their ethnic group, per-
petuating ethnic identiﬁcation patterns.
By the nineteenth century, modern
states and empires blanketed the globe. The
arbitrary boundaries of empires, and—in
the twentieth century—the subsequent
boundaries of newly independent nations
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 509 ---
ETHNICITY 433
in Africa and the Americas invariably left
confined minority populations among
dominant groups that controlled national
politics. This multicultural, multiethnic
challenge forced minority group members
to seek equality based on individual rights
or on outright political autonomy for their
people, the latter leading to a proliferation
of smaller enclaves with little political
power on the global scene.
Divisions within multicultural societies
habitually result in interethnic tension or
outright conﬂict fought over limited re-
sources. In 1985 George Simpson and
J. Milton Yinger identiﬁed six types of in-
terracial and interethnic relations deﬁned
along a continuum stretching from cooper-
ation to outright aggression. These rela-
tionships are (1) pluralism, (2) assimila-
tion, (3) legal protection of minorities, (4)
population transfer, (5) long-term subjuga-
tion, and (6) genocide. Despite the diver-
sity and differences in economic opportu-
nity among many plural societies in Africa,
ethnic groups such as the Wolof, Serer, and
Pulaar of Senegal strive to live together in
peace and harmony. The homogenizing
effects of nationalism and global culture,
however, eat away at diverse societies
through cultural, social, and physical inte-
gration and assimilation. By legally protect-
ing minorities through ofﬁcial policies such
as the civil rights laws in the United States,
subnational identities continue to provide
marginalized groups a political platform.
On the negative side, the belief that
one’s own culture is superior to others (eth-
nocentrism) can lead to long-term subjuga-
tion, ethnic conﬂict, ethnocide, and in its
extreme form, genocide. Ethnocide, often
an overt policy of colonial regimes, is the
application of political coercion and force
to pressure marginalized peoples to give up
their way of life. For example, the
Portuguese implemented a colonial policy
of Assimilação, in which subjugated peo-
ples could attain Portuguese citizenship by
owning land and speaking and writing the
colonizer’s language. This policy weakened
the deﬁning markers of the originally colo-
nized ethnic groups. Assimilationist prac-
tices like this still abound, where powerful
factions coerce ethnic minorities into
ﬁtting in with their dominant culture or,
alternatively, experiencing discrimination.
Within the United States, the end of
the treaty system signaled the erosion of
Native American sovereignty. A focus on
individual rights advanced assimilationist
government policy aimed at the Native
Americans from the 1880s to the 1930s.
The Dawes Act of 1871, popularly known
as the Indian Homestead Act, divided up
commonly held lands, portioning out pri-
vate allotments and, consequently, assimi-
lating Native Americans into American
society. For example, in February 1890, the
U.S. government broke a Lakota treaty by
carving up the Great Sioux Reservation of
South Dakota to accommodate homestead-
ers. In reaction against this discriminatory
policy, Lakota warriors of the Pine Ridge
Indian Reservation adopted a militant form
of Jack Wilson’s (Wovoka) Ghost Dance
religion. This religion was a syncretic mix
of Native American and Christian beliefs in
which ancestor spirits would avenge their
mistreatment by the whites. On Decem-
ber 29, 1890, while attempting to disarm
and relocate a downtrodden Lakota en-
campment, the U.S. Seventh Cavalry mas-
sacred more than 150 men, women, and
children at Wounded Knee, South Dakota.
This ethnic conﬂict escalated to its violent
end in large part due to a misunderstanding
of the Ghost Dance movement.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 510 ---
434 E VOLUTION,H UMAN
Genocide, or the systematic eradica-
tion of an entire people by force in pursuit
of political aims, is the outcome of ethnic
identity politics taken to extreme ends. The
Nazi-perpetrated Holocaust in Europe, the
Bosnian genocide in former Yugoslavia,
and the 1994 Rwandan genocide—where
two extremist Hutu militias slaughtered an
estimated one million T utsis and moderate
Hutus in less than four months—attest to
the power of group membership and exclu-
sion as a motivation for human behavior.
Additionally, the Darfur conﬂict that began
in February 2003 has been described by the
mass media as genocide, or “ethnic cleans-
ing.” The Janjaweed Arab militia groups in
Sudan are estimated to have killed more
than 400,000 non-Arab peoples in the re-
gion. Both sides of this conﬂict are Muslim,
and both sides are largely black in skin
color. Therefore, the animosity is described
by most scholars as largely ethnic (Arabs
collectively termed Baggara versus non-
Arabic peoples such as the Fur, Masalit, and
Zaghawa). Political and economic motives
spur on the Darfur conﬂict; competition is
ﬁerce over scarce resources such as arable
land and surface water between farmers and
nomadic pastoralists in the drought-prone
Sudan. Ethnicity and ethnic differences
alone are neither inherently a source of
cooperation or conﬂict between groups.
Rather, people’s desire to belong to a group
in conjunction with many other historical,
cultural, political, economic, and even en-
vironmental factors may help explain why
people interact in different kinds of con-
sensus, cooperation, or antagonism.
Brandon Lundy

EVOLUTION,H UMAN
Human evolution is British naturalist
Charles Darwin’s theory and documenta-
tion of the development of the human
species, originating in Africa. The similari-
ties between humans and chimpanzees hint
at an African origin of humans, and mo-
lecular evidence puts the split between the
lines leading to humans and chimpanzees
at roughly 5 million years ago. Soon after,
perhaps 4 million years ago, a precursor of
humans ﬁrst walked upright. One hypoth-
esis suggests that these animals foraged
with their hands and brought food to their
mates and children. This hypothesis im-
plies kin cohesion, as may the 3.6 million-
year-old footprints in Laetoli. These are
two sets in synchrony, one presumably left
by an adult and the second by a child. The
two had walked side by side and had per-
haps been parent and child. These animals,
some of which must have led to humans
and others to a dead end, lived in southern
and eastern Africa. The fossils from 4 mil-
lion years ago are too fragmentary to per-
mit full reconstruction of anatomy, but the
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 511 ---
EVOLUTION,H UMAN 435
fossils, particularly the skeleton dubbed
Lucy, that date to roughly 3 million years
ago provide anatomical detail. These
Australopithecines were diverse. Some were
slightly built, much as are humans, and
others were far more robust than humans,
implying great muscularity and strength.
The large, ﬂat teeth equipped the robust
Australopithecines to grind plants and
seeds, whereas the teeth of the gracile
Australopithecines, more like ours, may
indicate a diet that included meat. Females
were much shorter and lighter than males,
implying competition among males for
mates. Australopithecines, with a large
mandible and small cranium, must have re-
sembled chimpanzees more than humans,
at least in the face and head. The long arms
of Australopithecines suggest that they
climbed trees as well as walked on the
ground, putting them somewhere between
an arboreal and terrestrial existence.
Around 2.5 million years ago in eastern
and southern Africa, contemporaneous
with the Australopithecines and in their
haunts, arose a hominid with a small
mandible, ﬂat face, and a brain larger than
that of Australopithecines. Paleoanthropol-
ogists designate this new hominid the ﬁrst
of our genus, Homo habilis, and assert that
at least two species of Homo existed by
2 million years ago. With our genus, the
size difference between males and females
declined, implying that nearly all of these
hominids who reached adulthood mated.
These may have been the ﬁrst hominids to
fashion stone tools, presumably for the
butchering of carcasses. Whether they
hunted or merely scavenged remains open
to question. The use of stone tools may
have driven the increase in brain size, and
roughly 2 million years ago these precur-
sors of humans radiated into still other
species with even larger brains. These new
species, Homo ergaster and Homo erectus,
were the ﬁrst to use ﬁre, and Homo erectus
was the ﬁrst to migrate out of Africa. The
prevalence of animal bones in sites occu-
pied by Homo ergaster and Homo erectus
evidences a regular supply of meat that
could have come about only through hunt-
ing. Hunting implies cooperation among
networks of people and so implies social
cohesion. With Homo erectus, people began
their long trek around the globe. Despite
settling Asia, Homo erectus did not cross the
Bering Strait into the Americas. The ocean
then barred the ﬁrst migrants out of Africa
from the Americas.
As Homo erectus spread from Africa
into Eurasia, this species branched into
others. Over time these species developed
larger brains and a wider array of stone
tools, making it difﬁcult to determine
which populations were or were not human
in anatomy and behavior. Neanderthal, for
example, had a brain slightly larger than
that of modern humans, undermining the
caricature of him as a witless brute. More-
over, these populations of archaic sapiens
surely interbred, making it likely that genes
from these early inhabitants of Africa and
Eurasia persist in contemporary popula-
tions of humans. In a striking contrast with
earlier hominids, archaic sapiens, notably
Neanderthals, buried the dead, possibly
with ﬂowers and other items that bespeak a
ritual. Burial and the religious trappings
that surround it imply that archaic sapiens
were human in a meaningful sense, though
they did not make art and may not have
spoken a language.
Our species arose perhaps 130,000
years ago in Africa and, like Homo erectus,
settled Asia, replacing archaic sapiens wher-
ever he went. Homo sapiens crossed the last
cultural Rubicon, developing language and
art. During these last 130,000 years,
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 512 ---
436 E XODUS
human evolution has been less biological
than cultural. About 40,000 years ago
Homo sapiens settled Siberia and may have
immediately crossed the Bering Strait—
then land because the ocean had sunk as
the polar ice caps absorbed water—into the
Americas. Fossils of Homo sapiens in the
Americas, however, date only to the last
12,000 years, weakening the conjecture
that humans had entered the Americas ear-
lier. Having made the long journey from
Africa to the Americas, humans found
themselves isolated in the New World. The
retreat of the glaciers 10,000 years ago re-
turned the ocean to its present depth, once
more submerging the land bridge between
Asia and the Americas and preventing
humans from migrating between the conti-
nents. Independently from one another,
humans in the Old and New Worlds devel-
oped agriculture, cities, and writing.
Despite these similarities, people in the
Americas on one side of the Atlantic and in
Africa and Eurasia on the other side created
separate worlds. In contrast to the people of
Africa and Eurasia, the Amerindians do-
mesticated few animals, had no draught
animal, used the wheel only as a toy, and
had rudimentary metallurgy and ship-
building. Isolated from the rest of human-
ity, the Amerindians did not develop im-
munity to the diseases that swept Eurasia
and Africa. Christopher Columbus re-
joined the Old and New Worlds; began an
exchange of microbes, plants, and animals
between the two regions; and nearly oblit-
erated the Amerindians. Homo sapiens, in
the form of Africans and Europeans, re-
placed the aboriginal inhabitants of the
Americas as they had replaced archaic sapi-
ens in Eurasia.
Christopher Cumo

EXODUS
The Exodus, or departure of the Israelites
from Egypt of the Old T estament, has reli-
gious, social, and political significance
through its new application by colonized
peoples. The biblical story of Exodus tells
how Moses—adopted as a child by the
Egyptian royal family—makes common
cause with his fellow Hebrews (or Children
of Israel), who are toiling under the tyran-
nical regime of the Pharaoh, and draws on
special God-given powers to persuade the
Pharaoh to “let my people go.” Parting the
waters, Moses leads them across the Red
Sea with the promise of a land “ﬂowing
with milk and honey” they could call their
own, although they must spend many test-
ing years in the wilderness—and defeat
more adversaries—before they arrive at the
banks of the Jordan to take possession of
Canaan, under Moses’s successor, Joshua.
The narrative has proved an enduring
rhetorical resource for a wide range of
political projects. Not surprisingly, it has
been of particular service to settler societies,
whose pioneers—in New England and
South Africa, for instance—modeled them-
selves on the Hebrews of the Old T esta-
ment, who ﬂed the oppression of Egypt to
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 513 ---
EXODUS 437
build a new land, even if it meant displac-
ing those already living there.
If the story helps an emerging people
or nation to make sense of itself, the conse-
quences may vary considerably. It can en-
courage complacency and justify conquest;
but it can also provoke self-doubt, as the
would-be Israelites wonder if they could
ever equal their elected forebears and if per-
haps they are not actually divinely “chosen”
at all. But more complex, ambivalent uses
of Exodus are evident among those who
ﬁnd themselves ruled by those settlers,
whose “milk and honey” they are (often
violently) prevented from sharing.
In South Africa, where “Ethiopian”
churches seceded from mission churches
(notably in1896 and 1917), black religious
leaders often identiﬁed themselves as new
Moseses, with a mission to free their people
from white domination. A notable example
is Albert Luthuli, leader of the African
National Congress in the 1950s, who called
his autobiography Let My People Go (1962),
its title a Mosaic injunction addressed to
the Pharaoh-like guardians of apartheid.
But it is probably in North America
where Exodus motifs have been reworked
most extensively. Slaves in the antebellum
South appropriated the religious teachings
to which they were exposed in such a way
as to give prominence to the Old T estament
narratives that told of the political history
of the Jews. This made their Christianity as
much about secular as spiritual redemp-
tion, even though the secular message had
to take on coded and indirect forms in the
sermons and spirituals likely to be over-
heard by their masters. In My Bondage and
My Freedom (1855), Frederick Douglass
tells how, nevertheless, “a keen observer
might have detected in our repeated
singing of ‘O Canaan, sweet Canaan,/I am
bound for the land of Canaan,’ something
more than a hope of reaching heaven.”
If the Pilgrim fathers interpreted the
crossing of the Atlantic as a voyage from
bondage to freedom, a voyage metaphori-
cally repeated, as it were, in the War of
Independence (as the original proposals for
the Great Seal of the United States suggest),
for slaves it meant something different. For
them, neither the colony nor the republic
was a promised land but rather a new Egypt
to which they had been forcibly removed.
The authors of slave narratives frequently
invoked Exodus. Henry Bibb, for instance,
recalled in his Narrative of the Life and
Adventures of Henry Bibb, An American
Slave (1849), how he dreamt of escape to
Canada from Kentucky, but found “the
river Ohio was my limit. T o me it was an
impassable gulf. I had no rod wherewith to
smite the stream, and thereby divide the
waters.” Yet others found ways of yoking
this biblical rhetoric not to individual,
clandestine ﬂight but to collective direct ac-
tion. Thus, we ﬁnd it in the appeals to their
followers by the leaders of slave insurrec-
tions such as Gabriel Prosser (1800) and
Denmark Vesey (1822). An uncompromis-
ing twist is also apparent in Henry High-
land Garnet’s stark assertion, in his Address
to the Slaves of the United States of America
(1848), that there can be “no redemption
without the shedding of blood” for “the
Pharaohs are on both sides of the blood-red
waters!”
This divergence of interpretations
should remind us that the Exodus story may
be read in many different ways. A further
complication in African American cultural
history arises when the Egypt of Exodus (as
a land of slavery) coexists with the Egypt as
it is reconﬁgured in Ethiopianism, which
draws on other parts of the Old T estament
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 514 ---
438 E XODUS
(and other sources) in order to make Africa
into a symbol of a golden age of black free-
dom and achievement (as illustrated by
Edmund Blyden’s lyrical description of the
Pyramids). Those promoting black emigra-
tion to Liberia sometimes paradoxically
represent the return to Africa as a crossing
of the Red Sea back to Egypt.
The ﬁgure of Moses also often provokes
ambivalent reactions. Harriet T ubman, who
led thousands of slaves North on the Under-
ground Railroad, became affectionately
known as the “Moses of her People.” White
abolitionists sometimes acquired a similar
distinction—John Brown and Abraham
Lincoln, for instance. But Lincoln’s igno-
minious successor, Andrew Johnson, was
found rather less worthy of the compari-
son. As Charles Sumner remarked: “They
should have had a Moses as a President; but
they had found a Pharaoh,” indicating the
ever-present danger that a powerful leader
always poses, however well-intentioned
(cited in Du Bois, 1956, 314). 
Many twentieth-century black ﬁgure-
heads have donned the mantle of Moses,
from Booker T . Washington and W . E. B.
Du Bois, through Joe Louis, to civil rights
leaders of the 1960s. The best illustration,
perhaps, is Martin Luther King Jr.’s famous
ﬁnal speech, on the eve of his assassination:
“Because I’ve been to the mountaintop. . . .
And I’ve looked over. And I’ve seen the
promised land.” Whether such a “Messiah
complex” is politically empowering for the
masses who are meant to follow remains a
matter of considerable debate.
In 1917 Robert S. Abbott, the pub-
lisher of the Chicago Defender, coined
slogans (“The Flight Out of Egypt”) and
promoted songs (“Bound for the Promised
Land,” “Going into Canaan”) in an attempt
to encourage southern blacks to migrate to
the North. And the Exodus motif has
proved an enduring strain in African Amer-
ican popular music. Consider, for example,
the many recorded versions of “Go Down
Moses” (by the Fisk Jubilee Singers, Paul
Robeson, Duke Ellington, The Golden
Gate Quartet, and Archie Shepp, among
others). Consider, too, the persona cele-
brated by Isaac Hayes on his album Black
Moses (1971) (wittily dissected in Chester
Higgins’s biblical liner notes) or Joe
Smooth’s inspirational deep house anthem
“Promised Land” (1989).
There are memorable reworkings of
Exodus in literature, too, above all, per-
haps, in poems that draw on the idioms of
the black preacher. “Ante-bellum Sermon”
(Paul Lawrence Dunbar) and “Let My
People Go” (James Weldon Johnson) are
the best-known examples. Melvin B.
T olson’s planned volumes after Harlem
Gallery (1965) were to have been: Egypt
Land, The Red Sea, The Wilderness,and The
Promised Land. But the most extended
treatments have been the verse narrative,
Moses, a Story of the Nile(1869), by Frances
E. W . Harper, and Zora Neale Hurston’s
novel, Moses, Man of the Mountain (1939).
In daring to make Moses an Egyptian,
Hurston at once confronts the vexed rela-
tionship of race and political leadership in
the United States (for her allegory makes
Moses a black man) and foregrounds the
inﬂuence of Africa on black Christianity in
the New World (for, at a more literal level,
we understand that he is heir to pagan
traditions of healing and magic, such as
voodoo). “Africa has her mouth on Moses,”
she writes, and Hurston is more aware than
most of the black Atlantic signiﬁcance of
the biblical ﬁgure, who also appears in the
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 515 ---

syncretic religious formations of Haiti,
for example, where he is fused with the
Dahomean god Damballa.
Perhaps the most popular “Black
Moses” of the diaspora was the Jamaican
Marcus Garvey, leader of the United Negro
Improvement Association. At the height of
his fame in the 1920s, he could boast mil-
lions of followers in a vast network of polit-
ical, cultural, and entrepreneurial initiatives
worldwide. Garvey continues to be invoked
as a mythic ﬁgure in contemporary Rasta-
farianism and is no doubt known to many
through reggae lyrics. At the turn of the
twenty-ﬁrst century, however, his global
reach has certainly been surpassed by his
fellow countryman, the Jamaican singer-
songwriter Bob Marley. It is salutary to
consider the striking discontinuity between
the self-aggrandizing and racially exclusive
“back to Africa” rhetoric of Garvey and the
inclusive and joyous ﬁrst-person plural
exhortations of the title-track of Marley’s
Exodus (1977)—a glimpse, perhaps, of an
open-ended narrative of liberation, in
which leaders do not become heads of state,
and where the point is not to secure terri-
tory but to keep on moving.
Alasdair Pettinger

EXPLORATION AND
EXPLORERS,A FRICA
Exploration in Africa, done for goods and
resources, the dissemination of religion,
political domination, and adventure, has
had an impact on all parties involved. After
a brief overview of the earliest explorations
of Africa, this entry looks at Central Africa
as the location that exempliﬁes the domi-
nant goals and perspectives of European ex-
plorers of Africa. Following this will come a
brief discussion of East, West, and southern
Africa, and ﬁnally the Sahara.
The reference in Herodotus’s ﬁfth-
century BCE work, Historiai (The Histories),
to a three-year circumnavigation of Africa by
“a Phoenician crew” under Egyptian king
Neco (610–595 BCE) documents the earli-
est known exploration of the continent.
Hellenistic interest in what Herodotus
knew as “Libya” is reiterated in the second-
century CE Geo¯graphike¯hyphe¯ge¯sis (Guide to
Geography) of Ptolemy, which places the
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 516 ---
440 E XPLORATION AND EXPLORERS,A FRICA
Nile’s source in the Lunae Montes (Moun-
tains of the Moon).
The fourteenth-century Rihlah
(T ravels) of Ibn Battu ¯ta in West Africa, the
sixteenth-century Descrittione dell’ Africa
(1550; A Geographical Historie of Africa)
of Moroccan traveler, Leo Africanus
(c. 1490–c.1554), who twice visited West
Africa, a few accounts of Ethiopia, and
records of coastal explorations (typically
emphasizing commerce and navigation)
constitute the major literary records of sub-
Saharan Africa before the eighteenth cen-
tury. It is important to remember, however,
that from at least the mid-ﬁrst-millennium
CE, traders (usually Muslim) had been
traveling back and forth across the Sahara
from North Africa to West Africa as well as
by sea from the Arabian Peninsula to East
Africa. Because the bulk of accounts of
African exploration are from Europeans,
however, we will focus on Europe’s explo-
ration of that continent, beginning with
Central Africa.
In the Western imagination, the
essence of the continent that has stood for
“darkness” has been—as Joseph Conrad’s
Heart of Darkness (1902) attests—Central
Africa. Europe has perceived Central Africa
as the most primitive, most savage, and
thus most “other” location within the land-
mass that German philosopher G. W . F .
Hegel, in his Vorlesungen über die Philoso-
phie der Geschichte (1837; The Philosophy of
History), describes as “compressed within
itself . . . enveloped in the dark mantle of
Night . . . . [where lives] man in his com-
pletely wild and untamed state. Such pre-
sumptions have made Central Africa the
antipode against which European differ-
ence—and supposed physical, intellectual,
and spiritual superiorities—could best be
proven. Europeans associated Central
Africa with Herodotus’s description of
Africans as “dog-headed,” other Africans as
“headless . . . with eyes in their breasts,”
and still others who “squeak like bats.” But
Central Africa might also hold the answer
to what Herodotus stated as “the Nile and
the riddle of its source,” so it is no wonder
that perhaps the three most famous
explorers of Africa—David Livingstone
(1813–1873), Sir Richard Francis Burton
(1821–1890), and Henry Morton Stanley
(1841–1904)—distinguished themselves
there.
Explorers sometimes approached this
cartographically blank region from the
north, as with Heinrich Barth (1821–1865),
who traveled from 1850 to 1855, and
Georg Schweinfurth (1836–1925), who
traveled from 1868 to 1871. But more typi-
cally they came from the south, as did David
Livingstone, who traveled in 1850–1856,
1858–1864, and 1866–1873, and from the
east, usually setting out from Zanzibar, as
John Hanning Speke (1827–1864) and
Richard Burton (1821–1890) did for their
1856–1858 expedition and later with James
Augustus Grant (1827–1892) and Speke for
their 1860–1863 travels.
Scottish missionary David Livingstone
set much of the tone and goals of nineteenth-
century travel in Central Africa when he
abandoned the proselytizing of missionary
work to focus on the “Commerce and
Civilization” that Livingstone declared in
his Missionary Travels (1856) would “open”
the continent to both Christianity and the
abolition of slavery—the proclaimed
raisons d’être of much European involve-
ment in sub-Saharan Africa. The impor-
tance of rivers to commerce catalyzed not
only the quest for the source of the Nile but
also the quest to map the major rivers of
the region.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 517 ---
EXPLORATION AND EXPLORERS,A FRICA 441
The nineteenth-century traveler in
Central Africa typically carried a noblesse
oblige air of paternalism, typified by
Burton’s description of indigenous people,
in The Lake Regions of Central Africa
(1860), as “of those childish races.” Explor-
ers’ texts and accompanying illustrations
magniﬁed the crisply dressed European,
whose stature and faraway gaze signiﬁed an
ability to lead, and these scenes typically
included a national ﬂag as Central Africa
became an arena in which not only men
but, metonymically, nations competed to
prove themselves and their “natural” supe-
riorities. Livingstone may have declared
himself a “pioneer of Christianity,” but
“grop[ing] in the interminable forests” for
the source of the Nile, he “stuck to it like a
Briton,” as reported in Livingstone’s Africa
(1872). What these explorations opened
Central Africa to, however, was not enlight-
enment, but approximately 10 million
deaths under the exploitative and brutal
rule of Belgian king Leopold II
(1835–1909), sovereign of the État
Indépendant du Congo (Congo Free State)
from 1885 to 1908.
In addition to ﬁnding the source of the
Nile, the “grail” of Central African travel
was to pass through it and escape alive
(akin to the Greek heroes who visited
Hades and returned to tell the tale), a feat
ﬁrst accomplished by Stanley, as told by
him in his Through the Dark Continent
(1878). In East Africa, however, the goal
was most certainly to answer the riddle set
out by Herodotus by ﬁnding the Nile’s
source. Speke solved this more than 2,000-
year-old riddle in 1858 and published the
answer (Lake Victoria) in his Journal of the
Discovery of the Source of the Nile (1863).
In West Africa the main goals were to
map that region’s major river, the Niger,
and to visit the fabled center of commerce
and learning, Timbuktu. Expeditions
generally traveled either south from T ripoli
(Libya) or east from Senegal. It was largely
poor Irishmen (Daniel Houghton) and
Scotsmen (e.g., James Bruce, Mungo Park,
Walter Oudney, Hugh Clapperton, and
Alexander Gordon Laing) who represented
Britain in early nineteenth-century
expeditions to West Africa. It was the desti-
tute Frenchman, René August Caillié
(1799–1838), who took the guise of a
Muslim to become, in 1828, the ﬁrst
European known to enter Timbuktu—and
thereby win a prize from the French
Geographical Society. He described his
journeys in his Journal d’un voyage à
T emboctou, dans L ’Afrique Centrale(1830;
translated as Travels through Central Africa
to Timbuctoo [1830]). Of particular impor-
tance to West Africa were the travels of
Scottish botanist Mungo Park (1771–1806),
who, although he died during his second
exploration of the Niger River, set scientiﬁc
and ethnographic standards of observation
that inﬂuenced many who followed. At the
other end of the century, Mary Kingsley
made two trips to West Africa, and her
account in Travels in West Africa (1897)
showed not only that English etiquette,
including “a good thick skirt,” could be
maintained in “the African forest,” but that
grit and courage were not characteristics
solely of men. More importantly, Kingsley
proved herself a sympathetic ethnographer
attuned to detail and to the lives of women.
Perhaps because of the early and
spreading presence of Europeans in the less
“glamorous” southern Africa, the explo-
rations there are, for the general reader, the
least interesting. Lacking the great rivers,
mountains, and fabled cities of the farther
north, and with more of a focus on setting
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 518 ---
442 E XPLORATION AND EXPLORERS,A FRICA
up mission stations and studying the ﬂora
and fauna, narratives such as Missionary
Labours and Scenes in Southern Africa
(1842), by Robert Moffat (1795–1840),
are slower and more intimate.
Also slower in pace are the narratives of
Sahara Desert exploration, but with these
comes a grandeur and often an inspiring
spirituality. While early-nineteenth-century
travelers to West and Central Africa typi-
cally saw the Sahara as something to “get
through,” in the mid-nineteenth century
this desert increasingly became a goal in
and of itself. The best early example of this
is Heinrich Barth’s detailed and highly
observant ﬁve-volume Reisen und Entdeck-
ungen in Nord- und Central-Afrika in den
Jahren 1849 bis 1855 (Travels in North and
Central Africa: Being A Journey of an
Expedition Undertaken Under the Auspices
of H. B. M.’s Government in the Years
1849–1855, published in 1857). As with
the exploration of the dense Congo
(or Zaire) River basin of Central Africa, the
goal to a great extent has been to explore
this greatest of all deserts and return to tell
the tale. But additional focal points of the
Sahara include the veiled T uareg men,
the nearly time-halting serenity of oases,
the rock art, and encountering (or even
joining) caravans.
Of all the continents, Africa is the one
most associated with exploration and
explorers. Africa has long been a place to
explore and ﬁnd things: the source of the
Nile, fabled cities, the Mountains of the
Moon (the Ruwenzoris), snow-capped
mountains on the equator, Stanley ﬁnding
Livingstone. It has been a continent of
beauty, stark contrasts, and a diversity of
articulate and developed cultures largely
unappreciated by early explorers. Africa has
often been the primitive “foil” against
which the Western explorer, and by exten-
sion the Western world, has deﬁned itself.
Exploring Africa has also often been trans-
formed into a trope for either traveling
back to a more primitive time or for de-
scending into the primitive unconscious of
the human id. What this tells us is that the
exploration of Africa has long been more
about the traveler than about the place
called “Africa”; it has been about using that
continent to deﬁne or inspire or test or
enrich explorers and the Western cultures
those explorers stood for. In this sense,
Africa has “served” not only the West’s
economic needs—though cheap labor and
natural resources—but also the West’s
psychological needs.
Kevin M. Hickey

FALASHA (BETA ISRAEL)
Falashas, Ethiopic for “strangers,” is the
name given to black Jews who lived in the
northwestern part of Ethiopia. According
to tradition, the Falashas (or Beta Israel, as
they call themselves) are the descendants of
Menelek, the son of Solomon and the
queen of Sheba. While the origin of the
Falashas is a mystery, it is likely that they
descended from Jews who immigrated to
Ethiopia during the early years of the
Christian era. It is certain, however, that
they broke away from mainstream Judaism
before the Mishnah was completed around
200 CE. The Falashas, a religious minority
in a Christian country, had a complex rela-
tionship with Ethiopian Christians. The
two groups were culturally and racially sim-
ilar in many ways, and the two religions
had a long history of inﬂuencing, convert-
ing, ﬁghting, and sharing with each other.
Judaism as practiced by the Falashas was
very different from other forms of Judaism.
Whereas they kept the Sabbath and Passover
and practiced dietary restrictions and cir-
cumcision, Falashas were unaware of the
Mishnah and Talmud traditions. They did
not use Hebrew as their sacred language and
did not celebrate Purim and Hanukkah.
Their Judaism was also different in that
Falashas incorporated certain conventions of
F
the Ethiopian Christians into their religious
practices. They had a common calendar,
they used the same sacred language (Ge’ez),
they observed circumcision of both males
and females, and they divided their places of
worship in the same manner. The Christian
institution of monasticism also played an
important role in their religious and secular
life for nearly a century and a half after its in-
troduction by a ﬁfteenth-century Christian
monk who converted to Judaism. Since the
Christianity practiced by Ethiopians had
strong roots in many Judaic inﬂuences and
in the Old T estament rather than the New,
there were even instances of Falasha lay cler-
ics relying on Ethiopian Orthodox churches
for their education and the production of
their sacred texts.
In Ethiopia most Falashas made their
living in agriculture—but only as tenant
farmers, since land ownership was limited
mainly to Christian government ofﬁcials
and military ofﬁcers. Other Falashas were
blacksmiths, weavers, potters, and con-
struction workers.
The Falashas were recognized as Jews by
the Sephardi chief rabbi in 1973 and the
Ashkenazi chief rabbi in 1975. This recogni-
tion allowed them automatic citizenship in
Israel. As a result of famine, civil war, and the
Falashas’ desire to emigrate, Israel, with
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 520 ---
444 F ANON,F RANTZ
diplomatic assistance from the United States,
lobbied the Ethiopian government to allow
them to relocate to Israel. On May 24 and
25, 1991, the Israeli military airlifted over
14,000 persons in Operation Solomon. An
earlier, clandestine attempt in 1984, Opera-
tion Moses, had airlifted to Israel over 8,000
individuals. In 1992, 4,000 more left
Ethiopia for Israel. T oday, all but a handful of
Falashas have immigrated to Israel. Unfortu-
nately for the Falashas, however, Israel has
not proven to be a paradise, as evidenced by
their major demonstration in 1996 to protest
the racism manifested against them.

FANON,F RANTZ
(1925–1961)
Frantz Fanon was a Martiniquan-born sol-
dier, psychiatrist, and a pan-African scholar
and activist. He was one of the foremost
scholars on the psychology of oppression.
Although born in the Caribbean nation of
Martinique, Fanon is perhaps most closely
identiﬁed with the African nation of Algeria,
for which Fanon fought during the latter na-
tion’s war for independence from French
colonial rule. Furthermore, although he was
trained as a psychiatrist, Fanon probably is
best-known as a pan-African scholar-activist,
thanks largely to such classic anticolonial
treatises as The Wretched of the Earth(1965),
Black Skin, White Masks (1967), and A
Dying Colonialism (1970).
At ﬁrst glance, it might seem ironic that
Fanon chose to attend medical school in
France, the nation that had colonized not
only his birthplace of Martinique but also
his future adoptive home of Algeria. How-
ever, Fanon was adept at mastering the tools
of the colonial power (e.g., French lan-
guage, French education) and subsequently
using those tools to subvert colonialism.
Fanon’s unique psychiatric perspective, in-
fused with black militancy, was so revolu-
tionary in scope that even the left-leaning
existentialist perspectives of such French in-
tellectuals as Jean-Paul Sartre—who wrote
the preface to Fanon’s The Wretched of the
Earth—were tame in comparison.
Psychoanalyst Frantz Fanon was a leading intellectual
of the anticolonial and Black Power movements of the
1950s and 1960s. He also worked with the National
Liberation Front during Algeria’s struggle for
independence. (Algerian Ministry of Information)
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 521 ---
FANON,F RANTZ 445
According to Fanon, the negative ef-
fects of colonialism can be seen in the racist
attitudes and corresponding behavior of
many persons of European descent toward
persons of color, as well as the self-hatred
and corresponding behavior of many per-
sons of color toward each other. This is not
to say that all persons of European descent
are racist, or that all persons of color engage
in self-hatred. Nevertheless, Fanon argued,
so many persons of European descent and
so many persons of color accept the prevail-
ing racial hierarchies in colonized nations
around the world that in general, race rela-
tions were, are, and always will be marked
by gross social inequities—that is, unless
persons of color rise in armed struggle
against their white oppressors.
In his writings on the pan-African con-
cept of Négritude (i.e., afﬁrmation of one’s
physical and cultural blackness as a coun-
tervailing force against antiblack racism),
Fanon provided an intellectual bridge be-
tween the concept of “Africanisms” among
black Americans (proposed by sociologist
W . E. B. Du Bois at the beginning of the
twentieth century) and the concept of
racial identity development among black
Americans (proposed by such post–civil
rights era, post–black power era psycholo-
gists as William Cross). Fanon did not in-
vent the concept of Négritude. (The con-
cept already had been championed by Aimé
Césaire, whom Fanon admired at one
time). Nevertheless, Fanon’s writings on
Négritude helped deﬁne the subject matter
of black studies in general (and black psy-
chology in particular) during the 1960s.
Like Du Bois, Fanon was renowned as
a scholar-activist. Unlike Du Bois, Fanon
explicitly and consistently advocated the vi-
olent overthrow of colonial regimes around
the world. One might be tempted to con-
clude that the difference between the
approaches of Du Bois and Fanon to elimi-
nating social inequities around the world is
akin to the difference between the ap-
proaches of Martin Luther King Jr. and
Malcolm X to eliminating social inequities
speciﬁcally in the United States. However,
just as Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm
X were more similar in ideology than one
might imagine, so too in hindsight were Du
Bois and Fanon. Both Du Bois and Fanon
believed that sustained political action was
necessary to achieve social equality.
Among personality theorists in the dis-
cipline of psychology, Fanon’s originality ri-
vals that of Sigmund Freud, Carl Jung, and
Alfred Adler. However, authors of main-
stream personality textbooks rarely mention
Fanon and never accord him the same status
as Freud, Jung, or Adler. In contrast, schol-
ars in the multidisciplinary ﬁeld of black
studies frequently draw upon Fanon’s in-
sights regarding the impact of colonialism
upon black personality development. With
the possible exception of Du Bois, no other
social scientist has mounted as formidable
an intellectual challenge to mainstream
views on race and personality as has Fanon.
Stanley O. Gaines Jr.

FARRAKHAN,L OUIS (1933–)
Louis Farrakhan is the current minister and
leader of the Nation of Islam. Farrakhan,
who leads the Nation of Islam movement,
calls on African Americans to rise into a po-
sition of power, one that whites, he be-
lieves, will never concede willingly. Blacks
must achieve agency through abstemious-
ness, devotion to Allah, discipline, self-
reliance, and pride in their African roots.
Born to West Indian parents in Roxbury,
Massachusetts, Louis Eugene Walcott was
raised in a strict Episcopalian milieu in the
Boston area, where he spent most of his
boyhood after his father’s early death. He
excelled in music (he is an accomplished
violinist), track sports, and academic sub-
jects. His racial consciousness was raised
in the 1950s, when the struggle against
segregation reached a heightened level of
intensity; he came to doubt the sincerity
of Christianity, thinking that no godly
religion could have tolerated whites’ age-old
racism. Farrakhan—calling himself “The
Charmer”—pursued a singing career that
changed dramatically in 1955. In that year
he heard the Nation of Islam leader, Elijah
Muhammad, speak at a Chicago club and
decided instantly to convert to Islam.
Committed to the Nation, he became Min-
ister Louis X, preaching at the Boston
mosque. He recorded propagandistic songs
and also wrote dramatic presentations such
as The Trial, in which “The White Man” is
found guilty of innumerable crimes.
Farrakhan remained with Elijah
Muhammad’s faction of the Nation when
Malcolm X split from the movement in
1964. Farrakhan suggested that Malcolm
deserved to be shot for his alleged treachery.
Soon after, Malcolm X was assassinated,
but no direct link between Farrakhan and
the gunmen has ever been proved. But the
apparently coincidental sequence of
Farrakhan’s outburst followed by Malcolm’s
murder fuels much of the continual ﬁre of
controversy and insinuation that follows
Farrakhan everywhere. A defendant in the
murder trial notoriously announced that he
considered Farrakhan’s remarks to be a state-
ment of instruction. Farrakhan carries bag-
gage from the assassination, but for many
years he has revered Malcolm publicly and
has sought reconciliation with Malcolm’s
relatives. T o Farrakhan’s dismay, Elijah
Muhammad’s son, Warith Deen Mohammad,
was named as the new leader of the Nation
when the old leader died in 1975. In 1977
Farrakhan revolted against Warith, form-
ing a new Nation of Islam. Since then,
Farrakhan has been the Nation’s public face.
Louis Farrakhan addresses his followers at the Nation
of Islam’s Saviour’s Day Convention at the University
of Illinois-Chicago Pavilion on February 23, 1997.
The convention included a live speech via satellite from
Libya’s Muammar al-Qaddaﬁ and taped messages
from the leaders of Ghana and Nigeria. In his speech
Farrakhan condemned American values and said that
African Americans should form a nation of their own.
(AP/Wide World Photos)
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 523 ---
FAUSET,J ESSIE 447
Farrakhan’s public proﬁle has been
vastly enlarged since 1984, when the
Nation’s policy of political abstention
changed to allow support for Jesse Jackson’s
presidential bid. Farrakhan also became
highly conspicuous as a ﬁgure of hatred for
Jews, in particular, as he articulated bla-
tantly anti-Semitic sentiments and made
comments about Adolf Hitler’s supposed
merits. Farrakhan has colorfully attacked
Jewish “bloodsuckers” who worship in
“synagogues of Satan.” Such hateful
rhetoric has ensured that Farrakhan is in-
ternationally notorious. Since 1986 he has
been banned from entering Britain by the
United Kingdom’s Home Ofﬁce, ostensibly
because his more extreme remarks may
cause violence between Britain’s Caribbean,
Jewish, and Muslim populations.
Although tested by prostate cancer,
Farrakhan remains a loud oppositional
voice in America. He organized the spectac-
ular Million Man March on Washington,
D.C.’s Capitol Hill in 1995 and has vocifer-
ously supported Iraq against the U.S. mili-
tary attacks of 1991 and 2003. Farrakhan is
feared by many whites, who see him as a
vicious proponent of a dangerous black
supremacy; many African Americans worry
that black self-esteem is harmed by his in-
sistence on the race’s victim status and his
rigid stress on the importance of collective
black goals. Other critics complain that
Farrakhan attacks the political system from
the outside when he could perhaps achieve
more by engaging with it. His many sup-
porters, however, maintain that Farrakhan
is a latter-day prophet who can lead African
Americans from a position of abject subju-
gation to one of righteous domination.
Kevin De Ornellas

FAUSET,J ESSIE (1882–1961)
Jessie Fauset was the most published black
female novelist of the Harlem Renaissance.
As literary editor of The Crisis, the ofﬁcial
journal of the National Association for the
Advancement of Colored People (NAACP),
from 1919 to 1927, Fauset also discovered
and promoted many leading black artists,
although much of the credit has been
wrongly attributed to W . E. B. Du Bois.
Her own work has generally been dismissed
as assimilationist.
Born in 1882, the daughter of an
African Methodist Episcopal minister in
Philadelphia, Fauset was the ﬁrst black
woman to graduate from Cornell Univer-
sity with a Phi Beta Kappa key, having been
rejected by Bryn Mawr on account of her
race. She later gained a masters degree in
French at the University of Pennsylvania
and also studied at the Sorbonne in Paris.
Fauset spent fourteen years teaching
French at the famous M Street High School
in Washington, D.C., during which time
she worked on NAACP discrimination
suits in the still-segregated capital. A fre-
quent contributor to The Crisis, she moved
to Harlem to work as literary editor on the
journal in 1919.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 524 ---
448 F ÉDEONREBELLION
Fauset published four novels: There is
Confusion (1924), Plum Bun (1929), The
Chinaberry Tree (1931), and Comedy:
American Style (1933). In her fiction,
Fauset offers a commentary on the trials of
being a black woman in America. She sug-
gests that there are alternatives for women
beyond marriage and children and depicts
numerous successful, economically inde-
pendent, and sexually conﬁdent women.
Fauset works toward a “feminist” alterna-
tive, where her heroines, though not always
successful, are almost always aware of the
obstacles that have been placed in their way
because of both their race and their gender.
Although well reviewed by much of the
black and white press at the time, Fauset’s
novels have since been heavily criticized be-
cause of a tendency among black literary
critics to glorify proletarian and folk tradi-
tions while disparaging those who depict
the middle class. More recently, feminist
critics have argued for a sympathetic con-
sideration of the progressive aspects of
Fauset’s novels, especially her implicit criti-
cism of the conventions of black women’s
romance novels. Moving beyond her novels
to her short stories, poems, and articles for
The Crisis and the black children’s maga-
zine, The Brownies Book, critics have devel-
oped a better understanding of the Pan-
African consciousness in her work.
Fauset supported the Pan-African Con-
gresses organized by Du Bois, and in 1919,
as one of the few black women in atten-
dance at the second Congress, she delivered
an address in which she sent a greeting
from the black women of America to the
women of Africa. When Fauset left The
Crisis in 1927, she taught at De Witt
Clinton High School in New York City
and continued to teach and publish after
her marriage in 1929. Like many black
women writers, she was unable to recapture
her earlier literary success after the Harlem
Renaissance. She moved to New Jersey in
1940 and died in 1961, long before her lit-
erary contribution was fully recognized.
Kate Dossett

FÉDEONREBELLION
On the Caribbean island of Grenada in the
late eighteenth century, the Fédeon Rebel-
lion was an antislavery, anticolonial insur-
rection led by both whites and blacks. On
March 2–3, 1795, an alliance of free col-
oreds, white French, white British, and
enslaved Africans launched one of the most
spectacular, sustained, bloody but ulti-
mately unsuccessful antislavery, anticolo-
nial, proto-nationalist struggles of the Age
of Revolution. Led by Julien Fédeon, the
free colored owner of Belvidere estate,
which was the revolutionary headquarters,
the rebels controlled all Grenada’s territory
except the capital, St. George’s, for nearly
two years until Lieutenant General Ralph
Abercromby’s British Expeditionary Force
suppressed this incipient revolution. The
liberated territory had its own capital,
Gouyave—re-named Port Libre—and other
rudiments of a polity. Chattel slavery was
abolished and residents were considered
citizens of the French Republic.
Actual planning began in 1793, but the
rebellion originated in more than a century
of slave resistance and also in French discon-
tent over British rule since 1763, but partic-
ularly after Grenada’s restoration to Britain
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 525 ---
FEMINISM AND WOMEN’S EQUALITY MOVEMENTS,AFRICAN 449
in 1783, which followed a short-term
French occupation begun in 1779. Between
1784 and 1795, the British Protestants used
the state apparatus to repress the French
Catholics. In 1793 the appointment of the
Catholics’ chief persecutor, Ninian Home,
as lieutenant governor of Grenada precipi-
tated the revolution.
Preparations were advanced before
Victor Hugues arrived at Guadeloupe from
France in 1794 to implement the National
Convention’s decree that abolished French
slavery and extended French citizenship to
all in her colonies. This was part of France’s
strategy to regain her eastern Caribbean
empire and capture British-held territory.
Hostilities began with simultaneous at-
tacks on the towns of Grenville and
Gouyave. Within twenty-four hours,
Home and important members of the
British establishment were captured. After
the British refused to surrender the colony
to General Fédon and the revolutionaries,
Grenada experienced internal war. Home
and the others remained prisoners at
Belvidere until April 8, when a bungled
British attack resulted in the execution of
Home and forty-seven others.
T ensions between Hugues and the
Grenadians over the conduct of the inter-
nal war eventually split the revolutionary
forces into two, with units of the French
republican army at Port Libre and the
Grenadians at Belvidere. By early 1796,
Grenada was virtually an independent
black republic. After Abercromby’s arrival
in the Caribbean in March, the balance
tilted permanently against the revolution-
aries. On June 10 the French surrendered.
Belvidere fell on June 19.
Those revolutionaries captured alive
were found guilty of high treason, hanged,
and decapitated. Their properties were con-
ﬁscated. Others were transported to Central
America. It was the end of French social
power in Grenada.
Fédon was neither captured nor made
to suffer an ignominious death. He is be-
lieved to have escaped to Cuba, where, oral
tradition holds, he died. He is a legend and
inspiration to Grenada’s artists, national-
ists, and revolutionaries. Fédon’s Rebellion
deﬁes categorization. The involvement of
free coloreds and white British and French
made it an insurrection against British
rule. The participation of thousands of
mostly African-born enslaved made it a
slave rebellion. The French military and
civilian presence made it an episode of St.
Lucia’s 1797 Brigands’ War. The Fédeon
Rebellion failed to abolish slavery and cap-
ture Grenada for republican France, but
British rule and slavery were shaken to
their very foundations.
C. M. Jacobs

FEMINISM AND WOMEN’S
EQUALITY MOVEMENTS,
AFRICAN
African feminism has had a complex intel-
lectual history in a postcolonial sociopolit-
ical context. Although it is clear that
women throughout Africa, from ancient
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 526 ---
450 F EMINISM AND WOMEN’S EQUALITY MOVEMENTS,A FRICAN
times on, worked to effectuate their own
power and agency within traditional
African societies, a conscious or ofﬁcial
“women’s movement” did not emerge in a
substantial way until the twentieth cen-
tury. Feminism often emerged in tandem
with independence movements and thus,
in Africa, has often been tied to larger
questions and problems of postcolonial
economic development and the fight
against imperialism. In turn, women in
Africa have expressed their needs and
sought equality in a complex relationship
of dialogue, support, tension, and conﬂict
with feminisms from the West, especially
the United States.
T wo phases may be seen in the devel-
opment of women’s movements in Africa
from the time of independence onward.
The ﬁrst phase is what is called a “Women
in Development” approach. A good deal of
scholarship in the 1970s and 1980s dealt
with women and their role in the develop-
ment of Africa. Women’s organizations
were tightly tied to the newly formed na-
tional governments and, after the United
Nations’ Decade for Women, to those of
their members who were given formal posts
within the government to work on women’s
development. Because of these close ties,
however, the efforts of many women’s
groups were hobbled by the agendas of the
political parties to which they were linked,
and women’s issues were sidelined in favor
of the larger project of getting votes for the
party. This began to change in the late
1980s and early 1990s, when women’s orga-
nizations began to assert their independence
from governmental organizations. Partly,
this was the result of the increasing presence
of multiparty systems in many parts of
Africa. In addition, there was growing em-
phasis on fund-raising through the creation
of independent organizations, many of
which availed themselves of the increased
funds poured into Nongovernmental
Organizations (NGOs) by industrialized
nations. These NGOs became more willing
to fund causes like women’s liberation,
which allowed many of the women’s groups
arguing for their rights to make more
efﬁcacious statements. The inﬂuence of the
international feminist movement, and
particularly the 1995 Beijing Women’s
Conference, helped to mobilize women in
Africa into new organizations. These orga-
nizations tended to be local in origin and
in agenda, speaking to the varied needs
of women throughout Africa and not at-
tempting to be larger, overarching organi-
zations dealing with all of women’s needs.
In addition, rather than attempting to
work with developmentalist agendas, these
groups more often found themselves lobby-
ing for politically strategic issues that
directly impacted women’s lives—issues
such as increased access to education and
political ofﬁce for women as well as domes-
tic violence, rape, and other matters requir-
ing legal protection for women. These
groups were also able to mobilize women
across ethnic divides. For example, the
Women’s National Council in South Africa
was a group able to cut across traditional
boundaries between groups in order to voice
more powerfully the concerns of women.
Women’s concerns, then, have come to
be addressed in increasingly diverse ways in
many parts of Africa, and in ways often dif-
ferent from the approaches of Western, in-
cluding U.S., feminists. For instance, many
African feminists use the idea of mother-
hood with which to gain moral authority to
argue for the collective rights of women.
Additionally, tensions along class lines
among women have been visible. With an
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 527 ---
FEMINISM AND WOMEN’S EQUALITY MOVEMENTS,A FRICAN 451
increasing number of women having access
to university educations since indepen-
dence, there is sometimes a divide between
those with and without university educa-
tions and between older and younger gen-
erations of feminists. Overall, however,
these differences have not stemmed the tide
of women’s organizing.
Several key voices and publications
provide examples of the diversity of African
feminisms. Combining photographs, data,
and commentary, Buchi Emecheta and
Maggie Murray’sOur Own Freedom (1981)
emphasizes the many social roles that
African women play. Emecheta and Murray
assert the need for women in Africa to
arrive at their own versions of freedom,
while reminding women of the West of the
need to understand the everyday lives of
women in Africa before making interven-
tions in African matters that, though well-
intentioned, are often ineffectual and
sometimes even harmful to the women
they are trying to help.
Florence Abena Dolphyne, a former
chair of the National Council on Women
and Development in Ghana, observes that
Western women and African women who
had joined together in solidarity through-
out the 1970s and 1980s often found
themselves at odds regarding how to argue
for the rights of women in Africa. Many
Western feminists found themselves argu-
ing for the right of women to be free of
what they saw as the patriarchal institutions
of polygamy, child marriage, female cir-
cumcision, and the birthing of too many
children. However, many women from
Africa found themselves on the defensive
over these matters, trying to explain the
deep cultural roots that some of these prac-
tices had. While Western feminists argued
for immediate governmental action via
legislation, African feminists argued for
more gradual approaches that included ed-
ucation programs and the improvement of
overall living conditions for many of the
women, often rural, who experienced these
practices in their everyday lives. In addi-
tion, Western feminists seemed to want to
avoid issues of international political im-
port to women in Africa—issues such as
South African apartheid and conﬂicts in
the Middle East—while women in Africa
argued that these issues, too, touched the
lives of women very deeply and should be
meaningfully addressed by women. They
were not, for the African women, a distrac-
tion, but a very vital part of liberating
women from the oppression they faced, op-
pression that in some cases implicated the
global imperialist system. Dolphyne argues
that economic survival and development
are of primary concern for African women,
and that education combined with sound
economic policies and goals will help Africa
and Africa’s women to move forward in
their own liberation.
In African Feminism (1997), Gwen-
dolyn Mikell attempts to explain the differ-
ences that keep U.S. and African feminists
from uniting. Mikell argues that African
feminism emerged under different condi-
tions and with different goals because
African feminism comes out of a resistance
against Western hegemony in Africa and
not out of a bourgeois capitalist context.
Because of these different circumstances,
the “rights” focus of U.S. and European
feminism ﬁnds little place in the emerging
African feminism. Instead, Mikell argues,
African feminism is heterosexual and pro-
natal in emphasis and is more concerned
with daily issues of survival, such as food,
housing, and the power relations that un-
derlie how resources are distributed. Thus,
