the types of community formed through
African feminist alliances tend to be less in-
dividualistic and more closely related to
shared cultural experiences and these al-
liances’ links to political power. Because of
these different forms and emphases, there
have been a number of difﬁculties between
Western and African feminists in forming
links to ﬁght women’s inequality. Contro-
versies over female circumcision in Africa,
for instance, are viewed differently from the
Western feminist point of view than they
are in many places on the African conti-
nent. In addition, women’s reproductive
rights and capacities have been areas of
conﬂict among U.S. and African feminists,
as Mikell asserts that African women do
not view reproduction and their roles as
mothers as oppressive and stultifying, in
contrast to some early U.S. feminist theo-
rists. Instead, many African feminists see
the roots of their oppression in their lack of
control over the economic circumstances of
their lives due to Western interventions
both during and after the colonial period.
Oyèrónké Oy˘ ewùmí argues that West-
ern feminists have too long sought to deﬁne
African women and their relation to  moth-
erhood in terms that are imperialist and
inaccurate. Instead of the metaphor of sis-
terhood, for instance, Oy˘ ewùmí argues that
alliances across the idea of motherhood are
more appropriate in light of familial and so-
cial relations within Africa. Because what
most women share in Africa is motherhood,
she argues that this should be the basis of
identiﬁcation among women. African femi-
nism must be united around the varying
identities held by all members of African so-
ciety, not just a biological consideration of
gender, which, despite inroads of Western
imperialism, remains secondary to other
identity markers such as age, status, and
class. In addition, she complicates the rela-
tionship between black American feminists
(or womanists) and Africa, noting that they
often partake in many of the same imperial-
istic discourses as their white American
counterparts in relation to Africa, and that
they allow their own image of Africa to
override the realities of life in Africa.
Overall, African feminism might be
said to be charactized by an interest in the
common struggle with men against the im-
perial exploitation of Africa by Europe and
the United States; a recognition of in-
equities springing both from traditional
African institutions and those that have
been added through colonialism; and a be-
lief that the local material conditions of
women’s lives must dictate the goals of the
African feminist movement. Rather than
simply importing Western feminist agen-
das, African feminism seeks to determine
which institutions need to be changed
within African society for the betterment of
women. African feminism also seeks to re-
spect the economic autonomy of African
women and works to establish their contin-
ued prosperity in connection with collec-
tive action for the beneﬁt of all women. It
draws critically on traditions from both the
West and its own communities to create
equality and empower women.
Kelly O. Secovnie

FEMINISM AND WOMEN’S
EQUALITY MOVEMENTS,
TRANSATLANTIC
Women’s transatlantic equality movements
refer to woman-centered struggles, political
drives for legal equality, and coalitions de-
parting from mainstream political and class
cultures that oppress minorities. For cen-
turies, women have played integral roles in
challenging and resisting oppression in
Africa and the Americas. Though the strug-
gle for gender equality involves countless
individual leaders and organizations, some
of its general motivations and characteris-
tics become clearer when examined
through the unique lens of the transat-
lantic. From colonial rebellions to current
political battles for legislation, the efforts of
women’s equality movements tell a com-
plex story of perseverance and desire. Their
narrative is one of coalition, of building
bridges, and of creating communities that
reﬂect the multilayered and complex inter-
ests of different interest groups. At the same
time, the histories of African feminists and
their movements also reveal their connec-
tions with and departures from U.S. femi-
nism as they demand their own places in
dialogues revolving around transnational
women’s movements.
During the colonial period that dis-
placed Africans to the Caribbean, women
were extremely active in the maintenance
of African traditions and spiritual expres-
sion, and they used these aspects of their
heritage to subvert oppressive systems of
power. While many slaves practiced their
religious rituals under the auspices of
Catholicism, enslaved women in Peru
rejected their European masters’ faith in the
sixteenth century. Thus, African women
retained powerful positions as priestesses,
persons with extremely important societal
value. Often, they used religious practices
like obeah to challenge the oppressive
power structures. African female slaves ﬁg-
ured prominently in eighteenth-century re-
bellions as well. For instance, Jamaicans
still talk about the legendary slave priestess,
Grandy Nanny, who ran away to the Blue
Mountains and led a guerrilla resistance
against the British. Women were also active
in antislavery movements in the Spanish-
speaking Caribbean. Mariana Grajales, for
example, is a widely known figure of
protest in Cuba. During the T en Years’ War
from 1868 to 1878 in which Cuba fought
for its independence from Spain, Grajales
organized a hospital for the wounded and
was then exiled at the end of the war. These
speciﬁc examples of women ﬁghting for in-
dependence are emblematic of a larger
trend in Africa and its diaspora of resistance
against not only hegemonic systems of pa-
triarchy but also more general sources of
racist, classist, and misogynist governmen-
tal and institutional oppressions.

For instance, many women’s equality
movements have united people from differ-
ent class strata to ﬁght against the very polit-
ical and class structures that would divide
them. In the two years of 1921 and 1922,
working-class women in El Salvador, aligned
with the growing Labor movement, rebelled
against their government and called for the
Meléndez administration to release political
prisoners. Women have worked across class
lines in Chile as well, forming coalitions like
the Centros de Belén de Zárraga in 1913 to
protest the exploitation of women workers
in the mining industry. In Mexico, women
from various class strata united to resist
Cortez’s conquest and later to play active
roles in the nineteenth-century Mexican
wars of independence. Jamaican women also
fought together to enact sociopolitical
change. They were involved in the Morant
Bay Rebellion of 1865, and they later con-
tributed to the decolonization movement
that was ideologically fueled by leaders like
Marcus Garvey in the 1920s. This ongoing
demand for equal rights persisted in the sus-
tained suffrage movements of the twentieth
century. Even though women did not win
the right to vote in Nicaragua until 1955,
they lobbied for suffrage rights as early as
1932, when the U.S. military administra-
tion denied the request. And in El Salvador,
women’s voting rights were constitutionally
recognized in 1938, though women did not
actually vote until 1950. The alliances
among women traversed class status. Every-
one was thus able to play a part in achieving
a more egalitarian society. While women
from the upper and middle classes used
their positions to write about sociopolitical
ills, women workers were able to use land
to gain more social autonomy in their rela-
tionships with men, as well as economic
autonomy.
Like these women freedom ﬁghters in
the Americas, African women have also
uniﬁed themselves across class strata to ad-
vance their struggle for equality. Rural
women in places like South Africa histori-
cally have been discriminated against, com-
monly being accused of witchcraft. One of
the interventions by women came in the
form of social organizations that bound
women together. For instance, in the early
twentieth century, Zenzele Clubs worked
to establish autonomy for women in an op-
pressive society controlled by a white hege-
mony. These clubs were based on the
African Women’s Self-Improvement Asso-
ciation and the Bantu Women’s Home Im-
provement Association, both of which
taught domestic skills to women from rural
and working-class areas. During their run
from the 1920s through the 1950s, these
organizations played integral roles in main-
taining equal rights efforts of poor women.
Much of the focus of these women, despite
their backgrounds, involved an opposition
to a broad, boundary-crossing sense of so-
cial injustice that permeated class, race, and
gender. Thus, women played an active part
in the Kenyan revolts against colonial pow-
ers in the mid-twentieth century, risking
imprisonment and even death at the hands
of their enemies in order to exact social
change.
Along with the alliances they formed in
a general resistance to governmental oppres-
sion, African women have come together
through their roles as mothers. During the
colonial period in Zimbabwe, motherhood
was extolled both by European missionaries
and by African women themselves. For the
missionaries, maternity perpetuated Chris-
tian ideals of womanhood. For the women,
bearing children ensured more social oppor-
tunities both politically and economically.

This common elevation of motherhood
helped to form connections even between
African politics and European religion.
Women employed Methodist prayer circles
in attempts to bolster their fertility. Also, in
the mid-twentieth century, a religious sect
called the Mai Chaza Church branched off
from the Wesleyan denomination and em-
phasized the sacred position of mother-
hood. The maternity that bonded women
despite class or racial variance became a
prominent factor of uniﬁcation of women
in Central and South America and the
Caribbean as well.
Perhaps the most well-known of the
coalitions formed out of a sense of maternal
duty is the Madres de la Plaza de Mayo
(Mothers of the May Plaza) in Argentina.
This group was founded in 1977 by moth-
ers who crossed paths when frantically
searching for their children who had gone
missing after the government sanctioned
their “disappearances.” These women used
their common agenda to demand their
children back from the state that had
terrorized them. Though they had not pre-
viously been politically active, the Madres
became a strong and effective societal force.
Like women in Zimbabwe, the Madres
used their social position as mothers to
stimulate political change. The historically
esteemed role of maternity in the transat-
lantic is one of the ways in which women’s
movements in Africa and the Americas
have distinguished themselves from tradi-
tional U.S. feminism. Maternity has not
been a source of obligatory marginaliza-
tion. Rather, it has been channeled as a pos-
itive force for coalition building that has
demanded respect, even from government
leaders. However, several associations have
found feminism a useful rallying point
around which to organize their agendas.
First published in 1976, the Brazilian news-
paper Nós Mulheres (We women) was the
ﬁrst to identify itself as “feminist.” Signiﬁ-
cantly, many of the equality movements
and groups in the latter half of the twen-
tieth century consisted of women from
working-class, urban areas. Again, empha-
sis on gender has not limited equality
movements to resistance against misogyny;
rather, these movements have spread their
domain into the broader concerns of hu-
manitarianism. Nós Mulheres, for example,
dealt with concerns of working-class
women but still retained strong support
from the domestic women of the middle
class.
In the latter half of the twentieth
century, more and more formal groups and
alliances throughout the Americas adopted
feminist afﬁliations and agendas as part of
their overall objectives. Gender was a
singular political issue in the preparatory
meetings leading up to the International
Women’s Year Conference in Mexico City
in 1975. Then, beginning in 1981, women
began to meet at biannual encuentros
(encounters) to discuss feminist concerns as
distinctly politicized ends unto themselves.
With each encuentro taking up new and
speciﬁc issues like race, sexuality, and auton-
omy, feminists—or feministas—mapped
out aims and motivations in a unique
vision of women’s equality. Women main-
tained the practice of working with other
women of different ethnicities and classes
to attain their general goals. Throughout
the 1970s, they protested governmental op-
pression and worked to provide their own
solutions to meet the needs of marginalized
women. In Brazil, rural and urban women
alike worked for greater ownership rights
and equality in working conditions. Race
became a central issue for Afro-Brazilian

women, and they created the United Black
Movement (Movimento Negro Uniﬁcado ,
MNU) to counter racist ideologies. The
1970s and 1980s also saw the rise of proj-
ects like the Feminine Amnesty Movement
(Movimento Feminino pela Anistia, MFA)
and the Cost of Living Movement (Movi-
mento contra a Carestia ). Such activity in
Brazil has led many to pinpoint
1979–1981 as the peak years of organized
women’s equality struggles, as evidenced by
groups such as the First Paulista Women’s
Congress.
The 1970s and 1980s proved important
decades for African women’s movements as
well. Feminists in South Africa organized
Rape Crisis in 1976, one of the oldest orga-
nizations of its kind, in Cape T own. It re-
ceived an enormous response from women
who formerly had no place to turn. Another
pivotal coalition at this time was WAG, the
Women’s Action Group, formed in 1983 as
a resistance to the Zimbabwe government’s
Operation Clean-up, a discriminatory ef-
fort by the government to clear out prosti-
tutes and the homeless from the streets.
The attempt soon got out of hand as the
military and police began arresting urban
professionals like teachers and nurses, most
of whom were black women. WAG inter-
vened by publishing documents concern-
ing the excessive arrests and presenting
them to the prime minister. They also in-
sisted that victims of Operation Clean-up
receive reparations from the government to
alleviate their losses. Although the women
who were arrested never received any ﬁnan-
cial consideration, WAG’s unrelenting
efforts contributed to the government’s
eventual termination of the program. After
the successful end of Operation Clean-up,
WAG organized a meeting attended by
women from various class strata in 1984.
Out of that gathering came the widely
read but unpublished r eport, Women of
Zimbabwe Speak Out (1984), which spoke
to many of the social concerns of American
women. WAG has remained active in Zim-
babwe, jump-starting initiatives like the
1990 Women’s Writers Project and main-
taining a focus on creating coalitions and
intersections of women from various back-
grounds and experiences. The late 1980s
also saw the surfacing of another focus for
African women—the vast number of mis-
treated female Somali and Sudanese
refugees. In the early 1990s women worked
to end South African apartheid, and during
1994 they not only witnessed the results of
their efforts in the region’s ﬁrst democratic
elections, but also wrote the Women’s
Charter for Effective Equality, which shed
light on violence toward women. More re-
cent dialogues and movements in these
areas of women’s concern have included at-
tempts to bring attention to women’s rights
in the midst of sociopolitical and religious
unrest in the Sudan.
Coalitions have played important roles
in the past two decades in the Americas as
well. Chilean women with socioeconomic
concerns united in the early 1980s to pub-
lish the notable socialist magazine Furia.
Other concerns have begun to be addressed
by feminists in the 1990s. For example, the
United Nations Conference on the Envi-
ronment in 1992 received valuable infor-
mation and support from transnational
feminist ecologists who formed the Planeta
Femea, or Women’s Planet, as distinct space
for women. Other groups and organiza-
tions with diverse supporters but common
goals include the Iniciativa Feminista,
which began in the early 1990s out of the
Latin American and Caribbean Feminist
Encounter held in Argentina. In Nicaragua,

women united in 1996 to form the
National Coalition of Women, which gave
a common initiative to women with vari-

Women have tirelessly worked
throughout the T ransatlantic World to at-
tain power through numbers and to achieve
equal rights in areas of gender, race, class,
and sexuality, to name a few. Their efforts
are numerous and span Africa and the
Americas, and the vast majority of them
maintain a focus on celebrating diversity
through coalitions and bringing women of
varying background together to work for
common goals. These goals cover a lot of
ground, from the revolutionary call in
1994 of the Zapatista Army of National
Liberation for gender equity to the interna-
tional summits and conferences that have
published documents chronicling women’s
status around the world and enumerating
their continued efforts. The strong and en-
ergetic work of feminist and women’s
equality movements has carried on into
new generations of transatlantic coalitions,
and women are still today carving out vital
spaces for themselves on an international
level. Bringing differences of identity and
experience  to the fore and disrupting the
hegemonic systems that would marginalize
them, women’s movements in Africa and
the Americas continue to use their histori-
cal struggles as a foundation of unity and a
means of speaking all the more powerfully
to a global audience.

FEMINISM AND WOMEN’S
EQUALITY MOVEMENTS, U.S.
The feminist and women’s equality move-
ments in the United States developed over
two centuries in what are known as ﬁrst,
second, and third wave feminisms; this his-
torical development has had a complex rela-
tionship to the interventions of various
groups, including African Americans, les-
bians, and feminists from around the At-
lantic World. The intersection of the
African Diaspora and feminism and the
pursuit of both racial equality and gender
equality in the United States has involved
positive cross-racial engagement, but also
exclusions of various parties with agendas
that have been considered either too special-
ized, unrelated, or in direct competition with
a speciﬁc feminist movement’s goal. Many
strands of both African American and inter-
national feminist thought have emerged in
response to the exclusions of feminist move-
ments that limited their involvement with

458 F EMINISM AND WOMEN’S EQUALITY MOVEMENTS, U.S.
race issues. These strands of response have
resulted in the promotion of stronger cross-
racial engagement on issues of equality.
First Wave
In Feminist Theory (1985), Josephine
Donovan cites the Enlightenment as the
start of American feminist thought, noting
Abigail Adams’s efforts to include women’s
concerns in the country’s new Constitution
along with the contributions of such ﬁgures
as Judith Sargent Murray, Mary Woll-
stonecraft, and Sarah Grimké, who crafted
“On the Equality of the Sexes,” A Vindica-
tion of the Rights of Women, and Letters on
Equality respectively, in accordance with
the natural rights theory of the Enlighten-
ment that had originally been offered only
to white, propertied males. The Declara-
tion of Sentiments, drafted by Elizabeth
Cady Stanton and others in July 1848 at
Seneca Falls, New York, was also based on
natural rights theory and, accordingly,
mimicked the tone of the Declaration of
Independence. Using natural rights theory
as a model for their demands, the women
of this era asserted their rights under the
rubrics of rationality, the equality of
women’s and men’s souls, the need for edu-
cation, and the right of the individual to
pursue her own agenda independently from
others. These Enlightenment values led to
the demand for political rights within the
American system.
The other strand of nineteenth-century
feminism was what Donovan calls cultural
feminism. Once again grounded in En-
lightenment values, this strand stressed the
broader changes that needed to take place
in the culture for women to be considered
equal and rational citizens. At the same
time, unlike the more politically minded
reformers, who emphasized the similarities
between men and women, the cultural
feminists (Margaret Fuller being a prime
example) stressed the differences between
them in an effort to show how women’s
unique cultural qualities could bring about
social reform. A good deal of the challenge
to the cultural domination imposed on
women came through questioning the
Christian Bible and the ways that it was
used against women. Elizabeth Cady Stan-
ton’s The Woman’s Bible and Matilda
Goslyn Gage’s Woman, Church, and the
State both critiqued the Bible and its use in
women’s oppression. Throughout the nine-
teenth century, then, we ﬁnd a dual empha-
sis on culture and politics and a demand for
the expansion of women’s natural rights at
both levels.
One of the large controversies surround-
ing the ﬁrst wave of the feminist movement
resulted from its initial alliance with the
abolitionist movement and its subsequent
distancing from that movement. In White
Women’s Rights (1999), Louise Michelle
Newman traces the feminist’s alliance with
abolitionists as a surface alliance that, in fact,
depended on the devaluing of black women
(and men) in order that white (which she de-
ﬁnes as meaning, in nineteenth-century par-
lance, a conﬁguration of persons who were
Anglo-Saxon, American, Caucasian, civilized,
Protestant, etc.) women could afﬁrm their
rights alongside white men. The philosophy
that bolstered this afﬁrmation was Social
Darwinism and later an imperialist philoso-
phy that was taking hold in the United States 
in the late nineteenth and early twentieth
centuries. These discourses offered only to-
kenism to black women within the move-
ment, a tokenism that was most popularly
acknowledged in Sojourner T ruth’s speech
in 1851 titled “Ar’n’t I a Woman?” Along
with other African Americans of the day,
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 535 ---
FEMINISM AND WOMEN’S EQUALITY MOVEMENTS, U.S. 459
Sojourner T ruth theorized the ways that
white women were excluding black women
from the movement and thus drew attention
to the discourse on race that feminism was to
encounter again and again throughout its
history.
Although many white women in the
early feminist movement were exposed to
the ideas of T ruth and others, they stead-
fastly refused to address the needs of black
women in any programmatic way. Instead,
the elevation of black women was said to be
their own problem, one that would come
along with their civilization’s evolution.
With whiteness as the preeminent category,
then, all other hierarchies of race, class, and
even religion fell into place beneath it. As
white women sought their liberation from
the white male patriarchy, they nonetheless
held their privileged possession of white-
ness as their birthright and as an evolution-
ary beneﬁt that should accrue to them
alongside the white men from whom they
demanded their rights. The civilizing of the
rest of the world could take place when
white women were granted their right to
“bring up” the uncivilized portions of the
world right alongside of white men. Thus,
the discourses of Christianity, imperialism,
and social Darwinism worked together to
create what Newman calls the racial origins
of the feminist movement.
The movement for black (men’s) suf-
frage, which did not include women’s right to
vote, caused a rift and controversy between
early leaders of the feminist movement and
some of black male suffrage’s earliest propo-
nents, such as Frederick Douglass. When
black male Americans achieved the vote
with the passage of the Fifteenth Amend-
ment in 1870, many of the women who had
worked for abolitionist causes felt betrayed.
It would be another ﬁfty years before the
ﬁrst wave of feminists achieved their ulti-
mate political goal of representation through
enfranchisement, but the lingering effects of
the debate within feminism on the issue of
race would continue.
Second Wave
Josephine Donovan applies the term “radical
feminism” to the resurgence of the women’s
movement in the United States in the 1960s
and 1970s. In this era, too, the movement
was connected to the struggle for the rights
of black Americans, as many of the women
who later became part of the feminist move-
ment were involved in the Civil Rights
Movement that was taking place in the
1960s. These women, both black and
white, having played vital roles in the radi-
cal movements of the New Left of that
decade, but not having received equal treat-
ment with the male activists, found them-
selves with the skills and wherewithal to
argue for their own rights as women along
similar lines that civil rights workers had
argued for their rights as African Americans.
Nonetheless, until recently this back-
ground was not the focus of most research
on the origins of the second wave of the
feminist movement. Instead, the focus has
been on some of the “germinal” works of
the movement, such as Kate Millett’s Sexual
Politics and Betty Friedan’s The Feminine
Mystique. The former attempts to theorize
patriarchy through an examination of the
ways that relationships between men and
women are not simply intimate matters,
but also political matters. Millett uses the
analogy of the relationship between the races
in the United States, noting that the rule by
one “collectivity” over another (e.g., whites
over blacks) has been acknowledged as
political, while that same type of rule,
when applied to women, is seen as solely
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 536 ---
460 F EMINISM AND WOMEN’S EQUALITY MOVEMENTS, U.S.
personal. She suggests, then, that while
racism is going the way of rule by aristoc-
racy in the United States, the issue of men’s
rule over women is urgently important to
recognize as a political reality in need of
reformation. Backing up the claim that the
personal is a matter for politics, Betty
Friedan’s The Feminine Mystique (1963) at-

no name” (p. 15). This problem, she stated,
was encompassed in the various ways that
American women were moving backward in
the ﬁelds of education, marriage, the world
of work, and relations with men. Friedan
names the problem as that of the suburban
housewife, the American wife who is sup-
posed to be the envy of the world but who
has no sense of her own fulﬁllment, only
the mystique of that fulﬁllment through
the entrapment of material goods to make
her life comfortable. This work, along with
Millett’s, forms the locus of early feminist
interventions, which encompassed the idea
of raising women’s consciousness of their
oppression, of naming the personal as
political, and of ﬁghting for the rights of
women to make their own destinies.
Another aspect of the second wave of
feminism was the expression of sexuality
and the ways that it was implicated in the
patriarchal system that ruled women’s lives.
Coming in the wake of the so-called sexual
revolution, feminists began to question the
roles that they as women were expected to
play as sexual objects. This questioning
produced a great deal of resistance to the
feminist agenda, with those opposed to the
women’s movement labeling feminists “les-
bians” as a way to insult them. A number of
opponents of the women’s movement
sought to discredit it through this attack on
women’s assertion of a sexuality free from
male oppression.
Unfortunately, a number of feminists
responded to this attack by targeting les-
bians within their own organizations as
scapegoats. Although the gay rights move-
ment had been developing alongside the
feminist movement, and many lesbians
were avid advocates of women’s rights, they
sometimes were rejected by the larger
movement organizations. Over time, les-
bians began to form their own feminist or-
ganizations and to theorize the relationship
between heterosexual oppression and patri-
archy. Eventually, mainstream feminist or-
ganizations began to incorporate gay rights
as part of their platforms, recognizing the
relevance of the struggle of lesbians to the
struggle of all women.
Third Wave
“Third wave feminism” is a sometimes con-
troversial term, both from the viewpoint of
some of the women who would consider
themselves modern proponents of women’s
rights and by those feminists who came of
age in the 1970s. On the one hand, some
third wave feminists are uncomfortable
with the label “feminist,” while some sec-
ond wave feminists see the third wave as
nontheoretical, uncommitted, or both and
question the need for a new “wave” when
there is much work to be done to advance
the revolutionary social change begun by
second wave feminists. A good deal of dia-
logue and thought has gone into theorizing
the third wave, and not without some con-
ﬂict. In Catching a Wave (2002), Rory
Dicker and Alison Piepmeier argue that
there is a great need for a third wave of fem-
inism, as inequities in U.S. society con-
tinue, especially at the higher levels of
power. Some bill this sort of feminism as a
reversion to individualism and see the need
for organization and consciousness raising
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 537 ---
FEMINISM AND WOMEN’S EQUALITY MOVEMENTS, U.S. 461
of the kind that was done in the second
wave. In short, the status of third wave
feminism is still, in some ways, under
debate.
The backlash against second wave
feminism has played a part in third wave
feminist agendas, with some wishing to
embrace the aspects of the second wave
that were useful, like raising consciousness,
while rejecting those that were not, like
conformity and racism. From the perspec-
tive of some second wave feminists, third
wave feminists come across as ungrateful
and as lacking in knowledge. Typically,
then, the relationship between second and
third wave feminists has been framed as a
sort of intergenerational conﬂict. Writers
like Dicker and Piepmeier, though, argue
for the continuity between the two groups
and for the possibilities of a reinvigorated
feminist movement that addresses the is-
sues of inequality that continue to plague
American women into the twenty-first
century. Rather than perpetuating what
they see as a type of martyr motif in earlier
feminist movements, third wave feminists
seek to exercise individual agency over their
personal behavior. In addition, the third
wave strongly emphasizes everyday activism
to empower women and men for political
and social change.
African American Feminist 
Interventions
By the early 1980s many women of color in
the United States were arguing against
some of the racist and classist assumptions
made by the mainstream women’s move-
ment. Theorists like Angela Davis, bell
hooks, and others criticized white femi-
nism as a middle-class institution that did
not take into account the experiences of
black women in America. Davis’s Women,
Race, & Class (1981) insisted on the histor-
ical investigation of the black woman’s ex-
perience during slavery as a prerequisite for
understanding black women’s struggle for
social emancipation. Since many black
American women still existed in working
conditions akin to those of slavery, Davis
argued, much can be learned about black
female experience in America today by
looking at the historical precedents that
controlled how black women could work,
and thus survive, in American society.
Through examining the ways that women’s
lives intersect via their class and racial sta-
tus as well as their status as women, Davis
hoped to move the discussion of black
women’s liberation forward.
In addition to Davis, bell hooks has
been one of the early and continuing inﬂu-
ences in the feminist movement. Her book
Ain’t I a Woman: Black Women and Feminism
picks up on Sojourner T ruth’s theme from
the ﬁrst wave of feminism and expands on
it to help readers understand the very spe-
ciﬁc histories of African women during the
time of slavery. She also examines the
dynamics within colonial American society
that contributed to the psychological
trauma of slavery, not just for black men,
but also (and perhaps especially) for black
women.
Among other considerations, black
feminists differed from white feminists of
the second wave because they attempted to
fight on several fronts against sexism,
racism, and class oppression. This multi-
tiered agenda created both an opportunity
for alliance and a challenge. African Amer-
ican feminists admitted to difﬁculty in
gathering support from both black women
in ﬁghting sexism. One of the central rea-
sons for their resistance, the black feminists
argued, was the limited resources black
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 538 ---
462 F EMINISM AND WOMEN’S EQUALITY MOVEMENTS, U.S.
women possessed simply to survive. Also,
ﬁghting the system would also involve a
risk to many black women’s fragile sense of
stability within American society. Never-
theless, black feminists continued to argue
for a feminism that would overthrow the
patriarchal and capitalist status quo in order
to ﬁght the battle for equality. In this sense,
the black feminists brought a different focus
to the feminist movement, moving it from
an argument for individual rights to an
argument for the collective rights of women
while recognizing the particularities of ex-
perience encountered by the various groups
of women in the United States.
During this same period of time, a
number of lesbians, black and white, began
to speak out against the heterosexism that
they saw both in society at large and within
the ranks of the women’s movement. They
argued that compulsory heterosexuality as
it was practiced co-opted both women and
men into roles that oppress women
through their forced identiﬁcation with
men, an identiﬁcation that is in no way
natural, but is constructed to support the
patriarchy.
In Personal Politics (1980), Sara Evans
notes that the two major waves of U.S.
feminism, that of the 1830s and 1840s and
that of the 1960s, were intimately con-
nected with the movements against racism.
The ﬁrst went hand in hand with the abo-
litionist movement, in which a number of
white women participated, and the second
was linked to the Civil Rights Movement,
in which, similarly, a number of white
women were involved. Thus, she argues
that the movements for women’s rights and
for the rights of black Americans were inti-
mately connected throughout the feminist
movement. Many burgeoning feminists
learned lessons from the organizational and
community and political activities involved
in the ﬁght for the rights of black Ameri-
cans, she argues. Likewise, black women
were instrumental in bringing issues of
women’s power to the fore of discussions
within and outside the movement.
Transatlantic Connections
Through the interventions of African
Americans and other women of color as
well as from lesbian feminists, the feminist
movement in the United States has faced a
good deal of criticism as being connected
with the patriarchal power it has sought to
overthrow, particularly as it relates to white
and heterosexual privilege. Recent research
has begun to plumb the depths of the
American feminist movement’s involve-
ment with other parts of the world, includ-
ing Africa, to look at the ways that imperi-
alist discourses have impacted on the efforts
of U.S. feminists to bring a more global
slant to their analysis. T racey Jean Boisseau’s
White Queen (2004), which examines the
life of May French-Sheldon, an early
American feminist and explorer of Africa,
provides a model for this type of historical
research. By looking at the ways that
French-Sheldon positioned herself in relation
to Africa, the imperialist endeavor, and the
new American presence on the international
scene of colonialism from the 1890s
through the 1920s, the study attempts to
theorize the rise of feminism in the United
States with the colonial and imperialist
impulse in Africa and thus to show the ways
in which women’s subjectivity, even in a
seemingly radical era for women’s rights in
the United States, was dependent on the very
imperialist structure that oppressed women
(and men) in Africa. As opposed to the more
standard histories of American feminism,
which sees it as linked mainly to Europe, this
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 539 ---
FEMINISM AND WOMEN’S EQUALITY MOVEMENTS, U.S. 463
study is one of recent import that attempts
to examine the history of U.S. feminism
through the lens of national and interna-
tional events concurrent with colonial and
imperial domination and the rise of the U.S.
role in international politics.
Likewise, Karen Sacks’s “An Overview
of Women and Power in Africa” (1982) af-
ﬁrms the way that later colonialism of the
ﬁrst half of the twentieth century had an
impact on African women’s lives. Her
analysis focuses largely on the responses of
African men and women to the imperial-
ism of the West and on the ways that
women found to resist those aspects of cap-
italism that did not suit them. Sacks asserts
that African women have their own forms
of kinship and sisterhood that deﬁne their
resistance to oppression and that Western
forms, contrary to what many, including
many feminists, might think, introduced
and reproduced oppression for women in
African societies.
Sacks contends that the power of West-
ern hegemony has been and continues to
be so strong that feminists have reproduced
the Africanist discourses of the nineteenth
century well into the twentieth and twenty-
ﬁrst centuries. This Africanist feminist dis-
course involved not only a universalizing of
all women as subject to patriarchy, regard-
less of time or place, but also placed its
agenda in the privileged position of saving
the world’s women from a victim status
that Africanist feminism, paradoxically,
promoted. Thus, second wave feminism
took on its civilizing mission in a different
form, attempting to socialize the women of
Africa and other parts of the third world
into feminist ideology and to save them
from themselves. The author argues that
these attitudes have done a great deal of
harm and reveal the ways that Western
feminism needs to evaluate its own theory
before attempting to understand the lives
of women in Africa.
In addition to focusing on the imperial
mindset and its conjunction with U.S.
feminists, many recent studies have at-
tempted to ground their analysis in a more
materialist theoretical framework. By fo-
cusing on the lives of women in Africa,
Asia, and Latin America, for example, these
studies attempt to take an approach to the
feminist concerns of women in the third
world by looking at the ways that women
work, both within family structures and in
the developing modernization that has
been occurring in these areas of the world.
By examining the means of production,
they attempt to address the inequalities
that women throughout the world face on
an everyday basis, showing how their wel-
fare impacts all of the world’s poor people
and how the threat to their autonomy
harms the whole world.
International Feminism
In an attempt to forge new theories that
take into account the lives of women in
Africa, many have proposed a more inter-
national feminist orientation. Theorists
have pointed out, however, that work needs
to be done to bring together U.S. feminism
and its concerns and African feminism with
its issues. Tani Barlow’s “International Fem-
inism of the Future” (2000) looks at the
growing movement of international femi-
nism coming out of the United States. She
argues that more often than not, interna-
tional feminism comes to be associated
with capitalist and neoliberal policies that
actually reinforce the inequities that they
purport to remedy. In addition, Barlow sees
the movement as more about consolidating
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 540 ---
464 F EMINISM AND WOMEN’S EQUALITY MOVEMENTS, U.S.
epistemological power within a U.S. frame-
work than really choosing to understand
the lives and feminisms of those living else-
where in the world. In order to create a
truly international bond, she argues, femi-
nists in the West need to interrogate the
basis for their behavior toward Africa and
other places in the world.
Georgina Ashworth’s A Diplomacy of
the Oppressed(1995) attempts to interrogate
U.S.-based international feminism to
bridge the apparently wide gaps between
what she calls women of the North and
women of the South. Warning against con-
descending maternalism, Ashworth asks the
women of the North to try to understand
the conditions that, in part, have been cre-
ated through their own nations’ imperialist
policies in the so-called third world. At the
same time, she warns women of the South
to not fall into a victim status and to ﬁght
practices that have been justiﬁed as cultural
but which are, in fact, damaging to women,
such as female genital mutilation. Through
coalition building and ﬁerce and honest
self-examination, Ashworth argues, an in-
ternational feminist movement can work to
change the lives of women all over the
world if only feminists of all areas will come
to understand the parts they play in chang-
ing their own lives, communities, nations,
and international politics.
The Future of Feminism
All of the conﬂicts engendered among
various groups making claims on a feminist
perspective seem to point to a continued
relevance for the ideas, ideals, and actions of
feminists around the world. Though the
deﬁnitions change from context to context,
the theorizing of U.S. feminism in the
twenty-ﬁrst century seems to be one that is
likely to lead to more understanding and
connection with Africans on the continent
and in the diaspora. Because of the coura-
geous interventions of black feminists both
in the United States and abroad, U.S. femi-
nism has grown to embrace the concept of
intersectionality—that is, the recognition
that every woman possesses her own rela-
tionship to the concept of gender based
upon her experiences. The understanding
of these experiences has gone beyond the
assumption that “woman” means white,
middle-class, Protestant, Anglo-Saxon women
of the United States and into the recogni-
tion that identity, whether formed through
the rubric of race, class, religion, colonial
context, sexuality, or other factors, is a mat-
ter of both personal and political import. In
that sense, U.S. feminism demonstrates a
continuity despite all of the conﬂicts within
which it was (and is) formed. This continu-
ity exists in the mantra that the personal is
political. The deﬁnition of the personal,
thanks to the interventions of many
throughout the centuries, has helped to
delineate a richer, more real relationship
between the personal and the political.
Kelly O. Secovnie

FETU OF CAPE COAST
The Fetu, inhabitants of present-day
Ghana, were peoples with a long tradition
of trading with Europeans. They played an
important role in enabling Britain to estab-
lish itself along the Gold Coast in the eigh-
teenth century and remained allied with
Britain into the nineteenth century.
Fante and Ga traditions state that the
Fetu were already established, probably by
the thirteenth century, along the coast
when they arrived. The Fetu originally set-
tled around ten miles inland from Cape
Coast—in modern Efutu, Ghana—and
then expanded to the coast. When the
Portuguese arrived in the late ﬁfteenth cen-
tury, Cape Coast was one of many Fetu
ﬁshing villages. The Fetu not only ﬁshed
but engaged in agriculture and salt and
palm wine production and traded with
various inland states and peoples. The Fetu
quickly developed an economic relation-
ship with the various Europeans states that
arrived on the Gold Coast and which, by
the sixteenth century, utilized Akan
weights for their gold trade. In the seven-
teenth century, the coastal importance of
the Fetu expanded as the English, Dutch,
and Swedes competed for their interests. In
1649 the Englishman Thomas Crispe ob-
tained from the Fetu king the right to
build at Cape Coast, but nothing came of
this at the time. In 1688 the Dutch at
Elmina convinced the Fetu king to attack
Cape Coast Castle, but when he was
driven back, the English supported a new
king, thus strengthening the relationship
between the English and the Fetu. It is
around this time that the Fetu capital
moved from Efutu to Cape Coast, thus in-
creasing the bonds between the Fetu and
English. By the early eighteenth century, as
the struggle between the Fante and Asante
began, the Fetu controlled important trade
paths between the coast and the interior.
One of these paths gave the Fetu access to
the Asante. As the Fante worked to control
the trade between the inland and coastal
peoples, in 1708—having defeated the
Asebu—they then attacked the Fetu and
took King Ahen Pompa prisoner. Sir
Thomas Dalby of the Royal African Com-
pany decided to intervene for economic
reasons and attempted to make Aguebah
Brasso the new queen of Fetu. In 1717
Fetu acquired a new king and this was fol-
lowed, in 1720, by another Fante attack.
While the Fante never ofﬁcially conquered
the Fetu, because of the changing coastal
political situation the latter—along with
the increasingly powerful Asante—were
integrated into the Fante confederation.
Within all of this, the Fetu, because of
their long history and experience with
Europeans, were very effective traders and
cross-cultural brokers and played an im-
portant economic role within the Fante
confederation.
Ty M. Reese

FILM (AFRICA)
African ﬁlm is a ﬂedgling industry, seeking
an identity and struggling to free itself from
the dominance of Hollywood and European
ﬁlms, which monopolize African media.
Africa does not have a centralized ﬁlm in-
dustry like that in the United States, and
access to modern ﬁlm production technol-
ogy is limited. Most early ﬁlms produced in
Africa have American or European ﬁnan-
cial backing and exhibit a predominantly
Western ideological perspective. The very
ﬁrst motion picture made by an African was
Ain el Ghezal (The girl from Carthage), a
1924 ﬁlm by T unisian director Chemama
Chikly. Under South African apartheid
(legalized racism), whites controlled all
aspects of African art and music by regulat-
ing the programming of visual media as
well as the release and performance of pop-
ular music. In 1931 South Africa enacted
the Entertainment Law, which essentially
forbade any artistic freedom of expression
from a black point of view, and blacks were
forbidden by law to view any uncensored,
unapproved ﬁlms.
Though a few ﬁlms were made in the
thirty-odd years after Ain el Ghezal, African
ﬁlmmaking did not truly gain momentum
until the late 1950s and early 1960s.
African cinema is divided into two primary
regions: north (francophone) and south
(anglophone) of the Sahara. Much of early
African cinema corresponded to the political
independence of African states and the
founding of the Organization of African
Unity (OAU) in 1963. That same year, one
of Africa’s premier directors, Ousmane
Sembene from Senegal, made his ﬁrst ﬁlm,
Borom Sarret, a twenty-minute short that
changed the trajectory of the ﬂedgling
African ﬁlm movement.
In the context of post-colonialism,
African ﬁlm seeks to view Africa, her
peoples, and cultures though an African
lens rather than through the distorted lens
of the Western colonial powers. Films
made by black Africans reﬂect the world of
Africa from an African perspective, which
seeks to communicate to the African
viewer the more identiﬁable realities, expe-
riences, and desires of African societies.
Sembene’s Borom Sarret presented the ﬁrst
alternate view in ﬁlm of Africa from an
African perspective and introduced the
possibility of a distinct African identity,
separate and independent from postcolo-
nial hegemony. But with the end of the era
of colonial domination in Africa came an-
other form of Western imperialism: cul-
tural imperialism. 
Most ﬁlms shown in Africa are from
America or Europe. Hollywood dominates
the African ﬁlm and television scene, inun-
dating African societies with American
ideologies and values and advertising
American products. The majority of movie
houses in Africa are owned and operated
by American or European corporations
and they control the ﬁlms that are pre-
sented, privileging ﬁlms from the United
States and Europe. Indigenous African
ﬁlms, even if they are of high quality, can-
not compete with the power of Hollywood
for distribution rights and unfortunately
are not widely viewed by African audiences.
Three principal styles of cinema are shown
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 543 ---

in Africa: Hollywood cinema (which rein-
forces colonial hegemony); third-world
imitation Hollywood (mostly action or ro-
mance ﬁlms from India and low-budget
kung fu ﬁlms); and what is called African
“radical” or “liberation” cinema—films
made by black Africans that challenge the
Hollywood depiction of black African
characters as derogatory Western stereo-
types, that carry sociopolitical messages,
that reﬂect and engage in a black cultural
discourse, and, most importantly, that pre-
sent uniquely African stories told from an
African point of view.
Radical African ﬁlmmakers do not
view ﬁlm as simply a means for entertain-
ment but also as an important tool with
which to engage in a discourse that exam-
ines and critiques the political, social, his-
torical, and modern realities of African so-
ciety. Modern Africa faces a cultural crisis
from the saturation of U.S. and European
ﬁlms and popular television that import
Western values and ideologies, which are
replacing and damaging traditional African
beliefs and values. T o combat this cultural
imperialism, African filmmakers use
Africa’s vast resource of traditional myths
and stories to comment on the African
experience in contrast to Hollywood and
European models. Some of the common
themes in African films are: the quality
of life; poverty; political instability; loss of
infrastructure; apartheid; the conflict
between traditional and modern life; the
commodiﬁcation of traditional art objects;
the unchecked inﬂuence of Western cul-
ture; the questioning of traditions that are
exploitive or harmful; gender roles and
such practices as polygamy, religion, and
the caste system; the questioning of histor-
ical narratives and the presentation of an al-
ternative African view; the environment
and its exploitation by the West; and the
continuing anticolonial struggle. But be-
cause of limited resources and a lack of pro-
duction and post-production facilities,
many ﬁlmmakers in Africa look to the West
for ﬁnancial support and use of production
resources. That support unfortunately
comes with a price, namely, giving the
backer the right to control the creative
output of the project, which comes into
play particularly if the ﬁlm is too critical
of the West or of capitalism and capitalist
structures.
African ﬁlmmakers present their work
at ﬁlm festivals worldwide, which counters
the negative portrayal of black Africans that
dominates Western media and provides
African filmmakers with a vehicle for
broader distribution outside the domi-
nance of those media. Some notable
African ﬁlmmakers and their ﬁlms are:
Ousmane Sembene’s La Noire de . . . (Black
Girl) (1965), Mandabi (1968), Xala
(Impotence) (1973), Ceddo (Outsiders)
(1977), Emitai (God of Thunder) (1971),
and Camp de Thiaroye (The Camp at
Thiaroye) (1988); Saﬁ Faye’s Kaddu Beykat
(Letter from My Village) (1975); Idrissa
Ouèdraogo’s Poko (1981), Wend Kuuni
(God’s Gift) (1982), and Yaaba (1989);
Kwaw Ansah’s Love . . . Brewed in the
African Pot (1981); Amadou Saalum Seck’s
Saaraba (Utopia) (1989); Moussa Sene
Absa’s Yalla Yaana(1995); Jilali Ferhati’s La
Plage des enfants perdus (The Beach of Lost
Children) (1991); Soraya Mire’s Fire Eyes
(1994); Dikongue-Pipa’s Muno Moto
(Somebody Else’s Child) (1974); and Che-
ick Oumar Cissoko’s Guimba (Guimba
The Tyrant) (1995). The greatest challenge
facing postcolonial African ﬁlmmakers is
to create a new black African identity that
reﬂects African values and ideologies, not

FILM (ATLANTIC)
The term “Atlantic ﬁlm” refers to the no-
tion of a diasporic, transnational space rep-
resented in the cinema of the Americas, the
Caribbean, Africa, and Europe. The con-
cept of the Atlantic as a location for a
multinational culture that transcends the
nationalist paradigms traditionally em-
ployed in the ﬁeld of cultural studies is de-
veloped in Paul Gilroy’s seminal work The
Black Atlantic (1993). For Gilroy and other
writers, terms traditionally used to discuss
the black diaspora such as “syncretism,”
“creolization,” mestizaje (miscegenation),
and “hybridity” all point to the ways in
which the Atlantic itself signiﬁes a spatio-
temporal unit of intercultural exchange
(between various cultures on both sides of
the Atlantic) that reaches beyond the bor-
ders of the national.
This notion of the Atlantic as a spatio-
temporal unit is exempliﬁed in the chrono-
tope. A concept developed by Mikhail
Bahktin to discuss the conﬂuence of space
and time in the novel, the chronotope is
fundamental to Gilroy’s theory of the black
Atlantic. Gilroy argues that modern black
culture has been preoccupied with the ex-
ploration of roots, while the paradigm he
proposes regards issues of identity not as
ﬁxed in time or place, but as ﬂuid and in
ﬂux. Rather than rootedness, Gilroy looks
to rhizomorphic and transnational connec-
tions—that is, to lateral connections that
displace traditional horizontal hierarchies
limited by national boundaries. As such,
the transoceanic travels of black people
serve as an important trope or ﬁgure for the
interconnectedness of the Atlantic World.
For Gilroy, ships themselves serve as the op-
erative metaphor, and the “Middle Pas-
sage,” a term that refers to the transporting
of slaves across the Atlantic, is key in illus-
trating the ﬂuidity of both time and place.
Some critics of Gilroy’s work, however,
object to the way his theories privilege ﬁrst-
world consciousness and give little atten-
tion in particular to the Caribbean. Still
others, such as Hamid Naﬁcy in his An Ac-
cented Cinema (2001), caution against see-
ing the global without considering the con-
tribution of national consciousness to
diasporas. He argues that the relationship
between the national and the diasporic
must not be overlooked, and that the re-
ductive view of a single black diaspora
would have to correlate to an equally re-
ductive single Other.
While transatlantic migration has led
to an exilic cinematic production (cinema
produced by ﬁlmmakers in exile from their
native countries) in the cinemas of Africa,
the Caribbean, Europe, and the Americas
that challenges the dominant theories and
aesthetics of mainstream cinema, many of
these ﬁlms share a sense of multiple identi-
ﬁcation of race, gender, class, language, and
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 545 ---
FILM (ATLANTIC) 469
nationality, all of these intersecting in ways
that are sometimes contradictory and op-
positional. The multilinguality of these
ﬁlms alone and the increasing numbers of
co-productions have led to a questioning of
ways to position exilic, diasporic cinema in
a global context. In “South American Cin-
ema” (2000), Julianne Burton-Carvajal
points to the term “transculturation,”
coined by Cuban anthropologist Fernando
Ortiz, to emphasize the reciprocity of con-
tact between cultures and the ways exile
serves to redeﬁne the national. A case in
point is British ﬁlmmaker Stephen Frears’s
Dirty Pretty Things (2002), a ﬁlm that in-
verts the marginalized position of an illegal
Nigerian immigrant. Okwe, a doctor by
profession, is relegated to working nights in
a hotel. He develops a relationship with a
T urkish maid, and the two ﬁnd a way to
turn the tables on the exploitation they are
suffering at the hands of a society that
keeps them in their marginalized status. In
the process, Frears explores a side of
London that has remained largely invisible
in the dominant discourse.
The motivation of Latin American cin-
ema to bolster its sense of nationalism
while also responding to postcolonial ideo-
logical and political hegemony (that is, the
cultural dominance of the former colonial-
ist powers) is shared by ﬁlmmakers in
Africa and the Caribbean. The process of
decolonization in Latin America and the
Caribbean (and indeed, Africa), marked by
the upheaval represented by the Cuban
Revolution, led to a project of recovering
the histories of the voiceless, in particular
the African and indigenous populations
in the Americas subjugated by the colonizers.
Cuban ﬁlmmaker T omás Gutiérrez Alea’s
masterpiece, La Última Cena (1976; The
Last Supper), presents a stinging indictment
of the hypocrisy of Spanish slave owners
who professed to be Christian while bene-
ﬁting from the inhumanity of slavery. The
films of Afro-Cuban filmmaker Sergio
Giral—El otro Francisco (1974; The other
Francisco), Plácido (1986), Maluala
(1979), and Rancheador (1977; Bounty
hunter)—likewise deal with attempts to
reframe the slavery and racism of the colo-
nialist past.
Gloria Rolando’s ﬁlm, Hijos de Baraguá
(My Footsteps in Baraguá) (1996), uncov-
ers the syncretic phenomena of African
cultures and practices in present-day Cuba,
as does the Puerto Rican documentary, The
King Does Not Lie: The Initiation of a
Shangó Priest (1993), by Judith Gleason
and Elisa Mereghetti, which illustrates the
ritual initiation of a priest into the Afro-
Caribbean religion of Santeria.
Recovering African heritage through
family and local ﬁliations is the theme of
Daughters of the Dust (1991), by African
American ﬁlmmaker Julie Dash, and Sugar
Cane Alley (1983), by Euzhan Palcy, from
Martinique. Palcy’s ﬁlm draws attention to
the prevalent themes of Euro-African ten-
sion in the Caribbean by underscoring the
issues of race and gender. José, the young
protagonist, is mentored by a village elder
who stands for the absent patriarchal Africa,
while in a subplot, the dynamics of a white
European patriarch and a  black-Creole
mother are played out. Written and directed
by Haile Gerima, Sankofa (1993), a title
that means going back in time in order to
go forward, uses the ﬁgure of an African
American fashion model transported from
modern-day Ghana to a Jamaican planta-
tion, where she becomes a slave.
Carlos Diegues’s Quilombo (1984) tells
the story of the quilombo (a settlement of
runaway slaves) in the Palmares region of

470 F ILM (CARIBBEAN)
Brazil. Set in the seventeenth century, the
poetic and fantastic meet in this ﬁlm to re-
count what is ultimately the tragic story of
the Portuguese colonization. The themes of
colonialism and postcolonialism are also
felt in modern Senegal in Camp de Thiaroye
(1987), by Senegalese ﬁlmmaker Ousmane
Sembène, considered by many to be the
father of African cinema. The ﬁlm exposes
the French colonialist mentality through
the story of colonial troops returning to
Africa in 1944 after ﬁghting the Germans
in France. T emporarily detained at Camp
de Thiaroye, the troops ﬁnally learn what
being an African in the French Empire re-
ally means when they are slaughtered by
the French themselves.
In the Hollywood ﬁlm Amistad (1997),
possibly the most commercially successful
ﬁlm in the United States to take on the
theme of Africans’ forced exile into slavery,
Steven Spielberg offers his perspective on the
Middle Passage. The plot revolves around
the uprising aboard the slave ship Amistad in
the year 1839 and the subsequent trial that
takes place in New England. The powerful
scenes of the mutiny, however, are marred by
the graphic images of the captive Africans
murdering the Spanish slave runners. Spiel-
berg unwittingly perpetuates the stereotype
of the black savage taking brutal revenge on
his captors. But the ﬁlm’s greatest disap-
pointment lies in Spielberg’s inability to
make the Africans the subjects and focal
point of the movie. The ﬁlm, nonetheless,
succeeded in introducing an important as-
pect of U.S. history to a large audience.
María Cristina Saavedra

FILM (CARIBBEAN)
Many Caribbean ﬁlms are made by directors
of Afro-Caribbean descent, whether living in
the Caribbean or abroad, while some ﬁlms
about Afro-Caribbean culture are made by
white and Asian directors. The Caribbean is
deﬁned as the islands in the Caribbean Sea
excluding Cuba, Puerto Rico, and the
Dominican Republic, which are covered in
the article on Latin American ﬁlm. Belize is
included in this article, despite its geographic
location in Central America, because its cul-
ture and history are more similar to other
former British colonies in the Caribbean
than to the Spanish-speaking countries of
Central America.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 547 ---
FILM (CARIBBEAN) 471
Films have been shot in the Caribbean
for more than a century, but development
of an indigenous ﬁlm industry dates only
from the 1970s. The growth of Caribbean
film has been impeded by the small
economies of most Caribbean countries,
which have inhibited development of the
infrastructure necessary for a ﬁlm industry,
and by the lack of opportunities for most
young Caribbeans to study ﬁlmmaking.
The English-speaking Caribbean
The ﬁrst Anglo-Caribbean ﬁlms were pro-
duced by white and Asian directors and
were influential in presenting Afro-
Caribbean culture to the world. Music was
central in these ﬁlms: in fact, their sound-
track is sometimes their best feature.
The ﬁrst T rinidadian ﬁlms were di-
rected by the Indian émigré Harbance
Kumar. Probably his best ﬁlm was Bim
(1975), which focused on an Indian boy
growing up in Port of Spain, T rinidad, and
T obago. T wo of Kumar’s ﬁlms are notable
primarily because they recorded perfor-
mances by major calypso musicians: The
Caribbean Fox (1970) and Man from Africa
(1982).
The ﬁrst Jamaican feature ﬁlm, The
Harder They Come (1972), directed by the
white Jamaican Perry Henzell, stars reggae
singer Jimmy Cliff as a young man who
leaves the countryside to try to make it as a
singer in Kingston. This ﬁlm brought reg-
gae music and the Rastafarian culture to
the attention of a worldwide audience. In-
terest in reggae and the Rastafarian culture
prompted the creation of three more ﬁlms
centered on Jamaican Rastafarians in the
next decade: Rockers (T ed Bafakoulos,
1978), Children of Babylon (Lennie Little-
White, 1980), and Countryman (Dickie
Johnson, 1982).
A signiﬁcant body of Afro-Caribbean
ﬁlm has been created by émigrés to England.
Horace Ové was born in T rinidad and edu-
cated at the London International Film
School. His ﬁlm Pressure (1975), the ﬁrst
British Film Institute–funded ﬁlm by a
black director, focuses on T rinidadian im-
migrants living in London. He also di-
rected the comedy Playing Away (1987)
and several documentaries including Reg-
gae (1971). Burning an Illusion (1981), by
the Barbadian-born Menelik Shabazz, was
also funded by the British Film Institute
and centers on a young Caribbean-British
woman’s awakening to her African heritage.
Isaac Julien, whose parents migrated from
St. Lucia to London, was a founding mem-
ber of the black ﬁlm and video collective
Sankofa and directed a number of ﬁlms ex-
amining black culture, including Looking
for Langston (1988), Young Soul Rebels
(1991), Frantz Fanon: Black Skin, White
Mask (1996), and Baadasssss Cinema
(2002).
Garifuna Journey (1998), by the Amer-
ican directors Andrea E. Leland and Kathy
L. Berger, is a documentary about the
Garifuna people of Belize, whose culture
incorporates links to their African past. Do
You See What I See?(Suzette Zayden, Debbie
Lisbey, 2004) is a documentary shot in
English and Kriol (a language used in Belize
that combines elements of English and
several West African languages) about
young people growing up in Belize.
The French-speaking Caribbean
Martinique and Guadeloupe (both French
overseas departments), despite their small
size, have produced outstanding Afro-
Caribbean directors. Martinique-born Eu-
zhan Palcy achieved international renown
with her ﬁrst feature ﬁlm, Rue Cases-Nègres

(1983; Sugar Cane Alley ), which tells the
story of a poor black family living in Mar-
tinique in the 1930s. Her other ﬁlms in-
clude A Dry White Season (1989), set in
South Africa in the 1970s, and Aimé
Césaire: A Voice for History(1994), a docu-
mentary about the Martiniquan poet and
playwright. Christian Lara, born in Guade-

directed a number of French-language ﬁlms

Bitter sugar), concerning a freed slave who
became a commander in the army of
Napoleon Bonaparte. Willie Rameau and

Despite Haiti’s poverty and frequent
periods of political repression, Afro-Haitian
directors have produced an impressive
body of work. Rassoul Labuchin’s Anita
(1980), the ﬁrst ﬁlm made in the Haitian
creole language, tells the story of a young
girl working as a domestic servant in Port-

Naïve art and repression in Haiti), Duva-

Duvalier Condamné (1974; Duvalier con-

Zenglendo (1999; Piwouli and the thug).
Both Labuchin and Antonin were forced
into exile by the Duvalier regime. Elsie
Haas, born in Haiti and educated in
France, directed several inﬂuential docu-
mentaries about Haiti, including La Ronde
des Vodu (1987; The voodoo dance). The
innovative documentary Krik? Krak!
(1988), directed by Jac Avila and Vanyoska
Gee, focused on the effects of the Duvalier
regime on impoverished Haitians. Raoul
Peck’s feature, L ’homme sur les Quais(1993;
The Man on the Shore ), set in Haiti in the
1960s, was the ﬁrst Haitian ﬁlm released in
theaters in the United States. His other
ﬁlms include Haitian Corner (1988), a
drama about the Haitian community in
New York, and Lumumba: La morte du
prophète (1992; Lumumba: Death of a
Prophet) and Lumumba (2000), a docu-
mentary and feature film, respectively,
based on the life of the Congolese leader.

FILM (LATINAMERICA)
Latin American ﬁlm is from those countries
in the Western Hemisphere that share as-
pects of a common culture based on the
Spanish language and a history of coloniza-
tion by Spain. This includes Mexico, Cen-
tral America except for Belize, most of South
America, Cuba, the Dominican Republic,
and the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico.
Brazil, a Portuguese-language country, is in-
cluded in the entry Film (South America).
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 549 ---
FILM (LATINAMERICA) 473
Belize, a former British colony, is included in
the entry Film (Caribbean) because it has
closer historical and cultural connections
with other former British colonies than with
the countries included in this article.
Cuba
Among the Latin American countries,
Cuba has the greatest output of ﬁlms con-
cerned with Afro-Caribbean heritage and
life. This is not surprising, since ﬁlms have
been made in Cuba for over 100 years and
because Cuba has a substantial population
of citizens with some African heritage.
However, ﬁlm direction and production
has been dominated by persons of Euro-
pean descent. This situation improved
somewhat after the Cuban Revolution of
1959, and many white Cubans have dealt
sensitively with racial issues in their ﬁlms,
but only a few Afro-Cubans have estab-
lished themselves as directors.
Cuban ﬁlmmaking before the Revolu-
tion largely dealt with the interests of white
Cubans, who dominated the ﬁlm industry
and comprised the preponderance of the
ticket-buying audience. Afro-Cuban life
generally was referenced only in relation to
Santeria or in the stock characters of for-
mulaic comedies. Shortly after the Revolu-
tion, the Instituto Cubano del Arte y la In-
dustria Cinematográficos (ICAIC) was
formed and took over all aspects of Cuban
cinema, resulting in state-supported cen-
sorship of ﬁlmmaking. 
Post-Revolution white Cuban directors
made a number of ﬁlms that included race
or slavery as a theme. La Última Cena
(1976; The Last Supper), directed by T omás
Gutiérrez Alea, is based on a historical slave
revolt on an eighteenth-century Cuban
plantation. Cecilia (1981), directed by
Humberto Solás, tells the story of a mulatto
woman in nnineteenth-century Havana.
Octavio Cortázar’s Acerca de un personaje
que unos llaman San Lázaro y otros llaman
Babalú (1968; About a personage whom
some call Saint Lazarus and some call
Babalú) documents religious festivities hon-
oring Saint Lazarus, whom many Afro-
Cubans regard as their divinity, Babalú Ayé.
In addition, several documentaries made by
non-Cubans or outside Cuba are important
for their presentation of Afro-Cuban music;
these include Yo soy, del son a la salsa(1997;
From Son to Salsa), directed by Rigoberto
Lopez, and The Buena Vista Social Club
(2000), directed by Wim Wenders.
José Massip, an Afro-Cuban, directed
La decisión(1965), which tells the story of
two mulatto brothers during the regime of
Fulgencio Batista. Sergio Giral is an Afro-
Cuban director who has made a number of
ﬁlms examining Cuba’s heritage of slavery,
including El otro Francisco (1974; The
Other Francisco), Rancheador (1977; Slave-
hunter), Maluala (1979), and Plácido
(1986). The Afro-Cuban director Sara
Gomez produced a number of ﬁlms in her
short life (she died from an asthma attack
at age thirty-one). Her documentaries in-
clude . . . Y tenemos sabor (1968; And we
have taste) and Ire a Santiago (1964; I will
go to Santiago), and her feature ﬁlm, De
cierta manera (1977; One Way or Another )
explores class and race prejudice in the
Miraﬂores neighborhood of Havana. More
recently, the Afro-Cuban Gloria Rolando
directed Raices de mi Corazon (2001; Roots
of my Heart), about the 1912 massacre of
members of an Afro-Cuban political party.
Other ﬁlms by Rolando include the docu-
mentaries Los hijos de Baragua (1996; My
footsteps in Baragua), and Los marqueses de
Atarés(2003; The marquesses of the neigh-
borhood of Atares).

The Dominican Republic 
and Puerto Rico
Because of the close association of the
United States with both the Dominican
Republic and Puerto Rico, American ﬁlms
are included in this section. The American-
produced documentary Change Up (2002),
directed by Loren Mendel and Tiller
Russell, deals with racial issues in the
Dominican Republic through the story
of two young Dominicans (one light-
skinned, one dark-skinned) hoping to play
major league baseball. T wo other American-
produced films, Washington Heights
(2002), directed by Alfredo de Villa, and
Raising Victor Vargas (2002), directed by
Peter Sollett, also include Afro-Dominican
characters.
The documentaries Amor por el Baile
(1998; Love of the Dance), directed by 
Eric Delgado, Jesus Burgos’s Del Africa a el
Caribe (1996; From Africa to the
Caribbean), Plena: Canto y Trabajo (1989;
Plena is Work, Plena is Song ), directed by
Pedro Rivera and Susan Zeig, and Ismael
Rivera and Fran Ferrer’s Concierto Mayor de
los Soneros (1978; Concert for “El Sonero
Mayor”) deal with African-influenced
music and culture in Puerto Rico. Sharon
Simon’s Mi Puerto Rico (1995; My Puerto
Rico) is a documentary that explores
Puerto Rico’s African, Taino, and Spanish
heritage. Every Child is Born a Poet: The
Life and Work of Piri Thomas (2002), di-
rected by Jonathan Robinson, is a docu-
mentary about Piri Thomas, the Afro-
Caribbean author of Down These Mean
Streets (1967), who explored the internal-
ized racial hatred of his father and de-
scribed his own quest to understand his
racial identity as an Afro-Puerto Rican in
this autobiography.
Mexico and Central America
Although no directors of African descent
from these countries have achieved world
renown, a few ﬁlms by white directors have
dealt with racial themes. The feature ﬁlm
La Negra Angustias (1949; The black An-
gustias), by the Mexican director Matilde
Landeta, is based on the life of a mulatto
woman who served as a colonel under
Emiliano Zapata. The Spanish-born direc-
tor Luis Bunuel, who worked in Mexico
for the second half of his career, made an
English-language ﬁlm on the theme of
racial injustice; his The Young One (1960)
tells the story of a African American man
who is falsely accused of rape and seeks
refuge on an island off the coast of South
Carolina.
South America
The director José Agustín Ferreyra, often
referred to by the nickname “El Negro”
because of his African heritage, was a
pioneer of Colombian cinema. His ﬁlms
include Palomas rubias (1922; Blonde
doves); Odio Serrano (1924; Mountain
hatred); Muñequitas porteñas (1931), the
ﬁrst Argentinian sound ﬁlm; Ayudarme a
vivir (1936; Help Me to Live ); and La
Mujer y la Selva (1941; The Woman and the
Jungle). His ﬁlms are notable for their
frequent focus on the favelas (slums) of
Buenos Aires. Palenque: Un Canto (1992;
Palenque: A Song), by the Colombian direc-
tor Maria Raquel Bozzi, is a documentary
about the village of Palenque de San
Basilio, founded by escaped slaves. Salto al
Atlantico (1990; Jump across the Atlantic ),
directed by María Eugenia Esparragoza, is a
documentary focused on the cultural simi-
larities between an African village in the
Belgian Congo and an Afro-Venezuelan

FILM (NORTH AMERICA)
United States
African Americans have been a part of the
American ﬁlm industry from the begin-
ning, but until the 1960s they participated
primarily as actors and actresses, typically
in a limited range of roles including ser-
vants, musicians, and dancers. Exceptions
include many roles acted by Paul Robeson,
in ﬁlms such as Dudley Murphy’s The Em-
peror Jones (1933), and Canada Lee, in
ﬁlms such as Lifeboat (1944), directed by
Alfred Hitchcock, and Body and Soul
(1947), directed by Robert Rossen.
One alternative to the mainstream
American film industry was the “race
movies” produced in the ﬁrst half of the
twentieth century. These ﬁlms used entirely
African American casts and were marketed
primarily to African American audiences.
Some race movies simply mimicked Holly-
wood genres such as slapstick, Westerns,
and gangster ﬁlms, while others took a seri-
ous look at issues such as racism and class
prejudice. Oscar Micheaux, who directed
forty ﬁlms between 1919 and 1938, was
the ﬁrst African American to produce a fea-
ture-length ﬁlm, The Homesteader (1919),
and a sound film, The Exile (1931).
Micheaux also wrote and produced most of
his ﬁlms and directed Paul Robeson’s ﬁrst
movie, Body and Soul (1925). George and
Noble Johnson founded the ﬁrst African
American production company in Amer-
ica, the Lincoln Production Company in
1916. Among their ﬁlms were The Realiza-
tion of a Negro’s Ambition(1916), A Trooper
of Troop K (1917), and A Man’s Duty
(1919), all directed by Harry A. Gant. Hol-
lywood picked up on the idea of all-black
casts for several musical ﬁlms that were not
intended exclusively for the African Ameri-
can market, including Hallelujah! (1929),
directed by King Vidor; Stormy Weather
(1943), directed by Andrew L. Stone; and
Carmen Jones (1954), directed by Otto Pre-
minger. Many African American perform-
ers also appeared in “soundies,” short musi-
cal ﬁlms created in the 1940s to be played
in public places such as bars or restaurants
by a coin-operated machine similar to a
jukebox.
The ﬁrst Hollywood ﬁlm directed by
an African American was Gordon Parks’s
The Learning Tree (1969), an autobio-
graphical account of growing up in the
1920s. The 1970s saw an explosion of ﬁlms
featuring, and sometimes directed by,
African Americans. Melvin van Peebles di-
rected the comedy Watermelon Man in
1970 and the runaway hit Sweet Sweetback’s
Baadasssss Song in 1971, in which he also
played the title character. The latter is gen-
erally considered the ﬁrst “blaxploitation”
ﬁlm, although some argue that Cotton
Comes to Harlem (1970), directed by Ossie
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

476 F ILM (NORTH AMERICA)
Davis, deserves that distinction. Blaxploita-
tion ﬁlms centered on the activities of black
characters, usually in an urban ghetto; in-
corporated contemporary African Ameri-
can popular music; and often featured
scenes of exaggerated violence and sex. The
quality of these ﬁlms varied greatly, and
some African Americans considered the
genre racist. Other works in this genre in-
clude Shaft (1971), directed by Gordon
Parks; Superﬂy (1972), directed by Gordon
Parks Jr.; Black Caesar (1973), directed by
Larry Cohen; and Coffy (1973), directed by
Jack Hill.
Spike Lee was the ﬁrst of a number of
young African American directors to bring
a distinctive directorial voice to American
cinema in the 1980s: his ﬁlms include She’s
Gotta Have It (1986), Do the Right Thing
(1989), and Malcolm X (1992). Robert
T ownsend’s ﬁlms include Hollywood Shufﬂe
(1989), a satire about his experiences in
Hollywood, and The Five Heartbeats
(1991). John Singleton’s Boyz n the Hood
(1991) and Matty Rich’s Straight Out of
Brooklyn (1991) both take an unsentimen-
tal look at African American life in impov-
erished neighborhoods. Women directors
in this generation include Julie Dash,
whose Daughters of the Dust (1991) focuses
on a family living off the South Carolina
coast in 1902, and Leslie Harris, whose Just
Another Girl on the IRT (1993) follows the
life of a female high school student in
Brooklyn, New York.
Canada
Afro-Canadians did not play a large part
in their nation’s ﬁlm industry until 1995.
In that year, the ﬁrst two feature ﬁlms pro-
duced by Canadians of African descent
were released: Clement Virgo’s Rude and
Stephen Williams’s Soul Survivor . Both
ﬁlmmakers are of Jamaican descent and
set their ﬁlms in the T oronto Jamaican
émigré community. The plot of Rude is
concerned with the intertwined lives of
several characters living in a housing
project. Soul Survivor ’s plot centers on a
young man who takes a job as enforcer for
a local moneylender. Stephen Williams
has worked primarily in television since
1995, while Clement Virgo has worked in
both television and ﬁlm; his later ﬁlms in-
clude The Planet of Junior Brown (1997),
Love Come Down (2000), and Lie With Me
(2005).
Several white Canadian directors have
also treated the culture and lives of persons
of African descent in their ﬁlms. The
award-winning animated short, Begone
Dull Care (1949), directed by Norman
McLaren and Evelyn Lambert, features the
music of the Montreal-born jazz pianist
Oscar Peterson. Director Gilles Groulx’s
Golden Gloves (1961) is a documentary
about aspiring boxers and their social mi-
lieu that includes the story of Ronald Jones,
a young Afro-Canadian living in Montreal.
Sitting in Limbo (1986), directed by John
N. Smith, concerns the lives of two
Caribbean-Canadian teenagers in Montreal
and features the reggae music of Jimmy
Cliff. Directed by Rebecca Yates and Glen
Salzman, Milk and Honey (1988) focuses
on a Jamaican woman who emigrates to
Canada to work as a domestic. The
T oronto-born Norman Jewison directed
several movies centering on the lives of
African Americans, including In the Heat of
the Night (1967), A Soldier’s Story (1985),
and The Hurricane (1999).
