FILM (SOUTH AMERICA)
The countries of South America vary
widely in geography, population, history,
and culture. Due to their common lan-
guage, the Spanish-speaking countries
share aspects of culture that they do not
share with Brazil (Portuguese-speaking);
Guyana (English); Suriname (Dutch); and
the French overseas department, French
Guiana (French). For this reason, the South
American countries in which Spanish is the
primary language have been included in
the article on Latin America, and this entry
discusses ﬁlms from Brazil, Guyana, Suri-
nam, and French Guiana.
Brazil
Brazil has been the major producer in the
Western Hemisphere, outside the United
States and Cuba, of ﬁlms including people of
African descent. This is due primarily to the
country’s large size and population, the fact
that it has had an active ﬁlm industry since
the early twentieth century, and the fact that
a large proportion of Brazilians (about 45
percent) have some African heritage. Afro-
Brazilian actors and actresses have appeared
frequently in Brazilian ﬁlms, particularly in
the chanchada, or Brazilian musical comedy
ﬁlms of the 1940s and 1950s, but have rarely
had the opportunity to play major dramatic
roles. Even fewer Afro-Brazilians have had
the opportunity to direct ﬁlms. However,
many white directors have explored aspects
of Afro-Brazilian history and life, and re-
cently more Afro-Brazilians have gained the
opportunity to direct their own ﬁlms.
Ironically, the ﬁrst impression many
movie audiences outside of Brazil received of
Afro-Brazilian culture was through the some-
what parodistic portrayals in ﬁlms by the
Portuguese-born singer and comedienne
Carmen Miranda, whose costume was
adopted from that worn by Afro-Brazilian
fruit sellers from Salvador de Bahia. She
made ﬁlms in both Brazil and the United
States, and her Hollywood ﬁlms in particular
were distributed more widely than any
Brazilian ﬁlms of the day. Her ﬁlms include
A Voz do Carnaval (1933; The Voice of the
Carnival), directed by Adhemar Gonzaga
and Humberto Mauro; Alô, Alô, Brazil
(1935; Hello, Hello, Brazil), directed by Wal-
lace Downey, Alberto Ribeiro, and João de
Barro; Week-End in Havana(1941), directed
by Walter Lang; The Gang’s All Here(1943),
directed by Busby Berkeley; and Copacabana
(1947), directed by Alfred E. Green.
More serious ﬁlms focusing on favela
(slum) life and featuring samba music in-
clude Rio Zona Norte (1957; Rio, North
Zone), directed by Nelson Pereira dos San-
tos, and Ofeu Negro (1959; Black Orpheus),
by the French director Marcel Camus,
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

which won the Academy Award for Best
Foreign Film. Another ﬁlm by Nelson
Pereira dos Santos, Rio, 40 Graus (1964;
Rio, 40 degrees), builds a portrait of Rio de
Janeiro by following ﬁve Afro-Brazilian
children through the city for a day. Re-

more realistic and less romanticized view of

(2002; City of God ), directed by Fernando
Meirelles and Kátia Lund, tells the story of
a group of boys growing up in a violent
housing project in Rio de Janeiro.
Several Brazilian directors have treated
the theme of slavery. Carlos Diegues di-
rected Ganga Zumba (1963) and Qilombo
(1984), which are about a village founded
by escaped slaves, and Xica (1976), which
is based on the life of a slave woman in
eighteenth-century Brazil. The story of
Qilombo is also told in the documentary
Aruanda (1960), directed by Linduarte
Noronha. Sinhá Moça (1953; The
Landowner’s Daughter), directed by T om
Payne and Oswaldo Sampaio; A Marcha
(1977; The March), directed by Oswaldo
Sampaio; and Chico Rei (1982), directed by
Walter Lima Jr., deal with events around
the year, 1888, that Brazil abolished slavery.
Haroldo Costa was the first Afro-
Brazilian director ( Pista de Grama [1958];
Grass T rack), but not until the late 1970s
did Afro-Brazilians in any number get the
opportunity to direct. The directors of this
generation had several things in common:
most were successful ﬁlm actors before they
got a chance to direct; most directed only a
single ﬁlm; and their ﬁlms have not become
part of the international repertoire. The
ﬁrst of these directors was Odilon Lopez,
who wrote and directed the comedy Um é
Pouço, Dois éBom(1970; Two is Better than
One). Waldyr Onofre directed the comedy
As Aventuras Amorosas de Um Padeiro
(1975; The Amorous Adventures of a
Baker) and worked as assistant director on
three other ﬁlms. Antonio Pitanga directed
Na Boca do Mundo (1978; In the Mouth of
the World) and also served as second unit
director on Carlos Diegues’s Qilombo.
One interesting documentary pro-
duced by Afro-Brazilian directors are Sil-
vana Afram’s Mulheres Negras (1986; Black
Women of Brazil), which focuses on Afro-
Brazilian women dealing with racism in
daily life. Another is Zózimo Bulbul’s ﬁlm
Abolição (1988; Abolition), which exam-
ines the situation of Afro-Brazilians one
hundred years after the abolition of slavery.
Guyana, Surinam,
and French Guiana
Guyana, Surinam, and French Guiana all
have ethnically mixed populations, includ-
ing a substantial number of persons with at
least some African heritage. Their national
languages reﬂect their colonial past: English
in Guyana, a former British colony; Dutch
in Surinam, a former Dutch colony; and
French in French Guiana, a former French
colony. Only a few ﬁlms have been made in
any of these countries. The ﬁrst Guyanese
ﬁlm, Aggro seizeman (1975), directed by
James Mannas and Brian Stuart-Young,
used an entirely Guyanese cast and focused
on the “seizeman” who repossesses goods
that are not fully paid for. The Guyanese
politician and author Rupert Roopnaraine
directed The T error and the Time (1979), an
experimental ﬁlm set in Guyana in 1953,
the time of the ﬁrst universal suffrage elec-
tions. Kean Gibson has made two ﬁlms

about African inﬂuences in Guyanese cul-

with his mother in Surinam. Le Bouillon

FIVE PERCENT NATION
The Five Percent Nation, also known as The
Nation of Gods and Earths, was founded in
Harlem in 1964 by Clarence 13X (Clarence
Smith [1929–1969]), a disaffected member
of the Nation of Islam. Clarence 13X, called
Allah by his followers, was a charismatic
Korean War veteran who at one time allied
himself with John Lindsay, the mayor of
New York, and was partially credited for
stemming violence in the wake of Martin
Luther King’s assassination in 1968.
Clarence 13X was himself assassinated in
1969. The group’s name refers to its funda-
mental belief that its members are the 5 per-
cent of the world that is civilized and have
knowledge of self, while 85 percent of the
world remains uncivilized and ignorant and
under the exploitation of devils that form
the remaining 10 percent.
The group’s additional name, The Na-
tion of Gods and Earths, is a reference to
the idea that each black man is God and
each black woman is the nurturing Earth.
The group renamed areas of New York City
with Islamic place-names: Harlem was
referred to as Mecca and Brooklyn as Me-
dina, for example. The Five Percenter mes-
sage gained popularity in the 1980s and
early 1990s through the lyrics of well-
known rap artists such as Rakim, Big
Daddy Kane, Brand Nubian, and Poor
Righteous T eachers. The use of rap music
as a medium, as well as the group’s colorful
catch phrases, numerology, coded lan-
guage, and message of empowerment con-
tinue to appeal to urban youth culture.
Brent Singleton

FLYINGAFRICANS
Popular and sacred myths depicting ﬂying
Africans are stories about New World
African slaves who could ﬂy back to Africa
rather than remaining enslaved. These
stories are related to eighteenth- and
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 556 ---
480 F LYINGAFRICANS
nineteenth-century legends, folktales, and
rituals, and twentieth-century ﬁlm and lit-
erary motifs originating out of the ethos of
the Middle Passage and transatlantic slav-
ery. Beliefs about Africans who had the
ability to ﬂy blended elements of West
African and Central African sacred myths
with the circumstances of slavery in the
Americas.
Legends incorporating the motif of the
ﬂying African have not only attracted the
attention of folklorists and anthropologists.
Contemporary writers have applied the
symbolic motif into their creative writing.
In twentieth-century African Diaspora lit-
erature, the once sacred myth of the ﬂying
Africans is expressed through secular motifs
of flight—birds of symbolic fortitude,
planes, pilots, people falling or jumping
from rooftops and cliffs, and prophetic
dreams of ﬂying. Thus, the ﬂight motif has
inﬂuenced the plot and characterization;
the thematic quest for freedom; the
“ancient properties” of the past; and self-
exploration in literary works such as T oni
Morrison’s Song of Solomon (1977), Earl
Lovelace’s Salt (1997), Gloria Naylor’s
Mama-Day (1988), Michelle Cliff’s Abeng
(1984), Esteban Montejo’s Autobiograﬁa di
uno schiavo (1966; The Autobiography of a
Runaway Slave), and Alejo Carpentier’s The
Kingdom of This World (1957). The motif
of the ﬂying African is also portrayed in
ﬁlms such as T omás Gutiérrez Alea’s La
Última Cena (1976; The Last Supper ) and
Gillo Pontecorvo’s Burn!(1969).
During the reign of the transatlantic
slave trade, the majority of African slaves
sent to the Americas came from the Slave
Coast, in the area of Senegambia and Cen-
tral Africa. Although peoples from along
the coast and from central areas of Africa
were diverse in their ethnic backgrounds,
they shared similar ontological beliefs.
Bantu-speaking peoples from these areas
had shared religious and traditional beliefs.
Despite the onslaught of transatlantic slav-
ery, these sacred beliefs survived the horriﬁc
conditions of the Middle Passage—the At-
lantic crossing—and became established in
the Americas through syncretic religions
such as Obeah, Santeria, Candomblé and
Voodoo.
The myth of ﬂying is also related to the
forbidden act of suicide. The Tiv of Nigeria,
for example, believed that committing sui-
cide was worse than committing murder.
Likewise among the Azande, Kanuri, Ibo,
and Hausa suicide was also forbidden. One
way in which to “correct” or “repair” the
taboo of suicide when it did occur was
through mythologizing or encoding the act.
If a suicide occurred, that individualistic act
had to be ritualistically cleansed by the liv-
ing in order that the individual’s soul could
ﬁnd peace in the spirit world and not roam
in various “shape-shifting” forms among the
living. One of the central ontological tenets
that existed among the early generations of
enslaved Africans who arrived in the New
World was that it was forbidden to take
one’s own life. According to extant oral his-
tory, the enslaved Africans who arrived in
the Americas during the early centuries of
slavery frequently dismissed, denied, or
concealed suicide by engaging the myth of
ﬂying. Thus, in the ethos of New World
slavery, to ﬂy would become a euphemism
for suicide. In “The Nkuyu: Spirit Messen-
gers of the Kumina” (1977), Maureen
Warner-Lewis draws attention to the rela-
tionship between suicide and the myths of
ﬂying among African peoples in the emerg-
ing New World cultures. The ﬂying African
motif not only implicated suicide, but it
was offered as a response for sudden and
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 557 ---
FLYINGAFRICANS 481
inexplicable feats of disappearance by slaves
from their masters.
Throughout numerous ancient West
African societies, the ability “to ﬂy” or to
have divine powers was directly correlated
with abstinence from salt. T raditions indicate
that such abstinence enhanced shamanistic
powers and enabled magico-religious prac-
tices. With the discipline to refrain from
adding salt to food, mystics and healers
separated themselves from the ordinary
members of the community. In preparing
the body and mind for healing and divina-
tion rituals, they would not consume salt.
There was also a widespread view that salt
could ward off evil because evil sorcerers
would not come near the salt.
Beliefs about the powers of salt absti-
nence persisted during the formation of
neo-African cultures in the Americas. The
early generations of African peoples coming
to the Americas as slaves forged circumstan-
tial reasons for their ontological beliefs, and
abstinence from salt became associated with
the brutality of slavery, submission to Chris-
tianity (salt was frequently given in Catholic
baptismal ceremonies), and collective mem-
ory of the traumatic Atlantic crossing. In
New World slave history, people of African
descent began to associate salt with unmiti-
gated death, misery, betrayal, and suffering.
Yet as spiritual people who had recent col-
lective memories of an African homeland,
they trusted that through death, their souls
would be able to “ﬂy” back to Africa if they
abstained from salt. The folklore and leg-
ends show that “ﬂight” in the context of
slavery in the New World represented the
hope, unity, and courage of African slaves
who could “rise into the air” and escape
back to the homeland in Africa.
Although slavery was eventually abol-
ished in the English, Spanish, French,
Portuguese, and Dutch colonies in the
Americas, sacred beliefs about the ﬂying
Africans and the connections to suicide de-
veloped into popular legends. These leg-
ends are part of the folklore in the English-,
French-, Spanish-, Portuguese-, and
Dutch-speaking communities in the New
World African Diaspora. Legends of the
ﬂying Africans have especially proliferated
in neo-African folklore in the United
States, the Caribbean, and Central America.
In The Book of Negro Folklore (1958), by
Langston Hughes and Arna Bontemps, for
example, “The Legend of the Flying
African” appears as a traditional story still
told among the Gullah people of the
Georgia Sea Islands. Some of the most well-
known twentieth-century references to
“folks ﬂyin’ back tuh Africa” can be read in
the oral narratives that were collected in
Drums and Shadows: Survival Studies
among the Georgia Coastal Negroes (1940)
during the 1930s. Emerging from many
different African ethnicities that converged
in the Americas during the momentum of
transatlantic slavery, the myth of the ﬂying
African has been revitalized by numerous
contemporary writers into legends of liber-
ation, empowerment, and freedom.
Angelita Reyes

FOLKLORE,A FRICAN
African folklore is part of the oral tradition
of black culture. They are oral traditional
tales of Africa that have survived and been
transformed by African American and
Caribbean storytelling and cultural prac-
tices. When they needed to write about the
literature of their ancestors, West African
intellectuals of the 1960s turned to the
griot to preserve the age-old traditions of
African storytelling. The griot, whose in-
herited wisdom was acquired through
legacy, age, and experience, was the only
person who could keep the African past
from falling into oblivion at a time when
modernization was casting its shadows over
the continent. A troubadour par excellence,
the griot was an erudite poet whose knowl-
edge and wisdom came not only from his
function of historian and genealogist, but
also from his role of diplomat and diviner.
He retained sacred knowledge of the un-
matched arts of praise-poetry, story collect-
ing, reciting, and negotiating.
The griot was traditionally a public ser-
vant, counselor, and artist at the service of
the royal authority and the people that it
governed. His fate depended on the sur-
vival and prosperity of the king or queen
next to whom he would walk, ride, and
run, even during wartime. This unity be-
tween the griot and royal personages was
manifested in the continuing relationships
between  the families of the griots and roy-
alty. In the empires that used to be in cur-
rent Mali, Guinea, Senegal, and the Gam-
bia, “it was understood that a son would
succeed his father as griot to a particular
line of kings.” When author Djibril Tamsir
Niane went to collect information about
the epic of Sunjata Keita, Guinean griot
Djeli Mamadou Kouyate told him, “The
hero’s father, Maghan Kon Fatta, the king
of Mali, had as his griot a certain
Gnankouman Doua; when the king died
and Sunjata succeeded to the throne, he in-
herited as griot the son of Doua, Balla
Fasseke Kouyate” (Niane, 1965, 9). Djeli
Mamadou Kouyate rendered the exact
words that Maghan Kon Fatta had spoken
to his son Sunjata before he died: “In Man-
den each prince has a griot; the father of
Doua [that is, Duga] was my father’s griot;
Doua is my griot; the son of Doua, Balla
Fasseke, is to be your griot” (cited in
Austen, 1999, 34). These statements
demonstrate the vital role that the griot
plays as a historian and keeper of oral tradi-
tion in Africa. By transmitting unwritten
knowledge of the past, the griot becomes
the purveyor of African oral tradition. Djeli
Kuyate’s repetition of the word griot, his
emphasis on names, and the distinctive
tonality, cadence, and rhythm in which he
narrates Maghan Kon Fatta’s last words to
his son are patterns of the old poetic tradi-
tion from which contemporary African oral
strategies derived. The manner in which
the griot recites or interprets traditional
epics, such as that of Sunjata, helps us un-
derstand the origins and characteristics of
African discursive strategies. In this epic,
Sumanguru Kante, king of Sosso, old Mali,
had a conversation with his new griot, Bala
Faasege, whom he had taken from his rival,
Sunjata. Sumanguru told Bala:
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 559 ---
FOLKLORE,A FRICAN 483
What is your name?
The griot replied, “My name is
Nyankuma Dookha.”
Sumanguru said, “I am going to take
your name from you;
And apart from those with special
knowledge,
No one will know your name any more.
I shall name you after my xylophone.
What I am going to do to you,
That is what I shall make your name.
The third will be your surname
Your ﬁrst name is Balo;
I will cut your Achilles tendons;
Your surname is Kuyate.”
They call him Bala Faasege Kuyate.
(cited in Austen, 1999, pp. 36–37) 
This epic, which was narrated by
Malian griot Demba Kanute in the early
1970s, reﬂects the importance of orality
and understated meaning in traditional
African poetry. As the tone of the conversa-
tion between Sumanguru and Bala Faasege
suggests, in traditional African epic poetry,
the importance of the word depends on the
way meaning is encoded and expressed in a
verbal exchange. When Sumanguru tells his
new griot Balla, “I am going to take your
name from you,” he intends to go further
than just removing the civil name and iden-
tity that Bala had in the past. Sumanguru
envisions to completely eradicate Bala’s pre-
vious status as griot of the Keita family by
transforming him into the bard of the
Kante household. This shift of identity re-
quires substituting Bala’s previous alle-
giance to the “Dookha” for a new commit-
ment to the “Kuyate.” Once complete, this
transformation of Bala’s status, which shifts
both his royal and ethnic loyalty, is irre-
versible. The unalterability of Balla’s new
social position accounts for the seriousness
and solemnity of Sumanguru’s tone when
he says, “I will cut your Achilles tendons.”
What Sumanguru does here is not to per-
form the act literally but to signify on his
intent to kill the old personality of his new
griot in the same way a knife would have
cut through the “Achilles tendons” of a per-
son. While he has no intent to hurt Bala,
Sumanguru wants to sever Bala’s “tendons”
metaphorically, signifying his affective con-
viction that no one other than Bala de-
serves to become his griot. The understated
meaning of Sumanguru’s words is a central
feature in African oral poetry. Behind the
literal aspect of words, the griots convey
subtle and implicit meaning through the
use of symbolic images.
Because of the transatlantic slave trade,
which resulted in the forced transportation
of millions of Africans to the Western
world, African folklore found its way in the
Americas. In order to preserve the memory
of their homelands, ancestors, and cultures,
the enslaved Africans held tightly to the
folktales and worldviews that they either
brought from Africa or learned from their
forbears in the Americas. These Africans
passed down knowledge of the tales from
generation to generation, making it possi-
ble for scholars to ﬁnd their traces in the
rich literature of blacks in the Americas.
The African inﬂuence in the folklore of
the Americas is visible in the similar ways
in which tales are told on both sides of the
Atlantic Ocean. A few examples are in Zora
Neale Hurston’s book of folklore, Mules
and Men (1935). Here, Hurston’s story-
tellers develop rhetorical devices that are
traceable to cultures and places in Africa.
Such devices include opening formulas and
calls-and-responses. Examples of opening
formula in Mules are the sentences, “Well,
once upon a time was a good time” in “The
T urtle Watch” (p. 84) and “Ah got to say a
piece of litery [literary] fust to git mah wind
on” in “How Jack Beat the Devil” (p. 47).
These phrases are analogous to the ones
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 560 ---
484 F OLKLORE,A FRICAN
used in Wolof and Fulani folktales, where
they serve to arouse the audience members
to listen attentively and participate in the
process of the storytelling. The Wolof sto-
ryteller begins his or her narrative in a sim-
ilar way with the formula “leb-on” (there
was a story) to which the audience re-
sponds “lup-on” (it happened here). 
Like the African American formula, the
Wolof version invites the audience to listen
attentively and participate actively in the
process of storytelling by answering to the
teller’s calls. In T alking and T estifying
(1977), Geneva Smitherman found in the
African American church a call-and-
response exchange in which the preacher
tells the audience, “Y’all don’t want to hear
dat so I’m gone leave it alone,” to which the
congregation responds by saying “‘Naw, T ell
it, Reb! T ell it! T ell it!” A similar verbal ex-
change occurs in Wolof storytelling. Here,
the teller establishes a rapport of communi-
cation by saying “Am-on a ﬁ” (it happened
here) to which the audience responds by
saying “da na am” (it was so). The sentence
“Naw, T ell it, Reb! T ell it! T ell it!” that
Smitherman described as a usual formula in
African American sermon, rap, comedy, and
storytelling is visible in James Baldwin’s Go
T ell it on the Mountain (1953), when the
congregation in the T emple of the Fire Bap-
tized responds to Gabriel’s call “Woe is me!”
by shouting “‘Yes! T ell it! Amen! You preach
it, boy.” This pattern of call-and-response in
the African American sermon is consistent
with the Wolof communicative exchange
described earlier.
Moreover, the African inﬂuence in the
Americas is visible in the trickster ﬁgures of
Brer Rabbit and Brer Dog that Hurston de-
picts in Mules to represent the unequal
power relations between planters and slaves
during slavery. One example is the tale
“What the Rabbit Learned,” in which Brer
Dog seeks revenge against Brer Rabbit, who
had taken the former’s girlfriend, Miss
Saphronie, from him and cut his tongue
during their previous conﬂict in “How Brer
Dog Lost His Beautiful Voice.” In “What
the Rabbit Learned,” Brer Rabbit and Brer
Dog were walking peacefully in the bush,
as if no grudge existed between them,
when, all of a sudden, the Rabbit heard the
sound of barking dogs. Noting that Brer
Rabbit was frightened by the sound of the
hounds, Brer Dog told the Rabbit, “Ain’t
we done held a convention and passed a
law dogs run no mo’ rabbits? Don’t pay no
’tention to every lil’l bit of barkin’ you hear”
(pp. 146–147). The Rabbit, who knew that
some trick was being played against him,
responded, “Yeah, but all de dogs ain’t been
to no convention, and anyhow some of
dese fool dogs ain’t got no better sense
than to run over dat law and break it up.”
Saying this, Brer Rabbit took off, remem-
bering the old-time saying “Run every time
de bush shake” (p. 147). 
The intelligence, charm, wisdom, and
verbal dexterity that Brer Rabbit exhibits in
his capacity to outsmart Brer Dog in the
bush signiﬁes on the subversive strategies
that slaves developed to outwit the slave-
holders and slave catchers who chased them
when they ran away from plantations. The
wisdom that makes Brer Rabbit “run every
time de bush shakes” alludes to the intelli-
gence that the African slaves in America
such as Frederick Douglass and Solomon
Northup demonstrated by running away or
hiding in secret places whenever they were
chased by cruel slave owners. Such subver-
sive strategies of resistance derive from the
vigilance that African tricksters like Leuk,
who is Brer Rabbit’s grandfather, used to
survive oppression in the mythological
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 561 ---
FRENCH EMPIRE 485
world of Ndoumbelane. In Birago Diop’s
“The T ricks of Leuk-the-Hare” (1966),
Leuk charmed a princess and escaped her
father’s plan to execute him by simply
telling the king, “Bour [your majesty] . . .
you cannot kill the father of your grand-
child!” (81). The wisdom and verbal skill
that Leuk used to subvert a stratiﬁed tradi-
tional Wolof society is the source from
which Brer Rabbit and the African slaves in
the Americas drew in order to outsmart
their oppressors.
African folklore has a rich history that
is traceable from the traditional epic of
Sunjata to the contemporary literature of
blacks in the Americas. In both Africa and
the Americas, folklore has served as an im-
portant means of entertainment, educa-
tion, and cultural survival. The Africans
who survived the Middle Passage have used
it to preserve their past and resist domina-
tion. In this sense, black writers of the
Americas have inherited the role of pre-
servers of the past that griots used to play in
Africa.
Babacar M’Baye

FRENCH EMPIRE
The French Empire grew rapidly in the At-
lantic between the sixteenth and the nine-
teenth centuries, competing heavily with
the British Empire. The French laid claim
to substantial territories in North, West,
and Central Africa, North America, and
the Caribbean, particularly what is now the
nation of Haiti. French merchants, in
search of new markets and potential
sources of raw materials, were attracted by
Africa and the New World. The French
Empire relied heavily on the transatlantic
trade started by European merchants in the
ﬁfteenth century and involving the export
of manufactured goods from Europe to
Africa, the shipment of African slaves to the
New World, and the sale of American-
grown crops to Europe.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 562 ---
486 F RENCH EMPIRE
The early voyages of Jacques Cartier
and other French explorers to the coasts of
the New World that they hoped to make
New France, as well as the frequent voyages
of French ﬁshermen to the Grand Banks of
Newfoundland throughout the sixteenth
century, were the precursors to French
colonial expansion. France’s ﬁrst major
American colony was established on July
27, 1605, with the foundation of Port
Royal in the colony of Acadia (present-day
Nova Scotia, Canada). In 1608 Samuel de
Champlain founded Quebec City, which
was to become the capital of New France
(later called Canada). Areas of French set-
tlement were generally limited to the St.
Lawrence River valley. The territories of
New France were developed as mercantile
colonies because at that time in France
there was relatively little interest in long-
term settlements. In the 1680s, Cavelier de
La Salle offered France another chance to
carve out an empire in the New World.
After several fruitless attempts, he reached
the fork of the Mississippi Delta with his
crew, and on April 9, 1682 he acquired the
territory of Louisiana. Colonization efforts
began in July 1684, but the region was so
inhospitable and the living conditions so
bad that French colonial ambitions ended
in failure.
At the same time, the French began to
build a smaller but more proﬁtable empire
in the West Indies to enhance their Ameri-
can expansion. Settlements along South
America’s northern coast in present-day
French Guiana began in 1624, despite
Amerindian hostility, widespread tropical
diseases, and malnutrition. In 1643 the
French colonists established a settlement at
Cayenne along with some small-scale plan-
tations. After the T reaty of Paris of 1763,
which deprived France of almost all her
possessions in the Americas other than
Guiana and a few Caribbean islands, in-
cluding Martinique, Guadeloupe, and St.
Lucia. Louis XIV sent thousands of settlers
to Guiana in the 1780s and 1790s. Exports
of sugar, hardwood, Cayenne pepper, and
other spices brought some prosperity to the
colony for the ﬁrst time. In these decades
Cayenne became surrounded by planta-
tions, some of which had several thousand
slaves brought in from Africa. 
The Compagnie des Îles de l’Amérique
(Company of the American Islands) colo-
nized in Guadeloupe and Martinique in
1635. The French took possession of
Guadeloupe, wiped out many of the native
Caribs, and annexed the island to the king-
dom of France in 1674. One indication of
Guadeloupe’s prosperity at this time is that
in the T reaty of Paris in 1763, France de-
cided to abandon its territorial claims in
Canada in return for British recognition of
French control of Guadeloupe. French con-
trol of Guadeloupe was ﬁnally acknowl-
edged in the T reaty of Vienna (1815). Mar-
tinique was colonized in 1635 by the
French occupying forces, who deported the
native Caribs from the island and banned
their return.
The most important French Caribbean
colonial possession was the colony of Saint
Domingue (later Haiti), which was the
western third of the Spanish island of His-
paniola. Saint Domingue was acquired in
1697, and soon afterwards French settlers
began importing African slaves, who be-
came the most numerous segment of the
population. In the eighteenth century,
Saint Domingue grew to be the richest
sugar colony in the Caribbean and the
French Empire’s most important territory.
The colony was ruled by a small minority
of Europeans and free people of color.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 563 ---
FRENCH EMPIRE 487
On August 14, 1791, the ﬁrst success-
ful slave revolt in the Americas began in
Saint Domingue. The slaves were led by
T oussaint Louverture and then, following
his capture by the French in 1801, by Jean
Jacques Dessalines. They defeated French,
Spanish, and British colonists and eventu-
ally achieved independence as Haiti on Jan-
uary 1, 1804. Haiti thus became the ﬁrst
black republic in the world. The Haitian
example inspired numerous slave revolts in
the Caribbean and the United States.
As with other French colonies in the
Americas, the settlers established large
food-producing plantations sustained with
a supply of African slaves. Though the Por-
tuguese were the pioneers of the slave trade
in Africa, Frenchmen later became active
participants. French merchants exchanged
brass, copper bracelets, and other Western
goods for pepper, beads, salt, ivory, gold,
and slaves, their most precious asset, who
subsequently became Africa’s most exten-
sive export industry; they were major com-
mercial commodities in the transatlantic
economic order. The growing demand for
sugar and other tropical crops (cane sugar,
tobacco, cotton, rum, cocoa, coffee, and
tea) in the 1630s caused French entrepre-
neurs to step up production, which re-
quired additional laborers. Thus, the
French became increasingly dependent on
cheap African labor for the exploitation of
their American plantations and estates and
the development of their colonies in the
Americas, especially in the West Indies and
in Latin America, which employed about
90 percent of all the Africans taken to the
New World.
At the same time that French expan-
sion was occurring in the Americas, French
involvement in Africa was also growing as a
consequence of economic expansion.
French merchants began trade relations
with African kingdoms in the late ﬁfteenth
century, and by 1624 they had begun to
establish trading posts along the African
coast. 
France had many African colonies,
most of which were acquired in the late
1880s after the Berlin Conference of
1884–1885 that led to the “scramble for
Africa.” Between 1880 and 1900, French
control was established over much of
Northern, Western, and Central Africa.
Burkina Faso (formerly Upper Volta),
Chad, Côte d’Ivoire, Dahomey (present-
day Benin), Gabon, Mali, Mauritania, and
Niger, as well as the east African coastal en-
clave of Djibouti (originally French Soma-
liland), were annexed as overseas territories
of France. They served as reservoirs of
needed raw materials and cheap labor for
French ventures in the Americas. While the
enclaved colonies provided the much-
needed raw materials and slaves, the coastal
territories, while also serving those pur-
poses, additionally provided embarkment
points for the Americas. Besides the re-
source potential and investment opportu-
nities offered by African territories, the
sugar cane and slavery-based economy of
the French possessions in the Americas jus-
tiﬁed French colonial ambition in Africa. 
The growing demand for slave labor in
the Americas, particularly in the French
West Indies, rapidly increased the volume
of slave trade. French slave traders were
particularly active in the Gulf of Guinea,
the Senegambia, and Kongo. The suppliers
of slaves for France’s New World colonies
included the prosperous kingdom of Da-
homey, which established slave trading rela-
tions with the French in the seventeenth
century; it became a French colony in
1892. The coastal part of the kingdom
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 564 ---
488 F RENCH EMPIRE
became known as the Slave Coast, with
Ouidah serving as one of the main supply
points for the much-needed cheap labor for
France’s West Indian plantations. Guinea
also served as a slave collection point from
the time Portuguese ﬁrst came to the area
and began the slave trade in the ﬁfteenth
century. Various European powers came to
the Senegal area from the ﬁfteenth century
onward until France gained possession of
Gorée in 1817, an important slave trade
departure point. Though Côte d’Ivoire was
not an active player in the transatlantic
slave trade, its coastal towns of Assinie,
Grand-Bassam, and San Pedro were impor-
tant collection points of slave labor in-
tended for American plantations owned by
the French. Even after the trade had been
abolished, some slave-trading activities per-
sisted along the Ivorian coasts, with several
African tribes and chiefs acting as agents for
French traders.
The coastal area of Kongo was a major
source for the transatlantic slave trade, and
French traders exported Gabonese slaves
well into the 1870s, long after the trade had
ended elsewhere on the West African coast.
The French had established a trade port on
the West African coast in what is present
day Senegal as early as 1659, and from the
mid-seventeenth to mid-nineteenth cen-
turies became participants in the transat-
lantic slave trade, which was largely under
the control of the British, Dutch, and Por-
tuguese. During this period France ex-
ported hundreds of thousands of slaves a
year to the Caribbean, Latin America, and
North America. 
French penetration into Central Africa
began in the late nineteenth century during
the scramble for Africa in an attempt to ex-
pand the French Empire. France wished to
expand the borders of the French Congo to
link up with French territories in West
Africa, North Africa, and East Africa and
ultimately maximize the exploitation of the
region’s human and natural resources.
The French extended their inﬂuence to
North Africa, establishing a protectorate
over Algeria (1830), T unisia (1881), and
Morocco (1911) because of the economic
potential of that region. The French colo-
nial empire also included colonies and ter-
ritories,  namely Indochina (modern Viet-
nam, Cambodia, and Laos) and the South
Pacific islands of New Caledonia and
French Polynesia. The French made their
last major colonial gains after World War I,
when they gained mandates over the for-
mer territories of the Ottoman Empire that
make up what is now Syria and Lebanon, as
well as most of the former German colonies
of T ogo and Cameroon.
When France abolished slavery in 1848,
the former slaves ﬂed into the rainforest and
set up communities similar to the ones from
which they had been stolen in Africa. These
Maroons formed a buffer zone between the
Europeans, who settled along the coast and
main rivers, and the unconquered, and often
hostile, native American tribes of the inland
regions. Since no prior arrangements were
made for their reintegration as free beings,
these former slaves and their place in society
became a pressing social issue. The French
subsequently repatriated some of the freed
slaves to France between 1859 and 1899 to
work in subordinate capacities and others to
resettlement communities in Cameroon,
Gabon, and Côte d’Ivoire. French mission-
aries, ﬁred by a profound enthusiasm and
concerned with the spiritual welfare of freed
blacks, established missions in these
communities.
The impacts of the French Empire in
both the Western Hemisphere and Africa
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 565 ---
FRENCH EMPIRE 489
were very profound. France’s expansionist
drive established signiﬁcant relations be-
tween Africa and the Americas. The actions
of the empire resulted in the creation of large
African communities in the Americas and
the West Indies. Armed with their African
cultural background, the slaves started new
ways of life, which entailed a combination of
African culture and American elements.
African settlements in the New World
helped to produce a host of synergetic cul-
tures that differ widely from one country to
the next (for example, Guadeloupe as op-
posed to Haiti) and within different regions
of the same territory (for example, southern
versus northern areas of Guadeloupe). This
acculturation operated in two directions,
and strains of African culture have decid-
edly inﬂuenced many of the emergent cul-
tures of the New World; master and slaves
were mutually influenced. Whites de-
pended on African skills to identify useful
ﬂora and fauna in Africa and the appropri-
ate methods of agricultural production for
African crops in America. Blacks also
learned from the Indians while teaching
them about medicinal herbs.
The Africans brought with them their
music, which has had a profound impact on
the musical heritage of the world. Haitian
popular music, for example, derives in large
part from the chants and rhythms of African
drums in the religious rituals of Dahomey
and from the daily life songs that were so
much a part of the African tradition. African
slaves likewise carried their dances across the
Atlantic. Many French Caribbean dances,
including the popular soukous dance, came
from African culture. Africans also left their
mark on the literature and folklore of the
New World. The popular tales and legends
as well as the folk literature and literary
works produced by Caribbean writers in
French are, in large part, of African origin.
There is also a signiﬁcant African inﬂuence
on the French language spoken in the
Caribbean, as demonstrated by the popular
creole languages. Finally, Africans brought
their religious beliefs—Voodoo, for exam-
ple—into the West Indies, where they
blended with Catholic Christianity.
The French Empire also had a pro-
found economic, social, cultural, and psy-
chological impact on African societies and
peoples. The French slavers deprived the
continent of a large proportion of its able-
bodied workforce, which was forcefully dis-
placed from its natural setting to a com-
pletely new environment and culture. The
psychological impact of this dehumanizing
process was crippling, and the loss and dis-
location of population to the transatlantic
markets were detrimental to the economy
of precolonial Africa.
The French Empire also disrupted in-
digenous societies by damaging the social
and economic fabric of the society and un-
dermined the conﬁdence of Africans in their
historical evolution, which militated against
economic progress and cultural develop-
ment. On the other hand, while certain
African areas suffered severely, others were
little affected, or even derived economic ben-
eﬁt from relations with France. The French
expansionist enterprise played a signiﬁcant
role in the capitalist transformation of North
America and the emergence of dependency
structures in Africa and the Caribbean by the
mid-nineteenth century. The process gave
rise to economic, social, and political struc-
tures and relations within which North
America became developed and industrial-
ized, while Africa and the Caribbean re-
mained underdeveloped and agrarian.
Thus, the effects of the expansionist
drive of the French Empire were mixed
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 566 ---
490 F UGITIVE SLAVE LAW
rather than entirely negative. Contact with
France and the Americas opened new im-
ages of the world for Africans and pre-
sented them with products of Western civ-
ilization (including language, education,
culture, goods, industry, and technology).
For example, between 1548 and 1583,
maize, manioc, tobacco and probably
beans, groundnuts, and other New World
plants were introduced into Africa. The
crops from the New World transformed
Africa’s agriculture in the seventeenth cen-
tury by increasing yields and improving
nutrition and health. These gains were,
however, bought at a terrible price, and no
balance sheet can ever present the full ac-
count of the role of the French Empire in
creating relations between Africa and the
Americas.
Philip A. Ojo

FUGITIVE SLAVE LAW
The Fugitive Slave Law of 1850 protected
U.S. slaveholding interests and increased
sectional tension leading to the Civil War.
The U.S. Constitution in its original form
protected some slaveholding interests in a
number of its clauses. Among them was the
Fugitive Slave Clause, which prohibited
free states from emancipating or harboring
escaped slaves and required that runaways
be returned to their owners on demand.
Some northerners feared that free blacks
would be unjustly conﬁned and sent into
slavery under the law. In response, many
northern states passed laws designed to give
accused fugitives legal rights to protect
them from kidnapping, and some prohib-
ited state ofﬁcials from assisting in captur-
ing fugitives.
As antislavery sentiment grew in the
North during the early nineteenth century,
public resistance to southern attempts to
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 567 ---
FUGITIVE SLAVE LAW 491
capture runaways increased, which was ex-
pressed in part by the creation of an under-
ground network of free blacks and sympa-
thetic whites who shuttled escaped
southern slaves to freedom. Southerners
looked to the federal government for fur-
ther support in regaining fugitive slaves
from free states. Recovery of runaways was
not simply a practical interest for slavehold-
ing southerners but a matter of principle, as
they accused northern states of violating
their constitutional responsibilities.
The Compromise of 1850, designed to
prevent secession by again balancing sec-
tional interests, included the Fugitive Slave
Law, which toughened provisions for recov-
ering slaves. This law required U.S. mar-
shals to help owners recover fugitives and
imposed ﬁnes on any person found guilty of
harboring a runaway. There was immediate
outrage in some northern communities,
particularly Boston, where vigilante groups
arose to protect and rescue fugitives from
capture.
Overall, the Fugitive Slave Law in-
creased tension between the North and
South leading to the Civil War.  It did so by
helping to perpetuate slavery as the most
volatile issue facing the country during the
mid-nineteenth century. 
Ian M. Spurgeon

FULANI
The Fulani are a nomadic Muslim ethnic
group located primarily in present-day
Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger. The Fulani
currently represent the largest nomadic
population in the world. An ethnic group
now spread across a large portion of West
Africa, the Fulani are believed to have orig-
inated in North Africa or the Middle East.
Converted to Islam by Arab jihadists, the
Fulani themselves pursued jihads against
the non-Muslim peoples in West Africa
until they displaced or assimilated large
portions of those populations. They estab-
lished two signiﬁcant empires in the ﬁrst
half of the nineteenth century: one cen-
tered in Massina, the other in Sokoto. They
are credited with creating many of the im-
portant trade routes across the interior of
West Africa.
As they entered new regions, the Fulani
established large cattle herds, driving them
from one seasonal pasture to another. T ra-
ditionally, cattle have been the measure of
wealth among the Fulani. But in recent
decades, their nomadic way of life has been
eroded by three factors: desertiﬁcation, in-
tensiﬁed by recurring drought, and the ex-
pansion of agriculture have combined to
reduce grazing lands and have increasingly
forced the Fulani into villages. Moreover,
the greater availability of motorized trans-
port has made the rhythms of the nomadic
life seem increasingly anachronistic.
The Fulani continue to adhere to a
fairly rigid caste system. The major castes,
in their order of stature, are the nobility,
the traders, the tradesmen, and the descen-
dants of slaves. The most prominent fea-
tures of the Fulani culture are their empha-
sis on the stoic endurance of pain and the
accentuation of beauty through tattooing.
As part of their initiation into adulthood,
Fulani boys traditionally endured a cere-
mony in which they viciously struck each
other with staffs and laughed to demon-
strate their contempt for the weapons being
used against them. Although this violent
ceremony has been banned in many places,
the practice of ritual tattooing continues
unabated. Fulani women especially stand
out because they typically dye their lips
black.
Martin Kich

GABON,R EPUBLIC OF
The African nation of Gabon, with a pop-
ulation of 1,425,000 and an area of
103,347 square miles (267 kilometers), has
been shaped by the interaction of Africans,
Europeans, and Americans. Gabon’s relations
with the Americas date back to between
1809 and 1815, when the Portuguese
shipped about 4,000 slaves from the Gabon
coast to the New World, in spite of British
and American antislave trade legislation at
that period. A former French colony,
Gabon became independent in 1960.
The growing market for slave labor in
the Americas, speciﬁcally in the Portuguese
islands, Brazil, Cuba, and the French West
Indies after 1860, acted as a stimulus both
to the enslavement process and the volume
of slave trade. Because of these new slave
markets and because of their proximity,
traders exported Gabonese slaves well into
the 1870s, long after the trade had ended
elsewhere on the West African coast. Slaves,
recruited from most of the interior tribes,
continued to be an important supplement
to the trade in wood, ivory, and other for-
est products in the region until the 1870s.
Nevertheless, a widely applied policy of
concluding treaties with indigenous ethnic
groups, combined with promoting British
land occupation projects in Gabon under
493
G
French protection, had the effect of severely
impeding the trafﬁc in slaves. 
Another sphere of signiﬁcant American
inﬂuence in Gabon was in the ﬁelds of ex-
ploration and evangelization. American ad-
venturers, explorers, and missionaries were
among the ﬁrst to investigate the mysteries
of the African interior. Among the most
notable was Paul Belloni du Chaillu, who
went to Gabon in 1855 for the express
purpose of scientiﬁc exploration in an area
that was still terra incognita to the world
at large. Du Chaillu penetrated the interior
of west-central Africa, starting from the
Gabon River, and then moved eastward.
Another important influence came
through missionary activities that related
to trade. Captain Richard Lawlin, a veteran
American trader, offered to take two
American missionaries, the Reverends John
Leighton Wilson and Benjamin Griswold,
on trading voyages down the coast to check
on possible new locations for missionary
activity in Gabon. These two American
missionaries, representing the Christian
foreign mission agency, American Board of
Commissioners for Foreign Missions, were
among the pioneers in the effort to bring
Christianity to the Mpongwe people of
Gabon. They landed with Lawlin on June 22,
1842 at Glass near the Gabon estuary, a

GABRIEL (1776–1800)
The black author of a failed slave rebellion
in eighteenth-century Virginia, the en-
slaved revolutionary known only as Gabriel
was born near Richmond, Virginia, at
Brookﬁeld, the Henrico County plantation
of Thomas Prosser. Most likely, Gabriel’s
father was a blacksmith, the occupation
chosen for Gabriel; in Virginia, the off-
spring of skilled bondpersons frequently in-
herited their parent’s profession.
Status as a craft artisan provided the
young blacksmith with considerable stand-
ing in the slave community, as did his abil-
ity to read and write. As Gabriel grew to be
an unusually tall young man, even older
slaves looked to him for leadership, a habit
uncommon in African culture. By the mid-
1790s, as he approached the age of twenty,
Gabriel stood at about six feet, and the
muscles in his arms and chest betrayed
nearly a decade in Brookfield’s forge.
According to the journalist James T .
Callender, blacks and whites alike regarded
him as “a fellow of courage and intellect
above his rank in life” (Callender to Jefferson,
Thomas, 17 October, 1800, cited in French,
Scot, 16). 
In the fall of 1798 Gabriel’s old mas-
ter died, and ownership of Brookﬁeld
passed to twenty-two-year-old Thomas
Henry Prosser. An ambitious young man
with a townhouse in Richmond and a lu-
crative auction business, Prosser increas-
ingly maximized his proﬁts by hiring out
his surplus slaves. Despite all of the work
to be done at Brookﬁeld, Gabriel spent a
considerable part of each month smithing
in Richmond for artisans long on orders
and short on labor. Although still a slave
under Virginia law, Gabriel enjoyed a
rough form of freedom. Indeed, his ties to
the plantation became so tenuous that sev-
eral historians erroneously have identiﬁed
him as a free man.
Emboldened by this quasi-liberty, in
September 1799 Gabriel moved toward
overt rebellion. Caught in the act of steal-
ing a pig, a delicacy slaves used to supply
their families with protein, Gabriel refused
to endure the verbal abuse of its owner, a
white neighbor. Instead, he wrestled his
tormentor to the ground and bit off the
better “part of his left Ear.” Under Virginia
law, slaves were not tried as whites. They
were prosecuted under a colonial statute of
1692 that created special segregated tri-
bunals known as courts of oyer and ter-
miner, composed of ﬁve justices of the
peace. No jury was empanelled and
there was an appeal to the governor. On
October 7 Gabriel was formally charged
with attacking a white man, a capital crime.
Although found guilty, Gabriel escaped the
gallows through an antiquated “beneﬁt of
clergy” clause that since the Revolution had
been denied to white defendants. Slaves
still possessed the right to beneﬁt of clergy,
which allowed them to avoid hanging in
exchange for being branded on the thumb
with a small cross if they were able to recite
a verse from the Bible.
Gabriel’s branding and incarceration
served as a brutal reminder that despite his
literacy and special status, he remained a
slave. By the early spring of 1800, his fury
began to turn into a carefully considered
plan to bring about his freedom, as well as
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 572 ---
496 G ABRIEL
the end of slavery in Virginia. As a literate
man who moved among urban artisans,
Gabriel surely knew that several states to
the north had recently passed laws for grad-
ual emancipation, and that New York had
ﬁnally approved such a statute in 1799. As
he explained it to his brothers, Solomon
and Martin, slaves and free blacks from
Henrico County would gather at Brookﬁeld
on the evening of August 30, 1800. As the
small but determined band of insurgents—
armed with crude swords fashioned from
scythes—neared Richmond, it would split
into three groups, each with clearly stated
objectives. Governor James Monroe, who
resided in the small executive mansion
adjacent to the capitol building, was to be
seized as a hostage but otherwise left un-
harmed. A small number of whites, includ-
ing Thomas Henry Prosser, were to die, but
most would live as hostages in order to
force the Virginia elite to grant the rebels’
demands, which included their freedom
and an equitable division of white property.
“Quakers, Methodists and French people,”
three groups who had earned a sometimes
undeserved reputation as foes of slavery,
were not to be harmed. Gabriel hoped that
the “poor white people,” who had no more
political power than did the slaves, “would
also join” the rebels. If Monroe and the
town leaders agreed to Gabriel’s demands,
the slave general intended to “hoist a white
ﬂag” and drink a toast “with the merchants
of the city” (Egerton, 1993, 26).
The uprising collapsed just before sun-
set on the appointed day, when a severe
thunderstorm hit the Richmond area.
Creeks rose, washing away fragile wooden
bridges and severing communications be-
tween Brookﬁeld and the city. Perhaps only
a dozen slaves reached the blacksmith shop.
The chaos of the storm convinced two
Henrico slaves, T om and Pharaoh, that the
revolt could not succeed. They informed
their owner of the conspiracy, and he hur-
ried word to Governor Monroe. As the state
militia closed in, Gabriel escaped south by
way of the swampy Chickahominy River.
Gabriel was ﬁnally betrayed by a slave, who
had heard of Monroe’s $300 reward for
Gabriel’s capture. Returned to Richmond
under heavy guard, Gabriel was quickly
tried and found guilty of “conspiracy and
insurrection.” On October 10, 1800, the
young revolutionary died with quiet com-
posure at the town gallows. He was twenty-
four years old. In all, twenty-six slaves,
including Gabriel and his two brothers,
were hanged for their part in the conspir-
acy. Another bondman allegedly hanged
himself while in custody. Eight more rebels,
including Gabriel’s chief lieutenant, Jack
Ditcher, were transported to Spanish New
Orleans; at least thirty-two others were
found not guilty. Reliable sources placed
the number of slaves who knew of the plot
to be between ﬁve and six hundred.
Douglas R. Egerton

GAMBIA,THE 497
GAMBIA,THE
The Gambia, located on either side of the
River Gambia, is surrounded on three sides
by Senegal and on the west by the Atlantic
Ocean. A ﬁfth of its surface area is occupied
by the River Gambia, and it has a largely
Muslim population of about 1.5 million.
The Gambia was colonized by the British
in the seventeenth century. In 1661 they
seized a fort built at the mouth of the river
by the duke of Kurland, from modern-day
Latvia, and renamed it James Fort. It was
controlled by various British chartered
companies and captured by the French in
1779, who returned it to the British in
1816. From 1843 until 1866 The Gambia
was a separate colony, but from 1866 until
1888 it was administered from Sierra
Leone. The latter did not work well, how-
ever, and from 1888 The Gambia was a
separate colony again. In 1894 it was en-
larged to include the “Protectorate,” land
further upriver. On February 18, 1965,
The Gambia became an independent re-
public within the British Commonwealth
as the Republic of The Gambia.
The Gambia was a major source of
slaves. The English established the Guinea
Company in the early seventeenth century,
which became known formally as the
Royal Africa Company in 1660 to trade
with the region. They were originally inter-
ested in gold, but after running up losses,
they quickly turned to the slave trade, and
the company may have been involved in
taking slaves to Virginia as early as May
1628. Those enslaved were then sold to
plantations there in return for tobacco,
which was brought back to England. The
Royal Adventurers Company, formed in
London during the 1660s, which included
Prince Rupert and his brother Maurice,
was also involved in the region, with the
prince (who had fought in the English
Civil War twenty years earlier) and his
brother  sailing to The Gambia. They were
the ﬁrst members of a European royal fam-
ily to visit West Africa, and the only roy-
alty to visit until the nineteenth century.
Once again, buying slaves and transport-
ing them to the Americas became a lucra-
tive business. Soon a new company, the
Gambia Adventurers, was also established,
and in 1672 the Royal African Company
was founded.
One of the slaves from The Gambia
who was transported to the Americas was
Kunta Kinte, from the village of Juffure. At
the age of sixteen he was taken on the Lord
Ligonier to Virginia where he was sold to a
planter. His story, and that of his descen-
dants, form the basis of Alex Haley’s
Roots (1977).
As the slave trade grew during the sev-
enteenth century, demand for slaves from
The Gambia continued unabated, as dis-
ease and overwork took the lives of many
slaves in the American plantations and even
as other sources of slaves became available. 
William Fitz William Owen (1774–
1857), a Canadian surveyor, charted the
Gambia River in the 1820s. In 1831 the
Barra War resulted from Britain’s determi-
nation to extend its inﬂuence upriver into
Ashanti territory; this same year, Britain
annexed these lands and designated them a
crown colony. From 1831 to 1841, Sir
Henry Vere Huntley (1796–1864) was
next-to-last lieutenant governor of The
Gambia; later, he became governor of
Prince Edward Island. The governor from
1847 until 1852, Richard Graves McDonnell
(1814–1881), who had been chief justice
of The Gambia from 1843, also later
served in Canada—in his case as lieutenant
governor of Nova Scotia in 1864–1865.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

The Gambia has had a variety of polit-

Gambia on his way to and again going

anniversary of The Gambia’s independence.
The delegation included George W . Bush,
later governor of T exas, and after his inau-
guration in 2001, the forty-third president
of the United States. It was one of only
three visits overseas made by Bush before
he entered politics. In his speech to the
United Nations on November 10, 2001,
Bush mentioned The Gambia, noting that
one of its citizens had been killed in the
September 11 attacks and that his wife
spent the following day, their fourth wed-
ding anniversary, helping look through the
debris for her husband. In the realm of
music, New York–based Gambian musi-
cian Foday Musa Suso, a prominent Kora
player, has helped popularize West African
music in the United States.
Justin Corﬁeld

GARVEY,A MY JACQUES 499
GARVEY,A MY JACQUES
(1885–1973)
Jamaican-born Amy Jacques Garvey served
Marcus Garvey’s United Negro Improve-
ment Association (UNIA) as secretary, legal
adviser, journalist, and associate editor of
the organization’s weekly newspaper, the
Negro World. In 1922 Jacques Garvey mar-
ried the movement’s leader, Marcus Garvey,
and when he was convicted of mail fraud
by the U.S. government and imprisoned in
1925, she took charge of his legal defense
campaign and the management of the
UNIA headquarters in Harlem. She was
widely regarded as the unofﬁcial leader of
the movement. Historians of the Garvey
movement that mention Jacques Garvey
have traditionally focused on her role as the
wife and helpmate of Marcus rather than
on her own intellectual contribution to
Black Nationalism. More recently she has
been seen as an important feminist leader.
Jacques Garvey’s own account of the move-
ment suggests that she chose to invest her
strength in Garveyism rather than the man.
Published in 1963, her Garvey and Garveyism
is essentially a memoir in which she claims
much of the credit for sustaining Marcus
Garvey’s legacy through his years in prison
and for much of the twentieth century.
Indeed, she compiled and edited a collec-
tion of Marcus Garvey’s speeches, The
Philosophy and Opinions of Marcus Garvey
(1922), which inspired scholars and leaders
of Black Nationalist movements across the
globe.
Born in Kingston, Jamaica, on December
31, 1895, Jacques Garvey’s great-great
grandfather was the ﬁrst mayor of that city,
the Jamaican capital, and her father,
George Jacques, had a secure managerial
position at La Paloma Cigar Factory. An
educated woman, Jacques Garvey’s mother,
Charlotte Henrietta, was the daughter of a
black woman named Jane and an English
farmer, Frank South. As a member of the
brown middle class, Jacques Garvey had an
elite secondary school education at the ex-
clusive Wolmers Girls’ School, an educa-
tion denied most Jamaicans. As a member
of the middle class, she also was exposed to,
and for a time internalized, the Eurocentric
and racist values of Jamaica’s caste system
from her distinct position in the hierarchy,
which incorporated eight categories rep-
resenting varying shades of blackness.
Indeed, Jacques Garvey later recalled her
shame at her father coming to her school
because of his darker color.
Jacques Garvey’s father was disap-
pointed that she was not a boy and educated
her as if she was, encouraging her intellectual
development through the reading of foreign
newspapers and study of current affairs. Al-
though Jacques Garvey was keen to enter the
law profession, her father was unwilling to
allow her to work in an ofﬁce where she
might be exposed to the wiles of young men
and so decided she would train as a nurse.
However, her father’s sudden death allowed
Jacques to work as a clerk in a legal ofﬁce
for four years before deciding to leave for
England in 1918. Prevented from sailing
there by World War I, Jacques Garvey chose
instead to go to the United States, a land
much spoken of by her father as one mixed
with opportunity and restrictions.
The circumstances in which Jacques
Garvey and her future husband met have
been buried beneath the contradictory re-
ports of his ﬁrst and second wives and sub-
sequent speculation on the part of biogra-
phers. Marcus Garvey’s ﬁrst wife, Amy
Ashwood, claimed that she and Jacques
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 576 ---
500 G ARVEY,M ARCUS
Garvey had been best friends in Jamaica,
while Jacques Garvey stated that she did
not know Ashwood until she moved to
America. Either way, Jacques served as Ash-
wood’s bridesmaid on the latter’s marriage
to Garvey just two and a half years before
her own marriage to him in 1922. The two
women remained enemies throughout their
lives.
It was between 1924 and 1927, the pe-
riod, signiﬁcantly, when her husband was
in prison, that Jacques Garvey edited the
Women’s page in the Negro World, titled
“Our Women and What They Think.” The
title was misleading, as Jacques Garvey
wrote much of the page herself while con-
tinually pleading with her readers to con-
tribute their poems, stories, and political
pieces. The page allowed Jacques Garvey to
articulate her burgeoning feminism and
draw attention to the liberation struggles of
black women across the world. Her editori-
als are generally regarded as her most im-
portant intellectual contribution.
Jacques Garvey campaigned for the
Pan-African cause throughout her life.
Returning to Jamaica with her husband
following his deportation, Jacques Garvey
supported her husband’s establishment of a
UNIA branch in London. She gave birth to
a son, Marcus, in 1930 and another son,
Julius Winston, in 1933. Marcus Garvey
relocated to London in 1935, while Amy
Jacques Garvey remained in Jamaica with
her two sons. Jacques Garvey continued to
promote Garveyism and her husband’s
legacy after his death in 1940. In addition
to editing a second volume of Garvey’s
Philosophy and Opinions in 1967, Jacques
Garvey continued to write and publish in
Pan-African magazines and in the 1940s
actively supported the People’s National Party
in Jamaica. She died in 1973, disillusioned
with postindependence Jamaican politics
but still promoting Garvey’s legacy.
Kate Dossett

GARVEY,M ARCUS
(1887–1940)
Marcus Garvey was a Jamaican-born black
cultural nationalist and the founder of the
Universal Negro Improvement Association
and the Black Star Line, a shipping ﬁrm.
Marcus Garvey was born in St. Ann’s Bay,
Jamaica, on August 17, 1887. He grew up
in a decaying environment and peasant
economy marked by poverty, hurricanes,
and weak family bonds of affection. In the
British colonial school that he attended
until just the sixth grade, Garvey was
exposed to racial separation and prejudice,
which inﬂuenced his consciousness. At the
age of sixteen he became an apprentice
printer in Kingston, Jamaica. There, he be-
came impressed with the power of oratory
and developed an interest in political orga-
nization and struggle. During the Jamaican
printers’ strike of 1907, he was blacklisted
and ﬁred for being the only foreman who
supported the workers.
Following the vast emigration of
Jamaicans to South America and Europe in
the 1910s, Garvey arrived in Britain in 1912.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 577 ---
GARVEY,M ARCUS 501
In England he attended Birkbeck College
and met with members of Britain’s cos-
mopolitan black elite, including the
Guianese T . Ras Makonnen and the
Sudanese-Egyptian Mohamed Ali. These
men taught Garvey the importance of
wealth and knowledge for the development
of African people worldwide. Inspired by the
teachings of Makonnen and Ali, Garvey
founded the Universal Negro Improvement
Association and African Communities
League in Jamaica on August 1, 1914. The
goal of the organization was to promote fra-
ternity, assistance, Christian worship, educa-
tion, commerce, and industry among blacks.
On March 23, 1916, Garvey arrived in
Harlem to seek support from African
Americans. Booker T . Washington, whom
he greatly admired, had died in 1915 with-
out having met or given support to Garvey.
Despite unsuccessful attempts to convince
African American leaders such as W . E. B.
Du Bois and A. Philip Randolph to help
him fund his projects, Garvey continued
to give public lectures, at which he was
often booed. The catalyst of Garvey’s polit-
ical fame in North America was the vio-
lence that blacks faced in northern cities
during the early twentieth century. Follow-
ing the migration of thousands of African
Americans from the South during World
War I, poor northern whites felt greater
hostility toward newly arrived black mi-
grants whom they were taught to perceive
as the cause of their predicament of low
wages or unemployment and poor living
conditions. From these circumstances
emerged a white racism that resulted in a
deadly riot in East St. Louis on July 2,
1917. Angry white mobs attacked defense-
less black migrants whom they accused of
taking their jobs in the city’s industrial
plants. The riot ended after thirty-nine
blacks and nine whites were killed. Garvey
intervened promptly by denouncing the
massacre as part of “America’s continuous
round of oppression of black people who
for three hundred years had given their life
blood to help build the republic” (Levine,
1993, p. 118). 
Garvey’s activism in the United States
was curtailed as J. Edgar Hoover led a
campaign accusing him for mail fraud. In
January 1922 Garvey and three of his asso-
ciates were arrested and, in February, were
indicted “on twelve counts of fraudulent
use of the mails to sell Black Star stocks”
(Levine, 1993, p. 134). Garvey was tried in
June 1923 and was imprisoned until
December 1927, when he was deported as
an undesirable alien. On June 10, 1940,
Garvey passed away at his West Kensington
residence in London.

GATES JR., HENRY LOUIS
(1950–)
Henry Louis Gates Jr. is the Chair and the
Alphonse Fletcher University Professor of
the Department of African and African
American Studies at Harvard University and
also the director of the W . E. B. Du Bois
Institute for African and African American
Research. As such, he is one of the most
inﬂuential writers and thinkers concerning
“race” in contemporary America. Indeed,
Time magazine considered Gates to be one
of America’s most inﬂuential people, placing
him within the top twenty-ﬁve.
Born in the quiet mill town of Piedmont,
West Virginia, Gates demonstrated an
academic prowess that was to be exercised
during his candidature at Yale. Graduating
summa cum laude in 1973 in the ﬁeld of
history, he was to return brieﬂy to Yale as
an assistant professor in both the English
and African American Studies departments
after completing his PhD in English at
Cambridge University on a Mellon
Fellowship.
Gates’s scholarship has always been
premised on a deep interest in his own fam-
ily’s genealogy and history. The descendant
of slaves exported from Africa to America,
Gates has made it clear that he feels an
immense loss at not being able to trace his
genealogy through an African history that
deﬁnes so much of his personal identity. In
his PBS documentary, Wonders of the African
World (1999), Gates explains how this in-
herited distance from Africa and African
history came at the hands of America’s
Eurocentric ideological imperative. Since
the European tradition was considered the
only signiﬁcant contributor to America’s in-
tellectual cultural life—a point that Gates
critiques in his well-known revision of the
“white” canon of literature, Black Literature
and Literary Theory (1984)—many aca-
demic disciplines exhibited an unacknowl-
edged Eurocentricism that, at worst, mani-
fested itself as a kind of institutionalized
racism. So it was that such unmediated
racism in the academy resulted in genera-
tions of Americans being taught erro-
neously that history began for the African
American only with the ﬁrst footfall of
African slaves on the soil of the New World.
T o ask what lay before the artiﬁcial his-
torical marker of the ﬁrst slave ship, or to
want to understand the kind of history that
Africa offers the African American, is to
join the project of recovery that has domi-
nated Gates’s professional and private life.
For Gates’s personal interest in recovering
his own family’s history translates into the
grander act of reclaiming the production of
history from the marginalizing and impov-
erishing dictums of Eurocentric thought. It
is perhaps for this reason—of exposing the
artiﬁciality of historical markers while also
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 579 ---

reclaiming the act of its production—that
Gates still considers his 1983 rediscovery of
Harriet E. Wilson’s novel, Our Nig (1859),
his ﬁnest achievement among the numer-
ous books, articles, essays, and reviews that
he has published. Certainly, it is one of his
most signiﬁcant publications since the re-
discovery of what is considered the ﬁrst
novel published in America by an African

literary tradition by more than thirty years.
It was a feat of literary detection that Gates
improbably repeated in 2001 with his ac-

the earliest known novel by a female
African American slave, The Bondswoman’s
Narrative: A Fugitive Slave Recently Escaped
from North Carolina, by Hannah Crafts.

GAY,L ESBIAN,B ISEXUAL,
AND TRANSGENDER
MOVEMENTS,AFRICA AND
AFRICAN DIASPORIC
All too frequently, gay, lesbian, bisexual,
and transgendered (GLBT) movements are
characterized as Western or white, but that
stereotype, however unfortunately true at
times, ignores the array of African and
African diasporan contributions to global
efforts at expanding the deﬁnition of per-
son and citizen, regardless of sexual orienta-
tion or gender identity. That stereotype has
its roots in the persistent myth that African
societies were and are inherently free of ho-
mosexuality and androgyny. This miscon-
ception was created by European pundits
after Atlantic contacts had begun in the
ﬁfteenth century and was rooted in the
mischaracterization of Africans as savages
living close to nature. Since universal
heterosexuality was considered the epitome
of being uncorrupted by luxury and
civilization, the perceived backwardness of
Africans was supposed to inoculate them
from civilized vices such as sodomy. This lie
has been ironically recast by African na-
tionalists such as President Robert Mugabe
of Zimbabwe to this day to distinguish
themselves as being morally and inherently
superior to effete colonizers and their west-
ernized dupes.
Given this entrenched discourse of
misinformation, it is important to note
that sexual and gender diversity were toler-
ated and celebrated in long-standing
African traditions, which generally featured
same-sex relationships marked by differ-
ences in rank, age, and gender identity. Fre-
quently, unlike in contemporary north-
western European and North American
cultures, such same-sex relationships are
complemented by participation in hetero-
sexual marriage and parenthood. For
instance, in the Hausa city of Kano, as
anthropologist Rudolf P . Gaudio has
observed, the transgendered and transves-
tited prostitutes called the ‘dan daudacarry
on pre-Islamic religious possession prac-
tices in the heavily Muslim city, while the

k’wazo, older, straight-acting, and wealthier
men who are the penetrators, and their
younger and anally passive partners, baja,
maintain patron-client connections that re-
main alongside heterosexual familial obli-
gations and love maintained by both k’wazo
and baja. Only sex between two ‘dan dauda
is frowned upon in part because such inti-
mate behavior requires at least one person
acting as a man privately and, much more
importantly, publicly. Even sex between
k’wazois not seen as a problem as long as
both participants act in a conventionally
masculine way outside the bedroom. While
the Hausa are nearly unique in having male
homosexuality stratiﬁed by both age and
gender identity or appearance, most
African societies would feature such rela-
tionships based either on perceived differ-
ences of age or gender identity or appear-
ance. Examples of cultures with male
homosexuality organized by one partner
being conventionally masculine and the
other dressing and acting as a woman
would include the Akan, Dahomey, Fanti,
Mombasan, Umbundu, Yoruba, and Zulu.
Examples of cultures with male homosexu-
ality organized by both partners being pub-
licly masculine, with the younger partner
presumably acting as the woman in private,
would include the Anyin, Eritrean, Mossi,
Nzema, Ondonga, Rwandan, Tsonga, and
Zande. Stateless hunters and gatherers with
the least social stratiﬁcation had the most
egalitarian relationships between men hav-
ing sex with men.
Female homosexuality in traditional
African cultures, however less documented,
was no less ubiquitous and varied. For in-
stance, among the Nandi of Kenya, the fe-
male husband, generally an older and
childless matron, would be promoted to
male status without completely dressing as
a man. Occasionally a conventional wife
earlier in her life, the female husband
would allow her younger partner to have a
male consort in order to have children.
Relations between the female husband and
her wife resembled and still resemble that
of a Victorian romantic friendship in
Britain or America, yet that outward
chastity never necessarily ruled out genital
sex between the women in private. Like
male homosexuality, lesbian relationships
in Africa tended to rest upon inequalities of
power based upon age and/or gender iden-
tity and appearance, with older and more
masculine women holding the upper hand.
This was and is especially true of the
Mummy-Baby couplings among boarding-
school girls in Lesotho. In those cultures
such as the Mombasan, where female ho-
mosexuality was the most prevalent—if still
stratiﬁed by age and/or gender identity or
appearance—female status and autonomy
was the greatest.
Slave trades within Africa and, in par-
ticular, the transatlantic slave trade did
nothing to diminish this sexual and gender
diversity. In Cuba, for example, enslaved
Africans paired the Yoruban warrior-god
Shango with Catholic Saint Barbara or
even changed him into her, in part because
both ﬁgures triumphed over slavery and
death through the force of their spiritual
convictions. Both of their transcendent
journeys involved lightning and ﬁre; both
the African orisha and the Catholic saint
were thus connected to the colors white
and red. Both stories involved overly dra-
matic familial tragedies: father killing
daughter and, in Shango’s case, brother pit-
ting brother against brother. Yet their sto-
ries also displayed the functional aspects of
androgyny. In Barbara’s case, she was a
young woman who acted as men should; in
