Shango’s case, he was a male god who tem-
pered his manly zeal for truth with “femi-
nine” mercy. For instance, Barbara was a
demure, “feminine” virgin who had the
“masculine” strength to die for what is
right; Shango was a strong, “masculine”
monarch who is redeemed by “feminine”
virtue.
The implications of Shango’s pairing
and/or sex change show the inventiveness
of the enslaved Africans confronted with
dealing with a strange new monotheism. It
was expedient for those confronted with ac-
cusations of heresy and witchcraft in colo-
nial Latin America to hide or to mix their
worship of Shango with their devotion to
Barbara. Yet for many, this pairing and/or
transformation was not merely a cover for
illegal activity, but a deepening of the rele-
vant meanings embedded in both the
Yoruban and Catholic narratives. Good
spirits can come in many forms, whether
male or female. All those who believe can
overcome slavery and death. It makes no
difference whether they are male or female,
white or black.
This pragmatic and unexacting stance
was in opposition to the orthodox doc-
trines put forth by the Roman Catholic hi-
erarchy. T o the hierarchy, women priest-
esses, “false” and foreign gods, direct
contacts with the dead and divine while
still alive, and androgyny in general was
just plain evil. T o the ofﬁcial church, evil
was absolute evil and was not a necessary
balancing force in the universe. T o the ofﬁ-
cial church, these Afro-Atlantic heresies
threatened to turn their world of ﬁxed cat-
egories upside down, with slaves triumph-
ing over slaveholders, women acting as
men, and men acting as women. Although
the Inquisition was far easier on suspected
“witches” drawing from the Yoruban orishas
than its Protestant contemporaries, its
court records frequently show the con-
tempt and fear of Catholic authorities faced
with Shango becoming Saint Barbara.
Unlike ofﬁcial Christian teaching and
like the Afro-Atlantic religions, some Native
American cultures shared this positive view
of spiritual androgyny. As historian Ramon
A. Gutierrez has noted in When Jesus Came,
the Corn Mothers Went Away (1991), even
though men in many Mesoamerican,
Arawak, and Andean cultures kept women
away during religious ceremonies as not to
be distracted, they needed a feminine entity
present during worship to maintain the
essential balance of gender characteristics
in the universe. The “third-sex” berdache
in these cultures appeared to meet this
need, a berdache being both a spiritual
leader and a homosexual male who took on
the appearance and work of an adult
woman.
Gay and transgendered men served
similar purposes in many cultures of west-
ern and central Africa. The best summon-
ers of the divine were women, but men liv-
ing as women were perfectly acceptable.
The transatlantic slave trade made their
role even more signiﬁcant than before be-
cause it enslaved far more men than
women, especially during the sixteenth and
seventeenth centuries. Thus, spirit medi-
ums themselves embodied the legitimacy
and indeed the necessity of androgyny, of
which the Shango-to-Barbara transforma-
tion was the most famous and conventional
example. Even more revealing are other sex
changes in Afro-Brazilian Candomblé that
did not require the presence of a Catholic
saint. As historian James Sweet reports
in “Male Homosexuality and Spiritism in
the African Diaspora: The Legacies of a
Link” (1996), two deities—Oxumare and

Logum-Ede—are men for six months and

then turn back into men. Logum-Ede, in
particular, is a macho hunter who lives
alone in the forest and who suddenly and
regularly becomes a ﬂirtatious and vain

Christianity and creolization tended to
turn African diasporan cultures homopho-
bic in the Americas. For example, a
strongly heterosexual former slave, Estaban
Montejo, recalled in 1963 that male homo-
sexuality was organized by gender identity
or appearance and age in Cuba before
emancipation. Passive and effeminate part-
ners would act as housewives and garden-
ers, while the masculine husband would sell
the couple’s produce at market. While the
womanizing Montejo was never challenged
by these couples, he did ﬁnd that older
men in slave communities hated the same-
sex couplings. Montejo concluded that this
distaste among the older and presumably
less acculturated slaves indicated that these
practices had not been found in Africa. Just
the opposite was true, however. These prac-
tices with male homosexuality stratiﬁed by
gender identity or appearance and age were
widespread throughout western Africa. In-
ternalizing Catholic stigmas surrounding
sodomy was just a small part of the
European cultural baggage accumulated
after the Middle Passage. Christianity and
creolization would both strengthen and,
eventually, weaken slavery, but the associa-
tion of homosexuality with possession cults
and uneven sex ratios of barracks-like sugar
plantations made it very unattractive to
those blacks seeking both approval from
and equality with middle and upper class
whites and justiﬁcation in the context of
their own nineteenth-century ideology of
heterosexual domesticity.
Corresponding urbanization, neverthe-
less, tended to facilitate clandestine homo-
sexual coteries of all kinds, and this was
particularly true of the largest American
city, New York. African American migra-
tion to New York accelerated after 1900
and turned the Harlem district of Manhat-
tan into a primarily African American
neighborhood. Because of the links be-
tween urbanization and organized gay
communities, the Harlem Renaissance
became both a black and homosexual
movement, as the noted literary critic
Henry Louis Gates Jr. has discerned. These
elements of race and sexuality were care-
fully intertwined. As critic A. B. Christa
Schwartz has uncovered, the poet laureate
of the Renaissance, Countee Cullen, mixed
various tropes in his works to appeal to dif-
ferent kinds of people: traditional white
and black elites who liked his attachment
to traditional form over modernist chaos;
race men and women who appreciated his
explicit exploration of the humiliation cre-
ated by Jim Crow; and homosexuals of any
race who applauded his daring verses about
same-sex love. Both Langston Hughes and
Claude McKay, however sexually ambigu-
ous, also dared to include relatively positive
versions of gay and bisexual men in their
search for black manhood. Richard Bruce
Nugent went further in pushing the enve-
lope of sexual dissidence and was rewarded
by posthumous obscurity. 
Lesbians were portrayed in a much
more negative light by gay and bisexual
male Renaissance writers, even if Alain
Locke, the almost openly homosexual guru
of “the New Negro,” endorsed feminist
tones in the writings of Zora Neale
Hurston; nevertheless, there was an under-
current of Sapphic voices, such as those of
Angelina Weld Grimké, Georgia Douglas

While the Harlem Renaissance was
both black and gay if largely male, the next
cycle of literary and cultural creativity after
World War II would eventually lead to un-
restrained celebrations of blackness and
queerness of whatever gender, if not always
side by side. In the 1950s and 1960s, two
gay African American men—novelist James
Baldwin and organizer Bayard Rustin—as
well as playwright Lorraine Hansberry
(who wrote A Raisin in the Sun [1959])
would contribute to the civil rights move-
ment that, in turn, would help to shape the
modern gay rights movement in America.
Black drag queens led the ragtag rebels at
Stonewall in 1969, the iconic epiphany of
gay liberation. Jamaican wordsmith Audre
Lorde would inspire feminist zeal and
Sapphic introspection. Mel Boozer, the
African American head of the mainly white
Gay Activist Alliance in Washington, D.C.,
became the ﬁrst openly GLBT person to
run for vice-president at the Democratic
National Convention in 1980. Congress-
woman Barbara Jordan of T exas, however
closeted, was an anchor of 1970s sensibility
whose baritone voice stood for the oppressed
and downtrodden.
Yet that did not prevent gay whites,
whether men or women or transgendered,
from discriminating against their compatri-
ots who happened to be African American.
As late as the 1970s, for example, white-
owned gay bars in Norfolk, Virginia, dis-
couraged black customers with higher
cover charges and requests for multiple
forms of identiﬁcation. These discriminatory
practices, long after the Civil Rights Act of
1964, were not restricted to this region,
however. Such persistent and pervasive
racism among white gays and lesbians led
to the development of organizations that
looked out for the interests of queer African
Americans, one being the National Coali-
tion of Black Gays that became the
National Coalition of Black Gays and
Lesbians. On the local level during the
1970s, these were complemented by
UMOJA-UNITY in Norfolk and the
Memphis Committee in T ennessee. By the
1980s, Black and White Men T ogether still
held out the promise of integrated inti-
macy, but it became less political and more
social as the years went by. Most recently,
the National Black Justice Coalition has
advocated on behalf of marriage rights for,
among others, same-sex couples, mobiliz-
ing African American clergy, journalists,
and other opinion shapers to combat right-
wing white attempts to prevent the exten-
sion of equality by courting conservative
black churches.
Indeed, while dealing with the Scylla
of exceptionally virulent racism among
some white gays, GLBT movements
among peoples of African descent have
also had to confront the Charbydis of espe-
cially rabid homophobia in their own
communities. In the United States, from
Adam Clayton Powell through the young
Moleﬁ Asante (who changed his views in
the 1990s) through the Nation of Islam
(until very recently), influential black
nationalists and Afrocentrists have used
GLBT identities as a useful foil in creating
the universally heterosexual and, thus,
“superior” Pan-African identity. As the sex-
ual and gender diversity of African cultures
is more widely known now in America than
even a decade ago, however, this extreme

However fractured by class, gender,
gender identity, and race, GLBT move-
ments in America and Europe would ﬁrst
spread to South Africa and then, after
1995, go continentwide in Africa. In
South Africa, the ﬁrst GLBT movements
emerging after the late 1960s were re-
stricted to middle- and upper-class whites,
reﬂecting the apartheid mores of the P . W .
Botha regime and the National Party.
Their apolitical avoidance of racial issues
rendered them politically irrelevant both
before and after the fall of apartheid in the
early 1990s. Among middle-class blacks,
gay male and, less frequently, lesbian
groups sprang up in the wake of the
Soweto revolt in 1976. A decade later,
these groups embraced the Freedom
Charter of the African National Congress
(ANC), opposing discrimination of all
kinds. The ANC repaid its GLBT support-
ers by ﬁrst formally acknowledging their
right to legal equality. Then, it supported
the inclusion of sexual orientation among
the basic rights of all human beings to be
shielded from legal disabilities in the in-
terim constitution of December 1993 and
then in the new Bill of Rights of May 1996.
With the passing of the great Nelson Mandela
from the scene and his replacement as
president by the much more cramped
Thabo Mbeki, who has denied the etiology
of HIV/AIDS, the ANC’s support for
GLBT rights has diminished somewhat.
Only Desmond T utu regularly places ho-
mosexual rights alongside other expressive
freedoms; nevertheless, South Africa under
black leadership was the ﬁrst country in
the world to guarantee GLBT peoples legal
equality in its constitution.
Most other African nations have been
far less willing even to tolerate self-
identiﬁed GLBT cultures, let alone move-
ments; they have used old British colonial
laws or made new ones to hassle and to per-
secute. A witch’s brew of traditional and
Christian opposition to perceived sexual
deviancy has shored up flagging secular
dictatorships in Z imbabwe and Namibia.
Gays and Lesbians of Zimbabwe (GALZ),
with it estimated 300 members, still con-
tinues to meet and to speak out despite the
obvious danger of state-sanctioned pogroms.
Most recently, in Nigeria, the Archbishop
Peter Akinola and the Nigerian Anglican
Church have joined with that country’s
president, Olusegun Obasanjo, to draft a
law that would make same-sex relationships
or the act of defending them by any hetero-
sexual person crimes punishable by an au-
tomatic ﬁve years in prison. The Gay and
Lesbian Humanist Association of Nigeria
has courageously opposed this curtailment
of civil rights, but it has few supporters in
the religiously and ethnically polarized
country. Indeed, the Anglican bishops of
Uganda have been equally as active in en-
shrining discrimination against GLBT
peoples at home as they violently opposed
the consecration of an openly gay Episcopal
bishop in America in 2003. Elsewhere,
there have been few victories for GLBT
movements. In 2005 Cameroon witnessed

periodic detention of young men on

The HIV/AIDS pandemic has both
weakened and galvanized GLBT move-
ments in both Africa and the Americas. In
the United States, AIDS service organiza-
tions such as Us Helping Us in Washington,
D.C., were founded in the 1980s, and some,
such as US Helping Us, were led by middle-
class black gay men and provided education
and case management to their largely
African American clients. HIV/AIDS took
an increasing toll among African Americans
by the turn of the century as it became the
leading killer of young black adults and was
especially virulent among black gay and
bisexual men. One of the recommendations
by black GLBT leaders to this phenomenon
is for those men having sex with men to
avoid the “down-low” stance of denial or
self-denial that encourages risky behaviors,
a stance predicated on trying to cater to
heterosexual supremacy. In African coun-
tries such as Zimbabwe and Botswana, in
which the general population has been
ravaged by HIV , GLBT organizations have
been at the forefront in trying to distribute
medicine and information to prevent
national collapse. While enemies such as
President O basanjo still see homosexual
and transgen dered people as scourges in
themselves that are most un-African, the
GLBT movements have been instrumental
in drawing global attention to HIV/AIDS,
a plague that threatens African civilizations
to the core. Thus,  these movements could
be no more biblical, Christian, and, yes,
traditionally African in their community
service.

GENOCIDE
Genocide refers to the systematic eradica-
tion of a people who are identiﬁed by some
set of shared racial, national, linguistic, re-
ligious, or political attributes. The word
was coined in 1943 by Raphael Lemkin in
response to the Holocaust and given politi-
cal weight by documents such as the UN
Convention on Genocide of 1948. Geno-
cide has been a part of colonialism and its
aftermath on both sides of the Atlantic.
The problem of genocide, in Africa and
elsewhere, in the postcolonial era has raised
the question of whether or not interna-
tional powers, particularly the United
States, have either the duty or the capacity
to intervene effectively in genocidal con-
ﬂicts. Genocidal strife in Rwanda, in 1994,
and the Darfur region of Sudan, at the start
of the twenty-ﬁrst century, have made visi-
ble the transatlantic importance of the
problem of genocide at a time when the
United States has placed a high priority on
African stability and development.
Although the bulk of conflicts in
Africa, Latin America, and North America
have not been genocidal, the histories of
European colonialism, westward U.S. ex-
pansion, and postcolonial Africa are, never-
theless, punctuated by conﬂicts that were
either overtly genocidal or resulted in the
destruction of peoples. No single explana-
tion can be given for why genocides have
taken place. Beginning in the ﬁfteenth cen-
tury, early Spanish colonialism in the New
World was often genocidal, either through
deliberate conﬂict with indigenous peoples,
as in the case of the conquest of the
Caribbean documented by the monk
Bartolemé De Las Casas in his Brief
Account of the Devastation of the Indies
(1542), or unintentionally, by the transmis-
sion of European diseases such as smallpox,
against which many indigenous peoples had
no immunity. According to some estimates,
many indigenous groups lost 90 percent or
more of their population, effectively de-
stroying them as viable cultural or social
entities. Writing in the early sixteenth cen-
tury, Las Casas noted that the indigenous
population of the island of Hispaniola,
now the nations of Haiti and the Domini-
can Republic, had been reduced from ap-
proximately 400,000 to a mere 200 within
a few decades of Spanish rule. One conse-
quence of such destruction was the subse-
quent importation of African slaves as a
new source of labor in New World mines
and plantations.
It is difﬁcult to measure the destruc-
tion of the indigenous populations of the
Americas over the centuries of colonialism
and westward U.S. expansion, from the ﬁf-
teenth through the nineteenth centuries.
Rough estimates suggest a reduction of 70
percent or more of the indigenous popula-
tion, estimated at between 40 and 50 mil-
lion people, with many groups completely
destroyed. In assessing the history of the
westward expansion of the United States,
considered by some scholars a form of colo-
nial expansion, much controversy exists
over whether or not U.S. government poli-
cies toward Native North American peo-
ples were deliberately genocidal. Nonethe-
less, in many instances, those policies were
genocidal in their consequences, even if the
extermination was neither intended nor de-
sired by the federal government. In 1824
President James Monroe created the Ofﬁce
of Indian Affairs (later the Bureau of Indian
Affairs) within the Department of War.
Congress passed the Indian Removal Act in
1830, and the ﬁrst major task of the Ofﬁce
of Indian Affairs became the removal of
Native Americans from the southeastern
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 587 ---
GENOCIDE 511
United States. A well-known example of the
removal process was the forced relocation
of the Cherokee people from their land in
Georgia in 1838, resulting in what has be-
come known as the “T rail of T ears.” Several
thousand died en route. Other destructive
policies included the extermination of the
buffalo, a central part of the economic and
cultural life of the Lakota, and the erasure
of Native American cultures through
Indian boarding schools and other educa-
tional institutions, from the 1880s to the
1930s, that severed the ties of Native
American children to their cultural, reli-
gious, and linguistic heritage. Because these
policies entailed the destruction of group
identities, as well as the loss of life, some
scholars classify them as genocidal in their
consequences.
In the modern era, mass killings by
governments in Latin America, while they
are frequently intended to suppress politi-
cal opposition and are not intentionally
genocidal, often indirectly target ethnic
groups such as Mayans or economically
marginalized groups such as peasants. In
the twentieth century, the fear of Commu-
nist insurgency played a signiﬁcant role.
Prior to the cold war, the military govern-
ment of El Salvador in 1932 slaughtered re-
bellious peasants, often Mayan high-
landers, who were viewed as Communist
insurgents.
The most visible genocides in the
Americas in the cold war era have taken
place in Guatemala. Beginning in the late
1960s, the military pursued people per-
ceived as Communist insurgents, resulting
in mass killings in outlying villages that
were seen as potential recruiting grounds,
resources for guerillas, or hiding areas. Ap-
proximately 100,000 people were killed be-
tween 1966 and 1968.
In 1976 a large earthquake rocked the
region and Guatemala saw the growth of
new, nonviolent popular groups focused on
recovery efforts. These efforts led to broad
collective interactions between Latino and
indigenous groups, as well as between city
dwellers and rural farmers. Authorities saw
this new, broad union, which empowered
the impoverished and helped educate others
on the growing gap of power and proﬁt be-
tween rich and poor, as a danger to their
power. Violence resumed in 1978, when
counterinsurgency death squads began pre-
emptive killings, assaulting a wide range of
groups perceived as insurgents and their al-
lies. Over the next ten years, Guatemala
witnessed massacres of campesino villages.
New, radical death squads formed, the
most notorious being the Ejercito Secreto
Anti-Communista (ESA), which existed in-
dependently of government operations, re-
lying on direct guidance from Guatemala’s
head of state, General Romeo Lucas García.
Roving death squads proceeded on a sys-
tematic destruction of the indigenous
highland population in a total scorched-
earth policy. This aggressive policy claimed
the lives of between 100,000 to 150,000 of
Mayan Indians and campesinos.
The history of genocide in Africa dif-
fers from genocide in the Americas in terms
of the perpetrators, causes, and victims;
however, genocides in Africa have also been
part of the broader context of the violence
inherent in colonialism and the problems
of cold war-era political violence. The
colonial period in Africa ran from the late
nineteenth century to approximately the
early post-World War II era. In contrast to
the experience of native peoples in the
Americas, African peoples often became
subjugated as a colonial labor pool. In a
sense, this was a colonial continuation of
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 588 ---
512 G ENOCIDE
transatlantic slavery, with African peoples
nominally free, but often removed from
their own land and engaged in forced labor
under brutal conditions with few rights or
protections. Systematic genocide entered
the history of colonialism in Africa with the
extermination of the Herero people in
German South West Africa (now Namibia).
Responding to the brutality of German set-
tlers, a Herero rebellion took place in 1904;
farms were attacked and some 100 German
settlers were killed. German soldiers, led by
General Lothar von T rotha, appointed by
Kaiser Wilhelm II, retaliated by driving ap-
proximately 65,000 Herero out of Namibia
to the edge of the Kalahari Desert. Many
Herero who attempted to escape were
killed by machine guns, while those who
remained at the edge of the desert died of
thirst and starvation. Only some 15,000
survived. Some captured Herero were also
sent to labor camps in which over half of
the prisoners died.
In the post–World War II era of the
cold war and African independence, the
majority of African and Latin American
genocides have been the result of conﬂicts
erupting from failures to transfer power
peacefully  or from the expression of a rul-
ing group’s dominance. In Sudan, conﬂicts
have originated from the divisions between
north and south; the north, close to Egypt
and the Red Sea, is primarily Muslim,
while the south is home to many diverse
cultures and languages. While this division
is not a recent development, under British
colonialism rifts between the two were
forged. The north disregarded the south’s
agricultural and industrial development.
When faced with an uprising from the
south over the control of water, grazing
lands, and development funds, the north
responded with repressive civil war. The
ﬁrst such war lasted from 1952 to 1972,
and ﬁghting resumed in 1983. In 1989,
following a military coup, the northern
government declared Sudan an Islamic
state and instituted the severe repression of
Christians and animists. Peace talks began
in 2005, by which time between 100,000
and 500,000 people were dead or dis-
placed. The second war led to over 2 mil-
lion deaths, and despite peace talks the
ﬁghting continues.
Since 2003, further conﬂict has arisen
in Sudan’s Darfur region in the west. Rebel
groups rose up in Darfur, citing discrimina-
tion against black Africans in favor of Arabs
and a neglect of regional development by
the government. The Sudanese regime re-
taliated by creating the militia known as
Janjaweed (in Arabic, a man with a gun on
a horse), which began a wide-scale slaugh-
ter of black African men and women. The
conflict in Darfur has claimed over
200,000 lives and displaced approximately
3 million people. A large number of young
survivors ﬂed to Kenya. Aid workers la-
beled many of the young orphans the “Lost
Boys of Sudan”; several thousand of the
young men were subsequently sent to the
United States and Europe.
In some instances, xenophobia and the
attempt to consolidate power have led to
forms of genocide. Tanzania, Nigeria, and
Uganda offer examples of this path to
genocide at the end of the colonial era.
Though Tanzania is approximately one-
third Muslim and Arabic is a widely spoken
language, a purge of Arabs occurred in
Zanzibar shortly before its merger with
Tanganyika in 1964. They were seen as a
threat to the young African nation’s auton-
omy. Nigeria witnessed true genocide
from 1966 to 1970, when the dominant
group of Hausa-Fulani Muslims mobilized
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

GENOCIDE 513
as the Nigerian Federal Military Government
(FMG). Thousands of Ibo in the east were
massacred after a failed coup. Their perse-
cution by Hausa-Fulani Muslims acting
with federal power led to a short-lived
Ibo secession as the nation of Biafra. The
nation collapsed due to a lack of food and
support. An estimated one million starved
to death, while hundreds of thousands
more were internally displaced.
In Uganda during the early 1970s, Idi
Amin’s dictatorship was characterized by
mass killings of indigenous peoples; Asians;
Catholic clergy; the Karamojong, Acholi,
and Lango tribes; and any political oppo-
nents. Mass deportations of Asians also
took place. Half a million people were
butchered by Amin’s regime. In 1972 the
United States cut off aid to Uganda in
protest against Amin’s violence. Nonethe-
less, the unique diversity of Asian-Ugandan
culture was completely eliminated during
Amin’s regime. Following his departure in
1979, Milton Obote’s rule would see the
genocidal persecution of the Baganda,
Madi, and again the Karamojong people,
stopping only when the existence of a sta-
ble workforce was threatened. At least
50,000 were killed.
The 1994 genocide in Rwanda of the
T utsi people by the Hutu is Africa’s most
visible genocide of the postcolonial era, no-
table for both its sheer size as well as the
speed with which it took place. Under
Belgian colonialism, T utsis were favored,
politically and economically, over the Hutu
majority. The Rwandan genocide was pre-
ceded by the overthrow of T utsi monarchic
rule in 1959, while Rwanda was formally
still a Belgian territory. At that time, thou-
sands of T utsis were slaughtered and
150,000 were exiled into neighboring
Burundi. Many T utsi leaders did not ﬁnd
safe haven in Burundi and were extermi-
nated when that nation fell into civil war
between 1965 and 1973, and again following
the assassination of its ﬁrst democratically
elected president in 1993. These conﬂicts
led to the formation of the predominantly
T utsi Rwandan Patriotic Front (RPF) in
Burundi, which engaged in periphery com-
bat in Rwanda in 1990.
Although the scale of the killing in
1994 was unprecedented, a climate of
chronic violence against T utsis existed in
Rwanda well before the genocide. Rwandan
Hutu leaders began arming selected indi-
viduals in each town and village in 1991;
created the Radio des Milles Collines
(Radio of a Thousand Hills), an ambitious,
countrywide radio network, the only such
network for the expedient broadcast of pro-
paganda, command directives, and other
strategic information; and conducted mili-
tia training for several years. A supremacist
ideology called “Hutu Power” was actively
espoused by the government.
On April 6, 1994, a plane carrying the
presidents of Rwanda and Burundi was shot
down over the Rwandan capital of Kigali.
This resulted in the mobilization of the
trained Hutu militias, causing the immedi-
ate killing of from 40,000 to 50,000 in
Kigali, including both T utsis and moderate
Hutus. Immediate localized exterminations
occurred in the northeastern and eastern
regions of Rwanda, areas of RPF activity;
this was evidence of a well-prepared and
well-communicated strategy formed by the
Hutu leaders. Violence continued through
July 1994, with 800,000 T utsi and moder-
ate Hutu lives lost, a massive extermination
when one considers that previously, the
T utsi made up only some 14 percent of the
nation of 7.5 million residents. Subse-
quently, the Rwandan Patriotic Front, led
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

514 G ENOCIDE
by Paul Kagame, invaded Rwanda and took
control of it following the cessation of the
initial conﬂict. Some 2 million Hutus ﬂed
the country, fearing reprisals.
The history of European colonialism
and the U.S.’s economic, military, and
political prominence in the Western
Hemisphere has raised substantial ques-
tions about the Western responsibilities
for genocide in Africa and the Americas.
Although the U.S. Bureau of Indian Affairs
has issued an apology for the destruction of
native North American peoples, the federal
government as a whole has not yet issued
one. Whether any form of reparation for
North American genocide is possible
remains an open question. In the case of
Guatemala, questions have been raised as
to whether or not the United States can be
considered complicit in supporting death
squads because of the military aid given to
the government, despite an awareness of
the death squads’ actions. In September
2004 U.S. secretary of state Colin Powell
deemed the conﬂict in Sudan’s Darfur re-
gion to be a genocide, against the objec-
tions of the Sudanese government and in
contrast to a subsequent UN report that
failed to identify the conﬂict in Darfur as
genocidal. The U.S. declaration was given
in the context of lingering concerns over
the United States’ inaction a decade earlier
in the case of the Rwandan genocide.
The U.S. relationship to the Rwandan
genocide was part of a larger context of
diplomatic activity and the prior interven-
tions of the United States into Africa.
Although on April 11, 1994, a memo
warning of the impending mass slaughter
was sent to Undersecretary of Defense
Frank Wisner, the U.S. called for UN peace-
keepers to be withdrawn from Rwanda on
April 14. In the subsequent week, the UN
Security Council voted to do just that.
Although mass killings were underway, a
Pentagon memo was issued in May cau-
tioning against the use of the term “geno-
cide.” The memo noted concern that such
a ﬁnding could obligate the United States
to intervene militarily, according to the UN
Convention on Genocide of 1948. This
military reluctance was attributed, by
some, to the recent memory of the U.S.’s
disastrous military intervention in Somalia’s
capital, Mogadishu, in 1993. Part of larger
military and humanitarian operations dur-
ing Somalia’s civil war, an attempt to cap-
ture supporters of the warlord Muhammad
Aideed led to a seventeen-hour battle in
which eighteen U.S. Army Rangers and
many Somalis were killed. In this larger
context, the  responsibility of the United
States for addressing the problem of
genocide remains an open question.

GEORGIA’S SEA ISLANDS
Also known as Georgia’s Golden Isles, the
Sea Islands of Georgia are semitropical
barrier islands that stretch from Cumberland
Island near Florida up to Ossabaw Island
near Savannah. The islands house a distinct
fusion of African and American language,
and cultural practices developed there as a
result of slavery, including Gullah culture
and language. Functioning today as pristine
wildlife sanctuaries and as tourist hubs
complete with luxurious resorts, Georgia’s
Sea Islands boast beautiful beaches, diverse
ﬂora and fauna, and a rich history that ex-
tends back to Native American inhabitants
and the 1500s, when Spanish exploration
of the New World ﬂourished. Due to their
abundant plant and animal resources, their
immense agricultural possibilities, and
their potential to serve as both defensive
barriers and trading outposts, the Spanish,
English, and French laid claim over the
centuries to various Sea Islands until the
American Revolution landed them securely
in American hands.
As early as 1749, the year that Georgia
lifted its ban on slavery, African slaves began
arriving in Georgia’s Sea Islands to cultivate
such labor-intensive crops as rice, indigo,
sugar cane, and the world-renowned sea
island cotton. Wealthy plantation owners
like Major Pierce Butler, from whom
Butler Island takes its name, often required
hundreds of slaves to convert marshlands
into lucrative cash crops. So many Africans
were brought to the islands, in fact, that
by 1860 slaves outnumbered whites on
Cumberland Island by a ratio of seven to
one. These proportionately large African
populations, as well as several absentee
owners who lived much of the year on the
mainland, allowed Sea Island slaves to
maintain more of their West African tradi-
tions and languages than their mainland
counterparts. By November 1858, when
the Wanderer deposited the U.S.’s last
shipment of slaves on Jekyll Island, the
Gullah—also referred to as Geechee—
culture and language were already ﬁrmly
rooted throughout the Sea Islands. The
Wanderer was the last ship to bring human
cargo from Africa to the Americas. Sapelo
Island, for instance, is still home to a
Gullah village founded in 1834 called Hog
Hammock. Comprising over 400 acres,
Hog Hammock was evacuated during the
Civil War, but once emancipated, freed-
persons returned to Sapelo and built a re-
markable village that combined some
American customs, especially Christian
religious practices, with the freedpersons’
West African heritage so that a distinct
language and tradition emerged.
Under the leadership of T unis G.
Campbell, the Freedmen’s Bureau encour-
aged former slaves to resettle in the Sea
Islands after the Civil War, but the process
was largely undermined by entrenched
white supremacy and natural disasters. For-
mer slaves who returned to Skidaway Island
after the Confederate defeat, for example,
were forced to abandon it again after a tidal
wave in 1889 ruined the fresh water supply
and rendered the land infertile. Also com-
plicating the reestablishment of African
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 592 ---
516 G HANA
Americans, wealthy northerners began to
buy Sea Islands that would make good pri-
vate hunting grounds and winter homes.
Jekyll Island sold in 1886 for $125,000 to
a group of powerful millionaires, the so-
called Jekyll Island Club. Names on the
club’s roster included Rockefeller, Macy,
Vanderbilt, Morgan, Pulitzer, and
Goodyear. Likewise, Wassaw Island was
purchased by New England businessman
George Parsons in 1866 as a getaway for his
family and guests. Now it serves as a na-
tional wildlife refuge and is a safe haven for
the endangered loggerhead sea turtle.

GHANA
The present-day African nation of Ghana
was an economically pivotal location for
the transatlantic slave trade. Later, it was an
important part of the history of African
colonialism and independence as a British
crown colony that gained its independence
in 1957, under the leadership of Kwame
N’Krumah and his Convention Peoples’
Party (CPP). The country took its name
from the ancient precolonial kingdom of
the western Sudan as it became the ﬁrst
European colony south of the Sahara to
achieve its independence. Generally con-
sidered one of the best administered and
stable countries in West Africa, Ghana has
not suffered as extensively from ethnic or
civil conﬂict as some of its neighbors, but
neither has it been without historical
turmoil.
Prior to European arrival, the region
was dominated by a number of powerful
precolonial states, including the Akan king-
dom of Bono, the Mamprusi kingdom, the
coastal kingdoms of Ga and Ewe, the Fante
kingdom, and the powerful inland Akan
kingdom of Asante. Hausa traders were
also active among these kingdoms from the
north. The Portuguese were the ﬁrst to ar-
rive on the coast in 1471, quickly establish-
ing a fort to trade ﬁrearms and slaves for
gold. The wealth of the inland gold ﬁelds
quickly drew other Europeans to the re-
gion, the Dutch in 1642 and the Danes in
1670. In the latter year, England estab-
lished a trading fort on the coast. The re-
gion quickly was incorporated into the
growing transatlantic slave trade as
Europeans traded ﬁrearms for slaves, re-
sulting in increased conﬂict in the region to
fuel the trade via prisoners of war.
As a result of the growing instability
and the introduction of ﬁrearms, a central-
ization of power resulted in the Akan king-
dom of Akwamu expanding into the coastal
regions and the emergence of the Asante as
a major power. In the coastal cities an inde-
pendent African merchant class emerged as
intermediaries between Europeans and the
inland kingdoms, which further connected
the region to the transatlantic economic sys-
tem. Intermarriage between European
traders and local women resulted in a com-
mercial class that was westernized and par-
ticipated in the development of plantation
agriculture and manufacturing on the coast.
The region was deeply integrated into the
transatlantic slave economy as the vast
majority of the slaves taken from Africa
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 593 ---
GHANA 517
came from the region where Ghana,
Cameroon, Angola, and Congo are located.
The region became known as the Slave
Coast and was quickly incorporated into a
slave trade that transformed the practice of
slavery in Africa and widened the number
of groups susceptible to being enslaved. So
extensive was the slave trade in the region
that when it was ultimately banned by
Britain, the result was an economic and
political crisis and a power shift from the
coast inland to the Asante. Coastal states
lost their economic mainstay and access to
ﬁrearms due to abolition and the British
demand for a transition to legitimate trade.
The Asante, who had never fully transferred
the main focus of their economy to slaving,
still had gold ﬁelds to ﬁnance continued im-
ports. By the 1880s the Asante Empire con-
trolled most of the territory of what is today
modern Ghana. Able to rely on their con-
trol of inland gold ﬁelds, the Asante traded
with Europeans in the south and Muslims
in the north.
The Asante’s hegemony over the re-
gion, however, was challenged by a growing
European presence along the coast. The
British had established a series of settle-
ments along the Gold Coast from the early
nineteenth century on. The Asante began
to resent the increasing interference of Great
Britain in the region, especially with the in-
troduction of legitimate trade. When the
British took over administrative control of
the Gold Coast settlements from the
African Company of Merchants, the two
powers came into direct conﬂict. Direct
hostilities broke out with the ﬁrst British-
Asante War (1822–1826). A peace treaty in
1831 eased tensions temporarily as the
Asante agreed to withdraw their coastal
claims, which opened the coastal region up
to increased trade and Christian missionary
activity. The British continued to consoli-
date their hold upon the coastal area by ne-
gotiating a protectorate treaty with the
Fante in 1844 and by buying out Danish
interests in the region in 1850. The British
established the seat of colonial government
in the coastal port of Accra. The two pow-
ers came into conﬂict again as the British
moved into Asante inland territory. The
Second British-Asante War was fought
over a ten-year period between 1863 and
1873. The ﬁnal result was a British victory
as its troops pushed into the Asante capital
of Kumasi and burned it to the ground.
The British formally annexed the coastal
states and declared the Gold Coast a crown
colony. Despite the burning of their capi-
tal, the Asante refused to accept British
protectorate status and refused to pay the
reparations demanded by Britain from the
second war as laid out in the 1874 treaty.
The British forced the Asante king into
exile but were faced with a third conﬂict in
1900, organized by Yaa Asantewa, an Asante
noblewoman. The British defeated the
Asante and exiled the leadership of the re-
bellion and the kingdom. In 1902, without
organized opposition, the British annexed
the Asante kingdom and its northern terri-
tories. The British consolidated their con-
trol over what is today the entire territory
of modern Ghana after World War I, when
Germany’s former colonies were divided
among the Allies, Britain gaining a part of
German T ogoland.
The Gold Coast colony’s economy was
based on British investment in the extrac-
tion of gold, diamonds, manganese, baux-
ite, and timber and on the Gold Coast’s
role in the slave trade, which provided the
basis of England’s industrial development.
The indigenous economy focused on palm
oil until the 1890s and cocoa after 1890.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

518 G HANA
Commercial agriculture was introduced
and tended to beneﬁt those who controlled
the land: chiefs and lineage heads of fami-
lies. The coastal elite continued to western-
ize, sending its children to missionary
schools and producing a class of profession-
als who generally found work as mid-level
civil servants in the colonial bureaucracy.
The northern territories of the colony, lack-
ing any easily extractable resource, were ne-
glected by the colonial administration, and
the economy there remained underdevel-
oped and dependent on subsistence agri-
culture. Colonial economic infrastructure
development focused on the extraction of
raw materials. The ﬁrst railway was built in
1898 to connect the inland gold ﬁelds to
the coast and expanded in the 1920s to
connect Accra to cocoa-producing regions.
In 1928 the British constructed the Gold
Coast’s ﬁrst deepwater port at Takoradi and
extended the road system through the
1930s. The Gold Coast colony was consid-
ered by the British to be the model colony,
and after World War I they felt that it
would move slowly and naturally toward
independence under British tutelage.
It was in the 1920s, however, that
the ﬁrst signs of nationalist opposition to
colonialism began to emerge in the colony.
T o slow the process and ensure continued
colonial control, Britain introduced indi-
rect rule, empowering even more the “tra-
ditional” authorities. While this did not
have much impact in central and northern
regions, it upset the coastal mercantile and
professional elites who became increasingly
frustrated with the lack of social and polit-
ical advancement in the colonial system.
Desire for independence continued to grow
through the 1940s. The British seemed
open to the process, and in 1946 a new
constitution for the colony provided for a
legislative council with an elected majority.
But the slow transition to independence hit
a roadblock in the form of World War II.
The resulting high commodity prices and
shortage of consumer goods created discon-
tent, and when the cocoa industry was dev-
astated by a virus that killed the trees, pub-
lic suspicion arose that the colonial
government was out to ruin farmers while
European merchants beneﬁted from high
prices and market shortages. Added into
the mix were the returning Africans who
had served in Britain’s military and who
had listened to the wartime rhetoric of
democracy and liberty. Such experiences
certainly challenged notions of colonialism,
in addition to which two world wars had
produced generations of veterans who had
witnessed the barbarity and uncivilized be-
havior of Europeans in the theaters of war.
When India and Pakistan sought indepen-
dence, their efforts and successes were in-
spirational. Politicized Africans acquired a
growing audience as increasing urbaniza-
tion concentrated mounting numbers of
people in cities, where they found shrink-
ing opportunities for advancement. Riots
and boycotts became common.
Merchant A. G. Grant and newspaper
editor Joseph Danquah and other national-
ists founded the United Gold Coast
Convention (UGCC) in 1947. They were
arrested for sedition, but the time was not
yet ripe for a popular challenge to the sta-
tus quo. The UGCC needed someone who
could bridge the gap between their elitist
and exclusive leadership and the growing
discontent of the masses. The British re-
sponse to increasing disturbances included
setting up a number of investigative com-
missions. The Coussey Commission actu-
ally concluded that the process of bringing
independence to the Gold Coast was too
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 595 ---
GHANA 519
slow and that the British should establish
representative and responsible government
as soon as practically possible. Fearing the
loss of leadership, the UGCC invited
Kwame N’krumah to lead the campaign for
self-government. N’Krumah, a charismatic
and natural leader, had been active in
England, co-organizing the Fifth Pan-
African Congress and advocating radical
populism and African socialism. N’Krumah
sought to push the independence move-
ment forward through organizing the
popular classes and crippling the colonial
system through strikes and boycotts. Under
the banner “Self Government Now,”
N’Krumah quickly radicalized and nation-
alized the movement, much to the alarm of
the more conservative UGCC leadership.
When a 1948 strike turned violent and
British troops ﬁred on demonstrators, riots
broke out. The colonial authorities moved
against the UGCC, jailing N’krumah,
Danquah, and others. As a result, N’krumah
left the UGCC and a split emerged in
the independence movement. N’krumah
founded his own political party in 1949,
the Convention People’s Party (CPP). Ulti-
mately, 70 percent of Gold Coast voters, in
a national plebiscite held in 1956, chose
the CPP’s vision of independence, and in
1957 the Gold Coast gained its indepen-
dence and emerged as the newly named
country of Ghana under the presidency of
Kwame N’Krumah.
Ghana achieved its independence dur-
ing the cold war, and Kwame N’Krumah
ﬁrmly placed the new nation in the non-
aligned movement. Domestically, he imple-
mented a kind of African socialism, nation-
alized foreign holdings, and pursued
industrialization and infrastructure devel-
opment. He oversaw the construction of
the Akosombo Dam to develop Ghana’s
hydroelectric power. He expanded the state
through the provision of health and social
services and free and compulsory primary
education programs. Internationally,
N’Krumah became a powerful and vocal
advocate for Pan-Africanism, playing an
instrumental role in the creation of the
Organization of African Unity in 1963.
During the 1950s, Ghana’s rich mineral
resources sustained the economic demands
of N’Krumah’s policies, but when the price
of cocoa dropped in the 1960s and the
popularity of the CPP wore away, such
policies were harder to maintain. Patronage
and mismanagement were rife and the na-
tional debt soared while living standards
declined. N’Krumah, sensing his vision
endangered, responded with increasing
restrictions on opposition parties, which
joined in the United Party under Koﬁ
Busia. The political climate deteriorated as
N’Krumah became increasingly autocratic
and government critics found themselves
subjected to detention and torture. T o
offset the growing political turmoil and to
consolidate his political hold over the
country, N’Krumah declared Ghana a
republic in 1960 with himself the head of
the state and head of the government. He
was in sole control of the CPP and banned
all opposition within the party. Final con-
solidation of N’Krumah’s control occurred
in a 1964 referendum that declared Ghana a
one-party state under the CPP . With polit-
ical opposition banned and economic crisis
growing, N’Krumah was overthrown in
1966 by a joint military-police coup d’état.
This inaugurated many decades of mostly
military rule in the country.
At ﬁrst, the new National Liberation
Council (NLC) appeared sincere in its at-
tempts to stabilize the country. While the
NLC suspended N’Krumah’s projects, it

released detainees, investigated political
corruption, and returned Ghana to market
capitalism. In response to pressure from the
International Monetary Fund (IMF) and
the World Bank, the NLC implemented an
austerity program but in doing so caused
unemployment and economic hardship for
lower classes. The country was rocked in
1968 and 1969 by a series of worker strikes
and demands for the return to democracy.
The NLC agreed to draft a new constitu-
tion for the return of civilian government
and in 1969 elections were held, although
N’Krumah and his supporters were banned
from running.
In 1969 Koﬁ Busia was elected prime
minister in an election that banned
Nkrumah’s supporters, and with a coalition
of southern elites and traditional Akan
chiefs, he perpetuated the conservative
NLC’s economic policies. The 1971 drop
in cocoa prices, however, facilitated another
round of unrest and ﬁnancial crisis, and the
following year, the military once again in-
tervened. The National Redemption
Council (NRC) was established under the
leadership of Colonel Ignatius Kutu
Acheampong.  The new government ex-
cluded the leadership of the earlier military
junta of the NLC. Acheampong’s govern-
ment nationalized a number of private
companies in 1972, including the largest
gold mining ﬁrm in Ghana, and declared
a moratorium on Ghana’s foreign debt.
Opposition was suppressed in the name of
national security and stability. In 1975
Acheampong consolidated his control
through the Supreme Military Council
(SMC), excluding his NRC rivals from its
membership. Like those before him,
Acheampong’s government was character-
ized by corruption, mismanagement, and
environmental and economic crisis. In
response, students and professionals para-
lyzed the country with a series of strikes
and work stoppages in the late 1970s, again
demanding a return to civilian rule. While
the military dictatorship initially agreed to
new elections, in 1978 it rigged a referen-
dum to retain power. Another wave of
strikes led to an internal coup as General
Frederick Akuffo replaced Acheampong
that year and appointed a constitutional as-
sembly calling for elections for the upcom-
ing year. But Ghana’s return to civilian rule
would not be a peaceful one, as on the eve
of the 1979 elections, a group of young
army ofﬁcers lead by Flight Lieutenant Jerry
John Rawlings overthrew the government
and formed the Armed Forces Revolutionary
Council (AFRC). While elections took place,
the AFRC purged the bureaucracy of SMC
appointees and oversaw the executions of
Acheampong and Akuffo.
Ultimately, civilian rule was restored,
but the new government under Hilla
Limann inherited a ruined economy and
was poorly prepared to deal with another
drop in cocoa prices. Inﬂation skyrocketed
and food shortages resulted in famine. The
country verged once again on bankruptcy
and political chaos. In 1981 Ghana, despite
its hopeful beginnings, looked like another
failed African state, and in response Lieu-
tenant Rawlings staged a second coup. Ini-
tially a self-styled populist, Rawlings
pledged to end corruption and in 1982 es-
tablished the National Defense Council,
but in doing so he also dissolved parlia-
ment, banned all political parties, and ap-
pointed radical leftists to his ruling council.
Local government was turned over to Revo-
lutionary Defense Committees. This did lit-
tle to stabilize the country. In addition to
continued political and economic turmoil,
environmental disasters of drought and

wildﬁres led to widespread famine. As op-

and courted the International Monetary
Fund. He introduced market economy re-
forms and a strict austerity plan to curb gov-

slowed Ghana’s economic decline, the aus-

Most importantly, they were not accompa-

munity to reestablish democracy in Ghana.
As a result, he promised to restore parlia-
mentary democracy to the country and na-
tional elections were held in 1992, followed
by a referendum on a new constitution. In
what were called “free and fair” elections by
a report of the Commonwealth Observer
Group, released before all ballots had been
accounted for, Rawlings and his National
Democratic Congress (NDC) defeated the
National Patriotic Party (NPP). The new
constitution committed Ghana to a multi-
party system and a free press. Once again
the euphoria accompanying a return to
democracy was diminished as Ghana expe-
rienced budget deﬁcits, political patronage,
and growing poverty. Rawlings held on to
power but the opposition charged him with
fraud and corruption. Rawlings stabilized
the country’s economy through increased
foreign investment, and as the country ex-
perienced renewed economic growth, polit-
ical opposition decreased. T ensions over
land issues in the northeastern region of the
country took on ethnic overtones and broke
out in violent clashes, but generally Ghana
began to stabilize. Harkening back to
Ghana’s regional and continental inﬂuence
during the N’Krumah and Pan-African
era, Rawlings sought to increase Ghana’s
inﬂuence by taking on high proﬁle peace-
keeping roles in the Economic Community
of West African States (ECOWAS). Ghanaian
peacekeeping troops have been deployed
in the Côte d’Ivoire, Liberia, Sierra Leone,
and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
As the 1990s came to a close, Ghana was no
longer considered a failed state but rather a
model of successful reform.
Despite such successes, Rawlings and
the NDC were again charged with corrup-
tion, and the NDC experienced internal
dissent, and, after the 1996 elections, had
to contend with the formidable Parliamen-
tary opposition bloc, the breakaway New
Patriotic Party. Rawlings responded to stu-
dent demonstrations with repression. His
term as president ended, and at the end of
2000, Vice President John Atta Mills faced
off against the NPP’s John Kufour. Kufour
and the NPP won the election and oversaw
the ﬁrst democratic transfer of power since
independence. But the euphoria again was
short lived as the country experienced fur-
ther national and natural disasters. Exten-
sive ﬂooding in Accra and ethnic violence
in the north inaugurated a state of emer-
gency that lasted until August 2004. Again
an IMF and World Bank debt relief plan
was negotiated, and Kufour dedicated his
government to regaining economic stability
and maintaining Ghana’s regional leader-
ship role in ECOWAS. One of the most
progressive acts of Kufour’s government
was the establishment of a reconciliation
commission to investigate alleged human
rights abuses during military rule. Former
president Rawlings was called to testify in
February 2004. Perhaps as a result of the
inquiry, a group of army personnel were de-
tained on suspicion of planning to destabi-
lize the government prior to national
elections. The plot was foiled, and Kufour

was reelected to a second term in 2004.
T oday, Ghana appears to have regained its
economic and political stability and is
showing the characteristics of a modern
democracy. Its nascent economic recovery
and political stability, however, was endan-
gered during April and May of 2005 by a
ﬂood of T ogolese refugees displaced by po-
litical violence in their homeland. Ghana
clearly has an interest in decreasing the in-
stability and political violence in West
Africa and most likely will continue to play
a leading role in developing regional solu-
tions through agencies such as ECOWAS.
T ransatlantic connections have been
and continue to be strong between North
America and Ghana despite some periods of
tension, primarily during the 1980s. Ghana
received the ﬁrst Peace Corps workers from
the United States in 1961 and the two coun-
tries have long-standing economic and trade
ties formalized through cooperative agree-
ments and treaties. Ghanaian immigrants
are among the largest African groups settling
in the United States, and their vibrant West
African culture and music have become in-
creasingly popular globally. Ghana has be-
come a “motherland” of sorts for returning
diasporan visitors and repatriates. In 2001
Ghana’s parliament passed legislation that al-
lows any person of African Diasporan de-
scent to live and work in Ghana indeﬁnitely,
although this has not always resulted in
seamless integration or acceptance.

GHANA EMPIRE
The Ghana Empire was a West African em-
pire that was built on trade in salt and gold.
It is difﬁcult to trace the exact origins of the
empire, but most historians believe the
Soninke people started to build it during
the fourth century AD. The empire’s gov-
ernmental system depended on a strong
central authority controlled by a king, who
was believed to be semidivine by the
Soninke people. The security of the Ghana
Empire was dependent on a strong military
force, which was needed to guard its bor-
ders from enemies and maintain Soninke
control over neighboring tribes. The gov-
ernment of the Ghana Empire was able to
develop the power of its military by collect-
ing tribute and soldiers from the tribes
under its control. A strong military and
central government formed the foundation
for the future growth of the Ghana Empire,
as these institutions guaranteed traders a
certain degree of security when conducting
business within its territory.
The rise of the Ghana Empire is attrib-
uted to the trade conducted with the Mus-
lims who resided in the Maghreb during
the eighth century AD. It was this trade that
led to the further development of the em-
pire, as the central government was able to
collect taxes on imports and exports.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 599 ---
GILROY,B ERYL AGATHA 523
Salt and gold were two of the main re-
sources used by the Ghana Empire to amass
its wealth. The central government insti-
tuted a monopoly on all of the gold found
in order to control the circulation of this
precious metal within the empire.
After 1050, the wealth of the Ghana
Empire attracted a number of enemies who
came to plunder. Muslim Berbers, who were
called the Almoravids, also declared a reli-
gious war against the Soninke pagans and
captured the capital of Ghana in 1076. This
led to a great deal of instability in the empire
as the states of Takrur, Diara, and Kaniaga
broke away from the central government’s
control. A division among the Soninke peo-
ple allowed the nation of Susu to conquer
Diara and the city of Kumbi Saleh, but the
Susu were not able to maintain control over
this land. The Susu were defeated in 1235 by
a tribe from Mali, which captured the capi-
tal of Ghana in 1240.
Brian de Ruiter

GILROY,B ERYL AGATHA
(1924–2001)
Beryl Gilroy was a Jamaican-British novel-
ist, essayist, and educator. Gilroy is well-
known in Britain as a pioneering black
teacher. In her writing, she explores indi-
vidual histories of persons in the African-
Caribbean diaspora and pursues the theme
of cultural identity. Her son, Paul Gilroy,
would later deal with this issue theoretically
in The Black Atlantic: Modernity and Dou-
ble Consciousness (1993). Like many of her
contemporary colonial Caribbean migrants,
she invested in the future through radical
writing for children. She also published
ﬁction, autobiography, poetry, and reminis-
cences and analyzed her own writing in a
collection of essays, Leaves in the Wind
(1998). British critics have been reluctant
to appraise her creative output; she has
received much more recognition in the
United States, where she was honored by
the Association of Caribbean Women
Writers and Scholars in 1996 in Florida.
Her ﬁnal novel, The Green Grass T ango, was
published shortly after her death in 2001.
Born in then-British Guiana in 1924
into a gifted family, she was inspired to
write by her maternal grandmother’s story-
telling. She attended Georgetown’s teach-
ers’ training college, leaving with a ﬁrst-
class diploma in 1945. Later, she went on
to gain a bachelor of science degree in psy-
chology in 1956, took a masters degree at
Sussex University in 1970, and was
awarded a PhD in ethno-psychology
from Century University in New Mexico
in 1987. Recognized as a gifted teacher in
British Guiana, she traveled to London
University in 1951 to study for an ad-
vanced diploma in child development,
awarded in 1953. In London during the
early 1950s, she had little choice but to
support herself through menial jobs in a
factory, as a maid, and as a dishwasher at
Joe Lyons Café. Institutional racism fueled
her determination to ﬁnd employment as a
teacher, and she was eventually sent to a
poor Catholic school where Gilroy wrote
her groundbreaking autobiography, Black
T eacher (1976). She became the first
black principal in 1969. Fueled by anger,
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 600 ---
524 G ILROY,B ERYL AGATHA
Gilroy’s woman’s version of her black expe-
rience as an educator, presented in Black
T eacher,is still much less well-known than
the contemporary experience of E. R.
Brathwaite as described in his T o Sir With

Gilroy’s refusal to teach from middle-
class Eurocentric materials led her to pub-
lish over sixteen award-winning readers for
children throughout the 1960s and 1970s.
Gilroy’s services to education were marked
by an honorary doctorate from the Univer-
sity of North London in 1995. Her drive
for professional recognition was matched
by a battle to get her work accepted by the
patriarchal publishing houses of the 1960s.
Publishers rejected her work at a time
when Caribbean ﬁction from writers like
Sam Selvon, George Lamming, and V . S.
Naipaul was blooming. Her writing was
“out of place” in publishers’ lists and
rejected for being colonial and unknowing
as well as psychological and strange. She
refused to ﬁctionalize her reminiscences,
Sunlight on Sweet Water (eventually pub-
lished in 1994), and thereby preserved her
memory of life in an African-Guyanese vil-
lage for future generations of British-born
Caribbean children. She also submitted a
“ﬁnal passage” novel, in the 1960s, depict-
ing the migration of the Caribbean colonial
subject to the metropole of London, but
the book had to wait over thirty years to
ﬁnd a publisher. In Praise of Love and Chil-
dren (1996) brings a focus on the transfer
to London through a female protagonist,
Melda Hayley, who nurtures the damaged
children of her fellow black settlers in
Britain of the 1950s. When publishing
opportunities opened up for women in the
1980s, her ﬁctional concerns marked her as
an innovative writer, and she began to at-
tract some critical attention. Frangipani
House (1986), which won the Greater
London Council’s Literature Prize, explores
the theme of ageing when traditional
Caribbean models of caring have been dis-
placed by patterns of transnationality. Boy
Sandwich (1989) is the story of Tyrone
Grainger, a nineteen-year-old black British
male and his family’s return to Guyana.
Later, she was able to pursue her interest in
historical ﬁction through Stedman and
Joanna—A Love in Bondage (1991) and
Inkle and Yarico (1996). The novels are
based on narratives of encounters between
slaves and Carib Indians from the seven-
teenth and eighteenth centuries. She exper-
imented with form in an epistolary novel,
Gather the Faces (1996). Her creative explo-
rations have been matched by a practitioner
element in her authorship and her life.
Both in her writing and through her later
work as an ethno-therapist in London, she
attempted to heal some of the deep psychic
wounds inﬂicted by the African diasporic
condition.
Sandra Courtman

GLISSANT,E DOUARD (1928–)
Eduoard Glissant is Martinique’s most
prestigious novelist and an important poet,
theorist, and academic, celebrated for his
theories of relationality and of antillanité
(Caribbeanness). Glissant has successfully
challenged Aimé Césaire’s claims that
Caribbean identity has African “roots,” but
without denying the fundamental impor-
tance of slavery and Africa in Caribbean
historical consciousness.
Indeed, despite his celebration of di-
versity, Glissant is, as Peter Hallward has
argued in Absolutely Postcolonial: Writing
Between the Singular and the Speciﬁc(2001),
a profoundly Hegelian thinker concerned
with founding a new notion of totality,
which Glissant has called “relation.” In op-
position to Césaire’s metaphor of roots—
evident as much in the Cahier d’un retour
au pays natal (1939; Notebook of a Return
to the Homeland) as throughout Césaire’s
work—Glissant’s monumental and mam-
moth essay, Caribbean Discourse (1981)
openly borrows from French philosophers
Gilles Deleuze and Felix Guattari the
competing metaphor of the “rhizome.” The
rhizome metaphor suggests that beneath
singularity, diversity, and speciﬁc identity
(in Glissant’s case, antillanité), there lies a
more fundamental relational link. Thus,
Glissant is quick to see this relation as part
of a wider Caribbean and Atlantic identity,
pulling in the pre-Columbian Americas as
well as Louisiana. He is also critical of the
burying of Caribbean folklore and the dis-
paraging treatment of creole language, for
all their attachment to African culture.
But Glissant’s theories and novels do
not fall into a cultural hermeticism that is
abstracted from real historical determi-
nants: not only does he cautiously extend
the metaphor out of and away from créolité
to embrace the tout-monde (whole world)
of human interculturalism, but he also ne-
gotiates the speciﬁcity of Caribbeanness in
relation to Atlantic history. Thus, his sec-
ond novel, The Fourth Century (1964)—
winner of the Charles Veillon Prize in
1965—though it is a proto-Roots search for
Caribbean history, opens with a powerful
narrative of two African slaves on board a
slave ship who are dueling before reaching
the Caribbean. It then recounts their ma-
rooning exploits and their progeny over
two centuries: two Martinican families’
intertwined genealogies are thus traced
back to a foundational (though not all-
determining) moment of Middle Passage
history. The characters in the novel, one an
African-style oral storyteller, recur at regu-
lar intervals in Glissant’s prose ﬁction. A
later novel, Malemort (1975), works
through history in the other direction,
backwards, looking for the mythical ﬁgure
of Odono, transported from Africa.
Glissant’s most recent writing celebrates
chaos and posits a world free from conﬂict.
Though Glissant is often heralded as
the contemporary champion of Caribbean-
ness, his theoretical and creative work regu-
larly engages with what he has called
“detour.” Following T oussaint Louverture’s
move across the Atlantic toward imprison-
ment and subsequent death in Napoleon’s
dungeon in the Jura region of France,
Glissant—in his play, Monsieur T oussaint
(1961)—recognizes the importance of
climbing back through history, of going
through the triangular trade backwards,
from the Caribbean to Africa, and then
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 602 ---
526 G LOBALIZATION
from Africa to Europe (in his case, France,
where he was a left-wing intellectual in the
1950s arguing for Caribbean indepen-
dence), as a way of deﬁning the speciﬁcity
of Caribbeanness. He has a deeply ambiva-
lent link to the ocean that carried its
human cargo from Africa and into chains:
“The Atlantic which we must cross is the
chaotic darkness which our very own lights
make” (1998 ), he says of Caribbeans con-
templating their ancestry. This is linked to
today’s realities in the French-dominated
region of Martinique and Guadeloupe. He
thus uses “slave trade in reverse” to describe
the large movement of Caribbeans toward
France in a further exile to ﬁnd jobs, but
insists that this Atlantic voyage is—like its
Middle Passage counterpart in the other
direction—a crucial moment in their dis-
covery of Caribbeanness.
This deeply Atlanticist consciousness is
of course not an impediment to his theory
of “relation,” of intercultural connected-
ness. Quoting “The Sea is History,” by
Saint Lucian poet and Nobel Prize–winner
Derek Walcott, Glissant has recently incor-
porated the Middle Passage into his literary
work in his short story, “The First Voyage”
(1994). Thus, it is not surprising that
Glissant’s earliest poetry, during the early
1950s, owes much to the oceanic conscious-
ness of a Saint-Jean Perse. His Atlanticist
consciousness has remained remarkably
constant throughout his literary and theo-
retical voyages.
Andrew Stafford

GLOBALIZATION
Globalization refers to a large set of eco-
nomic, social, cultural, and political trans-
formations that lead to the lives and
environments of people living in distant
places becoming intimately connected.
Globalization is a signiﬁcant dimension of
the transatlantic experience beginning,
some suggest, with the emergence of colo-
nial slavery. Cultures, environments, and
economic systems in Africa and the Americas
were dramatically transformed through the
European transatlantic slave trade and
colonialism. Globalization also refers to
processes of transformation speciﬁc to the
late twentieth century, after World War II.
In this second sense, globalization refers to
processes of change and connection across
political boundaries that are tied to the  siz-
able cultural, economic, and political role of
the United States in the transatlantic world.
Through slavery and colonialism, new
plants, agricultural methods, economic sys-
tems, social structures, and diseases were
brought to the New World and spread
rapidly. Some of these early transforma-
tions have been typically called the
Columbian Exchange. Additionally,
Africans further transformed the cultural
landscape of the Americas by creating new
religious traditions, such as Santeria and
Candomblé. Africans also brought new
technologies, knowledge, and skills, adapt-
ing them to New World conditions.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 603 ---
GLOBALIZATION 527
In terms of more recent changes, since
the end of World War II the United States
has spearheaded the effort to diminish
trade barriers between national and other
political boundaries. The Bretton Woods
Agreement of 1944 outlined a global eco-
nomic order that would promote free trade
economics internationally, including both
Latin America and Africa. In the cold war
period of the twentieth century, U.S. com-
mercial ambitions were threatened by
conﬂicts that drew in developing Latin
American and African nations. However,
when the Soviet system collapsed in 1991,
U.S. commercial goals became dominant
in global politics. Rapid deregulation and
mass privatization of state-owned enter-
prises took place in formerly Communist
and socialist economies. Competitive market
forces, unfettered by government controls,
contributed to globalization. T echnological
advances created rapid changes and con-
nections. By 2006, the global distribution
of goods such as satellite dishes and cellular
phones had reached many rural parts of
Africa and Latin America. U.S. culture was
exported through television programs,
music, the Internet, and movies. Innova-
tions in telecommunications dramatically
reduced social and cultural barriers and
offered foreign investors unprecedented
Latin American and African commercial
opportunities.
Major African and Latin American
cities such as Johannesburg, Cairo, Rio de
Janeiro, and Buenos Aires, alongside North
American cities such as Los Angeles, New
York, Mexico City, and T oronto, are now
“global” cities, with complex international
migration patterns, substantial foreign
investments, and a multitude of cultures.
The ease of transport assists migration,
immigration, and resettlement activities.
Increasing numbers of Latin Americans
have either lived in Europe or North
America. For Africa, increased immigration
from South Asia has occurred. African im-
migration to the U.S. has also grown.
Globalization carries signiﬁcant com-
plications and costs that include issues
involving security, sovereignty, the environ-
ment, and national identity. Some argue
that because of the vast economic disparities
between the United States, Africa, and
Latin America, economic and cultural glob-
alization is a new form of colonialism, often
termed neocolonialism, in which wealthy
nations exploit the lower labor and resource
extraction costs and the lack of regulation
found in poorer nations. T ransatlantic
human migration has meant that public
health issues now can cross geographic bor-
ders with relative ease. Rapid economic
changes have led to substantial environmen-
tal concerns that nations are not always
prepared to address. In Africa, many states
cannot initiate environmental reforms
because of more immediate problems of
basic subsistence and political turmoil.
Such pressures can also provide oppor-
tunities, however. In recent years, Latin
American countries such as Bolivia and
Venezuela have become increasingly aware
of their ability to contribute their natural
resources to the global economy. Some
African states realize the value of their spe-
cial wildlife resources and have increased
attempts to preserve them. Loss of species
from Amazonian and Congo deforestation
are substantial environmental concerns.
At the social level, losses of traditional
cultural identity are often feared. Globaliza-
tion increases social exchanges and intensi-
ﬁes racial and ethnic intermingling. This
leads local and national cultures to recon-
sider their collective identity. In Africa, for
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 604 ---
528 G OOD NEIGHBOR POLICY
example, traditional cultural forms such as
African music have been dramatically mixed
with cultural forms from abroad such as
hip-hop. What counts as “African music” is
then greatly transformed. T raditional and
isolated tribal life, as well as life in cities, is
becoming more connected to global net-
works of cultural and economic exchange.
Cultural and social changes also pro-
vide opportunities. The mixing of tradi-
tional music with Pan-American forms of
music such as reggae, rock, and hip-hop and
access to new communications and record-
ing technology has meant new creative op-
portunities and a global visibility for
African music and musicians. Globalization
has also meant the transatlantic circulation
of new ideas about feminism, fair trade
practices, gay and lesbian rights, human
rights, and public health and education,
particularly concerning HIV prevention.
The global circulation of ideas makes it pos-
sible for people to explore common, as well
as divergent, political, social, and economic
interests across vast geographic divides.

GOOD NEIGHBOR POLICY
The Good Neighbor Policy is the early-
twentieth-century U.S. foreign policy to-
ward Latin America that was based on the
principle of nonintervention and recogni-
tion of nations’ sovereignty. In his ﬁrst in-
augural address in 1933, Franklin D. Roo-
sevelt told the American people, “I would
dedicate this nation to the policy of the
good neighbor—the neighbor who res-
olutely respects himself and . . . respects the
rights of others . . . the neighbor who re-
spects his obligations and respects the sanc-
tity of his agreements in and with a world
of neighbors” (Roosevelt, Franklin D.
“First Inaugural Address, March 4, 1933.”
The Avalon Project at Yale Law School).
U.S. foreign policy toward Latin America
would now be based on the principle of
nonintervention and a respect for neigh-
boring nations’ sovereignty.
The real architect of this policy, how-
ever, was Henry Stimson, President Herbert
Hoover’s secretary of state. During 1927 in
Nicaragua, Stimson had seen ﬁrsthand how
the almost continual deployment of U.S.
troops there had failed to advance long-
term American interests in the region. In
Stimson’s assessment, the “Big Stick” policy
of President Theodore Roosevelt’s Roosevelt
Corollary not only violated the Monroe
Doctrine of 1823 but also led to instability
and rising anti-American sentiment in the
region. In 1928 Reuban Clarke, legal coun-
sel for the U.S. State Department, formal-
ized Stimson’s rethinking of U.S. foreign
policy in the 1928 Clarke Memorandum. It
stated that the U.S. should not automati-
cally send troops into civil conﬂicts in Latin
America, even if the lives and property of
U.S. citizens were endangered.
It was upon this foundation that FDR
developed his Good Neighbor Policy. The
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 605 ---

new policy was based on neutrality, with-
out abandoning U.S. national interests in
Latin America. Instead of invasion and oc-
cupation, U.S. interests in the region were
pursued through reciprocal trade agree-
ments, formal military bases, shared mili-
tary intelligence, and closer personal ties
cemented through multilateral meetings
and mutual defense treaties.

GOYEMIDE,E TIENNE
(1942–1997)
Etienne Goyemide was a versatile African
writer who wrote novels, short stories, plays,
and poetry in French and who won the
competition for the best francophone short
story on several occasions. Born in 1942 in
Central African Republic (RCA), he studied
education science, earned a Certiﬁcate of
English, and pursued a career in education.
Goyemide was a secondary school principal
who then served as the RCA’s general direc-
tor of education and its minister of educa-
tion and research. His two best-known
novels, both set in rural areas of his country,
are Le silence de la forêt (1984) and Le dernier
survivant de la caravane (The Last Survivor
of the Caravan) (1985).  The ﬁrst narrates
the initiatory journey of a top civil servant
who, after many years of study and estrange-
ment, decides to leave civilization to travel
through the forest, hoping to ﬁnd his real
self and give his life meaning through an en-
counter with the Babinga pygmies. It is also
an explorer’s study of the Babinga as well
as an intercultural narrative revealing the
deleterious effects of Western education on
Africans and encouraging a return to tradi-
tional values. The ﬁlm made from the novel
was the only African ﬁlm presented at the
Cannes festival in 2003 and was awarded the
jury’s prize at the Namur festival in Belgium
the same year. The second novel, a mythical
story written like an oral epic and inter-
twined with folktales, songs, and speeches, is
set in the last years of the nineteenth century
and records a dark episode of the age-old
northern slave trade. Through the last words
of a griot to the displaced children he has
been addressing, the conclusion of the novel
identiﬁes Goyemide’s targeted public as a
generation keen to know its history—a clear
allusion to a wide diaspora in search of its
roots and of a lost identity.
Françoise Parent Ugochukwu
