GREEN REVOLUTION
Historians term the increase in crop yields
in the developing world between 1960 and
2000 the Green Revolution. As early as
1917, scientists bred hybrid corn. Further
efforts yielded corn, rice, and wheat with
sturdy stalks to prevent lodging of insects,
and with resistance to pathogens and in-
sects. Agronomists coupled these crops
with fertilizers, insecticides, herbicides, and
irrigation to double yields on test plots.
The prospect of extending these gains to
farmers worldwide led the Rockefeller
Foundation and the Mexican Ministry of
Agriculture in 1943 to fund what would in
1966 become the International Center for
Wheat and Maize Improvement (known by
its Mexican acronym, CIMMYT) in Mexico.
In 1960 the Rockefeller Foundation
founded the International Rice Research
Institute in the Philippines and in 1967 es-
tablished the International Institute of
T ropical Agriculture in Nigeria.
The achievements of the Green
Revolution were not uniform. Between 1961
and 2000 the yield per acre of grains, root
crops, tubers, and legumes increased 2.5 per-
cent per year in sub-Saharan Africa; 2.4 per-
cent in Mexico, Central and South America,
and the Caribbean (Latin America); and
2.3 percent in North Africa. These data re-
fute the perception that the Green Revolu-
tion bypassed sub-Saharan Africa. Rather,
sub-Saharan Africa lagged behind Latin
America and North Africa in yield gains
until 1980. Between 1961 and 1980 yields
per acre increased 3.1 percent in Latin
America and 2.5 percent in North Africa,
whereas they increased only 1.7 percent in
sub-Saharan Africa. After 1980, however,
sub-Saharan Africa surpassed Latin Amer-
ica and North Africa. Between 1981 and
2000, sub-Saharan Africa tallied annual
gains in yields per acre of 3.2 percent com-
pared to 2.1 percent in North Africa and
1.6 percent in Latin America.
Biology, politics, and geography ex-
plain the initial success of the Green
Revolution in Latin America and North
Africa. From the outset, the Mexican Min-
istry of Agriculture gave CIMMYT money
to establish experiment stations and test
plots throughout Mexico. Scientists used
these stations to breed varieties of corn and
wheat speciﬁc to local environments. The
performance of these crops on test plots en-
ticed farmers to plant them in their ﬁelds.
North Africa and the lower South of the
United States share similar latitudes, easing
the transfer of high-yielding cultivars from
the latter region to North Africa. These cul-
tivars yielded well in North Africa, a region
of few crop diseases.
Since 1980, biological and ecological
constraints have slowed the increase in crop
yields in Latin America and North Africa.
First, several decades of breeding have
brought corn, wheat, and rice near the
maximum yield. Even under ideal condi-
tions, new varieties of corn boost yields
only 2 percent per year; wheat and rice cul-
tivars increase yields 1 percent per year.
Second, the evolution of new strains of
pathogens has checked yields. A new strain
of the fungal disease Late Blight of Potato,
for example, originated in Ecuador in 1997
and has spread throughout South America.
Annual losses total 15 percent of the potato
crop and the aggregate loss is $3 billion.
Third, intensive farming has brought the
land near maximum productivity. Farmers
have saturated the land with fertilizers, the
excess leeching into groundwater. Farmers
have already brought good land under cul-
tivation. Marginal land remains on average
only half as productive as fertile land.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 607 ---
GREEN REVOLUTION 531
In contrast to Latin America and
North Africa, sub-Saharan Africa beneﬁted
little from the Green Revolution before
1980. Until the 1990s cultivars were vul-
nerable to the pathogens and parasites en-
demic to sub-Saharan Africa. The parasitic
plant witchweed, for example, reduced the
yield of grains and legumes by as much as
two-thirds in sub-Saharan Africa. The need
for control of pathogens and parasites made
essential the establishment of experiment
stations for the breeding of resistant crops.
Unlike Mexico, the countries of sub-
Saharan Africa were slow to build a net-
work of stations. Political instability further
hampered the initial efforts of the Green
Revolution. CIMMYT refused to conduct
research in nations it deemed unstable.
Only in 1995, for example, did it begin re-
search in Mozambique. Moreover, research
in the 1960s and 1970s focused on corn,
wheat, and rice rather than on teff,
sorghum, millet, and yams, crops grown by
small farmers in sub-Saharan Africa.
Poverty compounded these problems. Poor
farmers could not afford the agrochemicals
that boosted yields.
Although tardy, the Green Revolution
has come to sub-Saharan Africa. In 1986
Japanese industrialist Ryoichi Sasakawa cre-
ated Sasakawa Global 2000, a philan-
thropic organization to fund agricultural
research in sub-Saharan Africa. In 1991
agronomists bred the ﬁrst high-yielding
sorghum and in 1995 the ﬁrst witchweed-
resistant sorghum. In 1999, some 200,000
farmers in twelve sub-Saharan countries
grew witchweed-resistant sorghum. At the
twentieth-century’s end, Sasakawa Global
2000 had established 400,000 experiment
stations and test plots throughout sub-
Saharan Africa for the breeding of crops.
A student at the African Center for Crop Improvement of the University of Kwa-Zulu-Natal, South Africa,
inspects her maize project in July 2006. The Center is supported by the Rockefeller Foundation. (Sharon
Farmer/Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation)

GRONNIOSAW,U KAWSAW
(CA. 1710–?)
Ukawsaw Gronniosaw authored A Narra-
tive of the Most Remarkable Particulars in
the Life of James Albert Ukawsaw Gronnio-
saw, an African Prince(1772), the ﬁrst slave
narrative in English. Alongside John
Marrant, Ottobah Cugoano, Olaudah
Equiano, and John Jea, Gronniosaw is con-
sidered a pioneer in the development of
slave narratives during the Enlightenment
period. He told his life stories to a young
lady in England, who committed them to
writing for her private satisfaction. Then,
in 1772, they were published in book form
for the ediﬁcation of Christian readers.
The Narrative records the author’s tur-
bulent lifelong journey, including his birth,
childhood, and youth; his enslavement; and
his spiritual growth. He was born in the city
of Baurnou in Nigeria as a grandson of the
reigning king. At age ﬁfteen he was sold in
Guinea to a Dutch captain, who trans-
ported him to Barbados. Thereafter, he
lived in New York, the Netherlands, and the
English towns of Colchester and Kidder-
minster, ﬁrst as a slave and then as a poverty-
stricken head of a household.
As a child, Gronniosaw was skeptical
of his native religion and became con-
vinced of the existence of a sole creator that
transcends the visible world. The Narrative
is an account of how God providentially
led him to Christ through enslavement and
numerous afﬂictions. Isaiah 42:16, which is
used as the epigraph, ﬁttingly summarizes
the theme of Gronniosaw’s narrative: God’s
deliverance from darkness into light and
His divine protection of the faithful.
John J. Han

GUILLÉN,N ICOLÁS
(1902–1989)
Nicolás Guillén was the most inﬂuential
Caribbean Spanish-language poet of the
twentieth century and one of the leading
literary ﬁgures of the African Diaspora. A
proponent of the Négritude movement in
the 1930s and 1940s, Guillén emerged as the
poet laureate of the Cuban Revolution in the
1960s. The author of more than a dozen col-
lections of poetry invoking social justice and
racial equality, Guillén remains the island’s
most celebrated writer since José Martí.

GUINEA 533
Born in Camagüey, Cuba, in 1902 to
parents of Afro-Hispanic descent, Guillén’s
social convictions were inﬂuenced at an
early age by the political activism of his
journalist father. It was during this period
that Guillén published his ﬁrst poems, com-
positions reﬂecting the Modernist aesthetic
of Rubén Darío. In 1926, after moving to
Havana to work in the civil service, Guillén
began to develop the poetic style for which
he would become best known. Drawing on
the West African–based popular dance
known as son, he combined rhythmic form
with the speech and folklore of the island’s
black population to create the collection
Motivos de son (1930; Motifs of Son). He
further articulated his Afrocentric vision of
Cuba with the more polemical Sóngoro
consongo: poemas mulatos (Songoro Cosongo:
Mulatto Poems) (1931). 
Following Fulgencio Batista’s coup in
1952 and subsequent U.S. military inter-
vention, Guillén raised the banner of anti-
imperialism and pan-Caribbean nationalism
in West Indies, Inc. (1934) and Cantos para
soldados y sones para turistas (1937; Songs
for soldiers and sones for tourists). Now a
signiﬁcant ﬁgure in the leftist intelligentsia,
Guillén spent much of 1937 attending rev-
olutionary congresses in Spain and Mexico,
where contact with such politically com-
mitted writers as Pablo Neruda and Diego
Rivera brought him to the Communist
Party. Over the next two decades, he de-
voted himself almost entirely to politics, in-
cluding an unsuccessful campaign for
mayor of his native Camagüey in 1940 and
editorship of the leftist newspaper Hoy
from 1941 to 1945.
With the end of World War II and the
onset of the cold war, Guillén’s Communist
afﬁliations forced him into self-imposed
exile. He traveled to Haiti to meet Jacques
Roumain, one of the seminal ﬁgures of fran-
cophone Négritude, and championed the
cause of Pan-Caribbean Afrocentrism in the
subsequent collection, El son entero (1947;
The complete son). Now widely viewed as
one of Communism’s most powerful voices
in the nonaligned world, Guillén saw his
status conﬁrmed when he was awarded the
Lenin Peace Prize in 1954.
Following the triumph of the Cuban
Revolution in 1959, Guillén returned
home to lend his support to the new
regime. Elected president-for-life of the
Union of Cuban Artists and Writers
(Unión Nacional de Escritores y Artistas
Cubanos) in 1961, he played a central role
in the revalorization of the country’s
African heritage. Among his later collec-
tions, Elegías (1958; Elegies), T engo(1964;
I have), and La rueda dentada (1972; The
toothed wheel) contain some of Guillén’s
most powerful polemics against the legacy
of slavery in the Western Hemisphere.
Eric L. Reinholtz
See also: Afrocentrism; Caribbean Literature;
Cuba; Latin American Literature; Martí,
José; Négritude
References
Márquez, Roberto, and David Arthur
McMurray. Man-Making Words. Amherst:
University of Massachusetts Press, 1972.
Smart, Ian Isidore. Nicolás Guillén: Popular
Poet of the Caribbean. Columbia: University
of Missouri Press, 1990.
GUINEA
The Republic of Guinea was previously
French Guinea, occupied by the Compag-
nie de Sénégal, a French chartered com-
pany of the eighteenth century. Guinea has
a population of 9,246,000, most of whom
live in rural areas. For many centuries
“Guinea” was a generic term for any place
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 610 ---
534 G UINEA
on the West African coast between Senegal
and the Côte d’Ivoire—with several places
being designated with the name “Guinea,”
such as Portuguese Guinea (Guinea-Bissau)
and Spanish Guinea (Equatorial Guinea).
Over several centuries, many people were
enslaved in Guinea and transported to
the Americas, and a signiﬁcant number of
the early English voyagers to the Americas
had been to Guinea.
Guinea is connected to the Americas
through patterns of slavery and early explo-
ration. Martin Frobisher (ca. 1539–1596),
who sought out the “Northwest Passage”
in the late sixteenth century, had spent the
1550s sailing off the coast of Guinea and
in 1554 had been held as a hostage by a
local chief. Francis (later Sir Francis) Drake
(c. 1540–1596) went to South America and
on his return passed Guinea. Sir Bernard
Drake (c. 1537–1586), who led the English
expedition to Newfoundland in the 1580s,
managed to capture a French ship from
Guinea with a signiﬁcant amount of gold
on board.
French connections between Guinea
and the Americas were also important.
Morillon du Bourg (d. 1670) was the French
commissioner who carried out negotiations
for the T reaty of Breda in French Canada.
He died on a subsequent voyage to Guinea.
Joseph de Fleury de la Gorgendière
(1676–1755) was a prominent merchant in
Canada who probably made his early for-
tune from the slave trade with Guinea.
Jean-Baptiste Curatteau (1729–1790) and
Jacques Bedout (1751–1818) both made
trips to Guinea as teenagers in the 1740s
and 1760s, respectively. The former be-
came a prominent religious ﬁgure in Mon-
treal, and the latter a French naval ofﬁcer
involved in the siege of Yorktown, Virginia,
in 1781. Mention should also be made of
Olivier Le Jeune (d. 1654), a slave who
probably came from Guinea (although
some sources claim he was from Madagas-
car) and was the ﬁrst black to live in the
St. Lawrence Valley in Canada.
From 1850 the French government
managed to make treaties with local rulers,
and these pacts became formalized between
1882 and 1893 as the Rivières du Sud, a
colonial division, which became French
Guinea in 1893. Camille Lucien Xavier
Guy, who was lieuteant governor of French
Guinea from 1910 until 1913, went on to
become governor of Martinique in the
Caribbean; his successor, Jean Jules Émile
Peuvergne, had been governor of Guade-
loupe before moving to French Guinea.
Robert Paul Marie de Guise, who was the
penultimate lieutenant governor of French
Guinea, had served in the West Indies, in
his case as governor of Martinique.
After World War II it was clear that—
despite attempts to retain their colonial
empire—the French would have to negoti-
ate an agreement with African nationalists.
The plan was drawn up by General Charles
de Gaulle and the former French ambas-
sador to Argentina, Bernard Cornut-Gentille,
who had been appointed minister of Over-
seas France. It set up the framework for
referendums to be held in French Africa. In
the 1958 referendum, Guinea was the only
French colony to vote for complete and
immediate independence. It became the
independent Republic of Guinea on Octo-
ber 2, 1958.
The nationalist hero who led Guinea
to independence was Sékou T ouré
(1922–1984), a longtime trade unionist
who formed the Democratic Party of
Guinea in 1947 and rose to become mayor
of Conakry, the city that became the capi-
tal of Guinea. Sékou T ouré led his country
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 611 ---
GUINEA DANCE 535
as it confronted France several times, with
the former colonial master being impli-
cated in a 1960 coup attempt. The govern-
ment also managed to survive an invasion
by exiles ten years later. By that time Sékou
T ouré was a leading spokesman for the
third world and viewed by many as a sup-
porter of the Soviet Union, which had
awarded him the Lenin Peace Prize in
1960.
The government was increasingly ac-
cused of becoming out of touch with the
people, and in 1971 Karim Bangoura,
Guinea’s ambassador to the United States
from 1969, was arrested and executed,
without a trial, the following year for his
role in an attempted coup in 1970 that
was led by Guinean exiles and assisted by
Portugese troops. He was replaced as am-
bassador by Sékou T ouré’s distant cousin,
Sadan Moussa T ouré (d. 1988). In 1976
Boubacar T elli Diallo, who had been
Guinea’s ﬁrst ambassador to the United
States, was arrested for involvement in a
plot to topple Sékou T ouré. He died in
captivity after fourteen days in prison.
Eight years later, in March 1984, Sékou
T ouré traveled to the United States for
medical treatment but died of a heart
attack on March 26, 1984, during surgery
at a hospital in Cleveland. In recent years
trouble in neighboring Sierra Leone has
sent many refugees into Guinea, where
U.S. and Canadian aid groups have been
active.
Justin Corﬁeld

GUINEA DANCE
Guinea dance illustrates the development,
fusion, and dispersal of African art forms
throughout the continent and to the Amer-
icas through dance. Guinea dance is well-
known for its highly stylized, exciting, and
virtuoso movement while being less-known
for its subtle, reserved, yet simplistic spiri-
tual dance. The dynamism and powerful
images of African dance owe much to
Guinean traditions and to its status as
home to the ﬁrst national dance company
for all of Africa, Les Ballets Africains. Les
Ballets Africains was created out of a need
to preserve African culture and counter the
denigrated and maligned images of Africa
as the “dark continent.” The creation of Les
Ballets Africains later spawned other na-
tional ballets of Africa, introduced the
djembe drum orchestra and dance to the
world, and helped father a rhythm nation
in Guinea that gave birth to creative fusions
of African movement. These fusions  have
added resources to the research, preserva-
tion, pedagogy, performance, practice, and
entertainment of African cultural art forms
through out the world. 
Out of his disappointment with Euro-
peans’ stereotypic criticisms of Africa as sav-
age and oversexualized, Keita Fodeba of
upper Guinea envisaged creating a vehicle
that would send the right message from
Africa. First studying in Senegal and then in
France, Fodeba was a poetry student,
dancer, choreographer, and musician.
While in France, shortly after 1948 he
began a poetry group consisting of 
Africans of the diaspora from Guadaloupe,
Martinique, Guinea, Cameroon, and so on.
This group gradually transformed itself into
a drum, dance, and storytelling group that
called itself the African Theater Ballet of
Keita Fodeba and which was renamed in
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 612 ---
536 G UINEA DANCE
1954 as Les Ballets Africains de Keita
Fodeba. Among the ﬁrst members were
Kante Facely, composer and choreographer;
Raphael Wigbert, who later became a diplo-
mat; Conte Seydou; and T oure Ismael.
The African Theater Ballet of Keita
Fodeba traveled throughout Europe as an
African theater. In the early 1950s notable
artists were recruited, such as Italo Zambo
of Guinea and Papa Ladji of Mali, the latter
being one of the most famous drummers of
Mali (and later to become the ﬁrst teacher
of djembe drum and its dances in the United
States). Between 1951 and 1955, they trav-
eled to Holland, Luxembourg, Denmark,
Norway, Germany, Italy, Spain, Austria,
France, Belgium, and Switzerland, and later
they expanded the tour. Les Ballets Africains
ﬁrst visited the United States in 1953.
Fodeba also took a political stance and
was involved in ﬁghting for Guinea’s inde-
pendence. He became famous throughout
West Africa, with taxi drivers carrying his
picture in their windows and his lyrical po-
etry played on radio. The songs composed
by Fodeba, which celebrate the history and
culture of Africa, became true classics, for
example, “Minuit,” “Aure Africaine,”
“Chanson de Djoliba,” and “SineMory.”
Les Ballets Africains de Keita Fodeba ac-
quired so much wealth that Fodeba was
able to make substantial contributions to
Guinea’s economy. When Guinea became
independent in 1958, Keita Fodeba ofﬁ-
cially declared Les Ballets Africains a gift to
Guinea, and from then on the ballet be-
came a national symbol.
At the time of Guinea’s independence
the nation’s leader, Ahmed Sékou T ouré,
emphasized the preservation of African cul-
ture through a broad rehabilitation of the
arts and the reinstitution of traditional lan-
guages, dance, art, and drumming in the
school curriculum. In 1962 T ouré created a
second ballet, Ballet Djoliba. Even a mili-
tary ballet was established in 1958. It had
no commercial function, its purpose being
purely educational, to serve as a commen-
tary on social wrongs and rights for the
well-being of the people of Guinea and
West Africa; it ended with the conclusion
of T ouré presidency. The Ballet Djoliba was
created with purposes similar to those of
Les Ballets Africains: to represent the cul-
ture of Africa by being an ambassador of
love and truth through presenting the folk-
lore of Guinea to the world, preserving the
traditions that were being forgotten by
urban city youth, and reuniting peoples
across ethnic barriers. 
The ballets were effective in creating a
strong national identity that integrated
elements of different ethnic dance forms in
a way that established uniformity and
provided a criteria or standard of African
theater performance that has served as a
model for all of Africa. Members of Guinea’s
national ballets helped create other African
national dance troupes, such as the National
Ballet of Senegal, whose ﬁrst director, from
1959 to 1961, was Guinean Italo Zambo,
who has been the artistic director for Les
Ballets Africains since 1987.
Although the primary repertoire of the
ballets draws from the legends and folklore
of Guinea, the repertoire has also reﬂected
rhythms and dances from other countries
in West Africa—Mali, Mauritania, Senegal,
The Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, Sierra Leone,
Liberia, Cote d’Ivoire, and Burkina Faso—
that date back to the thirteenth century of
the old Malian Empire. As part of the
process of preparing artists, acrobats re-
ceived training in other countries such as
Russia, China, and Korea. A notable artist,
choreographer, and director, Sekouba
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 613 ---
GUINEA DANCE 537
Camara—who performed with Djoliba
and later became its artistic director—
reported training as an acrobat in China. In
1966 Djoliba spent six months studying
Chinese acrobats and integrated their style
with its own. At the same time, an ex-
change in the cultural arts took place, with
the Africans teaching their Chinese coun-
terparts to sing in Malinke and Sousou.
General modiﬁcations in the dances
and rhythms have been made, such as lim-
iting those aspects of ritual dances desig-
nated inappropriate, while assuring dy-
namic stage presentations. A mélange of
movements from various ethnic dances
were incorporated inside the choreography
of a particular dance. For example, inside
of Dundunba (a Malinke dance of the
strong man, strong woman), movements
from Jolie, Sorsorne, Kassa, and other
dances are placed within its choreography
for stage. Progressively, the national ballets
have modernized Guinea folklore, empha-
sizing style and artistic license in creating
new dance versions and fast rhythmic com-
positions. In comparison, village tradition
continues to preserve ritual dance that is
evolving to reﬂect the youth’s reinvention
and assertion of their folklore.
Lamban is a dance that perfectly exem-
pliﬁes changes in presentation for stage.
Lamban is traditionally a dance of the
griots, the oral historians and praise singers
who recite family lineages and serve as
keepers of the traditional arts using the art
of the spoken word. In its village context,
Lamban is played for weddings and is also
a ritual healing dance, with movements and
tempo that are graceful, simple in form and
sound. But as adapted for the stage, Lamban
becomes highly vigorous, with an exagger-
ated nuance of spinning head motion and
postural movement and abrupt, staccato
rhythmic accents. These changes in move-
ment bring out the accents and nuance of
the dance, making it more visible for stage,
while emphasizing an up-tempo cadence.
These changes illustrate how the national
ballets are increasingly integrating modern
influences into African dance theater
presentation.
Although ofﬁcially, Guinea folklore
came with the touring of the national bal-
lets, the presence and initial appearances of
African arts in the Americas came with the
dispersal of Africans in bondage during the
Atlantic slave trade. Early forms of African
dance are seen in showgirls’ dancing, the
Charleston, the Lindy Hop, the Black
Bottom, and other popular dances. In fact,
Jazz Dancing in particular contains Guinean
retentions. Derivatives of Guinea dance can
be found in the Haitian, Cuban, Brazilian,
and diasporic African cultures spread
through out the Americas. In Haiti, for
example, a relatively signiﬁcant amount of
Guineans were enslaved, and retentions are
therefore reflected in Haitian dance;
Katherine Dunham’s technique, an infusion
of modern and traditional Haitian dance,
represents the connection. Correlations
have been made between Cuban rhumba
and salsa dance forms to, for example,
Macarou and Koukou of the Sousou and
forest peoples (Sekouba and Camara) of
Guinea. In Brazilian samba movement there
is a resemblance to a Malinke marchlike
movement in a dance called Saa of upper
Guinea. Today, the Umfundalai technique
of Kari amu Welsh Asante represents an
African-inspired and modern dance fusion.
With the Civil Rights Movement and
the Black Power Movement taking place at
the same time that the independence
movement was giving birth to Les Ballets
Africains and the Djoliba National Ballet,

538 G UINEA DANCE
black youth and practitioners of the arts
made connection with the African dance
that these companies presented as a part of
reclaiming their heritage and rights to an
African identity and sense of self. When Les
Ballets Africains ﬁrst came to the United
States, it was immediately received with
great enthusiasm by its African American
counterparts. Strong connections across
cultural and linguistic barriers were made
with the ﬁrst appearances of the national
ballets of Guinea.
The ﬁrst pioneer of the Guinean master
teachers to come to the United States was
Papa Ladji Camara, who came to the
United States in 1958. Starting in 1959 he
had encounters with artists like Chief Bey
and Charles Moore. In 1962 Katherine
Dunham of the Bamboise Dance Company
invited Papa to perform with that troupe.
Papa since then has worked with Babatunde
Olutunji, Pearl Primus, Constance Santi
De, Yusef Lateef, Mango Santamaria, Nina
Simone, Art Blakey, and many more. His
message of “African people for Americans
and Americans for Africans” reached many
across all ethnic barriers. Papa Ladji has the
distinction of being the ﬁrst master artist
and folklorist of Guinea to base himself in
the United States and teach the folklore and
rhythms of the djembe drum. The protégé
student of Papa Ladji, the late Babatunde
Olutunji, led the ﬁrst generation of tradi-
tional African folk artists and djembe players
to teach the ensuing generations. 
Papa Ladji taught his students only
from the folkloric traditions of his people
in Norussaba, Guinea, and Mali. A focus
on the repertoires of the national ballets
would come later, but Papa Ladji taught
ancient ritual folklore called by many
“fetish” music and dance. He was also one
of the ﬁrst to teach other nationalities and
women the secrets of the drum. Protégé
students of Papa Ladji were left to carry on
his mission to disseminate the ancient heal-
ing ritual magic of the drum and dance.
Aziz Ahmed continues to teach from Papa
Ladji’s repertoire of folklore with Nanfoule,
a name given to his group by Papa himself.
The ﬁrst traditional African cultural
arts schools emerged out of the Pan-African
movement. One of the ﬁrst schools or
dance companies to come out of this era of
African decolonization and independence
movements was the International African
American Ballet (IAAB), established
around 1974. The IAAB consisted of mem-
bers who would later spread out through
the country and become master teachers
Baba Olukose Wiles was a founding mem-
ber, senior artistic director, and music di-
rector of the group. The current artistic
director for Muntu Dance Theater of
Chicago, which started up in 1972, is
Amaniyea Payne, a former member of
IAAB; so is Chuck Davis, who is the
founder of Dance Africa and the African
American Dance Ensemble, started in
1968 and based in Durham, North
Carolina. Melvin Deal’s African Heritage
Dancers and Drummers is another example
of a generation that has taught youth since
the early 1960s. African American legends,
such as Baba Robert Crowder, Arthur Hall,
the Ishangi Family African Dancers, and
other related djembe traditional ensembles,
have raised the appreciation for African
culture in the U.S.
Although it was Guinea that played the
leading role in introducing the djembe
drum and dance traditions to the world,
groups based in other West African nations
where the djembe orchestra is featured have
made vast contributions. The djembe drum
originates from within the Mande world,

which includes the ethnic groups who
speak a Mande language as their mother
tongue and those interacting with them:
Bamana, Malinke, Baga, Sousou, Dyula,
Soninke, Konyaka, Loma, Kpelle, and
Koranko, as well as Wolof, Fula, Senufo,
Minianka, Dogon, and Gur, among others.
Artists from these ethnic groups were in
prominent dance troupes such as the
National Ballet of Senegal; Ballet Africaines
de Diebel Guee of Dakar; and dance groups
from Mali, Sierra Leone, Liberia, Côte
d’Ivoire, and other countries, which began
to spread themselves throughout the world.
In the United States, Mor Thiam, Abdul
Kunta, Assane Konte, Dan Gueye, Zack
Diof, Marie Basse, the late Djibi T raore of
Senegal, and Papa Djimo Kouyate’s Mem-
ory of African Culture Inc. school are
signiﬁcant in the establishing of African
cultural centers.
As the government for Guinea changed
after the death of Ahmed Sekou T oure in
1984 and Lansana Conte’s liberation of po-
litical prisoners and encouragement of ex-
iles to return, the nation also opened its
doors to the world for interested artists
from outside to enter and study. In 1986
Mohammed Kemoko Sano—director of
Ballet National Djoliba from 1973 to 1986
and dynamic choreographer for Les Ballets
Africains—founded Les Merveilles de
Guinee, composed of master Guinean
artists. Mamady Keita, a former artistic di-
rector and lead percussionist of the Djoliba
National Ballet, and Famadou Konate, a
master of Malinke drumming and former
lead djembe soloist for Les Ballets
Africaines, burst on to the world scene in
the mid-1980s, establishing themselves as
teachers and performers in Europe, spread-
ing universal messages about the power of
the djembe drum, and attracting many
people to Guinea. In 1991 a documentary
titled Djembefola, about Mamady Keita’s
return to his native village after twenty-six
years, brought him international acclaim as
an artist while increasing awareness of the
djembe. Mamady Keita has recorded several
compact discs on the Fonti Musicali label:
Nankama, Wasolon (1989), Mogobalu
(1995), Hamanah (1996), and Afo (1998).
New CDs of his are continually coming
out. Keita also founded a percussion
school, Tam Tam Mandingue, in Belgium,
and eleven other schools in Europe, Japan,
and the United States. In a conversation
with the author in 1998, Keita talked about
the music of the djembe having the power
to open a person up and bring out whatever
is inside. He has also written a book titled
My Life with the Djembe: Traditional
Rhythms of the Malinke (1999). Artists like
Keita have brought the djembe to the
world, the result being that numerous
groups have emerged on the world scene
playing djembe music and performing
Guinea repertoire in collaborative fusions
of African diasporan music and dance. Fatala
from Guinea and Faraﬁna of Burkina Faso
are two such djembe-based groups.
The latest addition of national artistic
companies began in 1987 when a French
percussionist, François Kokolaea, came to
Guinea by way of Brazil to study djembe
drumming. The following year he became
the ﬁrst manager of Les Percussion de
Guinee, consisting of the seven best percus-
sionist of Guinea. The artistic vision of the
national companies of Guinea is now follow-
ing the vision of  Mamoudou Conde, who is
the ofﬁcial representative of Les Ballets
Africaines, to continue the great legacy of
Guinea’s ancestral heritage that Keita Fodeba
so wanted to proclaim to the world. The
continued challenges of language barriers,

misconceptions or misinterpretations across
cultural barriers, and minimal codiﬁcation
of oral traditions play a role in the continued
ignorance  of African cultural art forms and
their accessibility through teaching. Further
understanding and awareness about tradi-
tional African drum and dance traditions
has been promoted by notable percussionists
or dancers turned scholars. Eric Charry of
the United States, Yaya Diallo of Mali,
Alphonse Tierou of Côte d’Ivoire, and many
other practitioners of these arts have begun
to document the deeper signiﬁcance, healing
attributes, and critical idiom of the arts, thus
translating orally based traditions into
codiﬁed forms. Their efforts substantiate a
communal as well as academic means of
facilitating continued preservation and
teaching of the African and African dias-
poric aesthetic of rhythm and movement.

GUINEA-BISSAU
The Republic of Guinea-Bissau has approx-
imately 1.4 million people (2005) living in
an area of 13,948 square miles (33,700
square kilometers), 5,046 square miles of
which is water. This small West African
country, with its capital in Bissau, has cul-
tural ties extending well beyond its national
borders; it is a member state of several inter-
national institutions, including the African
Union (AU), Economic Community of
West African States (ECOWAS), Comu-
nidade dos Países de Língua Portuguesa
(CPLP; Community of Portuguese-Speaking
Countries), and the French “franc zone.”
Population displacement, colonial “paciﬁca-
tion,” revolutionary independence, and
political and economic insecurity have
contributed to the shaping of this country.
Guinea-Bissau achieved independence
from Portuguese colonial rule on
September 10, 1974. João Bernardo “Nino”
Vieira successfully ousted Luís Cabral,
Guinea-Bissau’s ﬁrst president after inde-
pendence, in a 1980 coup d’état. The coup
broke up the union of Cape Verde and
Guinea-Bissau in part due to Guinea-
Bissauan resentment toward the protracted
legacy of Cape Verdean political domina-
tion. Disputes over economic policies led
to another political crossroads. After nine-
teen years of authoritarian rule, the former
chief of military staff, Ansumane Mané,
overthrew Vieira. In 2005 Guinea-Bissau
returned to multiparty, democratic elec-
tions, restoring Vieira’s power after he had
spent six years exiled in Portugal. Coups and
attempted coups, military putsches, and a
bloody civil war in 1998–1999 hindered po-
litical development and economic stability. 
Guinea-Bissau is one of the poorest
countries in the world, ranking 172 out of
the 177 countries listed on the United Na-
tions Human Development Index of 2005.
Fifty-nine years of Portuguese colonial rule,
followed by three decades of national insta-
bility, crippled Guinea-Bissau’s economy
and infrastructure. Agriculture continues
to dominate the economy and is estimated
to have contributed 62 percent of the
country’s gross domestic product (GDP) in
1999, with rice as the main staple crop.
Guinea-Bissau’s production and export of
cashew nuts ranks among the top ten in the
world. Fishing, timber, and tourism are all
avenues of future development. As of 2002,
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

GUINEA-BISSAU 541
mining played an insigniﬁcant role in the
country’s economy, although potential
mineral deposits include phosphate in the
Farim district, bauxite from the Boé dis-
trict, diamonds, and offshore oil. The
1998–1999 civil war was partially insti-
gated by a dispute over offshore oil rights
between Senegal and Guinea-Bissau; the
conﬂict led to a sharp drop in the latter’s
GDP . Structural adjustment programs
(SAPs) and international aid from the
World Bank, International Monetary Fund
(IMF), and United Nations Development
Program (UNDP) have been ﬁnancing the
country’s restabilization since December
2003. Physical and social isolation from its
former French colonial neighbors is also a
factor influencing Guinea-Bissau’s eco-
nomic development.
Guinea-Bissau’s eastern and southern
areas border on the Futa Jallon highlands
and the much larger Republic of Guinea,
while Senegal’s Casamance region runs
along its northern reaches. Guinea-Bissau is
bisected by numerous rivers that are regu-
larly ﬂooded along the ria, or sunken coast-
line. The offshore islands, islets, inlets, and
estuaries, such as the Bissagos Archipelago,
have promoted transatlantic anchorage and
trade since the ﬁfteenth century. The harsh
environment of Guinea-Bissau, including
thick forests, a humid climate, and a com-
plex river system has contributed to ram-
pant disease (including a 2005–2006
cholera epidemic affecting 25,000 people).
This geography, with its complex river
system, is what ultimately encouraged the in-
ﬂux of refugees from the hinterland seeking a
safe haven from invaders: the Mandinka of
the kingdom of Kabu, a Mali Empire tribu-
tary persisting from the eleventh century to
the eighteenth century, and Islamic Fula
from the southeast by the thirteenth century.
Guinea-Bissau has approximately thirty-
three different ethnic groups, the ﬁve largest
being the Balanta, Fula, Mandinka, Manjaco,
and Papel. Long-term population displace-
ment has left ethnolinguistic settlement
patterns marked by overlapping culture and
history, including a shared lingua franca
(Kriol), although Portuguese remains the
ofﬁcial national language.
As early as 1441, Portuguese explorer-
traders such as Nuño T ristão were able to
reach the West African coast on behalf of
state and religious backers such as Prince
Henry the Navigator. Scattered data from
European accounts describe Guinea-Bissau
as a hodgepodge of ethnic groups, languages,
sociopolitical structures, and religious afﬁlia-
tions. The country remains diverse today.
The legacies of Portuguese creolization
(linguistic and cultural), indigenous non-
centralized religious and political structures,
a historical precedence of blurred, ﬂuid cul-
tural group boundaries, and the ideology
of inclusion of the African Party for the
Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde
(Partido Africano da Independência ga
Guiné e Cabo Verde) (PAIGC), established
in Guinea-Bissau’s constitution of 1984 all
highlight the paradoxical nature of Guinea-
Bissau’s civil society.

GULLAH
Gullah is a term that describes the language
and the descendants of African slaves who
live in the Carolina low country and on the
coastal islands off South Carolina and
Georgia. In 1680 African slaves were ﬁrst
brought from the West Indies to these areas
for a number of reasons. Foremost was the
need for labor on land that was ideally
suited for the cultivation of rice, indigo,
and cotton. Since there was a limited sup-
ply of American-born slaves, African-born
slaves supplied the demand. They were not
only available, but many had a knowledge
of rice cultivation as well as a natural im-
munity to tropical diseases.
From their ﬁrst arrival, African slaves
had limited association with whites and,
consequently, minimal contact with
European culture. Plantations required a
large number of slaves but only a small
number of white overseers. After the Civil
War, when former slaves were allowed to
purchase land from the Freedmen’s Bureau
at $1.25 per acre, many of the Gullah became
landowners and were thus further isolated
from white inﬂuences. Gullahs were also ge-
ographically isolated; until roads and bridges
were built in the 1930s, many of the Sea
Islands could be reached only by boat. Be-
cause of this isolation, however, the Gullah
people have maintained much of their
African heritage, and over time they have
developed their own culture and language.
The Gullah language is a combination
of English and West African words. Its
unique characteristics come not only in the
use of African words and expressions, but
also in the employment of various aspects
of African grammar. For example, the lan-
guage makes use of pronouns that are not
gender speciﬁc, verbs that do not indicate
tense, and nouns that do not use standard
plural forms.
Aside from language, other instances of
African inﬂuences abound in Gullah cul-
ture. Family life reﬂects distinctive African
concepts of the extended family. Gullah re-
ligious practices—which include spirituals,
shouting, clapping, and foot stomping—
are mostly a mixture of African ceremonies
and Baptist beliefs. African traditions are
reﬂected in burial customs by the manner
in which graves are decorated with shells
and broken household items, as well as in
the way graves are positioned. African in-
ﬂuences can also be found in the many
trickster tales found in Gullah storytelling.
Various techniques and forms brought
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 619 ---
GUYANA 543
from Africa are retained in crafts, such as
coiled sweetgrass baskets. Another impor-
tant feature of African inﬂuence is seen in
the foods that are prepared, such as benne
(sesame), okra, rice, yams, peanuts, and
black-eyed peas.
T oday, Gullah is considered an endan-
gered culture. Rising taxes on Sea Island
property are forcing many people to sell
their land, often below its value, and to
move away. Also, as many Gullah go to the
mainland seeking work, they lose touch
with their distinctive language and culture.
Efforts, however, are being made to pre-
serve Gullah history and culture for future
generations—for example, by the Penn
Center, originally one of the ﬁrst schools
for freed slaves on St. Helena Island.
Kathy A. Campbell

GUYANA
Guyana sits on the north-central coast of
South America, east of Venezuela, north of
Amazonian Brazil, and west of Suriname.
The population is about 706,000, roughly
half of them Christian, 35 percent Hindu,
and 10 percent Muslim.
Much of the coast of Guyana was
under Dutch colonial rule until the
Napoleonic Wars of the early nineteenth
century. These settlements were economi-
cally dependent on sugar plantations and
slave labor, with Demerara sugar becoming
a household name around the world.
Guyana’s terrain allowed for a substantial
number of slaves to escape bondage and
form autonomous communities, often re-
ferred to as Maroon communities (from
“maronnage,” the Spanish word for escape).
Maroons waged a form of guerilla war
against planters. The possibility of resis-
tance against slavery was substantial, and in
1763, slaves in Berbice took part in a major
revolt that undermined the whole of the
Dutch plantation system, leading to its de-
cline and fall in the latter half of the eigh-
teenth century.
After the Napoleonic Wars, the British
took over the settlements of Berbice,
Demerara, and Essequibo. The British began
recording the numbers of slaves in 1823
and found 34,462 African-born slaves and
39,956 creole black slaves (slaves born in
the Americas). These numbers suggest that
very large numbers of slaves had been
brought to the area during the early years of
the Napoleonic Wars despite Britain’s abo-
lition of the importation of slaves from
Africa in 1807.
The three settlements taken from the
Dutch were merged in 1831 to form the
colony of British Guiana. Seven years later,
slavery was abolished in the British Empire.
Planters in Guiana fought the abolition of
slavery, but many former slaves left the
plantations to establish their own small-
holdings. This led to a shortage of labor on
the sugar plantations, forcing some planters
to offer land near plantations in return for
men to work on the sugar cane. Many of
the newly emancipated established small
villages of sixty or seventy people by pool-
ing their resources to buy an abandoned
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 620 ---
544 G UYANA
plantation and divide up the land. These
“free Negro villages,” as they were called,
led to a dramatic change that enabled many
to work on self-sufﬁcient farms. Plantation
owners tried importing German, Portuguese,
and Irish laborers and eventually organized
a large-scale migration of Chinese and Indian
laborers.
British Guiana gained its indepen-
dence on May 26, 1966, becoming the Co-
operative Republic of Guyana. Its ﬁrst
prime minister was Forbes Burnham.
T oday, many families of African descent in
Guyana still live in the villages established
in the years after emancipation, between
1838 and the 1850s.
Justin Corﬁeld

HAIR
The essential qualities of black hair tend to
include coarse texture and a ﬁnely-spiraled
curl. Described as kinky, because the hair
is inclined to wrap around surrounding
strands, its matting properties lend them-
selves to an array of hairstyles. The Nuer of
East Africa use mud to ﬂatten the curl.
Masaai men in Kenya braid their hair into
long tendrils and women shave theirs clean.
These styles reﬂect ethnicity, lifestyle, and
worldview. From pastoral groups to desert
nomads to nation-state urbanites, and
coastal dwellers, hairstyles underscore
group distinctions. They carry symbolic
meanings as invocations of the head where
power resides, part of a cultural statement
that encodes social, economic, and moral
status. They can indicate one’s age group,
marital status, or family lineage. Female
powers are invoked among the Tchrkin of
Brazil, where reproductive status is con-
veyed through hair. Nigerians consider
newborns with matted hair a sacred gift
and refer to them as Dada children.
Associated with costuming, hairstyles
sometimes serve as a communicative fea-
ture with ancestors. They illuminate social
ideas that employ concepts of nature and
architecture, the engineering of mathemat-
ical patterns found on pineapples, baskets,
or beehives. The Ibo and Yoruba ritualize
headdress in festivals to the river goddess.
The cylindrical shaped braids of the West
African Mangbetu duplicate their statue
art. Bakonga people symbolize their spiri-
tual worldview in styles that resemble the
kodya shell’s spiral. In Zaire, coiffures are
named after signiﬁcant ﬁgures.
These practices have origins in ancient
eras when young Egyptian rulers wore a
single braid on their scalp called the “lock
of youth.” The goddess Isis, generally de-
picted wearing braids, is described in The
Book of the Dead as the “lady of hair.”
Braiding is one of Africa’s most universal
creations, traveling across cultures through-
out history. Hindu women braided their
straight hair to create waves. Braids were at-
tributed to women’s power over karma in
Homer’s “Circe of the Braided T resses,”
and appear as early as the twelfth century
in drawings of European women. A resur-
gence of braided styles in twentieth-century
America led to what some call “ancient-
future designs,” contemporary innovations
on tradition. A transcultural exchange is
evident as women of the Diaspora share
and borrow ideas. Microbraids, twists,
dredlocks, and goddess braids have become
practical alternatives to pressing or relaxing
kinky locks.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 622 ---
546 H AITI
Professional athletes and entertainers
who don Afrocentric hairstyles have in-
creased their fashionable popularity around
the world. For many, these styles reduce
negative associations generated in folk be-
lief of curly hair as badand straight styles as
good. A holdover from racial oppression,
social acceptance in many societies afforded
more privileges to blacks with straight hair.
Modern technologies in the eighteen and
nineteen hundreds made these styles read-
ily attainable. In the United States, African
Americans built fortunes in the hairdress-
ing trade. Marie Laveau, Annie Malone,
Anthony Overton, and C. J. Walker em-
ployed techniques that beautiﬁed black
hair. Walker, a woman, most noted for cre-
ating a line of hair growers, cosmetics, and
straightening combs, is celebrated as the
one of the ﬁrst self-made millionaires.

HAITI
Haiti, a country located on the western
part of the Caribbean island of Hispaniola,
with San Domingo on the east, is a former
French colony that achieved independence
in 1804. With the exception of pre-
Columbian times, the history of Haiti and
that of its African inhabitants are virtually
undistinguishable. T oday, about 90 percent
of the seven million Haitians are of pure
black ancestry (called authentiques, or
nègres), while the remaining 10 percent are
mulâtres (mulattos). The native Indian
population disappeared within forty years
of Christopher Columbus’s ﬁrst voyage in
1492; most European settlers ﬂed or were
executed shortly after the declaration of
independence in 1804.
The ﬁrst shipment of African slaves
arrived in Hispaniola in 1510. They and
their successors were put to work in the
mines and on plantations. Slave imports
continued throughout Spanish rule, partly as
a result of the local Indian population’s dwin-
dling numbers, partly to heed Spanish priest
Bartolome de las Casas’s advice that slavery
was a humane way to alleviate the Indians’
woes. But with the conquest of Mexico and
Peru, Hispaniola became a backwater area of
the Spanish Empire, and the number of
slaves stagnated at a few thousand in the
western part of the island.
The number of Africans living in the
island increased dramatically with France’s
takeover of the western third of Hispan-
iola, which was renamed Saint Domingue.
French smugglers and buccaneers had been
present in the island throughout the 1600s
(particularly at La T ortue), but the ofﬁcial
takeover took place at the T reaty of
Ryswick on September 20, 1697. The
French, initially reliant on hunting and pri-
vateering, soon turned to the cultivation of
sugarcane, coffee, cacao, indigo, bananas,
and cotton, most of which were then ex-
ported to Europe.
Since these crops were labor intensive,
the slave trade reached signiﬁcant propor-
tions, particularly during the late eigh-
teenth century. Numbering 4,000 in the
1720s, annual slave imports grew to
10,000 in 1771, 27,000 in 1786, and
40,000 in 1789. As a result of this rapidly
growing trade, according to Moreau de
Saint Méry, who visited Saint Domingue
on the eve of the revolution, 60 percent of
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 623 ---
HAITI 547
all French slaves in the Americas lived in
Saint Domingue by the 1780s; of those,
two-thirds were born in Africa. Slaves came
primarily from the Congo and Angola, fol-
lowed by modern-day Guinea, Nigeria, and
Ghana.
Since French women were in limited
supply, particularly in the early years of the
colony, miscegenation was widespread. As
described by Saint Méry, people of African
ancestry were classiﬁed according to a com-
plex taxonomy that held that each human
being’s blood is made of 128 equal parts
(corresponding to the number of great-
great-great-great-great grandparents). Based
on the content of white blood, Haitians
could be described as sacatra, griffe, marabout,
mulâtre, quarteron, métis, mamelouque,
quarteronné,or sang-mêlé(from blackest to
whitest, respectively).
The vast majority of Haitians were
slaves, numbering half a million by 1790.
They were theoretically regulated by the
relatively benevolent Code Noir, promul-
gated by Louis XIV in 1685; but, in prac-
tice, abuses ﬂourished as slaves were left at
the mercy of each individual planter. Nu-
merous accounts relate stories of slaves
being burned alive in boiling sugarcane, de-
voured by red ants, mutilated, and branded.
The need to constantly import new slaves
vividly illustrates the high death rate the
slaves suffered.
Despite the appalling cruelty, the slave
system proved economically efﬁcient, and
Haiti became France’s most profitable
colony, widely known as the Pearl of the
Antilles. Slaves enjoyed little of this pros-
perity, but free blacks and mulattos (ap-
proximately 30,000 people in 1790), many
of whom owned slaves, often rivaled whites
(about 20,000 people) in wealth. They
complained, however, that as their ranks
swelled in the eighteenth century, racial
discrimination turned them into second-
class citizens forced to provide free military
service, banned from many public positions,
and suffering from numerous inequities in
the courts. In 1791, Vincent Ogé led a
failed mulatto revolt that aimed at gaining
full citizenship rights.
As slaves came to outnumber the free
ten to one, resistance was always a feature
of colonial Saint Domingue. Some slaves
chose suicide; others marooned; others
poisoned their masters. In 1758, Mackandal,
a maroon and houngan (Voodoo priest),
organized a slave network that managed
to poison several hundred planters before
Mackandal was arrested and executed. The
largest, and only successful, revolt broke out
on August 21, 1791, when the Jamaican-born
slave and Voodoo priest Dutty Boukman
organized a ceremony at Bois Caïman,
outside Cap Français (today’s Cap Haïtien)
during which slaves vowed to revolt against
their masters. Over the following days, a
thousand planters were killed in the neigh-
boring plains, marking the beginning of
the Haitian war of independence.
The conﬂict, lasting until November
1803, pitted white planters nostalgic of the
old regime against French revolutionary
and Napoleonic troops, Spanish and
British expeditionary forces, slave armies
led by T oussaint Louverture, Jean-Jacques
Dessalines, and Henri Christophe, and
mulatto armies led by André Rigaud,
Alexandre Pétion, and Jean-Pierre Boyer
(actual alliances shifted over time). By the
time the victorious slaves declared the
country’s independence in January 1804,
renaming it Haiti in the process, at least
200,000 people had died in a conﬂict that
was particularly brutal even by the stan-
dards of the time. Most white Frenchmen
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 624 ---
548 H ALEY,A LEX
who had not ﬂed by that time were killed
in the spring of 1804.
Racial and national pride was high
after independence, as the former slaves
had defeated Spain, England, and France
(including 50,000 of Napoleon’s best
troops), then proceeded to found the ﬁrst
independent black republic in the world.
Revivals of such racial nationalism took
place in the 1930s with the Noirisme
movement, in the 1960s under François
Duvalier, and the 1990s under Jean-
Bertrand Aristide.
Independent rule, however, proved a
political and economic disappointment.
Haiti was ruled by a series of dictators, in-
cluding Henri Christophe (1807–1820),
Faustin Soulouque (1847–1859), François
Duvalier (1957–1971), and Jean-Claude
Duvalier (1971–1986). Political instability
was endemic, with 102 revolts, civil wars,
and revolutions from 1843 to 1915 alone.
Racial tensions persisted, as the black major-
ity (mostly poor, but frequently able to seize
the top ofﬁce) resented the economic and
political inﬂuence of the mulatto minority.
The United States occupied Haiti twice
(1915–1934, 1994–2000). Haiti, once the
richest colony in the Western Hemisphere, is
now the hemisphere’s poorest country (with
a per capita gross domestic product [GDP]
of approximately $400) and suffers from a
variety of development woes (AIDS, emigra-
tion, land erosion, cocaine trafﬁcking, polit-
ical stalemate, and child slavery).
Philippe R. Girard

HALEY,A LEX (1921–1992)
Alex Haley was an African American author
of the landmark texts The Autobiography of
Malcolm X (with Malcolm X) and Roots.
Alexander Murray Palmer Haley was born in
Ithaca, New York, on August 11, 1921. He
spent his childhood in Henning, T ennessee,
before enlisting in the Coast Guard in 1939.
Haley began writing short stories in his early
twenties and eventually became chief
Scenes from the television miniseries,Roots, based on

television miniseries and the book brought stories of
African American life during and after the era of slavery
into American popular culture. It remains among the
most-watched programs in the history of television.

journalist of the Coast Guard before retiring
in 1959. Haley then began a career as an au-
thor, working as a feature writer for Reader’s
Digest and Playboy. In 1965, he wrote his
ﬁrst book, The Autobiography of Malcolm X:
As T old to Alex Haley, which was translated
into eight languages and made Haley an in-

Made into a television miniseries in 1977,
Roots was at the time the highest rated pro-

which chronicle the history of African
Americans in the antebellum United States.
Queen is Haley’s attempt to tell the story of
his paternal ancestors. He died of a heart at-
tack in Seattle on February 10, 1992.

HANSBERRY,L ORRAINE
(1930–1969)
Lorraine Hansberry was an African Ameri-
can female dramatist, activist, and educator,
and the author of A Raisin in the Sun, the
ﬁrst play by an African American woman to
reach Broadway. Lorraine Vivian Hansberry’s
work was the by-product of a protest tradition
that took root in the 1940s. She was born in
Chicago on May 19, 1930, to Nannie Perry,
a former schoolteacher and Republican ward
committeewoman; and Carl Hansberry, an
inventor and former U.S. deputy marshal
who later ran for Congress. Her family lived
in a segregated ghetto of Chicago—the
setting of A Raisin in the Sun (1959)—since
rigid housing segregation confined all
blacks to the same neighborhood regardless
of economic status. The reality of American
racism also hit Hansberry in the Jim Crow
grade schools she attended, and, in 1948,
at the University of Wisconsin, Madison,
where she fell victim to restrictive housing
policies. So, rather than ﬁnd shelter and
comfort within personal luxuries, Hansberry
developed a dramatic vision that dealt with
Lorraine Hansberry, a playwright and civil rights
activist, wrote the ﬁrst play by an African American
woman to appear on Broadway. (Library of Congress)

550 H ANSBERRY,L ORRAINE
African American themes, but she did not
restrict her focus to this subject.
Hansberry was deeply inﬂuenced by
her parents’ promotion of race pride, com-
mitment to civil rights programs, and in-
volvement with the NAACP and the Urban
League. Although she was acquainted with
political movements at her family home,
Hansberry’s personal political life began in
1948 when she was a student at the Univer-
sity of Wisconsin. She came in contact
with political groups, one of which was the
Young Progressives of America (YPA), and
joined the campus chapter of YPA in 1949.
Dissatisﬁed with the educational prospects
offered by the University of Wisconsin, she
departed for New York where, between
1950 and 1963, Harlem offered a huge in-
tellectual and cultural attraction. The cul-
tural and artistic consciousness promoted
by the Harlem Renaissance, about thirty
years earlier, still seemed to have a powerful
pull on the community.
During her Harlem years, especially
1961 through 1964, Hansberry spoke at an-
tiracist street corner rallies and marched in
picket lines. In 1964, while hospitalized in
failing health, she completed the text for a
photographic document on the Civil Rights
Movement titled The Movement: Documen-
tary of a Struggle for Equality(1964).
In 1951, Hansberry joined the staff of
Freedom, a monthly newspaper founded the
same year in New York by renowned black
actor, Paul Robeson. The paper became a
voice of, and political weapon for, the
masses of blacks and all progressive Ameri-
cans. Hansberry remained on the staff of
the magazine for nearly ﬁve years. Aside
from encouraging Hansberry’s commitment
to desegregation and equal opportunity,
Robeson aroused her interest in African af-
fairs and, between 1951 and 1953, she
wrote a number of articles that focused on
reconciling Africa and black America.
Through the offices of Freedom
Hansberry met with and had lengthy dis-
cussions with students and politicians from
Southern Africa, Kenya, Ghana, Sierra
Leone, and Nigeria. In the early 1950s,
when the ofﬁces of the Council on African
Affairs were located in the same building as
Freedom, Hansberry maintained close con-
tact with Robeson, W . E. B. Du Bois, and
distinguished Africans, all of whom had a
powerful political, intellectual, and philo-
sophical impact on her dramatic vision.
When, therefore, Africa is encountered
in Hansberry’s drama, the reference is sup-
ported by her genuine interest and pro-
found research on the arts, histories, poli-
tics, and traditions of a number of its major
ethnic groups. Rejecting the notion of
Africa as an obscure region, Hansberry be-
came more emotionally attached to the
continent in the 1950s when, because of its
independence struggles, it had become
more visible in black American literature
and politics.
In two of her works, A Raisin in the Sun
and Les Blancs (1970), Africa materializes as
a direct aesthetic and sociopolitical symbol,
while in a third play, The Drinking Gourd
(1960), Africa emerges indirectly through
oral traditions. In spite of the angle through
which it is presented, Africa is either con-
jured as a distant myth or as a tangible
socio-geographic setting in relation to a
number of related subjects. These include
the essence of the region to Hansberry, its
political and cultural relevance, relations be-
tween Africans and African Americans, and
the adaptation of African values that serve
key theatrical and cultural roles.
A Raisin in the Sun marked the begin-
ning of a more confrontational era in the
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 627 ---
HANSBERRY,L ORRAINE 551
black theater. In the play, Hansberry calls
on Africans and diasporic blacks to develop
the sense of belonging to a cohesive family.
Set in the South Side slums of Chicago, the
play is about the economic and social ef-
fects of racism on members of the Younger
family who strive to attain fulﬁllment
through singular aspirations. Against this
background, the play is structured on African
images and family values that recapture this
inﬂuence.
A direct reference to Africa is reached
through the Nigerian character, Asagai,
who represents the ﬁrst appearance of an
intellectual African as a major character in
black American drama. Asagai introduces a
relatively new insight on Africa. Through
him Hansberry creates a particularized
African whom she uses to dissipate the
myth that Africa does not accept its descen-
dants in America.
At the other extreme is George
Murchison, the African American who
spurns Africa. He personiﬁes those conven-
tional and uninformed facts about Africa
that are still largely predictable, and is the
classic victim of cultural rape. Irrespective
of how laudable some of the images of
Africa are in A Raisin, Hansberry does not
romanticize the yearning for a culturally
rich, viable, and spiritual homeland. In the
end, Africa also surfaces as a background
afﬂicted by political and neocolonial weak-
nesses that have existed for generations,
many of which continue to exist.
Hansberry began drafting Les Blancs
(The Whites) as early as 1960. But it was
not until 1970 that Robert Nemiroff, her
ex-husband, put together the published
version of the play. In Les Blancs Hansberry
expands on the attention given to Africa in
A Raisin. The play is the ﬁrst major play by
an African American to translate into
dramatic form the European exploitation
of the lands and peoples of Africa, and the
ensuing rebellion against European rule.
WhenLes Blancswas drafted in 1960, African
nationalist movements had assumed vast
and powerful proportions.
In recreating an African colonial scene
in the play, Hansberry advances the need
for dialogue between the oppressed and the
oppressor, yet insists on action and com-
mitment, and advocates the attainment
of sovereignty at any cost. The play does
not resolve any issue but raises thought-
provoking questions about history, Africa,
America, anger, and confrontation. Hansberry
ﬁnally argues for humanism even as she
visualizes the genesis of a new black world
and directs her themes through a predomi-
nantly African historical and socio-artistic
experience.
African-based folklore, customary
practices, chanting, drumming, and danc-
ing in Les Blancs energize the action and
tempo of the plot, heighten the tone and
moods disseminated through dialogue,
and celebrate indigenous African practices.
Herein lies the peculiarity of Hansberry’s
dramatic vision: her success at re-evoking
and reenacting history through an essen-
tially Western model, yet ritualizing and
mythologizing history through the use of
certain African cultural and folkloric para-
digms. Like A Raisin, Les Blancs expands
thematically, ﬁnally addressing global con-
cerns along with black issues within and
beyond Africa.
Without making direct references to
Africa in The Drinking Gourd, Hansberry
exploits African-based aesthetic and indige-
nous forms by using folk material for con-
temporary dramatic creativity. Whereas
characterization and setting sustain a tangi-
ble African presence in A Raisin and

Les Blancs, the crux of Drinking Gourd lies
in Hansberry’s ability to recapture African
sensibilities within an ancestral oral experi-
ence. Published a year after A Raisin, Drink-
ing Gourd shifts from issues of the family,
integration, and colonialism to the rele-
vance of communal art and slave freedom.
The recreation of a slave world in Drinking
Gourd is anchored to a folk background and
group consciousness that are fortiﬁed by the
components of folk article. This folk idiom
is realized in music, song, and dance-drama.
As she keeps slave history alive, Hansberry
also highlights the rich musical tradition
arising out of this history.
Movement, music, folksongs, spiritu-
als, and folklore are thus used to reinvigo-
rate the overall tone of Drinking Gourd. Al-
though African American like African
drama has steered from its rudimentary
source, the innovative importance of folk
material has not been lost. In Drinking
Gourd this truth is apparent in a musical
tradition where song, music, and dance are
tools for the type of group participation
that strengthens communal bonding, espe-
cially in the face of a crisis. Action and
rhythm are direct results of dance and
music in the play, and unfold not only as
key elements of folk drama but as factors
that intensify the themes and overall the-
atricality of the play.
Because she invokes Africa from differ-
ent perspectives, Hansberry has succeeded
in opening up a channel through which
several themes affecting Africans and
African Americans are inquired into. Be-
yond her appreciation of the region, she is
able to tap aesthetically from it and exploit
thematic and stylistic elements commonly
absent from white plays of the same period.
In the end, and in spite of her initial
and precise attention to African American
life, Hansberry’s drama is not restricted to
this motif. T rue, Africa is artistically and
culturally symbolic. But while nurturing
the sociopolitical well-being of blacks,
Hansberry’s plays also serve as a metaphor
for surveying broad-based human issues.
Phillip Efﬁong

HARLEM RENAISSANCE
The Harlem Renaissance, also called New
Negro movement, refers to the period of out-
standing literary and artistic creativity among
African Americans between the 1920s and
the mid-1930s. It was centered in the vast
black residential area of Harlem, New York
City, where emerging African American writ-
ers produced works imbued with a new-
found racial pride. Writers associated with
the Harlem Renaissance deﬁed both literary
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 629 ---
HARLEM RENAISSANCE 553
conventions set by white authors and the two
earlier African American literary types—the
writing of the plantation tradition and the
black dialect poetry. Instead, they portrayed
black American life and culture based on the
philosophy of Pan-Africanism. Some writers
also adopted the rhythms of the spirituals,
blues, and jazz in their works to reﬂect dis-
tinctly black ethos.
The Harlem Renaissance writers were
mentored by several prominent black intel-
lectuals. W . E. B. Du Bois—one of the
founders of the National Association for
the Advancement of Colored People
(NAACP), author of The Souls of Black
Folk (1903), and editor for The Crisis—
advocated black racial pride through redis-
covering the cultural heritage of Africa. Par-
ticularly inspiring to younger black writers
was his idea of the duality of the African
American identity: “One ever feels his two-
ness—an American, a Negro; two souls,
two thoughts, two unreconciled strivings;
two warring ideals in one dark body, whose
dogged strength alone keeps it from being
torn asunder” (Du Bois, 1903, p. 9). James
Weldon Johnson preﬁgured the Harlem
Renaissance with his celebrated novel The
Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man
(1912), which invoked Du Bois’ idea of
“two-ness.” Johnson is best remembered for
his God’s Trombones (1927), which com-
prises seven black sermons in free verse.
Founder of the Universal Negro Improve-
ment Association and leader of the “back-
to-Africa” movement, Marcus Garvey pro-
moted black separatism. His philosophy
was conveyed to younger black writers
through his newspapers, the Negro World
and the Blackman. Alain Locke edited The
New Negro: An Interpretation (1925), a
landmark anthology of the Renaissance, for
which he contributed several critical essays
offering new directions for black American
writing. The Renaissance was also signiﬁ-
cantly supported by white donors and writ-
ers including Carl Van Vechten, author of
the novel Nigger Heaven (1926).
Although the Harlem Renaissance
writers never formed a uniﬁed school, they
generally explored in their works the es-
trangement of African Americans, the kin-
ship of blacks in all continents, and the
beauty of blackness. Countee Cullen at-
tracted critical attention to the Renaissance
with his compendium Caroling Dusk: An
Anthology of Verse by Negro Poets (1927).
Cullen also published the poetry collec-
tions Color (1925) and Copper Sun (1927)
and the novel One Way to Heaven (1931),
all of which reflect his radical self-
consciousness. Langston Hughes published
his ﬁrst collection of verse, The Weary Blues,
in 1926, and his novel Not Without Laughter
in 1930. Among his well-known works are
the poems “The Negro Speaks of Rivers”
(1921) and “I, T oo” (1932) and the critical
essay “The Negro Artist and the Racial
Movement” (1925). An immigrant from
Jamaica and follower of Garveyism, Claude
McKay is noted for his collection of verse
Harlem Shadows (1922) and the novel
Home to Harlem (1928). These and his
other works reﬂect his racial pride, left-wing
ideology, and anticolonialism. Jean T oomer
authored Cane (1923)—an experimental
work blending the forms of fiction,
sketches, poetry, and drama—which ex-
plores black American experiences and the
ambiguous identity of diasporic blacks on
American soil. Wallace Thurman was a
unique ﬁgure in his critical perspective on
the New Negro movement. His novels The
Blacker the Berry: A Novel of Negro Life
(1929) and Infants of the Spring (1932) sat-
irized the excesses of the Harlem Renaissance.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

554 H AUSA (PEOPLE)
Thurman also collaborated with William
Jourden Rapp on the play Harlem (1929).
Zora Neale Hurston’s novel Their Eyes
Were Watching God came out in 1937,
which some critics contend marked the
ﬁnal year of the New Negro movement. Ac-
cording to other critics, the movement
ended in 1940 with the publication of
Langston Hughes’ autobiography The Big
Sea and Claude McKay’s treatise Harlem:
Negro Metropolis. Either way, with the ar-
rival of the Great Depression in 1929, fund-
ing from white sponsors decreased and
Harlem was unable to continue to sustain
its status as the heart of black American cre-
ativity. The Harlem Renaissance was instru-
mental in the development of cultural black
nationalism and the Black Arts Movement.

HAUSA (PEOPLE)
The Hausa are the principal inhabitants of
the northern regions of Nigeria, which is
often referred to as Hausaland or the Hausa
States. There are also signiﬁcant numbers
of Hausa in Benin, Cameroon, Ghana,
Niger, and as far away as Sudan. There is no
clear-cut deﬁnition for who belongs to the
Hausa ethnic group. This designation may
derive from a single attribute as well as a
combination of attributes, namely, those
people whose family can be traced to tradi-
tional Hausa bloodlines, those who speak
Hausa as a primary language, individuals
who are acculturated or assimilated into
Hausa life and religion, or those who sim-
ply have roots in Hausaland (no matter
their original ethnicity). Hausas make up
the largest ethnic group in West Africa and
have migrated throughout the region. Eth-
nicity is passed from the father to his chil-
dren, which has allowed Hausa traders to
marry in distant lands and spread their cul-
ture and language. Over 35 million people
speak Hausa as a ﬁrst or second language,
and it is used extensively as a language of
trade and commerce throughout parts of
the Sudanic region.
The Hausa are mainly Muslims. Islam
has played a signiﬁcant role in their soci-
etal development as well as the Hausa lan-
guage, which borrows heavily from Arabic.
Islam most likely came to Hausaland in
the fourteenth century, but did not gain a
strong foothold until the ﬁfteenth and six-
teenth centuries. At about this time, Hausa
legend describes the establishment of the
original Hausa states: Daura, Garun
Gabas, Gobir, Kano, Katsina, Rano, and
Zazzau. Despite their common language
and history the Hausa states were dis-
united for various political and economic
reasons. The squabbling between states al-
lowed neighboring kingdoms, such as Song-
hay and Bornu, to claim the Hausa as part
of their empires or at least as vassal states.
In the early nineteenth century, the Fulani
inhabitants of Hausaland, led by Uthman
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 631 ---
HEAD,B ESSIE 555
dan Fodio, engaged in a prolonged jihad
against the rulers of the Hausa states. The
jihad was not directed at converting the
Hausa, who were already Muslim, but
rather at realigning the rulers’ Islamic prac-
tices toward a more orthodox interpreta-
tion. After Hausaland was under the con-
trol of dan Fodio, the Sokoto Caliphate
was established and Hausaland was united
under a local central government for the
ﬁrst time in its history.
One result of the jihads and decades
of further internal and external warfare
was that many Hausa prisoners of war
were enslaved and sent to various parts of
Africa and the Americas. The Hausa were
guilty of similar practices toward their en-
emies. T races of the Hausa presence in the
New World are found throughout the
Americas, but their legacy is particularly
well documented in Brazil. The Hausas
are known to have played a role in several
Brazilian slave uprisings, most notably the
1835 revolt in Bahia where African Mus-
lims of many ethnicities banded together
in a failed attempt to overthrow the slave
system.
Brent Singleton

HEAD,B ESSIE (1937–1986)
Bessie Head was a South African-born nov-
elist and essayist who lived and wrote from
living in exile in Botswana. Born on July 6,
1937, Head was an unwanted girl of a scan-
dalous union between a middle-class white
woman and unknown black man. Whereas
people in the United States were racially di-
vided into two groups, white and nonwhite
(or colored), under the strict system of
racial segregation based on appearance,
social acceptance, and descent, South
Africans were classiﬁed into three groups,
white, black (Africans), and colored. The
colored referred to mixed race and included
Indians and Asians. Because of her mixed
heritage and English-speaking colonial ed-
ucation, Head experienced not only racism
but also alienation from a predominantly
Afrikaans-speaking colored community. In
1964, after an unsuccessful marriage, Head
moved into Serowe, Botswana, with her
son and lived in exile. She suffered from
chronic insomnia, nightmares, and halluci-
nations and struggled with poverty, injus-
tice, and oppression throughout her life. By
reﬂecting psychologically traumatic experi-
ences in a racist and sexist society, Head’s
novels, When Rain Clouds Gather (1969),
Maru (1971), and the autobiographical A
Question of Power (1974), subtly embody
her creatively complex vision of Pan-
African community beyond racial, class,
national, and gender boundaries. In the short
stories of The Collector of Treasures (1977),
drawing upon her research on precolonial
Africa and oral tradition in Serowe, Head
richly portrays ordinary village people and
the strange complexities of everyday life in
relation to larger historical events, political
struggle, religious conﬂict, traditional cul-
tural values, and modern development. In a
powerless social position as an exile colored
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 632 ---
556 H EALTH,P UBLIC
woman, Head powerfully engages in a di-
alectical investigation of the colonial history
and cultural representation to reconstruct a
new cultural identity, one that provides a
sense of belonging and a vision for a hope-
ful African future. On April 17, 1986,
Head died of hepatitis and was buried in
Serowe.
