HEALTH,P UBLIC
Public health is the science and practice of
protecting and improving the health of a
community. In the early nineteenth century,
life expectancy in the healthiest countries was
slightly higher than forty years, while the un-
healthiest countries’ life expectancy was in
the low twenties. A “mortality revolution”
occurred in Europe and North America, at
ﬁrst due to improvements in agricultural
production and transportation which pre-
vented localized famines, and then later
from improvements in public sanitation,
and ﬁnally from modern antibiotics. Life ex-
pectancy in these nations increased from
46 years in 1900 to 70 years in 1950. The
world’s richest countries today are converg-
ing on a life expectancy between 75 and 80
years. Likewise, life expectancy in sub-
Saharan Africa increased to 50 years in
1990, a 36 percent increase from 1950.
Since 1990, however, life expectancy in sub-
Saharan Africa has decreased to 46.5 years,
primarily due to HIV/AIDS. Sub-Saharan
Africa ranks last in the other major metric of
public health—maternal mortality—where
hemorrhage and sepsis are the leading causes
of maternal death. Although South America
on average has better public health statistical
measures, there are important issues of in-
equality across nations and within societies,
usually along racial and urban/rural divides.
Historically, the epidemiology of Africa
has shaped relations between Africa and the
Americas. Disease vectors systemic to tropi-
cal Africa prevented North American and
European colonial expansion and settlement
in tropical Africa until the late nineteenth
and early twentieth centuries. Conversely,
the resistance of Africans to Eurasian dis-
eases made possible their exploitation for
slave labor when these diseases decimated
native American populations. T ransatlantic
voyages and the production of sugar and its
related products led to the emergence of yel-
low fever and malaria as diseases limiting the
growth of European colonies in the tropical
regions of the Americas. In the twenty-ﬁrst
century, U.S. government policies and in-
ternational organizations have a substantial
role in shaping the future of public health
worldwide.
Controversy exists over the cause of
disparities in life expectancy between
North America and Africa. Some attribute
this gap to unique ecological conditions
and the lack of economic development.
Others focus on aspects of European colo-
nialism and relationships of economic de-
pendency as factors which create these poor
health conditions.
Epidemiologically, Africans, with the
notable exception of the Khoisan near the
Cape of Good Hope, shared the primary
diseases of the Eurasian peoples and thus
were not decimated like the Americans and
aborigines of Australia upon their initial
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 633 ---
HEALTH,P UBLIC 557
contact with Eurasians. The most promi-
nent of these diseases were smallpox,
measles, bubonic plague, cholera, and tu-
berculosis, all of which historically ravaged
populations in Africa, as they did in Eura-
sia. At the same time, the tropical zones of
Africa contained diseases not prevalent in
North America and Europe; the most sig-
niﬁcant of these diseases were malaria, try-
panosomiasis, and lymphatic ﬁlariasis.
T ropical Africa’s mosquitoes are the
most effective transmitters of malaria in
the world. More than 95 percent of infec-
tive bites in tropical Africa are from three
species of anthropophilic mosquitoes,
whose traits enable them to thrive in a wide
variety of tropical conditions.
The parasite that causes malaria comes
in three groupings of species. The parasites
enter liver cells, multiply for ﬁve to ﬁfteen
days, and then enter the bloodstream and
invade red blood cells. They rupture the red
blood cells, reenter the bloodstream, and
invade other red blood cells. At this stage,
the ﬁrst symptoms of fever, chills, and nau-
sea appear.
In malaria-endemic regions, children are
inevitably infected. Those who survive past
age ﬁve acquire apparent immunity, al-
though many suffer from neurocognitive se-
quelae and anemia. The parasite remains in
the liver, but the person suffers no severe clin-
ical symptoms as long as reinfection comes
from the same parasitical species. Areas of
unstable transmission may suffer malaria epi-
demics with high mortality, since even adults
may lose their acquired immunity. Shifts
in climate, movements of populations, or
human-induced environmental changes may
all introduce or reintroduce a species of the
parasite and a vector to an area.
People in malaria-endemic regions of
Africa have high rates of sickle cell and
thalassemia traits because these and other
genetic adaptations provide some protec-
tion against malaria. The sickle cell trait is
recessive, meaning that when both parents
have the sickle cell trait, there is a 25 per-
cent chance that the child will not have
the trait, a 50 percent chance the child
will have the trait, and a 25 percent
chance that the child will have a sickle cell
disorder. Sickle cell disorders often result
in death in childhood or early adulthood.
The World Health Organization (WHO)
in 1983 estimated that 100,000 infants
were born annually with sickle cell disease
in Africa, 1,500 in the United States,
1,600 in the Caribbean, 140 in the United
Kingdom, and 4,000 in South America.
In malaria-endemic regions, children with
a sickle-cell disorder rarely survive to
adulthood because the disorder (as opposed
to the trait) weakens resistance to malaria.
The absence of sickle-cell disorders in adult
Africans led some North American and
European medical researchers in the early
twentieth century to assume that sickle
cell disorders were the result of the mixture
of races in their countries, a reﬂection on
the dominance of racial theories in science
of that time.
Medical improvements for people of
European descent in tropical regions in the
ﬁrst half of the nineteenth century con-
sisted primarily in the use of quinine for
treatment and prophylaxis of malaria, re-
ducing exposure to mosquitoes by choosing
bases with higher elevation or anchoring
ships farther from shore, and eliminating
harmful medical practices such as bloodlet-
ting and mercury, which exacerbated
malarial dehydration, and administering
opium. The development of effective anti-
malarial drugs was given great urgency
during World War II, when many Allied
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

soldiers entered malaria-endemic areas.
Chloroquine, Primaquine, Proguanil, (all
brand names), as well as amodiaquine, and
sulfadoxine/pyrimethamine were devel-
oped during this time, and they are still
widely used to treat those who can access
them upon the development of symptoms
or as prophylaxis.
The World Health Organization
launched a malaria eradication program in
1955 using dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane
(DDT) but excluded Africa, arguing that
the local health infrastructure was inade-
quate to support the program. This program
greatly reduced the impact of malaria in
other regions, but environmental concerns
associated with DDT have curtailed these
vector-eradication programs. In the ﬁrst
decade of the twenty-ﬁrst century, malaria
has reemerged in areas where spraying was
halted.
As of 2006, an estimated 1.5–2.7
million people worldwide die annually from
malaria, primarily children in Africa. An-
other 500 million are infected. Estimated
yearly economic loss due to malaria is about
$12 billion, accounting for a crippling
1.3 percent annual loss in GDP growth in
endemic countries. The 2000 Abuja Targets
included increasing the percentage of chil-
dren with access to effective treatment
within 24 hours of the onset of symptoms,
increasing the number of children and preg-
nant women using insecticide-treated nets,
increasing the number of pregnant women
with access to appropriate malaria chemo-
prophylaxis or presumptive intermittent
treatment, and detecting epidemics within
two weeks of onset and responding within
two weeks of detection. Despite increasing
parasitic resistance to many of the ﬁrst-line
antimalarials, the main barrier to ﬁghting
malaria in sub-Saharan Africa is systemic,
not technical. Human resources develop-
ment, ﬁnancial investments, and systemwide
initiatives to increase the reach, coverage,
and equity of essential services to meet the
Millennium Development Goals developed
by the United Nations will require an esti-
mated $40–60 billion annually. Meeting
the more modest Abuja targets will require
$1 billion per year. Current spending is
$200 million per year.
The public health community has
shifted away from the search for the “magic
bullet,” single-disease, approach because of
its failure to develop the health infrastruc-
ture of trained assistants, local dispensaries,
and usable and transferable skills. The
WHO Alma Ata Conference of 1978 rec-
ommended that public health programs
demonstrate equitable distribution, com-
munity involvement, a focus on preven-
tion, appropriate technology, and a multi-
sectoral approach.
Yellow fever is caused by a virus trans-
mitted by the mosquito Aëdes aegypti, the
anthropophilic variety of which breeds in
open containers of water. Symptoms of se-
vere infection begin three to six days after
infection. These include high fever, chills,
headache, muscle aches, vomiting, and
backache. After a brief recovery period, the
infection can lead to shock, bleeding, and
kidney and liver failure. Liver failure causes
jaundice (yellowing of the skin and the
whites of the eyes), which gives yellow fever
its name. The mosquito lives up to four
months, but it cannot ﬂy more than 100
yards. Urban epidemics thus spread slowly,
one street at a time. T o survive, the virus
needs a number of nonimmunes within its
vector’s ﬂight range.
Some researchers believe that the ﬁrst
written record of yellow fever are Mayan
texts describing cases of the disease occurring
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 635 ---
HEALTH,P UBLIC 559
in the 1480s. Researchers disagree over
whether the virus’s origin is African or
American, but it seems that the migration
of Aëdes aegypti westward across the
Atlantic, presumably through the slave
trade, spread this more effective vector for
the virus. Yet, the ﬁrst conﬁrmed yellow fever
epidemic occurred in 1648 in Guadeloupe
and in Yucatan in Mexico, and the ﬁrst
recorded African epidemic occurred in
1778. As of 2006, Aëdes aegypti has never
appeared in Asia and Australia, leading
some researchers to posit that sugar produc-
tion was the third piece of the puzzle in the
development of yellow fever as an epidemic
urban disease. Aëdes aegypti can survive and
reproduce on a diet of sugar. The seven-
teenth-century Caribbean sugar production
process provided year-around sucrose and
open containers of water which enabled the
population of Aëdes aegypti to thrive in the
cities of the American tropics.
Children under the age of fourteen in
endemic regions generally survived yellow
fever and thereby gained lifetime immu-
nity, so it quickly became known as a dis-
ease of immigrants and strangers. Because
of its life span, it was able to survive
transatlantic voyages on sugar-laden ships
and cause outbreaks throughout the Atlantic
region. European army garrisons were thus
perfect populations for yellow fever epi-
demics, best illustrated by the decimation
of the French army sent to Saint Domingue
to suppress Haitian independence. Of the
59,000 soldiers sent to Haiti between 1791
and 1803, only 10,000 returned to France,
with yellow fever being the chief cause of
casualties.
Aëdes aegypti mosquitoes infected with
the yellow fever virus caused outbreaks in
port cities in the United States, the last one
being an outbreak in New Orleans in 1905.
These outbreaks were often occasions to
reinforce color lines or restrictions against
immigrants. During the 1793 yellow fever
epidemic in Philadelphia, the city’s European
American inhabitants called on the free
African Americans to provide medical per-
sonnel and other needed services, claiming
that Africans had a resistance to the disease.
Despite African Americans’ succumbing to
the disease at nearly the same rate as others,
accusations that they exploited whites dur-
ing the epidemic poisoned the city’s racial
climate years afterwards.
Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, experienced yel-
low fever epidemics throughout the second
half of the nineteenth century. Medical
experts were divided into two camps, those
infectionists who believed the disease was
contagious and those who believed the dis-
ease originated from local environmental
causes. The infectionist position generated
support for ending the importation of slaves.
European immigrants experienced
such high mortality that Brazilians believed
that yellow fever was deterring Europeans
from immigrating. As slave importation
ceased and emancipation approached,
Brazilians in the late 1800s hoped that
increased European immigration would
“whiten” the country. Local governments
cleared away large areas of lower-income
housing from downtown Rio de Janeiro in
their efforts to limit yellow fever epidemics.
Even though smallpox, tuberculosis, and
cholera killed Afro-Brazilians in large num-
bers, no public health efforts were made to
alleviate these diseases.
The demographics of the British
colonies in North America and the
Caribbean and the struggle to complete
the Panama Canal illustrate the impact of
the combination of malaria and yellow
fever in the American tropics. If European
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 636 ---
560 H EALTH,P UBLIC
migrants to the Caribbean had multiplied
at the same rate as their counterparts in
North America, the population of the British
West Indies in 1760 would have outnum-
bered the 1.7 million North Americans by
nearly 1.3 million.
Dr. William Gorgas, who led military
public health efforts during the U.S. occu-
pation of Cuba in 1898 and the construc-
tion of the Panama Canal in the ﬁrst
decade of the 1900s, estimated that the
French lost 22,189 laborers from 1881 to
1889 before giving up on the project. It
was only through extreme martial-law san-
itation measures in the canal zone, based
on the late nineteenth-century identiﬁca-
tion of the mosquito as a disease vector,
that the United States was able to complete
the canal.
Yellow fever is endemic today in tropi-
cal Africa and South America. The exis-
tence of an effective vaccine has reduced its
mortality. South American countries have
achieved an 80–90 percent coverage rate
with the vaccination, while most African
nations’ rates are less than 40 percent. 
T rypanosomiasis, or sleeping sickness,
was recorded by the fourteenth-century
historian Ibn Khaldun, who wrote that
lethargy killed Sultan Djata of the King-
dom of Mali. A mosquito of the Glossina
species (commonly know as the tsetse ﬂy)
transmits trypanosome, a parasite, to
human and bovines. After infection, a
chancre, a painful red sore, develops.
Within one to four weeks, symptoms ap-
pear such as fever, severe headache, irri-
tability, extreme tiredness, swollen lymph
glands, aching muscles and joints, weight
loss, body rash, confusion, personality
changes, slurred speech, seizures, and difﬁ-
culty in walking and talking. Left un-
treated, the patient dies.
From the 1920s, colonial governments
began devoting resources to the control of
trypanosomiasis. Despite inadequate fund-
ing, incorrect understanding of the disease,
and the reluctance of pharmaceutical com-
panies to support research into new drugs
to combat the increasing resistance of the
parasites to the older drugs, sustained sur-
veillance and control almost eliminated the
disease by 1965. In 2000, disruption of
health services due to war, population
movement, and ecological devastation
caused a resurgence of the disease. Mortal-
ity estimates from the former Zaire equal or
exceed those of the 1920s. The World
Health Organization estimates that 55–60
million people are at risk of infection, yet
only 4 million have access to health centers
with reliable diagnostic capability.
The East African trypanosomiasis epi-
demics of the early twentieth century pro-
vided the earliest arguments for those who
emphasized human culpability in high
African disease rates. Colonial restrictions
on gun use and hunting and declining culti-
vation due to colonial government labor de-
mands expanded habitats for the tsetse ﬂy
and other wild animals. Poorer nutrition due
to the abandonment of food crops in order
to grow the cash crops necessary to pay colo-
nial taxes left populations exposed to sleep-
ing sickness and inﬂuenza after WWI.
Trypanosoma cruzi is a related parasite
endemic in areas of tropical South America.
When it infects a human host through the
bite of Reduvidae bugs, it causes Chagas
disease, also known as American try-
panosomiasis. More than 10 million people
are afﬂicted with the disease and 100 mil-
lion people are at risk. Approximately 10
percent may die in the acute stage of the
disease. Those whose cases progress to a
chronic stage die prematurely, primarily
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 637 ---
HEALTH,P UBLIC 561
due to cardiac complications. Existing drug
treatments have severe side effects. Some
Latin American countries have vector con-
trol programs using insecticides with
pyretroids.
Lymphatic ﬁlariasis, caused by the par-
asite Wuchereria bancrofti, is also spread by
mosquitoes. The parasite damages the
lymph system, causing ﬂuid to collect and
arms, breasts, legs, and male genitalia to
swell. The resulting hardening and thicken-
ing of the skin is called elephantiasis. It also
reduces immunity to other infections.
Lymphatic ﬁlariasis annually infects 120
million people and causes 5 million lose
disability adjusted life years (DALY), sur-
passed only by malaria and tuberculosis.
The WHO has recommended apply-
ing annual single-dose mass chemotherapy
with a combination of two drugs (chosen
from among diethylcarbamazine, ivermectin,
and albendazole) to entire endemic com-
munities for the duration of the mean
reproductive lifespan of the adult worm,
believed to be four to six years. This would
eliminate the parasite from the area, as
these drugs eliminate the microﬁlaria from
the blood of infected people, and hence
mosquitoes would not become infected
when they bit humans. Some researchers
believe that a vector control program
should accompany the chemotherapy and
continue afterwards.
Some of public health’s greatest suc-
cesses in Africa have been the reduction in
polio, the use of oral rehydration therapy
(ORT) to prevent death from diarrhea, and
the use of invermectin to treat onchocerci-
asis. While polio is still transmitted in sub-
Saharan Africa, immunization is widespread.
Worldwide, cases have declined by 95 per-
cent. A recent setback took place in northern
Nigeria when some Muslim religious ﬁgures
urged people not to have their children
immunized, claiming that the immuniza-
tions were designed to sterilize the children
and spread AIDS. Later, in 2004, outbreaks
of polio occurred in that region and have
since spread to other countries.
ORT is a simple solution of sugar,
salts, and water mixed in proper propor-
tions to prevent death by diarrheal dehy-
dration. World health experts in the late
1970s estimated that the approximately
500 million annual episodes of diarrhea in
children under the age of ﬁve resulted in at
least ﬁve million deaths. Physicians in the
developed world used intravenous solu-
tions that would not work in the ﬁeld con-
ditions of the developing world. Various re-
searchers throughout the twentieth century
identiﬁed components of what would even-
tually become ORT , but the medical estab-
lishment in Europe and North America was
dismissive of oral liquid treatments and
held on to an improper understanding of
diarrhea and recommended a “starvation”
or fasting therapy. An international group
of researchers and clinicians in East
Pakistan (later Bangladesh), many of whom
were afﬁliated with U.S. institutions, devel-
oped ORT and tested it in the terrible con-
ditions of the Bangladesh War of Indepen-
dence in 1971. The developing world
adopted the technology quickly and re-
duced dramatically mortality from diar-
rheal dehydration. Although cholera is not
the only cause of diarrhea, the adoption of
ORT has dramatically reduced the lethality
of cholera epidemics.
Onchocerciasis, or river blindness, is
caused by infection with Onchocerca volvulus,
a parasitic worm living in the human body.
Adult female worms live for up to ﬁfteen
years. They produce millions of micro-
scopic larvae (microﬁlaria), which migrate
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 638 ---
562 H EALTH,P UBLIC
to subcutaneous (just beneath the skin) tis-
sue. Upon death, they cause skin rashes, le-
sions, intense itching, and skin depigmen-
tation. They also migrate to the eye and
cause visual impairment and blindness. In-
fected blackﬂies (Simulium spp.) transmit
immature larval forms of the worms from
human to human. Onchocerciasis is found
in thirty-ﬁve countries; 99 percent of in-
fected people live in twenty-eight nations
in tropical Africa. The disease results in an
estimated one million DALY annually.
Merck, Sharpe, and Dohme (MSD),
which developed invermectin for veterinary
medicine, collaborated with WHO, the
Special Programme for Research and T rain-
ing in T ropical Disease (TDR), and the
Onchocerciasis Control Program in West
Africa (OCP) to research if invermectin
would be as effective against Onchocerca
volvulus as it was against a parasite found in
horses, Onchocerca cervicalis. When it was
found to be effective, MSD decided to
offer the drug for free to prevent river
blindness. TDR developed a “community-
based treatment” program to administer
the drug. Affected communities organized
their own drug distribution and treatment:
they received tablets from district health
posts, delivered them to eligible patients,
and reported to health authorities, meeting
all costs themselves.
On the other hand, public health cam-
paigns can have unintended tragic conse-
quences. Egypt’s campaign of parenteral (by
injection) antischistosomal therapy (PAT)
did not practice adequate equipment steril-
ization, resulting in the creation of a reser-
voir of chronic hepatitis C viral infection.
Some of Africa’s public health chal-
lenges are “man-made.” Dependency theo-
rists talk about brain drain and pharmaceu-
tical patents impeding access to medicines
as examples of serious public health prob-
lems. According to the International Orga-
nization for Migration (IOM), a UN
agency, Africa has already lost one-third of
its human capital. As a result of the emigra-
tion of 20,000 skilled professionals every
year between 1996 and 2006, there are
more African scientists and engineers in the
United States than there are in Africa. In
particular, Africa’s health and social service
professionals’ emigration threatens the very
existence of the country’s health services,
according to the Kenyan Medical Associa-
tion. One-third of Ethiopia’s medical doc-
tors, 80 percent of Zambia’s, and 60 per-
cent of Ghana’s graduating doctors have left
the country.
One of the characteristics of interna-
tional free trade agreements is stronger
claims to intellectual property made by insti-
tutions and government regimes. The top 15
developed countries received 32,703 med-
ical patents from the U.S. Patent and T rade-
mark Ofﬁce from 1997 to 2001 while the
top 15 developing and transition countries
received 954 patents in the same period.
Patent holders seek to prevent pharmaceuti-
cal companies from manufacturing generic
versions of their drugs for export, and in
some cases, for domestic consumption. In
2000, the market cost in some countries for
an antiretroviral regimen using patented
drugs exceeded $10,000 per patient per year.
Without an affordable and stable supply of
treatments, there is less incentive to set up
public health systems. At the same time,
conglomerate international pharmaceutical
companies pay no intellectual property
rights when they exploit indigenous peoples’
knowledge of herbal medicine.
Other man-made threats to public
health include land mines and other war-
related pathologies, tobacco consumption,
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 639 ---
HIP-HOP 563
narcotic drug use, and practices which
harm female reproductive health, such as
female genital cutting and child mar-
riage. Modern, developed world diseases
like heart disease and diabetes are in-
creasing in Africa’s cities as upper class
Africans adopt more sedentary lifestyles.
Research into mental and geriatric ill-
nesses confirms their similarity to such
illnesses in the developed world, al-
though Africans may have different social
interpretations. Other public health chal-
lenges on the horizon include “new” dis-
eases, such Ebola and avian influenza.
Another threat is environmental degrada-
tion. Aside from the loss in production,
loss of forest areas may eliminate oppor-
tunities to discover beneficial therapies
by eliminating the people with the herbal
knowledge or by eliminating plant and
animal species.
Different routes to improving public
health have been proposed. Some stress
promoting investment in health care and
strengthening female autonomy as the best
ways to improve public health. Others
stress population control, technological ad-
vancement, and economic growth.
Even as modern medicine practices be-
come more available, “traditional” medical
practitioners continue to be widespread.
Some of their practices are efﬁcacious while
others are useless or even harmful. Yet the
continued lack of access to standard med-
ical care and the traditional healers’ fulﬁll-
ment of social roles make it likely that this
segment of Africa’s public health system
will remain active.

HIP-HOP
Hip-hop is the moniker for an artistic cul-
ture of rap music, grafﬁti art, and break
dancing that has risen from obscurity in an
African American community to become
one of the most popular and recognizable
in the world. Hip-hop’s focuses on aesthetic
innovation and reinvention and connection
to community have made it an attractive
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 640 ---
564 H IP-HOP
form of political and artistic expression for
people on nearly every continent. Hip-hop
culture is generally considered to be a syn-
thesis of four diverse elements: grafﬁti, 
b-boying, DJing, and emceeing.
Hip-hop as a musical form is consid-
ered to have begun in New York City, in
the deeply impoverished South Bronx of
the mid-1970s. Local DJs set up sound sys-
tems outside and played records for block
parties in scenes reminiscent of open-air
sound systems playing in Jamaica. The DJs
discovered that the instrumental “break” in
a song was what really got audiences ex-
cited; they began switching and mixing
records to take advantage of those “breaks.”
The popularity of the new sound eventu-
ally shifted from block parties to discos
to the avant-garde scene. DJs such as
Jamaican immigrant DJ Kool Herc, Grand-
master Flash, and Afrika Bambaataa (both
children of Caribbean immigrants) were
innovators of the new music and soon
became legends in New York.
Grafﬁti writing or “tagging” developed
as a culture alongside hip-hop. Grafﬁti
writers slipped into forbidden territory and
covered surfaces with nicknames or murals.
The act of tagging was inherently and bla-
tantly rebellious and political; writers
tagged street signs, walls, overpasses, and
train and subway cars with large, vivid
compositions, even in the face of noisy
public “anti-grafﬁti” campaigns and great
personal risk. The tags announced their ex-
istence to a world that seemed to want to
Hip-Hop pioneers The Sugarhill Gang perform live on stage in the mid-1970. (Getty Images)
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 641 ---
HIP-HOP 565
ignore the young, the poor, and the disen-
franchised. A “b-boy” (break-boy) or “b-girl”
was a dancer and an avid follower of 
hip-hop culture. They often traveled to
parties in groups called “crews,” challeng-
ing other crews with acrobatic dances.
From the b-boys and b-girls came one of
the most recognizable markers of hip hop
culture: break dancing. Brought to the
mainstream in movies such as Beat Street
(1984) and Breakin’(1984), break dancing
captivated the attention of the American
public and helped introduce hip-hop
culture to a world outside the African
American community.
Originally, the DJ was the focal point
of the musical hip-hop experience. Eventu-
ally, attention turned to the “emcee.” The
emcee kept the audience’s energy high by
speaking over the beat, often in inventive
rhymes, a technique known as “rapping.”
The focus on the emcee as primary vehicle
was solidiﬁed in 1979, when Sugarhill
Records released “Rapper’s Delight” by the
Sugarhill Gang. Instead of a live DJ, “Rap-
per’s Delight” was backed by a sample from
the hit disco record “Good Times” by Chic.
There had been little effort to record hip-
hop before; it was generally considered by
detractors as a fad, as well as by advocates as
a phenomenon that did not translate well
to recording. The emphasis had been on
the DJ’s inventiveness in creating sound
and ability to keep a crowd moving, which
had to be experienced live. When hip-hop
records became popular, however, the at-
tention shifted from the DJ’s skill to the
emcee’s ability to rhyme.
“Rapper’s Delight” was the ﬁrst com-
mercially successful hip-hop record. Its suc-
cess proved that recorded hip-hop was a po-
tentially proﬁtable endeavor, and other
independent labels attempted to capitalize
on the new music. The recording of hip-hop
ensured the continuance of the music, mak-
ing it portable and transferable; but it also
moved the attention ﬁrmly away from the
DJs that originated it to personalities of
the emcees, or “rappers.” The DJ moved to
the background. With the use of widespread
sampling in the late 1980s, the DJ has been
largely supplanted in much popular hip-hop
by the “producer,” the person who engineers
beats not in front of a live audience, but in a
studio.
Although it began in New York as
an underground phenomenon, hip-hop
spread like wildﬁre. Local hip-hop scenes
emerged in many cities across the United
States, each developing its own unique
sound and aesthetic, turning it into a di-
verse national phenomenon with innumer-
able styles and subgenres. Although it is
important to note that hip-hop’s musical
landscape has always been diverse, the
dominant style of hip-hop has shifted over
the decades. The party-style raps of the
1970s and early 1980s gave way to more
socially conscious music in the late 1980s
and early 1990s. The music of this era, con-
cerned with the decimation of African
American communities by poverty and
drugs and informed by the ongoing struggle
to overthrow apartheid in South Africa,
openly criticized the plight of black Ameri-
cans in the United States. The viewpoint
was strongly Afrocentric. Much of it fre-
quently referenced the troubled history of
black oppression in the United States.
Sometimes artists turned to African history
as an important and unacknowledged part
of the African American past. Artists like
Afrika Bambaataa, Public Enemy, KRS-
ONE, and Queen Latifah sought to educate
listeners and inspire a sense of history and
pride in African culture. They hoped that
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 642 ---
566 H IP-HOP
reminding listeners of the long-established
civilizations, great accomplishments, and
many struggles of African peoples would
call African Americans to action, encourag-
ing public protest and social action in
American communities.
That same era (1980s–1990s) wit-
nessed the rise of “gangsta rap,” especially
from locations outside of New York, most
notably in California and the American
South. In the mid-1990s, as hip-hop cul-
ture skyrocketed in popularity outside the
black community, party-style raps again
became popular. Hip-hop, whether ac-
tively “conscious” or not, has always been
highly inﬂuenced by politics and sociolog-
ical realities; even the 1970s block parties
were a reprieve from the grinding poverty,
gang warfare, and virulent institutional
racism of the South Bronx. “Gangsta rap”
is often viliﬁed for its violence and misog-
yny, but it was a response to the violent,
poverty-stricken, drug-decimated commu-
nities that arose in the wake of the crack
cocaine epidemic and eradication of gov-
ernmental support programs in the 1980s.
Public debate over the right to free speech
was reignited in the United States when
Miami rap group 2 Live Crew, led by
Haitian-American Luther Campbell, faced
obscenity charges and were banned from
performing in many venues because of
graphic sexuality in their music.
As hip-hop traveled across the United
States, it also traveled across the oceans.
Young people across the world have been at-
tracted to its rebellious aesthetic, social
commentary, and trendsetting. Hip-hop
artists have emerged on every continent
from the favelas of Rio de Janeiro to the
suburbs of Paris. These artists use an African
American art form to express local realities
with culturally speciﬁc content, sound, and
aesthetics in forms such as South Africa’s
kwaito music or Brazil’s baile funk.
At the dawn of a new millennium,
hip-hop has come farther and become
more popular than almost anyone could
have imagined. Yet that popularity has en-
gendered troubling concerns about the
current purpose and future direction of the
culture. The most popular hip-hop music
is often accused of being empty of mean-
ing, overly preoccupied with crass materi-
alism, laden with pointless violence and
misogyny. American hip-hop, once an
almost exclusively local, underground phe-
nomenon distributed by independent
labels, is now largely controlled by major
labels. This control allows distribution on
a larger scale that ever before, but also lim-
its the diversity of the music; major labels,
concerned with the bottom line, market
what is almost ensured to succeed and are
less interested in experimenting with the
new. The nonmusical elements of hip-hop
culture have been deﬁnitively pushed aside
in favor of the music. Finally, as the culture
has gone global, international artists and
enthusiasts who still see hip-hop as a viable
and vital tool for protest and rebellion take
issue with what they perceive as a danger-
ously and distressingly limited worldview
in much popular American hip-hop.
American artists are accused of being unin-
formed and uninterested in the plight of
blacks across the Diaspora. Even “con-
scious” rappers come under ﬁre for sub-
scribing to an outdated, romanticized view
of Africa and only being superﬁcially inter-
ested in transatlantic events. Now moving
into its thirties, the future of hip-hop
seems to be at a cr ossroads. How can the
culture retain its rebel stance if it is so
widely accepted, and if it seems to take that
acceptance for granted? Can popular art
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

also be revolutionary? Has hip-hop aged
beyond youthful rebellion?
Kristina D. Bobo

HIP-HOP,C UBAN
Cuban hip-hop, like its African American
counterpart, encompasses dance, music,
grafﬁti art, and a philosophical worldview.
Although a post-1990 phenomena, Cuba
has over 500 rap groups and has held an-
nual festivals that feature international stars
from the United States, Europe, Africa, and
Latin America. With the collapse of the
Soviet Union and increased cultural ex-
changes between the United States and
Cuba, hip-hop’s inﬂuence grew dramati-
cally as the island went into an economic
nosedive known as “the Special Period.” As
Cuba decriminalized the holding of dollars
and tourism became the main earner of for-
eign exchange, Cuba’s Afrodiasporic rap di-
alogue intensiﬁed, with U.S. organizations
like Black August and conscious rappers
like Roots and Common visiting the island.
Cuba’s economic crisis hit its black pop-
ulation hard, since many did not have fam-
ily abroad that could send them money, and
despite tourism’s takeoff, many African-
Cubans were discriminated in job hiring.
Alamar, a housing project east of Havana, is
credited with being the birthplace of Cuban
rap and is still one of the main locations for
both the festival and concerts. Initial govern-
ment reaction to the music was hostile; rap
was considered “foreign” and “antisocial.”
But eventually it was seen as a too large and
popular force to put down, so instead the
government tried to co-opt and contain it.
Now there is an ofﬁcial responsible for rap in
the Ministry of Culture, which also has pub-
lished the island’s ﬁrst rap magazine,
Movimiento. In addition, the Cuban Rap
Agency was formed to promote, record, and
help in the musical training of rappers.
Cuba’s rappers have strongly afﬁrmed
their Afro-Cuban roots, be it musically or
religiously, and are adamant in their denun-
ciation of racism, discrimination, and social
inequality. Cuban rappers have clearly de-
bunked the myth of Cuba’s self-image as a
racial democracy. Songs about prostitution,
street life, poverty, domestic violence, obses-
sion with money and class differences, and
the lack of spiritual and ethical values
abound, and their biting, poetic criticism is
a refreshing antidote to the island’s lifeless
press. Despite this predominantly socially
aware viewpoint, Cuban rappers also sing
about partying, sex, and having fun.
Though Cuban rap uses programmed
drumbeats and round bass lines, samples
Public Enemy, Jay-Z, and Vico C, and
throws in words in English, it also draws
heavily on the island’s deep Afro-Cuban
musical traditions of ritual music, rumba,
son, and the guaracha . Some groups have
used the batá drums, others sample old
songs like “Quirino” or “Lágrimas negras,”
and some use Cuban choteo (an irreverent
humor where nothing is sacred), similar to
signifying. All these variations make Cuban
hip-hop an extremely rich and layered ex-
ample of a genre that is conversant with
Cuban and non-Cuban history, culture,
poetry, and music.
Orishas, the best-known Cuban rap
group lives in Paris but performs frequently
on the island. However, most groups reside
on the island, still struggling to make ends
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

meet, with scant technical resources and
rarely appearing on radio or TV , unless they
have a more “commercial sound.” Yet
groups like Hermanos de Causa, Anónimo
Consejo, Las Krudas, Obsesión, Los
Paisanos, Papo Record, Cubanitos en la
Red, 100 Percent Original, Explosión
Suprema, Eleyó, Junior Clan, Grandes
Ligas, Madera Limpia, and Alto Voltaje
perform widely and have a signiﬁcant fol-
lowing among black, brown, and white
Cuban youth.

HIP-HOP,W OMEN IN
Hip-hop culture, encompassing dance,
music, grafﬁti art, and a philosophical
worldview, has deﬁned male and female
gender roles; women innovators have trans-
formed these roles through their art.
While hip-hop culture has been inher-
ently patriarchal since its inception, women
have always made powerful contributions
to the four essential elements of the genre.
Women have sprayed walls with paint as
grafﬁti writers, spun records as DJs, twisted
and turned their bodies as break dancers,
and, of course, moved the crowd with their
own voices as emcees. In the 1970s women
began to form a distinctly female voice at
hip-hop’s origination in the Bronx, New
York. In the new millennium, hip-hop
women impact cultures worldwide. Young
women have been cultural workers of the
same caliber, level of inﬂuence, and spirit of
innovation as young men. Despite this
truth, women in hip-hop have not always
garnered the same respect as men. Ironi-
cally, hip-hop women who have earned re-
spect from their male and female peers have
often generated work critical of the very pa-
triarchal structures that would limit their
abilities to excel.
Hip-hop has drawn on the same ability
to syncretize the dominant European sys-
tem of control, Native American culture,
and the foundational African ontology that
has formed black cultures in the West. The
original hip-hop artists are the children of
Caribbean immigrants, African Americans
that either participated in the Great Migra-
tion or descended from runaway slaves that
had escaped to the north, and the New
York Puerto Rican, or Nuyorican, popula-
tion that began to signiﬁcantly increase
mid-century. These diverse populations,
united in their shared oppression as people
of color and the shared elements of dias-
poric cultures, intermingled in the 1950s,
1960s, and 1970s. In the Bronx and
throughout the four other New York City
boroughs, these people of African descent
gave birth to the black and Latino youth
who created hip-hop, the new cultural
form that would, like jazz, become the new
American musical form.
It is important to recognize hip-hop as
a cultural retention that survived the Mid-
dle Passage and slavery. The history of oral
expression among women of African de-
scent is rooted on the continent itself,
where queen mothers, female griots, and
other women voiced their experiences in
the public realm. Documented poems that
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 645 ---
HIP-HOP,W OMEN IN 569
were sung or chanted, often by groups of
African women, explore themes of roman-
tic love, initiation to adulthood, family life,
and work. While these traditions continued
in the West, slaves often veiled authentic
African cultural forms to trick white
slaveholders.
Afro-Brazilian slaves veiled martial arts
training with what appeared to white sys-
tem controllers as dance, giving birth to
capoeira. Similarly, the New York Police
Department repressed early break-dancers
because their aggressive movements seemed
too gang-like in appearance.
Afro-Haitians and Afro-Cuban slaves
syncretized African religions with European
Catholicism, assigning African orishas the
names of Catholic saints and creating the
New World religions Voodoo and Santeria.
A hip-hop form of this legacy continues in
the use of street names, or tags, among graf-
ﬁti artists who must shield their identities
from police authority while communicating
authorship of their work to others in the
hip-hop community. Women grafﬁti artists
sometimes spray-painted images generally
accepted as exclusively female, like cosmetic
makeup, to identify themselves as women.
Early hip-hop grafﬁti artists who created
vast murals on New York subway trains
risked imprisonment, beatings, and even
death as the Metropolitan T ransit Authority
spent millions to eradicate the work these
artists were sharing with the public for free.
Simultaneously, artists who co-opted hip-
hop styles but worked on canvas and dis-
played their work at downtown New York
for-proﬁt art galleries were rewarded with
commissions and favorable attention from
mainstream media.
Afro-American slaves sang songs of
liberation and escape, though white slave-
holders believed singing slaves were only
trying to “steal away” or “ﬂy away” to Jesus.
Emcees also use “black code” in the form of
ever-changing colloquial expressions in their
lyrics. Hip-hop artists communicate directly
to their peers, just as their forebears commu-
nicated to fellow slaves, even when system
controllers have access to their music. In-
deed, gifted DJs’ layered use of sampling re-
conﬁgures recorded song, creating new con-
tent and new meaning. DJs and emcees also
faced oppression when, in the absence of
studio space, these artists practiced and per-
formed in government housing, city parks,
and public playgrounds.
As hip-hop is in line with the perpetu-
ation of African musical forms in the West,
so too is hip-hop’s struggle to express au-
thentic black art. Slaveholders criminalized
the talking drum, that most ubiquitous el-
ement of African sound, because of its
provocative use in slave rebellions. Like-
wise, early hip-hop artists fought for legiti-
macy and continue to struggle to deﬁne
the terms of authentic diasporic expression.
Women hip-hop artists have shared this
struggle against ofﬁcial efforts to silence
their work with men. However, these
women, unlike their male counterparts,
also struggled for legitimacy and freedom
within the patriarchal structure of the hip-
hop community.
In the early 1980s, women break-
dancers were often relegated to female-only
contests, or battles, as women breaking
against men was too often derided by par-
ticipants and the viewing audience. While
male members of the famous Rock Steady
Crew supported her movement art, female
member Daisy “Baby Love” Castro rarely
joined them in battles with other men.
Though girls traditionally excelled at chal-
lenging double Dutch jump rope move-
ments, many early male breakers felt their
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 646 ---
570 H IP-HOP,W OMEN IN
art demanded greater upper body strength
than women were perceived to have.
Although female grafﬁti artists risked
the same ofﬁcial efforts at repression as
men, male grafﬁti artists often discredited
their female peers by attacking their sexual
reputations—and ignoring their work.
Sandra “Lady Pink” Fabara and Gloria
“Lady Heart” Williams resisted both sexism
and racism with overtly political work and
deliberately feminine styles.
Perhaps the most famous expression of
female resistance in hip-hop is Lolita
Shante Gooden’s 1984 classic single “Rox-
anne’s Revenge.” Both women and men in
the hip-hop community embraced and cel-
ebrated her deﬁant anthem, which was a re-
sponse to UTFO’s 1984 hit song “Roxanne
Roxanne.” This moment in hip-hop repre-
sents the ﬁrst widely disseminated public
battle where a young woman held her own
against a group of men.
New York radio relegated hip-hop to
special late-night and weekend segments
until WQHT became the ﬁrst station to
play hip-hop on a regular basis. Angie
Martinez, a top-rated radio personality at the
station, used her inﬂuence to launch “Ladies
Night.” This Friday evening program fea-
tured women DJs, making their work more
accessible to a wider audience and celebrat-
ing the presence of women in hip-hop.
As hip-hop grew into a multibillion
dollar business through the 1990s, female
presence in the culture extended to media
and public relations, artist legal and man-
agerial representation, stylists, hairdressers,
makeup artists, designers, graphic artists,
and studio executives. These behind-the-
scenes workers often came to the business
of hip-hop with a powerful love for the
music and a concerted mission to help
preserve the integrity of hip-hop culture
while empowering themselves through
their careers. Like the female artists with
whom they labor, these women workers
struggle with sexism and misogyny in rap
while simultaneously preserving their al-
liance with black and Latino men and the
overall black and Latino community. Their
diminished presence in the music industry
relative to men renders this balancing act
and their positions even more precarious.
The most popular element of hip-hop
culture is, of course, the work of the emcee,
and celebrated female emcees have rhymed
about the liberation of people of color and
women’s empowerment. Though many
female emcees have garnered critical and
commercial success, few approach the sales
ﬁgures and critical attention paid to men.
In 1978 emcee Lady B became the ﬁrst
woman to record on wax. Lady B, once a
top-rated radio DJ on Philadelphia’s WUSL,
founded and worked as editor-in-chief of
the ﬁrst popular magazine devoted to hip-
hop and rhythm and blues, Word Up!
Salt-N-Pepa’s 1986 debut album, Hot,
Cool, and Vicious, reached double platinum
sales status as it celebrated female sexual
freedom and offered cautionary tales on
dating and male-female relationships.
Much like the blues singers that helped
form the foundation for their art, this pio-
neering female duo and their female DJ,
Spinderella, explored freely expressed fe-
male sexuality as an essential component of
authentic liberation.
In six months and with no radio play,
hip-hop icon MC Lyte sold over 125,000
copies of her powerful response to male de-
ception in male-female relationships, 1988’s
“Paper Thin.” MC Lyte would continue to
rhyme about a ﬁctional character, Sam, and
through her work explore themes of love,
violence, and the 1980s crack epidemic.

While Miss Melodie offered lyrics in

Women gained employment at private

scenes workers in hip-hop. Other women

Full Disclosure, a newsletter informing un-
dereducated hip-hop artists of the intrica-

multinational record companies. Bynoe
also founded Urban Think Tank Industry
to combine her love of hip-hop and mem-
bership in the hip-hop community with
activist work.
As hip-hop helped fuel the spoken
word movement of the 1990s, some
women generated explicitly political work
that challenges misogyny and the white-
controlled industry that now structures,
packages, and sells rap. Poet Ninety-Nine’s
“For the Brothers That Ain’t Here” publicly
castigated California-based Ice Cube for his
celebrity endorsement of St. Ides liquor.
Poet Sarah Jones’s “The Revolution” was
banned from public radio play by the
Federal Communications Commission, even
though Jones’s poem challenged the explicit
denigration of women and female sexuality
that prevails in much of today’s rap music.
Poet Jessica Care Moore, founder and pub-
lisher of Moore Black Press, has published
a collection of diasporic hip-hop writing
generated by male and female culture
workers titled The Poetry of MCs.
Female emcee Lauryn Hill has con-
sciously remembered Africa in her collabo-
rative work with overtly political male MC
Nas. Even before the release of her multi-

Education of Lauryn Hill, her duet with
Nas, “If I Ruled the World,” promised to
realign the black collective with the Mother
Continent. Indeed, Lauryn symbolically
represents the power of Africa herself as she
plaintively calls to her brothers. She
promises to “free all my sons” because “I
love ’em, love ’em, baby.” Indeed, women
have worked with the same persistence and

HUGHES,L ANGSTON
(1902–1967)
Langston Hughes was an African American
poet, playwright, and essayist. Though
known primarily for poems, short stories,
and plays that offer perceptive portrayals of
black life and music in the United States
between the 1920s and 1960s, Langston
Hughes also wrote many works that reﬂect
his travels along Africa’s West Coast and in
the Americas. Working aboard the S.S.
Malone freighter in 1923, Hughes visited
Senegal, Nigeria, Cameroon, the Belgian
Congo, Angola, and Guinea, observing the
palm groves and mango trees and listening
to the tom-toms and the songs of African
boatmen. These happy images of fertility
and singing natives appear in poems, such
as “African Fog,” “Call of Ethiopia,” and
“Danse Africaine,” but they contrast
sharply with the themes that Hughes’s
Africa poems address. For instance, Hughes
protests the wholesale exploitation of
African resources and labor in the poem
“Johannesburg Mines,” and he draws paral-
lels in numerous other poems between the
racism endured by blacks in America and
the European imperialism under which
Africans suffered. Further, with his copper-
toned complexion and relatively straight
From the 1920s through the 1960s, Langston Hughes
wrote poetry, ﬁction, and plays that sought to express
black experiences, struggles, and aspirations in
America. (Library of Congress)
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 649 ---
HUMAN IMMUNODEFICIENCY VIRUS AND PREVENTION 573
hair, Hughes quickly discovers that the
Africans ostracized those of mixed blood,
and in “African Morning,” the short story
that Hughes claims as one of his best, he
exposes the uniquely lonesome position of
the mulatto in Africa. However, in spite of
his mixed heritage, Hughes was invited
back to Dakar, Senegal, in 1966 and hon-
ored as a historic artistic ﬁgure at the World
Festival of Negro Arts.
Though Africa appears more frequently
in his work, Hughes also demonstrates
more than a passing interest in those regions
of the Americas to which he traveled. Partic-
ularly in the West Indies where many de-
scendents of former slaves reside, Hughes
encountered many important writers and
artists, and a cross-pollination between
these ﬁgures and Hughes occurred. When
Hughes visited Cuba in 1930, for example,
he obtained material for such poems as
“Soledad” and “Caribbean Sunset,” but he
also came into contact with Nicolás Guillén,
an Afro-Cuban poet who so much admired
Hughes’s use of jazz and blues characteris-
tics in poems that he wrote Motivos de Son
(1930). Reﬂecting the island’s mixed her-
itage, son is a style of music developed in
Cuba, which combines the Spanish canción
and Spanish guitar with African rhythms and
percussion instruments. Thus, like jazz and
the blues, son represents a popular blend of
Western and African musical traditions and
so provides a useful vehicle through which
to comment upon race relations. Guillén’s
ﬁrst major work, Motivos de Son adopts
many of Hughes’s other techniques and
themes as well, such as the utilization of the
language of poor blacks and the castigation
of imperialist ideologies.
One year after his visit to Cuba, Hughes
spent time in Haiti, where he encountered
the author Jacques Roumain and developed
the leftist philosophies that inﬁltrate his sub-
sequent works. From his experiences in
Haiti, Hughes produced the children’s book
Popo and Fiﬁna: Children of Haiti (1932),
the historical drama Troubled Island(1936),
and the translation of Roumain’s novel enti-
tled Gouverneurs de la rosée (1945). And in
1947, while on vacation in Jamaica, Hughes
met several prominent writers, including
Roger Mais and Vic Reid, and was so im-
pressed by their work that he included their
poems in an anthology called The Poetry of
the Negro, 1746–1949 . In “Broadcast to
the West Indies,” Hughes himself summa-
rizes the commonalities between blacks in
the United States and blacks in the
Caribbean: “I, Harlem, say:/HELLO,
WEST INDIES!/You are dark like me,/
Colored with many bloods like me,/. . . . It’s
a long ways/ From where you live to where
I/ live—/ But there’s a direct line/ From your
heart to mine.”
Dana Nichols

HUMAN IMMUNODEFICIENCY
VIRUS AND PREVENTION
Since being identiﬁed in the early 1980s,
human immunodeﬁciency virus (HIV) and
its consequence, acquired immune deﬁ-
ciency syndrome (AIDS), has become one
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 650 ---
574 H UMAN IMMUNODEFICIENCY VIRUS AND PREVENTION
of the major epidemics in both Africa and
the Americas. Prevention efforts in Africa
and in the United States have some impor-
tant parallels, but also many important dif-
ferences, as a consequence of culture, poli-
tics, and economics. Crucially, in the
relations between the United States and
Africa around HIV and AIDS, U.S. poli-
cies and practices regarding sexual/repro-
ductive health have had widespread effects
on the messages, programs, services, and
educational efforts toward the prevention
of HIV in Africa.
Although just 10 percent of the world’s
population resides in sub-Saharan Africa,
64 percent of all HIV-positive people
worldwide live there, as do 76 percent of all
HIV-positive women worldwide. More
than 20 percent of all adults in Swaziland,
Botswana, Zimbabwe, Lesotho, Namibia,
and South Africa are HIV positive. More
than 2 million people are HIV positive or
have AIDS in Latin America and the
Caribbean combined. In this area of the
world, the highest prevalence rate among
adults is in Haiti (5.6 percent). The adult
prevalence rate in the Caribbean (over
440,000 people) is second only to sub-
Saharan Africa (more than 25 million peo-
ple). In North America the prevalence rate
is 0.6 percent.
The epidemic takes different forms in
different areas and regions, and disparately
affects people even in regions with compar-
atively much higher or lower overall rates of
prevalence. Countries in Africa are not uni-
formly affected, and there is a signiﬁcant
difference in infection rates among African
nations, as is the case in other areas
throughout the world as well. Prevalence
rates are signiﬁcantly lower in western and
eastern Africa, although some countries
such as Nigeria, Burkina Faso, and
Cameroon have experienced recent surges
in prevalence. There is also signiﬁcant vari-
ation in when initial cases of HIV/AIDS
were ﬁrst recognized in African nations,
ranging from early in the recognition of the
virus such as in Uganda and South Africa to
much later in countries such as Namibia.
Thus some countries have had some
amount of lead time to plan and initiate co-
ordinated education prevention responses,
while others are still in the throes of the ﬁrst
waves of generational infection, with the
bulk of those infected and affected yet to
come in successive cohorts. In these coun-
tries, a prevention education response de-
pends not just on the planning and design
of the initiative itself, but on desperately
needed and rapidly depleting human re-
sources—people in their economic and ed-
ucational prime—to plan and implement a
response. Globally, less than one in ﬁve in-
dividuals is able to access prevention ser-
vices, and those disparately affected by ac-
cess barriers include youth and women.
HIV education prevention efforts reach
about 8 percent of youth in southern Africa.
The role of education efforts in HIV
prevention is crucial, and particularly for
young people may be one of the most effec-
tive since even in the most affected areas
schoolchildren have the lowest rates of in-
fection. Components of effective education
efforts in Africa provide HIV/AIDS and
sexual/reproductive health information
and advocacy (especially for underserved
groups) as well as building institutional ca-
pacity and leadership around HIV/AIDS.
Such efforts also address people’s sexual
health needs while concurrently addressing
the extent to which individuals may exer-
cise free and informed choices about these
needs without coercion, discrimination, or
violence.

Support and resources for many of
these programs originate from abroad. For
instance, the United Nations Population
Fund (UNFPA)–sponsored “Geração Biz”
in Mozambique provides youth-friendly
services to in- and out-of-school youth to
increase their sexual/reproductive health
literacy through improved access, counsel-
ing, and peer education programs that en-
courage HIV prevention strategies.
Prevention efforts among youth and
adults have been most effective when car-
ried out in speciﬁc areas with priority pop-
ulations. For instance, the prevalence rate
among female sex workers fell signiﬁcantly
in Côte d’Ivoire as a result of local targeted
long-term prevention efforts. Other local-
ized efforts, such as programs for pregnant
women under twenty in South Africa and
for urban men in Zambia, have shown
promising initial results. In T ogo, a unique
effort involves motorcycle taxi drivers who
are trained to become “behavior change
agents,” and in South Africa young soccer
players share HIV prevention information
with other teams in schools and the com-
munity.
Namibia provides one example of the
opportunities and the challenges of effec-
tive prevention education efforts. The ﬁrst
HIV/AIDS case in Namibia was recorded
in 1986. A high-proﬁle national social mar-
keting media campaign aimed at educating
Namibians about HIV/AIDS began several
years ago. It is coordinated by the Ministry
of Health and Social Services, in collabora-
tion with many corporate and community
partners. The campaign includes public
service announcements on radio and televi-
sion, full-page ads in periodicals and news-
papers, bumper stickers, and billboards
placed throughout the country. Attractive
full-color posters featuring the president of
Namibia urging citizens to learn about the
virus were also a component of the 2003
campaign, which were displayed promi-
nently in public gathering places including
post ofﬁces and other high-trafﬁc locations.
Although the ofﬁcial language of Namibia
was declared to be English at the time of in-
dependence in 1990, campaign materials
are produced in many languages and di-
alects so as to have the greatest impact in
this nation of diverse peoples.
In some ways this campaign mirrors ef-
forts in the United States, yet in other ways
it is quite different. The national nature of
the campaign, with uniﬁed messages, copi-
ous funding to provide for attractive mate-
rials ubiquitously placed throughout all
forms of media, and with such broad scope,
is a signiﬁcant departure from approaches
in the United States which consist of vari-
ous private organizations, local and state
health departments, federal agencies, and
other entities all engaging in various de-
grees of these but without one coordinated
message.
National media campaigns are also un-
derway in other countries, including the
Lovelife initiative in South Africa which in-
corporates HIV education messages into
newspapers, television, sport, and radio
media. A new era in large-scale HIV educa-
tion media campaigns occurred in 2005,
when leaders in broadcasting from through-
out Africa met to discuss past media
HIV/AIDS education efforts and to de-
velop a more uniﬁed and coordinated strat-
egy for the future. At this meeting, the new
pan-African African Broadcast Media Part-
nership Against HIV/AIDS was created.
This new collaborative approach aims to
make HIV/AIDS central to programming
and business plans of broadcasters across
Africa. Organized under an initiative of the

UN Secretary General, co-conveners repre-
sented both African and U.S. sponsors—
including the Henry J. Kaiser Family
Foundation, the Southern African Broad-
casting Association, and the Nelson Mandela
Foundation.
In Namibia, in addition to the national
social marketing campaign, the Namibian
Planned Parenthood Association recruits
and trains youth to be HIV/AIDS peer ed-
ucators. These youth are equipped with
both concrete information about HIV and
the presentation skills to make their efforts
most effective. The association also began
using interactive peer theater in 2002, in
which youth create and produce their own
skits about HIV/AIDS for use in educating
other young people. The peer corps in-
cludes youth from many regions of the
country, who (after training and with con-
tinuing opportunities for professional de-
velopment) carry messages of HIV aware-
ness and prevention to their home
communities. Since they are most in touch
with cultural norms and values as well as
the local language of their home communi-
ties, they function as effective ambassadors
of education and information about access
to testing and treatment as well as a host of
other issues of sexual and reproductive
health. Bicycles donated by several interna-
tional organizations carry volunteers to
provide HIV outreach into more distant
areas and those inaccessible to public trans-
portation.
The peer component of HIV preven-
tion efforts is currently very strong and
rather similar to efforts in the United States
in the early 1990s. Peer educators, usually
youth, are recruited and trained, and then
do outreach in a number of formats.
Namibian youth report that they applied to
the peer program to build their resumes
and make them more marketable in the
workplace, to provide them with activities
to ﬁll their time (especially for out-of-
school youth or young people older than
18 but without further higher education or
employment opportunities), and to enjoy
increased social status among their peers
and elders as one who is bettering them-
selves with professional development op-
portunities and as a leader in the commu-
nity. Peers also report enjoying the
opportunity to meet other like-minded
youth through the program, and greatly
enjoy being an innovative part of the solu-
tion to the AIDS crisis in their country.
The Namibian peer education approach is
not just youth-focused but youth-driven;
the peer leaders participate in informa-
tional and leadership building activities fo-
cused on helping them develop their skills
to decide in what direction the actual pro-
gram should go, which approaches are
working, and what new ideas might be of
interest in the communities. The U.S. ap-
proaches use many messages, approaches,
and priorities that are adult-produced and
driven; the Namibian approach gives ulti-
mate control over the agenda to the youth
themselves.
Other countries have also initiated peer
education programs, including South Africa
and Cameroon. Differences in prevalence
rates, as well as cultural norms and values,
dictate in what ways these strategies are
structured. In communities where there are
strict taboos against discussing sexual issues,
peer education and peer theater may use
more hyperbolic or abstract story lines or
messages; in regions where relatively fewer
adults are infected and ailing, some pro-
grams recruit and train adults (rather than
youth) to do adult-to-adult peer educating.
Countries with lower overall prevalence

Strategies to provide outreach efforts
to the many ethnic and cultural groups in
Namibia also include examining ways to
provide information in the most appropri-
ate cultural context for each community.
Prevention efforts that take into account
cultural norms and values include a study
of several cultures in which existing ap-
proaches commonly used in Namibia and
many other African countries (including
the “ABC” approach—abstinence, be
faithful, use condoms) are not as relevant
or useful to non-Christian, nonmonoga-
mous societies. Some research has been
done into ways sexuality is constructed in
these groups, toward the goal of crafting
more culturally competent and accessible
HIV/AIDS prevention campaigns in these
regions. Other approaches mirror those of
African nations that have had success in
slowing the rate of infection. For instance,
providing messages of both abstinence
and condom availability in tandem has
been key in reducing Uganda’s rate of
infection.
In Namibia, condoms are widely avail-
able, and advertising and public service
billboards sponsored by corporations and
businesses about this availability are visible
throughout the country. HIV prevention
materials and condoms have even been ob-
served at national park visitor centers,
placed strategically next to the visitor sign-
in books. World AIDS Day is marked
throughout the country in observances that
take place in each region (the country has
been divided into regions speciﬁcally for
HIV prevention efforts). 
Another feature of the African land-
scape of HIV prevention is an absence of
prevention messages and efforts aimed at
lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender
(LGBT) people. Nearly all information (ex-
cept in South Africa, a notable exception) is
aimed speciﬁcally at a heterosexual audi-
ence because in much of southern Africa
(and the continent overall) homosexuality
is not just discouraged but illegal and
sometimes punishable by imprisonment,
deportation, or execution. This lack of in-
formation puts LGBT people at distinct
and disparate risk, as an overlay onto their
already persecuted identities.
Discrimination against those who are
HIV infected or those thought to have
AIDS is widespread and complicates pre-
vention efforts. As of 2006, no public ﬁg-
ure or celebrity in Namibia has come out as
being HIV positive. Although public
health messages abound, the HIV preva-
lence rate nationwide is 22.5 percent (and
upwards of 40 percent in some regions),
and much of the population is very much
affected if not infected. HIV/AIDS is a
topic squarely in the public eye yet a taboo
topic of conversation in the everyday life of
most Namibian people.
A Namibian National AIDS Quilt has
been created, similar in concept and design
to the U.S. Names Project Quilt. Friends
and family members of people who have
died commemorate their loved ones in quilt
panels they create to honor them. One
striking difference between the U.S. and
Namibian projects, however, is that nearly
none of the Namibian quilt panels display
the given names of those memorialized.
Panels “to my schoolmates,” “to my beloved
husband,” and “for my daughter” are com-
mon. Panels that include the actual name of
the person in whose honor the panel was

created are virtually nonexistent. In a simi-
lar fashion, the obituary pages in the na-
tional newspaper are ﬁlled with notices of
the deaths of young people every day, but
almost all omit the cause of death of these
young people. Conversely, some obituaries
prominently note those who have died in
catastrophic non-HIV related ways, such as
auto accidents and hunting mishaps. The
stigma surrounding people who have AIDS,
and their families, is profound.
Overall, a comparison of African and
U.S. HIV prevention indicates several
important issues. In general, prevention
efforts must be not merely translated into
other languages, but into other cultures.
Offers of assistance (in the form of ﬁnancial
aid or educational materials) from the
United States—speciﬁcally those with con-
servative agendas or from faith-based
organizations—must be assessed for their
relevance to cultures and populations that
do not share the same worldview. In some
instances those approaches might be not
only irrelevant but dangerous. As an exam-
ple, in Namibia many women who are mar-
ried experience pressure to have sex with
their husbands without condoms, while
single women feel more power to negotiate
condom use with partners. For this reason,
some approaches espoused by the United
States, such as encouraging marriage and
discouraging condom distribution and ne-
gotiation skills, not only fall short but could
cause potential harm to women.
More generally, U.S. policies on sexual
and reproductive health can have wide-
spread effects on the messages, and the very
existence, of such prevention efforts in
Africa. The United States’s Mexico City
Policy restrictions (more widely known as
the “Global Gag Rule”) denies funding to
any family planning program abroad that
uses its own money to provide abortions,
abortion counseling, or advocacy. The
George W . Bush administration later
extended the gag rule to HIV/AIDS pro-
grams throughout the world unless they are
abstinence-only-until-marriage programs.
The United Nations Population Fund
(UNFPA) provides population assistance to
developing countries around the world,
including those in Africa most affected by
HIV/ AIDS; all U.S. funding for UNFPA
was cut in 2002.
Additional U.S. policy requires HIV/
AIDS organizations to pledge opposition to
sex trafﬁcking and prostitution or be dis-
qualiﬁed from receiving funding. This policy
was immediately implemented for interna-
tional programs as well, and now also affects
private American groups providing HIV/
AIDS services abroad. In addition, the policy
requires fund recipients to discuss condom
failure rates and considers applicants for
funding that have religious or moral objec-
tions to particular HIV/AIDS prevention
methods or treatment programs—such as
condoms and needle exchanges. Some
countries view this requirement as a chal-
lenge to their sovereignty and therefore
refuse to agree. Others ﬁnd the language of
the pledge problematic—it is unclear
whether programs that serve those involved
may actually be disqualiﬁed from funding—
although these programs may represent the
best hope for women and children to escape
sex trafﬁcking.
Ongoing controversy and legislation
about sex education in the United States
have implications for decisions about fund-
ing such programs abroad. For instance, a
request for funding proposals released in
January 2006 by the U.S. Department of
Health and Human Services for Community-
Based Abstinence Education programs

described more stringent and curriculum-
speciﬁc criteria for U.S. programs that
would qualify for such funds than ever be-
fore. The RFP criteria excluded funding to
all programs that included information
about contraceptives, left concerns about
the medical accuracy of information unad-
dressed, and re-traumatized survivors of
rape and sexual abuse by stating that absti-
nence is a choice over which young people
have complete control.
The revised criteria also speciﬁcally ex-
cluded provision of any information of rele-
vance to gay and lesbian people or their fam-
ilies, and included a deﬁnition of marriage
directly from the 1996 Defense of Marriage
Act; the criteria also recommended that ab-

because they are shameful and unable to be-
come happy—despite research to the con-
trary. Given the past trend of many U.S.
policies being extended to U.S. organiza-
tions doing work abroad, and then directly
to foreign programs, this development may
greatly impact how and what HIV educa-
tion efforts may remain eligible for contin-
ued funding in Africa in the near future.
These largely ideologically based re-
strictions undermine critical prevention ef-
forts. After President George W . Bush rein-
stated the Global Gag Rule, the impact of
the policy change was felt not just on repro-
ductive health but on HIV/AIDS preven-
tion efforts too. Under the policy, no U.S.
aid can be provided to foreign nongovern-
mental organizations (NGOs) that use
funding from any other source to perform
abortions in cases other than rape, incest, or
threat to life of the woman, provide referral
or counseling about abortion, or lobby for
legalized or more accessible abortion in
their own country. Those not complying
lose funding from the U.S. Agency for
International Development. For example,
the Lesotho Planned Parenthood Associa-
tion refused to agree to these restrictions
and no longer receives any USAID supplies,
including condoms—and Lesotho is one of
the areas of Africa most affected by HIV .
The policy has signiﬁcant effects on
HIV/AIDS prevention efforts, especially
those coordinated through reproductive
health providers. In Kenya, the effect of the
“Global Gag Rule” forced a clinic to close
in the province where HIV prevalence is
highest overall in the country. This effec-
tively ceased HIV testing and counseling
for more than 300,000 people who have no
other access to health care. At the same
time, these cuts also caused the clinic to re-
duce by half the number of trained out-
reach workers who bring HIV prevention
education efforts to local communities and
priority populations such as youth and
rural people. Also in Kenya, a creative pro-
gram that coordinated service delivery of
both HIV prevention education and repro-
ductive, maternal, and child health services
was forced to end—seriously threatening
this integrated and innovative approach as
well as the lives of the thousands of women
it reached.
In a similar situation in Ghana, a clinic
closure due to loss of USAID funding left
almost 700,000 people without access to
HIV prevention education, counseling,
and testing. In Ethiopia and Zambia
(where the average life expectancy in now
34 years old), loss of funds to providers has
severely reduced those countries’ capacity to
continue HIV education outreach through
trained community workers to outlying
areas and at-risk populations. Cameroon was
forced to close a youth center that provided
programs on HIV prevention education and
parenting.

In 2005 the U.S. international HIV
prevention abstinence budget was increased
to $295 million. In 2003 the $15 billion
AIDS law required at least a third of preven-
tion monies to be granted to abstinence-
only-until-marriage programs. In 2005,
that level was increased so that two-thirds of
the funding was required to go directly to-
ward abstinence-only-until-marriage pro-
grams. This approach does nothing to ad-
dress the needs of the millions of married
women at risk for HIV—up to four-ﬁfths
of HIV-positive women in sub-Saharan
Africa have been infected by their husbands,
who are their sole sexual partners.
T welve of the ﬁfteen focus countries
which received USAID grants for absti-
nence efforts from the 2004 “HIV/AIDS
Prevention through Abstinence and Health
Choices for Youth” program were African
nations—Botswana, Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia,
Kenya, Mozambique, Namibia, Nigeria,
Rwanda, South Africa, Tanzania, Uganda,
and Zambia. Of the eleven organizations
that won the ﬁve-year grants, nine were
faith-based in nature. These grants provided
a total of $100 million in abstinence-
centered grants under the Emergency Plan
for AIDS Relief and were directed to the
fifteen countries worldwide which are
home to more than 50 percent of people
with HIV infection worldwide.
In Uganda, the dangerous effects of
this approach are already being felt. A shift
in U.S. dollars to an abstinence approach
resulted in a shortage of condoms, with
those available having tripled in cost. Also
in Uganda, U.S. inﬂuence has changed the
focus of Uganda’s previously highly success-
ful strategy to one centered solely on absti-
nence. Inaccurate information about con-
dom effectiveness has been added into the
school curriculum, while at the same time
information about the risk of HIV in mar-
riage and the effectiveness of condoms has
been removed. This altered focus closely
parallels changes being made in some cur-
ricula in the United States as well. Since
Uganda is viewed as a model program by
the current U.S. administration, Uganda’s
approach to HIV prevention could have
devastating effects in Uganda and also
other countries receiving U.S. funding.
Other challenges to prevention efforts
include ﬁnancial and political forces within
Africa. Access to treatment remains difﬁ-
cult at best, and even in places where na-
tionwide treatment has been implemented,
such as Botswana, results have thus far been
mixed. At times there is a signiﬁcant lag
between when financial resources are
promised from countries such as the
United States and when they actually
become available on the ground. In other
instances, policies may serve to delay or
prevent monies from being distributed at all.
Under the Global Gag Rule, U.S. funding
to nongovernmental organizations provid-
ing HIV prevention efforts has been cut in
instances when those NGOs have also dis-
cussed family planning and other sexual/
reproductive health services; in several cases,
these cuts have affected NGOs whose pri-
mary purpose is to provide additional life-
saving services. In one such instance, some
African afﬁliates of the Red Cross were
completely shut down in this manner,
although they were the primary organization
addressing infant mortality, primary health
care and immunization programs, hunger,
and other critical health issues.
Access to medication to prevent
mother-to-child transmission has just be-
come available since 2004 in some African
countries. Some of these countries are ad-
dressing the protocols for who will qualify
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868
