for treatment; others are negotiating meth-
ods to transport needed medications into
more remote areas. Issues of training for
healthcare workers, enrolling eligible peo-
ple into treatment, and addressing infra-
structure challenges have also impacted the
success of these medication rollouts. In
many areas access to any medication is sim-
ply not available.
The prevention component of testing
and counseling can also be confounded by
numerous factors. Discrimination against
people who have AIDS, myths about trans-
mission and prevention, gender differences
in education, power, and inﬂuence, and
differences in approaches between tradi-
tional healers and Western medical practice
can all hinder testing and other prevention
efforts. With the additional layer of lack of
access to medication, there is little per-
ceived beneﬁt to being tested and knowing
one’s status.
The socioeconomic impact of HIV
and AIDS are varied and widespread. Mil-
lions of children are orphans due to AIDS,
and many children struggle to raise
younger siblings—the next generation—
without beneﬁt of parents, grandparents, or
extended family and community. Life ex-
pectancy is below 40 years of age in many
areas; thus, the sector of workers which
fuels nations and economies—teachers,
doctors, nurses, business and industry lead-
ers, civil service workers—is being steadily
wiped out. In some areas, open employ-
ment positions are being “double-ﬁlled”:
two employees are hired for one job, with
the employer knowing that at least one
of the candidates will have died before the
training period has ended. With the next
generation struggling with basic survival
needs and without beneﬁt of elders, hopes
for educational and economic advances
becomes dim. In many cases, these impacts
of HIV/AIDS not only strain current sys-
tems, but reverse previous positive trends in
the health, education, and economic sec-
tors. In turn, this trend creates a dynamic of
stunting economic growth in Africa at the
very time economic resources are most
needed to address HIV . The workforce in
some African countries will be up to 35 per-
cent smaller in 2020 because of HIV/AIDS.
The life expectancy has declined in thirty-
eight countries as a result of HIV/AIDS,
and in some countries an estimated 50 per-
cent of all health care workers die of AIDS.
The disparate effect on the young, and
on girls and women, is signiﬁcant also.
Women and girls, already at disadvantage
in many areas, balance cultural expecta-
tions against perceived opportunities. The
age of marriage for girls overall is younger
than for men, and with the added eco-
nomic pressure of having no family support
system or extended community due to
HIV impacts on the family, marriage may
appear the best option for some. The “sugar
daddy” phenomenon also lends itself to
girls caught between coexisting difﬁcult
choices. Engaging in sex for money for
food or for school uniforms in order to
continue one’s education is commonplace
in some areas.
More broadly, many African programs
that provide HIV/AIDS education preven-
tion also provide other critical health and
social service delivery to people in these
areas. The U.S. impact on the dissemina-
tion of sexual and reproductive health in-
formation can also affect access to other
vital services such as prenatal and perinatal
services, basic health care, and schooling
and feeding programs that may all be
housed within one service delivery system
or umbrella organization.

High rates of unemployment, unequal
distribution of wealth, and sometimes war-
fare, migration, and famine often further
complicate an already dire situation across
the continent. Concurrent increases in
other infections as a result of HIV infec-
tion, such as tuberculosis, further strain
health, family, and economic systems. The
emotional toll of such complications on
individuals and communities can be even
higher, as in situations such as an HIV-

hungry, and has nothing to eat.”

HUMAN RIGHTS
Human rights are core human values such
as the dignity of human beings, their essen-
tial equality, the right to live in a commu-
nity, mutual respect, and individual liberty.
The development of human rights was in-
ﬂuenced heavily by the history of transat-
lantic slavery and abolitionism. These
rights are, to varying extents, embraced in
the major philosophical and religious tradi-
tions. It is only since the post World War II
era,  however, that they have begun to re-
ceive legal recognition. Contemporary in-
ternational organizations with a signiﬁcant
transatlantic presence, such as the United
Nations, have been important vehicles for
the articulation of human rights.
Intellectuals in the United States and
Western Europe originally pioneered the de-
velopment of human rights in the eigh-
teenth and nineteenth centuries. Human
rights were a domestic concern and a matter
for domestic law. It was not until World War
I and, more signiﬁcantly, World War II that
human rights became an international issue.
Human rights are now not only a concern of
major Western governments but also of de-
veloping nations in Asia, Africa, and South
America as well as for intellectuals and non-
governmental organizations (NGOs).

The last half of the twentieth century
witnessed a dramatic internationalization
of human rights, but there continues to be
a signiﬁcant gap between principles of
human rights and the corresponding prac-
tices of states. The enduring issue in the
late twentieth century, therefore, was the
extent to which nations had been, and con-
tinued to be, willing to curtail their na-
tional sovereignty in order to promote an
international regime for the protection of
human rights.
The Development 
of Human Rights
Early transatlantic human rights move-
ments were primarily concerned with the
abolition of slavery. These early movements,
with some exceptions, tended to be national
rather than international. In 1806, Thomas
Jefferson argued in front of Congress that
citizens of the United States should not par-
ticipate in “those violations of human rights
which have so long continued on the unof-
fending inhabitants of Africa.” In Britain,
the Society for the Abolition of the Slave
T rade mobilized public opinion to such an
extent that the British Parliament was
forced to debate and to consider the com-
mon rights of humanity. In 1807, the U.S.
Congress passed an act that outlawed the
foreign slave trade. A similar act was passed
in Britain, which made it illegal to trade in
or purchase humans for the purpose of slav-
ery. International efforts to end the slave
trade were led by English reformers and fo-
cused on the Congress of Vienna in 1815.
The congress proclaimed that the interna-
tional slave trade was repugnant to the prin-
ciples of humanity and universal morality
and provided that the slave trade should
be abolished as soon as practicable. This
proclamation represented the ﬁrst time that
nations had acknowledged their collective
duty to protect and defend humanity.
Revolutions in communication and
transportation meant that by the late
nineteenth century the world was more
connected than ever before, and the pe-
riod saw a corresponding increase in the
recognition of the existence of interna-
tional human rights. Individual states
were increasingly willing to protest human
rights violations. Austria, France, Britain,
and the United States, for example, made
official protests to the Romanian and
Russian governments in respect to the dis-
crimination and persecution of their Jew-
ish populations. The period also saw the
establishment of an increasing number of
NGOs. In 1901, for example, the Ligue
des Droits de l’Homme articulated a vi-
sion to promote basic human rights on be-
half of all humanity.
Early human rights activists were pri-
marily concerned with the problem of
racial discrimination. In 1900, the ﬁrst
Pan-African Congress met in London. At
that congress, the black activist W . E. B.
Du Bois argued: “The problem of the
twentieth century is the problem of the
color line—the relation of the darker to
the lighter races of men in Asia and Africa,
in America and the islands of the sea”
(Lauren, 1998, p. 77).
Activists also turned their attention to
halting the process of imperialism, and to
protecting the rights of women, particu-
larly in the areas of marriage, education,
property, working conditions, birth con-
trol, and suffrage. The International
Woman Suffrage Alliance was founded in
1902; by the end of 1920, it had afﬁliated
societies in thirty countries throughout the
world, with its headquarters in London.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 660 ---
584 H UMAN RIGHTS
The outbreak of World War I acceler-
ated the evolution of international human
rights. At the Paris Peace Conference in
1919, nations pledged to endeavor to se-
cure fair and humane conditions of labor,
the just treatment of native inhabitants of
territories, enforcement of agreements re-
lating to the trafﬁc of women and chil-
dren, and to take steps for the interna-
tional prevention and control of disease.
The T reaty of Versailles was notable, how-
ever, for its exclusion of a racial equality
provision, which led to widespread inter-
national demonstrations, particularly in
Africa and Asia.
The period after World War I saw the
continued development of international
human rights. NGOs and individual human
rights activists increasingly saw themselves
as part of an international human rights
movement. International organizations such
as the Women’s International League for
Peace and Freedom, the International
Woman Suffrage Alliance, the International
Council of Women, and the International
Alliance of Women sought to advance the
rights of women around the world. The
Great Depression of the 1930s led to a
renewed discussion of human rights, partic-
ularly those rights relating to class, social,
and economic rights. The International
Labor Organization was responsible for a
number of conventions dealing with trade
unions, forced labor, working hours, insur-
ance, and antidiscrimination.
By the eve of World War II, this grow-
ing culture of rights was still primarily con-
ﬁned to Western states. One exception was
the growing movement to promote racial
equality and self-determination, which was
primarily driven by activists in Africa and
Asia and directed against Western colonial
powers.
Development of the 
United Nations
World War II was an important turning
point in the evolution of international
human rights in three main respects.
Firstly, while the protection of human
rights was becoming an increasingly impor-
tant international issue, it was still regarded
as a domestic issue. War exposed the danger
of allowing nations to justify their actions
by reference to their exclusive domestic
jurisdiction. Secondly, the war hastened the
process of internationalization and con-
ﬁrmed the international presence of the
United States. Finally, the war spurred the
major powers of the day to agree on funda-
mental principles on human rights and to
make public and global pledges to protect
these rights.
In 1941, British Prime Minister Win-
ston Churchill and U.S. President Franklin
D. Roosevelt announced a joint statement
of war aims in their “Atlantic Charter.” The
charter proclaimed important principles,
such as self-determination, labor standards,
economic advancement, and social security,
and, most importantly, contained an assur-
ance that people should live in freedom
from fear and want. The allied nations
agreed to abide by the principles outlined
in the Atlantic Charter and pledged to pre-
serve human rights and justice in their own
lands as well as overseas.
Despite growing concern for the pro-
tection of human rights, the reality was that
racism, colonialism, and persecution per-
sisted on both sides of the Atlantic. Individ-
uals and NGOs continued to lobby for the
protection of human rights. The issues of
primary concern were decolonization, the
fate of indigenous peoples, the treatment of
people of different races, classes, and castes,
and the rights of women and children.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 661 ---
HUMAN RIGHTS 585
At the conclusion of the war, the key
human rights issue for national govern-
ments was to provide an adequate safeguard
for human rights without impinging too
much on national sovereignty. Initial drafts
of a United Nations Charter failed to in-
clude any meaningful human rights provi-
sions. The British were concerned, for ex-
ample, that a general statement assuring the
protection of fundamental freedoms might
provide a starting point from which control
of its empire might be endangered. The
early drafts created feelings of shock and
anger, particularly in Africa, South America,
and Asia, where self-determination was seen
as fundamental to peace.
The UN Charter was signed two
months after the United Nations Confer-
ence on International Organization was
held in San Francisco in October, 1945.
The preamble to the charter sets down one
of the United Nations’ objectives:
T o reafﬁrm faith in fundamental human
rights, in the dignity and worth of the
human person, in the equal rights of men
and women and of nations large and small.
Article 1(3) provided that one of the
purposes of the UN was:
T o achieve international co-operation in
solving international problems of an
economic, social, cultural, or humanitarian
character, and in promoting and encouraging
respect for human rights and for fundamental
freedoms for all without distinction as to race,
sex, language, or religion.
The UN Charter also dealt more
speciﬁcally with a broad selection of eco-
nomic and social rights, as well as ensuring
the political, economic, social, and educa-
tional advancement of people and their just
treatment and protection against abuses.
The charter was an important step in
the evolution of international human
rights. Its weakness was that it did not
deﬁne the important human rights terms
with any degree of speciﬁcity. It also failed
to provide for adequate enforcement of
these rights and included an “escape clause”
in Article 2(7) which provided that “noth-
ing contained in the present Charter shall
authorize the United Nations to intervene
in matters which are essentially within the
domestic jurisdiction of any state.”
This clause undermined the charter’s
provisions on human rights. The develop-
ment of an international mechanism for
the protection and enforcement of human
rights had “smashed against the rock of na-
tional sovereignty” (Lauren, 1998, p. 198).
The period after the signing of the char-
ter saw a number of individuals and NGOs
criticize abuses of human rights both in their
home countries and abroad. Apartheid in
South Africa, immigration policies of
Canada, Australia, and New Zealand, and
the treatment of blacks in the United States
all received national and international atten-
tion. The charter was also used as a tool to
challenge human rights abuses. For example,
in 1945 the High Court of Ontario in Re.
Drummond Wren relied upon the human
rights provisions of the charter as part of the
public policy of Canada in refusing to en-
force covenants based on racial origin.
Human Rights in the Second
Half of the T wentieth Century
In 1946, the United Nations created the
Commission on Human Rights. The com-
mission’s ﬁrst goal was to seriously consider
the underlying philosophy of human rights
and to create a document that embodied uni-
versal norms. The members of the commis-
sion were forced to transcend their individual
political, cultural, religious, and philosophi-
cal ideals to put forward “universal rights”
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 662 ---
586 H UMAN RIGHTS
that should be guaranteed to all people of the
world. This document was submitted for
consideration by the General Assembly and
was adopted on December 10, 1948. The
Universal Declaration was not designed to be
a narrow legal document, but it was revolu-
tionary in the sense that it was the ﬁrst inter-
national document to proscribe normative
standards for human rights and quickly came
to assume moral, political, and even legal
force.
It became clear, however, that many
states that were willing to adopt nonbind-
ing declarations of principle were not simi-
larly willing to accept binding conventions
that might limit their national sovereignty.
Nations, such as Britain, were reluctant to
accede to anything that might jeopardize
their colonial interests. Similarly, the Soviet
Union and the United States, the super-
powers of the Cold War, shared the com-
mon fear that UN measures might restrict
their national sovereignty.
The Cold War affected the continued
development of human rights. In the late
1940s and early 1950s, the United States
found it convenient to use human rights
rhetoric as a weapon against the Soviet
Union, but with the rise of McCarthyism
in the United States and increasing criti-
cism of its domestic human rights record,
the United States began to view the devel-
opment of international human rights as a
threat to its national security. In 1953,
President Eisenhower proclaimed that the
United States would not be a party to any
human rights treaty approved by the
United Nations. It was not until the Civil
Rights Movement in the 1960s and the
Vietnam War that human rights were once
again on the U.S. public agenda.
The second half of the twentieth cen-
tury also saw an increased presence in the
United Nations of newly decolonized na-
tions. There were only four African mem-
bers of the United Nations during the
1950s. The destruction of the colonial
empires in Africa altered the nature and
composition of the United Nations. In par-
ticular, issues of racial equality and self-
determination became important issues on
the UN agenda. Indeed, the new African
and Asian states were particularly impor-
tant because their votes were instrumental
in breaking the Cold War deadlock and
precipitated a new array of international
legal mechanisms.
In the two decades after the adoption
of the Universal Declaration, the Human
Rights Commission was concerned with
drafting treaties to develop the basic cate-
gories of rights that were outlined in the
Universal Declaration. In 1966, the United
Nations adopted two treaties: the Interna-
tional Covenant on Civil and Political
Rights (ICCPR); and the International
Covenant on Economic, Social and Cul-
tural Rights (ICESCR). These covenants,
along with the Universal Declaration, com-
prise what is colloquially referred to as the
International Bill of Rights.
Civil and Political Rights
Since the second half of the twentieth cen-
tury, human rights have been categorized as
belonging to one of three generations: the
ﬁrst generation consists of civil and politi-
cal rights that can be derived from “natural
rights” philosophy; the second generation
consists of economic, social, and cultural
rights; and the third generation  includes
collective rights.
The ICCPR was designed to protect
first-generation individual rights and broadly
provides for the right of self-determination;
the enjoyment by minorities of their own
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 663 ---
HUMAN RIGHTS 587
cultures; protection of the individual’s
physical integrity; procedural fairness when
an individual is deprived of his or her liberty;
equal protection norms; freedoms of belief,
speech, and association; and the right to
political participation.
Economic and Social Rights
The ICESCR protects second generation
rights, such as the rights to work; just and
favorable conditions of work; rest and
leisure; trade unions; social security; strike;
protection of the family; and an adequate
standard of living.
The ofﬁcial UN position is that the
ICCPR and ICESCR are indivisible and
equally important. This position masks the
disagreement that exists over the two
treaties, which was fueled by the Cold War.
At one extreme, a number of states, most
notably the former Soviet Union and
China, took the view that economic and
social rights were superior to civil and po-
litical rights. At the other extreme, some
states, such as the United States, considered
civil and political rights to be paramount.
African states have overwhelmingly
committed themselves to protecting eco-
nomic, social, and cultural rights by widely
ratifying the ICESCR, and in some cases
entrenching these rights in their constitu-
tions. The ambivalence of Western states,
however, is one of the challenges facing the
development of economic and social rights.
The United States, for example, is yet to
ratify the ICESCR. In practice, “no group
of states has consistently followed up its
rhetorical support at the international level
with practical and sustained programmes of
implementation” (Steiner and Alston,
2000, p. 250).
In addition to the “core” treaties de-
scribed above, the international human
rights legal architecture includes a number
of other treaties which include conventions
dealing with the rights of women, slavery,
torture, racial discrimination, children, mi-
grant workers, genocide, and apartheid. In
addition to these binding treaties, there is a
developing body of nonbinding UN
human rights standards. Various regional
arrangements supplement the international
treaties, such as the European Convention
for the Protection of Human Rights and
Fundamental Freedoms, the African Char-
ter of Human and Peoples’ Rights, and the
American Convention on Human Rights.
The development of human rights is at
different stages on either side of the Atlantic.
The African system is perhaps the least
developed of the regional human rights
regimes. The African Commission on
Human and Peoples’ Rights, developed
from the UN charter, has few powers and,
for the most part, has been hesitant to exer-
cise any power that it does have. In contrast,
Europe is perhaps the most developed region
in terms of human rights. The United King-
dom, for example, has acceded to the major
international human rights treaties, accepts
rulings of the European Court of Human
Rights and the European Court of Justice,
and enforces European human rights law in
its domestic courts. The United States, on
the other hand, continues to exhibit reluc-
tance to be bound by international human
rights law. Even when it has ratiﬁed treaties,
it has done so with signiﬁcant and impor-
tant reservations. It is easy, however, to over-
state the failings of the United States. Since
the end of the Cold War, the United States
has consistently advocated the prosecution
of human rights violations and has been in-
strumental in setting up international crim-
inal courts for Yugoslavia, Rwanda, Iraq,
Cambodia, and Sierra Leone.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 664 ---
588 H UMANITARIANASSISTANCE
Human rights law has also been criti-
cized for having too much of a Western
focus. During the Cold War, Western and
communist states clashed over the univer-
salism of human rights. More recently,
some Islamic and East Asian states have ar-
gued that the international human rights
movement has not adequately considered
the cultural traditions of these states. Cul-
tural distinctiveness is also a key feature of
the African Charter on Human and Peo-
ples’ Rights which refers to “taking into
consideration the virtues of historical tradi-
tion and the values of African civilization.”
The issue of cultural relativism is an impor-
tant challenge facing the international
human rights movement through the
twenty-ﬁrst century.
Despite the tremendous advance in
human rights in the past half-century,
human rights violations continue to be a
problem. The 1990s saw human rights
problems such as ethnic cleansing, indis-
criminate bombing of civilians, govern-
ment brutality, and systematic violence
against women in many countries. The
challenge for the twenty-ﬁrst century is to
translate the emerging consciousness of
human rights into a global reality. The
goals of the human rights movement are far
from being realized and there continues to
be a signiﬁcant gap between principles of
human rights and the corresponding prac-
tices of states.
Simon Chapple

HUMANITARIANASSISTANCE
Humanitarian assistance is aid given to
people in emergency situations caused
either by natural disasters or human-made
situations (such as famine and conﬂict) in
order to prevent loss of life and livelihood.
This assistance can take a number of forms,
including food, medical supplies, tempo-
rary shelters, drinking water, and cash. It
can come from donations by both private
sources and governments. Humanitarian
assistance is delivered by different kinds of
organizations. Much of it is delivered by
governmental organizations such as the
U.S. Agency for International Develop-
ment (USAID), as well as private voluntary
organizations (also called nongovernmental
organizations or NGOs) such as CARE
and Oxfam. Multilateral organizations
such as the United Nations’ World Food
Programme (WFP) and the Ofﬁce for the
Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
(OCHA) also play a very important role.
Finally, some African governments have
humanitarian or disaster response ofﬁces
to mobilize local resources and coordinate
the efforts of their international partners.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 665 ---
HUMANITARIANASSISTANCE 589
Despite the existence of many humanitar-
ian organizations, it often takes a large pub-
lic outcry in the West to initiate major hu-
manitarian campaigns; this was as much
the case for the 1984–1985 famine in
Ethiopia as it is for Darfur, Sudan, twenty
years later. While humanitarian assistance
has traditionally been given on the basis of
neutrality and impartiality, this aspect of
the humanitarian ethic has been called into
question since the early 1990s, particularly
following the inadequate international re-
sponse to the 1994 Rwandan genocide.
A History of Humanitarian 
Assistance in Africa
Prior to achieving independence, most
African colonies were dependent on colo-
nial administrations and their own re-
sources for relief from famine and other
disasters. There was nothing to compel
colonial administrations to develop system-
atic policies for responding to what are
now considered humanitarian emergencies.
Famines and other disasters certainly oc-
curred, some of them caused or worsened
by colonial policies or practices, but the
colonial powers saw relief measures as an
administrative obligation at best, and often
did little to ease hardship.
Meanwhile, in Europe and the United
States, several organizations emerged to
help Europeans survive the ravages of
World War II, including the Cooperative
for American Remittances to Europe
(CARE) in America and the Oxford Com-
mittee for Famine Relief (later Oxfam) in
the United Kingdom. In addition, the
United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation
Administration was formed in 1943 for
the same purpose, though its operations
were taken over by the International Refugee
Organization, which then became the
Ofﬁce of the United Nations High Com-
missioner for Refugees (UNHCR) in 1952.
While these organizations initially focused
on rebuilding war-torn Europe, they even-
tually turned their attention to Asia and
Africa in the 1960s and 1970s, primarily to
ﬁll gaps that newly independent govern-
ments were unable to ﬁll. 
Following independence, few African
governments gave priority to antifamine
measures because the promise of economic
development seemed to make them unnec-
essary. However, a number of humanitarian
crises arose that made several governments,
as well as the international community, re-
assess the need for more systematic disaster
prevention and preparedness. One of these
disasters was the famine in Biafra, a state
which had tried to secede from Nigeria.
The Biafran famine became widely known
in 1968 following reports by journalists
that included photographs of starving chil-
dren. As there was no United Nations pres-
ence there, the relief effort was run by
NGOs. Joint Church Aid ran a major air-
lift, and the International Committee of
the Red Cross (ICRC) also participated
until it agreed to pull out following a con-
ﬂict with the Nigerian government. The re-
lief efforts continued for eighteen months,
until the war ended with Nigeria retaining
Biafra. The Biafra crisis was the training
ground of an entire generation of humani-
tarian aid workers, and saw the creation of
new private humanitarian organizations,
such as the Irish NGO Concern. It also
prompted the French physician Bernard
Kouchner to found Médecins Sans Fron-
tières (Doctors without Borders). More-
over, the crisis was an ethical watershed
for contemporary humanitarianism. At
the time of the crisis, the NGOs accepted
the Biafran assertion that they would be
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 666 ---
590 H UMANITARIANASSISTANCE
massacred by Nigerian federal troops if they
did not receive international assistance.
However, years later, analysts began to ac-
knowledge that the humanitarian interven-
tion had actually prolonged the war and
therefore the suffering of the Biafrans. The
Biafra experience has been painfully recalled
each time the international community has
had to decide whether to provide humani-
tarian assistance in situations of civil war.
Another major disaster was the 1974
famine in Ethiopia and the West African
Sahel. This famine resulted in the prolifer-
ation of disaster relief organizations within
both Africa and the international commu-
nity. Despite the creation of the United
Nations Disaster Relief Ofﬁce (UNDRO)
in 1971, the World Food Programme,
Food and Agriculture Organization, and
World Health Organization all established
their own emergency response ofﬁces in
1974–1975. The Ofﬁce of Sahelian Relief
Operations was established, and many
European governments as well as the United
States created special disaster relief agen-
cies, either within or in addition to their
development agencies. African countries es-
tablished relief agencies as well, such as
Ethiopia’s Relief and Rehabilitation Com-
mission (now the Disaster Prevention and
Preparedness Commission). The number
of humanitarian organizations and actors
thus multiplied considerably during the
1970s.
Recent Changes in 
Humanitarian Assistance
There have been a number of global
changes that have affected humanitarian as-
sistance to Africa since the 1980s. These in-
clude the increasing privatization of foreign
aid beginning in the 1980s, as well as the
end of the Cold War. Furthermore, the role
of humanitarian intervention in the 1993
collapse of Somalia and the 1994 Rwandan
genocide has called into question the
notion of humanitarian neutrality.
Through the 1970s and 1980s, NGOs
played an ever greater role in humanitarian
interventions in Africa. During the Cold
War, these organizations provided assis-
tance in countries or parts of countries that
were “on the other side.” A good example
of this was the work of the church-based
NGO consortium known as the Emer-
gency Relief Desk, which provided relief
aid to provinces in northern Ethiopia that
were engaged in civil conﬂict with the cen-
tral government and that suffered greatly in
the 1984–1985 famine. The NGOs were
able to bypass the Ethiopian government
by working from across the border in
Sudan. In fact, NGOs were increasingly
used to channel assistance from the West
around African governments that were seen
as corrupt or inefﬁcient, in effect “privatiz-
ing” what used to be ofﬁcial government
assistance. NGOs are not subject to profes-
sional regulation and have very little ac-
countability, beyond convincing their
donors that they are doing what they claim
to do in order to continue receiving sup-
port. Therefore, the turn to NGOs to avoid
corruption and inefﬁciency may just re-
place one set of problems with another. T o
address this problem, humanitarian agen-
cies and groups have begun developing sets
of standards to improve humanitarian prac-
tice and accountability. For example, the
Sphere Project based in Geneva, Switzer-
land, has developed the Humanitarian
Charter outlining disaster victims’ rights.
With the end of the Cold War, internal
conﬂict in Africa increasingly became cause
for humanitarian assistance. African na-
tions were no longer the pawns of the two
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 667 ---
HUMANITARIANASSISTANCE 591
superpowers, and national sovereignty
began to be eroded, particularly during
times of internal strife or conﬂict. There-
fore, humanitarian action came to be seen
(among the international community, at
least) as driven by a universal obligation to
help people who are suffering, rather than
interference in the internal affairs of sover-
eign nations. More crises came to be char-
acterized as “complex political emergen-
cies,” or crises in which politics were the
primary cause of suffering. There was also
greater concern for civilian suffering in
conﬂict situations, and the obligation to al-
leviate it through such measures as Opera-
tion Lifeline Sudan, which brought hu-
manitarian assistance to victims of civil war
in southern Sudan through the 1990s. This
shift placed humanitarian workers in con-
ﬂict situations, and also increased the hu-
manitarian role of national and UN mili-
tary forces. For example, the military forces
that intervened in Rwanda in 1994 at-
tempted to protect humanitarian workers,
assist humanitarian agencies in their work,
and deliver relief supplies directly to con-
ﬂict victims.
However, these changes in the role of
humanitarian assistance have caused many
people to question the neutrality and im-
partiality of humanitarian organizations.
T wo major humanitarian crises in particu-
lar necessitated a critical examination of
late twentieth-century humanitarianism:
the collapse of Somalia in 1993, and the
genocide in Rwanda in 1994. In the former,
humanitarian agencies called for the mili-
tary occupation of Somalia to facilitate
humanitarian response to a major famine
there. This situation happened to coincide
with U.S. government interests and with
the UN Secretariat’s desire to increase its
mandate. The result was the dramatic
collapse of the Somali state, which has
taken over a decade to rebuild. In Rwanda,
humanitarian neutrality prompted agencies
to call for a ceaseﬁre by the Rwandese
Patriotic Front (RPF), which was ﬁghting
the genocidal government. This ceaseﬁre
would have, in effect, prolonged the geno-
cide, as the victory of the RPF is what
ended it. The two catastrophes of Somalia
and Rwanda led to greater recognition of
the political role that humanitarian agen-
cies play during crises, whether they intend
to or not. Even so, there remains a lack of a
policy or ethics framework for humanitar-
ian agencies who insert themselves in polit-
ical and military situations.
Critiques of Humanitarian 
Assistance
Numerous critiques of humanitarian assis-
tance have emerged over the years. They
have focused on both motives and methods
of humanitarian efforts. For example, there
has tended to be an emphasis on food in
humanitarian responses in Africa at the ex-
pense of other major concerns, such as pro-
vision of clean water and health supplies.
This emphasis on food is all the more trou-
bling as most deaths during famines are
caused by disease rather than hunger.
The prominence of food aid has some
historic roots in the U.S. food aid program.
This program was formally institutionalized
by the Agricultural T rade Development and
Assistance Act of 1954, also known as
Public Law (PL) 480, which effectively sep-
arated food aid from other types of foreign
aid. It also established three forms of food
aid: that to be sold in recipient countries;
that earmarked for famine and other emer-
gencies, and that to be provided to U.S.
private voluntary organizations for distrib-
ution in the United States and overseas.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 668 ---
592 H UMANITARIANASSISTANCE
This structure exists today. From the begin-
ning, the link between the food aid pro-
gram and the need to dispose of U.S. agri-
cultural surplus was obvious, as was the
desire to develop commercial markets for
U.S. commodities, and led to some criti-
cism of the program. However, the Ameri-
can public (particularly farmers and agri-
cultural interest groups) preferred giving or
selling food aid to offering ﬁnancial assis-
tance. There is concern that giving away
“free food” creates a situation of depen-
dency, where African food producers be-
come dependent on food aid rather than
their own production. Other types of
humanitarian interventions have been de-
signed to try to solve this problem, as well
as address the effects of food aid on local
agricultural markets in Africa where food
producers find themselves unable to
compete with free food from America or
Europe. Some agencies, such as the WFP ,
buy more food aid locally to support
African markets. Food-for-work programs,
in which recipients engage in public works
projects in order to receive their rations,
have been another solution. Yet another
type of program that is increasing in popu-
larity is cash-for-work, whose advocates
recognize the importance of boosting local
markets during times of crisis, particularly
when the problem is not lack of food on
the market but people’s lack of income to
buy the food.
Finally, there is a question of what moti-
vates humanitarian agencies, particularly as
humanitarianism has become more of a busi-
ness driven by market forces with an increas-
ing number of organizations competing for
available resources. These market forces cause
some humanitarian emergencies to receive
inordinate amounts of aid, while others go
virtually unnoticed. Moreover, the new “war
on terror” launched by the United States has
made U.S. national security interests a major
part of the humanitarian landscape, particu-
larly as the crises in Iraq and Afghanistan
draw huge amounts of resources away from
emergency responses elsewhere. T o critics,
these factors signal the demise of the tradi-
tional humanitarian ethic of helping people
altruistically and impartially.
Jericho Burg

HURSTON,Z ORA NEALE
(1891–1960)
Zora Neale Hurston was an African Amer-
ican novelist, dramatist, and anthropologist
whose best-known work draws heavily on
the vernacular folk culture of her home
state, Florida. But she also traveled widely
in the Caribbean, and she brought a com-
parative diasporic perspective to her reﬂec-
tions on cultural forms, such as Voodoo
and biblical allegory, while the ethical and
political issues raised by emancipation
(from slavery and colonialism) are never far
from the surface.
She was born in Notasulga, Alabama,
but she grew up in the black town of
Eatonville, Florida. She attended school
there and in Jacksonville, then joined a
traveling theater company, before continu-
ing her education at Morgan Academy
(Baltimore, MD) and Howard University
(Washington, DC), where she was encour-
aged as a writer by Alain Locke.
Hurston moved to New York City in
1925, where she published a number of
stories and plays inspired by the Eatonville
of her childhood and became a leading ﬁg-
ure of the Harlem Renaissance, impressing
her associates with her gift as a storyteller
Harlem Renaissance author Zora Neale Hurston, famous for her 1938 novel, Their Eyes Were Watching God.
(Library of Congress)
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 670 ---
594 H URSTON,Z ORA NEALE
and mimic. At the same time, she studied
anthropology at Barnard College, obtain-
ing a BA, and, with the encouragement of
Franz Boas, undertook several folklore-
collecting trips in Florida, the Gulf Coast,
and the Bahamas between 1927 and 1931.
These trips were largely ﬁnanced by the
philanthropist Charlotte Osgood Mason,
who imposed conditions on Hurston’s re-
search. It was only in 1931 after her con-
tract came to an end that Hurston was free
to publish her ﬁndings. Over the next few
years her writing diversiﬁed to embrace a
variety of literary forms—scholarly essays,
sketches, musical revues, and her first
novel, Jonah’s Gourd Vine (1934)—as she
sought to devise new ways of presenting the
material she remembered and collected.
These experiments with different liter-
ary forms culminated in Mules and Men
(1935). The book presents her research
ﬁndings in the form of a ﬁrst-person narra-
tive that foregrounds the relationship be-
tween the author and her informants, and
it includes an account of her initiation as a
“hoodoo” practitioner in New Orleans.
This book was followed by Their Eyes Were
Watching God (1937), a novel set in
Florida. Written in the third person, the
narrative voice adopts the idiom and per-
spective of Janie Crawford, telling her story
as she returns home after the death of her
third husband.
Both works were praised for their vivid
rendering of the vernacular, but some
found their apparently exclusive emphasis
on rural humor and self-reliance detracted
from the harsher realities of the segregated
South. Famously, the young Richard
Wright accused its author of having her
characters ‘“swing like a pendulum eter-
nally in that safe and narrow orbit in which
America likes to see the Negro live, between
laughter and tears” (Gates and Appiah,
1993, p. 17). Hurston, in turn, lampooned
his didacticism, anger, and poor grasp of
dialect.
A Rosenwald Fellowship to pursue a
doctorate was suddenly cut back in 1935,
but a Guggenheim Fellowship the following
year funded a research trip to the
Caribbean which provided material for
Hurston’s next book, T ell My Horse: Voodoo
and Life in Haiti and Jamaica (1938). In
the eyes of some reviewers, it was a mix of
jaunty reportage, scientiﬁc pretensions, and
offhand political analysis. Her third novel,
Moses Man of the Mountain (1939), carni-
valistically rewrites the story of Exodus,
bringing to it her knowledge of hoodoo
practices, classical myth, and Egyptology.
By making Moses an Egyptian, which, in
the terms of the African American allegory
she reworks makes him a white man, is a
controversial move that has generally been
overlooked.
Hurston’s wartime autobiography, Dust
Tracks on a Road (1942), was a commercial
success, partly because of its refusal to dwell
on racial discrimination (although passages
cut from the published version are more
openly critical of U.S. society). She re-
turned to Florida for the setting of her
fourth novel, Seraph on the Suwanee
(1948), a sensitive study of the marriage of
a poor white couple, Arvay and Jim
Meserve. It did not sell well, however. A
projected ﬁfth novel, a ﬁctionalized study
of the life and times of Herod the Great,
was never completed, and only parts of the
manuscript have survived. 
Hurston’s political journalism of the
1950s betrays conservative Republican
sympathies, including an opposition to de-
segregation, which alienated her from pre-
vious readers. During this period she found
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 671 ---
HUTU 595
it increasingly difﬁcult to earn a living by
writing, and took jobs as a secretary,
teacher, and maid. Her health deteriorated
and she died in Fort Pierce, Florida, in
1960.
After more than thirty years of neglect,
Hurston’s work was rediscovered in the
1970s. With her ear for the vernacular cul-
ture of the black South, and her strong fe-
male characters, works such as Their Eyes
inspired a new generation of writers such as
Alice Walker and T oni Morrison. Critics of
the 1980s began to pay more attention to
Hurston’s technical innovations as a writer,
and in the 1990s she was widely recognized
as having anticipated many of the concerns
of post-modern ethnography.
Where previously Dust Tracks, for in-
stance, had been condemned as unnecessar-
ily elliptical about her personal life, it is
now more usually considered to address
head-on some of the contradictions and
pitfalls of autobiography. And far from ig-
noring the harsh realities of Jim Crow, her
“Southern” writings are these days more
often admired for the way they both record
and enact cultural strategies of resistance.
The conviction that Hurston’s best work
is rooted in the romanticized black commu-
nity she is deemed to have grown up in is less
powerful than it once was. Some critics have
endeavored to stress her appreciation of her
home state as a multicultural space, riven by
racial, class, and gender conﬂicts, as evident
in her contributions to the Florida Federal
Writers’ Project. T ell My Horseand Moses are
beginning to be reappraised for their innova-
tive exploration of themes of diasporic signif-
icance, such as African “survivals,” syn-
cretism, national liberation, and postcolonial
reconstruction. Above all, perhaps, there is a
growing recognition that previous attempts
to recruit Hurston to prevailing orthodoxies
has failed to take account of her anarchic
humor, radical individualism, and delight in
provocation.
Alasdair Pettinger

HUTU
The Hutu are the most populous ethnic
group in the Great Lakes region of central
Africa, including the current nations of Bu-
rundi, Rwanda, and eastern Zaire. They
settled in the region about 2,000 years ago,
dominating the indigenous T wa, a people
related to the pygmies. The Hutu gradually
cleared the forested hills and established
agricultural communities. The major social
unit in Hutu society was the clan, and at
the height of Hutu power in the ﬁrst half of
the second millennium, the clans united
under petty kings known as bahinza.
In the sixteenth century, the T utsi, a
people culturally and linguistically related
to the Hutu, migrated from Ethiopia into
central Africa and soon achieved hegemony
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 672 ---
596 H UTU
over the more numerous but very loosely
uniﬁed Hutu. A more physically imposing
people (on average about four inches taller
than the Hutu, who average ﬁve feet ﬁve
inches in height), the T utsi were favored by
the Belgian colonial regime. At the time of
independence, the Hutu constituted about
85 percent of the population of Burundi
and almost 90 percent of the population
of Rwanda, and yet in both new nations
the T utsi were politically and militarily
dominant.
In the late 1950s, the early 1970s, and
the mid-1990s, the tensions between the
Hutu and the T utsi erupted into terrible
violence, taking tens of thousands of lives
in each instance. In the mid-1990s, the
Hutu prosecuted an especially vicious
genocide against the T utsi and against
fellow Hutu whose loyalties had fallen into
question. The world community was ap-
palled by the carnage but very slow to inter-
vene. In particular, the United States,
which had recently intervened to stop the
Serbian genocide against Bosnian Muslims,
was criticized for intervening in Europe but
failing to do so in Africa. By the time that
the T utsi were able to reassert military con-
trol, the level of brutality and the body
count approached what the Khmer Rouge
had inﬂicted on their countrymen during
their reign of terror in Cambodia.
In the end, because of their excesses,
the Hutu lost most of the international
support for their efforts to achieve self-
determination. War-crimes trials have been
initiated against the perpetrators of the
worst acts of violence during the genocide,
and large numbers of Hutu have been
forced into a harrowing existence in impro-
vised refugee camps in neighboring Zaire
and Tanzania.
Martin Kich

IGBO
Igbo, which earlier colonial and diasporic
discourse inaccurately writes as “Ibo,”
“Iboh,” “Ebo,” “Eboe,” and “Eboh,” deﬁnes
an ethnic people of Nigeria, a person of Igbo
descent, as well as the language of the people.
The word is both singular and plural, with a
collective variant, “Ndigbo,” which refers to
the global nation as a whole. The Igbo are a
nation of forty-ﬁve million people whose
traditional homeland is located in southeast-
ern Nigeria, on the West African Bight of
Biafra off the coast of the Atlantic Ocean.
One creation myth asserts the heavenly
descent of the Igbo progenitor, Eri, at the
present Nri site. Modern historians, how-
ever, trace centuries of migratory patterns
between Igbo ozo (sacred courts) and Igbo
abamaba (secret cults) that, in one in-
stance, began with the Hebraic dispersal
from Israel, through Egypt and Sudan
across northern Nigeria to Nri. The oldest
kingdom in Nigeria, Nri is “the heart of
Igbo nationality.” The eze-nri (priest-king)
is a spiritual head and potentate. Igbo dis-
tinctions in ritual, leadership, commerce,
scholarship, scientiﬁc advancement, and
adventure are traceable to the unifying
forces of the priestly northern Igbo Nri
hegemony and the fraternal southern Igbo
ekpe and okonko.
In the colonial era, the Igbo were the
biggest exporters of palm oil in the world.
In the modern era, an abundance of oil in
southern Igbo land has made Nigeria the
ﬁfth biggest exporter of petroleum in the
world. Ninth-century Igbo-Ukwu bronze
casting and the Nsibidi script laid the foun-
dations for the high culture of bronze
technology and the writing alphabet in
West Africa. 
American-trained Igbo Nnamdi
Azikiwe (also known as Zik Azikiwe) led the
expulsion of British colonialism in Nigeria
and became the country’s ﬁrst president and
coined an African nationalism speciﬁc to
Nigeria that was known as “Zikism.” The
Zikist global African decolonization project
and the trans-African journalism of Zik’s
African Morning Post and West African Pilot
aided the Pan-Africanist vision of Kwame
N’krumah and Nelson Mandela. Nigeria’s
genocide against the Igbo and General
Ojukwu’s Biafran War (1966–1970) are
landmarks of the Igbo’s continuing struggle
for universal black emancipation. The post-
colonial signiﬁcation of Chinua Achebe’s
Things Fall Apart (1958) exempliﬁes Igbo
cultural interventionism in contemporary
black experience.
Igbo emergence as a “global tribe”
began with the Middle Passage. As a densely
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 674 ---
598 I KE,VINCENT CHUKWUEMEKA
populated ethnic group with the highest
birthrate in Africa, Igbo were the worst hit
by the transatlantic slave trade. Igbo slave
revolts were historic in Belize, Haiti, Jamaica,
Martinique, and much of the West Indies.
In the United States, Igbo slaves generated
legendary controversies with the 1732 poi-
soning death of President James Madison’s
grandfather, Ambrose Madison, at his
Montpelier slave plantation in Virginia, and
the 1803 drowning of ten of them at Igbo
Landing on St. Simons Island, Georgia,
after their revolt on a slave ship drowned
three white overseers. The legends of such
Igbo slaves and descendants of Igbo slaves as
Edward Blyden, Olaudah Equiano, Frantz
Fanon, James Horton, Ja Ja of Opobo,
T oussaint Loverture, Archibald “Aneaso”
Monteath, and Booker T . Washington
demonstrate the story of the black Diaspora
as the story of the rise of global Igbo
civilization.

IKE,VINCENT
CHUKWUEMEKA (1931–)
Born in 1931 in Ndikelionwu, in Awka,
Anambra State, eastern Nigeria, Vincent
Chukwuemeka Ike is a prominent novelist
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 675 ---
IMBUGA,F RANCIS D. 599
and administrator who has contributed sig-
niﬁcantly to the progress of Nigerian and
West African education. He is representa-
tive of a whole generation of Nigerians
who trained at elite secondary schools,
the University of Ibadan, and abroad, and
then pursued prestigious careers. Ike at-
tended the Government College, Umuahia,
before studying at the University of Ibadan,
graduating in 1955. T wo years at Stanford
University in the United States brought
him into close contact with the American
education sector. On his return to Nigeria,
he became assistant registrar of the Univer-
sity of Ibadan in 1957, and then registrar at
the University of Nigeria, Nsukka (UNN)
in 1963. UNN, founded in 1960 with the
help of Michigan State University, was the
ﬁrst indigenous university and the ﬁrst
U.S. land-grant type university in Africa.
The Nsukka course structure, entirely
American, was very different from the
British colonial higher education system,
and a number of black Americans were on
the staff. For Nigerians at home, this was
the ﬁrst real contact with African Ameri-
cans and Black Nationalism. After the civil
war in 1970, UNN reopened and Ike led
its restoration. He next served as registrar
of the West African Examinations Council
before becoming pro-chancellor of the
University of Benin in 1980. In 1983–1985,
he was visiting professor of English and
writer-in-residence at the University of Jos.
Ike’s interest in education and his desire
to encourage local publishing led him to
found the Nigerian Book Foundation in
1991. He is best known for his novels, espe-
cially T oads for Supper (1965), The Naked
Gods (1970), The Potter’s Wheel (1974),
Sunset at Dawn (1976), Expo 77 and The
Chicken Chasers (1980), and The Bottled
Leopard and The Search (1991). The novels
are inspired by Ike’s personal experience
of the social and political development of
Nigeria; they combine a satire of public in-
stitutions and an appreciation of traditional
values and oral literature. Several have been
on school programs for decades and some
have been translated into foreign languages.
Ike’s only U.S.-set novel, To  My
Husband from Iowa (1996), is the ﬁctional
account of the writer’s experience at the
International Writing Program, University
of Iowa, a residency program founded in
1967 that brings together established writ-
ers from all over the world. The Nigerian
female protagonist narrates her experience,
ranging from casual observations to a re-
ﬂection on the American way of life, to
show how developing countries can emu-
late Western values while keeping their own
traditions. Writing in English, Ike has at-
tracted a vast readership abroad, but he also
translated one of his novels, The Potter’s
Wheel, into Igbo. 
Ike is an Honorary Fellow in Writing,
University of Iowa: an Honorary Fellow,
City and Guild of London Institute; and
UNN made him a Doctor of Letters. In
2001, he got an award from the National
Council for Arts and Culture (NCAC) in
Abuja for his leading role in the cultural
sector.
Francoise Parent Ugochukwu

Imbuga was born on February 2, 1947,
in Wenyange Village in the western part of
Kenya. His experiences as a youth with
Kenyan culture and life helped to form his
disdain for city elites who were seemingly
out of touch with traditional Kenyan cul-
ture and values. Imbuga gained distinction
as a writer and actor early on in his life. As
a high school student in 1969, he was a ﬁ-
nalist in the Kenya National School’s
Drama Festival. From this platform of suc-
cess Imbuga became a writer and actor for
the Voice of Kenya television series from
1970 to 1973. As he wrote and acted on
television, Imbuga gained his BA in educa-
tion (1973) and later his MA in drama
(1975) at the University of Nairobi.
Imbuga’s professional experience as a writer
helped him gain a lectureship at the Uni-
versity of Nairobi in 1976 and later at
Kenyatta University. In 1988 Imbuga
moved to the United States to pursue his
PhD in literature at the University of Iowa,
which he completed in 1991.
Imbuga’s important plays include The
Burning of Rags (1989), Aminata (1988),
M a no fK a ﬁ r a(1984), The Successor (1979),
Betrayal in the City (1976), The Married
Bachelor (1973), andThe Forth Trial(1972).
His plays with the most interest to African
and North American scholars and readers are
Aminata and Betrayal in the City. Betrayal in
the City is Imbuga’s most famous and most
controversial play. The play takes place in
Kaﬁra, a ﬁctional postcolonial country situ-
ated in Africa, and it highlights the corrup-
tion of elites in the city who are not respon-
sible to the citizens of the country. Originally
the play was used in public schools across
Kenya, but it was later banned because it was
too subversive and education ofﬁcials wor-
ried that it might inculcate a hatred of the
Kenyan political elites. Aminata is Imbuga’s
attempt to call attention to the often-
repressed role of women in African society.
The play features a woman lawyer who is em-
inent in her ﬁeld but is not allowed to inherit
her father’s lands because she is a woman.
Imbuga is one of many prominent
Kenyan writers who have made a profound
impact upon postcolonial literature. His
examination of the intersection of Kenyan
and Western cultures has helped to recon-
ceive what it means to be “Kenyan.” There
are numerous scholarly books and articles
written about Imbuga in Africa and
America. Imbuga’s importance continues
to grow as African studies grow at North
America universities.
Brett Bennett

IMMIGRATION,U NITED STATES 601
IMMIGRATION,U NITED
STATES
Free people of African descent have been
migrating to lands now part of or associ-
ated with the United States for five
centuries—directly from Africa, from the
Caribbean, and elsewhere in the Americas,
and in lesser numbers from elsewhere in
the world. The numbers who have mi-
grated, their reasons for migrating, and
how they have migrated have varied widely.
Prospective immigrants have decided to
migrate, not to migrate, and how to mi-
grate based upon such things as their prior
knowledge of the United States; its indige-
nous or colonial predecessors; political,
economic, and other conditions where they
were living before; their understandings of
the experiences of relatives, friends, or
others who previously migrated; the encour-
agement or discouragement of relatives,
friends, or others; their own prior exposure
to U.S. citizens and residents; restrictions
on immigration and naturalization; the
availability and cost of transportation; the
available means of transportation; their
economic situations; and myriad other in-
dividual and family factors. Immigration of
people of African descent to the United
States has been increasing. More blacks
have migrated to the United States since
1945 than were ever brought into the
United States and its predecessor colonies
as slaves.
The Colonial Era
During the age of European exploration
and colonial expansion, ship crew members
were the ﬁrst free Africans to view lands
later to become parts of or associated with
the United States. Free black seamen
worked on Spanish and Portuguese ships,
and the crews of Columbus’s ships are
known to have included free blacks when
he and they explored the island then called
Boriquen (now Puerto Rico) in 1493. Vin-
cent Yanez Pinzon’s crew likewise included
blacks when their ship was blown off
course by a Caribbean storm and landed on
Boriquen in 1500. They had been attempt-
ing to return to their base on Hispanola
(Haiti) after becoming the ﬁrst people of
the Eastern Hemisphere to discover the
mouth of the Maranon (Amazon) and
South America’s northern coast. When
Juan Ponce de Leon led voyages from
Hispanola to explore and then colonize
Boriquen (which he renamed) in 1508 and
1509, those accompanying him included
Juan Garrido, an aristocratic black who had
migrated to Lisbon from his West African
birthplace. Garrido went with Ponce on
another voyage in 1513, during which they
and the others in their party made the ﬁrst
reported European discovery of Florida,
and again in 1521 when Ponce made a
fatal—for him—attempt to colonize
Florida.
In those years, the only restriction on
migration to Puerto Rico and Florida was a
practical one: whether the indigenous resi-
dents were able to ﬁght off prospective
colonists. The native residents of Puerto
Rico were not, and an all-male Spanish
colony, including Garrido, was established
there in 1509. The native residents of
Florida were able to ﬁght, so Ponce and
his Florida colonizing party retreated to
Havana, where Ponce died in July 1521 of
an arrow wound. Garrido was more seaman
and soldier than colonist. After retreating
from Florida with the wounded Ponce, he
quickly joined Hernando Cortes in Mexico
in time to participate in the siege and con-
quest of T enochtitlan in August 1521, if his

subsequent application for a Spanish pen-
sion is believed.
Others of African origin who soon
reached areas now part of the United States
included a black West African ship captain,
more recently from Portugal, whose
Spanish-ﬂagged ship and crew explored the
area of present-day New York harbor in
1526, and a black Moor of North African
origin who unexpectedly landed with his
surviving crewmates on the T exas coast in
1528, after their ship was blown off course
by a storm over the Gulf of Mexico.
In the colonial period, more free peo-
ple of African origin immigrated once per-
manent colonization of the lands now con-
stituting the continental United States
began. Some came as already free people.
Others came of their own choice as inden-
tured servants, becoming free after com-
pleting agreed-upon periods of service.
Some were slaves who received their free-
dom upon arriving.
The ethnic origins of the soldiers and
settlers who established Spain’s colonies in
Florida in the 1560s, New Mexico in the
1590s, T exas in the 1710s, and California
in the 1760s and 1770s are unclear. What
is known, however, is that Florida’s settlers
came from areas of Spain with meaningful
percentages of mulattos and blacks, and
that a Spanish viceroy warned a leader of
the Florida colonization effort to be careful
of the “half-breeds” and “mulattos” in his
midst. Also known is that colonial New
Mexico, T exas, Arizona, and California
were largely populated by a combination of
mixed bloods, blacks, and indigenous con-
verts to Catholicism—with mulattos iden-
tifying themselves as mixed bloods. Few
colonists identiﬁed themselves as espanols.
The policies of Spain toward further
immigration to its colonies varied. Within
two weeks of stepping ashore to take pos-
session of Florida and found St. Augustine,
Spain’s adelantado, or governor and mili-
tary leader, led an attack on the residents of
a nearby French Huguenot settlement es-
tablished the year before, slaughtering as
many as 300 of the “evil Lutherans.” On
the other hand, Spain later offered freedom
to any escaped slaves migrating to Florida
from England’s colonies to the north, if
they were willing to become Catholics.
Spain’s North American colonies to the
west were isolated, and so lightly populated
(except for New Mexico where there were
approximately 25,000 settlers by 1780), that
immigration to them as such was not a sig-
niﬁcant issue. Spain’s major concern was
with preserving its monopoly on trade with
its colonies. T o that end, it attempted to
keep non-Spanish traders away from them.
At times, at the request of the church fathers
who were usually a part (if not the leaders)
of its colonization efforts, it also made ef-
forts, typically unsuccessful in the end, at
religious-based exclusions of non-Catholics.
Spanish New Orleans, ceded to Spain
by France in 1763, had a free black popu-
lation of only 99 in 1769. One free black
who passed through New Orleans in the
1760s was Jean-Baptiste Point du Sable. He
then went north, established his home and
a trading post on the western shore of Lake
Michigan, and is now viewed as the
founder of Chicago.
In comparison, there were no legal re-
strictions on migration into England’s
North American colonies until 1763. Im-
migration was generally encouraged by
colonial legislatures and governors and the
English and British crowns, sometimes
with economic inducements. Occasional
efforts by colonial legislatures to limit
immigration in times of economic or
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

IMMIGRATION,U NITED STATES 603
cultural stress, primarily directed against
Scotch-Irish, Germans, and Catholics, were
vetoed by royal governors.
Restrictions on immigration to the
colonies enacted by the British Parliament
in 1763 responded to concerns over the de-
fensibility of new settlements on the
colonies’ western frontier. Parliament even-
tually banned all immigration to the
colonies, as strains between Britain and the
colonies mounted, but not until 1774.
Small communities of free blacks, in-
cluding immigrants, gradually developed in
the English and British colonies’ eastern
seaports during the colonial period. By
1790, the free black population of the new
United States was 59,511, with 27,054 free
blacks in the North (from Pennsylvania
north), 30,258 in the Chesapeake and
Upper South (Maryland and Delaware to
North Carolina), and 2,199 in the Lower
South (South Carolina and Georgia). The
largest numbers were 12,866 in Virginia,
8,043 in Maryland, and 6,537 in Pennsyl-
vania. Those numbers included manumit-
ted slaves as well as blacks who were free
when they migrated.
1776–1870
The United States removed all restrictions
on the immigration of free people to places
within its territorial jurisdiction upon be-
coming an independent nation. However,
the numbers of free blacks migrating to the
United States before the Civil War was rel-
atively small, except for two surges in the
1790s and 1808–1810. Pre–Civil War U.S.
Congresses chose not to regulate the immi-
gration of free people, notwithstanding
anti-immigration sentiments vigorously
asserted by some political groups and eco-
nomic interests from time to time.
The only pre–Civil War restrictions on
U.S. immigration, enacted in the ﬁrst
decade of the 1800s, did not affect free
blacks. They merely prohibited the import-
ing of slaves. Importing of slaves into some
states became illegal under U.S. federal law
effective April 1, 1804, speciﬁcally, into
those states which had already prohibited
the importing of slaves on their own. Some
states had enacted such prohibitions even
before independence was declared. Effec-
tive January 1, 1808, ship owners and oth-
ers transporting people into the rest of the
United States were similarly limited to
bringing in only free people.
However, the very ﬁrst U.S. Congress,
in its act of March 26, 1790, did prevent
free black immigrants from becoming U.S.
citizens by limiting naturalization of new
immigrants to “free white people.”
Later on, some states attempted their
own form of regulating immigration, but
in response to an inﬂux of impoverished
Irish ﬂeeing the potato famine, not blacks.
Those efforts were challenged in the courts
and failed. In The Passenger Cases (1849), a
5–4 majority of the U.S. Supreme Court
held that Massachusetts and New York laws
placing a per person tax on foreign passen-
gers arriving in those states by ship improp-
erly usurped the congressional power over
foreign commerce. The Supreme Court
majority’s opinion observed that if such a
tax were allowed without federal permis-
sion, states could prohibit ships from
bringing foreign passengers into the United
States altogether—a result it thought in-
conceivable. Proslavery Chief Justice Taney
wrote the dissent.
Despite the “free white” restriction on
U.S. citizenship, the number of free black
immigrants coming into the United States
increased in the 1790s. The increase was

largely because of slave uprisings in the
then-French colony of Saint Dominique
(Haiti). The refugees migrating to the
United States from Saint Dominique in-
cluded white slave owners and free gens de
couleur (men of color) and their slaves.
They largely settled in Atlantic seaport
towns, including Norfolk, Charleston, and
Philadelphia.
Approximately 500 of the Saint Do-
minique refugees in Philadelphia were gens
de couleur. But although blacks were
hardly a new phenomenon there, and
Philadelphia already had an elite African
American community, the new gens de
couleur received little sympathy or assis-
tance. Free black émigré men became im-
poverished, and free black émigré women
notably became paid companions of male
Americans and male refugees from France’s
own revolution—including the malleable
French diplomat Charles Maurice de
Talleyrand during his 1794–1796 U.S.
exile—as well as male white immigrants
from Saint Dominique.
The later years of the next decade saw
a second surge of immigrants from Saint
Dominique, this time largely into the Gulf
ports of Pensacola, Mobile, and New
Orleans. These francophone refugees had
ﬁrst gone to Cuba in the 1790s and early
1800s, only to been expelled in 1808 after
war broke out between France and Spain
when they refused to swear their allegiance
to Spain’s temporarily deposed Ferdinand
VII. Napoleon had replaced Ferdinand VII
on the Spanish throne with his brother
Josef Bonaparte. Some 3,102 Saint Do-
minique gens de couleur arrived in New
Orleans from Cuba in 1809 alone. As a
result, the 1810 U.S. census showed
29 percent of New Orleans’s population as
being free persons of color.
The gens de couleur and other Saint
Dominique refugees played major parts in
defeating the British in the Battle of New
Orleans. The Second Battalion of Free Men
of Color was almost entirely made up of
free black Saint Dominique refugees. Over-
all, over 600 of the approximately 3,000
U.S. soldiers who opposed the British were
free blacks. The white refugees who played
important roles in New Orleans’s defense
after being driven from Saint Dominique
included the Laﬁttes and other privateers
who provided gunners and soldiers. Other
white refugees made up a signiﬁcant per-
centage of the Battalion of Orleans.
Just before the Civil War started, a mi-
gration of African-Portuguese Cape Verde
islanders to the United States began. The
U.S. Navy’s African Squadron had been
based in the Cape Verde Islands off West
Africa’s coast, from 1843 until 1859. New
England whaling ships frequented them
too, and whaling captains soon began to re-
cruit the islanders as seamen. Some of the
recruited seamen then decided to migrate
to the United States, with the ﬁrst arriving
in New Bedford, Massachusetts, in 1860.
1870–1921
The U.S. Congress became more active on
questions of immigration and naturaliza-
tion after the Civil War, enacting qualitative
restrictions and some racial restrictions (but
not of African-origin blacks), for the ﬁrst
time. During those same years, the number
of immigrants to the United States, both
white and black, signiﬁcantly increased.
Congress began by passing the Nation-
ality Act of 1870, which added “persons of
African nativity and African descent” to
those eligible for U.S. citizenship. U.S.
Senator Charles Sumner of Massachusetts, a

IMMIGRATION,U NITED STATES 605
radical Republican, introduced bills propos-
ing to simply delete the words “free white”
from U.S. naturalization law in 1868, 1869,
and 1870. Sumner’s bills failed, but a com-
promise amendment proposed in 1870 by
radical Republican Senator Willard Warner
of Alabama, an Ohio-born former Union
Army general, was enacted.
Five years later, in 1875, Congress
passed the Page Act, the ﬁrst federal restric-
tion on immigration since importing slaves
was prohibited in 1804 and 1808. The
Page Act outlawed both the importing of
women for purposes of prostitution and the
immigration of persons convicted abroad for
nonpolitical felonies.
That same year, federal supremacy over
immigration matters was reconﬁrmed by
the Supreme Court, this time unanimously,
in Henderson v. Mayor of New York . New
York’s legislature had responded to the
Court’s decision in The Passenger Cases by
amending its state law to require either the
posting of a per person bond on allforeign-
ers arriving as ship passengers, or payment
of the same per person tax on arriving for-
eign passengers already disallowed in The
Passenger Cases. The Court’s decision in
Henderson struck down the amended law as
still impinging on Congress’s power over
foreign commerce, along with a similar
Louisiana law.
Later in 1875, in Chy Lung v. Freeman,
the Supreme Court struck down a California
law requiring bonds for some but not all
arriving foreign passengers—allegedly lewd
and debauched women—as another state
usurpation of Congress’s foreign commerce
power.
Congress enacted another federal im-
migration law in 1882. This time it barred
from immigration “lunatics,” “idiots,” and
“any person unable to take care of himself
or herself without becoming a public
charge.” It also placed a new federal per
person tax on arriving foreign ship passen-
gers. In The Head Money Casesof 1884, the
Supreme Court upheld that tax as a proper
exercise of constitutional power to regulate
foreign commerce, because it had been en-
acted by the body with that power—the
federal Congress.
The 1882 law was amended over Pres-
ident Woodrow Wilson’s veto in 1917. One
amendment added a new exclusion from
eligibility for immigration of those over six-
teen who could not read English or another
language. The 1917 amendments also in-
corporated a number of other exclusions
which had previously been added to U.S.
immigration law by other statutes enacted
after 1882. They had included epileptics,
alcoholics, sufferers from tuberculosis or
other “loathsome diseases,” polygamists,
anarchists, and those advocating violent
overthrow of the U.S. government as
among those ineligible for immigration.
The 1917 immigration law was the
ﬁrst to recognize refugees as entitled to spe-
cial consideration. It waived the new liter-
acy requirement for those able to show that
they were “seeking admission to the United
States to avoid religious persecution.”
A number of laws passed between 1882
and 1917 included racial restrictions on
immigration too. But the racial restrictions
had little effect on the immigration of
blacks because they applied only to immi-
grants from China, some other areas of
Asia, and some Paciﬁc islands.
The reported foreign-born black popu-
lation of the United States increased from
approximately 10,000 in 1870 to 54,737 in
1900. It is estimated that about 200,000
blacks migrated to the United States be-
tween 1865 and 1930, most before 1921.

Approximately 35,000 of the new
black immigrants came from the Cape
Verde Islands, the largest number between
1900 and the 1920s. Most were men who
worked in maritime-related trades and ﬁsh-
ing and as unskilled factory laborers and
crop pickers in southeastern Massachusetts
and Rhode Island. There they created their
own social institutions after ﬁnding them-
selves unwanted in local Portuguese and
Madeiran society.
Most other black immigrants between
1865 and 1930 came from the Caribbean.
Many of the ﬁrst were Cubans, who came
to cities on the Gulf and East Coast in the
decades before the Spanish-American War
of 1898, where their activities included ag-
itating for Cuban independence and the
abolition of Cuban slavery. Darker-skinned
Cubans tended to settle in and around
Florida. Some black Dominicans came to
the United States too, primarily to New
York City.
Other Caribbean blacks came after
1900, either directly or after working in the
Canal Zone or Central America. Many
ﬁnanced their migrations with their earn-
ings as laborers on the Panama Canal. The
largest numbers came from the British
colonies of Jamaica and Barbados, where
there was little industry or available land.
Other islanders had the same concern.
One-ﬁfth of the population of the Bahamas
migrated to Florida between 1900 and
1920.
1921–Present
U.S. immigration law radically changed in
1921 when Congress passed the so-called
Quota Act. In place of open immigration
with limited exclusions, Congress created
numerical caps on immigration. Altered
versions of those caps remain in place
today. The Quota Act further recognized,
for the ﬁrst time, the importance of family
uniﬁcation, which remains a fundamental
principle of U.S. immigration law.
The caps created by the Quota Act of
1921 temporarily limited, with certain ex-
ceptions, the number of people from out-
side of the Western Hemisphere “who may
be admitted...t o  the United States in any
ﬁscal year...t o  3  p e rcentum of the num-
ber of foreign-born persons of [their]
nationality resident in the United States
as determined by the United States census
of 1910.” There was no cap, however,
placed on immigrants from the Western
Hemisphere. Others excepted from the
Quota Act included the minor children of
U.S. citizens, who were likewise allowed to
migrate to the United States in unlimited
numbers.
The Immigration Act of 1924 kept the
temporary caps and made them perma-
nent, but reduced the percentage of each
nationality’s annual immigration quota to
2 percent, changed the determining census
date to 1890 (when there were fewer resi-
dent immigrants), and, most importantly
for black migration, cut back the Western
Hemisphere exemption by limiting it to
persons born in independent nations,
Canada, Newfoundland, or the Canal
Zone.
From then on, until Europe’s colonies
in the Caribbean and Central and South
America became independent, natives of
those colonies could only migrate to the
United States under the quotas for their
parent countries.
Other parts of the 1924 law set prefer-
ences for the distribution of each national-
ity’s quota and required prospective
immigrants to obtain quota visas at U.S.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 683 ---
