consulates abroad before coming to the
United States. Prospective immigrants
could no longer simply arrive in the United
States and present themselves to immigra-
tion authorities.
Recognizing the principle of family
uniﬁcation, the 1924 law made some
family members of U.S. citizens exempt
from the quota system altogether, and
thus still able to enter in unlimited num-
bers. As for other family members, the
1924 law made 50 percent of each nation-
ality’s visa quota ﬁrst available to the for-
eign husbands of U.S. citizens and the
foreign parents of adult U.S. citizens.
Within that 50 percent, foreign husbands
and parents skilled in agriculture, and
their wives and non-adult children, were
given preference. The other 50 percent of
each nationality’s quota, and unused por-
tions of the husbands’ and parents’ 50 per-
cent, was ﬁrst made available to certain
family members of legal immigrants already
in the United States, their minor children,
and their wives.
Under the 1924 law, the total number
of Eastern Hemisphere–born and colonial
Western Hemisphere–born people who
could obtain quota visas was 164,667 per
year. The annual quota for African-born
nationals, reflecting the comparatively
small numbers of African-born U.S. resi-
dents in 1890, was 1,200 per year.
The overall total of quota visas was re-
duced to 150,000 in 1929, with each for-
eign nation’s quota being adjusted to re-
ﬂect the number of inhabitants of the
continental United States attributable to
that nation by “birth or ancestry” as of
1920. U.S. immigrants from the Americas,
their descendants, and “slave immigrants”
were excluded when those computations
were made.
Since 1929, the history of U.S. immi-
gration policy has been one of adjusting
caps and quotas and adding to the classes of
prospective immigrants who can enter the
United States outside of caps or quotas.
Displaced persons acts enacted in 1948
and 1950 enabled more than 400,000 im-
migrants to come to the United States after
World War II. Then in 1953, at President
Dwight Eisenhower’s urging, Congress
enacted the United States’ ﬁrst Refugee
Relief Act, which allowed 214,000 refugees
and escapees from communist countries to
immigrate.
Following that precedent, subsequent
refugee, escapee, and asylum acts have al-
lowed political and religious immigration
outside of regular caps or quotas from every
continent except Australia—including
refugees from the Congo, Ethiopia, Egypt,
Kenya, Liberia, Somalia, the Sudan, Cuba,
and Haiti.
Similar acts have modiﬁed the require-
ments for refugees seeking citizenship. The
Haitian Refugee Immigration Fairness Act
of 1998, for example, allowed some es-
capees from Haiti to apply for permanent
U.S. residence and eventual U.S. citizen-
ship without ﬁrst obtaining a visa at a U.S.
consulate.
In 1952, U.S. naturalization law signif-
icantly changed when the McCarran-Walter
Act (Immigration and Nationality Act of
1952) removed the remaining racial restric-
tions on U.S. citizenship. The McCarran-
Walter Act also simpliﬁed the implementa-
tion of the family reuniﬁcation principle
by simply allowing all spouses of U.S.
citizens—irrespective of gender or race—
and all minor children of U.S. citizens to im-
migrate without regard for caps and quotas.
Preferences for quota visas were revised
in light of the elimination of any need for a

preference for spouses and children. Highly
skilled immigrants with urgently needed
skills, and their families, were given ﬁrst
preference instead.
One part of the 1952 law had particu-
lar temporary signiﬁcance for black immi-
gration from the Caribbean. Although
the annual worldwide cap on quota immi-
grants was slightly increased above
150,000, quotas for European colonies
were capped at 100 immigrants per colony
per year. The result was decreased migra-
tion into the United States from Jamaica
and Barbados and increased immigration
into England, until Jamaica became inde-
pendent in 1962 and Barbados became in-
dependent in 1966.
Congress scrapped the national immi-
gration caps on annual immigration in
1965, replacing them with hemispheric
caps: 120,000 quota visas were made avail-
able for immigration from the Western
Hemisphere, and 170,000 for immigration
from the Eastern Hemisphere. The new
caps did not apply to spouses, minor chil-
dren, and parents of U.S. citizens. Some
17,400 preference visas were set aside for
refugees from communist countries and the
Middle East.
The hemispheric caps were, in turn, re-
placed by a single global immigration cap
of 290,000 in 1976.
The Immigration Act of 1990, still in
effect, revamped the overall system of quo-
tas and of preferences within quotas. It cre-
ated a ﬂexible overall cap of 675,000 immi-
grants per year from everywhere beginning
in 1995, to be allocated among three new
classes of family-sponsored immigrants
(480,000 per year), employment-based im-
migrants (140,000 per year), and diversity
immigrants (55,000 per year). The exemp-
tion of spouses, minor children, and
parents of U.S. citizens from caps and quo-
tas remained.
The available ﬁgures show that migra-
tion to the United States from Africa has
been markedly increasing. After lulls dur-
ing the Depression, World War II, and the
early Cold War years, 39,300 Africans mi-
grated to the United States in the 1960s,
91,500 in the 1970s, 192,300 in the 1980s,
338,100 in the 1990s, 44,731 in 2000, and
53,948 in 2001. Some 70 to 75 percent of
the new African immigrants are estimated
to have been black, with that percentage in-
creasing. The sub-Saharan African popula-
tion of the United States was estimated at
more that 537,534 in 2000, 80 percent of
it being foreign born. African immigrants
have settled all across the United States,
with notable concentrations in New York
City and California. 
Prior to the 1970s, educated Africans
had primarily migrated to Europe. That
changed as Europe tightened its restrictions
on immigration and restrictions on migra-
tion from Africa to the United States were
reduced. The 1990 U.S. census showed
African immigrants, without regard to race,
as having the highest levels of education of
foreign-born U.S. residents. Notwithstand-
ing their diplomas and degrees, many
African immigrants have taken nonprofes-
sional jobs in the United States, especially
upon their arrival.
The largest numbers of sub-Saharan
African immigrants have come from
Ethiopia, Nigeria, Ghana, and since the
1990s, Somalia, reﬂecting the political,
racial, ethnic, and religious turmoil of those
countries. Africa has produced more
refugees than any other continent since the
early 1990s.
Approximately 3,800 young male
refugees, called the Lost Boys of Sudan,
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 685 ---
IMMIGRATION,U NITED STATES 609
came to towns across the United States as
refugees in 2000 and 2001. The Lost Boys
had been driven from their homes and fam-
ilies by warfare in southern Sudan as young
children and had wandered by themselves
for months before reaching the safety of
Kenyan refugee camps. Their lives after
reaching the United States have been the
subjects of newspaper articles, an essay on
the Red Cross’s Web page, ﬁlms, and at
least one book.
The available figures on migration
from the Caribbean to the United States
are similar. They show 519,500 Caribbean
migrants coming to the United States in
the 1960s, 759,800 in the 1970s, 892,700
in the 1980s, and around 1,200,000 in the
1990s.
In the 1960s and 1970s, the largest
number of Caribbean immigrants was from
Cuba: 258,600 in the 1960s and 276,800
in the 1970s. The largest numbers in the
1980s were from the Dominican Republic
(251,800), Jamaica (213,800), Cuba
(159,200), and Haiti (140,200). The num-
ber of migrating Haitians rose during the
1990s to approximate the number of mi-
grating Jamaicans.
Studies of immigrant Dominicans have
shown that their reasons for migrating to
the United States are largely economic, al-
though the number of Dominican mi-
grants has brieﬂy spiked after political tur-
moil. Dominicans in the United States
have largely congregated in the New York
City area.
The numbers of immigrants coming
from Jamaica and Haiti have roughly corre-
lated with political and economic events in
those countries. Jamaican immigrants have
settled all along the East Coast of the
United States, with some concentration in
the New York area. Haitian immigrants
have typically stayed in and around Florida,
but with a good number also coming to
New York.
The reasons for Cuban migration have
been more complex. The migrations of
Cubans in the 1960s certainly began with
refugees from Fidel Castro’s rule, but many
later immigrants seem to have come for
mixed family, political, and economic rea-
sons. Most Cuban immigrants have like-
wise stayed in and around Florida, espe-
cially in the Miami area where they have
considerable political and economic
power. A fair number are in the New York
area too.

IMPERIAL GERMANY,B LACK
ENTERTAINERS IN
The presence of black entertainers in impe-
rial Germany led to the transformation of
art forms (composition and performance,
music and vaudeville) through their contri-
bution of black cultural forms.
Not all blacks in Germany arrived
from America. Germany had colonies in
East, West, and Southwest Africa. Some in-
dividuals came from those lands to be
trained as missionaries, others pursued a
profession, others came to complete their
education, while still others were exhibited
as circus Africans until this was formally
forbidden. Thus, blacks in Germany were
not an uncommon sight. Of course, the av-
erage Germans’ perception of their
colonies, and of the natives from the
colonies, was guided by racist clichés. Dis-
crimination was effective enough to bar
blacks from most professions, except, like
their brothers in the United States, music
and vaudeville.
Areas of folk and traditional music
which did not ﬁnd their way onto record-
ings have all but disappeared from history:
those melodic lines which have been used
in orchestral works, published in books,
noted by instrumentalists, and described by
folklorists lack the intensity of recordings.
This effect is particularly dramatic when
considering the innumerable dancers,
singers, instrumentalists, comedians, and
actors of African descent active in Europe
prior to World War I. Negro spirituals,
published in England from the 1870s, have
the words, the melodic line, and piano ac-
companiment, but nothing of the qualities
that live performance (captured on record-
ings) reveals. And since most of the early
authors of scholarly books and discogra-
phies on blues and jazz were Europeans,
whose only contact with the music was
through recordings, the prehistory of jazz
and blues has also tended to disappear from
history. Even less well documented are as-
pects of the cross-cultural fertilization:
German musicians playing for audiences—
including black audiences—in the United
States in the nineteenth century.
Prior to the emergence of the Tin Pan
Alley music business, musical life in the
United States had for some 200 years been
dominated by Europe. Apart from folklore
there was little else but European—and for
that matter much German—musical reper-
toire. In fact, Germany was the center of
music, musical instruments, and music
publishing from the last decades of the
nineteenth century. Its tutors, instrumen-
talists, and publications were well known
outside Germany. Ambitious musical peo-
ple traveled to Germany for lessons and
study, including African Americans such as
Will Marion Cook, who was a pupil of fa-
mous violinist Joseph Joachim in Berlin in
1887–1889.
The ﬁrst American orchestra, black or
white, to tour Europe left the United States
as early as 1837. All the members of this
brass band, led by Frank Johnson, were
Afro-Americans. And, of course, this black
band played an exclusively European reper-
toire. American novelty dance tunes, many
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 687 ---
IMPERIAL GERMANY,B LACK ENTERTAINERS IN 611
of which had some African American back-
ground, did not appear in print until the
last decade of the nineteenth century when
they were made popular by the tunesmiths
of Tin Pan Alley. They had competition
from Germany, as German musicians
played to entertain American audiences.
Vast parts of Germany were extremely
poor. Apart from the option of military ser-
vice, many became itinerant musicians,
earning their living in England and the
United States, as well as North Africa and
the Far East. Stretches of Germany became
known as the “musicians’ belt” ( Musikan-
tenland ). Musicians from the very remote
rural hinterland were exposed to Africans
and African music. During their travels in
the United States, they by no means catered
exclusively to white audiences, as evidenced
by surviving photographs.
As professional musicians these German
artists had to be able to play the entire
repertoire by sight, and that repertoire had
to include ragtime, cakewalks, two-steps,
and any other fashionable American dance
tune of Afro-American influence. And
there is proof of this, as some of the local
museums keep the original collections of
notated music (Stimmbücher ).
In the Black Forest and other poor
neighborhoods, German musicians spent
the winter manufacturing mechanical mu-
sical instruments for export. People who
had not even heard of St. Louis or Sedalia
produced authentic cakewalk and ragtime
music for piano rolls and metal disc Sym-
phonions. Although some textbooks say
that the “March King” John Philip Sousa
introduced the cakewalk in Europe, the
claim is not supported by factual evidence.
On the contrary, Sousa had an apparent
aversion to African American inﬂuences in
music. Long before Sousa came to Europe,
Afro-Americans had come with their ban-
jos. Afro-American song and dance enter-
tainers performed buck, sand, and tap
dances, as well as cakewalks, for entirely
white audiences.
The institutionalization of discrimina-
tion following the abolition of slavery in
the United States illuminates the socioeco-
nomic motives for Afro-Americans to visit
Europe, as does the establishment of the Ku
Klux Klan only two years after the end of
slavery. Discrimination reached such levels
that this period is remembered as the “T er-
rible Nineties.” Lynchings were announced
in newspapers, as if people were being in-
vited to attend a picnic or some other form
of entertainment. At the same time, there
was a strange parallel development occur-
ring in the music world: while poor
German musicians migrated to the United
States, poor Afro-American musicians and
song and dance artists migrated to Germany.
In one year alone, 1896, more than one
hundred Afro-American individuals can be
identiﬁed in the major magazine devoted to
German traveling musicians and entertain-
ers, underscoring their national presence
and inﬂuence on German culture. And this
number could be only a small percentage
of the actual number touring. Some blacks
arrived as members of large troupes, such
as William Foote’s African Character
Concert Company, which set foot on
German soil at Hamburg in 1891. When
the troupe broke up, many of the members
remained in Europe and can be traced all
over Europe, from Madrid to Nischny
Nowgorod.
In Europe, too, people of African de-
scent were often disregarded and despised
as a racial minority—but nowhere as seri-
ously as in the United States. Many racially
mixed acts traveled as “black and white”
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 688 ---
612 I MPERIAL GERMANY,B LACK ENTERTAINERS IN
performers. Quite a few African Americans
married German women and appeared on
stage as racially mixed duets. This integra-
tion would have been virtually impossible
in the United States. As late as the mid-
1930s, John Hammond (a white man) cre-
ated a sensation when he organized his ﬁrst
Carnegie Hall concert featuring black and
white performers on the same stage. Dixy
Davis and husband Richard Davis, like
innumerable others, presented their perfor-
mances thirty to forty years before the
Carnegie Hall event.
Some performances by black visitors to
Germany were captured on ﬁlm. There is a
Pathé ﬁlm showing unidentiﬁed black and
white performers doing the cakewalk on
stage. Other Afro-American performers
recorded cylinders and disc records during
their stay in Europe. Besides Pete Hampton
and Arabella Fields, other pre–World War I
recording artists include the Four Black Di-
amonds, the Darktown Entertainers, man-
dolinist Seth Weeks, the Four Black T rou-
badours (also known as the Colored
Meisters), and the London-based banjo-
playing Afro-Canadian Bohee Brothers,
James and George.
Hampton and his fellow artists stand
in for the hundreds who unfortunately left
no trace on ﬁlm or disc. Perhaps the most
important of these is the husband and wife
team of Charles Johnson and Dora Dean.
The couple is said to have introduced the
cakewalk at New York’s old Madison
Square Garden in 1895. They are also said
to have been the ﬁrst dance team, black or
white, to wear evening clothes on the stage
(1901, at Hammerstein’s Roof Garden).
Despite their success in the United States,
they made Europe their permanent home
and only returned to the United States
when World War I broke out in 1914,
forcing them to disband their Ragtime Sex-
tette (which also included the dance team
of Rufus Greenlee and Thaddeus Drayton,
pianist Louis “Kid” Coles, and drummer
Peggie Holland). Long before Josephine
Baker reached European shores the impec-
cably dressed and beautiful Dora Dean was
a society event in Europe and the Germans
looked forward to her annual appearances
at the prestigious Berlin Wintergarten.
In the ﬁeld of music and vaudeville,
Europeans, including the Germans, truly
admired their visitors, and contemporary
reviews make it clear that audiences per-
ceived that what they were being offered
was not only professional but distinctive.
Rainer E. Lotz

INDUSTRIALIZATION
Industrialization ﬁrst appeared in Great
Britain in the 1780s and gradually made its
way across the North Atlantic to parts of
Western Europe and the United States, by-
passing much of Africa and the Americas,
until emerging on a limited scale by the late
nineteenth century. In the northern
Atlantic, the process of industrialization
generated incremental yet large-scale
changes. These included the expansion of
towns and cities, the construction of
factories, the liberalization of credit, and
the extension of transportation and com-
munication networks. This “industrial
revolution,” as historian Arnold T oynbee
termed it, was one of the most important
changes in human history. It took place
over several decades and did not affect all
of Europe and the rest of the world at the
same time. Indeed, in 1850, in many parts
of Europe, the number of agricultural
workers still outpaced those in manufactur-
ing although this gap narrowed signiﬁ-
cantly by 1914 when industrialization
expanded even more.
In explaining the conditions under
which the Industrial Revolution took place
in Great Britain, scholars generally point to
several key domestic phenomena: the ad-
vent of new inventions and technologies,
the availability of capital and credit, popu-
lation growth, and the expansion of agri-
cultural production. Looking at industrial-
ization on an international scale, however,
it probably would never have occurred in
its nineteenth-century context without the
commercial linkages forged by merchants,
planters, and colonial regimes within Africa
and the Americas during the sixteenth
and seventeenth centuries. Furthermore,
African and American societies impacted
and were impacted by industrialization in
several key areas: the establishment of
cross-Atlantic markets, or the so-called
“triangular trade” in certain commodities
(including molasses, rum, sugar, and cot-
ton); the expansion of large-landed estates
in Latin America and eventually Africa; and
the limited transfer of industrialization to
those regions in the early twentieth century.
Export commodities produced by
African laborers in Spanish America, Por-
tuguese Brazil, British America, French and
Dutch America, and the United States
stimulated Atlantic commercial exchanges
and industrialization in the long term. By
the early sixteenth century, European impe-
rial powers, such as Spain, Great Britain,
France, Portugal, and the Netherlands, estab-
lished colonial outposts in the Americas in
order to extract raw materials from the re-
gion. The reciprocal demand for resources
and the lack of sufﬁcient numbers of
Amerindian laborers led Western European
powers to turn to African slave laborers on
a larger scale by the seventeenth century.
Europeans tapped into a slave trade that
had already existed on the west coast and
interior of Africa; yet, one of the most
devastating long-term consequences of the
Atlantic slave trade was that European and
American demands for slaves drastically
depopulated several areas of the continent.
Between 1500 and 1850, millions of
African laborers endured the grueling long
voyages to the agricultural and mining sec-
tors of the Americas where they were put to
work in the production of gold, silver,
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 690 ---
614 I NDUSTRIALIZATION
diamonds, sugar, rice, tobacco, indigo,
henequen, and cotton. T rading certain
commodities was more proﬁtable than oth-
ers at several different times during the
colonial era. Gold and silver, for instance,
were important commodities in the six-
teenth and seventeenth centuries, but
dwindling returns led to the eventual de-
cline of these mining sectors. Proﬁts for
sugar production ﬂuctuated throughout
the seventeenth, eighteenth, and nine-
teenth centuries depending on demand and
competition. Cotton consumption grew
exponentially from the late eighteenth to
the early nineteenth centuries when it was
shipped to English factories, but the open-
ing of cotton plantations in Egypt, for ex-
ample, hurt this trade in the American
South.
Despite the proliferation in the trade of
commodities and slaves by the late eigh-
teenth century, there is still no consensus as
to what extent African slaves and the Atlantic
slave trade impacted industrialization. Karl
Marx was one of the ﬁrst intellectuals to
establish a link between the proﬁts earned
by merchants from the use of slave labor
with the accumulation of capital investment
in Britain’s industrial sector; subsequently,
others, such as Lowell Ragatz and Eric
Williams, in the early twentieth century
applied this idea speciﬁcally to the British
Caribbean as a case study. In his seminal
work Capitalism and Slavery (1944), Eric
Williams, a T rinidadian-born and Oxford-
educated scholar, argued that proﬁts earned
by merchants and traders from African
slavery helped to promote British industri-
alization and economic development.
According to this view, African slaves them-
selves and the raw materials that they pro-
vided for the Atlantic markets were sold by
merchants for a proﬁt, which were, in turn,
reinvested into other commercial and in-
dustrial endeavors, such as machinery and
factories. Moreover, not only did the raw
materials that African slaves produced spark
cross-Atlantic trade, but the English (and
later New England) cotton mills would not
have had a market to sell their manufac-
tured products nor a cheap source of cotton
to use as raw materials had it not been for
the demand in the Americas. Critics of the
“Williams thesis” have argued that proﬁts
from the slave trade were not a key source of
capital accumulation in Great Britain.
Proﬁts from the Atlantic slave trade ﬂuctu-
ated and were not that high (at least not for
European traders). In addition, the revenues
that the slave trade and slaves generated
were not large enough to constitute a major
factor in British capital formation. These
critics concede that some Atlantic mer-
chants secured handsome returns from their
participation in the slave trade and put
these dividends into factories, but they also
argue that the sum of these investments
were inconsequential at best in ﬁnancing
the industrial revolution. Finally, another
fault that critics ﬁnd with Williams’s argu-
ment occurs when comparing the industri-
alization experience of Great Britain with
those of Spain, France, the Netherlands,
and Portugal. These countries never indus-
trialized to the extent that Great Britain had
and thus, as the rebuttal goes, slavery and
the slave trade were not important variables
in the industrialization process. Despite the
objections raised, however, the Williams
thesis remains incredibly resilient and has
greatly inﬂuenced subsequent generations
of scholars until today.
What most scholars agree on is that the
production of agricultural commodities,
the transportation of raw materials, manu-
factured goods, and African slaves greatly
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 691 ---
INDUSTRIALIZATION 615
lubricated interoceanic commercial trans-
actions on a scale never before seen. This
“triangular trade,” as many historians call
it, caused changes within state institutions,
affected regional and city growth, and
helped to nourish new industries whose de-
pendence on export markets for sustained
growth was evident even before the close of
the eighteenth century. These factors
boosted the development of shipping and
ﬁnancial institutions, raised incomes, stim-
ulated new demands, and created a vastly
expanded market for British goods and ser-
vices, which resulted in the search for new
methods of production. T ransatlantic slav-
ery and all of the maritime and commercial
transactions associated with it, including
the issuance of shipping licenses, brokerage
and port fees, taxes, and other associated
transportation costs, led to the further ex-
pansion of the Atlantic system. Revolutions
in maritime navigation and shipbuilding
also cut down on transportation time and
cost. Within this context, one could argue
that a nascent form of industrialization ap-
peared in Great Britain in the eighteenth
century associated with interoceanic trade.
The rise of ports, shipbuilding and docking
companies, insurance ﬁrms, and reﬁneries
are all evidence of this. Moreover, in the age
of mercantilism, European empires created
bureaucracies to tax and regulate these
commercial exchanges. State involvement
was also enhanced by the fact that Euro-
pean governments invested heavily in con-
structing naval ﬂeets, fortresses, and paying
soldiers and ofﬁcers in order to protect
their extractive enterprises in Africa and the
Americas. Indeed, Atlantic port cities, like
Boston, New York, Bristol, and Liverpool,
ﬂourished in the late eighteenth and early
nineteenth centuries as they were geared to-
ward trade with Africa and the Americas.
Within these rising urban centers, the mid-
dle classes sought to expand their wealth
and social status. This led to the increased
volume of commercial transactions, such as
billing, insurance, and the development of
banking and other ﬁnancial and credit
schemes and institutions, that were vital to
industrialization. In fact, banking institu-
tions in the northern Atlantic shifted from
tight to liberal lending policies beginning
in the late eighteenth to early nineteenth
centuries.
The decline of slavery in Africa and the
Americas also took place within the context
of industrialization. As its wealthier popu-
lation built more factories and employed
more domestic laborers, Great Britain
passed the Act for the Abolition of the
Slave T rade in 1807. This decision was all
the more important because the British
Empire had the most powerful navy in the
world and could thus enforce its decree to
a great extent. Indeed, the slave trade and
chattel slavery continued into the 1880s,
but thanks in large measure to British en-
forcement, the volume of slave transactions
declined precipitously. In 1833, Great
Britain also became one of the ﬁrst indus-
trialized countries to abolish slavery, and
African-descended slaves in the Caribbean
directly beneﬁted from this action. Still,
scholars, including Eric Williams among
others, have often wondered why British
attitudes toward slavery and the slave
trade changed so abruptly in the early
nineteenth century. On the eve of Great
Britain’s decision to abolish slavery, sugar
plantations continued to be quite prof-
itable. Explanations abound ranging from
the rise of homegrown evangelical and abo-
lition movements, the decline in sugar
revenues, and industrialization itself. How-
ever, it is clear that the decisions to abolish
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 692 ---
616 I NDUSTRIALIZATION
the slave trade and slavery itself were all po-
litically and ideologically connected, rooted
in industrialization. By the late eighteenth
century, slaveholders and Atlantic mer-
chants lost support and power within the
British government as it competed with a
growing number of industrialists commit-
ted to the laissez-faire principles of Adam
Smith. These new, middle-class proponents
of abolition became increasingly hostile to
colonial monopolies and viewed slavery as
part of an outdated mercantilist system
that, they argued, should be dismantled. At
the same time, however, abolitionism also
gave Great Britain’s industrialized ruling
classes an opportunity to claim moral lead-
ership even as it exploited domestic workers
in their factories. These industrialists
sympathized and lent their support on a
variety of levels to evangelical movements
that based their opposition to slavery on
religious and humanitarian principles. By
the end of the Napoleonic wars in 1815,
the abolitionist movement had become a
potent national force, and slaveholder and
planter interests in Great Britain were
becoming politically subordinate.
By the middle to latter part of the
nineteenth century, huge changes also took
place in Africa and the Americas not only
because they continued to be the centers
for extraction of natural resources for
European powers but also because they
constituted the primary markets for
European, especially British, manufactured
products. Colonies in the Americas, for
example, stimulated demand for textiles,
ceramics, furniture, and other items. It is
equally important to stress that Europeans
attempted to saturate African markets with
their manufactured goods. At the same
time, there is ample evidence that the rise
of European factories undermined African
and American industries that might have
competed with them. T extile producers
in Latin America, for example, were put
out of business when English factories
ﬂooded the Atlantic markets with wool
and cotton products. As a result, the British
Caribbean, northern South America,
Mexico, and the American South special-
ized primarily in the production and sale
of agricultural commodities, such as cotton,
sugar, and coffee, for European markets.
Even as these agrarian-based societies
imported industrial technology during the
mid- to late-nineteenth century, this was
done to improve crop yields rather than
create competition with European facto-
ries. When railroads and railroad lines were
built in Cuba in the 1850s, for example, it
emerged as one of the largest sugarcane
suppliers in the world. Yet, the beneﬁts
that steam engines and railroads could
bring to the Americas could not save the
sugar economy as it continued a slow
decline into the nineteenth and twentieth
centuries. Indeed, the importation of
industrial technology and know-how by
the end of the nineteenth century did not
change the fundamental relationship
between the northern Atlantic industrial
centers and the societies of Africa and the
Americas.
By 1870, industrialization in Europe
and the United States beneﬁted greatly
from numerous scientiﬁc and technological
innovations. These shaped the supply and
demand of goods and services on a global
scale throughout the late nineteenth and
early twentieth centuries. The harnessing of
electricity, the use of the internal combus-
tion engine, and the invention of chemicals
and synthetic dyes spawned industries in
their own right and widened the gap be-
tween developing and developed countries
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 693 ---
INDUSTRIALIZATION 617
even more. Moreover, the number of in-
dustrialized nations expanded to include
Belgium and Germany, and these countries
increasingly demanded more foodstuffs for
their populations and raw materials for
their factories. They also sought the ex-
ploitation of new minerals, such as copper,
zinc, and nitrate, for use in the technologi-
cal, industrial, and military complexes of
the Western world.
Thus, industrialization had profound
consequences for Africa and the Americas.
Key agricultural and mining sectors of
these new national economies either re-
mained or eventually were turned over to
foreign industrial interests. This occurred
even as more and more nation-states de-
clared their independence from European
colonial powers, such as Portugal and
Spain, after 1820. This is often labeled by
some scholars as the birth of neocolonial-
ism, whereby Latin American governments
remained politically independent but eco-
nomically dependent on industrialized
countries for markets and technology. In-
deed, the wealthiest, more industrialized
countries of the West, such as Great
Britain, France, Germany, and the United
States, dominated the agricultural and min-
ing sectors of Latin American states. In
Central America, U.S.-owned plantations
grew bananas and other tropical fruits for
the expanding global market. In addition,
Brazilian landowners cultivated sugar, cof-
fee, and citrus. In Mexico until the 1930s,
the United States and Great Britain owned
a large number of mines and oil ﬁelds. For-
eigners also took over Peru’s guano industry
and Chile’s nitrate and copper enterprises.
In fact, Peruvian guano was utilized pri-
marily as a fertilizer and was responsible for
initiating an agricultural revolution in
Europe in the nineteenth century.
In Africa, the slave trade had already
precipitated the economic backwardness of
the continent, but aggressive European
colonialism in the late nineteenth and early
twentieth centuries aggravated this prob-
lem. At the height of the slave trade in the
mid-1700s, European merchants estab-
lished mutually beneﬁcial commercial rela-
tions with African middlemen and African
producers. By the 1850s, however, the de-
cline of the slave trade left Africa, also de-
pendent on the slave trade as a source of
revenue, in an inferior position relative to
European industrialized countries. Reduced
demand for commodities from Africa be-
cause of the onset of an economic depres-
sion in Europe in 1867 left African com-
mercial interests in turmoil. European and
African merchants competed for diminish-
ing shares of the market, but Europeans had
the advantage of military and technological
power in acquiring access to new markets.
With the ups and downs of the business
cycle, industrial powers searched for new re-
sources and markets. On an unprecedented
scale and with rapid speed, European pow-
ers made forays into the interior of the
African continent where they began seizing
large tracts of land in what scholars often
call the Scramble for Africa. By the end of
the nineteenth century, Great Britain, Ger-
many, France, Italy, and Belgium estab-
lished colonial regimes in various parts of
Africa. In the tropical and more temperate
zones of Africa, Europeans established
large-sized rubber, palm oil, and peanut
plantations. By the 1890s, Africa was begin-
ning to be drawn further into the Atlantic
network with the expansion of mining ac-
tivities in South Africa and the Belgian
Congo. This expansion continued until the
1960s when the African nation-states began
to declare their independence in increasing
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

numbers, yet African nations were still un-
derdeveloped and failed to industrialize to
any great extent.

INSURGENCY AND
COUNTERINSURGENCY
Insurgency is the armed opposition to a
government, often with the purpose of
overthrowing the government or gaining
independence from it. In Africa and the
Americas, insurgent movements have arisen
in Angola, Mozambique, Algeria, Sudan,
Burundi, Rwanda, Namibia, Nigeria,
Eritrea, Liberia, Sierra Leone, Uganda, the
Democratic Republic of Congo, Colombia,
Cuba, Guatemala, Nicaragua, Peru, and El
Salvador, among others. They have been
driven by a number of causes. In Peru,
Cuba, Guatemala, El Salvador, and
Colombia, Marxist movements sought to
take control of the government. In Angola,
Mozambique, and Nicaragua, anticommu-
nist groups sought to overthrow Marxist
governments. In Algeria, Sudan, Namibia,
Nigeria, and Eritrea, anticolonial or sepa-
ratist movements sought to achieve inde-
pendence. Religion or ethnicity has identi-
ﬁed rebel movements in Burundi, Rwanda,
Liberia, Uganda, Algeria, Sudan, and the
Democratic Republic of Congo. In recent
wars in Sierra Leone and Colombia, the
goals of organizations are less clear than
the political, religious, ethnic, or separatist
movements preceding them. In each of these
cases, government-led counterinsurgencies,
representing opposing political, religious,
and ethnic positions, fought against the
insurgents.
Insurgencies, unlike coups, are long-
term actions, often lasting many years.
Wars in Colombia, Guatemala, Angola,
and Sudan, for example, lasted more than
two decades. This length is due, in part, to
the strategy most insurgent movements
choose to use in their struggle: guerrilla
warfare. Guerrilla war is a strategy of the
weak. It is designed to allow a poorly
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 695 ---
INSURGENCY AND COUNTERINSURGENCY 619
manned and equipped faction to survive
long enough to gain recruits, equipment,
and experience. However, due to their
weakness, insurgents (also called rebels or
guerrillas), cannot readily defeat govern-
ment forces; on the other hand, govern-
ment forces (i.e., counterinsurgents) can-
not readily defeat guerrillas. The guerrillas’
ability to hide or melt into the population
makes them hard to ﬁnd; their ability to
win popular support makes their move-
ment difﬁcult to eradicate. Thus, the aver-
age guerrilla war has far more longevity
than a conventional war.
Insurgents almost always begin their
military opposition to a government lack-
ing much of the power of the ruling body.
The government occupies a territory and
has access to its resources, possesses a
trained and equipped (at least to a degree)
military, and has a population that funds it
through the normal workings of taxation
and the economy. Moreover, the govern-
ment possesses at least some level of inter-
national legitimacy. The opposition, on the
other hand, often lacks a territory, and its
armed forces are considerably smaller than
those of the government and typically more
poorly trained and equipped. At the very
beginning of the conﬂict, the opposition
often lacks any signiﬁcant funding source
and has little, if any, foreign recognition.
Capable rebel leaders recognize their
weakness and understand that meeting
government forces on the battleﬁeld will re-
sult in certain defeat. Instead, guerrillas en-
gage in hit and run attacks, striking the
enemy when it is weak and then ﬂeeing. T o
do this successfully, guerrillas must have a
base that is largely secure from attack.
Other countries may provide such havens,
as Uganda did for the Rwandan Patriotic
Front in the early 1990s. In other cases,
rebels ﬂee to areas characterized by terrain
inaccessible by the government’s military as
Fidel Castro did during his rebellion
against the Batista government in Cuba.
For this reason, most insurgencies have
been rural.
If the guerrillas go fully underground,
they may survive indeﬁnitely; however,
they pose little danger to the government
and have little hope of success. Guerrillas
must function among the population. It is
the main source of the guerrillas’ strength,
providing intelligence, weapons, food, hid-
ing places, and personnel. Without the
support of the population, the guerrillas
have no chance to win the war. Similarly, if
the government lacks that same support, it
too will lose the conﬂict. Thus, counterin-
surgents and insurgents are ﬁghting to win
over the same thing: the people.
Violence against the population has
been used by both governments and guer-
rillas to force the people’s acquiescence and
assistance. The Chilean government under
Augusto Pinochet arrested, killed, and “dis-
appeared” thousands of Chilean citizens it
believed sympathetic to the leftist rebels in
the country. The Revolutionary United
Front in Sierra Leone, fighting a war
against the government in the 1990s, sev-
ered the limbs of men, women, and chil-
dren to prevent them and dissuade others
from aiding government troops. The guer-
rillas have an additional incentive to use vi-
olence against the population. By demon-
strating their ability to act seemingly
unchecked, the guerrillas can diminish the
government’s legitimacy—the perception
that it has the right to rule.
Ideology is a second tool used by guer-
rilla groups to try to win the support of the
population. Mao Zedong and Che Guevara
both argued that, to succeed, guerrilla
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 696 ---
620 I NSURGENCY AND COUNTERINSURGENCY
groups must have a political goal with
which the people can sympathize. Whereas
Mao and Che focused on political
ideology—speciﬁcally forms of Marxism-
Leninism—other leaders and groups have
utilized religion, such as the Lord’s Resis-
tance Army in Uganda, and ethnicity, the
Interahamwe in Rwanda and the Demo-
cratic Republic of Congo, to deﬁne their
organizations’ causes and try to rally the
population. Religious and ethnic ideologies
have a key drawback: it is difﬁcult, if not
impossible, to convert those not part of the
group before the war. Anyone, on the other
hand, can change their political beliefs,
making it easier for the guerrillas to lure
former supporters of the government away.
These ideologies, whether political, reli-
gious, or ethnic are often a reﬂection of
and an answer to the perceived lack of
provision by the government. They are re-
sponses to groups’ feelings of being dis-
criminated against or ignored by the state’s
government.
T o combat the rebellion, governments’
counterinsurgent operations must focus
on responding to these feelings of discrim-
ination and neglect. The immediate re-
quirement for counterinsurgent forces is
providing security to the population.
Governments must hunt down and cap-
ture, kill, or isolate guerrillas so that they
do not pose a military threat, particularly
to the population. Governments must be
careful to avoid too much military force.
Indiscriminate attacks alienate those whose
families have been killed and property
damaged, encouraging them to shift
their allegiance to the rebels. Successful
counterinsurgency tactics focus on small
units, carefully trained, that are drawn
from and live among the population. These
troops have the potential of gaining the
population’s trust and therefore increase the
likelihood the people will provide intelli-
gence on guerrilla whereabouts and inten-
tions to the government.
Military force is necessary, but not suf-
ﬁcient, for a successful counterinsurgency.
T o combat insurgents, the government
must “win the hearts and minds of” the
same population the guerrillas are seeking
to win over. The government must prove
itself the legitimate ruler of the state. In
addition to providing security, the govern-
ment can provide goods and services,
improve infrastructure, build schools and
hospitals, and provide necessary food and
medicines to improve the view that the
government cares for its population. The
government must take steps to respond to
the reasons underlying the conﬂict, includ-
ing corruption; economic, political, and
social injustice; and ethnic and religious
discrimination. Only by responding to the
underlying sociopolitical issues can the
counterinsurgency succeed. Only by react-
ing to these issues can the government win
over the population that may otherwise
support the guerrillas.
The insurgencies that occurred to free
nations from colonial rule took place over
nearly two hundred years in the Americas
and Africa. The American Revolution was
the ﬁrst, in the late eighteenth century.
The Americans combined conventional
attacks—facing British armed forces on the
battlefields and oceans—with guerrilla
attacks, including the ambushes and sniper
attacks on British forces as they left Con-
cord for Boston in 1775; the British
suffered nearly 20 percent casualties in that
retreat. Thirty years later, in the early
1800s, several of the colonies of South
America fought under Simon Bolívar for
independence from Spain.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 697 ---
INSURGENCY AND COUNTERINSURGENCY 621
It was only in the mid-twentieth cen-
tury that the African states gained indepen-
dence from their colonial rulers; some, like
Algeria, undertook guerrilla warfare to ac-
complish this goal. From 1954 to 1962, the
FLN (National Liberation Front and its
armed wing, the ALN [National Liberation
Army]) waged an insurgency against
French rule. By 1957, the guerrillas were
striking Algerians and French, civilian as
well as military, in the Battle of Algiers. The
French responded violently, arresting,
killing, and torturing thousands of sus-
pected terrorists and their supporters. Such
response failed to end the insurgency. In-
stead, it galvanized the population to op-
pose French rule. The French counterinsur-
gency, at this time, was unsuccessful. It
relied heavily on garrisons—opening the
countryside to the guerrillas—and on ter-
ror to force compliance from the people.
By the time French military tactics im-
proved and the military began to pacify the
countryside as well as stop incoming
weapons and personnel from T unisia and
Morocco, the French government was tired
of the ﬁght. The FLN, which had been se-
riously depleted in the ﬁghting with the
French, also agreed to negotiations; the two
sides agreed to a four-year plan to allow the
Algerian people to decide their own fate. In
1963, Algerians would vote overwhelm-
ingly for independence and be granted it.
Even after the decolonization of Africa,
insurgencies on that continent did not stop.
Within a number of African countries there
were independence movements as one eth-
nic or tribal group sought independence
from the state. In Nigeria, 1967–1970, the
Biafran War saw a rebellion by the Ibo peo-
ple put down by the Nigerian government.
In Sudan, from 1955 to 1972 and again
from 1983 to 2005, the southern Sudanese
fought a long insurgency attempting to se-
cede from the Arab, Islamic government in
Khartoum. The more recent war ended in a
stalemate, with the signing of the Compre-
hensive Peace Agreement and the inclusion
of southern Sudanese in the government.
Like many insurgencies, this one ended
with the agreement of the factions to share
power, rather than with the victory of any
one group.
While each of these insurgencies failed
to achieve independence, two other con-
ﬂicts were successful. In Namibia, SWAPO
(South West African People’s Organization)
fought against South African forces begin-
ning in 1966, using both guerrilla and ter-
rorist tactics. In 1990, Namibia was de-
clared independent. The Eritreans fought a
more than three-decade war against the rul-
ing Ethiopian government, gaining inde-
pendence in 1993.
Most of the insurgencies during the
Cold War, in both Africa and the Americas,
were over political ideology rather than
border lines or national autonomy. That is
not to say that ethnic identity had no place
in the wars between Marxists, Maoists, or
socialists and their opponents; indeed, nu-
merous guerrilla groups were dispropor-
tionately drawn from ethnic minorities in
states, including the T upac Amaru in Peru.
However, these were wars in which factions
identiﬁed themselves by political leanings
and who fought to decide the political ide-
ology that would rule the state. In
Guatemala, following a U.S.-sponsored
coup in 1954, left-wing rebels would ﬁght
against successive anticommunist govern-
ments until peace accords were signed in
1996. In Colombia, too, wars were fought
between various anticommunist govern-
ments and leftist rebels. The most recent
war, beginning in 1984, featured two main
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 698 ---
622 I NSURGENCY AND COUNTERINSURGENCY
rebel groups, FARC (Revolutionary Armed
Forces of Colombia) and ELN (National
Liberation Army), that continued to com-
bat the government into the post-Cold War
period. In Africa, similar wars were fought
between communists and noncommunists
in Angola and Mozambique.
Communist groups were not mono-
lithic. They varied in ideological underpin-
nings and in their sources of support. In
Angola, the Chinese-supported FNLA
(National Front for the Liberation of
Angola) fought against the Soviet-sponsored
government headed by the MPLA (Popular
Movement for the Liberation of Angola),
which had won. The Maoist Sendero
Luminoso and Marxist T upac Amaru waged
wars with the Peruvian government,
espousing competing beliefs and using dif-
ferent tactics. T upac Amaru, in particular,
relied heavily on terrorist actions rather
than classic insurgency activities. In both
cases, the 1992 crackdown by the Peruvian
government weakened the groups’ ability
to wage war dramatically.
A characteristic common to many of
these conﬂicts was outside interference.
Most of these conﬂicts, particularly those
revolving around political ideology, saw
U.S., Soviet, Chinese, or Cuban inﬂuence.
These insurgencies became proxy wars in
the Cold War as the United States and
the communist countries sought to counter
one another. Through most of the Cold
War, the United States and its allies sup-
ported the counterinsurgents, seeking to
contain the expansion of communism,
while the Soviets, Chinese, and Cubans
supported rebel groups. This traditional
stance would change in the 1980s as Presi-
dent Ronald Reagan’s policy of rollback
led the Americans to support rebel move-
ments combating Marxist governments in
Nicaragua and Angola. Also in Africa, the
South African government assisted rebel
groups in Angola and Mozambique. Follow-
ing the Cuban revolution in 1959, the
Communist government under Fidel Castro
funded groups throughout Latin America. A
key ally in the war against the Batista govern-
ment, Che Guevara, would set up training
camps in Cuba for revolutionaries and go to
Congo in 1965, where he sought to train a
rebel army. He then traveled to Bolivia to try
to create an insurgent movement; he would
be captured and killed in 1967.
The clearest example of external inﬂu-
ence was the 1975–1992 Angolan civil war.
The Soviets provided assistance and Cuban
ground forces (up to 18,000 by October
1975) to the MPLA, who would soon win
control of the government. It was opposed
by UNITA, supported by the United
States, and FNLA, aided by China. South
Africa sent more than 5,000 troops to
combat the MPLA, which was also being
supported by Namibian rebels.
The end of the Cold War resulted in
two major shifts in insurgencies in Africa
and the Americas. First, external assistance
shifted from partisan aid to peacekeeping.
Soviet, Cuban, and American aid to war-
ring factions mostly ended by the early
1990s. This end was particularly noticeable
in Africa. American aid continued in Latin
America, particularly to the Colombian
government in its battle against FARC and
ELN. The collapse of apartheid in South
Africa and the removal of the white govern-
ment there also lessened the role of South
Africa in the wars of southern Africa.
A second shift was the decline in polit-
ically based insurgencies. Instead, insur-
gents organized themselves along ethnic
and religious lines. While groups—such as
factions in Burundi and Rwanda—had
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 699 ---
INSURGENCY AND COUNTERINSURGENCY 623
long been explicitly aligned along tribal
and ethnic lines, there was a decline in the
number of groups claiming pure political
motives. Islamist movements increased
their activities throughout northern Africa,
most notably in Algeria where, in 1992, the
Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) won elec-
tions. The military conducted a coup
shortly thereafter, leading to a seven-year
war with Islamic rebels, including the
Armed Islamic Group (GIA) and a break-
away group, the Salaﬁst Group for Preach-
ing and Combat (GSPC). This war led to
the deaths of more than 70,000 people.
While the war largely ended in 1999, ter-
rorist attacks by these two groups continue.
Other religious groups include the
Lord’s Resistance Army in Uganda, which
seeks to restructure society based on the
T en Commandments. Ethnic insurgent
organizations have included the Rwandan
Patriotic Front (RPF) in Rwanda, a pri-
marily T utsi group which came to power
following the 1994 genocide conducted by
the Hutu government.
Regardless of ideology, groups are in-
creasingly turning to self-ﬁnancing, often
through the production and sale of illicit
items. The RUF (Revolutionary United
Front) in Sierra Leone and UNITA in
Angola relied heavily on diamond sales.
Actions by FARC and ELN in Colombia
are increasingly divorced from their com-
munist ideology as they have increasingly
engaged in the narcotics trade, becoming
two of the wealthiest guerrilla organizations
in the world.
The increasing self-sufﬁciency of some
insurgent operations and the shift from po-
litically based to religious- and ethnic-
based organizations has effects for both the
insurgencies and the ability of governments
to counter them. The self-ﬁnancing by
organizations increases their likelihood of
survival. Unlike groups dependent on out-
side support and sanctuary, these groups
are not reliant on other governments, dias-
poras, or sympathizers in other countries.
However, only groups located in areas con-
ducive to the growth, mining, or drilling of
valuable items are able to ﬁnance their own
wars. The ethnic and religious component
of organizations also increases their chance
of survival as their members are less likely
to be converted to the government’s—or to
other groups’—way of thinking. Ethnicity
is not easily shifted. Thus, counterinsur-
gents are less able to defeat the insurgen-
cies. On the other hand, the identiﬁcation
by ethnicity or religion inherently limits
the ability of the guerilla group from ex-
panding its base of support. It limits the
likelihood the group will win the hearts
and minds of the population outside the
early base of supporters. The insurgency is
less likely to overthrow a government in a
multiethnic or multireligious state. These
new wars are likely to continue indeﬁnitely,
with insurgents and counterinsurgents
both stalemated.
Andrea M. Lopez

INTERNATIONAL
DEVELOPMENT
President Harry S. T ruman announced
on January 20, 1949, the U.S. commit-
ment to help poor countries develop their
economies. Amid the tensions of the Cold
War, the United States wanted to use for-
eign aid to woo the unaligned nations of
Africa, Latin America, and Asia. American
policymakers also foresaw that, if robust,
the economies in these regions would be
able to afford U.S. exports. In May 1950,
Congress passed the Act for International
Development, empowering the president
to authorize programs that aimed to help
poor nations strengthen their economies,
and that September, T ruman created the
T echnical Cooperation Administration
(TCA) to oversee the nascent development
programs. The TCA focused its early efforts
on improving agriculture, health, and
education.
Among the ﬁrst efforts were those of
Florida extension agent Frank Pinder in
Liberia and New England teacher Albion
Patterson in Paraguay. Both men had been
in the ﬁeld before Congress passed the Act
for International Development and so were
able quickly to make good the promise of
economic development. Pinder helped
Liberians grow rice, and Patterson taught
Paraguayan farmers to use the steel plow, a
cultivator, and a method for plowing under
velvet beans to increase the fertility of soils.
Contemporary with these efforts was a pro-
gram in Chile to purify water, build sewers,
and stockpile vaccines against typhoid and
smallpox. Plan Chilean sought to teach
farmers to use machinery and conserve soil.
In the mid-1950s, the University of
Chicago began to help the Catholic Uni-
versity of Chile develop a curriculum in
economics with the aim of graduating men
and women knowledgeable about and sym-
pathetic toward capitalism, and the two
universities began to exchange students and
scholars. In 1953, President Dwight D.
Eisenhower sharpened TCA’s focus on im-
proving trade between the United States
and the third world by loaning money to
underdeveloped nations. American policy-
makers initially favored the World Bank as
the originator of these loans, but the mag-
nitude of the proposed economic aid and
the World Bank’s insistence on short-term
loans spurred the United States to devise
alternatives to it. In 1957, Congress created
the Development Loan Fund to provide
long-term loans to developing nations and,
in 1959, the Inter-American Development
Bank to loan money to Latin America.
In 1961, Congress, at the urging of
President John F . Kennedy, created the U.S.
Agency for International Development
(USAID), which along with the Inter-
American Development Bank and the
World Bank loaned the countries of Latin
America $22 billion between 1961 and
1970. In concert with these loans, govern-
ments throughout Latin America con-

iffs to protect nascent industries. These
actions boosted gross domestic product
(GDP) on average in Latin America 6.5 per-
cent in 1969, though growth in agriculture
was only 2.5 percent. Between 1962 and
1972, USAID and the World Bank loaned
Nigeria $900 million in the belief that
Nigeria was the African nation most able to
beneﬁt from aid and with the aim of in-
creasing the production of food 45 percent

and of manufactured goods fourfold. GDP
rose on average 5 percent through 1965, but
political turmoil thereafter undid this
achievement.
More successful was aid to increase
food production in Latin America and
North Africa. The use of fertilizers, irriga-

By the mid-1990s, Uganda, T ogo, and

boosted GDP 10 percent per year.
Other countries in Africa and Latin

INTERNATIONAL
MONETARYFUND
In July 1944, representatives from forty-
four countries meeting in Bretton Woods,
New Hampshire, founded the International
Monetary Fund (IMF) to promote free
trade. In pursuit of this aim, the IMF sets
currency exchange rates among nations and
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 702 ---
626 I NTERNATIONAL MONETARYFUND
offers their central banks short-term loans.
In 1952, the IMF adopted the principle of
conditionality in claiming the right to re-
quire economic reforms of a country as a
condition of its receiving a loan. The IMF
ﬁrst made a conditioned loan to Peru in
1954. The IMF in 1958 required as a con-
dition of a loan that Argentina reduce the
power of its trade unions in hopes of slow-
ing the increase in wages and thereby
dampening inﬂation. In 1959, the IMF
obliged Chile, as it had Argentina, to slow
the growth in wages. Between 1954 and
1970, Latin American countries received
164 loans from the IMF . During the 1970s,
however, the number of loans to Latin
America declined as the region found itself
awash in capital. The oil crisis of that
decade slowed the growth of the U.S. econ-
omy, discouraging investment in it. Capi-
tal, ﬂeeing from the United States, found a
home in Latin America, allowing its na-
tions to forgo IMF loans. That is, loans
from the private sector replaced loans from
the IMF .
In 1978, the IMF obliged Sudan as a
condition of receiving a loan to devalue its
currency to make its exports cheaper on
the world market and thereby to earn for-
eign exchange. In pursuit of this goal, the
IMF steered Sudanese agriculture toward
groundnuts and cotton, traditional ex-
ports. T o curb inﬂation, the IMF required
Sudan to restrain the growth in wages and
to weaken price controls in the belief that
the free market would set prices lower than
would government. Devaluation of the
currency, however, increased the price of
imports, forcing Sudan to borrow money
and thereby driving up the deﬁcit to more
than $10 billion by 1982. The spike in the
price of imports elevated already high pe-
troleum prices. The result was inﬂation at
25.7 percent by 1982. Industry ﬂoundered
amid high inﬂation, skewing Sudan toward
the production of cash crops, as had been
the case during colonialism. In 1983, Nigeria
negotiated with the IMF for a $2.4 billion
loan but balked at the proposed reforms. In
1986, however, petroleum, Nigeria’s princi-
pal export, dipped below $10 barrel,
prompting private banks to withhold loans
from the country for fear it would default.
With few other sources of capital, Nigeria
accepted an IMF loan. Nigeria’s president
credited IMF reforms with turning a $79.4
million trade deﬁcit in 1986 to a $60.1 mil-
lion surplus in 1987. Between 1990 and
1992, the production of cotton increased
ﬁve times and of cocoa 50 percent. The
director general of the Nigerian Institute of
Social and Economic Research, however,
charged that the increase in cash crops came
at the expense of food for sustenance. More-
over, farmers received less than half the price
of their crops with the rest covering trans-
port to market. Like the Sudan, Nigeria saw
its economy tilt back toward the export of
cash crops and petroleum as had been the
case during colonialism. In 1985, the IMF
rescheduled the repayment of $1 billion due
between 1986 and 1991 in Zambia. Even so
Zambia paid 26 percent of export earnings
to service its debt. Judging that the IMF had
imposed too draconian a series of reforms,
Zambia in 1986 ended them, causing the
IMF to suspend loans to Zambia and raising
the possibility that the country might de-
fault on its debt. The next year the Organi-
zation of African Unity proposed the cre-
ation of an African debt club to lobby the
IMF to reschedule the repayment of debt
throughout Africa.
Zambia neared the precipice of default.
Mexico plunged over the edge, suspending
debt repayment in 1982, followed over the
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 703 ---

next two years by nearly every other debtor
in Latin America and Africa. The IMF in-
tervened, extending loans to ﬁfteen coun-
tries in Latin America in 1983, whereas it
had doled out loans to only ﬁve countries in
the region in 1981. Excepting a dip in the
number of loans in the mid-1980s, the IMF
remained active in Latin America, offering
loans to fourteen countries in the region in
1995 and to thirteen in 1996. Yet debt rose
between 1980 and 1995 from $11.2 billion
to $21.8 billion in Chile, from $27 billion
to $35.2 billion in Venezuela, from $27.2
billion to $90 billion in Argentina, from
$50.7 billion to $161.1 billion in Mexico,
and from $64 billion to $164.9 billion in
Brazil. Debt in Sudan stood at $24 billion
in 2003; in Argentina at $147 billion in
2004; and in Nigeria at $33 billion in 2005.
Brazilian debt totaled 51.3 percent of gross
domestic product in 2005. Rather than
restoring prosperity, IMF loans have coin-
cided with high debt.

IRONWORKING
Ironworking and bronze casting were part of
life in what are now central Nigeria and
Benin, and African slaves brought the
hearth, de cadinho (the crucible), and the
African forge to the Americas. In Brazil, they
are even credited with having been tutors to
their captors, working the iron directly in
the crude early forges of Minas Gerais.
Iron smelting and forging were sacred
in Africa, and this belief was preserved by
many Africans in America. An iron furnace
found in the sacred forest of the Akan dates
back to the ninth century. In the Mande
area of Upper Guinea, iron makers were
hereditary clans with considerable power.
Ironworking, and blacksmithing and
mining more generally, were the focus of
patterns of resistance to slavery. A metal
helmet made in the 1,000-year-old meth-
ods of the Nok was found in Palmares, the
seventeenth-century society of fugitives
and Indians in Brazil, a society that lasted
nearly a hundred years. Among descen-
dants of Ngola (Angola), iron or clay pots
were carefully fashioned into powerful reli-
gious objects. In Mexico, African miners
became a force in the Revolution of 1810,
which abolished slavery in Mexico. In Vir-
ginia and Maryland, forges were places
trusted, as in Congolese culture, as sanctu-
aries. A high proportion of successful fugi-
tives in America were associated with iron-
working and blacksmithing.
The iron industry in the southern
United States remained dependent on en-
slaved black labor until the middle of the
nineteenth century and the destruction of
the Civil War. After Emancipation, African
American ironworkers worked on railroads
and in the growing steel industry, making
rails in Pittsburgh. Black ironworkers re-
mained strong in the southern ironworks in
Richmond and Birmingham until the mid-
dle of the twentieth century.
Jean Libby

ISLAM,A FRICAN AMERICAN
African American Islam demonstrates the
spread of Muslim faith and peoples in
the New World as a consequence of the
transatlantic slave trade; it also describes
transatlantic political and religious ex-
changes, New World inventions of Islam,
and African American cultural identity. It is
generally acknowledged that Africa has en-
joyed a long and profound connection with
the religion of Islam dating back to the
eighth century. From North Africa, Islam
spread through the Sahel region as a result
of trade and commerce, and it put the peo-
ples of this region into contact with the
ﬂourishing Mediterranean world. In turn,
Africans were awakened to invisible forces
beyond their borders and introduced to
historical developments that make up the
ancient history of Western civilization.
A signiﬁcant number of African Mus-
lims were captured and sent to the Americas
during the Atlantic slave trade. In Brazil,
Surinam, and Haiti, Muslims were in
the vanguard of organized rebellion. Their
efforts in seceding from these colonial states
to establish independent “African” societies
in the New World inﬂuenced the overall
character of slavery even in the United
States where traders and planters con-
sciously suppressed all manifest signs of
“alien” religion in order to better control
their slaves.
The earliest African Muslims in America
and their resistance to the fate of slavery
are known through the experiences of
Yarrow Mamout, Job Ben Solomon, Abdul
Rahahman, Bilali Muhammad, and Lamen
Kebe—all Muslims—brought to North
America aboard slave ships from Sahelian
Africa in the eighteenth century. The reli-
gion of these slaves provided a ﬂedgling
ideology of opposition to subjugation
under the twinned yoke of slavery and New
World Christian dominion. As descendants
of elite Muslim lineages of African tribes,
they were often literate in Arabic and im-
pressed their white slave masters by their
leadership abilities on the plantation. In
this way, some Muslim slaves earned noto-
riety as drivers and a few even gained man-
umission.
Accounts of organized rebellion by
Muslim slaves in U.S. territories are scarce.
However, in the Caribbean world and par-
ticularly in northern Brazil, religion pro-
vided a singular ideological rallying point
for revolt. Muslim conspirators played a
cardinal role in the slave uprisings of Bahia,
earning for Muslims throughout the
Americas a special reputation for rebellion.
Their renown emanated from Brazil to
Surinam and throughout the Caribbean,
inspiring the successful revolt of T oussaint
Louverture and Jean Jacque Dessalines in
Haiti as well as several uprisings in Jamaica.
However, the role, if any, played by
Muslims in the U.S. Civil War and post-
Emancipation society remains unknown.

--- PAGE 705 ---
ISLAM,A FRICAN AMERICAN 629
With the exception of a few individual
testimonies, African Islamic traditions
appear not to have survived the transition
from slavery to freedom.
In the 1880s, Edward Blyden, a scholar
and churchman from St. Thomas, Virgin
Islands, published a treatise entitled Chris-
tianity, Islam and the Negro Race (1887,
reprinted 1967). This work was based on
Blyden’s years of travel in Africa and the
Levant on behalf of the Methodist-backed
American Colonization Society, which had
long sought to spread Christianity to Africa
by repatriating freed slaves. Blyden ex-
plained that the reasons Africans often
chose Islam over Christianity was because
the Qur’an had protected the black man
from self-depreciation in the presence of
both Arab and European colonizers.
When Blyden died in Sierra Leone he
was accorded a Muslim funeral. T o this day
the question of his conversion to Islam re-
mains a mystery. Nevertheless, he became
an important symbol linking Islam to pan-
African nationalism. His thought res-
onated with young black leaders like the
Jamaican Marcus Garvey, who was further
inﬂuenced by Duse Mohammed Ali, a
London-based Egyptian who published
The Africa Times and Orient Review, the
ﬁrst periodical devoted to the Afro-Islamic
Diaspora. Garvey apprenticed with Duse
Mohammed in London and eventually in-
corporated his mentor’s convictions into
the motto of his Universal Negro Improve-
ment Association (UNIA), “One God,
One Aim, One Destiny,” expressing the
Islamic principle of tawhid (unity or one-
ness). The logic of a separate destiny for
Americans of African descent espoused
therein was essentially a political impulse
that found its most articulate expressions
in religious discourse.
When disillusionment and despair
overwhelmed the black masses streaming
into northern cities during the Great
Migration (1914–1919), it was this reli-
gious discourse which prevailed among the
most destitute and heart-broken individu-
als who found little comfort in the tenor of
assimilation and status consciousness of the
Methodist and Baptist churches. Thus for
the growing African American urban popu-
lation, religious movements became sanc-
tuaries for autonomous thought and proto-
nationalist ideas. As these movements
began to respond to human needs for
protection, employment, food, money, and
shelter, the material foundations for nation-
alism solidiﬁed.
The period between 1890 and World
War II was one of luxuriant growth and de-
velopment for many forms of black religion
in the United States. In this time span,
three Islamic movements came to promi-
nence in urban America. They were the
Moorish Science T emple, the Ahmadiyya
Movement in Islam, and the Nation of
Islam. Understood as a whole, they repre-
sent a movement based on three themes:
the struggle for equality, interest in Africa,
and attachment to land. All those who
joined were somehow inﬂuenced by the
secular nationalism of Marcus Garvey’s
UNIA and the issues which gathered
around the rising tide of self-consciousness
and the will to discover and recreate a new,
urban identity.
Reformers and proselytizers of this pe-
riod depicted Islam as an alternative to
Christian ethics as well as a way to reestab-
lish a spiritual discourse with the world of
nonwhite peoples outside the United
States. During this time the elementary
principles of Islamic education, lifestyle,
and worship were established. Thereafter

they would remain the foundations of
African American Islam.
First organized in Newark, New Jersey,
in 1913 then revived in Chicago, Illinois,
in 1919, Nobel Drew Ali’s Moorish Science
T emple maintained an uncertain continu-
ity with the vestigial religious traditions
handed down from the slave generations.
In his amalgamation of Islam, Christianity,
Oriental mysticism, and gnosis, Noble
Drew Ali drew upon the folk beliefs of slav-
ery where Old and New T estament
prophets could be fused into a singular and
powerful symbol of resistance to oppres-
sion. The text of the identity cards distrib-
uted to the Moors reveals a conscious at-
tempt at syncretism.
In addition to their identity cards,
members of the Moorish Science T emple
sufﬁxed Arabic titles to their names, El or
Bey. They wore red fezzes and beards and
practiced abstinence from “unclean” foods,
cosmetics, and “theatrical, licentious enter-
tainment.” Segregation of the sexes was in-
stituted in the Moorish T emples, while at
the same time, Noble Drew Ali preached
monogamy and a stable family structure.
The greeting “Peace!” or “Islam!” was
adopted by the Moors, demonstrating
through a simple gesture the powerful ap-
peal and collective solidarity of the African
Diaspora to which Drew assimilated his
followers. As a way of attracting new con-
verts, those who professed to carry piety in
their breasts—no matter how faint and un-
clear their beliefs resonated—were invited
to eschew the “white God of the white
man.” Noble Drew Ali even authored his
own “Holy Koran,” drawing on passages
from the real Qur’an, the Bible, Garvey’s
sayings, anecdotes of Jesus, and his own
ideas. By the late 1920s, Noble Drew Ali
was celebrated as a black messiah anxious
to redeem his fellow African Americans.
His unorthodox teachings employed Islam
to counter the systematic dehumanization
of blacks brought about by the prolifera-
tion of Jim Crow laws. His considerable
following demonstrated a proclivity to op-
pose all Eurocentric ideologies and pre-
saged modern Afrocentric tendencies. Be-
yond doubt, the Moorish Science T emple
paved the way for the Nation of Islam.
Almost simultaneously Islam was mak-
ing inroads in other black communities
thanks to a group of Punjabi missionaries.
Founded in India by a self-proclaimed re-
deemer of Islam named Ghulam Ahmad,
the Ahmadiya Movement in Islam has an
important theological preoccupation with
the Christian gospel and its succession of
prophets and promise for the Second Com-
ing. Its appeal to many African Americans
lies in its criticism of the Bible as a forgery
and its apocryphal refutation of the cruci-
ﬁxion of Jesus. Around the turn of the
twentieth century, the Ahmadis created a
vigorous worldwide missionary movement.
Having determined to become the harbin-
gers of Islam in the West, they brought
ideas of Islamic social justice to bear upon
the reality of North American ghettos.
This synthesis was fortuitous, as
demonstrated by the experience of Walter
Gregg, a young T exan who migrated to St.
Louis, Missouri, in 1924. There, this pen-
sive young man, interested in books,
religion, and the problems of his race, met
another black convert to Ahmadiya who
offered him a solution: “Change your name,
get your language, follow your people and
you won’t be a Negro anymore.” He
changed his named to Wali Akram and
studied the Qur’an intensively. By 1933 he
had broken with the Ahmadiya and estab-
lished the First Cleveland Mosque as a

An era of rhetorical confrontation
began during the 1930s in Detroit. Under
the guidance of Master Fard Muhammad
and the stewardship of the Honorable
Elijah Muhammad, the Nation of Islam
(NOI) became the foremost non-Christian
religious movement among African Ameri-
cans. So great was the appeal of Elijah
Muhammad that the movement inﬂuenced
blacks in practically every major city in the
United States. The ideology of the Nation
of Islam played to the apprehensions of a
dislocated black population, victims of
racial segregation, economic exploitation,
and Cold War repression. Black Muslims
abandoned their “slave names” and re-
placed them with an “X,” indicative of
their “lost-found” Afro-Asian ancestry ac-
cording to Elijah Muhammad. Spiritual
uplift came to many blacks who were down
and out. Some were redeemed felons like
Malcolm X, who rose from “the dead level”
to the highest rank in the NOI. By his elo-
quent “straight talk,” Malcolm X articu-
lated many repressed feelings of the black
man which were ignored by leaders of the
Christian church. It was not the black man
but the Church which had fallen from
grace. So, whether from the conﬁnes of a
prison cell or the pews of a Baptist Church,
an individual could regain his humanity,
simultaneously redeeming his family and
enslaved ancestors, by being reborn into
the worldwide Islamic ummah.
Malcolm X’s defection from the Na-
tion of Islam profoundly affected the devel-
opment of orthodox Islam in America. Not
only was it a decisive blow to the power of
Elijah Muhammad’s organization, but it
also spelled an end to the idiosyncratic in-
terpretation of Islam which theretofore had
dominated public conception of the reli-
gion among many Americans. This rejec-
tion of the unorthodox practices of the Na-
tion of Islam, which had led to widespread
misperceptions of Islamic theology, paved
the way for discussions of Islamic belief and
inaugurated a period of rich diversity from
1965 until the present.
The decade 1965–1975 was a period
of transition from “temples” to “mosques”
and Islamic community centers. Leading
the way were the Mosque of Islamic Broth-
erhood in Harlem and the Dar ul-Islam
Movement founded at Yasin Mosque in
Brooklyn. Both were inspired by African
American Muslims who, like Malcolm X,
had traveled to Mecca and experienced for
themselves the racial plurality and interna-
tional appeal of Islam. Sheik K. Ahmad
Tawﬁq, founder of the Mosque of Islamic
Brotherhood, had studied at Al-Azhar
University in Cairo, where he was strongly
influenced by the Egyptian Ikwan al-
Muslimun (Muslim Brotherhood). Ac-
knowledging the internationalist character
of “true” Islam, Tawﬁq kept enough of the
“nationalist” logic within his grasp to make
sense to his African American audience.
Yasin Mosque led by Imam Yahya
Abdul Karim in Brooklyn was an out-
growth of Sheik Daoud Faisal’s Islamic
Mission to America, which was located on
State Street not far from the immigrant

Arab community on Atlantic Avenue.
Muslim emissaries, businessmen, and United
Nations diplomats from the world over fre-
