For years this interaction galvanized a solid
core of African Americans who mingled
with the foreign visitors. Arabic scholar-
ship, knowledge of Islamic law, and pil-
grimages to the Middle East were the priv-
ileges of this association. In the decade of
1965–1975 the African Americans resolved
to take their experience back into the
streets, uniting with their brothers who had
independently found the path to righteous
Islam. The target was Bedford-Stuyvesant
where they used Islamic zeal to recover a
gang-infested neighborhood. Their Islam
was infused with activism and their ac-
tivism was informed by sharia (Islamic
law). Inspired by tradition, they established
a dormitory ( suffa) for homeless and psy-
chically dislocated young men. T o rehabili-
tate convicts, they helped establish Masjid
Sankore, the ﬁrst orthodox prison mosque
recognized by the New York State Depart-
ment of Corrections. T o set an even greater
example, they put into motion a nation-
wide movement, the Dar ul-Islam.
Simultaneously, there were Islamic
movements underway in Philadelphia,
Washington, D.C., and Atlanta. Imam Talib
A. Dawud, an Antiguan jazz trumpeter and
lapsed Ahmadi convert, founded the Mus-
lim Brotherhood of America in Philadel-
phia. His movement influenced many
bebop-era jazz musicians, including Art
Blakey, Yusef Latif, John Coltrane, Rashied
Ali, Randy Weston, and Pharaoh Sanders,
who created an aura of popular culture for
African American Islam.
The Islamic Party of Washington, D.C.,
and Atlanta, Georgia, made inroads into
the black middle class because its founder,
Yusuf M. Hamid, attracted university stu-
dents searching for new formulas after the
demise of Black Power, the antiwar move-
ment, and Marxist politics. The movement
was organized according to Islamic popular-
political principles and combined com-
munal living with the spirit of hijrah, the
migration of the Prophet Muhammad from
Mecca to Medina to establish the ﬁrst
Muslim city-state in 622 BCE. The Islamic
Party’s ﬁnal goal, evoking this historic mi-
gration, was the establishment of an Islamic
state or caliphate somewhere in North
America. In an address to the Philadelphia
Muslim Conference in 1970, Hamid ar-
gued eloquently for unity with the Dar 
ul-Islam movement, but this initiative
failed after two years.
While imprisoned in New York for po-
litical crimes in the early 1970s, the Black
Power leader H. Rap Brown came into con-
tact with chaplains from the Dar ul-Islam
movement. He committed himself to Islam
and changed his name to Jamil Al-Amin.
Following his conversion to Islam and pa-
role from a New York prison in 1976, Al-
Amin made a pilgrimage to Mecca and
then settled in Atlanta’s West End, where
he founded the Community Mosque of At-
lanta. His congregation was the basis for
the National Community, a coalition of
thirty North American mosques that
sought to revive Brooklyn’s Dar ul-Islam
movement in spirit if not name. Presiding
as imam and civic leader for more than two
decades, Al-Amin was credited for resusci-
tating a dying ghetto by ridding the area of
drug dealers and prostitutes, thereby mak-
ing it safe for children and families.
Other activists who discovered Islam
while imprisoned were members of the
Black Panther Party and the Black Libera-
tion Army. Their use of Islam as a tool for

resisting the ennui of prison created a ﬁerce

There are a number of gleaming
Islamic centers across the American
landscape: Los Angeles, Chicago, T oledo,
Washington, Atlanta, and New York.
Wherever large immigrant communities
are established, there is usually an Islamic
center that has been funded partially
through local contributions but mainly by
organizations such as the Muslim World
League. Based in Saudi Arabia, the Muslim
World League is dedicated to promoting
the Wahabi dynasty’s claim over the holy
sites at Mecca and Medina. There are many
controversial aspects to the work of this or-

ism is another contentious issue. Moreover,
there is deep concern about the Islamic
propriety of Muslims investing in expensive
mosques while ignoring the needs of their
destitute brothers living in urban slums.
One emphatic conviction shared by
most African Americans who have made
their pilgrimage to Mecca is the rapture
felt by communing with the multitude of
humanity who circles the holy kaaba, the
cube-shaped structure predating the
Islamic presence in Mecca which became a
sacred sanctuary under Muhammad’s rule
and around which al-Masjid al-Haram is
built. This pilgrimage often becomes the
central experience in their lives and pro-
duces a contagious effect at home. In this
encounter, African American Muslims ex-
perience directly the heterogeneous ways
of Islam. As a consequence of this immer-
sion, other tendencies of Islam receive
new legitimacy. Signiﬁcantly, the experi-
ence reties the knot with African Islam,
thereby attracting those seeking a more
esoteric religious experience to the Suﬁ
traditions of the Sudan and West Africa.
So pilgrimages act as an impetus toward
Afrocentrism among many African Amer-
ican Muslims.
There are Muslims among blacks in al-
most every major American city. New York
is only one of the areas that has experienced
enormous growth in the number of
Muslims. There are 112 mosques in the
state of New York, with 71 in the ﬁve bor-
oughs of New York City. Chicago has at
least 40 mosques. In addition, Los Angeles,
Washington, Atlanta, Detroit, Cleveland,
and T oledo are cities where one might ex-
pect to see 10,000 Muslims celebrating the
Eid al-Fitr, the celebration marking the end

of Ramadan, communally. In total there are
almost 600 mosques nationwide.
The South-Central area of Los Ange-
les, scene of the 1992 riots in reaction to
the decision in the Rodney King trial,
counts dozens of small storefront mosques
of various afﬁliations and beliefs. There
was even a Shia mosque, al-Rasul, whose
black imam espoused jihad until he moved
to Iran in 1989. Local Muslim activists
proselytized among the notorious Crips
and Bloods long before the riots gave fur-
ther cause to the idea of unity. The activists’
efforts were based upon the belief that
gangs represent a “primitive” stage of cul-
tural nationalism whose logical culmina-
tion lies in adherence to Islam as the “true”
religion for people of African descent. Due
to the persistence of this minority of parti-
sans in the cause of Allah throughout the
past decades, it is often said that every
black youth grows up in proximity to some
notion of Islam.
For this reason, perhaps, almost 90 per-
cent of the converts to Islam in the United
States are African Americans, a trend whose
meaning has not been lost to prominent
Arab- or Asian-American Muslims who de-
sire to build a political coalition with the
goal of enhancing their position in Ameri-
can society. The alliance of the Muslim
Political Action Committee with Jesse Jack-
son’s 1988 presidential campaign was a ten-
tative gesture in this direction.
However, political differences surfaced
in 1991 on the occasion of the Gulf War.
Middle-class immigrants joined the fol-
lowers of Warith Mohammed in patriotic
support of the U.S.-led military coalition
to drive Iraqi forces from Kuwait. On the
other hand, many African American Mus-
lims, both Sunni orthodox and Nation of
Islam, dissented together with a large
number of pious, working-class immi-
grants who opposed foreign military pres-
ence in the sacred land of Islam. The war
also spurred a wave of conversion among
African American soldiers who were tem-
porarily based in Saudi Arabia and exposed
to intense religious proselytization by ul-
traconservative Wahabi clerics.
In the emotionally charged atmosphere
following the events of September 11,
2001, and subsequent American military
retaliations in Afghanistan and Iraq,
African American Muslims weathered occa-
sional though often persistent allegations of
disloyalty and subversion. However, there
was no evidence of mass collaboration with
terrorist cells as alleged by some media and
law enforcement ofﬁcials who seemed de-
termined to resurrect criminal stereotyping
and political witch hunts in the manner of
hysterical anti-Communism. In pursuit of
national security, the police regularly mon-
itor Friday sermons and special events at
mosques throughout the country. Some
Muslims allege harassment at their jobs and
discrimination in schools. While such per-
secution has failed to diminish their zeal, it
has fostered a new sense of unity among
indigenous and immigrant Muslims in
America. Another likely inﬂuence on the
future of Islam in America will be the reli-
gious choice made by thousands of young
African Americans returning home from
combat and military service in the Muslim
world.

JACOBS,H ARRIET ANN
(1813–1897)
Harriet Jacobs was an escaped female slave
and the author of Incidents in the Life of
a Slave Girl (1861). Jacobs was born in
Edenton, North Carolina, in 1813 to
Delilah and Elijah Jacobs—both slaves of
mixed racial ancestry. In her important nar-
rative, Jacobs discloses that she did not
know she was a slave until the age of six
when her mother died. Her mother’s mis-
tress took in Jacobs and taught her to read,
spell, and sew. Upon her death six years
later, the mistress conferred Jacobs on
her three-year-old niece, Mary Matilda
Norcom, whose father, Dr. James Norcom,
sexually harassed Jacobs for seven years. At
sixteen, when Norcom threatened Jacobs
with concubinage, she began an affair with
neighbor Samuel Sawyer, a young, white
attorney, and became pregnant to thwart
Norcom’s advances. She bore two children,
Joseph and Louisa Matilda. Norcom per-
sisted, and in 1835, Jacobs ran away and
hid for seven years in a three-foot high attic
crawl space above her grandmother’s home.
There, she watched over her children, who
lived with her grandmother, a freedwoman.
In 1842, Jacobs escaped to the north
where she worked as a nursemaid and then in
an antislavery reading room over Frederick
637
J
Douglass’s North Star. She reunited with her
children and, shortly thereafter, met Amy
Post, a Quaker feminist and abolitionist,
who encouraged Jacobs to publish her story.
Incidents is remarkable, for, unlike
male-authored slave narratives, it fore-
grounds the sexual violence female slaves
endured at the hands of their masters, the
disastrous effects of such exploitative prac-
tices upon slave mothers and their children,
and the problems racial mixing posed for a
system of inequity based upon skin color.
Initially Incidents was considered a
ﬁction: it was published under the pseudo-
nym Linda Brent; edited by Lydia Child, a
northern abolitionist, novelist, and political
pamphleteer; and shares some generic con-
ventions of Harriet Beecher Stowe’s novel
Uncle T om’s Cabin, which like Incidents, was
written in response to the Fugitive Slave Law
of 1850. In the 1980s, scholars conﬁrmed
Jacobs’s identity and her text’s authenticity
through manuscript and historical research.
Jacobs devoted her life to abolition,
before, during, and after the Civil War, and
died in her Washington, D.C., home March
7, 1897. She is buried in Mount Auburn
Cemetery, Cambridge, Massachusetts.
Wendy Weise
See also: Slave Narratives; Stowe, Harriet
Beecher

JAMAICA
Jamaica is an island of the Caribbean, 90
miles (145 kilometers) south of Cuba and
100 miles (161 kilometers) west of Haiti. It
is a former British colony with a history of
enslavement of its indigenous and African
peoples and of Afro-Jamaican rebellion
against domination through dance, reli-
gion, and outright confrontation. The orig-
inal inhabitants of Jamaica, prior to
Christopher Columbus landing there on
May 5, 1494, were the Arawak Indians
who gave the island its name, Xaymaca.
The Spanish took over Jamaica in 1496,
and they remained in power until 1655,
when the British gained control. The harsh
treatment by the Spaniards along with ex-
posure to foreign illnesses resulted in the
Arawak’s extinction. T oday, 90 percent of
the island’s population is of West African
descent. African natives we re in Jamaica
150 years before the B ritish arrived; after
the British landed on the island, though,
their culture became a dominant ﬁxture
of the island’s social mix.
African natives were brought to Jamaica
as slaves in 1517. In 1655, in a battle
between the Spanish and the British (called
the Western Design) for control of Jamaica,
the slaves sided with the Spanish, who in
turn gave them their freedom. After the
Spanish defeat, the freed slaves, now referred
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 715 ---
JAMAICA 639
Maroon War in the 1790s caused some of
the Maroons to be exiled to Canada and
then to Africa.
The Consolidated Slave Act of 1781
declared that a slave’s work day was to be
11 hours long and that each slave would get
a day off every other week. As the act
began, missionaries and leaders took up
residency to provide religious instruction as
well as support to the slaves. One such
leader was Moses Baker, a black Baptist
preacher. He and George Lisle, an emanci-
pated slave who became a preacher, saw
the need for religious enlightenment for the
slave population. They wanted to reach the
Afro-Jamaican population by combining
Christianity with their African practices of
religion. In 1792, a missionary society was
founded; the London Missionary Society
followed in 1795 and the British and
Foreign Bible Society in 1803. The mis-
sionaries’ role was to befriend the slaves,
teach them the tenets of the Christian reli-
gion, and to expose the immorality of slav-
ery. The missionaries gave the slaves more
determination to rebel for their freedom by
preaching the injustices of slavery. William
Wilberforce was instrumental in eliciting
a response from the Society for Gradual
Abolition of Slavery through his writings
showing the inhumanity and injustices of
slavery; in 1830, emancipation was
strongly recommended.
In 1831, one of the most violent rebel-
lions occurred. This uprising is referred to
as the Baptist War, or the Christmas Rebel-
lion, and was led by Sam Sharpe (it is
sometimes referred to as Sam Sharpe’s Re-
bellion). The rebellion, which lasted four
months, began peacefully but quickly esca-
lated into widespread violent unrest. This
rebellion, though, brought about a quick
response. Sam Sharpe was executed by
hanging May 23, 1832. Sharpe was de-
clared a national hero by the rebels, who
continued to revolt in the name of free-
dom until 1833 when emancipation was
declared.  However, emancipation did not
truly come to fruition in 1834.
August 1, 1834, is remembered as the
day of freedom and is commemorated by at-
tending a religious service called the “Divine
Services.” The Abolition Act declared that
all slaves’ children under the age of six or
born afterwards were considered free. De-
spite the Abolition Act, there was a condi-
tion to the slaves’ freedom: they had to par-
ticipate in an apprenticeship for six years.
This apprenticeship did, however, allow the
workers to argue against unjust treatment.
Missionaries organized the meetings for the
apprentices. The work and requirements for
those working in the ﬁelds (“praedials”) was
six years and differed from those in domes-
tic positions (“non-praedials”), which were
for four years. The apprenticeship program
lasted until August 1, 1838, when Britain
decided the program had become a hin-
drance. Education was awarded to the freed
slaves but only in a limited manner. Op-
pression was a constant factor in all aspects
of the slaves’ lives, including education and
religious reforms which appeared in the
guise of freedom.
In 1840, things began to change when
voting rights for Afro-Jamaicans were
granted. The emphasis was still on proﬁts
and the upper class; however, some of the
middle-class residents were granted political
seats on the council. Despite the positive
outcome, however small, in 1846, Britain
passed the Sugar Duties Act, which caused
the sugar industry in Jamaica to falter.
Riots and demonstrations increased and
with the Morant Bay Rebellion, extreme
restrictions were placed upon Jamaica.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 716 ---
640 J AMAICA
Once again Afro-Jamaican freedom
was tested when, on October 11, 1865, an
incident occurred that involved a man
who was sent to prison for trespassing on a
plantation that was considered abandoned.
This injustice caused ire in Afro-Jamaican
communities. Protesters marched to Morant
Bay to show their anger. This protest was
led by Paul Bogle and George William
Gordon. The result of this rebellion was
that Jamaica became a Crown Colony
under British rule.
Despite the governmental change, Afro-
Jamaicans were still considered a minority
and extremely oppressed. Under the new
government, Afro-Jamaicans were in dire
straights. The sugar industry was on the de-
cline and replaced with the banana industry
now controlled by the United Fruit Com-
pany. Because of the governmental actions,
the Afro-Jamaicans were immigrating to
other areas of the country for employment.
After the Morant Bay Rebellion,
Jamaica settled into a time of prosperity.
Afro-Jamaicans began to accumulate land
and there was a rise in the middle class. De-
spite this prosperity, Afro-Jamaicans were
still contained and oppressed by the white
majority. The Morant Rebellion demon-
strated to the white majority that Afro-
Jamaicans were capable of protesting
against unfair treatment and making a
strong statement against the whites.
From the late nineteenth century
through the 1930s, Afro-Jamaicans were
still not fairly recognized in government, so
they turned away from it and returned to
their religious heritage as a means of shap-
ing social protest and change. Movements
designed to confront the social injustices
experienced by Afro-Jamaicans include
Bewardism, Garveyism, Ethiopianism, and
Rastafarianism. Not only did these move-
ments choose to expose and address the
horrific conditions suffered by Afro-
Jamaicans, they also inspired the lower
classes to call for social and economic re-
forms. The People’s Political Party founded
by Garvey in 1929 was considered the ﬁrst
anticolonial political party. In 1935,
Alexander Bustamante created the Jamaica
Workers and T rademen’s Union (JWTU).
Three years later, Bustamante headed the
Bustamante Industrial T rade Union
(BITU) and Norman Manley created the
People’s National Party (PNP). All of these
parties were created to aid the peasants in
pushing for reforms. Another party that
was formed by Bustamante in 1943 was the
Jamaica Labour Party (JLP). A year later an
election was held and the Jamaican Labour
Party won with Alexander Bustamante as
the ﬁrst chief minister.
August 5, 1962, saw the creation of the
Dominion of Jamaica. At the celebration,
the motto of Jamaica (“Out of Many, One
People”) was instituted. At the ﬁrst session
of Parliament, Princess Margaret gave Sir
Alexander Bustamante the appropriate doc-
uments in recognition of the new com-
monwealth. Despite the celebration, Busta-
mante and Norman Manley both warned
the people of the challenges that were fac-
ing them as an independent nation.
In the 1950s, Jamaica took the newest
discovery of bauxite and coupled it with
the tourist industry to beneﬁt the econ-
omy. During this time, Afro-Jamaicans
beneﬁted from the recovering economy.
Yet political friction persisted and ﬂowered
in the 1960s as the leadership of  Edward
Seaga altered the social and political land-
scape of Jamaica. Seaga, who would be-
come leader of the Jamaica Labour Party
(JLP) in 1974 and Prime Minister of
Jamaica from 1980 to 1989, advanced an
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 717 ---

anticommunist and procapitalist model of
governance, and he was viewed by some as
emphasizing the business success of the
Afro-Jamaicans as individual initiative to
the detriment of viewing such successes as
part of a collective advance of their social,
economic, and political status. 
Afro-Jamaicans have had to face severe
poverty, discrimination, and oppression in
order to service and succeed as a culture. T o
preserve their heritage, they are working to
revitalize art, language, stories, music,
dance, and religion. One of the dance
forms that still exists in Jamaica is the jun-
conoo. Jamaica is also known as the birth-
place of Bob Marley and reggae music.
The deﬁnitive themes throughout Afro-
Jamaican culture are African heritage, reli-
gion, and struggles for freedom. 
In the twenty-ﬁrst century, Jamaica is
faced with high rates of crime, corruption,
and poverty. Drugs and drug trafﬁcking
play a big part in the country’s social and
political problems.  Jamaica is a land of ex-
tremes in terms of economic prosperity. A
major resort island, tourists driving to the
resorts go past people living in poverty.
And the Afro-Jamaicans are still ﬁghting to
receive the beneﬁts of their homeland.

JAMAICA,WOMEN’S ROLE IN
Jamaican women have been participants
and leaders in slave resistance and rebellion
and have shaped intellectual, cultural, and
political life in the Caribbean, Britain, and
the United States. From the ﬁrst arrivals in
the mid-seventeenth century till the pres-
ent, women of African descent have played
a key role in the socioeconomic, cultural,
and political development of Jamaica. Slave
women, of whom there were 160,000 on
the eve of Emancipation, constituted the
bulk of the ﬁeld labor force on the sugar
plantations. As they resorted more to covert
forms of resistance to improve their living
and working conditions, such as feigning
illness and slacking, than such overt forms
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 718 ---
642 J AMAICA,WOMEN’S ROLE IN
as running away and revolt, few slave
women have entered the ofﬁcial records.
A notable exception is Nanny of the
Maroons, a slave woman who became the
leader of a community of runaway slaves
and successfully used guerrilla warfare
against the British in the 1720s and 1730s.
Like their enslaved ancestors, the ﬁrst
generation of Afro-Jamaican women born
in freedom used a variety of strategies to
combat oppression. They played a visible
part in the 1865 Morant Bay Rebellion,
which followed several decades of planter
practices and colonial policies that aimed
to curb the legal rights of the ex-slaves.
Sarah Johnson and Ann Thompson raided a
police station and stores in order to obtain
gunpowder and cutlasses, while Elizabeth
Taylor beat a black man who had volun-
teered to put down the rebellion for having
betrayed his mother and race. These
women have not received as much atten-
tion in studies on the immediate post-
emancipation period, however, as Mary
Seacole. Having gained experience nursing
invalid soldiers in her mother’s lodging-
house, Seacole went to England in 1854 to
be sent as an army nurse to the Crimea.
When the War Ofﬁce rejected her on the
color of her skin, she made her own way to
the Crimea where she set up a medical store
and hostel near Balaclava.
Afro-Jamaican women in the post-
emancipation period not only tried to im-
prove their own lives and those of future
generations of black women by taking part
in protests but also by working within a
wide range of organizations. In the late
nineteenth and early twentieth centuries,
several middle-class Afro-Jamaican women
not only joined but also founded social
welfare organizations aimed at women and
children, such as the Jamaica Save the
Children Fund. After World War I, Afro-
Jamaican women became members of exist-
ing trade unions and set up unions that
catered speciﬁcally to women. The educa-
tor and social reformer Amy Bailey, for
instance, was the ﬁrst woman to join the
Jamaica Union of T eachers and cofounded
the Women T eachers’ Federation. While
most female union members were active as
rank-and-ﬁle members, a small number en-
tered the middle leadership, chaired com-
mittees, or worked as secretaries of unions.
Gladys Longbridge (Lady Bustamante), for
example, served as both secretary and trea-
surer of the Bustamante Industrial T rade
Union in the late 1930s.
Some Afro-Jamaican women also
played an active role in (semi-) political or-
ganizations. Born in Jamaica in 1897, Amy
Ashwood Garvey became a follower of
Marcus Garvey at the age of 17 and helped
him found the Universal Negro Improve-
ment Association (UNIA). When Garvey
left for the United States in 1916, she left
for Panama but eventually joined Garvey
and married him in 1919. Until their mar-
riage broke down in 1922, she played an
important role in the UNIA’s New York
branch. During World War II, she returned
to Jamaica where she founded the J.A.G.
Smith Political Party, which did badly in
the polls. In 1944, she went to the United
States, where she campaigned to persuade
the government to offer war work to
Jamaican men and women. In the late
1940s and 1950s, she was active in the Pan-
African movement and cofounded the As-
sociation for the Advancement of Coloured
People in the United Kingdom.
Garvey’s second wife, Amy Jacques
Garvey, is also remembered as a woman
who fought for the freedom and equality of
black people in Africa and the Diaspora.

JAMAICA,WOMEN’S ROLE IN 643
Born in Kingston in 1896, she moved to
the United States in 1918. She met Garvey
in 1919 and married him in 1923. She oc-
cupied key roles in the UNIA, was instru-
mental in organizing the ﬁfth Pan-African
Congress, put pressure on the United Na-
tions to issue an “African freedom charter,”
and wrote numerous letters, essays, and
speeches on black liberation. She was also
involved in local politics. Shortly after their
return to Jamaica in 1927, she helped Gar-
vey set up the People’s Political Party, and
in the 1940s, she worked for Norman
Manley’s Peoples National Party (PNP),
which was instrumental in bringing about
Jamaica’s independence. Jacques Garvey was
not the only Afro-Jamaican woman, how-
ever, who believed that self-government was
an essential precondition for the full equal-
ity of people of African descent in Jamaica
and actively fought toward this goal. Dur-
ing a visit to Britain in 1938, Amy Bailey
spoke about self-government to the secre-
tary of state for the colonies and also ad-
dressed the issue at a major peace confer-
ence in Glasgow.
Afro-Jamaican women in the interwar
years were not just concerned about class
and racial oppression but also about gender
oppression. Una Marson was one of several
women who criticized persisting Victorian
ideas about the place and roles of women
and the male domination of the political
processes. She voiced her opinions, amongst
other Afro-Jamaican women critical of these
pervasive and limiting ideas, in the maga-
zine The Cosmopolitan, which she edited
from 1928 till 1931. Marson is not only
known as Jamaica’s ﬁrst woman editor-
publisher but also as the ﬁrst major woman
poet of the Caribbean. In her poems, as
much as in her journalistic work, she encour-
aged Afro-Jamaican women to undermine
the Victorian ideal of womanhood and take
pride in their African heritage.
One of the factors that enabled Afro-
Jamaican women to play a more prominent
role in politics after World War I was the
extension of the franchise in 1919 to prop-
ertied, literate women over twenty-ﬁve.
It was not until 1939, however, that the
ﬁrst Afro-Jamaican woman stood for local
election. Mary Morris Knibb, an active
member of the Women’s Liberal Club,
won a seat that year on the council of the
Kingston and St. Andrew Corporation.
The granting of universal adult suffrage in
1944 enabled women also to stand for the
Legislative Council. In 1944, Iris Rhudella
Collins, a community worker, was the ﬁrst
woman elected to this political body. The
advancement of Afro-Jamaican women in
politics in the 1940s and 1950s was se-
verely hindered, however, by a strong ideol-
ogy of female domesticity, articulated by
the colonial government, unions, and polit-
ical parties. Some Afro-Jamaican women
did manage to cross the barriers and enter
politics. Daphne Campbell, for instance,
was one of several women active in Left
politics in the 1950s. She was an active
member of the PNP until 1952 when
Marxists were expelled from the party. She
then joined the People’s Educational
Organisation (PEO) and the People’s Free-
dom Movement, of which she became an
executive member in 1955. Campbell
worked especially toward the advancement
of Jamaican women. She set up the Jamaica
Women’s Assembly, an auxiliary of the
PEO, which was concerned with the plight
of working-class women.
The granting of independence in 1962
was not accompanied by a signiﬁcant im-
provement in the socioeconomic status of
Jamaican women. From the late 1960s

onward Afro-Jamaican women discussed
the deplorable status of women in Jamaican
society and proposed schemes to alter it.
The proposals put forward by several femi-
nist-oriented women in the PNP Women’s
Auxiliary, including the well-known scholar
Lucille Mathurin-Mair, led the government
to set up a Women’s Bureau in 1973 which
oversees the development of women in
Jamaica. The activities of feminist-oriented
Afro-Jamaican women also led to the cre-
ation of several nongovernmental organiza-
tions, including the Association of Women’s
Organizations of Jamaica, an umbrella or-
ganization of thirty different groups that
has done important work in the ﬁeld of
crimes against women.
T o improve the quality and quantity of
female representation at the highest level of
political decision making, the Jamaica
Women’s Political Caucus (JWPC) was set
up in 1992. It trains potential candidates
on relevant topics, such as fundraising and
presentation skills, and has achieved some
successes. In the 2002 elections, for exam-
ple, Afro-Jamaican women for the ﬁrst time
served as party leaders. The educator
Hyacinth Bennett led the National Demo-
cratic Movement, while talk-show host
Antoinette Haughton represented the
United People’s Party. The JWPC has,
however, a long way to go to increase the
proﬁle of Jamaican women in politics. As of
2004, women hold only 13 percent of the
parliamentary seats, 12 percent of the seats
at the ministerial level, and 22 percent at
the subministerial level.
Afro-Jamaican women have made more
inroads in culture than in politics since in-
dependence. They have played a key role in
the development of one of Jamaica’s most
well-known export products: reggae. Rita
Marley, Judy Mowatt, and Marcia Grifﬁths
formed the I-threes, the support group of
Bob Marley and the Wailers. Rita, who
gained the title “Queen of Reggae” in 1982,
has enjoyed a successful career in her own
right, both before and after her husband’s
death. She largely retired from music in the
mid-1980s and has devoted her energies
since to a number of causes. She looks after
her husband’s legacy, fosters the career of
Ziggy Marley and the Melodymakers, sup-
ports young talent, and is benefactor of a
number of humanitarian causes, including
the ﬁght against drugs. Another well-known
female Jamaican cultural icon is Louise
Bennett-Coverly, or Miss Lou as she is bet-
ter known. She has written and performed
in creole in the theater and on TV and radio
since the 1950s. Through her publications
and international tours of lectures and per-
formances, Miss Lou has done much to pro-
mote Jamaican culture worldwide. In 2001,
her role as ambassador of Jamaican culture
was formally recognized when she was ap-
pointed Member of the Order of Merit. For
four centuries, then, women of African de-
scent in Jamaica have used a variety of
strategies and techniques to ﬁght race, class,
and gender oppression and have helped to
develop the island and raise its proﬁle
abroad.

JAMES,C YRIL LIONEL ROBERT
(1901–1989)
Cyril Lionel Robert James was a T rinida-
dian scholar and intellectual and a proliﬁc
author whose works focus on Pan-African
and Pan-Caribbean politics. The mark of a
true intellectual often lies in his or her abil-
ity to anticipate historical change with such
depth and engagement that he or she re-
mains always of the moment, able to speak
to audiences in multiple times and loca-
tions. If the African American intellectual
and statesperson, W . E. B. Du Bois, was
one such ﬁgure, T rinidadian scholar and
intellectual C. L. R. James was another.
James’s life and journeys as a colonial intel-
lectual can be seen as emblematic of many
of the great changes that have shaped both
the previous empires of Europe and their
colonies in the African Atlantic over the
course of the twentieth century. His work
continues to serve as a model of intellectual
engagement with the world we live in. An
early predictor, for example, of the geopo-
litical events and effects of globalization,
James’s scholarship and theoretical analyses
lay at the forefront of providing new schol-
ars with ways to recognize the importance
of the framework of the African Atlantic
for analyzing the geopolitical events that
shaped the twentieth century, and for pre-
dicting the events and historical changes in
the century to come.
Between his birth in T rinidad on Janu-
ary 4, 1901, and his passing in May 1989
in Brixton, South London, James lived
multiple lives. His trajectory began as a boy
growing up in a small colonial society,
trained to be a Victorian gentleman scholar.
James sailed to England at the age of 31 to
become a novelist. Though he had already
published his ﬁrst and only novel, Minty
Alley in 1928, in London the young immi-
grant intellectual’s activities expanded to
include his political involvement with T rot-
skyism, and his writing and organizing for
Pan-African liberation between 1932 and
1938. James ended what was to be the ﬁrst
of many phases of his life in England as a
historian, publishing in 1938 his classic ac-
count of the ﬁrst black revolution in Haiti,
The Black Jacobins: T oussaint L ’Ouverture
and the San Domingo Revolution . In 1938,
James traveled to the United States on a
speaking engagement for the T rotskyite
movement. There he would live as an un-
derground revolutionary until 1956, when
he became a deportee and victim of
McCarthyism in the 1950s. During his time
in the United States, James wrote texts that
have now become classics in American intel-
lectual history, the expansive Notes on Amer-
ican Civilization which he began in 1949,
and his polemical Mariners, Renegades, and
Castaways, published in 1953, an original
study of Herman Melville’s American
classic Moby Dick that included an indict-
ment of the U.S. government for its treat-
ment of James as a political prisoner in-
terred on Ellis Island while awaiting his
deportation decision. Upon his deportation
from the United States in the late 1950s,
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 722 ---
646 J AZZ AND THE BLUES
James’s attention would turn to Pan-
African and Pan-Caribbean politics. 
Back in his homeland of T rinidad in
1958, James become a political journalist
and organizer until he was once again
detained as a political prisoner, this time
under house arrest in T rinidad in March
1965. During his years spent traveling
throughout the Caribbean and speaking on
issues central to Caribbean and African
politics, such as federation and decoloniza-
tion, James wrote his autobiographical
meditation on cricket, Beyond a Boundary.
This 1963 text, published a year after
T rinidadian national independence, has
since become a classic in postcolonial and
Caribbean literature. James returned to the
United States in the late 1960s, where he
spent more than a decade teaching in
American universities and speaking to in-
tellectual audiences. It was in this role that
he often served as an elder radical statesper-
son and interlocutor for the newly radical-
ized youth of the Black Power Movement
in the United States. During these years he
also anticipated the emergence of black
feminism in American cultural and intel-
lectual circles in the 1980s. Posthumously,
James is seen as a leading ﬁgure in postcolo-
nial and Caribbean studies and as a model
for intellectual and scholarly work in a
newly reconceived postnational, transat-
lantic, American study.
Michelle Stephens

JAZZ AND THE BLUES
Jazz and the blues are African American
musical forms that have had tremendous
cultural impact on other American musical
forms. Perhaps the art form that has bene-
ﬁted most from the melding of African and
American sensibilities is music, and this
mutual inﬂuence is clearest in the genres
commonly referred to as jazz and the blues.
Although scholars differ on exactly how to
deﬁne “jazz” and “the blues” and which
types of music they include within each
deﬁnition, there is enough common agree-
ment to allow fruitful discussion. The roots
of both jazz and the blues lie in Africa, but
the genres were developed in the Americas
by African slaves and their descendants,
and have returned to Africa as well as the
rest of the world as popular contemporary
music forms. Additionally, the inﬂuence of
jazz and the blues is evident in many types
of popular music, including rhythm and
blues, reggae, calypso, and bossa nova.
The Blues
The term “the blues”—or simply “blues”—
refers both to the speciﬁc musical form also
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 723 ---
JAZZ AND THE BLUES 647
known as “the twelve-bar blues” due to its
characteristic chord progression over twelve
bars, or musical measures, and to a range of
musical techniques such as this chord pro-
gression and the blues scale. The blues
developed in the United States from the
ﬁeld chants, spirituals, and work songs of
African American slaves, and displays sev-
eral characteristics which may be traced
back to African musical traditions. One is
the call-and-response format, in which per-
formance of a song alternates, often line by
line, between a leader (the call) and a group
(the response). Another is the blues scale,
with its lowered third and seventh tone
(and sometimes lowered ﬁfth tone as well),
and the use of melisma and “sliding” around
and between notes. Some scholars trace these
melodic characteristics back to the Muslim
music of West Africa. This is one version of
the notes of the blues scale, in the key of C:
C–D–E♭
F–G–A–B ♭–C
Of course, blues performers do not
conﬁne themselves strictly to those notes as
deﬁned in Western classical music. Al-
though the blues uses many different struc-
tures, the most common today is that
known as the twelve-bar blues, which
evolved around 1900 partially due to the
influence of American popular music.
The characteristic chordal structure of the
twelve-bar blues in the key of C would be:
C–CCC
FFCC
GFCC
Once again, this structure is only a basic
framework, which in performance is altered
according to the taste of the individual mu-
sician. T raditional twelve-bar blues lyrics
have a characteristic format which may be
notated as A–A´–B, meaning a ﬁrst line,
repetition with variation of the ﬁrst line,
and a second line. This structure is evident
in a stanza of the “St. Louis Blues” by W . C.
Handy (1914; Dover, 1990):
I hate to see the evenin’ sun go down
Hate to see that evenin’ sun go down
’Cause my baby done gone and left this
town.
T rying to devise rules to classify which
songs qualify as blues is difﬁcult and proba-
bly ultimately pointless: music is a living
art, not a collection of blueprints. Many
songs that are not strictly twelve-bar blues
incorporate some blues elements, and many
others include the term “blues” in the title
without using any blues elements at all.
However, it is useful to consider two blues
styles that developed over the years be-
cause they represent many of the opposing
tendencies in modern blues performance.
One style, commonly called “country blues,”
remains closer to the rural roots of the music
and is often performed by a single singer
backing himself on guitar. Outstanding
performers in this tradition who lived in
the era of recorded sound include Blind
Lemon Jefferson, Leadbelly (Huddie
William Ledbetter), and Mississippi John
Hurt (John Smith Hurt). A more modern
style of blues performance is often called
“city blues” or “urban blues” because it
incorporates musical elements that per-
formers were often ﬁrst exposed to in
urban areas. Music in the more modern
blues style is often performed by a singer
plus a small band including instruments
such as the electric guitar, piano, trumpet,
saxophone, and traps. Some of the most
inﬂuential performers in modern blues
include Muddy Waters (McKinley
Morganﬁeld), Buddy Guy (George Guy),
and Howlin’ Wolf (Chester Arthur
Burnett).

Jazz
Jazz was developed around 1900 in the
United States, largely by African Americans
who combined aspects of traditional forms
such as the blues with Western forms such
as marches and popular songs. The term
“jazz,” or “jass,” was ﬁrst used in New
Orleans and this city is often considered
the birthplace of jazz. New Orleans offered
ideal conditions for the birthplace of a new
African American art form: performances
by slaves at the legendary “Congo Square”
familiarized both whites and free African
Americans with African music and dance,
and many free African Americans living in
New Orleans were also educated in Euro-
pean musical traditions. Many of the
fathers of jazz came from New Orleans,
including Kid Ory (Edward Ory), King
Oliver (Joe Oliver), Sidney Bechet, and
Louis Armstrong; the latter is considered
by many to be the greatest jazz musician of
all time. Their early style is sometimes
called “Dixieland” and is characterized by
constant, simultaneous improvisation and
the use of the blues scale with its “bent”
notes outside the Western system of
pitches. The term Dixieland was popular-
ized in part by a band of white musicians
from New Orleans called The Original
Dixieland Jass Band, which made the ﬁrst
jazz recordings in 1917.
Jazz spread from New Orleans across
the United States; New York and Chicago
were particularly important centers of
activity. The increasing availability of jazz
on the radio and on sound recordings
helped to spread its inﬂuence. The decade
1920–1930 in the United States is often
termed the Jazz Age, attesting to the popu-
larity of the music and its acceptance, for
better or worse, as a metaphor for life in the
United States during those years. For some,
jazz symbolized the newfound freedom and
optimism of American society after World
War I, while for others it was the perfect
symbol of contemporary societal degener-
acy and decay.
Big band or swing music, which in-
cluded much larger instrumental ensem-
bles, was popular in the 1920s into the
1950s. The size of bands varied: Paul
Whiteman’s band sometimes included
twenty or more musicians, while twelve play-
ers was a more typical size for most bands.
The larger ensembles required a change in
style toward music which was more com-
posed or arranged and in which only one
instrument improvised at a time. White
bandleaders and musicians played a major
role in big band music. Important white
bandleaders included Benny Goodman,
Artie Shaw, T ommy Dorsey, and Jimmy
Dorsey. Important African American big
band leaders included Count Basie, Jay
Blues musician Muddy Waters in 1964. 
(Library of Congress)
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

McShann, Duke Ellington, and Bennie
Moten. Although the big band music, like
much of American life, was largely segre-
gated, there was also some collaboration.
For instance, Benny Goodman made a
point of including African American musi-
cians in his band and performing arrange-
ments by African American composers.
The modern jazz style known as bebop
developed in New York City in the 1940s,
although it did not become widely known
until a decade later because there were few
recordings from those early years. Musi-
cians working in this style developed a new,
more complex vocabulary of melody, har-
mony, and rhythm; indeed, some critics be-
lieve bebop was deliberately developed as a
more exclusive jazz for connoisseurs that
would not have the broadly popular appeal
of earlier styles. Bebop groups also returned
to the small ensembles characteristic of
early jazz, rather than the large bands of the
swing era. Early leaders in bebop include
Charlie Parker (Charles Christopher
Parker, Jr.), Dizzy Gillespie (John Burks
Gillespie), Thelonius Monk, and Max
Roach. More recent jazz musicians who
were inﬂuenced by bebop include John
Coltrane, Miles Davis, Charles Mingus,
and Ornette Coleman.
In the 1960s a style known as “free
jazz” was developed by a number of young
musicians who deliberately distanced
themselves from the conventions of tradi-
tional or “mainstream” jazz, such as pre-
dictable melodies and chord progressions.
Leaders of this movement included
Pharoah Sanders, Cecil Taylor, and Don
Cherry. Although popular among a small
circle of listeners, and inﬂuential among
Musician Louis Armstrong, one of the twentieth century’s leading jazz innovators. (Library of Congress)

music critics, this style of music did not
have wide popular appeal. Most jazz musi-
cians performed in more traditional styles,
often combining aspects of several histori-
cal styles with their own innovations. In
fact, the ready availability of recordings by
the 1960s meant that a typical musician
could be exposed to music from many dif-
ferent historical periods and geographical
regions, and this inﬂuenced many young
performers toward an eclectic jazz style
drawing on many inﬂuences.
The dissemination of jazz around the
world has been greatly aided by the con-
temporaneous development of mass media,
in particular the spread of radio broadcast-
ing and phonograph recording. This inﬂu-
ence was seen ﬁrst in European countries
that had more access to the new technolo-
gies; but by the 1940s, radio broadcasting
and phonograph records were reaching
many regions in Africa, Asia, and Latin
America as well. T ouring American bands
also helped popularize jazz, and again this
inﬂuence was felt ﬁrst in Europe. Will
Marion Cook was a pioneer in this regard,
and his most important single act may have
been introducing the saxophonist and clar-
inetist Sidney Bechet to Europe, and
Europe to Bechet. When Cook’s concert
band, the Southern Syncopated Orchestra,
toured England in 1918, their repertoire
was primarily concert (non-improvised)
works. However, their programs included a
few improvisational, blues-influenced
works featuring Bechet, which were re-
ceived with great critical acclaim. Bechet
went on to have a distinguished interna-
tional career as a jazz musician, touring
throughout Europe, the United States, and
the USSR before settling in France, where
he spent the last years of his life. Other
American jazz musicians toured extensively
in Europe and some chose to live there, a
choice that may have been inﬂuenced not
only by the availability of work due to the
popularity of jazz but also, in the case of
the African American artists, by the greater
social and political freedoms enjoyed there
compared with in the United States where
racial discrimination was legal in many
parts of the country.
Jazz became popular in Africa also, al-
though a few decades later than in Europe.
By the 1940s radio and phonograph tech-
nology was available in many regions of
the continent, and distinctive local styles
developed that combined elements of jazz
with traditional music. Musicians from
the Republic of South Africa were among
the ﬁrst to achieve worldwide recogni-
tion, including Hugh Masakela, Miriam
Makeba, and Dollar Brand (Abdullah
Ibrahim). Caribbean jazz inﬂuenced the
music of many other African forms; for
instance, the highlife style popular in
Ghana and Nigeria was heavily inﬂuenced
by calypso.
As jazz became known in Europe and
among classical musicians in America,
many classical composers tried incorporat-
ing aspects of jazz into their music. For
the most part, these classical works did
not include the improvisatory element
that lies at the heart of jazz performance,
but incorporated speciﬁc jazz-inﬂuenced
elements such as melodic motifs and
chord progressions into classical music
forms. The French composer Darius
Milhaud was among the ﬁrst well-known
classical composer to deliberately incorpo-
rate jazz elements into a concert work
with his La Creation du monde (The
Creation of the World; 1923). Other
early classical works that make extensive
use of jazz elements include the German

JAZZ,A FRICAN
Although jazz is no longer the most widely
played form of contemporary music, it is
still breaking new ground and combining
and recombining in different forms of
African popular music. There is still a core
of practitioners and fans interested in highly
experimental modern jazz, and a constantly
changing group of musicians fusing jazz
idioms with contemporary popular music
genres. This fusion is visible in African pop-
ular music, where many artists combine
elements of jazz, local rhythms, and modern
forms of electronic dance music.
The development of jazz music in South
Africa illustrates the way American jazz in-
ﬂuenced African jazz. South Africans had
their ﬁrst formal contact with African Amer-
ican music on June 19, 1890, when the min-
strel troupe of Orpheus Myron McAdoo’s
Virginia Jubilee Singers from Hampton,
Virginia, presented a series of concerts in
Cape T own. Their appearance created a sig-
niﬁcant impact upon the music scene, as it
introduced innovative new harmonic con-
cepts and structures that would play a cru-
cial role in the development of South
African jazz. The formal introduction of jazz
into South Africa took place shortly after
World War I, when American merchant sea-
men brought some of the early jazz record-
ings to Cape T own. In the middle 1920s,
Queenstown became known as “Little Jazz
T own” because of the many New Orleans–
style bands that were resident there.
Ragtime shifted into Dixieland jazz in
some areas. Many local Dixie bands were
formed in South Africa, like the Dark T own
Strutters and the Big Four of Johannesburg;
ragtime became part of the black urban
marabi music of the 1920s and 1930s. The
dance style called marabi evolved in the
black urban centers, where different tribes
met with former slaves from the Americas.
It was originally a humble form of music,
but it became similar to the jazz played by
swing bands in the United States when the
relatively wealthy and free blacks of Sophia-
town adopted it. In Ghana, Dixieland be-
came part of the repertoire of 1920s bands
such as the Jazz Kings of Accra.
Much of South African music of the
1950s was born at the crossroads of
American jazz, African American choral
styles, and African folk music. For example,
vocalist Miriam Makeba and her husband
trumpeter Hugh Masekela recorded in a
pop-jazz style. Furthermore, the 1950s were
a great age of jazz development in South
Africa. South Africans used jazz as a platform
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 728 ---
652 J OHNSON,C HARLES R.
and became deeply involved in the struggle
for democracy on a creative level by using
the music as a clarion call for liberation. As
a result of the bebop revolution in the
United States, a new strain of jazz began to
emerge, which contained a greater Ameri-
can inﬂuence. T ours by African American
artists such as Louis Armstrong and jazz sax-
ophonist Paul Winter became inspirations.
Jazz pianist and educator John Mehegan
served as a jazz mentor in South Africa.
American jazz inﬂuenced highlife music,
the Ghanaian and Nigerian ballroom music,
which absorbed many elements of jazz, espe-
cially in ordinary orchestras of wind and
string instruments. Fela Anikulapo-Kuti was
deeply impressed by American artists, which
led him to use jazz as a stepping-stone to
African music, and subsequently used
African music to play jazz. In 1968, he
coined a new style of music, Afro-beat, by
combining James Brown’s funk music, high-
life, and jazz with Nigerian beat. American
jazz and the Black Power Movement inﬂu-
enced him during a ten-month promotional
tour in the United States. His intricate
music, which might arguably be called Afro-
jazz, blends African rhythms and jazz horn
lines with sociopolitical lyrics that defend
the rights of the common people.
Manu Dibango, Africa’s best-known
jazz saxophonist and heir to jazz and
rhythm and blues, fused African rhythms
and melodies with jazz in his legendary
jazzy-sound album Soul Makossa (1972).
This recording was followed by African
Soul, a mixture of jazz, rumba, and Latino
rhythm. In 1983, Dibango recorded Elec-
tric Africa, an extraordinary mixture of jazz,
rap, and traditional music, with help from
great jazz musicians Bill Laswell, Bernie
Worrel, and Herbie Hancock. Moroccan
Maleem Mahmoud Ghania collaborated
with jazz giant Pharoah Sanders on Trance
of Seven Colors (1994), while Hassan Hak-
moun created fusion tracks of trancey
gnawa, rock and American dance music on
Trance (1993). Benin’s Gangbé Brass Band
explores the rich Voodoo culture and an-
cient songs of their country, which are
combined with jazz melodies to produce a
powerful contemporary sound.
Philip A. Ojo

JOHNSON,C HARLES R.
(1948–)
Charles R. Johnson is known as a journalist,
illustrator, scriptwriter, playwright, essayist,
ﬁction writer, biographer, and philosopher.
Johnson’s elevation to the stage of na-
tional and international fame came with
publication of his novel Middle Passage
(1990). However, his road to fame as a cre-
ative writer and scholar-teacher holding the
S. Wilson and Grace M. Pollock chair in
Creative Writing at the University of Wash-
ington since 1990 came by way of a varied
path. Born April 23, 1948, in Evanston,
Illinois, Johnson remained rooted to his
state through both his bachelor’s degree in
journalism (1971) and master’s degree in
philosophy (1973) at Southern Illinois
University. From the time he was employed
as a reporter and political cartoonist for the
campus newspaper, The Southern Illinois-
ian, and his stint as a stringer for The
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 729 ---
JOHNSON,J AMES WELDON 653
Chicago Tribune (1968), it appeared that
Johnson was heading for a long-term career
in journalism. But he changed directions at
the master’s level and went on to receive a
Ph.D. in philosophy from State University
of New York in 1998 that positioned him
squarely in academia, where he still re-
mains, even while periodically writing
scripts for television and publishing two
books of drawings—Black Humor (1970)
and Half-Past Nation Time (1972).
Author of two books of literary criti-
cism, ﬁfteen television scripts, and sixty-
three essays, Johnson is widely recognized
for his early novels Faith and the Good Thing
(1974) and Oxherding T ale(1984), and two
short-story collections, The Sorcerer’s Ap-
prentice (1986) and Soulcatcher and Other
Stories (2000). However, the catalyst of his
career came with the 1990 publication of
Middle Passage. The book’s 1830s ﬁctional
hero, Rutherford Calhoun, is a freeman who
undergoes a reverse middle passage out of
New Orleans on a slave ship, which lands at
Senegambia to pick up a cargo of mysterious
Africans. At sea Calhoun experiences a
body/soul division, after which he transforms
into a philosophically grounded, morally
based, and spiritually rooted personage—all
at the old age of twenty-three. Through
metamorphosis, he becomes a philosophical
composite of Everyman—the best shorn of
the worst ideas among the transatlantic slave
triad of Europe, Africa, and America—
emerging from Johnson’s own training and
sustained interest in philosophy as expressed
in Being and Race (1970) and Turning the
Wheel: Essays in Buddhism and Literature
(2003). Although Johnson’s 1998 novel
Dreamer and coauthored work King: The
Photobiography of Martin Luther King, Jr.
(2000) illustrate his reverence for the great
leader, neither has surpassed the attention
garnered by Middle Passage, which earned
Johnson the National Book Award in 1990,
two honorary doctorates, and a host of other
state, national, and international awards of
distinction.
Virginia Whatley Smith

JOHNSON,J AMES WELDON
(1871–1938)
James Weldon Johnson was an African
American poet, novelist, lyricist, historian,
educator, activist, and diplomat. He was the
eldest son of James Johnson, an American
freeman, and Helen Louise Dillett, a native
of Nassau, the Bahamas, who was educated
in New York. In his autobiography Along
This Way (1933), he described his mother’s
forebears as Haitians displaced by the years
preceding the Haitian Revolution of 1804
and a French army ofﬁcer in Haiti, who re-
located with them to the Bahamas. A native
of Jacksonville, Florida, Johnson became
familiar to America as a lyricist and poet—
having written the lyrics to “Lift Ev’ry Voice
and Sing” (also known as the “Negro Na-
tional Anthem”) and the collection of poetic
sermons God’s Trombones—and as an ac-
tivist in national politics. Johnson served as
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 730 ---
654 J OHNSON,J AMES WELDON
ﬁeld secretary and later executive secretary
of the National Association for the Ad-
vancement of Colored People (NAACP).
Johnson’s 1906 appointment as
American diplomat ﬁrst to Venezuela and
then Nicaragua was the result of President
Theodore Roosevelt’s Progressive Era ad-
ministration, which gave some government
positions traditionally reserved for whites
to a handful of African Americans. As
American diplomat to these countries,
Johnson gained a comparative perspective
on black cultural identity and racial atti-
tudes in the Americas. He noted in partic-
ular the different attitudes toward complex-
ion in the diverse black populations and
the difference in Venezuelan attitudes to-
ward racial and cultural assimilation. John-
son used some of these observations about
the cultural distinctiveness of black culture
versus the merits of its assimilation into a
national identity in his ﬁrst book-length
work, The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored
Man (1912), composed mostly during his
consular appointment in Venezuela. In this
work, Johnson used a narrator who could
“pass” as white to explore the cultural
meaning of blackness in the American
North and South as well as in Europe.
As diplomat to Venezuela and
Nicaragua, Johnson also observed these
countries’ resistance to American expan-
sionist policies, and worked on behalf of
the U.S. government to quell a revolution
in Nicaragua. Johnson sought promotion
to a consular position in Switzerland,
which he was stoutly denied under President
Woodrow Wilson’s administration in 1912.
Johnson resigned from his post the same
year.
Taking up the position of ﬁeld secretary
to the NAACP in 1916, Johnson was re-
sponsible for signiﬁcantly increasing the
membership of the ﬂedgling organization,
especially in the South, to make the NAACP
a national power. In this new position,
Johnson became another type of diplomat—
one who represented the concerns of black
people throughout the world, from African
nations to the Caribbean nation of Haiti.
As a correspondent for the NAACP ,
Johnson investigated American outrages in
Haiti under the U.S. Marines’ occupation,
initiated by the American government in
1915 and lasting until 1934. The results of
his investigation were published in a four-
part series called “Self-Determining Haiti”
in The Nation (1920). In this and other
writings of the World War I era, Johnson
reminded his readers of the hypocrisy of
the Woodrow Wilson administration’s slo-
gan claiming U.S. participation in the
Great War was to “make the world safe for
democracy.” Although black troops fought
with distinction in the war, they were
Author and civil rights activist James Weldon Johnson
was a leading ﬁgure of the Harlem Renaissance.
(National Archives)
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 731 ---
JOHNSON,L INTON KWESI 655
denied the rights and privileges of full and
equal citizenship in their own country.
Moreover, they were the victims of what
Johnson called the “Red Summer” of 1919,
when postwar race riots swept through
twenty-two cities and caused the deaths of
hundreds of African Americans.
In his investigative writing for the
NAACP , Johnson revealed the mentality of
the Southern populace that shaped Ameri-
can segregationist and expansionist prac-
tices. Johnson described the Haitian situa-
tion as one where the ignorance and the
racism of the American South were inad-
vertently exported to Haiti. As the ﬁrst
black nation to gain independence from its
French colonizers in 1804, Haiti was a
symbol of black pride and self-determinacy
to black people throughout the world. In
Haiti, he reminded his readers the majority
of marines stationed and leading the effort
of occupation had been passed over for par-
ticipation in World War I. These marines
were Southern, poorly trained and poorly
educated, and steeped in the conviction of
race hatred—a hatred that motivated the
very instances of extreme brutality that
Johnson was investigating.
Here and elsewhere in his diplomacy
and writings on behalf of the NAACP ,
Johnson supported the national outlook
and participation in the war, especially the
effort to defend democracy. He used the
very deﬁnitions of American patriotism,
however, to alter the policy of excluding
African Americans from the nation’s life in
art, letters, and politics. In fact, Johnson
often argued that African Americans were
more American than whites in their artistic
and cultural contributions as well as in
their patriotism and love of freedom.
In his political activities and in his
writing, Johnson was interested in the
broad concerns of the black Diaspora—
African decolonization, Haitian self-
determination, and so on—from a staunchly
nationalistic, American perspective. Like
many other African American leaders of
his day, Johnson rejected the alternative
vision of a cultural homeland for blacks
that Marcus Garvey provided in his Uni-
versal Negro Improvement Association.
Johnson saw Garvey’s program of repatria-
tion to Liberia as a threat to the NAACP’s
strategies of interracialism and integration
as the means to achieving civil rights for
African Americans.
Noelle Morrissette

JOHNSON,L INTON KWESI
(1952–)
Linton Kwesi Johnson was born August 24,
1952, in Chapelton, Jamaica, and has lived
in London since the age of 10. He is a poet,
performance poet, and dub poet. 
Johnson is the acknowledged godfather
of dub poetry, and because of his focus on
reggae music and themes, and his use of
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 732 ---
656 J OHNSON,L INTON KWESI
Jamaican creole, he also is known as the
world’s ﬁrst reggae poet. Dub poetry is po-
etry infused with musical rhythms. John-
son himself gave name to the “dub-lyricist”
in the article “Jamaican Rebel Music,”
which he authored for the publication Race
and Class in 1976. In Johnson’s perfor-
mances of dub poetry, he gives meaning to
the Rastafari notion that “word sound ’ave
power.” His notable poems, “Street 66,”
“Five Nights of Bleeding,” and “Inglan Is a
Bitch,” give realistic accounts of rough
times in 1970s England. Often the narrator
expresses the feeling of helplessness at hav-
ing apparently no means of escape from the
blues party culture that ends with the po-
lice showing up; but there is also a sense of
pride that comes with living through these
experiences, a righteous pride that serves as
catharsis for the audience. Johnson’s poems
run the gamut of human emotion. His
“Reggae ﬁ Dada,” for example, has been
called the “ﬁnest creole elegy to date”; the
poem addresses not only the loss of a father
but is also an indictment of the violence
and ﬁnancial hardships of Jamaican society.
While attending Goldsmith’s College,
University of London, in the 1960s, John-
son joined the Black Panthers and appar-
ently helped to organize a poetry movement
within the group. By the early 1970s, he was
published in Race T oday and honored as a
writer-in-residence; he later worked at the
Keskidee Center, noted for being the ﬁrst
home of black theater and art.
Johnson is published by Race T oday pub-
lications, Bogle-L ’Overture, Island Records,
and on his own label, LKJ. His poetry is an-
thologized in numerous publications such as
The Routledge Reader in Caribbean Literature
and Dub Poetry: 19 Poets from England and
Jamaica. His LKJ Records began production
in 1981 with two singles by Mikey Smith,
another Jamaican dub poet. In 1981–1982,
Johnson produced From Mento to Lovers
Rock, a radio series on BBC1. In the 1980s,
he continued to produce other Caribbean
poets, such as Jean Binta Breeze and Shake
Keane, as well as tour with the Dennis
Bovell Dub Band.
In 1990, Johnson was honored in Italy
for his accomplishments in poetry, with the
XIII Premo Internazionale Ultimo Nove-
cento. He also has received fellowships
from the University of Warwick in 1985
and Wolverhampton Polytechnic in 1987,
and from his alma mater of Goldsmith’s
College in 2003.
Perhaps because of Mikey Smith’s pre-
mature death in 1983, Johnson has become
an outspoken advocate for Smith’s work,
giving lectures on Smith for scholarly com-
munities. Johnson lectured at the Second
Conference on Caribbean Culture, held in
Jamaica in 2002, and was an honorary
visiting professor of creative writing at
Middlesex University in London in 2004.
Johnson has performed his poetry in
Europe and Africa, at the Queen Elizabeth
Hall in London, in 1984 and 1996, and on
a Broadway stage in New York City as part
of the “Russell Simmons Presents Def Po-
etry” in 2003, which aired on HBO.
For comparative purposes, one should
hear other dub poets, such as Benjamin
Zephaniah, Mutabaruka, Oku Onuora,
Mikey Smith, and Jean Binta Breeze.

JONES,C LAUDIA
(1915–1964)
Claudia Jones was a radical journalist, poet,
and political activist. She is an important
but neglected political and cultural ﬁgure of
black transatlantic experience. She made
wide-ranging contributions to the Commu-
nist Party of the United States (CPUSA),
including campaigns against the Italian fas-
cist occupation of Abyssinia and against the
unjust rape trial of nine black youths, “the
Scottsboro boys.” After deportation to
Britain, she joined the Communist Party of
Great Britain and began to publish a black
newspaper, the West Indian Gazette.
Jones was born Claudia Cumberbatch
in Port-of-Spain, T rinidad, in 1915; her
family emigrated to the United States when
she was nine. They settled in Harlem and
lived at the epicenter of many antiracist
movements, including the Marcus Garvey-
led Universal Negro Improvement Associa-
tion, which suffered brutal attacks. Her
mother was a garment worker who died of
exhaustion when Claudia was twelve; her
father became unemployed as a result of the
Great Depression. Jones became politicized
at an early age, and in 1936 she joined the
Young Communist League. She was a
gifted child who was forced to leave school
during the depression. After an intense pe-
riod of self-education, she took up a tech-
nical post on the Daily Worker, the U.S.
newspaper of the Communist Party. In the
United States, her activities were regarded,
along with those of other notable black ﬁg-
ures such as C. L. R. James and Paul Robe-
son, as subversive, and she was denied U.S.
citizenship. Between 1948 and 1955, she
was arrested several times and imprisoned
on Ellis Island under the 1940 Smith Act.
T reated as an undesirable alien, she was de-
ported from the United States in 1955. As
she urgently needed medical attention, and
T rinidad was reluctant to allow her return,
she sought asylum in Britain.
Following racist attacks and riots in
Nottingham and Notting Hill in 1958,
Jones organized the ﬁrst black indoor carni-
val, held in St. Pancras T own Hall in the
winter of 1959. Jones’s experience cam-
paigning for civil rights in the United States
enabled her to calm a volatile situation in
London following the murder of Kelso
Cochrane. The idea of organizing a carnival
was politically astute and signaled that the
migrant community would assert itself
through its culture, countering racial op-
pression with positive self-deﬁnition and an
assertion of the presence of black culture’s
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 734 ---
658 JOURNAL OF NEGRO HISTORY
presence in Britain. Subsequent carnivals at-
tracted performers, such as the calypsonian
the Mighty Sparrow, and evolved into the
London Notting Hill Carnival, which now
attracts over a million participants. 
In the course of a day in London, Jones
might have written for the West Indian
Gazette, intervened in the case of a home-
less immigrant, and advised a visiting polit-
ical ﬁgure of the standing of Norman Man-
ley and Martin Luther King Jr. She lived
and died during a time of intense activity—
antiracist movements in the United States,
independence struggles in the colonies, and
conﬂicts arising from mass migration to
Britain. She was determined to ﬁght op-
pression and provided leadership in the
black communities of the United States
and Britain in spite of frequent hospitaliza-
tions for heart problems.
One of Jones’s greatest achievements
was that she was able, through tenacity and
charisma, to bring together very different
groups of people in spite of conﬂicting in-
terests. In the struggles against imperialism,
she united African, Asian, and West Indian
factions who could be divided over Cuba,
Vietnam, Aden, and Ghana. In London,
writers, performers, artists, activists, and
workers met at political rallies organized by
her, including a march on the U.S. Em-
bassy in support of Martin Luther King Jr.
She kept a divided and frightened migrant
community fully informed of national and
international civil rights matters through
the West Indian Gazette. The paper, edited
by Jones and Amy Garvey, was ﬁrst issued
in March 1958 and reﬂected broad inter-
ests. It carried information of cultural de-
velopments and reviews of new creative
projects, in addition to political news.
Jones was able to communicate with a
range of people and important West Indian
ﬁgures often sought her political and cul-
tural analysis when they visited Britain.
The West Indian Gazette was written,
printed, and circulated against considerable
odds and it survived only two issues after
her death. Periods of imprisonment and
poverty, together with the effort associated
with production of the Gazette, con-
tributed to Jones’s deteriorating heart con-
dition. She was discovered dead in her ﬂat
on Christmas Day in 1964. Some private
papers were removed and the autobiogra-
phy that she was writing, which she had
read to friends, disappeared. The literary
work of Claudia Jones survives in ﬁfteen
poems that appeared occasionally in the is-
sues of the West Indian Gazette.
Sandra Courtman

1916. Woodson also was the founder of the

incorporated primary source material. The
use of primary source material was one of
the early outstanding features of the publi-
cation. Through primary research, black
scholars and white alike dispelled the be-
lief that primary data relevant to the
African American past did not exist.
Diaries, letters, and oral testimonies were
utilized, among other sources, to accom-
plish the task of educating the American
populace about the history of blacks in
American society.

JUANA INES DE LA CRUZ,
SOR (1651–1695)
Several of the nun Sor Juana’s literary works
celebrate the African voices heard in Colo-
nial Mexico. While Sor Juana Ines de la
Cruz and her works have primarily been as-
sociated with and analyzed from a proto-
feminist point of view, a number of her
writings also reﬂect a consciousness of the
African presence and inﬂuence in seven-
teenth-century Mexico. African voices re-
verberate in her villancicos, religiously
themed, songlike polyphonic poems with
festive or burlesque features, as well as her
play Los empeños de una casa (The House of
Trials). These articulations forge a multidi-
mensional image of the Other in Spanish
America as seen through their linguistic,
cultural, and historical contributions to
New World society.

Native Americans at the margins of Creole
society in the villancicos of Sor Juana. She

marginalized tongues highlights the signif-
icance and rise of the Creole nation within
the Old World imperial project. As a re-
sult, the nun’s writings reﬂect a cultural
synthesis that is uncommon during the
time period: “Sor Juana represents the sprit
of cohabitation among different races
under the banner of a single faith” (Orel-
lana, 1990, p. 85).
In the theatrical piece Los empeños de
una casa, the character of Castaño, whose
name translates as “chestnut” and alludes to
his skin color, ﬁgures as the comic relief
providing gracioso. However, as some critics
have pointed out, Castaño can alternatively
be seen as a “comic hero” (Johnson, 2001)
and operating as a tool of satire, assess-
ments that equally reafﬁrm the character’s
range and agency.
Sor Juana’s writings exhibit not only an
interest in the marginal voice of women but
also deal with questions of racial identity
and integration in the fabric of Spanish
America.
Bonnie L. Gasior
