JUDAISM
The history of Judaism, the monotheistic
religion of the Jewish people that draws its
spiritual and ethical principles from the
Bible and the Talmud, also encompasses
the history and historiography of Jewish
ethnicity and African identity. The search
for Jewish traces in Africa has long been a
stimulus for colonial fantasies. Until the
mid-twentieth century, European ethnog-
raphers had a tendency to Judaize any
African civilization that did not ﬁt their
conventional representations of blackness.
They based their assertions on such ques-
tionable clues as biometric measurements
(the famous “Semitic nose”), backed
vaguely with linguistic speculation: Ntoro,
the Ashanti spirit, for example, apparently
came from the T orah; Yam, their supreme
being, was said to derive from Yahweh the
god of Israel. The Fulani, Maasai, T utsi,
Igbo, Soninké, and Wolof, among others,
were thus credited with mysterious Jewish
origins.
Current claims of Jewish roots are by
far less numerous. They are also better doc-
umented, even though the descent of King
Solomon, who built the First T emple of
Israel in the tenth century BCE, remains a
puzzling issue. According to Kebra Nagast
(the Ethiopian national saga), Makeda, the
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 737 ---
JUDAISM 661
Queen of Sheba, bore a son to Solomon,
and this son, Menelik, founded the
Solomonic dynasty in Aksum. Ethiopian
Jews, claiming descent from Menelik, call
themselves the Beta Israel (House of Israel,
in Hebrew), a name which they prefer to
the derogatory term Falasha (“gone into
exile,” “landless ones” in the ancient Ge’ez
language). Some historians rather consider
the descendants as the tribe of Dan, one of
the ten tribes dispersed after the Assyrian
conquest in 721 BCE. Others believe they
were Judaized at a later date through con-
tact with Jewish merchants from Yemen.
In any case, their Judaism predates the
Talmudic commentaries that are the inspi-
ration for most contemporary Jewish ritu-
als. The religious observances of the Beta
Israel are directly prescribed by the T orah.
They ignore festivals and rituals based on
rabbinical traditions. Their religious leaders
are not rabbis but cahenat, a priestly caste,
just like in biblical times.
The Balemba, in southern Zimbabwe
and the Limpopo Province of South Africa,
also claim Solomonic descent. Their sym-
bol is an elephant in the middle of a Star of
David, and their diet, marriage ceremonies,
burial rites, musical instruments, agricul-
tural patterns, and harvest festival (Utu-
runga) seem manifestly Hebrew in origin.
A genetic study carried out in the 1990s
found a set of DNA sequences in the
Balemba that is distinctive of Jewish priests
believed to be the descendants of Moses’s
brother, Aaron. This genetic signature
(Cohen Modal Haplotype) is particularly
common among men of the Buba clan.
Unlike the Beta Israel in Ethiopia, the
Balemba gradually converted to Christian-
ity over the centuries, but this genetic study
has prompted a wave of reconversions to
Judaism.
Conversions to Judaism, a religion
generally hostile to proselytism, are uncom-
mon, but the case of the Balemba is not an
isolated one. In the 1920s, subsistence
farmers from eastern Uganda, the Abayu-
daya, founded Kibina Kya Bayudaya Ab-
sesiga Katonda (the Community of Jews
Who T rust in the Lord) and remained Jew-
ish even under the repressive regime of Idi
Amin Dada. The Abayudaya, numbering
about 3,000 before the destruction of their
synagogues and the persecutions of the
1970s, are in 2004 only about 500, but
they have rebuilt their synagogues where
they sing Jewish chants in Luganda and
Hebrew. Other collective conversions oc-
curred at the beginning of the twentieth
century in Rusape (eastern Zimbabwe),
and more recently in western Ghana, where
the House of Israel community of Sefwi
Wiawso and Sefwi Sui was founded in
1976. Several synagogues were also built
throughout the 1980s and 1990s in
Nigeria, Cameroon, and Malagasy. Their
founders declared they had had a “vision”
revealing that their peoples belonged to the
Lost T ribes of Israel. Since these are fairly
recent conversions, their rites bear the most
resemblance to western forms of modern
Judaism.
Substantial migrations into North
Africa began after the Babylonian armies
destroyed Jerusalem and its First T emple
(586 BCE), and they increased further
when the Romans destroyed the Second
T emple (70 CE). Over the centuries, North
African Jews have for the most part re-
mained in contact with other Jewish com-
munities around the world, while at the
same time incorporating Berber, Arab, and
Spanish customs. Moroccan Judaism, inﬂu-
enced by the Talmud from the time of
its writing between the second and fifth
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 738 ---
662 J UDAISM
centuries, became an important center for
kabbalistic teaching. T wo important events
occurred in the seventh century: ﬁrst, the
Arab Conquest, marked by the resistance
and defeat of the Kahina, the legendary
queen of the Aures who reigned over the
Jarawa, a tribe of Jewish Berbers; and next,
the ﬁrst expulsion from Spain, decreed in
694 by the Council of T oledo. North
African Jewish communities, swelled by the
arrival of Spanish Jews, would in the future
be reduced to the status of dhimma: toler-
ated in the land of Islam but discriminated
against and sometimes also persecuted.
The second expulsion from Spain, in
1492, generated the last and largest wave of
Jewish migration to North Africa. Some
families went farther south, assisted by
Jewish artisans and traders who had settled
along the trans-Saharan routes for cen-
turies. The best-known example is the Ka’ti
family, who founded several villages that
still exist around Timbuktu. Although
under threat from Askia Muhammad, who
forbade Judaism in the Songhay Empire,
the Timbuktu Jews practiced their religion
in secret for several generations before con-
verting to Islam.
Portugal waited until 1497 to expel its
Jews. Before this expulsion, it applied a dis-
criminatory head tax with the purpose of ﬁ-
nancing its colonial expansion. In 1493, as
not all Jews were able to pay, King Manuel
deported about 2,000 of their children,
aged two to ten, to São T omé. The aim was
both to “punish” the Jews and to “whiten
the race,” as the king put it. Only 600 chil-
dren survived—and when they grew up,
they continued to practice their religion,
much to the anger of the Portuguese bishop.
T oday there are no practicing Jews in São
T omé but the memory of this tragic episode
remains keenly felt. Other Portuguese Jews
ﬂed to Cape Verde to escape the Inquisition
and gradually converted to Catholicism
over the centuries. The Malian and Cape
Verdean descendents of Spanish and Por-
tuguese Jews are today rediscovering this
aspect of their history through community-
based learning programs.
North African Judaism, along with
Ethiopian Judaism, died away during the
second half of the twentieth century with
the massive emigration to Israel, Europe,
and North America. T oday, only a few
thousand Jews remain in Morocco, and a
few thousand also in Ethiopia, in Addis
Ababa and the region around Gonder, on
the border with Sudan. From the end of the
1940s, there were several waves of anti-
Jewish riots, and communities that had
been settled for thousands of years in Libya
and Egypt were totally wiped out. Jewish-
Arab relations and, as a result, Judaism in
Africa would today be very different if the
Zionist movement in Europe had accepted
the proposal by the British secretary of state
for the colonies, Joseph Chamberlain, to
create a national Jewish homeland on the
uninhabited Uasin Gishu plateau (in pre-
sent-day western Kenya). Theodore Herzl,
the founder of modern Zionism, was per-
sonally in favor but the Russian delegates to
the Sixth Zionist Congress, held in Basle in
1903, were ﬁercely opposed.
South Africa now has the largest Jewish
community in Africa; they are considered
part of the white minority. The community
was formed after the 1880s with the arrival
of European immigrants, mainly from
Lithuania. A few white South African Jews
distinguished themselves in South Africa’s
liberation struggle, such as Joe Slovo and
Ronnie Kasrils, but for the most part they
tended to adapt, collectively, to apartheid.
This attitude, coupled with the extensive
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

cooperation between Israel and the
apartheid regime, contributed to the in-
crease in negative representations of the Jews
and Judaism in Africa and the Americas.
The irony is that until the mid-1960s, Israel
often voted against South Africa in the
United Nations. Relations between the two
countries only improved after the Six-Day
War in 1967, when most African states, in a
movement of solidarity with the Arab cause,
broke off diplomatic relations with T el Aviv.
Political processes in the Middle East,
South Africa, and the United States have
greatly shaped black-Jewish relations since
the 1970s. The common bond of suffering
that once brought the two peoples together
has now loosened. The Judeophile attitude
of the ﬁrst African American Pan-African-
ists, such as Edward W . Blyden, W . E. B.
Du Bois, or Marcus Garvey, who saw in
Zionism a model for a return to Africa, is
now just a memory.

JUNETEENTH
Juneteenth is an African American holiday
commemorating the emancipation of all
slaves. Major General Gordon Granger
along with Union soldiers arrived in
Galveston, T exas, with the announcement
that the Civil War had concluded and all
slaves now were free on June 19, 1865,
which commenced the celebration of
Juneteenth and led to the holiday’s name.
General Order Number Three included the
following: “The people of T exas are in-
formed that in accordance with a Procla-
mation from the Executive of the United
States, all slaves are free. This involves an
absolute equality of rights and rights of
property between former masters and
slaves, and the connection heretofore exist-
ing between them becomes that between
employer and hired laborer.”
The announcement, greeted with
thanksgiving and jubilation by slaves, came
almost two-and-a-half years after President
Lincoln had signed the Emancipation
Proclamation. The reason for the delay
possibly had to do with a combination of
factors, including General Lee’s surrender
in April 1865 and a shortage of high-
ranking Union troops in T exas. But scholars
have disagreed upon why it took so long. As
the holiday developed, celebrations moved
from church grounds to public accommo-
dations like Emancipation Park in Houston,
T exas, and Booker T . Washington Park,
Mexia, T exas, where thousands annually
celebrated.
In 1980, Juneteenth was recognized
as an ofﬁcial T exas holiday, as a result of
the leadership of Al Edwards, an African
American state legislator. In recent times,
national Juneteenth organizations have
contributed to an increase in cultural
awareness, ofﬁcial state recognition beyond
T exas, and the resurgence of the oldest on-
going African American celebration of
emancipation. The celebration has taken
on a variety of expressions from parades
and commemoration programs to cookouts
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 740 ---
664 J UNETEENTH
and dances. Yet a prominent feature has
remained the reading of the Emancipation
Proclamation and reﬂection upon the sig-
niﬁcance of freedom.
Roland Barksdale-Hall

KANEM-BORNU EMPIRE
Kanem and Bornu were two ancient Islamic
empires populated chieﬂy by the Kanuri
ethnic group and located in the Lake Chad
region of West Africa, in modern-day
Nigeria, Chad, Cameroon, Niger, and Libya.
The empires, throughout their history,
amalgamated and separated several times,
but were always closely associated. Mai
Idris Alawma (r. 1570–1603) united and
expanded the empires in the sixteenth cen-
tury, and by the eighteenth century Bornu
had established itself as a major power in
the Sudanic region.
Around the turn of the nineteenth cen-
tury, the Fulani jihads and establishment of
the Sokoto Caliphate in neighboring
Hausaland began having an impact on the
western border of Bornu. Fulanis in Bornu
attacked major cities in hopes of incorpo-
rating the empire into Sokoto. The ruling
Mai sought aid from Kanem and the forces
of Muhamad al-Amin al-Kanemi responded
by repelling the Fulani onslaught. Although
Kanem-Bornu was largely populated and
ruled by Muslims, the Fulani jihadists in-
sisted that paganism and the persecution of
Fulanis were rife in Bornu. Years of hostili-
ties followed, but ultimately the Sokoto
Caliphate and Bornu came to a compro-
mise whereby the most westerly provinces
became part of Sokoto and the balance
665
K
remained Bornu. After preserving Bornu,
al-Kanemi became its ruler, but less than a
decade after his death Kanem-Bornu came
under control of the Sultanate of Wadai in
1846.
A major effect of years of internecine
warfare and the larger jihad in Hausaland
was the enslavement of captives on both
sides, who were often sent to other parts of
Africa or the Americas.
Brent Singleton

Kenneth Kaunda was the ﬁrst president of
Zambia, a position he held from 1964
to1991. He was born at the Lubwa Mission
in Chinsali, Northern Rhodesia, now
Zambia.
Kaunda’s long political career was
launched in 1950 when he formed the

KENTE CLOTH
Kente cloth is a striking, colorful textile
woven by the Ashanti people of Ghana.
Silk and cotton are the main raw materials,
and it is traditionally woven by men on
narrow horizontal looms. Strips of woven
fabric three to four inches wide and seven
to ten feet long are sewn together to make
the cloth—eight to ten strips sewn together
for women’s garments, and twenty to
twenty-ﬁve strips for those of the men.
Colors are symbolic: gold represents royalty

The UNIP went on to win fourteen seats in
the Legislative Assembly in 1962 and
Kaunda was named minister of Local Gov-

Kente has played an important role in
the lives of the Ashanti. Thousands of dif-

events, and sayings. It is also used ritually
to indicate royalty, wealth, and status.
Historically, kente was worn by the
king and his court, but beginning in the
early twentieth century, wealthy merchants
dealt commercially in the cloth, and it
became a widespread commodity. Kente,
however, is still treasured by the people of
Ghana, who wear it on special occasions.
Kwame N’krumah, the ﬁrst president
of Ghana, was instrumental in introducing
kente to the United States by wearing it on
ofﬁcial state visits. Later, during the 1960s,
African Americans adopted the cloth as a
symbol of black pride and unity. Presently,
kente is used not only in ethnic fashions
but also on ceremonial occasions.

KENYA
Located on the east coast of Africa, the
Republic of Kenya has a population of approx-
imately32,022,000. The country is bisected
by the equator and has always been rich
agricultural land. For many centuries Kenya
was a rich trading area for Arab and later
European merchants. In 1827 Charles Millet,
a merchant from Salem, Massachusetts,
arrived on the brig Ann and became the
ﬁrst American trading captain to visit the
East African coast. He traded in the port
of Mombasa. By the 1840s and 1850s,
American traders came to dominate the
Kenyan coast. Many of them brought with
them the unbleached cotton cloth woven
in Massachusetts, which is still known as
merikani in Swahili. During the American
Civil War, Confederate raiders attacked U.S.
merchant ships with the CSS Alabama
sailing along the Kenyan coastline. These
raiders caused major losses to the U.S. mer-
chant navy, not only in ships physically lost
at sea but also to those having to be sold or
“reﬂagged” owing to massive rises in insur-
ance premiums. By the late nineteenth cen-
tury, British, and to a lesser extent, French
ships, dominated the East African coast.
The British had originally taken over
Kenya under the auspices of the Imperial
British East Africa Company, with, from
1890, a protectorate over the sultanate of
Witu. Some missionaries, such as Ohio-
born Willis Hotchkiss and Wisconsin-born
John Stauffacher, came to Kenya during
this period. In 1906 the area was put under
the control of the British Colonial Ofﬁce
with a governor appointed to administer
the region. Although there were a few
settlers from before World War I, after
1920 large numbers of British settlers, and
also some other Europeans and Americans
(including big-game hunter Paul Rainey
from Cleveland, Ohio), started migrating
to Kenya. There were large farms available
and the central highlands was quickly dom-
inated by large white-owned farmsteads
which grew tea, coffee, and bred cattle.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 744 ---
668 K HOISAN
By this time signiﬁcant numbers of
British and American tourists had started
taking safaris in Kenya. Theodore Roosevelt
was one of the more celebrated visitors
when he toured Kenya in 1910, his account
being published as African Game Trails. An-
other famous American to tour Kenya was
Ernest Hemingway, who went on a safari in
the mid-1930s and this experience was
incorporated in his novel Green Hills of
Africa (1936). He also used the trip to write
The Snows of Kilimanjaro (1936)— Mount
Kilimanjaro being in Tanzania. Others had
been inspired by ﬁlms and also by traveling
exhibitions such as those organized by
American James Barnes as far back as the
1920s. U.S. physician George Crile, after a
safari in 1927, established a laboratory at
Maji Moto, where he was able to research
comparative anatomy in animals. There was
also trade, with Berry Boswell Brooks buy-
ing cattle in Kenya and taking them back to
Arkansas and T ennessee. However, after
World War II, increasing nationalist agita-
tion led to the Mau-Mau Uprising and
attacks on white-owned farms. Eventually,
with escalating violence and the British
clearly unable to maintain law and order,
negotiations began and on December 12,
1963, Kenya gained its independence. Jomo
Kenyatta, a key ﬁgure in the Pan-African
movement, would become the nation’s ﬁrst
prime minister and then its ﬁrst president.
When Kenya became independent, the
United States provided £3,206,000 in ﬁnan-
cial aid to the new country, and the United
States has remained on good relations with
Kenya ever since. It has maintained a con-
sulate in Mombasa since at least 1916, and
in Nairobi from at least 1919. The ﬁrst U.S.
ambassador to Kenya was William Attwood,
a former journalist who had been ambas-
sador to Guinea from 1961 to 1963. He was
in Kenya from 1964 until 1966, describing
his experiences in The Reds and the Blacks
(1967). This period saw a massive increase
in U.S. tourists visiting the country. Writer
Elspeth Huxley, whose famous The Flame
Trees of Thika(1959) encapsulated the life of
the British in Kenya, had studied at Cornell
University. Her books increased interest in
Kenya in the United States, as did Joy
Adamson’s famous Born Free(1960), about
Adamson’s life with a lioness. It was made
into a ﬁlm in 1966 by American ﬁlm pro-
ducers Sam Jaffe and Paul Radin.
In addition, many U.S. academics
researched in Kenya, with Irven Devore
and Richard Borshay Lee writing on the
primates of Kenya, and Herbert Friedman
working on the birds of Kenya. Kenya still
remains popular with U.S. and Canadian
tourists, and with increasing numbers from
South America.
Sadly, a grimmer transatlantic connec-
tion was created in August 1998 when the
U.S. embassy in Nairobi was bombed. Some
247 people were killed and 5,000 injured. It
caused a massive increase in security at all
U.S. embassies around the world and atten-
tion being focused on Osama bin Laden,
who was identiﬁed as the perpetrator.
Justin Corﬁeld

to the original woman from whence all
mankind emerged, also known as the
Mitochondrial Eve.
Although widely studied by cultural
anthropologists and linguists alike, they
remain one of the most misunderstood
cultural/linguistic groupings in the world.
Much of the misconception surrounding
the Khoisan ﬁnds its roots in the historical
legacy of racially and culturally biased
observations of colonial explorers and mis-
sionaries. The term has been used to describe
groups of people—including but not
limited to the Khoikhoi (also referred to as
Khoi; pejoratively referred to as Hottentot)
and the San (derogatorily referred to as
Bushmen)—as if they were one people. In
actuality, the Khoikhoi, translated to mean
“the real people,” were historically nomadic
herders of cattle and sheep who lived in
large groups, whereas the San, translated to
mean “outsider,” were hunter-gatherers
who lived in much smaller groups. Interest-
ingly, anthropologists report that because
the hunter-gatherers did not have a collec-
tive name for themselves in their own lan-
guage, they prefer to be called “Bushmen,”
as the term “San” was used by the Khoikhoi
as an insult. What is more interesting is that
if such accounts are accurate, the group
seemingly fails to recognize the insult inher-
ent in the term “Bushmen.”
Khoisan has also been used to refer to
a linguistic family reductively characterized
by its use of “click consonants.” Early
Dutch colonialists, bafﬂed by the intricate
sounds of the language, created the term
“Hottentot” to describe what they had
heard. Hottentot is actually the translitera-
tion of the Dutch words hateren (to stam-
mer) and tateren (to stutter), and as such
labels the people stutterers. The most dys-
functional manifestation of European
misconceptions about the Khoisan recorded
to date is the case of “Hottentot Venus,”
Saartjie (Sara) Baartman, who in life was
put on exhibition throughout Europe dur-
ing the nineteenth century, and after death,
whose skeleton, preserved genitals, and
brain were displayed in Paris Musee de
l’Homme until 1985.
Yaba Amgborale Blay

KINCAID,J AMAICA (1949–)
Jamaica Kincaid is an author of short sto-
ries, novels, and essays. She was born Elaine
Potter Richardson on the island of Antigua
in 1949. Kincaid was educated in the
British colonial system. At age seventeen,
Kincaid left Antigua for New York to be-
come an au pair. Kincaid also worked as a
staff writer at several magazines including
The Village Voice and The New Yorker,
where her ﬁrst short stories were published.
These short stories were compiled later into
her ﬁrst book At the Bottom of the River
(1992). The ﬁrst essay in this collection,
“Girl,” addresses colonial dominance and
dominion, and speciﬁcally female imposi-
tions in a patriarchal society and sets the
stage for Kincaid’s later works. Written
from the point of view of the mother
(although she is not mentioned once), this
essay chronicles the complicated and
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 746 ---
670 K INCAID,J AMAICA
complex love-hate relationship between a
mother and her daughter. Underlying this
personal relationship, fraught with ambiva-
lence, is a political one. The mother-daughter
dichotomy bears symbolic resonance to
the relationship between the self and the
colonial mother (country), England. This
theme is further developed and given full
critical attention in Kincaid’s ﬁrst novel,
Annie John (1986).
In Annie John Kincaid exposes the ills
of British colonial education, underscoring
colonial indoctrination and subjugation.
This book also incorporates African ances-
tral practices inhabited in the myth of the
Flying African, embodied in the grand-
mother and spiritual healer and ancestress,
Ma Chess, who miraculously appears and
disappears on the island as she bridges the
gap between Old World and New World.
A Small Place (1988) is Kincaid’s most
poignant critique of colonialism and colo-
nialist ventures. Detailing the harsh pres-
ent conditions in her lost paradise, Antigua,
Kincaid addresses the double colonization,
formerly by England and presently by the
United States, of the island and its inhabi-
tants. America has replaced Britain in its
imperialist ventures as tourism becomes
another, though subtler, form of coloniza-
tion. Duped, the inhabitants have begun
to see themselves through Western eyes;
therefore it becomes increasingly difﬁcult
to distinguish between the victor and the
vanquished. The shameful legacy of
Antigua’s colonial past lives on; there is no
visible difference between the colonialists
and the existing government that mimics
and duplicates imperialist tendencies—
political and economic exploitation and
subjugation—of the colonials. Kincaid’s
critique of America as present imperial power
is given ample weight in her reference to
the 1983 Grenada invasion by the U.S.
government.
The actual events of Kincaid’s second
novel, Lucy (1991), unfold in America, the
colonial mother (country). America’s might
is both asserted and questioned in this
novel as Kincaid repeatedly poses the ques-
tion: “How do you get to be the sort of vic-
tor who can claim to be the vanquished
also” (1991, p. 41). This position of “privi-
lege,” of being both victor and vanquished
is only available to a “chosen” few (the
powerful), a point Kincaid underscores in
her comment about explorers who had
crossed the seas in search of not only riches
but also freedom: “On their way to free-
dom some people ﬁnd riches, some people
ﬁnd death” (1991, p. 129). The pervasive
mother-daughter motif that forms the crux
of the novel is employed as a subtext for
the colonial relationship, the relationship
between the powerful and the powerless.
In The Autobiography of My Mother
(1996) Kincaid returns to the Caribbean
landscape, to her mother’s homeland
Dominica (although often stating that her
works are a combination of ﬁction and
truth, her truth, one cannot help but notice,
is the recurrent autobiographical references
in Kincaid’s works). In this third novel the
theme of motherlessness occupies center
stage and the notion of surrogacy is ﬁercely
interrogated. The absence of the biological
mother or mother ﬁgure lends to the rejec-
tion of the motherland. The barren state
that categorizes Dominica is representa-
tional of the devastation that has afﬂicted
many of the islands. While the mother
(land), the Caribbean landscape, is obfus-
cated, imagery of an imagined colonial
past, England, is ever present. This colonial
presence (in spite of self-governance) is
maintained and epitomized in the “father,”
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 747 ---
KING JR., MARTIN LUTHER 671
whether present or absent. It is this
“reserved” male power that Kincaid refers
to when she writes that the lives of men
always could be found in the pages of a
book (Lucy, 1991, p. 95).
In her memoir, My Brother (1997),
awarded the Prix Fémina in 2000, Kincaid
offers a searing and uninhibited account of
her brother’s death related to AIDS and her
mother’s indifference to his impending
death. The personal life story of her brother
is the story of her family, the hardships they
endured on the island of Antigua, and
speciﬁcally about her mother who adopts
the powerful suffocating image of a colo-
nial mother. This text also chronicles
Devon’s (Kincaid’s brother) relationship to
the Caribbean community and its relation-
ship to him and the disease AIDS. In Mr.
Potter (2002) Kincaid returns to her obses-
sion with the island of Antigua. The ﬁc-
tional story of Mr. Potter is the story of an
impoverished community. His struggles are
emblematic of the community’s continued
struggles. Amidst these struggles Mr. Potter
is obsessed with acquiring power, a symbol
of status and a male preoccupation as
Kincaid suggests.
Language is another obsession of
Kincaid. It is a symbol of both empower-
ment and disempowerment. Illuminating
the disempowering effects of a colonial
(adopted) language forced upon a people
who were deprived of their original tongue,
Kincaid sees the orphans and orphanages
left behind as a result of this disenfranchise-
ment: “the millions of people . . . made
orphans: no motherland, no fatherland, no
g o d s... and most painful of all, no tongue.
(For isn’t it odd that the only language I
have in which to speak of this crime is the
language of the criminal who committed
the crime?” (A Small Place , 1988, p. 31).
Yet, Kincaid “chooses” to use the language
of the criminal (evidence of her position as
a member of the “powerless” for she hasn’t
a choice), not to detail the “goodness” of
his deeds, but to curse him, to chronicle the
horror, the abuse, the injustices, the agony,
and humiliation inﬂicted upon the weak
and powerless.
Simone A. James Alexander

KING JR., MARTIN LUTHER
(1929–1968)
Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. was the most
important leader of the black freedom
struggle during the 1950s and 1960s
known as the Civil Rights Movement. King
grew up in Atlanta, Georgia, and received a
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 748 ---
672 K ING JR., MARTIN LUTHER
bachelor’s degree from Morehouse College
before moving north to earn his PhD in
theology, which he received in 1955. A year
earlier, King had returned to the South to
preach at Dexter Avenue Baptist Church in
Montgomery, Alabama. It was the same
year that the U.S. Supreme Court, in
Brown v. Board of Education, declared seg-
regation illegal.
On December 1, 1955, Rosa Parks, an
African American native of Montgomery,
was arrested for refusing to yield her seat on
a city bus to a white person. Local blacks,
led by King, began to boycott the city’s
buses not only in an effort to change things
in their town but to test the nation’s commit-
ment to enforcing the Supreme Court’s
ruling barring segregation. After more than
a year of struggle both on the streets and in
the courts, the city of Montgomery deseg-
regated its public transportation system.
Blacks nationwide, inspired by the example
set by King and his charges, organized simi-
lar protests, and these spiritually connected
crusades were coined the Civil Rights
Movement.
In 1957 King was named president of
a confederation of black ministers that
would come to be known as the Southern
Christian Leadership Conference. This po-
sition, combined with King’s heroic efforts
during the Montgomery campaign, secured
his place as one of the nation’s most impor-
tant leaders, a moral voice whose courage
and speaking ability gave the black freedom
struggle nationwide credibility. A year later,
King published his ﬁrst book, Stride T o-
wards Freedom, which further publicized
the urgency of the cause.
Although he was not a black nationalist,
and believed that freedom and morality
would be won through integrated coopera-
tion between American blacks and whites,
King always had an interest in the world-
wide underpinnings of racism and poverty.
He believed that the same systems that kept
African Americans from ﬁrst-class citizen-
ship were similar and connected to those
that had maintained the subjugation of
Asia and Africa under European powers. In
March 1957, King traveled to Ghana to at-
tend the inauguration of Kwame N’krumah,
whose ascent to power marked the country
as the ﬁrst African nation to achieve inde-
pendence from colonization.
As the Civil Rights Movement wore
on, King more explicitly began to tie events
and historical processes in Africa and the
Caribbean to things that were happening in
the United States. In his December 1964
speech accepting the Nobel Peace Prize,
King drew parallels between the ﬁghts by
blacks in Africa and America for political
power. In a January 1965 interview with
Playboy, King mentioned repeatedly the
Martin Luther King Jr. led the African American civil
rights struggle before his assassination in 1968. His
powerful speeches, writings, and ideals of equality have
inspired people internationally. (Library of Congress)

connections between Africa and America,
claiming that black Americans were the
cultural and spiritual descendants of Africa
and that their struggles for freedom and in-
dependence were mutual. In one of his
most famous works, the 1967 book Why

Had he not been murdered in 1968, it is

KONGO
The word Kongo refers to both the
Bakongo, a population group from West
Central Africa, and to an array of cultural
and religious practices shared by large
numbers of people in Central Africa and
the Americas since the era of the Atlantic
slave trade.
In the fourteenth and ﬁfteenth cen-
turies, the Kongo group consolidated a
large territory of vassal provinces around
their capital of Mbanza Kongo, under the
leadership of their king, the manikongo .
This kingdom extended from south of
today’s Gabon to the northern parts of
Angola and east into the actual Democratic
Republic of Congo’s interior. Its political
system was formally organized, hierarchi-
cal, and centralized in the hand of the
manikongo. In 1482, with the arrival of the
Portuguese explorer Diogo Cam, the Kongo
kingdom entered into European history.
The manikongo adopted Catholicism as
its state religion and built economic and
diplomatic links with Portugal and the
Papacy. Soon after, however, the kingdom
started to suffer from the combined disrup-
tive effects of waves of invasions, civil war,
and the growing Atlantic slave trade. Follow-
ing the decisive battle of Mbwila (1665),
lost by the Kongo to the Portuguese, the
kingdom crumbled into small warring chief-
taincies. This situation lasted through the
following centuries up to the nineteenth
century Belgian colonization.
As a part of the larger Bantu cultural
and linguistic area, the Kongo share with
the populations around them key religious,
linguistic, and social features. Kikongo, the
language of the Bakongo is a Bantu idiom
related to the adjacent Swahili and Shona
and to a small extent mutually understand-
able. Kongo religion is centered on ancestor
worship and a belief in the close relation-
ship between the world of the living and
the world of the dead. The centuries-long
relationship with European traders and
missionaries has had some bearing on the
Kongo belief system and religious art, both
of which integrate in their discourse traits
and icons of Christianity. Socially, one of
the long-lasting effects of the mixing of
Christianity and Kongo worldviews has
been the proliferation of prophetic or mes-
sianic politico-religious movements from
the early eighteenth century Antonians to
1920s Kimbanguism.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 750 ---
674 K RU SAILORS
Central Africa has been one of the
main gateways for the deportation of
Africans to be sold as slaves in the Americas.
On the foreign continent, Bantu slaves
from Central Africa have recreated a cul-
ture based on the common traits of their
groups of origin and identiﬁed by the word
Kongo. Kongo has taken different forms in
various parts of the Western Hemisphere,
but has remained the vibrant manifestation
of shared beliefs. Practicing and employing
paquets congo in Haiti or prendas in Cuba is
believing in the agency of the same spirits
that the bottle-trees from the United States’
South try to capture. Kongo also serves to
describe sociocultural space of empower-
ment among the members of the African
Diaspora. In Brazil as well as in Cuba or
Haiti, distinct groups have formed calling
themselves Kongo Nations and symboli-
cally electing their own kings.
Cecile Alice Fromont

KRU SAILORS
The name “Kru,” also spelled “Kroo,”
refers to the West African ethnic group who
originated in eastern Liberia and migrated
and settled along various points of the West
African coast, notably Freetown, Sierra
Leone, but also the Ivorian and Nigerian
coasts. Kru people also migrated to the
British port cities of Liverpool, London,
Cardiff, and elsewhere. Throughout the
nineteenth and twentieth centuries, the
name Kru became synonymous with seafar-
ing in West Africa, though its associations
with the sea stretched back much further.
Initially, Kru people developed maritime
skills through their work as ﬁshermen and
traders along the Liberian coast. These skills
allowed them to secure work on European
ships as sailors, navigators, and interpreters.
By the eighteenth century, Kru people were
invaluable in shipping the live “cargoes” from
shore to ship in lighters along the treacherous
Liberian coast. Evidence also suggests that
Kru people were involved in the actual trad-
ing of slaves with Spanish traders. Kru sailors
also worked aboard slave ships bound for the
Americas; they were employed as inter-
preters, navigators, and as stevedores loading
and discharging cargoes. Kru people were
more valuable as traders and sailors on slave
ships than as slave labor. T o ensure their sta-
tus as “freemen,” they initiated the practice
of tattooing their foreheads and the bridge of
their nose with indigo dye to distinguish
them from slave labor.
With the abolition of the slave trade,
Kru sailors sought alternative economic
opportunities and many migrated to Free-
town to work on British vessels trading
there. They also were able to ﬁnd work
aboard American and British warships
operating out of Freetown that were used
to combat the illegal trade in slaves. Free-
town became the British headquarters of
the Royal Navy’s antislave trade squadron.
Many factors operated in the decision
to employ Kru people as sailors on British
ships. Initially, they were used to ﬁll labor
shortages left by white crews who had died
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 751 ---
KRU SAILORS 675
or fallen sick on the malaria-infested West
African coast. Secondly, they were used as
laborers or stevedores on the coast to save
white labor from the arduous task of load-
ing and discharging cargoes in the steamy
climate of tropical West Africa. Kru labor
was also cheaper to employ and were slower
to organize in trade unions.
Kru seamen and auxiliaries were em-
ployed on U.S. trading ships on the Wind-
ward Coast of West Africa in the 1830s and
1840s. Evidence suggests they were fre-
quent visitors to America from at least the
nineteenth century. Kru labor and other
African people became an important part
of the Atlantic working class. They
emerged as a direct result of the historical
evolution of Atlantic capitalism. Europe,
Africa, and the Americas became inextrica-
bly linked in a triangle of Atlantic global
trade. There were many actors in this trade:
the wealthy and powerful, and those who
had only their labor power to sell. The
Kru’s involvement as workers in this
transatlantic system of trade transported
them not only up and down the West
African coast as well as farther aﬁeld to
Europe and America. Thus opportunities
for waged employment not only existed
along the West African coast in Freetown
and elsewhere but also in Britain and the
Guianas in the Caribbean.
Migration from Liberia in search of
waged work saw relations between the Kru
people and the Settler-Liberian govern-
ment (also referred to as Afro-Americans)
break down over the introduction of taxes
at all ports on labor and commodities in
the 1840s and 1850s. The American Colo-
nization Society had colonized Liberia in
1821, and then proceeded to settle freed
American slaves there. In their struggle
against the Liberian government, the Kru
began to trade arms and gunpowder in
preparation for armed conﬂict with the
Liberian state. Waged labor on board ships
became a means of buying arms to resist
Liberian encroachments on Kru land and
the introduction of taxes on Kru leaving
and entering Liberia. By 1910, different
Kru communities were at war with the
Liberian government. The latter had at
their disposal the Liberian militia, the
Frontier Force, and the American cruiser
Birmingham. In addition, in an attempt to
crush the Kru, the United States sent to
Liberia weapons and ofﬁcers to lead the
Frontier Force. The Birmingham was
used to bombard Kru settlements on
the coast, while others inland were burned
to the ground. Around 100 miles (161
kilometers) of this coast became involved
in the Kru revolt—an armed struggle
against the American-backed Settler-
Liberian government.
Established Kru communities have
grown up in Freetown, Sierra Leone, and
in Liverpool and Cardiff in the United
Kingdom. Such communities emerged out
of the need of British capitalism to utilize
free waged labor during the slave trade, and
later during colonization and postcoloniza-
tion. With the demise of world shipping,
the introduction of containerization, and
the use of cheaper Far Eastern crews, Kru
people are no longer prominent in shipping
conducted from West Africa. In Liverpool,
the Kru community is not being replen-
ished with the settlement of Kru migrants.
This community consists of a mere handful
of elderly Kru men (with even fewer Kru
women). The children of ﬁrst-generation
Kru often identify themselves in the con-
text of Liverpool with the larger group
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 752 ---
676 K RU SAILORS
identity of “black British” or Liverpool-
born black or “black of African descent.”
Such identities often indicate an ancestry of
mixed heritage which might include
African-Irish, African-English, African-
Caribbean, African-Arab, African-Chinese,
or in some cases a heritage that incorpo-
rates several of these over three or more
generations.
Diane Frost

LAING,KOJO (1946–)
Kojo Laing is a contemporary Ghanaian
novelist writing in English. From the mid-
1980s, Kojo Laing has been recognized as
one of the most innovative African writers.
Drawing inspiration from ancestral cultural
forms, he pushed the boundaries of the
novel to unexplored extremes and (along-
side other authors like Ben Okri and Syl
Cheney-Coker) contributed to the devel-
opment of a speciﬁc kind of West African
magical realism, which departs from Latin
American authors.
Born of an educated middle-class
Ghanaian family, he studied in Scotland
from 1957 to 1968, graduating with an
MA in political science and history. There
he also published his ﬁrst poems, expressing
his feelings of alienation in the face of
European racism through a concrete and
graphic conception of language. Back in
Ghana, he worked as a district administra-
tive ofﬁcer in various regions and at the
University of Ghana. From 1984 he has
dedicated himself to managing some sec-
ondary schools (a family enterprise), keeping
aloof from academic and intellectual circles.
His ﬁrst novel, Search Sweet Country
(1986), focuses on a variegated group of
characters struggling to deﬁne their personal
identities between 1975 and 1977, during
Acheampong’s military rule. Laing’s lyricism,
his insertion of neologisms and of terms
from several languages reproducing Accra’s
multilingualism, his use of formal devices
from the oral tradition, his magic realism
mixing spirits and witches amidst the living,
and his concentrated imagery won Laing
isolated praises and a few awards, and also
puzzlement and neglect.
Laing’s following novels continued this
search for a new identity capable of harmo-
nizing ancestral traditions and Western
culture, spiritual and material dimensions,
through even bolder literary experiments.
Woman of the Aeroplanes (1988) is set in
the other-dimensional town of T ukwan,
Ghanaian and invisible at the same time,
inhabited by immortals who long for a
multicultural identity and therefore visit
the immortal Scottish town of Levensvale.
Anything can apparently happen in the
novel, such as characters swapping parts of
their bodies and the town sage blowing
pipe smoke in the shape of words. Rather
than magic realism, Woman builds a world
approaching cartoons, or an outlandish
folktale dimension; Laing has always iden-
tiﬁed nonrepresentational art, African and
European, as one of his major inspirations.
This dimension is also evident in his only
collection of poems, Godhorse (1989), sim-
ilarly marked by a humorously disrespectful
attitude toward language and meaning.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 754 ---
678 L ATINAMERICAN LITERATURE
Laing’s novel Major Gentl and the
Achimota Wars (1992) constitutes another
carnivalesque enterprise, this time with a
science-ﬁction strain. Set in 2020, it narrates
the “Wars of Existence” between the greedy
Western nations and a Ghana where only
the eponymous town is still existing, whereas
the rest of the country has mysteriously
vanished. Laing turns symbols into concrete
images (symbols and shadows actually
become real characters in the novel), and the
disappeared land is to be seen as a ﬁctional
rendering of today’s ideological assault on
Africa. The success of Achimota’s strategy
becomes tangible when pieces of the van-
ished land ﬂoat back from the Atlantic: on
one small plot, a Ghanaian man is found
constantly moping—“his favourite occupa-
tion was refusing” (p. 123), an obvious
reference to Herman Melville’s Bartleby, the
Scrivener (1856), the emblematic victim of
Western civilization’s sterility.
Pietro Deandrea

LATINAMERICAN LITERATURE
The European presence in Latin America
has always been accompanied by an African
presence, and this is the case with Latin
American literature. When Christopher
Columbus was arriving in the New World on
the Santa María, an African named Pedro
Alonso Niño was serving as the pilot of La
Niña. By 1502, things had quickly changed;
no longer working as pilots, blacks were
arriving in Hispaniola as Spanish-born
(ladino) domestic servants. With the number
of dying enslaved Amerindians rising and
the number of black slaves from Spain
diminishing, African slaves (bozal ) were
sought to ﬁll the gap in free labor left by the
dead Amerindians. Blacks were eventually
moved from Africa to the islands and ulti-
mately on to the mainland where they
occupied a gambit of roles from domestics
to hard laborers, and sometimes their roles
even included being co-conquistadors. There
are reports of blacks traveling with Hernando
Cortés in 1519 to Mexico, with Francisco
de Montejo in 1521 to Yucatan, and also
with Pedro de Alvarado to Guatemala in
1524 and later to Peru in 1534.
It was not until circa 1569 that blacks
were ﬁrst represented in Latin American lit-
erature. In Alonso de Ercilla y Zúniga’s La
araucana that was published in three
installments in 1569, 1578, and 1589, there
is a black slave who functions as a would-be
executioner of an Araucanian Indian chief
who ostensibly executes himself rather than
be the victim of the slave. Next, the black
slave is seen in Sylvestre de Balboa’s poem
“Espejo de Paciencia” (1608), where he
rescues a Spanish bishop from French
pirates and is ultimately granted his freedom
as recompense for his good deed. Balboa’s
work does more than simply reinterpret
the black slave as a character with some
redeemable qualities; it also discusses the
themes of slavery and freedom while pre-
senting the idea that the enslaved may wish
to be something other than victimized.
This concept is revisited and further explored
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 755 ---
LATINAMERICAN LITERATURE 679
throughout the Latin America canon. In
1806 Pantaleón Rivarola produced a ballad-
like work “Romance de la Defensa” in which
he recounts the tale of the courageous slave
Pablo Jiménez, who kills two English soldiers
in his effort to rescue his brother.
In 1821 Juan Francisco Manzano
offered Poesías líricas (Cantos a Lesbia) as
the ﬁrst published book of poems by a
black author in Cuba. After gaining his
freedom in 1836, Manzano published
Autobiografía (1840) in London, but the
work had been circulated in manuscript
form from 1835 until its publication. In
Autobiografía,Manzano discusses the tragedy
of slavery from the slave’s perspective, and
that telling directly criticizes the cruel sys-
tem of slavery along with the perpetuators
of the system in the way of its slaveholders.
His indictment is so scathing that only the
ﬁrst portion of his work survived his former
master’s friends’ wrath and destruction.
This work serves as a great example
of the intrinsic tensions that exist between
those who wish to have freedom, especially
the literate marginados (marginalized), and
all other parties involved with the slavery
system. For the oppressed, the literature—
while not always intentionally political—
ﬁnds itself being seen as a polemic docu-
ment opposing the powerbrokers atop the
economic, political, and social hierarchy.
The black artist, just as other artists of that
time, may have tried to use art as a possi-
ble means of expression, a form of therapy,
or a mode of ﬁnancial advancement; but
this marginalized voice of artistic expres-
sion relating his view of the world was in-
terpreted as a blow against the well-deﬁned
establishment. Gabriel de la Concepción
Valdés, a free black in Cuba, writing under
the pseudonym Plácido, wrote verses that
gently challenged Spanish autocracy and
consequently caused his imprisonment.
Later he was sentenced to death because of
his rumored connection with the Conspir-
acy of the Ladder slave revolt. Ultimately it
was determined that Plácido and his works
were too volatile to be allowed to continue,
so he was ﬁnally executed.
The tragedy beyond Valdés’s death rests
with the effect it had on Manzano’s literary
aspirations. Manzano was reminded that
his written thoughts were in fact in diametric
opposition to the beliefs and desires of the
rulers of the kingdom of slavery. His earlier
plan of writing a novel detailing the most
horriﬁc elements of slavery that he omitted
from his diary died with Valdés. These two
virtual contemporaries—one enslaved and
one free—laid the paradigmatic groundwork
for many future writers. One functioned as
the individual working to improve the per-
sonal lot of one (Manzano), while the other
functioned as the individual working to
improve the lot of the masses (Valdes);
both, however, used literary expression as
the means for advancement. Through their
efforts, they left a long-lasting imprint
on Latin American literature and culture.
Directly to Manzano’s credit is the imitation
by white intellectual/abolitionist writers who
saw his work and attempted to recreate
works similar to his in an effort to shift
thoughts about slavery. This imitation pre-
sents the greatest irony in that the white
modeling of the slave narrative functions as
the nexus where the two worlds of Manzano
and Valdes met; Manzano’s attempt to
improve his personal lot becomes the means
by which the collective lot of many may be
improved.
In 1845 Martins Pena produced his
theatrical works treating the everyday life
of Rio de Janeiro Brazilians. While Afro-
Brazilians did not function as the primary
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 756 ---
680 L ATINAMERICAN LITERATURE
theme of his work O Cigano, they did
appear in marginalized roles. Pena presents
blacks as stupid and easily manipulated. In
his work, three principal characters run a
smuggling ring in which they convince
slaves to leave their present place of servitude
to work in the mines of Minas Gerais. This
happens by the promise that eight days of
mine work will grant slaves their freedom.
In 1850 Agrario de Meneses presented a
play with Brazil’s ﬁrst protagonist of color
entitled Calabar, based on a true story of
Calabar, a mulatto. Calabar, who begins as
a Portuguese ofﬁcer, betrays the Portuguese
army during the Dutch Wars because he is
a scorned lover; when the woman he loves
loves another within the Portuguese ranks,
he allies himself with the Dutch in order to
seek revenge. He has no great loyalty to
either side because both forces essentially
represent the same thing—a European
presence in Brazil.
Between 1851 and 1855, when José
Mármol presented his Amalia, blacks in
Argentina are presented as an economically
depressed but free group of individuals who
in a muted way contribute to the political
structure under the dictator Juan Manuel
de Rojas. In 1860 José de Alencar gave the
world his play Mãe in which a slave cares
for a successful young man who does not
initially realize that the slave is his mother,
but the truth is eventually uncovered. In
1867 Jorge Isaac published his work Maria
in which the reader sees the conditions of
Colombian slaves during the early portion
of the nineteenth century. In 1877 the
Afro-Colombian poet Candelario Obeso,
also known as the “Colombian Othello,”
published the controversial Cantos populares
de mi tierra, which functioned as the pre-
cursor to Poesía negra (Black Poetry). His
works, just like his life, were focused
around his frustrations of living within a
racially oppressive environment. In 1881
Arthur Azevedo’s Brazilian play O Liberato
has a slave as the central character, but he
never actually enters the stage. While all of
the other characters talk about him and his
fate, he dies before being able to direct his
own life.
By 1884, the issue of slavery and sexu-
ality began to surface in Latin American
literary works, with Arthur Azevedo treating
the theme in O Escravocrata, where the black
protagonist Lourenço fathers his mistress’s
child. Elsewhere, black women in Latin
American literature in a fashion moved into
the company of corrupted white men and
women from both Europe and the United
States. With the publishing of Tradiciones y
Leyendas Mexicanas, the world hears of
“The Mulatto of Córdoba,” the beautiful
woman of black blood who makes a deal
with the Devil. After being discovered, she
is punished by the community; this story is
slightly reminiscent of the Faust legends
and the Salem Witch T rials.
During the period of the 1880s, Cuban
writers actively began to use literature as a
means of political protest and critique.
Through the hard work of Domingo del
Monte, authors such as Alselmo Suárez y
Romero and Cecilia Villaverde were encour-
aged to pr esent slavery realistically and to
examine slavery as a formal theme. Works
by these Cuban writers, coupled with
Brazilian abolitionist works like Joaquim
Manuel de Macedo’s As Vítimas Algozes
(1869), Júlio Ribeiro’s A Carne (1888), and
Aldolfo Caminha’s Bom-Crioulo (1895),
actively worked to present the horrors of
slavery in such a way as to eventually attract
the attention of the Western world.
By the beginning of the twentieth cen-
tury, blacks and their literature were being
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 757 ---
LATINAMERICAN LITERATURE 681
considered in terms of their collective sim-
ilarities and not necessarily in terms of
strict geographical conﬁnes. Europe began
to evaluate Africa and its descendants in a
very new way; they were no longer only a
means for free labor but a source of an
alternative culture. This culture extended
itself beyond offering simple self-sustenance;
it was a viable contributor to the Western
world. In 1910 Leo Frobenius published
The Black Decameron and in 1917 Oswald
Spengler published Decline of the West. Not
only offering a theme for European writers
but also for the visual arts, Africa was having
an inﬂuence on Apollinaire’s African statues
as well as Pablo Picasso’s “The Damsels from
Avignon,” where he presents black imagery
in cubist form. Europe in a sense was looking
for and ﬁnding itself in parts of Africa.
By the 1920s a major shift took place
with respect to black writers and whites’
appreciation for African contributions to the
Latin American landscape in the way of the
literary movement known as negrismo.
Negrismo, also known as black poetry or
Afro-Antillan poetry, initially began as a
literary movement in which white writers,
such as Puerto Rican Luis Palés Matos,
Cubans Emilio Ballagas and Ramón Guirao
y Zacarías Tallet, among others, offered a
folkloric, primitive, and exotic vision of
blacks. They attempted to integrate their
impressions of Africa into literature through
an overt and intentional placement of
blackness and Africanism within poetry
through the use of true and morphed African
lexicons that sometimes created Spanish
neologisms.
Negrista works from white authors
provided a framework or a literary corpus
to embody and present the theme of Africa
to the mainstream, but it was not until the
entrance of black practitioners like Nicolás
Guillén that negrismo came to possess and
reﬂect the authentic spirit of the African
within the movement. Later in the 1930s
the negritude movement, an intellectual
conduit for black French speakers, began to
take root. Both negrismo and negritude
celebrated African ancestry, and both
showed the historical progress of the African
descendant while simultaneously forecasting
the possibility for future writers wishing to
tackle the themes and challenges historically
associated with African inﬂuences in Latin
American literature. After Guillén’s publi-
cations, there seemed to be a virtual explo-
sion of works treating the theme of the
African and his descendants in the Latin
American world. No longer the slave to
whom the Aruacanian Indian chief refuses
to submit himself for execution, the African
descendant is praised; and the African de-
scendant is praising his own heritage. He is
no longer only the subject but he is the
agent evaluating his history and himself.

LEAGUE OF COLOURED
PEOPLES
The League of Coloured Peoples (LCP)
was the largest British pan-African organi-
zation in the 1930s and 1940s. It was
founded in London in March 1931 by
Dr. Harold Moody and modeled on the
National Association for the Advancement
of Colored People (NAACP). League
membership was multiracial, but the lead-
ership was exclusively in black hands, pre-
dominantly West Indian and African. The
LCP aims were to promote the welfare of
“coloured peoples in all parts of the world”
and to improve race relations. Effecting
these aims involved lobbying government
and private institutions to end racial dis-
crimination that was widely practiced in
Britain and in the colonial Empire. The
LCP quarterly journal, The Keys, ﬁrst pub-
lished in 1933, reﬂected James Aggrey’s
aphorism that both the black and the white
keys of the piano had to be played together
for effective melody. Throughout its life the
league was always plagued by lack of money
and overreliance on voluntary workers.
League funds were supplemented from
Moody’s pocket and much of the work
undertaken by his family—to the extent
that the LCP was often accused of being a
Moody family affair.
Initially the league was mainly con-
cerned with social and welfare activities and
was unfairly thought to represent only the
interests of professional and middle-class
black people. In 1935 it began an effective
enquiry into discrimination by shipowners
and trade unions that deprived black colo-
nial and British seamen of work by labeling
them as “aliens.” More widely, the LCP
lobbied over the Scottsboro Boys and
protested various colonial policies. One of
Moody’s aims was to cultivate the support
and good will of inﬂuential people as a
means of bringing about change in racial
policies and attitudes. He was probably more
successful in the former than the latter.
At times the league cooperated with
other black organizations in London, such
as WASU (West African Students’ Union).
Relations with WASU were soured by a
dispute over the control and direction of a
student hostel largely funded by the Colonial
Ofﬁce. The LCP was also accused by radical
black spokesmen, such as the Marxists
George Padmore and C. L. R. James, of
being conservative and too closely identiﬁed
with ofﬁcial, particularly Colonial Ofﬁce,
interests, although both men and other
radicals wrote for The Keys and respected
Moody.
The LCP was radicalized in the mid-
1930s by the Italian invasion of Abyssinia,
became more pan-African, and began to
cooperate with other black radical groups
to denounce British weakness in the face
of fascist aggression. That cooperation
continued over labor unrest in the British
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 759 ---
LEAGUE OF NATIONS 683
Caribbean with a league resolution demand-
ing radical social and welfare changes, self-
government, and federation for the British
West Indies. The LCP also campaigned for
black Britons to be eligible for commissions
in the armed forces, against land alienation
by white settlers in Africa, and denounced
Nazi and fascist policies on race.
League membership and influence
reached its zenith in 1943 with several
branches in Britain and the colonies.
Britain’s black population increased in
wartime as people from the empire came
to join the armed forces and to work in
industry and agriculture. The presence of
large numbers of black GIs and the racial
discrimination policies of the U.S. armed
forces often exerted a baleful inﬂuence on
British people and institutions. The LCP
campaigned to break down racial barriers
and to end racial discrimination in hotels,
public houses, restaurants, and dance halls.
It also argued for changes in the school
curriculum. The twelfth annual general
meeting of the LCP in Liverpool in 1943,
attended by 500 people, agreed to a “Charter
for Colonial Freedom.” In 1944 a more
strongly worded “Charter for Coloured
Peoples” called for “full self-government at
the earliest opportunity” for colonial peoples,
and for legislation to end racial discrimina-
tion in employment and in public places
in Britain. Although the LCP had discussed
a future pan-African congress, it played
only a minor role in the congress held in
Manchester in July 1945, largely because of
Moody’s hostility to its leftist focus. Thus
the LCP , the main pan-African organization
in Britain, bypassed an opportunity to bring
its inﬂuence to bear on a gathering that is
now seen as having considerable political
signiﬁcance. Largely under the thumb of
Moody, LCP policy was mainly concerned
with establishing cultural centers in a number
of cities that would provide accommoda-
tions for black people and promote good
race relations.
Moody died in April 1947. Robbed of
his leadership and his many ofﬁcial contacts,
the League of Coloured Peoples became a
less effective body. There were internal dis-
putes over policies, ﬁnance, and leadership.
Although it had become more radical in
voice, by the early 1950s the LCP was
greatly reduced in members and was only
one organization among several seeking to
represent the interests and claims of a black
population that was growing steadily as
a result of new immigration from the
Caribbean.
David Killingray

LEAGUE OF NATIONS
The League of Nations was a post–World
War I organization formed to prevent inter-
national conﬂicts. At the end of World
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 760 ---
684 L EAGUE OF NATIONS
War I (1914–1918), the idea surfaced
among world leaders that such an organiza-
tion was needed to prevent international
conﬂicts. At the Paris Peace Conference in
January 18, 1919, U.S. president Woodrow
Wilson chaired the committee with the
responsibility of drawing up a covenant for
such an organization. In a speech, Wilson
framed his Fourteen Points for a new world
order that resulted in the League of
Nations. The co venant, ratiﬁed as part of
the Versailles Peace T reaty, instituted the
league on January 10, 1920, with head-
quarters in Geneva, Switzerland. The
league began with forty-two members; at
its peak in 1934, it had ﬁfty-eight member
states participating.
The league’s assembly consisted of rep-
resentatives of its members; a council, which
included permanent members and members
elected by the assembly; and a secretariat.
The ﬁve world powers, Britain, France, Italy,
Japan, and the United States, were to make
up the permanent members of the council;
however, Wilson failed to get the Versailles
Peace T reaty ratiﬁed in the senate and so
the United States did not participate in the
league. The league was further weakened in
the 1930s when Japan and Germany with-
drew their membership in 1933, and with
Italy following in 1937. The Soviet Union
(USSR) was elected as a permanent member
in 1934 but was expelled in 1938 after it
attacked Finland.
Exiled Ethiopian leader Haile Selassie speaks before the League of Nations in 1936, urging the group to renounce
Italy’s claim on Ethiopia. Selassie had previously appealed to the League in 1934, when Italian and Ethiopian
forces ﬁrst clashed. Conﬂict was followed by a full-scale invasion of Ethiopia by the forces of Italian dictator Benito
Mussolini. (Library of Congress)
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 761 ---
LESOTHO 685
Various articles made up the charter of
the league. The covenant contained 26
articles, most of which were dedicated to
maintaining peace and promoting inter-
national cooperation. Other articles, such
as number ten, stipulated that sovereignty
and independence of individual states
would not be undermined by the league.
Article twenty-three dealt with securing
humanitarian rights, while twenty-ﬁve made
provisions for Red Cross societies. The
league also made provisions for handling
diseases, drug addiction, and trafﬁc in
women and children worldwide. Its judicial
branch, the Permanent Court of Interna-
tional Justice (PCIJ) at The Hague, which
arose out of article fourteen of the covenant,
heard 65 cases and successfully reached 37
judgments. In addition, the International
Labor Organization (ILO) was also suc-
cessful in improving working conditions
worldwide.
However, the league had weaknesses. It
wielded no considerable military force and
attempted to impose economic sanctions
on offenders that were largely ineffective.
Most poignantly, the league was unable to
prevent any of the events that led to World
War II. Where Africa and the Caribbean
region were concerned, the league was only
indirectly related to the extent that it
wielded theoretical power over the nations
that claimed parts of Africa and the
Caribbean for themselves. Article twenty-
two, for instance, mandated that colonies
taken from the defeated powers should be
turned over to other members of the league
for administrative purposes, since it was felt
that these peoples could not successfully
govern themselves. However, the body was
hardly able to protect these so-called
embryonic territories from outside distur-
bances. For instance, in 1935 the league
sanctioned Italy for attacking Abyssinia
(Ethiopia) but failed to prevent the invasion.
The success of the league relied heavily on
the ability of the “great powers” to unite
and enforce disarmaments and impose mil-
itary sanctions on aggressors. Only Britain
and France remained permanent members
throughout the life of the league, and this,
among other factors, undermined its peace-
keeping ability.
The league was dissolved on April 19,
1946, and replaced by the United Nations.
While the league did not prevent conﬂicts
from occurring, it did play an important
role in world politics and created a model
for the United Nations, which continues to
have a role in international peacekeeping
and arbitration.

LESOTHO
A landlocked country entirely surrounded
by South Africa, the Kingdom of Lesotho
has a population of about 1,865,000. It was
originally the British colony of Basutoland,
which was established when Moshoeshoe,
the Sutu ruler, concluded a treaty with the
British to protect his country from the
Boers. Initially, British government agents
oversaw the protectorate, but after the
Disannexation Act of 1883, a resident
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 762 ---
686 L EWIS,M ARY EDMONIA
commissioner was appointed. He served
under the high commissioner for South
Africa until South Africa became a republic
in 1961.
During the Second Anglo-Boer War
of 1899–1901, Canadian soldiers served
alongside the British and other British
Empire soldiers, and some were garrisoned
in Basutoland. In 1910 Basutoland refused
to be incorporated into South Africa, and
retained its separate identity.
As with all colonial administrations,
many civil servants in British Africa previ-
ously served in the Caribbean. T wo of the
governors of Basutoland previously served
in the West Indies: Edwin Porter Arrowsmith,
who was governor from 1951 until 1955,
was governor of T urks and Caicos Islands
and Dominica in 1946 and later governor
of the Falkland Islands; and Alexander
Falconer Giles, governor from 1961 until
1966, had been governor of St. Vincent.
Basutoland was granted independence
on October 4, 1966, and became the
Kingdom of Lesotho. Being a member of
the British Commonwealth, there were rel-
atively few contacts with the Americas. The
U.S. Peace Corps started work in Lesotho
in 1967; the Presbyterian Church in the
United States from the 1970s; and the
Congo Inland Mission from 1973. One of
the major works on the country, The Guide
to Lesotho, ﬁrst published in 1974, was
written by David Ambrose, a British-born
schoolteacher who had studied at the
University of Colorado. 
During South Africa’s era of apartheid,
Lesotho supported activities against
apartheid, including taking in refugees
from South Africa. In turn, Lesotho became
visible to the United States in the context
of antiapartheid activities. It also became a
relatively small trading partner, with Lesotho
exports to the United States largely being
textiles.

LEWIS,M ARY EDMONIA
(1845–1911?)
Mary Edmonia Lewis was the ﬁrst African
American woman to gain recognition as an
artist and as a sculptor both in the United
States and internationally. Her most famous
works include Death of Cleopatra (1875)
and Forever Free (1867). Unfortunately, little
information remains about Lewis’s life and
career. Her father was an African American
freeman, and her mother was of Ojibwa
(Chippewa) and African American descent.
Born in upstate New York, she was orphaned
at a young age. T wo aunts, who belonged to
a Mississauga Chippewa band, “adopted”
her and her siblings. Lewis claimed that her
Chippewa name meant “wildﬁre.” Her older
brother was a gold miner, and he sent Lewis
to New York Central College and Oberlin
College.
Oberlin was a major center for aboli-
tionists, and the college accepted African
Americans and women as students. How-
ever, the artist confronted racism in this
liberal setting. During the winter break of
her third year at Oberlin, the artist was
accused of poisoning two young women.
Lewis supposedly gave them spice wine
before they went on a sleigh ride. During
the ride, the girls suffered stomach pains,
and the artist was accused of foul play. Soon
after she was accused, Lewis was abducted
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 763 ---
LIBERATIONTHEOLOGY 687
and beaten. The charges against her were
dropped because of insufﬁcient evidence.
Lewis suffered emotional scars because
of this incident, and she moved to Boston.
She apprenticed under Edmond Brackett
and eventually opened a studio. After gaining
a successful reputation, Lewis sailed to Italy
in 1865. She moved to Rome where she
established another studio and continued
her studies. She joined many expatriate
artists in Rome. During her stay in Rome,
Lewis was inﬂuenced by the Greco-Roman
sculpture. Thus, her work represented her
transatlantic experiences with European
styles and American subject matter. Her
Forever Free was carved in marble, and its
ﬁgures wore dress reminiscent of classical
Roman attire. It was the ﬁrst sculpture to
celebrate the Emancipation Proclamation
that freed America’s slaves. Her Death of
Cleopatra was famous and notorious inter-
nationally and nationally. This sculpture
was neoclassical, and it captured the moment
of Cleopatra’s death. Cleopatra represented
black identity because Egypt was the symbol
for black Africa in the nineteenth century.
Lewis’s masterpiece was noted as an afﬁr-
mation of African American identity.
In Rome, Lewis sculpted altarpieces for
the Roman Catholic Church. In 1874, Lewis
returned to the United States and was hon-
ored for her international success. One critic
claimed that she was the most interesting
representative of America and he hoped
other American artists would follow her
example. In 1876, Lewis’s sculptures were
well received at the Centennial Exposition
in Philadelphia. After 1876, her artwork
declined in popularity, and she sank into
obscurity. Her remaining sculptures repre-
sent her amazing transatlantic journey as an
artist.
Kelly J. Baker
