LIBERATIONTHEOLOGY
The term liberation theology was popular-
ized by the Roman Catholic Peruvian the-
ologian Gustavo Gutiérrez Merino and is
often used in reference to a movement
within Latin American Roman Catholicism.
However, the terms liberation theology or
theologies of liberation are now regularly
employed to refer to a number of other
related theologies that seek to integrate an
active concern for social justice with a belief
in Christianity. Liberation theologies have
developed in both Africa and the Americas,
including Latin American liberation theol-
ogy, Latino/Latina liberation theology,
mujerista theology, black theology, South
African liberation theology, and womanist
theology.
All liberation theologies are contextual
theologies that take into account the partic-
ular social, political, historical, and cultural
settings of religious inquiry. Not all contex-
tual theologies are theologies of liberation,
however. Theologies of indigenization and
enculturation, for example, also take cultural
setting into account. These theologies seek
to more adequately ﬁt Christianity to a par-
ticular culture and in this way effectuate a
more thorough process of religious conver-
sion. Theologies of liberation, however, are
not primarily concerned with evangelization,
but with overcoming oppression and injus-
tice. Liberation theologians promote earthly
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 764 ---
688 L IBERATIONTHEOLOGY
as well as heavenly justice for those who are
oppressed. Thus, theologies of liberation
emphasize the importance of both spiritual
and physical freedom.
The birth of Latin American liberation
theology is often located either during the
creation of the Latin American Episcopal
Conference (CELAM) in the 1950s or
during the Second Vatican Council
(1962–1965) initiated by Pope John XXIII.
Nevertheless, many of the ideas that con-
tributed to the growth of the movement in
the late twentieth century have been present
in Latin America for centuries. In fact, Latin
American liberation theologians recognize
the Spaniard Bartolomé de las Casas as a
predecessor to contemporary practitioners
of liberation theology. Las Casas, whose
father traveled to the Americas with
Christopher Columbus, participated in the
conquest of Cuba and joined the Domini-
can order of the Catholic Church in the
early sixteenth century. Las Casas was one
of the ﬁrst people, if not the ﬁrst, to be
ordained to the priesthood in the Americas.
Las Casas, who became bishop of
Chiapas, used his position to vocally con-
demn the abuses committed by the
Spaniards against the indigenous people
of the Americas. His famous Brevissima
Relacion de la Destruycion de las Indias (Very
Brief Account of the Destruction of the Indies)
published in 1552 and the posthumously
published in 1875–1876 Historia de las
Yndias (History of the Indies) made his views
public and cemented his reputation as
defender of the Indians. Las Casas did not
initially condemn the treatment of enslaved
Africans, and even suggested that the
importation of African slaves could help to
alleviate the burden the Spanish had placed
on Native Americans. Las Casas later re-
gretted this suggestion, however, and his
unrelenting indictment of Spanish atrocities
in the Americas demonstrated a lifelong
commitment to ﬁghting injustice. 
Those who practice Latin American
liberation theology, like Las Casas, have
dedicated themselves to exposing injustices
and improving the lives of the subjugated
and the underprivileged. Camilo T orres
Restrepo, a Catholic priest from Colombia
who later became a guerilla commander, is
often cited as a predecessor of liberation
theology. He was a professor who cofounded
the sociology department at the National
University in Colombia before he died in
an armed struggle against the Colombian
military. He is one of a number of priests
who took up arms to defend the cause of
liberation for the poor in Latin America.
While many liberation theologians have been
politically active, most have used peaceful
methods to promote social change.
One of the most inﬂuential theologians
and practitioners of liberation theology was
Brazilian archbishop Hélder Pessoa Câmara.
In 1967, he led a group of bishops who
published a message promoting a “prefer-
ential option for the poor.” This phrase
would later become synonymous with the
goals of Latin American liberation theology.
In 1971, Gustavo Gutiérrez Merino, consid-
ered the founder of liberation theology by
many, published his monumental Theology
of Liberation and the term he had coined a
few years earlier began to receive extensive
international recognition. The Brazilian
Leonardo Boff, one of the founders of
liberation theology along with Gutiérrez,
published Church: Charisma and Power in
1981. In 1985, the Vatican condemned
Boff to silence and removed him from
religious duties for the ideas he expressed in
this book. In 1986, the decision was reversed
after an outpouring of international support
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 765 ---
LIBERATIONTHEOLOGY 689
for Boff. However, facing renewed criticism
by the Vatican in 1992, Boff made the
decision to leave the Franciscan order and
continue his struggle as a lay theologian,
writer, speaker, and professor.
Other important ﬁgures in the devel-
opment of liberation theology include the
Argentinean Miguel Ramondetti, founder
of the Movement of Priests for the Third
World (MSTM), the Brazilian Hugo
Assmann, author of Oppression-Liberation
(1971), and the Uruguayan Juan Luis
Segundo, author of The Liberation of
Theology (1975). Additional well-known
ﬁgures from Latin America associated with
liberation theology include the Nicaraguan
priest and poet Ernesto Cardenal Martínez,
the Salvadoran Archbishop Óscar Arnulfo
Romero, assassinated in 1980, and the for-
mer Haitian president Jean-Bertrand Aris-
tide. Noted practitioners of Latin American
liberation theology who are not Roman
Catholics include the Methodist minister
José Miguez Bonino from Argentina, author
of Doing Theology in a Revolutionary Situation
(1975); the Presbyterian Rubem Alves from
Brazil, author of A Theology of Hope(1969);
and the Presbyterian Elsa Tamez from
Mexico. A noted theologian, professor, and
author of Through Her Eyes: Women’s Theol-
ogy from Latin America (1989), Elsa Tamez
incorporates the insights of both liberation
theology and feminist theology in her work.
Based in Costa Rica, Tamez has successfully
encouraged other liberation theologians to
give greater consideration to the importance
of women’s voices and women’s lives. Tamez,
Miguez Bonino, Alves, Gutiérrez, L. Boff
and his brother Clodovis Boff, author of A
Church for the Next Millenium (1998), are
among the many theologians who continue
to actively promote and practice liberation
theology in Latin America.
Latino/Latina liberation theology in
the United States, also known as U.S. His-
panic theology, maintains strong ties to
Latin American liberation theology. How-
ever, while some theologians, such as James
Cone, have argued that contemporary
Latin American liberation theology contin-
ues to marginalize issues of racial and
ethnic oppression in favor of focusing on
political and economic oppression, Latino/
Latina liberation theology has kept issues of
ethnic discrimination in the forefront along
with the continuing problems of economic
oppression. Latino/Latina liberation theol-
ogy’s most prominent contemporary theo-
rist and practitioner is Virgilio Elizondo. A
Mexican American born and raised in San
Antonio, T exas, Elizondo is a Roman
Catholic priest, theologian, and author of
many books including A God of Incredible
Surprises: Jesus of Galilee (2004). Founder of
the Mexican-American Cultural Center
(MACC) and former rector of San Antonio’s
San Fernando Cathedral, Elizondo was in-
ﬂuenced by the Second Vatican Council and
is a coeditor of the collection T eología y
Liberación(Theology and liberation) pub-
lished in 1991. Elizondo’s interest in libera-
tion theology is apparent in his concept of
the Galilean Jesus. Elizondo analyzes the
speciﬁc multicultural context of Jesus’s life
in Galilee and the prejudice Jesus was
exposed to as an ethnic outsider in order
to better understand the contemporary
context of Mexican-American communi-
ties. Other inﬂuential theologians in this
area include Arturo Bañuelos, Orlando
Espín, Roberto S. Goizueta, and Justo L.
González.
Mujerista theology, or Latina feminist
theology, is a growing ﬁeld of inquiry that
has also contributed signiﬁcantly to the
development of Latina/Latino liberation
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 766 ---

theology. Mujerista theology attempts to
enable Latina women to liberate themselves
as members of a shared Latino/Latina com-
munity and also strives to have a positive
impact on mainstream theologies. This the-
ology was ﬁrst elaborated by Ada María
Isasi-Díaz in her book En la Lucha: A
Hispanic Women’s Liberation Theology
(1993). Isasi-Díaz, a Cuban-born Catholic
theologian and the leading proponent of
mujerista theology, promotes the impor-
tance of creating bridges between various
groups of Latinos and Latinas. Isasi-Díaz
expanded her earlier work in La Lucha
Continues: Mujerista Theology (2004).
Other key ﬁgures in Latina feminist theol-
ogy include María Pilar Aquino, Daisy L.
Machado, and Jeanette Rodriguez.
Black theology in the United States
highlights issues of racial and ethnic dis-
crimination. Unlike Latin American and
Latina/Latino liberation theologies, which
are largely though not exclusively Roman
Catholic, black theology has been primarily
produced and practiced within Protestant
communities. While many date the devel-
opment of black theology to the Civil
Rights and Black Power Movements of the
late twentieth century in the United States,
others locate black theology’s roots in the
great revivals of the eighteenth and nine-
teenth centuries, and some situate it still
earlier in the arrival of enslaved Africans to
the American continent in the sixteenth
century. Prominent predecessors to con-
temporary black theology include the
slave rebellion leader Nat T urner, the aboli-
tionists David Walker, Sojourner T ruth,
and Frederick Douglass, as well as the
African Methodist Episcopal bishop Henry
McNeale T urner.
James H. Cone, African Methodist
Episcopal minister, theologian, professor,
and author of numerous books, including
Black Theology and Black Power(1969), was
the ﬁrst to formulate a systematic black
theology, and he continues to play an active
role in the ongoing dialogue on black the-
ology. Other highly inﬂuential proponents
of varieties of black theology include J.
Deotis Roberts, author of Liberation and
Reconciliation: A Black Theology (1971;
1994); William R. Jones, author of Is God
a White Racist?: A Preamble to Black Theol-
ogy (1973; 1997); Gayraud S. Wilmore,
author of Black Religion and Black Radical-
ism (1983; 1998); Kelly Brown Douglass,
author of The Black Christ (1994);
and Dwight Hopkins, author of Heart
and Head: Black Theology Past, Present, and
Future (2002).
South African liberation theology or
black theology shares many parallels with
U.S. black theology. While contextual
Christian theologies in other countries of
the African continent have tended to em-
phasize issues of enculturation and African-
ization rather than liberation, numerous
South African Christian theologians re-
sponded to the evils of apartheid and the
lingering inequality between whites and
blacks in South Africa with a strong appeal
to political mobilization against oppres-
sion. Even as the Black Power Movement in
the United States helped prepare the
ground for the emergence of black theology
in the late 1960s, the black consciousness
movement, founded by Steven Biko in
South Africa in 1977, helped to pave the
way for a uniﬁed response to apartheid.
Anglican bishop Desmond T utu, win-
ner of the 1984 Nobel Peace Prize and the
ﬁrst black general secretary of the South
African Council of Churches, has made
equal rights and a shared educational sys-
tem the center of his campaign against

inequality in South Africa. His sermons,
speeches, and other statements have been
collected in edited volumes, including Cry-
ing in the Wilderness: The Struggle for Justice
in South Africa (1982). In postapartheid
South Africa, the T ruth and Reconciliation
Commission met from 1996 to 1998
under Bishop T utu’s leadership. Alan
Boesak, president of the World Alliance of
Reformed Churches from 1982 to 1991, is
the author of the inﬂuential Farewell to
Innocence: A Socio-Ethical Study on Black
Theology and Black Power (1976). Boesak
has argued for a worldwide theology of lib-
eration and dislikes the tendency among
certain U.S. black theologians to employ
blackness as the symbol of oppression.
Roxanne Jordan, author of “Black Feminist
Theology in South Africa” from We Are
One Voice (1989) identiﬁes a common
struggle against white supremacy, shared by
blacks in the United States and South
Africa. Other key ﬁgures in South African
liberation theology include the Lutheran
bishop Manas Buthelezi and the Pente-
costal reverend Frank Chikane, a pastor in
the Apostolic Faith Mission.
Womanist theology seeks to address
some of the blind spots in the previously
mentioned theologies of liberation. Devel-
oped around Alice Walker’s concept of a
womanist as a black feminist or feminist of
color, womanist theology focuses on the
necessity of eliminating all forms of oppres-
sion, including race and gender discrimina-
tion. Womanist theologians include Katie
Cannon, author of Black Womanist Ethics
(1988); Jacquelyn Grant, author of White
Woman’s Christ, Black Woman’s Jesus: Femi-
nist Christology and Womanist Response
(1989); Dolores Williams, author of Sisters
in the Wilderness: Womanist Theology
(1993); and Diana L. Hayes, author of
Hagar’s Daughters: Womanist Ways of Being
in the World (1995). Womanist theologian
Renee Hill was the ﬁrst to criticize the lack
of attention paid to sexuality and particu-
larly to lesbianism in womanist theology.
Hill argued that issues of sexuality cannot
be divorced from womanist concerns about
community and survival. Kelly Brown
Douglass, also inﬂuential in the area of
black theology as noted above, is another
contemporary practitioner of womanist
theology who has written on the subject of
sexuality. An Episcopal priest, she has
employed womanist theology to address
the issue of sexual orientation, most no-
tably in Sexuality and the Black Church: A
Womanist Perspective (1999).

LIBERIA
Liberia, whose name means “free,” is an
African nation with a history of relations
with the United States from nineteenth-
century abolitionism and repatriation plans
to current political and economic issues. The
long relationship has inﬂuenced the history,
politics, and culture of Liberia’s people,
making Liberia the African nation most no-
ticeably connected to the United States.
History
Ofﬁcially known as the Republic of Liberia,
the tropical country was once a trading post
for Portuguese explorers in the 1400s. Its
location on the western side of Africa, just
north of the equator, makes Liberia an eas-
ily accessible port of entry from the Atlantic
Ocean. The Portuguese traded ivory, spices,
and slaves from the interior.
In 1822, the repatriation movement of
the American Colonization Society (ACS)
established Liberia as a colony for freed
African slaves. This colony was the begin-
ning of Liberia’s close connection to the
United States. The ACS consisted primarily
of Quakers and slaveholders. The former
believed in the abolition of slavery and the
latter believed that the freed slave would
destroy the American economy. They both
agreed that freed slaves and free-born
blacks should be taken to Africa, despite
opposition from blacks. Over the next forty
years, 19,900 African Americans, a few West
Indians, and about 5,000 Africans recap-
tured from slave ships settled in Liberia.
After being ruled by the ACS for
25 years, Liberia gained independence on
July 26, 1847, making it today Africa’s old-
est independent nation and the second old-
est independent nation of primarily black
citizens (Haiti is the oldest). Liberia is one
of only two African countries never colo-
nized by a European country; Ethiopia is
the other. Liberia became an example of in-
dependence to the many African countries.
Its independence was ﬁrst recognized by
England and France in 1848 and 1852, re-
spectively, but was not recognized by the
United States until 1862, after slavery in
the United States had been abolished.
Most visibly tying Liberia to the United
States is its ﬂag. Known as the “Lone Star,”
it has six red and ﬁve white alternating
stripes and a white star in the upper left cor-
ner against a blue canton. For many years,
Liberia used American currency, but as the
Liberian economy declined and was bur-
dened by foreign debt in the early twentieth
century, particularly after World War I, the
American dollar became scarce. However,
the United States continued to provide ﬁ-
nancial support in loans to its African ally
for years to come.
Politics
Liberia’s political values stem from U.S.
colonization. As a result, Liberia is a repub-
lic: it has a constitution, with a bill of
rights, that divides the government into
executive, legislative, and judicial branches;
the Supreme Court heads the court system.
Descendants of the freed slaves who
settled in Liberia are known as Americo-
Liberians. After gaining independence,
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 769 ---
LIBERIA 693
Americo-Liberians led both the govern-
ment and the economy even though they
represented a very small percentage of
Liberia’s population. This small percentage
controlled the government for many years
through the T rue Wig Party (TWP). A
free-born black raised in America, Joseph
Jenkins Roberts was Liberia’s ﬁrst president.
The political division between the em-
igrants and indigenous people was revealed
through the division of labor—for years the
indigenous people did most of the menial
labor and were not allowed the educational,
housing, and political opportunities or rep-
resentation they deserved. As a result, there
was increasing tension between ethnic
groups. The TWP was in power until 1980
when Samuel K. Doe, of the Krahn ethnic
group, led a successful coup d’état during
which President William R. T olbert was
assassinated. When Doe was officially
elected in 1985, the 133-year-long rule by
Americo-Liberians was ended by the
People’s Redemption Council (PRC).
However, from the time Doe took control
in 1980, his rule was brutal and continued
to distance ethnic groups from each other.
Doe eliminated his political rivals by en-
forced exile or assassination. Members of
his cabinet were primarily Krahn even
though Krahns made up only 5 percent of
Liberia’s population.
Liberia’s civil war began on December
24, 1989, when Charles Taylor, leader of
the National Patriotic Front of Liberia
(NPFL), invaded Liberia from its neigh-
boring country, Côte d’Ivoire. On Septem-
ber 9, 1990, President Doe was assassinated
by rebel forces led by Prince Johnson, who
was once a member of the NPFL and had
formed the Independent National Patriotic
Front of Liberia (INPFL). By October
1990, Liberia’s Interim Government of
National Unity (IGNU) was established.
Amos C. Sawyer was named president of
Liberia, but Charles Taylor continued the
war, refusing to cooperate with the new
government. While civil war continued,
the Cold War ended and Liberia was no
longer a strategic interest to the United
States, which was concentrating on Iraq’s
invasion of Kuwait. As a result, Liberia’s
most prominent international supporter
was not eager to physically intervene
though it gave $500 million in humanitar-
ian assistance. Peacekeeping efforts by the
Economic Community of West African
States Cease-fire Monitoring Group
(ECOMOG) were ignored by the NPFL
and challenged by the Economic Commu-
nity of West African States (ECOWAS),
which was divided over intervention.
On July 19, 1997, elections were held
after the United States, United Nations,
Africa Union, and ECOWAS successfully
negotiated disarmament and demobiliza-
tion of the warring factions. It was the ﬁrst
election in twelve years. Taylor won the
election, but six years later, Liberia had not
seen much improvement. Taylor aided the
Revolutionary United Front (RUF) in
Sierra Leone; his actions led to the resurrec-
tion of armed ﬁghting against him from his
adversaries, and corruption and social
unrest continued.
As a result of Taylor’s support of the
RUF , the United Nations imposed sanc-
tions against Liberia in 2001. Relations be-
tween the United States and Liberia were
already strained, especially since the United
States was hesitant to supply much inter-
vention during Liberia’s civil war. After a
considerable amount of pressure from the
international community, Charles Taylor
resigned on August 11, 2003. He was
granted asylum in Nigeria, an act that
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 770 ---
694 L IBERIA
caused dissension between Liberians who
wanted Taylor tried in a court in Sierra
Leone and the United States who helped
negotiate Taylor’s exile.
The National T ransitional Government
of Liberia was established on August 21,
2003. Gyude Bryant was chair and Wesley
Johnson was vice chair of this two-year rul-
ing body. In October 2005, Liberians voted
for their next president. In preparation for
the election, a team of election monitoring
experts was sent from the United States to
Liberia. Funded by the U.S. Agency for
International Development (USAID), the
team spoke favorably about the successful
voters’ registration led by the National Elec-
tions Commission (NEC) and the United
Nations Mission in Liberia (UNMIL).
Over a million Liberians registered to vote
and the registration process was effective
and free of any major concerns. Liberians
elected Ellen Johnson-Sirleaf, who became
the ﬁrst woman president in Africa. 
Culture
Liberia’s cultural landscape reveals its close
connection to the United States even
though Americo-Liberians are the only
people who have a direct connection to the
United States. They are the channels
through which much of America’s social,
political, and economic values have been
transmitted to the rest of Liberia’s popula-
tion. Christianity is one of those values.
Some 30 percent of the population is
Christian, while 60 percent is animist and
10 percent is Muslim. Ninety-ﬁve percent
of Liberia’s population is from indigenous
African tribes: Kpelle, Bassa, Gio, Kru,
Grebo, Mano, Krahn, Gola, Gbandi,
Loma, Kissi, Vai, Dei, Bella, Mandingo,
and Mende. T wo and a half percent are
Americo-Liberians and 2.5 percent are
Congo people (descendants of immigrants
from the West Indies who had been slaves).
Bordered by Sierra Leone, Guinea, and
Côte d’Ivoire, Liberia’s indigenous ethnic
groups have much in common with groups
in those countries, language being one.
However, because of American inﬂuence,
English is Liberia’s ofﬁcial language, mak-
ing it one of a few African countries to
which English is pervasive. Nevertheless,
most of the population speaks at least one
language from the Niger-Congo language
group of about twenty languages. The more
widely spoken languages are Mande, West
Atlantic, and Kwa, none of which are
unique to Liberia.
Education is one aspect of Liberia’s
culture that was signiﬁcantly disrupted by
the civil war. With an unemployment rate
of 85 percent in 2003, and a literacy rate of
57.5 percent in 2005, Liberia’s government
faced the need to implement plans that
would provide the schooling, healthcare,
and other basic services needed by all its cit-
izens. In February 2004, the United States
cohosted an international reconstruction
conference on Liberia during which over
$524 million was pledged in total aid.
Some of this aid is helping rebuild
Liberia’s schools, many of which were badly
damaged or completely destroyed during
the war. Liberia’s educational system began
during its early years as settlers and mis-
sionaries built schools and universities
modeled after schools in the United States.
Cuttington University is one of Liberia’s
most prestigious institutions, previously
attracting Rhodes scholars from around the
world. Founded in 1889 by an Episcopal
bishop, Cuttington is known for primarily
teaching Liberia’s elite. Much of the school
was destroyed during the war, including
parts of its Africana Museum, a prominent

learning center. As Cuttington and other
schools reopen and plans are made to make
education free on the elementary and sec-
ondary levels, more of Liberia’s citizens will
get the education they need to continue the
country’s journey toward stability.
Michaela V . Lawrence

LIBYA
A former Italian colony, Libya became an
independent kingdom under Idris I in
1951. The discovery of signiﬁcant petro-
leum resources in 1959 rapidly expanded
the Libyan economy. In 1969, Colonel
Muammar al-Qaddaﬁ deposed King Idris.
Libya’s relations with the United States have
often been tense under the leadership of
Qaddaﬁ. The new Libyan republic pro-
moted Arab unity, and Qaddaﬁ advocated a
personal brand of Islam-inspired socialism
that he articulated in a three-part book en-
titled The Green Book (1975). Already frag-
ile relations with the United States became
worse in the 1980s when the U.S. govern-
ment accused Libya of producing chemical
weapons and condemned Qaddaﬁ’s support
for international terrorist organizations.
Meanwhile, Qaddafi became close to
African American groups such as the Black
Panthers and, in particular, Louis Abdul
Farrakhan’s Nation of Islam.
The tension between the U.S. and
Libyan governments increased after U.S.
bombing raids on the major cities of T ripoli
and Banghazi in 1986. Following the os-
tensible involvement of Libyan terrorists in
the destruction of Pan Am Flight 103 over
Lockerbie, Scotland, in 1988, the United
States and the United Nations applied a
series of economic sanctions against Libya.
Most of these sanctions were dropped in
2003 when Libya formally acknowledged
responsibility for the destruction of Pan
Am Flight 103 and agreed to open its
weapon programs to U.N. inspectors after
announcing that it would stop producing
chemical weapons.
Ziad Bentahar
Reference
Qaddaﬁ, Muammar. The Green Book. Ottawa,
ON: Jerusalem International Publishers,

LITERATURE,A FRICAN
African literature encompasses the mutual
exchange between African American and
African writers and intellectuals linking
literature and politics through transatlantic
cultural connections. The history of African
written literature can be divided into four
periods: the pioneers’ era (1910–1930), the
negritude period (1930–1960), the decolo-
nization and its aftermath (1960–1990),
and the postcolonial legacy (1990 onward).
These near one hundred years have seen a
constant and fruitful exchange between
writers and an enduring American inﬂuence.
It was in the United States that blacks
ﬁrst awoke to the consciousness of their
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 772 ---
696 L ITERATURE,A FRICAN
condition and started writing about it. The
Middle Passage was part of the process of
identity transformation that turned Africans
into African Americans, and slave narratives
thus became one of the earliest forms of
African American culture, dating back to
the 1760s and Olaudah Equiano’s autobiog-
raphy (1789). More narratives were pub-
lished in the 1850s, drawing on plantation
oral narratives, trickster tales, and myths of
slave ﬂying and transmigration.
In the early years of the twentieth
century, ﬁctional works appeared that still
drew on slave legends, plantation songs,
jazz, and blues. Booker Washington, W . E.
B. Du Bois, and Marcus Garvey had so-
ciopolitical agendas that proved to be an
enduring part of African literature. Garvey
greatly inﬂuenced theorists of African inde-
pendence and was instrumental to the birth
of the negritude movement. Literature
ﬂourished in this context. James Weldon
Johnson published the Book of American
Negro Poetry in 1922. In 1925 Alain Locke
drew together major voices of the Harlem
Renaissance with The New Negro, an an-
thology that gave a place to writers like
Langston Hughes, Claude MacKay,
Sterling Brown, Countee Cullen, and Jean
T oomer. Born in the Virgin Islands in
1832, Edward Blyden traveled to the
United States in 1850 before settling in
Liberia in 1851. He exerted a great
inﬂuence on Garvey, Kwame N’krumah,
George Padmore, and others; laid the foun-
dation of West African nationalism and
Pan-Africanism; was an ambassador to
Britain and France in the 1880s; and is con-
sidered as an example of a new transatlantic
reality or a black Atlantic, in which bonds
were forged among English-speaking
West Africans, between African countries,
between Africa and the Diaspora, the
Christian and the Islamic world, and Africa
and the West.
West Indian writers played a major
part in the development of African litera-
ture, joining Paris-based African students
in using journals as a means of disseminat-
ing their ideas. They were actively involved
in the Revue des griots (1915), La Race
nègre (1927), Lucioles (1927), La Revue
indigène(1927), Le Cri des nègres (1931), La
Revue du monde noir (1931), and Légitime
défense(1932), Most of these journals were
short-lived, yet they achieved their aim of
bringing African students and writers of all
horizons together and helping the black
Diaspora to discover its identity.
Poet Nicolás Guillén brought the Afro-
Cuban voice to the movement in the1930s.
In Martinique, Aimé Cesaire in the 1940s
propagated the new ideas in his journal
Tropiques, encouraging new writers like
Frantz Fanon, Glissant, and Zobel and
strengthening links with Central and South
America. Authors now expressed them-
selves in different ways, with literature and
politics often side by side, as in Maran’s
Batouala (1921), considered as the ﬁrst
African novel, Jean Price-Mars’s Ainsi parla
l’oncle (1928), and Jacques Roumain’s
Gouverneurs de la rosée(1946).
After West Indian nations began to
gain independence, West Indian writers
separated into three groups, and while
some continued identifying with the negri-
tude movement, others focused on the
Creole identity. A third group, including
Maryse Condé, shared a multiple identity,
equally close to African, West Indian,
and American literatures. Pan-Africanism
started out as an ideology of blacks in the
United States in the 1920s, with Du Bois
organizing the ﬁrst and second Pan-African
Congresses in Paris. At that time, the
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

coming of Leopold Senghor, Aime Cesaire,
and Alioune Diop to the French capital
encouraged the pan-African movement. The
journals Légitime défense and L ’Etudiant
noir spearheaded by Cesaire and Senghor,
united black writers, focusing on black
identity and on the ﬁght against European
colonial assimilation. For many years, Paris
served as the rallying point for black writers
from all horizons, cutting across the lin-
guistic divides and facilitating a mutual dis-
covery, either through personal meetings or
through the reading of each other’s works
in the original or in translation. Senghor
acknowledged being indebted to Sterling
Brown and Claude MacKay. Diverse
writers including Senghor, Aime Césaire,
Richard Wright, and Jean-Paul Sartre gath-
ered around Alioune Diop to support the
new Présence africaine journal, launched in
Paris in 1947. In France, the Communist
journal Nouvel Age, devoted to African
American songs and poetry, published in
1930 and 1931, and Senghor’s anthology
of New African and Malagasy Poetry in
French in 1948, contributed to the discov-
ery of black American literature. The ﬁrst
two congresses of black artists and writers
in Paris (1956) and Rome (1959), orga-
nized by Présence africaine, and the black
arts festival held in Dakar in 1966, brought
African and West Indian writers together
once more and paved the way for the inclu-
sion of African literature in French univer-
sity programs in the 1970s.
Very early on, African writers formed a
united front, encompassing geographical,
linguistic, and cultural barriers along with
transatlantic slavery as a common history.
In Africa, works published in European
and African languages have been depicting
the national experiences of slavery since the
early days, through Nigerian Yoruba plays
and to the ﬁrst Igbo novel, Pita Nwana’s
Omenuko (1933). Later, African literature
would flourish with the publishing of
Yambo Ouologuem’s Le devoir de violence
(1968), Ayi Kwei Armah’s The Beautiful
Ones Are Not Yet Born (1969), and Koﬁ
Awoonor’s Comes the Voyager at Last, a T ale
of Return to Africa (1992), around the same
time that American black literature such
as Booker Washington’s Up from Slavery
(1901) and Olaudah Equiano’s Interesting
Narrative (1789) were being translated, the
ﬁrst into Yoruban in 1966, the second into
French in 2002. The struggle for emancipa-
tion, inherited from slavery and drawing
more recently on similar experiences like
that of Native Americans, has been a recur-
rent theme of African Diaspora writing
since the Negro spirituals and the poetry of
Harlem Renaissance, with some writers—
Richard Wright ( Native Son, 1940; Black
Boy, 1945), Lorraine Hansberry ( A Raisin
in the Sun, 1959), and James Baldwin (The
Fire Next Time , 1963)—close to political
movements such as the Civil Rights
Movement. Other related themes—exile,
dispossession, hybridity, and a search for
ancestral roots—have equally inspired
many writers, including David Diop,
and, more recently, Alex Haley and TsiTsi
Dangarembga.
The gradual fragmentation of black
African literature into national units de-
prived writers of the global platform that
had brought them together, with African
American and Caribbean literatures growing
as literatures on their own merit while
women writers like T oni Morrison emerged.
Yet the plot, characters, and scenes of many
African novels still testiﬁed to the mobility
of their authors, and in the 1990s, Anyidoho
and Awoonor both chose the Diaspora as
the theme of their poetry, using images of
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

698 L ITERATURE,A FRICAN AMERICAN
slavery, suffering, dispossession, and disloca-
tion as their primary material.
From the start, higher education played
a major part in the development of African
literature as Anglophone writers tended
to look toward British and, increasingly,
American universities for support. The years
1945–1975 saw American assistance for the
development of higher education in Africa;
the opening of departments of Anglophone,
African, and American studies in European
countries; an increased involvement of
African writers in American universities; and
the development of black studies and
African American literature in the United
States. Since then, most of the leading
African writers have either studied or lec-
tured there: Chinua Achebe, Chukwuemeka
Vincent Ike, Valentin Mudimbe, Ngandu
Nkashama, Niyi Osundare, Wole Soyinka,
and Adaora Lily Ulasi. This led to a growing
American presence in their works, such as
with Mudimbe’s Carnets d’Amérique(1976)
and Ike’s T o My Husband from Iowa(1990).
If the black protest of the 1960s paved the
way for the development of black studies in
American universities, this development has
been sustained and facilitated since the
1980s by an intellectual migration, often
controversial, from African universities.
Recent years have witnessed a shift in
African writers’ location, with the United
States, Britain, and France as new centers of
African literary activity.
A new African literature has emerged as
well, a literature of several worlds by black
writers of African descent born either in
Europe or in the United States. Their work,
informed by the authors’ lives and diasporic
contexts, differs considerably from that of
Africa-based writers, while sharing with
them the themes of migration and exile.
One hopes that this development will not
eclipse the writings of the many black
African writers still on African soil.
Francoise Ugochukwu

LITERATURE,A FRICAN
AMERICAN
African American literature speciﬁc to the
United States has had ties to Africa and to
Europe since its inception in eighteenth-
century America. Its earliest poets and
authors had cultural roots in Africa. Phillis
Wheatley, for example, was born in Africa
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 775 ---
LITERATURE,A FRICAN AMERICAN 699
and survived the Middle Passage before
writing her poetry in America. Other
eighteenth-century authors possessed a
memory of Africa passed down by their
forebears through the survival of oral tradi-
tions and other cultural practices. While
eighteenth-century authors of African
American literature had ties to Africa,
nineteenth-century authors such as Frederick
Douglass, William Wells Brown, Josiah
Henson, and other fugitive slaves who pub-
lished their narratives carried their antislav-
ery message to Europe, traveling in lecture
circuits to Britain, Germany, and France
and making the ethical issue of slavery and
the slave trade a worldwide concern.
T wentieth- and twenty-ﬁrst-century African
American authors have incorporated an
African past into their works in an active at-
tempt to revalue their African andAmerican
heritage, to conceive of themselves as mem-
bers of a black Diaspora with roots in Africa,
and to reevaluate their current status as citi-
zens of another land and another nation.
African American literary history tells
the story of the African Diaspora that was
forcibly created by the transatlantic slave
trade. Through its earliest authors we see
African and African-descended peoples
demonstrating the cultural retentions, cul-
tural adoptions and adaptations, and New
World cultural creations that deﬁne the
shared experiences of the black Diaspora.
Christianity, one of the major subjects of
early African American literature of the
eighteenth century, was used by authors
such as Phillis Wheatley and Jupiter
Hammon in poetry as a tool through
which to create an empathetic bond with
their white, Christian audience, but more
importantly as a way of expressing their hu-
manity. They emphasized that their conver-
sion to Christianity had made them better
people in introducing them to a Christian
God, but that, perhaps more signiﬁcantly,
their adoption of it transformed Christianity
into a better form of itself, representing the
true ideal rather than the corrupted form of
American Christianity that accommodated
slavery (see, for example, Phillis Wheatley’s
“On Being Brought from Africa to
America,” published in 1773). By mere
virtue of learning how to write, these
authors’ writings entered into the political
debate about the ethics of slavery; at the
same time, because of its content, their
poetry forever transformed the American
literary tradition.
This theme of literacy was developed
further in nineteenth-century African
American literature. In fact, literacy—the
experience of acquiring it, prevalent in
most of the slave narratives—was directly
connected to the transnational debate
about African and African-descended
people’s capacity for learning, which was
correlated with their relative humanity. The
revolutionary values of the Enlightenment
that led to the American Revolutionary
War and the founding of the United States
of America—liberty, justice, equality—
were at odds with the practice of enslaving
African Americans, a contradiction that
could be justiﬁed only by categorizing
African Americans as something other than
of the civilized humanity of the European
world. Literacy was the barrier separating
Africans and African-descended peoples
from a shared standing with Europeans and
European-descended people. According to
the values of the Enlightenment, the ability
to read and write demonstrated the level of
one’s humanity; the ability to write poetry
set a writer apart for his or her “genius” in
shaping language into art. But proving
the humanity of Africans and African
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 776 ---
700 L ITERATURE,A FRICAN AMERICAN
Americans would consequently undermine
the slave system as unethical, and the econ-
omy of colonial America and the United
States rested on slavery.
Therefore it was inevitable that the
literary accomplishments of African
Americans in the eighteenth and nine-
teenth centuries enter into the realm of
politics, not just art. Their productions
took on a symbolic value whose meaning
changed depending on the reader’s disposi-
tion toward ethics of slavery. Learning how
to read and write, a central episode in many
slave narratives, simultaneously described
the author’s transformation from spiritual
darkness to revelation and to manhood or
virtuous womanhood; the very act of
describing this process demonstrated the
author’s success. (“Written by herself” and
“written by himself” were frequently subti-
tles of the narratives, asserting the author’s
status of full humanity in authoring his or
her life story in an unmediated narrative
voice.) These nineteenth-century narratives
written by escaped slaves, directed largely at
a northern reading audience, were used in
the abolitionist cause. Many such authors
(such as Frederick Douglass and Harriet
Jacobs) observed, however, the overbearing
power of the abolitionist cause over their
personal narratives, and the attempts of
such prominent abolitionists as William
Lloyd Garrison and Harriet Beecher Stowe
to dominate and thus control their words
and attitudes to ﬁt their own political plat-
form. Virtually every escaped slave’s narra-
tive was published with a preface authored
by a leading abolitionist who, while afﬁrm-
ing that the author’s story was indeed true,
also suggested the signiﬁcance of his or her
life story in the abolitionist cause. Because
of this, escaped slaves felt themselves mov-
ing from one system of control to another,
each depriving them of their individual
voice and authority over their own lives.
The symbolic value of African Ameri-
can literature in a transatlantic context—
the meaning and signiﬁcance of its works
in the formation of a literary tradition—
has been continually assessed and redeﬁned
by its literary critics and creative writers.
Over the course of the twentieth century,
these writers have described the ways in
which being black and being American
operate in contradiction, or at least in
tension, with one another. (The issue of
choosing loyalty to race or to nation
emerges in early twentieth-century African
American literature, in works such as James
Weldon Johnson’s Autobiography of an 
Ex-Colored Man.) These tensions, reﬂected
in literature, also represented a political
reality: choosing between national culture
and cultural nationalism, in other words,
between Americanism and cosmopolitan
black identity. W . E. B. Du Bois acknowl-
edged this tension as it resided in African
Americans and proposed that it be main-
tained so that nothing was lost through as-
similation to “African” or “American” values.
The early twentieth-century push for African
American civil rights—emblematized by the
National Association for the Advancement
of Colored People (NAACP) and the
National Urban League—was linked with
democratic concern for Africa. The issue of
world democracy, raised by World War I
and President Woodrow Wilson’s vow to
make the world “safe for democracy,” was
taken up by the NAACP and other organi-
zations and applied to African Americans
within the United States, who had the
status of second-class citizens. But an
upwardly mobile, race-conscious African
American middle class also sought to sup-
press those aspects of black creative culture
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 777 ---
LITERATURE,A FRICAN AMERICAN 701
that were considered shameful—too work-
ing class, too close to stereotype. Writers of
the early- and mid-twentieth century, such
as Langston Hughes, Sterling Brown and
Zora Neale Hurston, called for recognition
of the value of African American folk
culture, distinct from a rising African
American middle class that mimicked
white values. In valuing folk culture, these
writers afﬁrmed working class forms of ver-
bal, musical, and physical expression such
as blues music and the Black Bottom dance
that originated in rural, southern, and
largely uneducated communities.
Writers of the New Negro Renaissance
era of the early twentieth century, in con-
ceiving of a worldwide black cultural iden-
tity, shaped and were shaped by emerging
artistic and political movements in other
countries, from communism—speciﬁcally
Marxism—to negritude. Writers of this era
traveled to the Soviet Union, France,
Britain, Spain, Morocco, Liberia, and other
parts of Africa. W . E. B. Du Bois studied at
the University of Berlin, Germany, later be-
came an admirer of Marxism and the Soviet
Union, and renounced his American citi-
zenship and became a citizen of Ghana in
1963, one year before his death; Langston
Hughes, Jamaican-born Claude McKay,
and T rinidadian C. L. R. James traveled to
the Soviet Union and had afﬁliations with
the Communist Party; Richard Wright,
who embraced Marxist ideology if not al-
ways the party itself, permanently relocated
to Paris, where he lived and wrote from
1945 to 1960. These national, political,
and cultural exchanges resulted in the de-
velopment and use of the concept “art as
propaganda” in these writers’ works.
The Negritude Movement, founded in
the 1930s by Senegal’s Léopold Senghor,
Guyana’s Léon Gontran-Damas, and
Martinique’s Aimé Césaire, sought to afﬁrm
and celebrate peoples of African descent and
their cultures. Emphasizing intercultural
exchange between African and Caribbean
writers, the Negritude Movement devel-
oped as a response to the colonial domina-
tion of black lives in virtually every aspect:
political, intellectual, educational, and
psychic. Its major authors sought the
spiritual and actual reclamation of an
African past, one that embraced plurality,
dynamism, and tensions of culture.
Negritude may have given formal status to
meaningful exchanges that were already
occurring as a result of African American
and Afro-Caribbean writers interacting—
for example, the Haitian poet Réné Maran
and Langston Hughes.
The Black Arts Movement, active from
the 1960s to its peak in the mid-1970s, was
formed in the context of and in response to
the political upheavals of the Korean and
Vietnamese Wars and the assassinations of
John F . Kennedy, Malcolm X, Martin
Luther King Jr., and Robert Kennedy. This
movement developed the internationalism
of New Negro Renaissance era writers by
identifying itself with third world subjects
and explicitly developing the link to
African nations such as Nigeria, Senegal,
Ghana, Kenya, and Tanzania. Its aesthetic
program ran parallel to the Black Power
Movement and asserted the exclusive use of
literature as a political platform, even a
weapon. (Amiri Baraka famously called for
“poems that kill” in his 1969 poem “Black
Art.”) Radical works were authored in the
ﬁelds of essay, poetry, and drama, literary
forms that were seen to be the most useful
platforms for the political exigencies of the
time. The movement radically revised the
notion of audience for its works, directing
them at a mass black audience. At the same
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 778 ---
702 L ITERATURE,A FRICAN AMERICAN
time, Maulana Karenga and others intro-
duced the concept of Afrocentrism as an
educational corrective to blacks’ wide-
spread poor self-esteem.
Black Arts helped shape the discourse
on African American culture, social identity,
and political rights into which the following
decades of African American literature en-
tered. The polemical and reﬂective literature
of autobiography, modeled by Malcolm X
(with Alex Haley) in 1965 was deepened by
autobiographies by Gwendolyn Brooks,
James Alan McPherson, and Alex Haley—
all of whom traveled to parts of Africa
and reﬂected on their identity both through
the continent and outside of it. Black
feminism—or womanism, as Alice Walker
called it—grew not only out of the Black
Arts Movement but also in response to it, as
it sought to recover a black female creative
tradition that had been devalued by male-
dominated deﬁnitions of “tradition,” be
they black or white. Alice Walker’s novel,
The Color Purple, features a return trip to
Africa for African Americans as missionar-
ies. T oni Morrison’s novel Song of Solomon
incorporates the myth of the ﬂying African
as a central motif, and she explores the
rupture of memory caused by the transat-
lantic slave trade and slavery itself in
Beloved.
African American writers have ad-
dressed the issue of cultural rupture (as a
result of the transatlantic slave trade) and
the question of homeland and belonging
through the theme of the Middle Passage in
literature that ranges in form from poetry
and ﬁction to criticism and theory. The
Middle Passage as a theme helps to explore
rupture and connection in the paradoxical
situation of African Americans, who are
depicted as outsiders to, and yet part of,
both African and American cultures.
Robert Hayden’s poem “Middle Passage”
explores the way in which history lives in
and through African Americans. T oni
Morrison’s novel Beloved shows how that
history is, and must be, passed on. Alex
Haley’s Roots explores the unspeakable na-
ture of the Middle Passage and relates it
directly to his family’s history. John Edgar
Wideman begins his Homewood Trilogy
with the short story “Damballah,” which
traces the history of two families through
generations from enslavement and memory
of an African homeland through the 1970s.
These authors use the Middle Passage to
articulate the tensions of location, home-
land, and literary traditions. Moreover,
Caribbean authors whose parents immi-
grated to the United States have con-
tributed to this theme’s development—
authors such as Paule Marshall, June
Jordan, Edwidge Danticat, and Michele
Cliff—so that national distinctions of
authors as “American” or “Caribbean” be-
come blurred. (For example, Marshall, in
Praise Song for the Widow, carries her
protagonist from the United States to the
Caribbean, and from tourist-deﬁned vaca-
tion spots through a “middle passage” expe-
rience to a cultural homeland on a remote
Caribbean island.)
Literary critics such as Derek Walcott,
V . S. Naipaul, and Paul Gilroy have used
the theme of the Middle Passage to articu-
late new critical-theoretical paradigms for
the study of African American, Caribbean,
African, and black British culture. Derek
Walcott looks to “The Sea as History.”
Arguing that modernism need not be a
nationally defined artistic movement,
Paul Gilroy shows that in fact black intel-
lectual modernism predated American and
European forms and that the forced,
continuous movement of black peoples
throughout the world has created this
condition. These critical paradigms focus

on the importance of memory in the cre-
ation of a homeland.
Mid-twentieth-century African writers
have been inﬂuenced by African American
and Caribbean writers as well. As African
and Caribbean independence movements
occurred and discussion of decolonization
were placed on the table, authors from these
regions wrote about each other and used
each other’s political models to understand
their current situations. Derek Walcott
wrote about the Mau Mau rebellion in
Kenya in his poem “A Far Cry from Africa.”
Jamaican author Victor Stafford Reid used
the Mau Mau rebellion as a parable for
Jamaican independence. Kenyan-born
Ngugi wa Thiong’o used lines from Derek
Walcott’s poem “The Swamp” for the epi-
graph to his novel Petals of Blood.
Thus African American writers forged
connections between aesthetic and politi-
cal movements, nationally and interna-
tionally: the New Negro Renaissance and
the ﬁrst push for civil rights for African
Americans in the early twentieth-century;
negritude and African and Caribbean
anticolonialism; Black Arts and Civil
Rights, Black Nationalism and African
decolonization.
Noelle Morrissette

LOCKE,A LAIN LEROY
(1886–1954)
Alain LeRoy Locke was an African
American scholar, intellectual, and editor
of The New Negro. Born on September 13,
1886, to Pliny and Mary Hawkins Locke in
Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, Locke, after
graduating from high school, attended
Alain LeRoy Locke was a major philosopher and
supporter of the arts during the Harlem Renaissance.
(National Archives)
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 780 ---
704 L ONG ISLAND:AFRICAN AMERICANS AND NATIVE PEOPLES
Harvard University in 1904, graduating
magna cum laude and Phi Beta Kappa in
three years. Locke was the ﬁrst African
American Rhodes scholar, and in that
capacity spent three years at England’s
Oxford University, graduating in 1910.
He began a long, distinguished career at
Howard University in Washington, D.C.,
in 1912 as an assistant professor of English
and philosophy. Locke completed his doc-
torate at Harvard and returned in 1918 to
Howard as a professor of philosophy,
eventually becoming the chair of the
Philosophy Department in 1921, a posi-
tion he held until his retirement in 1953.
In 1924, Locke took a research sabbat-
ical with the French Archeological Society
in Cairo, Egypt, after the discovery of the
King T utankhamen tomb. This experience
allowed Locke to explore the richness and
diversity of African art in Egypt and in
Paris, which was the center of European art
and culture at that time. Locke was one of
the ﬁrst Americans to amass a collection of
African art. He wrote about the importance
of African art, urging African American
artists to look for inspiration from their
ancestral homes. Locke urged the Howard
University administration to institute a
comprehensive African Studies program,
one that would focus on anthropology, cul-
ture, and history. Although such a program
was not instituted until after his death,
Locke was instrumental in the reorganiza-
tion of the liberal arts department at
Howard, which resulted in the inclusion of
programs and courses centering upon
African society.
Locke felt strongly that the African
heritage of the American black must be
explored and should become central to the
future works of black artists, “an artistic
vanguard.” A prolific writer, Locke
published over 300 essays and articles on
blacks, African politics, and the arts. He was
the editor of The New Negro, published in
1925. A mentor of great inﬂuence for
various artists, The New Negro featured
the works of Langston Hughes, Zora Neale
Hurston, Countee Cullen, Aaron Douglas,
and other artists of the Harlem Renaissance.
Locke was a member of the Interna-
tional Institute of African Languages and
Culture, an international exchange professor
in Haiti in 1943, and an honorary fellow in
the Sociedad de Estudios Afro-Cubanos.
Locke died in 1954 of heart failure.

LONG ISLAND:AFRICAN
AMERICANS AND NATIVE
PEOPLES
Long Island has had cultural encounters in
forced labor and has made cultural and
political efforts to raise awareness of this
history. Interactions between Africans and
American Indians on Long Island predate
the arrival of slavery in the area. Jan
Rodrigues, described as a free mulatto from
Santo Domingo in the employ of explorers
seeking to dominate the area’s fur trade,
spent the winters of 1613 and 1614 with
the East Rockaway Indians and reportedly
fathered some children among them.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 781 ---
LONG ISLAND:AFRICAN AMERICANS AND NATIVE PEOPLES 705
Soon after that, Africans and Long
Island Indians encountered each other in
situations of forced labor. African slaves,
shipped north from Virginia, were im-
ported to New Netherland by the Dutch
West India Company as early as 1626 in an
attempt to bolster the agricultural develop-
ment of the colony. By the late 1640s, New
Netherlanders were privately importing
slaves from Angola and the Dutch colony
of Curaçao, where slaves had already been
conditioned to plantation existence and
were therefore in far more demand than
those coming directly from Africa. In 1664,
the area came under the control of the
English, whose policy was to promote the
importation of African slaves. Some Long
Island Indians were enslaved alongside
Africans, and many more were forced into
indentured servitude. Enslavement of Long
Island Indians was ofﬁcially prohibited in
1679, but continued for much longer.
Enslaved Indians and Africans were
allies in some recorded incidents of resis-
tance against whites. In 1657, a group of
Shinnecock men were accused of burning
down several homes in Southampton, and
later they implicated a fellow slave, an
African woman, in planning the arson. In
1708, two slaves, one an African woman
and the other an Indian man, were con-
victed of murdering their owner and his
family. Later, four blacks and two Indians
were taken into custody under suspicion of
having played a role in the plot. Both inci-
dents led to legal measures on the part of
the colonial government that further lim-
ited the freedoms of blacks and Indians.
In addition to slaves, Long Island had a
population of free blacks who had gained
their freedom by working off periods of
indenture, were manumitted by owners, or
had purchased their freedom. They also
intermarried with Long Island Indian
populations, so much so that in the late
1700s local and tribal governments occa-
sionally enacted laws to prevent blacks
from settling on Indian reservations. In the
1780s, the Mohegan missionary Samson
Occom led many Long Island and New
England Christian Indians to upstate New
York in what is known as the Brothertown
Movement. Blacks and Indians with black
ancestry were speciﬁcally excluded from
this migration.
The end of slavery in New York began
in 1799 with the passing of the Gradual
Manumission Act, which freed those slaves
born after July 4, 1799, once they reached
the age of twenty-eight (males) or twenty-
ﬁve (females). The Act of 1817 declared
that slaves born before that date would
gain their freedom July 4, 1827. In addi-
tion to the slave population, New York had
a large class of free blacks throughout this
time.
During the ﬁrst half of the 1800s,
blacks and Indians continued to interact in
many ways. Neighborhoods made up of
free blacks and off-reservation Indians
sprang up in many towns, including Lake
Success in Manhasset and the Freetown
neighborhood in Easthampton. Excluded
economically from many opportunities
available to whites, blacks and Indians on
eastern Long Island found work on whaling
ships. In many cases, blacks and Indians
came together in the sphere of Christian
worship. African Methodist Episcopal Zion
churches founded by black and Indian
congregations existed in Manhasset and in
the Eastville section of Sag Harbor. Some
of these churches are said to have sheltered
runaway slaves traveling the Underground
Railroad on their way to New England.
Black preachers that traveled a circuit on
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 782 ---
706 L OPES,H ENRI
Long Island also reported visiting black and
Indian congregations.
Intermarriage between the two groups
continued through the 1700s and 1800s,
leading some whites to conclude erro-
neously that Long Island’s Indians were
extinct. While Long Island Indians contin-
ued to recognize themselves as American
Indians and maintained some traditional
cultural practices, to outsiders they were
often perceived as black, and therefore no
longer Indian. Popular beliefs about race
led many whites to conclude that black
“blood” essentially erased any remaining
Indian characteristics. While many African
American Long Islanders have American
Indian ancestors, and many Long Island
Indians have African ancestry, the racial
categories used by whites in the nineteenth
and twentieth centuries also incorrectly
made it appear that the two groups, African
Americans and American Indians, had
conﬂated into one general “colored” popu-
lation. For example, the census taken on
the Unkechaug reservation in 1860 records
several families as Indian. In the 1880 cen-
sus, the very same families are identiﬁed as
“black” or “mulatto.” Clearly, the percep-
tions of the census taker changed, not the
ethnicity of the family. This belief that
Long Island’s Indian heritage had been di-
luted or erased by intermarriage with blacks
was also exhibited in newspaper articles and
early ethnographic studies that focused on
the physical appearance of individuals
rather than on continued indigenous cul-
tural practices.
These attitudes often had disastrous
consequences for the tribes. In 1910, the
Montauk tribe ﬁled a lawsuit against the
developers of the Long Island Rail Road,
charging them with treaty violations. The
developers’ defense rested heavily on the
argument that the Montauks had intermar-
ried with blacks to the point that they were
no long Montauk, and the judge agreed
with them. The Unkechaug faced similar
legal challenges to their identity as Indians,
one involving educational aid from the
state and one involving residency on
the reservation. In both cases, the Indians
were challenged on the basis that they were
black, not Indian.
Since the 1970s many of the surviving
Indian communities on Long Island have
begun cultural and political revitalization
efforts, raising awareness of their survival
on Long Island.
Lisa Bier

LOPES,H ENRI (1937–)
Henri Lopes, a poet, writer, and political
figure, was born in Leopoldville on
September 12, 1937. As a writer and poet
in Congo (Brazzaville), he speaks about
the struggles in modern African society
and of people in the African Diaspora. He
is a mulatto through his mother and
deﬁnes himself as “sans identité ﬁxe” (i.e.,
without stable identity). As a francophone
writer and diplomat, he is convinced that
French unites Africans and has become an
African language; his work explores the
unities of Africans on both sides of the
Atlantic.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 783 ---
LOPES,H ENRI 707
Lopes spent his childhood in Brazzaville,
where he attended school before moving to
Bangui and Nantes. At Paris-Sorbonne he
completed an MA in history. He taught in
France for two years before returning to the
Congo in 1965. He then taught at the Ecole
Normale Supérieure in Brazzaville. He was
appointed national director of education be-
fore becoming minister of the same depart-
ment in 1969. Lopes was prime minister of
the Congo from 1973 to 1976, ﬁnance min-
ister from 1977 to 1980. After leaving his
national posts, he worked for sixteen years as
deputy director, then director general of
UNESCO in Paris. Since 1998 he has been
ambassador of the Republic of Congo to
France, England, Spain, Portugal, and the
Vatican.
Lopes’ literary career started in 1966
with a collection of poetry, but he soon
opted to write prose. His topics are in-
spired by the ordinary life of modern
African society and include dictatorship,
the illegal enrichment of leaders and the
elite, corruption, and the misery of the
masses. His characters are striking, such as
the desperate poor, the smart prostitute,
and the inhumane tyrant. His aim is to
moralize in what he thinks to be a deca-
dent society. Tribaliks: Contemporary Con-
golese Stories (1971) presents eight novellas
describing society and individuals; it won
the Grand Prix Littéraire d’Afrique Noire
in 1972. Nouvelle Romance (1976) is a
novel about the condition of women. Sans
T am-T am(1977) can be seen as an attempt
to decolonize the mind. Pleurer-Rire
(1982), translated as The Laughing Cry: An
African Cock and Bull Story (1987), de-
scribes the abusive rule of President Bwaka
Mabé who came to power by putsch. Le
chercheur d’Afriques (1990) is the story of
André Leclerc, a young mulatto student
whose father, a former colonial agent in
Africa, lives in Nantes, formerly a center of
the slave trade. Sur l’Autre Rive (1992) is
an artistic and existential quest for identity
of a young lady torn between Africa and
America. The Lily and the Blazing (1997)
tells the life story of Simone Fragonard, di-
rectly linked to the mulatto community
living across the banks of the Congo River.
Dossier classé (2002) follows a similar
theme.
In 2003, Lopes published an autobio-
graphical work, Ma grand-mère bantoue et
mes ancêtres les Gaulois: Simples discours,
which fully opens up a dialogue of cultures.
Deﬁning himself as a citizen of the world,
he describes his afﬁnity with the African
Diaspora of the United Sates and the
Caribbean represented by writers such as
Richard Wright, Langston Hughes, James
Baldwin, and Nicolàs Guillén: “Ils con-
stituent une partie des Afriques que décou-
vre le ‘chercheur’ d’un de mes romans.”
[They are part of the Africas that the
‘seeker’ of one of my novels discovers.] 
(Ma grand-mère, 2003, p. 16). Borges and
Pessoa inspire him as well.
In Sur l’Autre Rive the narrator is the
writer himself in the skin of a female artist.
Marie-Eve, a young Congolese, immigrates
to Guadeloupe and presents herself as a
Caribbean artist. The protagonist, by so
doing, disqualiﬁes Africa from its pedestal
as the native land of all blacks and gives up
her African heritage to adopt a Caribbean
identity. From an inner dream, the journey
becomes real when the artist joins the other
shore.
In his career Henri Lopes has received
many prominent awards, such as the Fran-
cophonie Prize of the French Academy,
and many international distinctions. He
is a member of the High Council of

LORDE,A UDRE (1934–1992)
Audre Lorde was an African American les-
bian poet and essayist whose works engage
multiple female cultures of the African
Diaspora. For the poet and feminist Audre
Lorde, writing was an act of war against
hegemonic racial and gendered discourses.
As a black lesbian, speaking from the
vantage point of one doubly negated in
American society, Lorde deﬁned her life as
a revolutionary endeavor. She believed the
search for the self involved at the profound-
est of levels a war against those forces that
would prevent one from naming that self.
Lorde found both the strength and the
words to wage that war in multiple female
and feminist traditions of the African
Atlantic, including the Caribbean Creole
heritage of her Grenadian mother from
which she renamed herself in her 1982
autobiography Zami: A New Spelling of My
Name.
Audre Geraldine Lorde was born in
1934 and raised in New York by parents
who had migrated from Grenada ten years
earlier. They were a working-class couple
with a strong marriage and very clear ideas
about raising their American-born daugh-
ter in a manner rooted in the cultural her-
itage of their Caribbean past. Like many
other Afro-Caribbean women writers of the
eighties, Lorde had a mother who played an
early and formative role in the poet’s com-
mitment to writing. In her autobiography,
Lorde described her teenage struggles with
her mother as the ﬁrst engagement of many
battles to come, in this instance, a battle to
assert her own deﬁnitions of self and home
against her mother’s experiences and per-
ceptions shaped by a life of exile. Writing
became both the means by which Lorde
ﬁrst distanced herself from her mother’s
strong inﬂuence and then later, the very
bridge that reconnected her to multiple fe-
male cultures of the African Diaspora from
which she could draw new cultural and
spiritual meanings.
These very meanings shaped Lorde’s
feminist politics and poetics. Cited by
many as a central voice in the development
of contemporary feminist theory, Lorde’s
contributions to the ﬁeld lay in her insis-
tence in placing American feminism, as
practiced by both black and white women,
in dialogue with the feminisms of other
women throughout the African Diaspora,
and in dialogue with a gay politics of
sexuality. Lorde ﬁrst dared to question the
“politics of location” of white American
feminism in the 1980s, interrogating white
feminists’ inability to locate themselves
and their own gendered and racialized
politics vis à vis women in Africa, the
Caribbean, and closest to home, African
America. Throughout her career Lorde
ceaselessly traveled, both physically and
psychically, integrating into her own life
and work the different experiences of black
women throughout the African Atlantic,
in locations as disparate as Mexico,
Grenada, Ghana, Germany, and Russia.
Her black feminist poetics has become a
bridge connecting women in far-flung
places across the Diaspora. In addition to
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 785 ---
LOST BOYS OF SUDAN 709
her critical contributions to and expansion
of American feminist theory and practice,
Lorde should be considered one of the
central foremothers in an emerging
transnational network of feminists of
color, women across the colonial and
postcolonial worlds who have been able to
share and understand their diverse experi-
ences while discovering together the tools
to dismantle the oppressions that continue
to master them.
The “black woman warrior poet” (as
Lorde ﬁrst named herself) fought her ﬁnal
battle in 1992, dying of liver cancer at the
age of 58. In her battle with cancer, Lorde’s
writing became her weapon and armor.
Accustomed to using her words to ﬁght the
enemy without, from the mid-1970s Lorde
turned to ﬁghting the enemy within, pub-
lishing The Cancer Journals in 1980 and
adding breast cancer survivor to her list of
names and identities. Lorde’s account of
her deeply personal battle to face down
despair in the face of her own mortality
provided new lessons in the use of words as
tools to ﬁght the oppressions which, still
too silently, constrain the lives of women
in communities throughout the African
Atlantic.
Michelle Stephens

LOST BOYS OF SUDAN
The Lost Boys of Sudan are the approxi-
mately 20,000 orphaned refugees, both
young men and women, left behind in the
aftermath of north-south conflict in
modern-day Sudan. Many young men were
sent abroad to the United States and
Europe, where they sought greater eco-
nomic opportunities, but also experienced
many cultural conﬂicts. In 2001, a group of
about 3,600 Lost Boys, all young men,
arrived in the United States.
In the late 1980s, the Khartoum-based
northern government of Sudan proclaimed
itself an Islamic state and named Christians
and non-Muslims enemies of the state. The
Islamic government identiﬁed and pursued
the Dinka people of southern Sudan as
“separatists” and conducted raids on
villages in the south. In the attacks, men,
women, and children were assaulted and
murdered. Many thousands of young men
and women ﬂed for hundreds of miles over
difﬁcult terrain with few supplies and in
constant danger. Those who escaped were
taken to refugee camps in Kenya. Aid orga-
nizations described them as “Lost Boys,” a
reference to Peter Pan’s crew of orphans.
Many young men were subsequently sent
abroad to the United States and Europe.
Abroad, they experienced the strain of cul-
tural adjustment and of loyalties divided
between those who remained in the refugee
camps and to their new “home.” The

they sought sometimes proved elusive.
