LOUVERTURE,TOUSSAINT
BRÉDA(CA. 1743–1803)
T oussaint Bréda Louverture, a leader of the
Haitian Revolution, was born a slave in
Saint-Domingue (modern-day Haiti) and
became a general in the French army and
the governor of Saint-Domingue before
dying in exile in France. He became a
heroic symbol of black emancipation from
colonial rule for African Americans and the
African Diaspora.
Louverture’s Upbringing 
(ca. 1743–1789)
Louverture was born around 1743 in Saint-
Domingue, which from 1697 to 1804 was
a colony of France. Louverture’s father was
the second son of Gaou-Guinou (or Gaou-
Guinée), chief of the Arada (or Allada)
nation in Dahomey (modern-day Benin).
Louverture’s father was captured in com-
bat, sold as a slave, and fathered ﬁve sons
and three daughters (Louverture was the
eldest son). Louverture himself was born
near Cap Français and thus qualiﬁed as an
American-born Creole (as opposed to the
African-born bossales).
The young Louverture worked as a
slave on the Bréda plantation and may have
belonged either to its absentee owner, the
Comte de Noé, or to its manager, Baillon
de Libertat. While a slave, T oussaint mar-
ried black freedwoman Suzanne Simon-
Baptiste, who already had a son, Placide,
from a mulatto called Séraphin. Louverture
adopted the mixed-blood Placide and had
two more sons, Isaac and Saint-Jean.
Louverture’s exact physical appearance
remains uncertain, for the many portraits
that depict him lack consistency (he was
given the nickname fatras bâton, which ap-
plied to lanky men). Spared the strenuous
ﬁeld tasks associated with sugarcane culti-
vation, Louverture oversaw the plantation’s
draft animals (contemporaries described
him as a coachman or as a veterinarian).
Louverture spoke French, some un-
speciﬁed African language, and the local
creole. He may have been taught to read
before the revolution, but his written
French remained tentative throughout his
T oussaint L ’Ouverture led the Haitian uprising that
gave rise to the ﬁrst independent black nation in the
Western Hemisphere. He became and remains an
important symbol of liberation for peoples throughout
the African Diaspora. (Library of Congress)
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 787 ---
LOUVERTURE,TOUSSAINT BRÉDA 711
life and he later relied on white secretaries
for his correspondence. T radition has it that
he was inspired by Abbé Raynal’s Histoire
philosophique et politique des établissements
et du commerce des Européens dans les deux
Indes (1774), in which Raynal predicted
that a black Spartacus would one day lead a
slave revolt in the Caribbean. Recent re-
search, however, indicates that Louverture
was freed in 1776 and settled down on a
plantation of his own as a free-colored
planter exploiting slave labor. His alleged
aristocratic ancestry, local birth, education,
marriage, and early emancipation made
him one of the more privileged elements
among Saint-Domingue’s black population
on the eve of the French Revolution.
Louverture’s Participation 
in the Revolt against France
(1791–1794)
The beginning of the French Revolution in
1789 had important implications in Saint-
Domingue. White republicans fought
conservative monarchists afraid of the
revolution’s increasingly radical tone. Free
mulattos, inspired by the 1789 Declaration
of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen,
fought against segregation rules that treated
them as second-class citizens. The slaves,
representing 90 percent of the colony’s pop-
ulation, revolted in August 1791 following
a Voodoo ceremony in Bois Caïman on the
Le Normand plantation in Morne Rouge.
Within a few weeks, 100,000 slaves were in
arms on Saint-Domingue’s northern plain.
Louverture later depicted himself as a
lifelong advocate of freedom to appeal to his
black brethren, but his conduct in the early
days of the slave revolt was far more cau-
tious. A devout Catholic, he probably did
not attend the Voodoo gathering at Bois
Caïman. Instead, he helped his former mas-
ter Baillon de Libertat and his family escape
unharmed from their plantation. Only then
did he join the ranks of the slave army as a
surgeon. The rebel army’s leadership initially
consisted of Dutty Boukman, who was
quickly executed by the French, Jeannot
Bullet, who was executed by his own for ex-
cessive cruelty, Jean François, Jean-Jacques
Dessalines, and Georges Biassou.
Louverture, acting as Biassou’s aide-de-
camp, helped draft a proposal in December
1791 to halt the revolt in exchange for a
few concessions, but the planters of Cap
Français rejected the plan and the ﬁghting
continued. Louverture, Biassou, and
Dessalines joined the Spanish forces of
Santo Domingo (modern-day Dominican
Republic) as auxiliaries when Spain de-
clared war on France in 1793. Spain pro-
moted Louverture to colonel and gave him
his own troops. Great Britain, also at war
with France, seized the major ports of
Saint-Domingue in 1793–1794.
Faced with monarchist opposition, a
slave revolt, and two foreign invasions,
French commissioner Félicité-Léger Son-
thonax abolished slavery in Saint-Domingue
on August 29, 1793. This bold move, which
the French National Assembly ratiﬁed and
extended to other French colonies on
February 4, 1794, was designed to attract
black soldiers into French ranks, but
Louverture fought for Spain until May 1794.
Only then did he turn against his Spanish
patrons and rally to the French army. He
may have switched sides because his rela-
tionship with his superiors had deteriorated
to the point that Jean François brieﬂy threw
him in prison in 1793; or he may ﬁnally
have become a convert to the idea of general
emancipation.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 788 ---
712 L OUVERTURE,TOUSSAINT BRÉDA
General and Governor of 
Saint-Domingue (1794–1802)
Continued instability in France and the
high death rate among white ofﬁcers in the
tropical climate quickly made Louverture
and his black soldiers France’s most potent
military force in the Caribbean. In his
memoirs, Louverture emphasized that he
had been injured seventeen times and that
a cannon ball had knocked off his front
teeth (the gap in his teeth is one of the rea-
sons given for his nickname l’ouverture,
French for “opening”). But accounts of in-
dividual battles in which Louverture was
involved do not support the claim that he
was an exceptionally gifted general. His
political acumen, however, was keen.
Louverture befriended General Etienne
Laveaux, who promoted him to brigadier
general, and then division general, which
made him the highest-ranked nonwhite
ofﬁcer in the island. Louverture cleverly
maneuvered to send white generals and
civilian commissioners, including Laveaux,
Sonthonax, and Gabriel d’Hédouville, back
to France under various pretexts.
In August 1798, Louverture single-
handedly negotiated a treaty with Brigadier
General Thomas Maitland under which
England, whose losses in Saint-Domingue
had reached 13,000 dead, would turn over
British-occupied towns to Louverture’s
army. In exchange, Louverture allowed
British merchant ships in the colony despite
France’s mercantilist trade rules and its on-
going war with England. Louverture also
undermined French plans to attack British
Jamaica for fear this would divert troops
from the Saint-Domingue theater. Maitland
secretly suggested that Louverture should
break from France and declare himself king
of Saint-Domingue under British protec-
tion, but Louverture declined the offer.
Despite France’s quasi-war with the
United States (1798–1801), Louverture
also signed an April 1799 agreement with
the United States that put an end to French
privateering and opened Haitian ports to
U.S. ships. In exchange, Louverture ob-
tained crucial U.S. naval support during
the siege of Jacmel in the War of the South
(1799–1800). The bloody war, which pit-
ted Louverture against mulatto general
André Rigaud, ended in the defeat of the
powerful mulatto party that had domi-
nated the south of Saint-Domingue.
Afraid that France could use Spanish
Santo Domingo as a base to attack Saint-
Domingue and remove him from ofﬁce,
Louverture invaded Santo Domingo in
1800. Philippe Roume de Saint-Laurent,
France’s last white civilian commissioner,
was increasingly marginalized for opposing
the invasion, imprisoned, and then ex-
pelled in 1801. That year, Louverture in-
structed his supporters to draft a constitu-
tion that made him governor-general for
life and gave him the right to choose his
successor. Louverture now controlled Saint-
Domingue quasi-independently, though he
continued to pay lip service to the colony’s
links with France.
Convinced that continued production
of sugar and coffee was essential to the
economic survival of Saint-Domingue,
Louverture kept some of the features of the
prerevolutionary social order. The 1801
constitution institutionalized a system of
forced labor under which former black
slaves, now known as cultivateurs, were
forced to remain on their plantations in ex-
change for a share of the crop. Louverture
also incited exiled white planters to return
to Saint-Domingue because their technical
and managerial expertise was essential to
the revival of sugar exports.

LUMUMBA,PATRICE 713
Capture, Exile, and Death
(1802–1803)
Afraid that the 1801 constitution was the
ﬁrst step on the path to Saint-Domingue’s
independence, First Consul Napoléon
Bonaparte summoned a massive expedition
as soon as a temporary peace with England
made it possible to ship French troops
across the Atlantic. The expedition, num-
bering 20,000 men and led by Bonaparte’s
brother-in-law General Victor Leclerc,
landed in Cap Français in February 1802.
French troops were ofﬁcially instructed to
reinforce Louverture’s, but Louverture ac-
cused them, with good reason, of coming
to Saint-Domingue to remove him from
power and restore slavery. He instructed his
men to ﬁght holding battles, to destroy
buildings and supplies, to retire to the
island’s mountainous interior, and to wait
for yellow fever and malaria to take their
toll. Intense ﬁghting followed, most notably
during the siege of Crête à Pierrot, after
which Louverture and Leclerc signed a
ceaseﬁre (May 1802).
Louverture was allowed to retire to his
plantation at Ennery, but the French ac-
cused him of plotting a second uprising
and captured him in June 1802. Exiled on
board the Héroswith his family, Louverture
was sent to Brest, then to the Fort de Joux
in the Jura Mountains. There, he experi-
enced humiliation and mistreatment moti-
vated in part by his refusal to reveal where
he had hidden the funds he had accumu-
lated as governor. Hungry, cold, and old, he
died of pneumonia in his cell on April 7,
1803. But his strategy ultimately paid off
when the French, decimated by tropical
fevers and guerilla warfare, abandoned Cap
Français in November 1803.
Louverture was a complex character,
torn between his African roots, French
ideals of the Enlightenment, and the reac-
tionary colonial order. But in death, he was
lionized as a single-minded martyr of free-
dom in various works by the poets William
Wordsworth and Alphonse de Lamartine,
the abolitionist Victor Schoelcher, and the
historian C. L. R. James.
Philippe R. Girard

LUMUMBA,PATRICE
(1925–1961)
A political leader and popular hero of African
liberation struggles, Patrice Lumumba was
born in the Kasai province of what was then
the Belgian Congo. Despite receiving only an
elementary education as a child, Lumumba
went to work in Leopoldville (now Kinshasa)
and Stanleyville (now Kisangani) as a
journalist.
In 1955 Lumumba joined the Belgian
Liberal Party. He also became regional pres-
ident of a Congolese trade union associa-
tion. In 1958 he increased his political
involvement, helping to found the
Mouvement National Congolais (MNC).
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 790 ---
714 L UMUMBA,PATRICE
The MNC emerged from the local elec-
tions of December 1959 with a strong
majority, despite the fact that Lumumba,
the MNC leader, was under arrest. The
1959 elections were crucial given that
Belgian authorities had just announced a
ﬁve-year timetable for Congo’s indepen-
dence. During the 1960 conference in
Belgium to establish the terms of indepen-
dence, Lumumba played an important part
in pushing the Belgians to move up the
date of independence to June 1960, follow-
ing May elections to establish a govern-
ment. On June 23, 1960, the MNC
formed the independent Congo’s ﬁrst gov-
ernment, with Lumumba as the country’s
ﬁrst popularly elected prime minister and
Joseph Kasavuba as president.
Lumumba’s leadership was immediately
opposed by the Belgian colonialists, as well
as the U.S. government and corporations
with interests in the Congo’s vast resources.
In June 1960, the mineral-rich Katanga
province, under Moise Tshombe, backed by
the Belgians, seceded from Congo. With
few alternatives, and facing U.S. opposition
within the United Nations to his rule,
Lumumba turned to the Soviet Union for
aid. While Lumumba’s politics were those
of a social democrat, the turn to the Soviets,
a move made out of practical necessity,
strengthened the view, especially among
Patrice Lumumba speaking with supporters in Congo on October 15, 1960. The ﬁrst prime minister of the
Democratic Republic of Congo, Lumumba inspired many as a voice of African national independence and
anticolonialism. (Library of Congress)

U.S. government leaders, that Lumumba
was a communist. Documents later released
reveal that the view of Lumumba as a com-
munist contributed to Eisenhower’s call for

In September, after only 67 days in
ofﬁce, Lumumba was illegally dismissed
from ofﬁce by Kasavubu. On September

Mobutu Sese Seko, who would terrorize
the country for three decades. Lumumba

was taken to Katanga province and turned
over to his archenemy Tshombe. A Soviet
resolution before the UN Security Council
calling for Lumumba’s release was defeated
eight votes to two. On January 17, 1961,
Patrice Lumumba was executed by a
squad consisting of Belgian ofﬁcers and
Katangan authorities.
A martyr for African liberation upon his
death, Lumumba remains a powerful sym-
bol of anticolonial and anti-imperialist
struggles. His principled opposition to
exploitation and oppression have made
Lumumba an icon for resistance movements
globally.

MAD MULLAH (1864–1920)
“Mad Mullah” is the term the British gave
to Mohammed bin Abdullah Hassan, a
ﬁgure central to Somalia’s national war of
liberation, and who is seen as an early
jihadist. He was born in the Ogaden region
of what was then called British Somaliland.
T utored by his father and other sheiks
in childhood, Hassan, as a young man,
went on trading voyages. In Egypt he was
inspired by stories of the Mahdi in the
Sudan. While in Mecca for the hajj he
joined the Salihiya tariqa, a puritanical Suﬁ
sect with strict beliefs and dervish practices.
In the 1890s, Hassan returned to Somalia.
He settled in the Nogal Valley where his
preaching, conducted with great rhetorical
and poetic skill, made him the mullah of
the Salihiya, and the leader of a movement
to expel the inﬁdel from Somalia. In 1899,
he attacked Burao, a trading center, begin-
ning his ﬁrst jihad.
In October 1902, the British defeated
the Mullah’s forces at Erigo. On February
22, 1903, the Mullah defeated a British
force at Bumburu. In subsequent battles,
the Mullah’s dervishes were usually de-
feated by British forces. In early 1905, the
Mullah was driven into Italian Somalia and
forced to sign a peace agreement.
In 1907, the Mad Mullah launched his
second jihad against the British. Fighting
M
continued, with victories and defeats on
both sides, until 1920, when the British
brought a squadron of airplanes from the
Western Front. After his headquarters at
Taleh was bombed, he ﬂed to Ethiopia
where he soon died. However, the death of
the Mad Mullah did not stop his inﬂuence.
He has been enshrined in Somali lore as an
early hero of Somali liberation.
Andrew J. Waskey

MADAGASCAR
The fourth largest island in the world, the
Republic of Madagascar has been a long-
standing trade partner of the United States
and is of strategic importance because of
its proximity to the island of Diego Garcia
in the Indian Ocean. It has a population of
approximately 18,400,000. The nation
was a French colony beginning in 1896
and gained full independence in 1960 as
the Malagasy Republic. It was renamed
Madagascar in 1975.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 794 ---
718 M ADAGASCAR
Madagascar’s ﬁrst contact with Euro-
peans began in 1500 because of the slave
trade. In the nineteenth century, under the
rule of the Merina monarchy, Madagascar
developed strong diplomatic relations with
the United States. T rade with the Americans
increased along with American inﬂuence in
the region’s whaling industry.
In the 1950s, American aid was of-
fered, including an economic survey of the
Lake Alaotra region. After independence,
Malagasy ofﬁcials visited the United States
in search of private investments. American
scientiﬁc and trade missions also visited
Madagascar. In July 1963, the United
States agreed to support American private
investments in the island. While some of
the island’s legislators were skeptical of
American motives, many Malagasy were
pleased to have investment from beyond
their former colonial rulers.
In 1964, Madagascar took on new
importance as an alternative location for an
American satellite-tracking station that was
removed from Zanzibar. Subsequently,
American ﬁnancial aid to Madagascar grew
to about $3.5 million in value. The aid
promoted rural-welfare programs, trained
manpower, helped in secondary-road
building, and equipped the gendarmerie, a
paramilitary force. This massive American
aid was meant to preclude Soviet and
Chinese communist inﬂuences in the region
and protect Western security. Nonetheless,
from 1978 until 1991, Madagascar aligned
with socialist and radical regimes, includ-
ing Cuba, Libya, Iran, and North Korea.
In the 1980s, Madagascar abandoned
communism in favor of a market economy
and a democratic constitution. Successful
political and economic reforms in the
1990s resulted in renewed U.S. support.
Madagascar further strengthened ties with
Canada, Brazil, and Europe. The U.S.-
funded Leland Madagascar Ground Sta-
tion, inaugurated in 1997, is one major
fruit of the cooperation between the
United States and Madagascar. Because of
the Leland project, the telecommunica-
tions sector in Madagascar is now equipped
with modern technology.
Several American trade delegations
have visited the island since 2003 and U.S.
trade missions have signed twelve commit-
ments with the government of Madagascar
to explore investment opportunities. With
the United States as one of its principal
trade partners, Madagascar was the ﬁrst
country to beneﬁt from the Millennium
Challenge Account (MCA), an American
aid program.
Madagascar is also important to the
United States because of the military base
on Diego Garcia, northeast of the nation.
Diego Garcia was a key military facility
during the Cold War and is now indispens-
able for American interventions in the
Middle East.
Philip A. Ojo

MADHI (1844–1885)
The Madhi is the name for a historical ﬁg-
ure, Muhammad Ahmad, who successfully
waged a war of liberation for Khartoum in
1881, as well as an eschatological ﬁgure in
both the Sunni and Shi’a traditions of
Islam. The historical ﬁgure was born in
1844 as the son of boat builders. Ahmad
pursued religious studies and held a strong
interest in Suﬁsm. In both the Sunni and
Shi’a abstractions of Islam, the Madhi was
viewed as a redemptive ﬁgure or deliverer
on par with Christ in their respective escha-
tological frameworks. 
In 1871, Ahmad moved to Aba Island,
where he built a mosque. Subsequently he
traveled throughout Sudan for ten years,
where he noted the Sudanese people’s ha-
tred of the Ottoman Egyptians who ruled
Sudan. In 1881, Muhammad Ahmad pro-
claimed himself al-Mahdi al-Muntazar and
raised an army known as the Ansar, in def-
erence to the residents of Medina who wel-
comed the Prophet Muhammad during the
Hijrah. For three years, Ahmad won battles
throughout the Sudan and consolidated his
power. Charles George Gordon, who had
been appointed governor-general of Sudan
by Khedive Ismail, was placed in the pre-
carious position of trying to organize a
withdrawal of Khartoum while fending off
Ahmad. Khartoum fell and Gordon was
killed in January 1885, at which point the
Madhi formed a government. Ahmad re-
quired that all Muslims add to their statement
of faith, the Shahada, that “Muhammad
Ahmad is the Mahdi of God and the repre-
sentative of His Prophet,” in effect equat-
ing him with the Prophet Muhammad.
This requirement would be short-lived as
Ahmad died from typhus six months after
the fall of Khartoum. However, the career
and movements of the Mahdi would be
carefully studied by Islamist intellectuals,
such as Abdullah Azzam, Safar al-Hawali,
and Ayman al-Zawahiri, as they formulated
their own eschatological framework which
would be carried out by their Mahdi heir
apparent: Osama bin Laden.
Ojan Aryanfard

Islamic Understanding of Death and

MALAWI
The land-locked Republic of Malawi was
originally the British protectorate of Nyasa-
land. Surrounded by Zambia, Tanzania,
and Mozambique, the eastern part of the
country is dominated by Lake Nyasa (or
Lake Malawi). Malawi has a population of
approximately 11,907,000. Historically,
U.S. and British missionary activities have
been prominent in the country. British
missionary activity started in 1874 and a
consul was appointed nine years later. In
1889 a small protectorate was established,
and enlarged in 1891 to cover the western
shore of Lake Nyasa. From 1893 until
1907, it was called the British Central
African Protectorate, but then reverted to
its original name of Nyasaland, which it re-
tained until independence. U.S. missionar-
ies were always active in Malawi, with the
National Baptist Convention sending staff
from 1895; the African Methodist Episcopal
Church from 1900; the Assemblies of God
from 1930; the Church of the Nazarene
and the United Presbyterian Church of

In the early twentieth century, two

in about 1889, arrived in the United States

went to Indiana University and then to the
University of Chicago, graduating in 1931.
He then went to Meharry Medical School,
afterward moving to Britain, where he was
a physician in Liverpool during World
War II.
In 1938, the Rhodesia-Nyasaland
Royal Commission was established to in-

between Northern and Southern Rhodesia
and Nyasaland. It included in its members
Patrick Ashley Cooper, who subsequently
moved to Argentina where he became the
chairman and managing director of the
province of Buenos Aires Waterworks
Company Ltd., director of the Argentine
T ransadine Railway Company Ltd., and
member of the Argentine Chamber of
Commerce Advisory Board.
In 1953, Nyasaland was joined with
Northern Rhodesia and Southern Rhodesia
to form the Federation of Rhodesia and
Nyasaland. However, Nyasaland was a re-
luctant member. This reluctance led to the
dissolution of the federation in 1963.
Malawi gained status as an independent
member of the British Commonwealth on
July 6, 1964, and two years later, on July 6,
1966, became the Republic of Malawi,
with Hastings Banda as its ﬁrst president.
Initially relations between the Banda
government and the United States were
good. However, the U.S. Peace Corps,

MALCOLM X (1925–1965)
Malcolm X was a minister for the Nation
of Islam, a convert to orthodox Islam, and
a world leader of the cause of African
Americans. Malcolm Little was born in
Omaha, Nebraska, in 1925 to an active
Baptist preacher whom white supremacists
killed in 1931. Malcolm had a troubled
beginning in life. He withdrew from
school at age 15 because of discrimination.
He was put into many foster homes due
to his behavior, later joining his sister
in Boston. He worked at several places in
Boston and New York. He also engaged
in many criminal activities, which landed
him in jail in 1946 for carrying ﬁrearms,
larceny, and burglary. It was at the prison
that he had his salvation. There, he joined
the Nation of Islam (NOI), which
preached that blacks were superior to the
white men who were devils and that Islam
was the religion of the blacks. In prison,
Malcolm X, an African American Muslim leader
during the civil rights era, gave voice to ideals of
African American and Pan-African self-determination
through economic and cultural independence. He
was assassinated on February 21, 1965. (Library
of Congress)
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 798 ---
722 M ALCOLM X
Malcolm learned and improved himself
educationally before his release in 1952.
On leaving prison, he worked at several
jobs in Detroit and became active in the
NOI. He was shortly appointed a minister
at the NOI due to his fervent energy and
his electrifying oratorical skills. He changed
his name to Malcolm X and made it his
mission to ﬁght against racism, cruel treat-
ment of blacks, and shaking off the yoke of
slavery imposed upon blacks.
Malcolm was imbued with the idea of
Black Nationalism, which he had inher-
ited from his father, a follower of Marcus
Garvey, the Jamaican activist who insisted
that Africans abroad should go back to
Africa and build it. Malcolm saw a great
connection between African Americans
and Africans: in his view they were the
same people who shared the same culture
and heritage, and yet were subjugated col-
lectively by white people. He believed that
freedom for Africans in the Diaspora was
tantamount to freedom for all blacks all
over the world; they were one people sep-
arated against their will. They shared the
same values, culture, arts, music, and
identity, and therefore, they needed to
work together to liberate themselves.
Malcolm also argued that since many of
the slaves brought to the New World were
Muslims, African Americans should em-
brace Islam because it is the religion of
their ancestors. 
Malcolm’s unconditional love for
blacks and his fervent desire to unite
Africans led him to visit Ghana, Nigeria,
Morocco, and Senegal in 1959 to
strengthen his relationship with African
peoples and their leaders and to afﬁrm their
common heritage and culture. He believed
that black Americans and Africans would
prosper and resume their respected roles in
world affairs if they united. T o put this
belief into practice, he helped establish the
Organization of the African Unity (OAU)
in Addis Ababa to unite all Africans. As he
described it in his autobiography, African
leaders and the masses received him warmly
and accorded him great respect, something
he had never enjoyed before. The Africans
actually regarded his visit a blessing, and
they were so impressed with him that they
nicknamed him “omowale”—“a son who
returns home.”
In America, Malcolm had been an
ardent follower of Elijah Muhammad, the
leader of the NOI. The relationship broke
down after Malcolm made derogatory
comments about the death of President
John Kennedy. Malcolm felt stiﬂed by the
authoritarian organization of the NOI and
decided to leave the group rather than
being silenced by Elijah Muhammad after
his excommunication for ninety days. He
founded his own movement in Harlem in
1964 and called it Muslim Mosque.
In April 1964, Malcolm visited Mecca
and performed the Islamic pilgrimage. The
journey was a spiritual discovery and en-
lightenment for him. At Mecca, he joined
millions of Muslims in prayer, standing
shoulder to shoulder and wearing the same
gown to show the equality of all human be-
ings before God. He confessed that he had
never before seen sincere and true brother-
hood practiced as he witnessed it in Mecca,
for all pilgrims related to one another
peacefully regardless of their color. He
found that Islam was not exclusively for
the blacks, but for all human beings. Thus,
he renounced his previous erroneous
charges against white men that they were
devils. He boldly and publicly apologized
for his previous misjudgment of all the
white people.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 799 ---
MALE REVOLT 723
Upon his return to America in July
1964, Malcolm preached a new message of
peace, accommodation, and tolerance. He
became a witty person, a reformed leader,
who perceived all human beings as equal.
He reverted to the true orthodox Islam
and adopted a new name, El-Hajj Malik
El-Shabazz. He was aﬁre with new spiritual
insight. He welcomed the white men in his
movement and fought for the rights of
blacks and oppressed people.
However, Malcolm’s openness to the
white men, his accommodation of all blacks,
and his change from a racist to a nationalist,
humanist liberator for all the oppressed peo-
ple angered some members of the Nation of
Islam who did not share his universal and ac-
commodative approach to the problems of
the blacks. Thus, he was brutally killed on
February 21, 1965, in Harlem, New York.
With his death, black Americans lost one of
their most able leaders and spokesmen.
Malcolm X was a humanist, an ambas-
sador of peace, a soul-saving leader, and a
revolutionary person who followed the
truth wherever he found it. Many books,
articles, autobiographies, ﬁlms, and doc-
toral dissertations have been written and
produced about him and his legacy, which
survives as part of a collective culture of
blacks in the modern world. Malcolm X
has been described as a shining prince. He
will never be forgotten in the history of
Africans in America. He was and still is the
source of pride for many Americans.
Yushau Sodiq

MALE REVOLT
The Male Revolt is the second largest re-
volt of freed and enslaved Africans in the
Americas, after the Haitian Revolution.
The Male Revolt happened in the city of
Salvador in the state of Bahia, Brazil, in
1835. In the conﬂict, about 70 Africans
died and about 500 were taken prisoner.
The early nineteenth century was a
period of economic decline and political
turmoil in Bahia. As a consequence, be-
tween 1816 and 1835, there were many
smaller revolts in the region. Yet, the Male
Revolt was truly extraordinary, since the
most common form of slave resistance in
Brazil was taking ﬂight instead of engag-
ing in armed revolts. The Male Revolt was
an African movement and not merely a
slave revolt. In fact, it involved both slaves
and ex-slaves almost equally in terms of
numbers.
Salvador was an urban slave society and
all of the slaves who participated in the re-
volt were wage earners. In this sense, they
had the freedom of movement to pass on
messages to individuals in other areas of the
city and the state. One characteristic of this
movement was the involvement of large
numbers of Muslim Africans. In fact, the
term “male” means African Muslim and it
probably derives from the Yoruban word
imale, meaning any African who adopted
the Islamic religion. Islam functioned as a
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 800 ---
724 M ALI
unifying force among the rebels. Muslims
organized the movement and enforced dis-
cipline in the group. They were a unifying
factor in a nonuniﬁed community. How-
ever, the rebels were not spearheading a re-
ligious revolution in the region. The Male
Revolt was not a religious war. The move-
ment had as its objective to take power
from the established elite and to give it to
the African population. Muslim slaves be-
came common in Salvador only in the ﬁrst
half of the nineteenth century, when the
slave trade to Brazil increased signiﬁcantly.
Muslims comprised an elite group within
the slave society, as some of them were reli-
gious leaders and possessed knowledge of
reading and writing. However, it seems that
they were also feared and hated by other
blacks. News of the impending revolt was
leaked to the authorities by two freed-
women, both African-born, and the revolt
was crushed at its inception. This event
illustrates the fact that there was little cohe-
sion among the African population in the
Americas. The African community in
Salvador, as well as in many other parts of
the Americas, was unable to overcome all of
its differences and divisions. Slave masters
were eager to exploit these differences in
order to prevent the uniﬁcation of a strong
group of Africans.
The people participating in the Male
Revolt believed that their enemies were not
only the whites but all of the Brazilian-born
population regardless of their race. So, any
Brazilian-born black was also considered an
enemy. The plan was to kill everyone in
Bahia who was not an African, including
whites, blacks, and mulattos. Apparently,
the mulattos who were not killed were to be
enslaved. One of the results of the revolt
was a wave of violence and racism toward
Africans in Bahia. Many peaceful Africans
were killed and persecuted by the domi-
nant population. In fact, fear of a black re-
volt was a very real aspect of Brazilian life
during the colonial period and during the
ﬁrst half of the nineteenth century. The vi-
olent slave revolution that began in Haiti in
1792 terriﬁed whites living in the many
slave societies of the Americas for many
years after the event. When the sovereignty
of the ﬁrst slave-run nation was declared in
1804, it seemed possible that a similar re-
volt could occur anywhere where enslaved
people outnumbered whites. The Male
Revolt of 1835 reinforced this fear by
clearly revealing the threat under which
Brazilian whites were living.
Rosana Barbosa

MALI
Located in West Africa, the Republic of
Mali is landlocked, dominated by the
Sahara desert, and has a population of
about 11,957,000. In medieval times, the
Mali Empire covered much of inland West
Africa. It was founded in the thirteenth
century and its capital, Timbuktu, became
a byword for a location that was remote
and inaccessible. In the late sixteenth cen-
tury, the empire started to decline but the
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 801 ---
MALI 725
aura of the place remained, although most
Europeans only had the description of a
Spanish moor, Leo Africanus, to go on.
This changed in 1816 with the publication
of The Narrative of Robert Adams, a Sailor
Who Was Wrecked on the Western Coast of
Africa, in the Year 1810, Was Detained
Three Years in Slavery by the Arabs of the
Great Desert, and Resided Several Months in
the City of T ombuctoo. The author was not,
in fact, called Robert Adams but Benjamin
Rose, an African American sailor who had
been born in Hudson, New York, and in
1813 managed to see the British Consul at
Mogador (now Essaouira, Morocco). He
said that he had been held as a slave and
wanted to return to the United States but
instead was sent to the U.S. consul at
Tangier, from where he begged his way to
London. There he met a man who had
been told that he (Rose) had seen
Timbuktu. Rose then “became” Robert
Adams. Rose/Adams was illiterate, so his
book, which described Timbuktu in nega-
tive terms, was ghost-written by Samuel
Cook, a member of the British African
Company. The book was published in Lon-
don in 1816, and republished in the fol-
lowing year in Paris and then Boston. Some
corroboration for his story emerged, and
academics still disagree on whether or not
Rose/Adams ever reached Timbuktu.
After the decline of the empire of Mali,
the French made inroads and established
the Upper River Colony, which ran from
1880 until 1890. It then became French
Sudan from 1890 until 1899. After becoming
Upper Senegal and Middle Niger for three
years, it was renamed Senegambia-Niger for
three years, and then Upper Senegal-Niger
until 1920 when it was renamed French
Sudan. The French used it for expanding the
growing of cotton. During World War I,
large numbers of men from Mali were re-
cruited into the French colonial forces and,
in the last two years of the war, some
fought alongside U.S. servicemen on the
Western Front.
As with many other colonial services,
ofﬁcials rotated around the empire and
three of the French lieutenant governors of
French Sudan had either served in, or were
to serve in, Martinique in the West Indies.
Louis Albert Grodet, lieutenant governor
of the French Sudan from 1893 until 1895
had been in Martinique 1887–1889; Louis
Jacques Fousset, governor of French Sudan
from 1931 until 1935 went on to become
governor of Martinique; and his successor,
Mathieu Maurice Alfassa, was in Martinique
when he was appointed governor of French
Sudan, a post he held until 1936.
Few people visited the French Sudan
during this period without some attempt to
get to Timbuktu. From October 1912 until
May 1913, an American, D. W . Berty, and
men of his American T rans-Saharan Expe-
dition visited the city. The house they
stayed at has been preserved and is almost
opposite the T omboctou-Boy Batouma
Museum. T wo U.S. religious groups sent
missionaries: the Christian and Missionary
Alliance in 1924; and the Evangelical
Baptist Missions from 1951. In addition,
in the early 1950s, just before the colony
became independent, U.S. anthropologist
Peter B. Hammond conducted research in
the country.
In 1958, the French Sudan voted to
become an autonomous member of the
French community, and two years later, on
September 22, 1960, became independent
as the Republic of Mali. The United States
sent Thomas Kenneth Wright to Bamako,
Mali’s capital, and he was succeeded in
1961 by William Jules Handley. One U.S.

diplomat, E. G. “Jay” Ruoff, from Cincinnati,
Ohio, wrote of his experiences in Mali
in his book Making a Difference (1997).
During the late 1990s an American gui-
tarist, Banning Eyre, went to Mali where he
immersed himself in Mali’s music, which
formed the basis of his book In Griot Time
(2000). Other musicians include those who
made up the group Afro-Jazz de Ségou,
which was popular in Cuba in the 1950s.
Cuban music was popular in Mali during
the 1960s. Since early 2000, the U.S.
government has supported Malian troops
defending the government against attack
by T uareg rebels, who have been ﬁghting
for greater recognition, developmental aid,
and political autonomy to the northern
desert region they inhabit since the early
1990s.

MANDELA,N ELSON (1918–)
Nelson Mandela is a Nobel Peace Prize re-
cipient, dismantler of apartheid, and was
the president and architect of South Africa’s
liberal constitution. Nelson Rolihlahla
Mandela was born on July 18, 1918, in
Umtata, T ranskei. Expected to follow his
father, a T embu chief, into high tribal
ofﬁce, Mandela chose rather to become a
lawyer. Expelled from one university for
joining a protest boycott, he went on to
complete his law degree and later opened
South Africa’s ﬁrst black law ﬁrm. In 1944,
Mandela joined the African National
Congress (ANC) and helped form its Youth
League (ANCYL), becoming its president
in 1950. Mandela was central to the ANC’s
adoption of a radical “Programme of Ac-
tion” which advocated civil disobedience,
strikes, and boycotts in order to attain di-
rect parliamentary representation and equal
rights for nonwhites, thereby ending
apartheid rule. In 1952, Mandela was given
Nelson Mandela was South Africa’s ﬁrst black president
(1994–1997) and a Nobel Peace Prize recipient. A
leader in the struggle to overturn South Africa’s system
of white domination and racial segregation known as
apartheid, Mandela was known throughout both Africa
and the Americas. Mandela spent 28 years as a political
prisoner in South Africa under the apartheid
government. (Courtesy: Embassy of South Africa)

a suspended sentence of nine months’ hard
labor under the Suppression of Commu-
nism Act (1950) for leading the “Deﬁance
Campaign.” Elected deputy national presi-
dent of the ANC later that year, Mandela
faced banning, arrest, and imprisonment.
He was among the accused (all of whom
were acquitted) in the protracted T reason
T rials (1956–1961). Following the Sharpeville
Massacre (1960), the government banned
the ANC and the Pan-Africanist Congress
(PAC). Debarred from peaceful political
activity, the organizations went under-
ground. Living in constant fear of arrest,
Mandela helped to organize a mass strike
and to forge, as its commander-in-chief,
the ANC’s military wing—Umkhonto we
Sizwe (“Spear of the Nation”)—in order to
mount an organized armed struggle. Hav-
ing illegally left the country, Mandela was
arrested on his return to South Africa in
1962 and was sentenced to fiv e years’ im-
prisonment. When police arrested a num-
ber of prominent ANC leaders in 1964,
Mandela, still serving his previous sentence,
was sentenced to life imprisonment—
together with seven others—for planning
armed resistance. In spite of the conﬁnes of
his Robben Island cell, Mandela (and his
then wife, Winnie, herself a political
activist) became an internationally recog-
nized symbol of the ﬁght against apartheid.
Mandela repeatedly refused a commuted
sentence or release in exchange for a public
acceptance of certain apartheid policies and
a renunciation of violence. Under F . W . De
Klerk’s presidency, Mandela was released
on February 11, 1990 (after 27 years in
prison). In 1991, he was elected president
of the ANC and in 1993 accepted the
Nobel Peace Prize, which he shared with De
Klerk. A landslide victory for the ANC in
the ﬁrst democratic elections in 1994 saw
Mandela, with De Klerk as his deputy pres-
ident, form the “Government of National
Unity.” As president, Mandela assisted the
peaceful transition to racial equality, with
the emphasis always on reconciliation and
nation building, and was largely responsi-
ble for South Africa’s liberal constitution.
Mandela also intervened in a number of in-
ternational disputes (particularly in Africa,
Asia, and the Middle East), and personally
set about attracting foreign investment
back to South Africa. Despite retiring as
president in 1999 and from public life in
2004, Mandela, who remains one of the
most revered statesmen of all time, has led
major campaigns against poverty and
HIV/AIDS.

MANZANO,J UAN FRANCISCO
(1797?–1854?)
Juan Francisco Manzano was a Cuban
Creole mulatto born into slavery. At an
early age, he learned how to read and write
in his ﬁrst master’s house. Subsequently, he
went on to publish a collection of poetry,
expressing the suffering that dates back to
the sixteenth century when the ﬁrst African
slaves were imported into Cuba from Africa,
and also an autobiography that vividly
describes the everyday life of African slaves
in mid-eighteenth century Cuba.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 804 ---
728 M ANZANO,J UAN FRANCISCO
There is much debate as to the key
dates in Manzano’s life: his birth, his man-
umission, the writing of his autobiography,
and his death. Critics such as José Luciano
Franco place his birth in 1797, whereas
José Fornario and Joaquín Luaces believe it
was 1806 or 1807. As to the date of his
freedom, Franco gives 1837 and the critic
Cintio Vitier establishes it as 1836, a year
after he began to write his autobiography.
He died in Havana, a free man with a
broken spirit, either in 1853 or 1854.
Until he was able to purchase his free-
dom, Manzano’s existence was consumed
with a desire for independence. Thereafter,
the driving force in his life became the de-
sire to be recognized and respected by the
ruling white society. In this effort to iden-
tify with the white culture, he rejected his
African heritage, and consequently his own
self-worth.
The ﬁrst opportunity for recognition
came Manzano’s way in 1836 when the
wealthy intellectual and patriot Domingo
del Monte took interest in Manzano’s writ-
ings and invited him to read some of his
poetry at one of his renowned literary gath-
erings. Manzano’s poetry expressed the
hardships and humiliations of a slave’s exis-
tence. Such insight into a slave’s psyche
was valuable material for the abolitionists
of Manzano’s time. After the reading, del
Monte put together a volume of Manzano’s
poems in hopes that sales of the volume
would bring in enough money to buy the
slave’s freedom, and they did. Shortly
thereafter, del Monte asked Manzano to
write an autobiography recounting the life of
a slave.
Published in England in 1840, Manzano’s
Autobiografíais the ﬁrst text in Cuban litera-
ture written by a slave. It is very important to
keep in mind that Manzano was still a slave
when he began to write his autobiography.
This fact explains why the narrator’s voice
appears to be so timid and reluctant at times.
Ivan Schulman points out that Manzano
never broaches the question of slavery’s im-
morality or questions the codes of the master
discourse. Instead, Manzano centers his at-
tention on his personal experiences and feel-
ings such as his love for his ﬁrst masters, his
privileged childhood, his fear of his second
mistress, the ambivalence of the slave’s
psyche, what appears to be his innate servil-
ity, and the circumstances that forced him to
become a runaway slave. The critic William
Luis believes that Manzano’s account served
as an “ur” text for the early slave writers, and
Salvador Bueno demonstrates that the Auto-
biografíainspired the Cuban slave narratives
that followed. José Luciano Franco, who
edited Manzano’s complete works in Spanish
in 1937, points out that Manzano’s efforts
were among the ﬁrst to incorporate blacks
into Cuban letters.
At the end of the Autobiografía,
Manzano promises a second part to his
story. That text was lost soon after it was
corrected, never to be found again.
Beatriz Rivera-Barnes

MARLEY,R OBERT NESTA
(1945–1981)
Robert “Bob” Nesta Marley was a musician
and cultural ﬁgure of Jamaican reggae and
Rastafarianism. No single ﬁgure has done
more for the promotion of Jamaican reggae
music and the Rastafarian religion world-
wide than Bob Marley. He was born in the
parish of St. Ann in Jamaica, West Indies,
on February 6, 1945. By the time of his
death in 1981, Marley and his music had
spread across the African Atlantic from
America to Zimbabwe. As a musician
Marley contributed much to the formal
development of reggae as a musical form.
As a cultural ﬁgure Marley represented
Rastafarian lifestyles, thought, and religious
practices to a wider world. Marley’s leg-
endary status, however, beneﬁted most di-
rectly from the ability of his music to cap-
ture and express a century-long tradition of
black freedom struggle across the Diaspora,
from Africa to the Caribbean and through
the United States, from the maroons of the
colonial period to the buffalo soldiers of
the nineteenth century, from the days of
slavery to the decolonization movements in
Africa of the late twentieth century.
Born to Captain Norval Marley, a
white quartermaster in the British West
Indian regiment, and Cedella Booker, an
eighteen-year-old Jamaican woman, Marley
was known locally as a Creole “pickney,” a
designation of mixed cultural and racial
status which also describes the space of his
Caribbean homeland and the very process
by which reggae developed as a musical
form. Marley and his mother’s move to
Kingston, the capital city, when he was 10
was the ﬁrst of many movements that
would mirror the larger migration patterns
of other black and Caribbean subjects in
these middle years of the twentieth century.
As Jimmy Cliff portrayed in the ﬁlm The
Harder They Come, many Jamaican youth
found themselves leaving the rural, peasant
communities of their childhood for the
newly developing world and job opportu-
nities to be found in the urban city of
Kingston. Many of those youth would ﬁnd
their best means to express that migration,
and the conditions they would ﬁnd in the
ghettos of Kingston, in music.
Reggae was created in the streets of
Kingston from a combination of African
American jazz and rhythm and blues beats,
Jamaican music and dance steps such as
those found in the folk-form mento and
the popular music ska, and African
rhythms practiced in the drumming and
Jamaican reggae musician and composer, Robert Nesta
Marley (Bob Marley) was a pioneer whose songs about
oppression and struggle made him an international
anticolonial hero. He remains a symbol of freedom
struggles globally and his music continues to be
artistically inﬂuential on both sides of the Atlantic.

chanting rituals of Rastafarian musicians.
In the ghetto trench towns of Kingston,
Marley came under the mentorship of lead-
ing ﬁgures such as the singer Joe Higgs,
who held lessons for up and coming singers
in the tenement yards. Marley’s ﬁrst signif-
icant move was to join with his stepbrother
Bunny Wailer and friend Peter T osh to
form the Wailing Wailers. They signed up
with record producer Clement “Sir Coxsone”
Dodd, whose Studio One was the site where
ska, an early form of popular Jamaican music
from which reggae derived, was invented.
Here the Wailers recorded their ﬁrst single,
“Simmer Down,” a tune that became a “rude
boy” anthem for Jamaica’s urban male youth
of the early 1960s.
By February 1966, Marley met and mar-
ried singer Rita Anderson, a local singer in
the girl group the Soulettes. Hardship, how-
ever, soon led Marley to join his mother who
had immigrated to America in 1964. Marley
would stay in Wilmington, Delaware, for six
months, earning money to take back to sup-
port himself on the island. In this respect, he
followed the migration route of transna-
tional, seasonal Caribbean workers that de-
ﬁned the Caribbean region throughout the
twentieth century, as many traveled to
America looking for work and the income to
help them make a better life for themselves
in the West Indies. Marley used his hard-
earned cash to ﬁnance his own record label
when he returned to Jamaica in October.
His second important musical step was
to combine with another legendary pro-
ducer, Lee “Scratch” Perry, a ﬁgure instru-
mental in transitioning Jamaican popular
music from ska and rock steady to reggae
proper. While both earlier musical forms
took the conventional four beats to the bar
of classic rhythm and blues and added an
accentuated after-beat, reggae musicians
added an additional half-note to the classic
after-beat of the ska/rock steady formula.
By 1968–1969, reggae had emerged as the
new sound of Jamaican popular music, and
Marley’s tunes and lyrics were at the center
of that transformation. By the early 1970s,
the Wailers had secured recording contracts
in Britain and it was in the spring of 1972,
while recording in London, that Marley
had his third fateful encounter with a
record producer, this time with Chris
Blackwell, the Jamaican founder of the in-
ternational label Island Records. As when
he worked with previous producers, Marley’s
music evolved; while working with Black-
well, his music both initiated and then re-
ﬂected its development as an international
form. Under the Island label, reggae and
Marley’s music became both part of a world
market and important in the development
of a now multinational music industry. On
his ﬁrst record with Island, Catch a Fire,
Marley played with Jamaican musical
forms even further by incorporating rock
and other elements of American music
popular in the 1970s. Adding elements of
soul, blues, and funk, Marley basically in-
corporated modern electronic sounds from
a more metropolitan form of urban music.
Marley’s ﬁrst successful American tour, in
1973, included the Wailers opening for
Bruce Springsteen and playing support for
Sly and the Family Stone.
By 1976, Marley and the Wailers were
international stars. However, Marley was
also at the center of a tense political situa-
tion in Jamaica, which destabilized even
further in December 1976 when the gov-
ernment’s call for an election precipitated
violence between warring political factions.
On the eve of a planned free concert to
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 807 ---
MARRANT,J OHN 731
emphasize the need for peace in the streets
of Kingston, Marley was shot and
wounded, and though he deﬁantly ap-
peared on stage brieﬂy and returned to the
Jamaican stage once again in April 1978 to
play at another concert for peace, the polit-
ical situation was so fraught that he never
returned to Ja maica. Unable to return to
his island homeland, his interests turned to
Africa, and he produced two African-
inﬂuenced albums, Survival and Uprising,
within nine months of each other over
1979 and 1980. In April 1980, Marley was
ofﬁcially invited to perform at the indepen-
dence celebrations in Zimbabwe, cement-
ing his stature as an international, black,
third world superstar. Later that year, after
performing two shows at Madison Square
Garden as part of his American Survival
tour, he collapsed while jogging in New
York’s Central Park on September 21,
1980. Bob Marley died on May 11, 1981,
in a hospital in Miami, from complications
developed from a cancer that had ﬁrst been
identiﬁed in the big toe of his right foot in
July 1977. His musical legacy and heirs
continue to proliferate.

MARRANT,J OHN
(1755–1790?)
John Marrant was a Methodist preacher
and author of A Narrative, a spiritual auto-
biography and captivity narrative. Marrant,
who was born a free man in New York in
1755, made an impact on black communi-
ties during his lifetime through his preach-
ing; he continues to make an impact
through his two important published
works. After his father’s death, Marrant was
brought to Florida, and then Georgia,
undergoing considerable education until
moving to South Carolina at the age of 11.
He became a Christian at the age of 13 after
hearing George Whiteﬁeld, a Methodist
evangelist, preaching. His family disap-
proved of Marrant’s committed devotion to
prayer and study, causing Marrant to leave
home.
In young adulthood, Marrant preached,
mainly to slaves, incurring the displeasure of
their owners. After many adventures and
perils, survival from which he credited to
divine providence, he moved to Bath, west-
ern England, and was ordained a minister
in the Huntingdon Connexion, a sect
that followed a Calvinist-like version of
Methodism. Marrant’s motivation for this
ordination was the pleading of his brother,
who suggested that English loyalists in
Nova Scotia needed Christian guidance.
In 1775 he moved to Nova Scotia and be-
came a much-revered preacher. But Mar-
rant, suffering ﬁnancially, left for Boston
in 1787, serving African Masons in the
capacity of lodge chaplain. He married
Elizabeth Herries, a daughter of black
loyalists, in 1788, and returned to England
in 1790. He preached in east and
south London, dying in Islington in 1791,
aged 35.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 808 ---
732 M ARSHALL,PAULE
Marrant’s ﬁrst book, A Narrative, was
ﬁrst published in 1785; highly successful,
many editions followed. The book is a
compelling account of Marrant’s spiritual
journey, telling of his ﬂight from his family,
his search for God in the woods, his cap-
ture by Cherokees, and his trying to con-
vert the Native Americans who once con-
sidered killing him. Part spiritual
autobiography and part captivity narrative,
the book is renowned as a stirring account
of the subjugated black experience in
America during a period of immense
change. Its factual details are questionable;
for example, Marrant’s claims about being
forced to serve as a musician in Britain’s
Royal Navy cannot be supported by con-
temporary documentation. But the work is
a seminal African American text, and has
been reprinted and studied attentively
since the 1970s. Marrant’s second major
work, A Journal, was ﬁrst published in
1790. This second book is celebrated as an
important account of the black missionary
life in late-eighteenth-century America. It
complements A Narrative,as Marrant again
stresses that black communities must main-
tain dignity in the face of never-ending
hardships and maltreatment by domineer-
ing whites and become regenerate through
God.

MARSHALL,PAULE (1929–)
Paule Marshall is a novelist and essayist
whose work explores American-Caribbean
cultural connections and conﬂicts through
female protagonists. Marshall was born
Valenza Pauline Burke on April 9, 1929, in
Brooklyn, New York. The daughter of ﬁrst-
generation West Indian immigrants from
Barbados, Marshall was raised in a close-
knit West Indian community, a factor that
inﬂuences and informs all her works. Not
only is Marshall’s work infused with the
Caribbean (Diaspora) culture but also her
fascination with the Caribbean “nation
language” is strikingly obvious in all of her
writings. Marshall attended Brooklyn
College where she earned a ﬁrst degree in
English literature. After graduating in
1953, she worked as a writer and researcher
for Our World, an African American maga-
zine, at which time she began working on
her ﬁrst novel, Brown Girl, Brownstones .
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 809 ---
MARSHALL,PAULE 733
Since then, Marshall has assumed several
professorships at academic institutions,
such as Yale, Columbia, Cornell, and
Virginia Commonwealth universities, and
has won numerous prizes and awards, in-
cluding in 1992 the prestigious MacArthur
Fellowship and an American Book Award.
Set in Brooklyn against the backdrop of
the Great Depression and World War II,
Marshall’s autobiographical novel Brown
Girl, Brownstones(1959) depicts the real-life
struggles of an Afro-Caribbean immigrant
community in search of the American
dream. This novel, while it speaks of com-
munity and kinship, or lack thereof, is also
a coming of age story for the young female
protagonist, Selina Boyce, who in addition
to becoming embroiled in the struggle for
selfhood independent of the Caribbean
community, is also enmeshed in an ongoing
struggle with her powerful mother, Silla, for
autonomy. The brown girl, Selina, stands in
stark opposition to white Eurocentric values
symbolized by the brownstones that the
mother, Silla, and others members of the
Barbadian Homeowners Association, on
the ride to upward mobility, purchase as a
means of not only acquiring wealth but also
status. In this novel Marshall questions the
relentless pursuit of material possessions
and the lack of spirituality and spiritual
consciousness. Acknowledging her dual her-
itage, Afro-Caribbean and African American,
Selina makes her own way, returning to
her motherland, Barbados, enacting both a
physical and spiritual return as a means of
bridging the two communities, African
American and Afro-Caribbean. This depar-
ture for the motherland is a marker of
transatlantic connections.
Marshall’s collection of four novellas,
Soul Clap Hands and Sing (1961), which
won the Rosenthal Award of the National
Institute of Arts and Letters, is arguably a
“detour” from her other works in which the
leading characters are women, distinctively
black women. In these short stories, geo-
graphically titled Barbados, Brooklyn,
British Guiana, and Brazil, the leading
characters are all middle-aged men who
relentlessly pursue fame and wealth at the
expense of love and companionship. In her
own words, Marshall undertook this proj-
ect in order to explore if she could write
convincingly about men. In this short story
collection, Marshall once again addresses
the surrendering of one’s spiritual essence
and the inexorable pursuit of material ac-
quisitions, as she demonstrates the devas-
tating effect of this “obsessive pastime” as
each man eventually confronts a hollow and
meaningless existence in spite of material
wealth and/or personal success.
The Bournehills community in The
Chosen Place, the Timeless People (1969) is
marked by its deep-seated sense of commu-
nity and communal kinship while it refuses
to relinquish its ancestral inheritances to
modernization/Westernization. In this sec-
ond novel, as in all of her works, Marshall
is engaged with what Kamau Brathwaite
calls the literature of recognition (of an
African presence). Resisting and renounc-
ing colonial intervention, the Bournehills
inhabitants proudly embrace their past, their
roots. Honoring their dead hero, Cuffee
Ned, the Bournehills inhabitants restage
and participate in an annual reenactment
of the slave rebellion that Cuffee initiated
years ago in Pyre Hill, now famously
known as the Pyre Hill Revolt. This return
to the past is both spiritual and physical for
the main character, Merle Kinbona, who at
the novel’s end is embarked on a journey to
Africa to reclaim her lost daughter. In the
process of reclamation, she will reclaim
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 810 ---
734 M ARSHALL,PAULE
herself, mending her disparate selves and
the community. History and memory are
here employed as tools of empowerment.
Marshall’s next novel, Praisesong for
the Widow (1983), which was awarded the
Before Columbus American Book Award
in 1984, explores the theme of diasporic
continuity and connectivity as the middle-
aged African American woman protagonist,
Avatara (Avey) Johnson, voyages inad-
vertently to the off island of Grenada,
Carriacou. This novel traces Avey’s spiritual
unmooring, her rootlessness, and relin-
quishment of things ancestral to her return
to self and embraces ancestral inheritances
as she eventually is able to “call her nation”
by invoking the ancestors. Consumed by
materialism in White Plains, New York,
Avey is able to reclaim herself, under the
direction of Mothers, on the chosen island
of Carriacou, where homage is paid reli-
giously to the ancestors and African oral
traditional practices are proudly practiced
and preserved. The Mothers who redirect
Avey’s wanderings and stage her rebirth
are Marshall’s Mother Poets who have
double vision and could see in more ways
than one.
Marshall’s collection of essays, Reena
and Other Stories (1983), includes the in-
troductory groundbreaking autobiographi-
cal essay “The Making of a Writer: From
the Poets in the Kitchen.” In this essay
Marshall chronicles her emergence into a
writer which began in her mother’s kitchen,
where her mother and other women of the
Barbadian community concocted their
art—domestic chores as well as political
issues—for they themselves were poets in
the making. The common, everyday lan-
guage used by these women poets are the
“true” markers of their identity. The spoken
word served as a refuge as well as functioned
as a weapon according them visibility and
empowerment.
Daughters (1991) details the spiritual
and physical journeys of an African Ameri-
can daughter, Ursa, who after living and
working in the United States for several
years, upon her mother’s request, returns to
the ﬁctitious Caribbean island T riunion to
assist her prime minister father with his re-
election campaign. Once an ardent histo-
rian who ﬂaunted his historical knowledge
and ties to the island, the incumbent prime
minister, Primus McKenzie, in his quest for
reelection, abandons his past oral tradi-
tions, surrendering not only his rights but
also the community’s right to U.S. imperi-
alist interests. Ursa eventually comes to
self-realization as she merges with the an-
cestress Congo Jane and dedicates her life
to community activism. Merging with the
ancestress is suggestive of a possible conver-
gence between the two worlds, T riunion
and the United States, presently at odds.
On the verge of achieving wholeness, Ursa
returns not only to her homeland but also
to her thesis project in T riunion, rejected
earlier in the United States, documenting
the lives of slaves in the New World and
their resistance to enslavement in the
United States.
Marshall returns to the theme of
bridging communities and communal rela-
tionship in The Fisher King (2000). The
concept of binary oppositions, or opposing
forces (a common feature in Marshall’s
works), that is at the center of the novel
highlights the need for synthesis—the
need to unite disparate selves. Here again
dual heritage, African American and Afro-
Caribbean, is celebrated in the young male
protagonist Sonny, the Fisher King, who
has a pivotal role to play in uniting and
preserving family ties (the Holy Grail).

their combined heritage, Afro-Caribbean

MARSON,U NA (1905–1965)
Una Marson was a poet, playwright, and
activist, who devised the London-based
radio program Caribbean Voices.
Born in Jamaica, Marson authored
four volumes of poetry: Tropic Reveries
(1930), Heights and Depths (1931), and
The Moth and the Star(1937), all published
by the author in Kingston, and T owards
the Stars (1945), published in London by
University of London Press. Her poetry
continues and extends the pioneering work
in the vernacular of her countryman
Claude McKay. Her correspondence with
James Weldon Johnson and Langston
Hughes, who would publish several of her
poems in his 1949 anthology Poetry of the
Negro, demonstrates that Marson was also
inﬂuenced by the poets of the Harlem Re-
naissance, the blossoming of African
American cultural expression in the 1920s
of which McKay is often described as the
initiator.
Marson lived in London in the 1930s
and 1940s, working for Dr. Harold Moody,
founder of the League of Coloured Peoples.
Poems such as “Quashie Comes to London”
and “Little Brown Girl” are early evocations
of the Caribbean immigrant experience; the
latter focalized through the female perspec-
tive that characterizes much of Marson’s
writing. Her feminist journalism and
lifelong commitment to the international
women’s movement complements the
womanist blues that Marson developed in
poems such as “Kinky Hair Blues.” Marson
subsequently worked with the exiled Haile
Selassie, accompanying him to the League
of Nations in 1935. Her ﬁrst play, At What
a Price,was staged in Kingston in 1932, and
the following year made history as the ﬁrst
black colonial production to be staged in
London’s West End; her second play,
Pocomania, performed in Kingston in
1938, anticipates much postcolonial
Caribbean writing in its exploration of folk
materials as cultural resistance.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 812 ---
736 M ARTÍ,J OSÉ
In the 1940s Marson was employed by
the British Broadcasting Corporation,
where she devised Caribbean Voices, the
radio program that would prove “the single
most important literary catalyst for
Caribbean creative and critical writing in
English” (Brathwaite, 1984, p. 87).
On her return to Jamaica, Marson
worked for the Daily Gleaner and the Pio-
neer Press, where she encouraged new
writers, among them the young Andrew
Salkey. H er considerable contribution to
Caribbean and international culture was
recognized in 1977 in a special “Caribbean
Woman” issue of the journal Savacou,
which was dedicated to the memory of this
“poet, pioneer, patriot and people-person.”
Nonetheless, Marson’s books remain out of
print, although selections from her poetry
appear in the Penguin Book of Caribbean
Verse in English.

MARTÍ,J OSÉ(1853–1895)
Born on January 28, 1853, in Havana
Cuba, José Martí is an important political
ﬁgure of Hispanic America and is known as
a national hero of Cuba. His face, life, and
memory are commemorated on stamps, in
books, and in statues all across the world.
Martí died on a Cuban battleﬁeld at 42,
after he and the Cuban Liberation Army
launched an invasion of Cuba to ﬁght
against Spanish forces on May 19, 1895.
Martí was a revolutionary, a journalist, a
poet, a scholar, a teacher, a politician, a mo-
tivational speaker, a mentor, and a hero. As
a teacher, Martí believed that race prejudice
had no place in democracy or in education.
He taught in New York City from 1891 to
1895 at La Liga (The League), a place
where blacks and whites could study to-
gether. As a political activist, Martí wished
to unite Latin nations and people together
under a common goal of universal har-
mony and simultaneously build the Cuban
nation. He spoke for the disenfranchised,
believing everyone, no matter the color of
one’s skin or the class they were born into,
had the right to learning and wisdom. He
was a nation builder.
Martí’s revolutionary spirit began early
in life. At sixteen, he became involved in
antigovernment activity and his beliefs
(written in numerous political writings in
his school newspaper) led to his imprison-
ment for six years of hard labor and his de-
portation from his homeland. Exiled to
Spain, Martí graduated from the University
of Saragossa and founded the Cuban Revo-
lutionary Party in 1892, which fought for
the unity of Latin America against U.S. an-
nexation and imperialism. As a journalist,
Martí wrote for many newspapers, covering
criminal trials, labor strikes, art exhibits,
political turmoil, and elections all over the
Americas, and wrote about such inﬂuential
individuals as Ralph Waldo Emerson, Walt
Whitman, and Jesse James.
Martí began publishing at an early
age. His ﬁrst poem was published in 1868,
at the age of 15. He wrote many social
and political pieces, including Nuestra
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 813 ---
MASAI 737
América, Mi Raza, El presidio politico en
Cuba, Versos Libres, Madre América, and
Ismaelillo, and was also known for writing
children’s pieces. In 1889, Martí published
“A Vindication of Cuba” in the New York
Post in response to an unjust criticism of his
country and his people in the Philadelphia
Manufacturer. This metaphorical response
is a dialectical one about the struggle be-
tween defending one’s nation against the
prejudices of the United States and the
guilt and love that commingle in the desire
of a patriot to see his land free from the
unjust criminals who pretend to be leaders
but are in reality thieves. At the same time,
he defends his people against allegations of
effeminacy and idleness, by historically re-
counting the many soldiers, builders,
teachers, writers, thinkers, and metaphori-
cal giants who fought in wars, built rail-
roads, ate roots from the land, and died
with honor in their hearts ﬁghting for what
they believed. Martí emphasizes that simple
cowards would strike people down with
machetes and unjust words and not raise a
hand to help a fellow man and friend defeat
the enemies that stand on their land.
Versos Sencillos, written in 1891 and
known as Simple Versesin English, is one of
Martí’s most powerful writings and his last
book of poetry. Evoking the ideological, so-
cial, and political struggles of Cuba, Martí
employs the metaphor of nature to suggest
that ties bind us to our countries not just
through birth, but through death. As the
plant grows and survives, so does mankind
and Cuba, even in the light of betrayal and
indignity of frost or government oppres-
sion. For Martí, mankind needed to evoke
the spirit of the land in order to gain the
spirituality necessary to conquer external
demons (government oppression) that
threatened one’s livelihood. At the same
time, one needed to conquer the internal
demons that struggled to dominate the
mind-set of Cubans far greater than tyrants
could. Martí was bound to the land, and
there he struggled for solace against op-
pressive regimes, the materialism that
brought man down, and the curtailment of
human rights, which he felt most subju-
gated and silenced the black working class.
In his poems, he speaks of the death of
ﬂowers, of repression, of pompousness, and
the light that will shine through every
morning bringing life and joy once again to
Cuban liberators.
On that battleﬁeld is where Martí held
his last stand in life and death, ﬁghting for
his principles that Cuba be free and liber-
ated against racism, imperialism, and the
control of other countries. Martí will be
forever known as a revolutionary, whose
commitment to cultural and spiritual
strengthening will be remembered for cen-
turies to come.
Rosa E. Soto

MASAI
The greeting of “I hope your cows are well”
illustrates the pastoral character of the
Masai. Tall, slender, and garb characterized
by bright red cloaks and elaborate bead-
work, the Masai are descendants of one of
three eastern Nilotic-speaking peoples who
migrated out of Sudan into the Rift Valley
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 814 ---
738 M ASAI
of what is today Kenya and Tanzania during
the ﬁrst millennium BCE. By the seven-
teenth and eighteenth centuries CE, they
dominated the Rift Valley from Mount
Kenya to Mount Kilimanjaro. Masai society
was and is polygamous, patrilineal, and or-
ganized around age grades. The basic social
unit is the polygamous family compound
(kral ). The Masai live in circular villages
called enkangs, which are made up of nu-
merous krals. Political and social authority
is exerted by elders, shamans (laibon), or
senior warriors.
Young men become warriors (moran )
once they undergo circumcision at approx-
imately 13 years of age. At this time, they
leave the enkang and move to a warrior
village ( manyatta) for up to eight years.
Moran responsibilities are to defend their
communities and their cattle. T raditionally
known as lion hunters, the moran use only
a club against a lion and such encounters
bring great status to the individual. When
the moran reach their late teens or early
twenties, they are initiated as junior elders,
return to the enkang, and establish their
own families. Ultimately they transition to
senior elder status.
Masai women are also organized by age
grade and undergo a circumcision cere-
mony. They are not allowed to own cattle,
but do own other livestock such as donkeys
and goats. Women build the distinctive
dome-shaped homes and are considered to
own the houses they build and live in.
The central ﬁgure in Masai religious
life is the laibon, whose activities include
healing, prophecy, and divination. The
Masai are monotheistic and refer to Enkai
as the creator. It was Enkai who sent cattle
to the Masai when the earth and sky sepa-
rated. As a result of Enkai’s gift to them, the
Masai believe all cattle in the world belong
to them—a strong justiﬁcation for raid-
ing the herds of non-Masai neighbors to
“regain” Masai property. Both cattle and the
grass upon which cattle graze are sacred to
the Masai and provide further justiﬁcation
for their pastoralist culture. The Masai be-
lieve that farming scars the earth. Reinforc-
ing their interdependent relationship with
their cattle, the mainstay of the Masai diet is
saroi, a mixture of cow’s milk and blood.
During the nineteenth century, com-
petition over grazing lands, pressures of
agriculturalists on grazing lands, and popu-
lation migrations farther south along the
Rift Valley led to the Masai Civil Wars, an
internecine conﬂict for dominance in the
region. The Masai cattle herds were deci-
mated by disease in 1880 and a serious
drought in 1881 resulted in famine. It was
at this time Europeans began to establish
control over East Africa and the Masai
found themselves subject to British control.
In 1904 the Masai were divided among two
districts and then reunited in 1911 in a sin-
gle territory termed “Masailand” overlap-
ping the boundary between Kenya and
Tanzania. Even today, the Masai move rela-
tively unimpeded across this national
boundary. T oday, while their opportunity
to hunt lions is curtailed, the Masai have
been able to maintain their distinctive
cattle-based seminomadic lifestyle to a
great extent. Modern Masai move between
village and city with relative ease, but the
urban dress is quickly shed for the tradi-
tional scarlet cloak upon return to the
enkang or manyatta.
Heather Thiessen-Reily

MAURITANIA
Mauritania is located in the northwest of
the African continent, north of Senegal and
Mali, and south of Morocco and Algeria;
nearly half of the country is desert, al-
though it has a lengthy coastline. Maurita-
nia has a population of about 2,999,000,
with a quarter of the population living in
Nouakchott, the capital. In early medieval
times, it was a part of the empire of Mali
and the Kingdom of Morocco. During the
sixteenth century, the Portuguese used
Mauritania as one of their sources of slaves
for Brazil and their other colonies, but they
did not occupy any part of the country. In
the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries,
Mauritania attracted a few merchants from
the Americas, mainly because of the trade in
gum arabic. One of these merchants was
James Riley, who was shipwrecked off the
Mauritanian coast and survived to write An
Authentic Narrative of the Loss of the Ameri-
can Brig Commerce, which was published in
1847 in Hartford, Connecticut, and has
been republished many times since then.
From 1857, the British had recognized
French rights to Mauritania, on the west
coast of Africa, but apart from occupying
some of the coastline, the French made lit-
tle attempt to control the hinterland until
1900. Much of this had been achieved by
1914, and in 1920 Mauritania became a
part of French West Africa. The main
port of Mauritania was St. Étienne (now
Nouadhibou). From 1928 until 1929,
Alphonse Paul Albert Choteau was governor
of Mauritania, later moving to the
Caribbean as governor of Guadeloupe. The
pilot Antoine de Saint-Exúpery was involved
in some ﬂights around Mauritania (he later
ﬂew in Argentina). Interestingly, the French
colonial authorities in Mauritania often used
horses imported from Argentina.
Mauritania was administered from
Senegal until 1958, when it voted to remain
autonomous within the French Commu-
nity. On November 28, 1960, it became
independent as the Islamic Republic of
Mauritania. The United States recognized
Mauritania, and its ﬁrst ambassador was
Henry Serrano Villard. The U.S. Peace Corps
sent volunteers to Mauritania from 1967 to
1968 and again from 1972.
Since independence, there have been a
number of U.S. researchers who have
studied Mauritania, including James L. A.
Webb, coeditor of an extensive bibliogra-
phy on Mauritania, author of Desert Fron-
tier: Ecological Change, Atlantic Commerce,
and Regional Economy in the Western Sahel
1600–1850 (1995), and coauthor of
Mauritania: Transformation in a Desert
World, and Anthony G. Pazzanita, author
of Historical Dictionary of Mauritania
(1996). In 1984, the African Studies Cen-
ter at Michigan State University published
an anthology of oral tradition of precolo-
nial Mauritania. Three Canadian scholars
have also completed theses on Mauritania
at the University of Montreal: Amadou
Ba worked on aspects of demography;
Amadou B. Sarr studied the political
economy of Mauritania; and Sadio T raore
wrote on the nomadic population between
1965 and 1976.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

Mauritania’s relations with the United
States have been uneven. The country
opposed U.S. policies in the Middle East in
the ﬁrst Gulf War of 1990–1991. Since
then, however, it has supported the United
States in the 2003 invasion of Iraq.
