MAURITIUS
The Republic of Mauritius occupies a single
small island east of Madagascar with a popu-
lation of 1.2 million. The government of
Mauritius has also laid claim to a number of
smaller surrounding islands, including Diego
Garcia, the major U.S. military base for op-
erations in the Indian Ocean region. Diego
Garcia is part of the archipelago called the
Chagos Islands and is under British adminis-
tration. Like many African island nations,
Mauritius’s history has been tied heavily to
transoceanic trade. Arab and Indian Ocean
sailors visited the island early in its history.
Portuguese sailors reached it in the sixteenth
century. Subsequently, the island passed
through several colonial hands, claimed by
the Dutch in 1598, taken and settled by the
French in 1715, and taken over by the
British in 1810 during the Napoleonic wars.
Mauritius remained a British colony until in-
dependence in 1968. T oday, Mauritius is a
peacefully multiethnic nation composed of
people of African, Arab, East Asian, South
Asian, and European descent.
Settled by successive waves of traders,
merchants, planters, slaves, and laborers,
Mauritius prospered economically under
both French and British rule, and since in-
dependence. Sugar plantations are a major
feature of the island’s landscape. French
and British cultural and linguistic inﬂu-
ences are strong; however, there are also
many Muslim, Indian, and African cultural
and religious inﬂuences.
Mauritius is one of Africa’s strongest
economies and is a member of various inter-
national organizations, including the African
Union and the World T rade Organization. It
has been a peaceful, multiparty democracy
since independence. Much of Mauritius’s
export earnings are from sugarcane, a tradi-
tional crop; however, the nation has been
rapidly modernizing, becoming a site of light
manufacturing, especially textiles, and of
banking and international ﬁnance for coun-
tries in the Indian Ocean region.
The independence of Mauritius in the
1960s was complicated by competing
claims over the Chagos Islands, including
Diego Garcia, some 1,200 miles (1,931
kilometers) west of the main island. The
British refused to consider the indepen-
dence of Mauritius without retaining con-
trol over the islands. The British had, in
relative secret, already agreed to lease the
island of Diego Garcia to the United States
in order to construct a supply base for air
and naval forces. The United States saw
Diego Garcia, located near the center of the
Indian Ocean, as critical to maintaining a
strategic presence in the Indian Ocean,
against the much closer communist pres-
ences of the Soviet Union and China.
While U.S. diplomatic and economic
relations with Mauritius are strong, Diego
Garcia continues to be a point of signiﬁcant
contention. Mauritius continues to claim
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 817 ---
MAYS,W ILLIE HOWARD 741
ownership of the Chagos Archipelago.
Among the issues also raised by the con-
struction of Diego Garcia was the forced
relocation, by the British at the request of
the United States, of approximately 2,000
people already living in the Chagos Islands.
With the end of the Cold War, this issue
has resurfaced as the descendants of those
Chagos islanders, many of whom live in
poverty in Mauritius, have demanded the
right to return to the islands. Historical
scholarship suggests that the United States
was heavily responsible for organizing and
ﬁnancing the forced relocation. Since the
late 1990s to 2007, the base at Diego Garcia
itself has become a focus of Mauritian
concern. Protesting the militarization of
what they perceive to be part of Mauritius,
the Mauritian organization Lalit, along
with other national, British, and American
groups, have sought to close the base on
Diego Garcia.

MAYS,W ILLIE HOWARD
(1931–)
Willie Mays is widely considered the great-
est all-around baseball player of the 1950s
to 1960s. Mays started his professional
career with the Birmingham Black Barons
of the Negro National League in 1948, was
acquired by the New York Giants in 1950,
and reached the majors in 1951. Along
with his great baseball skills, including
power, speed, and a strong throwing arm,
he exhibited an infectious enthusiasm for
the game that he never lost. By the time
that he retired from the New York Mets, he
was ﬁrmly positioned as one of the greatest
players in baseball history.
Mays learned baseball young, as his fa-
ther had played in the industrial leagues
near Birmingham, Alabama. Only seven-
teen when he signed with Birmingham, he
quickly developed his baseball skills and
while still a teenager attracted the attention
of the New York Giants. After parts of two
seasons in the minors, Mays was summoned
to the parent club in 1951 and earned Na-
tional League Rookie of the League honors.
He then missed most of 1952 and all of
1953 while serving in the U.S. Army. Re-
turning in 1954, Mays led the National
League in batting with a .345 average and
topped the league with 13 triples. He also
Baseball star Willie Howard Mays (left) with Roy
Campanella (right) in 1961. (Library of Congress)
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 818 ---
742 M AYS,W ILLIE HOWARD
hit 41 home runs and drove in 110 runners
to win the Most Valuable Player Award in
the National League. That magical season
concluded with the pennant and a World
Series triumph for the Giants over the fa-
vored Cleveland Indians, who had set an
American League single-season record with
111 victories.
The turning point in the 1954 series
occurred in the eighth inning of the ﬁrst
game with the score tied. Cleveland’s Vic
Wertz slugged a long drive to deep center
ﬁeld. Mays raced after the ball with his
back to home plate, made an outstanding
over-the-shoulder catch, whirled, and riﬂed
a throw back into the inﬁeld that prevented
one of the two base runners from advanc-
ing. The game remained tied, and the
Giants went on to win in extra innings,
their first victory in a four-game sweep.
Along with his remarkable play in the
1954 series, from then on known simply as
“the Catch,” Mays’ enthusiasm helped to
establish fans’ perception of him. Mays
loved baseball, and when he was not per-
forming in a major league park, he might
be participating in stickball games on the
streets of Harlem. His zest for the game and
his penchant for welcoming people with
“Say hey” led to a lasting nickname—the
“Say Hey Kid.”
Yet Mays’ popularity and rise to baseball
immortality did not make him immune to
racism. Although he escaped the harsh treat-
ment and overt hatred that Jackie Robinson
endured, he faced more subtle aspects of
racism. The grace and ease with which he
played led people to view him as an instinc-
tive ballplayer who did not need to work at
the game, a conclusion they would not have
arrived at regarding multitalented and grace-
ful white players such as Joe DiMaggio.
Similarly, many white writers saw his good
humor as a childlike simplicity, viewing him
as an eternal child, a boy wonder, rather
than the dedicated, sensitive, and intelligent
man he really was. In fact, the “Say hey”
greeting was a thoughtful adult’s substitu-
tion for people’s names that he did not re-
member, and hence an attempt to avoiding
insulting them. And the stickball he played
on the streets of New York was an attempt to
please his fans, by later standards an effective
marketing tactic. Mays reﬂected seriously on
his identity as an African American, remark-
ing that scouting reports customarily identi-
ﬁed African American players as a Negro
ﬁrst and a talented player next. In his case,
he said that the reports talked ﬁrst about his
ability and then noted his race. The talent
may have come ﬁrst in the reports, but there
was no overlooking his racial identity.
Mays played in the majors through
1973, compiling a lifetime .302 average
with 3,283 hits and 660 home runs. At the
time, only Babe Ruth and Hank Aaron had
hit more home runs. T wice he earned Most
Valuable Player honors, and throughout
most of his career seldom a year went by
without his leading the league in at least
one major category. The Sporting News
selected Mays as the greatest player of
the 1960s, and in 1979, in his ﬁrst year of
eligibility, he was enshrined in the National
Baseball Hall of Fame.

MCKAY,C LAUDE 743
MCKAY,C LAUDE
(1889–1948)
Claude McKay was a Jamaican-born poet
and novelist writing in the New Negro Era.
McKay was born in the Clarendon region
of Jamaica, where his father was a relatively
prosperous farmer. Although McKay re-
tained a lifelong love of the soil, he chose to
work not on the land but in the Jamaican
constabulary, or police force, and it was
during his time as a “constab” in 1912 that
he published his ﬁrst two collections of po-
etry, Songs of Jamaica and Constab Ballads.
These were the ﬁrst books of verse to be
published in the Jamaican vernacular, a
medium in which the young McKay was en-
couraged to write by an expatriate English
folklorist, Walter Jekyll, the ﬁrst of a series
of white male mentors who would include
Frank Harris and Max Eastman. With ven-
erable exceptions, such as Lloyd Brown’s
West Indian Poetry, McKay’s dialect volumes
have long suffered critical condescension or
plain neglect; rehabilitated to critical discus-
sion by Michael North in his groundbreak-
ing Dialect of Modernism, these poems may
now be read not as crude apprentice work
but as an essential if controversial part of
McKay’s career as a writer. The most re-
markable of the dialect poems are creole
monologues, like “A Midnight Woman to
the Bobby,” and subtle subversions of the
iniquities of colonialism, like “Quashie to
Buccra.” Written in the Jamaican vernacular
but in traditional form, the dialect poems
lack, for commentators like the Barbadian
poet-critic Kamau Brathwaite, an authentic
environmental expression.
Yet all of McKay’s writing is driven by
internal tensions. His poetry in standard
English is characterized by a guiding ten-
sion between traditional, inherited forms,
like that of the sonnet, and an urgent, often
topical, subject matter. The most famous of
these sonnets, “If We Must Die,” was writ-
ten amid the race riots of the Red Summer
of 1919, and yet the poem has been coun-
termanded to other occasions and other
causes: it was allegedly quoted, without
attribution to the author, by Winston
Churchill during World War II. McKay
had left Jamaica for the United States in
1912, intending to study agronomy at the
T uskegee Institute in Alabama; he did not
complete his studies, working instead as a
waiter and on the railroads and eventually
as a journalist. Although he would never re-
turn to the Caribbean, much of the poetry
McKay wrote in the United States is in-
ﬂected with nostalgia for his native place:
writing from New York City about his is-
land home, McKay’s major mode other
than protest is that of urban pastoral.
McKay is frequently described as a
prime mover within the Harlem Renais-
sance of the 1920s, the burgeoning of black
culture at that time in New York and other
Northern cities; however, McKay was at
best equivocal in his response to the intel-
lectual architects of the Renaissance. His in-
spiration came from the masses, from the
ordinary folk, while his primary social and
intellectual contacts in New York were with
members of the white literary Left, princi-
pally Max Eastman, for whose journal the
Liberator McKay was for a time the coeditor
as well as a regular contributor. McKay
spent a lengthy sojourn in England in
1920–1921, when he worked for the ex-
suffragette Sylvia Pankhurst’s radical news-
paper the Workers’ Dreadnought. Moving in
radical circles in London, he highlighted the
prejudice afﬂicting black people, especially
seamen, in Britain and made common
cause between Irish, Indian, and African
American nationalisms. On meeting his
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 820 ---
744 M CKAY,C LAUDE
idol, George Bernard Shaw, McKay was dis-
appointed that the Irishman did not share
his perspective on the connections between
various anticolonial causes; McKay was
further disenchanted when Shaw advised
him that as a black man he would be bet-
ter advised to give up poetry to pursue a
career as a boxer. Notwithstanding this,
McKay published his ﬁrst book of poetry in
standard English, Spring in New Hampshire,
in England in 1920; the majority of the
poems from that volume were subsequently
reproduced in his ﬁrst American book pub-
lication, Harlem Shadows, in 1922.
McKay did not remain long on his
return to the United States. A self-styled
vagabond wanderer, he traveled in 1922 to
the then Soviet Union as a delegate to the
Fourth Congress of the Third Communist
International, and after a prolonged stay in
the USSR, went on to France and thence to
North Africa, not returning to the United
States until 1934. He vividly documents
his 12-year absence in his autobiography,
A Long Way from Home (1937). McKay
published two of his three novels in the
1920s, Home to Harlem in 1928 and Banjo
in 1929. Home to Harlem was regarded by
such pillars of the Harlem Renaissance
establishment as W . E. B. Du Bois as a
scurrilous exposé of the seamy underside of
black American life, and therefore at odds
with the philosophy of positive racial repre-
sentation favored by Du Bois and other in-
ﬂuential Harlemites. (Du Bois stated he felt
like taking a bath after reading it.) McKay’s
two major characters, Jake and Ray, repre-
sent the warring elements of the author’s
own personality, the easygoing and natural
drifter (Jake) versus the intellectual and
Caribbean exile (Ray). Ray reappears in
Banjo in much the same role and ﬁnds in
that novel’s eponymous hero another version
of Jake, the natural man, to offset his own
intellectual and introspective propensities.
Set in the French port of Marseilles, Banjo
celebrates the international and transna-
tional quality of black experience; in this
respect, the novel would prove a crucial in-
ﬂuence upon the Négritude movement led
by the Martinican poet and statesman
Aime Cesaire and the Senegalese writer and
leader Leopold Sedar Senghor. In Home to
Harlem and Banjo, McKay returns to the
black vernacular and develops in both nov-
els a version of the black picaresque—
Banjo is subtitled “A Novel without a Plot.”
Banana Bottom (1933), McKay’s third
and ﬁnal novel (he published a collection of
short stories, Gingertown, in 1932), is quite
different. Set in Jamaica, with a female pro-
tagonist, Bita Plant, the novel celebrates
closure, with the marriage of Bita to Jubban,
a peasant farmer who symbolizes the land
on which he works and embodies the cul-
mination of the organic metaphors that are
found throughout McKay’s writing.
McKay’s life, like his writing, is ﬁlled
with often ﬁerce contradictions: a Com-
munist and then an equally fervid anti-
Communist, who converted to Catholicism
in the 1940s; born a British citizen in colo-
nial Jamaica, he has frequently been seconded
to the canon of African American literature
despite the emphatically international con-
tours of his career and experience. As an exile
from his native Caribbean, McKay would
long be regarded as an outsider to the indige-
nous culture of that region. And yet, as
Kamau Brathwaite has pointed out, it is
“McKay the exile” who is the founder of a
Caribbean literary tradition characterized by
migration and exile from home.
Lee M. Jenkins

MÉDECINSSANS FRONTIÈRES
Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF)/Doctors
Without Borders is the world’s largest inde-
pendent medical relief organization. It was
founded in 1971 by a group of French doc-
tors and journalists returning to Paris from
a Red Cross mission to the Biafran War in
Nigeria. MSF provides emergency medical
assistance to people affected by armed con-
ﬂict, epidemics, natural or man-made dis-
asters, or excluded from health care. Realiz-
ing that more than 90 percent of all death
and suffering from infectious diseases oc-
curs in the developing world with insufﬁ-
cient health care systems, MSF rehabilitates
hospitals and dispensaries, establishes rural
clinics, provides vaccination and drugs,
and trains local staff. MSF consists of not
only doctors, but nurses, water and sanita-
tion specialists, nutritionists, epidemiolo-
gists, logisticians, administrators, plumbers,
radio operators, lawy ers, mechanics, and
accountants working alongside skilled local
staff ensuring that the essential medicines,
food, fuel, personnel, vehicles, water blad-
ders, and tools are delivered to those in the
heart of the emergency. T o maintain its inde-
pendence, nearly 80 percent of MSF’s oper-
ating funds comes from the general public—
individuals, foundations, corporations, and
nonproﬁt organizations worldwide—while
20 percent comes from international agen-
cies and governments.
MSF’s decision to intervene in any cri-
sis is based solely on an independent assess-
ment of people’s needs. When MSF learns
of a developing crisis, it sends an inspection
team to assess the situation, and based on
the team’s recommendations, volunteers
and equipment are dispatched within hours
to the troubled zone. Its large-scale logisti-
cal capacity ensures that emergency teams
arrive with medical kits and equipment
needed to start saving lives immediately.
The teams accept responsibility for a range
of medical interventions that include pro-
viding basic health care as well as preven-
tion of epidemics, constructing water and
sanitation facilities, providing supplemen-
tary foodstuffs to vulnerable groups, and
training local health workers. For longer-
term programs, MSF provides medical and
psychological care to patients with infec-
tious diseases such as tuberculosis, sleeping
sickness, and HIV/AIDS.
MSF addresses obstacles preventing
people in the developing world from ob-
taining affordable treatments for diseases
such as HIV/AIDS, malaria, and tubercu-
losis. Through its Campaign for Access to
Essential Medicines, MSF advocates to
overcome trade and other barriers to treat-
ments, lower drug prices, and to stimulate
research and development of new treat-
ments. Worldwide, MSF staff raises public
awareness by speaking at conferences and
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 822 ---
746 M ERCANTILISM
showing traveling exhibitions. It also orga-
nizes special public education projects to
address the stark realities of living without
access to medicines and the devastation
caused by war.
Many critics, however, believe MSF is
used as a convenient smokescreen to hide
the lack of willingness of the international
community to intervene in crises (the inci-
dent in Rwanda was a case in point).
Esther F . Ojo

MERCANTILISM
Mercantilism is the political design of gov-
ernments to encourage a favorable balance
of trade with competing nations. Mercan-
tilist strategies for a favorable balance of
trade included granting monopoly privi-
leges and tax incentives, restricting the out-
ﬂow of gold and silver coin, and securing
colonies as sources of gold and silver, slaves,
and raw materials for commodities. In the
sixteenth through eighteenth centuries, the
colonialist governments and merchants of
Europe collaborated to expand mercantile
networks linking Asia, Africa, and the
Americas.
An illustrative example of the connec-
tion between Africa, the Americas, and mer-
cantilist notions about money is the manner
in which the English slave trade developed.
In 1663, King Charles I licensed a slave-
trading monopoly. T o commemorate the
event, the Royal Mint issued a new gold
coin “in the name and for the use of the
Company of Royal Adventurers of England
trading with Africa.” The coin was the
guinea, named after that part of Africa, and
it continued to be minted until 1813. The
company was created to encourage colonial
development and raise money for the
Crown. Less than 10 years later, however,
the slave trade was given to a new monop-
oly, the Royal African Company. More
successful than many other colonial ven-
tures, the company greatly supported the
colonies in the West Indies and North
America. Among its many subscribers were
the king, other members of the royal fam-
ily, merchants of London and Bristol, and
the famous philosopher of liberty and
property, John Locke. Later, in 1695,
Locke participated in a major debate about
the supply of and demand for silver specie
in England, after which he was asked to
join the Crown’s Board of T rade. In 1698,
Locke’s board ended the Royal African
Company’s monopoly, opened the slave
trade to independent merchants, and al-
lowed the slave trade to expand and to be-
come an essential element of Great Britain’s
transatlantic economy.
Although the word “mercantilism” is
usually used to refer to either the economy
or the economic thought of the sixteenth
through eighteenth centuries, it was ﬁrst
coined in the nineteenth century, adapted
from Francois Quesnay and Adam Smith’s
analyses of the “mercantile system.” In The
Wealth of Nations (1776), Smith explained
that the popular understanding of the bal-
ance of trade committed the bullionist—or
Midas—fallacy by confusing wealth with
money. Indeed, one mercantilist writer,
Thomas Mun, argued in 1623 that precious
metals were indispensable to a nation’s
wealth and power, and if a nation did not
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 823 ---
MERCANTILISM 747
have access to such metals, then it should
attempt to export more than it imports by
encouraging and protecting domestic pro-
duction. Smith’s critique of the mercantile
system argued that protectionist policies
designed to encourage the ﬂow of money
into the nation inhibited trade and in turn
decreased productivity.
Historians of economic thought have
questioned the characterization of mercan-
tilist economics as bullionist because
Smith’s position was much closer to that of
many early economic thinkers than he ad-
mitted. Hence the term “mercantilism” has
been called a historiographic red herring
because it obscures the diversity of early
economic thought, exaggerates differences
between free-market thinkers and mercan-
tilists, conﬂates histories of thought, policy,
and economic activity, and locates mercan-
tilist thought within a determinate histori-
cal timeframe. In practice, the term mer-
cantilism has been used differently to
describe a historical period, a political pro-
gram, and a set of ideas.
Historically, the period after feudalism
and before modern capitalism has been de-
scribed as mercantilist. The growing mer-
chant class, a more mobile labor force, and
the development of secure lending institu-
tions challenged feudal ties to land. Spanish
and Portuguese ventures for territory and
gold in the Americas and the African coast
opened up new opportunities for their
merchants as well as merchants from Italy
and later from the Netherlands, France,
and England. The period was marked
by an almost constant state of war fought
over the control of resources and trade, the
seventeenth-century Anglo-Dutch Wars
being a paradigmatic example. European
states without access to gold and silver
mines attempted to achieve a favorable
balance of trade by promoting industry at
home and the slave trade abroad or by ac-
cessing new markets such as the fur trade in
North America. An increasingly integrated
world economy of cash crops (notably
sugar, tobacco, indigo, and tea), gold and
silver mines, banks, slave labor, naval
stores, food, and ﬁnished goods emerged.
Politically, mercantilism means the
policies and strategies of nation building.
States became increasingly centralized, mil-
itarized, and absolutist as they sought to
make merchants dependent on the state for
protection, thus ensuring tax revenue.
States developed increasingly efﬁcient and
strict bureaucracies to enforce lucrative cus-
toms duties on cash crops and African
slaves as well as to centralize the ﬂow of
information. Merchants sought to gain
protections for their interests from the
state, but at the same time, they often com-
plained about the limitations imposed upon
them, especially restrictions on with whom
they could trade. The dominant ideology
was that of the “common good,” in which
merchants deﬁned their interests as identi-
cal with the public interest. Mercantilist
propaganda urged the state to protect
domestic industry and trade because, they
argued, it would effect a general improve-
ment of the national economy as well as
make the labor force more industrious. Tax
incentives and monopoly licenses were
created to promote nascent industries and
settlement in the colonies. Policies such as
England’s famous Navigation Acts forbade
manufacturing and the development of
ﬁnancial institutions in the colonies, which
were seen as a captive market as well as a
source of raw materials.
Intellectually, nineteenth-century laissez-
faire thinkers had more in common with the
earlier mercantilists than they admitted. As
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 824 ---
748 MERCOSUR
early as the Salamanca school in mid-
sixteenth century Spain, scholastics began
to question the feudal acquisition of treasure
and the moral teleology of the Christian
state. They concluded that the inﬂux of
American and African gold into Spain
along with a corrupt and bureaucratic court
had caused inﬂation, the underdevelop-
ment of Spanish industry, and a growing
dependence on foreign merchants. For the
next 200 years, different writers debated
about the elasticity of supply and demand
and the economic principle of comparative
advantage, advocated commercial invest-
ment in domestic industry, encouraged the
state to engage in commercially useful pro-
jects such as building roads and canals, and
gave moral legitimacy to private interest,
thus overturning the Renaissance Human-
ist belief that a republic ought to safeguard
the moral virtue of its citizens from the cor-
ruption of the marketplace. The tendency
of mercantilist authors was toward empiri-
cal and materialist explanations of human
and social behavior rather than religious or
Aristotelian notions about the “good” cor-
responded with the rise of the “new sci-
ence” associated with Francis Bacon.
In terms of thought and policy, laissez-
faire economics differs from mercantilism
in four respects. First, although most mer-
cantilist authors did not subscribe to the
naïve bullionist position often ascribed to
them, they did see a ﬁscally liquid nation as
more capable of successfully waging wars,
engaging in trade, and dominating the
market. Second, although mercantilists un-
derstood the elasticity of supply and de-
mand, their focus on achieving a favorable
balance of trade still privileged production
over consumption and advocated protec-
tionist policies. Against this understanding,
Adam Smith argued that the market was
self-correcting; therefore, the state ought to
limit its domain to the rule of law, to secur-
ing basic property rights, and to providing
necessary services, because ad hoc mercan-
tilist policies that favored corporate mo-
nopolies interfered with the market and
corrupted the state. Third, while mercantil-
ism emphasized the wealth of a nation as a
competition with other nations, free-
market economists argued that an open
trade beneﬁted the people of all nations.
And fourth, while both mercantilist and
free-market economists posited the utility
of rational, private interest, mercantilists
were more likely to see state intervention as
necessary for promoting the public good.
Steven W . Thomas

MERCOSUR
MERCOSUR (Mercado Común del Sur, or
Common Market of the South) is a trade
organization formed by Argentina, Brazil,
Paraguay, and Uruguay. MERCOSUR was
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 825 ---
MERCOSUR 749
created under a treaty signed on March 26,
1991, in Asunción, Paraguay, with a provision
that the common market was to be formed
by December 31, 1994. MERCOSURseeks
to signiﬁcantly extend the global economic
reach of its member countries by creating
ties to other developing markets around
the world, including African nations.
MERCOSUR is closely behind NAFTA and
the European Union in economic power
due to its members’ combined population
of over 200 million. The most visible compe-
tition for MERCOSUR is the proposed for-
mation of a Free T rade Area of the Americas,
which has been under discussion nearly as
long as MERCOSUR has been in existence.
The T reaty of Asunción contains ﬁve
annexes outlining trade liberalization pro-
visions: the elimination of duties and other
charges among the members; product
rules of origin; dispute resolution; safeguards
against economic damage to a member
caused by unusually high imports of given
products from other members; and ten
working groups to advance the facilitation
of these economic and sector-based poli-
cies. Three other documents set out further
elements of how MERCOSUR is to oper-
ate: the Ouro Preto Protocol on the Institu-
tional Structure of MERCOSUR (“Ouro
Preto Protocol”); the Brasilia Protocol on
the Resolution of Controversies; and the
Olivos Protocol for the Resolution of Con-
troversies (“Olivos Protocol”). Additional
protocols set out rules for MERCOSUR
in more speciﬁc areas such as intellectual
property, competition, and government
procurement.
T wo of the institutions making up
MERCOSUR, the Common Market Coun-
cil (or Council of the Common Market) and
the Common Market Group, are considered
by the T reaty of Asunción. The Ouro Preto
Protocol speciﬁes those two institutions plus
four more: the MERCOSUR Commerce
Commission, the Joint Parliamentary Com-
mission, the Socio-Economic Consultative
Forum, and the Administrative Secretariat.
The Olivos Protocol provides for a Perma-
nent Appellate T ribunal, and the Committee
of Permanent Representatives is an addi-
tional institution formed by the Council as
allowed under the terms of the Ouro Preto
Protocol.
Chile and Bolivia entered into separate
Economic Complementation Agreements
with MERCOSUR on June 29, 1996, and
December 17, 1996, respectively. These
agreements do not make Chile and Bolivia
members of MERCOSUR in the usual
sense. The countries do not participate in
meetings or other activities of MERCOSUR.
Rather, the agreements give a 10-year goal
for the development of a free trade area with
Chile and Bolivia and contemplate the es-
tablishment of judicial and institutional
frameworks as well as the physical infrastruc-
ture needed to accomplish economic coop-
eration with the two countries. From August
12, 1999, through December 16, 2003, the
Andean Community and various combina-
tions of its component states of Colombia,
Ecuador, Peru, and Venezuela entered into
several Economic Complementation Agree-
ments with MERCOSUR.
MERCOSUR has also reached out to
countries in other world regions to form
trade alliances, signing an agreement with
India on January 25, 2004, and beginning
discussions with Canada in early 2005. The
organization entered into an agreement on
December 16, 2004, with the Southern
Africa Customs Union (SACU), composed
of Botswana, Lesotho, Namibia, South
Africa, and Swaziland. The agreement with
the SACU provides for mutual tariff
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 826 ---
750 M EXICO
between the two groups except in cases of
duties charged for items in new industries.
MERCOSUR also signed a framework
agreement with Egypt on July 7, 2004, as
the start of formal negotiations toward a
trade agreement with that country; Paraguay
and Uruguay have since ratiﬁed this member
agreement in 2005 and 2006, respectively,
and Argentina and Brazil are expected to
complete the same process of ratiﬁcation by
2007–2008.

MEXICO
Mexico has a history of race and African
peoples from Spanish exploration through
the slave trade and the abolition of slavery
to current cultural forms expressive of an
African past. People of African descent have
a rich heritage in Mexico in spite of the
country’s emphasis on its indigenous and
European pasts. The ﬁrst Africans arrived
there as acculturated servants and explorers
during the conquest period of Spanish
America’s history (1519–1540). The most
notable were Estevanico, considered to be
the ﬁrst Spaniard to explore what is today
the American Southwest, and Juan Garrido,
a conquistador who accompanied Hernán
Cortés’s expeditions to defeat the Aztec
Empire. The existence of Africans in the re-
gion prior to European arrival is a source of
controversy. Scholars have pointed to stone
carvings and ﬁgures with so-called African
features related to the T ezcatlipoca cult, but
these assertions have been largely rejected
by and large by the scholarly community. In
the immediate aftermath of Mexico’s con-
quest, subsequent generations of Spanish
settlers augmented their labor supply with
a small but steady importation of African
slaves; by 1570, however, the demand for
slave labor increased dramatically. Disease
decimated the region’s indigenous popula-
tions, and reformers, such as Bartólome de
las Casas, argued that African slaves would
help alleviate the harsh conditions of
Spanish rule. As a result, the Spanish
Crown sanctioned the importation of thou-
sands of mostly male African slaves as the
best alternative to the chronic shortage of
labor in the mining, ranching, ﬁshing, and
plantation economies of the Viceroyalty of
New Spain. In 1580, the entire colony had
a population of over 30,000 African slaves,
and by 1640, it had imported the largest
number of slaves in Spanish America. By
1790, the total number had grown to more
than 200,000, and most of these passed
through the port city of Veracruz, which
ﬂourished as a slave trading center.
As the number of slaves imported from
Africa increased, so too did concerns among
authorities that slave revolts could poten-
tially disrupt the colonial framework.
Indeed, slaves often demonstrated their
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 827 ---
MEXICO 751
capacity to resist by breaking tools, slowing
down the output of their labor, or simply
escaping. Moreover, the worst fears of Span-
ish colonists were realized when the num-
bers of both violent slave rebellions and ma-
roon, or runaway, settlements increased
during the eighteenth century. Amapa,
Mandinga, and Yanga became critical
refuges for escaped slaves. These develop-
ments, coupled with the fact that native
populations had recovered, compelled the
Spanish Crown to restrict the importation
of African slaves to New Spain and order at-
tacks on free settlements. Surviving ac-
counts, such as the one by Juan Laurencio,
a Jesuit priest accompanying Spanish sol-
diers, provide vivid recollections of the mil-
itary campaigns against Yanga. Yet, runaway
settlements often thrived in spite of hostile
colonial actions. African slaves had devel-
oped a strong sense of racial identity and
ability to reconstitute family and kinship
ties. Located in the state of Veracruz, for ex-
ample, Mandinga was founded by runaways
and gradually evolved into a legal township
during the nineteenth century. As the legal
status of its residents changed and a degree
of social and political stability was estab-
lished, Mandinga attracted outsiders.
Generalizing about the daily lives of
Afro-Mexican slaves is difﬁcult. The typical
African slave had some experience with a
wide range of life-altering phenomena such
as revolts, suicides, violence, witchcraft,
and slave communities. In addition, Spanish
lawmakers tried to restrict the upward
mobility of blacks by developing a sistema
de castas, or caste system, a racial categoriza-
tion scheme that ranked Africans at or near
the bottom of the social ladder. This system
meant that African slaves had few rights:
they were not allowed to receive an educa-
tion, marry, or possess weapons. Penalties
for violating any of these laws were espe-
cially inhumane. Nevertheless, slaves pur-
sued outlets of manumission provided by
the vagaries of the colonial legal system.
Early forms of manumission were outlined
in the Siete Partidas,or royal codes that reg-
ulated how African slaves should be treated.
Beyond these laws were various paths to
freedom including manumission by mas-
ters, self-purchase, and race mixture. As in
other parts of Spanish America, slave own-
ers in New Spain could grant freedom to
their slaves in wills or allow their slaves to
earn a free wage in order to buy freedom.
Still, the most common route to emancipa-
tion was through blood or marriage ties.
Race mixture and acculturation was has-
tened by the limitations of marriage choices
in so far as the number of male slaves
greatly outnumbered female slaves by more
than three to one. This had the effect of
freeing them or their offspring. From the
early 1700s, the percentage of the popula-
tion who were considered “African” de-
clined dramatically. The fact of race mixture
is clear evidence that colonial authorities
utterly failed to keep Africans and indige-
nous groups segregated. Repre sentations of
race mixture may be seen in various casta
paintings that adorned elite houses in New
Spain. Although the depictions of mixed race
couples and their offspring were ﬁctitious,
they add rich historical detail about colonial
notions of blackness, racial classiﬁcation, and
family life.
People who had African blood and
were denied opportunities for social ad-
vancement sought to improve their social
standing by enlisting in colonial military
units. The Spanish Empire welcomed this
new source of recruits as it struggled to
maintain its colonial defenses. Mulatto en-
listed men enjoyed some beneﬁts, including
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 828 ---
752 M EXICO
exemption from paying taxes; yet, they
were denied others, including the beneﬁts
of the fuero militar, deﬁned as special priv-
ileges granted to military personnel. Pro-
posals to weaken or disband mixed-race
units were met with resistance by Spanish
ofﬁcers. The conscription of black soldiers
in Veracruz was part of a larger initiative by
the Bourbon monarchs to reorganize
Spain’s defenses in response to defeats in
Cuba, the Philippines, and elsewhere in the
empire between 1760 and 1810. However,
when it came to promoting ofﬁcers, the
opportunities of light-skinned over darker-
skinned blacks prevailed.
During the wars of independence from
Spain (1810–1821), Afro-Mexicans fought
on both sides in various regional battles, es-
pecially in the Costa Chica on the western
coast of Mexico. Fathers José María Morelos
and Miguel Hidalgo, considered to be the
founders of Mexico’s independence move-
ment, encouraged Mexicans of all races and
classes to participate in attacks against
Spanish colonial garrisons and towns. A
troop of mixed race Africans, the Batallón de
los Morenos, helped to prolong Hidalgo’s
movement before Hidalgo was captured by
Spanish forces and executed. As the wars
wore on, most Afro-Mexican communi-
ties strongly favored independence. This is
probably because Mexican revolutionaries
called for an end to a variety of colonial
institutions, including racial classiﬁcation
systems and slavery. After this tumultuous
period, Vicente Guerrero, Mexico’s second
president, successfully ended chattel slavery
in 1829. Because of his accomplishments
and his ability to rally nonwhites, Guerrero
was also known as “El Negro Guerrero.”
Among his accomplishments, Guerrero
banned racial discrimination by law and
eliminated race as a category in census
counts. These measures have had the nega-
tive effect of limiting social scientists’ efforts
to compile more accurate statistical proﬁles
of Afro-Mexicans, including patterns of race
mixture. Still, an African presence in Mexico
during the nineteenth century may be seen
in novels, short stories, and poems. José
Joaquín Fernández de Lizardi’s El Periquillo
sarniento is considered by many scholars as
the ﬁrst antislavery tract in the Americas.
Fernández de Lizardi vividly tells the story
about an educated Afro-Mexican who de-
fends his race in a debate with a British
official convinced that white Europeans
are intellectually superior.
The newly independent Mexican gov-
ernment formally abolished chattel slavery
in 1829. Still, the new nation-state experi-
enced problems with slave owners from the
southern United States, who sought new
ways to expand slavery. Constant political
problems among T exas, the United States,
and Mexico arose over the issue of fugitive
slaves crossing into Mexico during the early
nineteenth century. In the mid-nineteenth
century, for example, a border crisis
erupted between the United States and
Mexico when 200 Seminoles, most of
whom were descendants of runaway African
slaves, attempted to settle in Mexico. Dur-
ing the U.S. Civil War, some Confederate
states attempted to relocate freed Afro-
American communities to Mexico. Later in
the nineteenth century, various colonization
projects to resettle black Americans were ex-
panded to include both Mexico and Central
America, but all of these efforts failed.
Contemporary estimates of the entire
Afro-Mexican population range from as low
as 0.5 percent to as high as 5 percent of
Mexico’s more than 110 million inhabitants.
Although Afro-Mexicans continue to live
among people of other races, there is strong
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 829 ---
MEXICO (AFRO-MEXICAN IDENTITY) 753
biological and physical evidence that African
descendants exist in various parts of Mexico.
This is why linguists, ethnomusicologists,
anthropologists, biologists, artists, journal-
ists, and literary critics continue to frequent
small Afro-Mexican townships around Ver-
acruz, the Costa Chica in western Mexico,
Coahuila in the north along the United
States-Mexico border, and the Yucatán
Peninsula. Life within these areas is still dif-
ﬁcult as villagers face poverty with little hope
of improvement. Still, African cultural traits
remain strong in local celebrations and festi-
vals. More scholars are teaching, researching,
and publishing on the Afro-Mexican experi-
ence than ever, and there appears to be no
sign that their activities will slow down in
the coming years.
Jesse Hingson

MEXICO
(AFRO-MEXICAN IDENTITY)
Afro-Mexican identity is deﬁned by the
cultural retention and transformation of
African identities and the experience of
racial classification and race-mixing in
Mexican society. The formation of Afro-
Mexican identity since the sixteenth cen-
tury until today is linked to miscegenation,
social stratiﬁcation and mobility, the degree
of African cultural retention, and modern
inﬂuences.
As soon as large numbers of slaves ar-
rived directly from Africa in the sixteenth
century, their status and mobility were re-
stricted by New Spain’s colonial regime.
These lawmakers set up a ranking system,
or sistema de castas, that determined legal,
social, and economic rights for all races in
the colony. Broadly speaking, Europeans
were ranked the highest depending on
wealth while indigenous peoples were
ranked lower. Africans were considered the
lowest. This scheme mostly failed to oper-
ate as Spaniards had intended because it
did not take into account other factors that
might enhance a person’s standing in the
colonial world. Africans arriving on slave
ships, for example, were immediately sepa-
rated by how skilled they were: bozales, or
those slaves described as non-Christian,
non-Europeanized Africans, ranked lower
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 830 ---
754 M EXICO (AFRO-MEXICAN IDENTITY)
while ladinos were considered more valu-
able because they knew European customs
and languages.
Moreover, the process of mestizaje, or
race mixture, served to undermine New
Spain’s racial classification system. As
Spaniards made laws regulating commu-
nity and sexual relations between Africans
and other races, almost nothing could be
done to prevent people of different races
from interacting with one another. Also,
miscegenation accelerated because the
number of male slaves greatly outnum-
bered female slaves by more than three to
one. At the least, this had the effect of free-
ing the offspring of mixed-race unions.
Thus, from the early 1700s onward, the
percentage of the population who were
considered “African” declined dramatically,
thereby increasing the number of freed
people. From this evidence, one could
argue that the colonial structure was based
more upon class distinctions where greater
socioeconomic mobility prevailed across
racial lines. While racial stratiﬁcation ap-
peared weak, racial barriers remained. The
presence of racial barriers was especially
true for Afro-Mexicans who enlisted in
colonial military units. Mulattos, for exam-
ple, enjoyed some beneﬁts, including not
having to pay taxes, yet were denied others,
including the fuero militar, deﬁned as legal
exemptions for military personnel. Light-
skinned soldiers almost always won promo-
tions over darker-skinned soldiers. Overall,
Afro-Mexicans failed to achieve any kind of
racial unity even in the face of a hostile
European-dominated legal system.
Eventually, the social structure of
Mexican society shifted around the time of
independence from inequality based on
race to a new system founded upon class
distinctions. After Mexicans achieved their
independence from Spain, leaders sought
to dismantle colonial laws, particularly
racial categorization. In this effort, race
was eliminated as a category in census
counts.
T oday, the legacy of racism continues
as Afro-Mexicans still live in impoverished
conditions, concentrated mostly on the east
and west coasts. Within these areas, run-
away slave communities were formed at
Yanga and Mandinga in relative isolation.
People in those areas usually emphasize
their African cultural traits, including
music, dance, and religious practices, de-
spite the fact that their heritage is more
racially mixed. Festivals, such as the one
celebrating Yanga, are held annually. In
Cuajinicuilapa, a town near Mexico’s
west coast, a museum dedicated to Afro-
Mexican history and culture has been
erected. Pride in their African heritage is
homegrown, but an important factor in
Afro-Mexican identity has been contact
with outsiders who visit these villages
wanting to see traces of African culture.
Jesse Hingson

MICROFINANCE
The provision of ﬁnancial services to low-
income people who are operating small
businesses has become known in develop-
ment literature as microﬁnance. Many of
the current microﬁnance programs are pat-
terned after indigenous associations in
Latin America (CorpoSol in Colombia,
Emprender in Argentina); Africa (Zambuko
T rust in Zimbabwe, CVECA Pays Dogon
in Mali); and Asia (Bank Rakyat in Indone-
sia, Self-Employed Women’s Association in
India). Poor microentrepreneurs, especially
women, have had limited access to ﬁnancial
services offered by commercial banks.
Widespread recognition of this lower acces-
sibility to formal credit has led to recent en-
deavors to target the poor through develop-
ment programs that provide financial
services.
Microﬁnance services target poor peo-
ple who operate at least one microenterprise.
Poor is deﬁned as living on less than $2 per
day. Using this deﬁnition, poor people rep-
resent approximately 40 percent of sub-
Saharan Africa population and 24 percent of
Latin America and Caribbean population.
Microenterprises (employing 1–5 people)
are a vibrant component of developing
country economies, providing a wide range
of goods and services. Often these goods and
services are provided in the informal econ-
omy that exists without formalized rules or
regulations by market vendors, microbus
and taxi drivers, small-shop owners, and
small-scale artisans. The informal economy
can represent as much as 50 percent of na-
tional economic activity and working hours
in a developing country. The importance of
microenterprises as a vital source of house-
hold income for the urban and rural poor is
often masked because their economic con-
tributions are not counted in national
macroeconomic statistics.
The need for microﬁnance programs that
target the poor in Africa and Latin America is
threefold: private sector ﬁnancial institutions
are unwilling or unable to provide ﬁnancial
services to the poor; microentrepreneurs
(especially women) are underserved by ﬁnan-
cial services provided by commercial banks;
and negative economic environments (high
inﬂation, corruption, lack of formal jobs) in
many developing countries make it difﬁcult
for microentrepreneurs to access ﬁnancial ser-
vices. The provision of ﬁnancial services to
poor people is costly and entails high levels of
risk due to potential clients not having a
ﬁnancial history, not having formal collateral
to secure a loan, and high transaction costs
(by both the client and the ﬁnancial institu-
tion) in deposit mobilization and loan alloca-
tion. Frequently, poor clients are interested in
depositing numerous small sums outside reg-
ular banking hours in rural or semi-urban
areas, and requesting small loans using no for-
mal collateral. These types of transactions are
expensive for commercial banks. Clients are
often required to leave their business and
travel great distances, conduct transactions in
foreign languages and observe customs unfa-
miliar to them, and pay additional fees
(referred to as speed money) to attempt to ac-
cess ﬁnancial services. These types of transac-
tions are expensive for clients.
There are two approaches to programs
that provide ﬁnancial services to the poor:
institutionalist and welfarist. The institu-
tionalists focus on creating sustainable
microﬁnance programs as part of a larger
system of ﬁnancial deepening (i.e., increased
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 832 ---
756 M ICROFINANCE
accessibility to ﬁnancial services by all eco-
nomic sectors). In this approach, microﬁ-
nance programs are just one layer in a mul-
tilayered ﬁnancial system that includes
informal, semiformal, and formal banking
institutions. Proponents of this system in-
clude the World Bank, the Ohio State Uni-
versity Rural Finance Program, and the U.S.
Agency for International Development.
The welfarist approach focuses on the
need of microﬁnance programs to reach the
poorest of the poor. They are less interested
in sustainability issues and the ﬁnancial
deepening potential of microﬁnance pro-
grams. Proponents of the welfarist approach
include the Grameen Bank in Bangladesh
and the Foundation for International
Community Assistance (FINCA) programs
in Latin America and Africa.
Depending on which approach a mi-
croﬁnance program embraces could deter-
mine the clients it selects to participate in
its program (e.g., poor vs. the poorest of
the poor), the type of delivery system it uti-
lizes (e.g., lending to groups vs. lending to
individuals), and how it ﬁnancially supports
the services it provides (e.g., ﬁnance compa-
nies or community banks or donor-funded
social service nongovernmental organiza-
tions [NGOs]).
The institutionalist approach is often
synonymous with the “best practices”
phrase. This phrase refers to a constellation
of recognized practices that the most suc-
cessful microfinance programs employ
worldwide. Best practices include formation
of a credit group consisting of individual
members, each of whom owns and operates
an established microenterprise producing a
weekly cash ﬂow; group guarantee of small
initial loans made to each member on a
rotating basis; use of a market interest rate
supporting program administrative costs;
mandatory savings requirement; weekly
mandatory group meeting for loan repay-
ment and information dissemination;
demonstrated high repayment rate; and the
ability of the program to service signiﬁcant
numbers of individuals. Best practices are
intended to substitute traditional loan col-
lateral (e.g., property) with information on
client creditworthiness (e.g., character refer-
ences, business reputation, ability to save on
regular basis), which reduces the risk of pro-
viding ﬁnancial services to microentrepre-
neurs. They are also intended to reduce the
costs of saving and borrowing (ﬁnancial
transaction costs) both from a client and an
organization standpoint.
As part of a strategy to alleviate bottle-
necks to private sector development, donor
agencies/institutions (e.g., World Bank, U.S.
Agency for International Development) have
provided ﬁnancial and technical support to a
number of organizations (e.g., Freedom from
Hunger, FINCA, Grameen Bank) providing
microﬁnance services to poor microentrepre-
neurs. These organizations vary in terms of
target clientele, maximum loan size, program
strategies, geographic coverage, size of loan
portfolio, and ﬁnancial security.
Microﬁnance delivery programs have
grown exponentially. In 1997 there were
approximately 600 microﬁnance institu-
tions serving 13.5 million clients. By 2002
there were more than 2,500 institutions
reaching over 67 million clients. The ma-
trix of credit sources for the poor in Latin
America and Africa usually excludes formal
ﬁnancial institutions such as commercial
banks. Semiformal nonbank ﬁnancial insti-
tutions include credit unions, various non-
governmental organizations such as savings
and loan companies, and programs such
as FINCA and the Promotion of Rural
Initiatives and Development Enterprises
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 833 ---
MICROFINANCE 757
(PRIDE). These ﬁnancial NGOs are fre-
quently located in rural areas, small towns,
or within urban markets. Often semiformal
ﬁnancial institutions offer ﬁnancial services
tailored to their low-income customer base.
These services include photo-ID passbooks
for illiterate customers, extended service
hours for market women, collection per-
sonnel who circulate in the market for cus-
tomers who cannot leave their businesses,
acceptance of small savings deposits, and
extending loans less than $100.
Informal nonbanking ﬁnancial sources
include individuals and informal associations
organized by ethnicity, kin, or neighborhood
who collect savings and may extend small
loans on a rotating basis. These informal
ﬁnancial sources are known in Latin America
as rotating savings and credit associations
(ROSCAs), in Africa as Savings and Credit
Associations (SCAs), or by various indige-
nous names (e.g., susu, esusu, katapila).
Microﬁnance programs reach low-
income households in both rural and urban
areas. They enable female microentrepre-
neurs, who access ﬁnancial services, to de-
velop ﬁnancial management, decision-
making, and leadership skills. Micro loans
are used to expand the wealth base of house-
holds and enterprises. Additionally, microﬁ-
nance programming results in clients trying
new practices and informing others about
such practices.
While providing microﬁnance services
alone is unlikely to raise clients out of
poverty, it is recognized as one of the neces-
sary development steps in alleviating poverty.
Microﬁnance programs in Zimbabwe and
Peru have enabled clients from poor house-
holds to better cope with negative economic
environments and incrementally improve
their living conditions. Participants have more
income-earning opportunities and are better
able to provide education expenditures to
educate their children than nonparticipants.
Since the mid-1980s, there have been
successful examples of microﬁnance services
replication in industrial countries. Accion
International programs, begun in Latin
America in 1961, are now established in
Chicago, New York, and San Antonio in the
United States.
One of the limitations of microﬁnance
delivery systems is their inability to service
clients who have successfully borrowed
smaller amounts from them and are now
ready to “graduate” to larger loans on an
individual contract basis. In Africa, this type
of progressive lending involving larger busi-
ness loans ($500 to $1,000) at competitive
interest rates for longer periods of time (e.g.,
18 months to 1 year) are difﬁcult for many
microﬁnance clients to access. A form of
ﬁnancial intermediation which integrates
deposit mobilization and loan allocation
services between informal and semiformal
ﬁnancial sources and formal ﬁnancial insti-
tutions is one method of increasing access.
In dealing with poor clients, financial
NGOs could collect small deposits and
disseminate smaller loans for commercial
banks for a fee. One projected result of this
integration would be the “graduation” of
qualiﬁed microﬁnance clients and the micro-
ﬁnance programs themselves to formal sector
banking. The clients would graduate by be-
coming customers of commercial banks, and
the programs would graduate by becoming
regulated ﬁnancial institutions able to sustain
themselves as commercial banks. Approxi-
mately 40 ﬁnancial NGOs have converted to
private commercial banks. Examples are more
prevalent in Latin America (BancoSol in
Bolivia and Mibanco in Peru) than Africa
(K-Rep is only African example).
Gayle A. Morris

MIDDLE PASSAGE
The term “middle passage” refers to the
transatlantic voyage experienced by
Africans who were being shipped from
Africa to America as human cargo in the
slave trade. It was given this name—middle
passage—because the journey from Africa
to America represented the middle leg of
the three-step trading network set up by
the Europeans. The trip started in Europe
with the ships transporting a cargo of rum,
brandy, weapons, metalware, and other goods
to Africa. Once in Africa, the European goods
were exchanged for slaves who would be
then shipped to America. The increasingly
agriculture-based American society was in
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 835 ---
MIDDLE PASSAGE 759
need of cheap labor. The colonial popula-
tions were small and grew slowly, and there
was, therefore, a shortage of ﬁeld labor.
In America, the enslaved Africans were
exchanged for sugar, tobacco, and other
products that would be taken on the return
trip to Europe. Slaves thus played a central
role in the European economy and to what
was called the “triangular trade.”
Forms of slavery had been in existence
for a long time, but the scale of the Atlantic
slave trade from its inception in the seven-
teenth century was something new in the
seventeenth century. It was also distin-
guished by its severity and the decimation
of the African population, as well as by the
great distances that separated slaves from
their homes, which increased their cultural
alienation and legal vulnerability. The ﬁrst
European power to organize the Atlantic
slave trade was the Portuguese empire in
the sixteenth century. However, the English
replaced them as the most powerful slave
trading nation in the late seventeenth and
eighteenth centuries. It is estimated that
the British ships transported more people
in their Atlantic voyages that any other
European nation.
African society was disrupted by
transatlantic slavery since it created a radical
break within African society. While Africans
could be enslaved in different ways by
African societies, the European economy
altered the established practices in the ex-
change of slaves. First, most slaves were sold
by African chiefs themselves to European
traders in exchange for European goods.
These slaves were usually debtors, people in
debt, criminals, or captured enemies. The
African chiefs participated actively in selling
other Africans to Europeans, rather than re-
taining them for their own society, because
the trade goods they received in return
enhanced their prestige and brought them
more followers. The other source of slaves
was direct capture by Europeans, as de-
scribed by the former slave Olaudah
Equiano’s account of his experience as a
child: “One day, when all our people were
gone out to their works as usual, and only I
and my dear sister were left to mind the
house, two men and a woman got over our
walls, and in a moment seized us both”
(Andrews, ed., 2000, p. 211).
Once captured, traders chained the
slaves together and forced them to march
to seaports to wait for the ship that would
carry them to America. Often for months
at a time, the enslaved men and women
were kept in dungeons—barracoons—
distributed along the African coast. It is
calculated that of the millions of African
people sold into slavery, approximately
half of them died before reaching the
African coast. T raders branded slaves with
hot irons as if they were cattle and restrained
them with shackles. Some of these Africans
had never seen white people, ships, or the
ocean itself.
The middle passage was psychically
traumatic and the conditions atrocious.
Male slaves were usually chained in pairs by
the ankle and placed in the space provided
for them below decks. Female slaves and
children, usually fewer in number than
African males, were left untied on the upper
dock. According to historian Hugh Thomas,
this segregation was intended to keep the
women from being seduced by the men or
to prevent women from inciting male slaves
to rebellion. The slave merchants involved in
the Atlantic trade wanted to optimize their
use of deck space. They added broad
shelves between each deck on which the
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 836 ---
760 M ILITARYFORCES
enslaved men lay, thus nearly doubling the
number of slaves who could be transported
in a single shipment. A well-known repre-
sentation of this is the plan of the English
slave ship Brookes, with the slaves packed
against each other and distributed all over
the different levels of the ship. The space in
slave ships was so crowded that the Africans
could hardly move and had to sleep on top
of each other. Sometimes there was neither
adequate ventilation nor enough space to
put buckets for the slaves’ body wastes. The
heat and the stink were insufferable, the air
totally unbreathable. If the weather was
good, slaves were forced to ascend to the
upper deck and “dance” to exercise and
prevent muscular atrophy.
The unhygienic conditions within the
ships caused the spread of all types of
illnesses, particularly smallpox, dysentery,
the ﬂux, scurvy, and dehydration. Most of
these illnesses were caused by the lack of
vitamins or adequate drinking water. In
the late eighteenth century, English traders
began to have their slaves inoculated
against smallpox before carrying them on
their ships. Besides illness, there were
other factors that threatened the integrity
of the ships’ human cargo. Suicide was
common: some slaves preferred to die
rather than cope with their present circum-
stances, endure what they were going
through, or because they did not know
what awaited them at the end of the
journey. Many jumped overboard and
drowned. Others refused to eat, but were
force-fed with a speculum orum, an instru-
ment designed to keep the slaves’ mouths
open while food was forced down their
throats. Many deaths were also caused by
violence and rebellion. Slave uprisings took
place from time to time and usually ended
in bloodshed. The rebellions were brutally
crushed and, once the crew regained con-
trol, the leaders immediately executed.
Scholars estimate that, in total, around
11 million Africans were shipped to the
Americas between 1450 and 1900 to become
slaves.
Laura Gimeno-Pahissa

MILITARYFORCES
Colonial heritage shaped the formation and
development of military forces in Latin
America and Africa. Additionally, much of
recent African and Latin American military
history can be seen as a series of proxy battle
grounds between powerful external political
forces, including former imperial powers
and the United States and Soviet Union
during the Cold War. As a consequence of
political instability caused by military con-
ﬂicts, many countries may be said to be in a
state of continual revolution.
From 1945 to 1992 in Latin America
and from the end of World War II to the
present in Africa, internal revolutions have
periodically spilled over to neighboring
countries when one side of the conﬂict
retreats into another country or turns to
another country for assistance. At present,
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 837 ---
MILITARYFORCES 761
Latin America is largely demilitarized, but
African conﬂicts may be growing.
As a result of the Panama Canal, world
powers had a great deal of interest in Latin
America and sought to gain better footholds
on isthmian trade dealings. At the start of
the twentieth century, the United States
supervised the security of its investments by
enacting legislation and agreements with
regional governments with the clear goal of
quelling revolutions and other disruptions
that would affect their trade dealings. At
this point, military forces in the region
were comprised of professional armies
loaded with weapons acquired through free
trade or direct military assistance, most
often from U.S. suppliers.
Both Latin America and Africa con-
tributed military forces in World War I and
World War II. During the Cold War, Latin
America and Africa also experienced numer-
ous military operations. In particular, World
War II heavily inﬂuenced Latin American
and African military force development.
Much of Africa was directly involved in
World War II combat while Latin American
military forces beneﬁted from land lease
programs and favorable trade terms with
the United States.
When World War II began, the U.S.
military, under extensive land-lease programs,
gave training and supplies to the military
forces operated by recognized Latin American
governments. Latin American militaries
were provided with strategical training and
developed a strong logistical infrastructure.
During the Cold War, Latin American
powers underwent a U.S.-backed stasis.
Many weapons were transferred to guerillas,
primarily because of U.S. and communist
adversarial relations between the countries.
The Latin American military alignment
with the United States improved their
ﬁghting forces. By simply extending the
progress afforded by U.S. war dollars, nations
modernized not only their military forces
but provided a model to synthesize resources
to ﬁght other forces. The combination of
updated training methods, experience, the
synthesis of logistical models, and across-
the-board skills improvement in language
ability, industrial processes, and maintenance
of complex weapons systems, such as aerial
or naval craft, were great assets for Latin
American military force development.
Between World War II and the end of
the Cold War, Latin American military
forces were of two kinds: the ofﬁcial, recog-
nized military forces which received aid
from the United States; and the secondary,
revolutionary forces that were formed due
to internal conﬂict and were often aided by
the Soviet Union and its allies. Revolutionary
forces also found their funding through
security contracts with drug producers and
trafﬁckers in the region, especially after the
Cold War. Notably, their supply line is
extremely well-organized and often follows
the same channels as the trafﬁc of illegal
drugs.
While military forces in Latin America
are characterized by the dichotomy between
ofﬁcial government defense forces and rev-
olutionary forces, with sharp contrasts in
organizational structure, logistics, and aid,
African military forces offer a different pic-
ture. In sub-Saharan Africa, military con-
ﬂicts take place primarily as a means to
promote or settle a governmental system in
a situation where none exists or there exists
an openly corrupt and brutal regime based
on military rule. Africa’s continual internal
military struggles have resulted in more
than ninety military coups since 1963.
Following African decolonization in
the 1960s, the United States, China, the
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 838 ---
762 M ILITARYFORCES
Soviet Union, and Islamic nations funneled
military aid to promote their political ori-
entation within the region and to secure
markets for trade and exploitation. As a
source of great mineral wealth, and as a
jumping-off point for the Indian Ocean,
Africa is of great strategic value and is rid-
dled with internal and external conﬂicts.
Colonial and postcolonial economic inter-
ests, communism, Islam, tribal inﬁghting,
and various forms of neocolonialism all
inﬂuenced the creation and purposes of late
twentieth- and early twenty-ﬁrst century
African military groups.
African military forces lack organized,
well-supplied professional ﬁghting regiments.
Most military powers are formed from
tribal or national conﬂicts, which consist of
small arms and light artillery. In many
cases, the army acts as the police, and vice
versa. Soldiers serve for many reasons, but
most often in order to provide a living for
themselves. Except for those motivated by
Islamic unity, the typical African soldier is
not driven by deep ideological underpin-
nings and are, generally, soldiers of fortune,
siding with whomever pays the most or
with whom they believe is the likely winner
of a conﬂict.
African military forces rely almost
exclusively on small arms. Few big-budget
items like tanks or jet ﬁghters exist. For
example, in 1979, the only tanks found in
independent sub-Saharan Africa were in the
Ivory Coast (5 French), Guinea (12 Soviet),
Ethiopia (50 U.S.), Somalia (150 Soviet),
and Mali (10 Soviet). In sub-Saharan
Africa, jet fighters could be found in
Guinea (8 Soviet), Mali (6 Soviet), Nigeria
(15 Soviet), Ethiopia (26 U.S./Great
Britain), Somalia (18 Soviet), and Uganda
(7 Soviet). Most African states lack techno-
logical, logistical, and ﬁnancial abilities to
maintain complex weapon systems. In many
parts of Africa, the variation in terrain
complicates large-scale operations. There-
fore, most African armies are designed to
perform mainly localized functions.
Other military forces present in Africa
include external peacekeeping forces and
occasional mercenary armies. United Nations
forces provide mediation, security, and
pressure toward the cessation of hostilities.
Private mercenary groups such as Executive
Outcomes provide security to foreign
companies and government leaders. While
private mercenary groups are not wide-
spread, their presence does signiﬁcantly
impact Africa’s geopolitical and commercial
landscape.
Latin American forces are typically
defenders of established governing bodies
and operate in a modern fashion, drawing
upon the weapons and skills of larger inter-
national powers, such as the United States.
Although most of the small arms used by
African militaries come from outside powers,
particularly from the era of the Cold War,
African force structures and military opera-
tions are based more on survival and local-
ized conﬂicts, rather than ideological con-
ﬂicts. Latin America’s military experience is
heavily inﬂuenced by a single large external
power: the United States. In contrast,
Africa’s many newly independent nations
and their armed forces have a much more
fractured and tumultuous relationship to
external powers.

MILLER,S AMUEL T. (FL. LATE-
NINETEENTH CENTURY)
Samuel T . Miller was an African American
teacher and missionary to Angola. Miller
was born into slavery in Burkeville, Virginia,
and grew up there before being emancipated
at the end of the U.S. Civil War. Unfortu-
nately, his birth date as well as his death
date are unknown. After the war ended,
Miller attended Hampton Institute in
Virginia, training to become a teacher.
In 1879, the American Board of Commis-
sioners for Foreign Missions (ABCFM), a
Congregational mission society based in
Boston, decided to establish a mission in
West Central Africa (Angola) and selected a
three-man team comprised of two white
ordained ministers and Miller. At the time
of his selection, Miller was working as a
teacher and serving as a local Baptist church
leader in Virginia. From the ABCFM’s
perspective, Miller was an extremely attrac-
tive candidate given his status as a freed
slave and as an educated African American
with teaching experience. As a result of the
ABCFM’s selection and his willingness to
comply with the request, Miller was to be-
come the ﬁrst African American missionary
to serve in Angola.
The team arrived in the colonial capital
of Luanda in 1880, but it was not until the
following year that the team was able to
establish their mission at Bailundu, some
190 miles (306 kilometers) inland from
Benguela, a major entrepôt on Angola’s
southern coast. Miller immediately identi-
ﬁed more closely with Africans than with
his associates, fueling his colleagues’ racist
attitudes. Undeterred, Miller wasted little
time in establishing a school for local
children. After a series of walking tours
through nearby villages to recruit students,
the school opened on January 1, 1882, and
Miller was soon teaching six days a week,
ﬁve hours a day. Miller labored tirelessly to
learn Umbundu, the local language, and
resisted students’ requests to learn Portuguese,
insisting that classes be conducted in the
vernacular. Miller was so committed to this
approach that he produced one of the ﬁrst
Umbundu grammar books, which came
to be used by both his students and later
arriving missionaries. Again vexing his col-
leagues, Miller pedagogically instituted an
industrial education strategy in which
manual labor was employed in order “to
uplift” the African students. In this senti-
ment, Miller appears to have been a product
of his background, for Hampton—“the
wellspring of industrial education”—was a
center of the industrial school of thought.
For Miller, the stress on labor and industries
was part and parcel of the evangelization
process, while for his associates it had no
place in conversion endeavors.
Due to differences with the regional
king, Ekuikui, in 1884, the mission was
forced to abandon its post and return to the
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 840 ---
764 M OHAMMED,WARITH DEEN
coast. Upon reaching Benguela, Miller and
a colleague opened a station while others
appealed to American and Portuguese ofﬁ-
cials to use coercion to facilitate the mission’s
return to the interior. After considerable
Portuguese persuasion, Ekuikui apologized
and invited the missionaries back, ensuring
their safety and calling for their hasty return.
However, at this point Miller opted to
return to the United States, citing insur-
mountable differences with his colleagues.
It is in letters that Miller sent to the board
at the time of his departure in December
1884, and after his arrival in Boston in the
New Year, that Miller ﬁrst offers a glimpse
into the hostile environment in which he
had been serving. His candidness and con-
demnation in these letters exists in sharp
contrast to his acquiescent and upbeat tone
in letters from the ﬁrst four years of his
service. Once home, Miller petitioned the
board to send him back to Angola to oversee
his own mission station, explicitly expressing
his unwillingness to work with his former
colleagues. Upon notiﬁcation of denial,
Miller severed his ties with the board for
good. By 1886, Samuel Miller was in
charge of his own school of approximately
50 students near his place of upbringing in
Burkeville, Virginia, and it is at this point
that he disappears from the historical
record. It was not until 1890 that another
African American missionary, Susan Collins,
would serve in Angola.
T odd Cleveland

MOHAMMED,
WARITH DEEN (1933–)
Imam Warith Deen Mohammed, also
known as W . D. Mohammed, is the current
leader of Mosque Cares. The son of Elijah
and Clara Muhammad, he was born
October 30, 1933, in Hamtramck, Michigan.
After the death of Elijah Muhammad in
February 1975, W . D. Mohammed was
unanimously chosen as the subsequent
leader of the original Nation of Islam
(NOI). Mohammed transformed the NOI,
which basically was a proud black nationalist
organization, into an Islamic organization
following orthodox Islam’s ideals, beliefs,
and practices. He introduced and taught
the Qur’an as the guide for followers, along
with the Five Principles of Islam and the
Six Articles of Faith. Mohammed changed
the group’s annual fast from the month of
December to coincide with the universal
fast in Ramadan (the ninth month of the
Muslim calendar). For the ﬁrst time, all
other races and ethnic groups were allowed
to enter NOI mosques (formerly called
temples) and join the Nation of Islam as
members. He abolished the titles and posi-
tions of minister, captain, and secretary.
Ministers became imams and assumed the
primary roles of leading the prayer and
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 841 ---
MONROE DOCTRINE 765
conducting other spiritual and ceremonial
functions on behalf of the community.
Mohammed also eliminated the central
authority in Chicago and made each
mosque autonomous and independent. In
1978, when the community was called the
World Community of Al-Islam in the
West, Minister Louis Farrakhan broke with
W . D. Mohammed and left the organization
along with some other members. They res-
urrected the Nation of Islam again in ideas,
principles, and practice. Although Imam
Mohammed ofﬁcially resigned in Septem-
ber 2003, many still recognize him as their
leader in the Islamic outreach organization
he directs, The Mosque Cares, which recog-
nizes the doctrine of orthodox Islam while
afﬁrming the social and cultural diversity of
Islam’s practitioners.
Besides his position with Mosque Cares,
Mohammed is an international leader and
a spokesman and member of several mul-
tireligious and peace-focused councils and
organizations. In February 1992, he was
the ﬁrst Muslim to deliver an invocation at
the opening session of the U.S. Senate in
Washington, D.C. In February 1992, he
toured the Pentagon and addressed Muslims
and chaplains in the U.S. military. In January
1993, he delivered an address before the
Los Angeles-based World Affairs Council.
On March 3, 1992, he delivered an address
on the ﬂoor of the Georgia State Legislature,
the ﬁrst ever given by a Muslim. In Septem-
ber 1992, he was presented with Egypt’s
highest religious award, the Gold Medal of
Recognition. In January 1993, he partici-
pated in the inaugural Interfaith Prayer
Service for President William Clinton.
During Clinton’s second term, Mohammed
served on the president’s Religious Advisory
Council and attended breakfast sessions for
religious leaders at the White House. In
December 1994, he was awarded the Cup
of Compassion from Hartford Seminary. In
February 1995, he was invited by the reli-
gious community and Dallas city ofﬁcials,
along with Rev. Martin Luther King III
and Rosa Parks, to ofﬁciate at the ﬁrst “Acts
of Kindness Week.” On March 6, 1995,
Imam Mohammed delivered the keynote
address at the Muslim-Jewish Convocation.
In 1996 he met with Pope John Paul II at
the Vatican. He continues to encourage
interfaith dialogue and tolerance, and
speaks regularly at the annual convention
of The Mosque Cares.
Muhsin Shaheed
