MONROE DOCTRINE
The Monroe Doctrine was a U.S. policy
on Latin America declaring that European
powers that did not already have a presence
in the Americas would not be allowed to
colonize this region. The Monroe Doc-
trine, named for President James Monroe,
was a response to the geopolitical issues
brought about by the shared American
continent. Following the War of 1812,
there were still disputed land claims in the
western North American continent and a
power vacuum left throughout Latin
America by the departure of Spain.
Monroe and his cabinet were worried
about the inﬂuence of European political
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 842 ---
766 M ONROE DOCTRINE
turmoil spreading to the Americas. The
Napoleonic Wars had taken a signiﬁcant
toll on most of Western Europe and left
the continent in shambles. Civil wars in
Piedmont, Neopolitan, and Sicily (pre-
uniﬁcation Italy), as well as the Greek war
for independence beginning in 1821, were
violent affairs militarily and the cause of
contentious debate throughout American
and European politics.
In late 1823, Great Britain and the
United States discussed how to approach
disputed territories and a new approach to
Latin America. These negotiations ﬁrst led
to an agreement to state jointly that neither
side would meddle with the affairs of Latin
America. However, Secretary of State John
Quincy Adams, as well as others in Monroe’s
cabinet, was worried that the Americans
would lose face by partnering with Great
Britain, their former colonizer.
President Monroe agreed with Adams
and in his December 1823 address to
Congress, the president announced the
United States policy toward Latin America.
The United States, on its own, declared
that European powers that did not already
have a presence in the Americas would not
be allowed to colonize or prospect.
James Polk, elected president in 1844,
campaigned on a promise to annex T exas
from Mexico, attain most of what would
become the American Southwest, and gain
the Oregon T erritory from the British. The
term utilized during the Polk presidency by
supporters of the annexation policy was
Manifest Destiny; however, this policy was
merely a morally charged extension of the
Monroe Doctrine. Polk was successful in
achieving all of his goals, going to war with
Mexico to ensure the annexation of T exas
and the American Southwest. He negotiated
U.S. Marine Corps patrol boats on the Ozoma River, Santo Domingo, ca. 1919. The United States maintained a
military presence in the Dominican Republic from 1916 until 1924. (National Archives)
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 843 ---
MONTAIGNE,M ICHEL DE 767
with the British to attain the Oregon T erri-
tory. However, there were plenty of critics of
Manifest Destiny and the true purposes of
annexation. The Monroe Doctrine encoun-
tered signiﬁcant protest from abolitionists
and small government proponents.
Presidents Theodore Roosevelt and
William Howard Taft were also responsible
for differing interpretations of the Monroe
Doctrine. Roosevelt, a leader in the Spanish-
American War, felt that the United States had
a responsibility to act as a guardian to Latin
America and enumerated such responsibility
in his corollary to the Monroe Doctrine.
William Howard Taft’s Dollar Diplomacy
was an attempt to utilize America’s economic
power as leverage in dealing with Latin
American leaders.
The Monroe Doctrine was utilized by
Woodrow Wilson in sending troops to
Haiti in 1915 and by the Republican pres-
idencies in the 1920s to take actions in
nations like Panama and Venezuela. President
Franklin Roosevelt attempted to relinquish
the United States of the responsibilities
of guardian by enacting law to release the
Philippines from U.S. control and promising
no undue activity in Latin America. This
noninvolvement, however, was temporary.
The onset of World War II and the ideolog-
ical conﬂicts of the Cold War caused Latin
America to be a battleground between de-
mocratic and communist leaders.
Nicholas Katers

MONTAIGNE,M ICHEL DE
(1533–1592)
The French humanist and skeptic thinker
Michel de Montaigne is best known for his
Essais, ﬁrst published in 1580. His work
inﬂuenced how the Enlightenment would
portray both Native Americans and Africans
and presents a critical contemporary per-
spective on beliefs about primitiveness that
are important to studies of human rights.
Montaigne was born to a rich chevalier,
Eyquem de Montaigne, and to Antoinette
de Louppes, of Spanish Jew origin. Eyquem
was a soldier in Italy during his youth, and
there had met humanist thinkers who
deeply inﬂuenced him, to the point that he
planned his son’s education according to
their humanist principles. The newborn
baby was thus sent to live with a poor peas-
ant family to get an early experience of the
hardest life. When three years later he came
back to Montaigne Château, strict orders
were given to his tutor, the family, and the
servants: the child had to be addressed only
in Latin and never forced to learn, instead
his natural curiosity was to be carefully
stimulated. Montaigne later studied law in
T oulouse and was a brilliant counsellor of
the Parliament. He served at the court of
Charles IX from 1561 to 1563.
His marriage and the birth of his ﬁve
daughters were no obstacle for his ﬁrst and
early retreat from public life. In 1571,
Montaigne chose to isolate himself with a
vast library in the tower of the château,
where he was to write his famous Essais. He
would leave his tower 10 years later to
travel around Switzerland, Germany, and
Italy. His Journal de voyage, in which the
thinker records his experiences in the three
countries, evidences Montaigne’s huge in-
terest in the customs of the diverse peoples
that he met. On his return, he was offered
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 844 ---
768 M ONTAIGNE,M ICHEL DE
the post of mayor of Bordeaux. The experi-
ence, though, ended sourly for Montaigne
when the citizens censured him for having
taken refuge in his castle during the plague
crisis in 1585. Weary and ill, Montaigne
retired deﬁnitively to the château, where he
died seven years later.
The topics of the Essais, which deal
with the most diverse aspects of the life of
a Renaissance chevalier—education, fam-
ily life, health, interests, and even clothes
and food—served as an excuse for deeper
reﬂection on essential themes. With the
detachment of a modern anthropologist or
ethnographer, Montaigne wrote about
ethics, politics, religion, law, and the cus-
toms of both his compatriots and foreign
peoples.
Montaigne condemned openly the
colonial project in America in “Des
Coaches,” an essay in which he claimed that
Europeans had destroyed earthly Paradise
to get pepper and some pearls. Both in “Des
Coaches” and in “Des Cannibales,” though
not only in these two, Montaigne con-
denses his discursive approach to the other-
ness of the American peoples. The essay en-
titled “Des Cannibales” deals in particular
with the Brazilian tribes that French explor-
ers were encountering at that time. Like
the vast majority of authors dealing with
America, Montaigne obtained information
from explorers’ accounts and chronicles,
including those of Francisco Lopez de
Gómara, Jean de Léry, André Thevet, and
Girolamo Benzoni. He stands above other
authors, however, because he personally
met and interviewed, with the help of an
interpreter, three T upinamba Indians who
had been brought to France in 1562.
Montaigne’s essay on the Brazilian men
is, according to Hayden White, a Renaissance
version of Tacitus’s Germania, which had
been written to contrast the virtue of
the simple, noble life in the forests of the
Germani to the dissolute and decadent way
of living of the Romans. Through the com-
parison, thus, the virtually neutral depiction
of a foreign nation becomes a denunciation
of the vices of Tacitus’s society. Montaigne
supports the recovery of the values of nature,
as civilization has failed to eradicate violence
and barbarism from European societies.
Horriﬁed by the bloody slaughter during
the religious wars between Catholics and
Huguenots, Montaigne, in his Essais,rejects
the validity of the antithesis “natural vs.
artiﬁcial,” or “savage vs. civilized,” in both
sophisticated and “primitive” societies. The
distinction between good and evil is equally
unclear, and the concepts themselves—as
in fact, culture and even knowledge—are
relative to the highest degree. Roger Celestin
points out that Montaigne somehow decon-
structs the notion of a center of knowledge
as he writes about the T upinambas. Instead
of incorporating them in the structures of
knowledge of Montaigne’s sixteenth-century
France, which would amount to digest-
ing the T upinambas, it would seem that
Montaigne acknowledges that a cultural
“other” only makes sense in an open process
of negotiation with one’s self. 
“Des Cannibales” inspired Shakespeare’s
Caliban character in The T empest;the Essais
were part of the dramatist’s known library.
Virginia Fernández Canedo

MONUMENTS AND MEMORIALS,S LAVERY 769
MONUMENTS AND
MEMORIALS,S LAVERY
Since Henry Wyatt raised an arch to com-
memorate the abolition of slavery in the
British Empire in 1834 at the entrance to
his home near Stroud in Gloucestershire, a
handful of monuments and memorials
concerning slavery and abolition have been
erected in North America, the Caribbean,
and Africa. Famous ones include the U.S.
memorial to the Amistad rebellion, Africa
Rising at the African Burial Ground in New
York City, Caribbean monuments to the
Maroons and slave uprisings, and slave
forts in Africa, which were once transit
points in the transatlantic slave trade.
Several prominent memorials are in the
United States. In New Haven, Connecticut,
an impressive 14-foot bronze-relief statue
sculpted by Ed Hamilton in 1992 memori-
alizes the 1839 rebellion on the Amistad.
The discovery in the early 1990s of the
remains of an African burial ground in
New York City led to the creation of the
African Burial Ground as a major memorial
site and a place for historical education
about slavery. Barbara Chase-Riboud was
commissioned to construct a monument.
Called Africa Rising, it was installed on
Lower Broadway in 1998. This magniﬁcent
20-foot bronze statue with silver patina is
topped out with a ﬂowing African female
ﬁgure.
Chase-Riboud was spurred on by
the success of this memorial and lobbied
Congress for a permanent federal memorial
speciﬁcally to commemorate the victims of
the Middle Passage. However, her efforts
and those of others have had little success.
In 1999, the Homeward Bound Foundation
did manage to have constructed a monu-
ment to the dead of the transatlantic slave
trade, which was deposited on the ocean
bed 265 miles (427 kilometers) off New
York facing Africa.
In the Caribbean there has been rela-
tively more remembrance activity. Espe-
cially prevalent are memorials to slave rebel
leaders and Maroons, rather than to victims
of the slave trade. In the British Caribbean,
the most noteworthy monument is the
Emancipation Statue in Barbados. Erected
in 1985 and sculpted by Karl Broodhagen,
it depicts a male slave ﬁgure breaking
his chains. Many on the island relate the
sculpture to the slave rebel Bussa, who led
400 rebels against the Crown in 1816.
Later, a memorial to Nanny, leader of the
rebels in the First Maroon War, was raised
in National Heroes Park, Kingston, Jamaica.
An interesting feature of the memorial to the
Asante-descended warrior is that it repro-
duces the sound of the abeng, an instrument
used by the ﬁghters. Maroons also feature
in many memorials in Dutch Suriname and
Curaçao and French Martinique; they show
the ubiquitous ﬁgure of the slave casting off
his chains. The national T ula monument in
Curaçao commemorates the slave rebellion
of 1795. Sculpted by Nel Simon and
erected in 1998, it shows three leaders of
the rebellion using a hammer and an anvil
to set themselves free.
Much of the memorial activity in
Africa is centered on the slave forts of the
west coast in Senegal and Ghana. A slavery
interpretation center/memorial on Goree
Island off Senegal was planned with the
help of the UNESCO Slave Routes Project,
which also gave impetus to many other
memorial activities throughout the Atlantic
triangle. Smaller-scale memorials include
works of art and statuary collected at the
old slaving post of Albreda in the Gambia.
Benin has been in the forefront of monu-
mental activity, especially at Ouidah. In
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 846 ---
770 M OODY,H AROLD
addition, Benin was presented with the
Reconciliation Sculpture by the City of
Liverpool in 2005. Around 13 feet (4 meters)
high, the sculpture includes iconography
from and information about the slave
trade. Rochester, Virginia, will also receive
a copy of the sculpture as atonement for
Liverpool’s history of enslaving Africans
and transporting them to the Americas.
Alan Rice

MOODY,H AROLD
(1882–1947)
Harold Moody was a founder of the League
of Coloured Peoples and an outspoken
critic of colonialism. Moody was born in
Kingston, Jamaica. His mother was the
major inﬂuence on his early life. As a
teenager Moody became a Christian, a faith
that was to be the mainspring of all his sub-
sequent activities. From 1904 to 1911 he
studied medicine at King’s College, London,
but after graduating he was refused hospital
posts because of his color. He set up a pri-
vate medical practice in south London and
married a white English wife. For the rest
of his life, Moody lived and worked in
London, returning to Jamaica for only
three brief visits.
Harold Moody had little to do with
politics between 1912 and 1929. He
concentrated on raising his six children,
building up a prosperous medical practice,
preaching, and church work. However, he
was all too aware of racial prejudice from
his own experience and by intervening on
behalf of black doctors and nurses denied
entry to hospitals. Eventually Moody real-
ized that the “color bar” in Britain was not
going to be combated by preaching or per-
suasion but required more direct action.
Also by the late 1920s he had become
much more conscious of his African her-
itage and that confronting racism was a
pan-African cause.
In 1931 Moody established the League
of Coloured Peoples (LCP), a multiracial
organization led exclusively by black people.
He regarded the LCP as primarily a
Christian organization. Moody persistently
lobbied for black civil rights, by letter and
delegation, to urge change on private insti-
tutions and government. Moody’s nation-
wide preaching increasingly dealt with race.
He believed that steady pressure, reasoned
argument, and evidence of black responsi-
bility would gradually end racial discrimi-
nation in Britain. His lack of radicalism and
willingness to cooperate with the Colonial
Ofﬁce inevitably earned him the scorn of
radical blacks.
Moody’s close contact with leading
West Indians and Africans, the Italian inva-
sion of Abyssinia in 1935–1936, and the
labor unrest in the West Indies all fueled his
criticism of colonialism. Moody was not
opposed to the British Empire; rather he
demanded that it should be democratic and
color-blind. However, by 1943–1944 he
supported the League’s Colonial Charter
for Coloured People, which demanded
colonial self-government and economic
development. Before World War II, Moody
argued for a future pan-African meeting
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 847 ---
MORANT BAY REBELLION 771
but in Africa. In 1944 he corresponded
with W . E. B. Du Bois about the 5th Pan-
African Congress that eventually met in
Manchester, England, in 1945. Moody did
not attend and the LCP had only a token
presence, a serious miscalculation. Moody
was suspicious that socialists might dominate
the congress, and he also saw it repeating
what the League had already agreed to in its
1944 charter. By 1946 Moody’s focus was
on gaining support for a Colonial Cultural
Centre in central London (also to be the
headquarters of the LCP) where black and
white people could meet each other. T o
raise money he visited New York and the
West Indies in 1946–1947. Moody returned
home in poor health and died within ten
days.
Moody was a large man and an impres-
sive speaker with great energy and organizing
skills. At his death it appeared little had
been done to change racial attitudes in
Britain. Nevertheless he had given voice to
black demands for equal civil rights and
helped prepare the way for changes in social
attitudes as well as the law. He wrote a
number of pamphlets but no major book.
David Killingray

MORANT BAY REBELLION
The Morant Bay Rebellion of Jamaica that
began on October 11, 1865, changed the
political conﬁguration of Jamaica, set off
heated political debates in England and
America, and created a historical event that
continues to inform and inspire African—
especially Caribbean—peoples today.
By 1865, the apprenticeship system
that followed the 1834 abolition of slavery
in Jamaica had been over 28 years. During
those nearly three decades, former slaves
had largely left the sugar plantations to set
up their own small-scale farming commu-
nities. Plantation owners suffered not only
from the loss of their formerly cheap and
abundant labor but also from reduced
proﬁts because the price Jamaicans received
for sugar was no longer protected by the
British. In addition, the American Civil
War both disrupted the Jamaican economy
and strengthened calls for justice and equal
rights for all people. Frustrated plantation
owners exacerbated worsening tensions in
Jamaica by placing high tariffs on imported
goods typically purchased by the ex-slave
population; 1865 was also the second year
of a drought.
What ignited this situation into rebel-
lion was escalating tensions surrounding a
case of trespassing that, itself, was more
about ongoing conﬂicts over rent and land
ownership than the actual trespass. On
October 11, 1865, approximately 500 black
Jamaicans confronted a militia of some 30
men guarding the Morant Bay Courthouse
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 848 ---
772 M ORANT BAY REBELLION
(southeastern Jamaica). Women began
pelting this militia with stones and bottles,
and the militia responded with shooting,
killing seven blacks. By the end of the day,
the crowd had responded by killing 18mili-
tiamen. In the following days, two planters
were also killed.
Similar to the Haitian Revolt (1792–
1804) under T oussaint Louverture, the
Morant Bay Rebellion was preceded by the
writing of letters and petitions to ﬁgures of
colonial power. Paul Bogle, a Native Baptist
church deacon and leader of the Morant
Bay Rebellion, wrote to Edward John Eyre,
governor of Jamaica, declaring that as loyal
subjects of Queen Victoria, Jamaica’s ex-slave
population deserved better treatment. And
once the rebellion began, Bogle declared
that the rebellion was not against the queen
but against injustice. From documents, it is
known that at least some African Jamaicans
believed that the queen did not support the
actions of those representing the Crown in
Jamaica, and it was presumed that replace-
ments sent out from England would
support the goals of revolting Jamaicans.
(T oussaint Louverture had professed a sim-
ilar conﬁdence toward France.)
The response from Governor Eyre,
however, was not justice but the killing of
nearly 500 largely innocent people. Paul
Bogle was among those killed. Particularly
incendiary in Britain was the execution of
Jamaican House of Assembly member
George William Gordon despite the lack of
any evidence linking him to the rebellion.
Immediate results of the Morant Bay
Rebellion included Governor Eyre’s re-
moval from ofﬁce and his return for trial in
England. Pro- and anti-Eyre camps quickly
formed primarily along the lines already
drawn by the contentious Carlyle-Mill
“Negro Question” debate that had begun
when Thomas Carlyle published “Occa-
sional Discourse on the Negro Question”
(1849), followed by John Stuart Mill’s
response “The Negro Question” (1850),
and then Carlyle’s revised essay “Occasional
Discourse on the Nigger Question” (1853).
The pro-Eyre side included Charles Dickens
and Alfred T ennyson. The anti-Eyre side
included Herbert Spencer, T . H. Huxley,
and Charles Darwin.
In general, the Morant Bay Rebellion
conﬁrmed already-held positions in the
United States. As stated in the December 2,
1865, issue of Harper’s Weekly, those who
supported slavery saw it as proof of “the
inevitable consequences of emancipation
and the conferring of civil rights upon men
of colored blood,” while abolitionists and
reconstructionists saw it as the inevitable
results of “utter destitution” and “injudi-
cious legislation.” T oday the Morant Bay
Rebellion and, especially, Paul Bogle remain
symbols of resistance to the injustices
of colonialism and neocolonialism as evi-
denced, for instance, in Bob Marley’s song
“So Much Things to Say” (1977).
Kevin M. Hickey

MOREJÓN ,N ANCY 773
MOREJÓN ,N ANCY (1944–)
Cuban poet Nancy Morejón has a deep
understanding of the African dimension of
Cuban history, society, and culture. The
rhythm and the contents of her poetry
incorporate the music and language of
Afro-Cubans and reveal the everyday life
of the Cuban people, particularly of the
Afro-Hispanic woman. Her particular
interest in the fusion of the Spanish and
African cultures makes her a literary de-
scendant of the renowned Afro-Cuban poet
Nicolás Guillén. Author Alice Walker ﬁnds
it refreshing and almost unheard of to read
the poems of a black woman who is at
peace with her country.
Born in 1944 in Havana, Cuba, Morejón
is a poet, a scholar, a teacher, a theater
critic, an editor, a dramatist, and a translator.
Unlike many of her contemporaries, she
opted to remain in Cuba where she has
lived most of her life. The city of her birth
is forever present in her poems. She still
lives in the old neighborhood where she
grew up and writes that she walks on
Cuba’s sidewalk as a revolutionary and
constantly afﬁrms this identity of a black
woman formed in the Revolution. Mutismos,
her ﬁrst book of poetry, was published
in 1962.
In the preface to a bilingual (Spanish-
English) collection of Morejón’s poetry
published in 1985 entitled Were the Island
Sleeps Like a Wing,Miguel Barnet points out
that Nicolás Guillén considered Morejón’s
poetry to be as black as her skin. One of the
poems in this collection, “Richard trajo su
ﬂauta,” celebrates the Afro-Cuban by evok-
ing black independence heroes and African
gods, and alluding to African-inspired
music. In the section of this collection
entitled “Mujer Negra” (Black Woman),
Morejón focuses on slavery, poverty, and
the afﬁrmation of the Afro-Cuban since
Castro’s revolution by emphasizing the
point of view of the slave and of the black
woman. The ﬁrst poem, “Looking Within,”
expresses in four simple lines how the
suffering dates from the sixteenth century
(date of the arrival of African slaves in
Cuba) and how the nightingale has always
sung this suffering. The second poem,
“Elegua’s Eyes,” is in honor of the African
orisha Eleggua, warrior, lord of the iron,
who is represented in Afro-Cuban lore as a
coconut with cowrie shells for eyes.
The critic and translator Kathleen
Weaver points out that the poem “Negro”
(Black Man) is in honor of the dignity and
suffering of millions. The poem begins by
alluding to the black man’s hair and how
some thought that it was the devil’s own
hell, then to his smile, to his footprints,
and ﬁnally to his bronze spirit. Finally, in
“Mujer Negra,” the poem that gives the
section its name, the black woman can still
smell the foam of the sea that she was
forced to cross but cannot remember the
night or her ancestral language. Cuba is the
land where the black woman, represented
as a collective consciousness, suffered and
where she stopped dreaming of the road to
Guinea. Finally, she wonders if it was
Guinea, or Benin, or Madagascar, or Cape
Verde that marked her homeland. In 2002
Morejon published a bilingual edition of
her selected poetry from 1954 to 2000.
Beatriz Rivera-Barnes

MOROCCO
Located on the northwest coast of Africa,
with a long Atlantic seaboard, the King-
dom of Morocco has had extensive links
with the Americas. The Norwegian sailor
Thor Heyerdahl suggested that it was pos-
sible that, in ancient times, men could have
sailed from Morocco to the Americas,
putting the idea to the test with his Ra
Expeditions when, in 1969–1970, Ra I and
later Ra II sailed from Morocco for the
West Indies, reaching Barbados on the sec-
ond attempt. Whether or not such travels
actually took place in the ancient world,
the longstanding presence of Americans in
Morocco’s main port, Tangier, reﬂects the
historical and modern connections be-
tween Morocco and the United States.
Morocco has a population of approximately
31.6 million.
During the medieval and early modern
period, Morocco managed to preserve
much of her independence, although the
Portuguese, Spanish, and brieﬂy the British
occupied several ports. In 1777 the sultan
of Morocco made moves to recognize the
United States, and six years later when
the U.S. brig The Betsy was captured by
Moroccans and taken to Tangier to force
the issue, arrangements for full diplomatic
relations resulted with Morocco becoming
the ﬁrst country to recognize the new
United States of America after the War of
Independence (a few countries recognized
the United States during the war). Thomas
Barclay became the ﬁrst U.S. consul in
Tangier, and in 1820 the U.S. consulate there
became the ﬁrst property abroad purchased
by the U.S. government.
There were some early American visi-
tors, not least Benjamin Rose, who as
“Robert Adams” became famous for having
visited the city of Timbuktu in Mali. An
African American born in Hudson, New
York, Rose was traveling on the ship Charles
when it was attacked by Moors. He became
a slave of the Arabs for three years until he
managed to escape to Mogador (modern-
day Essaouira) from where he was able to
make his way, after many more difﬁculties,
to London.
There also were early connections be-
tween Morocco and Argentina. In the early
1790s, José de San Martín, later the inde-
pendence hero of many countries in South
America, served in the Spanish Army in
modern-day Morocco and Algeria and was
involved in the attack on Oran in Algeria
in 1791. San Martín died in France but
was subsequently buried in Buenos Aires.
Moroccans also had connections with
Buenos Aires. Charles William Simpson,
born in Tangier in 1822, moved to Buenos
Aires in 1851 or 1852, where he was regis-
tered with the British consul as a “busi-
nessman.” He was secretary to the British
Hospital in that city and died on March 12,
1856. He was buried in the Victoria
(Protestant) Cemetery in Buenos Aires, and
when it was cleared, his gravestone was
saved and taken to the British Cemetery at
Chacarita where it survives. Morocco still
maintains an embassy in Argentina.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

MOROCCO 775
As Morocco prospered during the late
nineteenth century, many Europeans but
also a few people from the United States
and Brazil moved to the country; their
interests were represented by consuls in
Tangier. The number of Americans in
Morocco was never high, but their proﬁle
was out of proportion to their numbers.
The United States often sent in warships to
protect even the smallest of U.S. interests.
For example, Ion Perdicaris, a millionaire
who had become fascinated by Morocco,
was to cause a great deal of trouble in 1904
when he and his stepson, Cromwell Varley,
were abducted from their estate near Tangier
and held for ransom. After U.S. warships
intervened, the two were released.
The United States supported maintain-
ing Moroccan sovereignty when the issue
was raised at the Conference of Madrid in
1880, but was outvoted by the European
powers.
The American community grew in the
1920s and 1930s, especially in Tangier, an
“international city” where many Americans
settled to enjoy a relatively freewheeling
existence without having to worry about
many laws or taxes. U.S. citizens also had
extraterritorial rights, meaning that the
United States claimed jurisdiction over its
citizens abroad. There was even an American
school in the city, although most of the
children attending were not Americans.
Most people still identify wartime Morocco
with the ﬁlm Casablanca(1942). Humphrey
Bogart played the ﬁctional Rick Blaine,
who runs Rick’s Bar in the Atlantic port of
Casablanca, through which many people
are trying to escape to Lisbon and then to
America, and employs a black musician
Sam (played by Dooley Wilson). The ﬁlm
ends with premonitions of Operation T orch
(November 1942). This Allied offensive,
carried out by thousands of U.S. and
Canadian soldiers, and a number of Britons,
of whom there were more than 480 casual-
ties, captured Morocco from Vichy France,
of whom there were more than 1,346 casu-
alties. Eight Canadian airmen are buried at
Casablanca (four having previously been
buried at T etuan) and two more at Ceuta,
formerly a Moroccan port, but occupied by
Portugal and then Spain since 1415. In
2004, former U.S. diplomat Sally Kriger
opened Rick’s Café in Casablanca modeled
after the one in the ﬁlm.
After World War II, Tangier regained
its international status with some American
writers moving to the city, and others
to Casablanca on the Atlantic coast. Paul
Bowles, the New York-born novelist and
translator, moved to Tangier in the late
1940s with his wife, and the two rapidly
became central ﬁgures in the Tangier artistic
society that emerged. After independence
in 1956, a large number of the expatriates
in Tangier left. There are many American
graves in the cemetery at St. Andrew’s
Anglican Church, and the cemetery and
other sites in Tangier are regularly visited
by thousands of American tourists who
visit Tangier and other cities in Morocco
each year. Ahmed Laraki, the Moroccan
prime minister from 1969 until 1971, had
previously been ambassador to Washington,
D.C., as was Ahmed Osman, who was prime
minister from 1972 until 1979. After the
September 11, 2001, attacks on the United
States, Morocco tried to introduce tougher
security legislation modeled on George W .
Bush’s Patriot Act; however, this legislation
did not pass until after the May 16, 2003,
terrorist attacks in Morocco, in which
members of the Al-Qaeda-afﬁliated terrorist
organization Salafia Jihadia committed
a series of suicide bombings targeting
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

Spanish- and Jewish-owned hotels and
restaurants, as well as attempts to bomb a
Jewish cemetery and the Belgian consulate.
In 1980, there were 9,896 Morocco-born
people resident in the United States.
T en years later the ﬁgure was 15,541, and
by 2000 it had reached 38,000. Smaller
numbers of Moroccans live in Canada and
South America.

MORRIS,M ERVYN (1937–)
Born in 1937 in Jamaica, Mervyn Morris is
a poet, scholar, literary and cultural critic,
and editor of numerous collections of West
Indian literature and criticism. A graduate
of the University of the West Indies (UWI),
Morris also attended Oxford University on
a Rhodes scholarship in the early 1960s.
Morris retired from teaching at UWI in
2002. He still lives in Jamaica.
In 1964 Morris became an early advo-
cate for oral literature and the orality of
Jamaican poet Louise Bennett’s work. In his
essay in the Jamaica Gleaner, “On Reading
Louise Bennett, Seriously,” Morris argues
that creole is a valid Jamaican language and
Bennett’s work represents well this cultural
heritage; he thus avoids the “mental slavery”
of viewing Jamaican creole as something
uncouth or “less than” Standard English.
Morris has since edited numerous collections
of Bennett’s poetry. He is also an acknowl-
edged mentor to successful Jamaican poets,
such as Mutabaruka and Mikey Smith.
Morris’s poetry is widely praised.
His collections include The Pond (1973),
Shadowboxing (1979), Examination Centre
(1992), and On Holy Week (1993). The
majority of his poetry is concise, restrained
to one or two pages. He gained acclaim for
the poem “The Day My Father Died,” which
gave him the label “personal poet” (as
opposed to the more political Caribbean
poets of the late 1960s and early 1970s
of the Caribbean Artists Movement, such
as Edward Kamau Brathwaite and John
La Rose). Yet his poetry addresses many
personal, social, political, national, and
international issues. For example, “Case
History, Jamaica” narrates the life of “X,” a
representative nameless Jamaican, who il-
lustrates the cultural consequences of a her-
itage of slavery and colonialism. In 1993
and 1994, Morris served as the director of
the Poetry Workshop at the University of
Miami’s Summer Institute for Caribbean
Creative Writing. For his work as a poet,
scholar, and leader in the community, he has
received various honors, including the Silver
Musgrave Award (1977), the Institute of
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

Jamaica’s Centenary Medal (1979), and the
Una Marson Award for Literature (1997).
Is English We Speaking(1999) is a collec-
tion of Morris’s critical articles that focuses
on the usage of oral and scribal creativity and
the variations of Standard English and creole.
Subjects of his essays range from Louise
Bennett’s poetry to the deﬁning points of
“dub poetry,” to broad explorations of vari-
ous Caribbean authors’ works, including
Claude McKay, Jean Rhys, Derek Walcott,
Mutabaruka, T revor Rhone, Mikey Smith,
Linton Kwesi Johnson, and Sam Selvon. His
article in Disappointed Guests: Essays by
African, Asian, and West Indian Students
(1965) is a critical and earnest response to his
education and living environment while at
Oxford University. In Making West Indian
Literature(2005), Morris explores the creative
variations of West Indian authors’ works.
Morris also is the editor or coeditor of
the following collections: Voiceprint: An
Anthology of Oral and Related Poetry from
the Caribbean (1989); The Faber Book of
Contemporary Caribbean Short Stories(1990);
and Progressions: West Indian Literature in the
1970s (1991). He continues to publish po-
etry in esteemed journals such asCalalloo.

MORRISON,TONI (1931–)
T oni Morrison is an African American
novelist, essayist, educator, and a recipient
of the Nobel Prize for Literature. Morrison
was born Chloe Anthony Wofford on
February 18, 1931, in Lorain, Ohio. Her
parents were G eorge and Ramah (Willis)
Wofford. Morrison was the second of four
children (two girls and two boys). She
encountered many obstacles growing up, but
her parents expected much of her anyway.
She married Harold Morrison, an archi-
tect, in 1958 and had two sons, Harold
Ford and Slade Kevin. She and her husband
divorced in 1964, and from that time on
she was solely responsible for the upbringing
of her sons.
Morrison received a B.A. from Howard
University in 1953; it was during this period
of her life that she changed her name to
T oni. She earned an M.A. in English from
Cornell University in 1955. After a brief
stint (1957–1964) at Random House as
an editor, she taught at numerous colleges
and universities and eventually accepted a
faculty position at Princeton University,
where she has been since 1989.
Morrison never intended to write pro-
fessionally, but she has been publishing
novels, plays, nonﬁction, and song lyrics
since 1969. Among her novels are The
Bluest Eye (1969), Sula (1973), Song of
Solomon (1977), T ar Baby(1981), Beloved
(1987), Jazz (1992), Paradise (1998), and
Love (2003). A ﬁlm version of Beloved was
released in 1998. In addition, Morrison has
written a play, Dreaming Emmett, that was
ﬁrst produced in Albany, New York, in
1986. With her son Slade Morrison, she
has written the following books for chil-
dren: The Big Box (1991), The Book of
Mean People (2002), The Book of Mean
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 854 ---
778 M ORRISON,TONI
People Journal (2002), The Lion or the
Mouse? (2003), The Ant or the Grasshopper?
(2003), and The Poppy or the Snake?
(2004). Her nonfiction pieces include
Playing in the Dark: Whiteness and the Lit-
erary Imagination (1992) and the text of her
Nobel Prize acceptance speech, The Dancing
Mind (1996).
T ransatlantic themes are common in
Morrison’s novels. In Beloved, for example,
the narrator moves back and forth across
the Atlantic, offering perspectives of African
life both pre- and postslavery. An African
American folktale focusing upon slaves
with the ability to ﬂy and who can return to
Africa if they desire provides the foundation
for Song of Solomon. Paradisebrings together
the Americas and Africa via Afro-Brazilian
religious beliefs, Roman Catholicism, and
African American folk Christianity that
inﬂuence a principle character. Morrison’s
work also frequently reﬂectsAfrican American
experiences in both the northern and
southern United States and the roles history
and cultural roots play in the lives of
African Americans.
One of the most signiﬁcant U.S. authors of the twentieth century, T oni Morrison’s novels and critical writings have
brought an African American feminist voice into the center of American literature. In 1993, Morrison was
awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, a recognition of her international inﬂuence. (Getty Images)

MOVIMENTO NEGRO
UNIFICADO
Originally the Movimento Negro Uniﬁcado
Contra a Discriminação Racial (Uniﬁed
Black Movement Against Racial Discrimi-
nation), the Movimento Negro Uniﬁcado
(MNU) was formed to address civil rights
and the right to freedom of expression.
Because of its history, continuous activity,
and present relevance, the MNU is the
most important black organization in
Brazil, being the heir of the Frente Negra
(Black Front, 1931–1937) and central to
the overall history of the Brazilian Black
Movement—a movement that today com-
prises more than 5,000 groups of all sorts.
The MNU was founded on June 18, 1978,
in São Paulo at the culmination of a rally
protesting the death under torture of black
worker Robson Silveira da Luz at the police
headquarters of Guaianases, a district in
São Paulo; the expulsion of four black ath-
letes of the Tietê sport club; and the killing
of black worker Nilton Lourenço by a po-
liceman. At that time Brazil was still ruled
by a military dictatorship that curtailed
civil rights and freedom of expression,
which partially explains the radical origins
of the MNU, born as it was in a twofold
struggle against political and racial oppres-
sion. Unlike other black movements,
which favored a sheer cultural agenda, the
MNU engaged from its inception in con-
crete social activism. This meant that its
members had to ﬁght on two fronts, both
against an unjust regime and against other
oppositional groups that failed to give the
racial question its due importance. T orture,
for instance, was viewed by MNU members
not only in the scope of the military
regime but also in the broader context
of Brazil’s colonial past and the violence
inﬂicted upon slaves.

780 M OZAMBIQUE
From the very beginning, the MNU
was inserted in an international network of
black militancy, which is still at work today.
C. L. R. James’s collaboration with Leon
T rotsky was a key source of inspiration for
some of MNU’s founding members, who
became voices heard in intercontinental
meetings. And MNU activists, inﬂuenced
by trends of black thought, have contributed
to overseas debate about Brazil’s sui generis
kind of racism, a hegemonic belief that color
is not a hindrance to social and cultural
interaction.
Right after its founding, the MNU
started to foster so-called Centros de Luta
(Fighting Centers), regional groups supposed
to act locally. They were ﬁrst organized in
big urban centers as Rio de Janeiro, Salvador,
and Belo Horizonte, but soon expanded to
others cities as well. Despite its aim to pro-
mote the debate on racial issues in Brazil,
the MNU has been criticized for its intel-
lectualist, middle-class nature because it has
had little or no penetration in poor neigh-
borhoods, or favelas (jerry-built shacks on
the outskirts of big cities), or in the interior
of the country. On the other hand, the
movement has managed to be remarkably
consistent and coherent in its views and
opinions during its existence. Among MNU
activists are some of the most important
Brazilian black thinkers and academics, such
as Clovis Moura, Abdias do Nascimento,
Milton Barbosa, and HamiltonCardoso.
After the gradual reestablishment of
democracy in Brazil in the late 1980s, the
MNU moved to a more institutionalized
political practice, ﬁghting for policies of
afﬁrmative action at schools and universities,
compensation for Afro-Brazilians, acknowl-
edgment of theirimportance for the country,
and land rights for quilombo-descending
populations. The MNU remains an impor-
tant agent in Brazilian civil society and a
fundamental organization in the struggle
against racial inequality.

MOZAMBIQUE
Located on Africa’s east coast, Mozambique
has a population of roughly 19,500,000.
Portuguese explorers ﬁrst occupied the land
that is now known as Mozambique in the
1490s. Initial contacts were made with
Arab trading settlements that had existed
in coastal areas for centuries. Portuguese
traders soon established forts and trading
posts at these settlements, making them
important ports in Portugal’s eastward
expansion.
In Mozambique, the Portuguese initially
maintained a limited presence, relative to
its more prized colonies in Brazil and Angola.
Investment in Mozambique was severely
limited as the Portuguese government
chose to focus attention and resources on
the more lucrative colonization of Brazil.
This period established lasting cultural
connections between Mozambique and the
Americas. Among these inﬂuences is the
growth and use by Mozambique’s many
small-scale farmers of crops, such as maize,
that are native to the Americas.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 857 ---
MOZAMBIQUE 781
In the early years of colonialism,
Mozambique was used by the Portuguese
primarily as a source of gold and, more
signiﬁcantly, of slaves. Often, the ﬁnal des-
tination of slaves from Mozambique was
the quickly growing plantations of Portugal’s
primary colony, Brazil. Mozambique’s slave
trade continued past the early nineteenth-
century abolition of slavery in Portugal’s
other major African colony, Angola. The
slave trade from Mozambique, while reduced
in numbers, continued as that colony’s slave
exports were simply redirected toward the
networks of the Indian Ocean. Thus slaves
from Mozambique were forced into the
unacknowledged slavery of “contract labor”
systems in French sugar-planting colonies
or the slave markets of eastern Africa. This
shift in Mozambique’s slave trade from an
Atlantic to an eastern orientation would
continue until the last decades of the
1800s. The use of slaves from Mozambique
as contract labor on French plantations
lasted until the practice was abolished by a
decree from Napoleon III in 1864.
Portuguese colonialism paid little
attention to economic development in
Mozambique. The horrible treatment of
Africans, including forced contract labor,
spurred struggles against the colonial powers.
In 1962 the Front for the Liberation of
Mozambique (FRELIMO) brought together
several anticolonial movements. FRELIMO
initiated a campaign of armed resistance
against Portuguese colonial rule in 1964, a
struggle that continued until Mozambique
gained independence following the over-
throw of the Slazar regime in Portugal
in 1975.
Following independence, the FRELIMO
regime established itself as a single-party
government allied to the Soviet-led socialist
bloc, which included Cuba. The nominally
Marxist FRELIMO government provided
support to liberation movements in neigh-
boring South Africa (African National
Congress) and Zimbabwe (ZANU). At the
same time, the apartheid governments in
South Africa and Rhodesia (now Zimbabwe)
funded and armed a right wing rebel move-
ment, the Mozambican National Resistance
(RENAMO), which ignited a civil war that
lasted for almost two decades. The civil war
claimed over a million lives and made almost
two million refugees seek asylum outside the
country.
In the ﬁrst decade of independence,
Mozambique, like its former colonial cousin
Angola, became deeply embroiled in Cold
War struggles. Like Angola, Mozambique
faced destabilization efforts launched by
the apartheid regime in South Africa.
While Mozambique did not face the same
threats of formal military invasion that
Angola suffered, the South African regime
provided ﬁnancial and military support for
the reactionary rebel forces of RENAMO
in its lengthy campaign against the govern-
ment. Mozambique also faced threats from
the Ian Smith government in Rhodesia,
which attempted to topple Mozambique’s
government following its decision to support
UN sanctions against Smith’s racist govern-
ment. Since the defeat of Smith’s govern-
ment and the independence of Zimbabwe
in 1980, Mozambique has developed
friendly, if at times strained, relations with
the country.
Diplomatic relations between
Mozambique and South Africa were only
initiated with the Nkomati Accord of
1984. This process left South African sup-
port for RENAMO intact, however. The
process of developing friendly ties between
the two countries could only begin in
earnest with the fall of the apartheid
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 858 ---
782 M ULLEN,H ARRYETTE
regime. Full diplomatic relations with
South Africa were only established in 1993.
In the years immediately following
independence, Mozambique relied largely
on socialist bloc countries, including Cuba,
for political, economic, military, and social
support. However, Mozambique never
enjoyed the same level of military or civil
support that characterized Angola’s rela-
tionship with Cuba, for example. The rela-
tionship with the socialist bloc began to
change with Mozambique’s involvement
with the World Bank and the International
Monetary Fund beginning in 1984. This
change initiated a dual shift as Western aid
came to replace Soviet assistance and as the
conditions placed on ﬁnancial aid, such as
the privatization of social programs and
institutions and restrictions on spending,
compelled Mozambique’s governments to re-
organize on a neoliberal capitalist basis. With
the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1989,
the break became complete. Mozambique’s
primary sources of support outside of Africa
now include Sweden, Norway, Denmark,
Iceland, Italy, and The Netherlands. Thus,
Mozambique’s international focus has fur-
ther moved toward Europe and the East
rather than the Americas.
In recent years Mozambique has devel-
oped strong and friendly relations with
its neighbors, most notably, Zimbabwe,
Zambia, S outh Africa, and Tanzania. As
well, the country retains close relations with
Angola and other Lusophone countries,
including Brazil.

MULLEN,H ARRYETTE (1953–) 
Harryette Mullen is a contemporary African
American female poet and educator. Mullen
was born in Florence, Alabama, raised in
the T exas border town of Fort Worth, and
educated at the University of T exas, Austin,
and the University of California, Santa Cruz,
where she took her PhD. Since earning her
doctorate, she has taught creative writing
and African American literature at Cornell
University and the University of Southern
California, Los Angeles. She has produced
six volumes of poetry—Tree T all Woman
(1981), Trimmings (1991), S*PerM**K*T
(1992), Muse & Drudge (1995), Blues
Baby: Early Poems and Sleeping with the
Dictionary (2002) (a ﬁnalist for both the
National Book Award in Poetry and the
National Book Critics Circle Award in
Poetry)—as well as the scholarly study
Freeing the Soul: Race, Subjectivity, and
Difference in Slave Narratives (1999).
African and African American poetry, folk-
lore, slave narratives, feminism—each is a
scholarly concern for Mullen and all invari-
ably inform her creative work, which remains
a highly allusive affair. A typical Mullen
poem playfully manipulates advertising
jingles, slang, black vernacular, diasporic
idioms, pigeon, blues lyrics, nursery rhymes,
and any number of other discourses in an
attempt to deconstruct the essentially oral
African American literary tradition pro-
pounded by Henry Louis Gates Jr. and to
refashion it into a multivoiced, participatory,
intertextual poetics. Taking inspiration
from the dictionary word game S/H110017, a
mathematical composition technique of
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 859 ---

the international literary avant-garde group
Oulipo (Ouvroir de littérature potentielle ),
as well as the all manner of constraint-based
wordplay—acrostics, anagrams, homo-
phones, puns, oronyms, palindromes—
Mullen’s work is decidedly experimental.
Never merely exuberant for its own sake,
Mullen’s language teases out perceived social,
cultural, and political divides and in doing
so, celebrates the inherent mongrel character
that is contemporary American culture.
Her intertextual parodying reimagines the
African American’s relation to Anglophone

wide praise, receiving, among other acco-

MUSEUMS AND
TRANSATLANTIC SLAVERY
The museum’s practice of collecting and
exhibiting African and African American
cultural objects and practices, as well as the
cultural practice of slavery and the slave
trade, reveals the contentious issues sur-
rounding historical engagement with, and
acknowledgment of, the slave past. Since
the 1990s a number of museums across the
world have begun to explore the subject of
transatlantic slavery and the slave trade as
part of a trend to engage in meaningful
debates on difﬁcult subjects that had tradi-
tionally been marginalized.
In the past, museums have avoided
controversy and either ignored issues related
to slavery or have only dealt with aspects
that are comfortable. For instance, in many
museum structures, African artifacts are in-
cluded within natural history collections in
an anthropological and ethnological con-
text. While there have been many good and
interesting displays, such an approach does
not allow for proper integration within
wider historical themes or develop the in-
teraction between Africans, Europeans, and
white Americans when exploring such
issues as slavery or colonization. Similarly,
the history of black people within the Dias-
pora has rarely been considered worthy of
notice, just as the contributions of most
working people are ignored.
Probably the earliest museum to
approach the subject of slavery was
Wilberforce House in Hull, England, the
family home of William Wilberforce,
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 860 ---
784 M USEUMS AND TRANSATLANTIC SLAVERY
which opened to the public in 1906. At
that time and for many years afterward, the
principal focus was on Wilberforce’s per-
sonality and the displays related to him and
his abolition campaigns. A few artifacts,
such as whips and shackles, were included.
Some of the earliest developments in
terms of slavery were related to the inter-
pretation of historic sites. Although black
people constituted about half the population
of Virginia’s capital, Williamsburg, in the
eighteenth century, visitors to Colonial
Williamsburg saw no black faces and almost
no reference to black workers until 1975.
Gradually black interpreters and a wide range
of programming addressing these topics
were introduced. A major development was
the reconstruction of the slave quarters on
the nearby plantation at Carter’s Grove,
which opened to the public in 1989. Here
visitors see not only the physical conditions
of the enslaved but face up to uncomfort-
able issues, including slavery, racism, and
discrimination.
The wider museum world began to
explore some of the issues surrounding
slavery during the 1980s and early 1990s.
New displays were installed in Wilberforce
House in 1986, but these were limited in
interpretation and execution and had little
impact. T emporary exhibitions on the local
black population in Britain were held in
Liverpool, Nottingham, and London, and
in 1992 the T rophies of Empire series of
exhibitions in Liverpool, Bristol, and Hull
explored the legacies of Britain’s colonial
past with particular reference to slavery. A
major exhibition on the French slave trade
opened in Nantes under the title Les
Anneaux de la Mémoire in 1992. At about
the same time, a number of exhibitions
were developed in museums in the United
States. Among the most comprehensive was
A House Divided: America in the Age of
Lincoln organized by the Chicago Historical
Society in 1990. This exhibit placed the
issue of slavery at the heart of the display.
In 1991 Richmond’s Museum of the Con-
federacy addressed related issues in its exhibit
Before Freedom Came: African American
Life in the Antebellum South. This exhibit
later toured and a smaller version was
incorporated into the museum’s permanent
displays. The traveling exhibit A Slave Ship
Speaks was based on the artifacts that have
been recovered from the wreck of the slave
ship Henrietta Marie.
However, the ﬁrst major museum dis-
play to examine the transatlantic slave trade
and its associated slavery was the T ransat-
lantic Slavery: Against Human Dignity
Gallery at the Merseyside Maritime Museum
in Liverpool. This three-year project began
in 1991 with the support of the Peter
Moores Foundation, a private charitable
organization, and culminated with the
opening of the gallery in October 1994.
This groundbreaking initiative, which has
attracted international attention, is based
on extensive academic and community
research and consultation.
Other permanent exhibits on the
British slave trade and slavery have opened
since then. A temporary exhibition on
Bristol’s slave trade in 1999 was later incor-
porated into the city’s Maritime and Indus-
trial Museum as a result of public demand
pending the realization of plans for a new
Museum of Bristol. In the same year, the
National Maritime Museum’s T rade and
Empire Gallery included a signiﬁcant sec-
tion on black seafarers and on the slave
trade. The Empire and Commonwealth
Museum, which opened in Bristol in 2002,
also addresses the subject in a frank and
open manner.

--- PAGE 861 ---
MUSEUMS AND TRANSATLANTIC SLAVERY 785
These projects have not been completed
without comment and controversy. The
Liverpool development involved a prolonged
discussion with the black community, locally
and farther aﬁeld, over wide-ranging issues
of ownership, project structure, interpreta-
tion, and content. The T rade and Empire
Gallery was subject to a sustained campaign
in parts of the British press outraged that
the museum should be raising issues
that questioned the traditional view of the
Empire.
Inevitably some museums are reluctant
to deal with the subject and this reluctance
has also extended to funders. With a few
notable exceptions, the major developments
have been undertaken by public institutions
with ﬁnancial support from public bodies.
Certainly there has been little commercial
sponsorship.
In the United States there are few
major museums that have substantial dis-
plays devoted to transatlantic slavery. The
most extensive development is the Museum
of African-American History in Detroit,
which includes a 70-foot replica of a slave
ship and cast ﬁgures representing slaves.
This display has proved to be controversial
because the casts were taken from local
schoolchildren whom critics argue are too
healthy and well nourished to represent the
enslaved. Few attempts have been made to
examine the trade itself and show visitors
the origins of the African American popu-
lation. The traveling exhibition Captive
Passage, originated by the Mariners’ Museum
and developed from the Liverpool gallery,
was the ﬁrst signiﬁcant examination of the
trade.
In many museums and historic sites
the subject matter is largely ignored. A
2002 survey of nearly 200 plantation
museums and sites in the American South
concluded that slavery was inadequately
presented. In the vast majority of cases, the
subject was ignored or trivialized. Plantations
were seen in terms of their owners, the
interior decoration, and the often luxurious
contents with no reference to the people
whose labor produced the lifestyle—the
black laborers and servants. Only black-run
sites and a handful of white-organized sites
treat the experience of slavery with any
measure of competence.
Many of the museums that do attempt
to treat the subject in a direct, frank, and
holistic manner are to be found in West
Africa, the Caribbean, and South America.
However, they are rarely able to present dis-
plays to the standards found in museums in
Europe and North America because of the
lack of resources, facilities, and investment.
In West Africa, the main such displays are
found in buildings associated with the trade
itself. The historical museum in Ghana is
housed in the former Cape Coast Castle
and the former fort at Elmina is also main-
tained as an historic site. In Senegal, there
are displays in the former Old Fort and
Maison des Esclaves on the island of Goree.
Limited support has been given by interna-
tional organizations such as UNESCO and
by some European and American museums.
Similarly, in the Caribbean there are few
major museums and few displays on slavery
and its impact. Probably the most substan-
tial display is found in the Kura Hulanda
Museum in Curaçao, which has been pri-
vately funded. Under the title the African
Holocaust, this display examines the trade
from a mainly non-European perspective
and places it against displays of African
artifacts and replicas. There are plans for
museum displays in a number of coun-
tries, including Barbados, J amaica, and
the Bahamas, and the potential of many
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 862 ---
786 M USIC,A FRICAN
historic sites across the region is being
examined.
There is no doubt that the issue of slav-
ery presents difﬁculties for museums. Some
of these are structural ones: who does it?
who pays for it? where do you do it? who
organizes and controls the process? Some
are emotional ones: slavery is not an ordi-
nary subject and with its adjunct racism, it
is still potent, controversial, and raw. But
the challenges go wider. In practical terms
there are other difﬁculties. Lack or imbal-
ance of collections is one. Many European
museums have larger and more compre-
hensive African collections than their coun-
terparts in Africa, but they often have very
little relating to their own black communi-
ties. There are interpretative problems. For
instance, many African artifacts have tradi-
tionally been seen from a European per-
spective; the information recorded is often
poor, inaccurate, and partial. There are few
images and few representations of Africans,
and frequently the Africans are depicted in
subservient or debased positions relative to
European images. For example, most dis-
plays show European material produced for
the antislavery campaigns, which often
silences an African perspective on the expe-
rience of slavery while empowering and
elevating European agency. So museums
have to be careful how they use the so-called
material evidence and to think carefully
about the messages that they promote. Fur-
thermore, the need for cooperation between
museums and other agencies across the
Diaspora is vital to ensure that resources
are shared more equally.
Anthony Tibbles

MUSIC,A FRICAN
African music contains vast musical
forms—not just drumming—extensive
variation, and demonstrates dynamic cul-
tural exchanges within Africa and between
African and African American musical
forms. It is sometimes thought that before
colonizers came, Africa was totally isolated
from the rest of the world. Yet, in precolo-
nial times, Africa had trade connections
with countries of the Mediterranean, the
Near East, and Southeast Asia, as well as
China and India. Indigenous Africans have
long encountered people and music of
other societies within Africa itself, in the
East Horn, the Sudanic belt of West Africa,
eastern areas of the continent, and on the
island of Madagascar.
During the Islamic period of African
history, which began in 741 CE, Islamic
and Arabic culture were widely dissemi-
nated on the continent. People in many of
these Islamized areas continue to perform
music today that has recognizable Arabic
traits. In North Africa the music is heavily
Arabic.
Since Arabic music belongs to the
Oriental family of modal music and is
markedly different from the indigenous
African music that preceded it, the two
families cannot be treated effectively as one
branch of the same musicology. And yet, in
spite of these disparities, North African
music is still unequivocally “African
music,” whether it “sounds African” or not.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 863 ---
MUSIC,A FRICAN 787
The same is true of certain kinds of
Western music that have inﬂuenced indige-
nous African music, particularly in southern
portions of Africa where there has been a
European settler population plus a core of
Western-oriented African people. And the
long history of intercontinental communi-
cation across the Atlantic Ocean between
Africans and their descendants in the New
World has resulted in hybridized popular
music and dance forms that continue to
prosper in Africa and beyond. Varied as the
preceding kinds of music are, however,
their existence on African soil means that
they too qualify as “African music.”
In the early decades of the twentieth
century, when pioneer musicologists in
Africa and the West ﬁrst began serious
research into sub-Saharan African music,
they noticed a cluster of musical character-
istics that seemed to be continent-wide and
to have remained intact despite centuries of
countless African catastrophes. Even a hun-
dred years later, these characteristic traits
are still alive and well in Africa, sometimes
unchanged, sometimes diluted, reﬁned, or
otherwise modiﬁed, but always recognizable
for their uniqueness as compared with
other world music.
Language in Africa has had a strong
connection to music. In fact, no serious
study of sub-Saharan music should over-
look the fact that Africa is the most multi-
lingual continent in the world. Estimates
indicate more than 2,000 distinct languages
and as many as 8,000 dialects are spoken.
However, the majority of these languages
are tone languages, which explains the
inextricable unity of language and music in
Africa. In tone languages, the highness or
lowness of the syllables in words contributes
to meaning. The same word of only two
syllables can mean as many as four different
things, depending upon selection of high-
or low-pitched syllables. Africans learning
these languages as children can soon distin-
guish subtle differences in intonation, and
the melodic tones contribute to aspects of
music as well.
Africans have put their unique tonal
languages into practical use through a
number of speech surrogate musical instru-
ments that can “speak” words of praise (or
condemnation); chronicle history; recite
poetry, proverbs, and epics; warn of danger;
and more. Most commonly these remarkable
instruments are drums with membranes or
made of wood or metal, but xylophones,
trumpets, bells, and other instruments capa-
ble of at least two pitches are also used.
Another distinctive characteristic of
African traditional music is its extreme
importance to society as a whole. Music is
everywhere in Africa and has multifarious
uses. There are speciﬁc songs for everything
imaginable: for rowing upstream, and for
rowing downstream; for educational pur-
poses; to accompany cooperative labor; of
political commentary; essential to rites of
passage; of worship; for celebrating the loss
of a child’s ﬁrst tooth; for chiding a child
for bed-wetting; and for a beautiful cow.
The Zulus have a praise song to honor a
valiant (if defeated) enemy, and in Ghana
there is a special song for hanging.
At gatherings, which most often occur
out-of-doors, it is often difﬁcult to differ-
entiate African performers from the audi-
ence, since both are closely interwoven.
The audience is apt to sing along, clap, pop
ﬁngers, or dance enthusiastically, making
everyone present at a performance an active
participant. In short, African music is
communal.
“Moving to music” is an essential con-
comitant of African music, observable not
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 864 ---
788 M USIC,A FRICAN
only everywhere in Africa, but highly visible
in distant locations when people of the
African Diaspora assemble for worship, or
just to share their energizing music. African
music is spectacularly kinesthetic, and
appears to incite some kind of physical
response—usually dancing.
Not only are music and dance insepa-
rable in Africa so are the arts in general
treated as total art. Often in festivals or
other events that include music, there is also
dancing, poetry, costumes, pageantry, role-
playing, storytelling, and imaginative visual
effects. If opera is deﬁned as “sung drama,”
Nigerians were staging genuine operas long
before having contact with the West.
All universal categories of musical in-
struments, grouped according to how they
produce sound, are found in abundant
variety in Africa: membranophones (vibrat-
ing skin), chordophones (vibrating strings),
aerophones (vibrating air), and idiophones
(the vibration of the instrument itself).
Some of these instruments that were origi-
nally indigenous to Africa, such as the mbira
(hand piano), kora, and banjo, besides any
number of percussion instruments, are fast
spreading to other parts of the world. Africa,
in turn, has enthusiastically embraced
Western electronic instruments, guitars in
particular.
In fact, there are parts of Africa where
there are no drums whatsoever, but Africa
is home to endless varieties of idiophones
that vibrate when they are struck, scraped,
stamped, or shaken. When sub-Saharan
Africa is considered as a whole, the most
universal percussion instruments—ones
always available—are clapping hands. 
Although all world music consists of
the same elements, namely rhythm, melody,
harmony, texture, form, and timbre, the
nature of these elements and their uses
differ widely from culture to culture. In
Africa, rhythm takes precedence over all the
other elements. African rhythm is so unique,
so unimaginably complex, yet so com-
pelling, that this factor alone must account
for the popularity and global inﬂuence of
Africa on popular music, folk music, and
myriad dance forms.
Nowhere else in the world is rhythm as
rousing and sophisticatedly complex as in
Africa. A single rhythm is almost nonexis-
tent, as was observed by early scholar A. M.
Jones. All over Africa, he said, there are
always two simultaneous rhythms going
on, or even three, four, or ﬁve rhythms
occurring at the same time.
Initially, when musicologists tried to
understand and analyze the bafﬂing intrica-
cies of African rhythm, they unsuccessfully
applied concepts of Western music theory.
They had been trained to read printed music
that represents sound by notes, measures,
bar lines, staves, key signatures, time signa-
tures, dots, rests, clefs, and additional
dynamic markings. Because of time signa-
tures, Western music tends to have regu-
larly recurring accents. The positive side of
this means that performers can play together
in a coordinated manner, but the downside
is that if accents are followed too religiously,
music can end up sounding unduly rigid.
In the West, time is divided into rhythmic
units (notes) that have constant ratios and
are simple fractions of each other. In other
words, two quarter notes always last as long
as one half note; and a sixteenth note
always lasts as long as half an eighth note.
Although this system, known as “divisive
rhythm,” does not cover every situation, it
has proved to be fairly adequate when
Western music is concerned.
In Africa, however, there is no written
body of music theory. Music traditions are
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 865 ---
MUSIC,A FRICAN 789
passed along orally for generations. Fur-
thermore, additive rhythms dominate most
African music, meaning that time is divided
into units (beats or pulses) that are added
together, rather than divided. The crucial
words, additive and divisive, pinpoint a
fundamental and important distinction
between African and Western rhythms.
However, the polyrhythmic texture of
African music is of even greater signiﬁcance.
In West Africa, for example, there are
“time lines,” frequently consisting of 12
pulses (or beats) that are added as units and
repeated as cycles throughout a given work.
Usually a double bell with two pitches
reiterates the time line, but this is often
reinforced by a large rattle. T ogether these
instruments maintain the underlying pattern
of the time line. A very common example
from Ghana is 2/H110012/H110011/H110012/H110012/H110012/H110011. Note
that this does not suggest any of the stressed
beats implicit in Western time signatures.
Although it is difﬁcult for Westerners
to comprehend how extremely complex
polyrhythms can be regulated by a time
line, African musicians use them almost like
a metronome might serve a Western musi-
cian, the exception being, however, that a
metronome regulates practice, whereas a
time line is an essential part of performed
African music.
Once the time line has been established
by the double bell, the other musicians
enter at their own pace and commence
their individual rhythmic patterns. An un-
informed Western-trained conductor, how-
ever, might try in vain to get the assembled
musicians to start on a downbeat. (There
are no downbeats in indigenous African
music.) Once launched, intricately inter-
woven polyrhythms continue in a collective
performance that often continues for a sus-
tained period of time.
Africans also show a marked interest in
that element of music known as timbre.
Any number of vocal sounds, in addition to
musical tones, are cherished and exploited,
including yodeling, grunting, hissing, ulu-
lating, falsetto, growling, clicking, and a
thick quality sometimes referred to as
“threadiness.”
In instrumental music as well, an addi-
tional noise factor is frequently added in
the form of small attached, or enclosed,
seeds or small stones or bits of metal that
hum, rattle, buzz, or even blur the main
tone. For Africans, noise embellishing a
tone is as much appreciated as a tone.
Although African music uses melody
in the many songs that are part of African
culture, melody, in general, plays a subordi-
nate role to rhythm. However, short
melodies, blended with the characteristic
vocal “call-and-response” form, are every-
where in Africa, as well as in far distant
parts of the world where there has been an
African presence or secondary inﬂuence.
There are myriad variations of call-and-
response (antiphony) used for instrumental
as well as vocal music, but the song arche-
type involves a lead singer whose initial
phrase is answered immediately by a chorus.
Back and forth the pattern continues
throughout an entire work, often with the
leader improvising or overlapping his/her
call phrase before the ending of the choral
phrase—an “Africanism” that results in dense
and fascinatingly interwoven sounds that
some scholars see as symbolizing the com-
munity and closeness of African society.
Americans are indebted to people of
African descent for creating the music forms
that give this country its very identity, no-
tably spirituals, ragtime, blues, jazz, rhythm
and blues, hip-hop, rap, and gospel. Myriad
original dance forms are also associated
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 866 ---
790 M USIC,A FRICAN POPULAR
with the music forms. The same phenome-
non continues in the Caribbean, South
America, and elsewhere on the planet.
Such a triumphing of the arts, despite
severe adversity, testiﬁes to the enormous
power of culture to survive and afﬁrm itself.
In this case, individual genius and imagina-
tive use of African-derived polyrhythms,
syncopation, call-and-response, and unusual
timbres have made it all possible.
In fact, at this very moment in time,
young people the world over are listening
to, dancing to, or performing popular music
whose relentless and ubiquitous accents on
the second and fourth beats continue to
speak in a subversive African voice. In a
strange way that never could have been
imagined or consciously maneuvered,
African people have managed to “colonize”
the world from within, via their extraordi-
nary, life-afﬁrming music and dance.
Carol Lems-Dworkin

MUSIC,A FRICAN POPULAR
Contemporary African popular music has
many elements contributing to its evolution
and development, the most significant
being the rich eclectic cultural diversity of
the continent’s inhabitants and the inﬂuence
of foreign cultures. American music styles
such as rumba, jazz, blues, funk, reggae,
soul, and rock have been the most inﬂuen-
tial. Just as Africa impacted the music of
the New World in the aftermath of the
transatlantic slave trade, the Americas have
reciprocated by strongly inﬂuencing the
music of Africa. Music styles, musical
thought, and musical technology from
North America, Brazil, and the Caribbean
have had a great impact on African popular
music. This impact is due, in strong part,
to the ways in which Africans can easily
relate to the historical experience of blacks
throughout the Americas. Furthermore,
African musicians often see in the aesthetics
of their American counterparts outstanding
models to emulate.
Popular music is an expressive practice
and performance in African daily life. This
reservoir of African cultural values is a por-
trait of local realities, the motor of society,
and the soul of the people. Apart from en-
tertainment and identity formation, popular
music has become a tool against socioeco-
nomic and political injustices in contempo-
rary African societies. It portrays social
problems and offers possible solutions
through lyrics that focus on such issues as
politics, economy, health, literacy, working
conditions, nutrition, urbanization, and
agriculture. Most importantly, popular
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 867 ---
MUSIC,A FRICAN POPULAR 791
music expresses people’s hope and desire for
change.
While most musicians use local themes
and rhythms, improved communication
and transportation have led to inﬂuences
across continents and cultures. The product
of this process in Africa is a popular music
that combines local and foreign rhythms
and instruments, which has led to renewed
creativity and a wider audience, while re-
taining an African ﬂavor. African musicians,
aware that their music draws strength from
syncretism and enticed by the prospect of
international sales, are very receptive to for-
eign rhythms, particularly American styles.
There has been a fusion of African local
music styles and American music traditions
such as rumba, jazz, gospel, funk, reggae,
and rock. These American inﬂuences have
been enhanced by electronic media such as
radio, television, the Internet, and satellite
broadcasts.
Many factors contribute to American
inﬂuences on popular music in Africa.
Most notable are the long-standing transat-
lantic connections that have kept Africans
in the Diaspora connected. Black inﬂuence
from the Americas started with the policy
of returning freed slaves from the United
States, Brazil, and the Caribbean to Africa
in the early nineteenth century. These re-
turnees brought with them dance music
styles originally from Africa but adapted to
the New World, and then fed back into the
mainstream of African music. African
American and Caribbean sailors who
visited African ports—Monrovia, Free-
town, Cape Coast, Accra, Lagos, and Cape
T own, in the mid-nineteenth century in-
troduced calypso, meringue, ragtime, and
minstrelsy to the continent. Caribbean
regimental bands stationed in West African
forts, American warships refueling along
African coasts during the American Civil
War in 1862, and the inﬂux of American
troops during World War II comple-
mented this early American inﬂuence. In
most cases, there was a small contingent of
African Americans on board who served as
cleaners and stewards and also provided
musical entertainment for the crew. In ad-
dition, as African native churches began to
separate from those of the white missionar-
ies and take on an independent existence,
special styles of music were developed.
One source for these was the American
Negro spiritual which became an inspira-
tion for Africans early in the twentieth
century.
With increasing urbanization, new music
styles that combined African and American
elements emerged in Accra (Ghana), Lagos
(Nigeria), Nairobi (Kenya), Dar-es-Salam
(Tanzania), Kinshasa (Democratic Republic
of Congo), and the black townships of South
Africa. These were cities that provided lead-
ership during the 1950s and 1960s and
brought about social, economic, and politi-
cal change in Africa. These new forms in-
clude West African highlife, which had
Caribbean traits, Congolese popular music,
which reﬂected Latin American inﬂuences,
and Southern African sabasaba and kwela,
both of which drew on American swing and
jive music.
In the 1970s and 1980s, many African
artists and musicians migrated to Europe
and the Americas to pursue professional
careers. Many traveled to the United States
to study at various institutions, including
the Manhattan School of Music in New
York. In the process, they were inﬂuenced
by American sounds and new recording
technologies that had emerged rapidly
since the 1950s. These artists subsequently
reinvented African music.
