792 M USIC,A FRICAN POPULAR
Similarly, visits and tours by African
American artists, such as jazz musician
Louis Armstrong in 1956 and 1962, jazz
saxophonist Paul Winter, trombonist
T rummy Young, and clarinetist Edmund
Hall, among others, were a source of inspi-
ration. Those visits afforded African musi-
cians ﬁrsthand experience with American
artists.
In the postwar years, highlife and
calypso transformed the musical scene in
English-speaking Africa. In the 1970s,
American soul and rock music spread in
West Africa where it was adapted to local
realities to produce highlife. Highlife music
is the Ghanaian and Nigerian ballroom
music. Its instrumentation consists of
Western instruments, such as saxophones,
trumpets, trombones, ﬂutes, and electric
guitars, combined with a rhythmic ensemble
of African drums, bells, xylophones, mbiras
(thumb-pianos), flutes, and sometimes
rattles, which back up the melody instru-
ments. In order to produce rhythms that ﬁt
more easily into a Western musical scheme,
many highlife bands have come to use
Latin American rhythms. Among the early
pioneers of Ghanaian concert parties and
highlife are King Bruce and his Black Beat,
E. T . Mensah and his Ramblers dance
band, Roy Chicago, Ashanti Brothers,
Nana Ampadu, City Boys, and Hi-Life
International. T rumpeter Victor Olaiya and
guitarist Bobby Benson led highlife music
in Nigeria in the 1960s. Besides bringing
calypso to West Africa, in 1948 Benson also
formed a band called Bobby Benson Jam
Session Orchestra, which played pop,
swing, ragtime, jazz, and later highlife
music. Other inﬂuential Nigerian highlife
bands include Rex Lawson’s Mayors Dance
Band, Osita Osadere’s Soundmakers Inter-
national, Oriental Brothers International
Band, Orlando Owoh’s Omimah Band,
Oliver de Coque’s Expo ’76 Ogene Super
Sounds. Ebenezer Obey modernized juju,
the African equivalent of American folk-
rock, derived from the samba and intro-
duced to Nigeria by the descendants of
freed Brazilian slaves, by drawing on high-
life. “King” Sunny Ade, a key ﬁgure in
juju music, emphasized the techniques of
Jamaican dub and sonic details. Indicating
their American connections, highlife bands
often take their names from American mod-
els; for example, the Ramblers, the Comets,
the Stargazers of Kumasi, the Black Beats,
the Modern King Stars, and the Ambas-
sador Springboks. Many use the big-band
styles of jazz and Western pop that were
prominent in the 1940s.
Highlife was later influenced by
American jazz, rock, reggae, and hip-hop. It
absorbed many elements of jazz, especially in
ordinary orchestras of wind and string
instruments. It also had many aspects of
Afro-calypso and reggae taken from guitar
and Caribbean inspiration. The introduction
of soul and reggae in the late 1960s and
1970s ushered in a very creative era in
African popular music, bringing about
Afro-rock, Afro-reggae, and Afro-hip-hop.
The black American soul message
“Black and Proud” was taken up by a gen-
eration of Africans listening to American
soul music, spirituals, and jazz. Soul stimu-
lated a new crop of creative musicians,
including Nigerian Fela Anikulapo-Kuti,
Ghanaian Osibisa, and Cameroonian
Manu Dibango. Fela Anikulapo-Kuti was
deeply impressed by American artists,
which led him to use jazz as a stepping-
stone to African music, and subsequently
used African music to play jazz. In 1968, he
coined a new style of music, Afro-beat, by
combining James Brown’s funk music,
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 869 ---
MUSIC,A FRICAN POPULAR 793
highlife, and jazz with Nigerian beat. The
Black Power Movement inﬂuenced him
during a ten-month promotion tour in the
United States. His intricate music, which
might be called Afro-jazz, blends African
rhythms and jazz horn lines with sociopo-
litical lyrics that defend the rights of the
common people.
Manu Dibango, Africa’s best-known
jazz saxophonist and heir to jazz and
rhythm and blues, became famous as a
result of his legendary jazzy sound Soul
Makossa (1972). This album was followed
by African Soul, a mixture of jazz, rumba,
and Latino rhythm. He fused African
rhythms and melodies with reggae, notably
on Gone Clear (1979) with American artists
Robbie Shakespeare and Sly Dunbar, and
funk on Waka Juju (1982). Dibango also
popularized makossa, which combines
Western and African instruments and con-
fronts sociopolitical issues. In 1983, he
recorded Electric Africa, an extraordinary
mixture of jazz, rap, and traditional music,
with help from jazz musicians Bill Laswell,
Bernie Worrel, and Herbie Hancock.
Rumba, originating from Latin America,
surfaced in the Congo Basin area in the
1940s and 1950s. Its spread was made
possible by the prevailing cosmopolitanism
and a relatively booming economy. It was
immediately embraced to enrich the existing
musical heritage with numerous variations
ranging from rumba-sukumu at the begin-
ning of World War II to rumba-kara, rumba-
boucher, rumba-sukusu, and rumba kiri-kiri
or soukous, which is one the most popular
music and dance styles today in Africa. A
decade later, the region was invaded by
American rock and Cuban salsa. The
Cuban rumba fused with African rhythms
to produce the ﬁrst distinct syncretic dance
style in Francophone Africa, Congo music.
Congo music later went electric and incor-
porated a brass front line, creating the pop-
ular Congo jazz style. The most prominent
Congo jazz groups are Joseph “Grand
Kalle” Kabasselleh’s African Jazz, Jean Serge
Essous’s O.K.Jazz, Orchestre Bella Bella,
and “Franco’s” (François Luambo Makiadi)
T .P .O.K.Jazz. In addition, Tabu Ley
Rochereau’s African Fiesta played Latin
rhythms on the drums of rock music and
Papa Wemba’s Viva La Musica was inspired
by Puerto Rican star Ray Barreto Otis
Redding’s sweet soul.
As rumba penetrated some places, rag-
time was shifting into Dixieland jazz in other
areas. Many local Dixie bands were formed
in South Africa, like the Dark T own Strutters
and the Big Four of Johannesburg. Ragtime
became part of the black urban marabi
music of the 1920s and 1930s. In the black
urban centers where different tribes met
with former slaves from the Americas, the
marabi dance style evolved. It was originally
a humble form of music, but it became
similar to the jazz music played by swing
bands in the United States when the rela-
tively wealthy and free blacks of Sophiatown
adopted it. Much of South African music
of the 1950s was born at the crossroads of
American jazz, African American choral
styles, and African folk music. For example,
vocalist Miriam Makeba and her husband
trumpeter Hugh Masekela recorded in a
pop-jazz style. Meringue became the national
music of Sierra Leone, where it is called
maringa. In Ghana, Dixieland became part
of the repertoire of 1920s bands such as the
Jazz Kings of Accra.
In the 1960s another imported dance
style became popular in Africa: the popular
music explosion among urban youth ignited
by rock and roll and the twist, both origi-
nating from black Americans. The decade

witnessed the formation of many African
popular bands, such as the Avengers of
Ghana, the Heartbeats of Sierra Leone, and
the Cyclops of Nigeria, with their own
unique styles. In 1979, an American pro-
duction outﬁt invited Congolese musicolo-
gist Ray Lema to work in the United States,
where he learned studio sound-recording
technique. In 1983, Lema released Kinshasa-
Washington DC–Paris, an album that sums
up his career and reﬂects a mixture of inﬂu-
ences: rumba, rock, funk, reggae, jazz, tra-
dition, and modernity.
Zouk, invented by the group Kassav,
fused Caribbean musical inﬂuences with
funk and rock to produce an unusual,
rhythmic cocktail, and brought it to Africa.
The group’s ﬁrst tour of a dozen African
countries was a huge success, and many
African artists sought to emulate the band.
There were numerous guest performers on
Apollo 95 (400 percent Zoblazo) by Ivorian
Frederic Desire Ehui (Meiway), including
Jacob Desvarieux of Kassav from Martinique.
Ehui’s Extratrerrestre features Cuban musi-
cians playing the brass and cord section,
spiced with Latino touches. This develop-
ment was no doubt a reﬂection of the
growing recognition for Caribbean culture.
Many African artists have undertaken
pilgrimages to Jamaica, home of many
excellent recording studios. For example,
Côte d’Ivoire’s Alpha Blondy, known as an
African Rasta who creates Jah-centered
anthems, made a pilgrimage in 1983 to T uff
Gong Studios in Kingston, Jamaica, where
he recorded the Jerusalem album with the
Wailers. He became the ﬁrst African star of
reggae with Jah Glory(1983). Ivorian Tiken
Jah Fakoly, who has established himself as
one of the leading artists of the new reggae
scene in Côte d’Ivoire, had a series of con-
certs in 1999 in New York and Philadelphia
with a Jamaican backing band. Tiken’s
Cours d’Histoireand Françafrique(2000) were
mixed in the legendary T uff Gong studios in
Jamaica and fused reggae beat with hard-
hitting lyrics.
African music experienced a boom in
the 1980s as it absorbed elements of rock
and pop music. This absorption led to ex-
perimentation with various aesthetic inno-
vations in which musicians took advantage
of Western studio techniques while remain-
ing faithful to their African roots by per-
forming traditional instruments. Malian
musicians T oumani Diabate and Ali Farka
T oure played African versions of the blues,
while Issa Bagayogo updated the traditions
of Mali to the age of electronic dance music
in the 1990s. Ethiopian Aster Aweke
adapted her extraordinary voice to a reper-
toire of soul-jazz-rock. Salif Keïta’s repertoire
includes Afro-Cuban numbers, Mandingo
blues-rock fusion as well as songs with jazz
orientation salsa and zouk.
Senegalese Youssou N’Dour founded
mbalax (Cuban music performed with
Western aesthetics and supplemented with
African polyrhythms) as a major form of
dance music, just as Senegal’s Orchestra
Baobab successfully mixed Cuban music
and African music on Pirate’s Choice
(1982). Benin’s Angélique Kidjo does a
mixture of Afro-punk, reggae, samba, salsa,
jazz, rumba, zouk, and makossa. Sudanese
singer-songwriter Rasha invented a mish-
mash of jazz, pop, reggae, and American
dance music in Sudaniyat (1997). Moroccan
Maleem Mahmoud Ghania collaborated
with jazz giant Pharoah Sanders on Trance
of Seven Colors (1994), while Hassan
Hakmoun created fusion tracks of trancey
gnawa, rock, and American dance music on
Trance (1993). Benin’s Gangbé Brass Band
explores the rich Voodoo culture and ancient

MUSIC,A FRICAN POPULAR 795
songs of their country, which are combined
with jazz melodies to produce a powerful
contemporary sound.
Hip-hop, too, has had a tremendous
inﬂuence on African popular music. This
urban American form has been absorbed
and transformed by African youth, and led
to the birth of an African rap. Notably, few
African artists adopt the sexist language and
violent imagery favored by some American
rappers. The end result is a sound that is
distinctly hip-hop with an African ﬂavor.
Original hip-hop has emerged in Nigeria,
South Africa, Cameroon, Senegal, Tanzania,
Ghana, Mozambique, Kenya, Angola,
Congo, and Mali. Hip-hop groups often
rhyme in Wolof, Malinke, Dioula, Baoule,
French, English, Fon and Yoruba, and
Jamaican patois; they sing in both R&B and
jail styles, which are fused with the tones of
the kora and ngoni harp-lutes and balafon
xylophone. Senegal’s Positive Black Soul
updated a classic Orchestre Baobab rumba
with skittering beats, reggae-inflected
flows, and spicy Manding-style guitar
sound on Boul Ma Mine . Similarly, South
African rappers have a style known as kwaito:
a thumping hybrid that draws from hip-
hop, house music, and dance hall reggae,
alongside a mixture of local traditions,
including Zulu praise poetry. They rap in a
Soweto-bred form of slang called tsotsi taal,
which draws from Zulu, Afrikaans, English,
and other languages. Many rap groups have
emerged, including 1549, Parlement,
Supreme Posse, M.A.M., Negromufﬁn, and
R.A.S. Many artists note that they are
inﬂuenced by the music of Bob Marley,
Michael Jackson, MC Solaar, Youssou 
N’Dour, and Alpha Blondy.
Starting at the end of the 1990s, a
modern dazzling rap based on the multitude
of Benin’s traditional rhythms and melodies
was created. Benin’s most popular rappers,
Sakpata Boys, have incorporated chants,
dances, and practices of the Voodoo reli-
gion into their performance. H2O Assouka’s
production is a combination of local in-
struments and rhythms, interwoven with
smooth rap. Ardiess started out in 1997 as
a purely modern rap group, basing their
music on American rap heard on the radio
and seen on television, but it later added
some traditional instruments, rhythms, and
melodies. Many groups have adopted
American names: DaBrains in Senegal;
Da Fugitivz in Gambia; Big Daddy Kane,
K-Solo, Biz Markie, Gangstarr, Alasko
Deejay, and Ras Goody Brown Côte
d’Ivoire, and Big Melody, Dave II, Fuzajay,
Magic, L ’archange, Melcky, S II B, R. Man,
and Surah in Benin. In 1999, conﬁrming
hip-hop’s transatlantic and disaporic na-
ture, the Pan African Hip-Hop Festival
was held in Cotonou, Benin, and these
connections and collaborations continue
to 2007.
Philip A. Ojo

MUTABARUKA (1952–)
Mutabaruka (Rwandan for “one who is
always victorious”) is one of the “new wave”
of poets that emerged during the Jamaican
social turmoil of the early 1970s. Born
Allan Hope in Kingston, Jamaica, he
changed his name in his twenties to reﬂect
his afﬁliation as a Rastafarian and to cast
off the shackles of his Anglophone name.
Mutabaruka’s poetry was ﬁrst published
by Swing magazine in 1971. His thoughts
about Black Power and the Back to Africa
movement are paramount themes in his
early poetry, and uplifting messages to the
African Diaspora pervade his poetry and
music to this day. He has published numer-
ous reggae CDs and poetry books, and he
has a successful radio show in Jamaica
where he reasons with his audience about
wide-ranging cultural concerns.
His early poetry is infused with popular
culture and social concerns. “Nursery Rhyme
Lament” (1973) is a humorous revision of
traditional Western children’s tales—such
as Jack and Jill and Humpty Dumpty—
that appeals to the Jamaican community’s
social concerns. “dis poem” (1992) is one of
Mutabaruka’s crowd pleasers that asserts a
complex Jamaican identity that refuses the
audience’s attempts to simplify it. The
poem further slyly infuses the audience into
the poem. T o read the poem, or to hear it
performed, is to be a willing participant in
its themes, thoughts, and accusations. The
success of “dis poem” is indicated further
by its inclusion in The Routledge Reader in
Caribbean Literature (1996).
Mutabaruka has traveled the world
performing his poetry, usually in full
Jamaican folk r egalia. He performed “dis
poem” on stage in New York City for the
“Russell Simmons Presents Def Poetry”
show, which aired on HBO in 2003. In
early 2005, he republished First Poems as a
dual collection with Next Poems.
David W . Hart
See also: Black Power Movement; Caribbean
Literature; Jamaica; Johnson, Linton Kwesi;
Morris, Mervyn; Reggae; Smith, Mikey

N’KRUMAH,K WAME
(1909–1972)
Dynamic and charismatic, N’Krumah led
the Gold Coast colony to independence,
became the ﬁrst president of Ghana, and
fostered the Pan-African movement. Born
Francis Nwiakoﬁe Nkrumah and educated
in Catholic mission schools, he trained as a
teacher near Accra. He spent 1935 to 1945
in the United States continuing his educa-
tion at Lincoln University and the Univer-
sity of Pennsylvania. He studied economics,
sociology, and philosophy. It was in the
United States where N’Krumah was intro-
duced to the writings of Pan-Africanist
Marcus Garvey. N’Krumah traveled to
Britain in 1945 to pursue doctoral studies
in philosophy and law, became a political
activist in the African student movement,
and took the name Kwame.
N’Krumah returned to the Gold Coast
colony in 1947 and was appointed secre-
tary of the United Gold Coast Convention.
However, he felt the group’s leadership was
not moving quickly enough to dismantle
colonial control of the colony. Considered
a radical nationalist, N’Krumah had al-
ready begun developing an African form of
socialism, which drew heavily on precolo-
nial traditional communal values. In 1949
N’Krumah established the Convention
People’s Party (CPP), the ﬁrst real popular
political party in Africa, to push for inde-
pendence. Under N’Krumah’s leadership,
the CPP organized a general strike and
boycott to pressure colonial authorities in
the Gold Coast colony. As a result,
N’Krumah was jailed for sedition.
N’Krumah continued to be a popular
political ﬁgure, though, and in 1951 he
and the CPP won the ﬁrst Gold Coast
general election. In March 1957 the Gold
Coast colony was granted independence
and became Ghana. Under N’Krumah’s
leadership Ghana became the inspiration
for independence movements across the
continent. N’Krumah dedicated himself to
African independence from all forms of
foreign domination and was fundamental
in the establishment of the Pan-African
movement. As president, N’Krumah ulti-
mately implemented an authoritarian one-
party state and his own personality cult.
Economic pressures and political discon-
tent resulted in his overthrow by a police-
army coup d’état in 1966. N’Krumah went
into exile and died of cancer in 1972.
Despite the ignominious end of his presi-
dential career, N’Krumah is remembered as
a powerful symbolic figure in African
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

798 N AIPAUL,VIDIADHAR SURAJPRASAD
decolonization and a passionate advocate
for African unity who dedicated much of
his life to Pan-Africanism.
Heather Thiessen-Reily

NAIPAUL,VIDIADHAR
SURAJPRASAD (1932–)
Vidiadhar Surajprasad Naipaul is a
T rinidadian-born novelist and travel writer
who addresses African, Caribbean, and
British themes in his works. He is a recipi-
ent of the Nobel Prize for Literature.
Naipaul, of East Indian heritage, was born
in Chaguamas, T rinidad, on August 17,
1932, to Seepersad Naipaul and Dropatie
Capildeo. He left the Caribbean on an
academic scholarship and obtained his B.A.
from Oxford in 1953. While studying in
England, Naipaul met fellow black West
Indian writers, including George Lamming.
They formed a part of the Caribbean mi-
gratory writers traveling overseas. Naipaul’s
early texts, The Mystic Masseur (1957), The
Suffrage of Elvira (1958), Miguel Street
(1959), and A House for Mr. Biswas(1961),
take place in T rinidad andexamine West In-
dian social and political issues. Many of
these issues are inﬂuenced by the strong con-
nection of the West Indies to Africa, such as
the role of the matriarchal family and signif-
icance of community.
After examining life in T rinidad,
Naipaul broadened the geographical scope
in his next texts. He uses his migration
from T rinidad to England as the basis of the
novel The Enigma of Arrival (1987). In
addition, Naipaul examines the effects of
colonialism and nationalism in what he
considers the “third world societies” of
T rinidad, British Guiana, Surinam,
Jamaica, and Martinique in The Middle
Passage (1962). Naipaul’s other travel
writings explore the history of colonialism
and postcolonialism in Indian society in
An Area of Darkness (1964) and India: A
Wounded Civilization (1977) and the nega-
tive effects of religion in the Muslim coun-
tries of Indonesia, Iran, Pakistan, and
Malaysia in Among the Believers (1981) and
Beyond Belief (1998). Naipaul garnered the
prestigious Booker Prize in 1971 for his
novel, In a Free State (published that same
year). Critics praised his depiction of post-
colonial Africa’s fall to violence and chaos
after the end of European control. Naipaul
also illustrates Africa in his novel A Bend in
the River (1979) and “Crocodiles of
Yamoussoukro” in Finding the Center
(1984). Both texts describe politics in
Africa and draw from Naipaul’s observa-
tions of when he traveled to Africa.
Naipaul’s other series of writings are
mostly autobiographical. In A Turn in the
South (1989), Naipaul retells his experience
of traveling through the southern United
States and notes the similarities of the
American South to T rinidad. His memoir
Reading and Writing (2000) details his
process of becoming a writer in London
and his father’s inﬂuence on his career
choice. Naipaul’s relationship with his
father is also expressed in Between Father
and Son (2000).
In 2001, Naipaul won the Nobel Prize
for literature. Many critics hailed him as
the top novelist from the Anglophone
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 887 ---
NAMIBIA 799
Caribbean and commended his range of
texts, from ﬁction to travelogues. After
receiving the Nobel Prize, Naipaul wrote
the novel Half a Life (2001) and its sequel,
Magic Seeds (2004). Like Naipaul, the
novels’ main character travels to India,
England, and Africa and notes the historic
consequences of colonialism. Naipaul lives
in England with his second wife, Nadira
Khannum Alvi.
Dorsía Smith

NAMIBIA
The republic of Namibia is a large country
in southwestern Africa covering an area of
318,321 square miles (824,116 square kilo-
meters). The country borders South Africa
to the south, Botswana to the east, and
Zambia and Angola to the north. T o the
west, arid land separates most of the main-
land from a long Atlantic Ocean coastline
of approximately 975 miles (1,570 kilome-
ters). Its history as an independent nation is
linked to global intervention and United
Nations efforts to curb South African dom-
ination. With a population of approxi-
mately 1.83 million (2001 census),
Namibia has one of the lowest population
densities of any country in the world (2.1
persons per square kilometer). Although
urban areas have been growing since
independence, 67 percent of the popula-
tion still lives in the rural areas, mostly in
the north. Namibia has a large number of
youth, with 40 percent of the population
less than 15 years of age. Nonetheless, the
population composition is changing sig-
niﬁcantly, with growth slowing as a result
of lower fertility and life expectancy due
to AIDS.
Namibia became the ofﬁcial and inter-
nationally recognized name of the country
only after achieving independence on
March 21, 1990. Formerly known by its
colonial name, South-West Africa, the
current name was adopted by the liberation
movement and dominant political party,
the South-West Africa People’s Organiza-
tion (SWAPO), in the early 1960s and by
the United Nations in 1968.
Bordered by the Namib Desert to the
west and the Kalahari Desert to the east, the
landscape is for the most part ﬂat and dry.
Groundwater from aquifers provide much-
needed water in a country where high tem-
peratures cause rainwater to evaporate fast.
Over 50,000 boreholes have been drilled to
supply water for ﬁeld irrigation as well as
livestock and human use throughout the
country. The Okavango, the Zambezi,
and the Kwando, the largest of Namibia’s
perennial rivers, ﬂow from Angola and
Zambia, shaping distinctive landscapes in
the northern r egions. As a result of heavy
rainfall in their catchment areas, seasonal
ﬂooding occurs in the Caprivi plains, where
many people grow crops. Farther west, in
the country’s most densely populated
north-central regions, heavy rains allow for
agriculture, ﬁshing, and cattle to thrive in
the Cuvelai areas. This drainage system con-
sisting of shallow reservoirs, or oshanas,that
periodically ﬁll with water has attracted set-
tlers for centuries.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 888 ---
800 N AMIBIA
Namibia’s economy depends primarily
on the use of natural resources for farming,
mining, ﬁshing, and tourism. Livestock
and crop farming is an important activity
for many Namibians in the freehold, gov-
ernment, and northern communal areas.
Deposits of diamonds, uranium, copper,
gold, zinc, and lead are exploited and ex-
ported overseas, making the country’s in-
come largely dependent on the general
state and trends of the global economy.
Thanks to the rich Benguela Current,
ﬂowing northward and distributing rich
nutrients along the coast, a prosperous
fishing industry generates employment
and income, mainly through processing
and exports. Rich geological formations,
abundant wildlife, and pristine skies make
Namibia attractive to tourists and scien-
tists alike.
Painted rocks representing wildlife and
hunting and gathering populations from
circa 27000 BCE have been found in
Namibia. Although human migration to
and across this land goes back hundreds of
thousands of years, most of the current
population descends from groups that
arrived in Namibia in the last 600 years.
Cultural diversity reﬂects in more than a
dozen languages spoken in the country and
different identities, histories, and tradi-
tional organizations. Although probably
not the original inhabitants, the oldest
groups still living in Namibia are the San.
Later on, the Nama and the Damaras
arrived. The Owambo, currently the largest
ethnic group in the country, did not enter
Namibia probably until the ﬁfteenth cen-
tury. In 1486 Diego Cão from Portugal
arrived at Cape Cross. This event marked
the beginning of a European presence in
search of land, wealth, and souls to
Christianize. However, it was not until the
early nineteenth century that several mis-
sionary groups followed the path set by the
London Missionary Society, establishing
themselves in the country. Their presence
and interaction with the autochthonous
population caused signiﬁcant social, eco-
nomic, and cultural changes.
The British ﬁrst established a station in
Walvis Bay to buy cattle from the local
population, mainly to supply St. Helena
during Napoleon’s exile. Later on, as the
guano trade grew and more British nation-
als invested in the area, Britain declared it
to be its territory. The Heligoland-Zanzibar
T reaty (1890), signed by Britain and
Germany, established boundaries with
British South Africa and Bechuanaland and
transferred the island of Zanzibar to British
hands in exchange for the Caprivi Strip,
giving Germany access to the Zambezi
River. The German rule (1884–1914) over
South-West Africa (except Walvis Bay,
which remained under British control)
soon encountered active resistance. The
resistance struggle by the Ovaherero and
the Nama culminated in what historians
consider to be the ﬁrst genocide of the
twentieth century. Between 1904 and
1907, 65,000 Ovaherero, more than
10,000 Namas, and an unknown number
of San were massacred by order of the com-
mander of the German imperial forces in
the country, General Lothar von T rotha.
Many were killed by shooting or died from
starvation, disease, and overwork in the
desert or in labor camps.
During World War I, South African
troops fought and settled in South-West
Africa. The Peace T reaty of Versailles (1919)
transferred the full administration and legis-
lation of former German Southwest Africa
to South Africa, which administered it as a
League of Nations mandate territory. After
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 889 ---
NAMIBIA 801
World War II and the League supersession
by the United Nations, South Africa re-
peatedly opposed requests to place the ter-
ritory under UN trusteeship, administering
it as one of its provinces instead. In the
1960s, when many African countries were
gaining independence, and the SWAPO
started mobilizing guerrilla military resis-
tance against South Africa to pressure it to
grant independence to Namibia, the UN
General Assembly revoked South Africa’s
mandate. However, South Africa would
continue to administer Namibia for three
more decades—and SWAPO would con-
tinue to lead the struggle for independence
from bases in Zambia, southern Angola
(since its independence in 1975), and sev-
eral industrialized countries.
In spite of international condemnation
and growing internal resistance by churches,
students, and other associations, the South
African government extended to South-
West Africa its own system of apartheid:
the policy of ethnic and spatial separation.
The recommendations of the Odendaal
Commission Report (1964) reﬂected a
clear opposition to policies of social, politi-
cal, and economic integration and equality.
Under the policy of “Native reserves” and
the creation of ethnic “homelands,” South
Africa secured a supply of cheap labor and
better controlled the land and its popula-
tion. Seven homelands were created in
1968, namely, Ovamboland (renamed
Owambo in 1972), Okavangoland (re-
named Kavango in 1972), Damaraland,
Hereroland, Kaokoland, Namaland, and
Eastern Caprivi. The policy of ethnic frag-
mentation forced the relocation of urban
blacks into “locations” on the periphery of
white towns. In addition, it systematically
used ethnicity as the criterion for the uni-
lateral distribution of goods, services, land,
and rights, facilitated control, and rein-
forced relationships of subordination at all
levels.
SWAPO’s armed wing, the People’s
Liberation Army of Namibia (PLAN)
started operating from the Caprivi Strip in
1971–1972, at the same time that black
contract workers went on strike for the
abolition of the contract labor system, free-
dom of movement and employment, in-
creased wages, and permission to reside
with their families in the urban areas.
While these events opened the way for
strengthened links between churches, orga-
nized labor, and the liberation movement,
repression also followed. Nonetheless, in re-
sponse to UN pressures, the South African
government granted self-government to the
“Native Nations” and established an
advisory council for South-West Africa in
1973. This body, comprising the different
ethnic leaders in Namibia, turned two years
later into the T urnhalle Constitutional
Conference, which was central in the polit-
ical process to independence.
In 1978, the diplomatic efforts of
Canada, France, West Germany, the
United Kingdom, and the United States
(known as the Western Contact Group) led
to the presentation of Security Council
Resolution 435 proposing what was known
as the UN Plan. The Plan called for demo-
cratic elections in Namibia under UN
supervision and the cessation of all military
activities by all parties. Shortly after, how-
ever, in line with the Reagan Administra-
tion’s “Constructive Engagement” policy
for southern Africa, South Africa refused to
implement UN Security Council Resolu-
tion 435 until Cuban troops withdrew
from Angola, and the latter’s ruling part,
the Popular Movement for the Liberation
of Angola (MPLA), withheld its support to
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 890 ---
802 N ANNY
SWAPO. During this time, South Africa
sent more troops to Angola, intensifying its
support for the National Union for T otal
Independence of Angola (UNITA). A
decade of intense negotiations between all
stakeholders followed under the leadership
of the UN secretary general’s special repre-
sentative, Martti Ahtisaari.
It was not until the ﬁrst group of
Cuban troops left Angola in early 1989
that South Africa ofﬁcially began adminis-
tering the territory’s transition to indepen-
dence. During this period, amnesty was
granted to political prisoners, South
African troops were withdrawn, discrimi-
natory legislation was repealed, and the re-
turn of more than 40,000 refugees was co-
ordinated with assistance of the UN High
Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).
Many of the current political leaders re-
turned from exile holding degrees from
renowned universities in Europe and the
Americas. “Free and fair” elections gave
power to SWAPO in November 1989.
The Constitutional Principles developed
in 1982 served as a framework for a new
constitution (1990) establishing three
independent branches of government, a
multiparty system, and a bill of rights. On
March 1, 1994, Walvis Bay and 12 off-
shore islands were transferred to Namibia
from South Africa. Sam Nujoma, the ﬁrst
president of Namibia, was later reelected
for two more terms. He was replaced as
president by Hiﬁkepunye Pohamba, the
SWAPO ofﬁcial candidate in the elections
of November 2004.
The many Cuban doctors and agricul-
ture technicians, as well as Peace Corps
volunteers, working in the country, and
numerous development efforts funded
through bilateral agreements and the UN
Global Fund to ﬁght AIDS, are a clear
reminder of the support Namibia received
to achieve its independence.
Monica Ruiz-Casares

NANNY (CA. 1700–1740)
During the eighteenth century, Nanny of
the Maroons was an important leader
of the Maroons in their rebellion against
British occupation. Also known as Granny
Nanny, today she stands out as the only
recognized female Jamaican national hero.
During the days of Spanish settlement
on the island of Jamaica, Africans went into
the mountains and created communities in
an attempt to escape their enslavement.
These runaways were called Maroons, a term
derived from the Spanish word cimarrón,
which means “wild” or “untamed.” Maroon
communities became larger as more and
more slaves were brought to the island.
Maroons played an important role in
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 891 ---
NATION OF ISLAM 803
combating the institution of slavery; they
would periodically come down from the
mountains, taking back with them fellow
Africans as well as supplies of food. They
engaged in combat with Spanish settlers,
and later with the British, and as legend has
established, they were successful in defeat-
ing and keeping these settlers at bay.
Maroons also played an important role in
maintaining the cultural heritage of the dis-
placed African community, preserving tra-
ditions, customs, and ideals that they
brought with them from Africa.
Although there are many legends sur-
rounding Nanny, she is often described as
an Asante warrior. Despite her small
stature, she took on a leadership role both
within the Maroon military as well as in the
Maroon village communities. Her military
prowess played an important role in help-
ing to develop the legend of Nanny; she
was recognized for her strong military
techniques that often created havoc and
catastrophe for British forces. Nanny is re-
membered in both legend and documents
that call attention to her supernatural skill,
a characteristic that links her to obeah.
Nanny’s greatest strength was her ability to
organize the Eastern Maroons and to effec-
tively keep at bay the British attempting to
overpower their mountain community.
Documentation from British accounts of
the First Maroon War (1720–1738) suggests
that the British troops were often ﬂabber-
gasted by the abilities of the Maroons
under Nanny’s leadership.
As a leader in her village community,
Nanny played an important role in main-
taining the connection between the Jamaican
diasporic community and its African her-
itage. She passed down legends from Africa
to the community and ensured that the
community maintained the customs and
traditions that they had brought with them
from Africa.
In Jamaica today, Nanny of the Maroons
remains a symbol of unity and strength and
she continues to be an inspiration to her
people. Although legends suggest that
Nanny was one of many women who took
on leadership roles among the Maroons,
Nanny is most remembered because of her
insistence, sometimes in opposition to other
Maroon leaders, that the Maroons must
struggle to maintain their independence and
never submit to subjugation.
J. A. Brown-Rose

NATION OF ISLAM
The Nation of Islam (NOI) is an Islamic
movement founded in 1930s America by
Wallace Fard, a white man. The original
name of the movement is the Lost Found
Nation of Islam in the Wilderness. Wallace
Fard’s origin is controversial because he
claimed to have been born in different
countries, and little is actually known
about him. Around 1930, Fard appeared in
Paradise Valley, a black neighborhood of
Detroit, Michigan. He invited people to
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 892 ---
804 N ATION OF ISLAM
Islam and told them that their original
religion was not Christianity but Islam.
Within a short time, he won a few follow-
ers. He claimed that their origin was
Asiatic, that white men were descendants of
Yacub, and that blacks were superior to
whites, whom Fard called devils because of
their historic enslavement and mistreat-
ment of black people. Fard preached for
four years and laid the foundation of the
NOI, established training schools for the
girls, launched the Fruit of Islam, a guard
for protecting the leaders of the NOI, and
established the University of Islam. He
then disappeared in 1934. Little is known
about what happened to him after 1934 or
how or where he died.
However, before his disappearance, he
had chosen one of his able followers, Elijah
Poole, to lead the movement. Fard might
have disappeared when he could no longer
control or manage the movement. A con-
tributing factor may have been that all his
members were black people in whom he
had instilled a hate for white people and
he was a white person. His disappearance
gave ample chance to Elijah Poole to re-
structure the Nation of Islam, which be-
came one of the largest black nationalist
movements in the United States.
Elijah Poole was born in Sandersville,
Georgia, in October 1897. He worked sev-
eral jobs before moving to Detroit in 1919,
where he worked at the Chevrolet auto
plant for six years. He was introduced to
Islam through Wallace Fard. He admired
Wallace Fard’s explicit discussion of the
psychological damage that slavery had done
The Nation of Islam was led in its early years by Elijah Muhammad. (Library of Congress)
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 893 ---
NATION OF ISLAM 805
to black Americans. Fard appointed Poole
his minister in 1933. Poole changed his
surname to Muhammad and requested that
black converts change their surnames to X
to eradicate their slave names. He had
considerable success in converting blacks
into Islam. Muhammad became leader of
the Nation of Islam in 1934 when Wallace
Fard disappeared. He opened temples in
Chicago, Philadelphia, New York, and
Washington, D.C. Muhammad also moved
to Chicago and restructured the NOI as a
separatist nationalist black movement.
Muhammad helped black Americans
under the umbrella of the Nation of Islam
to understand who they were and how
white men had murdered, brutalized, and
enslaved them. He gave blacks new identi-
ties and encouraged them to be self-
disciplined and economically independent.
In his outlines of the goals of the NOI, he
declared that what the NOI wanted for
black Americans in general were freedom,
equal opportunity, an end to police brutal-
ity and mob attacks against blacks, equal
education, and equal justice under the law.
He discouraged his followers from using
drugs, consuming alcohol, eating pork, or
borrowing on credit.
Muhammad was jailed from 1942 to
1946 for draft evasion. He continued to
lead his followers from prison through his
wife and his ministers and found the prison
fertile soil for recruiting new members into
the NOI. After his release, he devoted his
attention to the economic development of
the NOI. He purchased 140 acres of farm-
land in Michigan and invested greatly in
farm products to boost the economic con-
dition of his followers. A few years later, the
NOI established groceries, clothing stores,
restaurants, trucking companies, schools,
bakeries, and banks. Muhammad provided
jobs for his followers and taught them, as
the backbone of the African American
community, to be independent and re-
spectful of their families.
The success of Elijah Muhammad can
be attributed to many factors. First, he em-
phasized economic self-sufﬁciency. He be-
lieved that any group that relies on others
financially will never attain prosperity.
Second, despite continued police hostility
and brutality against black people, he did
not preach the overthrow of the govern-
ment or violence. Third, he did not shun
Western and modern technology as did his
mentor, Fard. Rather, the NOI under
Elijah Muhammad invested in radio, pub-
lications, farms, and businesses. Muhammad
embraced the mass media in order to pro-
mote the NOI. Even those people who did
not agree with him were sympathetic to his
sincere attempts to assist and protect black
people. Muhammad believed strongly that
for blacks to succeed in America they must
have total economic independence. He en-
couraged education, hard work, frugality,
and the avoidance of drugs.
Despite these great accomplishments
as a separatist nationalist black movement,
the NOI as an Islamic movement had
ﬂaws. The NOI taught the supremacy of
blacks over whites, when Islam preaches
equality of all humans before God. The
NOI also taught that Wallace Fard was
God incarnated; this claim contradicts the
Islamic declaration of faith, which asserts
that only Allah is God.
When Elijah Muhammad died, his son
Imam Warith Deen Mohammed (also
known as Wallace Dean Mohammed) be-
came the leader of the NOI. He struggled
to move the NOI from its racist and sepa-
ratist ideologies into mainstream Islam,
which recognizes all races as human and
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 894 ---
806 N ATION OF ISLAM
equal before God. He revived the NOI and
redesigned its policies and doctrines to
represent both Wallace Fard and Elijah
Muhammad as people. He changed the
temples into mosques, dissolved the Fruit
of Islam, did away with the mythology of
Yacub, allowed white and immigrant
Muslims to join the NOI, and decentral-
ized the hierarchical structure of the NOI
by allowing each local imam to be respon-
sible for running the affairs of the Muslims
in his locale. Some older members of the
NOI resented those changes and thus left
the movement. But Mohammed fervently
continued his revival, which won him
recognition in the Muslim mainstream in
the United States. Mohammed ofﬁcially
resigned from the leadership of the NOI in
November 2003, but he continues to serve
the organization.
One of the African American Muslim
pioneers, who served the NOI until shortly
before his death, was Malcolm X. Born in
Nebraska as Malcolm Little, he dropped out
of school at an early age because of discrim-
ination. He went to prison for burglary and
converted to the Nation of Islam while he
was incarcerated. He became an inﬂuential
member of the Nation of Islam after his
release from prison. Elijah Muhammad ad-
mired him for his eloquence and charisma
as a speaker, and promoted him to the high-
est level of authority in the NOI and
appointed him his spokesperson on several
occasions. Malcolm opened many temples
for the NOI across the United States and
won many African American youths to
Islam. Malcolm fought against racism, yet
followed Muhammad’s teaching that white
people were devils for enslaving blacks and
maltreating them. 
One of Malcolm X’s greatest contribu-
tions to the NOI was his founding of the
publication Muhammad Speaks, a news-
paper that featured articles concerning
the doctrines of the NOI, its beliefs, its po-
litical stance, its activities, and messages
from Elijah Muhammad. The newspaper
had a circulation of more than 600,000 at
its peak. Its publication helped to provide
jobs and training to thousands of NOI
members.
Disagreements between Elijah Muham-
mad and Malcolm X led to the latter’s
excommunication for 90 days due to com-
ments Malcolm made about the assassina-
tion of President John Kennedy on
November 22, 1963. Malcolm X broke
away from Muhammad and established his
own movement, the Muslim Mosque, in
New York in 1964. The same year he made
the Islamic pilgrimage to Mecca. Learning
from his experience at Mecca about Islamic
brotherhood changed Malcolm’s life.
Enlightened with new spiritual insights, he
became a reformed person with a different
outlook. He retracted all his derogative
comments about white people, he reverted
to orthodox Islam, and adopted a new
name, El-Hajj Malik El-Shabbaz. Malcolm
X continued to ﬁght for the rights of the

NDEBELE
Ndebele are a people of South Africa de-
ﬁned by their language and their cultural
and political contributions to South Africa
before and during apartheid. The name
Ndebele is best explained by pointing out
that the term ndebele is really a category
word used by Sotho-speakers to deﬁne
Nguni-speakers in general (usually in the
Sotho form matebele). The Ndebele peoples
of South Africa probably came by the name
because their language is one of the Nguni
languages spoken by peoples living near the
South African coast.
In the 1800s, when the Ndebele mi-
grated inland into the eastern part of
Mpumalanga Province (traditionally Sotho-
speaking territory) the surrounding Sotho
noted their different language and customs.
They referred to these foreigners as mate-
bele or “strangers from the east.” Gradually
the Sotho term matebele changed into
ndebele, the Nguni form of the term.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 896 ---
808 N DEBELE
Thus there are several South African
and Zimbabwean groups called Ndebele,
but they are different societies with differ-
ent histories. They differentiate themselves
by adding an important chief’s name,
such as Ndzundza (the largest group) or
Manala, or a geographical location, such
as T ransvaal (a former province in South
Africa). In Zimbabwe they are called
Mzilikazi Ndebele after their famous chief
who led them there.
The Ndzundza Ndebele of South
Africa had been a signiﬁcant force before
their tragic 1883 war with the Boers when
the white farmers laid siege to their rocky
fortress for nine months to win their rich
land. When starved out of their retreat, the
chief was ﬁrst sentenced to death but later
life imprisonment, along with many coun-
cil members. Each victorious Boer ﬁghter
was given ﬁve families of the vanquished
Ndzundza to use as tenant farmers to work
for ﬁve years on their scattered white farms
with very little, if any, pay.
The Manala Ndebele, not involved in
the war, found their way to Wallmansthall
Mission, not far from Pretoria, and have a
calmer history than the Ndzundza. The
Mzilikazi Ndebele, passing through the
former T ransvaal Province from the coast,
had ﬁerce encounters with the Ndzundza as
they traveled into Zimbabwe, where even-
tually they settled.
The Ndzundza Ndebele felt a strong
need to distinguish themselves from other
Ndebele because the war’s aftermath left
them scattered far and wide throughout the
T ransvaal Province. For years they tried to
gather at different farms, but the govern-
ment feared if they grouped together they
would again become a danger.
The Ndzundza became world-famous
because of their unique and colorful wall
art (beginning around 1945) identifying
their mud homesteads. The women created
this distinctive identity marker annually,
composing striking geometric designs that
resembled the elaborate beadwork on their
traditional dress. Over the years, the hand-
some decorations, originally done in earth
colors and washing bluing, gradually
changed into more durable acrylic-painted
designs, if the owner could afford it. Visit-
ing tourists who wanted a portable artifact
reminding them of the Ndzundza color-
fully decorated homesteads purchased
beaded art forms, such as dolls and toy
animals. But sadly, the wall art almost dis-
appeared as the apartheid government
relocated the Ndebele into a desolate home-
land at end of the 1970s.
Both of the South African Ndebele
groups, and other Africans, were deeply
affected by South Africa’s apartheid system.
Apartheid (which means “apartness” or
“separate” in the Afrikaans and Dutch
languages) was a scheme of the National
Party government that came into power in
1948. It was used to justify a system that
determined where people lived, went to
school, and worked and insured that white
people stayed at the top and Africans re-
mained at the bottom economically, so-
cially, and politically. Apartheid was ofﬁcial
until the 1994 elections replaced the
National Party with the African National
Congress and a multinational government
headed by Nelson Mandela.
The 1980s stand out among those
46 difﬁcult years of enforced apartheid.
The decade was extremely violent, with
hundreds of people jailed, tortured, and
killed. The Ndebele were one of the
African groups that suffered the most
because of their fierce resistance to
forced relocation into one of the ten
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 897 ---
NÉGRITUDE 809
government-organized homelands, Kwa
Ndebele, and so-called independence.
Kwa Ndebele administration was
headed by a group of African businessmen
who were appointed by the South African
government. The Kwa Ndebele leadership
manipulated lesser chiefs and headmen to
go along with the homeland independence
proposition, which would enrich them but
deprive all inhabitants of their South
African citizenship.
However, the paramount chief David
Mahlangu, members of the royal family of
the Ndebele, and a majority of Africans
successfully battled this disaster at a great
loss of lives, with the dedicated help of
elders and youths from both inside and
outside the territory. Their success, and the
resistance of other Africans, plus the ex-
treme economic and political disarray
within the entire country by 1981, became
one of the ﬁnal blows dismantling the
apartheid government.

NÉGRITUDE
The concept of négritude identiﬁes a liter-
ary and cultural movement that was
founded in the 1930s in Paris by three
major black poets: the Senegalese Léopold
Sédar Senghor, the Martinican Aimé
Césaire, and the Guyanese Léon Gontran-
Damas. The term refers to the ideology of
cultural afﬁrmation, celebration, and revi-
talization that emerged from the exchange
of ideas between African and Caribbean
intellectuals who were searching for a cure
to the acculturation that European colo-
nization had created in the lives of people
of African descent.
Many blacks of Africa and the
Caribbean, who were at home or abroad,
felt exiled in their own homelands. They
felt that they had succumbed to the power
of Western civilization that had separated
them from their original African selves. In
order to resist this feeling of separation
from Africa, Césaire, Senghor, Gontran-
Damas and their followers wrote books of
poetry in which they reclaimed their
African past. In Return to My Native Land,
Césaire cast out the mirage of the Western
civilization that had separated him from
blacks of other continents. In Return,
Césaire states:
my race pitted with macula
my race ripe grapes for drunken feet
my queen of spittles and of lepers
my queen of whips and of scrofulas.
This passage reﬂects the strong inﬂu-
ence that the difﬁcult historical conditions
of blacks in the Americas had on Césaire’s
poetry. Césaire’s representation of his race
as the people that have been “pitted with
macula,” forced to grind grapes with their
“drunken feet,” spat on, infected, and
whipped helps him suggest the atrocious
experiences of the Africans who had been
enslaved in the Americas during the
transatlantic slave trade. The passage antic-
ipates Césaire’s denunciation, in his later
works, of how the economic development in
the West was partially built on the tortured
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 898 ---
810 N ÉGRITUDE
and murdered bodies and souls of the en-
slaved Africans and their descendants.
One of the challenges of scholars of
négritude is to explore the complexity, mu-
tability, and radicalism of the movement
without portraying its ideologies as black
cultural fundamentalism and mysticism or
as inferiority complex. In The Historian in
Tropical Africa: Studies Presented and Dis-
cussed at the Fourth International African
Seminar at the University of Dakar Senegal
1961 (1964), Jan Vansina decried how
négritude has been inappropriately inter-
preted as a myth in which the writers had a
common goal of stressing the speciﬁcity
and particularity of black culture, history,
and social and cultural inventions. This in-
terpretation of the goals of the négritude
movement fails to point out the idea of
multiculturalism and connections between
races and civilizations that its proponents
defended in their works.
Négritude has both internal and exter-
nal values. On the one hand, it is spiritual-
ist and existential; on the other, it is a
practical assessment of black people’s con-
nections to politics, culture, class, and hu-
manity. One of the most celebrated studies
of négritude is Jean-Paul Sartre’s essay
“Orphée Noir” (Black Orpheus) in which
the French existentialist philosopher
praised the movement for being the literary
expression of the soul and being of black
people. Although he perceived négritude
as a search for the collective soul of black
folk, Sartre did not see the movement as a
return to unchanging traditions, a myth, or
a racially exclusive philosophy. Instead, he
saw négritude as a progress toward equality
and universalism, and a continuous jour-
ney without end. Sartre’s interpretation of
négritude anticipated the blend of African
and Western values that Senghor used to
create a perfect synthesis in his négritude.
The fusion of values in Senghor’s négritude
is noticeable in the introduction of Ce Que
Je Crois: Négritude, Francité et Civilisation
de l’Universel(1989), where Senghor clearly
states: “I believe, above all, in Negro-
African culture, that is to say, in Négritude
and in its expression in poetry and arts...
I also believe in francophony, and, more ex-
actly, in francité that is integrated in Latin
culture and in the Civilization of the Uni-
versal, where Négritudehas begun to play a
very important part.” Senghor’s négritude
embraced the fusion of modern African
and Western cultures. By learning to better
appreciate Senghor’s hybrid vision of his
own culture and place in history, scholars
can arrive at a better understanding of the
complex history of négritude from the na-
tive Africans’ point of views.
The négritude movement was a multi-
faceted literary movement that aimed at
improving the conditions of people of
African descent. As one of the most voiced
poets of the movement, Césaire gave négri-
tude a concrete historical background by
using his poetry to represent the traumatic
effects of slavery on the enslaved Africans
and their descendants. Working with
Césaire, Senghor and the other contribu-
tors of the movement, such as Gontran-
Damas and Sartre, suggested the human-
ism of the movement, which was visible in
its acceptance and blending of all races and
civilizations for the good of mankind.
Babacar M’Baye

NEGRO LEAGUES
The Negro leagues, as they were com-
monly called, featured outstanding African
American baseball players throughout ap-
proximately the ﬁrst half of the twentieth
century. The Negro leagues attracted large
crowds to their games as baseball became
an important part of black culture and,
during the 1930s and 1940s, the largest
black-owned industry in the country. The
desire for the same opportunity to achieve
fame and fortune that white players en-
joyed led eventually to integration of the
major leagues in 1947. Once the major
leagues were open to African American
players, the Negro leagues went into a
sharp decline as the best black players,
given a choice, trained their sights on the
majors. By the end of the 1960 season, the
ﬁnal Negro league had died.
The Negro leagues grew out of a long-
standing passion for baseball on the part of
African Americans that originated during
slavery, when slaves played versions of the
game with a ball made from a piece of cloth
wrapped around boiled chicken feathers.
From the beginning, baseball had been
largely, though not entirely, segregated. The
ﬁrst professional team, the Cincinnati Red
Stockings of 1869, excluded blacks, as did
the ﬁrst professional league, the National
Association of Professional Base Ball Play-
ers, created in 1871.
Despite their exclusion from much of
white baseball, at least a few African
Americans played on predominantly
white teams in the National Association
of Base Ball Players, an association of
amateur teams that was formed in 1858,
even while all-black teams were develop-
ing in the 1860s. An occasional African
American made it into white professional
baseball, such as Bud Fowler, born, ironi-
cally, in Cooperstown, New York, site of
the future National Baseball Hall of
Fame. The most notable exception to the
all-white rule was Moses Fleetwood
Walker, a gifted athlete who caught in
1884 for T oledo of the American Base
Ball Association, at the time a major
league. Even the minimal integration that
had occurred came to an end in 1887
when Cap Anson, the player-manager for
the Chicago White Stockings, refused to
compete against Newark of the Interna-
tional League, for whom Walker was play-
ing. Newark benched Walker rather than
lose the revenue from the game. By 1889,
the last few African American players in
organized ball were gone, and a gentle-
men’s agreement to exclude blacks would
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

812 N EGRO LEAGUES
remain in force until the signing of Jackie
Robinson.
The result of this exclusion was not the
end of African American interest in base-
ball but rather formation of all-black teams
and leagues. A leading Negro league pio-
neer was Rube Foster, a great pitcher who
received his nickname form outpitching
the ace of the Philadelphia Athletics, Rube
Waddell. Foster, the manager as well as a
player for the Chicago Leland Giants, led
his team in 1909 into the Park Owners
Association, so named because teams were
required to own their own ballparks. The
following year, Foster formed his own
team, the Chicago American Giants, which
remained the most powerful team in the
association and continued its dominance
during the early years of the Negro
National League, which was formed in
1920. Foster was the primary architect of
the National League and served as its ﬁrst
president.
In 1923 a new league, the Eastern
Colored League, was formed, permitting
Negro League World Series play from 1924
through 1927. The new league disbanded
in 1928, and the National League, hit hard
by the Depression, folded in 1931. Negro
league veteran Cum Posey organized the
East-West League in 1932, and in the same
year the Negro Southern League was de-
clared a major league, but neither effort
survived beyond that year.
Gus Greenlee led formation of a new
Negro National League in 1933, and this
league caught on. In the same year, the
East-West All-Star Game was inaugurated
and proved a huge attraction, even out-
drawing the white All-Star contest by
more than 15,000 spectators in 1944. The
Negro American League was added in
1937, permitting restoration of a Negro
League World Series. The Negro leagues
during these years enjoyed tremendous
success, featuring players the equal of any
in the white major leagues and becoming
the largest black-owned business in the
United States. Baseball became, as poet
James Weldon Johnson said, part of the
black cultural expression. Black America
took special delight in seeing Negro league
teams defeat teams of white major leaguers
in exhibition contests. John Holway’s
research indicates that Negro league teams
won a large majority of those contests.
Certain Negro league teams proved espe-
cially successful. The Homestead Grays
(1912–1950) won the National League
pennant every year from 1937 to 1945
and again in 1948, along with the World
Series in 1943–1944 and 1948. Cum
Posey began as a Homestead player in the
Grays’ inaugural season and eventually be-
came the team’s owner. Catcher and
legendary slugger Josh Gibson and ﬁrst
baseman Buck Leonard were among the
top players on the team. After the Na-
tional Baseball Hall of Fame started in-
ducting stars of the Negro leagues, both
men were enshrined, appropriately in the
same year, 1972.
The Kansas City Monarchs (1920–
1950) also featured many stars, none big-
ger than pitcher Satchel Paige, and won
pennants steadily throughout its history.
The Pittsburgh Crawfords, owned by Gus
Greenlee, had a shorter life (1931–1938),
but the mid-1930s team, featuring Paige,
Gibson, and center ﬁelder Cool Papa Bell,
is often considered the greatest Negro
league team of all time. The Newark
Eagles (1936–1948), born as a fusion of
two teams, the Brooklyn Eagles and
Newark Dodgers, was owned by Abe and
Effa Manley. Effa, reared in an African

for African American players, but oppor-

ﬁeld managers remain limited even into
the twenty-ﬁrst century.

NEOCOLONIALISM
Neocolonialism is a term used to describe
the continued existence of colonial rela-
tionships in today’s world. In discourses
that are critical of global economic, polit-
ical, and cultural restructuring of the con-
temporary world, it is held that colonial-
ism is not a matter of the past but rather it
continues in new forms. The term began
to be used in reference to African coun-
tries following their decolonization after
World War II. The term was ﬁrst used by
Kwame N’Krumah, Ghana’s first post-
independence leader, in the 1960s.
N’Krumah and other voices critical of in-
ternational relationships after decoloniza-
tion have drawn attention to a new type of
colonialism in which ex-colonizers as well
as some other industrialized, developed
First World countries exploit ex-colonies
and other nonindustrialized, developing,
less developed, and underdeveloped third
world countries, this time by economic
and cultural inﬂuence rather than by di-
rect political control as in the old form of
colonialism.
Although neocolonialism largely indi-
cates a new world order since World War II,
it is argued that neocolonial practices ﬁrst
began in Latin America well before the
mid-twentieth century. Latin American
colonies such as Greater Columbia, Mexico,
Peru, Argentina, and Cuba gained their
independence from the dominant colonial
authority in the region, Spain, throughout
the nineteenth century. Yet, especially the
United States, which itself fought an inde-
pendence war against the British Empire
only a couple of decades earlier than some
Latin American independence struggles,
gained economic and thereby political
control over many economically weak and
needy Latin American countries in the
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 902 ---
814 N EOCOLONIALISM
nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.
Therefore, the argument goes that in the
years following World War II, the United
States was much better prepared than
other developed countries in the world to
implement neocolonial policies.
According to critics of neocolonialism,
the major actors in neocolonial world order
are multinational corporations (MNCs),
multinational enterprises (MNEs), transna-
tional corporations (TNCs), international
organizations that supply foreign aid to
needy countries, the local entrepreneurial
middle class, as well as local leaders who are
friendly to foreign investors. TNCs are very
large companies whose ofﬁces, factories,
and branch plants are located in different
developing countries around the world.
Their headquarters, however, are in the
metropolises of developed countries such as
the United Kingdom, United States, and
Japan. The opponents of these huge com-
panies hold that although they bring jobs
to the region in which they are established,
TNCs exploit the raw materials and cheap
labor force in that region, and they also
destroy the environment. Some TNCs are
much richer than many third world coun-
tries, and their wealth entails political
power over the poor country. They may
force a country to change the laws they ﬁnd
inconvenient instead of conforming to the
laws. Therefore, TNCs are attacked because
they threaten the independence of local
governments, and it is held that TNCs
merely have replaced the colonial armies of
the old colonial period. Some argue that in
the twenty-ﬁrst century, TNCs, rather than
nation-states, are the dominant political
and economic forces. Others draw atten-
tion to the contribution of TNCs to the
economy of their home countries as a result
of which the First World nations do not
only maintain but also strengthen their
power over the rest of the world.
The international rules of trade are
deﬁned by the World T rade Organization
(WTO), a transnational organization
whose ultimate aim is to abolish interna-
tional trade barriers such as customs duties
and trade taxes. Free trade and export-
oriented growth are encouraged by organi-
zations such as the International Monetary
Fund (IMF) and the World Bank (WB),
too. The critics of these organizations argue
that the loans given by the IMF and WB to
needy countries aim to make the latter
more and more dependent on the former
rather than improve the poor country’s
economy. The foreign aid supplied by the
IMF and WB requires that the recipient
country participate in the Structural
Adjustment Plans designed by these organi-
zations. Adjustment Plans aim to integrate
developing countries into the capitalist
economic system; therefore, they impose
privatization and export-oriented produc-
tion on the developing country as major
goals to achieve. According to the oppo-
nents of the Adjustment Plans, the decrease
in state help, especially for health and
education, and a production policy indif-
ferent to a country’s own needs undermine
that country’s self-sufﬁciency and political
autonomy. Furthermore, it is argued that
the high interest rates of the loans given by
the IMF and WB enslave the debtor in that
many third world countries today have to
pay back much more to these organizations
than the amount of money they received
from them.
The critics of neocolonialism also pin-
point cultural colonization of the third
world, mainly via media and education.
They argue that media companies in devel-
oping countries promote consumerism and
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 903 ---
NETHERLANDS ANTILLES 815
Western lifestyles so that they can be assim-
ilated easily into the new world order. As
for education, they hold that Eurocentric
design of the curricula and course books as
well as the promotion of trade-oriented
schools in developing countries perpetuate
neocolonialism. Especially since the 1990s,
the critics of neocolonialism all around the
world have come together in global solidar-
ity to raise their voices, particularly against
the WTO. The riots in Seattle in 1999,
those in Bangkok, Washington, D.C.,
Prague, Davos, Salzburg, Seoul, Melbourne,
and Bologna in 2000, and in Montreal,
Naples, and Genoa in 2001 are all indica-
tive of the worldwide opposition to what is
seen as the neocolonial world order.
Elif Oztabak-Avci

NETHERLANDS ANTILLES
The Netherlands Antilles consist of six
islands in the Caribbean. St. Martin (which
is partly Dutch and partly French), St.
Eustatius, and Saba are in the Leeward
Islands, while Curaçao, Bonaire, and Aruba
are in the Windward Islands (Lesser
Antilles) and are situated some 559 miles
(900 kilometers) from the Leeward Islands
close to the mainland of Venezuela. The
islands today have an autonomous position
within the kingdom of the Netherlands,
which is made up of the three countries:
Aruba, the Netherlands Antilles, and the
Netherlands.
From 1568 to 1648 the Dutch were at
war with Spain. In 1580 Spain conquered
Portugal and expelled Dutch traders from
the country. This expulsion meant that the
Dutch had to ﬁnd an alternative for the
Portuguese salt that was used in the herring
industry. They decided the Caribbean was
a good alternative. At the end of the
sixteenth and in the ﬁrst decades of the
seventeenth centuries private Dutch mer-
chants and privateers were active in the
Caribbean. The Dutch government sup-
ported the foundation of the Dutch West
India Company (WIC) in 1621 to regulate
the trade to Africa and America. However,
the main aim of this company was to ex-
tend the war against Spain. After the com-
pany occupied a part of northern Brazil
(1624–1654), slave trading became a major
factor in WIC’s history. Seeking strong-
holds in the Caribbean in the struggle
against Spain, the WIC conquered the
island of Curaçao in 1634. The neighbor-
ing islands of Aruba and Bonaire followed.
In the Leeward Islands, St. Martin, St.
Eustaius, and Saba also became Dutch
colonies. In 1648 St. Martin was divided
between the Netherlands and France.
During the Brazilian experience, the
Dutch conquered the Portuguese slave cen-
ter Elmina on the West African coast in
1637, which accelerated the nascent Dutch
slave trade. From Elmina many Dutch slave
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 904 ---
816 N ETHERLANDS ANTILLES
ships crossed the Atlantic Ocean to Brazil,
Surinam, Curaçao, and St. Eustatius.
Elmina was one of the more than 20 Dutch
trading posts in West Africa in the seven-
teenth century. Curaçao and St. Eustatius
were crucial staple markets for the Dutch
slave trade from Africa. Dutch slave exports
from Africa from 1620 to 1803 totaled
approximately 550,000, or 5 percent of the
whole transatlantic black Diaspora. Some
64 percent of these slaves were men. Most
slaves came from the Gold Coast, the Slave
Coast, and the Loango-Angola region. The
Dutch West Indian islands were not really
suitable for large-scale plantation produc-
tion. The WIC saw more possibilities sell-
ing slaves from Curaçao and St. Eustatius
to the Spanish and English colonies in
the Caribbean. About 92,000 slaves were
transported to Curaçao and 29,000 to
St. Eustatius from where they were sold to
the Caribbean region.
Compared with most of the sugar-
producing Caribbean colonies, the percent-
age of slaves in the Netherlands Antilles
population was low and the ratio of whites
to slaves atypical. In 1789 the Dutch
Leeward Islands had about 4,256 whites,
785 free nonwhites, and 9,400 slaves. The
slaves formed 65 percent of the total popu-
lation and the ratio of whites to slaves was
1 to 2.2. On Curaçao the numbers in 1789
were 3,564 whites, 4,560 free nonwhites,
and 12,864 slaves. The slaves made up 61.3
percent of the population and the ratio of
whites to slaves was 1 to 3.6. This meant
that many slave owners were in direct and
personal contact with their slaves. On the
largest island, Curaçao, more than 60 per-
cent of the slave owners possessed less than
ﬁve slaves in the period 1735–1863. In
1764 this island counted 534 owners and
5,534 slaves, but only ﬁve masters had
more than 100 slaves. Compared with
Surinam, the slave population in the
Netherlands Antilles saw a continuous nat-
ural increase in the nineteenth century. This
increase is in sharp contrast with the large
plantation societies in the Caribbean. The
reasons for this increase were the labor con-
ditions, the nature of slavery, and a higher
level of fertility of the female slaves. A proof
of these favorable factors are ﬁgures from
a reliable 1845 source that reports that 70
percent of slave children on C uraçao
reached the age of 12, while in Surinam
only 50 percent survived to this age.
The plantations on the Netherlands
Antilles did not produce for a world market
and that made a big difference in the con-
ditions and treatment of slaves. Dutch trav-
elers of the time reported that slaves of
Curaçao were afraid to be sent to Surinam
where slaves were treated far worse. Al-
though the slave situation on these islands
was atypical compared to the sugar planta-
tion societies in the West Indies, the social
stratiﬁcation was almost the same. The
white elite was formed by protestant
Dutchmen and Sephardic Jews on Curaçao
and by British and Dutch settlers in the
Dutch Leeward colonies. Most of them
were civil servants, military men, mer-
chants, and planters. Free nonwhites and
blacks were important for the economy. In
1789 they formed 20 percent of the
Curaçao population and in 1863 it was
50 percent. They worked on the land, in
the harbors, or were artisans or sailors. At
the bottom of the social ladder were
slaves. They produced corn and sorghum
for their masters and the black commu-
nity, took care of the cattle, did the hard
work in the salt pans of Bonaire and
St. Martin, and served their masters in
crafts and in their homes. On St. Martin
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 905 ---
NETHERLANDS ANTILLES 817
and St. Eustatius slaves also were active on
the small sugar plantations. In 1863 slavery
in the Dutch colonies was abolished.
In a process of adaptation, mingling,
and integration, slaves developed local forms
of music, traditions, cooking, stories, and a
sort of common African language, guené,
that long existed as an underground slave
language on Curaçao. This process of cre-
olization was not identical in the six islands
because the demographic, social, and eco-
nomic context was different. The Lesser
Antilles had more commercial contacts with
Spanish-speaking colonies and these small
societies were inﬂuenced by Spanish, Dutch,
and African cultural trends. On Aruba,
where slavery was not as important as on
Curaçao, African inﬂuences were not really
signiﬁcant. Latin and Indian features domi-
nate on this island. The African beat and
rhythm in dances like tambú and tumba in
the Lesser Antilles and the belief in evil
ghosts, orzumbis and eszé(related to Haitian
Voodoo), show up a more sustained African
connection. In the context of this slave soci-
ety and in communication with the whites,
a new language, Papiamentu, started to de-
velop on Curaçao in the seventeenth cen-
tury. In this language the Nanzi stories of the
spider as a trickster ﬁgure were recounted
and adjusted to the local situation.
The Calvinist Dutch Reformed Church
was not really interested in baptizing the
slaves. The administration tolerated that
preachers of other religions did the religious
teaching of the slaves. This practice was
even stimulated in the nineteenth century.
On Aruba, Bonaire, and Curaçao, many
slaves became Roman Catholics, and on the
Leeward Islands, Methodists, Anglicans,
and Roman Catholics. The white elite
considered these inferior slave religions. On
the Leeward Islands, many British settlers
inﬂuenced the culture and language of the
Dutch colonies. In the nineteenth century,
Caribbean English became the common
language of society. In culture and religion,
the Dutch Leeward Islands show many
similarities with the surrounding English-
speaking West Indies.
In the Netherlands Antilles there were
three substantial slave uprisings. In 1750
and 1795 slaves of some plantations re-
belled on Curaçao. The 1750 uprising
lasted only one day, although 59 slaves and
one white overseer were killed by the rebels.
The 1795 revolt began August 17 and was
more serious. More than 2,000 slaves took
part in the rebellion under the leadership of
a slave named T ula. After two weeks of
negotiations and battles, Dutch soldiers
assisted by civilians and groups of free
coloreds and blacks defeated the rebellious
slaves. After both revolts the punishments
for the slave leaders were harsh and cruel.
In 1848 the 1,100 slaves of St. Eustaius de-
manded their freedom. The leaders of the
uprising referred to the abolition of slavery
in the British and French colonies. After
some skirmishes the slaves returned to the
plantations.
Although their revolts were not as large
as those in Haiti or Jamaica, the slaves of the
Netherlands Antilles were not always com-
pliant. The many laws to control and regu-
late the behavior of slaves had to be ofﬁcially
announced periodically to remind the white
settlers of the black threat. Regulations to
prevent slaves from fleeing to foreign
colonies were especially strict. Nevertheless,
hundreds of slaves ﬂed from the Lesser
Antilles to Venezuela. In 1760, 400 ex-
slaves from these islands lived in a city quar-
ter of Coro, Venezuela, where Papiamentu
was the language commonly used.
Ronald Donk

NIAGARA MOVEMENT
The Niagra movement was an early-
twentieth-century organized protest move-
ment of African American men and a pre-
cursor to the formation of the National
Association for the Advancement of
Colored People. In 1903, Atlanta University
professor William Edward Burghardt
(W . E. B.) Du Bois published The Souls of
Black Folk, which included an argument
against Booker T . Washington’s acceptance
of segregation. T wo years later, in February
1905, Du Bois met with Monroe T rotter,
John Hope, and others in Buffalo, New
York, to further develop that argument.
The meeting led to a larger one at Niagara
Falls. Since no hotel on the American side
of the falls accepted African Americans, the
group met on the Canadian side. From
July 11 to 14, 1905, 29 men developed a
protest movement named after its meeting
place, with Du Bois as general secretary.
The Niagara movement called for immedi-
ate universal manhood suffrage, equality of
economic opportunity, equality in educa-
tion, and equality before the law for African
Americans. Members distributed pamphlets
decrying the accommodation proposed by
Washington and lobbied against Jim Crow
legislation. The group metagain the follow-
ing year in Harper’s Ferry, West Virginia.
Though it established 30 branches, a lack
of both permanent headquarters and con-
sistent ﬁnancing kept it from garnering a
large following. Though the movement’s
call for suffrage only included men, and
though T rotter opposed female member-
ship, Mary White Ovington, a socialist set-
tlement house worker, became the group’s
ﬁrst white member in 1908. Other liberal
intellectuals from the white community
soon joined her, leading directly to the
establishment of the National Association
for the Advancement of Colored People
(NAACP) the following year. Du Bois
served as editor of the NAACP’s journal,
The Crisis, but his executive duties with the
Niagara movement ended when the group
disbanded in 1910.
Thomas Aiello

Du Bois, William Edward Burghardt;
Washington, Booker T .
