W . E. B. Du Bois. New York: Garland, 1993.
Rudwick, Elliot. W . E. B. Du Bois: Voice of the
Black Protest Movement. Urbana: University
of Illinois Press, 1982.
NICARAGUA
The largest country in Central America,
Nicaragua shares borders with Honduras
on the north and Costa Rica to the south.
Nicaragua has undergone signiﬁcant politi-
cal, economic, and social changes since the
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 907 ---
NICARAGUA 819
late 1970s. As a result, Nicaraguans have
had to contend with serious challenges
posed by natural disasters—such as earth-
quakes and hurricanes—and unstable and
corrupt governments. Comparable in size
to the state of New York, the vast majority
of the population (approximately ﬁve mil-
lion) is located in the Paciﬁc lowlands
around Managua, the capital city. Most
Nicaraguans are mestizo (of mixed Indian
and Spanish descent), but there is a large
African inﬂuence on the Atlantic coast.
In addition, most Nicaraguans are Roman
Catholics, although Protestantism is grow-
ing. Nicaragua is home to several volcanoes
(many of which are still active) and the
two largest freshwater lakes in Central
America—Managua and Nicaragua. Lake
Managua gives the capital city a beautiful
picturesque quality and Lake Nicaragua has
the only freshwater sharks in the world.
Nicaragua’s economy is based largely on the
production and export of agricultural goods.
The most important export crops are cof-
fee, cotton, various hardwoods (such as
mahogany), cattle, and seafood. However,
in recent years dropping world prices for
agricultural commodities, coupled with
the effects of a decade-long civil war in the
1980s, rampant corruption, and Hurricane
Mitch, has wreaked havoc on Nicaragua’s
already weak economy.
During the 1980s, Nicaragua was the
subject of a foreign policy debate in the wan-
ing years of the Cold War. The Sandinistas—
who had close ties to Cuba and the Soviet
U.S. marines in 1932 hold the ﬂag of Augusto Sandino, a liberal Nicaraguan leader who engaged the U.S. forces
in guerrilla warfare for many years. The marines were withdrawn in 1933. (National Archives)
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

820 N ICARAGUA
Union—were engaged in a destructive
civil war against the contras (counterrevolu-
tionaries supported by the Reagan adminis-
tration). Unfortunately, scholarship on
Nicaragua has focused on explaining the
domestic and international sources of polit-
ical instability in Nicaragua; few scholars
have explored the Afro-Caribbean culture
on Nicaragua’s east coast and its larger ex-
periences in the Atlantic World. The Afro-
Caribbean community in Nicaragua is
located in what is known as the Mosquito
Coast. For centuries, the Mosquito Coast
was under British control as Great Britain
established beachheads in the strategically
important Central American isthmus.
Hoping to connect the Atlantic and Paciﬁc
oceans, European—and later American—
powers sought to control the vital passage-
way because it would ensure military and
economic inﬂuence for the entire Western
Hemisphere. In the late nineteenth cen-
tury, the Liberal Party in Nicaragua—
under the leadership of José Santos
Zelaya—gained control of the government
and with the aid of the United States,
Nicaragua militarily regained control of the
Mosquito Coast (roughly one-third of
Nicaragua’s territory). The Afro-Caribbean
community in Nicaragua thus dealt with
Spanish, British, U.S., and Nicaraguan
efforts to control their destiny.
The ﬁrst Garifuna to arrive in Nicaragua
came to Pearl Lagoon, on the Caribbean
coast, in 1880. That year Joseph Sambola,
believed to be a descendant of a Carib chief,
founded the ﬁrst ofﬁcial Garifuna commu-
nity of San Vicente in honor of their ances-
tral home. In 1892 Sambola also founded
Ebo Point, while his descendants founded La
Fe in 1901 and Justo Point and Orinoco (the
largest Garifuna community in Nicaragua
today) in 1907. The Garifuna in Nicaragua
were involved in various aspects of the local
economy, including cutting mahogany and
working on sugar plantations and saw mills.
The African presence on Nicaragua’s east
coast, however, has a much longer history
that precedes the arrival of Joseph Sambola.
African slaves had been brought to the
Mosquito Coast (named so after the Miskitu
Indians in the region) since 1633, by the
British living on the island of Providence,
about 100 miles (1.6 kilometers) off the
Caribbean coast of Nicaragua, who sent
them to work on the sugar plantations. The
slaves brought to Nicaragua were primarily
from the modern states of Gambia, T ogo,
Ghana, and Benin. By 1787 there were
roughly 1,800 slaves on the coast. With
its commercial presence on Nicaragua’s
Caribbean coast, Great Britain established
the Kingdom of Mosquitia under the aus-
pices of the governor of Jamaica. From
here, Afro-Nicaraguans carved out their
own unique way of life mediated by outside
pressures from the United States and the
government in Managua.
On February 10, 1894, Nicaragua re-
gained control of the Mosquito Coast.
Comprising one-third of Nicaragua’s na-
tional territory, the Mosquito Coast had,
for over 300 years, been outside the limits
of Spanish then Nicaraguan authority. By
the late nineteenth century, the Mosquito
Coast, under the stewardship of Great
Britain, was thriving economically. The re-
gion had become successful producing ba-
nanas, rubber, and gold. Economic reasons
alone can account for why Nicaragua wanted
to control its territory. The Mosquito Coast
was the scene of a dramatic struggle over
the future course of the region. Nicaraguan
elites wanted to control the rich economic
assets but viewed the inhabitants of their
newly acquired land with suspicion. These
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 909 ---
NICARAGUA 821
fears were well founded as the Creoles and
Garifuna (who by virtue of their experi-
ences under British control and tutelage)
viewed themselves as English and superior
to their Hispanic neighbors. By contesting
the process of state formation, the Afro-
Caribbean populations of Belize and
Nicaragua showed how larger political and
economic structures impacted daily life for
these populations and how, in turn, the
Garifuna and Creoles inﬂuenced the polit-
ical, economic, social, and cultural institu-
tions. These struggles are still very much
prevalent in present-day Nicaragua. These
struggles are most evident in the participa-
tion of the Afro-Caribbean community in
the civil war that resulted in the overthrow
of Zelaya, and later to the contra’s war
against the Sandinistas.
The Afro-Caribbean community on
Nicaragua’s Mosquito Coast had a long his-
tory of being the center of contested strug-
gles between empires seeking to control their
land and its rich economic potential. When
Nicaragua gained control of the Atlantic
coast, policymakers in Managua confronted
a foreign land. After centuries of British cul-
tural inﬂuence, Afro-Nicaraguans resented
their Spanish-speaking ofﬁcials and the
government in Managua. At ﬁrst, Managua
tried to culturally incorporate the Mosquito
Coast but found resistance among the
Afro-Caribbean. This resistance has made
Nicaragua’s Atlantic coast a unique window
with which to explore larger issues of state
and nation formation within the context of
the Atlantic World. The Mosquito Coast
was at the center of various power struggles
between Spain, Britain, the United States,
and Nicaraguan authorities. The uniqueness
of their culture (funneled through centuries
of British inﬂuence), and the region’s eco-
nomic importance made certain that the
Atlantic coast would be at the center of in-
tense political intrigue. History has shown
that Afro-Nicaraguans have taken an active
part in determining their own destiny, of-
tentimes resulting in armed struggle to
maintain their autonomy. (They have been
very successful in this regard as the
Mosquito Coast, formerly known as the
Department—or state—of Zelaya has been
divided into two autonomous regions.)
Afro-Nicaraguans were an important factor
in the overthrow of Zelaya in 1909 and in
the civil war that engulfed Nicaragua in the
1980s. The experiences of Afro-Nicaraguans
thus show the lasting impact the African
Diaspora had in the process of state and na-
tion making in their new homelands. More
than passive recipients of historical processes,
Afro-Caribbeans in Nicaragua were active
participants who helped shape the modern
Nicaraguan state.
Alberto Nickerson

NIGER
This landlocked country in West Africa has
a population of approximately 11,361,000
people, all of whom live in the capital and
scattered oases. More than two-thirds of
Niger is uninhabited desert. It was the
source of slaves in the early days of the
European slave trade. Captives were brought
down the Niger River for sale to European
slavers on the West African coast. Later,
exploration of Niger and the Niger
River would be significant to African
Americans when the Niger Valley Explor-
ing Party, which included Martin R.
Delany, a black nationalist who had
founded the ﬁrst black newspaper west of
the Alleghany Mountains and was a strong
advocate of black emigration, sought possi-
ble settlements for African Americans.
Their explorations would eventually lead to
the establishment of Liberia.
The French gradually took control of
land east of the Niger River by signing
treaties with rulers of individual ethnic states
in the 1890s, and creating Niger in 1911.
For 11 years, the area was under military
rule, and in 1922 became the French colony
of Niger. The French lieutenant governor
from 1932 until 1933 was Théophile
Antoine Pascal T ellier, who had come from
the West Indies where he had been governor
of Guadeloupe from 1929 to 1931.
In the early twentieth century, U.S.
missionaries became active in the region,
with the Sudan Interior Mission starting
work in Niger in 1924 and the Evangelical
Baptist Missions in 1929. Ties with the
United States would grow signiﬁcantly
afterward.
In 1958 Niger voted to remain au-
tonomous within the French Community,
and became independent on August 3,
1960, as the Republic of Niger. The ﬁrst
president, Hamani Diori, ruled the country
for the next 14 years. The United States
immediately recognized the new country,
appointing R. Borden Reams as their ﬁrst
ambassador.
From the 1980s Niger’s main exports
were uranium, coal, and gold. It rapidly
became the ﬁfth-largest uranium producer
in the world. In the run-up to the U.S.-
led invasion of Iraq in 2003, there was
much controversy in the United States
over claims made by President George W .
Bush that Iraq was sourcing supplies of
uranium from Niger, which, although found
to be based on faulty intelligence, focused
U.S. and international attention on the
country.
Justin Corﬁeld
See also: Delany, Martin Robinson; French
Empire; Liberia
Reference
Decalo, Samuel. Historical Dictionary of Niger.
Lanham, MD: Scarecrow Press, 1997.
NIGERIA
Nigeria is the largest country in West
Africa, a land of diverse cultures, and a na-
tion of many peoples with rich religious
traditions. The name Nigeria was given to
the country by the British Lord Luggard’s
wife in 1914. Nigeria consists of different
peoples and cultures, including the primary
ethnic groups: the Fulani-Hausa, the
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 911 ---
NIGERIA 823
Yorubas, and the Igbos, among many
others. Nigeria is located in West Africa
and bordered in the north by Niger, in the
south by Gulf of Guinea, in the west by
Benin, and in the east by Cameroon and
Chad. Its present population is about 132
million within an area of 356,669 square
miles (572,926 kilometers). Its climate
varies from area to area and generally there
are dry and wet seasons with different tem-
peratures too. Nigerians speak different
languages, among which are English, the
ofﬁcial language, Hausa, Igbo, and Yoruba.
There are many other dialects. Nigerian
currency is called Naira. Major holidays in
Nigeria are New Year’s Day, Good Friday
and Easter, Eid a-Fitr and Eid al-Kabir
(Muslim festivals), Independence Day, and
Christmas Day.
Government
Nigeria is a federal republic. It won its in-
dependence from Britain in 1960 and be-
came a republic in 1963. It has 36 states
with a federal capital at Abuja. Nigeria has
a long and rich history that goes back more
than 3,000 years. It boasted major empires
in Africa with very rich traditions and cul-
tures. Among its past empires were Oyo,
Igbo, Bornu-Kanem, and Hausa-Fulani.
Each empire had its distinctive administra-
tive structure and system of governance. In
1914, the British merged the empires and
formed a cohesive government known as
Nigeria. The integration has not been suc-
cessful, in part because the country was
divided into states after independence. A
citizen of one state cannot become a gover-
nor or senator in another state. Hence, the
sense of unity or patriotism among all
Nigerians is always challenged.
Religion
Although Nigeria claims to be a secular
state, religious issues permeate all aspects
of Nigerians’ private and public lives. Re-
ligion shapes both local and federal poli-
cies to a large extent. Nigeria has three
major religions: Islam, which is predomi-
nant in the north; Christianity, which is
predominant in the east and many parts
of the west; and African indigenous reli-
gions, which have minority followers in
many parts of Nigeria. Muslims compose
about 48 percent, Christians 40 percent,
and African traditional and other religions
12 percent. Both Christianity and Islam
are perceived as intolerant religions
because of their contempt for indigenous
religions, which they arrogantly label as
paganism. Christianity and Islam are ex-
clusive religions; they rival one another
and occasionally resort to violence to
achieve their missionary goals. The adher-
ents of indigenous religions are the small-
est group, yet they inﬂuence Islam and
Christianity because many people resort
to these indigenous beliefs during the
time of crisis. One of the causes of tension
between Muslims and Christians is the in-
troduction and application of the Shari’ah
(Islamic law) in 12 northern states. The
issue of the application of Islamic law is
yet to be resolved. There are other impor-
tant causes of unrest in Nigeria, including
like tribal and ethnic crisis, corruption,
and unemployment.
Politics
Politically, Nigeria is a recovering demo-
cratic country. It witnessed 29 years of
brutal military dictatorship, from 1966
to 1979 (under four different military
dictators who were either deposed and/or
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 912 ---
824 N IGERIA
killed) and again from 1983 to 1999 (under
three different military dictators who were
deposed or resigned). Nigeria has also en-
dured many years of corrupt civilian
rule. After its independence in 1960, it
went through many changes of govern-
ment, from the British parliamentary sys-
tem to the American presidential democra-
tic system, from civilian to military
dictatorial rule, until May 29, 1999, when
the people chose an elected leader, Olusegun
Obasanjo. Under his leadership, Nigeria be-
came relatively stable and peaceful, even
though there are occasional religious turbu-
lence, ethnic crisis, civil demonstrations,
and cult disturbances in colleges all over
the country. The government tries to solve
these crises amicably, but its failure to
tackle the roots of the problems hampers
its efforts. The roots of the problems are re-
ligious intolerance among the Muslims and
Christians, the high rate of unemployment,
mismanagement of the country’s resources,
and corruption of the elected leaders.
Nigeria had and continues to have a
good relationship with its neighbors, par-
ticularly with African countries. It main-
tains trade relationships with nearly all
countries of the world and has embassies in
those countries. It has membership status
in many international organizations and
leads the world in international peacekeep-
ing. Unfortunately, Nigeria has a bad image
abroad due to the corruption of a few
Nigerians who engage in fraud and interna-
tional drug trafﬁcking. Nigeria has pro-
duced great leaders who have contributed
to its development. Among them are Sir
Abu Bakar Tafawa Balewa, Chief Obafemi
Awolowo, Major General Muhammad
Muritala, and former president Olusegun
Obasanjo.
Economy
Nigerians are very hard-working people
who believe strongly in capitalism. They
are naturally entrepreneurial, especially the
Yorubas and Igbos, and engage in all types
of businesses and travel to any part of the
world for trade. Women are the backbone
of business in Nigeria because they control
the local markets. However, they are under-
represented in the public sector and in pol-
itics despite representing more than 50 per-
cent of the voters in the 2003 general
election.
Economically, Nigeria is extremely
rich in natural and human resources but
is laden with corruption and mismanage-
ment. Nigeria is the sixth-largest crude
oil producer in the world and 90 percent
of its budget comes from oil revenue.
Before the oil boom of 1973, Nigeria’s
economy relied exclusively on agricul-
ture; afterward it switched its reliance to
the exportation of oil. Lack of adequate
technological development has made
Nigeria an underdeveloped country
despite its abundant resources. The
past civilian and military governments
did not invest in the infrastructure of
the country during the oil boom.
Major public needs like electricity, good
roads, and communications were not
developed.
Since the election of President
Obasanjo, inroads have been made to de-
velop the Nigerian economy by combating
government corruption and mismanage-
ment and building the infrastructure
through foreign investment. The commu-
nication system has been improved the
communication system and many govern-
ment companies privatized to boost their
productivity and efﬁciency.

NIGERIA 825
Education
Nigerians value education and the nation
has produced many scholars, educators,
and artists in all ﬁelds of science, technology,
law, religion, history, engineering, and so
forth. Nigerian professors, doctors, artists,
educators, and lawyers are all over the
world. Even though there is still some illit-
eracy in Nigeria, the government continu-
ously strives to provide free primary and
secondary education for its citizens. Nigeria
today has more than 48 universities,
hundreds of technical schools, colleges of
education, polytechnics, and thousands of
elementary and high schools with more
than 18 million students in schools and
colleges in the year 2000. 
Nigerians begin their informal educa-
tion at home and formal education at age
six at school. They spend six years in ele-
mentary, three years in junior high, and
three years in senior high. Interested stu-
dents pursue higher education at one of
the government or private universities,
which lasts for four years. Every graduate
student from university enrolls in one year
of national youth community service after
graduation. Many Nigerians study abroad,
and after completion of their degrees,
some return home while others stay abroad
to work.
Culture
Nigeria is a country of diverse cultures.
Each ethnic group boasts its own culture
and way of life. Although these cultures
are similar, and sometimes identical, each
has its own unique features that may not
be shared by others. For instance, the
sculptures of the Nok people of Jos
Plateau and Zaria are a distinct art form
that is collectively admired by Nigerians,
as are the bronze works of the Yoruba in
Ile-Ife and Benin. Each group maintains
unique ceremonies. Egungun, Gelede,
Bori, and other entertainments like mask,
Sakara, Fuji, Apala dances, and boju-boju
(“cover the eyes”games) are sources of
pride and amusement for the spectators.
In addition, marriage, birth, and funeral
ceremonies in each community differ from
one another. Nigerians make decorative
carvings from wood, calabash (from Oyo),
stone, ivory, and bones. These art forms
are found in many regions and reﬂect an-
cient traditions of Nigeria. Furthermore,
some Nigerians have received interna-
tional recognition for drama and litera-
ture. Wole Soyinka won the Nobel Prize
for literature in 1986 for The Lion and the
Jewel, and Chinua Achebe has had his
novel Things Fall Apart translated into
many languages.
Yushau Sodiq

826 N IGERIA,D RAMA IN
NIGERIA,D RAMA IN
The origin and development of drama in
Nigeria has global political and cultural im-
portance since it bears connections to play-
wrights of the African Diaspora. Drama in
Nigeria has its origins from the indigenous
traditional practices of the people and has
developed through three major phases: the
traditional/oral, the popular/itinerant, and
the modern/written stages. These dramatic
phases cohere with the developmental
stages of the Nigerian nationhood—
precolonial/preindependence, postinde-
pendence, and the modern/contemporary
Nigeria. Even though these dramatic
phases can be studied independently, they
are in an intricate, symbiotic relationship
with one another, indicating a continuum
from the early to the contemporary times.
Easily a microcosm of drama in Africa,
Nigerian drama serves as a model to dra-
matic practices and norms in other parts of
Africa. There are certain beliefs and values
that underlie and inform Nigerian drama.
They include the fact that all the people
come from a common ancestor, the belief
in the central unifying factor called tradi-
tion, the recognition of the sacredness of
man and the immutability of humanity,
and the argument that an umbilical cord
links the worlds of the unborn, the living,
and the dead. These beliefs and values con-
stitute a corpus by which the three phases
of Nigerian drama relate and are identiﬁed
and they set guidelines for the exponents
and practitioners over the years.
T raditional drama in Nigeria, being a
derivation of the folk tradition and practiced
by people who, though not literate, yet are
revered as the custodians of the commu-
nity’s spiritual essence, is an integration of
the religious and the secular. It delineates
ethical codes for the people and manifests
in rituals such as sacriﬁces, initiation, birth,
funeral, mourning, and circumcision rites
and festivals like coronation, seasonal and
occupational celebrations, dances, songs,
tales, mimes, and music. Its mode of trans-
mission is oral and its setting is natural and
realistic, with high audience participation.
T oward the late eighteenth and early
nineteenth centuries, organized troupes,
called traveling or itinerant theatres,
emerged primarily in the southwestern
(Yoruba) region of Nigeria and attached
professionalism to the art. Pioneered by the
Alarinjo Theatre, and later by The Popular
Theatre of Hurbert Ogunde, itinerant the-
ater entertained audiences mainly in the
king’s palace or court. The texts embodied
the praises of genealogies of royals. The
traveling theatre employed the language of
the people, incorporating traditional
speech items and nuances into the dramatic
performances. Thus it gained high popular-
ity among the people.
Between the nineteenth and mid-
twentieth centuries, Nigeria was colonized
by Britain and the Christian religion im-
posed on its people. The religion con-
demned all forms of traditional drama as
heathen, an entertainment that would
only lead people to hell. As a result, dra-
matic practices were abandoned by many
Nigerian artists as the dominant trend was
to become converted to Christianity. How-
ever, in the 1940s Ogunde introduced a
unique concept that involved the careful
use of the Christian rhythm to render
traditional songs. Having been a church
choirmaster, Ogunde used traditional
musical instruments to accompany familiar
Christian songs and introduced into his
theater Western theatrical features such as
scripting of the lines, the use of a set stage,
and microphones. Ogunde’s theater was
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 915 ---
NIGERIA,D RAMA IN 827
greatly concerned with the sociopolitical is-
sues that were then threatening the corpo-
rate status of the post-independence
Nigeria. It actually marked the beginning
of what is today called the Modern or Con-
temporary Nigerian Drama. There were
various types of performances in southern
and southeastern Nigeria, but the north
could hardly develop a dramatic form,
since the spirit of Islam rejects all forms of
imitative and representative art.
Modern drama in Nigeria emerged in
credible forms in the 1960s when many
Nigerians who studied abroad were re-
turning home. These scholars, inﬂuenced
by ancient European literary features,
which they studied in colleges, applied
them in their creative works. A major ex-
ponent, Wole Soyinka, the 1986 Nobel
Laureate in Literature, pioneered modern
theater development in Nigeria. Accord-
ing to Osoﬁsan, “Before Soyinka, there
was no professional theatre company to
undertake the production of plays in
English” (154). While Soyinka’s pedestal
was the University of Ibadan School of
Drama, of which he was chair, Ola
Rotimi’s was the University of Ife. Other
pioneer Nigerian playwrights include J. P .
Clark and Wole Ogunyemi. Their plays
served as a medium for sociopolitical crit-
icism, the condemnation of retrogressive
and debilitating norms and trends, as well
as the projection of an ideal society. Zulu
Sofola was the first female Nigerian
dramatist; her Wedlock of the Gods was
published in 1972.
There are generations of playwrights
in Nigeria. The general characteristic
among them is the careful integration of
elements of traditional life into drama. The
elements—songs, myths, legends, dances,
incantations, chanting, rituals, tales, and
traditional speech devices—are the forms
through which drama is made manifest.
The close relationship between human life
and drama justiﬁes the critical relevance
of drama among Africans. The incidence of
these elements in the dramatic practices of
Africans in the Diaspora is therefore ex-
plicable. It is apparent that the African
slaves in the New World went with their
African traditional beliefs and practices—
the songs, tales, dances, celebrations, folk
beliefs and myths, and rituals. These have
been handed down through the genera-
tions of blacks in the New World and ac-
count for the similarity in the themes
deployed by playwrights in Africa and the
New World. The theaters of Derek Walcott
in the Caribbean, Langston Hughes, Lor-
raine Hansberry, and the contemporary
Suzan-Lori Parks and others in America,
reveal a meticulous transfer of African dra-
matic modes into modern American the-
ater. Obviously, in spite of their forceful
dislocation and slavery, the African slaves
succeeded in sustaining their African her-
itage and practices. This connectedness
stresses the common background of black
people the world over.
Ini Uko

828 N IGERIAN TRADITIONAL DANCES
NIGERIAN TRADITIONAL
DANCES
Nigerian dance combines cultural and
artistic forms—religious and theatrical, vi-
sual and musical arts—that reﬂect and de-
velop the diverse traditions of Nigeria. The
diverse cultural characteristics of Nigeria
are manifest in not only the more than four
hundred languages and dialects spoken
there but also in theatrical arts that are
from nature and holistic in concept. A typ-
ical cultural performance is a symbiosis of
dances, drama and music, and visual tradi-
tional arts and crafts. The crafts include
costuming, carving, musical instrumenta-
tion, and craftsmanship. T raditional per-
forming arts in Nigeria are composed of
both religious and theatrical elements, but
historically, traditional dances are linked
more closely to the traditional religious sys-
tem. As a result, there are as many dances as
there are gods and goddesses. But many
dances also can trace their origin to occupa-
tional movements. Dances represent the
manifest presence of Nigerian traditional
performances because they have always
been a very prominent feature of expression
of a rich traditional repertoire across the di-
verse groups.
Some Nigerian traditional dances show
and possess unique characteristics, and at
times they share identical characteristics
with other dances of communities that are
poles apart, stressing the concept of unity
in diversity. However, whether unique or
similar, certain characteristics have been
observed representing the dominant move-
ment styles of African, and by implication,
Nigerian traditional dances.
. . . the dominant movement styles include
tilting of trunk, bent knees, angular arms,
ﬂat foot, earthbound movements, twisting
of the waist, isolation of body parts,
syncopated movements, acrobatic steps,
expressive movements, shaking of the body
(buttocks in female), improvisational
movements resulting in poly-rhythmic
movement style.” (Ugolo, 1998, p. 65)
Gelede
Gelede is a sociocultural cult that repre-
sents the total and holistic nature of
Nigerian theatrical performance. Gelede is
one of the masking traditions (mask
dramaturgy) of the Yorubas, which occurs
mainly in the western coastal areas of
Nigeria. Although it is holistic in context,
dances form the climax of this rich theatri-
cal performance. It is mainly entertain-
ment in nature, but it still retains its
socioreligious function of improving the
lot of individuals. The dance may cleanse
the society of pestilence, induce rain, enrich
human fertility, or enlist the support of
supernatural forces and the “powerful
mother” in crucial times (e.g., wartime).
The typical gelede dance performances
consist of masked and unmasked dancers
dancing side by side. The masked perform-
ers are two identical masquerades that
dance in unison and also alternate to the
Woro musical ensemble. The rhythm is pe-
culiar; so also are the dances of both the
masques and the male and female dancers.
The movements vary, but the predominant
one has to do with the wriggling of the
entire body in a combination of ﬁshlike
and snakelike movements. Movement is
punctuated with isolation of body parts to
beats and other improvisational move-
ments resulting in polyrhythmic move-
ment style.
A typical gelede ensemble is made up of
eighteen members, including drummers,
singers, and two or three masked dancers.
The masked gelede dancer/performer is cos-
tumed beautifully. The costume comprises a
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 917 ---
NIGERIAN TRADITIONAL DANCES 829
painted wood carving communicating di-
verse messages and meanings, carved female
breasts, and beautiful masquerade cloths,
usually of variegated colors. Bangles made
of brass or iron add to the beauty, as well as
the music of the gelede. A nocturnal cere-
mony of “Efe,” an all-night concert or night
of fun, is the climax of a typical gelede
performance. The Efe male mask (the
humorist) entertains the supernatural world
and the general public with songs, poetry,
dance, and satire. Gelede performance is
highly rated among the Yorubas, to the ex-
tent that a proverb is devoted to it: “Oju ti
o ri gelede ti ri opin iran,” meaning that an
eye that begets a gelede performance has
seen the ultimate in entertainment.
Swange Dance
Swange is a dance of the Tiv people of the
hinterland in northern Nigeria. Though
dissimilar, it has identical choreographic
structure with the coastal gelede. Swange
dance steps include the vigorous twisting of
the body in a snakelike form with expres-
sive movements of the hands. This dance is
accompanied by swange music produced
by membrane drums, aero phone, and per-
cussion musical instruments. Dancers are
clad in white and black striped wrappers
with white tops and wear anklets that pro-
duce sound to accompany the music.
Ugho Dance
Ugho is a royal ceremonial dance originally
performed by both male and female mem-
bers of the Benin royal family that later
moved outside the royal courts. Except
when performed in the palace by members
of the royal family, female performers are
banned from adorning their heads with the
full royal hairdo decorated with coral
beads. The dancers stand in a straight line,
holding white handkerchiefs in both hands,
with beads on their necks, arms, and ankle.
The ladies adorn their heads with beads in
a hairdo called okunkun. The dancers move
one leg and a hand at the same time and
look at that direction (e.g., the left leg and
the left hand to the left). At regular inter-
vals, they squat slightly and shake the but-
tocks with their hands stretched out.
The dancers wear the traditional attire
of either white wrapper or the red velvet
clothes; the women cover the body from
the shoulder to the ankle while the men are
well padded from the waist to appear as
royal chiefs in the Obas palace. The musi-
cal ensemble is made up of metal gongs,
membrane musical instruments, as well as
some rattle guards (maracas).
Atilogu Dance
The atilogu dance is indigenous to the Igbo
people of eastern Nigeria. It consists of en-
ergetic movements that entail the effective
use of the hand, leg, and waist, with the lat-
ter two most emphasized. Such dance vo-
cabularies as hops, twist, jumps, turns, and
shaking of the body in response to drum-
beats are expressed in this dance. The musi-
cal ensemble includes big and small metal
gongs, the wooden gong (ekwe), membrane
drums, and traditional ﬂute (ajah).
Bata Dance
Bata dance is a very rigorous Yoruba dance
executed with mathematically accurate ex-
pressive movements and accompanied with
praise poems. There are as many as eight
variants of this dance, the most prominent
of which is the fast tempo gbamu. Bata can
be claimed to be the source from which
such popular Western “break” and “electric
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 918 ---
830 N OIRISME
shock” dances took their roots because of
their identical features with bata. Bata
music, which is produced by bata drums, is
usually associated with the worship of
Sango the Yoruba god of thunder. The fero-
cious sound of the beats and the rugged
and intimidating shape of the instruments
are in attunement with the ferocious dispo-
sition attributed to Sango in Yoruba history
and mythology.
The tempo of the dance is dictated
by the lead drum ( iya ilu), followed by
the gentle caressing rhythmic sound of the
small drum (omele abo), backed by the
sharp sound of male or triple drums (omele
ako or omele meta ). A base drum ( ijin)
might be played to lessen the work of the
lead drum.
Imole Oloba Ritual Dance
This dance is performed annually during the
Oloba festival by the Yoruba people of Ado-
Ekiti. Oloba is the goddess of fruitfulness,
peace, and prosperity. About eight to twelve
maiden initiates of the goddess perform it
after a ritual preparation in the shrine.
The lead performer, who represents the
chief priestess, falls into a trance during the
course of the dance while the other per-
formers serve as chorus and dancers. Cos-
tumes depict the characters represented by
each dancer. The veiled lead performer
wears a beaded crown with a beaded bottle
at its pinnacle. She puts on heavy coral beads
from her neck to her breasts and around the
waist as an ornamental short skirt over a
cloth worn underneath. A breast band cov-
ers her body decorated with traditional
white chalk, and she wears beaded bracelets
on her wrists with metal rattles on her knees.
She normally holds pigeons in both hands as
a symbol of peace and progress.
The dancers representing two minor
priestesses wear beads and rattles with ban-
gles made of cowries, have their faces de-
signed with native white chalk, and carry
efﬁgies of the goddess while holding two
white horsetail flywhisks. The other
dancers carry pots of glowing ﬁre.
Nigerian dances are as numerous as the
ethnic diversity of the country and the
above are just a few of the scores of other
traditional dances still extant. While most
of these dances often are performed outside
their original context, their existence as tra-
ditional cultural entity is still retained and
their rich traditional elements have sur-
vived adaptation.
Nawar Al-Hassan Golley

NOIRISME
Noirisme (also known in Haiti as
“Africanisme,” “Haïtienisme,” or “négritude”)
is a Haitian black nationalist movement
that emerged during the ﬁrst U.S. occupa-
tion of Haiti (1915–1934), but many of its
roots lay in Haiti’s racial past. Racial rela-
tions have long proved contentious in
Haiti. During colonial times (1492–1791),
the white minority (Spanish, then French)
enslaved Haiti’s majority (Amerindian,
then African). A few months after Haiti ob-
tained its independence in January 1804,
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 919 ---
NOIRISME 831
Governor-General for Life Jean Jacques
Dessalines ordered all whites to be exe-
cuted, with the exception of non-French
foreigners (Poles, Americans) and skilled
individuals (doctors, priests). The white
population in Haiti has been small ever
since. Many Haitians complain that colo-
nial domination was replaced by Western
economic and military domination (the
United States invaded Haiti in 1915 and
1994).
Relations between Haitians of pure
African descent (authentiques, or noirs, or
nègres) and their lighter-skinned compatri-
ots (mulâtres, or jaunes) have also been
tense. Many mulattoes were free during
colonial times and owned black slaves.
During the war of independence, mulatto
generals such as André Rigaud shifted
alliances, and black generals such as
T oussaint l’Ouverture sometimes fought
them. After independence, mulattoes
played the leading economic and political
roles even when they did not occupy the
presidency. T oday, with the exception of
some rich blacks ( gros nègres), most rich
Haitians are mulattoes.
When the United States invaded Haiti
in July 1915, ostensibly to bring an end to
the country’s extreme political instability,
Haiti became, in reality if not in name, a
U.S. protectorate patrolled by U.S.
Marines and a U.S.-trained constabulary,
the gendarmerie. Americans and gen-
darmes forced Haitians to work for free on
road improvement projects, a system remi-
niscent of slavery. U.S. occupation ofﬁcers,
all of them white, brought with them the
racial prejudices prevalent at that time and
frequently disparaged Haitian character
(even mulattoes were treated as second-
class citizens). T wo revolts led by the mostly
black force of mercenaries and bandits
known as cacos (1915, 1918–1920) failed
to oust U.S. forces. During the latter, U.S.
troops killed caco leader Charlemagne
Masséna Péralte. Noirisme, the intellectual
equivalent of Péralte’s military revolt, was a
reafﬁrmation of Haitians’ love for their
country, pride in their African heritage, and
conﬁdence that the country’s failures were
accidental, not a product of a national and
racial inferiority. In practical terms, noiristes
sought to study the country’s African
roots, including the French-African dialect
(Creole), the Catholic-Animist religion
(Voodoo), and popular folklore, all of
which had been disparaged by foreigners
and the European-trained mulatto elite as
inferior, barbaric, and satanic.
Jean Price-Mars, the most famous
Haitian intellectual and noiriste, is best re-
membered for the inﬂuential Ainsi parla
l’Oncle (1928), in which he accused the
Haitian elite of looking up to European
culture while denying Haiti’s African past.
He also founded the Society of Haitian
History and Geography (1922) and the In-
stitute of Ethnology. Fellow ethnologists
Lorimer Denis and François Duvalier
founded the review Les griots in 1938.
Price-Mars’ protégés, like Jacques Roumain
and Jean Brierre, strove to create a gen-
uinely Haitian literature. Roumain, whose
world-famous Gouverneurs de la rosée was
published in 1944, also founded the Revue
indigène in 1927 to encourage the study
of Haitian folklore. In parallel, Selden
Rodman’s Renaissance in Haiti played a
great role in popularizing Haitian art, once
derided as naïve in foreign countries.
Even though the bulk of the noiriste
movement must be associated with the
ﬁrst U.S. occupation of Haiti and its
immediate aftermath, a mix of racial pride
and Haitian nationalism has underpinned
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

various regimes in Haiti’s history. Faustin
Soulouque’s regime (r. Haiti 1847–1859)
was one of them, as were those of François
Duvalier (in power 1957–1971) and
Jean-Bertrand Aristide (in power 1991,
1994–1996, 2001–2004). Other blacks
inspired by Price-Mars and noirisme in-
clude Stokely Carmichael, Léopold Sédar
Senghor, and Aimé Césaire.

NON-ALIGNED
MOVEMENT
The Non-Aligned Movement (NAM)
emerged during the Cold War as a group of
nations not formally allied with either the
United States or the Soviet Union and in-
cludes key nations in Latin America, the
Caribbean, and Africa. The movement was
founded at a summit meeting in Belgrade
in 1961 to address concerns of third world
nations such as decolonization, human
rights, and disarmament. T oday, the NAM
consists of over 100 nations that continue
to discuss issues of polarization between the
global North and South.
Origins of the NAM
The 1950s and 1960s were a time of in-
creasing interest in regional and global co-
operation among emerging nations, and
were marked by the formation of regional
groups such as the Organization of American
States and the Organization of African Unity.
Other more expansive regional groupings,
such as the 1955 Bandung Conference,
brought together African and Asian states to
discuss colonialism, economic development,
and world peace.
The sense of community among emerg-
ing nations engendered at the Bandung
conference helped lead to the formation of
the NAM. The founding ﬁgures of the
movement were Yugoslavia’s Josip Broz
Tito, Indian prime minister Jawaharlal
Nehru, and Egyptian president Gamal
Abdel Nasser, along with Indonesian presi-
dent Sukarno and Ghanaian president
Kwame Nkrumah. Yugoslavia, India, and
Egypt had worked closely together since
two formative events of 1956, the Suez
Canal crisis and the Soviet Union’s invasion
of Hungary. These events encouraged
Yugoslavia, India, and Egypt to collaborate
in the face of superpower interests.
Another factor leading to the emer-
gence of the NAM was the rapid decolo-
nization of Africa in the late 1950s and
early 1960s. The year 1960 has often been
called the “Year of Africa,” since in this year
16 African states became independent and
joined the United Nations. This year also
marked the emergence of apartheid into
global consciousness, when South African
police fired into a crowd of peaceful
demonstrators in Sharpeville, killing 69
and leading to international condemnation
of the country’s systematic segregation and
oppression. In addition, war in Algeria was
ongoing, and the government of the Congo
had rapidly broken down within a few
weeks of the granting of independence.
Superpower support of Congolese factions,
along with events such as the shooting
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 921 ---
NON-ALIGNED MOVEMENT 833
down of an American U2 spy plane over
the Soviet Union, led to heightened Cold
War tensions in which it seemed increas-
ingly difﬁcult to avoid choosing sides in the
Cold War.
In this Cold War environment, Tito
visited Ghana, T ogo, Liberia, Guinea, Mali,
Morocco, T unisia, Sudan, and the United
Arab Republic (later Egypt and Syria) from
February 13 to April 23, 1961, to garner
support for a conference of states amenable
to maintaining their own national identi-
ties and interests. From September 1 to 6,
1961, the leaders of 12 Asian countries,
eleven African countries, Cuba, and
Yugoslavia met in Belgrade, Yugoslavia, at
the ﬁrst NAM summit.
Objectives of the NAM
The goals of the NAM, as articulated at the
summit, were both economic and political.
Economically, these nations wanted effec-
tive international cooperation and eco-
nomic development (discussed in terms of
the unequal balance of trade between the
North and South). Politically, the states de-
sired independence for colonized peoples
and international peace and security.
Speciﬁc matters discussed included disar-
mament, self-determination, Palestinian
rights, and condemnation of apartheid.
Neutrality, or nonalliance with either the
United States or Soviet Union, was seen as
the way to achieve these goals.
In the 1960s and 1970s, it seemed pos-
sible that the nonaligned states could form
a power bloc challenging the dominance of
the superpowers. In the United Nations
General Assembly, nonaligned nations
often voted as a bloc. Contradictions, how-
ever, existed within the movement. Some
nonaligned countries were in practice
aligned with one of the superpowers, as in
the case of Cuba’s alignment with the Soviet
Union. The NAM’s positions were not al-
ways consistent; while it advocated global
disarmament, in the 1970s nonaligned
countries such as Cuba and Egypt were
among the top weapons exporters in the
third world. The Soviet Union’s invasion of
Afghanistan in 1979 split the movement.
Afghanistan, a NAM member, was occu-
pied by one of the superpowers. The NAM’s
rotating leadership at that time rested with
Cuba, and the movement’s sixth summit
had just been held in Havana. In the United
Nations General Assembly, the majority of
NAM countries voted to condemn the
occupation and call for the withdrawal of
Soviet troops from Afghanistan. Cuba and a
dozen other NAM members opposed the
condemnation.
The NAM T oday
Since 1970, member nations of the Non-
Aligned Movement have met at a summit
approximately every three years, often in
Southeast Asia, but also in the African and
American states of Algeria, Egypt, South
Africa, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Colombia, and
Cuba. Some NAM members have left the
movement since the end of the Cold War, yet
today NAM nations make up almost two-
thirds of the United Nations’ membership
and represent over one-half of the world’s
population. While the NAM did not emerge
as a viable third bloc acting outside the bipo-
larity of the Cold War world, the economic
and political objectives of the NAM have
consistently focused on promoting develop-
ment and opposing neocolonialism.
Patricia G. Clark

NOTTING HILL CARNIVAL
IN LONDON
The Notting Hill Carnival is a London-
based celebration of African folk memory,
rooted in T rinidadian Carnival and repre-
senting diverse and multicultural identities.
Notting Hill Carnival—originally trans-
ported to London by Afro-Caribbeans,
mostly T rinidadians—takes place the last
Monday in August, over a bank holiday
weekend. What began as a nostalgic cele-
bration of folk memory has proliferated to
such an extent that it now has the potential
to be used as a model for multicultural in-
tegration and instruction in other large
European cities. Although this carnival has
been acknowledged as “Europe’s largest
street festival,” it is not celebrated as na-
tional culture in London or Europe. It
takes place primarily in Notting Hill, in
London’s peripheries—or out of urban
space. Yet it transforms those very margins
into center spaces, which paradoxically
reclaims another type of identity for Afro-
Caribbean and other marginal groups. Fur-
thermore, the carnival has contributed to
London’s image as a world city because of
the economic boost it provides through
tourism and its highly professional aes-
thetic content jointly facilitated by carnival
artists from London’s different multiethnic
groupings.
Notting Hill Carnival is rooted in
T rinidadian Carnival: African slaves publicly
celebrated emancipation in 1834 by taking
to the streets, reinstituting their African
cultural forms yet simultaneously adopting
European festival forms. This historical
legacy was transplanted to the global city of
London when West Indian migrants began
arriving in London in the early 1850s.
However, the literature is sparse and con-
tradictory regarding the actual genesis of
the Notting Hill Carnival. Stuempﬂe states
that as early as 1951, a group of 11 steel
band players, the T rinidad All Steel Percus-
sion Orchestra, was invited from T rinidad
and T obago to represent T rinidad by parti-
cipating in the Festival of England (1995,
p. 94). This festival engendered the space
for the steel band to become a dominant
art form in “Caribbean Britain,” since it
created the possibility not only for home-
sick T rinidadians to display T rinidadian
culture but also to give public prominence
to steel band as a Caribbean musical form
in Britain. This was further developed by
Claudia Jones, a black T rinidadian writer
and activist, who organized dances and par-
ties at her home in Notting Hill. T rinidadi-
ans continued to come together, to drink
rum, and “beat pan.” The creation of “rum
shop culture,” in the late 1950s, at St.
Pancreas, marks the genesis and the ofﬁcial
birthplace of carnival in Britain.
The 1960s saw the carnival adopting
other features. As early as 1964, a social
worker invited the steel band players to
participate in the “Notting Hill Festival.”
Notting Hill, a poor, migrant slum, adja-
cent to the wealthy streets of Kensington,
with their “place-style” houses and expen-
sive shops, was to become the ofﬁcial site
for the celebration of carnival.
In 1965, Notting Hill Carnival ap-
peared in this area for the ﬁrst time,
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 923 ---
NOTTING HILL CARNIVAL IN LONDON 835
although there was no ﬁnancial support
from the prestigious Borough of Kensing-
ton and Chelsea for this migrant and other
lower-class peoples’ street festival. Rhaune
Lazlett, a London-born woman of
Amerindian and Russian descent, orga-
nized this multiethnic community event.
Russell Henderson and other T rinidadians,
all members of TASPO (T rinidad All Steel
Percussion Orchestra) took to the streets
with a few masqueraders to celebrate this
community event in T rinidadian style. In
this way the steel band reclaimed public
space for itself in Britain, thereby placing
the carnival at Notting Hill, and initiating
Notting Hill Carnival, as it is known today.
At the beginning of the 1970s there
were growing racial tensions between the
police and Afro-Caribbean youths living in
Notting Hill and Ladbroke Grove, espe-
cially during the carnival celebrations. This
hostility culminated in the race riots at
Notting Hill. Numerous investigations re-
vealed not only opposition from the au-
thorities but the more serious problem of
cultural fragmentation within the different
Caribbean groupings, and the clash be-
tween black British-born Jamaican youths,
who introduced reggae music to the carni-
val. Reggae music is associated with Rasta-
farianism while soca music is overtly associ-
ated with T rinidadian Carnival’s diverse
forms of celebration. With this cultural
fragmentation, Notting Hill Carnival
began to experience a slow transformation
from its initial traditional, T rinidadian
Caribbean forms of celebration into a
transnational, global site of struggle that
was culturally different and differentiated.
Nonetheless, the ofﬁcial threat to remove
the carnival from the streets reverberated
deeply among these groups, with the
carnival providing the forum for these
various groups to coalesce. This coming
together facilitated a marking out and a
shaping of new collectivities and multiple
ethno-Caribbean identities in the British
mainstream context.
Notting Hill Carnival, although be-
coming a highly politicized event, assumed
other features. In 1978 a commission was
formed to develop and promote the carni-
val, to raise its proﬁle as a multidiversiﬁed,
holistic art form embodying dance, music,
theater, as well as all the visual arts.
At the start of the 1980s, the carnival’s
reputation began to change as other cele-
bratory forms were introduced. The addi-
tion of sound systems created publicity for
Carnival, so that by 1986 a large number of
white British youths attended. This
changeover happened as a result of the pop-
ularity of Arrow’s calypso song “Hot Hot
Hot,” since it introduced the white British
population to soca music from T rinidad
and T obago’s carnival. Black Caribbean dis-
placed culture began its slow trek out of its
urban space to the center of global society
in London.
The presence of the white youth popu-
lation also impacted the carnival in other
ways. Jamaicans were delegated a special
space to play their Jamaican music, so that
they no longer formed a part of the parade
route. The organizers for masquerade
bands developed a special route. Carnival
artists were invited to develop an education
program for schools to depict the culture of
carnival and carnival arts. Artists taught
steel band, calypso, and soca music and
costume-making skills in schools. Carnival
at the end of the 1980s was one of the most
successful for the police, schools, and the
organizers.

The 1990s saw economic development
of the Notting Hill Carnival. As early as
1995, the carnival became known as The Lilt
Notting Hill Carnival sponsored by Coca-
Cola. In an attempt to raise the national
proﬁle of the carnival, the Arts Council of
Britain provided ﬁnancial support in col-
laboration with Roehampton Institute,
London, to develop and compile a publicly
accessible National Carnival Database of tex-
tual and visual information. The council also
provided support to carnivalists.
Notting Hill Carnival, enacted out of
place in the urban metropolitan setting, has
paradoxically transformed its urban place
into a highly politicized space that has facil-
itated the actual development of a culture
of carnival in the United Kingdom. This
model has been used in many other cities
in Britain as well as other European coun-
tries such as Sweden, Rotterdam, Greece,
T enerife, and Paris. The German Carnival
of Cultures, celebrated in Berlin, Bielefeld,
and Hamburg, is one example of how Not-
ting Hill Carnival has been utilized as a
multicultural, multidiversiﬁed form of cel-
ebration in a homogenous society.

NOVA SCOTIA,A FRICAN
AMERICAN DIASPORA IN
The African American Diaspora in Nova
Scotia is the migration, voluntary and in-
voluntary, of blacks from the United States
to this British North American colony
during the late eighteenth and early nine-
teenth centuries when two separate African
American migrations—black Loyalists and
black refugees—took place. By 1784, fol-
lowing the American Revolutionary War,
3,500 black Loyalists had migrated to Nova
Scotia and, in addition, hundreds of slaves
were brought to the colony by their white
Loyalist owners. The black Loyalists re-
ceived small allocations of land in a num-
ber of widely separated locations (the
largest population concentration was in
Birchtown on the colony’s south shore) and
some of them endured racial violence in
1784 as local whites attacked blacks for ac-
cepting lower wages from employers. They
faced discrimination in terms of employ-
ment and an unfair judicial system. In
search of better opportunities, nearly 1,200
left for Sierra Leone in 1793 with the aid of
British abolitionist John Clarkson. Under
similar circumstances during the War of
1812, 2,000 black refugees migrated to
Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. Beset by
poverty, government inaction, and the hos-
tility of the local white population, the
refugees were forced into menial labor jobs
while attempting to farm unfertile land.
Both the Loyalists and the refugees came
north because of British military proclama-
tions offering freedom, risking their lives in
escaping from slavery and ﬁghting for the
British during the wars. Yet there is one
important difference between these groups.
Unlike the leadership of the black Loyalists,
the refugee elite opted to stay in Nova
Scotia. Thus, despite numerous offers
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 925 ---
NOVA SCOTIA,B LACK REFUGEES IN 837
from the colonial government, 94 percent
of the refugee population remained in
Nova Scotia.
It is important to understand the black
Loyalists and the black refugees in the con-
text of the African American Diaspora.
These migrants brought many of their
experiences and cultural values to Nova
Scotia, such as African churches, the
Gullah language, burial ceremonies, and
cooking styles. Moreover, African Nova
Scotians were keenly aware of events in
Afro-America. For example, although slav-
ery had ended in Nova Scotia in the early
nineteenth century, the black population
founded the African Abolition Society in
1846. This society’s mission focused on the
plight of long-lost relatives and friends still
laboring in Georgia, Maryland, and
Virginia. As events unfolded during the
American Civil War, some African Nova
Scotians attempted to aid the cause of free-
dom through service as seamen. The link-
ages between Afro-Nova Scotia and Afro-
America continued throughout the latter
half of the nineteenth century in at least
three ways. First, preachers from southern
and northern states plied their trades in
Nova Scotia’s black churches. Second, after
the Civil War, African Nova Scotians mi-
grated to New England, generally and
speciﬁcally to Boston, in search of better
economic opportunities. Lastly, William
H. Golar, born during the mid-nineteenth
century in Nova Scotia to African Ameri-
can parents, moved to North Carolina and
eventually became a professor and later
president of Livingston College in North
Carolina.

NOVA SCOTIA,B LACK
REFUGEES IN
The black refugees were American slaves
who migrated to Nova Scotia during and
after the War of 1812. These African
Americans were primarily from the
Tidewater Chesapeake region and the
Georgia Sea Islands. During the conﬂict,
British ships regularly raided the American
coastline in hope of encouraging slaves to
abscond from their owners. In April 1814,
Admiral Alexander Cochrane issued a
proclamation promising settlement in
British colonies to any Americans willing to
switch sides. This promise resulted in the
moderate trickle of escaped slaves becom-
ing a virtual ﬂood as nearly 3,500 slaves
ﬂed to British ships. Of that total, over
2,000 had arrived on the shores of Nova
Scotia by the end of 1818. Some 400 of
these people went to New Brunswick. The
remaining 1,600 settled in Nova Scotia.
Once in Nova Scotia, the black
refugees faced a host of problems, includ-
ing but not limited to poverty, sickness, a
postwar economic depression, and hostility
from the local white population. Nova
Scotia’s government was unprepared, and
in some ways, unwilling to provide the
refugees with the support that an indigent
immigrant population required. For exam-
ple, Lt. Governor John Sherbrooke failed to
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 926 ---
838 N WAPA,F LORA
institute the imperial government’s provi-
sions for the care of former slaves. Instead
many refugees spent their ﬁrst months in
Nova Scotia searching for employment,
shelter, and medical attention. Eventually,
the colonial government decided to settle
the refugees on 10-acre farms at Hammonds
Plains and Preston (about 12 and 9 miles
[20 and 15 kilometers] respectively from
the colony’s urban center Halifax) in hopes
that the new settlers would be able to pro-
vide for their own subsistence. Yet this plan
was flawed from the beginning. The
refugees were placed on some of the worst
land in the colony and the small size of
their lots made commercial farming impos-
sible and subsistence farming tenuous. The
refugees also obtained tickets of location as
opposed to freehold grants. Thus they
could not sell their land in order to raise
capital to facilitate a move to another part
of the colony. The failure of the govern-
ment’s land settlement policy caused the
refugees to seek government provisions as
their small farms never produced enough
foodstuffs to feed the communities.
Indeed, throughout the refugees’ ﬁrst 25
years in Nova Scotia, they faced starvation
and malnutrition.
Despite the challenges the refugees
faced economically, they were able to create
tightly knit communities that emphasized
religious unity, as seen in their establish-
ment of African churches, and mutual sup-
port in a racist environment that placed
them at the lowest rung of the social ladder.
In 1821, the government attempted to per-
suade the refugees to leave Nova Scotia for
T rinidad. But barely 6 percent of them
accepted this offer. They valued freedom in
Nova Scotia despite the limitations placed
on it by economic circumstances and white
hostility. After 1821, the refugees developed
separate black churches, political organiza-
tions, community associations, and an abo-
lition society.
Harvey Amani Whitﬁeld

NWAPA,F LORA
(1931–1993)
The Nigerian writer Flora Nwapa
Nwakuche was an important participant in
the global effort at redeﬁning womanhood
in the twentieth- and twenty-ﬁrst century.
She made history in 1966 when she pub-
lished Efuru, the ﬁrst novel in English by a
woman from black Africa. With this
groundbreaking act, she altered a tradition
of publishing male-oriented and male-
authored works. She also rejected the estab-
lished literature’s conventional representa-
tions of women in secondary, trivial, or
unrealistic positions. Nwapa’s versatile and
proliﬁc output is evident in her literary
achievements: six published novels, two
collections of short stories, one collection
of poetry, three plays, as well as 10 chil-
dren’s books.
Nwapa’s Efuru commenced the process
of reconﬁguring the African (and particu-
larly Nigerian) female image from the dis-
torted portrayals in male-authored literature.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 927 ---
NWAPA,F LORA 839
The monumental and unprecedented im-
portance of this novel in world literature
accounts for its translation into French
(1986) and Dutch (1991).
Except in some of her short stories and
children’s stories, Nwapa assesses the
woman within the context of marriage.
This setting allows her to reafﬁrm support
for the marriage institution as an authentic
African value and offers a framework within
which the woman encounters the most se-
vere forms of dehumanization, subjugation,
relegation, and injustice. Her major preoc-
cupations include defending the integrity of
Nigerian and African womanhood, project-
ing means of empowerment for women,
and giving credibility to the female essence,
while attempting not to denigrate men. She
places the woman against the pervasive
backdrop of feminism from which she
weaves an authentic African dimension that
is tangential to its Western counterpart. In
her plays, as Emenyonu notes, “Nwapa por-
trays women who are no longer content to
wait for their oppressors to bequeath free-
dom on their own (men’s) terms....[ S h e ]
shows ﬂickers of hope, of restoration and of
rebirth” (1998, p. 385). Nwapa demon-
strates the prospect of resilience in different
types of women—the traditional, Muslim,
literate and illiterate, the primitive, as well
as the sophisticated. She stresses that given
the opportunity and right conditions, the
Nigerian woman can excel, whether or not
she is married or has children. Nwapa advo-
cates female economic independence as a
means for female transcendence of the
immanent and age-long male sexism that
preserves the deplorable status of the
woman in a decadent, morally bereft soci-
ety with a highly insensitive and corrupt
leadership.
Nwapa expresses her concern about the
fate of the black woman, whether in Africa,
North America, or the Caribbean in her
writings. This preoccupation is also evident
in literature of the black diaspora, indicat-
ing at its root the commonality of experi-
ence. Writers such as Alice Walker and
Maya Angelou echo Nwapa in One Is
Enough. In the novel, Amaka abandons her
marriage to escape domestic violence and
brutality, moves to the city, applies herself
properly, becomes wealthy, and gives birth
to a set of twin sons by a Reverend Father,
thus debunking the notion of her barren-
ness. Her economic independence and crit-
ical impulse empower her to choose moth-
erhood but not marriage, arguing that the
latter and female debasement and enslave-
ment should be mutually exclusive.
The legacy of this writer can easily be
deduced from her inﬂuence and facilitation
of the enhanced ideas of female selfhood
and assertiveness in Nigeria and all of
Africa. Buchi Emecheta, perhaps the most
proliﬁc African female writer today, has
said she was motivated to write after she
read Nwapa’s Efuru. Nwapa’s publishing
company, Tana Press, was the ﬁrst to be es-
tablished and run by a woman in Africa. It
helped give voice to women who hitherto
had no access to publishers, and also in-
spired Emecheta to establish her publishing
company in England. Nwapa evolved
themes in her writings that many other
writers on both sides of the Atlantic are still
developing.

Emenyonu, Ernest N. “Portrait of Flora

OBEAH
Widely believed to have African origins,
Obeah is a New World folk religion that
employs sorcery, using spells as conduits of
power. The word’s real origin is dubious,
but the general consensus regarding its
etymology points to the Egyptian word for
serpent, oph. There is also thought to be a
relationship between the term “obeah” and
the Ashanti word Obayifo, meaning a wiz-
ard or witch. Prevalent in the West Indies,
Obeah mingles shamanism and African
spirituality along with Christianity, com-
bining folk mystic and Spiritual Baptist
religions. Its heterogeneous foundations
also involve ancient powers of the occult
passed down through oral traditions, as
well as African factions of sorcery and
voodoo. Obeah is practiced throughout the
Caribbean and is most concentrated in
areas populated by descendants of Ashanti-
speaking West African slaves. Various reli-
gious groups, such as Christians, Muslims,
and Hindus, adopt aspects of Obeah into
their own religious doctrines and texts,
however. There is an emphasis on blood
and sacriﬁce within Obeah, which leads
many to assume that it dabbles only with
evil and death. While many dismiss it as a
pejorative form of witchcraft, practitioners
see it as extending into the everyday
concerns of health, domesticity, and love,
among other things. 
A religious leader, called an Obeahman
or Obi, can be a woman or a man and is
greatly respected. All spells or practices
must occur through an Obeahman, who
can divvy out spiritual help or harm. These
shamans have abilities that stem from spir-
itual knowledge, and their powers extend
from healing to casting/undoing spells to
mediating between the living and dead.
They often use elements from nature, in-
cluding herbs and roots, to concoct a mix-
ture for a spell. Obeah practitioners often
wear charms to protect themselves from
danger or evil. These are so widespread that
the word “obeah” can actually be used to
describe a charm or talisman that one wears
in the practice of the religion. Along with
actively engaging in casting spells and com-
municating with spirits, an Obeahman also
serves as a religious advisor for people who
desire insight into the everyday and/or the
supernatural. 
Thus, Obeah reaches far beyond the
evil, “black magic” stereotype imposed on
it. This reductive view, however, is what
caused colonial slave owners to forbid its
practice. A report written in London in
1789 by a committee on trade and colonial
plantations revealed the European anxiety
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 930 ---
842 O’F ARRILL,ARTURO “CHICO”
over the etymology of Obeah regarding
serpents. Called Ob or Aub in the Egyptian
language, a serpent represented original sin
and evil to European Christians. In the
Bible, Moses does not even allow the
Israelites to ask about Ob, the name con-
noting wizardry and sorcery. This 1789
report reduced Obeah merely to antiquated
and distant African spiritual rituals that
Jamaicans pretended to practice so as to
threaten white rule. The colonialists
accordingly regarded Obeah as an insubor-
dinate or rebellious practice.
After British colonialists noted the
prominence of Obeah on their sugar plan-
tations in the seventeenth century, they
perceived its practice as a threat because
of the potential for insurrection and ret-
ribution. Obeah provided for the slaves
an interpersonal social order and an impor-
tant sense of autonomy apart from their
European masters. Wielding the ability to
ensure personal self-interest through the
manipulation of certain rituals and sub-
stances, slaves used their religious practices
as fuel for resistance. In the Jamaican rebel-
lion of 1760, for example, Obeah played an
important role by providing inspiration to
the leader Tacky, who claimed to have been
aided by an Obeahman in the struggle.
Because of the threat of uprisings, British
slave masters did not hesitate to outlaw
Obeah’s practice. 
After becoming illegal, Obeah rituals
were forced to be performed in secret. They
are still against the law today in most parts
of the Caribbean, but they tend not to be
prosecuted. Still, however, Obeahmen
must work inconspicuously, usually hold-
ing individual consultations from their
homes or from storefront spaces. Obeah is
still not considered an “organized” religion
like Haitian Voodoo and other Creole
faiths because it does not have ofﬁcial or
recognized rituals due to its legal marginal-
ization. Despite European efforts to erase
the religious rituals of the African Diaspora,
however, Obeah still remains a powerful
force among its practitioners throughout
the Caribbean today.
Merinda Simmons

O’FARRILL,A RTURO
“CHICO” (1921–2001)
Chico O’Farrill was one of the three great
pioneers of Latin Jazz—along with Mario
Bauzá and Machito (Francisco Grillo).
O’Farrill was expected to go to law school,
but his love for big band music made
him take up the trumpet. He studied with
Cuban classical composer Félix Guerrero
and played with the Orquesta Bellemar.
By 1948 he was in New York ghost com-
posing for Gil Fuller, then wrote a hit for
Benny Goodman (“Undercurrent Blues”).
O’Farrill later wrote for Dizzy Gillespie,
Noro Morales, Stan Kenton (“Cuban
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 931 ---
OGUN 843
Episode”), and Machito. O’Farrill aban-
doned the trumpet and dedicated himself
to composing, directing, and arranging.
His “Afro-Cuban Jazz Suite” (1950), a rec-
ognized masterpiece of the genre, was fol-
lowed by a “Second Afro-Cuban Jazz Suite”
(1952) and the “Manteca Suite” (1954),
where he added three movements to the
Gillespie-Pozo original to form the suite.
From 1951 to 1954, he released six land-
mark recordings of Latin big band jazz,
which included the Afro-Cuban suites, as
well as “Cuban Blues.” Although compos-
ing proliﬁcally and still popular in the
ﬁfties, O’Farrill moved to Mexico in 1957,
where he composed “The Aztec Suite”
(1959). His son Arturo, an accomplished
pianist, was born in Mexico.
O’Farrill returned to the United States
in 1965, and from 1967 to 1994 did not
record as a band leader, but instead
arranged extensively for La Lupe, Cal
Tjader, Count Basie, Ringo Starr, Clark
T erry, Charles Mingus, David Bowie, and
Gato Barbieri, among others, and also
wrote music for TV commercials. O’Farrill
made a comeback in the mid-nineties with
three extraordinary recordings, the ﬁrst
being Pure Emotion (1995), which won a
Grammy nomination, and features a
twelve-minute version of “La Cucaracha”
that mixes in Ellington with show tunes
and twelve-tone passages. Heart of a Legend
(1999) features vintage work in different
Afro-Cuban genres and Carambola (2000)
is a ﬁtting end to a proliﬁc career. With his
classical training, O’Farrill showed a re-
markable handling of form that always
seemed effortless and elegant, buoyed by
infectious rhythms. He was comfortable
composing songs, cha-cha-chas, rumbas,
guajiras, as well as blues and jazz, often
going from genre to genre within a song
almost unnoticeably. Featured in Fernando
T rueba’s ﬁlm on Latin Jazz, Calle 54,
O’Farrill also wrote classical compositions,
from symphonies to chamber pieces.
Alan West-Durán

OGUN
Ogun is a Yoruba divinity. He is god of
metallurgy (iron) and war. He is an
Orisha—an agent of God Almighty,
Olodumare. In the Yoruba pantheon he is
next to Orisha-nla, the archdivinity. He is
the guardian spirit of all metalworkers,
smiths, warriors, and all who deal in metal-
lic objects. In modern Yoruba religious
thinking, he is the guardian spirit of driv-
ers, engineers, pilots, and all who operate
machinery of one kind or another.
In Yoruba religion and culture, there
are two traditions regarding the person of
Ogun. He is sometimes portrayed as a
primordial deity created by Olodumare, or
God Almighty. According to oral tradition
Ogun—as a hunter divinity—came down
from the heavens on a spider’s web in the
company of other divinities to possess the
earth. During their descent to earth, they
became stuck in a forest. Ogun used his
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 932 ---
844 O IL
magical sword to clear the way and this
enabled them to proceed. The Yoruba
therefore regard Ogun as a problem-solver
who clears the way for humans in all areas
of life here on earth.
According to another tradition, Ogun
is one of the numerous sons of Oduduwa,
progenitor of all Yoruba people. Thus,
Ogun is a real human being transformed
into a deiﬁed ancestor because he led an
exemplary life; was elevated to a titan (as in
Greek mythology) in the culture. He lived
as a valiant warrior, inventor of agriculture,
and founder of cities. Ferocious and unfor-
giving, Ogun had a propensity for carnage.
He had a destructive temper; causing him
to destroy the very things he created. His
favorite drink was the palm wine. Legend
has it that after a drunken and destructive
binge, Ogun, ﬁlled with remorse, attempted
to restore what he had destroyed. 
Symbolically Ogun represents the cre-
ative, benevolent, as well as the evil and
destructive forces of nature. He can be
compared to Cain of the Judeo-Christian
tradition. Ogun shares the creative and de-
structive attributes of the T rimurti of Hindu
tradition—Brahma , Vishnu, and Shiva. In
Greco-Roman mythology, Ogun is the
equivalent of Mars and Ares—god of war
and iron. Devotees of Ogun must make
ritual sacriﬁces to him before embarking on
any project. This ritual usually includes a
dog, a ram (ritually slaughtered), palm oil,
palm wine, yams, and kola nuts. Ogun is
also celebrated during annual festivals.
In the Americas, Ogun is venerated in
diverse forms in the Afro-Caribbean reli-
gions of the southern United States, Cuba
(Santeria), Brazil (Candomble), and Haiti
(Vodun; popularly known as Voodoo). The
tradition of worshipping Ogun and other
African deities in these places is clear
evidence of the survival and resilience of
African religions and cultures in the New
World.
’BioDun J. Ogundayo

OIL
Numerous sedimentary basins with oil de-
posits exist in the Americas and in Africa.
The oil industry connects nations and is a
focus of a great deal of economic and polit-
ical activity in the modern era. Oil has a
long history. In the middle of the 1800s,
oil was found in western Pennsylvania. At
ﬁrst the oil was extracted from hand-dug
shallow wells, a method used since ancient
times. On August 27, 1859, the ﬁrst cable-
drilled well was brought in on Oil Creek,
near Titusville, Pennsylvania, by Colonel
Edwin Drake. The well initiated the mod-
ern oil industry.
On January 10, 1901, a rotary drill on
Spindletop, a small hill near Beaumont,
T exas, brought in a gusher. Soon many new
discoveries were made in T exas. The East
T exas oil ﬁeld (1930) was America’s largest.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 933 ---
OKIGBO,C HRISTOPHER 845
Many ﬁelds were also drilled in Oklahoma
at places like Bartlesville and on Indian
reservations. Other early important oil ﬁelds
were in California. Great oil companies
developed to ﬁnd and sell oil—Standard
Oil of California, T exaco, Standard Oil of
New Jersey, Phillips Petroleum, and many
others. Eventually oil was found in great
abundance in Louisiana, Kansas, Michigan,
and other states including Alaska.
Canada’s oil industry began when
Imperial Oil brought in its first well
on February 13, 1947, at Leduc near
Edmonton, Alberta. Oil has been found
in a number of Canadian locations since.
Oil has been discovered in several Latin
American countries. Drilling produced the
ﬁrst commercial well in Mexico in 1901.
By 1910 exploration deﬁned several ﬁelds
in central Mexico near T uxpan. New
sources have continued to be discovered.
Since 1911 Mexico has been an oil ex-
porter. Both Mexico and the United States
have exploited oil under the Gulf of Mexico
using offshore oil platforms and rigs.
Venezuela’s ﬁrst commercial well began
producing in 1917. Lago de Maracaibo is
the center of the oil industry. Farther south
great deposits of oil have been found in
Patagonia and in the Pampas and Grand
Chaco regions of Argentina and Paraguay. 
After World War II oil was found in
the Sahara Desert by French petroleum
engineers. In Algeria, oil was found in the
1950s. Libyan oil ﬁelds were brought on-
line soon afterward. The challenges of the
Sahara desert have made locating and pro-
ducing oil a challenge. Far more difﬁcult
have been the political struggles that have
threatened peaceful business operations. In
southern T unisia, oil has been found in
several locations including the Ghadames
Basin. Northwestern and southeastern
Egypt and Sudan have been the locations of
new oil ﬁelds. 
The Niger River delta is the location of
Nigeria’s oil industry. The ﬁrst commercial
well was drilled in 1956 at Oloibiri in
present-day Bayelsa State. Likely African
prospects are in the coastal regions of
Western Sahara, the coastal regions of the
Congo and Angola, and in southern Sudan
and southward.
The modern search for petroleum has
intensiﬁed in Africa because of political
instability in Venezuela. The industrial
areas of the United States and Canada are
in need of greater supplies of oil than are
available domestically. However, the devel-
opment of oil ﬁelds in Africa has in recent
decades been accompanied by political
tensions. Some of these have been caused
by the failure of local elites to share oil
revenues. In other cases the search for oil in
Africa has environmentally impacted the
local populations. The quest for oil by
American oil companies has made many of
the African oil ﬁelds into global hot spots.
Andrew J. Waskey
