OKIGBO,C HRISTOPHER
(1932–1967)
Christopher Okigbo was one of the leading
poets of African decolonization. In the
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 934 ---
846 O KIGBO,C HRISTOPHER
second half of the 1960s, as Africa began
to truly understand the signiﬁcance of its
political and economic independence from
colonial rule, and as Nigeria fell into a
terrible civil war, the work of a generation of
African poets—Wole Soyinka, J. P . Clark,
Koﬁ Awoonor, Lenrie Peters, Okot p’Bitek,
Dennis Brutus, and Christopher Okigbo—
announced a new and powerful voice in
English poetry. Articulating the sensibility
of a decolonized Africa, Okigbo composed
a poetry that skillfully blended European
and African narrative themes and forms. It
was an uncompromising and difﬁcult po-
etry that forced American and European
scholars to reconsider the manner in which
they approached and judged not just the
poem form but literature as a whole.
Okigbo was born in the village of
Ojoto, Anambra State, Nigeria, in 1932.
Educated at Government College in
Imuahia and the University of Ibadan in
Nigeria’s west, Okigbo met and became
friends with such notable Nigerian writers
as Chinua Achebe and Wole Soyinka. Con-
sidered an excellent student, Okigbo com-
pleted his degree in Classics in 1956. After
holding various administrative positions
for the next ten years in Nigeria’s major
towns, Okigbo, like many other Nigerian
intellectuals of his day, responded to the
worsening political situation in Nigeria’s
east by choosing to return home to help in
the eastern provinces’ drive for secession
from the nation-state of Nigeria. Taking
the rank of major in the newly formed
Biafran army, Okigbo opted to lead the
struggle for independence from the front.
He was killed in the Nigerian military’s
assault on the town of Nsukka in 1967, at
the age of 35. 
His death at such a tragically young
age deprived the world, in the words of
Donatus Ibe Nwoga, of one of Africa’s
most original, distinctive, and important
poets. However, the initial response to
Okigbo’s poetry in the West was not so
favorable. Along with the work of the other
Ibadan poets, Okigbo’s poetry was consid-
ered to suffer from an “overdose”—as
Gerald Moore and Ulli Beier saw it—of
Ezra Pound, Gerard Manley Hopkins, and
T . S. Eliot. It was an “afﬂiction” that Ken
Goodwin saw in most African poetry. In
his study of ten African poets in the early
1980s, Goodwin concluded that much
African poetry did little more than imitate
the American and European poetry upon
which it was clearly modeled. As such, the
African names that obviously populated
much African poetry were devalued as
inauthentic expressions lacking the origi-
nality of their European counterparts.
However, as American and European
critics began to understand how formal
poetry worked in terms of African oral
traditions, the response to Okigbo’s poetry
changed dramatically. Forced to acknowl-
edge the important role played by previ-
ously unrecognized traditional African
disciplines—such as the Yoruba praise
song—in Okigbo’s poetry, Western aca-
demics began to admire the skill with which
Okigbo managed to weave together the
disparate European and African narrative
forms. The result was an African voice that
drew worldwide attention to the artistic,
cultural, religious, and political concerns of
the postcolonial Nigerian nation.
Grant Hamilton

OKRI,B EN 847
OKRI,B EN (1959–)
Ben Okri is a London-based Nigerian
novelist, born in 1959 in Minna, Nigeria,
to Igbo and Urhobo parents. He spent his
early years in London, where his father was
studying law, returned to Lagos, the then
capital of Nigeria, in 1965, and perma-
nently relocated to England in 1976.
While Okri seldom reveals details
about his childhood, he has extensively
commented on his ﬁrst literary discoveries.
They range from the African tales and leg-
ends his parents used to tell him to Greek
and Roman myths, as well as European au-
thors such as Aristotle, Plato, Shakespeare,
Dickens, Ibsen, Maupassant, and Chekhov.
This double heritage, the intermingling of
African stories and European sources, and
the later inﬂuence of contemporary African
writers, was to become the major inspira-
tion for his work.
Okri began writing in 1976 while wait-
ing to get a place at a university in Nigeria.
When his application was rejected, he
moved to England, ﬁrst to work and write
in London, where he still resides, then to
study comparative literature at the University
of Essex.
His ﬁrst novel, Flowers and Shadows,
published in 1980, features a teenager’s dis-
illusionment with Nigeria’s corrupt society,
of which his own father turns out to be a
part. Okri’s second book, The Landscapes
Within (1981), which he was to rewrite
under the title Dangerous Love (1996), may
be considered an early artistic manifesto,
for it seems to reﬂect the author’s views on
language and creation, as expressed further
in the collection of essays A Way of Being
Free (1997).
The Landscapes Within, as well as some
of the short stories contained in Incidents
at the Shrine (1986) and Stars of the New
Curfew (1988), read as tales of a country,
Nigeria, struggling with poverty, corrup-
tion, and sometimes war. Some of these
thematic interests are also central in The
Famished Road (1991), for which Okri
won the Booker Prize. Based on the
Yoruba myth of the abiku (the spirit-child
who is born, dies, and is reincarnated end-
lessly), the novel is told from the perspec-
tive of Azaro, a spirit-child who has
decided to stay on earth. Throughout the
book, the constant interaction between
“reality” and the spirit world reminds one
of African folktales as well as twentieth-
century narratives inspired by the oral tra-
dition. Ultimately, the abiku, who is inﬁ-
nitely dying and reborn, is intended as a
symbol for the Nigerian nation. In 1993,
The Famished Road was followed by a se-
quel, Songs of Enchantment; the abiku tril-
ogy was later completed by Inﬁnite Riches
(1998). The 1990s also saw the publica-
tion of Okri’s allegorical novel Astonishing
the Gods (1995) and two collections of po-
etry, An African Elegy (1992) and Mental
Fight (1999). 
His 2002 novel, In Arcadia, recounts
a ﬁlm crew’s journey to Arcadia, a region
of Greece traditionally depicted as an
idyllic setting. The book explores, among
other themes, man’s everlasting quest for
happiness.
Daria Tunca

ORGANIZATION OF
AMERICAN STATES
The Organization of American States
(OAS) is the oldest regional security orga-
nization. It was established in Bogota,
Colombia, with the signing of its charter
on April 30, 1948. Its purpose was and is to
promote regional integration, cooperation,
and security among member states within
the Western Hemisphere. The original
twenty-one signatories to the charter were
Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Colombia,
Costa Rica, Cuba, Dominican Republic,
Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Haiti,
Honduras, Mexico, Nicaragua, Panama,
Paraguay, Peru, United States, Uruguay,
and Venezuela. Subsequent new members
are Barbados, T rinidad and T obago (1967);
Jamaica (1969); Grenada (1975); Surinam
(1977); Dominica, Saint Lucia (1979);
Antigua and Barbuda, Saint Vincent, and
the Grenadines (1981); Bahamas (1982);
St. Kitts and Nevis (1984); Canada (1990);
Belize, Guyana (1991). T oday all thirty-ﬁve
countries of the Americas have ratiﬁed the
charter. In 1962, despite the opposition of
the largest Latin American member coun-
tries, Cuba’s rights to participate and vote
in OAS activities were suspended. In recent
years, however, there has been some sup-
port among some Latin American members
to reinstate Cuba’s participation in the
organization.
The idea of regional integration and
cooperation did not originate with the
OAS. Latin American leaders such as
Simon Bolivar and intellectuals such as
Haya de la T orre previously advocated
Secretary General of the Organization of American States (OAS), Cesar Gaviria (right), inspects the collection of
signatures during a referendum in Caracas, November 23, 2003. (AFP/Getty Images)
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 937 ---
ORGANIZATION OF AMERICAN STATES 849
various forms of Pan-Americanism or
hemispheric unity. Practical attempts at
regional cooperation were made in the late
nineteenth century as represented by the
First International Conference of American
States held in Washington, D.C., in 1890.
In 1910 representatives of American states
established the International Union of
American Republics and its secretariat, the
Commercial Bureau of the American Re-
publics, which became the Pan American
Union in 1910. As the twentieth century
progressed, the U.S. State Department
became increasingly concerned with what
it termed “creeping communism” in Latin
America and the Caribbean. T o address
U.S. security concerns and protect U.S.
interests in the region, the Pan American
Union was transformed at the Ninth Inter-
national American Conference in 1948
into the OAS, resulting in the creation of
an inter-American collective security sys-
tem. The OAS charter, however, proclaimed
the more expansive principles of peace
and justice, collaboration and cooperation,
national sovereignty and independence,
nonintervention and noninterference,
and by the 1950s Latin American and
Caribbean members hoped the organiza-
tion would expand its interests beyond se-
curity issues to economic development. But
the Cold War had begun and the U.S. kept
the organization’s priorities focused on
hemispheric security.
The basic structure of the OAS in-
cludes the General Assembly, which sets
major policies and meets once a year. The
Permanent Council, whose ambassadors
are appointed by member states and who
hold regular meetings at OAS headquarters
in Washington, D.C., oversee the organiza-
tion’s ongoing policies and actions. T o en-
sure equal representation among member
states, the chairmanship of the Permanent
Council rotates every three months in
alphabetical order of member countries.
The OAS conducts its business in four ofﬁ-
cial languages (English, Spanish, French,
Portuguese) and generally seeks consensus
decisions in all matters. The OAS functions
on simple majority rule: one country–one
vote with no veto powers vested in any
member. But the United States has often
been able to marshal enough votes from
smaller members to push its interests and
priorities. An example of this was the 1954
Declaration of Caracas, which condemned
Marxist ideology as foreign and unaccept-
able in the Western Hemisphere.
In addition to the General Assembly
and Permanent Council, there is the
General Secretariat (GS), whose secretary
general and assistant secretary general are
elected by members for ﬁve-year terms. The
GS carries out programs and policies set by
political bodies of the OAS, which include
specialized units on democracy, trade,
tourism, social development, and educa-
tion. Other specialized agencies with head-
quarters throughout the hemisphere include
the Pan American Health Organization,
the Inter-American Children’s Institute, the
Inter-American Institute for Cooperation
on Agriculture, the Pan American Institute
of Geography and History, and the Inter-
American Indian Institute.
Over time the OAS has expanded its
agenda of concerns to include human
rights, poverty, drugs, and corruption.
Added to its specialized agencies in 1978
were the Inter-American Commission on
Human Rights and the Inter-American
Court of Human Rights. Interest in the
North American Free T rade Act (NAFTA)
fostered interest in the promotion of free
trade in the region and discussion of the
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 938 ---
850 O RISHA
potential of a Free T rade Zone of the
Americas. The 1980s also brought in-
creased concern to the organization about
hemispheric drug production and trafﬁck-
ing as well as political corruption.
In the 1990s, the subject of hemi-
spheric concern revolved around the pro-
motion and protection of democracy in the
region. Events in Haiti, Peru, Guatemala,
and Paraguay resulted in the OAS drafting
Resolution 1080, which established proce-
dures for collective reaction to threats to
democracy in the hemisphere. T o further
OAS goals, the First Summit of the
Americas was held in Miami in 1994. All
members but Cuba were invited and at-
tended. The purpose was to establish broad
political, economic, and social develop-
ment goals, which included revisions of old
policies as well as addressing new threats to
hemispheric stability and security includ-
ing corruption and illegal arms trafﬁcking
and production. In the 2000s, the OAS has
expanded its interested to address collective
action against terrorism. Coincidentally,
the membership signed the Inter-American
Democratic Charter on September 11,
2001, deﬁning democracy and establishing
further guidelines for collective member-
ship action. This led to the creation of
the Inter-American Committee Against
T errorism (CICTE).
As with most regional organizations,
the effectiveness of the OAS has been
undermined at times by the inherent con-
tradictions caused when its founding
principles of national sovereignty, nonin-
tervention, and democracy collide with the
national and hemispheric interests of its
members. Conflicting agendas between
major Latin American nations and the
United States have often added tensions
to the OAS and crises such as the
Falklands/Malvinas War between Britain
and Argentina, the U.S. mining of
Nicaraguan harbors, and U.S. invasions of
Panama and Grenada have highlighted
the conﬂict between national interest and
hemispheric unity. Finally, the status of
Cuba within the organization remains an
unresolved issue of the Cold War for OAS
members. 
Heather Thiessen-Riely

ORISHA
Orisha is the Yoruba term for a deity, or di-
vinity. It is also spelled as orisa, or orixa, in
Afro-Brazilian religions. These supernatural
beings are part of a well-articulated belief
system of the Yoruba that has existed for cen-
turies. In the past, Europeans in Africa and
the New World, out of ignorance and cul-
tural bias, tended to describe orishas as noth-
ing more than primitive mumbo-jumbo;
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 939 ---
ORISHA 851
they saw orishas as evidence of fetishism,
idolatry, or of Africans’ lack of spirituality
and cultural sophistication. However, this
attitude has changed. Orishas are in-
creasingly recognized as an important
part of the African religious Diaspora. In
Latin America, Brazil, and the southern
United States, unique and hybrid forms
of orisha worship and Yoruba religion can
be found in the practice of Santeria and
Candomblé.
Orishas are part of an elaborate theology
comparable to any in Western civilization.
In Yoruba traditional religion, Olodumare,
God the Almighty One, is at the helm of a
clearly established hierarchy of beings, both
spiritual and human. He is Oluwa Eleda,
self-created Lord of all creation, who re-
sides high in the heavens, and is also known
as Olorun, or owner of the heavens. He
does not intervene directly in human
affairs, but is believed to have created the
orishas to assist him in governing all of cre-
ation in its diverse forms and manifesta-
tions. On the other hand, orishas are highly
evolved beings who are directly involved in
the affairs of humans. Thus, they are inter-
mediaries between God and man. They
belong to a pantheon of divinities, spirits,
and deiﬁed ancestors. They constitute an
essential part of Yoruba cosmogony, indi-
vidual, and collective identity. 
Orishas are the Yoruba and African
equivalent of gods, goddesses, and saints in
Western culture. In Hindu and Buddhist
traditions, these are called devas . Just as in
Western or Eastern religions, there are
major orishas and lesser ones. For example,
higher orishas are Ifa, the orisha that fore-
tells and guides the destiny of humans;
Ogun, the deity of war and metallurgy; and
Shango (also spelled Xango or Sango), the
deity of thunder and lightning. Osun
(Oxun in Afro-Brazilian Candomblé), the
river goddess, and Aje, the goddess of com-
merce and prosperity, are lesser orishas.
However, for the devotees and adherents of
particular orishas, this categorization might
be pointless insofar as their spiritual and
existential needs are satisﬁed.
Thus, orishas can be considered to be
agents of Olodumare’s will and inﬂuence in
the affairs of humans. Because of their
importance in the daily lives of people, an
orisha is also seen by the Yoruba as an in-
separable part of each individual’s destiny
(or Ori, which is also an orisha) here on
earth. Sacriﬁces are often offered to propi-
tiate the orishas in order to gain their pro-
tection or support. Each orisha has speciﬁc
offerings and rituals peculiar to their quali-
ties. There usually are priests and priestesses
who specialize, through decades of train-
ing, in speciﬁc orishas and thus become tra-
ditional healers and counselors. In Yoruba
society, these agbalagba, or wise men and
women, play a preeminent role in the
maintenance of social and moral order.
Indeed, they are the glue that have held
Yoruba (and African) societies together
given the often negative consequences of
African encounters with Western systems
of thought.
In the context of the African Diaspora,
orisha worship can be seen as part of the
hybridization of African religions with
Western Christianity, especially Catholicism,
in the Americas. Its presence attests to the
enduring capacity of the African spirit and
imagination to survive despite the severing
of familial, cultural, and religious ties that
was part of slavery.
’BioDun J. Ogundayo

OROONOKO
Aphra Behn’s novelOroonoko; or The Royal
Slave (1688) is a heroic tragedy, courtly
romance, and travel narrative all rolled into
one. Oroonoko is a slave of noble birth, a
king, who falls victim to the tragedy of
British slavery and racism. Though
Oroonoko is enslaved, he never loses his
royal dignity nor his essence of virtue, even
in the face of his enslavement. Oroonoko
loves the beautiful Imoinda, who he even-
tually murders. He is betrayed by his own
people and meets a bloody and tragic end.
As the executioner cuts off parts of his
body, Oroonoko calmly smokes a pipe
until he “gave up the Ghost, without a
Groan, or a Reproach.” 
Oroonoko explores themes of human
nobility, slavery, and European inhumanity
to African slaves. Though her hero is black,
Behn emphasizes he is a person of “quality.”
Behn’s Oroonoko is one of the ﬁrst attempts
to portray the lives of African characters
from an African point of view, and one
of the ﬁrst attempts to explore the contra-
dictions between human dignity and
European racism.
Debbie Clare Olson
References
Behn, Aphra. Oroonoko. Catherine Gallagher,
ed. New York: Bedford/St. Martins, 2000.
Lipking, Joanna. Oroonoko: An Authoritative
T ext, Historical Background, Criticism. New
York: W .W . Norton, 1997.
OUSMANE,S EMBENE (1923–)
Born in 1923 in Ziguinchor, Casamance,
southern Senegal, Sembene Ousmane is a
major African writer and ﬁlmmaker, with a
long-term commitment to social justice
and a vision to reach African popular audi-
ences. He started his artistic career as a
poet, a short story writer, an essayist, and a
novelist, but is best known as a ﬁlmmaker.
Considered the father of sub-Saharan
African cinema, he is the most interviewed
Senegalese and African ﬁlm director so far,
and has received countless awards and dis-
tinctions. Since his ﬁrst poem, published in
1956 in Cahiers du Sud, a Marseilles-based
left-wing journal, he has produced ﬁve
novels, ﬁve collections of short stories, and
directed seven short ﬁlms, ten features, and
four documentaries. From traditional sto-
rytellers, he inherited a bold and indepen-
dent voice, unique communication skills,
and a passion for his country. While his
ﬁrst novels drew on his personal experience
of manual work, it was his concern for the
uneducated and the marginalized, born of
the same experience and practice of trade
unions and political activism, and his desire
to communicate with the ordinary people
of his country in a language they could un-
derstand, that led him to ﬁlm production.
His ﬁlms, written or subtitled in French,
Wolof, or Diola, but also in English,
French, German, Chinese, and Japanese,
are now reaching an international audi-
ence. They are mostly adapted from his
earlier novels or stories, which have been
on African high schools and universities’
curricula for decades. Moolaade,Ousmane’s
ﬁrst ﬁlm produced outside Senegal’s na-
tional borders, in Burkina Faso and in
Bambara, came out in 2003. Seven of his
ten published literary works have been
translated into English. Doctoral theses,
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 941 ---
OUSMANE,S EMBENE 853
master’s dissertations, and a vast number of
scholarly articles have been devoted to his
literary and ﬁlm work. 
The son of a ﬁsherman from Dakar,
Ousmane left school at age 15 but kept on
reading and acquired a vast knowledge of
culture. In 1938, he was already acquainted
with the power of pictures, but his career as
a ﬁlm producer really took shape in the
early 1960s when he went to study cinema
at the Gorki Studios in Moscow. The
feature and short ﬁlms he produced after his
return to Senegal range from satirical come-
dies to dramas and documentaries. They
project a distinct African voice and aesthet-
ics, and illustrate his vision of art and cul-
ture as a school to raise the political aware-
ness of his audiences, promote social justice,
and restore dignity to African people.
Ousmane offered Faat Kine to the national
Council of Senegalese Women (COSEF).
His ﬁrst short ﬁlm Borom Sarett won the
ﬁrst prize at the T ours festival. Ousmane’s
ﬁrst feature ﬁlm, La Noire de . . . , produced
in 1966, was the ﬁrst feature ever produced
by an African ﬁlmmaker and won the
Jean Vigo prize at the 1967 Cannes Film
Festival. Mandabi (1968) received the in-
ternational critique prize at the Venice Film
Festival in 1969. It was also shown as part
of the 7th Film Festival at the Lincoln Cen-
tre, New York. Camp de Thiaroye (1989)
was presented at the Hartford’s Spring Film
Festival in April 2002. 
The United States discovered Sembene
Ousmane at the time their African
American elite was reconnecting with its
African roots, and he has given the Dias-
pora a new understanding of Africa. In
1996, his work inspired Florence Ladd’s
novel Sarah’s Psalm, set in the 1960s in
Cambridge and Dakar. That same year a
weeklong screening of Ousmane’s work
at the University of Victoria, British
Columbia, gathered crowds of students,
ﬁlm critics, and cultural workers. On May
5, 2001, Ousmane received the Harvard
Film archive prize from Harvard University
in Cambridge, Massachusetts. On American
university and college campuses, and in
the Caribbean, he is now one of the most
studied and sought after African writers.
Francoise Parent Ugochkuwu

PAGEANT,THE AFRICAN
AMERICAN
The African American Pageant is an African
American communal dramatic form that
addresses links to Africa and forms a black
aesthetic. With the adoption and reapplica-
tion of the medieval pageant tradition, the
early half of the twentieth century wit-
nessed a signiﬁcant development in African
American drama. Following a history of
slavery, post-Reconstruction disappoint-
ments, and Jim Crow laws, black dramatists
identiﬁed in pageantry the opportunity to
reafﬁrm cultural identity, instill racial pride,
rectify history, and venerate black heroes
and heroines. Both ritualistic and regenera-
tive, emergent black pageants thus served to
relink culturally and artistically with Africa,
promote a black aesthetic, and counteract
ingrained stereotypes. Subsequently, they
became a propaganda tool and a means of
distinguishing black culture from the dom-
inant European.
Black pageants were partially an off-
shoot of changes in black economic, cul-
tural, and artistic life during the Harlem
Renaissance of the 1920s. The European
pageant, on the other hand, derived from
more auspicious circumstances, evolving
from religious ceremonies to more secular
performances where comedy, spectacle, and
the conﬁrmation of class were central at-
tributes. Even so, the pageant tradition
comprised fundamental elements that
were germane to the type of functional
theatre that blacks aspired for, includ-
ing communal involvement; performer-
audience interaction; improvisation; em-
phasis on movement, mime, dance, music,
and song; as well as ceremonial and
episodic arrangements.
W . E. B. Du Bois deﬁned the black
pageant as “a great historical folk festival...
with the added touch of reality given by
numbers, space and fidelity to truth”
(p. 231). Like its European antecedent, it
was not conﬁned to formal theatrical space,
but could be produced outdoors or in
churches, homes, and grand halls, thereby
attracting crowds and emerging as an ideal
public and communal medium for reaching
large African American audiences. How-
ever, a unique black experience demanded
stylistic and thematic changes in borrowing
and transplanting the form.
In its original European setting, the
pageant tradition underwent signiﬁcant
changes before black dramatists exploited
it. The liturgical roots of English drama
around the sixth century BCE ﬂowered into
the famous cycle plays beginning in the
tenth century. The cycle plays constituted
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 944 ---
856 P AGEANT,THE AFRICAN AMERICAN
major pageants during the medieval period,
having ﬁrst shifted from a strict preoccupa-
tion with biblical subject matter to more
secular themes and styles.
The pageantry of cycle plays gave rise
to other pageant traditions that made elab-
orate use of masks, movement, mime, and
improvisation, marginalizing the written
text and encouraging collective participa-
tion. They were subsequently more elabo-
rate, more vibrant, and more colorful than
their precursor cycle plays, and emerged
in the form of masques, mummings, the
Italian intermezzi, and fetes. This rich
legacy of post-cycle-play pageants remained
popular well into the nineteenth century and
was sustained during the festive and spir-
ited Elizabethan Age and reign of James I.
Weddings, canonizations, coronations,
funerals, military triumphs, and state visits
formed the bases for pageantries during
the Renaissance and Baroque periods. As a
medium of hospitality, the genre reﬂected
on and preserved the magnitude of status
and nobility, as was apparent in their ﬂam-
boyance and in the introduction of extrav-
agant feasts.
Operating within a more gloomy set-
ting and detached from the fanfare and
ostentation that informed the European
pageant, African American pageants incor-
porated black music and concentrated on
issues, themes, and characters that were
familiar to the black community. Stock
characters, common in Renaissance
pageants, for instance, would be transferred
to African American realities and remateri-
alize in the form of character-types like Art,
Invention, Literature, Business, Woman-
hood, Adventure, and Slavery, whose desig-
nations deﬁned their messages and roles.
Thus, unable to explore and preserve the
aristocratic space, splendor, and wealth of
European Renaissance pageantry, African
American dramatists were able to adopt cer-
tain components of the tradition that they
adjusted to their unique circumstances.
In general, black pageants, like their
medieval predecessor, were different from
conventional plays. Ranging from come-
dies to tragedies, they relied on sizable
casts, elaborate sets, outdoor or large space
performances, improvisation, and proces-
sional ﬁnales that featured historical ﬁgures
or qualities like T ruth and Freedom. Stan-
dard plot development was replaced with
episodic presentations that utilized pro-
logues, tableaux, and vocal or orchestral
musical interludes. Character depictions
were often symbolic of people and values
relevant to the community, while storylines
sometimes commemorated important
events that took place as recently as the year
of the production. Communal involvement
was reinforced by neighborhood participa-
tion in making costumes, painting sets,
posting notices, practicing musical scores,
researching histories and characters por-
trayed, and working onstage and backstage.
Shows were frequently advertised in The
Crisis, the ofﬁcial magazine of the National
Association for the Advancement of
Colored People (NAACP), making them
easily accessible to the people. Through
pageants, black audiences and performers
were thus offered opportunities to en-
counter and learn from familiar situations,
experiences, and characters.
Two Races [n.d.] by Inez M. Burke, a
pageant speciﬁcally written in the interest
of seventh and eighth grade children, sets
out to rewrite history and acknowledge
historic black achievers who are otherwise
excluded from standard educational curric-
ula. The pageant relies on a combination
of character-types that are conventional,
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 945 ---
PAGEANT,THE AFRICAN AMERICAN 857
symbolic, and allegorical. Typical of Re-
naissance pageants, action and storytelling
take precedence over dialogue in Two Races,
while music and song complement this
approach.
Dorothy C. Guinn’s pageant, Out of
the Dark (1924), which was written pri-
marily for high school students, lauds
African American ingenuity and provides
information generally lacking in main-
stream history books. Comprising a pro-
logue, four episodes, and an epilogue, the
pageant traces the history of African
Americans from Africa through slavery to
post-slavery and modern times, thus docu-
menting their exploitation, sufferings,
struggles, survival, and accomplishments.
The main characters represent key African
American heroes and heroines, as well as
sociopolitical and artistic facets of the black
experience. A truly composite piece exten-
sively employing the storytelling tradition,
pantomime, dance, music, song, poetry,
and tableaux, Out of the Dark is one of the
more elaborate African American pageants.
Frances Gunner’s The Light of the
Women (1930)—subtitled A Ceremonial
for the Use of Negro Groups —was mainly
written in the interest of junior high and
high school girls. Much like in a morality
play (a secularized offshoot of medieval
cycle plays), its characters—which are all
female—are allegorical and symbolic of
the historic achievements of black women
in America. Besides individual representa-
tions, a communal effect is delineated and
sustained through the presence of an active
crowd. The Light of the Women also relies
heavily on action, movement, music, song,
and storytelling, while keeping dialogue
to a minimum. None of the eulogized
women from the past or present have speak-
ing roles. Like imaginary, expressionistic
ﬁgures, they simply emerge and fade away
after their accolades are announced. While
hymns are sung to complement the sacred
dimensions of the drama, they also recap-
ture the soothing and inspirational role of
spirituals and gospel music throughout
African American history. In the end the
pageant becomes a ritual of rejuvenation
and hope, one that envisages limitless
possibilities for black women.
Edward J. McCoo’s pageantEthiopia at
the Bar of Justice (1924) employs perhaps
more dialogue than was common in African
America pageants of the 1920s. But the large
number of characters present, the allegorical
casting, the use of narratives, and the inter-
spersing of music and song in the pageant
retain the holistic and rite-of-passage attri-
butes that are typical of the form.
In spite of the secularization of drama
during European Renaissance and post-
Renaissance periods, religious ideals were
not completely lost even if they were not
strictly applied. African American pageants
also preserved a religious angle either in the
utilization of direct Christian principles or
in the creation of sacred icons and precepts.
Ultimately, a sacred ambiance was achieved
and presupposed the deliverance of blacks
through methods that were not just tangi-
ble but were also divine. This spiritual
paradigm would have a strong impact on
future African American drama, especially
during the critical periods of the 1960s and
the post-1960s. Dramatists like George
Wolfe, Barbara Ann T eer, Amiri Baraka,
Ntozake Shange, and George Houston Bass
subscribed to styles that leaned on ritualis-
tic patterns, some of which were similar to
those featured in earlier pageants.
Philip Efﬁong

PAIGE,L EROY ROBERT
(CA. 1906–1982)
Leroy “Satchel” Paige, a great pitcher in the
Negro Leagues and, near the end of his ca-
reer, in the Major Leagues, was known for
his control, fastball, showmanship, and
philosophical aphorisms. Born in Mobile,
Alabama, somewhere around 1906, Paige
earned his nickname by carrying luggage at
a railroad depot. He began playing semipro
baseball in the early 1920s and signed his
ﬁrst professional contract in 1926 with the
Chattanooga Black Lookouts of the Negro
Southern League. He played for some of
the greatest Negro League teams, establish-
ing his reputation as possibly the greatest
pitcher in the history of the Negro Leagues,
as well as the equal of the great major
League pitchers of his time. He ﬁnally was
given an opportunity to play in the major
Leagues, with the Cleveland Indians in
1948, one year after Jackie Robinson broke
the color barrier. Although well past forty,
he was still an outstanding pitcher, helping
the Indians win the American League pen-
nant and the World Series.
Paige starred for the Pittsburgh
Crawfords (teaming with catcher Josh
Gibson to give Pittsburgh one of the great-
est batteries in baseball history) and the
Kansas City Monarchs, and for a variety of
other teams, along with playing in Cuba,
the Dominican Republic, and Mexico. He
excited fans with such theatrics as sum-
moning his outﬁelders to sit behind the
pitcher’s mound while he struck out
the batter. He delighted in showing off his
control, for example, by repeatedly ﬁring
his fastball over a chewing gum wrapper
set on home plate. He liked to share philo-
sophical musings, most famously the
cautionary imperative “Don’t look back,
something might be gaining on you.” A
huge celebrity, especially in the South,
Paige even did some guest guitar playing
with Louis Armstrong’s band.
Despite being shut out of the Major
Leagues for most of his career, he often
faced the greatest of major leaguers in
exhibition games, and with great success.
Joe DiMaggio called Paige his toughest
pitcher to hit against, and the great major
league pitcher Bob Feller claimed that
Paige was the best pitcher that he ever saw.
In one especially memorable outing
against another Hall of Fame hurler, Dizzy
Dean, Paige outdueled Dean one to noth-
ing in a thirteen-inning game. In another
contest, he struck out Rogers Hornsby
ﬁve times.
Paige won six of seven decisions in his
ﬁrst season with the Indians, whose owner,
Bill Veeck, had integrated the American
League the year before by adding African
American outﬁelder Larry Doby to his
team. Paige later followed Veeck to the St.
Louis Browns, with which he made the All-
Star team in 1952 and 1953. He continued
to pitch effectively in the minors as late as
1961. In 1965, he was brought back to the
majors by the Kansas City Athletics to
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

pitch one game. He hurled three innings,
giving up only one hit. Satchel Paige was
inducted into the National Baseball Hall
of Fame in 1971, the ﬁrst individual who
played most of his career in the Negro
Leagues to be so honored.

PALM OIL
Palm oil is a local and export commodity
important to the economy of southern
Nigeria. The harvesting and processing of
palm oil (Elaeis guineensis) has long been
important to the economy of southern
Nigeria. The fruit of the mature palm can
be processed to make palm oil. The fruit is
steamed and pounded to remove the shell,
and oil is pressed from the pulp. Palm oil
was used indigenously as cooking oil, light-
ing fuel for lamps, and to make cosmetics
and medicines. Palm oil was also an export
crop, transported by European slave traders
and used for the manufacture of candles
and soap. The Industrial Revolution in
Britain increased the demand for palm oil
in the nineteenth century; it was used to
maintain factory machinery and make
cooking oils.
When the British slave trade ended in
1807, traders in southern Nigeria made a
rapid transition to the legitimate palm oil
trade. The trade centered upon Calabar,
New Kalabari, and Bonny, with shipments
from Calabar increasing from around
1,200 tons in 1812 to 4,500 tons by 1864.
The palm oil trade in Calabar was ex-
panded by traders such as Great Duke
Ephraim, who founded plantations in
Akpabuyo, east of the city. The plantations
were farmed by the large pool of labor that
formed with the end of the slave trade.
Palm oil was also gathered throughout the
hinterland regions of southern Nigeria.
Some was kept for domestic use, while the
rest was taken to the oil house to be boiled.
Each rural area had a market where pro-
duce was gathered from the area. T rading
stations developed in the interior measured
crops and put them in containers for trans-
port by river to the coast. At the coast the
oil was boiled again before export.
As the volume of oil increased, new oil
hulks, ships with a larger capacity, were
built by European traders. Initially, the
nineteenth-century palm oil trade contin-
ued to operate the “comey duty” and trust
trade system that had structured trade rela-
tions between Europeans and African
traders during the slave trade. Comey duty
was a levy paid by European traders to
Calabar kings, per ton of cargo, for the
right to trade within their territory. After
comey duty was paid, the traders would
“break trade”—hold open negotiations
with the exchange of gifts and dinners
served by Calabar kings in their palaces
and by European traders on board ship.
In the trust trade system, goods, such as
liquor, weaponry, cloth, and building
materials, would be advanced to Calabar
traders, who then organized the harvesting
and transportation of palm oil to the coast
for export.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 948 ---
860 P ALM OIL
The oil hulks would spend up to a
year moored offshore, negotiating trade,
unloading European goods, and loading
palm oil. The management of credit
and debt in the trust trade often led to dis-
putes, with some European traders becom-
ing known as “palm oil rufﬁans” due to
unscrupulous trading practices. Some
European traders in Calabar joined the
ekpe secret society to gain recourse to in-
digenous authority to recover trade debts.
With the establishment of the British
Consul in Calabar in 1861, shippers in-
creasingly called upon the intervention of
the consul to settle trade disputes.
In the colonial era, oil palm and oil
kernel became the main exports of
southeastern Nigeria. Palm kernels were
produced from the 1870s onward for ex-
port only and were used for the manufac-
ture of industrial oils and animal feeds.
Women provided much of the labor in the
local processing of palm kernels and con-
trolled the income from their trade. The
local trade in foodstuffs such as yams
meant that women could concentrate their
labor on oil and kernel production. How-
ever, in the early twentieth century the
export market price fell, and the British
colonial government began to intervene
and manage the marketing and processing
of palm oil.
The worsening trade conditions sparked
unrest, which became widespread in the
1929 Women’s War when women oil
producers protested against the impact of
falling prices, increased taxation, and
government marketing cartels. More than
ﬁfty women were killed when police ﬁred
on protesters. The colonial government
response to the protest was to reform the
corrupt “warrant chief” administration
system, in which local leaders had been
imposed by the government. Political ofﬁce
and administrative posts provided new
spheres of employment for men, while
women retreated from the palm oil export
trade to produce food for the household
economy and domestic markets.
A British monopoly over the palm oil
trade was secured when the United Africa
Company was set up in 1929. European
companies started to exert greater control
at local levels through taxation and produce
inspection. The processing of oil palm was
also removed from the control of local pro-
ducers when the colonial government in-
troduced large-scale mechanized presses.
After 1945 the government established
mechanized “pioneer palm oil mills,” or-
dering eighteen mills for the eastern
provinces of Nigeria. In the 1950s produc-
tion and processing were further central-
ized when bulk oil plants (BOPs) were set
up by the United Africa Company in con-
junction with the colonial government.
There were seven BOPs in Nigeria, and by
1958 the plants processed 177,800 tons of
palm oil. The marketing of oil became
controlled by the Commodity Marketing
Boards from the late 1940s onward, along
with the other main export crops in West
African colonies, namely cotton, ground-
nuts, and cocoa. By the mid-twentieth
century, palm oil processing for export in
southern Nigeria was completely controlled
by large ﬁrms.
The decline in the value of oil palm as
an export crop had started in 1914 and
continued into the 1960s. The dependence
of the agricultural economy of the region
upon a single export crop increased vulner-
ability to market shifts and meant
production increased even when prices fell.
Nigeria was the largest supplier of palm oil
to Britain until the 1960s, when East Asian
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 949 ---
PAN-AFRICAN CONFERENCE 861
oil producers started to supply the colonial
oil market. By the 1970s, the Nigerian
palm oil export industry had collapsed.
The impact on Nigeria’s gross domestic
product was muted by the growth of the
petroleum oil industry, but the economy of
the rural interior which had become struc-
tured around oil palm production was se-
verely damaged. The great wealth gener-
ated by both the palm oil and petroleum
trade, and its inequitable distribution, are
pervasive themes in contemporary Nigerian
popular culture. In the play All for Oil
(2000), Clark-Bekederemo draws parallels
between the way palm oil and petroleum
oil exports sustained the colonial and post-
colonial Nigerian state, and enriched
Nigerian and overseas traders, while im-
poverishing people in the oil-producing
regions and devastating the environment
that they inhabit.
Philippa Hall

PAN-AFRICAN
CONFERENCE (1900)
The Pan-African Conference was held from
July 23 to July 25, 1900, in London’s
Westminster Hall. It was organized by
members of the Pan-African Association,
led by Sylvester Williams as general secre-
tary, and comprised of a number of distin-
guished individuals, both of African and
European descent, who were devoted to ad-
dressing the issues facing persons of color
in the African Diaspora. The purpose of the
conference, then, was to bring together
blacks from all parts of the Diaspora to
discuss such topics as colonialism and dis-
crimination, while attempting to forge
solidarity among blacks. Among those in
attendance were delegates from North
America, the West Indies, Ethiopia, and
West Africa, including Liberia, Sierra
Leone, and Gold Coast (Ghana).
While a permanent body and plans for
further meetings were created, the most
tangible results of the conference consisted
of two notable statements. The ﬁrst was
a petition to Queen Victoria of England,
ostensibly to draw her attention to the
injustices suffered by Africans as a result
of imperialist activity. Indentured labor,
segregation, economic and political disen-
franchisement, and other forms of discrim-
ination were the subject of outrage among
the delegates. The petitioners appealed to
Queen Victoria to address the situation
affecting the African colonies and asked her
to recognize the humanity of the Africans
under her dominion.
The Pan-African Conference con-
cluded with an “Address to the Nations of
the World” given by African American
scholar and activist W . E. B. Du Bois. Du
Bois asked Europeans to work toward
“racial uplift” in Africa, which included
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 950 ---
862 P AN-AFRICANISM
working toward prosperous black states in
Africa and bringing an end to racial injus-
tice. However, much of his message was
geared toward peoples of African descent
themselves. Du Bois demanded that blacks
be responsible for their own uplift, and that
the states of Ethiopia, Liberia, and Haiti
provide positive examples of black self-
determination.
The discourse that emerged from the
Pan-African Conference continued in the
years to come as persons of color around
the world became increasingly aware of their
shared struggles. Furthermore, the meeting
served as a forerunner of a series of similar
conferences, known as congresses, in the
decades to follow, the last one being held in
1945.
Carmen Lenore Wright

PAN-AFRICANISM
Pan-Africanism describes the idea of unity
among people of African descent against
oppression. This spirit of solidarity
emerged during World War I when a group
of black intellectuals and political leaders
from the Caribbean, the Americas, and
Africa met in London to discuss the future
of blacks worldwide. While the list of
Pan-Africanists is long, it includes key
ﬁgures such as the African American W . E.
B. Du Bois, the Jamaican Marcus Garvey,
the Beninese Kojo Houenou-T ovalou, the
T rinidadian George Padmore, and the
Ghanaian Kwame N’krumah. These ﬁgures,
and many others, contributed greatly to the
ideological and political development of
the Pan-Africanist movement.
Du Bois was the most outspoken de-
fender of the idea of unity between blacks
of the Diaspora and Africa. According
to Du Bois, these blacks were united by
the social heritage of slavery and their
close connections with Africa. Du Bois
envisioned Pan-African kinship to be not
just a slogan of brotherhood and sister-
hood between blacks but the expression of
a true political and economic unity be-
tween blacks. In order to put his ideas into
practice, Du Bois helped organize the Pan-
African Congresses of 1919 (held in Paris)
and of 1921 (held in London, Paris, and
Brussels). These congresses allowed black
leaders from Africa, America, and the
Caribbean to meet in the West to discuss
the predicament that colonization had
created in their nations and propose ways
in which they could achieve equality,
democracy, and economic and political
development. The most salient aspect of
Du Bois’s Pan-Africanism was its descrip-
tion of the physical suffering, the loss of
life, and the devastation of land that
European imperialism brought about in
Africa. Du Bois lamented how European
colonialism opened the way from the
Sahara to the Cape of Good Hope for
marauding masses of Bantu warriors and
for committing relentless aggression and
conquest. In this sense, Du Bois’s Pan-
Africanism was a strong denunciation of
the impact of European colonization of
Africa.
Garvey’s Pan-Africanism took a differ-
ent turn than Du Bois’s did, because it
centered not just on the idea of unity be-
tween the black Diaspora and Africa but
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 951 ---
PAN-AFRICANISM 863
also on the belief that such unity would
lead to a return of all people of African
descent to Africa. Garvey’s motto—which
later became a rallying slogan for black
nationalists of the 1960s in the United
States, the Caribbean, and Africa—was one
of the strongest expressions of cultural and
political solidarity between blacks. The
essence of Garvey’s Pan-Africanism was his
theory of re-Africanization that urged
blacks of the Diaspora to go back to Africa
and use their skills to help develop it.
Garvey interpreted this return as a recon-
nection with the continent that great kings
and queens used to rule in ancient times.
In the 1920s, Garvey collaborated with
an African political ﬁgure named Kojo
T ovalou-Houenou, who was a ﬁrm backer
of his Pan-Africanism. T ovalou-Houenou’s
support of Garvey’s Pan-Africanism is
visible when, in his address at Carnegie
Hall, he endorsed not only Garvey’s immi-
gration project in Liberia but also his plans
to extend his inﬂuence across the African
continent. T ovalou-Houenou was im-
pressed by Garvey’s perception of Liberia
as a black Zion that symbolized African
liberty. In this sense, T ovalou-Houenou was
one of the strongest validations Garvey
received from a highly educated African
intellectual of the 1920s.
T ovalou-Houenou’s views on Garvey
contradict the unsubstantiated notion that
Garvey was an imperialist or a colonialist.
Like Garvey, T ovalou-Houenou recognized
the importance of racial alliance in the
development of nationhood and techno-
logical advancement in Africa. Although
he was proud of the forms of cultural and
industrial development that already existed
in traditional Africa, T ovalou-Houenou
admitted that Africans could take advan-
tage of the intellectual, artistic, and
scientiﬁc know-how of the black Diaspora.
Referring to the delegations of UNIA
members that Garvey had sent to Liberia
in the 1920s, T ovalou-Houenou said: “You
will bring to your brothers in Africa the arts
and industries of the world...y o u  will
bring all the education and morality and all
that you have learned...and there shall be
a fusion and community of ideas and spirit
in our great motherland, Africa.” T ovalou
Houenou’s statement reﬂects a very practi-
cal concept of solidarity between blacks of
the Diaspora and Africa. Instead of just
mentioning such unity, he points out the
need to concretize it in the Diaspora’s use of
its manpower and intelligentsia to give ac-
tual support to Africa. T ovalou-Houenou
envisions the union between blacks of the
West and Africa as a blending between the
people, ideas, and spirit that could uplift
the conditions of blacks worldwide. Both
Garvey and the UNIA admired this part of
T ovalou-Houenou’s nationalism. In its
edition of August 30, 1924, the Negro
World praised T ovalou’s Pan-Africanism as
a call for blacks from around the world to
march back to their homeland and wrest it
from its oppressors.
Pan-Africanism would not have had a
strong meaning without the contributions
that the Ghanaian Kwame N’krumah and
his close friend George Padmore made in
its development. After completing his stud-
ies at Lincoln University, between 1939
and 1942, and at the University of
Pennsylvania, in 1942 and 1943, N’krumah
returned to Ghana to become the secretary
general of the West African Secretariat, an
organization that was founded at the ﬁfth
Pan-African Congress to fight for the
independence of European colonies in
West Africa. In I Speak of Freedom: A State-
ment of African Ideology (1961), N’krumah
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 952 ---
864 P AN-AFRICANISM
developed his thesis that the freedom of
Ghana would not mean anything unless it
was linked with the total liberation of the
entire continent of Africa. Earlier, he had
said that the independence of West Africa
required the speedy liberation of all depen-
dent territories in Africa from colonialism,
imperialism, and racialism.
N’krumah’s Pan-Africanism expands
the concept of African independence and
self-determination, which was at the core
of Padmore’s philosophy. In Pan-Africanism
and Communism (1956), Padmore de-
scribed what he viewed as a growing politi-
cal consciousness among Africans that what
happens in one part of Africa has effects
on Africans living in different parts of the
world. Padmore ﬁrmly believed that this
awareness would lead to the creation of a
United States of Africa. Padmore’s concept
of a “United States of Africa” rejuvenated a
key ideology of Pan-African resistance that
had parallels in Garvey’s “Africa for the
Africans” slogan. Padmore had great inﬂu-
ence on N’krumah, especially during the
1960s when N’krumah thought to con-
vince the leaders of the independent
African states to unite with Ghana to form
a United States of Africa. N’krumah’s dream
has not been realized yet, but it continues
to inspire millions of people of African
descent worldwide toward the liberation of
their nations.
Pan-Africanism has a long history in
which many black intellectuals from both
Africa and the black Diaspora contributed
to defend Africa and its descendants world-
wide against oppression. The central ideol-
ogy of the movement is the unbreakable
bond between people of African descent.
These ties should be given concrete mean-
ing so that the noble development goals of
Pan-Africanism can transform the lives of
blacks worldwide. Many believe that the
ideals of Pan-Africanism will remain alive
as long as people of African descent con-
tinue to be denied the justice and equality
they have been ﬁghting for throughout the
history of the modern world.
Babacar M’Baye

PARAGUAY
Paraguay, a country of south-central South
America, has a history of African peoples,
spanning from its involvement in slavery
to its views on racial mixing as an indepen-
dent nation, and how its contemporary
African population operates in the nation’s
contemporary life and politics. Despite the
very modest presence of African descen-
dants living in Paraguay today, their
profound contributions to the country’s
history should not be ignored. African
slaves ﬁrst came to Paraguay during the
seventeenth and eighteenth centuries via
trade routes through Brazil, Uruguay, and
the port city of Buenos Aires. In the early
seventeenth century, some of the earliest
African slaves to enter the region accompa-
nied Jesuit missionaries to isolated frontier
settlements. Small numbers of slaves were
imported primarily because Paraguay
lacked large plantations and rich mines,
such as the one in nearby Potosí. This
insured that African slaves would not be
needed in great numbers to augment the
region’s labor supply. The consistent demo-
graphic decline of Guaraní due to epidemic
diseases did not compel the Spanish to
import slaves on a large scale. Still, the
African slaves that did arrive lived near
indigenous reducciones, or settlements orga-
nized by the Spanish to concentrate native
groups, and helped build farms, churches,
and roads during the entire colonial period.
This proximity assured that Europeans,
Africans, and indigenous peoples would
be in regular contact with each other in
spite of the Jesuits’ best efforts to keep
Europeans and Africans isolated from the
Guaraní. 
By the eighteenth century, hundreds
more slaves were brought in to cultivate
yerba mate, a tea grown primarily in
southern South America. This crop eventu-
ally became Paraguay’s most lucrative
export, and the Jesuits were particularly
adept at running productive estates. With
the blessing of royal authorities, some Afro-
Paraguayan settlements, like Emboscada,
Areguá, and Guarambaré, were founded.
Emboscada, in particular, was given the
unfortunate role of serving as a buffer
colony for the white populations against
raids from hostile indigenous groups. This
would not be the last time that African
peoples would be compelled to sacriﬁce
their lives in this way. Many slaves bought
as domestic servants lived primarily within
or near Asunción or Villa Rica. Compared
with the working conditions of slaves who
worked in the rural areas of the country,
these urban slaves lived much more inde-
pendently and were by far treated better.
They were also able to form stronger fam-
ily linkages within their own communities
and experienced modest natural growth.
In the mid-1780s, according to colonial
census records, both freedmen and slave
descendants of the ﬁrst Africans totaled
almost 15 percent of the population.
African peoples, also called pardos by
most Paraguayans at the time, declined in
number after 1811, when Paraguay
achieved its independence from Spain. At
ﬁrst, this was due in large measure to the
process of mestizaje, or race mixture. An
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 954 ---
866 P ARAGUAY
increasing number of free pardos lived
near and among indigenous communities
as skilled workers and farmers on state-
supported ranches. Moreover, the
Paraguayan state sanctioned miscegenation
by passing laws promoting the practice.
Dr. José Gaspar Rodríguez de Francia,
Paraguay’s dictatorial ruler between 1814
and 1840, promulgated a unique law in the
Americas that ordered local elites to marry
members of other racial groups, including
free pardos and mulattoes, as long as these
groups were similar in terms of socioeco-
nomic status. Dr. Francia also used the
power of the state to resettle a thriving
Afro-Paraguayan township called Tabapí to
the northern frontier region of the country.
The new settlement at T evegó would serve
to alert and perhaps stall any Brazilian
incursions into Paraguay. 
Modest yet significant sources of
African immigration came from Argentina
and Uruguay, respectively. Afro-Argentine
troops accompanied the Argentine indepen-
dence leader, Manuel Belgrano, in his
failed military campaigns in the region.
Also, after José Gervasio Artigas, an early
hero of Uruguay’s independence move-
ment, was forced into exile in Paraguay by
a combination of Brazilian and Argentine
forces, numerous Afro-Uruguayan soldiers
followed him. The descendants of these
veterans settled in Cambacuá (also spelled
Camba Cuá), located approximately 25
miles (40 kilometers) east of Asunción.
Paraguay’s government assisted these set-
tlers’ efforts to start a new community by
providing them with land grants, farm sup-
plies, and animals. Cambacuá ultimately
thrived as an independent community, and
their descendants still live there to this day.
Peculiar characteristics of the slave
system developed that had more to do
with the authoritarian features of the
Paraguayan state. First, slave purchases
and sales were tightly regulated by the state
because it emerged as one of the largest
owners of slaves. The ﬁrst rulers of an inde-
pendent Paraguay during the early nine-
teenth century would often confiscate
slaves from their political enemies and use
them in state-supported estates, factories,
and public works projects. Second, and
perhaps paradoxically, slaves were, as a gen-
eral observation, not treated as harshly as in
other areas of the Americas. In fact, on
state-run farms and factories, slaves were
often promoted to oversee other slaves.
Still, as was the case with Tabapí, the state
had the power to move large numbers of
pardos around the country whenever it
deemed necessary.
An abolitionist movement slowly
evolved in Paraguay beginning in the
1840s. In 1842, the government issued a
“free womb” legislation that led to the
emancipation of slaves when they reached
adulthood. As a result of this law, the free
Afro-Paraguayan population experienced a
growth spurt. In addition to those classiﬁed
as free and slave, these Libertos de la
República, as this new generation of freed-
men was called, created a third class of
Afro-Paraguayans. As in Brazil and Mexico,
for example, Paraguayan slavery ended
gradually in stages. A generation later, full
emancipation would be given to slaves in a
new constitution. By 1846, pardos consti-
tuted a little over 7 percent of the popula-
tion, and just under half of these remained
enslaved. Generally, however, their num-
bers continued to fall.
Race mixture was not the only rea-
son for the demographic decline of
Afro-Paraguayans. Many were killed as
soldiers in the War of the T riple Alliance

PARAGUAY 867
(1865–1870), considered by most scholars
as the most devastating total war in South
America’s history. The modernization
policies of Paraguay’s dictatorial leaders,
Antonio Carlos López (ruled 1840–1863)
and his son Francisco Solano López
(ruled 1863–1870), threatened Argentina,
Uruguay, and Brazil enough for them to
form a military alliance against the land-
locked nation. Solano López, in particular,
drafted pardo troops and placed them on
the frontlines and in the cavalry—some
have argued as cannon fodder. T o be sure,
the Paraguayan dictator’s act signiﬁcantly
thinned the numbers of male Afro-
Paraguayans. Paraguay maintained the
integrity of its borders as long as it could,
but it could not sustain the constant attacks
of its neighbors. Eventually, the war took a
dramatic turn for the worse. When Solano
López ran out of state-owned slaves, he
demanded and received others that were
privately owned. Nevertheless, most, if
not all, of these slaves were sent to their
deaths in desperate offensives. It should
be noted that Africans were disproportion-
ately represented as soldiers in the ranks
of Argentine, Brazilian, and Uruguayan
armies as well. Paraguay experienced high
casualty rates among its military and civil-
ian populations, and it eventually lost the
war. This costly conﬂict led to what seemed
like the certain disappearance of African
peoples (in both Paraguay and Argentina).
Because a disproportionate number of
Afro-Paraguayan males were sent to die
in the war, the result was that females
greatly outnumbered males. After the war,
Paraguay’s puppet government incorpo-
rated an abolition provision into the allied-
created Constitution of 1870, but few
Afro-Paraguayans, especially males, re-
mained alive to see the beneﬁts of freedom.
According to international figures,
Paraguay has a population of approxi-
mately 156,000 Afro-Paraguayans, repre-
senting 2 to 3 percent of the country’s pop-
ulation. This total is disputable since the
government does not ofﬁcially make it a
point to include pardos in its census counts.
Still, nongovernmental organizations have
veriﬁed these numbers. T wo communities
make up the largest concentrations of Afro-
Paraguayans: Emboscada and Cambacuá.
The municipality of Emboscada is now
primarily a mining community located
about 50 miles (31 kilometers) outside of
Asunción. Cambacuá is now incorporated
within the Fernando de la Mora municipal-
ity, an important suburb of Asunción. As
with the rest of the country, this commu-
nity suffered great losses as its male mem-
bers were drafted into the War of the T riple
Alliance. Since then, the Cambacuá com-
munity has been gradually dispossessed of
its lands to make way for urban sprawl and
development. The area’s impoverished con-
ditions and racial discrimination have
forced many Afro-Paraguayans to look for
jobs and housing elsewhere, but some have
remained. Those who have stayed face
unemployment, racism, poverty, and the
lack of educational opportunities. Still, a
strong sense of cultural pride exists within
the Cambacuá community. Evidence that
Afro-Paraguayans have maintained their
heritage is seen in the annual festival of
St. Baltazar, a Catholic patron saint, also
celebrated by many African descendants
in Uruguay and Argentina. This festival
represents a mixture of African-based and
Catholic rituals. Every January 6, the Ballet
Cambacuá demonstrates to outsiders that
a vibrant Afro-Paraguayan community
thrives despite its hardships. The painful
yet inspiring story of Afro-Paraguayans

PEACE CORPS
The Peace Corps is a U.S. governmental
agency established by Executive Order on
March 1, 1961. The Congressional Peace
Corps Act of September 22, 1961, formally
authorized the Peace Corps to foster world
peace and camaraderie. Congress passed
legislation making it an independent
federal agency in 1981. With a yearly bud-
get of about 1 percent of the U.S. foreign
operations spending, the Peace Corps’ rela-
tively small size and careful oversight by the
Ofﬁce of Inspector General (OIG) helps
the agency maintain ﬂexibility, effective-
ness, and efﬁciency.
By 2006, there were 7,810 Peace Corps
volunteers serving seventy-seven countries
in six program areas: education, youth
outreach, and community development;
health and HIV/AIDS; agriculture; envi-
ronment; business development; and infor-
mation technology. The purpose of the
Peace Corps is to have skilled Americans
living abroad for twenty-six months in
order to help foreign countries meet their
development goals. Volunteers learn the
host country language and live at a level
comparable to a host-country counterpart.
The overarching aim of every volunteer is
to transfer necessary skills to their counter-
part. The Peace Corps has worked hard to
ﬁnd the right programs to ﬁt each country’s
unique needs, though occasionally these
programs are not entirely successful.
Throughout its tenure, three goals
have consistently directed the Peace Corps’
mission: (1) to help the people of interested
countries in meeting their needs for trained
men and women; (2) to help promote a
better understanding of Americans on the
part of the peoples served; and (3) to help
promote a better understanding of other
peoples on the part of all Americans. Since
the program’s humble beginnings, the
Peace Corps has placed more than 182,000
volunteers and trainees in 138 countries,
48 of which are located in Africa alone.
In his 1960 speech at the University
of Michigan, Senator John F . Kennedy
challenged students to go abroad and
model U.S. values, promote development,
and share their expertise as a testament to
the American spirit. By March 4, 1961,
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 957 ---
PEACE CORPS 869
President Kennedy had appointed his
brother-in-law, Robert Sargent Shriver Jr.,
as the ﬁrst director of the Peace Corps.
Under Shriver’s leadership, 55 countries
invited more than 14,500 volunteers to live
and work outside the United States. By
June 1966, the Peace Corps had reached its
largest number of Americans serving
abroad at any one time, with 15,556
volunteers in 52 countries.
When volunteer training was out-
sourced to host countries in 1973, admin-
istrative diversity increased. Appointed by
President Ronald Reagan, Loret Miller
became the longest-serving director and
the second of only four women to hold
the post (the ﬁrst woman and the ﬁrst
African American director was Carolyn
R. Payton).
The 1990s saw even more diversity with
the initial deployment of volunteers to
Eastern Europe, the former Soviet Union,
China, and South Africa. As of June 27,
2000, all volunteers in Africa must be qual-
iﬁed as educators of HIV/AIDS prevention
and care. The Peace Corps also committed
an additional 1,000 volunteers worldwide
to work on HIV/AIDS-related activities as
part of President George W . Bush’s Global
AIDS Relief Package in 2003. (In that same
year, sixteenth director Gaddi H. Vasquez
made historic inroads in Mexico, providing
technical volunteers to the National Coun-
cil for Science and T echnology [CONA-
CYT].) By 2006, Ron Campbell became the
ﬁrst Peace Corps AIDS Relief Coordinator.
The range of diversity among volun-
teers is quite high. The biographical break-
down from a September 2005 Peace Corps
survey suggests that the average volunteer
is a 28-year-old single white female with an
undergraduate degree (with 58 percent
female, 9 percent married, 16 percent
minority, 6 percent over 50 years old [old-
est 79], 96 percent with undergraduate
degree, 13 percent with graduate training,
and a median age of 25).
This bipartisan institution (one senator
and six representatives have served as volun-
teers) continues to innovate. For example,
the Coverdell World Wise Schools program
(initiated by Director Coverdell) promotes
correspondence between thousands of U.S.
teachers and serving volunteers.
Director Mark Gearan’s 1995 Crisis
Corps initiative has recently gained world-
wide attention. It provides returned vol-
unteers with the opportunity to give
short-term assistance to victims of natural
disasters and humanitarian crises. In only
ten years, more than 900 Crisis Corps
participants have served special needs. For
example, 272 volunteers worked domesti-
cally for the ﬁrst time in Peace Corps
history alongside the Federal Emergency
Management Agency’s (FEMA) relief oper-
ation after the devastation of Hurricane
Katrina in the Gulf Coast region in
September 2005.
