870 P EACEKEEPING AND MILITARYINTERVENTIONS
PEACEKEEPING AND
MILITARYINTERVENTIONS
Peacekeeping is an international action
authorized under Chapter VI and Chapter
VII of the Charter of the United Nations
(UN), which invokes an array of measures
including forcible and nonforcible military
intervention by individual states or an
organized group of states in order to “main-
tain or restore international peace and
security.” T raditionally, peace enforcement
actions have been used to resolve interstate
conﬂict. However, with the sharp rise in
civil strife within countries in the post–
cold war years, peacekeeping operations
have increasingly been organized against
internal conﬂicts such as civil wars, massive
violations of human rights in ethnic strug-
gles, and state-supported or directed geno-
cide, as in Rwanda in 1994. In the case
of genocide, the Security Council can be
called upon by signatory states of the
Convention on the Prevention and Punish-
ment of Genocide (signed by the United
States in 1948 but not ratiﬁed by the U.S.
Senate until 1988) to take action to prevent
genocide by invoking Article VIII of the
convention. Efforts to organize an interna-
tional humanitarian intervention in Darfur
(Sudan) in 2006 by the United Nations or
other multilateral or unilateral force, such
as the United States, for example, empha-
sized the importance of enforcing the con-
vention. A small regional multilateral force
of some 7,000 African Union (AU) troops,
which had been dispatched to help enforce
a U.S.-brokered peace agreement, failed to
stop the genocide in Darfur. Furthermore, a
more forceful UN military action remained
stymied by the objections of the autocratic
Sudanese president Omar Hassan al-Bashir,
who rejected a foreign military presence as
a form of recolonization of his country.
Often international peacekeeping
forces must deal with sticky sovereignty
issues and negotiate the terms of interven-
tion. The Clinton Doctrine, proposed by
U.S. President Bill Clinton in 1999, and
subsequent legal opinions further asserted a
responsibility by the world community to
stop ethnic cleansing and genocide when-
ever and wherever it occurred.
In international relations, intervention
covers a wide range of international actions
that seek to influence and affect the
internal politics, processes, structures, and
conditions within another country. Gener-
ally, direct military intervention involves
the overt and limited use of military
personnel or special expeditionary forces,
short of outright, full-scale warfare.
However, the line between low-
intensity intervention and interstate war-
fare is often blurred, so that some authori-
ties consider the Vietnam War and the
Korean War direct military interventions
by the United States. Indeed, intervention
as a form of warfare is justiﬁed on legal and
political grounds under the Christian
theory of “just war,” and the international
legal principles of jus ad bellum and jus in
bello, which establish the appropriate rea-
sons for war and the correct means for its
conduct. Interventions, therefore, not un-
like wars, can be considered legitimate if
used as a last resort, conducted for a just
cause with limited force and protection of
civilians, and if sanctioned by a legitimate
authority, such as an international organi-
zation like the United Nations or regional
organizations like the Organization of
American States (OAS) or African Union.
Also, under both the charters of the de-
funct League of Nations and the United
Nations (and regional organizations such as
the OAS and the AU), the use of force,
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 959 ---
PEACEKEEPING AND MILITARYINTERVENTIONS 871
such as military intervention and outright
war, are permitted in self-defense and for
collective security. Nevertheless, unless
there is an uncontested just cause, unilat-
eral intervention by a powerful state is no
longer an accepted international norm. The
majority of contemporary interventions,
whether unilateral or multilateral, have
been conducted under (or in part appealed
to) the rubric of humanitarian interven-
tions. Human rights law mandates that
outside parties (national states and/or inter-
national organizations) have not only the
right but the obligation to intervene in the
internal affairs of another state to protect
a people against abuses by their fellow
citizens or own government.
Since the end of the Cold War, peace-
keeping operations and interventions of
every type have been on the rise. The major-
ity of interventions and humanitarian and
peace operations—both peacemaking and
peacekeeping—have been multilateral ven-
tures, or multinational force (MNF)
actions, requested by the local government
and/or sanctioned under the United
Nations Charter and Ofﬁce of Peacekeeping
Operations. Under Chapter VIII of the UN
Charter, member states can resort to re-
gional organizations to resolve international
peace and security issues. Although regional
enforcement methods and operations which
employ armed intervention and military
power require Security Council authoriza-
tion, this rule has been ﬂexibly applied.
Since the early 1990s, with the emer-
gence of new security threats, increased
armed conﬂicts globally, as well as greater
regional dimensions to conﬂict in Latin
America and especially Africa, there has
been a shift to greater regional peacekeep-
ing operations. Indeed, many contempo-
rary peace and humanitarian operations
have drawn on multiple sources for support
and legitimacy, including the UN Security
Council, regional organizations, informal
regional and subregional groups, and major
powers. The international community has
encouraged a greater capacity and proactive
posture by the African Union (as in Darfur,
for example), unlike the feeble role of its
predecessor, the Organization of African
Unity (OAU). Efforts are being made to
develop an African Standby Force (ASF),
and to have subregional organizations, such
as the Economic Community of West
African States (ECOWAS), take the lead
in such a force and in regional and subre-
gional peacekeeping and security issues.
The history of military interventions in
Latin America and Africa is quite extensive
and complex. During the ﬁrst half of the
twentieth century, and prior to the found-
ing of the United Nations, the majority of
interventions were unilateral incursions by
a superpower or a major or regional power
(often an imperial or postcolonial power).
In the Western Hemisphere, the United
States intervened repeatedly in the
Caribbean and Central America in order to
advance and protect its national interests
and national security. For example, the
United States conducted a series of military
interventions between 1898 and 1934 in
the Caribbean Basin in the name of pro-
moting “civilized behavior,” trade and in-
vestments (so-called “dollar diplomacy”),
and democracy. Such interventions in-
cluded Panama (1903–1914), Haiti
(1915–1934), the Dominican Republic
(1916–1924), Cuba (1917–1922), and
Nicaragua (1909–1925 and 1926–1933).
Other forms of interventions included
propaganda and misinformation and coer-
cive measures short of direct military action
such as economic sanctions. With the onset
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 960 ---
872 P EACEKEEPING AND MILITARYINTERVENTIONS
of the cold war after 1949, U.S. interven-
tions in Latin America and Africa often in-
volved such indirect and covert operations
by national security agencies such as the
U.S. Central Intelligence Agency (CIA)
and reflected the ideological struggle
against communism and potential Soviet,
communist Chinese, and Castroite inﬂu-
ence in the third world. Noteworthy cases
included Guatemala (1954), Cuba (1961),
Zaire/ Congo (1961–1964), Chile (1973),
and Angola (1975). Both Zaire and Angola
involved early UN peacekeeping operations
that were complicated by covert CIA inter-
ference and cold war rivalry among the
United States, the Soviet Union, and the
Peoples Republic of China. And since 9/11
and the War on T errorism, covert interven-
tions appear on the rise. In 2006, the
CIA secretly funded secular warlords in
unstable Somalia in order to marginalize
Islamist militias and forestall (unsuccess-
fully) their control of the country and
interim government.
On the other hand, several major U.S.
cold war interventions in the Dominican
Republic (1965) and Grenada (1983) were
direct, overt, and mobilized thousands
of predominately U.S. troops. Generally,
these interventions, like those before the
onset of the cold war, were justiﬁed as
“national self-defense,” “protecting lives,
liberty and property,” “maintaining law and
order,” and “restoring democracy.” Often
the actions were invited (and therefore
legitimated) by a domestic government or
faction and sanctioned under the charter of
the Organization of American States and/or
the United Nations Security Council. The
majority of post–cold war interventions,
such as Panama (1989) and Somalia
(1992–1994), have followed this pattern,
but have introduced new justiﬁcations such
as ﬁghting the drug war and humanitarian
relief, respectively (and most recently, the
global War on T errorism).
In Somalia in December 1992, the
United States became engaged in a major
peacemaking and peacekeeping operation.
Prodded by scenes of massive starvation
and criticisms of racism by UN Secretary
General Boutros Boutros-Ghali and pan-
African NGOs and interest groups in the
United States, a U.S.-led and dominated
humanitarian mission was dispatched to
Somalia by U.S. President George Bush.
At the time, the United States had limited
its involvement in the Balkans (Bosnia in
1995 and Kosovo in 1999) because inter-
vention there appeared difﬁcult and the
United Nations, European governments,
and NATO were willing to take the lead.
By contrast, the humanitarian mission in
Somalia was assessed as “do-able,” and the
humanitarian crisis, although grave, was
alleviated by a small-scale conventional
peacekeeping force. However, the U.S.-UN
intervention proved disastrous in the end,
evolving from its limited humanitarian
mandate to a wider peacekeeping, peace-
enforcement, and nation-building role.
Although the immediate problem in
Somalia was mass starvation, drought, and
environmental degradation, the underlying
problem was endemic religious, regional,
and clan conﬂict. After three years of civil
war in 1991, a coalition of clans toppled
Mohamed Siad Barre, who had seized
power in a coup in 1969 and had installed
a socialist-Islamic dictatorship. Within this
volatile context, the U.S.-UN humanitar-
ian rescue mission, “Operation Restore
Hope,” was successful initially, but soon
became hostage to the feuding among rival
warlords like the notorious General
Mohammed Farah Aidid. The intervention
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 961 ---
PEACEKEEPING AND MILITARYINTERVENTIONS 873
disintegrated into a nasty policing opera-
tion, resulting in hundreds of Somali casu-
alties and the sensational death of a small
contingent of U.S. Army Rangers (“Black
Hawk Down”) and the mutilation of their
bodies.
After the failed nation-building at-
tempt, U.S. forces ﬁnally pulled out in
March 1994, and the UN a year later. The
UN operation had cost billions of dollars,
and over a decade later the Somali state re-
mained near collapse, politically unstable,
and on the edge of one humanitarian crisis
after another. The main lesson for the U.S.
military and policymakers was to avoid
becoming overextended in intrastate and
ethnic conﬂicts, especially in Africa. The
hazard of another Somalia-type imbroglio
partly explained the U.S. and international
community’s failure to intervene in
Rwanda and Zaire/Congo from 1994 to
1997, and the general reluctance to do
more in Darfur in 2006.
The Somali case has also led to harsh
critiques of humanitarian intervention as a
form of legitimate and effective interven-
tion. Most post–cold war interventions
have been justiﬁed, at least in part, by hu-
manitarian claims, which provide a ready
moral escape clause to the international
legal principle of nonintervention. Critics
question whether this may dilute the mean-
ing of humanitarianism, and whether the
results of foreign military involvement en-
dure and provide long-term security. Thus
the term “humanitarian intervention,”
even when authorized by the UN Security
Council, has been challenged as a mis-
nomer. In other words, can a military oper-
ation be “humanitarian” in all its aspects:
motives, purposes, methods, and results?
Or can a humanitarian intervention do
more harm in the end than good?
Also, some question the “double-
standards” or political selectivity of some
operations over others, and argue that
under the UN charter humanitarian inter-
vention derives its legality from the exis-
tence of “a threat to international peace
and security.” Thus the UN Somalia Oper-
ations (UNOSOM I and II) were both
legally justiﬁed as security and peacemak-
ing and peacekeeping operations. Finally,
can a UN intervention occur against the
express opposition of the target state’s gov-
ernment, as in Darfur? In the Somali crisis
there was no effective government that
could provide or withhold consent. And,
fearing the establishment of a precedent
for intervention, the African states urged
cautious wording in Resolution 794 of
December 4, 1992, which authorized
Operation Restore Hope. The preamble to
the resolution speciﬁcally emphasized the
“unique character,” “extraordinary nature,”
and “exceptional response” in the Somali
case.
Nevertheless, since the ﬁrst peacekeep-
ing operation in 1948, the United Nations
has been active, if not always completely
successful in the prevention, management,
and resolution of conﬂicts around the
world. The majority of third world con-
ﬂicts have had similar instigating condi-
tions: histories of internal economic and
political oppression; colonial exploitation
and dependent development; severe re-
source scarcities, poverty, and ecological
and environmental degradation; ethnic,
religious, and nationalistic tensions; un-
equal minority-majority power relations;
and regional structural inequalities. In
many cases (such as the Sudan, Somalia,
and the Congo), local instability has
threatened regional and global peace and
security. As a consequence, multilateral
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 962 ---
874 P EACEKEEPING AND MILITARYINTERVENTIONS
interventions for peacemaking, peacekeep-
ing, and peace enforcement purposes have
expanded steadily, as have postconﬂict rec-
onciliation, rehabilitation, and reconstruc-
tion efforts in the third world. In these
efforts, a critical problem has been the
need for greater military force, which cre-
ated its own risks to peacekeepers and
civilians, and to the impartiality of the UN
missions.
In Africa, especially, these problems
have been endemic and severe. Indeed, a
majority of peacekeeping operations since
1999 are on the African continent: six in
Africa (the Democratic Republic of the
Congo; Ethiopia and Eritrea; Liberia; Ivory
Coast; Burundi; and the Sudan), compared
to one in the Caribbean (Haiti) and one in
Europe (Kosovo). And in 2006, the crisis
in Sudan—ethnic cleansing and over
2.2 million refugees—escalated further. A
concerned international community and
African Union (whose peacekeeping troops
were undermanned and besieged) appealed
to the UN Security Council to authorize
deployment of a 20,000-strong multina-
tional force under a Chapter VII mandate
to enforce the 2004 Darfur Peace Agree-
ment and to protect the civilians caught in
Sudan’s brutal civil war.
Peacekeeping results have been mixed
and highly dependent on the ﬁnancial
and political commitment and the mili-
tary and technical support of the interna-
tional community. In mid-2006, the
UN Department of Peacekeeping Opera-
tions (DPKO) was engaged in 15 peace-
keeping operations and three special
political and/or peace-building missions,
involving 108 contributing countries, more
than 72,000 uniformed personnel (that
is, troops, military observers, and UN
police), as well as several thousand
international and local civilian personnel
and UN volunteers. These were expensive
operations and a number of truce and ob-
server missions, established as early as the
late 1940s, remained ongoing for decades.
Since 1948, the estimated total cost of
peace-related activities approached $41
billion; and for one year alone, from July
1, 2005 to June 30, 2006, approximately
$5 billion was approved for peacekeeping
operations and missions.
The dominance of U.S. power in the
contemporary international system also has
meant greater pressures and opportunities
for U.S.-led military interventions. During
the 1980s, interventions involving U.S.
troops doubled over totals in previous
decades, and jumped further in the 1990s.
In the post-9/11 world, there has been a
new wave of interventions to counter ter-
rorism and the proliferation of weapons of
mass destruction (WMD). In this context,
peacekeeping and interventionist opera-
tions have taken on even greater signiﬁ-
cance. These operations demonstrate more
than ever that national security and global
security are interdependent and that both
entail progress in sustainable development
and human rights in the third world. State
collapse, civil wars, and governance vacu-
ums in Africa and Latin America not only
fuel humanitarian and refugee crises and
contribute to regional instability but may
provide safe havens for radical militias and
terrorist groups.
Nevertheless, the international com-
munity has learned a degree of caution.
Any intervention, even if well-intentioned
or for justiﬁable ends, such as the U.S.-
UN Somalia operation, can provoke local
resentment and opposition and further
complicate rather than decrease the “threat
to international peace and security.” On
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 963 ---

the other hand, the strong international
commitment to protect human rights and
prevent and punish genocide may con-
tinue to challenge and expand the notion
of a global security community and the
support for humanitarian intervention and
peace enforcement operations, at the ex-
pense of the traditional principles of
sovereignty and nonintervention.

PENTECOSTALISM
Pentecostalism is a Christian religious
movement that started in Los Angeles,
California, in 1906. Its origins lie within
African American culture because it was
founded by William Joseph Seymour, a
black preacher from Louisiana. He had
been taught religion by a man named
Charles Parham, a teacher of the Bible and
a leader of the T opeka Revival. After work-
ing under Parham, Seymour moved to
Indianapolis, where he learned even more
about what he would later call Pentecostal-
ism after he joined a church there. Seymour
then moved to Cincinnati and later to
Houston. In both cities he attended church
and learned about the Holy Spirit and
“speaking in tongues.” But it was not until
he moved to Los Angeles that he began
to preach on his own. There Seymour
preached in an old abandoned building on
Bonnie Brae Avenue to a small congrega-
tion that consisted “largely of black domes-
tic servants and washer women.” But the
makeup of his congregation would change
within a short time. Seymour eventually
moved his congregation to a church on
Azusa Street. Although Parham is believed
to have been the ﬁrst head of the church, it
is clear that within a short time Seymour
himself was in charge of the congregation.
For many historians of religion, Seymour’s
move to Azusa Street signiﬁes the birth of
Pentecostalism as a religious movement.
But the new religious movement that
was called “Pentecostalism,” and indeed
Seymour’s church itself, were the target of
media criticism. Reporters from the Los
Angeles Times, the Los Angeles Record, and
the Los Angeles Daily Times,for example, all
mocked the religious services that Seymour
and his followers performed. Indeed, other
churches were also critical. They were
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 964 ---
876 P ENTECOSTALISM
particularly critical of the tongues that
practitioners spoke in, and of the ecstatic
behavior that they witnessed. However,
what the reporters and other people did not
know was that Pentecostalism shared many
of the same religious elements found in
more traditional forms of Christianity: the
Bible, religious pamphlets, songs, and ec-
static behavior. They also were not aware of
the fact that ecstatic behavior was similar to
the shouting and dancing that were so preva-
lent in predominately African American
churches at the time. What was different
about Pentecostalism, then, was that unlike
other religious movements at the time it
attempted to embrace individuals from all
walks of life, from every social and eco-
nomic level, and from every racial and
ethnic group. Because of de jure segregation
at the time, however, it became difﬁcult to
maintain the racial and ethnic diversity that
was a part of the church when it began.
Within a short time, Seymour’s church
became almost entirely black.
Diversity also brought about a plethora
of different beliefs about the Holy Spirit,
church doctrine, and the religious services
themselves. Members who held different
views often departed to start their own
churches. Differences in views and segrega-
tionist practices were such that by 1906
there were nine Pentecostal assemblies in
Los Angeles. This process of breaking and
reorganizing continued throughout the
twentieth century. T oday, Pentecostalism
has managed to become the fastest-growing
Christian movement. It has a membership
estimated to be almost two billion.
But there are other factors that have
caused Pentecostalism to spread rapidly
around the globe. From the outset, those
who practiced Pentecostalism relied on im-
provisation and innovation; this, along
with cultural diffusion and syncretism,
helped Pentecostals to increase their mem-
bership not only in the United States and
in Europe but also in Latin America,
Africa, and Asia at a time when other
denominations such as Presbyterians,
Methodists, and Episcopalians have not
been able to do so.
The rise of African Pentecostalism is
directly connected to the healing of the
body that Seymour began in his church on
Azusa Street in Los Angeles, as the faith
promises a saved soul and improved health.
Early in the twentieth century, John
Alexander Dowie, a healing evangelist
who was a member of the Assemblies of
God, a newly organized movement that
broke away from Seymour’s church, led
missionaries to South Africa. However, it
was not until the 1970s that Pentecostal-
ism began to expand rapidly throughout
other parts of Africa. In fact, it has been
argued that Pentecostalism has experienced
its greatest growth in Africa as well as in
Latin America. The religious movement
has maintained its own distinctiveness in
Africa, and yet in some instances it has also
incorporated some of the religious prac-
tices found in the more traditional African
independent churches into its own doc-
trine and services. Overall, however, as
Pentecostalism continues to expand in
Africa, it likely will become the religious
movement that the majority of African
Christians worship.
The rising number of Caribbean im-
migrants from Jamaica and West African
immigrants primarily from Nigeria in-
creased the presence of black Pentecostal
churches in Britain. The construction and
expression of black identity played a role in
the formation of these churches. The desire
for black group solidarity and the need to
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 965 ---
PÉRALTE,C HARLEMAGNE MASSÉNA 877
be protected from racism were additional
reasons why blacks in Britain turned to
Pentecostalism.
Pentecostalism’s doctrine has been de-
ﬁned in two stages and in three stages.
Central to the two-stage doctrine is bap-
tism in the Holy Spirit, which also in-
cludes sanctiﬁcation by faith. Although
baptism in the Holy Spirit is important in
the three-stage doctrine, “speaking in
tongues” is important as well. The three-
stage doctrine encompasses justiﬁcation by
faith, sanctiﬁcation by faith, and healing
of the body; the premillennial return of
Christ; and baptism in the Holy Spirit.
Harvey Cox, in Fire from Heaven, cri-
tiques how doctrine is accomplished by
Pentecostals by focusing on the three di-
mensions of elemental spirituality. Accord-
ing to Cox, these three dimensions are
primal speech, primal piety, and primal
hope. Primal speech is about communica-
tion; it speciﬁcally includes glossolalia,
which is sometimes referred to as “speak-
ing in tongues.” One’s ability to speak in
tongues, then, is a sign that a person has
been baptized in the Holy Spirit. Primal
piety is also about communication, but
nonverbal communication. It points to the
resurgence in Pentecostalism of trance,
vision, healing, dreams, dance, and other
archetypal religious expressions. Primal
hope points to Pentecostalism’s millennial
outlook—its insistence that a radically
new world age is about to dawn. It should
be thought of as a ﬁnal mission for the
church and its members, which means for
Pentecostals the full restoration of this new
life and age will come in the next world,
in the afterlife.
Darrell Donnell Darrisaw

PÉRALTE,C HARLEMAGNE
MASSÉNA(1885–1919) 
Charlemagne Masséna Péralte was a Haitian
patriot who led an unsuccessful effort to oust
U.S. troops during the ﬁrst U.S. occupation
of Haiti (1915–1934). Born in Hinche on
October 10, 1885, Péralte studied at the
elite institution of St. Louis de Gonzague,
and then became a lawyer. Bright, well-
ducated, and handsome, Péralte would
probably have pursued a successful career in
the ranks of the elite (he served as diplomat,
judge, ofﬁcer, and mayor) had it not been for
the political turmoil affecting Haiti in the
1910s.
In the early twentieth century, political
instability increased in Haiti, with no less
than six different presidents from 1911 to
1915. Following an established pattern, the
mulatto elite would hire cacos (mercenaries
and bandits) to overthrow the sitting presi-
dent, raid the national treasury, then estab-
lish a new president—who was himself over-
thrown within a few months. The United
States grew concerned that chaos in Haiti
might help European powers (Germany, in
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 966 ---
878 P ÉRALTE,C HARLEMAGNE MASSÉNA
particular) take over the country, thus
threatening the Windward Passage and ac-
cess to the Panama Canal. U.S. president
Woodrow Wilson also concluded that
Haitians were incapable of ruling themselves
and that he, acting as a “benevolent” impe-
rialist, should preside over Haiti’s destiny
in order to teach Haitians how to elect
“good men.”
When President Vilbrun Guillaume
Sam was literally dismembered by a crowd
on July 28, 1915, Wilson ordered U.S.
sailors and Marines ashore to invade Haiti.
Cacos made an unsuccessful attempt to
expel U.S. troops from September to
November. The U.S. occupation force
proceeded to stabilize the country, and it
carried out its promises of building hospi-
tals, roads, and bridges, but Haitian na-
tionalists resented the humiliation of being
occupied by a foreign power. Public anger
focused on the corvée, which the U.S.
occupation force had reestablished in July
1916. A form of taxation originating in
medieval France, the corvée required peas-
ants to work for their lord without pay-
ment. The corvée was legal under an 1863
Haitian law, but it had been rarely enforced
prior to the U.S. arrival. Work gangs did
improve the country’s dilapidated road
system, but Haitians could not help but
associate this institution with slavery (in
some cases, foremen tied the workers with
ropes to prevent escapes).
In early 1918, Péralte was sentenced to
ﬁve years of hard labor for complicity in a
raid on the Hinche barracks. He managed
to escape in September 1918 while sweep-
ing a Cap Haïtien street. He started putting
together a 5,000-strong army of cacos,
occasionally supplemented by irregulars,
with which he attacked garrisons and towns
held by the U.S.-trained constabulary, the
gendarmerie. The abolition of the corvée
(October 1918) failed to bring the revolt to
an end. By early 1919, the United States
put several companies of Marines, backed
by World War I vintage “Jenny” planes, on
Péralte’s trail. Dozens of engagements
followed, most of them in the North and
along the Artibonite River. By bribing a
caco general, Jean-Baptiste Conze, U.S.
forces were ﬁnally able to ascertain where
Péralte would strike next. On October 31,
1919, as Péralte’s troops were attacking
Grande Rivière, Marine Sergeant Herman
“Hard Head” Hanneken, accompanied by
a small group of men disguised as cacos,
managed to slip into Péralte’s camp and
gunned him down. Marines then propped
up Péralte, tied him to a plank, and took a
photograph that they hoped would prove
to all Haitians that Péralte was dead. The
move proved less effective than initially
hoped, for it gave rise to a widespread be-
lief among Haitians that Péralte was cruci-
ﬁed and that he ended his life as a Christ-
like martyr. After killing Péralte, U.S.
forces went on the offensive and brought
the second (and last) caco rebellion to an
end by May 1920.
Dr. Philippe R. Girard

PERU 879
PERU
Peru, located on the west coast of South
America, is the third largest country on
that continent after Brazil and Argentina.
During the colonial period, Peru was one of
the most important centers of the Spanish
colonial economy in the Americas.
The African presence in Peru dates
from the ﬁrst years of the Spanish conquest.
African slaves were present with Fernando
Pizarro when his forces conquered the Incas
in 1532. From colonial time to emancipa-
tion in the mid-nineteenth century, the
owning of African slaves became wide-
spread in Peru, especially along the coast,
where the native population decreased sig-
niﬁcantly after the arrival of the Europeans.
Various social groups in Peru owned
slaves, including artisans, priests, mer-
chants, sailors, and even free blacks. Yet, it
is important to keep in mind that Peru was
never a major slave center in the Americas.
It has been estimated that about 100,000
slaves came to Peru from the early colonial
period onward.
Most slaves in Peru were personal
servants, even though signiﬁcant numbers
were also employed in agriculture and
mining. For instance, on the Peruvian
coast, African slaves worked on farms, es-
pecially on sugar plantations; they also
worked in artisan shops and as domestic
servants. In addition, many Peruvian slaves
were employed in mines, mainly gold
mines. In the rich silver region of the
Andes, the native population remained
fairly large, so they were the major labor
force in the silver mines. This labor force
makeup contrasts with the situation in
many other areas of Latin America and the
Caribbean, in that Peru never depended on
African slave labor for its most important
export economy.
In addition, African slavery in Peru was
very much an urban institution. Of all of the
slaves who arrived in Peru, about 40 percent
were kept in the city of Lima or in the
surrounding region. In Lima, from the late
sixteenth century through most of the sev-
enteenth century, blacks numbered the same
as Spaniards. The city also counted a large
number of free blacks and mulattos working
alongside the slaves.
The slave trade to Peru had to over-
come signiﬁcant obstacles. Slaves brought
from Africa, after surviving the perilous
Middle Passage, were landed at Cartagena
in modern Colombia where they were sold,
and then taken by sea and land to the
Paciﬁc, before being shipped again to Peru.
The mortality rate was consequently very
high and African slaves were frequently
bought from other Latin American regions
instead of directly from Africa.
The number of slaves in Peru began to
decrease from the late seventeenth century
as prices rose with the booming sugar econ-
omy of the Caribbean. Numbers increased
again toward the end of the eighteenth cen-
tury with the establishment of free trade
and the Spanish crown’s wish to stimulate
its colonies’ economies.
After Peru acquired its independence
from Spain in the 1820s, slavery in Peru
began showing signs of decline, in part due
to the inﬂuence of the new liberal ideas
propounded by leaders such as Jose de San
Marti and Simon Bolivar. In 1821, the
same year that independence was declared,
all children of slave mothers were declared
free. That same year the African slave trade
was abolished, thereby seriously weakening
the institution. Yet, total abolition came
only in 1855, around the same time that
other Latin American countries—such
as Colombia, Ecuador, Venezuela, and
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 968 ---
880 P ERU
Argentina—were also going through the
same process. The delay indicated the con-
tinuing strength of slavery and the slave
owners, despite the apparent commitment
to liberal values. The main argument for
the continuation of slavery came mostly
from landowners, who believed that the
economy of the country would suffer with-
out slave labor.
Nevertheless, slavery was in decline.
Various factors explain its eventual demise.
For instance, at the time of abolition, the
number of slaves had decreased signiﬁ-
cantly, from around 89,000 in 1821, to
about 25,000 in the early 1850s (or
1.3 percent of the population). The decline
was, in part, a result of slaves buying their
own freedom. At the same time, slave resis-
tance increased in the nineteenth century,
with the Haitian revolution remaining a
terrifying reminder to all slave owners
in the Americas of the possible fate await-
ing them. In addition, Peruvians were
looking for alternative sources of cheap
labor abroad and began importing signiﬁ-
cant numbers of Chinese coolies. Finally,
international pressure, mainly from Great
Britain, influenced Peruvians to end
slavery.
One aspect of slavery in Peru that was
common to other parts of Latin America
was the high level of race mixture among
blacks, Spaniards, and natives. As a conse-
quence, Peru always had a substantial pop-
ulation of free mulattos. This is not to say
that all mulatto children were born free, as
before the law of 1821, Afro-Peruvians
assumed their mother’s status. Since most
mulatto children were fathered by
Spaniards, remained slaves for the rest of
their lives. Nevertheless, a signiﬁcant num-
ber of these mixed children were freed by
their fathers.
However, these children of mixed race,
even if they were free, still suffered racism
in Peruvian society. As in many other
American states, the color of one’s skin de-
termined how one was accepted in society.
In this context, the lighter the color, the
easier it was for one to be accepted by the
white population. As a result, many blacks
in Peru viewed mixing with lighter skinned
people as a positive step in order to better
the social position of their offspring. T oday
only a small number of blacks can still be
found in Peru. Still, Africans have inﬂu-
enced Peruvian culture, and in the early
twentieth century, there was an acceptance
in the country of the inﬂuences from the
former slaves. For instance, the national
dance of Peru is the marinera, an Afro-
Peruvian dance.
Rosana Barbosa

PÉTION,ALEXANDRE SABÈS 881
PÉTION,ALEXANDRE SABÈS
(1770–1818) 
After playing a prominent role in Haiti’s
War of Independence (1791–1804),
Alexandre Sabès Pétion became president
of Haiti’s South and West provinces
(1807–1818). Pétion was born in Port-
au-Prince on April 2, 1770, the son of a
free mulatto woman and an unknown
white Frenchman (the name Pétion
stemmed from his childhood nickname,
pitchoun, or “little one.”) A soldier, Pétion
studied at the French military academy.
During the War of Independence, he
helped oust British forces, and then fought
a losing civil war against T oussaint Louver-
ture. Allying himself with the French when
they returned in 1802, he ﬁnally joined a
united Haitian front against the French.
After Jean-Jacques Dessalines was over-
thrown and killed on October 17, 1806,
Pétion drafted a new constitution that
would give extensive powers to the presi-
dent of the senate, a position he occupied,
and more limited powers to the president,
Henri Christophe, a black general and his
most dangerous rival. Civil war quickly pit-
ted Pétion against Christophe, with the
former in control of Haiti’s South and
West, and the latter in control of the North
province. After Christophe installed his
own independent government in the
North (February 17, 1807), Pétion had the
senate elect him president of the South
(March 9, 1807). Thanks to its tight con-
trol of the senate, Pétion was reelected in
1811 and 1815; he then became president
for life in 1816. Pétion faced numerous
military challenges throughout his presi-
dencies. Christophe repeatedly, though un-
successfully, attacked Port-au-Prince, hop-
ing to reunite the country under his rule.
Fellow mulatto soldier and revolutionary
veteran André Rigaud ruled a breakaway
state in the South. Jérôme-Maximilien
Borgella took over after Rigaud’s death on
September 18, 1811, and was ﬁnally ousted
on March 7, 1812. Around Grande-Anse,
Pétion also faced a long-running insur-
gency led by Jean-Baptiste Perrier (aka
“Goman”), and partly financed by
Christophe, which only ended in 1819.
Despite his weak democratic creden-
tials, Pétion was much less harsh than
Christophe was in the North. He founded
a pension for girls and a high school in
Port-au-Prince (now known as Lycée
Pétion). His land policies earned him the
nickname of “Papa Bon-Coeur” (“good-
hearted Daddy”). In stark opposition to
Christophe, who forced his peasants to re-
main on plantations under conditions rem-
iniscent of slavery, Pétion decided in 1809
to conﬁscate the French’s former planta-
tions and to distribute the land to Haiti’s
Undated portrait of Alexandre Sabès Pétion, president
of the Republic of Haiti from 1806 until his death in
1818. (Library of Congress)

inhabitants (soldiers, for example, were
given three carreaux, about nine acres).
However generous, this policy proved to be
the South’s (and later Haiti’s) ruin. Aban-
doning sugar, Haiti’s main export crop,
peasants turned to small-scale subsistence
farming, complemented by a few coffee
bushes. With the exception of coffee, ex-
ports, along with the country’s importance
in world trade, markedly diminished.
Pétion also provided a safe haven for Latin
American revolutionaries fighting wars
of independence against Spain. Most fa-
mously, in 1815 and 1816, Pétion twice
hosted South American patriot Simón
Bolívar and gave him money, weapons,
and a printing press (in exchange for this
help, Bolívar abolished slavery in South
America). Pétion died in Port-au-Prince
on March 29, 1818. Jean-Pierre Boyer suc-
ceeded him as president of the South.

PHILIP,M ARLENE NOURBESE
(1947–) 
Born in T obago, Marlene Nourbese Philip
immigrated to Canada to complete her
university education and to pursue a career
as a barrister; she abandoned the law for
writing in 1982. In addition to her poetry,
she has published two novels and two
books of essays that investigate racism,
colonialism, and the position of the woman
of color in Canadian cultural life. Philip
was awarded the Casa de las Americas Prize
for her 1989 poem sequence She Tries Her
T ongue, Her Silence Softly Breaks, a work
that Philip has described as “kissing
cousins” with North American language
poetry because of a shared interest in typo-
graphical experimentation and a common
foregrounding of the materiality of lan-
guage. What differentiates Philip’s poetic
from its American cousin and suggests a
closer, Caribbean, kinship is her concern
with voice; moreover, the major theme of
She Tries Her T ongue—that of the mother-
daughter relationship—recurs in much
Caribbean women’s writing, from Jamaica
Kincaid to Lorna Goodison. She Tries Her
T ongue is concerned with memory, origins,
and genealogy.
As Philip has stated, genealogy is “an
account of descent.” In She Tries Her
T ongue,Philip redeploys the myth of Per-
sephone’s descent into the Underworld as the
unwilling consort of Pluto or Dis and her
partial restoration to her mother to explore
her own experience of exile and separation
from her native T obago and the wider his-
tory of African transplantation. Philip, like
Kamau Brathwaite, has argued that lan-
guage was and continues to be one of the
most important sites of struggle between
the Old World and the New World, and
her Persephone also ﬁgures the “linguistic
rape and forced marriage between African
and English tongues.” Philip’s exploration
of displacement and marginality, and the
quest for reunion with the mother and the
retrieval or creation of a mother tongue, is
conducted with greatest intensity in a re-
markable triad of poems, “Discourse on the
Logic of Language,” “Universal Grammar,”
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 971 ---
PHILLIPS,C ARYL 883
and “The Question of Language Is the
Answer to Power.”
Lee M. Jenkins

PHILLIPS,C ARYL (1958–) 
Caryl Phillips is a novelist, travel writer,
and essayist, born on the Caribbean island
St. Kitts. He immigrated to Britain at the
age of 12 weeks in the arms of his mother
and grew up in white working-class
neighborhoods in Leeds, later Birming-
ham, “riddled with the confusions of being
Black and British,” as he puts it. Neither
his mother, who decided not to confront
her son with his past in order to facilitate
his integration into the new society, nor the
syllabuses of the educational establishments
he visited—including Queen’s College,
Oxford—provided any answers. As a cru-
cial experience in his life, Phillips therefore
often refers to his ﬁrst trip to the United
States where he came across the novels of
Richard Wright and Ralph Ellison, and dis-
covered in them a tradition that provided
him with a sense of belonging; this experi-
ence, eventually, also led to his decision to
confront his confusion and write.
Phillips’, career as a writer started in
1980 when his ﬁrst play, Strange Fruit, was
staged and published, followed by Where
There Is Darkness (1982) and The Shelter
(1984). After that, he continued to write
dramatic pieces (especially for the BBC)
and hung on to journalistic work (about
literature, music, and sports); this, how-
ever, he considered as his “other job” next
to what he truly intended to be, a novelist:
His ﬁctional debut The Final Passage was
published in 1985, followed by A State of
Independence (1986).
The unifying thematic core of Caryl
Phillips’s work fundamentally consists in
the human experience of uprooting and
displacement. Many of the themes he
traces in his novels were already addressed
in his dramatic work. The Final Passage,
covering the experience of a young West
Indian family emigrating to England, and
A State of Independence, whose protagonist
returns to the Caribbean after years of
English “exile,” for instance, closely link up
with the early plays. They also address
the tensions and turmoil both between ﬁrst-
and second-generation immigrants and
the West Indian and British cultures,
respectively.
Higher Ground (1989), his third novel,
marks a point in Phillips’s oeuvre when he
extends his (biographically influenced)
focus on the British-Caribbean axis to what
Paul Gilroy termed “the Black Atlantic.”
This is shown in the thematic scope of the
novel ranging from the sufferings of an
African collaborator in the last days of the
slave trade via the fate of a black prisoner in
the American South to the brief meeting of
a Caribbean immigrant and a Polish Holo-
caust survivor in London. It is, however,
also manifest in the novel’s rhizomorphic,
polyphonic structure that is to become a
fundamental characteristic of his later
work.
In Cambridge (1991), Phillips chooses
a singular setting on a Caribbean island in
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 972 ---
884 P LANTATIONS ANDPLANTATIONSYSTEMS
the early nineteenth century and essentially
juxtaposes the conflicting voices of a
planter’s daughter, Emily, and an elderly
educated slave, Cambridge. The poly-
phonic, fragmentary dimension of Cam-
bridge surfaces only at second sight, that is,
intertextually: the two narrative voices are in
fact pastiches, artistic recompositions of bits
and pieces of eighteenth- and nineteenth-
century travelogues on the one hand, and
slave narratives on the other.
With Crossing the River (1995) and
The Nature of Blood (1997), Phillips
continues his investigations of human dis-
placements in further historical depth and
aesthetically challenging forms. Crossing the
River comprises four fragments of narra-
tion, together spanning 250 years of black
Atlantic history: A tale of repatriation in
Liberia is followed by the experience of an
ex-slave in the American West; a slaver’s log
gives way to the diary of a white British
woman who falls in love with a black
American GI.
The Nature of Blood, while similarly
weaving four different narrative threads,
daringly juxtaposes issues of anti-Semitism
and racism. The majority of the novel is
dedicated to the Jewish girl Eva who goes
through the holocaust; her story, however,
is continually cut through by narratives
evoking Jewish victims of anti-Semitism in
ﬁfteenth-century Venice, Othello’s life in
Venice a century later, and ﬁnally the fate
of a young Ethiopian woman in Israel.
With his latest novel, Caryl Phillips has
returned to a contemporary setting some-
where in rural northern England. In A Dis-
tant Shore (2003), he stages the careful
mutual approaches of two social outsiders,
an aging English woman and a West
African refugee. It further testiﬁes to the
deeply political concern of Phillips’ art,
which nevertheless transports its messages
in lyrical, emotionally perceptive, and aes-
thetically complex forms. These qualities
also apply to the broad range of Phillips’s
nonﬁction. Notable publications in this
context are his travel writings in The
European Tribe (1987) and The Atlantic
Sound (2000), as well as his collection of
essays, A New World Order (2001).
Lars Eckstein

PLANTATIONS AND
PLANTATIONSYSTEMS
The variety of plantations and plantation
systems of Africa and the Americas devel-
oped between the early ﬁfteenth and late
nineteenth centuries. These large-landed
estates were mostly export-oriented enter-
prises, supplying sugar, rice, tobacco, in-
digo, and other key staples to northern
Atlantic markets. As the number of planta-
tions expanded after 1500, the demand for
laborers also increased, and European mer-
chants, planters, and colonial governments
turned to the forced enslavement of
millions of Africans.
It is difﬁcult to generalize about the na-
ture of plantations or plantation systems in
the Atlantic World because they evolved in
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 973 ---
PLANTATIONS ANDPLANTATIONSYSTEMS 885
a variety of climatic and regional zones.
Moreover, plantations differed in size, scale,
demographics, ownership, management,
living conditions, and what types of crops
were planted. Historian Philip D. Curtin
notes that the first plantations in the
Americas originated in the sugar-growing
estates of the Mediterranean and the
Madeira, Cape Verde, and Azores islands of
the eastern Atlantic. After 1500, Europeans
adapted these models to the soils and
climates of the Americas; still, variations
in the types of plantations increased even
more as Europeans cultivated newer
“American” crops, such as tobacco, coffee,
and cacao, although sugar production
dominated. The ﬁrst problem in establish-
ing plantations was that they were ex-
tremely labor intensive, often requiring
hundreds of laborers to function efﬁciently.
In certain parts of the Americas, Europeans
attempted to enslave Amerindian peoples,
but the indigenous populations declined
dramatically as a result of deadly diseases
that Europeans brought with them. In
response, Europeans imported African
slaves as the best and proven alternative to
chronic shortages of labor, yet they accom-
plished this on a much larger scale than had
been previously attempted.
Plantations and plantation systems
touched almost every aspect of economic
activity in the Americas. Living and work-
ing conditions varied greatly depending on
the region, and more often on the individ-
ual owner. African slaves not only worked
in various agricultural situations but also
near or within plantation households as do-
mestic servants, cooks, midwives, and arti-
sans. The vast majority of slaves that
worked on plantations originated from
West Africa, but they were commingled
with slaves from other regions even before
arrival to the Americas because slave traders
crudely mixed ethnic groups. In addition,
natural increases in slave populations were
rare due mainly to high death rates from
overwork, disease, and poor diets. Until
the early nineteenth century, planters
looked mostly to slave traders for addi-
tional workers. Crown and local authorities
enacted laws regulating the treatment of
slaves on plantations, but enforcement
depended in large measure on the behavior
of individual owners. In some regions of
Spanish and Portuguese America, for exam-
ple, slaves petitioned colonial courts for
freedom or recourse for excessive punish-
ments while others turned to religious
institutions. In addition, there is ample
evidence of planters manumitting slaves in
legal documents and wills. Still, laws gov-
erning plantation life tended to focus on
limiting the social, legal, sexual, cultural,
and political behavior of African slaves.
Legal codes in various parts of the Americas
indicate that plantation slaves had few
rights; they were more often not allowed to
receive an education, marry, or possess
weapons. Planters and local authorities
were particularly interested in keeping
Africans separate from other social groups
so that no class or racial alliances could
form to threaten the plantation system and
other colonial institutions. Penalties for
violating laws or rules were especially harsh
and inhumane, including whipping, beat-
ing, torture, rape, and death.
At the same time, policies designed to
control slave plantation laborers simply
could not be enforced because of the slaves’
resourceful ways of resisting. In the course
of their lives, African slaves resisted planta-
tion labor by employing a variety of non-
violent and violent resistance strategies. On
a broad level, personal confrontations (and
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 974 ---
886 P LANTATIONS ANDPLANTATIONSYSTEMS
not violent rebellions) were the most com-
mon expressions of slave resistance. Slaves
broke tools, allowed farm animals to es-
cape, and robbed crops or important agri-
cultural implements with much more
frequency than they engaged in violent
confrontations with their masters. Slaves
also escaped, and depending on the avail-
ability of mates, established sexual unions
with members of other racial groups. More
violent means of slave resistance included
spontaneous and organized revolts and
suicides. Rebellions occurred in Haiti and
Cuba that challenged plantation slavery. In
addition, the establishment of runaway (or
maroon) slave communities throughout
the Americas attest not only to the vitality
of slave resistance to plantation labor but
also the reproduction of cultural patterns
similar to those in Africa. Indeed, planta-
tions were sites for the retention and
mixture of African cultural traits. The resis-
tance that occurred on plantations affected
the trajectories of colonial politics and ex-
pended almost all of the resources, ener-
gies, and lives of both plantation owners
and slaves. The Spanish crown, for exam-
ple, decided to ban the importation of
slaves in some parts of the Americas be-
cause the cost of imposing authority upon
an increasingly resistant slave population
proved too much to bear.
Plantation slavery was clearly on the
decline in various parts of the Americas
by the nineteenth century, but plantations
were incredibly persistent, innovative,
dynamic, and adaptable institutions. In
Mexico, Colombia, and Argentina, planta-
tion slavery lasted until the early to mid-
nineteenth century after a long and
protracted death. In the United States,
Cuba, and Brazil, however, the plantation
system ended only in the latter part of the
nineteenth century. Moreover, the end of
the slave trade and eventually slavery in
the Americas did not mean the end of the
plantation system. In the West Indies, the
British abolished slavery in 1807, but
sugar plantations continued strong as colo-
nial authorities decided to import East
Indian and Chinese laborers to replace re-
cently emancipated black plantation work-
ers. In the late nineteenth and early twen-
tieth centuries, new sugar, cotton, and
rubber plantations emerged as European
powers took control of large swaths of
territory in Africa.
Jesse Hingson

POPULAR MUSIC,A MERICAN INFLUENCES ON AFRICAN 887
POPULAR MUSIC,A MERICAN
INFLUENCES ON AFRICAN
Contemporary African popular music has
had many elements contributing to its
evolution and development, the most
signiﬁcant being the rich eclectic cultural
diversity of the continent’s inhabitants and
the inﬂuence of foreign cultures. However,
American music styles, such as rumba,
jazz, blues, funk, reggae, soul, and rock,
have been the most inﬂuential. Just as
Africa impacted the music of the New
World in the aftermath of the transatlantic
slave trade, the Americas have reciprocated
by strongly influencing the music of
Africa. Music styles, musical thought, and
musical technology from North America,
Brazil, and the Caribbean have had a great
impact on African popular music because
Africans can easily relate to the historical
experience of blacks in the Americas. The
beats and rhythms of these imported styles
provide a visible link between Africa
and the Americas. African musicians see
in the discourse and aesthetics of their
American counterparts outstanding mod-
els to emulate.
Popular music is an expressive practice
and performance in African daily life. This
reservoir of African cultural values is a por-
trait of local realities, the motor of society,
and the soul of the people. Apart from the
entertainment and identity functions, pop-
ular music has become a singularly effective
weapon against socioeconomic and politi-
cal injustices in contemporary African soci-
eties. It speaks of social problems and prof-
fers possible solutions through its lyrics
that focus on such issues as politics, econ-
omy, health, literacy, working conditions,
nutrition, urbanization, and agriculture.
Hence, popular music may be described as
a powerful sense of people to name the
inequality they suffer from and recognize,
often with humor or bitter irony, their own
struggle and endurance, the desire for
change, and the belief in the possibility of
change.
In order to ensure relevance to the
needs of their immediate audience, most
musicians use local themes and rhythms.
However, with improved communication
and transportation, societies across conti-
nents and cultures have been and continue
to be tremendously inﬂuenced by one
another. Africa is no exception to this
trend, which entails conscious and/or
unconscious drawings from elements of
foreign cultures. The product of this
process is an African popular music that
combines local rhythms and tools with for-
eign music; it also leads to renewed creativ-
ity and a wider audience while retaining the
African ﬂavor.
Because African musicians realize that
their music draws strength from syn-
cretism, because they are eager to experi-
ment, and also because they are enticed by
the prospect of international sales, they are
very receptive to foreign rhythms, particu-
larly American styles. This receptiveness
has led to a fusion of African local music
styles and American music traditions, such
as rumba, jazz, gospel, funk, reggae, and
rock. These American inﬂuences result
from contacts between Africa and the
Americas, contacts that have more recently
been enhanced by the electronic media,
including radio, television, the Internet,
recordings, and satellite and cable
networks.
Many factors contributed to American
inﬂuences on popular music in Africa,
notably the long-standing transatlantic
connections that kept Africans in the Dias-
pora connected. Black inﬂuence from the

Americas started with the policy of return-
ing freed slaves from the United States,
Brazil, and the Caribbean to Africa in the
early nineteenth century. These returnees
had a tremendous musical effect on native
Africans. They brought with them dance
music styles originally from Africa but
adapted to the New World, where they cre-
ated an enormous impact before being fed
back into the mainstream of African music.
One of the earliest New World inﬂu-
ences on African popular music was that of
Afro-American and Caribbean sailors who
visited African ports—Monrovia, Free-
town, Cape Coast, Accra, Lagos, and Cape
T own, in the mid-nineteenth century and
introduced calypso, merengue, ragtime,
and minstrelsy to the continent. Caribbean
regimental bands stationed in West African
forts, American warships refueling along
African coasts during the American Civil
War in 1862, and the inﬂux of American
troops during World War II further spread
this early American inﬂuence. In most
cases, there was a small contingent of
African Americans on board who served as
cleaners and mess stewards, and also pro-
vided musical entertainment for the crew.
With increased urbanization and the
impact of Western culture, new music
styles that combine African and American
elements emerged largely in the cities that
provided leadership during the 1950s and
1960s in bringing about social, economic,
and political change in Africa—Accra
(Ghana), Lagos (Nigeria), Nairobi (Kenay),
Dar-es-Salam (Tanzania), Kinshasa, or
Leopoldville (Zaire), and the black ghettoes
of the cities in the Republic of South
Africa. These new forms include West
African highlife (showing certain
Caribbean traits), Congolese popular music
(reﬂecting Latin American inﬂuence), and
Southern African sabasaba and kwella (both
similar to American swing and jive music).
Additionally, Africa was not left out of
the great progress witnessed by the music
industry in the post–World War II years as
the art developed in different directions,
including style and technique. Manhattan
Research, the world’s ﬁrst electronic music
studio, was founded in 1946, and studios
started using magnetic tape for recording.
With the development of technology,
American electric and electronic instru-
ments spread, affecting the way musicians
played and having a repercussion on
African artists.
In the 1970s and 1980s numerous
African artists and musicians migrated to
Europe and the Americas to pursue a pro-
fessional career. Many traveled to the
United States to study at various institu-
tions including the Manhattan School of
Music in New York. In the process, they
were inﬂuenced by American sounds and
new recording technology, and subse-
quently they reinvented African music in
its contemporary form, with many varia-
tions and styles. The products of such
influences would create new rhythms
incorporating African sounds.
Similarly, visits and tours by African
American artists, such as Louis Armstrong,
veteran jazz saxophonist Paul Winter,
T rummy Young, and Edmund Hall, among
others, were a source of great inspiration.
Those visits afforded African popular musi-
cians to have ﬁrsthand experience with
American artists through exchanges and
personal contacts. Also, as African native
churches began to separate from those of
the white missionaries and take on an inde-
pendent existence, special styles of music
were developed. One source for these was
the American Negro spiritual, which

became an inspiration for Africans early in
the twentieth century.
Since then there has been a continuous
stream of American dance music styles to
Africa, bringing rumba, samba, conga
mambo, merengue, Dixieland jazz, bebop,
and pop music, including rock and roll,
soul, blues, twist, funk, and reggae, which
all became popular and made a tremendous
impact on African musicians. Local artists
began to imitate the newly introduced
American rhythms and styles; it was often a
matter of taking an African traditional style
or song and adapting it to American
sounds. In the postwar years (the 1950s
and 1960s), while highlife and calypso
transformed the musical scene in English-
speaking Africa, Latin American music and
Afro-Caribbean styles, particularly the
rumba and Afro-Cuban percussion, domi-
nated the French-speaking countries.
In the 1970s, American soul and rock
music spread in West Africa where it was
adapted to local realities to produce high-
life. Highlife music is the Ghanaian and
Nigerian ballroom music. Its instrumenta-
tion may consist of Western instruments,
such as saxophones, trumpets, trombones,
ﬂutes, and electric guitars, but there is
almost always a rhythmic ensemble consist-
ing of African drums, bells, xylophones,
mbiras (thumb-pianos), ﬂutes, and some-
times rattles, which backs up the melody
instruments. In order to produce rhythms
that ﬁt more easily into a Western musical
scheme, many highlife bands have come to
use Latin American rhythms. Among the
early pioneers of Ghanaian concert parties
and highlife are King Bruce and his Black
Beats, E. T . Mensah and his Ramblers
dance band, Roy Chicago, Ashanti Broth-
ers, Nana Ampadu, City Boys, and Hi-Life
International.
T rumpeter Victor Olaiya and guitarist
Bobby Benson led Nigerian highlife
music. Besides bringing calypso to West
Africa, Benson also formed in 1948 a band
called Bobby Benson Jam Session Orchestra,
which played pop, swing, ragtime, jazz, and
later highlife music. Other influential
Nigerian highlife bands include Rex Lawson’s
Mayors Dance Band, Osita Osadere’s
Soundmakers International, Oriental
Brothers International Band, Orlando
Owoh’s Omimah Band, and Oliver de
Coque’s Expo ’76 Ogene Super Sounds.
Ebenezer Obey modernized juju—the
African equivalent of American folk-rock,
derived from the samba, which was intro-
duced to Nigeria by the descendants of
freed Brazilian slaves—by drawing on high-
life. “King” Sunny Ade, a key ﬁgure of juju
music, emphasized the techniques of
Jamaican dub and sonic details. T o conﬁrm
their American connections, highlife bands
often take their names from American
models (e.g., the Ramblers, the Comets,
the Stargazers of Kumasi, the Black Beats,
the Modern King Stars, the Ambassador
Springboks), and they exhibit the inﬂuence
of the big-band styles of jazz and Western
pop that was so prominent in the 1940s.
Highlife was later influenced by
American jazz, rock, reggae, and hip-hop.
It absorbed many elements of jazz, espe-
cially in ordinary orchestras of wind and
string instruments. It also took on many
aspects of Afro-calypso and reggae
from guitar and Caribbean inspiration. The
introduction of soul and reggae in the
late 1960s and 1970s ushered in a very
creative era in African popular music,
bringing about Afro-rock, Afro-reggae, and
Afro-hip-hop.
The black American soul message
“Black and Proud” was taken up by a whole

Manu Dibango, Africa’s best-known

legendary jazzy sound on his album Soul
Makossa (1972). This album was followed

Rumba, originating from Latin America,
surfaced in the Congo Basin area in the
1940s and 1950s. Its spread was made pos-
sible thanks to the prevailing cosmopoli-
tanism and a relatively booming economy.
It was immediately embraced to enrich the
existing musical heritage with numerous
variations ranging from rumba-sukumu at
the beginning of the war to rumba-kara,
rumba-boucher, rumba-sukusu, and rumba
kiri-kiri or soukous, which is one of the
most popular music and dance styles today
in Africa. In the 1960s, the region was in-
vaded by American rock and Cuban salsa.
The Cuban rumba fused with African
rhythms to produce the ﬁrst distinct syn-
cretic dance style in Francophone Africa,
Congo music. Congo music later went
electric and incorporated a brass front
line, creating the popular Congo jazz style.
The most prominent Congo jazz groups
include Joseph “Grand Kalle” Kabasselleh’s
African Jazz, Jean Serge Essous’s O.K. Jazz,
Orchestre Bella Bella, “Franco” (François
Luambo Makiadi’)s T .P .O.K. Jazz, Tabu Ley
Rochereau’s African Fiesta (that played
Latin rhythms on the drums of rock
music), and Papa Wemba’s Viva La Musica
(that was inspired by Puerto Rican star Ray
Barreto and Otis Redding’s sweet soul).
As rumba penetrated in some places,
ragtime was shifting into Dixieland jazz in
other areas. Many local Dixie bands were
formed in South Africa, like the Dark
T own Strutters and the Big Four of Johan-
nesburg. Ragtime became part of the black
urban marabi music of the 1920s and
1930s. In the black urban centers where
different tribes met, and met with former
slaves from the Americas, a dance style
called “marabi” evolved. It was originally a
humble form of music, but it became sim-
ilar to the jazz music played by swing

1983, Lema released Kinshasa-Washington,
DC-Paris, an album that sums up his career
and reﬂects a mixture of inﬂuences: rumba,
rock, funk, reggae, jazz, tradition, and
modernity.
Kassav, the inventors of zouk, which
fuses Caribbean musical inﬂuences with
funk and rock to produce an unusual,
rhythmic cocktail, constitutes a signiﬁcant
factor in American inﬂuences on African
popular music. The group’s ﬁrst tour of a
dozen African countries was a huge success,
and many African artists emulated the
band. The interest in their music is no
doubt a reﬂection of the growing recogni-
tion for the culture of the Antilles, and for
Caribbean culture in general.
Many African artists have undertaken
pilgrimages in Jamaica, which boasts of
many excellent recording studios. For in-
stance, Côte D’Ivoire’s Alpha Blondy, who
calls himself an African Rasta and creates
Jah-centered anthems, made a pilgrimage
in 1983 to the legendary T uff Gong Studios
in Kingston, Jamaica, where he recorded
his phenomenal Jerusalem album with the
Wailers. He became the ﬁrst African star of
reggae with Jah Glory (1983). Ivoirian
Tiken Jah Fakoly, who has established him-
self as one of the ﬁgureheads of the new
reggae scene in Côte D’Ivoire, had a series
of concerts in 1999 in New York and
Philadelphia where he appeared on stage
with a Jamaican backing band. Tiken’s
Cours d’Histoire and Françafrique (2000)
were mixed in T uff Gong Studios and fused
reggae beat with hard-hitting lyrics. On
Apollo 95 (400 percent Zoblazo) by Côte
D’Ivoire’s Frederic Desire Ehui, known as
Meiway, are numerous guest performers,
including Jacob Desvarieux of Kassav from
the Caribbean island of Martinique. Ehui’s
Extratrerrestre features Cuban musicians
playing the brass and cord section and spic-
ing the album with Latino touches.
African music experienced a boom
in the 1980s as it absorbed elements of
American rock and pop music, including
musical rhythms, styles, and tools. This
absorption led to experimentations with
various aesthetic innovations in which musi-
cians incorporated elements of American
ﬂamenco, blues, soul, rock, jazz, reggae,
and funk and took advantage of Western
studio techniques, while remaining faith-
ful to their African roots by performing
traditional instruments. Malian musicians
T oumani Diabate and Ali Farka T oure
played African versions of the blues, while
Issa Bagayogo updated the traditions of Mali

to the age of electronic dance music in the

Several other African artists and groups

Senegalese Youssou N’Dour established

Hip-hop, the most ubiquitous musical
style in the world, is another African Amer-
ican cultural movement, which has had
tremendous inﬂuence on African contem-
porary popular music. This distinctly
urban American form has been absorbed
and transformed by African youth; it has
now led to the birth of an African rap,
including the original hip-hop of Nigeria,
South Africa, Cameroon, Senegal, Tanzania,
Ghana, Mozambique, Kenya, Angola,
Congo, and Mali. There are hundreds of
hip-hop groups in most African capitals.
They rhyme in Wolof, Malinke, Dioula,
Baoule, French, English, Fon and Yoruba,
and Jamaican patois; they sing in both
rhythm and blues and jail styles, which are
fused with the tones of the kora and ngoni
harp-lutes and balafon xylophone. How-
ever, very few of the African groups have
adopted the sexist language and violent im-
agery favored by some American rappers.
The end result is a sound that is distinctly
hip-hop with an African ﬂavor.
Senegal’s Positive Black Soul updated a
classic Orchestre Baobab rumba with skit-
tering beats, reggae-inﬂected ﬂows, and
spicy Mandingo-style guitar sound on Boul
Ma Mine. Similarly, South African rappers
have their own style known as “kwaito,” a
thumping hybrid that draws from hip-hop,
house music, and dance hall reggae, along-
side a mixture of local traditions, including
Zulu praise poetry. They rap in a Soweto-
bred form of slang some people call “tsotsi
taal,” which draws from Zulu, Afrikaans,
English, and other languages. In Abidjan,
hip-hop has become really important: the
youth listen to the rap sound and dress
in baggy jeans. Many rap groups have
emerged, including 1549, Parlement
Supreme Posse, M.A.M., Negromuffin,
and R.A.S., claiming they were inﬂuenced

by the music of Bob Marley, Michael

Starting at the end of the nineties, a

Ardiess started out in 1997 as a purely

American musicians continue to exert
an enormous inﬂuence on African musi-
cians even today. Contemporary African
popular music is a synthesis of cultures
(high and low), moods (upbeat, ecstatic,
melancholy, spiritual), genres (folk, elec-
tronic, jazz, classical, psychedelic), for-
mats (song, symphony, suite, jam), and
lifestyles (Western and Eastern). African
polyrhythms, Jamaican reggae and dub,
Brazilian pop music, and other forms have
all fully integrated. These developments,
made possible by the contacts that black
Africans have maintained with African
American societies in North and South

viable and ﬂexible, and by no means in
danger of imminent extinction. However,
given the social and cultural importance of
traditional music and dance, many African
countries are working hard to preserve and
protect them from undue American inﬂu-
ences. Indeed, as Ali Mazrui has stated,
Africa’s openness to new cultures is both its
strength and its weakness, demonstrating
its ability to learn from others and also sug-
gesting the danger of becoming dependent
and intellectually imitative.

PORTUGUESE EMPIRE
As the ﬁrst modern global empire, and the
last of the western European empires to
withdraw from its colonies, the Portuguese
empire established extensive connections
between Africa and the Americas based on
the slave trade. Portugal’s role in the T rans-
atlantic World, in terms of slavery and colo-
nialism, centered around its major colonies
of Angola, Brazil, and Mozambique. After
decolonization, Angola and Mozambique
became important sites of cold war conﬂict,
with their communist governments sup-
ported by communist governments in the
Americas, particularly Cuba, and insurgen-
cies supported by the United States.
The establishment of sugarcane planta-
tions in Brazil created a large demand for
African slave labor. This demand initiated
a lengthy, and brutal, connection between
Brazil and Portugal’s main African colony,
Angola, via the slave trade. Due to this
dependence on the Angolan slave trade,
Portugal abolished the slave trade in 1836,
quite late compared to other European
nations. For several decades the prohibition
against the slave trade was not enforced.
Portugal’s reliance on Angolan revenues
meant that there was little incentive to end
slavery.
Initially, the continuation of the slave
trade in Portuguese colonies was tied to
ongoing trade with Brazil, which was a
Portuguese colony until 1822. In Brazil,
the demand for slaves remained high into
the late 1800s. Although the Brazilian slave
trade was abolished in 1850, slavery
remained legal until the so-called “Golden
Law” of 1888 abolished slavery itself, mak-
ing Brazil the last country in the Western
Hemisphere to do so ofﬁcially.
Portuguese and Brazilian slave ships
traveled unhindered from African coastal
settlements until as late as 1845. Despite
the passage of an 1842 treaty with Britain
that declare the trade to be piracy, the slave
trade from Angola was continued with ship-
ments going to Brazil until around 1853
and to Cuba into the 1860s. An estimated
2 million slaves were transported from the
western coasts of Africa in the decades just
before and after 1850. Lacking local naval
bases, the British Royal Navy was ineffective
in interdicting slave ships and rescued only
around 3,000 slaves per year. Slave ship-
ments from the ports of Luanda and
Benguela on the Angolan coast continued
until the late 1860s, with Portuguese,
Brazilian, and Cuban slave traders replacing
British and French merchants.
The slave trade began to decline with
the closure of Brazilian slave markets.
However, the trade continued from Angola
to the islands of Sao T ome and Principe.
These shipments continued for decades,
disguised as contract labor to elude external
pressure against the trade.
Slavery was ﬁnally abolished ofﬁcially
in 1878. Nonetheless, many Africans
continued to suffer as slaves under ongoing
programs of contract and forced labor.
Many freed slaves had few options but to
remain with their former owners under the
same working conditions. Others who
attempted to maintain small farms were
pushed into forced labor, especially
through the use of taxes. Many labor
contractors and local authorities were for-
mer slave traders. Vagrancy laws made it
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 983 ---
POSTCOLONIAL STUDIES 895
possible for Africans not regularly em-
ployed to be drafted into labor without
remuneration. In effect, slavery and the
slave trade continued into the twentieth
century in Portuguese Africa.
After World War II, Portugal violently
resisted decolonization and African inde-
pendence. Beginning most forcefully in
1961, guerrilla movements in Portuguese
Africa, especially Angola, Mozambique,
and Portuguese Guinea (now Guinea-
Bissau) took a heavy toll on Portuguese
forces in the colonies and encouraged
domestic resistance in Portugal.
When the Salazar dictatorship in
Portugal fell in 1974, newly independent
Angola and Mozambique soon fell into
protracted civil wars. Their postindepen-
dence communist governments became
caught up in the proxy wars being fought
between the United States and the Soviet
Union during the cold war. In addition to
outright invasions by the South African
apartheid armies, communist governments
in Angola and Mozambique faced internal
insurgent groups supported by the United
States and its allies, including South Africa
and Zaire, now the Democratic Republic of
the Congo. During the cold war important
connections were created between newly
independent African countries and coun-
tries in the Americas. Nominally commu-
nist governments in the Americas, most
importantly Cuba, provided military, civil,
and technical support against what was
perceived as Western and U.S. imperialism.
Jeff Shantz
