POSTCOLONIAL STUDIES
Postcolonial studies is a theoretical term for
the analysis of the consequences of colo-
nialism, including but not limited to eco-
nomics, culture, and politics. Postcolonial
studies can only be deﬁned with an un-
derstanding of the term colonialism. The
strict deﬁnition of colonialism is the direct
or indirect rule of a country or region over
another by the means of political, military,
and economic institutions. The ruling
country or region is called the colonizer or
the metropolis, and the region being ruled is
called thecolony. Critical studies of the strict
deﬁnition of colonialism show how the in-
tricate relationship shared by the metropolis
and its colonies is based on bilateral but
unbalanced economic exchanges and the
displacement and marginalization of local
populations. However, colonialism can also
be understood in a broader sense. The broad
deﬁnition of colonialism is the unequal cul-
tural inﬂuence of a region over another by
its education, literature, or means of com-
munication. For instance, this deﬁnition
would identify the taste of Africa’s elite for
French literature or British poetry as a con-
sequence of colonialism, in which the
culture of the colonizer has had a strong
inﬂuence on the culture of the colonized.
In relationship to colonialism, then,
postcolonial studies is the analysis of the
consequences of this colonialist system, such
as economic exploitation, cultural marginal-
ization, and political exclusion. Postcolonial
studies are intrinsically linked with the global
process of reevaluating the relationship
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 984 ---
896 P OSTCOLONIAL STUDIES
between the metropolis and the colonies.
Postcolonial studies consist of three main
ﬁelds of work. The ﬁrst involves studies of
literature and poetry, such as the work of
Nigerian critic and poet Onwuchekwa Jemie
Chinweizu. The second involves studies
based on a variety of theories from philoso-
phy and social sciences, such as political
science, history, and sociology. This includes
the work of the Indian-T rinidadian writer
Vidiadhar Surajprasad Naipaul. The third
involves studies of works by visual and per-
formance artists, such as the work of Indian-
South African historian and art critic Sarat
Maharaj.
Much of postcolonial studies, especially
those of the twentieth century, focus on
how countries in Africa and the Americas
have “decolonized” themselves, since many
of these countries achieved governmental
self-determination in this era. Self-
determination is a process in which colo-
nized nations give themselves power over
their territories by the creation of their
own political institutions that are distinct
from those of the colonizer. The ways by
which these countries have acquired inde-
pendence can be classiﬁed in one of three
broad categories. The ﬁrst are countries
whose populations are mostly from the
metropolis, such as Argentina and, to some
extent, the United States. The second are
countries whose populations are of mixed
ethnic backgrounds, some from the colony
and some from the metropolis, such as
Brazil and South Africa. The third are coun-
tries whose populations consist of mostly
indigenous people that have either evacu-
ated their elite (who are from the metropo-
lis) from their land, or have ensured that the
political inﬂuence of the elite has declined
to almost none; this is the case for Congo or
Senegal.
Postcolonial studies are also interested
in structuration, a theory that implies that
the culture of colony, such as its literature,
food, and popular cinema, has a signiﬁcant
effect on the metropolis. More recently,
postcolonial studies have considered the
effects of structuration on Western Europe
and North America through the adoption
of exotic cultural products. Theorists such
as Edward Said have been very critical
toward this tendency. In fact, postcolonial
theorists argue that this interest for exotic
culture is only oriented around the advan-
tages it can bring to Western countries.
Postcolonial studies owe much to au-
thors of political science and philosophy.
In fact, the concepts of ideology, hege-
mony, and imperialism developed during
the twentieth century by political philoso-
phers Antonio Gramsci and Georg Lukacs
have been very influential. These two
European authors have been critical of the
role Western countries have had on the re-
gions of their empire. Ideology is an ensem-
ble of beliefs that determine the acts of a
government or a society. For postcolonial
theorists, it means that many actions from
the agents of the metropolis are inﬂuenced
by the ideology of colonialism. Hegemony
is the ideological and cultural domination of
the metropolis over the colonies. Imperialism
is deﬁned by Gramsci, Lukacs, and other
postcolonial theorists in a way very similar
to colonialism, having both a strict and a
broad sense. Indeed, the concepts of impe-
rialism and colonialism can be seen as in-
terchangeable. Imperialism is the result of
the actions taken by the metropolis—the
effects of colonialism on the metropolis.
For instance, the effects of imperialism can
be measured by the existence of a powerful
and authoritarian transportation industry
in the cities of the Northern Hemisphere
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 985 ---
POSTCOLONIAL STUDIES 897
or the broad availability of exotic fruits
in most groceries of countries of North
America and Western Europe. Colonialism,
on the other hand, is the result of this
power on the colonies—the effects of colo-
nialism on the colony. For example, the
noted presence of farmers of European
descent in South Africa remind people from
the former colonies the effects the metrop-
olis had on their countries during the
colonial period.
Since the end of World War II, the
works and actions of anticolonialist politi-
cal authors such as the Guinean theorist
and political activist Amilcar Cabral,
the Martiniquan poet and politician Aimé
Césaire, the Martiriquan psychiatrist Frantz
Fanon, the Argentine revolutionary Ernesto
“Che” Guevara, and the Vietnamese revolu-
tionary Ho Chi Minh have changed the re-
lationships between countries from North
America and Western Europe and former
colonies from Latin America, Africa, and
Asia. Their works and actions have there-
fore been very inﬂuential on postcolonial
theories and studies. Their work typically
involves stirring descriptions of the strug-
gles of the people from the colonies. Some
wrote against the terrible living conditions
in the colonies. Others were more radical
by staging political coups or revolutionary
movements against the occupation of the
colonies by Western countries. These anti-
colonialist political authors and their
followers were important forces in the
self-determination of colonies and serve
as inspirational examples to many natives
from former colonies throughout the
world.
In the 1960s, poststructural philoso-
phers such as the French Michel Foucault
and literary critics like Russian theorist
Mikhail Bakhtin built new theories that
connected written or spoken discourses to
the dynamics of power. These theories that
see discourse as a constructed conscious or
unconscious extension of politics have been
very instrumental for postcolonial studies.
For example, some scholars compare the
British writer Rudyard Kipling’s literature
to the interests of the British Empire in
India.
Even if the theoretical sources of post-
colonial studies owe a lot to international
philosophy and critical studies, currently,
postcolonial studies are overwhelmingly
dominated by English-speaking scholars
or by studies widely distributed among
English-speaking scholars. This is especially
true for postcolonial studies covering
Latin America. For instance, authors like
Uruguayan Eduardo Galeano and the
Mexicans Carlos Fuentes and Octavio Paz
criticize both the colonial past of Spain and
the inﬂuence of the United States over
Latin America, but their works are rarely
considered postcolonial. There are two
possible explanations for this fact. The ﬁrst
explanation is biographical: Their ancestors
were part of the elite ruling over the local
indigenous people. However, postcolonial
studies challenge this fact. The second,
more likely explanation, is cultural: Post-
colonial studies are associated with the
former British Empire more than any other
colonizing country. As a matter of fact,
most of the important postcolonial schol-
ars, such as the Palestinian-American liter-
ary critic Edward Said, the South Asian
feminist Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak, and
the Jamaican-British sociologist Stuart
Hall, are from countries or regions linked
to the British Empire. In addition, several
authors do not consider themselves as post-
colonialists because they feel that the cate-
gory is too restrictive for their work. This is
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 986 ---
898 P RE-COLUMBIAN AMERICA
true for Spivak, who has rejected the label
“postcolonial” because she ﬁnds it inade-
quate to refer to the contemporary situa-
tion of globalization.
One of the most signiﬁcant criticisms
against postcolonial studies is that it leads
to the general fragmentation of scholarly
knowledge. Marxist theorists claim that
most postcolonial studies focus on micro-
historical biographies, which are too
speciﬁc, and, as a result, are unable to be
inserted in the larger picture of colonial
history. Other theorists like Homi K.
Bhabha have criticized postcolonial studies
for focusing too much on the opposition
against the colonizer by the colonized. In
other words, postcolonial studies tend to
describe the colonized with speciﬁc features
while simplifying the colonizer.
Despite all the criticisms raised against
postcolonial studies, it is remarkable that
postcolonial theorists have been instrumen-
tal in the processes of decolonization and
emancipation after the second part of the
twentieth century. Postcolonial theorists
have also been inﬂuential not only in de-
centralizing the centers of study and
knowledge from Western countries to the
former colonies but in giving a voice to
the most marginalized scholars—the in-
digenous and women—from the former
colonies of European countries.
Dmitri della Faille de Leverghem

PRE-COLUMBIAN AMERICA
Despite some technological limitations,
a few Native American civilizations had
achieved a high level of development before
the arrival of European explorers. Long
isolated from outside inﬂuences, however,
local inhabitants suffered a demographic
catastrophe when European and African
diseases were introduced in the late
ﬁfteenth century.
Human Settlement
The Americas were the last major conti-
nents to be settled by humans. There is
ample archeological evidence proving that
humans were present in the Americas by
the end of the Pleistocene epoch 11,000
years ago. How and when humans entered
the continents, however, remain a matter of
debate. The prevailing theory holds that
Clovis hunters arrived in North America
c. 10,000 BCE using a land bridge then
linking Alaska to Siberia. The theory is
supported by the dearth of human remains
prior to that date, and physical and genetic
similarities between Native Americans and
East Asians. It is based on the assumption
that humans settled the entire North
America continent very quickly after they
moved into Alaska to account for skeletal
remains found in South America.
A rival theory, based on the discovery of
skeletons in Chile and Peru dated prior to
10,000 BCE, holds that humans entered
the Western Hemisphere earlier, or followed
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 987 ---
PRE-COLUMBIAN AMERICA 899
a different route. Some scholars believe that
humans crossed the Bering Strait before
the formation of a continental ice sheet in
Canada in 20,000 BCE. Others hold that
Paciﬁc Islanders could have reached the
Paciﬁc coast of South America by boat, thus
explaining the early presence of human
remains in that area.
North America
Despite their common ancestry, pre-
Columbian civilizations were marked by
remarkable cultural and linguistic diversity.
In North America, where 2 to 10 million
people lived by 1500, scholars have identi-
ﬁed six major geographic groupings. The
subarctic area covering much of Canada
was too cold to sustain agriculture, so it was
home to nomadic hunters, gatherers, and
ﬁshermen who followed herds of caribou.
Farther south, between the Atlantic Ocean
and the Mississippi River, inhabitants sup-
plemented deer hunting with the cultiva-
tion of corn, beans, and squash. They built
permanent, fortiﬁed villages and burial
mounds.
In the Great Plains, Native Americans
were divided between sedentary farmers
growing corn and living in earthen houses
and buffalo-hunting nomads traveling by
foot (horses were not introduced until the
Spanish voyages of exploration). Neighbor-
ing tribes in the Rocky Mountains area,
such as the Nez Percé and the Shoshone,
were limited by the dry, harsh environment
they lived in. In the Paciﬁc Northwest,
abundant wildlife and high rainfall sup-
ported a large population, such as the
Kwakiutl and the Nootka, who lived off
ﬁshing (salmon) and hunting (deer, seals)
and produced elaborate art. The American
Southwest is best remembered for the pres-
ence of Pueblo Indians living in communal
cliff dwellings, but their numbers dwindled
before 1500 due to climate change and
external attacks.
Mexico, Central America,
and the Caribbean
With the exception of the Incas, the
most advanced Native American civiliza-
tions were found in Mexico and Central
America. The city of T eotihuacán outside
Mexico City shows that a major urban
center ﬂourished around 300 to 900 CE.
The city’s large streets and market squares
suggests that it was at the center of a signif-
icant trade network. T eotihuacán’s massive
buildings, most notably the pyramids of
the Sun and of the Moon, also prove that
the city was home to an elaborate social
organization and religion. This civilization
was followed by the T oltecs (tenth to thir-
teenth centuries). Skilled in metal and
stonework, the T oltecs shared many charac-
teristics with their Aztec successors, includ-
ing human sacriﬁce, a 52-year calendar,
and worship of the sun and of the feathered
serpent Quetzalcoatl.
The Aztecs were the most powerful
entity when Spaniards, led by Hernán
Cortés, entered Mexico in 1519. They were
relative newcomers who had settled in a
swamp of Lake T excoco (under present-day
Mexico City) c. 1325. According to the
tradition, they chose the site because they
had seen an eagle devouring a snake on a
cactus and had interpreted it as a divine
omen. The area was already settled by more
powerful groups, so the Aztecs most likely
contented themselves with the least appeal-
ing plot. Despite such inauspicious begin-
nings, the Aztecs built a large capital
(T enochtitlán), which by the early six-
teenth century numbered a quarter million
inhabitants and was remarkable for its large
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 988 ---
900 P RE-COLUMBIAN AMERICA
pyramids, markets, raised ﬁelds ( chinam-
pas), canals, and causeways linking the
island city to the shores of Lake T excoco.
They allied themselves with neighboring
cities, then subdued them and created an
empire stretching from the Paciﬁc to the
Gulf of Mexico that encompassed ﬁve
million subjects by 1500.
Aztec culture, which incorporated many
local traditions inherited from T eotihuacán
and the T oltecs, was warlike and religious.
The Aztecs worshiped a variety of gods;
Quetzalcoatl was particularly popular with
the lower class as a redeemer god whose
return would bring an era of justice.
Most gods required human sacriﬁce, par-
ticularly the god of war and of the sun,
Huitzilopochtli. The Aztecs were afraid
that the sun might not return, particularly
at the end of the 52-year calendar cycle, so
they sacriﬁced dozens of thousands of
victims in the hope that blood offerings
would convince the sun to rise again.
Preferably, such victims were chosen
among prisoners captured during the con-
quest of neighboring cities or during battle
reenactments staged with already subdued
cities (Flower Wars).
Farther south in southern Mexico and
Central America, the Olmecs (1200–400
BCE) were renowned for their pyramids
and colossal statues made of basalt. Much
of the Olmec culture survived under the
Maya, whose classic period dates from 300
to 900 CE. Organized around independent
city-states such as Palenque, Tikal, and
Uxmal, the Mayas built steep stone pyra-
mids and magniﬁcent carvings. Agricul-
tural production was intensive, allowing for
high density of settlement in the classical
period and the use of cocoa beans as a form
of currency. The Mayas also had advanced
mathematics, a calendar, and a complex
writing system. The Mayas survived until
the Spanish conquest, though by the ﬁf-
teenth century large city centers had given
way to small villages.
With the exception of the Guanata-
habey, a people of western Cuba about
which little is known, Caribbean islands
were home to two major groups: the Tainos
and the Caribs. The Tainos, who inhabited
the Greater Antilles (Bahamas, Cuba,
Jamaica, Hispaniola, and Puerto Rico), re-
lied on ﬁshing and the cultivation of yams
and cassava to sustain a large population of
maybe 500,000 on Hispaniola alone. They
were organized in chiefdoms led by
caciques, practiced a ballgame in courts
called batey, and worshipped fetishes of
spirits and ancestors (zemis). The Caribs,
who occupied smaller islands such as
Guadeloupe in the Lesser Antilles, were
more warlike. Using canoes and bows, they
organized raids to Taino islands to seize
female captives.
South America 
Diversity also marked the human settle-
ment of South America. The area west of
the Andes, temperate and dry, hosted civi-
lizations far more advanced than those
found in the low-lying, humid basin of
the Amazon. The Arawak inhabitants of
Guiana and Venezuela were closely related
to the Caribs of the Antilles. The Amazon
basin itself was home to the Jivaros and the
T upi-Guarani, who lived off subsistence
agriculture and hunting in the difﬁcult
rainforest environment. First described by
Ferdinand Magellan in 1520, the T ehuelches
of Patagonia (Argentina) were known as tall
warriors and hunters. The inhospitable
area around Cape Horn harbored Fuegian
people surviving on small-scale hunting and
ﬁshing.

PRE-COLUMBIAN AMERICA 901
The Andean mountains of Peru and
Bolivia were home to the most advanced
civilizations of South America, including
the Chimu, the Mochica, the Nazca,
and most notably the Incas, who by the
fifteenth century had built an empire
stretching from Colombia to Chile and
numbered ten million people, including
the dominant Quechua. Like many other
Native American civilizations, the Incas
suffered from key technological drawbacks.
They pounded gold but did not smelt iron;
they lacked large draft animals (except
llamas and alpacas); they did not use the
wheel and gunpowder. Contrary to the
Aztecs and the Mayas, the Incas were illit-
erate and had to content themselves with a
memory aid (quipu).
Despite these limitations, the empire
was noted for its extensive hierarchy,
ranging from the emperor himself (also
called the Inca and claiming to be a direct
descendant of the sun-god Inti) to provin-
cial governors and village leaders. Dead
Incas were mummified, given living
quarters and servants, and consulted on
state matters. The imperial bureaucracy
ﬁnanced an army, an extensive network of
roads, state granaries, and public temples.
The empire’s organizational skills were
useful in transporting food when some
provinces experienced famine. They also
allowed the Inca to levy a labor tax, or
mita, which compelled peasants to work
on the Inca’s ﬁelds and on public monu-
ments. The Incas are famous for architec-
tural masterpieces such as the palaces
in the capital Cuzco, the fortress at
Sacsahuamán, and the mountain retreat
in Machu Pichu. The Incas also devel-
oped various strains of corn and potatoes
adapted to the many ecosystems encoun-
tered in the empire.
Contacts with the 
Outside World 
Human interaction with the American
continents began long before Christopher
Columbus “discovered” the New World. As
explained above, East Asians, and possibly
Paciﬁc Islanders, entered Alaska and Peru
over 10,000 years ago. Viking sailors, who
colonized Iceland and Greenland from
Scandinavia, claimed in their sagas that
Leif Ericsson visited Vineland (present-day
Newfoundland) c. 1000 CE. The story has
since been corroborated by archeological
evidence. European ﬁshermen routinely
ﬁshed cod in the Grand Banks off the
Canadian coast in the ﬁfteenth century. A
few scholars, such as Gavin Menzies in
1421: The Year China Discovered America
(2002) and Louise Levathes in When China
Ruled the Seas (1997), suggest that Chinese
navigators may have sailed to the Americas
before Columbus did, but evidence for this
latter claim remains sketchy.
Western exploration of the Americas
took off following Columbus’s 1492 voyage
to the Bahamas, Cuba, and Hispaniola.
Columbus undertook an additional three
voyages that reconnoitered the Caribbean
Sea and the coast of Central America. He
was followed in the ﬁrst three decades
of the sixteenth century by numerous
European explorers. Juan Ponce de León
explored Florida. Amerigo Vespucci sailed
down the coast of Brazil. Ferdinand
Magellan stopped in Argentina and
southern Chile on his way to the Paciﬁc
Ocean. Vasco de Balboa walked across the
Isthmus of Panama. Cortés conquered
southern Mexico. Francisco Pizarro con-
quered the Inca empire. Hernando de Soto
and Francisco de Coronado explored the
North American South and Southwest.
John and Sebastian Cabot sailed up the
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 990 ---
902 P RICE-MARS,J EAN
Atlantic coast of North America looking
for a Northwest Passage to Asia.
European interaction with pre-
Columbian civilizations proved generally
disastrous to the latter. Spanish explorers,
most notably Columbus in Hispaniola,
Cortés in Mexico, and Pizarro in Peru,
imposed Spanish rule by force and de-
stroyed local elites who refused to cooper-
ate. Awarded gifts of land and native labor
(encomienda and repartimiento), Spanish
conquistadors forced their subjects to work
for free in mines and on agricultural estates.
Such atrocities, well documented in
Bartolome de las Casas’sHistory of the Indies,
led Spanish king Charles V to outlaw future
encomiendas in his New Laws of the Indies
(1542). The ban indirectly led to European
reliance on white indentured labor, and, ul-
timately, African slave labor as a substitute
for forced Native American labor.
Cross-Atlantic interaction also led to
the exchange of germs, crops, and animals
between Europe, Africa, and America
(Columbian Exchange). The introduction
of smallpox, whooping cough, measles,
typhus, the plague, and later yellow
fever and malaria had devastating conse-
quences among Native Americans. In
North America, smallpox was occasionally
transmitted on purpose by settlers desirous
to rid themselves of local competitors; in
Latin America, Spaniards generally had
no intention of destroying a valuable labor
force. Whether intentional or not, the
Columbian Exchange resulted in the death
of 90% of the native population. In the
Caribbean, the Tainos had virtually
disappeared within 50 years of the Spanish
conquest. In some other countries, native
populations eventually rebounded and
there is a signiﬁcant portion of pure-
blooded or mixed blood Native Americans
(mestizos if they descend from Europeans,
zambos if they descend from Africans) in
Mexico (including Aztecs and Mayas), Peru
(Quechua), and Paraguay (Guarani). Pre-
Columbian populations also fared rela-
tively well in areas devoid of precious
metals and unsuited for plantation agricul-
ture, and thus unappealing to European
settlers. The Araucanians of southern
Chile opposed Spanish conquerors such as
Pedro de Valdivia and maintained their
independence until a war in 1880–1881.
Even today, Amazonian tribes continue to
live independently under the Brazilian gov-
ernment’s supervision.

PRICE-MARS,J EAN
(1876–1969) 
Jean Price-Mars, who served as a teacher,
ethnologist, historian, statesman, and
diplomat, was the foremost apostle of a
Haitian intellectual reawakening that
would acknowledge the country’s African
roots. Price-Mars was born on October 15,
1876, in Grande Rivière du Nord of Jean
Eléomont Mars, a planter and deputy, and
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 991 ---
PRICE-MARS,J EAN 903
Fortuna Delcour Michel. The name
“Price” was added in deference to Hannibal
Price, president of the Chamber of
Deputies and author of The Rehabilitation
of the Black Race by the Republic of Haiti
(1900). In a country where name recogni-
tion plays a great role, Price-Mars had a
distinguished heritage. On his maternal
side, his grandmother, Elizabeth P . Godart,
claimed that she was related to an epony-
mous mulatto who died with Vincent
Ogé’s 1791 rebellion. Jean-Baptiste Mars,
his father’s ancestor, was an African slave
who bought his freedom, fought with the
American revolutionaries at Savannah,
then represented Haiti’s blacks at the his-
toric February 4, 1794, French National
Assembly session that abolished slavery in
the French colonies. Price-Mars was also
related to Tirésias Simon Sam and Vilbrun
Gauillaume Sam, both of whom became
president of Haiti during Price-Mars’
youth.
At ﬁrst home-schooled by his father,
Price-Mars enjoyed an education few black
Haitians of his era beneﬁted from. He
attended the Collège Henri Grégoire in
Cap Haïtien, then the Lycée Pétion in 
Port-au-Prince, then studied medicine
in Port-au-Prince and Paris. While in Paris,
he met young nationalist Haitian intellec-
tuals such as Windsor Bellegarde, and was
appalled by the racist “science” then popu-
lar in European countries, most notably
Gustave Le Bon’s Laws of the Evolution of
Peoples (1894). A 1903 trip to the United
States brought home the reality that Haiti
had fallen technologically behind its pow-
erful neighbor. His family ties landed him
various posts in the Haitian Embassy in
Paris, Berlin, and Washington, an election
as deputy (1907), and a position as inspec-
tor of Haiti’s schools.
Price-Mars, who had already called on
fellow members of the elite to uplift them-
selves in the review L ’Essor (founded in
1912), was pushed to greater intellectual
activism by the July 28, 1915, U.S. inva-
sion of Haiti. Price-Mars considered the
U.S. occupation, lasting until 1934, to be a
humiliation. The invasion’s quick military
success seemed to prove the theory that
whites were inherently superior to blacks;
and Price-Mars’s relatives were partially
responsible for the political instability that
prompted the United States to intervene.
In parallel to his career as a history teacher
at the Lycée Pétion and as a country doctor,
Price-Mars delivered a series of lectures,
which, in addition to his world-famous
Ainsi parla l’Oncle (1928), established his
reputation as an intellectual. The Haitian
elite, he argued, was responsible for the
country’s decline because of its divided
Haitian author, Jean Price-Mars. (Library of Congress)

904 P RINCE,M ARY
loyalties as a racially African elite looking
up to European, particularly French,
culture.
A founder of the Society of Haitian
History and Geography (1922) and the
Institute of Ethnology, Price-Mars showed
that much of Haiti’s popular culture, in-
cluding Voodoo and Creole, were of
African origin, and that this was nothing to
be ashamed about. Animism shared many
of Christianity’s core values; Voodoo was
not a satanic cult, but a syncretism reﬂect-
ing Africans’ respect for their ancestors and
natural powers. The African race’s alleged
inferiority was a myth. Aside from Thus
Spoke the Uncle, Price-Mars published La
vocation de l’élite (1919), Une étape de
l’évolution haïtienne (1929), Formation
ethnique, folklore et culture du peuple haïtien
(1939), Jean-Pierre Boyer Bazelais et le
drame de Miragoâne (1948), La République
d’Haïti et la République Dominicaine
(1953), De Saint-Domingue à Haïti(1959),
Silhouettes de nègres et de négrophiles(1960),
and De la préhistoire d’Afrique à l’histoire
d’Haïti (1961).
The mulatto elite was offended by
Price-Mars’s prodding, but young intellec-
tuals, especially black ones, were respon-
sive. T wo of his students, François Duvalier
and Dumarsais Estimé, later became presi-
dents. Writer Jacques Roumain (author of
Gouverneurs de la rosée, 1944) was one of
his protégés. Abroad, personalities as di-
verse as Stokely Carmichael, Aimé Césaire,
and Léopold Sédar Senghor recognized
Price-Mars as a pioneer of Negritude. In
1956, admirers published a collection of
essays entitled Témoignages sur l’oeuvre et la
vie du Dr. Jean Price-Mars. Price-Mars’s ac-
claim as an intellectual was not matched
in the political arena. Failing several times
to be elected president, he had to content
himself with being a senator, foreign minis-
ter, minister of education, and ambassador
to the Dominican Republic and France.
Jean Price-Mars died on March 1, 1969, in
Pétionville. He had married Clara Perez in
1930; their daughter Marie-Madeleine was
born in 1932 (Price-Mars had also fathered
a son, Louis, in 1907).

PRINCE,M ARY (1788–?) 
Mary Prince was the Bermuda-born author
of The History of Mary Prince, A West
Indian Slave (1831), a slave narrative that
was a bestseller and inﬂuential to British
abolitionism. Most of the biographical and
historical information known about Mary
Prince comes from this account. Published
by the Anti-Slavery Society in London and
Edinburgh, it ran to three editions that year
alone and was crucial in rousing public
support for the abolitionist cause. In 1829
Prince had presented a petition to Parlia-
ment appealing for manumission from
her owner James Wood of Antigua. Lord
Stowell’s judgment in 1828 on the case of
Grace Jones meant that slave owners were
not obliged to manumit slaves brought to
Britain. Accompanied by a proposed bill
for the emancipation of all British slaves,
Prince’s petition was unsuccessful but was
part of a multipronged and powerful
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 993 ---
PRINCE,M ARY 905
campaign that was to culminate in the
passing of the Emancipation Act in 1833.
Mary Prince’sHistory remains unique,
being the only account published in Britain
by a female slave relating in ﬁrst-person nar-
rative the experience of West Indian slavery.
Her history was written while Prince was a
servant to Thomas Pringle, secretary of the
Anti-Slavery Society. Susanna Strickland,
later Susanna Moodie, transcribed the nar-
rative and Pringle, who was also a poet,
edited the transcription. The History is
therefore a collaborative and literary enter-
prise, crafted as a sentimental yet highly
effective piece of writing. Prince details the
emotional suffering of slavery, physical and
sexual abuse, as well as her many resistances,
thus exploiting the roles of both the “good
slave” and the “noble rebel.” Written in the
mode of Romantic abolitionist discourse,
the History achieves the effect of sounding
like the unmediated voice of Prince directly
appealing to the British public. She is rep-
resented as a truthful eyewitness and
spokesperson for all slaves, whose task is to
inform the public of slave suffering and of
the moral turpitude of the plantocracy.
Prince was born in Bermuda in the
Devonshire parish in 1788 into the owner-
ship of a farmer, Charles Myners. Her
mother was a household slave, her father
was a sawyer, and she had siblings. When
Myners died Prince passed into the posses-
sion of Captain Williams. Until the age
of twelve Mary was a companion to
Williams’s daughter. When the estate was
sold off, the Prince family was dispersed.
She was bought by Captain Ingham of
Spanish Point. After ﬁve years of severe
abuse, Prince was sold at her own request to
a Mr. D—. He owned land on the remote
T urk’s Island where the salt industry
supplied Bermuda with its main income.
For about ten years Prince labored in the
grueling salt ponds until D—returned to
Bermuda. At around the age of thirty,
Prince asked to be sold to the Woods family,
who took her to Antigua, a relatively liberal
environment for British slaves. The Woods’s
household was another violent regime, yet
Prince took steps toward freedom. She
saved money through huckstering and hints
at a relationship she had with a white man,
Captain Abbot, who tried to buy her free-
dom. Prince never mentions having any
children. She later joined the Moravian
Church, where she met her future husband,
a free black named Daniel James.
In her mid-forties Prince came to
England with the Woods family hoping
they would free her. However, the Woodses
were intransigent. Prince was forced to leave
them and came under the direction of the
Moravians and Anti-Slavery Society. Having
sustained many injuries incurred by her
masters’ violence, by her middle age Prince
had arthritis, was lame and going blind. She
is described in a court transcript of 1833,
in which the Woods family won a case of
libel against Thomas Pringle over the
History’s content. After this date there are no
further records of Mary Prince. It is uncer-
tain whether she was able to rejoin her hus-
band as a free woman in Antigua. Still, she
remains a key ﬁgure of slave resistance.
Kerry Sinanan

906 P UERTO RICO
PUERTO RICO
Like most of the Caribbean, Puerto Rico is
a racially mixed island whose populace is
descended from African, European, and
indigenous peoples. As a result, Puerto
Ricans acknowledge this tri-part past by re-
ferring to the “three roots” of Puerto Rican
culture, each of which is imagined to have
contributed something unique to the
historical and contemporary fabric of
Puerto Rican culture. From the African
root comes associations with labor, food,
and dance; from the Spanish, high culture,
learning, and Catholicism; from the indige-
nous, associations with folk traditions,
nature, and a pre-Columbian spirituality.
A brief consideration of these associations
reveals the vast differences between the
races in Puerto Rico in terms of power and
social position, with the Spanish compo-
nent occupying the highest position, the
indigenous the middle, and the African the
bottom. Though contemporary Puerto
Rican culture asserts a universal sharing of
these racial components (all Puerto Ricans
being some combination of all three roots)
and a color-blind social structure, both
history and recent scholarship calls this
into question.
Some scholars have argued that Puerto
Rico’s overlapping history of colonialism,
migration, and slavery up to the nineteenth
century resulted in a popular and national
culture that is fundamentally Afro-Mestizo
in character, not white-Creole as dominant
iconography would suggest. As Jose Luis
González points out in his text Puerto Rico:
The Four Storeyed Country, by the nine-
teenth century the colonial bourgeoisie
of Puerto Rico was not made up of native
born Puerto Ricans, but actually consisted
of first generation immigrants from
Corsica, Mallorca, the Canary Islands, and
other Caribbean and European locations.
As a result, González argues that the ﬁrst
Puerto Ricans—that is the ﬁrst people to
imagine themselves as being from Puerto
Rico—were not white-Creoles, they were
Afro-Mestizo Puerto Ricans. Part of the
reason for this, González argues, is that
Afro-Puerto Ricans were tied to the land in
a way that the foreign-born elite were not:
they were slaves, and they were the one
group of people who could not conceive of
home outside of the island.
Since Puerto Rico has a dual colonial
past as both a former colony of Spain and a
current Free Associated Commonwealth of
the United States, the issue of national
identity is one that is fraught and trouble-
some. The complications of a foreign-born
bourgeoisie and elite in the eighteenth and
nineteenth centuries (whose cultural iden-
tity and allegiance were tied to their places
of origin, as the continued use of their
native languages suggests) gave way in the
twentieth century to the implications of
U.S. citizenship. Consequently, the ques-
tion of Puerto Rican identity as a national
identity was left unanswered and in crisis.
As the United States exerted political
authority over the island in the twentieth
century, the issue of race and identity came
to the forefront. On the one hand, the
United States’s racial black/white binary, de-
lineated by one drop rules, had limited
if any applicability for the racially mixed
island. On the other hand, Puerto Rico and
its population came to be popularly repre-
sented and imagined as a white population.
In distinction to Cuba, for example, which
was often depicted as a dark, unruly, and
savage ﬁgure in the popular political car-
toons of the early twentieth century, Puerto
Rico was depicted as a white and domicile
ﬁgure, often taking the form of a white
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 995 ---
PUERTO RICO 907
child or woman in need of Uncle Sam’s
help and tutelage. What this use of imagery
suggested was that in order for Puerto Rico
to be part of the United States, the issue of
race needed to be resolved (or at least imag-
ined) in such a way that it could be a part
of the United States while remaining apart
from it, a move that the Supreme Court
called “foreign in a domestic sense.” This
resolution was accomplished by imagining
Puerto Rico and Puerto Ricans as a white-
Creole population, effectively obfuscating
African contributions by privileging the
indigenous and Spanish.
Though the ofﬁcial distance from the
African heritage of Puerto Rico is deeply
troubling, this is not to say that black Puerto
Rican identity is nonexistent. Jose Luis
González argues that though black Puerto
Ricans may be excluded from discourses of
high culture, the popular culture of Puerto
Rico is deeply indebted to its African roots.
Everyday examples of this abound, but the
most analyzed African-inﬂuenced contribu-
tions to Puerto Rican culture are tied to the
(stereotypically) sensual: food, dance, and
music. For example, Puerto Rican cuisine
popularly utilizes foods like yucca, which
have traditional African roots and were an
important part of the slave diet, while
rhythms and beats like bomba are heavily
indebted to African traditions.
Another important aspect of Afro-
Puerto Rican identity occurs within the
Puerto Rican Diaspora, in large urban
centers within the United States like New
York City, Chicago, and Philadelphia. The
major waves of Puerto Rican migration took
place between 1940 and 1970, when nearly
a third of the entire Puerto Rican popula-
tion migrated. This time also coincided with
a major crisis and shift in American racial
classiﬁcation and separation (typiﬁed by Jim
Crow laws). Since many Puerto Rican fam-
ilies consist of individuals who physically
demonstrate a wide range of racial charac-
teristics, some appearing white, others
trigueno (wheat colored), and others black,
the question of racial belonging becomes a
major issue in Puerto Rican identity. In his
classic memoir Down These Mean Streets
(1967), writer Piri Thomas deals with this
conﬂict by traveling through the Deep
South during Jim Crow as a black man who
is passing for white.
By the late 1970s and early 1980s, the
culture syncreticism and exchange between
African American and Puerto Rican cul-
tures found a voice in both literary pro-
duction and popular culture. The creation
and popularity of the Nuyorican Poets
Cafe, featuring writers like Pedro Pietri,
Miguel Piñero, and Miguel Algarín, fur-
ther underscored this link between African
American and Puerto Rican cultures by
emphasizing the racial and social similari-
ties of both groups. The works of the
Nuyorican (a term blending New York and
Puerto Rican) poets are gritty urban post-
cards, concerned with issues like poverty,
racism, oppression, drugs, cultural alien-
ation, and violence, which characterize
urban American ghettos. By the late 1980s
and into the 1990s, scholars like Juan
Flores emphasized the cultural connection
between the two groups through popular
urban art forms like salsa, hip-hop, bomba,
rap, and spoken word poetry. Scholars have
noted that while the two major Latino
groups in the United States—Puerto
Ricans and Chicanos/Mexicanos—share
many cultural similarities, an important
point of departure is the notable inﬂuence
of African culture in relation to Puerto
Ricans and indigenous culture in relation
to Chicanos/Mexicanos.

QADDAFI,M UAMMAR
AL- (1942–)
Muammar al-Qaddaﬁ, the leader of Libya
since September 1, 1969, was a supporter
of the Palestine Liberation Organization
(PLO) who subsequently renounced terror-
ism and weapons of mass destruction. Born
in Sirte as the son of a Bedouin tribesman,
Qaddaﬁ attended Sebha Preparatory before
attending the University of Libya and
Military Academy in Benghazi. During his
academic career, Qaddaﬁ desired to emu-
late Gamal Abdul Nasser, who orchestrated
the overthrow of the Egyptian monarchy in
1952. It was the principles of Arab social-
ism that would drive Qaddaﬁ to imitate
him. Qaddaﬁ would also develop friend-
ships with students from Sebha, who
would eventually assist him in his own
coup against King Idris I of Libya. In 1966
Qaddaﬁ was commissioned a Libyan Signal
Corps ofﬁcer. On September 1, 1969,
Qaddaﬁ led a group of ofﬁcers in over-
throwing Idris I and establishing the Revo-
lutionary Command Council, which still
rules Libya. For 35 years after coming to
power, Qaddaﬁ promoted Pan-Arabism
throughout the Middle East. Qaddafi
would also earn the disdain of the United
States because of his support for the PLO,
which was responsible for the Black
September massacre at the 1972 Olympics.
T ensions with the United States came to a
boiling point with Libya’s involvement in
the April 5, 1986, bombing of a German
nightclub that was a popular spot for U.S.
servicemen. The United States would retal-
iate with Operation El Dorado Canyon, in
which U.S. warplanes destroyed several key
military targets and inadvertently killed
Qaddaﬁ’s adopted daughter. Following the
1986 air strike, Qaddaﬁ avoided the inter-
national spotlight and focused on efforts by
Libya to work cooperatively with other
African states. He has been a prominent
ﬁgure in African organizations such as the
African Union. 
In 1988, belief in Libyan involvement
in the destruction of Pan Am ﬂight 103
over Lockerbie, Scotland, which killed 270
passengers, would lead to the isolation of
Qaddaﬁ from the West. Qadafﬁ’s responses
to the claims of the involvement of the
Libyan intelligence services and of the in-
dictment of Libyan citizens as suspects were
complicated, across the course of the inves-
tigation, trial, and appeals process, which
lasted some 11 years. Qaddaﬁ denied in-
volvement at the time, although in 2000 he
indicated that he would accept the decision
of the international court convened to try the
suspects involved in the ﬂight’s destruction.

QUAKERS 911
the Religious Society of Friends, developed
in England during the seventeenth century.
George Fox founded Quakerism on the no-
tion that the Inner Light of God exists in
the hearts of the bourgeoisie. Only those
who followed higher law principles were
capable of receiving God’s Inner Light.
George Fox began preaching in 1647 to
English civilians that sought peace during
British political turmoil. An English judge,
who referred to Fox as a shivering coward
when Fox advised the judge to tremble at
the Word of God, coined the term “Quaker.”
Fox’s statement suggested that the British
Empire’s disobedience of God’s law was the
origin of the political strife in England.
Instead of practicing speciﬁc creeds,
the Quakers advocated that a renewed spir-
itualism between God and Humanity
would inherently revamp forms of worship
and trade. Humanity was therefore to place
its trust in God and the clergy. The clergy
were believed to conduct the purest man-
ner of commerce because their goal was to
better the human condition. The Quakers
preached against the moneyed class and
advocated that humanity abolish slavery
across Africa and America immediately
without violence.
William Penn introduced Quakerism
to America in 1682. The colony of
Pennsylvania was established by Penn to
serve as an asylum for prosecuted English
Quakers to enter the New World. The
constitution of Pennsylvania safeguarded
the religious freedom of its citizens. Quaker
laws maintained a placid community that
from 1682 to 1756 required no military
and had only a small police force. Low
crime rates in Quaker settlements proved,
they believed, that the world could prosper
ideally where there was no tyrannical ruler
present.
By the 1700s, abolitionism was a full-
scale movement in Pennsylvania. Quaker
activists Anthony Benezet and John
Woolman pressured slaveholders to eman-
cipate their slaves on religious, moral, and
economic grounds. The Quaker message
was to spread internationally to convince
all slaveholding nations to disband their
colonies. Moreover, the message was that a
world without slavery would enhance the
individual talent of every nation.
Congress received various petitions
from the Quakers to end human bondage.
The petitions noted the hypocrisy of prac-
ticing slavery in a country that had recently
rejected oppressive British rule. The main
argument advanced by the Quakers was
that America was imposing the same
tyranny on Africa that Britain had placed
English Quaker William Penn founded the colony of
Pennsylvania. Following his faith, he regarded the
colony as a holy experiment in which religious and
civil liberties could ﬂourish. The Quakers were the ﬁrst
Christian denomination to abolish slavery in their
midst. (Library of Congress)

on America. Delegates published tracts that
urged Americans that it was their humani-

Quaker settlements still exist in the
United States, Africa, and various other
nations. The Religious Society of Friends
maintains that although life is sacramental,
observing special sacraments is not neces-
sary in practicing one’s faith. Contempo-
rary Quakers conduct business and wor-

Seventeenth-century Quakers practiced
their beliefs in camps that convened in any
location that offered periods of silence.
Long intervals of quiet were required in
order to have God’s Light bestowed upon
its supporters to have them comprehend
their responsibility to respond to interna-
tional suffering. Long periods of silence
were supposed to have large groups reach a
collective understanding of the human
condition.

QUAQUE,P HILIP
(1741–1816)
Taken from the Gold Coast enclave of
Cape Coast, in modern Ghana, to London
as a youth, Philip Quaque returned home
in 1766 to establish a mission and a school
for the Anglican Society for the Propagation
of the Gospel in Foreign Parts (SPG).
While his mission did not prove successful,
he is remembered for laying the foundation
for the development of the nineteenth-
century Gold Coast educational system.
Quaque was most likely a student of
the Reverend Thomas Thompson, also a
SPG missionary, whose lack of success and
failing health caused Thompson to create a
plan to send several Cape Coast youth, in-
cluding Quaque, back to England to be ed-
ucated and converted. Thompson believed
that an African missionary would be more
successful than a European missionary
because of their ability to relate to the local
peoples. Thompson, in consultation with
Cudjoe Caboceer the local de facto leader,
sent three boys to London; only one,
Quaque, survived his stay and returned
home. Cudjoe, whose son Frederick Adoy
had received an English education, saw the
beneﬁts of local boys obtaining new knowl-
edge within the context of the trans-
Atlantic slave trade. An English education
ensured them of company employment
along with the social, economic, and polit-
ical power that came from being a cross-
cultural broker. Of the three boys, Quaque
exceeded all expectations in his ability to
learn and in his conversion to Christianity.
In 1765, he was ordained into the Anglican
Church and then accepted positions with
both the SPG and the Company of
Merchants T rading to Africa. In the spring
of 1766, he arrived at Cape Coast with his
English wife and her female companion.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1001 ---
QUILOMBO 913
Quaque, who was very eager to begin, be-
lieved that the enthusiastic response of the
local peoples to his return marked their
desire to learn what he had to offer. He
quickly worked to establish his mission
and, like his predecessor Thompson,
focused on converting the local elite in the
belief that if they converted the others
would follow. Quaque quickly found that
the company, because of its involvement in
the slave trade, supported education over
proselytization. The same was true of the
local people. Quaque reacted by integrating
religion into the educational process by
teaching students to read and write from
various Anglican tracts. The problem was
that while the local people were initially
enthusiastic about the educational oppor-
tunity, and the resulting economic oppor-
tunities, the children and parents quickly
lost interest when they understood the
long-term commitment required. Quaque
made many efforts to permanently estab-
lish his school and mission, with his bright-
est moment arising in the early 1790s when
a group of European ofﬁcials joined together
and formed the T orridzonian Society. This
gentleman’s society pooled resources to cre-
ate a boarding school for local children,
many of whom were their offspring, and
placed Quaque in charge of educating and
converting them. As the slave trade came
under challenge from the abolitionist move-
ment, the society soon dissolved and with it
Quaque’s last hope for success. Quaque lived
out the rest of his life at Cape Coast in rela-
tive obscurity. While both his mission and
school were failures in that very few children
or adults were educated or converted, Philip
Quaque laid the foundations for the educa-
tional and missionary activity in Ghana of
the nineteenth century.
Ty M. Reese

QUILOMBO
The word quilombocomes from the African
Bantu linguistic root, where, written with
k, it means “settlement” and “union,” and
connotes slave communities formed in
resistance to slavery. In colonial Portuguese,
when it acquired the meaning of “fortress”
or “camp,” it referred to the place runaway
slaves would gather and to the resulting
community thus formed. The term is
equivalent to the English maroon, and
corresponds to the palenque or cume in
Spanish America. Quilombos and their
inhabitants, called quilombolas, were one of
the most important forms of resistance to
slavery in Brazil. T oday they represent a
salutary reminder that slaves did not accept
passively their plight but revolted when
they could do so. Successful quilombos
(i.e., those that were not very soon de-
stroyed by white slave owners) gave birth to
settlements, which could prove to be so
well organized, both in terms of adminis-
tration and internal hierarchy, that they
would resemble villages, in some cases even
establishing commercial ties with peddlers
and neighboring farms. Their population
was mixed, because in addition to black
slaves, native Brazilians and Mestizos of all
sorts could also be found there. It is inter-
esting to note that quilombos were present
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1002 ---
914 Q UILOMBO
in all periods of Brazilian history prior to
the abolition, and in all regions of the
country. Their size could range from a few
tens of people to the astounding 20,000 of
the Palmares quilombo. In the quilombos
ex-slaves reproduced many of the social
practices of their native Africa. Work was
highly collaborative, agriculture was varied,
the land was commonly worked on, and
livestock were not considered private
property, but owned by families or the
collectivity.
Settlements in forests and places of
difﬁcult access were called “breaking-away
quilombos” (quilombos de rompimento);
there were, however, two other kinds of
quilombos in Brazil: the urban and
the abolitionist quilombos. Already in the
seventeenth century, there were cities like
Salvador or Rio de Janeiro that were big
enough to conceal black people in the
crowds, but still small enough to have
somewhat dense vegetation surrounding
them. Urban quilombos were hiding places
where runaway slaves could stay when not
in the city. Relying on the solidarity of
freed slaves, as well as that of small shop
owners, who exploited their labor, runaways
managed to survive in a hostile environ-
ment. Abolitionist quilombos ﬂourished in
the nineteenth century. They were unhid-
den sites of confrontation supported by
abolitionists, both black and white, who
welcomed runaway slaves at a time when
slavery was already in decline. After aboli-
tion, quilombos became important centers
of Afro-Brazilian culture.
Even though repression was relentless
and all quilombos destroyed by slave own-
ers, their militias, or the government, there
are still as many as 750 communities in
Brazil, totaling 3 million people, which
are made of former quilombolas. These
quilombo-descended populations are now
struggling to keep alive their heritage and
cultural identity as well as to have full
rights over the land their ancestors invested
so much hope in.
Fabio Durao

RACE,H ISTORY OF
The history of race as it applies to humans
is the history of a largely Euro-American
(Western) idea that declares the existence
of a hierarchy of Homo sapiens races that,
although reﬂecting a geographical distribu-
tion (for example, Europe, Africa, Asia), is
ultimately biologically based. The creation
and development of this idea into the
theories (or stories) of race that continue
to have an impact on how many twenty-
ﬁrst-century people see themselves and
others, is the creation and development of
an idea responding to many inﬂuences, but
especially capitalism.
Racialism can be deﬁned as the idea
that the creation of human races occurs from
the biological transmission of not only
distinguishing physical but also intellectual,
moral, and spiritual characteristics. Racism
adds to racialism the idea that one race of
humans is superior to others, and this supe-
riority justiﬁes the superior race’s domina-
tion of those inferiors. In Western thought,
racism posits a race of white/Caucasian pu-
rity superior to impure, nonwhite races.
Current genetic research indicates that
today’s humans have descended from a
common father who lived approximately
60,000 years ago—a mere 2,000 genera-
tions. The human migration out of Africa
that resulted in the variety of skin colors
that exist today occurred only 40,000 years
ago. Although these exact dates may change
with future research, they indicate that skin
color is a superﬁcial adaptation whose vari-
ations do not distinguish human races.
Human skin color is an ever-changing
epidermal adaptation to sunlight. Skin must
balance between being light enough to allow
sufﬁcient production of vitamin D (vital
for strong bones) and dark enough to pre-
vent the destruction of folate (important to
fertility and fetal development). Increased
exposure to sunlight increases the skin’s
production of melanin, and this darkens the
skin. The production of melanin thus can
vary both in individuals over a lifetime, and
in populations over generations.
Not only are skin colors a recent devel-
opment in human evolution, but the idea of
categorizing humans by skin color is also a
recent development. Humans have long cat-
egorized others, and groups tend to evaluate
“others” as inferior. The supposed inferior-
ity of other groups, however, has tradition-
ally been based on such characteristics as
language, religion, and customs. Although
skin color has been an element of, for in-
stance, the caste system of India, skin color
as the primary basis for ranking groups (and
ranking all groups throughout the world) is
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1004 ---
916 R ACE,H ISTORY OF
a European invention that began during
Europe’s so-called Age of Discovery.
Europe’s exploration of the world began
in earnest in the ﬁfteenth century. Early
European travelers to Africa saw Africans
more as trading partners than as inferiors.
Europe’s usurpation of the Americas, how-
ever, resulted in the importation of enslaved
Africans, and this dramatically different
relationship with Africans required a new
“story”—the story of dark-skinned (espe-
cially African) inferiority. By the ca. 1603
production of Shakespeare’s Othello, skin
color had, for Europeans, become a marker
of difference.
During the seventeenth and eighteenth
centuries, the rise of European imperi-
alisms increased the need for this new story,
and the increasingly important ﬁeld of sci-
ence served this need with plant and animal
classiﬁcation systems, for example, Carolus
Linnaeus in 1735 and Charles Darwin in
1871, that included humans. During the
eighteenth and especially the nineteenth
century, a profusion of scientiﬁc studies as
well as philosophical and eugenicist argu-
ments strengthened European theories of
race (and racism) by interconnecting race
and skin color with both phenotypical vari-
ations (e.g., craniology) and with such ele-
ments as geography, nation, language, and
degree of development as measured by ma-
terial productivity, for example, Immanuel
Kant in 1775; G. W . F . Hegel in 1830; and
Arthur de Gobineau in 1853.
Europeans generally saw Africa as a
“dark” continent of childish, uncivilized
peoples whose limited potentials could be
approached only through the ﬁrm hand of
an enlightened “parental Europe.” The
“parental ﬁrmness” of slavery would bring
order and the “light” of Christianity to
Africans, and this would result in a more
productive and civil “African race.” This
parental ﬁrmness was eventually trans-
formed into such social interventions as
colonization, Jim Crow separation in the
United States (ca. 1877–1964), apartheid in
South Africa (1948–1994), and harsher
prison sentences for blacks vis-à-vis whites
with equal records. Although diminishing
since the 1960s, the belief that skin color
indicates important differences continues to
exist throughout the Americas, and during
times of perceived threat, race remains per-
haps the most powerful trope for producing
fear and anxiety among U.S. Americans.
The emotional power of race is partic-
ularly strong in the United States because
of that country’s long maintenance of bi-
nary ideas about race coupled with spatial
segregation. This segregation (e.g., ghetto
from suburb) has not only inhibited inter-
actions and mutual understandings but has
also helped maintain economic inequalities
that produce differences that are then taken
as results not of economic but of racial
differences.
How Africana peoples have responded
to Western ideas about race has varied.
During the eighteenth century, for instance,
the writers Phillis Wheatley and Olaudah
Equiano  generally worked within the dom-
inant white logic of race, maintaining the
ﬁction of African inferiority but with the
admonition that Africans—contrary to
thinking at the time—could approach
equality with whites under proper tutelage.
Although white abolitionists and post-
bellum reconstructionists were politically
nearest to African Americans, even this end
of the white political spectrum adhered to
what is probably the essential aspect of the
discourse of race, its foundation on a binary
logic that excludes African Americans from
the normativity of whites (an idea rooted in
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1005 ---
RACE,H ISTORY OF 917
the limpieza de sangre—purity of blood—
doctrine of ﬁfteenth-century Spain).
This is the logic of the hypodescent, or
“one drop,” theory of race—one drop of
black blood (i.e., one nonwhite ancestor)
makes a person black. Hypodescent pro-
duced such gradations as half black is mu-
latto, one-quarter is quadroon, one-eighth
is octoroon, one-sixteenth is mustaﬁna,
and one-thirty-second is a whitewash. That
white has no gradations indicates its purity,
and purity by deﬁnition is unattainable for
any lineage once contaminated. The ex-
treme nature of this binary logic is that it
maintains eternal separation.
As the nineteenth century drew to a
close, the deﬁnition of race began to strain
as it expanded to address the complexities
of a more global scope. W . E. B. Du Bois
wrote that the division of races between
white and black was also a division internal
to African Americans in that the sense of
being fully human is continually disrupted
by the binary logic that posits the African
American as lacking, as not human but
merely black human, not American but
Negro American. This Du Bois called
“double consciousness.”
The 1930s saw the development of a
Marxist (class-based) understanding that
race is a story used in capitalist systems to
divide and exploit workers. During the
1950s and early 1960s, such people as James
Baldwin and Martin Luther King Jr. pro-
moted the belief that the arts, religion, and
political coalitions could erase skin color
from the equation of human relations.
With the violence of white responses to
the Civil Rights Movement, this integra-
tionist vision of race was overtaken by a
return to more racialist thinking. During
the 1960s, Black Nationalism, Black
Power, Afrocentrism, and the Black Arts
Movement expressed a black pride pro-
moting a politics of racial separation and
competition. This binary understanding of
race, however, diminished by 1970 when
Africana identities became increasingly
complicated by gender, sexuality, ethnicity,
and religion, and “black” no longer equaled
“heterosexual black male.”
Thus since around 1970, U.S. ideas
about race have become more complex
and ﬂexible and thus more like the ideas
held elsewhere in the Americas. Space does
not allow distinguishing differences in
concepts of race among Caribbean nations,
American nations with prominent indige-
nous populations, Euro-Latin nations,
Canada, or African nations—particularly
South Africa and its Black Consciousness
Movement. But in Brazil, to provide one
example, race is not understood as an im-
mutable biological category but a classiﬁca-
tion that includes both appearance and
class; thus phenotypic variations can result
in different racial categories for siblings
from identical parents (impossible under
the genotypic deﬁnitions that have domi-
nated in the United States), and changes in
wealth over a person’s life can change that
person’s race. Also, many Caribbean na-
tions maintain highly complex systems that
rank multiple nonwhite groups of not only
African but also Asian and various mixed
ancestries using such terms as Creole,
métissage, métisse, mestizaje, and noiriste.
Since the 1960s, Africana scholars
(e.g., Cornell West, Paul Gilroy, Anthony
Appiah) have become prominent voices
discussing (and thus deﬁning) race as a so-
ciohistorical construction—a ﬁction. This
rejection of a biological basis to race, how-
ever, does not deny the existence of black
epistemological, social, musical, spiritual,
and other heritages and experiences from
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

which come outstanding examples of the
humanist tradition and vital resources for
everyone.

RADIO MARTÍ
Radio Martí is the most recent of several U.S.
government radio projects created speciﬁ-
cally to broadcast to Cuba. The ﬁrst was
Radio Swan, ﬁnanced by the Central Intelli-
gence Agency (CIA), which began broad-
casting after the Cuban Revolution of 1959.
Radio Swan, later renamed Radio Americas,
ceased operations in the 1970s. Voice of
America (VOA), a U.S. government-funded
program that broadcasts news and enter-
tainment to many countries of the world,
also began broadcasting to Cuba in 1959.
Radio Martí was created in 1985 as a spe-
ciﬁc program within VOA, and broadcasts
a variety of programming including news,
sports, and entertainment programs. No
official figures are available, but some
observers believe it is the most-listened-to
radio station in Cuba. The station was
named after Jose Martí, a leader in the ﬁght
for Cuban independence.
Although Radio Martí considers itself
to be unbiased, the Cuban government
considers it to be propaganda, and has at
times “jammed” the signal, that is, broad-
cast noise at the same frequency so the
Radio Martí broadcast could not be heard.
Many Americans have also raised issues of
news bias; their charges were supported in
1995 when a federal government investiga-
tion disclosed that chairman Jose Mas
Canosa and director Rolando Bonachea
had encouraged slanted news reporting
and punished employees who complained
about it. With the growing availability of
commercial radio broadcasting, Radio Martí
has attracted fewer listeners in Cuba. For
instance, it is estimated that in the 1990s
almost three-quarters of the Cuban popula-
tion listened to Radio Martí, while in 2005
a U.S. government survey revealed that less
than 2 percent of Cubans had listened to
Radio Martí in the previous week.
Sarah Boslaugh

RASTAFARI
The Rastafari movement is a cultural, reli-
gious, and political movement that began
in the early 1930s among the descendants
of African slaves in the Caribbean nation
of Jamaica. Its central tenets are liberation
from white oppression, black supremacy,
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1007 ---
RASTAFARI 919
and the doctrine of repatriation to Africa
for the Diaspora, as well as the divinity of
Haile Selassie, the former Ethiopian em-
peror. While the Rastafari tradition is not a
form of Christianity, and is in some cases
hostile to that faith, it incorporates some
Christian elements—for instance, the world
outside Africa is viewed as “Babylon,”
Africa is “Zion,” and God is “Jah” (from
“Jehovah”).
The movement grew out of longstand-
ing traditions in Jamaica—particularly black
resistance to oppression, which gave rise to
numerous revolts against colonialists, and
“Ethiopianism,” which traced black Africans’
lineage to the rulers of the ancient Egyptian
and Ethiopian dynasties and viewed Africa as
the promised land of the Bible.
Ethiopianism found its greatest
spokesman in Marcus Garvey, the Jamaican
union leader and founder of the Universal
Negro Improvement Association. Garvey
was a proponent of Pan-Africanism, the
goal of which was to unite people of color
against imperialism, and he launched the
Back to Africa movement in the 1920s. He
quoted Psalm 68 (“Princes shall come out
of Egypt and Ethiopia shall stretch forth its
hands unto God”) to emphasize the noble
destiny of Africans and their descendants.
He is also believed to have said “Look to
Africa for the crowning of a Black King; he
shall be the Redeemer.”
The crowning of Haile Selassie I as the
emperor of Ethiopia in 1930 was seen as the
fulﬁllment of Garvey’s prophecy, though
Garvey himself was critical of him. The
early Rastafari preachers declared Selassie to
be the messiah, the reincarnation of Jesus
Christ. Further evidence of the African
king’s divinity was his biblically inspired
title, which put him in the line of descent
from King Solomon: “King of Kings, Lord
of Lords, Conquering Lion of the T ribe
of Judah.” Rastafari is derived from the
emperor’s precoronation name, Tafari
Makonnen, and the Ethiopian (Amharic)
word for duke—ras .
Leonard Howell was the most promi-
nent of a handful of preachers who began
preaching the new religion. After traveling
in Africa and America, he returned to
Jamaica to spread his message of repatria-
tion and resistance in “street meetings” in
the slums of Kingston. The area was home
to many urban poor, mostly peasants who
had migrated from Jamaica’s rural areas over
the decades since emancipation (in 1834).
He and other ministers quickly gained
followings—as well as attention from the
government for their revolutionary views.
Howell was convicted for sedition in 1933
for abusing the government and sentenced
to jail, along with the three other major
Rastafari leaders of the time.
Following his release, Howell retreated
to the hills above Kingston, where he
oversaw Pinnacle—a community of be-
lievers numbering about 1,000, by some
estimates—from 1940 until 1954. Various
principles of the Rastafari movement crys-
tallized here, including the use of ganja, or
cannabis, as a religious sacrament. Ganja
was said to have grown on the grave of
King Solomon and was a major cash crop
for Howell’s group. He also preached
resistance to the established order, and Pin-
nacle became the target of raids and arrests
until it was destroyed by the government in
1954 and its followers dispersed in the
Shanty-T own or Back-O-Wall area of
Kingston. Howell was later committed to
Kingston Mental Hospital.
Other fundamental principles of the
tradition to emerge in its early years were
a vegetarian diet known as “i-tal” (which
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1008 ---
920 R ASTAFARI
means the “essence” or “nature of things”);
the prohibition of alcohol; the use of the red,
gold, and green colors (from the Ethiopian
flag); and the long, matted dreadlock
hairstyle, a custom that is dictated by the
biblical verse Leviticus 21:5 (“they shall not
make baldness upon their head”) and which
also connotes a rejection of social norms.
Other traditions include “reasonings,” or
philosophical discussion sessions, and cele-
brations known as “nyabingi” that involve
dance, drumming, and ganja. A distinctive
vocabulary known as “i-talk” is another hall-
mark of the movement. The words “me” and
“you” are never used, for instance; instead,
“I and I” expresses the concept of oneness.
“Irie” is another special term that denotes
positivity.
After the destruction of Pinnacle, a
new phase of Rastafari movement began.
Its adherents advocated militant resistance
to the establishment and the destruction of
“Babylon.” A series of violent clashes with
the government ensued in which Rastas
were sometimes killed, and often arrested
and forced to submit to having their locks
cut off. In 1958, hundreds of Rastas tried
to capture the city of Kingston in the name
of Haile Selassie. In 1959, an armed en-
campment was raided and its leader, the
Rev. Claudius Henry, arrested. In 1966,
with the Rastafari widely seen as a revolu-
tionary threat, the government bulldozed
Back-O-Wall, an area it had targeted for
development—resulting in the destruction
of several Rasta camps.
At the same time, while the Rastafari
displayed a general distrust of organized
politics, there were efforts made by some
members to bring about reforms. In 1960,
a government report was issued urging
that Rasta concerns be taken seriously, and
in 1961, an unofficial delegation was
dispatched to Africa to explore repatriation.
Ras Sam Brown, the ﬁrst Rastafari to foray
into politics with an unsuccessful run in
1961 at a Parliament seat, wrote up a man-
ifesto containing twenty-one points. In it,
he proposed that the movement take power
with the goal of “uplift[ing]...the poor
and oppressed,” and that a government be
set up under the “Repatriation and Power”
banner.
This focus on empowerment at home
was reinforced by the historic visit to
Jamaica in 1966 by Emperor Haile Selassie
I—his ﬁrst and only trip to the island na-
tion. Selassie himself was a member of the
Ethiopian Orthodox Church and strongly
discouraged ideas of his divinity. He also
earned a reputation as a despot, especially
after the Ethiopian famine of the 1970s,
when he made sure to keep his pet lions fed
while people were starving. He was de-
posed by the army in 1974. Still, he contin-
ued to be seen as divine by the Rastafari,
even more so after his death in 1975. On
the 1966 visit, the anniversary of which is
still celebrated by Rastafari, he brought a
message to the enthusiastic crowds that
came to greet him—that the Rastafari
should not seek to be repatriated before
they had succeeded in liberating the people
of Jamaica.
In the latter half of the twentieth cen-
tury, various waves of migration brought
the Rastafari movement (if not its sub-
stance, then its style) to Central America,
Cuba, England, Canada, and the United
States. The movement entered pop culture
in the 1970s with the emergence of Bob
Marley and the spread of reggae, which
touches on Rastafari themes and is inspired
by the Nyabinghi music. The Rastafari
movement’s adherents are now believed to
number about 1 million worldwide.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

Currently, the movement includes three
major groups, which are known as “houses”
or “mansions”: the House of Nyabinghi; the
T welve T ribes of Israel; and the Bobo
Ashanti. The House of Nyahbinghi is an as-
cetic sect whose motto is “Death to black
and white downpressors.” The T welve T ribes
of Israel, which took hold among middle-
class Jamaicans in the 1970s, revere their late
founder, Vernon Carrington, as a prophet.
(He was known as Prophet Gad.) The group
is the most doctrinaire of the three and
places a strong emphasis on the Bible. It also
has a stated policy of including all races. The
fundamentalist Bobo (pronounced Bob-bo)
Ashanti sect members wear turbans and
robes, and live in a utopian community
called Bobo Hill in Jamaica, where they raise
money by selling handmade brooms.
Charles Edwards, also known as Prince
Edward Emmanuel Charles VII, founded
the group in the 1950s and is seen as part of
a Holy T rinity that includes Haile Selassie
and Marcus Garvey.

REGGAE
Reggae was born in Kingston, Jamaica, in
the 1960s from the melding of musical
genres such as jazz, blues, rocksteady, ska,
calypso, and rapsodie. In 1968, Frederick
“T oots” Herbert, of T oots and the Maytals,
coined the term “reggae” in his ﬁrst album
entitled Do the Reggay. Yet the word reggae
may have derived from either “rega,” the
name of a Bantu-speaking people on Lake
Tanganyika in former Zaire; from the
Kingston slang term “streggae,” used to
identify a sex worker; or from the term
“rege,” which means “danse” in the Soninke
language of West Africa.
The development of reggae was the mas-
terpiece of three men: Robert (Bob) Nesta
Marley, Bunny Livingston (later known as
Bunny Wailer), and Peter T osh. These three
pioneers of reggae were the original members
of the Wailers band, which crafted a new
music that combined traditional rhythms
stemming from mento, calypso, and ska
with the new sound of American blues and
jazz, and rocksteady. The synthesis of these
musical genres was heavily inﬂuenced by the
cultures that enslaved Africans brought to
the Americas centuries ago.
Despite its multiple origins, reggae is
primarily a music coming from the people.
In a June 1976 interview, Bob Marley, the
legendary singer who popularized reggae,
said, “Reggae say[s] something. But it can
only mean something if it mean[s] some-
thing to the people who make it and the
people who listen.” Marley’s statement
shows that reggae is the property of the
masses, since its meaning is shaped by the
people who hear it, feel it, and live it. In this
sense, reggae is a universal music that has a
message that reaches people from all over
the globe. Yet, despite its universality, reggae
is primarily a product of African-Jamaican
identity, because it evolved from the local
resistance of black Jamaicans against racial,
economic, social, and cultural oppressions
since slavery. This message of resistance
against domination reaches out to black
people from the Americas, Africa, and other
parts of the world who continue to suffer
from the legacy of slavery and colonialism.
Reggae teaches the message of lib-
eration, resistance, respect, brotherly and
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1010 ---
922 R EGGAE,A FRICAN
sisterly love, and hard work that black peo-
ple have learned from centuries of hard-
ships in “Babylon,” a word that identiﬁes
the West and every other place where
black people continue to suffer. Following
on the footsteps of their pioneers, reggae
artists from Jamaica and around the globe
travel across the world on a regular basis,
spreading the message and wisdom of
Rastafarianism, which is a term that refers
to the philosophical and religious teachings
of Haile Selassie (of Ethiopia) and Marcus
Garvey (of Jamaica).
Babacar M’Baye
