REGGAE,A FRICAN
Reggae music in Africa owes its birth and
evolution to the African Diaspora, and to
the inﬂuence of Jamaican reggae. Just as
Africa impacted the music of the New
World in the aftermath of the transatlantic
slave trade, the Americas and Caribbean,
particularly Jamaica, introduced reggae to
Africa. Africans were receptive to this music
style because they could easily relate to
the historical experience of Jamaicans. The
beats and rhythms of reggae music are an
aesthetic link between Africa and Jamaica.
Reggae made its initial impact in Africa
during the mid-1970s, and since that time
it has served as a major force in urban pop
music scenes of numerous African nations,
especially Anglophone countries. The rea-
sons for the popularity of reggae in Africa
range from the structural and functional
afﬁnities that exist between indigenous
African musical forms and reggae, the eclec-
tic background and purpose of reggae, the
potent appeal of the music’s religiously in-
spired and sociopolitically charged lyrics,
and the eagerness on the part of young
people in Africa to identify with a black
transnational pop music idiom. Some have
argued that the popularity of reggae among
West African youth developed out of their
growing dissatisfaction with both the over-
produced, high-tech Western disco/rap/funk
pervasive in urban nightclubs and the per-
ceived stufﬁness and rigidity of traditional
music in the 1970s.
Africans can easily relate to the socio-
economic and political conditions in the
black Diaspora. African territories had to
ﬁght for freedom, and today the indepen-
dent states are ﬁghting against neocolonial-
ism, oppression, exploitation, corruption,
and material deprivation. The messages and
philosophies of reggae music are a means of
protest. As a result of the similarities between
the historical and contemporary realities
of Africa and Jamaica, the images and tribu-
lations found in the lyrics of reggae make it
very attractive to the African people. As with
Jamaican reggae, African reggae became a
medium for telling about the struggle of the
oppressed peoples of Africa—their stories
and their trials and tribulations. Soon the
music began to blossom in most parts of
Africa, including Burkina Faso, Côte
d’Ivoire, Gambia, Ghana, Mali, Nigeria,
Senegal, and South Africa.
Like everywhere across the globe, Bob
Marley served as the foremost apostle of
reggae on the African continent. African
reggae musicians frequently cite Marley as
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1011 ---
REGGAE,A FRICAN 923
their earliest and most enduring musical as
well as ideological inﬂuence, as evidenced
by the immense popularity he continues
to enjoy in African countries. The impact
of Bob Marley’s music and his media-
generated image on youth in Africa, and
on African Rastas in particular, cannot be
underestimated. Many African pop musi-
cians have either played reggae music at
one point in their careers or incorporated
reggae rhythms and/or Rasta-inspired lyrics
in their songs.
Throughout the continent one can ﬁnd
recordings by Bob Marley, Peter T osh,
Jimmy Cliff, and others, and recordings of
African reggae artists are on sale in record
shops and market stalls in both urban and
rural marketplaces. Reggae is also frequently
heard on local radio stations, in taxis, bars,
discos, on street corners, and everywhere
young people congregate. In fact, since
the mid-to-late 1970s, Africa has served as
a major international market for reggae
music. It is claimed that Marley is one
of the best-selling musical artists on the
continent.
Prominent African reggae musicians
include Ivorian artist Alpha Blondy, an
African Rasta who creates Jah-centered an-
thems and became the ﬁrst African star of
reggae with Jah Glory(1983); Ivorian Tiken
Jah Fakoly, who has established himself as
one of the leading artists of the new reggae
scene in Côte d’Ivoire and had a series
of concerts in 1999 in New York and
Philadelphia with a Jamaican backing
band; and South African Ermelo “Lucky”
Dube, who became the ﬁrst reggae star of
South Africa with Rastas Never Die (1985).
Another popular artist is Kush, a singer,
songwriter, arranger, and roots reggae and
African jazz musician from Côte d’Ivoire.
His music is a beautiful combination of
traditional roots reggae rhythms mingled
with African and jazz undertones. His work
contains poetic expression of Rastafarian
faith and wisdom as they relate to the cur-
rent sociopolitical crises.
Many African artists have also under-
taken pilgrimages to Jamaica, home of
many excellent recording studios. For in-
stance, Alpha Blondy made a pilgrimage in
1983 to T uff Gong Studios in Kingston,
Jamaica, where he recorded his phenomenal
Jerusalem album with the Wailers. Tiken Jah
Fakoly’s Cours d’Histoire and Françafrique
(2000) were mixed in the legendary T uff
Gong Studios in Jamaica and fused reggae
beat with hard-hitting lyrics.
The decor of the stage and the dress
style of most African reggae artists also re-
ﬂect the three symbolic colors of the black
race represented in the Ethiopian ﬂag and
used by Jamaican reggae stars: red, which
signiﬁes the memory of the spilt blood of
black peoples in defending themselves and
their ways; yellow, which stands for African
riches stolen by the imperialists; and green,
which represents the fertility of African
green ancestral land. These colors are often
used in conjunction with black, the color
that identiﬁes the African race.
Many Africans have adopted the
Rastafari way of life, including refusing to
cut their hair and wearing Rastafarian accou-
trements, such as the tam, a hat similar to a
beret but large enough to cover dreadlocks.
Marley’s dreadlocked profile stares out
from T-shirts and wall posters in African
market stalls, homes, and restaurants.
Along with Muhammad Ali, James Brown,
and Michael Jackson, Bob Marley ranks
among the most popular and inﬂuential
Pan-African heroes of all time—widely
known, listened to, admired, and idolized
by young people in Africa.

924 R ELIGION (AFRICA)
Overall, the most noticeable Pan-
American inﬂuences on reggae in Africa are
the creation of syncretic styles that fuse
Jamaican reggae and other American music
traditions, such as rumba, jazz, gospel, funk,
and rock, with African traditional rhythms.
For instance, in the 1970s, highlife music,
the Ghanaian and Nigerian ballroom music
that resulted from an adaptation of
American soul and rock music to West
Africa realities, absorbed many elements
of reggae to produce a faster and louder
highlife style. Manu Dibango, Africa’s best-
known jazz saxophonist, fused African
rhythms and melodies with reggae, most no-
tably on Gone Clear (1979) with American
artists Robbie Shakespeare and Sly Dunbar.
In 1983, Congolese musicologist Ray Lema
released Kinshasa-Washington DC-Paris, an
album that reﬂects a mixture of inﬂuences:
reggae, rumba, rock, funk, jazz, tradition,
and modernity. Benin’s Angélique Kidjo
mixed reggae, Afro-punk, samba, salsa,
jazz, rumba, zouk, and makossa. Sudanese
singer-songwriter Rasha invented a
mishmash of reggae, jazz, pop, and American
dance music in Sudaniyat (1997). Even
today, new styles of reggae are emerging
and becoming popular in Africa. These in-
clude dancehall and raga, also known as
raggamufﬁn. African reggae music is a beau-
tiful synthesis of moods (upbeat, ecstatic,
melancholy, spiritual), formats (song, sym-
phony, suite, jam), and lifestyles (Western
and Eastern), African polyrhythms, and
Jamaican reggae, all of which are fully
integrated.

RELIGION (AFRICA)
John S. Mbiti, the renowned scholar of
African religion, put it best when he de-
scribed Africans as notoriously religious.
Ever since the ﬁrst humans originated from
Africa, the continent has been home to
diverse religious beliefs and attitudes. From
ancient Nubian religions, to pharaonic
Egypt, to precolonial times, religion has
permeated every aspect of African life.
Africa was home to the major Western reli-
gions of Christianity, Islam, and Judaism
even before European contact. The histories
of these three religions clearly support this
fact. The Bible states that the Jews migrated
from Egypt to the promised land of Israel.
Before spreading to Europe, Islam ﬁrst ar-
rived in northern Africa in the seventh cen-
tury. Also, Bilal, a black African, was Islam’s
ﬁrst muezzin calling the faithful to prayer.
Early Christianity spread from the Arabian
Peninsula and southern Mediterranean on
its way to Europe. Moreover, Africans such
as Saint Augustine were among the pillars of
the early Christian church.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1013 ---
RELIGION (AFRICA) 925
As recently as a hundred years ago,
European colonizers and Western scholars,
out of cultural arrogance, racism, and igno-
rance, tended to describe African religions as
nothing more than primitive mumbo-
jumbo. For example, the term fetishism was
often used to describe religion on the
continent of Africa. This term is derived
from Portuguese feitiço, for a “made thing,”
something factitious or artiﬁcial . Used by
the Portuguese during their encounter with
Africans in the ﬁfteenth century, it described
the charms and amulets worn by Africans.
Thus, African religion was regarded as child-
ish or primitive. For the Europeans, it was
either the lowest form of religion or the
absence of any spirituality at all.
Recent works by African scholars of reli-
gion have contributed immensely in dis-
pelling the simplistic, and negative, presen-
tation of African religions as proof of African
backwardness. This current in scholarly
thought is partly the result of African schol-
ars, who, as both participants and experts in
their own cultures, bring their unique per-
spectives into their writings about African
religions. Furthermore, Western scholars
have become more culturally sensitive in
their discussion of African religion. T echno-
logical advances have also helped anthropol-
ogists to understand and explain that African
religions and religious symbols can be con-
sidered on their own as elaborate systems of
theology. Thus, in structure, content, and
purpose African religions are comparable to
any in Western civilization. It is simply the
mode and idiom by which these are propa-
gated that makes them different from but
not inferior to Western belief systems.
T oday, modern African religion, in the
broadest sense of the term, continues to
inﬂuence and shape Africans and African
cultures. Even the most modern and
atheistic African—who may profess no reli-
gious afﬁliation—is religious in outlook, es-
pecially in the manner in which they relate
to their environment, community, and the
world in general. For the African, everything
in the world—both visible and invisible—is
interconnected and imbued with the sacred.
Religion is too narrow a concept to de-
scribe Africans’ notion of ultimate reality.
In discussing or studying African religious
belief, cosmology would be a more appro-
priate term. For Africans, the concepts of
God, nature, community, family, life, birth,
death, ancestors, good, evil, soul, spirits,
symbols, religion, worship, ritual, rites of
passage, behavior, character, morality,
ethics, and language are all parts of an intri-
cate and interconnected reality. Most
Africans know that this reality is rooted in
the constantly expanding networks of
attitudes, concepts, and symbols that inﬂu-
ence their religious beliefs, which are the
foundation of all African cultures. They
also influence the daily lives of most
Africans. That is why the terms “religion”
and “theology” will not have the same reso-
nance for the average African as they would
for the average Westerner. But that does
not mean that African religions cannot be
studied or discussed, or even understood as
complete belief systems that have governed
the hearts and minds of Africans for
centuries before the arrival of Islam and
Christianity on the continent. In short,
African religions indicate that there is an
African worldview which the Westerner has
to ﬁrst understand in order to really know
the Bantu-speaking peoples of the African
continent. 
In modern times, Christianity and
Islam have become the dominant religions
in Africa. In most of north and West Africa,
Islam is the predominant religion, while
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1014 ---
926 R ELIGION (AFRICA)
Christianity is a very close second. Countries
like Algeria, Egypt, T unisia, and Morocco
have majority Moslem populations. In spite
of this, African traditional religion is still
practiced. For example, the Berbers of
Morocco practice a form of shamanism
called gnaoua, or gnawa, in which dance and
trances are used for healing.
In the western, central, and eastern
African countries of Ethiopia, Ghana,
Nigeria, and Kenya, Christianity seems to
be in ascendancy, even though these na-
tions do have sizable Moslem populations.
In Nigeria, the average Yoruba, Moslem or
Christian, will still consult or honor the
family’s orisha, or guardian deity, in times
of crisis. Also before any major undertak-
ing, the Yoruba will often consult the
babalawo, or seer—in addition to the spiri-
tual support of their local bishop or imam.
In Ghana, the Ashanti will invoke the an-
cestors and pour libation during an oath-
making ceremony. In southern Africa,
where Christianity has held sway for cen-
turies, people still practice their indigenous
religions. For example, in Lesotho, the
sangoma, or traditional priest and healer, is
often consulted by the people.
European colonization has been an
obvious factor in the spread of Christianity
in Africa. Early European settlers, while
seeking new territories, natural resources,
and raw materials, also sought to spread
their religion in Africa out of the belief that
Africans needed to be converted. Many
schools were opened by European mission-
aries as part of their bid to convert and
“civilize” Africans. Some of these schools
still exist today.
In Africa both Christianity and Islam
have taken on distinctive local ﬂavors. They
have incorporated elements of African
culture and traditional religion to produce
hybrid forms that differ greatly from their
original versions. The Mouride brother-
hood of Senegal is one good example. It is a
uniquely African adaptation of the Islamic
faith. It arose out of an eclectic combi-
nation of Wolof nationalism, Suﬁ Islam,
and African traditional religion during the
French colonial domination of Senegal. It
is a vibrant religion which has grown from
a membership of less than half to over 90
percent of Senegal’s population in recent
years. Almost all Senegalese belong to one
of the three major Suﬁ brotherhoods: the
Tijaniyya, the Mouride, or the Qadiriyya.
Suﬁsm is the mystical branch of Islam. It
shifts from the external rituals of Islam to a
spiritual focus that is more intensely emo-
tional, personal, and closer to the heart.
God is not regarded as a distant ruler but a
close friend. He is to be found through
submission to a guide, or marabout, who is
deemed to have supernatural powers.
The Mouride sect was founded in the
late nineteenth century by a charismatic
Islamic and Wolof leader, Sheikh Amadou
Bamba, who led the native resistance against
the Christian onslaught that accompanied
French colonization of Senegal. The found-
ing of the sect was also a response to the rise
of militant Islam in nineteenth-century
Senegal. Outside of Senegal there are over a
million followers today, scattered all over
the globe, especially in the United States,
where they actively engage in commerce. A
big portion of their proceeds are sent to
T ouba, Senegal, the world headquarters of
the brotherhood. The Senegalese immi-
grant community in Harlem is comprised
mainly of Mourides. The continuing
success of the movement is largely due to
the belief in supernatural powers attributed
to the founder, Amadou Bamba. He is the
great source of baraka, or blessing, which
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1015 ---
RELIGION (AFRICA) 927
eternally ﬂows to followers from one gener-
ation to the next. The sheikh is therefore a
guarantor of redemption for his followers.
Herein lies the comparison to ancestor
worship in traditional African religion. The
Mouride brotherhood requires total sub-
mission to a religious guide. The disciple,
or talibe, declares his total submission to a
sheikh, who in turn undertakes to intercede
for his followers. A disciple can be attached
to only one sheikh at a time. During an ini-
tiation ceremony, known as njebbel, the dis-
ciple comes before the sheikh, on his knees,
and swears this oath: “I submit my body
and my soul to you. I will do everything
you order me, and abstain from anything
you forbid me.” A blessing is given to the
new follower, and the sheikh becomes
the guarantor of the spiritual welfare of the
person, on condition of the disciple’s un-
questioning obedience and loyalty. Legend
has it that Amadou Bamba promised that
“whosoever he may be, he who becomes
my disciple shall be saved in this world and
the next. Any Mouride who seeks refuge
with me shall go to paradise and shall not
know the burning embers of hell.” This
complete submission to his will is generally
seen as being the only certain path to par-
adise. Every year Amadou Bamba’s burial
site in T ouba attracts hundreds of thou-
sands of followers who gather for a week-
long pilgrimage.
There are likewise Africanized versions
of the Christian religion. One of the best ex-
amples can be found in West Africa. The
Celestial Church of Christ, headquartered
in Nigeria, was founded by S. B. J. Oshoffa.
Oshoffa, a Methodist layman, reported
receiving a vision of an angel who instructed
him to teach people to trust in Jesus.
According to the church’s Web site, the
church “came into the world from heaven
by
DIVINE ORDER on the 29th of
September, 1947 in Porto Novo, Republic of
Benin.” The church has branches (organized
into parishes and dioceses) all over the
world. The church holds that the Bible is
perfect and without errors. Members are
taught that prayer can effect physical healing
and that they can prophesy under divine
inspiration. The church derives its hymns
from the words of those who have been so
inspired. It claims to have between ﬁve and
six million followers worldwide, including in
the United States. Some of their rituals, such
as cleansing baths in ﬂowing rivers and
streams, fasting, incense burning to purify
surroundings, the wearing of cassocks, and
sacriﬁcial offerings of symbolic items clearly
point to a blending of elements of African
traditional religion and Roman Catholicism.
The Celestial Church of Christ em-
braces the priesthood of women, who have
the same opportunities to be ordained as
men. However, women are required to
respect the Old T estament prescriptions
about purity; this means that they are not
allowed to approach the Holy Altar during
their monthly menstruation. The Celestial
Church of Christ is one of what are called
“African-instituted churches,” or AICs.
These are Christian sects without any di-
rect historical ties to the European mission-
aries of the late nineteenth and early twen-
tieth centuries.
The Celestial Church of Christ has ﬁve
ministries: pastor, prophet, evangelist, shep-
herd, and teacher. Prophecy is especially im-
portant, and some members of this ministry
are seers, dreamers, or “hearers of divine
voices.” Their role is clearly shamanistic.
The mode of worship is almost like that of
the Catholic Church because it is liturgical.
It consists of prayers, hymns, Bible readings
and sermons, offerings, and sacraments.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1016 ---
928 R ELIGION (AFRICA)
Unlike in orthodox Christian denomina-
tions, exorcisms, and miracles are common
and regular features in the Celestial Church.
These are not unconnected with the African
belief in witchcraft. Upon entering the
church, adherents take off their shoes and
bow their heads three times, touching the
ﬂoor with their forehead. They wear white
garments (this symbolizes priesthood for
all believers) and palm fronds, while the
clergy wear colorful garments. Holy water,
incense, and crosses are used during the
service and the Eucharist is celebrated
occasionally. The other two sacraments of
the church are baptism and marriage.
Polygamy, clearly an important element in
African culture, is accepted by the church.
The church does not oblige polygamous
new members to divorce their wives. Clergy
can also remain polygamous. Indeed, the
church frowns upon divorce.
There is a special ritual for new mem-
bers. They kneel down before a bucket of
water, holding a candlestick, which is lighted
by a priest who says prayers of forgiveness
and sanctiﬁcation. Next, the new members
take a ritual cleansing bath with the water,
after which they receive what the church
calls “Christian education.” All members
must be baptized at an appropriate time.
People coming from other denominations
undergo a second baptism because they are
believed to have been polluted. 
The Celestial Church’s founder, S. B. J.
Oshoffa, died in 1985. After several years of
battles for succession, his son, Emmanuel
Oshoffa, was chosen as worldwide leader of
the church in 2002.
Religion in Africa also has a darker,
sinister side. It has been a great source of dis-
cord in Nigeria, Sudan, Somalia, and Egypt.
For example, in Nigeria riots have broken
out between Muslims and Christians since
1999, causing the deaths of tens of thou-
sands of citizens. In Sudan, for several
decades civil war has ravaged the population
because an Islamic government has sought
forcibly to convert and rule the southern
half of the country—which is majority
Christian or animist. T ogether with ethnic-
ity, religion has been used by some of Africa’s
politicians to further their goals. The results
have usually been horrendous.
In the Americas, African traditional re-
ligions have been implanted thanks to slav-
ery and immigration. Over four centuries
of slavery resulted in the creation of new
and hybrid forms of African and Christian
religion in Brazil, Cuba, the United States,
and Jamaica and other Caribbean nations.
African slaves and their descendants created
new belief systems from African and
Christian religions. T oday, Afro-Caribbean
religions like Candomble, Macumba,
Obeah, Rastafari, Orisha, and Santeria co-
exist with mainstream Christian sects in the
New World.

RELIGION IN AFRICA AND THE
AMERICAS,D EMOGRAPHY OF
The demography of religion in Africa and
the Americas is the study of peoples and
their religious afﬁliations in these regions.
Africa: An Overview
Christianity and Islam are the two largest
religions in the world, with large popu-
lations in both Africa and the Americas.
These two world religions, both of
which originated in the Middle East, have
deep roots in Africa. In the beginning of
the twenty-ﬁrst century, Christians and
Muslims comprised over 50 percent of the
world’s population. Of the 6.2 billion
people in the world, Christians comprised
2,038,905,000 (32.9 percent), Muslims
comprised 1,226,403,000 (19.8 percent),
and Hindus comprised 828,130,000
(13.3 percent). Africa has been a big con-
tributor to the large numbers of Christians
and Muslims in the world. In the past
half century, while the populations of
Christians and Muslims in Africa have
increased substantially, the total number of
Africans who practice indigenous religions
has increased in absolute numbers but de-
clined in proportion to the continent’s total
population: “Between 1931 and 1951 the
number of Muslims in the whole of Africa
had risen from 40 million to 80 million in
comparison with a Roman Catholic rise
from 5 million to 15 million....O f
the total Black population estimated at the
time as being 130 million in Africa south
of the Sahara, 28 million were Muslim,
13 million were Catholics, 4 million were
Protestants, and 85 million still followed
their own indigenous religions, even though
some of these traditionalists were nominally
Muslim or Christian. Islam in Africa as a
whole, including Arab Africa, commanded
the allegiance of approximately 40 percent
of the continent’s population” (Mazrui,
1986, pp. 135– 136). Within the continent,
of the estimated 823.4 million Africans in
2001, those who practiced traditional or
indigenous religions were 137.8 million
(16.7 percent).
Christianity has been very successful in
converting Africans. As of 2001, there were
an estimated 304.3 million (36.9 percent)
Christians in Africa. Statistics show that
there were as many Catholics in Africa as of
2004 as there were Africans who practiced
traditional religions in 2001. There are an
estimated 130 million Catholics in Africa,
comprising 16 percent of the continent’s
population.
As for the total estimates of Muslims in
Africa in 2001, they comprised 371.4 mil-
lion (45.1 percent) of the total 823.4 million
people, thus making Africa the only conti-
nent in the world where proportionally
Islam has the largest number of followers.
Other religious groups comprised 9.8 mil-
lion (1.2 percent).
North Africa
Muslims are the majority in North Africa.
Of the estimated 182.9 million North
Africans in 2001, Muslims accounted for
166.9 million (91.2 percent). Some 9 mil-
lion (4.9 percent) of the North African

West Africa
In West Africa, Muslims also comprised the
majority, although their proportion was
not as high as that of North Africa. In the
17 countries and territories that comprised
West Africa, Muslims accounted for

In Central Africa, Christians constituted
the highest proportion in 2001. Of the
estimated 96.8 million people in Central
Africa, 61.8 million (64 percent) were
Christians. Africans who practiced in-

(21.6 percent). The estimated number of
Central Africans who practiced Islam was
13.5 million (14 percent). The people with
other religious beliefs made up 437,688

Christians comprised the highest propor-

Southern Africa
Christians accounted for the highest pro-
portion of the total population of Southern
Africa. Of the total population of 50.25
million Southern Africans, an estimated
34.2 million (68 percent) were Christians.
Southern Africans who practiced indige-
nous religions comprised 14.1 million
(27.9 percent). In Southern Africa, the
Muslim population was 871,722 million
(1.7 percent). Southern Africans who prac-
ticed other religions comprised 1.09 mil-
lion (2.1 percent).
Caribbean
The Caribbean, made up of 24 nations,
had a total population of nearly 37 million
in 2001. No less than 65 percent of the
people are of black African descent. The
region is overwhelmingly Christian
(90.38 percent of the total population).
Approximately 8.25 percent of the total
population practiced other religions in
2001.
Latin America
Like the Caribbean, Christians in Latin
America represent the overwhelming ma-
jority. Of the estimated 490 million people
in Latin America in 2001, people of black
African descent accounted for 19 percent.
Almost 9 out of every 10 (89.14 percent)
people in Latin America in 2001 were
Christians. Another 5.65 percent of the
total population during that same year
practiced other religions.

North America
Bermuda, Canada, and the United States
are three nations classiﬁed under North
America, with a combined black population
of nearly 40 million by 2004. Blacks in
these three nations comprise at least the na-
tional average within religious groups. Like
both the Caribbean and Latin America,
Christians account for the majority of
people in North America. For example, as of
2000 in Bermuda, Christians accounted for
85 percent; unspeciﬁed 1 percent; and those
with no religion accounted for 14 percent.
In Canada, as of 2001, Christians
comprised 70.3 percent; Muslims 1.9 per-
cent; other and unspeciﬁed, 11.8 percent;
and those with no religion accounted for
16 percent. In the United States in 2002,
Christians accounted for 78 percent;
Jews, 1 percent; Muslims, 1 percent; other,
10 percent; and those with no religion ac-
counted for 10 percent. African Americans
accounted for 42 percent of the estimated
5 million Muslims in the United States,
with another 5.2 percent comprising
African Muslims, including Africans of
any racial background. For blacks in these
three nations, within their populations,
they comprised at least the national aver-
age of the religious groups.
Christianity and Islam 
in Africa T oday
Christianity and Islam have grown rapidly
in numbers in Africa in the post–World
War II era. Both religions have been suc-
cessful in spreading all across the continent.
That impact is due to the fact that both
Christianity and Islam require a convert
to abandon most or all of his or her tradi-
tional beliefs or cultural practices. For ex-
ample, Muslim missionaries spread forms
of restrained behavior. In addition, political
leaders and governments inﬂuence prevail-
ing religions. Islam is now the ofﬁcial reli-
gion of several African nations. President
Frederick Chiluba of Zambia says that his
country is “a Christian Nation that will seek
to be governed by the righteous principles
of the word of God.” In Côte d’Ivoire, West
Africa, the late president Felix Houphouet-
Boigny spent $360 million to build in the
political capital, Yamoussoukro, the Basilica
of Our Lady of Peace, the tallest church in
the world. It boasts a huge gold dome and
bears a resemblance to St. Peter’s in Rome.
As Christianity and Islam grow in Africa,
the number of Africans who practice indige-
nous religions will probably continue to de-
cline, even though many African Christians
and Muslims will continue to incorporate
some of their traditional and philosophical
beliefs in their religious practices.

932 R EPARATIONS(SLAVERY ANDCOLONIALISM)
REPARATIONS(SLAVERY
AND COLONIALISM)
Reparations refers to movements in the
United States and other nations with slav-
ery and colonial histories that call for mon-
etary and nonmonetary compensation to
individuals or groups that are victims, or
the descendants of victims, of slavery, racial
segregation, and colonialism. Long consid-
ered an outrageous ideological concept,
reparations has in recent years emerged as a
legitimate, though still highly controversial,
political and social cause that can be linked
with global struggles for human rights.
On April 2, 1998, President Bill Clinton
ended his tour of six African countries by
delivering a speech at Gorée Island, off the
coast of Senegal, from which millions of
Africans were forced to embark on voyages
of no return to the Americas. Recalling
the historical links between this former
slave trading post and the United States,
President Clinton said that “America’s
struggle to overcome slavery and its legacy
forms one of the most difﬁcult chapters” of
that shared history. Although earlier on the
trip he had acknowledged that European
Americans were “wrong” in receiving “the
fruits of the slave trade,” Clinton failed to
make a formal apology for his nation’s in-
volvement in the transatlantic slave trade.
This failure was disappointing to many
African Americans, whose hopes for public
redress for slavery, if only in the symbolic
form of an apology, had been fueled ten
years earlier by a similar gesture to Japanese
Americans. In the Civil Liberties Act of
1988, the U.S. Congress ofﬁcially apolo-
gized for the violations of the civil liberties
and constitutional rights of Americans of
Japanese descent who had been relocated
and interned during World War II. Fur-
thermore, federal funds were allocated for
ﬁnancial compensation to interned indi-
viduals and for public education on the
internment. The virulent criticism Clinton
received from conservative Republicans
such as Pat Buchanan and T om DeLay for
even his moderate expressions of regret
during his tour of Africa made it clear,
however, that the cause of black reparations
was highly controversial. Nevertheless, in
the years following his visit to Africa, the
movement for slave redress gained momen-
tum, sparking a ﬂurry of debate on repara-
tions in the United States.
Contemporary reparations demands in
the United States have historical roots in
the post–Civil War era. Some previously
enslaved individuals, pressed by economic
hardship, lodged claims with former mas-
ters for unpaid slave labor. Invoking the
federal government’s broken promise to
give the freedmen “forty acres and a mule,”
more than half a million African Americans
petitioned Congress between 1890 and
1916 for slave pensions. Neither the indi-
vidual redress claims nor the collective
appeals to the government were successful,
however.
The modern black reparations move-
ment in the United States may be said
to begin with civil rights activist James
Forman’s interruption of a Sunday service
in New York City’s Riverside Church in
1969 to read a “Black Manifesto,” demand-
ing that white Christian churches and syn-
agogues pay $500 million as a “beginning
of the reparations due us as people who
have been exploited and degraded, brutal-
ized, killed and persecuted.” Although a
few white clergymen admitted the church’s
guilt and endorsed expressions of repen-
tance, Forman’s tactics were widely de-
nounced in the press and the manifesto
trivialized. However, the manifesto’s term
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1021 ---
REPARATIONS(SLAVERY ANDCOLONIALISM) 933
“reparations” would be adopted by later
activists as was the idea that the money be
used to develop black communities. The
most important link with the later move-
ment was the manifesto’s implicit idea that
recompense was due to African Americans
not just for slavery but also for the Jim
Crow system that replaced it in the
American South.
Institutionalizing racial segregation
and black disfranchisement, Jim Crow per-
petuated and institutionalized social injus-
tice and inequality and sanctioned racial
violence. In the case of Plessy v. Ferguson
(1896), the U.S. Supreme Court declared
that it was not unconstitutional to offer
separate facilities for people of different
races, provided these facilities were equal in
quality—the so-called “separate but equal”
doctrine. While the majority opinion in
this landmark ruling was that the U.S.
Constitution did not have the power to
enforce social equality and eradicate racial
prejudice, in a dissenting opinion Justice
John Marshall Harlan insisted that the
Constitution is “color-blind, and neither
knows nor tolerates classes among citizens.”
Arbitrary “separation of the citizens, on the
basis of race,” Justice Harlan argued, “is a
badge of servitude wholly inconsistent with
the civil freedom and the equality before
the law established by the Constitution.” It
was precisely the latter line of reasoning
that the Supreme Court was to follow
unanimously in 1954, in another landmark
decision. In Brown v. Board of Education of
T opeka,the Court ruled that “separate edu-
cational facilities are inherently unequal,”
producing in black children a feeling of in-
feriority and depriving them of the equal
protection of the laws guaranteed by the
Fourteenth Amendment. The 1954 Brown
decision implicitly overruled the Supreme
Court’s infamous decision of 1896, but it
took almost two more decades and a long
civil rights struggle before the Jim Crow
system was completely dismantled. For
more than a century after the abolition of
slavery, then, Americans of African descent
suffered the burden of social and political
inequality, which, combined with their
often bleak economic prospects, severely
restricted their opportunities to enjoy the
privileges of U.S. citizenship.
This long history of racial injustice,
both during and after slavery, and particu-
larly the fact that it was legally and consti-
tutionally authorized, became the basis for
“The Case for Black Reparations” made by
Yale law professor Boris I. Bittker in 1973.
Prompted by a question posed by a black
student, Bittker, a prominent white legal
scholar, tried to establish legal grounds for
reparations. Bittker’s study of existing law
designed to compensate groups for injus-
tices imposed on them led him to conclude
that, far from being an outrageous pro-
posal, black reparations is a concept that is
susceptible to ordinary legal analysis.
Raising important questions about individ-
ual versus group compensation, the prob-
lem of racial classiﬁcation to determine
eligibility for reparations, and the selection
criteria for black organizations that were to
administer reparation programs, Bittker
did not offer easy answers to what he de-
scribes as a “second American dilemma,”
but merely aimed to open a national debate
on these questions. Ironically, however,
Bittker’s book was largely ignored and little
debate ensued, though the analysis it of-
fered and the questions it raised still inﬂu-
ences and challenges reparations advocates
today.
Signiﬁcantly, Bittker’s book was ﬁrst
published in 1973 by T oni Morrison, then

an editor for the New York publisher
Random House and only at the beginning
of a literary career that 20 years later would
make her the ﬁrst African American author
to win the Nobel Prize for literature. Mor-
rison’s internationally acclaimed novel
Beloved (1987) was to make a major contri-

past. The heightened consciousness of the
shameful history of slavery, coupled with
an increasing awareness that the civil rights
legislation of the 1960s had failed to rem-
edy entrenched patterns of racial inequality
in the United States, helped to reenergize
the black reparations movement in the
1990s.
The first important event was
Congressman John Conyers’s attempt to
put reparations on the political agenda in
1989. Inspired by the government’s formal
apology and reparation payments to Japan-
ese Americans in 1988, Conyers, a black
Democrat from Michigan, introduced a bill
to establish a commission to study repara-
tion proposals for African Americans. Nam-
ing his bill “H.R. 40,” as a reminder of the
government’s unfulﬁlled promise of “forty
acres and a mule” to the freed slaves, Conyers
ﬁrst of all asked, as he writes on his ofﬁcial
Web site, that the federal government
acknowledge “the fundamental injustice
and inhumanity of slavery.” His bill further
proposed to establish a commission to study
slavery and subsequent racial and economic
discrimination against African Americans,
as well as the impact of those forces on
African Americans living today. On the
basis of this ofﬁcial study, the commission
would then “make recommendations to
Congress on appropriate remedies to redress
the harm inflicted on living African
Americans.” Couched in moderate terms,
Conyers’s bill aimed to launch “a national
discussion” on black reparations without al-
lowing the issue to polarize the Democratic
Party or the nation. But even though he has
reintroduced the bill to every Congress
since 1989, it has remained stalled on the
subcommittee level and as a result has never
yet come before Congress itself.
Founded in the late 1980s, the National
Coalition of Blacks for Reparations in
America (N’COBRA) has developed into
the largest grassroots organization of slave
descendants in the United States that exclu-
sively focuses on the issue. Besides support-
ing Conyers’s bill, the organization engages
in education campaigns aiming to put pres-
sure on state and municipal legislators to
support reparations and is involved in legal
action on reparations. Demanding repara-
tions from the U.S. and state governments
for the “500 years’ holocaust of Africans in
America,” N’COBRA employs a much
more strident rhetoric than any of the pre-
viously discussed reparations advocates and
its black nationalist leanings have prevented
it from receiving mass support in the
African American community.
Internationally, the Organization of
African Unity (OAU) took up the issue at
the initiative of Nigerian president Ibrahim
Babangia. In 1993, the ﬁrst Pan-African
Conference on Reparations, held in Abuja,
Nigeria, under the auspices of the OAU, is-
sued a proclamation that perhaps for the
ﬁrst time put the issue of reparations in an
international perspective, explicitly linking
slavery and colonialism. The Abuja
Proclamation calls upon “states and nations
whose economic evolution once depended
on slave labor and colonialism” to recognize
the “unique and unprecedented moral
debt owed to the African peoples which
has yet to be paid.” The views on repara-
tions artic ulated in the pr oclamation are

rather diffuse, presenting the cause both as

The role Africans played in the slave trade
is left unmentioned.
More important and inﬂuential was
the establishment in South Africa of the
T ruth and Reconciliation Commission
(TRC) in 1995. By allowing both the vic-
tims and the perpetrators of violence dur-
ing the apartheid regime from 1960 to
1994 to tell their stories before the TRC,
the new South African government aimed
to bring about reconciliation between the
various ethnic groups in the nation and
make possible the transition to a truly free
and democratic government. Appearing be-
fore the TRC in 1996, the last white presi-
dent of South Africa, F . W . de Klerk,
begged forgiveness for the years of
apartheid rule, but former president P . W .
Botha ignored a summons to appear before
the commission. After more than two years
of hearings and investigations into human
rights violations, the TRC published a re-
port of its ﬁndings in 1998. The report
deemed the South African government, the
civil service, and its security forces the pri-
mary perpetrators of gross violations
against human rights, but also held the
ANC and other liberation movements ac-
countable for human rights violations.
President Nelson Mandela addressed the
issue of reparations in the speech he deliv-
ered upon receiving the report: “It is for
those who have the means to contribute to
the efforts to repair the damage brought by
the past. It is for those who have suffered
losses of different kinds and magnitudes to
be afforded reparation, proceeding from
the premise that freedom and dignity are
the real prize that our sacriﬁces were meant
to attain.” It was only in 2003 and under
pressure from reparations activists, however,
that President Thabo Mbeki announced
that about 19,000 apartheid victims who
testiﬁed before the TRC would receive a
reparations grant of R30,000 (US$4,200),
substantially less than the amount of repara-
tions the TRC had recommended.
In the United States, the reparations
movement gained small successes on the
state level in the 1990s. In 1993, a group of
nine survivors of the 1923 race riot of the
all-black town of Rosewood, Florida, ﬁled a
claim with the state legislature of Florida to
compensate them for damages resulting
from the destruction of their community.
Having ordered an academic investigation
of the events of 1923, the Florida legisla-
ture in 1994 acknowledged that govern-
ment ofﬁcials had been responsible for
“some of the damages sustained by the
claimants,” and concluded that “a moral
obligation exists to redress [survivors’] in-
juries.” The state of Florida paid $150,000
to each of the survivors in compensation
for emotional trauma suffered during the
event and awarded compensation to fami-
lies in Rosewood that could demonstrate
property loss. Building on the success of
the Rosewood reparations claim, similar
claims were ﬁled in other cities, most no-
tably in T ulsa, Oklahoma, where at least
40 and perhaps hundreds of African Amer-
icans were killed and thousands of black
homes and businesses were burned or
looted by white mobs in 1921. In its 170-
page report, published in 2001, the state-
appointed Oklahoma Commission to Study
the T ulsa Race Riot of 1921 recommended
that survivors and their descendants be paid

reparations for damages sustained during

The 2003 lawsuit against the State of
Oklahoma was prepared by the Reparations
Coordinating Committee (RCC), an orga-
nization founded in 2000 by Charles
Ogletree, a Harvard law professor, and
Randall Robinson, former president of
T ransAfrica, an African American think
tank, and author of The Debt: What Amer-
ica Owes T o Blacks(2000). Since 2002 the
Reparations Coordinating Committee has
been involved in a number of lawsuits
against public institutions and private cor-
porations. The most widely publicized of
these legal actions was a class-action suit
ﬁled in New York by a group of lawyers on
behalf of Deadria Farmer-Paellmann and
millions of slave descendants against a num-
ber of major private corporations, whose
predecessor companies had proﬁted from
slavery. It was subsequently consolidated
with similar reparations lawsuits prepared
by the RCC and brought before the U.S.
District Court in Chicago. Ruling against
the plaintiffs, the judge in the Chicago case
suggested that slaver y reparations claims
should be directed at the legislative and
executive branches of government rather
than be addressed in court.
Although reparations activism has so far
had few concrete positive results on the po-
litical and juridical levels in the United
States, the cause has gained both in visibility
and credibility in the years since President
Clinton’s failed apology in Africa. African
American activist Deadria Farmer-Paellmann’s
research into private corporations’ historical
links with slavery caused insurance company
Aetna in 2000 to offer a public apology for
selling insurance policies on slaves to ante-
bellum slave holders. Moreover, Aetna,
based in Hartford, Connecticut, created a
minority internship program and invested in
other initiatives serving the African Ameri-
can community as forms of reparations for
its ﬁnancial gains from slavery. Aetna’s apol-
ogy made enough of an impact to receive
international media coverage.
Aetna’s apology prompted the Hartford
Courant, the oldest continuously published
newspaper in the United States, to investi-
gate its history, leading to a front-page
article in which the Courant apologized for
having published advertisements in its
pages for the sale of slaves in the eighteenth
and nineteenth centuries. As a result, many
major national and international corpora-
tions based or active in the United States
are now looking into their predecessor
companies’ involvement with slavery, if
only because a number of states and cities
(California, Illinois, Chicago, and others)
require all companies doing business there
to disclose links with slavery. An important
effect of these disclosures and apologies is
that they underscore the complicity of the
entire American nation in slavery. Slavery
was not simply an institution peculiar to
the American South, thus supporting U.S.
reparations activists in their claim that
reparations should be addressed on a
national or even international level.
Reparations advocates from various
parts of the world tried to put the repara-
tions issue on the international agenda dur-
ing the World Conference against Racism,
Racial Discrimination, Xenophobia, and
Related Intolerance held in Durban, South
Africa, in September 2001. Unfortunately,

this United Nations-sponsored conference

government has sought to make reparations
for the nation’s slavery past.
As a result of these national and inter-
national developments, the public debate
on reparations Bittker and Conyers had
called for ﬁnally started in the United
States. Public opinion polls taken around
the time of the lawsuit against Aetna and
other corporations in 2001 and 2002 show
that an overwhelming majority of white
Americans are opposed to reparations for
slavery, while a substantial majority of
African Americans support it. The most
controversial issue is the idea of cash repa-
rations payments. A CNN/ USA T oday
Gallup Poll taken in 2002 found that 90
percent of white respondents were opposed
to cash payments by the government to
slave descendants, while 55 percent of black
Americans were in favor of it. Somewhat
less controversial are other forms of repara-
tions: the same poll found that 34 percent
of whites and 68 percent of blacks sup-
ported the idea that companies that proﬁted
from slavery apologize, while 35 percent of
whites and 75 percent of blacks felt these
companies should set up scholarship funds
for American slave descendants. Among the
ten reasons against reparations for slavery
listed by conservative publicist David
Horowitz in his book Uncivil Wars (2002)
are ones most often given by opponents—
that only a minority of white Americans
owned slaves and that most living Americans
have no connection to slavery, particularly
those who themselves or whose ancestors
immigrated to the United States after the
Civil War.
Though the reparations issue has re-
ceived little media attention since 2002, in
academic circles it is widely debated. While
the public debate in the media focused on
reparations for slavery alone, legal scholars
and political theorists who support black
reparations agree with Bittker and Conyers
that reparations should be made also for
the era of racial segregation, whose damag-
ing effects can more easily be traced to the
problems that African American communi-
ties face today. On the one hand, some
liberal theorists, such as Wendy Brown,
warn against political organizing around
historically “injured” or marginalized
group identities because a preoccupation
with past injuries tends to obstruct eman-
cipatory aspirations and foster racial and
political divisiveness. P olitical theorist
Lawrie Balfour argues, however, that
people can effectively be mobilized politi-
cally around the identity-based issue of
reparations if they move beyond a feeling
of racial resentment and group interest.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

938 R EPRODUCTIVE HEALTH AND FAMILY PLANNING
What is at stake is not so much black
resentment about racial injustice; rather,
white opposition to the idea of black repa-
rations seems to be fed by resentment
about constraints imposed on white privi-
lege. Rather than dwelling in the past,
Balfour argues, reparation politics can
redeem the past by offering an avenue for
social change from which not only African
Americans can beneﬁt.
In the past few years, reparations for
slavery and segregation, though still mar-
ginal in the public discourse, has emerged
as a legitimate issue of social justice. In
Atonement and Forgiveness, Roy L. Brooks
emphasizes that “black redress” should be
forward-looking and directed toward racial
reconciliation. Proposing a model of repa-
rations that focuses on atonement rather
than on compensation, Brooks argues that
the U.S. government must ﬁrst acknowl-
edge its responsibility and apologize and
then provide slave redress in the form of
asset-building reparations such as an
atonement trust fund, a museum of slav-
ery, and other forms of community reha-
bilitation. Only then can black America
forgive the wrongs suffered and can the na-
tion as a whole move forward toward racial
reconciliation.

REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH AND
FAMILY PLANNING IN
AFRICA, U.S. INFLUENCE ON
The United States has been a leading donor
in funding family planning and reproduc-
tive health in Africa since the late 1950s.
These activities have led to a tremendous
decrease in the prevailing high population
growth rate in Africa. However, recent cuts,
restrictions, and the reimposition of the
“Mexico City Policy” likely will lead to a
signiﬁcant increase in unplanned pregnan-
cies, abortions, and death, which will ulti-
mately lead to an increase in the population
growth rate in the continent.
World population growth accelerated
after World War II, when the population of
less developed countries began to increase
dramatically. By the year 2000, half the
world’s poor were in Africa, and it is the
only continent to have become poorer in
the past 25 years. By 2100, Africa is
expected to capture the greatest share of the
world population. Throughout the region,
population has outstripped economic
growth since the mid-1970s. Population
growth is particularly rapid in Africa, where
women average anywhere from ﬁve to eight
children each. Africa’s current growth rate
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1027 ---
REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH AND FAMILY PLANNING 939
of 2.9 percent means that, if this rate con-
tinues unchanged, the continent will dou-
ble its population every 24 years. Fertility
rates in the countries of Africa remain at
high levels for traditional and cultural rea-
sons. Patterns of childbearing vary across
Africa, whose population accounted for 10
percent of the world population in mid-
1992. Despite much variation in language,
customs, and taboos, a common preference
for large families runs through much of
Africa; this tradition is fed by the perceived
economic beneﬁts families receive from
their children. For a long time, barriers to
family planning acceptance included high
illiteracy rates, high infant mortality rates,
the high economic and social value placed
on children in developing countries, and
religious beliefs.
Rapid population growth is also having
a serious effect on the natural environment
in Africa. Some 500 million hectares of
land have been affected by soil degradation
during the last half century, including as
much as 65 percent of agricultural land.
This degradation has been a major factor in
constraining food production in Africa to
only a 2 percent annual increase, well below
the rate of population increase. In many
regions, particularly the Sahel, population
growth has exceeded carrying capacity and
thus denied the development and security
that would encourage a fall in childbearing.
The number of undernourished people in
Africa has more than doubled and projec-
tions indicate that the region will be able to
feed only 40 percent of its population by
2025.
The varied socioeconomic develop-
ment and the government policies of sub-
Saharan African countries did not lend
themselves to a straightforward assessment
of the prospects for fertility decline. Family
planning was perceived by Africans as a
means of attaining accelerated develop-
ment. This emphasis on development
benefits led some Africans and their
governments to suspect the intentions of
the family planning initiative’s advocates,
both nongovernmental and governmental,
and prevented African governments from
adopting population policy. However,
economic stagnation during the 1980s
prompted many national governments to
recognize that rapid population growth was
hindering their socioeconomic develop-
ment. Realizing that rapid population
growth not only threatens the future wel-
fare of society as a whole but also impedes
economic development, these sub-Saharan
countries began to give active consideration
to population policies to reduce fertility
and high rates of population growth by
expanding family planning services, raising
the age of marriage, improving the status of
women, providing family-life education,
and incorporating economic incentives for
smaller families into the provision of social
services. African governments have increas-
ingly taken steps to address these social
problems and some have adopted vigorous
family planning programs.
In an unprecedented move, African
leaders collectively endorsed family plan-
ning and the need to integrate it into ma-
ternal and child health programs in the
1984 Kilimanjaro Action Program. Ac-
cording to Africa’s Population Challenge,
about two-thirds of the region’s countries
now have active family planning programs.
There has also been a fundamental shift in
people’s attitudes toward childbearing. This
shift is partly explained by the increasing
economic hardship for poor families
who, given government budget cuts, ﬁnd it
harder to afford the costs of educating more
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1028 ---

children. The use of family planning meth-
ods, though still at a low 18 percent for the
region, has risen sharply in some states,
particularly in southern and eastern Africa.
In recent years, most African govern-
ments, already burdened by rapid popula-
tion growth, forced to cut budgets to pay
their foreign debt and keep their economies
aﬂoat, and nudged by global advocacy ef-
forts and their family planning associations,
have come to accept that fewer, better-
spaced births lead to healthier children and
lower maternal mortality and morbidity. By
the time of the Third African Population
Conference, held in Dakar in December
1992 as part of the preparations for the
International Conference on Population
and Development (ICPD) in Cairo in
1994, delegates were speaking almost unan-
imously about the importance of family
planning, both as a human right and as a
development issue.
Many international conferences on
population and development have also fo-
cused on the crucial importance of people’s
reproductive health needs, including their
access to services that enable them to plan
their families, ensure healthy childbirth,
and prevent HIV/AIDS and other sexually
transmitted infections. Important confer-
ences and the initiation of these debates
began with the 1968 T eheran Conference
on Human Rights, the World Population
Plan of Action in 1974, the International
Conference on Population in 1984, the
Amsterdam Declaration of 1989, and the
Convention for the Elimination of All
Forms of Discrimination against Women.
These conferences addressed women’s needs
and rights in a holistic and integrated way
by ensuring male involvement and respon-
sibility in reproductive health and attending
to adolescent sexual and reproductive needs.
International human rights treaties af-
ﬁrm that reproductive rights, including the
right to health, the right to family planning,
the right to reproductive self-determination,
and the principle of nondiscrimination, are
human rights and that lack of ac cess to re-
productive health services and information
constitutes a violation of these basic human
rights principles. The rights to family plan-
ning and health were ﬁrst articulated in the
Universal Declaration of Human Rights,
and were reﬁned in subsequent human
rights treaties adopted by the international
community. The ﬁrst World Population
Conference (Bucharest, 1974) was a land-
mark in the debate on population and
development and the Plan of Action that
resulted emphasizes the key role of fertility
reduction in economic development. Since
then, directives and linkages to develop-
ment have placed population and family
planning services within primary health
care programs, or within community devel-
opment programs, with a focus on quality
services and the need for better services for
those being served. Issues such as high
maternal mortality rates and contraceptive
acceptability have also become factors
critical to the delivery and distribution of
contraceptives.
The second International Conference
on Population and Development (Mexico
City, 1984) was marked by the conservative
position of the United States, which, echo-
ing the policy of free markets, emphasized
“sound economic policies” as the key to
development and challenged the view
that rapid population increase was not
an obstacle to economic growth. Hence, in-
ternational development agencies began
to broaden their focus from reproductive
health to a more encompassing concept
that included not only fertility regulation
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1029 ---
REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH AND FAMILY PLANNING 941
and maternal child health but also sexually
transmitted diseases.
The World Conference on Women and
Empowerment held in Beijing in 1995 em-
phasized new attitudes toward family plan-
ning, reproductive health and rights, and
also put family planning, reproductive and
sexual health care, and women’s empower-
ment squarely in the context of develop-
ment, underlining their critical importance
to any social and economic progress. The
Program of Action highlighted the impor-
tance of gender equity to achieving repro-
ductive health and reproductive rights, and
broadened the mandate of reproductive
health programs to include customary laws;
traditional, cultural, and religious practices;
and policies and legislation.
The international conferences called
on governments to recognize that repro-
ductive health eludes many due to inade-
quate levels of knowledge about human
sexuality and appropriate or poor quality
reproductive health information and ser-
vices, the prevalence of high-risk sexual
behavior, discriminatory social practices,
negative attitudes toward women and girls,
and the limited power many women have
over their sexual reproductive lives. Hence,
the United Nations Population Fund
(UNFPA) included in its programs repro-
ductive health and family planning, popu-
lation policy and advocacy, along with its
commitment toward human rights. It has
the goals of providing universal access to a
full range of safe and reliable family plan-
ning methods and reproductive health ser-
vices; reducing infant, child, and maternal
mortality; and providing universal access to
primary education.
For people in African countries, espe-
cially women, the greatest risks to repro-
ductive health include sexually transmitted
diseases, early motherhood, and unwanted
pregnancy. Many, especially those in rural
areas, do not have access to risk-reducing
information related to reproductive health
and health services because health care is
inaccessible, inadequate, and unavailable to
large numbers of rural populations. They
have few choices about where and from
whom they receive health care. One of the
major factors affecting most Africans’
health status is low income. Poverty in-
creases health problems and is associated
with poor nutrition, inadequate housing,
and unsafe living conditions. Thus, poverty
not only increases their health care needs, it
also decreases their ability to have access to
health care.
The international communities, in-
cluding the United States, agreed to fund
family planning in developing countries
including those in Africa based on the
premise that when couples can choose the
number, timing, and spacing of their chil-
dren, they are better able to ensure there
are enough resources for each family mem-
ber to prosper and thrive, and as a result,
their children do not repeat the cycle
of poverty of their parents, communities
thrive, and in turn, countries fare better.
Realizing that the greatest deﬁcits in access
to health services can be found in the
poorest segments of the population, the in-
ternational communities decided that
channeling resources for family planning
activities would save lives, stabilize popula-
tion growth, slow the spread of AIDS,
reduce poverty, and improve women’s posi-
tion in society.
It is believed that family planning can
expand life choices for women and girls.
Postponing early marriage and childbirth
among girls and young brides by offering
family planning choices increases their
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

chances of receiving a good education,
which is vital not only to women’s individ-
ual development but to that of their
children as well as to the social, political,
and economic growth of their community.
International family planning and repro-
ductive health programs funded by the
United States through the United States
Agency for International Development
(USAID) population program and UNFPA
provide health care choices that assist
women in realizing their right to health,
including reproductive health care, and the
right to decide freely and responsibly on
the number and spacing of one’s children.
The United States began its population
assistance programs in 1965 with the
announcement that technical assistance
in family planning would be available to
countries requesting it. By 1968, the
United States was the primary source of
funding for international population and
family planning activities, with a budget of
nearly $35 million representing over 66 per-
cent of the total international assistance; by
1994, the USAID budget had reached
$463 million, providing assistance to over
60 countries. USAID’s family planning
program is one of the most successful com-
ponents of U.S. foreign assistance. Since
the agency began providing family plan-
ning services in 1965, the use of modern
family planning in the developing world
has more than quadrupled, going from less
than 10 percent to more than 40 percent.
In the countries with the largest USAID-
sponsored family planning programs, the
average number of children per family has
declined by one-third, from more than six
to less than four.
The need to stabilize the rapid popula-
tion growth rate is the primary objective
of USAID family planning programs in
Africa and grew out of concern that if
the continent’s growth rate continued un-
abated, problems of conﬂict, corruption,
and competition for limited resources
would be exacerbated. The programs are
based on the premises that when people
can control the size of their families, re-
sources will be available at the household,
national, and global levels for enduring
improvements in quality of life and that
improved health status of women can play
a critical role in family welfare, economic
productivity, and population stability.
USAID has therefore focused its efforts
on interventions that contribute to stabi-
lizing population and improving health
care, which are essential for sustainable
development.
The rationale for U.S. government
support was coupled with a strong concern
about rapid population growth as a destabi-
lizing factor in international order and
a threat to U.S. security, in part prompted
by the cold war atmosphere of the
period. U.S. interest in population assis-
tance stemmed from a combination of
strategic and humanitarian concerns, in-
cluding promoting a better life for people
in developing countries and enabling cou-
ples and individuals to decide freely on the
size of their families.
USAID is the lead donor in supporting
Africa’s efforts in increasing the use of volun-
tary family planning services and contracep-
tive prevalence. The agency has contributed
signiﬁcantly to increasing the use of modern
contraceptive methods, which have helped
to reduce high-risk pregnancies and abor-
tions and saved the lives of hundreds of
thousands of women.
USAID’s family planning programs
involve a range of programs, from health
to social to technical interventions and

REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH AND FAMILY PLANNING 943
assistance. USAID supports programs in
more than 60 countries in Africa, Asia,
Latin America, the Caribbean, Eastern
Europe, and the former Soviet Union at
the host government’s request. The
agency’s strategies for family planning are
to provide high quality, voluntary health
care services that are easily available to
many people. Essential elements of the
programs include counseling and services,
training of health workers, contraceptive
supplies and their distribution, ﬁnancial
management, public education and mar-
keting, and biomedical and contraceptive
research and development. USAID sup-
port is based on a broad reproductive
health approach, which emphasizes choice
among a wide range of contraceptives, im-
proved quality of care, and client-centered
services. USAID family planning programs
are increasingly integrated with other com-
munity-based efforts to improve maternal
and child health, enhance women’s status,
and prevent HIV transmission and other
infectious diseases.
USAID’s reproductive health programs
in Africa include training, capacity build-
ing, contraceptive logistics, contraceptive
social marketing, and behavior change
communication, with the objectives of
contributing to sustained and broad-based
economic growth by reducing the rapid
rate of population growth through sustain-
able reduction in unintended pregnancies,
increasing use by women of voluntary prac-
tices that contribute to reducing fertility,
and improving maternal and child health
by enabling women to space between births
and to limit family size. These activities are
all designed to improve the demand for
and access to quality family planning and
reproductive health services. In addition,
USAID supports awareness raising and
advocacy activities concerning the impact
of rapid population growth on all sectors of
society and on maternal and child health.
Working with private voluntary organi-
zations (PVOs), local nongovernmental or-
ganizations (NGOs), women’s groups and
networks, community-based organizations,
and private sectors, USAID supports the in-
tegration of family planning into existing
NGO health services and establishes net-
works for community-based distribution
of contraceptives and contraceptive social
marketing programs using radio advertise-
ments, ﬂyers, billboards, and peer educators
to spread family planning information in
communities. USAID works with commu-
nity NGOs to provide safe, affordable, and
quality family planning services in African
countries through community-based dis-
tributors and clinics and also provides
training to traditional birth attendants and
patent medicine dealers who sell family
planning products.
In spite of USAID’s successes in the
area of population reduction in African
countries, many feminist researchers assert
that concerns about high fertility and low
contraceptive prevalence in Africa have
stimulated policy and program efforts at
promoting family planning in the region
because health-related conditions impinge
on population policy. According to the
feminist researchers, relative failure of
family planning programs is in part a mea-
sure of the programs’ failure both to see
women’s lives in a cultural context and to
approach women as whole individuals
beyond their childbearing roles. Feminists
therefore advocate for family planning
efforts that would take into account exist-
ing sexual practices, patterns, and partner-
ship arrangement of the populations they
serve.

Though the United States has been a
supporter of international family planning
and population assistance since the late
1950s, in 1984, the Reagan administration
imposed restrictions on U.S. funding for
international family planning, and in
January 2001, President George W . Bush
reimposed the Global Gag Rule, or what is
popularly known as “Mexico City Policy,”
on USAID population programs. This pol-
icy restricts foreign nongovernmental orga-
nizations that receive USAID family plan-
ning funds from using their own, non-U.S.
funds to provide legal abortion services, or
even provide accurate medical counseling
or referrals regarding abortion even where a
woman’s physical or mental health is en-
dangered (the only exceptions are in cases
of rape, incest, or where the woman’s life is
endangered), lobby their own governments
to legalize abortion, or conduct public edu-
cation campaigns regarding abortion. In
addition, even the provision of services that
are “permitted” on paper, such as lifesaving
abortions and postabortion care, are often
curtailed because NGOs fear jeopardizing
their funding through any association with
abortion. Providers may even be reluctant
to dispense emergency contraception be-
cause of the Global Gag Rule. By sti-
ﬂing public debate and the ability of foreign
NGOs to lobby their governments, the
Global Gag Rule undermines NGOs’s right
to exercise freedom of speech. The Global
Gag Rule also forces health care organiza-
tions to make an immoral choice: either
give up desperately needed funds for family
planning and other reproductive health care
services, or give up their right to free speech
and to provide patients with full and accu-
rate medical information.
The Global Gag Rule also erects barri-
ers to the development of the democratic
process in other countries, the promotion
of civil society and development of NGOs
abroad, and the enhancement of women’s
equality and participation in the political
process. Furthermore, it inappropriately
challenges foreign governments’ sovereignty
by constraining their implementation of
national health care policy decisions. It will
decrease women’s ability to access preg-
nancy-related care, family planning, and
services for HIV/AIDS and other sexually
transmissible infections, and will lead to
higher rates of unintended pregnancy and
higher rates of abortion.
Because of its size and wealth, the United
States remains one of the largest bilateral
donors to international family planning
programs. However, the United States’s
continued insufﬁcient funding levels and
restrictions on family planning contravene
a principal goal of the foreign policy of the
United States in providing humanitarian
assistance and a better future for all. In
addition, these limitations severely curtail
the ability of low-income nations to ensure
their citizens’ rights to health, family plan-
ning, and reproductive health. The United
States has also been a leader in funding the
United Nations Population Fund, which
works in over 140 countries to provide
crucially needed funding for reprod uctive
health services. However, in 2002, Presi-
dent Bush eliminated funding for UNFPA
due to pressure from extreme anti-choice
legislators who claimed that the program
was involved with coercive abortion in
China.
Despite U.S. support for desperately
needed programs in developing countries,
especially in African countries, to ensure
reproductive rights, the nation’s participa-
tion has been inconsistent, insufﬁcient, and
mired with burdensome restrictions. Many

NGOs and the majority of nations receiv-

leadership to revitalize international repro-

ing for family planning and reproductive
health assistance. These nations and NGOs
believe that because family planning and
reproductive health programs are so impor-
tant for both health and demographic
reasons, it is essential that more, not fewer,
resources be invested in this area, especially
because the numbers of women in the re-

the proportions of those women who want
to use contraception. According to Nicole
Itano, there are nearly 1 billion women of
reproductive age in the third world (pro-
jected to rise to over 1.2 billion by 2010).
Unfortunately, with the laudable exception
of a few (mainly Scandinavian) countries,
most donor contributions have stagnated or
even decreased.
Moreover, there are other causes com-
peting for international funding, most
notably AIDS. At the time of the Cairo
Conference, 20 million people were in-
fected with HIV , the virus that causes
AIDS. Just over ten years later, that number
has doubled. Indeed, AIDS threatens to de-
rail the ICPD strategy. For, although bil-
lions of dollars are now pouring in to ﬁght
the disease, much of this money is going
into AIDS-speciﬁc programs that do not
address reproductive health more broadly.
Naﬁs Sadik, a former head of UNFPA and
now the UN secretary-general’s special
envoy for HIV in Asia, has observed often
that as few as ten years ago, those working
in family planning shied away from the
ﬁeld of HIV with its heavy burden of social
stigma. The roles have since reversed as
reproductive health is engulfed in a storm
of religious and political controversy. One
consequence is that organizations con-
cerned with ﬁghting AIDS are failing to
make use of valuable infrastructure and ex-
pertise already on the ground in places
where the disease hits hardest. Given that
more than half of HIV infections in Africa
are among women, and that for many
African women family planning services are
their main contact with the formal health
care system, such services need to be
drafted into the wider battle against HIV .
Many family planning clinics already
offer HIV testing and counseling, as well as
condoms for protection against un-
wanted pregnancy and HIV infection, and
also provide a broad-based message of
sexual health.
