RESTAVEK
The restavek, a Creole word derived from
the French reste avec, or “stays with,” is a
contemporary form of child slavery on the
Caribbean island of Haiti. Slavery has a
long history in Haiti, and by the 1780s,
half a million slaves lived in the French
colony of Saint-Domingue (present-day
Haiti). A successful slave revolt and war of
independence (1791–1804) led to the
abolition of slavery (temporarily in 1793,
permanently with the declaration of inde-
pendence in January 1804), but forms of
slavery lingered on. Haitian rulers T oussaint
l’Ouverture, Jean-Jacques Dessalines, and
Henri Christophe forced former slaves to
remain on plantations under a system
known as fermage. In 1863, a law legalized
the corvée, thus requiring local residents to
provide free labor to help keep up the road
system; seldom applied initially, the corvée
was revived extensively during the early
part of the ﬁrst U.S. occupation of Haiti
(1916–1918). Various twentieth-century
Haitian presidents, François Duvalier most
famously, received a per capita allowance
for each worker sent to the Dominican
Republic to help with the sugarcane har-
vest, or zafra (many Haitian workers were
then sent back to Haiti without receiving
the salaries they were promised).
Restaveks frequently originate as sons
and daughters (girls predominate) of poor
peasant families in Haiti’s rural areas who
are given away to an urban family in Port-au-
Prince (primarily), Jacmel, Les Cayes, or
Cap Haïtien in exchange for the promise
that they will be well taken care of and ed-
ucated. In reality, restaveks often end up as
household slaves. Households employing a
restavek are better off than the families the
children come from, though by no means
well off. Various reports estimate that there
are between 100,000 and 300,000 restaveks
in Haiti. Charged with menial chores such
as mopping, babysitting, cooking, fetching
water, and cleaning, restaveks rarely receive
the education they were promised (salaries
are nonexistent). Cases of malnutrition,
verbal abuse, and medical neglect are fre-
quent. Many also play a central role in
the sexual initiation of young men of the
household. Those who complain are typi-
cally beaten by their owners. When they
become pregnant or sick, or when they
reach their teenage years, restaveks usually
ﬂee (or are chased) from the household.
On August 15, 2002, Haiti signed the
UN Convention on the Rights of the
Child, which prohibits economic exploita-
tion of children (article 32). Under Haitian
law, no child under 12 may be employed
as a household servant. They must be
fed, clad, and provided medical atten tion.
Families hosting a restavek should re ceive
prior authorization from social services.
These legal provisions, like many others in
Haiti, are widely ignored. Popular and ofﬁ-
cial contempt for restaveks, along with
widespread hardships and poverty in
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1035 ---
RICE IN THE AFRICAN DIASPORA 947
Haiti, mean that many Haitians do not
even condemn child servitude. Despite
President Jean-Bertrand Aristide’s declara-
tions of sympathy for Haiti’s children, non-
governmental organizations remain the only
ones to actively combat restavek slavery.
Although restaveks seem to have existed
for at least a century, they ﬁrst received
international attention in the 1990s with
the publication of several reports, including
the UNICEF’s Les enfants en situation
spécialement difﬁcile en Haïti (1993), as well
as Jean-Robert Cadet’s Restavec: From
Haitian Slave-Child to Middle-Class American
(1998). Cadet, a former restavek, recounted
in his autobiography how he was aban-
doned by his father after his mother’s death,
raised as a restavek, then ﬂed to the United
States.

RICE IN THE AFRICAN
DIASPORA
The African agricultural contribution of
rice to the New World shaped patterns of
subsistence and identity throughout the
Americas. One of the enduring legacies of
the Atlantic slave trade is the failure to rec-
ognize the accomplishments of the enslaved
in the agricultural history of the Americas.
African slaves provided considerably more
than brawn to the New World, shaping
landscape and diet around subsistence pref-
erences. Nowhere is the African agricultural
contribution to the Americas more evident
than in the development of rice as a planta-
tion crop in late seventeenth-century
colonial South Carolina. Rice was ﬁrst
introduced to South Carolina shortly after
the colony’s establishment in 1670. It ini-
tially appeared as a crop Africans grew for
food. They planted it with the rains but also
in wetland environments, such as inland
swamps, along river ﬂoodplains, and in es-
tuaries. Its potential as a plantation crop
soon became evident, and by the eighteenth
century, rice was exported from Carolina
plantations to Europe. Decades later, the
cereal’s cultivation on the fertile ﬂoodplains
of tidal rivers made South Carolina the
wealthiest plantation economy in North
America, long before cotton became “king.”
The transformation of South Carolina’s
coastal plains to irrigated rice ﬁelds in such
a short period of time revealed a remarkable
grasp of tidal ﬂow and saltwater-freshwater
dynamics. Until the 1970s scholars cred-
ited the original English and French
Huguenot settlers with this stunning
achievement. In mastering the complexities
of paddy rice farming without any prior
familiarity with its cultivation, Carolina’s
founding fathers metamorphosed into in-
genious planters. Such views on rice history
as a product of European initiative began to
change when historians Peter Wood and
Daniel Littleﬁeld revealed that other mi-
grants to the colony already possessed con-
siderable experience growing rice. These
were Africans enslaved from the broad
region of West Africa where the cereal had
been cultivated for centuries. With prior
expertise growing rice in West Africa, the
enslaved capitalized on a body of knowl-
edge that guided rice’s establishment as a
preferred dietary staple in the Americas.
They transferred crucial cultivation,
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1036 ---
948 R ICE IN THE AFRICAN DIASPORA
processing, and cooking methods to the
New World. In South Carolina rice was
directly sown as in West Africa, and not
transplanted as in Asia. The irrigated rice
systems along the West African coast from
Senegal to Sierra Leone served as the proto-
type for the tidal plantations established
in South Carolina and later Georgia. The
wholesale African export of rice culture to
the Americas involved centuries-old prac-
tices of cultivation as well as consumption,
which became evident in the grain’s trajec-
tory from ﬁeld to kitchen and across the
Atlantic.
From where did Africans develop rice
culture? Until the twentieth century, schol-
ars believed the crop a recent introduc-
tion to West Africa, brought by Portuguese
mariners after the return voyage of ex-
plorer Vasco da Gama from India in 1498.
Thanks to Portuguese intercession, the ce-
real’s cultivation was formally established
along Africa’s Upper Guinea Coast. But
Africa’s colonization at the end of the nine-
teenth century caused such views to be
questioned. French colonial botanists in
West Africa began documenting distinctive
characteristics of the rice grown there, no-
tably its red color, upright growth pattern,
and tolerance of saltwater ﬂooding and
drought. In the early twentieth century,
they advanced the proposition that the rice
found in West Africa originated there, and
its presence long antedated the arrival
of the Portuguese. Research additionally
showed that the African rice did not diffuse
across the continent from Asia. It was al-
ready established when Asian rice arrived in
East Africa following the eighth-century
expansion of Islam. The international scien-
tiﬁc community had accepted the conclu-
sion that the rice grown in West Africa
was truly indigenous to the region. The
scientiﬁc name, Oryza glaberrima, distin-
guishes the African species from the domes-
ticated Asian cereal, Oryza sativa.
In the years since Wood’s groundbreak-
ing research, archaeologists Roderick and
Susan McIntosh found African glaberrima
present in one site along the ﬂoodplain of
the Niger River in Mali some 2,000 years
ago. Further, work in historical linguis-
tics supports a date of domestication for
African rice between 4,000 and 4,500 years
ago, probably by speakers of Mande lan-
guages, who possibly responded to drier
climatic conditions by domesticating the
cereal and sowing the grain in lowland
swamps. The cereal then diffused south to
the Guinean highlands, where ample rain-
fall permitted its cultivation as a rain-fed
crop, and westward to speakers of West-
Atlantic languages settled near the Atlantic
coast. Long before the arrival of Europeans,
West Africa’s indigenous rice region reached
along the Atlantic coast from Senegal to
Côte d’Ivoire and inland for more than one
thousand miles to the country of Chad.
Over this geographic expanse, African soci-
eties grew rice within sight of Saharan sand
dunes, Atlantic waters, and highland re-
doubts, adapting the crop to enormous
ecological variability.
Wherever rice is grown in West Africa,
it is associated with women. For centuries
the cereal has remained a crop principally
grown by women, or one with a distinct di-
vision of labor, where women carry out the
sowing, weeding, and seed selection. The
experience of cultivating rice in distinctly
different environments made the cereal a
valued food crop throughout the region.
Rice, along with millet and sorghum (two
other African domesticates), sustained the
successive African empires that formed be-
tween the Senegal and Niger Rivers in the
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1037 ---
RICE IN THE AFRICAN DIASPORA 949
millennium prior to the fatal dislocations
of the transatlantic slave trade. In the mid-
fourteenth century, one Muslim visitor, Ibn
Battuta, noted the importance of rice and
its availability in regional markets.
Africa’s red rice did not go unnoticed by
Europeans. The arrival of Portuguese car-
avels along the Upper Guinea Coast in the
mid-ﬁfteenth century initiated commen-
taries on the cereal’s widespread cultivation,
the diverse places where it was grown, and
the role of women in growing, processing,
and marketing the crop. Throughout the
four centuries of the Atlantic slave trade,
Europeans relied upon rice and the other
cereals grown by African societies to provi-
sion the slave ships that sailed across the
Middle Passage to the Americas. In this way,
rice was introduced to the New World.
Archival records reveal that slave ships
principally purchased rice “in the husk,”
meaning with the indigestible hulls still at-
tached to the grains. Any rice grain left un-
milled on a slave ship could serve as seed
rice. The African mortar and pestle proved
the only way to remove the hulls, a neces-
sary step to the cereal’s consumption. Unlike
wheat, oats, and barley, the cereals then
known to Europeans, rice demands a dif-
ferent milling method. The objective is not
to crush the grains into ﬂour but to leave
the grain intact while removing the hulls.
The hollowed out log and handheld wooden
pestle, traditionally used by African women
to process all cereals, was the only way to
mill rice without breakage. This method
was alien to European agricultural prac-
tices. Records in European archives reveal
that African females aboard slave ships were
put to this task, milling rice with their tra-
ditional technology, which remained the
only way to prepare and polish rice for con-
sumption. Mortar-and-pestle processing
remained ubiquitous until the last quarter
of the eighteenth century, when a success-
ful mechanical mill was developed.
The mortar-and-pestle milling per-
formed by African women was crucial for
establishing rice culture in the Americas,
for without a way to remove the hulls, rice
could not be eaten. The diffusion of the
mortar and pestle throughout the black
Atlantic provides additional testimony to
the importance of African women for es-
tablishing rice culture in the Americas.
The earliest introduced rice to the
Americas was likely African glaberrima.
Archival records in South Carolina report a
delivery of rice from a Portuguese slave ship
in the 1680s. Rice of a red color was also re-
membered as among the ﬁrst types planted
in the colony, even though higher-yielding
Asian rice replaced them as the rice planta-
tion economy consolidated. Rice of a red
color is also featured among the earliest
types described in Brazil. Shortly after its
colonization in the sixteenth century, and
one hundred years before South Carolina
was made a colony of England, rice was in-
troduced to Brazil from the Cape Verde
Islands near the coast of Senegal.The cereal’s
initial appearance is associated with slavery,
as slaves grew the cereal for subsistence in
the food ﬁelds of Brazilian sugar plantations.
While its establishment is unquestionably
attributed to Portuguese initiative, rice was
not grown in Portugal until the late eigh-
teenth century, centuries after its introduc-
tion to Brazil. From the 1750s, Portugal
developed rice plantations in the eastern
Amazon region, centered on Maranhão, lo-
cated south of the estuary. Modeled on the
successful Carolina system, the region’s rice
plantations developed on tidal rivers and
imported the high-yielding “Carolina gold”
seed variety (a sativa rice). Africans with
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1038 ---
950 R ICE IN THE AFRICAN DIASPORA
expertise growing rice along the Upper
Guinea Coast were enslaved and brought
directly to the region.
Rice also shaped patterns of subsis-
tence, resistance, and identity throughout
northeastern South America. It was planted
as a food crop in the former Guianas and
by runaways from plantation slavery
(maroons) who ﬂed to the rainforest to es-
cape a life of bondage. T o this day maroon
descendants grow rice, and the cereal re-
tains its African identity as a woman’s crop.
It was in this region that French botanists
found African rice in the 1940s and 1950s.
Female maroons in Guyane (French
Guiana) were still planting the seeds in the
decade following World War II. African
rice was also discovered growing wild on
the margins of a former sugar plantation in
El Salvador during the 1950s. Botanical
collections in Latin America may hold other
examples of African rice, but they have yet
to be analyzed for its presence.
It is thus unsurprising that the role of
enslaved African women in rice agriculture
is not forgotten in the historical memory of
slavery retained in some remote hamlets of
northeastern South America. From the
Guianas to Amazonic Brazil, maroon de-
scendants tell a legend about rice origins.
They recount the story of a female ancestor
who hides grains of rice in her hair during
the long, harrowing journey aboard a slave
ship. The precious seeds escape detection.
When she ﬂees the plantation that holds
her captive, she smuggles the rice grains in
her hair. She then plants them for food as a
maroon. This, say her descendants, is how
they came to grow rice.
The maroon narrative is faithful to
African women’s historic role in seed selec-
tion and rice cultivation, but it remains
signiﬁcant for additional reasons. The oral
history of rice introduction challenges the
longstanding view that European ingenuity
and initiative pioneered rice cultivation in
the Americas. While high-yielding Asian
varieties guided the transformation of rice
as an important and proﬁtable crop in the
eighteenth-century colonial system, the
maroons make claim to the prior knowl-
edge and agency of Africans in establishing
seeds from Africa. This oral history con-
trasts sharply with written accounts that
claim transoceanic seed transfers were
solely the outcome of European efforts to
disperse them. In the maroon narrative, the
usual agents of seed dispersal celebrated in
Western accounts—European navigators,
colonists, and men of science—are replaced
by an enslaved African woman whose de-
liberate effort to sequester grains of rice in
her hair enabled her descendants to survive
in plantation societies. The narrative pro-
vides a vivid memory of the transatlantic
slave trade, African initiative, and the dietary
preferences of the enslaved.
One enduring signature of the African
Diaspora is the manner of preparing rice
in the Americas. Asians prefer a rice bowl
where the grains adhere to one another.
The Spanish paella and Italian risotto bear
the Middle Eastern inﬂuence of the pilaf,
where rice is sautéed in animal fat or oil
and then cooked in a stock. The African
method of rice preparation favors cooking
the cereal so every grain is separate. It is
sometimes also mixed with greens, okra,
black-eyed or pigeon peas (additional African
plant domesticates). The popular converted
rice marketed globally (including under the
brand name Uncle Ben’s) is actually par-
boiled rice, a method of steaming newly
harvested rice that is not yet dry. Parboiling
the rice concentrates the nutrients, eases
removal of the husk, and reduces
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1039 ---
RICE IN THE AFRICAN DIASPORA 951
spoilage from microbes. Even the ubiqui-
tous image of Uncle Ben speaks to the
social memory of the African rice heritage
in the Americas.
Between the sixteenth and eighteenth
centuries the American, Asian, African, and
European continents experienced botanical
and ecological exchanges that were nothing
short of revolutionary. The intensity and
richness of these interchanges, among soci-
eties made unequal by the process of con-
quest and colonization, is revealed in a
body of literature known among scholars as
the Columbian Exchange. The name refers
to the intercontinental plant exchanges
during the centuries following the mar-
itime voyages of Columbus to the New
World. While improving historical under-
standing of the role of plants in shaping
global food systems and societies, there is
little attention to crops of African origin.
Emphasis remains on the role of plants
(the potato, tomato, maize) domesticated
by America’s native peoples, or those do-
mesticated in Asia, such as sugar cane and
rice, on societies elsewhere.
Africa—home to more than 2,000 na-
tive grains, roots, and fruits utilized as food
staples—receives little or no commentary
except as a recipient of introduced crops.
In part, this omission results from the fact
that many of its native plants are grown in
the tropics and not known or considered
unimportant by societies in northern tem-
perate societies. Most people are unaware
that the two most popularly consumed
beverages in the West derive from African
plants. Coffee originated in Africa, while
cola soft drinks rely on the African kola
nut. The lack of attention to African plants
represents a research bias that continues to
haunt the present. In the continent where
human beings evolved, three important
centers of plant domestication developed,
direct products of the civilizations that
developed there. That African rice was not
acknowledged as native to West Africa until
the second half of the twentieth century is
illustrative of the enduring ignorance of
African agricultural achievements.
It can be said that Africans actively
shaped the early modern Atlantic world.
Until the third decade of the nineteenth
century, they crossed the Atlantic in greater
numbers than Europeans, albeit being
forced to do so in chains. While Africans
and their descendants were central to the
economic development of the Americas for
more than three centuries, their role in agri-
cultural innovation and botanical exchanges
has received little acknowledgment. Among
the migrants to the Americas, they alone
possessed prior experience growing crops in
the tropics. Plants of African origin con-
tributed to survival, cultural identity, and
ritual. While Europeans purchased African
food surpluses to provision slave ships, it
was the victims themselves who took the
seeds of their dietary staples and planted
them in the ground for subsistence in the
colonies where they were forced to labor.
Futhermore, slaves deliberately established
many African foods, such as black-eyed
peas, okra, and sorghum, on plantation
subsistence ﬁelds.
The African Diaspora was one of
plants as well as people. Plants came across
the Atlantic in the holds of slave ships as
provisions, medicinals, or for their general
utility. The enslaved drew upon their
botanical knowledge to establish African
plants in new locales, thereby profoundly
shaping the cuisines of the U.S. South,
Brazil, Cuba, and other plantation
economies. The history of rice in the black
Atlantic provides one way to promote the
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1040 ---

historical recovery of the African heritage
in the Americas.

ROBINSON,J ACK ROOSEVELT
(1919–1972)
Jackie Robinson was a Hall of Fame baseball
player with the Brooklyn Dodgers, but more
importantly he was a prominent civil rights
pioneer. At a time when African Americans
were shut out of organized white baseball
and restricted to all-black leagues, Robinson
was recruited by Dodgers general manager
and co-owner Branch Rickey to become the
ﬁrst African American in modern times to
play in the Major Leagues. Robinson faced
enormous hostility from many players on
other teams, and even from some of his own
teammates, but he persevered, showing the
courage to resist ﬁghting back. Instead he
struck back with his bat, glove, and feet, be-
coming an outstanding hitter and helping
to bring a new type of play to Major League
games. He opened the door to hundreds of
other African Americans in baseball and
helped open the eyes of millions of white
Americans to the evils of racism.
Jackie Robinson was well prepared to
play his historic role. College educated, he
was an outstanding athlete at the University
of California, Los Angeles, starring in base-
ball, football, basketball, and track. During
World War II, he enlisted in the U.S. Army
and was made a second lieutenant. There he
encountered racism more directly than he
had at UCLA. While stationed at Fort
Jack Roosevelt Robinson (Jackie Robinson) is shown in
his Kansas City Monarchs uniform. Later, he would
sign with the Brooklyn Dodgers and, in 1947, became
the ﬁrst African American to play Major League
baseball. (Library of Congress)

Riley, Kansas, he was not permitted to play
on the football or baseball teams. Later, at
Fort Hood, T exas, on a July day in 1944,
Robinson boarded a bus and was ordered
to the back. He refused and was court-
martialed. Vehicles on military bases, how-
ever, had ofﬁcially been desegregated by
then, and Robinson was acquitted. After
that, ﬁghting for equal rights became a per-
manent and personal crusade for him.
After his military service, Robinson
played Negro League baseball for the Kansas
City Monarchs in 1945. His successes at bat
and on the bases, as well as his educational
background and maturity (he was 28 when
he played his ﬁrst Major League game), led
Rickey to conclude that he was the right
person to break the color barrier. Rickey
subjected Robinson to an exhaustive inter-
view process before signing him to play
with the Dodgers’s top Minor League team,
the Montreal Royals, in 1946. Robinson’s
Major League rookie season of 1947 was a
stunning success despite vocal opposition,
insults, and even threats by other teams not
to play a Dodger team with Robinson on it.
Although some teammates opposed having
a black teammate, many others supported
him, most importantly shortstop Pee Wee
Reese, the highly respected captain of the
team. Robinson won National League
Rookie of the Year honors as a ﬁrst base-
man. He batted .297 and led the league
with 29 stolen bases, introducing a style of
play based heavily on speed, stolen bases
(including stealing home, a Robinson trade-
mark), hit-and-run plays, and bunting. In
short, it was the type of play common in the
Negro Leagues. Attendance at Dodgers
games increased dramatically, as the team
set attendance records at several cities. Huge
numbers of African Americans came to see
Robinson and applaud his accomplish-
ments. Robinson shifted to second base in
1948, leading National League second base-
men with a .980 ﬁelding average. He had
his greatest season in 1949, leading the
league in batting average at .342 and stolen
bases with 37. It was the ﬁrst of six consec-
utive seasons in which he would bat over
.300. The 1949 season also brought with it
the National League Most Valuable Player
Award.
The Dodgers proved themselves one of
the best and most beloved teams ever
during Robinson’s years with them. The
club included such stars as Reese, center
ﬁelder Duke Snider, ﬁrst baseman Gil
Hodges, catcher Roy Campanella, and
pitcher Don Newcombe, the latter two
among many African Americans who fol-
lowed Robinson to the Dodgers. Robinson,
however, was widely perceived as the cata-
lyst for the team’s success. In his ten seasons
(1947–1956) with Brooklyn, the Dodgers
won six pennants and the 1955 World
Series, the team’s ﬁrst-ever World Series
Championship. In the other four years, the
Dodgers ﬁnished second three times and
third once. Robinson meanwhile proved to
be a versatile as well as talented player, as he
also spent considerable time at third base
and in the outﬁeld.
Robinson’s ﬁnal two seasons were less
successful than the others, with Robinson
batting .256 and .275. His entry into the
majors delayed by his military service and
the ban on African Americans, Robinson
was thirty-seven years old by his tenth sea-
son. In the winter of 1956, he was traded to
the New York Giants but decided to retire,
ﬁnishing with a career .311 batting average.
He was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame
in 1962. In later years, Robinson continued
to open doors of opportunity for African
Americans. As a businessman, he was an

executive with the coffee company Chock
Full o’ Nuts, which ran a chain of coffee

ways aided the Civil Rights Movement of

As the 1960s progressed, Robinson’s

there has been just one Jackie Robinson, so
would no other player ever again wear his
number.

ROSAS DE OQUENDO,
MATEO (1559–?)
Mateo Rosas de Oquendo’s writing reﬂects
the African presence in colonial Peru and
speaks judgmentally of the particular lust-
fulness of women of African descent.
Compared frequently to his peninsular
counterpart Francisco Quevedo, Rosas de
Oquendo worked in a similar literary vein
of satire. In his narrative poem Cosas que
pasan en el Piru, año de 1598 (Things that
Happen in Peru, 1598 ), he criticizes social
structures and Peruvian reality in the late
sixteenth century. Through double enten-
dre, he describes a decadent, (morally) cor-
rupt, socially pretentious Peru brimming
with sexual promiscuity. This literary de-
vice forges a carnivalesque atmosphere in
which charade (the ostentations of dress
codes) and deception (“false” virgins) reign.
His verses hint at the stereotypical com-
plexity of the New World and the instabil-
ity of the viceroyalty for tolerating such
behavior.
The brunt of Rosas de Oquendo’s satire
is directed toward those of African descent in
Lima, particularly women. There are some
fourteen direct references in Cosas que pasan
to negros, negras, and mulatas—members of
groups that are frequently associated with
dance and dalliance and comprise the bot-
tom rung of the social ladder. Through them
and those around them, Rosas de Oquendo
paints a picaresque Peru comprised of adven-
ture-seeking rogues, lascivious prostitutes,
and opportunistic go-betweens.
The poem, multifaceted and hybrid
in form, functions as a pseudo-historical
testimonial emanating from an agenda-
encumbered first-person narrator. But
given that the poetic voice in the author’s
text functions as a witness of events, it is
difﬁcult to determine allegiances, since his
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

tone vacillates between admonishing the
happenings—“things that happen in
Peru”—and advocating them.

ROYALAFRICAN COMPANY
Parliament established the monopolistic
Royal African Company (RAC) in 1672 to
expand England’s African trade and to en-
sure a constant ﬂow of African slaves into
its American plantations. The RAC created
the foundations of England’s slave trade
that would, by the eighteenth century,
displace the Dutch as the primary carrier
of slaves from Africa to the Americas. The
RAC’s creation was a response to the
growing European belief in the impor-
tance of the transatlantic slave trade not
only to the American plantation system
but to the development of individual state
economies. The RAC was a joint-stock
company designed, through its monopoly
in England’s African trade, which included
slaves, gold, ivory, and other African
commodities, to provide dividends to its
shareholders. While most of the early
shareholders included the king and nobil-
ity, it did not take long for England’s
growing merchant population to take con-
trol of the company. As the company
worked to establish itself on the Gold
Coast, by expanding the number of coastal
forts it possessed, the RAC quickly learned
of the ﬁnancial and logistical difﬁculties of
overseeing the slave trade. This trade in-
volved carrying a large supply of com-
modities from Europe to West Africa,
exchanging these commodities for slaves,
and then carrying the slaves to the Ameri-
cas. Within this, the RAC needed to meet
the demands of the American plantations
for slaves.
The RAC soon found it difﬁcult to
proﬁt and, within England’s mercantile
class, many were unhappy because they were
denied an opportunity to participate in
what they viewed as a very lucrative busi-
ness venture. This growing espousal of free
trade by English merchants, and the chal-
lenges it presented to mercantile thought,
caused Parliament, in 1698, to pass an act
that opened England’s African trade. The
Act of 1698, scheduled to expire in 1714,
allowed a larger segment of England’s mer-
cantile class to participate in the slave trade.
T o make up for the loss of proﬁts to the
RAC, the separate traders paid a 10 percent
duty on all goods that they imported into
West Africa. This opening of England’s
slave trade allowed it to expand and, while
in the years before the act’s expiration a de-
bate between the two sides ensued, the situ-
ation continued. The RAC continued to
work to maintain its coastal presence, yet
throughout the ﬁrst half of the eighteenth
century, its situation deteriorated. Finally, in
1750, Parliament decided to dissolve the
RAC and in its place created the Company
of Merchants T rading to Africa to oversee
the maintenance of England’s African trade.
Ty M. Reese

RWANDA
The Republic of Rwanda is a small and
mountainous country in central Africa
with a population of about 7,954,000.
Most inhabitants are either members of the
majority tribe, the Hutus, or the minority
T utsis. Rwanda was occupied by the
Germans during the colonial era and was a
part of German East Africa until World
War I. During the war, the British, aided
by French, Belgian, and some Portuguese
soldiers, invaded the region. After the war,
the region was annexed by the Belgians,
who ruled it under a League of Nations
mandate, and later as a United Nations
T rusteeship. Rwanda was granted indepen-
dence on July 1, 1962.
Very few Americans went to Rwanda
before independence. However, the Free
Methodist Church of North Africa started
missionary work in the region, called
Ruanda-Urundi, in 1935. The Presbyterian
Church in the United States started send-
ing missionaries to Rwanda in the 1970s,
and the U.S. Peace Corps started operating
in the country in 1975.
Rwanda has been the focus of important
primatological studies because of its gorilla
population. George B. Schaller’s The Year
of the Gorillawas the ﬁrst popular account of
Rwanda’s mountain gorillas. The work in-
spired many others, including the most fa-
mous American connected with Rwanda:
Dian Fossey. Born in San Francisco, she
studied at San Jose State College and then
Cambridge University, going on a safari in
Africa in 1963. Fossey returned four years
later to establish the Karisoke Research
Center in Ruhengeri, Rwanda. She spent
many years in close study of Rwanda’s
mountain gorillas in the Virunga Moun-
tains, living in close proximity to them. She
served as scientiﬁc director of the Karisoke
Research Center from 1967 to 1980, proj-
ect coordinator from 1980 to 1983, and
then scientiﬁc director again from 1983.
She opposed the hunting of gorillas and
was murdered by poachers in 1985. She
was the author of the internationally fa-
mous book Gorillas in the Mist, which was
later turned into a ﬁlm of the same name.
Rwanda returned to international visi-
bility in April 1994 when growing tensions
between the majority Hutu and minority
T utsis erupted from occasional massacres
into wholesale genocide. Hutu leadership
had, for many years, been promoting an
ideology of “Hutu Power” and had been
systematically organizing in preparation.
While many in the U.S. media attributed
the tensions and genocides to “ancient eth-
nic hatreds,” later scholarship noted that
there had been peaceful mixing of Hutus
and T utsis well up to the colonial era. The
tensions that led up to the genocide were,
many argued, a consequence of the prefer-
ential treatment of T utsis over Hutus by
Belgian colonizers in the twentieth century
and the resulting disparities in wealth and
economic power.
Despite warnings from the Canadian
general Roméo Dallaire, head of the United
Nations Assistance Mission for Rwanda, lit-
tle action was taken to prevent the massacres
by international bodies or Western nations.
A move to increase the number of UN
peacekeepers in the country before the mas-
sacre was blocked by the U.S. government.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1045 ---
RWANDA 957
Many T utsis ﬂed to neighboring Burundi.
Reorganized under Paul Kagame’s leader-
ship, the T utsi-led forces of the Rwandan
Patriotic Front returned to Rwanda to over-
throw the Hutu government and reestablish
order. By July, 800,000 Rwandans, both
T utsi and Hutu, had been killed.
Paul Kagame was made president in
2000 and reelected in 2003. During his pres-
idency, Rwanda has sought to reconcile
T utsis and Hutus. Among the critical parts of
the reconciliation process have been the cre-
ation of local courts, known asgacaca courts,
to prosecute those responsible for the geno-
cide. Some have proposed creating truth and
reconciliation commissions along the same
lines as South Africa’s postapartheid com-
missions, which seek to have perpetrators
publicly admit and atone for their crimes in
order to help communities heal.
The United States’s inaction during
the massacres has resulted in a national
revisiting of the question of whether or not
the United States should intervene militar-
ily in the case of genocide. The Rwandan
tragedy returned to public view in the 2004
ﬁlm Hotel Rwanda. The ﬁlm centered
around a hotel in Rwanda’s capital, Kigali,
which served as one of the few sanctuaries
for T utsis, Hutus, and foreigners trapped in
the midst of the genocide.

SADAT,M UHAMMAD ANWAR
EL- (1918–1981)
Muhammad Anwar el-Sadat, also known as
Anwar el-Sadat and Anwar al-Sadat, was
president of the Arab Republic of Egypt
(1970–1981) and the “architect of a new
Mideast.”
One of thirteen siblings, Sadat was
born on December 25, 1918, in Mit Abul-
Kum, a village in the Nile Delta north of
the Egyptian capital, Cairo, to a poor
Egyptian-Sudanese family. At the time,
Egypt was a British Colony. He studied at
the Royal Military Academy—a British
military school that ﬁrst opened its door to
the middle class in 1936. He developed anti-
colonial thoughts at an early age, as
demonstrated by his choice of study. Be-
sides studying traditional subjects, students
had to learn to analyze battles. Sadat chose
to study the Battle of Gettysburg, the turn-
ing point in the American Civil War. After
graduating from the Royal Military Acad-
emy in 1938, he was appointed to a remote
government base where he met Gamal
Abdel Nasser, who became Egypt’s idolized
president. Sadat was to become one of
Nasser’s Free Ofﬁcers who overthrew the
Egyptian monarchy headed by King
Farouk I as well as ended British rule in the
revolution of July 23, 1952.
Sadat was arrested twice by the British,
who accused him of assisting the Germans
during World War II. He was jailed from
1942 till 1944 and lived as a fugitive from
1944 till 1945. Having been stripped of his
rank, Sadat tried to resume civil life but
found himself back in anti-colonial activity.
He was arrested again in January 1946 and
held in solitary conﬁnement for eighteen
months. His imprisonment was to con-
tinue for another year and a half.
In 1950, Sadat was reinstated into the
army by Nasser, who was then in charge of
the Free Ofﬁcers Organization. During the
1952 revolution, Sadat was assigned the
task of overseeing the ofﬁcial abdication of
the king. He became the voice of the revo-
lution in his capacity as the editor of the
newspaper al-Gumhuriya (The Republic).
From 1955 on, Sadat held various govern-
mental positions, including serving as
Nasser’s vice president in 1964–1966 and
again in 1969–1970. In 1970, Sadat be-
came the president of Egypt on Nasser’s
death.
Sadat’s 11-year presidency was dra-
matic and controversial. On the domestic
front, Sadat was relatively unknown. Un-
like Nasser, whom the people adored and
supported unconditionally, Sadat had to
prove himself worthy of his position to
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1048 ---
960 S ADAT,M UHAMMAD ANWAR EL-
secure his rule. He ordered the arrest of
many rivals and potential opponents. How-
ever, to avoid infuriating the people, he or-
dered the release of many political prison-
ers. Sadat won some popularity from the
relative success of the 1973 October War
against Israel in which parts of the Sinai
Peninsula, which was occupied by Israel in
1967, were regained.
On the international stage, in 1972
Sadat ended a 15-year alliance with the
Soviet Union, expelling Soviet advisers
from Egypt and turning to the United
States for help and friendship. Diplomatic
relations between Egypt and the United
States were restored when the U.S. secre-
tary of state, Henry Kissinger, accepted
Sadat’s invitation to visit Cairo in December
1973. Under Sadat’s rule, Egypt became
the second-largest recipient of U.S. aid in
the world.
Sadat took Egypt and the entire Arab
world by surprise when, in 1977, he made
his historic visit to Jerusalem, proclaiming
his intention of making peace with the
country that had been Egypt’s foe for
25 years. His visit started a process that
culminated in 1978 with talks at Camp
David, Maryland, hosted by the American
president Jimmy Carter. Sadat, Menachem
Begin (the Israeli prime minister), and
Carter signed a peace accord at the end of
these talks. Sadat’s initiative for peace won
him and Begin the 1978 Nobel Peace
Prize; it also won him international
acclaim. At home, though, this initiative
cost him his life. Many Arabs saw Sadat’s
initiative as a sellout to the enemy. Sadat
was assassinated by Muslim fundamental-
ists within his own army on October 6,
1981, during the annual parade celebrat-
ing the victory in 1973. Three American

Who Dared. London: Frank Cass, 1996.
SAILORS
The African Diaspora followed shipping
routes out of Africa and dispersed free and
enslaved black sailors along those routes
throughout the ages of European coloniza-
tion of North America and American chat-
tel slavery. In the late 1600s, England dis-
placed the Netherlands as the dominant
maritime power in the Atlantic. This power
shift resulted in a corresponding shift in the
national, ethnic, and racial composition of
ships’ crews. England was a large and pow-
erful nation, but rapid expansion soon
nearly exhausted the supply of able-bodied
men available to serve in its Royal Navy.
Jails were emptied, towns and villages were
required to supply quotas of men, and press
gangs regularly kidnapped sailors of any
allegiance, race, or nationality. Coupled
with the fact that England was rapidly
expanding its enslavement of Africans, this
shortage made it a natural outcome that
some slaves would end up serving on
English ships.
Slaves were taken to sea for many
reasons. Sea captains often took slaves as
personal assistants. Slaveholders would send
slaves to sea so that they might collect their
slaves’ wages and prize money, or “shares”
that were paid to each sailor when his ship
captured an enemy ship. Far more slaves
were simply pressed into maritime slavery
in the way that other Africans were forced
into plantation slavery—by physical duress.
After they were aboard, slaves began to
learn the ways of the ship. This new knowl-
edge gave those slave-sailors a set of
portable skills they could take with them to
other ships. After earning, or escaping to,
their freedom, many black sailors remained
at sea because it provided them with a trade
that they could follow.
The reasons black sailors found them-
selves at sea were as diverse as the ships they
sailed. Though initially most black sailors
came into the seafaring trade through the
English Royal Navy, they eventually found
their way into the worldwide merchant ser-
vice, onto slave ships and pirate ships, into
the American whaling fleet, and into
sundry maritime-related trades ashore:
manual labor trades like loading and un-
loading ships, and skilled trades like ship’s
carpentry, caulking, painting, or black-
smithing. Black sailors were themselves a
diverse lot, and many became important
ﬁgures in the Pan-African world. They in-
cluded in their numbers Olaudah Equiano,
the famous abolitionist and writer; Crispus
Attucks, the American Revolutionary hero;
Denmark Vesey, the slave-revolt organizer;
Captain Paul Cuffe, organizer of the ﬁrst
black-led back-to-Africa movement; and
Robert Smalls, the ex-slave who became an
inﬂuential member of the U.S. Congress.
In fact, among this list is one—but not the
only—remarkable woman sailor “William
Brown.”
There were many good reasons free
and enslaved blacks wanted to remain at
sea. The social world of the forecastle,
where the common sailors lived secluded
from the ofﬁcers, was organized around a
sailor culture that was different from any
culture that existed ashore. Politically, the
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1050 ---
962 S AILORS
ship was organized from the top of the so-
cial order down—not unlike the world of
the shore. Sailors of all races and nations
were all held captive by their captains. In
some literal sense, after they left shore, they
were all the slaves of their captains. The
idea that sailors of all races and nations
were “all in it together” had a unique effect
on the social order of the ship that existed
among the “people,” as the common sailors
were called. This social solidarity promoted
unity and racial reconciliation to a degree
unseen in almost any other labor situation
in which diasporic blacks might have found
themselves. The physical danger of the job
they had to do also contributed to unity.
Ability truly meant something to sailors
who directly depended upon each other for
their physical safety.
Because ability showed itself in the
“wooden world,” as the ship was called, it
was a place for social advancement for
black sailors. Lacking opportunities on
shore, many black sailors had long careers
at sea. The skills and experience they
gained in a life at sea would often grant
them better wages and higher social status
than they ever could have achieved ashore.
T raveling the world from port to port gave
black sailors worldliness and experience un-
available to people living on shore. Their
mobility also granted them access to infor-
mation about Africa and the branches of
the African Diaspora; other blacks relied
on them as a valuable conduit of this infor-
mation. They regularly touched port around
the Atlantic and came into contact with
free and enslaved blacks who worked in the
maritime trades and lived in port cities.
The link they constituted back to Africa
and among widely dispersed black popula-
tions made black sailors important ele-
ments in the formation of a Pan-African
identity as well as in abolitionist move-
ments around the Atlantic world.
The decades preceding the Civil War
in the United States saw a sudden and dra-
matic decline in the number of black sailors
on American ships. Knowing that free
black sailors threatened the institution of
slavery in the American south, slaveholding
Southerners used Denmark Vesey’s alleged
conspiracy to institute severe restrictions on
the rights of black sailors. In December
1822, South Carolina passed the ﬁrst of a
series of restrictions on African American
sailors called the Negro Seamen Acts. These
acts amounted to a tax on free black sailors
who were taken into the South. They were
designed to price them out of the labor
market.
The de-integration of the maritime
trades was also hastened in the United
States by an inﬂux of immigrant labor,
mostly Irish, which was coincident with the
Negro Seaman Acts. The last refuge of large
numbers of African American sailors was
the Nantucket whaling trade, of which they
composed, at times, as many as half of
those involved in the trade. The American
South’s Civil War tactic of harassing the
Yankee whaling ﬂeet, however, was the nail
in the cofﬁn of that trade, which had begun
its decline with the discovery of oil in 1859
at Titusville, Pennsylvania. Shortly after the
Civil War, worldwide shipping became in-
creasingly mechanized, and with the
steamship came the end of the need for
large crews. By the turn of the twentieth
century, people of African descent had lost
almost all trace of their once-great seafaring
tradition.
Matthew D. Brown

SAINT KITTS AND NEVIS
Saint Kitts and Nevis, formerly colonized
by Britain and France, is a small federated
twin-island nation located in the north-
eastern Caribbean about 1,300 miles (2,092
kilometers) southeast of Miami, Florida.
Although Christopher Columbus encoun-
tered the islands in 1493, it was not until
1624 that the British, and the French a year
later, permanently colonized St. Kitts
(shortened form of St. Christopher). The
island became both European powers’ ﬁrst
colony in the Caribbean. However, in
1713, the T reaty of Utrecht ceded French
St. Kitts to the British. In 1628, the Caribs
of Nevis were killed and driven off, like the
Caribs of St. Kitts, and supplanted by
English settlers from St. Kitts.
The mainly European and overwhelm-
ing majority of African peoples would
come to dominant the population of these
islands. In St. Kitts, there were mainly
English, French, and Irish settlers. How-
ever, starting in the 1620s to the early
1800s, over 115,000 enslaved Africans
were forcefully brought to the island, with
large numbers coming from Nigeria and
West-Central Africa areas. In fact, there was
a town in St. Kitts called Angola T own be-
cause it was populated with hundreds of
Africans of Central Africa origins. Addi-
tionally, there were instances where
Congolese Christians from Central Africa
were recognized in St. Kitts.
On the other hand, in Nevis there were
mainly English and Irish European settlers.
More than 25,000 Africans were forcefully
brought to Nevis over the span of two cen-
turies. A large number of these individuals
came from the area that is known as Nigeria
today. In addition, an almost equal amount
of peoples came from the present-day area
of Ghana, pointing to Akan origins.
The institution of slavery dominated
most of the colonial history of St. Kitts and
Nevis. Other than a short period of white
indenture servitude, basically the small
numbers of Europeans of the territories
controlled the islands’ major political and
economic institutions. The colonial gov-
ernments, with varying degrees of subor-
dination to the metropolis, were headed
by the French and English colonists, with
governors, councils, and assemblies. The
control and ownership of farms of to-
bacco, cotton, indigo, and ginger, and the
mid-seventeenth century emergence of the
monoculture sugar industry, would enrich
European planters and help further the
development of the British, and for some
time, the French Empires. In most of the
eighteenth century, imports to England
from Nevis was almost double that of
the colonies of New York, and St. Kitts,
based on its population and size, and was
the single richest colony in the British
Empire.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1052 ---
964 S AINT KITTS AND NEVIS
On the other hand, besides a small
number of emancipated slaves, the vast ma-
jority of the peoples, who were of African
descent, were forced to perform the brunt
of the labor on the farms and plantations.
Many Africans found slavery to be intoler-
able, and there was resistance to enslave-
ment with acts ranging from damaging
property, running away, committing sui-
cide, to revolting. For example, in Nevis,
besides scores of runaways, there were re-
ports of Africans plotting to revolt in 1725
and in the early 1760s. It was similar in St.
Kitts. In 1639, a group of Africans on the
French side of St. Kitts temporally estab-
lished a maroon society in Mount Liamaiga
(formerly Mount Misery). In 1737, at the
St. Kitts harbor, about 100 newly imported
enslaved Africans chose to commit mass
suicide and jumped overbroad into the
sea. At least 33 drowned in order to escape
slavery. In 1770 and 1778, there were
reported plots of Africans’ attempts to
revolt. Up until near the end of the slave
era, the legendary leader Markus, along with
30 other maroons, roamed the woods of
St. Kitts.
The intermediate phase in the develop-
ment of the colonial societies comprised
the emancipation and postemancipation
period. Albeit, the English settlers and the
metropolis still had strong inﬂuence over
the political and economic institutions of
the societies. Although not drawing as
much wealth as it used to, the sugar indus-
try continued to be the main economic ac-
tivity of these islands up into the twentieth
century. In 1871, the separate colonies of
St. Kitts, Nevis, Antigua, British Virgin
Islands, Dominica, and Montserrat became
a part of the single colony of the British
Leeward Islands. In 1882, St. Kitts and
Nevis were jointed together to become the
single unit of St. Kitts-Nevis.
The ﬁnal stage of the colonial period
would bring reform and self-government
for the islands. St. Kitts-Nevis continued to
grow sugar, which accounted for close to 90
percent of the islands’ exports. Cotton was
introduced mainly in Nevis. By the 1930s,
Nevis was growing sugarcane and cotton
along with large areas of subsistence crops.
In spite of that, islanders continued to face
adversity. In 1935, the third of a series of
labor riots erupted in St. Kitts, with subse-
quent occurrences in other British
Caribbean territories. This development
gave rise to strong labor unions with mem-
bers who eventually entered the govern-
ment and directly inﬂuenced social, eco-
nomic, and political reform. At the same
time, the almost negligible population of
people of European descent continued to
decline. In St. Kitts-Nevis, similar to some
of the other British Caribbean territories,
many of the political leaders were of
African descent and came from working-
class backgrounds. One of such leaders,
Robert Bradshaw, a member of the Labour
Party, dominated politics from the late
1940s until his death in the 1978. In 1956,
the Leeward Islands Federation was dis-
solved. From 1958 to 1962, St. Kitts-Nevis
was united with nine other British colonies
to form the West Indies Federation. In
1967, St. Kitts-Nevis along with Anguilla,
became an associated state with internal
self-government.
St. Kitts-Nevis entered the postcolonial
period of its history on September 19,
1983. Thereby, the society became one of
the smallest and youngest African diasporic
states. Ninety-ﬁve percent of the estimated
40,000 citizens of the islands are of African
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1053 ---
SAINT KITTS AND NEVIS 965
descent; small numbers of minorities of
British, Portuguese, and Lebanese descent
make up the rest of the population. English
and English Creole are spoken by the
islanders. Most of the people are followers
of Christianity, mainly Protestant and
Roman Catholic denominations, with a
small minority of Rastafarians.
Kittitians and Nevisians’s cultural inter-
actions with other peoples have been
heightened with their historical and politi-
cal ties to other islands and with present
ties to intergovernmental organization such
as the Organization of Eastern Caribbean
States (OECS) and the Caribbean Com-
munity (CARICOM). Additionally, St.
Kitts-Nevis has one of the strongest migra-
tory traditions in the Caribbean, if not the
world, which deepens cultural interactions,
especially with other African diasporic mi-
grants, societies, and minority communi-
ties in other lands. This migratory tradition
began in the preemancipation period but
the movement continued and expanded to
include constant streams of substantial
migratory movement. Yet, there were many
returns and temporary sojourners, in the
nineteenth and twentieth centuries.
However, some of the more persis-
tence cultural practices are derived from a
shared African origin and a persistent
stream of diasporic interactions. This is
evident in many facets of the society.
Kittitians and Nevisians have a strong
kinship-based societal organization that
has merged with the nation-state. This is
similar to the organization in some other
Afro-Caribbean and African societies.
Similar to other diasporic societies, there
are the traditional community arrange-
ments of African-influenced shotgun
houses clustered together. The connection
to the land and agricultural practices of
animal rearing and farming, more so on
Nevis, parallels some traditional African
and Afro-Caribbean societies. Addition-
ally, there are some traditional utilities,
such as the mortar and pestle and the
yabba pot. Dietary meals eaten in Africa
and the islands share such ingredients as
cornmeal, okra, pigeon peas, plantains,
tamarinds, tannia, sorrel sorghum, water-
melon, and yams. Furthermore, there is
the traditional use of herbal remedies such
as jumbie beads (Abrus precatorius) and
periwinkle (Catharanthus roseus ) for health
and medical purposes.
African-descended persons in the
islands share with the wider African
Diaspora some musical traditions, such as
calypso performance and African banjo
and drum usage. Additionally, there are the
storytelling traditions, which include
Anansi stories. Furthermore, there are the
local crafts, such as the 300-year-old
African-derived pottery-making and
basket-making. Moreover, there is the
continued tradition of African-originated
Warri game-playing.
Finally, the traditional festivities, re-
ferred to in the islands as Christmas Sports,
share some similarities with Junkanoo
festivities in other islands. These festivities
include singing, dancing, acting, and story-
telling for about a two-week period around
Christmas time. Many aspects of these fes-
tivities have been institutionalized into the
annual Carnival in St. Kitts and Culturama
in Nevis.
Kittitians and Nevisians, after centuries
of struggle, have control of the major
political, social, and some economic insti-
tutions of the islands. Kittitians and
Nevisians, like other people of Africa

and African descent, have to continuously
negotiate their existence and survival
after many centuries of colonialism in a
world that is increasingly becoming more
globalized.

SAINT KITTS AND NEVIS
REVOLT (1639)
The Saint Kitts and Nevis Revolt was an
early slave uprising that set the precedent
for aggressive resistance to French slavery in
the Caribbean. At the birth of the French
Empire in the Caribbean, Africans, mainly
serving as slaves, were present. In fact, by
1626, about a year after the establishment
of the ﬁrst permanent French colony on the
Caribbean island of St. Kitts, enslaved
Africans outnumbered almost by double
the Frenchmen on the island. Indeed, as
the number of enslaved Africans increased,
so did their resistance to bondage. As else-
where in the Americas, African resistance in
St. Kitts varied from damaging property,
committing suicide, revolting, maronnage,
or a combination of all the above. Nevis, an
island separated from St. Kitts by a mere
two miles of narrow channel and claimed
under the sovereignty of England, would
develop a similar population of maroons
resisting slavery. 
Although information on the early
years of French colonial rule in the
Caribbean is sparse, a reported uprising in
1639 would set the precedent for an aggres-
sive form of resistance in the world of
French slavery. This insurrection of about
60 enslaved Africans occurred in the
Capesterre section of St. Kitts. These
Africans, including men, women, and chil-
dren, left the plantation and ﬂed to Mount
Liamaiga (formerly called Mount Misery).
From Mount Liamaiga, which was strategi-
cally located close to the Anglo-French bor-
der (British and French colonizers shared
the island), these Africans would raid the
small number of planters on the island.
Albeit the ultimate objectives of these
rebels are not clear, it was nevertheless a
courageous act by Africans to resist slavery.
Swiftly, in response to the insurrection,
Philippe, sieur de Lonvilliers de Longvilliers
de Poincy, the governor of French St. Kitts,
dispatched a military force of 500 men
to suppress the rebellion. Many of the
Africans, who were poorly armed, were
killed and those that were captured were
executed. However, according to scholar
Nellis Crouse, there remained a sole
African insurrectionist who lived apart
from the other rebels in order to elude cap-
ture. If the larger group’s intention was sim-
ilar to this rebel’s reported acts of deﬁance
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1055 ---
SAMBO’S GRAVE 967
to the French, his behavior indicated a con-
tinuation of resistance through a one-man
campaign against the French. Indeed, this
unnamed African reportedly served as a ral-
lying point for many enslaved Africans,
who held great respect for him and helped
him to evade the French. Although he
often was surrounded by French soldiers
who shot at him, the French were unable to
kill or apprehend him. The rebel continued
to successfully avoid capture. Many is-
landers began to believe he had supernat-
ural powers. However, the French contin-
ued their pursuit and after three years of
eluding the French, he was shot and killed
by a French soldier.
While many of the insurrectionists
were killed, it is thought that a few of the
rebels continued to roam the woods of
St. Kitts even into the 1660s. Insurrection,
revolts, and all forms of resistance would
persist in St. Kitts and everywhere the en-
slavement of Africans occurred in the
French Empire. However, it would be over
a century later, in another realm of the
French Empire—Haiti, when a long his-
tory of resistance would cumulate into full-
blown revolt. The Haitian revolt, unlike
the revolts in 1639, would not only cause a
minor interruption of the slave system but
would become the largest and most suc-
cessful slave revolt ever. The revolt would
eventually lead to the establishment of a re-
public, which earlier rebels could only
dream of, founded on the principle that all
men and women are free.
Mario Nisbett

SAMBO’S GRAVE
This extraordinary gravesite located at the
Lune Estuary on Sunderland Point near
Lancaster is one of the earliest slave graves
in Britain. It lies on unconsecrated ground
on the edge of a farmer’s ﬁeld. It is the grave
of an adolescent brought to England from
the West Indies by an unnamed captain
around the year 1736. The boy was left at
Sunderland Point while his master sailed on
to do business in town. It is reported that
after two days, when his master failed to
return, the young man became profoundly
distressed and died. It is more likely he died
from the combination of the vigors of the
voyage and sickness. The inhabitants of
Sunderland decided to bury him on the
point rather than in Overton churchyard
because he was not baptized. In 1796 the
Reverend James Watson wrote a sentimen-
tal elegy based on the story and raised
funds to place a plaque at the grave with a
portion of the elegy laid out. Since the early
1980s it has become a signiﬁcant tourist at-
traction. Flowers and stones with messages
are regularly laid at the grave. It memorial-
izes a black British presence established
long before the signiﬁcant post-1945 mi-
gration from the West Indies. As one of the
few slave graves positioned right at the
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

point of entry of the slave ships, it provides
a vivid reference point to the workings of
the transatlantic slave trade.

SANCHEZ,S ONIA (1934–)
Sonia Sanchez is a poet and educator inﬂu-
ential to the Black Arts Movement. She was
born Wilsonia Benita Driver in Birmingham,
Alabama. Her mother, Lena Jones Driver,
died when Sanchez was a year old; she
and her two siblings (Patricia and Wilson)
went to live with their grandmother, who
died when Sanchez was six. Her father
moved the family to New York three years
later.
After graduating from Hunter College,
Sanchez, who had been writing poetry
since her youth, became involved with a
new strain of black poets in the 1960s. She
and others published by Dudley Randall’s
Broadside Press, including Don L. Lee
(later Haki Madhubuti), Nikki Giovanni,
and Etheridge Knight, became known as
the “Broadside Quartet,” a group of young
poets deeply involved in the growing Black
Arts Movement and its emphasis on
Afrocentricity and Black Nationalism. Her
poetry uses nontraditional structures and
forms and incorporates the black vernacu-
lar tradition to make powerful statements
about poverty, racism, and sexism in the
lives of ordinary African American people.
The unconventional oral delivery of her
poetry seeks to emulate African language
patterns. Sanchez has also written highly
acclaimed plays (including 1970’s We a
BaddDDD People) and essays. She taught at
numerous colleges across the United States.
Sanchez retired in 1999 as professor of
English from T emple University. In 2001
she was awarded the Robert Frost Medal
for distinguished lifetime service to the art
form from the Poetry Society of America.
She continues to write and perform her
work, and released a CD in 2004 called
Full Moon of Sonia.
Kristina D. Bobo
See also: African Literature; Afrocentrism; Black
Power Movement

SANTOS ARRASCAETA,
BEATRIZ (1947–)
Beatriz Santos, songwriter, vocalist, human
rights activist, culturalist, journalist, chore-
ographer, writer, and teacher, is the niece
of the poet Juan Julio Arrascaeta, the
“Langston Hughes” of Afro-Uruguayan
poetry. Santos’s concern for racial justice
and the social and economic advancement
of black Uruguayan citizens embarked her
on a career as one of the most widely

known civil rights activists in Uruguay. She
is the founder and director of the Centro
Cultural por La Paz y la Integración (the

an organization whose goal is to combat all
forms of discrimination and to eradicate
the multiple oppressions that black
Uruguayans experience.
Since 1991, she has lectured in Brazil,
the Caribbean, the United States, and
Africa. After writing radio scripts and serv-

the black periodical Mundo afro, Santos
began to write poetry and short stories to

Uruguay. Subsequent to publishing her
work in local periodicals, her poetry
reached beyond the shores of Uruguay and
was published for the ﬁrst time in 1993 in
the Afro Hispanic Review . English transla-
tions of her short stories appear in Daugh-
ters of the Diaspora: Afra-Hispanic Writers
(2003), an anthology of works and essays
by and about black women in Spanish
America. As of 1993, Santos has published
three books and several short stories.
Her ﬁrst book, Historias de vida: Negros
en el Uruguay (Life Stories: Blacks in
Uruguay) (1994), coauthored with T eresa
Porzecanski, is a collection of testimonies
documenting black life in Uruguay. Santos
presents for the ﬁrst time the voices of
Afro-Uruguayans who tell their own story.
The collection of ten eyewitness accounts,
from informants ranging in age from 40 to
80, recounts their experiences past and
present of what it means to be black and
Uruguayan.
In 1994, Santos published Africa en el
Río de la Plata (Africa in the River Plate )
with Nene Lorriaga. A chronological
summary of the Afro-Uruguayan experi-
ence, the authors trace the history of 
Afro-Uruguayans from slavery to the
1990s. Santos’s third book, La herencia
cultural africana en las Américas (African
Cultural Heritage in the Americas) (1998), is
a collection of essays that treat a broad
range of issues such as racism, sexism, civil
rights, cultural heritage, and African tradi-
tions in the black Uruguayan community.
Of most signiﬁcance is the chapter on black
women’s creative achievements, which
demonstrates a range of literary talents that
explicate the politics of cultural production
and the ways in which black Uruguayan
women artists have formed their own liter-
ary tradition.
A talented singer and dancer, Santos
has performed in Africa, the Caribbean,
and the United States. In 1995 she starred
in El desalojo de la calle de los negros (The
Eviction of Blacks to the Street ), a ground-
breaking play of social protest by the black
Uruguayan playwright Jorge Emilio Cardoso.
The play brings to the public the contro-
versial governmental removal of poor black
Uruguayans from the conventillos, old colo-
nial mansions where black citizens resided
for years. As one of the lead actors, she sang
songs against this racist act, the devastating
impact it had on the residents of Barrio
Reus al Sur, the historic cradle of Afro-
Uruguayan culture, and the loss of commu-
nity. Her performance earned her high
marks from critics who praised her distinc-
tive and eloquent voice.
Motivated to change the political land-
scape of Uruguay, she sought election to
government ofﬁce in 1996. The ﬁrst black
Uruguayan to run for ofﬁce since the 1940s,
Santos was endorsed by the Colorado pres-
idential campaign. Despite all efforts, she
lost the election. However, Santos has
raised both the political and social con-
sciousness of Afro-Uruguay at home and
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1058 ---
970 S ÃO TOMÉ EPRÍNCIPE
abroad. T oday, she continues the struggle
for equality and justice in Uruguay while
targeting the education of underprivileged
and neglected youth. Working with
Colegio Cervantes, a local high school, and
the national library of Uruguay, her goal is
to make sure that every child has the same
educational opportunities. T o that end,
Santos, with her undying energy, embodies
the Afro-Uruguayan experience.
Caroll Mills Young

SÃO TOMÉ EPRÍNCIPE
The Democratic Republic of São T omé e
Príncipe is two islands in the Gulf of
Guinea, off the coast of West Africa. The
land is densely populated; although the
population is roughly 182,000, only 2 per-
cent of the land is arable. The island of São
T omé was ﬁrst recorded by the Portuguese
in 1469 and settled by them 16 years later.
The nearby island of Príncipe was occupied
15 years later. Both were quickly used for
sugar plantations, becoming, brieﬂy, the
largest sugar-producing area in the world
and generating much revenue for Portugal.
The many streams on the island proved
very effective for watermills to generate
power. However, there was a slave revolt in
1530 and many plantation owners left for
Brazil, where they established the planta-
tion system on a much larger scale and set
the scene for a massive increase in the slave
trade.
Slavery remained a cornerstone of the
economy of São T omé because, being an is-
land, it was a convenient place for slavers
from mainland Africa to bring their slaves
for transshipment to Elmina, a town and
slave port in present day Ghana, where they
could be sold to American slavers. It was es-
timated that during the sixteenth century a
slave ship carrying 100–120 slaves would
sail from São T omé to Elmina every 50
days. In 1553 some 500 slaves were taken
directly from São T omé to the Spanish
Indies. Gradually the governors of São
T omé and of Príncipe (they were initially
separately administered) established a
monopoly on the slave trade from the nearby
African coast.
São T omé generated massive wealth. It
was captured by the Dutch in 1641 and re-
taken by the Portuguese seven years later.
The Dutch did not, however, take Príncipe.
By this time the importance of São T omé
had diminished and Angola was the main
Portuguese source for slaves, with some of
these then being taken to São T omé for
transshipment elsewhere. It also became
common for some slaves to be taken from
mainland Africa to São T omé; after work-
ing there for a few years, they were
then sold to Brazilian slavers. When the
Portuguese court moved to Rio de Janeiro
during the Napoleonic Wars, São T omé
had declined in prominence so that the
Portuguese king felt the need to fortify the
island, as was the case with Angola.
After the abolition of the slave trade in
1830, there was still an illicit trade through
São T omé to Brazil, but that ended in 1888
when Brazil abolished slavery. However, the
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1059 ---
SARO-WIWA,K EN 971
economy of São T omé, through cocoa and
coffee plantations, was still reliant on
slaves. After the abolition of slavery in
1875, most of the ex-slaves remained on
the islands but agitated for civil rights and
then for independence. The main visitors
to the island over the next hundred years
were Portuguese civil servants and soldiers.
In 1953, São T omé was in the news after
over 1,000 plantation workers were shot by
Portuguese troops during a strike. Rapidly
much dissatisfaction with Portuguese rule
materialized, and there was some help pro-
vided to anti-Portuguese groups from some
countries, including Fidel Castro’s Cuba.
After the change of government in
Lisbon in 1974, a transitional administra-
tion was established in São T omé and
Príncipe, and independence was granted on
July 12, 1975. The United States immedi-
ately recognized the new country, and its
ﬁrst ambassador was Andrew L. Steigman.
São T omé remained heavily economically
reliant on Angola until the 1980s. It has
now begun promoting a tourist industry,
and in 2000 started drilling for oil. Work
was assisted by the United States, eager to
end its reliance on Middle Eastern oil.
Justin Corﬁeld

SARO-WIWA,K EN
(1941–1995)
Ken Saro-Wiwa was a leading voice of the
Nigerian people’s struggles for a just society
and a founder of the nonviolent and multi-
ethnic political pressure group Movement
for the Survival of the Ogoni People
(MOSOP). He was executed by the Nigerian
government in 1995. His death awoke
many in the United States and around the
world to the struggles of the Ogoni people
and of Nigerians in the oil-rich delta,
against violence and exploitation.
Born Kenule Beeson Saro-Wiwa in
1941, Ken Saro-Wiwa grew up in the small
town of Bori, near Port Harcourt, in Nigeria’s
east. Acknowledged as an exceptional
student, Saro-Wiwa received prestigious
government scholarships that gave him the
opportunity to attend Government College
in Umuahia and the University of Ibadan,
where he was soon to become a teacher.
However, his academic career came to an
abrupt end with the outbreak of Nigeria’s
civil war in 1967. At the beginning of hos-
tilities, Saro-Wiwa chose to ally himself
with the unitary nationalist policies of the
federal authorities of western Nigeria rather
than with the secessionist aims of his home
region in the east. Indeed, Saro-Wiwa be-
came one of the ﬁrst cabinet members of
the newly created Rivers State region in
eastern Nigeria in 1968. However, his asso-
ciation with the government came to a dis-
cordant end in 1973 when he left his cabi-
net position for reasons that are best
reﬂected in his acclaimed set of short stories
A Forest of Flowers(1986). Here Saro-Wiwa
talks of the Nigerian people’s struggle
against a corrupt government characterized
by its greed, sloth, ignorance, and merce-
nary self-interest. Indeed, it was this period
in the mid-1980s that saw Saro-Wiwa’s
writing ﬂourish. In addition to his two
radio plays of the early 1970s, he produced
more than 20 titles in all genres of litera-
ture: four novels, a poetry volume, two
books of short stories, three titles concern-
ing politics, two drama volumes, one on
folklore, and nine children’s books.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1060 ---
972 S CHOMBURG,ARTHUR ALFONSO
However, it was Ken Saro-Wiwa’s
deep-seated passion for exposing the
maltreatment and injustices suffered by
Nigerians at the hands of aggressive multi-
national oil companies, and the dictatorial
military regime that both depended on and
supported the invasive activities of oil com-
panies, that made him a most distin-
guished ﬁgure. His passion manifested
itself in numerous political pamphlets and
several addresses to the United Nations, all
of which revealed the ecological and
human cost of oil extraction in Nigeria’s
Delta region. As a founder of MOSOP ,
Saro-Wiwa petitioned for the increased
autonomy of the Ogoni people based on
the collection of a fair share of oil revenues
and remediation for the environmental
damage caused by oil investigation and
extraction to Ogoni lands.
His outspoken criticism of the com-
plicit relationship between government and
multinational oil companies led to Saro-
Wiwa’s arrest several times throughout the
early 1990s; the dictatorial regime could
not tolerate Saro-Wiwa’s kind of peaceful
political activity that forced Shell to cease
operations in the Ogoni region in 1993. In
May 1994, he was arrested for the last time
on charges of incitement to murder. The
announcement that he had been executed
by hanging on November 10, 1995, by a
specially convened military tribunal, which
Amnesty International had deemed to be
politically motivated and inequitable, was
met with outrage and condemnation by the
international community. The United
States withdrew its ambassadors while the
Commonwealth of Nations suspended
Nigeria’s membership. Noted Nigerian
writer Wole Soyinka questioned whether
such reactions were the consequence of a
global conscience being ﬁnally nudged
awake by Saro-Wiwa’s death. Such a con-
science was certainly being felt by the
Undergraduate Council of Harvard
University, which passed a resolution on
November 19, 1995, that called for a com-
plete corporate withdrawal from Nigeria
and for Harvard to divest fully from oil
companies that invested in Nigeria.
Given such forceful responses—which
were repeated worldwide—it was apparent
Ken Saro-Wiwa’s execution had not paci-
ﬁed oppositional voices to the government,
as the Abacha regime had hoped. Rather,
his premature death at the age of 54 only
served to force countries like the United
States to reappraise its relationship with
Nigeria and seriously reconsider the moral
and ethical responsibility of engaging in
corporate activity on foreign soil.
Grant Hamilton

SCHOMBURG,ARTHUR
ALFONSO (1874–1938)
Arthur (Arturo) Alfonso Schomburg was a
scholar and bibliophile inﬂuential to the
Harlem Renaissance. He was born in
Puerto Rico to a freeborn black mother and
a father of German descent. He studied
commercial printing at the Instituto
Popular in San Juan and black literature at
St. Thomas College in the Virgin Islands,
where he ﬁrst began collecting books. In
1891, Schomburg emigrated to New York,
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1061 ---
SELASSIE I, HAILE 973
where he worked a series of jobs, includ-
ing devoting several decades to Banker’s
T rust, and participated in Caribbean
decolonization groups such as Las Dos
Antillas.
Schomburg’s passionate belief that “the
American Negro must rebuild his past in
order to make his future” drove his distin-
guished work as a scholar and administra-
tor. He cofounded with journalist John
Edward Bruce the Negro Society for
Historical Research in 1911 and served as
president of the American Negro Academy
(ANA) from 1922 until its disbandment in
1929. He wrote for publications including
Crisis, Opportunity,and Survey Graphic, was
associated with the Harlem Renaissance,
the New Negro movement, and the
Universal Negro Improvement Association
(UNIA). Schomburg was close with such
writers and intellectuals as Walter Page,
James Weldon Johnson, and Claude
McKay.
Over the course of his life, Schomburg
amassed a huge collection of rare materials
including slave narratives, poetry, journals,
broadsides, artwork, abolitionist sermons
by ex-slaves, and the almanacs of Benjamin
Banneker. Currently housed in the
New York Public Library in Harlem, the
Schomburg Center for Research in Black
Culture contains more than 5 million items
and serves as the preeminent archive of the
African Diaspora.
