SELASSIE I, HAILE
(1892–1975)
His Imperial Majesty Emperor Haile
Selassie I, King of Kings, Lord of Lords,
and the Lion of Judah, was emperor of
Ethiopia from 1930 to 1974. He was born
Tafari Mekonnen but changed his name to
Haile Selassie (“Power of the T rinity”)
when he was crowned emperor on Novem-
ber 2, 1930. Because Ethiopia was never
colonized by a European power, except for
a brief occupation by the Italians from
1935 to 1941, Haile Selassie was a beacon
of hope for colonized countries throughout
Africa and the Caribbean, as well as for
African American activists in the United
States. Regarded as God incarnate, he in-
spired the Rastafari movement (from Ras
Tafari, his preimperial title and name)
among working-class blacks in Jamaica. In
an editorial following Selassie’s coronation,
Jamaican activist Marcus Garvey suggested
that Selassie was the answer to a biblical
prophecy of a kingdom reaching out from
the East. This essentially launched the
Rastafarian movement, which has since
spread worldwide. A devout Ethiopian
Orthodox Christian, and therefore uneasy
about the movement’s religious beliefs,
Haile Selassie was nevertheless touched by
Rastas’ desire to return to Africa and in the
1940s granted them a parcel of land in the
town of Shashamane, 150 miles (241 kilo-
meters) south of Addis Ababa. Some 200
Rastas, mainly of Jamaican and American
origin, continue to live there.
Considerable controversy surrounds
Haile Selassie’s reign—he is seen by some as
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1062 ---
974 S ELVON,S AMUEL DICKSON
a feudal despot and by others as a force for
enlightened modernization. As regent, be-
fore becoming emperor, he abolished slav-
ery so that Ethiopia could enter the League
of Nations in 1923. He toured Europe and
was inspired to begin a substantial modern-
ization program, including public educa-
tion and agricultural production. The
League of Nations then failed to lend sup-
port when Italy invaded Ethiopia in 1935,
and he went into exile in England until he
secured British assistance to oust the
Italians in 1941. Haile Selassie ruled until
he was deposed in a military-led Marxist
coup d’état in 1974. He died a year later,
still held under house arrest by the new
government.
Jericho Burg

SELVON,S AMUEL DICKSON
(1923–1994)
Samuel Selvon was a novelist, raised in San
Fernando, T rinidad, by his East Indian father
and half-Indian, half-Scottish mother. He
attended a local elementary school and then
Naparima College, a prestigious secondary
school, where his penchant for English
composition and literature became obvious.
Having grown up on the multiracial island
of T rinidad, Selvon regarded himself a
true T rinidadian Creole, evident in his re-
fusal to learn Hindi despite his predomi-
nantly Indian heritage. In 1939, at age 16,
he left school after his senior Cambridge
exams. He took a job at a garage, but then
moved on to the T rinidad oilﬁelds where
he worked as a safety inspector. During
World War II, he served in the Royal Navy
Reserves as a volunteer, working as a wire-
less operator on minesweepers and motor
torpedoes. At the end of the war, he moved
to Barataria, a place that serves as the
setting for some of his novels and where he
was a journalist with the Trinidad Guardian
for ﬁve years. He began as a reporter but
soon become subeditor and then the editor
of The Guardian Weekly,a literary magazine
in which numerous of his short stories and
articles appeared. These were printed under
pseudonyms, however, since employees
were prohibited from using their own
names. Selvon also sold some of his short
stories and poems to the BBC for the
radio pr ogram Caribbean Voices that was
aired in the West Indies from London in
the 1950s.
In 1950, Selvon emigrated to England,
traveling on the same ship as George
Lamming. Facing difﬁculties to get a job as
a journalist, he settled for a clerical job at
India House. During his time with the
company, he completed his ﬁrst novel, A
Brighter Sun (1952), for which he was later
awarded a Book Society Recommendation
and a fellowship worth about $4,800. This
was the ﬁrst novel in which T rinidadian
dialect was used in a major work of ﬁction
and has therefore earned Selvon an impor-
tant place in the development of West
Indian ﬁction. This novel was also impor-
tant as it dealt with the creolization process
that was taking place in T rinidad. Because
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1063 ---
SENEGAL 975
the use of dialect and the predominantly
West Indian themes prevented wide accep-
tance of his work, he consciously modiﬁed
the spelling to make his work more accessi-
ble to foreign audiences. His second novel,
An Island Is a World (1954), won him a
fellowship from the McDowell Colony in
New Hampshire, and the Guggenheim
Foundation Fellowship gave him a year in
the United States for creative writing.
While at the McDowell Colony, he wrote
the outline for The Lonely Londoners
(1956). This novel was a major achieve-
ment, being the ﬁrst Caribbean novel to
employ dialect in both dialogue and narra-
tive. The Plains of Caroni (1968), commis-
sioned by Caroni Limited, drew Selvon
back to his homeland and was the only
novel that was wholly written in T rinidad.
Some critics have divided Selvon’s
work into three categories—the peasant
novels, the middle class novels, and the
immigrant novels. Roydon Salick, for ex-
ample, observes that the peasant novels, in-
cluding A Brighter Sun, Turn Again Tiger
(1979), and The Plains of Caroni, are con-
cerned with the relationship between the
individual and the communal life of the
Indo-T rinidadian peasantry; the middle-
class novels, An Island Is a Worldand I Hear
Thunder (1963), deal with bourgeois
T rinidadians; and the immigrant novels,
The Lonely Londoners, The Housing Lark
(1965), Moses Ascending (1975), and Moses
Migrating (1983), deal with the West
Indian immigrants in London. This catego-
rization might be a useful and simple orga-
nization of Selvon’s work, but each category
is not exclusive of the other.
Selvon is the author of a stage play,
Switch, that was performed at the Royal
Court Theatre, London, in 1977. He coau-
thored the ﬁlm script for Pressure (1978),
a motion picture that dealt with the color
question in London. He has published 12
novels, children’s books, a collection of
short stories, radio and television scripts,
and numerous newspaper and magazine ar-
ticles. He was awarded numerous awards
throughout his career, including the dis-
tinction of being writer-in-residence at
both the University of Winnipeg and the
University of the West Indies. He was also
the holder of two honorary doctoral
degrees from the University of the West
Indies, St. Augustine (1985), and the
University of Warwick (1989). In 1978,
Selvon moved to Canada after 28 years in
England. Selvon died of a heart attack at
age 70 on April 16, 1994.
Gisele Ramphaul

SENEGAL
The Republic of Senegal is the western-
most country on the African continent.
Senegal’s strategic access to the Atlantic
Ocean has made it a major center for the
exchange of American, European, and
African commerce, culture, and politics.
Its borders include the Atlantic Ocean to
its west, Mauritania to the north, Mali
to the east, and Guinea and Guinea-Bissau
to the southeast. Gambia is almost
completely situated within the boundaries
of Senegal. The Senegal River separates
northern Senegal from Mauritania.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1064 ---
976 S ENEGAL
The Gambia River runs inside the bound-
aries of Gambia.
An estimated 11 million people live in
Senegal. Dakar, the capital, had 230,000
inhabitants in 1950. In the 1980s, it had
more than 900,000. In 2007, more than
2 million people resided in the greater met-
ropolitan area. Some of Senegal’s histori-
cally highly populated cities have included
Saint-Louis, Ziguinchor, and Thies. More
recently, T ouba, the headquarters of the
Sunni Muslim-inspired Mouride brother-
hood, has become the second largest city in
Senegal. There are a number of ethnic
groups in Senegal; the most prominent are
the Wolof, Pulaar, Diola, and Serer. The
Wolof ethnic group comprises 43 percent
of the population. The second largest
ethnic group is the Pulaar, who account for
24 percent of the population. Expatriate
communities from France, Lebanon, Cape
Verde, as well as additional parts of Africa
and the Americas account for 12 percent of
Senegal’s population. While French is the
ofﬁcial administrative language, the Wolof
language is the indigenous lingua franca.
Senegal’s geographical position and
history has aided its integration into larger
networks. Its democratic model of gover-
nance has been cited as an example to
neighboring countries. With a population
that is 94 percent Muslim, Senegal is also a
part of the Muslim Diaspora. The majority
of the Senegalese population converted to
Islam in the eighteenth and nineteenth
centuries. This period of Islamic conversion
coincided with the expansion of colonial
ofﬁcials throughout Senegal. The most
prominent of which were French.
For centuries, Senegal was the site of
local and regional precolonial political
blocs. These political structures facilitated
trade through long-established trading net-
works throughout much of the Sahel and
sub-Saharan West Africa. Senegal also par-
ticipated in various trade networks extend-
ing into the Sahara and into the northern
Atlantic. Horses, cattle, salt, gold, and iron-
work were among the many items traded.
The introduction and expansion of the
transatlantic slave trade would alter local
trading dynamics. It changed the orienta-
tion, destination, and items being traded.
In 1445, in addition to raw goods, the
Portuguese began importing Africans to
Europe. The British, Dutch, and French
soon began extracting Africans from the
region, and thus began a reconﬁguration of
local trade. As sugar, cotton, and coffee
plantations expanded in the Americas, the
numbers of slaves being exported increased.
This transformation of the local economy
had a negative impact on many local eco-
nomic, social, and political relationships.
The subsequent growth in European explo-
ration and colonization would further dis-
integrate most of the previously existing
networks.
While scholars debate the number of
slaves shipped from the Senegambia region,
they agree that the majority were shipped
during the seventeenth and eighteenth cen-
turies. The ﬁgures range widely from a few
thousand to more than twenty thousand
being shipped in a single year. Most of the
slaves shipped from Senegal actually origi-
nated in the Gambia. They were trans-
ported from sites in the Gambia by land or
boat to ports in Senegal. For example, ports
in Gorée, Dakar, Ruﬁsque, and Joal all
became sites for transatlantic transfers.
Slaves from Senegambia landed in destina-
tions as varied as Havana, Salvador, New
Orleans, and Charleston. It is estimated that
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1065 ---
SENEGAL 977
14.5 percent of U.S. slave imports origi-
nated in Senegambia.
Senegal has had a long and nuanced
relationship with France. Between the six-
teenth and nineteenth centuries, France
became quite familiar with Senegal’s
resources, cultures, and terrain. During the
European “scramble for Africa,” France
negotiated control for what is present-day
Senegal, Mauritania, Guinea, and Mali.
During this era, Senegal was one of France’s
most important colonies. The headquarters
of l’Afrique Occidentale Française (AOF)
was situated in Dakar. As the regional seat
of AOF , Senegal received signiﬁcant devel-
opment of infrastructure, such as roads,
railroads, medical facilities, schools, and
administrative buildings.
In particular, the educational system
included a series of primary and secondary
schools and universities. Colonial ofﬁcials
and missionaries managed the schools.
Modeled after the French educational sys-
tem, students were sent from other French
colonies to Lycée Faidherbe (Saint Louis)
and Lycée Van Vollenhoven (Dakar) to
pursue the baccalauréat. In 1918, one of
Africa’s earliest schools of medicine opened
in Dakar. This school was established in di-
rect response to World War I. The war
greatly impacted the French economy and
the colonial administrators wanted to ease
some of the burden on the metropole. As a
result, a number of Africans could now
complete higher medical degrees in Senegal.
Between 1918 and 1937, 400 doctors com-
pleted the four-year program. In subse-
quent years, the school would expand to
train pharmacists and midwives.
France was directly involved in the
affairs of its colonies. Citizenship was
extended to persons in certain areas that
met certain qualiﬁcations. In the four
communes of Senegal—Dakar, Gorée,
Ruﬁsque, and Saint Louis—inhabitants
who mastered certain educational and
French cultural standards were granted
French citizenship. Many of these citizens
became colonial bureaucrats. Others mi-
grated to France and some became deputies
in the French parliament. Some of the
deputies included Lamine Guéye and
Leopold Sedar Senghor. During World
War II, the role of African deputies became
increasingly important. They began to de-
mand better access to education, resources,
and political autonomy for their con-
stituents. In 1956, the loi-cadre began the
initial steps toward independence. In 1960,
Senegal received its independence from
France.
Postcolonial Senegal has been a player
in regional and international politics, aca-
demic discourse, and cultural exchange.
Leopold Sedar Senghor, Senegal’s ﬁrst pres-
ident, used his ties to local and French
politicians (including two-time president
Charles De Gaulle) to ease the transition to
nationhood. As the country progressed, he
continued to negotiate political linkages.
Born into a Catholic, Serer family, Senghor
pursued his studies in Senegal and France.
He taught French in France, became a par-
liamentary deputy, used his poetry to speak
to the importance of African cultures, and
later added “African” aspects to Senegal’s
postcolonial school system. Senghor allo-
cated huge sums of the government’s bud-
get in support of the arts and education.
Senghor was quite successful in mobi-
lizing intellectual communities. Along with
Alioune Diop and others, he helped coor-
dinate the 1956 Congress of Black Writers
and Artists in Paris, France. This major
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

conference included participants from
around the globe. Some of the noted guests
included Frantz Fanon (Martinique), Haile

(United States), and Richard Wright
(United States). He also initiated the 1966
Festival of Negro Arts in Dakar, Senegal.
This festival featured artists, writers, musi-
cians, and entertainers from Africa, the
Americas, and Europe. Some of the note-

Louis Armstrong, Duke Ellington, and
Katherine Dunham.
Abdou Diouf and Abdoulaye Wade
followed Senghor as presidents of Senegal.
Upon Senghor’s retirement, Abdou Diouf
became president in 1981. A career bureau-
crat, Diouf continued Senghor’s tradition
of maintaining strong relations with the
French. During the later years of his presi-
dency, Diouf increasingly engaged other
foreign powers in Western Europe and the
United States. A number of ofﬁcial delega-
tions made visits to the United States. In
1997, President Bill Clinton became the
ﬁrst sitting U.S. president to visit Africa.
His trip included a visit to Senegal.
In 2000, Abdoulaye Wade, a former
opposition leader, became the third presi-
dent of Senegal. Many members of his
cabinet are Senegalese citizens who have
worked or studied at universities in the
United States, France, or Canada. The
Senegalese minister of foreign affairs,
Cheikh Tidiane Gadio, is one such exam-

positions with a number of international
agencies such as the World Bank and
United Nations. Gadio received his doctor-

rather successfully marketed his goals to the
Senegalese expatriate communities in
Europe (particularly France) and the United
States. Since Wade has become president,
he has appointed a new Senegalese ambas-

bying ﬁrm to represent Senegal, and visited
President George W . Bush on numerous
occasions. In 2002, President Bush became
the second American president to make an
ofﬁcial visit to the African continent. Like
Clinton, Bush visited Senegal.
The relationship between the United
States and Senegal has grown closer over
the years. At the same time, Senegal’s per-
ceived political and economic allegiance to
France has diminished. George Bush
tapped Wade as an advisor and mediator on
African affairs. The Bush administration
also diversiﬁed its foreign assistance to
Senegal. In assisting the United States to
combat terrorism, Senegal has allowed one
of two West African FBI bureaus to be es-
tablished in Senegal.
In the 1970s and 1980s, more
Senegalese began migrating abroad; mem-
bers of the Mouride brotherhood are one of
the largest groups of emigrants. As of 2007,
about one-third of Senegal’s population are
afﬁliated with the Mouride brotherhood.
This powerful religious network has follow-
ers who trade and reinvest in the brother-
hood. Found in places such as Marseille,
Paris, Sydney, and Montreal, one of the
more recent sites of Mouride expansion is
the United States. New York City is one
such site. Senegalese engage in various in-

Harlem, and Brooklyn. There is presently
an African-styled market in Harlem as well
as numerous food shops, restaurants, hair
salons, and electronics stores. Harlem has
been dubbed “little Senegal”; a ﬁlm with
that title was released in 2001. Large num-

SENGHOR,L EOPOLD SEDAR
(1906–2001)
African statesman, poet, and cofounder of
Négritude, Leopold Sedar Senghor served as
president of Senegal from 1960 until 1980.
Born in Joal, Senegal, Senghor moved to
Paris on a scholarship, graduating from the
Lycee Louis-le-Grand in 1931. With the
outbreak of World War II, Senghor joined
the French army; he spent eighteen months
as a prisoner of war after being captured by
German forces. Following the war Senghor
turned to electoral politics, winning election
in 1945 to represent Senegal in the French
Constituent Assembly. Between 1946 and
1958 he won continuous reelection to the
French National Assembly.
In August 1960, following Senegal’s
separation from the Federation of Mali,
Senghor was elected the ﬁrst president of
Senegal. He would be reelected president in
Poet and statesman Leopold Senghor was a leader in
Senegal’s movement for independence. (Mychele
Daniau/AFP/Getty Images)
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1068 ---
980 S EYCHELLES
each of the elections of 1963, 1968, 1973,
and 1978.
In addition to his position as a promi-
nent postcolonial statesman, Senghor
gained international renown as a major
poet and cultural theorist. Along with
Aime Cesaire and Leon Damas, Senghor
developed the concept of Négritude, a
widely inﬂuential perspective on art and
culture that advocated cultural production
based in black African experiences against
pervasive colonial inﬂuences. Négritude, as
expressed by Senghor, espoused values
rooted in understandings of traditional
African societies and upheld the greatness
of African civilizations.
His vision of African Unity motivated
Senghor to play a large part in the forma-
tion of the Organization for African Unity
in 1963. In 1974 Senghor led Senegal into
the West African Economic Community.
Politically, Senghor advocated a mod-
erate form of African socialism, a material-
ist perspective based on local institutions
and community relations rather than mod-
els borrowed from the Soviet model of state
socialism. For Senghor, socialism in Africa,
far from being a foreign ideology, was
rooted in the communal practices of social
life that characterized precolonial African
societies. African and European socialism
represented two halves of a coming human-
ist world civilization.
Following his departure from politics
in 1980 Senghor moved to Normandy,
France, where he died in December 2001.

SEYCHELLES
Composed of 115 small islands, the
Republic of Seychelles lies some 500 miles
(805 kilometers) northeast of Madagascar
in the Indian Ocean. Its approximately
80,000 inhabitants live primarily on Mahe
Island, with a small percentage on Praslin
and La Digue islands; the remaining islands
are minimally populated or uninhabited.
As with many other African island-nations,
Seychelles has a complex colonial history
tied to maritime trade and exploration. Al-
though the rocky islands were not valuable
for agriculture, as the island of Mauritius
was, Seychelles offered an important port
for ships crossing the Indian Ocean. The
strategic position of the islands made them,
in the post–World War II era, a focus of
cold war rivalry between the United States
and the Soviet Union for inﬂuence in the
Indian Ocean. Since the end of the cold
war, Seychelles has become central to inter-
national efforts to study and preserve the
environments of Indian Ocean islands and
waters.
Already known to early Arab and Indian
Ocean sailors, the islands were reached
by the Portuguese in 1502. The French
subsequently claimed Seychelles in 1756.
However, it was not until 1770 that the
ﬁrst group of settlers arrived, a small group
of French colonists, African slaves, and
Asian laborers. The British seized control of
the islands in 1794. Able to supply ships
with water and food as they traveled the
Indian Ocean, the islands of the Seychelles
were a valuable prize in the competition
between European powers. Seychelles also
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1069 ---
SHABAZZ,B ETTY 981
served as a transit point in the trafﬁc of
slaves from Africa across the Indian Ocean.
Self-governing by the 1960s, Seychelles
remained technically a British colony until
independence in June 1976. Where the
islands had once been the focus of rivalry
between the naval powers of Britain and
France, Seychelles, after independence,
became the focus of rivalry between super-
powers. After independence, the islands
sought to remain neutral, becoming part of
the Non-Aligned Movement. Seychelles
found itself juggling U.S. and Soviet inter-
ests, at times to its advantage. In 1963, the
U.S. Air Force began to have a presence in
the country by building a radar tracking
station. The nation received substantial
economic aid from the United States.
However, it retained friendly relations with
the Soviet Union. In December 1981, two
Soviet warships docked on the nation’s
main island, Mahe. This event symbolized,
to some international observers and the
United States’s disquiet, the rising inﬂuence
of the Soviet Union and communism in
Seychelles and the Indian Ocean region
more generally.
Internally, Seychelles experienced
political turmoil after independence that
reﬂected some of the dimensions of the
cold war. In 1977, Seychelles’s ﬁrst postin-
dependence elected government was over-
thrown by a coup. Seychelles remained a
one-party state until multiparty elections
were restored in 1993. In 1982, a military
coup was put down with the assistance of
troops from socialist-led Tanzania.
In the post–cold war era, the country
remains part of the Non-Aligned Move-
ment, describing its own position as one of
“positive non-alignment.” The government
of the Seychelles is a supporter of what has
been termed the Indian Ocean Zone of
Peace, a project for the demilitarization of
the Indian Ocean region. Seychelles has
expressed support for closing the U.S. air
and naval base on Diego Garcia and for
Mauritius’s claims to the island, against
British ownership.
With the rise of environmental aware-
ness, Seychelles has become a central part
of international, United Nations, and U.S.
conservation and ecological research efforts
in the Indian Ocean. As with other African
islands, Seychelles is home to many unique
animals, plants, and habitats. The coral
reefs around the island of Aldabra, endan-
gered by the global warming of ocean
waters, have been designated a United
Nations World Heritage Site. With many
uninhabited islands, Seychelles has desig-
nated over 40 percent of its territory as na-
tional parks or environmentally protected
areas. The nation has also sought to de-
velop eco-tourism, whereby the ﬂow and
activities of tourists and the tourism indus-
try are managed so as to be ecologically
sustainable.
Richard Juang

SHAKUR,A SSATTA(1947–)
Assata Shakur (aka JoAnne Chesimard) is
an African American political activist living
in exile in Cuba, who was born JoAnne
Deborah Byron on July 17, 1947, in New
York, the older of two girls. She spent her
formative years in segregated Wilmington,
North Carolina, with her mother, aunt,
and maternal grandparents. Her grandpar-
ents owned and operated a restaurant-
waterfront enterprise for black citizens
called Freeman’s Beach where Shakur
worked as a youth. Largely inﬂuenced by
her mother, a schoolteacher, and her aunt,
attorney Evelyn White, Shakur was edu-
cated in various schools in Wilmington, in
New York, and by cultural excursions. She
attended and graduated from Manhattan
Community College. There she became
more politically involved and began read-
ing the works of socially conscious black
writers of the late 1960s. She began wear-
ing her hair in the “natural” style of that
period, rejecting the straightened, relaxed
hairstyles of African American women of
past years. She also attended the City
College of New York and was married
brieﬂy. She changed her name to “Assata,”
which means “she who struggles,” and
adopted the name “Shakur,” which means
“the thankful.”
Shakur joined the Black Panther Party
(BPP) in New York’s Harlem community
in the early 1970s, working with the Free
Breakfast for Children Program, with the
medical cadre, and to free the New York
Panther 21, a group of BPP members from
the eastern region who were charged with
conspiracy. She eventually became disillu-
sioned with decisions made by the Panther
leadership in Oakland, California. In May
1973, along with former Black Panther
Sundiata Acoli, Shakur, a target of U.S.
counterintelligence, was arrested on the
New Jersey turnpike. During the arrest,
New Jersey State troopers wounded her and
killed former Black Panther Zayd Shakur.
Ofﬁcer Werner Foerster was also killed.
Shakur was acquitted of criminal
charges of kidnapping and bank robbery,
but was convicted of the murder of the
state trooper even though testimony sup-
ports that she was incapable of ﬁring a gun
after being almost fatally wounded. She
gave birth to a daughter, Kakuya, while
incarcerated. She escaped from Clinton
Correctional Center in 1979. Often re-
ferred to as the soul of the Black Liberation
Army, Shakur was given political asylum in
Cuba and currently resides and remains
politically active there. She has written an
autobiography entitled Assata. She is the
subject of Gloria Rolando’s ﬁlm Eyes of the
Rainbow. In 2005, the Federal Bureau of
Investigation offered a $1 million bounty
for her return to the United States.
Joan McCarty

SHANGE,N TOZAKE (1948–)
Ntozake Shange is an African American
poet and playwright whose most famous
work, For Colored Girls Who Have Considered
Suicide/When the Rainbow Is Enuf (1975),
was the second play by a black woman to
open on Broadway. In 1976, the play
opened at the Henry Street Settlement’s
New Federal Theatre in New York, thrust-
ing Shange into immediate prominence;
that same year, and 17 years after the phe-
nomenal run of Lorraine Hansberry’s
A Raisin in the Sun, it reached Broadway.
Through this play, Shange popularized a
poetic style that sought to revive and
tap the nonverbal paradigms that inform
what she describes as her ancestral oral
Hip-hop artist Tupac Shakur. (Corbis)
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

SHANGE,N TOZAKE 985
traditions. They include music, song, dance,
mime, movement, poetry, and ritual. T o pre-
serve this ceremonial ideal, she devised an
avant-garde stage—the choreopoem—that
integrated such nonverbal resources to over-
come the limitations of dialogue and
realism. In her pursuit of a vibrant theatrical
form, Shange initiated a revolutionary phase
in the African American quest for a func-
tional theatre.
The task Shange speciﬁed for music
and dance is similar to the role of both in
African traditional performance. Apart
from helping to retain ties with Africa,
dance, like music, served as a cathartic
agent for Shange, a defense mechanism,
and an instrument of audience-performer
participation and interaction. T o fully
explore black music, dance, and other
nonverbal resources, Shange endorsed the
rejection of conventional theater practices
and the promotion of a rich interdiscipli-
nary form that appealed to all the physical
senses.
Reconstructing standard English
usage, Shange used language to reinforce
her theatrical liberty and further reject
standard practice. Using a colloquial,
metaphoric, and rhythmic style that agreed
with her poetry, she deliberately distorted
the English language by breaking away
from conventional spellings and pronunci-
ations. Using her chosen “language,”
Shange addressed a wide range of themes,
including, among others, racism, the
unique position of black women, stereo-
types, the black middle class, the disregard
for black artists, and black survival. Central
to her themes was a black feminist and Pan-
Africanist consciousness that emerged in
her anti-racism and anti-imperialism stance,
her rejection of Western cultural hegemony,
and her commitment to recuperating
marginalized black traditions. The intensity
of Shange’s drama is perhaps best expressed
in her adaptation of Frantz Fanon’s “com-
bat breath” theory. Her combat breathing
implies the opening of wounds that would
be left to bleed as part of a healing process,
inspiring solidarity and seeking the spiri-
tual transcendence of a corporal existence
where women are vulnerable.
Shange’s life and personal struggles had
an extensive impact on her as a writer. She
was born Paulette Williams to Paul T . and
Eloise Williams, a surgeon and a psychi-
atric social worker, in T renton, New Jersey,
on October 18, 1948. Her early childhood,
ﬁrst in upstate New York and later in
St. Louis, was extremely sheltered and com-
fortable. Shange was thirteen when her
family returned east to New Jersey, where
she completed high school. In New Jersey,
she became increasingly aware of the con-
straints imposed by sexism and racism.
Shange earned a bachelor’s (honors)
degree in Afro-American music and poetry
from Barnard College in 1970 and, in
1973, a master’s degree in American studies
from the University of Southern California.
It was also in 1971 that she dropped
Paulette Williams and adopted the African
(Zulu) name Ntozake Shange. Ntozake
means “she who comes with her own
things,” while Shange means “one who
walks like a lion.” The new names pointed
to her new identity and artistic direction.
From 1972 to 1975, Shange taught at
Sonoma State College, Mills College, and
the University of California Extension.
While teaching at Sonoma State College,
she began writing poetry in earnest. She
also found time to dance and perform her
poetry with the Third World Collective,
Raymond Sawyer’s Afro-American Dance
Company, the West Coast Dance Works,

techniques. This gradual shift is evident in
Colored Girls and four other dramatic
pieces by Shange: Boogie Woogie Landscapes
(1979), Spell #7 (1979), A Photograph: Lovers
in Motion (1977), and Daddy Says(1987).
Structured on the boogie-woogie,
Shange’s Boogie Woogie Landscapes is an ex-
pressionistic and fantasy representation
filtered through the random thoughts,
reveries, visions, hopes, combat breath, in-
ternal conﬂicts, and memories of the play’s
single “real” character, Layla. While
Landscapes is technically set in Layla’s bed-
room, the real landscape lies within her
head. This mental process, both conscious
and unconscious, grows out of a hostile
racist and sexist setting, and is relayed in
quick stream-of-consciousness succession,
suggesting speed and kinesis. Shange’s Spell
#7 is set in a St. Louis bar frequented by
largely unsuccessful or frustrated black mu-
sicians and artists. The black identities con-
structed within this exorcised space are free
of the dominant culture’s control and
stereotypes. In line with the choreopoem,
this play is structured on a nonlinear and
nonrealistic plot arrangement, narrative
patterns, and a stream-of-consciousness
and play-within-play formula. An improvi-
sational effect is sustained in what resem-
bles a spontaneous rendering and dramati-
zation of race- and gender-oriented stories
in several tonal voices by the characters. A
Photograph tells the story of Sean David, a
misogynistic, ambitious photographer and
the three women in his life—Michael, a
dancer; Nevada, an attorney; and Claire, a
model. While all three women are in love
with him, he merely needs them to satisfy
his ego. Sean pretends to be a strong black
male, but his façade is crushed when he is
rejected for a fellowship and a gallery exhi-
bition that would otherwise launch his
career. When Shange wrote Daddy Says, she
practically discarded her choreopoem style.
More than any of her dramas already dis-
cussed, this work resembles conventional
drama the most. Addressing the sexual and
social development of black women in the
play, Shange journeys into the American
Southwest where there has been a tradition
of black cowboys/cowgirls as active partici-
pants in horse and cattle driving. Daddy
Says readdresses a recurrent subject in ear-
lier Shange plays, which is the central
theme of sexism as it affects young black
women and girls; it is directed at the
freedom or lack thereof of women to make
vital choices for themselves.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1075 ---
SHARPEVILLE MASSACRE 987
Overall, Shange played a key role in
expanding the black literary focus on racial
and cultural identity so that it embraced a
sexual revolution. Having lost faith in the
ability of men to respond effectively to
female subordination, she furnished the
American stage with not just a signiﬁcant
black presence but a feminine one too.
Shange thus made pronounced contribu-
tions to the Black Aesthetics Movement
and its efforts to break down conventional
walls. Her structural and representational
choices show that while she confronted
critical themes and raised fundamental
questions, she also mourned the loss of an
indigenous culture whose strength was de-
pendent on rhythmic and religious prece-
dents. It is a culture that her theater strived
to recover.
Phillip Efﬁong

SHARPEVILLE MASSACRE
On March 21, 1960, white South African
police opened ﬁre on an anti-pass demon-
stration in Sharpeville T ownship, near
Johannesburg. Ofﬁcial ﬁgures, disputed by
many, recorded 69 dead and 180 injured,
of which many were shot in the back while
running away. The demonstration marked
the end of passive resistance to the racist
system of apartheid.
Pass laws, restricting the movement of
Africans, existent in some form since 1790,
multiplied with the inﬂux of Africans seek-
ing work in the rapidly industrializing
towns of the 1920s. By the 1960s, over
100,000 Africans were arrested for pass
violations annually. The Pan Africanist
Congress (PAC), a 1959 breakaway from
the African National Congress, led active
resistance to the hated pass laws. Robert
Sobukwe, PAC leader, called on Africans to
leave their passes at home and court arrest
in a day of national protest. On March 21,
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1076 ---
988 S IERRA LEONE
confrontations between police and
demonstrators occurred nationwide. In
Sharpeville, around 20,000 people gath-
ered outside the police station. When
police refused to arrest them, confusion
arose and, in the early afternoon, the police
opened ﬁre for about one minute. While
some commentators saw Sharpeville as an
example of state violence against a peaceful
crowd, others described a mob clearly in-
tent on violence. The brisk ofﬁcial inquiry
clariﬁed little.
A nationwide state of emergency and
the outlawing of all antiapartheid organi-
zations followed the temporary suspension
of the pass laws. Sobukwe was among the
11,503 people arrested and 6,800 jailed.
Repressive legislation increased. Sharpeville,
a watershed in twentieth-century South
African history, marked the end of passive
resistance, the beginning of the armed
struggle, and of the international condem-
nation of apartheid.
Laura Pechey

SIERRA LEONE
The Republic of Sierra Leone is in West
Africa, bordered on the north by Guinea,
on the south by Liberia, and on the west by
the Atlantic Ocean. Its current war-torn
state dates from British colonization. It was
originally named Sera Lyoa, Portuguese for
“Lion Mountains,” by the Portuguese ex-
plorer Pedro da Cintra, who landed there
in 1462. Sierra Leone was a major center
for the eighteenth-century slave trade. Like
neighboring Liberia, the country was set-
tled by former slaves, but unlike Liberia, it
became a British colony, only becoming in-
dependent in 1961. Sierra Leone is cur-
rently a republic with a president elected
every ﬁve years and a unicameral parlia-
ment. The country has only recently
emerged from a bitter civil war, lasting
from 1991 to 2002. The economy is based
on mineral exploitation, particularly dia-
monds, although little of the proceeds pass
through formal economic channels, and
funds from the “blood diamonds” fueled
the civil war. Most of the population, cur-
rently around 6 million, relies on agricul-
ture for their livelihood. There are twelve
main languages spoken, as well as English
and Krio (a Creole derived from English).
The majority of the population is Muslim,
followed by practitioners of indigenous
religions and a small percentage of
Christians.
Prior to European contact, people in
what became Sierra Leone participated in
well-established long-distance trade routes
that extended across the Sahara. From the
seventh century onward, Islam spread
along these trade routes. Following the
Portuguese arrival, Sierra Leone became in-
corporated into the European and Ameri-
can slave trade. The ﬁrst slaves in North
America came from Sierra Leone; they were
brought to the southern United States in
1652. Slaves continued to be taken from
Sierra Leone through the nineteenth cen-
tury; the famous Amistad rebellion in 1839
involved Mende who were eventually deter-
mined by the U.S. Supreme Court to have
been illegally seized from Sierra Leone.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1077 ---
SIERRA LEONE 989
They were returned to “Mendiland”
(current Sierra Leone) in 1842 by a group
calling themselves the Amistad Committee,
which also established a mission there
and became the American Missionary
Association.
Freetown, eventually to be the capital
of the modern state, was founded in 1791,
by a group of British abolitionists led by
Granville Sharpe, as a settlement for freed
or escaped slaves who had become “black
poor” living in London. Many of these ﬁrst
settlers died. Some 1,200 former slaves
who had settled in Nova Scotia following
the American Revolution also settled in
Freetown in 1792. The settlement was not
initially intended to be a British colony, but
the company that ran it went nearly bank-
rupt following attacks by the local T emne
kingdom as well as the French navy.
Freetown became a British Crown Colony
in 1808. It continued to be settled by liber-
ated Africans, or Krio, and the population
rose to 6,000 within a decade. The new res-
idents of Freetown embraced the English
language and Western culture, which pre-
saged the divide between the Krio, who saw
themselves as culturally superior, and the
ethnic groups of the interior. This divide
worked against attempts at national unity
throughout Sierra Leone’s history, and was
not mitigated when the British eventually
colonized the interior and established a
protectorate in 1896. The British often
played the Krio elite against the rest of the
population in their efforts to undermine
potential national unity.
Sierra Leone’s decolonization process
was lengthy, beginning with a new consti-
tution and elections in 1951 providing a
framework for the process. Dr. Milton
Margai, the ﬁrst medical doctor from the
protectorate, became chief minister in
1953, and then prime minister in 1960.
Sierra Leone obtained independence in
1961 and became a parliamentary democ-
racy within the British Commonwealth.
There were several political parties, includ-
ing Margai’s Sierra Leone People’s Party
(SLPP), as well as the People’s National
Party (PNP), launched by his brother
Albert in 1958. The All People’s Congress
(APC) was established in 1960 as an alter-
native party representing teachers and the
working classes. However, the SLPP , led by
Milton Margai, won the ﬁrst postindepen-
dence elections, and he was prime minister
until his death in 1964, when he was suc-
ceeded by his brother Albert.
The independent government of Sierra
Leone was not very stable, with a military
coup following the 1967 elections, a return
to civilian rule a year later, the adoption of
a republican constitution in 1971, and the
establishment of a one-party government
by the APC in 1978. Major General Joseph
Saidu Momoh, elected president in 1985,
reestablished multiparty rule under a new
constitution in 1991. However, Momoh
was deposed in a military coup the follow-
ing year. In the meanwhile, an ongoing
rebel war in eastern Sierra Leone, led by
Captain Foday Sankoh and the Revolu-
tionary United Front (RUF), was further
destabilizing the country, as was spillover
from the concurrent Liberian conflict.
Presidential and parliamentary elections
were held once again in 1996, because of
popular demand and international pres-
sure, and Ahmad T ejan Kabbah was elected
president. Kabbah was overthrown by the
military the following year, but was rein-
stated following a Nigerian-led interven-
tion by the Economic Community of West
African States Monitoring Observer Group
(ECOMOG) in 1998.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

990 S IERRA LEONE COMPANY
The RUF continued to ﬁght against
the government, attempting another coup
in 1999. Later that year, President Kabbah
and RUF leader Sankoh negotiated the
Lomé Peace Accord, but because another
rebel group calling themselves the West
Side Boys was not included in the negotia-
tions, the peace did not last. United
Nations peacekeeping forces and British
troops also worked to stabilize Sierra
Leone, but violence continued until 2002.
T ens of thousands had died, and roughly
one-third of the population was displaced,
but perhaps even more horrifying was the
rebels’ custom of mutilating civilians by
chopping off their hands. The Lomé
Accord had provided for a disarmament,
demobilization, and rehabilitation program
to assist all combatants’ return to society,
as well as a T ruth and Reconciliation
Commission (TRC). However, demobiliza-
tion was only signiﬁcantly implemented
following yet another peace agreement
signed in Abuja in May 2001; the TRC
began hearings in 2003. The UN peace-
keepers ﬁnally withdrew at the end of
2005. Sierra Leone’s stability remained
tenuous in 2007 as new national elections
were due, conditions were deteriorating in
neighboring Guinea, and a tentative new
peace was unfolding in Liberia.

SIERRA LEONE COMPANY
The Sierra Leone Company (SLC) was a
joint-stock enterprise of a group of British
philanthropists that took over the failing
colony of Sierra Leone in 1791 with the
intention of making it proﬁtable. Disease,
hostile indigenous neighbors, and a lack of
organization plagued the colony, and
despite new supplies and a small inﬂux of
settlers in 1788, the colony did not thrive.
Granville Sharpe set up the St. George’s
Bay Company to take control of the
foundering colony. This organization be-
came the Sierra Leone Company upon
receiving a charter from the British
government. Through its ﬁnancial support,
the SLC not only subsidized the colony but
essentially kept it alive. Self-government
transformed into company rule as the SLC
took over the administration of the colony.
The motives of the Sierra Leone
Company were not completely altruistic, as
company investors believed that the colony
would one day become proﬁtable. The
company felt the key to success was a large
settler population, and to that end orga-
nized the addition of a new population
group to the original black settlers from
England. In 1792, 1,200 former slaves who
had been freed by the British Army during
the American Revolution were transported
from Nova Scotia, Canada, to Sierra Leone.
Hopes for proﬁtability and a thriving
colony were quickly dashed as the settlers
faced difﬁcult times. Malaria led to a high
mortality rate. International conﬂict im-
pacted the new settlement of Freetown as
the Napoleonic Wars broke out in 1794,
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1079 ---
SISULU,WALTER 991
resulting in the French navy destroying the
newly established port. The Nova Scotian
settlers were becoming frustrated and felt
the SLC was not overseeing the colony
fairly. Promised equality in all things, they
found themselves shut out of government
and the decision-making process of the
colony. They complained that company
administrators were racially prejudiced and
ruled in an autocratic manner. Settlers
claimed they had been promised free land
when they agreed to repatriation, but the
company failed to provide it. And when
land was distributed, company ofﬁcials
imposed high rents. Settler discontent and
frustration came to a head in 1800 when
the Nova Scotia settlers rebelled. The ma-
jority of the colony’s population remained
neutral, but the rebels established a rival
government to the company’s and almost
overthrew the colony’s governor. The rebel-
lion was put down due to the fortuitous ar-
rival of British soldiers accompanying 500
Maroons—runaway Jamaican slaves who
had surrendered to British authorities in
1795. The Maroons had been transported
to Nova Scotia and then to the Sierra Leone
colony once they agreed to repatriation.
The suppression of the rebellion did
not result in the success of the colony
under Sierra Leone Company rule. The al-
ready hostile indigenous T emne peoples of
the region became further alarmed at the
inﬂux of the Maroons and the British
troops who accompanied them across the
Atlantic. Of the approximately 3,000 black
settlers, less than half had survived by
1807. The dreams of a proﬁtable colony
slipped away and investors in the company
began to dry up. In 1808 the Sierra Leone
Company turned the colony over to the
British government.
Heather Thiessen-Reily

SISULU,WALTER
(1912–2003)
Walter Sisulu was a South African anti-
apartheid activist and cofounder of the
African National Congress’s Youth League.
Walter Sisulu and his wife Albertina
devoted their lives to the struggle against
apartheid in South Africa. Born on May
18, 1912, in Ngcobo, to a black mother
and a white father, Walter left school at 15
and worked in low-paying jobs while also
organizing a strike, educating himself, and
writing articles on African heroes. Sisulu
joined the African National Congress
(ANC) in 1940 and cofounded its Youth
League (1943), which favored militancy. As
repressive legislation increased after 1948, a
new generation of black leaders emerged
(Sisulu among them), advocating a policy
of mass action. Sisulu helped lead the
Deﬁance Campaign (1952–1953), during
which 8,000 were arrested for violating
discriminatory laws. He, and others, were
banned from political activity and impris-
oned for months. Sisulu was tried for
treason, along with 155 other signatories of
the Freedom Charter, which sought equal
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1080 ---
992 S LAVE FORTS
rights for all races. Jailed throughout the
1960 state of emergency, which was de-
clared after a large group of black South
Africans refused to carry their passes, he
was eventually acquitted of treason in
1961. The Sisulus faced countless ban-
nings, arrests, and imprisonments. With
the outlawing of all antiapartheid organiza-
tions in 1960, Sisulu helped forge the
armed struggle for equality through the
ANC’s military wing. In 1963, he was
arrested and charged with ANC activity.
Released on bail, he disappeared under-
ground. In July 1963, Sisulu was one of six-
teen arrested at the ANC’s secret headquar-
ters and charged with planning sabotage.
Jailed for life in 1964 with seven others,
Sisulu was released shortly before the
decriminalization of the ANC in 1990.
Walter Sisulu served as ANC deputy presi-
dent 1991–1994. He died on May 5, 2003.

SLAVE FORTS
During the course of more than four
hundred years of transatlantic slaving, the
principal European powers involved built
many forts along the coast of Africa to help
sustain their part in the trade. Built partly
as military and political establishments to
protect their nation’s trading and commer-
cial interests, the forts also acted as opera-
tional centers for conducting the trade in
enslaved Africans. Although the forts were
never the main means of conducting the
trade or even overseeing it, their presence
was a powerful and symbolic reminder of
the European presence and involvement in
Africa.
There were three main types of
establishments—castles, forts, and
factories—which are generically called slave
forts. The castles were the grandest and
most elaborate structures, with signiﬁcant
fortiﬁcations. They were usually the seat of
the official representative of the main
European powers and fulfilled quasi-
diplomatic, military, and commercial
functions. Cape Coast Castle was the base
for the English Royal African Company
and Elmina Castle, captured from the
Portuguese by the Dutch in 1637, was the
residence of the governor of the Dutch
West India Company. The most numerous
establishments were the forts, the medium-
sized bases which also had combined
commercial and military functions typiﬁed
by such places as Dixcove. Factories made
up the ﬁnal category of slave forts. These
smaller commercial bases were often not
fortiﬁed and fulﬁlled a more local role.
The Portuguese began the ﬁrst fort at
Arquin (Mauretania) in 1448 and over the
next century and a half they constructed a
further 13 to 15 forts, including founding
Elmina in 1482. As the ﬁrst European
traders along the African coast, the Por-
tuguese were principally interested in gold,
ivory, spices, and wood rather than slaving,
though in a precursor of the transatlantic
trade, they did take enslaved Africans to the
Azores, Cape Verde Islands, and Madeira.
Indeed, until the late seventeenth century
Africans from Benin and São T omé were
brought into Elmina as slaves to produce
gold and to supply the overland slave trade
to North Africa.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1081 ---
SLAVE FORTS 993
The rapid development of sugar plan-
tations and the consequent demand for
labor in Brazil and the Caribbean from the
early seventeenth century saw the arrival of
the Dutch, then the English, French, and
Scandinavian powers on the African coast
anxious to get into the trade and supply
their own developing colonies on the other
side of the Atlantic. It was a period of ﬁerce
rivalry between the various national trading
companies, which spawned a spate of
building along the West African coast.
Between 1640 and 1710, more than 40
forts were built, two-thirds of them along a
186-mile (300-kilometer) stretch of the
coast of present-day Ghana. The forts
frequently changed hands as the European
powers battled for supremacy and to estab-
lish their spheres of inﬂuence.
The period from the early eighteenth
century saw a slowdown in building and
probably only 15 new forts were erected
during the ensuing century. By the early
nineteenth century, there were probably
some 70 to 80 signiﬁcant establishments
being maintained, though within only a
short time they were no longer being used
for their original purpose. Although the
Europeans had superior military power,
most castles and forts were built with the
agreement of local African leaders. Sites
were bought or rented. Although there
were occasional tensions and altercations
with the local population, the two generally
lived in a reasonable degree of cohabitation.
Until the mid-nineteenth century, there
was little attempt to colonize Africa itself;
the European presence was conﬁned to
the coast and Europeans had little or no
control over the hinterland or inland com-
munications. Virtually all the forts were
built on the coast itself, and even at
Ouidah, one of the few exceptions, the fort
was only some 3 miles (5 kilometers) from
the sea. 
A signiﬁcant number of slave forts still
survive. Much of what is known of their
original appearance comes from contempo-
rary European descriptions and engravings.
European travelers included references in
their various works and also printed de-
tailed engravings of some of the main forts.
In general, the design of the larger and
medium-sized forts followed a traditional
pattern of buildings placed around a cen-
tral courtyard protected by high walls and
regular bastions or towers. There were usu-
ally openings for cannons and small aper-
tures for small arms. Entry was via a gate on
the seaward side protected by a guard
tower. One of the key factors in locating
forts was a source of secure drinking water.
Most forts also had a separate area where
Africans lived either as servants or awaiting
transportation.
Life in the forts for the European in-
habitants was hard and difﬁcult. T o a large
extent they operated as isolated communi-
ties, surviving on self-sufﬁciency and de-
pendent for most of their supplies from
ships arriving from the home nation. The
day was a strictly controlled regimen of
work and discipline regulated by the bell.
The governors of the large forts exercised
absolute power. In such circumstances, mo-
notony and boredom were major problems,
and this often led to drunkenness and
violence. There were almost no European
women, and although relationships with
local women were forbidden, many re-
sorted to the temptations of illicit affairs.
The risk of disease and general health prob-
lems of living in a tropical climate, together
with the stresses and strains of surviving
in such conditions, meant that most
Europeans only spent relatively short tours
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1082 ---
994 S LAVE NARRATIVES
of duty, usually not exceeding two or three
years.
In the colonial and postcolonial eras,
the role and use of the forts has varied con-
siderably. Some were abandoned, left to fall
into ruins or even on occasion slip into the
sea. Several of the large forts continued to
be used as administrative centers or fulﬁlled
public functions as hospitals. A few govern-
ments made use of their fortiﬁed nature as
prisons. Some of the most well-known forts
have been converted into museums and/or
places of memory, becoming important vis-
itor attractions, especially for tourists.
Elmina and Cape Coast Castles have both
been declared World Heritage sites. This
designation has led to tension between peo-
ple who have tried to develop the sites’
tourist potential and those who see some
the consequences of development, for in-
stance, events or souvenir shops, as a viola-
tion of the memory of those who suffered.
Anthony Tibbles

SLAVE NARRATIVES
The slave narrative genre ﬁrst appeared
around 1760 and later, in the nineteenth
century, became one of the most signiﬁcant
forms of African American, and American,
expression set in print. Slave narratives
advanced the notion that no one could do
more justice to the slave than the enslaved.
Devising a set deﬁnition for slave narratives
is extremely difﬁcult given that diverse
writers had differing experiences with
bondage. Slave narrators sought to explicate
the uniqueness of their time in bondage.
The slave narrative form is a transatlantic
one that explores the forced separation of
Africans from their native soil.
Slave narratives are based on the
rhetorical supposition that the ability to
sustain a complex narrative is what makes
blacks equally intelligent as whites. The
slave narrator was thought of as a reliable
transcriber of the character of bonded
laborers. Although slave narratives are a
mode of self-deﬁnition, the deﬁnition that
the narrator ultimately achieves is not a
novel one, but one founded on the aware-
ness of an identity that has always existed—
an identity that is suppressed by slavery—an
identity that can ﬂourish only in freedom,
but that can never be fully attained because
white industrialists sustain a market econ-
omy driven by exploiting cultures they
term the “other.” The goal that slave narra-
tors had in mind was to explain that their
misery stemmed from their having been
forcefully transported from Africa to
America.
A primary feature of the slave narrative
is to show the contribution that Africa
made to the abolition movement. The Nat
T urner rebellion of 1831 in Southampton
County, Virginia, created a new generation
of abolitionists that declared their undy-
ing devotion to emancipation. Journalist
William Lloyd Garrison led abolitionist
camps across the United States. Free blacks
north of the Mason-Dixon Line con-
tributed to Garrison’s American Anti-
Slavery Society by editing newspapers,
organizing conventions, and circulating
pamphlets. Blacks and whites united to
sway public opinion toward accepting the
liberation of black Americans. The slave
narrative was the dominant form in Amer-
ican literature from 1830 to 1865. Slave
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1083 ---
SLAVE NARRATIVES 995
narratives were published en masse with the
intent of having America recognize the
brutality associated with the enslavement of
an entire continent. Americans were then
expected to feel guilty given that a slave
manufactured most consumable products.
Most fugitive slaves would cross the
Ohio River to gain freedom. Although
there are no existing records indicating the
exact number of slaves that escaped across
the Ohio River, it has been estimated that
approximately 60,000 slaves escaped their
masters. Of these 60,000 fugitive slaves,
some 6,000 wrote a narrative of their time
in captivity. The objective that slave narra-
tors attempted to accomplish was to prove
the wrongfulness of an economic system that
warranted their enslavement, by using the
printing press as a weapon to terminate
slavery. Slave narratives were written in
Africa as well as America. Striking similari-
ties in form and content among various
slave authors resulted in the ﬁrst printed
transatlantic African American genre.
White editors typically wrote introduc-
tory essays for slave narratives in order to
attest to the trustworthiness of the author,
prefatory material assured readers that the
text was a factual one authored by a fugitive
slave. Many often doubted that an author
who was a slave had the intellectual capac-
ity to produce an eloquent and complex
narrative; these doubters alleged that a
white abolitionist had written the manu-
script in order to make the fallacious case
that a slave was able to attain intelligence
when properly educated. Slave narrators
described slavery as a state of unbearable
physical, intellectual, emotional, and spiri-
tual torture. Escape was compelled by a
personal disaster caused by either the sale of
a loved one or an inner-conﬂict that forced
the slave to reclaim their sovereignty from
their master. Slave narratives proved that
slave masters were wrong to assume that
Africa was a degenerate territory that re-
quired slavery; they argued that Africans
were capable of producing a genre meant to
advance the notion that their forced re-
moval from Africa was unwarranted.
Abolitionists’ presses published slave
narratives and sold them at antislavery con-
ventions across the United States. A large
number of slave stories were printed in
several editions and sold tens of thousands
of copies. The immediate success of slave
narratives was due in great part to the tran-
scendentalist motif employed by ex-slave
writers of not romanticizing an event in
one period, but instead to demonstrate that
past actions will inherently have an effect
on the present and future. Slave narrators
demonstrated that bondage severed their
ancestral roots and that writing a narrative
about their captivity was the sole means of
keeping a connection with Africa. Slave
narratives forged a transatlantic relation-
ship not only among African Americans
but also among the white Americans who
were to discover that commerce must never
be placed ahead of humanity.
A major rhetorical device implemented
by slave narrators was the collective “we”
pronoun to unify bonded workers and
every individual that proﬁted from slavery.
Readers were asked to empathize with the
ex-slave subject’s tribulations. Slave narra-
tors used collective pronouns to have
humanity accept that forced servitude is an
infringement of God’s creed that everyone
is equivalent despite race, gender, or
economic class. Collective pronouns uni-
ﬁed the African American community so
that they would not dismiss slavery as a
normal practice and maintain the aspira-
tion of reviving an Africa way-of-life.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1084 ---
996 S LAVE NARRATIVES
Slave narrators adopted the Romantic
lyric “I” to have slave owners better under-
stand bondage and to efface any sense of
apathy that slave masters had toward forced
African Diaspora. The slave narrator’s deci-
sion to address a white audience was in-
tended to demonstrate that bondage was a
white-constructed power dynamic that
would cease only once the master/slave rela-
tionship was inverted. Abolition redeﬁned
Africa as a continent to be appreciated for
its cultural value instead of exploitable
labor.
The pioneering slave narrative was The
Interesting Narrative of the Life of Oladudah
Equiano, or Guastavus Vassa, the African
(1814). Oladudah Equiano’s saga was a
journey through a commercial system cre-
ated to serve white culture at the expense of
black submission. A double-consciousness
emerged that separated enslaver from en-
slaved. Africans were to adopt a white
Western mind-set if they were to gain
admission into a white-dominated world.
Equiano’s choice to appropriate into white
culture meant that he compromise his
black identity since this appropriation im-
plied that he admit his heritage was inferior
to white culture. Equiano’s narrative forged
a transatlantic relationship between Africa
and America that explained that many
Africans chose to follow a slave-based
market economy only to uphold their
livelihood.
The most widely read African Ameri-
can literary text of the nineteenth century
was The Narrative of the Life of Frederick
Douglass, an American Slave (1845).
Douglass’s narrative deconstructs the white
literary canon’s standard of what black
autobiography must entail. Stressing a pas-
sive voice to achieve credibility, the narra-
tive positions the slave in the role of the
antagonist and subject of the story in two
ways: by functioning antithetically against
racist charges toward black selfhood, and by
resisting the objectiﬁcation/fragmentation
that necessitated slaves to objectify them-
selves. Douglass retains authoritative power
by making his own choices. The enslaver
then becomes the object whose desires con-
tradict the requirements that constitute a
utopist nation. Objectifying the master
exemplifies how the American market
economy depended on the labor of bonded
Africans. Forced submission of salaries by
slaves to their masters demonstrated that
the riches held by most wealthy antebellum
industrialists were contingent on the work
of African Americans. Douglass gained
great fame and was invited to tour Great
Britain. He demonstrated that a writer of
African descent was capable of attaining in-
ternational acclaim. Globalizing the slave
narrative genre increased the marketplace
of African writers to spread their avowals of
the negative repercussions of slavery.
The twentieth century saw the emer-
gence of the neo-slave narrative—a form
that suggests that the implications of slav-
ery are beyond repair since they have left
unbridgeable gaps in African history. T oni
Morrison’s Beloved (1987) examines these
gaps through rememory, or the metaphoric
apparatus that rebuilds past realities by de-
picting events that parallel the human
psyche. Rememory has the reader consider
the mind’s activity of depending on and
accepting the integration of what has passed
and what is currently transpiring in order
to survive. Morrison therefore allows her
protagonist Sethe to complete the journey
from being a woman that identiﬁes herself
with motherhood only to a woman that re-
alizes her human qualities. Morrison’s novel
depicts a transatlantic connection between
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1085 ---
SLAVE REVOLTS/MARONNAGE 997
African psyche and American economics
that sustains nearly two centuries after
emancipation.
Slave narratives remain signiﬁcant in
the twenty-ﬁrst century for the reason that
they are the ﬁrst printed texts in African
American literature, and as such they are
both literarily and historically signiﬁcant.
Black authors of the American antebellum
era struggled to have their culture properly
integrated into the mainstream. In a con-
temporary context, slave narratives epito-
mize the role that literacy plays in preserv-
ing the intertwined histories of Africa and
America.

SLAVE REVOLTS/MARONNAGE
Organized resistance to slavery is as old as
slavery itself. Throughout the New World,
forms of slave resistance, from rebellion to
revolution, articulated the intolerable con-
ditions of enslavement and asserted the
rights of slaves to be free. That word of
such revolts spread to other slave commu-
nities demonstrates the inﬂuence of such
knowledge on other rebellions and revolts.
T o rebel against slavery is as frequent as the
institution itself, and rebellion includes a
range of responses, both covert and open.
In the transatlantic slave trade, hidden and
indirect forms of rebellion included day-to-
day resistance, such as work slowdowns,
deliberately poor work performance, attacks
on property, the creation of slave cultures,
and literacy practices. Methods of open
deﬁance included refusals to work, de-
mands for concessions, rejections of orders,
threats, violence, escape, and revolt. Slaves’
knowledge of revolts in other regions and
countries enhanced their own determina-
tion to rebel and seek liberation.
The earliest documented rebellion by
enslaved Africans in the Western Hemisphere
occurred at San Miguel de Gualdape in
1526, when slaves rebelled against the
Spanish, and the ﬁrst documented rebel-
lion in Mexico occurred in 1537. In Brazil
in the 1600s, a group of forty slaves re-
belled, burned the sugar cane plantations,
and killed the slave owners. They created a
community that ultimately had a popula-
tion over 20,000, and they are credited
with developing the martial art of capoeira.
Revolts took place often in the New World
because people could not accept being
enslaved. In Jamaica, an Asante warrior
named Queen Nanny, led guerrilla resis-
tance against the British, particularly dur-
ing the First Maroon War from 1720 to
1739, and became a legendary ﬁgure.
The slave uprising of Saint-Domingue,
beginning in 1791, was the largest and
most successful slave revolt in world his-
tory. The insurgency was on a massive scale
unprecedented in the Atlantic world, and
by 1792, the colony was engulfed in revo-
lution, due in part to the arming of slaves
by conﬂicting factions of whites and free
colored people with various alliances and
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1086 ---
998 S LAVE REVOLTS/MARONNAGE
goals. Saint-Domingue had half a million
enslaved Africans, comprising 80 percent
of the population. The 1793 emancipation
in Saint-Domingue was unusual in that it
provided immediate emancipation and
granted the former slaves citizenship as well
as freedom. T oussaint Louverture became
the leader of Saint-Domingue after emanci-
pation, and in 1804, the new republic of
Haiti signed its Declaration of Indepen-
dence. The Haitian revolution was a signif-
icant example for slaves globally and a
source of fear to all slave owners.
Information about the Haitian Revolu-
tion made its way to slaves in the United
States despite slave owners’ attempts to
control information that might encourage
insurgencies. The more restrictions upon
reading and news were increased through-
out the early nineteenth century, the more
the slaves sought information, literacy, and
allies. U.S. political leaders advised against
the public discussion of slave revolts, but
they could not suppress the messages about
freedom taught by the revolutions in Haiti,
France, and America. Freedom was not
only intended for Europeans.
The presence of Haitian refugees in
Virginia also contributed to slave unrest. In
1800, Gabriel Prosser, a literate blacksmith
knowledgeable about revolutionary politi-
cal currents, planned to capture Richmond,
Virginia. He gathered 900 people together
at one time, but the conspiracy unraveled
due to a torrential thunderstorm. Prosser
was reported captured, and along with ap-
proximately 30 fellow rebels, was hanged.
Several other slave rebellions in the follow-
ing decades became linchpin moments for
slaves working against the system that
oppressed them.
In 1811 in Louisiana, perhaps the
largest U.S. slave rebellion erupted. Now
known as the Louisiana Rebellion, it was
led by a Haitian native. An unknown num-
ber of black people, at least 180 and possi-
bly as many as 500, marched toward New
Orleans, but federal troops came in to quell
the rebellion.
In 1822, Denmark Vesey conspired to
take control of Charleston, Virginia, ulti-
mately gathering 600 to 900 supporters.
Vesey, a literate carpenter and sailor, had
been inspired by the Haitian Revolution,
and he had traveled widely in the
Caribbean. Although able to buy his own
way to freedom in 1800, Vesey was not
allowed to buy his family members out of
slavery. An active member of the African
Methodist Church, Vesey knew he had to
take action when white people closed down
his church in 1821. But the tremendous
number and diversity of recruits resulted in
an information leak that halted his efforts
to capture arms and ammunition and then
take Charleston, and Vesey was arrested,
along with other leaders. His story became
legendary.
Another major slave revolt was orga-
nized by Nat T urner in 1831 in Virginia.
After experiencing “a vision that his duty
was to end bondage,” T urner gathered 60
to 80 men and set forward to the ammuni-
tion stores of Southampton. Between 57
and 65 white people were killed along the
way, and vigilante retaliation by angry
whites killed over 200 black people, re-
gardless of their connection with Nat
T urner. Federal troops were sent in to
prevent additional slaves from joining
T urner’s Rebellion. After escaping capture,
T urner surrendered. His ﬁnal statements,
expressing his beliefs and reminding his
captors of how Jesus Christ had been cruci-
ﬁed, became famous. It is believed that Nat
T urner was incited to act by David Walker’s
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1087 ---
SLAVE REVOLTS/MARONNAGE 999
1829 “Appeal,” a long essay offering an ar-
gument against slavery and a call to revolu-
tion by the enslaved.
Because Nat T urner had been a
preacher and possessed reading ability,
Southern states tightened their laws against
literacy and put limits on black preachers.
The fear that T urner’s and Vesey’s rebellions
engendered brought long-lasting reprisals
against slaves. New laws made the manu-
mission or emancipation of slaves nearly
impossible. Slaveholders increased regula-
tions of free blacks, and they rejected any
situations that would increase the number
of free black people anywhere in the na-
tion. Southern state lawmakers instituted
curfews for slaves and free blacks and for-
bade slaves to assemble together for any
reason, even religious. Heightened tensions
contributed to slave owners’ hysteria about
the possibility of slave revolts, and slave
owners sought greater political power in
order to protect their investments in the
bodies of slaves.
Slave-trading ships also were subject to
revolts. In 1839, the Amistad was taken
over by Joseph Cinque and 54 Africans
during the Middle Passage. The slaves,
gaining the support of outspoken aboli-
tionists, were ultimately freed by a U.S.
Supreme Court ruling. Later that same
year, the U.S. domestic slave trade was dis-
rupted by a mutiny by 19 slaves on the ship
the Creole, sailing from Virginia to New
Orleans. All 135 slaves reached freedom in
the Bahamas.
While slaves who risked their lives to
join revolutionary movements challenging
slavery were important examples to other
slaves, there were other methods of resis-
tance. Uncountable numbers of slaves
operated individually or in clusters to create
secret patterns of everyday resistance, such as
poor work performance, misleading the
slave owners, and gaining skills of which
their masters were unaware. Slaves devel-
oped a range of ways to undermine the
slavery system. Ultimately, self-removal from
the slavery system was an important method
for slaves regaining ownership of themselves.
Running away to a place where slavery
was not legal was a common strategy.
The border states between slave and free
states—Virginia, Kentucky, T ennessee,
Maryland, and Delaware—had even more
freedom attempts than the Deep South.
Due to the inaccuracy of slaveholders’
records, an exact number of fugitives is not
known. Still, analysis of extant reports
about fugitive slaves shows that the average
runaway slave was a young black man in his
teens or twenties with such personality
traits as courage, determination, and 
self-reliance. Escape disguises and methods
were numerous and diverse, with slaves
masquerading as free blacks or as whites,
men posing as women, or women posing as
men. Most runaways set out alone or with
only a few others. Slave owners’ advertise-
ments for runaway slaves described them in
ways that reveal important details about the
fugitives, such as skills in trade, the ability
to read, write, and speak American Indian
or other languages, appearance, and attempts
to reach family members.
Helping others to gain freedom was an
important form of rebellion against the
slavery system. Harriet T ubman, after
liberating herself, helped over 300 men,
women, and children to escape in the
1850s. The Underground Railroad was a
loose consortium of different individuals
and organizations that served to connect
fugitive slaves with people who could help
them hide out along the way to freedom in
Canada. Because it had to operate in secret,
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1088 ---
1000 S LAVERY (ECONOMICS)
little historical information is deﬁnitively
known about the Underground Railroad.
Both white and black people helped slaves,
and people who had been assisted to
freedom worked to raise funds for their
escape and often stayed involved to deliver
others to freedom.
“Maroons” were groups of escaped
slaves living in regions inaccessible to out-
siders. The term probably comes from the
Spanish word cimarrón,referring to a wild
animal which had returned to the wild after
being domesticated. Petit marronage was
the French designation for slaves who left
for a limited amount of time, while grand-
marronage occurred when runaways formed
independent, permanent communities and
had no intention of returning to enslave-
ment. In Mexico, maroons formed settle-
ments called palenques. Runaways in the
United States who could not get to the free
states sometimes began maroon colonies in
places such as the Allegheny Mountains,
Blue Ridge Mountains, or Great Dismal
Swamp, and virtually every state had maroon
gangs of ten to 20 fugitive slaves.
The maroons were often on the move,
carrying weaponry and planning forays
into town. These gangs of outlying fugitive
slaves struck fear into the hearts of white
inhabitants. Slaves were constantly plan-
ning, and slave owners were always worried
about the revolts that were inevitable due
to the legal yet immoral and indefensible
institution that treated humans as property.
Amy Cummins
