SLAVERY (ECONOMICS)
The transatlantic importation of human
slaves as chattel, or personal property, was
essential to the expansion of Europe’s capi-
talist economy and its extraction of wealth
from the New World. There remains a fas-
cinating critical debate about the extent to
which proﬁts from the Atlantic slave trade,
along with the proﬁts from the sugar and
tobacco grown by slave labor, helped fund
Britain’s Industrial Revolution in the eigh-
teenth century.
In the slave trading system, the funda-
mental item of exchange was the person of
the slave, showing the falsehood of slave
owners’ claims to operate a “benign” or
kind institution. Auctions that sold slaves
to the highest bidder were the most com-
mon method of selling slaves. A vivid de-
scription of a slave auction appears in
William Wells Brown’s 1853 novel Clotel,
or the President’s Daughter,the ﬁrst African
American novel: “This was a Southern
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1089 ---
SLAVERY (ECONOMICS) 1001
auction, at which the bones, muscles,
sinews, blood, and nerves of a young lady
of sixteen were sold for ﬁve hundred dol-
lars; her moral character for two hundred;
her improved intellect for one hundred; her
Christianity for three hundred; and her
chastity and virtue for four hundred dollars
more.”
Despite being considered other peo-
ple’s property, slaves in the Caribbean and,
to a lesser degree, in Brazil could have some
measure of economic independence due to
managing “provision grounds” like gardens.
While slaves in Saint Domingue and
Jamaica were among black people, and serfs
in Russia lived in a peasant world avoided
by their masters, slaves in the Southern
United States lived in their masters’ worlds.
The internal slave economy in the South
was small because slave owners wanted to
keep their slaves in utter dependence.
Living conditions kept economic opportu-
nities among slaves to a minimum, although
slaves were able to develop some nurturing
forms of culture and education within the
slave quarter communities.
While the law stated that slaves had no
property rights, local custom often accorded
slaves the privilege of small garden plots.
Slave owners usually did not allow slaves to
control what they grew, and they strictly
limited the amounts of food available for
the slaves’ consumption and the clothing
slaves could wear. In the 1850s, between 5
and 10 percent of slaves were “hired out,”
usually for a one-year term, to work for
money paid by an employer to their master.
Some slaves skilled as mechanics or crafts-
men were able to “hire their own time,”
although the slave owners still kept most or
all of the money earned. Although it was
rumored that a slave had invented the
cotton gin credited to Eli Whitney, there is
no historical evidence for such a claim.
Nevertheless, it is known that a slave
named Barclay built the ﬁrst cotton gin in
Mississippi by following a traveler’s verbal
account and a simple drawing of Whitney’s
gin.
Southern slavery’s “commercial orien-
tation” was central to the South as a dis-
tinctive region and to the social values of
slavery. From colonial life onward, South-
ern agriculture focused on producing staple
crops for a regular market. By 1850, about
55 percent of Southern slaves cultivated
cotton; 10 percent grew tobacco; 10 per-
cent produced crops including sugar, rice,
or hemp ﬁber; 15 percent worked as ser-
vants inside houses; and the remaining
10 percent worked in industry or trades.
Cotton ultimately became the most impor-
tant crop for the region and nation. While
in the year 1800 cotton accounted for only
7 percent of the dollar value of all U.S. ex-
ports, by 1860 cotton was 58 percent of all
U.S. exports. Even the free states in the
North were economically implicated in the
institution of slavery, as the slave industries
supported the entire nation’s welfare.
The study of slavery in relation to
economics continues to be subject to many
political and ideological debates. The work
of one particular pair of econometricians in
the 1970s was published to immediate crit-
icism that largely discredited it. The misuse
and erroneous interpretation of data in
Time on the Cross: The Economics of American
Negro Slavery (1974) by Robert Fogel and
Stanley Engerman has been refuted by
Herbert Gutman in Slavery and the
Numbers Game: A Critique of “Time on the
Cross” (1975). For instance, Gutman ex-
plains how they underestimated the amount
of whipping as punishment, gave inﬂated
ﬁgures for the skills held by slaves, and thus
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1090 ---
1002 S LAVERY (ECONOMICS)
argued illogically that a steep decline in
slave skills followed Emancipation.
The interpretive argument of Time on
the Cross was also challenged by other
scholars, who said Fogel and Engerman
went beyond claiming the efﬁciency, prof-
itability, and professional nature of South-
ern slavery beneﬁted the economy to also
claiming that slave owners were instilling
modern work habits in their slaves and that
slaves had beneﬁted from the institution.
While it is fair to say that Southern slave
owners were aggressive in their aim to max-
imize proﬁts, it is not accurate to claim that
they were making slaves into productive
workers who helped slaves achieve a modi-
ﬁed version of the American Dream of
rising in status. The very nature of unfree
labor made that unfeasible by providing no
compensation for slaves’ labor, denying
slaves’ humanity, breaking up families, and
offering no real incentives for better work
quality. The Southern plantation owner
had fundamental differences from the
Northern industrialist.
Scholar James Oakes published a book
in 1982 that emphasized the aggressive and
greedy character of slave owners in order to
assert a fundamental similarity between the
Northern and Southern social orders dur-
ing the decades before the Civil War. But
Oakes corrected himself in his 1990 book
Slavery and Freedom, in which the author
repudiated part of his previous argument
and stated that while “a highly developed
market economy” was necessary for slave
society to develop, the relationship between
masters and slaves was essentially “a non-
market relationship.”
Using slaves to produce goods changes
the equation of production and consump-
tion. Under Southern slavery, relations of
exchange were determined by the market,
and commerce required transactions and
competition. But the relations of produc-
tion were not determined by the market
because slaves were unpaid and did not
even own themselves. The workers could
not negotiate for better treatment, al-
though slaves did resist the slave economy
in ways such as physical retaliation, subtle
sabotage, appropriation of goods they had
produced, or self-removal from the work-
force. The entire Southern economy was
predicated upon a system that did not com-
pensate its workers. Furthermore, the slaves
were not consumers who could buy goods,
which further inhibited economic exchange.
U.S. slavery was not fading out in the
decades preceding its abolition, and aboli-
tion was not an economic decision because
the institution was unproﬁtable. Slavery
was still proﬁtable at the time of the Civil
War, although it provided inadequate stim-
ulus to modernization, industrialization, or
urbanization. Some historians have over-
stated or understated the proﬁtability of
slavery. T o say that the Southern region in
1860 was the fourth most prosperous na-
tion in the world in 1860 is accurate in a
sense but overlooks the limitations of the
Southern economy, which relied on only a
few crops. Southerners kept planting more
and more cotton to export to Europe, a
tactic that gained money but did not build
a developed and robust economy. The
South’s economic development had fallen
behind the North’s, and its manufacturing
made up only 16 percent of the total for
the United States. Railroad construction,
literacy rates and schooling, and urbaniza-
tion also lagged behind the rest of the
country.
Southern intellectuals of the antebel-
lum era thought, and often feared, that
slavery would end due to market forces,
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1091 ---
SLAVERY (ECONOMICS) 1003
although scholars today realize the false-
hood of the belief that slavery could die out
on its own accord. The political economy
of Thomas Roderick Dew, a college profes-
sor and administrator, led him to believe in
the 1840s that, sooner rather than later,
free labor would become cheaper than slave
labor and thus cause a general emancipa-
tion of slaves. But Dew insisted that the
South’s social system was a good model for
a world order because only servitude could
guarantee stability and, for those in power,
liberty. Some people thought that the in-
evitable laws of political economy would
“do their work” without the help of
Northern agitation, and another claim was
that black people, if freed, could not thrive
independently.
The arguments by pro-slavery political
economists and apologists defending slav-
ery were steeped in racist beliefs and gener-
ally led to unscholarly, biased conclusions.
Proponents of slavery alleged that they were
providing slaves with security from birth
until death. Not only was this claim factu-
ally inaccurate, but it also contradicted
free-market theory. They did not take into
account the reality that most achievements
of the modern world had come from free-
labor economics and that genuine progress
was necessary for survival.
Slavery was the pivotal issue thrusting
the United States into Civil War, and the
related ﬁnancial proﬁts, a motivation in
most wars, also heavily inﬂuenced the
Southern states’ decision to secede from the
Union. Southern states could only retain
their economic and political power if slav-
ery continued in the South and expanded
into the new territories in the west. At the
beginning of the war, President Abraham
Lincoln stated in 1861 that the dispute be-
tween the North and South concerned the
expansion rather than the existence of slav-
ery. Taking effect on January 1, 1863, the
Emancipation Proclamation made the war
to preserve the union into a struggle to
make black people free, and it ended any
chance that Britain or France would pro-
vide ﬁnancial and military support for the
Confederate States of America. The South’s
failed cotton embargo also showed that the
slave-based economy was going to have to
change, by force and by law.
Amy Cummins

SLAVERY (HISTORY)
Slavery can be deﬁned as not owning one-
self, or what Stephan Palmie has called
“institutionalized human unfreedom.”
Scholars who study slavery identify two
criteria: the legal recognition of property
rights involving human beings, and the
slave’s position as an outsider from society.
There have been many forms and degrees
of slavery throughout the past 4,000 years
of world history, and slavery is believed to
have existed in all parts of the globe, in-
cluding classical Greece and Italy. Anthro-
pologist Jack Goody states that the earliest
legal documents record the sale of slaves,
and the earliest legal code of which scholars
have knowledge refers to the slaves’ con-
stant efforts to escape from slavery. The de-
sire for freedom from bondage has charac-
terized every society that held fellow
human beings in a state of “unfreedom.”
Documentation of the transatlantic
slave trade, which became the largest forced
migration in history, began in the year
1441. A Portuguese historian reported that
a group of sailors in Africa for oils and skins
decided to take “captives” to be human
merchandise valuable as servants. Yet even
before that time, Africans had been en-
slaved for work in the mines of the Gold
Coast, now Ghana, and the “market” for
slaves had already existed in late-medieval
Europe. There was extensive trade con-
ducted by Islamic nations and managed by
Sudanese horsemen due to the high demand
for slaves in Muslim countries from the
tenth through the fifteenth centuries.
T ransatlantic slave commerce developed
after a preexisting slave trade among the
Mediterranean, central Europe, and the
Black Sea regions.
Forms of slave trading and slavery had
existed on the African continent for thou-
sands of years. The process of African inter-
nal slavery involved acquiring people
through transactions such as raiding, kid-
napping, war, the selling of criminals, and
indentured servitude to avoid starvation
during famine. Historians argue that
African internal slavery was part of a “con-
tinuum of relations,” with family and kin-
ship ties on one end and the use of persons
as chattel, or personal property, at the other
end. Attesting to the difﬁculty of compar-
ing African with American slavery, data
show substantial variations in the treatment
and use of slaves in African societies, yet it
was undeniably the exploitation and subju-
gation of fellow human beings. Finally,
scholars still debate whether the rise of ex-
porting slaves was caused by European
slave trading or was a separate develop-
ment, but it is known that the trade relied
on partnerships between Africans and
Europeans.
European ships relied primarily on
“slave markets” in southwest Africa, the re-
gion between Senegal and Angola. First the
coastal regions then the interior of Africa
were raided for slaves. Such trade agree-
ments were devastating not only to the
slaves as individuals but also to the African
countries being depopulated. The early
modern slave trade, from the ﬁfteenth to
seventeenth centuries, sent most slaves to
Portugal and Spain; numbers exceeded
50,000 people but could have been double
that amount.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1093 ---
SLAVERY (HISTORY) 1005
The number of slaves exported from
Africa in the transatlantic slave trade is now
believed by economists to be not less than
12 million and not more than 20 million.
But there continues to be substantial de-
bate and new research about the estimated
numbers of imported Africans, resulting
in the numbers being revised upward.
Historian Edward Reynolds quantiﬁed in
1985 that an estimated 11,698,000 people
were exported from Africa to the New
World, and that 9,778,500 of them sur-
vived to arrive in the Americas. From
within that number, Reynolds estimated
that at least 596,000 people were imported
into what became the United States, but
the ﬁgures were probably much higher.
The Middle Passage denotes the jour-
ney from Africa across the Atlantic Ocean.
The average length of this trip was at least
sixty days, but it varied due to departure
and arrival points and weather. High death
rates were due primarily to dehydration,
the length of the voyage, and the spread of
contagious diseases in overcrowded, unsan-
itary living conditions. T reatment of the
slaves included branding to indicate owner-
ship, chaining by the ankles, removal of
clothing, and sexual abuse. Slaves torn
from their homelands usually did not know
where they were going or why they had
been taken. The desire to return to their
homelands led slaves to attempt rebellions
and suicide, despite harsh retaliation. Up to
one-third of slaves who survived the
Middle Passage died during the experience
of “seasoning,” a disciplinary process aimed
at breaking the spirits of the slaves so they
would be effective workers.
The demand for slaves beyond Africa
was due to the need for workers on planta-
tions for sugar, tobacco, cotton, and coffee,
and in mines. Reynolds estimates that, of
all the slaves who came from Africa, Brazil
imported 38 percent; the British Caribbean
17 percent; Spanish America 17 percent;
North America 6 percent; and the Dutch,
Danish, and Swedish Caribbean 6 percent.
In terms of scale, numbers, and cruelty,
slavery reached unprecedented levels in the
post-Columbian Americas. Greed and
domination led governments and individu-
als in power to seek great proﬁts without
paying workers any wages or acknowledg-
ing that they were human beings. Various
countries legally abolished, or outlawed,
slavery at different times in history, usually
after declaring incremental restrictions:
Britain in 1834, Denmark and France in
1848, the United States in 1865, Cuba in
1886, and Brazil in 1888.
The systematic importation of slaves
into British North America began in 1619,
and by the 1690s, slaves became cheaper
than indentured servants in the North
American colonies. Using slave labor al-
lowed for the mass production of tobacco,
rice, and indigo in the South. Slavery was
an important part of the economy at the
time of the U.S. War of Independence, or
American Revolution, even though slavery
contradicted the ideology that asserted
American self-determination and freedom
from Britain. In 1808, the U.S. Slave T rade
Act went into effect, prohibiting the im-
portation of slaves. Although U.S. partici-
pation in the transatlantic slave trade ofﬁ-
cially ended at that point, trafﬁcking in
slaves within the United States only in-
creased. The slave population of the United
States increased sevenfold between 1790
and 1860, and there were four million
enslaved people in the South by the time of
the Civil War.
The condition of slavery denied the
humanity of the slave. Laws stated that the
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1094 ---
1006 S LAVERY (HISTORY)
authority of the master must be complete
in order to render the submission of the
slave perfect. Slave owners who mistreated
and killed their slaves were not punished
because slaves were considered property
rather than fellow humans with human or
legal rights. For example, their marriages
were not considered legally binding, and
they could not own property or provide
legal testimony. Slave owners took sexual
advantage of female slaves, and the children
of slaves followed the condition of the
mother, remaining in bondage. Although it
was illegal to teach slaves to read or write,
many slaves still learned to read. Further-
more, the existence of slavery delayed the
development of public education in the
Southern states.
The dominant ideology in the South
stated that slavery was acceptable although,
in 1860, under 25 percent of the South’s
white population was in a slave-owning
family. Most Southern politicians were
slaveholders who, watching out for their
own interests, made support of slavery an
integral part of Southern politics. Race
prejudice also played an important role in
causing poorer whites to accept slavery.
Some people claimed that slavery was ben-
eﬁcial to blacks as well as to whites and that
masters could serve in a parental relation-
ship to their slaves. However, the institu-
tion of slavery cannot be beneﬁcial to the
slave subject because personhood is denied.
Slaveholders and their political allies in
the Southern states also alleged that the
Hebrew Bible supported their practice of
owning slaves. However, Christians of vari-
ous denominations were essential in lead-
ing the movement to abolish slavery in the
United States and other nations.
The Civil War, fought for a network of
reasons including the slavery debate, led to
the preservation of the Union and the abo-
lition of slavery. The ratiﬁcation of the
Thirteenth Amendment of the Constitu-
tion in 1865 abolished slavery in the
United States. Even after the process of
Reconstruction from 1865 to 1877 helped
bring some improvements in the living and
working conditions of American blacks,
the legacy of slavery and racism continued.
Writers and public speakers have his-
torically used the phrase “wage slavery” to
compare the condition of not owning one-
self with being economically discriminated
against in unjust working conditions. The
term came into use when the awareness of
economic class exploitation was rising. For
example, in antebellum America, Southern
defenders of the institution of slavery
claimed that their practices were no worse
than the wage slavery of Northern states or
of England. Nevertheless, not all ways of
extracting labor from subordinated individ-
uals are like slavery. Such a comparison can
be inadequate in light of the historical
realities and degradations people of African
heritage suffered under slavery in the
Americas. The institution of slavery still
persists in the twenty-ﬁrst century. It is be-
lieved that millions of persons suffer at the
present time from modern-day slavery or
other forms of unfree labor, but it is always
important to describe the terms and condi-
tions with any claim that people live in
slavery.
Amy Cummins

SMALLS,R OBERT
(1839–1915)
Robert Smalls was one of the ﬁrst African
American heroes of the American Civil
War, and later a prominent Reconstruction-
era politician in the South. Following cele-
brated military service in the Union Army,
he returned to his home in Beaufort, South
Carolina, where he parlayed his reputation
as a war hero into a brilliant political career
that spanned four decades. Smalls is,
perhaps, best known to historians for his
daring escape from slavery on May 13,
1862. Commandeering the Confederate
Portrait of Civil War naval hero Robert Smalls and captured Confederate ship Planter. Smalls’s capture of the
vessel allowed him to free a group of African Americans from slavery, including his wife and children. (Library of
Congress)
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1096 ---
1008 S MITH,M IKEY
ship Planter, on which he served as pilot,
Smalls saved 15 people, including his wife
and three young children. Having intimate
knowledge of the signal codes required for
moving in and out of Charleston harbor,
which was under intense Confederate
scrutiny and a heavy Union blockade,
Smalls was able to run safely out to the
blockade, providing the Union with the
full resources of the ship as well as key tac-
tical information about the harbor and
adjacent Fort Sumter. Following the war,
Smalls returned to Beaufort, purchased the
home in which he had served as a slave, and
won election to the South Carolina State
House of Representatives, serving from
1868 until 1870. In 1874, Smalls was
elected to the United States Congress,
where he served ﬁve terms. In 1890, he
took the position of Collector of the Port
in Beaufort, which he kept for 20 years,
remaining active and visible in the South
Carolina Republican Party. In 1910, at the
age of 71, he declined the position of am-
bassador to Liberia. He died on February
23, 1915.

SMITH,M IKEY (1954–1983) 
Mikey Smith was a Jamaican dub poet
whose early success included a drama de-
gree in 1980 from the Jamaica School of
Drama. His transatlantic concerns with
Africa and the Americas may be viewed in
the themes of his poetry, which ﬁnds sym-
pathetic ears worldwide; his poetry often
revolves around ironic elements of cultural
noise, social plight, variations of suffering,
and, especially, afﬁrmation of the present
day. His connection to his transatlantic au-
dience may also be viewed in his choice to
perform in London at the 1982 “Interna-
tional Book Fair of Radical Blacks and
Third World Books.” In 1981–1982 Smith
made more international connections by
touring Paris, Milan, Amsterdam, and
Britain, receiving great acclaim for his
highly crafted performances of his poetry.
He also toured the world with reggae singer
Gregory Isaacs.
Smith was such a success in London
that the BBC made a documentary about
him titled “Upon Westminster Bridge.” In
1982, Smith recorded his trademark poem,
“Mi Cyaan Believe It,” and eight other
poems for a CD of the same name. On the
disc he speaks his trademark “lawd”
(lord)—that is sometimes extended into
more of a howl, “lawwwwwwwwd.”
Kamau Brathwaite likens the sound effect
to the roar of a motorcycle engine. Carolyn
Cooper describes it as the afﬁrmative voice
of the suffering. The record was produced
in London by fellow Jamaican dub poet
Linton Kwesi Johnson.
Smith was just beginning to reap the
beneﬁts of his impressive creativity when
personal and political problems turned
against him. On August 17, 1983, he
found himself in an argument with sup-
porters of the Jamaican Labor Party, who
later stoned him to death, although it is un-
clear exactly what took place and why. He
died at age 29. In a prophetic poem titled
“Dem Naw Destroy I,” Smith makes the
case that he will continue to live through
life’s hardships. The poem was published
posthumously with his collection It a
Come, in 1986. And Smith does live on

anthologies like The Routledge Reader in

SMITHSONIAN AFRICAN
ART MUSEUM
The Smithsonian African Art Museum
(SAAM) began as a private educational in-
stitution and has been transformed into a
national museum supporting research and
education and playing a leading role in fos-
tering appreciation of African and African
American art. The Museum of African Art
was founded in 1964 by former U.S.
Foreign Service ofﬁcer Warren M. Robbins.
The museum initially began as a private
educational institution situated in what
was previously the residence of Frederick
Douglass—an ex-slave and prominent abo-
litionist during the early to mid-nineteenth
century. Until 1979 the African art
museum remained privately operated and
possessed a scant collection of paintings by
African American artists and an even
smaller collection of African art. The
Museum of African Art was absorbed by
the Smithsonian Institution in 1979 fol-
lowing a congressional act, and in 1981 was
renamed the National Museum of African
Art.
In 1983 Sylvia H. Williams became the
new director of the National African Art
Museum. In 1987 a new building was
erected on the National Mall to house the
museum’s growing art collections. The
National Museum of African Art currently
houses a distinctive collection of visual
art materials including sculptures, pho-
tographs, pottery, jewelry, furniture, and
musical instruments, among a number of
other artistic mediums acquired from
across the entire African continent. The
national art museum contains the largest
public collection of contemporary African
art in America.
In addition to its role as the leading
museum of African art in the United States,
the Smithsonian National Museum of
African Art fosters distinctive research facil-
ities and educational programs. The mu-
seum’s archives, named for famed photog-
rapher Eliot Elisofon, contain over 300,000
photographic images and transparencies
that visually portray dimensions of African
life. The archives also contain nontextual
records, such as documentary ﬁlms and
other videos relevant to African art and his-
tory. The museum’s library, named for mu-
seum founder Warren M. Robbins, is part
of the Smithsonian Institution libraries’
consortium and contains over 25,000
books and periodicals. Maps, videotapes,
and children’s literature are also included in
the library’s holdings. The repository is
catered toward adult and juvenile re-
searchers interested in exploring African
history, art, and culture.
The National Museum of African Art
encompasses a high-tech conservation
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1098 ---
1010 S OCCER
laboratory, and has been nationally recog-
nized as the leading conservation center for
the preservation of African art. African art
aﬁcionados often seek advice from curato-
rial staff on how to preserve and maintain
private collections. The public is also in-
vited to the conservation laboratory to have
objects identiﬁed and to deposit donations.
Since its inception the National
Museum of African Art has developed
into a superior museological institution,
research facility, conservation center, and
educational organization. The museum re-
lies heavily on its volunteers, interns, and
professional staff to create an entertaining
and enjoyable learning experience. The
museum continues to incorporate new and
exciting exhibitions that educate and
engage its viewing public.

SOCCER
Soccer—better known as “football” outside
the United States—is the most popular
team sport in Africa, Latin America, and
the Caribbean. More generally, it plays an
important part in the cultural, social, and
often the economic and political life of
these regions.
South American soccer is dominated
by Argentina and Brazil. The former has
won the Copa America, the oldest interna-
tional tournament in world football, orga-
nized by the South American Soccer
Federation (Confederatión Sudamericana
de Fútbol [CONMEBOL]), a total of 17
times (like Uruguay). In addition, the
Copa Liberatores, a CONEMBOL inter-
national club tournament, has been won by
Argentinean teams 20 times (as of May
2005). Brazil is the only team that has
qualiﬁed for all 17 FIFA (Fédération Inter-
nationale de Football Association, world
soccer’s governing body) World Cup tour-
naments and has won the championship a
record number ﬁve times. The Argentinean
and Brazil rivalry is mirrored by the ongo-
ing dispute on who is the all-time best
player of world soccer. Opinions are di-
vided between Brazil’s Pelé, three times
World Cup winner and former sports min-
ister of Brazil, and Armando Diego
Maradona, Argentinean World Cup winner
in 1986 and the only player known to have
inspired the foundation of his own church.
Soccer in the CONCACAF (Confed-
eration of North and Central American
and Caribbean Association Football) region
is dominated by Mexico. The Mexican
national team has won the CONCACAF
Gold Cup, a tournament held since 1963,
seven times, followed by three-time cham-
pion Costa Rica. African soccer is orga-
nized via the CAF (Confédération
Africaine de Football) and is dominated by
North and West African nations. Egypt,
Cameroon, and Ghana have all won the
Africa Cup, the tournament held biannu-
ally by the CAF since 1957, four times.
Cameroon and Senegal have both reached
the FIFA World Cup quarterﬁnals once,
which makes them the most successful
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1099 ---
SOCIALISM 1011
African teams internationally. The fact that
South Africa won the right to host the
FIFA World Cup in 2010 partly reﬂects
the augmented status of African soccer in
an increasingly global game.
In a globalized world, the best players
tend to follow the money. Their departure
has led to a phenomenon that could be de-
scribed as a continuous “leg drain,” similar
to the brain drain poor countries face by
losing their best academics to richer coun-
tries. The soccer leg drain is more ambiva-
lent. National teams can benefit from
recent developments of the game through
their players gaining insights at European
or rich South American clubs. Many Latin
American (and African) clubs increasingly
rely on transfer fees earned from selling the
most valuable players to ﬁnance themselves.
In Brazil the transfer system has created an
ownership model that makes it almost im-
possible for professional players up to a cer-
tain age to decide where to work. A rising
problem is the increasingly young age of
players who become subject to transfer
deals. FC Santos of Brazil, for example,
signed a nine-year-old boy from southern
Brazil, said to be the “new Pelé.” The FIFA
has declared its intention to change its
transfer rules to rule out such transfers.
Despite the economic pressures on the
game, soccer remains a strong focal point
for identity-building processes. Football
clubs and national teams deliver a symbolic
representation of an assumed origin (or
belonging) for people that usually lasts an
entire lifetime. Argentina is said to be
divided fairly evenly between fans of the
River Plate and Boca Juniors teams, and
support for either club is an important
characteristic of many Argentines’ self-
deﬁnition. These connections are consti-
tuted by personal origin (place of birth,
social status, etc.) and deﬁne whole com-
munities. They also help to strengthen the
ties of exile communities to their homeland.
U.S. Major League Soccer (MLS)
makes use of these ties by allocating star
players from South and Middle America to
clubs with a perceived spectator potential
in the local Latin community. For example,
Jorge Campos, long-time goalkeeper for
the Mexican national team, was signed
by the L.A. Galaxy team. Similarly, perhaps
the most skilled Colombian player ever,
Carlos Valderrama was tapped to play for
the Florida-based teams Tampa Bay
Mutiny and Miami Fusion. These efforts
were rather unsuccessful, and as a result,
Club Deportivo Chivas USA was created.
This team seeks to attract the Latin popu-
lation of California by signing mostly Latin
American players.

SOCIALISM
Socialism, broadly deﬁned, refers to some
type of collective ownership and control of
a society’s means of production, subsis-
tence, and exchange. Over time and in di-
verse contexts, the speciﬁc mechanisms of
control and practices of collective decision
making have ranged from state control of
the economy, as in numerous Soviet
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1100 ---
1012 S OCIALISM
systems, to libertarian control through
popular assemblies, as in the Zapatista
communities of Chiapas, Mexico. Social-
ism, in varying forms and different per-
spectives, has been widely inﬂuential in a
variety of national and regional contexts in
Africa and the Americas. For many in
poorer or developing countries, socialism,
and especially the example of the Russian
Revolution, has offered a model for the
coincidence of industrial/economic and
governmental/political revolutions. This
revolutionary model, in which a seizure of
national power has provided a lever for
rapid industrialization, held great appeal
throughout the twentieth century within
numerous countries of the global south.
As postcolonial governments looked
for means by which to catch up with the
industrial might of the former colonial
powers, the approach of socialism, espe-
cially statist socialism, seemed to provide
both a potentially effective political pro-
gram and an ideological justiﬁcation for
statist reorganization of the economy and
work. However, it should be noted that
many commentators suggest that in both
the Americas and Africa, many of the in-
digenous, or noncolonial societies, were
actually organized as socialist societies in
which the necessities of life were shared
within relatively egalitarian communities.
Movements or systems identiﬁed ex-
plicitly as socialist have a long history in
Latin America, ranging from the last
decades of the nineteenth century to the
present. Among the most important exam-
ples include certain indigenous and agrar-
ian movements during the Mexican
Revolution, the Cuban Revolution, and the
Sandanista uprising of Nicaragua. In the
twenty-first century significant socialist
projects include the Zapatista movement in
Chiapas, Mexico, the factory reclamation
movements of Argentina, and elected na-
tional governments formed as part of
the populist wave known collectively as the
Bolivarian Revolution. These include the
governments of Hugo Chavez in Venezuela
and Evo Morales in Bolivia.
The history of such explicit socialist
movements or societies is more recent in
Africa, dating especially to the movements
against colonialism from the middle or late
twentieth century. Important examples of
socialist movements and systems include
the MPLA (Popular Movement for the
Liberation of Angola), which formed the
ﬁrst postcolonial government in Angola,
and FRELIMO (the Liberation Front of
Mozambique), which took power in
Mozambique. Between 1974 and 1991 a
socialist government under Lieutenant
Colonel Mengitsu ruled Ethiopia. That
government’s survival in the face of a vari-
ety of opposition and independence move-
ments was dependent in part on aid and
military support from Fidel Castro’s social-
ist government in Cuba. In addition, nu-
merous socialist parties and organizations
have been active in several Africa countries,
including South Africa, where socialists of
various stripes played signiﬁcant parts in
the downfall of the apartheid regime.
African socialism refers to the perspec-
tive that traditional African communities
exhibit characteristics, including social rela-
tions and sharing of resources, which reﬂect
a form of indigenous socialism. Socialism
was viewed as an ongoing characteristic of
African communal life. Some African so-
cialists argued that indigenous forms of
socialism were key aspects of identity for
many Africans based on local community
experiences. African socialism was pre-
sented as an alternative to scientiﬁc, or
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1101 ---
SOCIALISM 1013
authoritarian, socialism based on models
borrowed from Soviet or Maoist regimes.
Many postindependence leaders advo-
cated some form of African socialism, al-
though their visions and the actual projects
they initiated to carry out their visions var-
ied widely. Socialism provided an alterna-
tive to the exploitative and oppressive polit-
ical economic regimes of imperialist rule.
At the same time, Western versions of
socialism, especially Soviet-inspired sys-
tems, were viewed as inapplicable to the
speciﬁc social circumstances of less industri-
alized countries whose labor base was often
concentrated in agricultural or resource
extractive industries. Similarly, advocates of
African socialism sought to draw upon local
governance practices in order to organize
social and productive change rather than
through the centralized statist models of
Sovietism.
Perhaps the most inﬂuential version of
African socialism was Julius Nyerere’s vi-
sion of ujamma (“villigization”) based on
cooperative work and living in organized
villages. Ujamma combined socialism and
communal life toward the cause of rural de-
velopment. The focus was on improving
society through the development of people
rather than ratcheting up production.
Despite gains in areas of health and educa-
tion, ujamma left many people worse off
materially. Nyerere’s works had much inﬂu-
ence on the perspective of the West Indian
Marxist C. L. R. James and his analyses of
working-class self-organization.
African socialism held out a promise of
self-sufﬁciency, equality, economic devel-
opment, and prosperity following locally
appropriate social practices. In practice,
most examples of African socialism failed
to deliver much in any of these areas. Many
leaders who had advocated African socialism
fell back on authoritarian forms of Soviet-
style government when attempting to
implement their policies. Among the most
notable proponents of African socialism, in
addition to Nyerere, are Amilcar Cabral
(Guinea-Bissau and Cape Verde), Samora
Machel (Mozambique), Thomas Sankara
(Burkina Faso), and Michel Micombero
(Burundi).
Perhaps the most important, and indeed
inspirational, direct connection between
socialism in Africa and in the Americas is
represented by the support given by Cuba
to the socialist forces of Angola in their
struggles, ﬁrst for independence and later
against the invasion forces of apartheid
South Africa. Cuban forces and materials
were deployed in support of the Marxist
MPLA during the liberation struggles of
1975 and played an essential part in their
ability to defeat the opposition movements
backed by W estern imperialist interests.
This support helped the MPLA become
Angola’s ﬁrst postindependence govern-
ment following the withdrawal of the
Portuguese colonial power.
The Cubans also came to the aid of
Angola in 1988 when a South African of-
fensive at Cuito Cuanavale in Angola
threatened to defeat forces of Angola’s
socialist government. In addition to send-
ing thousands of troops to reinforce the
Cuban forces already in Angola, the Cuban
government reduced their country’s own
anti-aircraft defenses by shipping its most
advanced weapons to Angola. Angolan and
Cuban troops, along with forces of the
South West Africa People’s Organization
(SWAPO), managed a stunning victory
over the apartheid army invaders. The
South African defeat forced that country’s
government to take part in negotiations
that eventually led to the independence of

1014 S OCIALISM
Namibia, and indeed played a major part in
the collapse of the apartheid regime only a
few years later. This crucial, world-altering
victory would not have been possible with-
out the alliance between the socialist gov-
ernments of Cuba and Angola.
The collapse of the Soviet Union and
the Soviet systems in Eastern Europe, along
with the passing of Maoism and the em-
bracing of capitalism in China, all dealt se-
vere blows to the socialist societies of
Africa. With the loss of aid and resources
from the Soviet economies, many socialist
governments in Africa became more des-
perate for aid from Western capitalist gov-
ernments and international organizations
like the International Monetary Fund and
World Bank. They also became more vul-
nerable to the pressures of Western capital-
ist governments and institutions to accept
programs of neoliberal structural adjust-
ment programs, including the privatization
of government works and lands. The im-
pacts of these programs were severe on local
populations and led governments such as
those of Angola, Mozambique, and Zambia
away from previous social commitments to
the people of those countries.
The collapse of the Soviet systems in
Eastern Europe did not have the same neg-
ative impact on socialist movements in
Latin America. In fact, alternative, and in
many ways novel, socialist movements have
emerged in several Latin American coun-
tries. These movements, whether the grass-
roots and libertarian Zapatistas in Mexico
or the electoral Bolivarian movements
in Venezuela and Bolivia, have offered
glimpses of potentially innovative move-
ments that do not refer easily to the forms
of socialism that have preceded them, espe-
cially the Soviet forms of statist socialism.
Few social movements have had the
global impact, either in symbolic terms as
heralds of new (post-) socialist politics or in
more practical terms as leaders in the global
struggle against neoliberal capitalism, than
the Zapatista Army of National Liberation
(EZLN, or simply the Zapatistas). Globally,
the Zapatistas have been upheld variously
as the heralds of a diversity of new politics.
Thus the Zapatistas have been presented as
examples of, to name only a few, postmod-
ern rebellion, anarchism, autonomous
Marxism, or the multitude. The Zapatistas
have perhaps posed the most organized and
convincing challenge to neoliberalism.
In an early statement following their
public emergence, on the day the North
American Free T rade Agreement took
effect, the Zapatistas argued that NAFTA
meant a death sentence for the indigenous
ethnicities of Mexico. The statement also
charged that under the modernization
program of the Mexican government of
the day, indigenous people were entirely
dispensable.
For many, the Zapatistas presented the
possibility of the ﬁrst postmodern revolu-
tion: a revolution challenging contempo-
rary notions of the nation-state and what is
meant by citizenship. From the longer-
term analysis of struggles, historically be-
tween the Mexican state and indigenous
people, the Zapatista uprising may be seen
as a predictable outcome of modernizing
(and globalizing) programs that have sup-
pressed the identity and aspirations of the
Mayan people for centuries.
The World Social Forum, a yearly
gathering of socialist movements, provides
a venue for socialists in the Americas and
Africa to come together to discuss strategies
for resisting capitalist globalization. The
World Social Forum was initiated in 1990
in São Paolo, Brazil, sponsored by the
Cuban government and the Communist
Workers Party of Brazil, which now forms

Brazil’s government. Since then the Social

African socialists, such as Patrice

SOKOTO CALIPHATE
The Sokoto Caliphate was an early 
nineteenth-century African Islamic kingdom.
The Sokoto Caliphate emerged from the
jihad of Shehu Usman Dan Fodio; jihad is
here understood as a struggle for the sake
of Islam against unbelievers. The Shehu
began preaching Islam in 1774–1775 to
the Hausa and Fulani in the northwestern
part of present-day Nigeria. In 1804,
Sokoto itself became the headquarters of
the Shehu’s son Muhammad Bello. The
Shehu died in 1817, and Bello became
caliph. But the caliphate lacked the cohe-
sion that it had under the Shehu. Bello sub-
sequently conducted 47 raids during his
lifetime. At the time of his death in 1837,
the caliphate had become solidiﬁed. It in-
cluded regions of what are now Nigeria,
Benin, Niger, and Cameroon. Politically,
the caliphate was a system of local emirates
that owed authority to the caliph in
Sokoto. The caliph controlled the appoint-
ment of the emirs, who were fairly inde-
pendent as long as they acted in accordance
with the caliphate. But Sokoto was
nonetheless the location of a centralized
administration. The emirs paid tribute to
the caliph, especially with the spoils of war,
and Sokoto settled internal disputes among
emirates. The emirates were usually able to
defend themselves from individual invaders
without the intervention of Sokoto. But
the caliphate could not resist the large-scale
movements of the British that began in
1900. In 1903, Sokoto fell to the British
West African Frontier Force under Frederick
Lugard.
Mahriana Rofheart

SOMALIA
Located on the northeast coast of the Horn
of Africa, Somalia has a population of
approximately 8,305,000. In a state of civil
war in the 1990s, Somalia has been the
focus of much U.S. military involvement
and international concern.
The vast majority of the population is
Muslim, most of whom are Sunni. Arabic is
commonly spoken. T rade with Europeans
began early, with Portuguese and British
traders operating from the port of Aden.
Subsequently, a small number of traders
from the United States also had contact
with Somalia, including Alexander I.
Cotheal, who traded on the Juba River in
southern Somalia in the 1850s.
Egyptian soldiers occupied Somalia be-
ginning in the 1870s. In 1884, the ﬁrst
British political agent was appointed to the
country. Somalia became a British protec-
torate called British Somaliland in 1885,
and was initially governed from India. In
the south, Italians sought to colonize the
land and establish plantations. In this colo-
nial context, American explorers went to
Somaliland in the 1890s. Best-known of
these American explorers was the Pennsyl-
vania-born A. Donaldson Smith. After in-
heriting a fortune in 1892, Smith went big-
game hunting in Somaliland. He later
explored under the auspices of the Royal
Geographic Society, publishing Through
Unknown African Countries: The First Expe-
dition from Somaliland to Lake Lamu in
1897.
International conﬂicts have been part
of Somalia’s history, partly because of its
proximity to European powers. In 1899, a
rebellion broke out in British Somaliland
led by Muhammad ibn Adb Allah Hasan,
known to the British as the “Mad Mullah.”
The revolt was gradually put down by the
British use of the Camel Corps led by
Richard Corﬁeld. Corﬁeld was killed at the
battle of Dul Madoba in 1913, but by then
the rebels had been largely defeated. Dur-
ing World War II, British Somaliland was
brieﬂy captured by Italy. The British retook
the region and also gained control of Italy’s
portion, placing the area under a British
military administration.
On July 1, 1960, Somalia gained inde-
pendence and the U.S. Peace Corps started
operations in the new nation in 1962. The
ﬁrst president was Aden Abdullah Osman
Daar, and he was succeeded in 1967 by
Abdirashid Ali Ahermarke. In 1969,
Abdirashid Ali Ahermarke was assassinated
and Mohammed Siad Barre came to power
through a coup. He would remain presi-
dent until 1991, although his power would
erode dramatically to the point where, by
the end, he controlled very little of the
country. Internal revolts led to rebel groups
taking over much of the countryside out-
side of the capital of Mogadishu. With
these internal problems, there was little
contact between Somalia and the Americas
throughout much of the 1960s; the United
States was, however, the largest donor of
nonmilitary aid.
U.S.-Somali relations were strained in
the 1970s when Somalia sought military
support from the Soviet Union. Soon after
the Ogaden War of 1977–1978, in which
Siad Barre sought and failed to seize the
Ogaden territory form Ethiopia, U.S.-
Somali relations became closer; however,
the United States remained critical of
Somali human rights abuses.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1105 ---
SONGHAY (MEDIEVAL EMPIRE) 1017
When Siad Barre was overthrown in
1991, chaos ensued. Aid convoys sent by
the international community were regu-
larly hijacked. Somalia became what is
known as a failed state, a country without
effective governance. On December 9,
1992, the United States sent in 28,000
troops accompanied by soldiers from the
French Foreign Legion, Canada, and many
other countries. The warlord Mohammed
Farrah Aidid was in power in Mogadishu.
Signiﬁcant conﬂict resulted. On July 12,
1993, a U.S. helicopter attack killed many
Somali clan leaders. On October 3, a team
of U.S. soldiers sought to capture two of
Aidid’s chief advisers. The attempt failed
and the soldiers were pinned down.
Eighteen were killed and seventy badly
wounded. That incident, because of the
helicopters the U.S. soldiers used, became
known as “Black Hawk Down,” leading to
a ﬁlm of the same name in 2001.
The United States would remain in the
country, but both U.S. and United Nations
forces would leave in 1995. Civil war con-
tinued for many years. As a failed state,
Somalia has been a central focus of U.S.
concerns about terrorism, with many fearing
that the country offers an effective sanctuary
for terrorists. Recently, the U.S. government
froze the assets of al-Barakaat, the major in-
ternational exchange in Somalia which was
suspected of being linked to Al Qaeda. As of
2006, the U.S. government has supported
the UN’s efforts to aid the newly-formed
Baidoa-based coalition government.
Justin Corﬁeld

SONGHAY
(MEDIEVAL EMPIRE)
The Songhay Empire was an African king-
dom that began in the ﬁfteenth century
and grew to prominence in the sixteenth
century. The three great kingdoms that
emerged in the western Sudan all took ad-
vantage of their strategic positions along
trade routes connected to international
commercial networks. The Berbers, an
T omb of Muhammad Ture (who took the name Askia),
ruler of the Songhai Empire from 1493 to 1528, at
Gao in present-day Mali. (Werner Forman/Art
Resource, NY)
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1106 ---
1018 S ONGHAY (MEDIEVAL EMPIRE)
indigenous people from North Africa, sold
goods from the western Sudan to North
African merchants, who in turn sold them
to Asians and Europeans. Imports from
abroad then entered West Africa. The
Sudan beneﬁted from the extensive com-
mercial activity, which led to the founding
of towns, cities, and states. Ghana arose
during the fourth century, peaked during
the eleventh, and fell to other conquerors
about 1240. Mali was established about
1230 and reached its height during the
fourteenth century. Songhay was the most
powerful. It appeared about 1468, and was
strongest during the sixteenth century. 
The Songhay Empire rose to eminence
with the reign of Sunni Ali. He was a great
general who defeated all of the fear-inspir-
ing warriors of the western Sudan; among
them were the Mossi, the Fulani, and the
Dogon. He then captured Timbuktu from
the Tauregs in 1468, and ﬁnally succeeded
in conquering the important trading city of
Jenne in 1473. These victories gave him
command of the trade routes and the Niger
Delta. Ali’s rule was a mobile military gov-
ernment created by conquest and main-
tained by force. He used military comman-
ders to govern his vast lands. Sunni Ali
organized a military ﬂeet on the river com-
prised of war canoes, and he used several
capitals as his bases of operations in order
to oversee his vast domains. He continued
to push the Songhay Empire, which now
included its predecessors, Ghana and Mali,
far into the northern desert. He governed
effectively by allowing the local rulers in
the more distant provinces to remain in
their positions, as long as they collected
taxes from the people and maintained
order. Because Ali carried on a relentless
pursuit of the Muslim Tauregs, and dis-
played little respect for Islam, he was
frequently criticized in Arabic sources as a
ruthless oppressor.
Sunni Ali was always guided by politics
and economics. He tolerated the Islamic
faith and exhibited public support for the
Muslim traders in his realm as the tradi-
tional source of economic prosperity in
West Africa. However, Ali, like his prede-
cessors, remained faithful to the old African
ways, realizing that the basis of power in
West Africa lay in maintaining the loyalty
of its indigenous peoples. His military
strength was dependent upon the support
of his people, the indigenous ﬁshermen and
farmers of the Middle Niger region. Ali did
not hesitate to punish the Muslim commu-
nity if he suspected them of disloyalty. For
instance, he persecuted the Muslims in
Timbuktu because they supported his ene-
mies the Tauregs. At heart, Ali was an
African priest-king in the old tradition, al-
ways cognizant of the religious needs of his
own people, and striving to balance the de-
mands of the old African traditions with
the new religion, Islam. Although the Mus-
lims may have viewed him as a tyrant,
Sunni Ali is today honored in Songhay oral
traditions as the founder of Songhay civi-
lization and as an authentic conquering
hero. Sunni Ali died in 1492.
Askia Muhammad (1493–1528) be-
came the next powerful Songhay king.
Known as Askia the Great, he led the em-
pire in its glory. He established the Askia
dynasty, and then went on to make intelli-
gent and subtle use of Islam in order to re-
inforce his power in the Sudan. In other
words, Askia the Great was most admired
for his diplomatic skills. His taking the title
“askia” instead of “sunni” was a symbol of
his new administration. Askia was a mili-
tary rank in the Songhai army, whereas
sunni had been the traditional royal title.

SONGHAY (MEDIEVAL EMPIRE) 1019
Just three years after his ascent to the
throne, Askia Muhammad undertook a
two-year pilgrimage to Mecca; the purpose
of his trip was to cement relations with the
key Muslim powers in North Africa. Like
Mansa Musa of Mali before him, he trav-
eled with a large caravan and distributed
much gold. The Egyptian caliph named
him the caliph of the Sudan, and he
received the support of a noted North
African Muslim cleric named al-Maghili,
whose works are still known in West Africa.
After he returned to Songhay Askia
Muhammad began to assert Muslim law
and learning in the empire, relying on the
guidance of al Maghili. Timbuktu and
Jenne were revived as important centers of
Muslim learning and culture. Leo Africanus,
the well-known traveler and writer from
Morocco, ﬁrst visited the Songhay empire
in 1510, and published a colorful account
of the region, vividly describing the town of
Timbuktu as a thriving center of learning
and commercial activity ﬁlled with learned
men like doctors, judges, and priests, as
well as bustling with many shops, mer-
chants, and craftsmen.
Askia Muhammad’s revival of cultural
centers like Timbuktu provided the basis
for a full ﬂowering of indigenous scholar-
ship. Native writers left valuable historical
records written in Arabic, which had be-
come the literary language of the western
Sudan. The works of scholars trained in the
religious and intellectual center at
Timbuktu make up some of the ﬁrst histo-
ries about the continent by indigenous
Africans. One of these early scholars was
Ahmed Baba. He completed about ﬁfty
works on Islamic law, compiled a biograph-
ical dictionary of Muslim scholars, and
collected an extensive library. Some of his
works are still used by contemporary
Muslims in West Africa. A historian pre-
dating Muhammad and Baba was the
Soninke born scholar Mahmud Kati. He
was born in 1468 and reportedly lived to be
125. He was a personal follower of Askia
Muhammad, beginning his long career by
accompanying the emperor to Mecca. Kati
began his major work, T arikh al Fattash
(The History of the Seeker of Knowledge ), in
1519 and his descendants completed the
text in 1665.
Askia Muhammad developed Jenne as
another important cultural and economic
center. The trade products were essentially
the same as they had been for Mali: salt and
gold dust. Jenne was an important link be-
tween the traders in Timbuktu and the pro-
ducers of gold in the forest regions of the
south. Salt blocks traveled by canoe from
Timbuktu to Jenne, where porters then
transported this valuable commodity to the
southern goldﬁelds. Gold was the main im-
petus for the trans-Saharan trade, as well as
kola nuts, and captured slaves for sale in the
Muslim north. Additional trade items were
luxury goods, horses for the military, and
cloth.
Jenne flourished as a prosperous
Muslim market and city under both the
Mali and Songhay empires. However, ar-
chaeologists have determined from studies
of its burial sites, that the city was ﬁrst es-
tablished by ancient Africans, not Muslims.
Jenne developed in the Niger ﬂoodplain,
and the evidence indicates that it was occu-
pied by Africans as early as the third cen-
tury BCE. T erracotta ﬁgures have been ex-
cavated that place Jenne within the ancient,
West African terracotta tradition along
with the Nok culture.
Askia Muhammad was an excellent
administrator. He made some appointments
based on merit while others were hereditary.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1108 ---
1020 S OUKOUS
He also governed with the help of Muslim
ofﬁcials and advisors. Each of the ﬁve
provinces in his empire was headed by a gov-
ernor. The governor was a royal appointee,
not a local ruler, so he was very much depen-
dent upon the emperor for his position.
Governors raised their own armies, which
were used to ensure the payment of tribute.
Askia Muhammad modernized the military
by organizing a permanent army, navy,
and cavalry. Still, the emperor recognized
traditional beliefs and customs. He never
forced the common people to accept Islam.
Many traditional customs were retained at
court, traditional leaders were acknowledged
at the village level, and Askia Muhammad
never conducted a jihad against unbelievers
in his realm.
He was not as effective, though, in the
matter of royal succession. The empire
began to disintegrate shortly after the rule of
Askia Muhammad was brought down in a
rebellion led by one of his own sons in 1528.
Years of civil war followed that undermined
the empire. Then the Moroccans emerged as
a very real threat. They intended to take over
the lucrative trans-Saharan trade. In 1590
they succeeded in crossing the Saharan
desert with a small army reinforced with Eu-
ropean muskets that were superior to bows,
spears, and swords. The Moroccans easily
defeated the Songhay in battle, and the inva-
sion was soon followed by political collapse.
The Songhay Empire split apart and its peo-
ple retreated to their original homeland
along the middle Niger River.
Earnestine Jenkins

SOUKOUS
Probably the most inﬂuential African mu-
sical style, and deﬁnitely the most popular
African dance music of the twentieth cen-
tury, soukous (often known in Africa as
“Congo music,” “Congolese rumba,” or
“Lingala music”) is the electriﬁed “rumba”
of Central Africa that developed largely in
the capital cities of Brazzaville, Republic
of Congo, and, especially, Kinshasa,
Democratic Republic of the Congo
(formerly Zaire).
Much as the African rhythms and call-
and-response traditions that left Africa with
the slave trade returned to Africa in the
form of rap music at the end of the twenti-
eth century (creating a profusion of African
rap styles); those same exported traditions
previously returned to Africa in the 1930s
in the form of the Afro-Spanish/Cuban
rumba music known as “son.” This music
Central Africa transformed into soukous.
In Brazzaville and Kinshasa—in
Africa’s equivalent of the musical syn-
cretism of New Orleans that produced
jazz—the rural Afro-Cuban dance music
son was combined with the indigenous
musical style known as maringa and jazz
inﬂuences from Europe and America to
create soukous. The most inﬂuential early
soukous groups included African Jazz, in
the early and mid-1950s, followed by the
group O.K. Jazz, with guitar great Franco
(François Luambo), and Rock’a Mambo.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1109 ---
SOULOUQUE,FAUSTIN 1021
Soukous bands are typically large and
include singers, one to four guitars, and
various percussive and brass instruments.
From the ﬁfties to the present, there has
been a general shift from a more acoustic
and melody-focused soukous to a faster-
paced, electric soukous with a “galloping”
rumba beat and extended electric guitar
passages that are distinctive in their bright
and ﬂowing sounds at the upper ends of the
guitar’s register. Each of these extended pas-
sages of instrumental jamming (guitars
often with saxophones and/or trumpets) is
called a sebene (pronounced “say-ben”) and
is a distinctive “dance” feature of soukous
that, in concert, can last upwards of half an
hour. Another distinctive feature of souk-
ous is that the lyrics are typically sung in
the melodious language of Lingala.
Kevin M. Hickey

SOULOUQUE,FAUSTIN
(1782?–1867)
Faustin Soulouque (aka Faustin I) ruled as
Haiti’s president-for-life, then as emperor,
from 1847 to 1859. Soulouque was born in
Petit-Goâve around 1782 (the exact date is
uncertain). His parents, both of whom had
belonged to the Mandingo tribe in Africa,
had been brought to Haiti as slaves when
Haiti (then known as Saint-Domingue) was
France’s colony. A professional soldier,
Soulouque served under André Rigaud,
Alexandre Pétion, Jean-Pierre Boyer, and
Jean-Baptiste Riché, charged with such sen-
sitive tasks as commanding the Presidential
Guard.
When President Riché died in February
1847, the Senate gathered to pick a succes-
sor. Deadlocked over two competing candi-
dates, senators chose Soulouque as a con-
sensual alternative for the presidency on
March 1, 1847. The light-skinned, elite
mulâtres (mulattos) traditionally picked
noirs (blacks) of pure African descent as
nominal leaders of the country, only to ma-
nipulate them when they reached ofﬁce.
Soulouque was round, jovial, illiterate,
seemingly uninterested in politics, and
many wrongly concluded that Soulouque
would be a harmless puppet.
Soulouque soon proved otherwise. Re-
lying on black generals he had befriended
during his years in the army, and on a para-
military force known as zinglins,Soulouque
spent 1848 rounding up prominent mu-
latto politicians in Port-au-Prince and the
south. Those who did not ﬂee in time were
harassed, arrested, and killed. A secret
police and further executions in later years
enforced a regime of terror that even
Soulouque’s dictatorial predecessors seldom
equaled. Other Haitian dictators had often
secretly believed in Voodoo while defend-
ing the Catholic faith in public; Soulouque
and his wife, Adelina, openly practiced
both religions, which helped cow potential
enemies into submission.
On August 26, 1849, Soulouque was
crowned emperor of Haiti under the name
Faustin I. The crown of gilded cardboard
Soulouque used for the occasion, along with
the colorful nobility he proceeded to ap-
point (there was a Comte de l’Ile-à-Vache,
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1110 ---
1022 S OULOUQUE,FAUSTIN
or Count of Cow Island, among others),
quickly made him the object of ridicule
among European diplomatic circles. Victor
Hugo, who despised French emperor
Napoleon III, compared Soulouque to a
black Napoleon III. A more elaborate coro-
nation ceremony, with crowns and gowns
brought from France at great expense, took
place on April 18, 1852.
Soulouque made repeated attempts
to conquer the neighboring Dominican
Republic. This goal had been pursued by
several of his predecessors (T oussaint
Louverture, notably), but it also had the
nationalist aim of warding off French,
British, and U.S. inﬂuence in Hispaniola
(foreign powers blockaded Haitian ports
in August 1851). A first expedition
(launched in March 1849) unexpectedly
faltered in April when Gen. Pedro Santana
routed Haitian troops near Ciudad Santo
Domingo. T wo other short-lived expedi-
tions followed in June 1850 and Novem-
ber 1855. Soulouque’s military proved
unsuccessful, but he nevertheless managed
to expand Haiti’s eastern border near
Hinche.
Foreign expeditions, the extensive po-
lice apparatus, royal pomp, and widespread
embezzlement were hard to ﬁnance. Many
Haitians (including Soulouque himself)
bypassed the customs house, greatly dimin-
ishing a traditionally important source of
government revenue. Extortion made up
some of the difference; the printing press
and default on foreign loans provided the
rest. Inﬂation ensued. The Spanish silver
piastre, which only bought one Haitian
gourde in the 1820s, bought ﬁve gourdes
by the time Soulouque took over in 1847;
when he left ofﬁce, the piastre was worth
20 gourdes. In 1856–1857, when a world-
wide deﬂation lowered the price of Haitian
cotton and coffee, a full-blown economic
crisis struck Haiti.
In January 1859, Fabre Nicolas Geffrard,
a Haitian general whom Soulouque had
turned against, raised an army that fought
its way from Gonaïves to Port-au-Prince,
the capital. Soulouque managed to escape
on a British ship that took him to
Kingston, Jamaica, and exile. Following the
fall of Geffrard in 1867, Soulouque re-
turned to Haiti as an apolitical retiree. He
died in Petit-Goâve on August 6, 1867.
U.S. and European contemporaries
scorned Soulouque for being a ridiculous,
bloodthirsty self-proclaimed king. T oday,
historians frequently criticize Soulouque
for passing few reforms of substance while
in office, and of seeking power for power’s
sake. The criticism is well deserved, but
Soulouque’s presidency and reign are rep-
resentative of a wider conflict in Haitian
society that pits black leaders (populists,
speakers of Creole, adepts of Voodoo, and
nationalists) against mulattos (elitist,
French-speaking, Catholic, and interna-
tionally oriented people). Soulouque,
who fought Dominicans, defaulted on
foreign debts, worshiped Voodoo, learned
French at a late age, and promoted fellow
blacks to the highest ranks of govern-
ment, clearly belonged to the former
school.
Philippe R. Girard

SOUTH AFRICA,H ISTORY AND POLITICS 1023
SOUTH AFRICA,H ISTORY
AND POLITICS
The history of the South African region
from the precolonial era to its present-day
republic includes a diverse portrait of in-
digenous and colonizing peoples, and a
painful account of the colonial practice of
apartheid, the long road to its dismantling,
and the current issues faced by the republic.
In the pre-Christian era, southern Africa was
inhabited by nomadic San hunter-gatherers.
Around 500 BCE, Khoikhoi pastoralists
began to move south and, despite some
resistance, to assimilate the San—hence the
term “Khoisan.” Agriculture came to the re-
gion with the slow southward drift of
Bantu-speaking peoples into the region
from around 500 CE. These Bantu-speaking
peoples gradually assimilated, expelled, or
killed the Khoisan. In 1652, a refreshment
station was set up at the Cape by the Dutch
East India Company, which soon began to
appropriate Khoisan land, encourage Euro-
pean settlers, and import slaves from Africa
and Asia. Meanwhile, the African kingdoms
were consolidating their power with in-
creasing violence, notably the Zulus under
Shaka, the Ndebele under Mzilikazi, and
the Sotho under Moshoeshoe. After re-
peated tussles with the Dutch, the British
secured the Cape Colony in 1806; 5,000
Britons were soon settled in the colony
(1820). Between 1835 and 1840, several
thousand Dutch-descended colonists, an-
gered by Britain’s emancipation of their
slaves, trekked north, in what has become
known as the “Great T rek.” In 1838, the
Zulus, refusing to relinquish their land,
massacred 70 trekkers, only to be defeated
at the Ncome River. Anxious to retain
power over Port Natal (Durban), the British
annexed the region (Natal) in 1842. After
lengthy wars, the British defeated the
Xhosas (1878) and Zulus (1879), forcibly
removing them from their land. By 1898,
when T ransvaal commandos conquered the
Venda, the region’s entire indigenous popu-
lation had been dispossessed and colonized.
Industrialization and urbanization in
southern Africa arrived with the discovery
of diamonds in the Northern Cape (1867)
and gold in the T ransvaal (1886). Africans
ﬂocked to work in the mines; color bars
were introduced to secure skilled work and
high wages for whites; pass laws restricting
the movement and employment of Africans
were tightened. Having recognized the
South African Republic (the T ransvaal)
(1852) and the Orange Free State (1854) as
independent Afrikaner states, and now anx-
ious to control the mines, Britain annexed
the diamond ﬁelds (1871) and reannexed
the T ransvaal (1877). In 1881, the T rans-
valers defeated the British and regained
qualiﬁed independence. Meanwhile, some
Dutch descendants began to standardize
“Afrikaans”—a Dutch Creole—and to call
themselves “Afrikaners.” T ension between
the Afrikaners and the British led to the
South African War (1899), during which
26,000 Afrikaner women and children died
from starvation and disease in British con-
centration camps. A peace treaty promising
the republics self-government was eventu-
ally signed in 1902. Following much nego-
tiation, the Union of South Africa was
founded in 1910 as a unitary state compris-
ing four provinces (the T ransvaal and
Orange Free State republics, and the Natal
and Cape colonies), with Dutch and English
as its ofﬁcial languages, and no extension of
the franchise to nonwhites.
Whites were by no means uniﬁed by
the Union: a group of radical Afrikaners
soon split to form the National Party (NP)
in 1914, and following World Wars I
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

1024 S OUTH AFRICA,H ISTORY AND POLITICS
and II—both of which South Africa entered
on the British side—Afrikaner Nationalists
again split to the right. When white
mineworkers revolted against the use of
cheap black labor (and 150 died), a
Nationalist-Labour coalition, led by J. B.
M. Hertzog, came to power promising to
ensure white workers’ rights. Meanwhile,
nonwhites were beginning to demand re-
form through various ﬂedgling organiza-
tions: the South African Indian Congress
(SAIC) (1923); the South African Native
National Congress (1912), later the African
National Congress (ANC) (1925); the
Communist Party of South Africa (1921);
and, in the late 1920s, the hugely success-
ful Industrial and Commercial Workers’
Union (ICU). The 1913 Natives Land Act,
limiting African landownership, left 7 per-
cent of South Africa’s land in the hands of
the black majority in the form of overpop-
ulated “reserves” (which served as reservoirs
of cheap black labor). Meanwhile, the
government attempted to curb the inﬂux
of Africans to the cities by setting educa-
tional standards for employment (1922),
tightening pass laws, and clearing slums
(1923). Crucially, in 1949, militant ANC
members—most famously Nelson Mandela,
Walter Sisulu, and Oliver Tambo—were
coming to the fore of the movement. A
major gold-miners’ strike in 1946 of be-
tween 60,000 and 100,000 Africans faced
brutal state suppression. In 1948, riding on
fears of black competition, the National
Party, led by D. F . Malan, came to power
under the slogan of “apartheid” (apartness).
Over the next forty-six years, the Na-
tional Party promoted Afrikaner interests
and white supremacy, while systematically
eroding all black participation in the politi-
cal system. However, while they feared the
black majority, their reliance upon cheap
black labor made total segregation undesir-
able. Instead, detailed discriminatory legis-
lation was passed, criminalizing interracial
relationships (1949, 1950); racially classify-
ing people as white, Asian, colored, and
Bantu (black African); allowing the govern-
ment to ban opponents without the right to
appeal; racially zoning living and working
areas; separating amenities; and extending
the pass laws (1952). Over 3.5 million peo-
ple were forcibly removed from “black
spots”—which generally became white
areas—to the reserves. The government
soon grouped the reserves into eight (later
ten) fragmented “tribal homelands,” creat-
ing the illusion of a white majority and
causing ethnic tensions among Africans,
and took over African education, imple-
menting curricula that limited African hori-
zons. In 1952, the ANC and SAIC
launched a national campaign of deﬁance
against the pass laws, and, in 1955, an al-
liance of anti-apartheid groups (including
the ANC and SAIC) adopted a “Freedom
Charter.” One hundred ﬁfty-six members
of the alliance were charged with (and, after
a ﬁve-year trial, acquitted of) high treason.
In 1959, the Pan Africanist Congress
(PAC) split from the ANC. When in early
1960 the PAC called on Africans to defy
pass laws, police shot dead 67 Africans in
Sharpeville. Countrywide protest erupted;
police arrested and jailed thousands; a state
of emergency was declared; and all African
political organizations were banned. The
ANC and PAC, debarred from political ac-
tivity and pushed underground, initiated
an armed struggle through new military
wings. In 1963, 17 leaders of the ANC’s
military wing—including Mandela—were
arrested by the police and sentenced to life
imprisonment. Prominent liberal politi-
cians and religious leaders continued the

public campaign against apartheid. On
June 16, 1976, 15,000 Soweto schoolchild-
ren peacefully protested against being
taught in Afrikaans: two black youths were
shot dead by police; unrest spread across the
country; over 575 people (mainly young
and black) died; and the security police bru-
tally murdered Steve Biko (ﬁgurehead of the
Black Consciousness Movement). South
Africa—which had declared itself a republic
and left the British Commonwealth in
1961—became increasingly isolated. Be-
tween 1976 and 1981, the government
foisted “independence” on the “homelands”
which the world refused to recognize. By
1978, the declining white and steadily
growing black populations, increased vio-
lence, sharp recession, foreign disinvest-
ment and criticism, and the collapse of
Afrikaner solidarity rendered the apartheid
system increasingly untenable. Under Presi-
dent P . W . Botha (1978–1989), palliative
reforms were made, while countless govern-
ment opponents suffered torture and deten-
tion without trial, scores dying in police
custody. In 1984, the government created a
new tricameral parliament consisting of
three uniracial chambers—white, Asian,
and colored (mixed race)—but carefully en-
sured its domination by whites. An interra-
cial alliance of 525 organizations, the
United Democratic Front (UDF) set about
(with the help of the increasingly militant
African trade unions) organizing boycotts,
sabotage, strikes, and disrupting the colored
(mixed race) and Asian elections. Violence
spiraled throughout the 1980s, including
a full-scale civil war between supporters of
the UDF/ANC and Inkatha (a Zulu na-
tionalist movement led by Chief Mango-
suthu Buthelezi and quietly armed by the
government). Between 1981 and 1989,
South African forces invaded Angola and
conducted hit-and-run raids on Lesotho,
Mozambique, Zimbabwe, and Zambia:
over one million died as a result. In 1986,
the government repealed the pass laws but
state repression soon redoubled in a nation-
wide state of emergency. In 1987, a pro-
tracted miners’ strike of over 250,000
prompted the government to ban the UDF
and 16 other organizations.
In early 1990, President F . W . De Klerk
unbanned the ANC, and all other pro-
scribed organizations, and released thou-
sands of political prisoners. On February
11, Mandela’s release from prison signaled
the beginning of the transition to democ-
racy. The government repealed apartheid
legislation, and the ANC suspended the
armed struggle. Formal talks among 19
political organizations collapsed following
the Boipatong massacre, in which the ANC
suspected police involvement. Negotiations
soon resumed and an interim constitution
was agreed upon in 1993. Following the
1994 elections, a Government of National
Unity (GNU) with full legislative pow-
ers—in which minority parties would be
included—was to devise a permanent con-
stitution, which would include universal
adult suffrage, a bill of rights, and an
independent judiciary. Negotiations faced
short-lived resistance from Inkatha, 
right-wing Afrikaner nationalists, and the
nominally independent homeland of
Bophuthatswana, which demanded a feder-
ation of sovereign states rather than the cen-
tralized state favored by the ANC. Civil
war continued in Natal; the far right
bombed ANC ofﬁces; scores were shot dur-
ing an Inkatha demonstration; ANC youth
leader Chris Hani was assassinated; and the
PAC gunned down 11 churchgoers. Under
pressure, Buthelezi ﬁnally agreed to enter
the elections. In April 1994, the country’s

ﬁrst and strikingly peaceful democratic elec-
tion gave the ANC a solid majority, and in
May, Mandela was jubilantly sworn in as
president of South Africa (alongside his
two vice presidents, Thabo Mbeki and De
Klerk). Framed under Mandela’s excep-
tional leadership, the South African consti-
tution remains one of the most liberal in the
world. However, despite a hugely successful
program of electriﬁcation, and controversial
land and afﬁrmative action legislation, re-
construction and development was frustrat-
ingly slow; and South Africa’s crime rates re-
main among the highest in the world. The
ANC’s invasion of Lesotho in 1998, its
arms deals, and high government salaries
also faced criticism. The T ruth and Recon-
ciliation Commission, cochaired from 1996
by Archbishop Desmond T utu and offering
amnesty from prosecution in exchange for
full disclosure, was more positively received:
thousands of victims and perpetrators came
forward but many apartheid functionaries
remained silent; and the ANC’s detention
camps were left unexamined. Following the
1999 general election (which the ANC
again won), Mandela stepped down and
Thabo Mbeki—prophet of an “African Re-
naissance”—became president. Mbeki (re-
elected in 2004) has increasingly attracted
criticism for his stance on HIV/AIDS and
for his failure to condemn Zimbabwean
president Robert Mugabe. While South
Africa boasts a growing economy, the
HIV/AIDS pandemic, exacerbated by the
poverty of millions of South Africans,
threatens to overshadow the country’s other
achievements.
Laura Charlotte Pechey

SOYINKA,WOLE (1934–)
Wole Soyinka is a Nigerian playwright,
activist, and educator. He is a recipient of
the Nobel Prize for Literature. Born in
Abeokuta, southwestern Nigeria, on July 13,
1934, Soyinka was educated at a govern-
ment high school and University College,
Wole Soyinka of Nigeria is known as a poet, novelist,
playwright, critic, and ﬁlmmaker of international
stature. In 1986, he became the ﬁrst black African to
receive the Nobel Prize for Literature. (AFP/Getty
Images)
