Ibadan, and at the University of Leeds,
United Kingdom. With about 40 pub-
lished books of plays, poetry, ﬁction, auto-
biography, criticism, and politics, Soyinka
is easily Nigeria’s most adventurous and
proliﬁc writer. Soyinka has held numerous
professorial positions in universities across
Africa, Europe, and America. An early story

emissary for his aunt, Funmilayo Ransome-

Soyinka cofounded the Pyrate Confraternity
to counter the perversion of Nigerian
youth education by the importation of
colonial foppery. Such unrelenting opposi-
tion to the excesses of institutionalized
power marks all of Soyinka’s lifelong ac-
tivism and writing. His representation of
Nigeria as a hopeless half-child in his 1960
independence drama, A Dance of the

country’s civil war. Soyinka occupies a

has been charged with treasonable felony
twice, by the military dictatorships of
Yakubu Gowon and Sani Abacha. The con-
ferment of the 1986 Nobel Prize for Liter-
ature on Soyinka was both an afﬁrmation
of his commitment to social justice and an
enduring recognition of the evocative deﬁ-

complexity.

SPANISH EMPIRE
For many decades before Christopher
Columbus arrived in the Americas in 1492,
Spain was commercially active in the
Mediterranean Sea and along the Atlantic
coast of Africa. The 1469 marriage of Ferdi-
nand and Isabella, which united Aragon
and Castile, helped pave the way for
Columbus. Because the South Atlantic had
been ceded to Portugal in the T reaty of
Alcáçovas (1479), the two monarchs realized
that it would be advantageous for Spain to
seek new areas of commercial and territorial
expansion. Upon the success of Columbus’s
ﬁrst voyage, Spain immediately ﬁnanced a
second. A combination of arms and disease,
against which native populations had no de-
fense facilitated this second conquest, which
in turn gave Spain a dominantly strong eco-
nomic position in Europe.
At the height of its imperial empire,
from about 1402 to 1824, Spain extended
its territories around the globe. In the
Americas, this expansion ranged from
Alaska through the northwestern United
States and California/Mexico; from the
northernmost border of the T erritory of
Louisiana to Central America; south to
Chile and Patagonia; and from present-day
Georgia south to the Caribbean islands,
Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bo-
livia, Uruguay, Paraguay, and Argentina. At
times, Spain occupied various African terri-
tories in the Western Sahara (Morocco) and
along the coast of what is now Equatorial
Guinea, including the offshore island of
Fernando Póo (Bioko). In Asia, Spain ruled

the Philippine Islands; Oceania (Guam,
Micronesia, Palau, and the Northern
Marianas); and the Caroline Islands.
In 1402, the Frenchman Jean de
Béthencourt claimed the Canary Islands for
Henry III of Castile; in 1492, Columbus
stopped at the islands on his voyage to the
New World. Spain did not ofﬁcially possess
the islands until 1479, and even then
before all three (Grand Canary, La Palma,
and T enerife) were conquered. Portugal
acquired the Azores, Madeira, Cape Verde,
and the São T omé islands, and focused on
spice trade with the East under Vasco da
Gama. Until the T reaty of T ordesillas
(1494), Spain and Portugal competed over
the South Atlantic. The treaty protected
Portugal’s exclusive route to India, and
Spain dominated the Americas.
After the conquest of the Canary Islands,
the Spanish imposed a new economic model:
expanding in the non-European world and
taking advantage of forced colonial
labor/servitude. Practicing single-crop cul-
tivation, they established plantations of
sugar cane, harvested by black slaves im-
ported from continental Africa. Mining
was also lucrative: silver could be easily
mined in Potosí (Peru) and in Zacatecas
(Mexico), thanks to the abundant supply of
native labor. Other proﬁtable exports from
the Americas included cacao, tobacco,
sugar, and animal skins. In 1503, the Board
of T rade (Casa de la Contratación) was es-
tablished to retain the trade monopoly with
the American colonies and to govern com-
merce. According to the Spanish royal edict
of repartimiento, settlers were allotted na-
tive Americans as possessions in the forced-
labor system known as encomienda.
After the successful settlement of His-
panola in the early 1500s, Spanish conquis-
tadors sought new territories. In 1508, Juan
Ponce de León conquered Puerto Rico; by
1515, Diego Velázquez conquered Cuba.
The ﬁrst settlement on the mainland was
Darién in Panama, founded by Vasco
Núñez de Balboa in 1512; later, in 1513,
Balboa sighted the Paciﬁc (South Sea).
By the early 1500s, Hispaniola, Puerto
Rico, and Cuba were Spanish possessions—
the most well-known Spanish colonies in
the New World—and also points from
which to set out in new directions. In 1507,
the New World was named America after
Amerigo Vespucci, an explorer whose letters
provided information useful to European
commerce.
The exploration and conquest of
Central America largely took place from
1522 to 1527. The fall of two major
cities—T enochtitlán in 1521 and
Atahualpa in 1533—facilitated the Spanish
conquest and settlement of Mexico. Juan
Ponce de León returned to Florida in 1521
with a second expedition, but failed to
establish a settlement. Perhaps the most
successful conquistador leader was Hernán
Cortés, who described his conquests in his
published Letters. In the campaigns of
1519–1521, with a small Spanish force
(and with the crucial support of around
200,000 Amerindian allies), Cortés de-
feated the formidable Aztec empire. Thus,
Mexico was brought into the empire as
New Spain. Similarly, Francisco Pizarro
conquered the Inca empire, which would
become the Viceroyalty of Peru from 1531
to 1533. This area was particularly rich in
gold and silver. 
During the reign of Charles I, Spain,
with its vast holdings in the New World,
became the most powerful state in Western
Europe. Renamed Charles V in 1519 upon
becoming Holy Roman Emperor, Charles
commissioned the voyage of Ferdinand

Magellan, a Portuguese explorer who found
a westward route to Asia. En route from
Asia to Spain, he was killed in a local war in
the Philippines; after Magellan established
claims in the East, the expedition reached
Spain without him in 1522. By the early
1530s, the Spanish explorers had gone
from Florida to Nova Scotia in North
America.
From 1537 to 1597, Spain had to
focus upon the defense of the Caribbean
from French, English, and Dutch attacks,
leading the Spanish to develop the transat-
lantic ﬂota system: two substantial ﬂeets
escorted by warships, one that left for
Veracruz, Mexico, and the other for
Panama. The Board of T rade in Seville gov-
erned commerce in the colonies. In 1543,
the Crown created a merchants’ guild (con-
sulado) to ensure a monopoly over trade
and establish a permanent Spanish military
presence. Fortiﬁcations were built to pro-
tect Havana, Santo Domingo, San Juan de
Puerto Rico, and Portobelo.
In 1559, the T reaty of Chateau-
Cambrensis brought recognition of Spanish
dominion over some of the regions of Italy
(Sicily, Sardinia, Milan, and Naples),
Flanders, and the Low Countries. Henry II
of France, an aggressive enemy of Spain,
died during the celebrations following
the treaty, thus removing France from com-
peting for power with Spain and the
Hapsburgs. Chronic civil war and religious
unrest further weakened France’s power.
Using New Spain as a point of depar-
ture, the Spanish then colonized the
Philippines, departing from Navidad,
Jalisco, in November of 1564. Miguel
López de Legazapi (also spelled Legaspi),
accompanied by his pilot, a missionary
named Andres de Urdaneta, arrived in
February 1565. The expedition returned to
New Spain by October 8, setting a record
for unprecedented speed and for crossing
the Paciﬁc from west to east. The Spanish
also settled Sant Agustín (Saint Augustine)
in 1565, protecting the northern ﬂank of
the empire from the French.
Meanwhile, the Council of T rent con-
vened (1545–1564) to create and approve
an agenda for reform of the Catholic
Church to counter the effects of the
Protestant Reformation. In a famous
debate in 1550, the ontology of native
Americans was called into question by Juan
Ginés de Sepúlveda (his position was that
they were like animals, without souls). The
priest Bartolomé de las Casas defended
their humanity and their human rights; his
ultimate aim, however, was to bring them
into the faith (but not by force). As a result,
enslavement was banned by law—but still
carried out in practice.
Another result of the Council T rent
was the Calvinist-led 1566 rebellion of the
Netherlands, the richest provinces in
Europe, that wanted autonomy from the
decrees of the Council of T rent. English
support of Dutch rebels led the Spanish to
plan a later, albeit unsuccessful, invasion of
England. In 1569, ofﬁces of the Inquisition
were authorized in Lima and Mexico City
by Philip II. Shortly thereafter, he rewrote
the royal decrees, replacing “conquest” with
“paciﬁcation.”
Spain defeated the Ottoman forces on
the island of Malta, strategically located
south of Sicily. When Sultan Suleiman the
Magniﬁcent died, leaving the sultanate to
his son Selim the Sot, Philip II of Spain
was emboldened to go to war with the
Ottoman Empire. In 1571, Spain defeated
the T urks at Lepanto in the famous battle
by that name, thus wresting control of the
Mediterranean from the Ottoman Empire.

1030 S PANISH EMPIRE
Another important event in 1571 was
the dispatching of the ﬁrst Manila galleons
to New Spain by López de Legazapi. Span-
ish ships then regularly crossed the Paciﬁc
between Acapulco and Manila, carrying
Mexican silver in exchange for Chinese
silks, ceramics, and other Asian products.
This proﬁtable trade route created a Span-
ish stronghold in Asia. In 1583, an audien-
cia (division of viceroyalties) made Manila
politically subordinate to New Spain.
The Spanish were less successful in
Northern Europe, with Dutch rebellions
in 1566 and 1572. The legendary 1588
defeat of the Spanish Armada in the
English Channel was also costly for Spain,
with losses of more than 30 ships and
15,000 men. This defeat in turn raised
shipping rates, bankrupting Spain. In 1596,
a retaliatory Anglo-Dutch fleet sacked
Cadiz, Spain, destroying 34 America-
bound ships and 4 million ducats worth of
freight.
Hostilities with the Dutch continued
until the truce of 1609, also known as the
T welve Years’ T ruce, or Pax Hispanica.
Peace with France was established with the
1598 T reaty of Vervins; a treaty with James
I of England in 1604 allowed Spain to
focus its attention—temporarily—on the
troublesome Dutch provinces. War broke
out between Spain and the Netherlands
again in 1621.
In the seventeenth century, Spain’s Eu-
ropean rivals of England, Holland, and
France began to encroach upon the vast
reach of Spain’s territories, planting
colonies in the Lesser Antilles, the Guianas,
and Central America. Economically, the
colonies profited from or survived on
piracy, sugar production based on slave
labor, and contraband trade with Spain.
The Portuguese claimed a much larger
part of Brazil than agreed upon the 1594
T reaty of T ordesillas. Spain gained the port
of Ceuta in 1668, but lost Gibraltar to
Britain in 1704 in the War of Spanish Suc-
cession. In the War of Polish Succession,
Spain took Naples and Sicily back from
Austria, and took Cuba during the War of
Jenkins’ Ear (1739–1742). Spain lost
territories to Britain but recovered them
during the American Revolutionary War
(1775–1783). In 1769, Spain began
mission planning in California. In 1777,
Portugal received what is now Uruguay
(then Colonia do Sacramento) in exchange
for the land currently called Equatorial
Guinea.
The Spanish Empire had declined, in
part due to the difﬁculty of maintaining its
colonies. Rivalry for wealth and power
caused tensions between the elites in Eu-
rope and in the colonies. The destruction
suffered by the Spanish ﬂeet at the hands of
the French at the Battle of T rafalgar (1805),
and the Peninsular War (1808) also con-
tributed to Spain’s declining power.
Similarly, in the eighteenth century, the
Industrial Revolution largely bypassed
Spain, causing its economy to decline. With
ﬁnancial troubles, a weak government, and
a declining navy, Spain could no longer
prevent a rapid expansion of contraband
trade with the colonies.
T wo conspiracies at the end of the
eighteenth century were harbingers of trou-
bles ahead. The Conspiracy of Minas
Gerais (1788–1789) and the Conspiracy of
the Tailors in Salvador da Bahía (1798)
were abortive attempts at revolt against the
Europeans, in this case, the Portuguese.
The conspirators were executed, but the
uprisings set other events in motion.
Inﬂuenced by Enlightenment ideals
and inspired by the French Revolution,

these attempts at rebellion foreshadowed

Each colony’s struggle for indepen-
dence was unique, but most of the
American colonies became independent in
the early 1800s. In 1806 and 1807, British
forces occupied Buenos Aires. The colonial
rebels, newly conﬁdent, rose up against the
Spanish authorities and other European
occupying powers in a number of strategic
locations: La Paz, Mexico City, Chihuaha,
Quito (now in Ecuador), Caracas (now in
Venezuela), Santa Fe de Bogotá (now in
Colombia), Granada, Santiago (Chile), Las
Piedras, Asunción (now in Argentina; then
in Paraguay), and Cuzco (Peru). Present-
day Argentina became an independent state
in 1816; Chile in 1818; New Granada,
under the legendary Simón Bolívar, in
1819; Mexico in 1821; Ecuador in 1822;
and the area that is now Venezuela,
Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia
(named after Bolívar) in 1825, then called
the Republic of Gran Colombia. Santo
Domingo declared independence in 1821
and, for a brief period of time, sought to be
included in Bolivar’s Republic of Gran
Colombia. Santo Domingo was occupied
and ruled by Haiti until a revolution in 1844.
The United States was the ﬁrst nation
to recognize Gran Colombia and Mexico,
in 1822. President James Monroe asserted
the famous Monroe Doctrine, stating that
European interference in the Americas
would endanger its “peace and safety.” In
1823, the United Provinces of present-day
Central America (Guatemala, El Salvador,
Honduras, Nicaragua, and Costa Rica)
declared independence from Mexico.
After the former British colonies in
America became the United States, Spain
ceded the Ohio Valley; in 1800, it returned
the Louisiana T erritory to France. In the
Louisiana Purchase of 1803, the United
States bought Louisiana from Napoleon,
and in 1819, acquired Florida by treaty.
After the wars of independence from 1810
to 1826, Spain no longer had a vast empire
in the Americas, only Cuba and Puerto
Rico; in North Africa, Melilla and Ceuta;
and in the east, the Philippines, Guam, and
the Micronesian islands.
Napoleon tried to take over Spain, but
had to face guerilla warfare and the upris-
ing of the Spanish people. This attempt was
followed by the Peninsular War, various
civil wars, a republic, and an unsuccessful
democracy.
From 1868 to 1898, Cubans fought for
independence and won with the help of
North America. In the Spanish-American
War of 1898, Spain had to contend with the
United States and Cuba. The United States
purchased Puerto Rico, Cuba, and Guam.
(Since 1959, however, Cuba has been under
the leadership of Fidel Alejandro Castro,
who overthrew the regime of Batista, be-
came prime minister of Cuba in February
1959, transformed Cuba into the ﬁrst
Communist state in the Western Hemi-
sphere, and has held effective power in the
country ever since. As of 2007, he is the
world’s longest-ruling head of government.)
In 1899, the Marianas and Marshall
Islands were sold to Germany, and at the
end of the nineteenth century, Spain had
only a few African holdings. Spain had

STOWE,H ARRIET BEECHER
(1811–1896)
Harriet Beecher Stowe was an abolitionist
author and activist whose antislavery novel,
Uncle T om’s Cabin,became America’s ﬁrst
bestseller in 1852. She was born on June
14, 1811, in Litchfield, Connecticut,
daughter to Congregational Church minis-
ter Lyman Beecher. Harriet received her
formal education at the Congregational
Church and at the Hartford Female Semi-
nary. Lyman Beecher moved his family to
Cincinnati, Ohio, in 1832 to serve as pres-
ident of the Lane Theological Seminary. In
1836, Harriet married Calvin Stowe, an in-
structor at Lane, and bore seven children
with him. Notable members of the Stowe
household included clergymen Henry
Ward and Edward Beecher, and reformer
Catherine Beecher.
Harriet Beecher Stowe’s texts deal pri-
marily with the repercussions of Puritanism
in New England during the eighteenth and

ister’s Wooing(1859); The Pearl of Orr’s Is-

STUDENT NONVIOLENT
COORDINATING COMMITTEE
Founded on February 1, 1960, the Student
Nonviolent Coordinating Committee
(SNCC) was created to encourage young
activists to use sit-ins and nonviolent anti-
segregation protests during the Civil Rights
Movement. The group was formed at the
suggestion of Ella Baker, who was then
the director of the Atlanta headquarters of
the Southern Christian Leadership Confer-
ence (SCLC). Perceived as more radical than
the SCLC, the political ideals of SNCC in
the early days were nonviolence and paci-
ﬁsm. But the continual threats from the
whites, particularly during SNCC’s com-
munity programs, and the rise of militant
black power with the election of Stokely
Carmichael as SNCC chairman persuaded
SNCC volunteers to resort to violence. In
addition to citizenship education drives,
SNCC led Freedom Rides and Freedom
Summer, in 1961 and 1964 respectively.
Freedom Rides were organized to desegre-
gate bus terminals throughout the South.
Along the way, many Freedom Riders re-
ceived death threats and were brutally
beaten by mobs. Eventually the U.S. Justice
Department sent federal marshals to pro-
tect the riders. Freedom Summer was an
effort to draw national attention to Missis-
sippi’s racism and to register black voters in
rural counties of the South. SNCC also
helped to create the Mississippi Freedom
Harriet Beecher Stowe, U.S. author and antislavery
advocate. She is most famous for her novel, Uncle
T om’s Cabin. (Library of Congress)

Democratic Party (MFDP) that functioned
as an alternative to the white-dominated
state Democratic Party. Furthermore,

and provided a model for the future femi-

SUDAN (DARFUR REGION) 
The Darfur region is the westernmost re-
gion of Sudan, where ethnically diverse
peoples have historically coexisted peace-
fully, but became the scene of ethnic ten-
sions and genocide. The Darfur region
shares an international border with Central
African Republic to the southwest, Chad to
the west and northwest, Libya to the north,
and Egypt to the northeast. It also shares a
border with three other Sudanese regions:
Shimalya to the northeast, Kordofan to the
east, and Bahr al-Ghazal to the south.
The population of Darfur is about seven
million people, who belong to more than 60
ethnic groups and whose members are
largely categorized as Zurga (blacks or in-
digenous population) and Arabs. Although
both categories of Darfur’s population are
black or brown, they have since the late
1970s been categorizing themselves, and
been categorized by outsiders, as Arabs and
indigenous Africans. The Fur outnumber all
other ethnic groups in the region. They are
the founders of a kingdom that lasted for al-
most four centuries (1640–1917). This
kingdom was a cultural and economic
meeting point for West Africa, Arabian
Peninsula, North Africa, and Africa south of
the Sahara Desert. Therefore, in addition to
its indigenous groups, such as Fur and Dajo,
other groups from Central, West, and North
Africa, the Nile region, and Arabian
Peninsula migrated and settled in Darfur.
Being a meeting point for the abovemen-
tioned regions, Darfur was probably
involved in the transatlantic slave trade, but
there is more documentation of its involve-
ment in the trans-Saharan slave trade.
The sultans of the Fur kingdom fol-
lowed an accommodating policy by which
they were able to integrate the groups and
individuals who constituted the population
of their kingdom. Most of the people who
migrated as individuals or small families set-
tled in the capital city of the kingdom, and
many of them worked in the administration
of the kingdom; some of them reached high
positions as ministers or governors of the
provinces. Those who migrated to the king-
dom in bigger groups were offered areas
where they settled. T o further the integra-
tion of the immigrating population, the
sultans were largely exogamous (they often
married non-Fur women).
The sultans divided their kingdom into
six big administrative units known as dars
(singular dar), which were like provinces or
regions. These provinces were Dar Fashir
and its surroundings (including the capital
city and neighboring areas); Dar Daali (also
known as Dar Ab-Asheikh), which included
the plains to the east of Jabel Marra until
Kordofan; Dar Abu Umong, which in-
cluded the whole region from central Jabel
Marra to the south and southeast up to Dar
Firti, which presently includes northern
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1123 ---
SUDAN (DARFUR REGION) 1035
parts of Bahr al-Ghazal and northwestern
parts of Central African Republic; Dar Abu
Dimang, which included western and
southwestern parts of Jabel Marra to the
west and southwest until Garcila (its center
was Zalingai and its surroundings); Dar 
al-Takanawi lying to the north of Fashir
(the capital) up to current southern fringes
of Libya; and Dar al-Garib, which included
the area to the west of Dar Abu Dimang up
to Waddie (current Chad). Several groups
were given autonomous status within these
provinces and on several occasions they
were directly accountable to the sultan in
Fashir. For example, dars such as Dar
Rizeigat, Dar Bani Halba, and Dar Fallata,
where Arab ethnic groups live today, were
initially parts of the big dars (provinces),
like Dar Abu Umong, but were marked off
by sultans as homelands of the groups
whose names they carry. The governor of
each province/region was known as abuand
he was responsible for the welfare of his sub-
jects. The governors collected taxes and trib-
ute and sent them to the sultan. In times of
war, the sultan asked the governors to send
young men, including their sons, to defend
the kingdom. In November 1916, the last
sultan of Darfur, Ali Dinar, was killed by
British and Egyptian armies and his king-
dom annexed to Sudan.
The accommodating climate that the
sultans prepared for their subjects made the
latter interact peacefully, often to the extent
that they developed complementary eco-
nomic niches and intermarried. In many
cases herders were dependent on farmers to
satisfy their needs of agricultural products
such as millet, sorghum, vegetables, and
fruits. The pastoralists also herded their ani-
mals on the stalks of millet, sorghum, toma-
toes, and other crops after the farmers had
harvested the farms. In addition to meat,
hides, butter, and milk, the farmers needed
animal manure to renew the fertility of the
farmlands. Herders left with friend farmers
their weak animals as well as heavy luggage
which they did not want to carry during the
long seasonal transhumance. On the other
hand, farmers entrusted pastoralists with
their animals during the rain seasons because
they were busy working the land.
As a result of these complementary re-
lationships, some pastoral people became
farmers and farmers became pastoralists
and lived in camps as if they were originally
herders. People also picked up each other’s
languages and their ways of life until it be-
came almost impossible to distinguish in-
digenous Africans from Arabs in some parts
of the region.
Since the late 1970s, however, the in-

its indigenous population because they are
seen as a block to further expansion of
Arabism into Africa south of the Sahara.
Thus the government ripped the Darfur
society to the extent that the return of

SUNDIATA
Born around 1202, Sundiata Keita is the
most beloved and celebrated hero in Mali
and was the ﬁrst emperor of Mali.
According to the oral tradition, the son
of Nare Maghan Konate, king of Mande,
and Sogolon Konde, nicknamed “Ke-
diougou,” which means “unattractive,” led
an extraordinary life ﬁlled with challenges he
overcame. As a child, Sundiata was paralyzed
and for years could not walk. But when
Sasuma Berete, his father’s ﬁrst wife, mocked
his mother for having a crippled son, Sundi-
ata in response to the insult that made his
mother cry, rose up and walked. During his
teenage years, Sundiata joined the hunter’s
community. There, he was taught the code
of honor and the esoteric science of the
hunters. He was an excellent hunter and
soon became a simbo, or master hunter.
After his father passed away, Dankara
T uman, Sasuma Berete’s son, became king.
At his mother’s request, Dankara sent Sundi-
ata and his family into exile. They found asy-
lum in Mema. When Sumanguru Kante and
his army invaded and took over Mande,
Dankara and his family were forced into
exile. Tired of living under Sumanguru
tyranny, the people of Mande sent for Sundi-
ata. His father’s throne was waiting for him.
In 1235, Sundiata and Sumanguro met for
the ﬁfth and last time in Krina. Sundiata de-
feated Sumanguru who, according to the
griot, disappeared inside a cave in Koulikoro.
After winning the war against Suman-
guru Kante, all the leaders of the Mandingo
coalition met to pledge allegiance to Sundi-
ata and proclaimed him emperor of Mande.
According to the oral tradition, it was during
this ceremony that Sundiata changed the
name of his empire from Mande to Mali.
During his reign that lasted more than
20 years, Mali became a peaceful, prosper-
ous empire. Sundiata Keita died under
mysterious circumstances in 1255.

SUNDIATAKEITA AND SUNDIATAEPIC 1037
SUNDIATAKEITA (1202–1255)
AND SUNDIATAEPIC
The Sundiata Epic is the oral tradition that
tells the story of Mali’s emperor Sundiata’s
rise to power. It is one of the oldest surviv-
ing epics. Sundiata Keita, also called “Lion
King,” was the founder of the Mali Empire.
According to the griot, the traditional his-
torians, oracles predicted Sundiata’s birth
and extraordinary life long before his par-
ents met. Even today in Mali, Sundiata is
still the most beloved and celebrated hero
of the country.
Sundiata was the son of Nare Maghan
Konate, king of Mande (a group of states
in West Africa), and Sogolon Konde, nick-
named “Kediougou,” which means unat-
tractive. According to the oral tradition,
Nare Maghan already had a wife, the
beautiful Sasuma Berete. But when So-
golon arrived in Mande, he married her
to fulﬁll the prophecy he had been told.
The prophecy said that the unattractive
woman would give birth to a son who,
“like the seed of a baobab tree—the
biggest tree in the savanna,” would be-
come one of the greatest emperors of West
Africa. Both wives gave birth to sons.
Sasuma Berete had Dankara T uman, while
the other wife had Sogolon Diata, which
became Sundiata.
As a child, Sundiata was paralyzed and
for years could not walk. One day, Sasuma
Berete, his father’s ﬁrst wife, mocked his
mother for having a worthless, crippled
son. In response to the insult that made his
mother cry, Sundiata rose up and walked.
During his teenage years, Sundiata joined
the hunter’s community. There he was
taught the code of honor and the esoteric
science of the hunters. He was an excellent
hunter and soon became a simbo, which
means “master hunter.”
After their father passed away, Sundiata’s
older brother Dankara T uman became king
of Mande. Fearing that her son would one
day be dethroned by Sundiata, Sasuma
convinced Dankara to chase Sundiata out
of Mande. Sundiata left with his mother
Sogolon, his two brothers, and his sister.
The road of exile took them to different
kingdoms. But in every territory, Sundiata
and his family were asked to leave. Finally,
they found asylum with his mother’s family
in Mema, where Sundiata was trained and
became an exceptional warrior. Meanwhile,
Sumanguru Kante, the “invincible king,”
and his army were taking over Mande. In
a desperate attempt to keep his throne,
Dankara T uman forced his sister, Nana
T riban, to marry Sumanguru. The union
didn’t save him. Sumanguru Kante and his
army invaded and took over Mande. This
invasion forced Dankara T uman and his
family to ﬂee into exile. Tired of living
under the tyranny of Sumanguru, the peo-
ple of Mande sent for Sundiata. His day
had come. His father’s throne was waiting
for him.
From 1232 to 1235, the armies of Sun-
diata and Sumanguru Kante fought ﬁve
times. Sundiata lost the ﬁrst battles, but
then support came. First, Nana T riban left
Sumanguru after discovering the secret
antidote to his invulnerability: the spur of
a white cock attached to an arrow. Then,
after his uncle Sumanguru betrayed him by
taking away his wife, Fakoli Kuruma and
his army joined Sundiata.
A legendary battle for Mande took
place in 1235 in Krina. Sundiata launched
the fatal arrow. It barely touched
Sumanguru but its effects were devastat-
ing. He lost all his powers. According to
the griot, Sundiata chased Sumanguru
who ran and disappeared inside a cave in
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1126 ---
1038 S URINAME
Koulikoro. The site where Sumanguru
Kante disappeared still exists in Mali and
is believed to be haunted by his spirit.
After winning the war, the 12 leaders of
the Mandingo coalition pledged allegiance
to Sundiata and proclaimed him emperor
of Mande. According to the oral tradition,
it is during this ceremony that Sundiata
changed the name of his empire from
Mande to Mali.
Sundiata then organized his nation.
The 12 leaders were nominated kings of
their respective regions. Every year they
paid the emperor’s taxes with agricultural
products (rice, millet, sorghum, beans,
cotton, peanuts). Taxes were also imposed
on such goods as silk, dates, and sugar im-
ported from neighboring countries,
sometimes as far as Egypt. Kola nuts and
salt were exported from Mali. All gold
mines belonged to the emperor. Gold was
used to buy horses, armaments for the
army, and to pay soldiers’ salaries. Gold
was also donated to poor families and of-
fered as gifts to distinguished guests. Dur-
ing his reign, that lasted more than 20
years, Mali became a peaceful, prosperous
empire.
Sundiata Keita died mysteriously in
1255. He left behind an empire that in-
cluded Mali, Mauritania, Senegal, Gambia
Burkina Faso, Ivory Coast, and Guinea.
The people of Mali consider him the father
of their nation.

SURINAME
The Republic of Suriname, on the north-
eastern coast of South America, has a pop-
ulation of about 437,000. It is religiously
diverse; nearly half are Christians, 27 per-
cent are Hindu, and 19 percent are
Muslim. Named Surinam during colonial
rule, it was renamed Suriname after inde-
pendence. In 1630, the English established
a short-lived settlement at T oriaca, near the
present-day capital of Paramaribo. In 1651,
English traders established another colony
on the Surinam River which was named
Willoughby, after Francis Willoughby from
Barbados. This colony included African
slaves in order to establish plantations.
These slaves seem to have come from Bar-
bados and other Caribbean islands rather
than directly from Africa. The colony was
captured by the Dutch 16 years later. The
T reaty of Breda in 1670 gave the Dutch con-
trol over what became Surinam in return
for the B ritish keeping New Amsterdam
(modern-day New York).
The African slaves in Surinam became
the subject of a book by the English
woman writer Aphra Behn. Behn wrote of
her early experiences in Surinam in the
novel Oroonoko, of the History of a Royal
Slave (1688). Based on an enslaved African
prince she met in Surinam, it described the
prince being transported to Surinam as a
slave. This story proved durable and popu-
lar across the eighteenth century.
The Dutch tried to develop Surinam
and established sugar plantations in the
eighteenth century, also importing African
slave labor. However, many of these slaves
easily escaped into the tropical forests and
swamps that covered much of the country.
These escapees became known as Maroons
or “Bush Negroes,” with some known as
the Ndjuka. These Maroons waged an
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1127 ---
SWAZILAND 1039
intermittent guerilla war against the Dutch
for years. Attacks by Maroons led to peace
treaties being signed with them in 1761
and 1762, in order to reduce the loss in
conﬁdence in Surinam by businessmen
in Amsterdam. A slave revolt took place
in Berbice in 1763. Some plantations were
abandoned or had their output reduced. It
was not until 1790 that the colony’s econ-
omy recovered. Among the many opera-
tions against the Maroons was one in 1772
that was recorded by John Stedman, an
English soldier, in his famous Narrative of
a Five Years’ Expedition against the Revolted
Negroes of Surinam.
The British occupied Surinam during a
part of the Napoleonic Wars, from 1804 to
1816. They recruited some of the Africans
into ﬁve companies of the Black Chasseurs
of Surinam. After the war, the British
helped inﬂuence the Dutch in reducing the
slave trade. In 1816, the authorities in Suri-
nam established a court to deal with mat-
ters concerning slaves. Seven years later, the
Dutch outlawed the slave trade and agreed
to the seizing of their ships if equipped for
slavery, even without slaves on board. On
July 1, 1863, slavery was ﬁnally abolished
in Surinam. Plantation owners were given
300 guilders per slave in compensation.
However, emancipation did not mean im-
mediate freedom: laws ensured that the
33,000 slaves who were declared free had to
work for another ten years, albeit in a plan-
tation of their choice. In an attempt to in-
crease the number of plantations from the
1870s, many Chinese and then Indian, and
ﬁnally Javanese laborers were brought to
work in the country, reducing the inﬂuence
of the African ex-slave population.
Nonetheless, sugar declined in importance.
In the period 1863–1873, sugar made up
80 percent of the exports of Surinam. This
fell in the next decade to half of all exports.
By 1939 it was only 6 percent of exports.
During the early 1930s, with rising
unemployment owing to the Depression,
Anton de Kom, a Creole, emerged as a
major nationalist ﬁgure. He and others
urged independence, and although he was
deported, others started protesting. On
November 25, 1975, Surinam became in-
dependent as the Republic of Suriname.
The descendants of African ex-slaves and
Maroons and people of Creole heritage are
major parts of the population today.
Justin Corﬁeld

SWAZILAND
The landlocked kingdom of Swaziland
borders South Africa and Mozambique
and has a population of about 1,161,000.
It was ruled by the king of the Swazis, ﬁrst
King Ngwane in the late eighteenth
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1128 ---
1040 S WAZILAND
century, later his grandson Sobhuza I in
the nineteenth century, and then Sobhuza’s
great-grandson Sobhuza II in the early
twentieth century, the second of whom
managed, against various colonial powers,
especially the British, to maintain the
Swazi kingdom’s independence. However,
by 1895 the land had become a dependent
territory of the Boer Republic of T ransvaal.
After the Anglo-Boer War of 1899–1902,
the area was placed under the British
colony of T ransvaal. Finally, in 1906 it was
placed directly under the rule of the high
commissioner of South Africa; the follow-
ing year a resident commissioner was ap-
pointed to the protectorate of Swaziland.
The king of the Swazis still controlled
much of the country, with the people
ﬁercely loyal to him.
Many U.S. Christian missions were
established in Swaziland: the Evangelical
Alliance Mission (as the Scandinavian
Alliance Mission of North America) from
1892; African Methodist Episcopal Church
from 1904; the Church of the Nazarene and
the Wesleyan Methodist Church of America
Missionary Society from 1910. One of the
ﬁrst of the missionaries was Petra Mallena
Moe, who was born in Norway but moved
to the United States when she was 19 and
left for South Africa when she was 29. A
year later she moved to Swaziland and
worked at the Bethel Mission there until her
death in 1953. Others included Harmon F .
Schmelzenbach from northern Ohio, who
worked in Swaziland from 1910 until his
death in 1929; and Joel C. Rogers from
Battle Creek College, who opened a mission
station in Swaziland in 1919.
On September 6, 1966, Swaziland be-
came independent while remaining within
the British Commonwealth. The country
was immediately recognized by the United
States, Canada, the British Caribbean, and
most other countries in the Americas.
Charles Joseph Nelson was the ﬁrst U.S.
ambassador appointed to the country (in
1971), and was succeeded by David
Benjamin Bolen in 1974 and Donald
Richard Norland in 1976. The U.S. Peace
Corps has operated in Swaziland since
1969. With the increase in world attention
on South Africa during the late 1970s and
1980s, and various levels of sanctions
brought against the country for King
Sobhuza II’s suspension of the constitution
and banning of political activity in order to
prevent multi-party elections in 1973, the
United States and other countries con-
centrated some effort in ensuring that
Swaziland remained stable. Some Americans
in South Africa, keen not to have their
children educated in the segregated South
African school system, sent them to inter-
national schools in Swaziland.
The Swazi royal family took the sur-
name Dhlamini (or Dlamini) and six
members moved to the United States. G. P .
Dhlamini studied at Harvard University
and James M. Dlamini studied at Columbia
University. Phonius M. Dlamini gained a
doctorate from the University of Manitoba
in Canada with his thesis “Cost-Beneﬁt
Analysis on Simunye Sugar Project: The
Case of a Resettlement Scheme in
Swaziland.” Political life in the country
is still centered on the king and the royal
family.

TANNER,H ENRY OSSAWA
(1859–1937)
Henry Ossawa Tanner was an American
artist, an expatriate, and a painter of interna-
tional acclaim. He was born in Pittsburgh,
Pennsylvania, in 1859, and he lived most of
his young life in Philadelphia. His father,
Benjamin, was a bishop for the African
Methodist Episcopal Church. Tanner grew
up in an intellectual and spiritual household
that impacted the themes for his art. From
1879 to 1885, he intermittently attended
the Pennsylvania Academy of Fine Arts
under the instruction of Thomas Eakins.
Unfortunately, he faced racism at the acad-
emy and in his life because he was an African
American artist in a white-dominated art
world. The artist struggled for his art to be
judged on artistic merit rather than his racial
heritage. In 1891, Tanner traveled to Europe
to study in Rome; however, the artist chose to
study in Paris at the Académie Julian. In
Europe, Tanner experienced freedom from
racism, and he lived in France for the rest of
his life, returning to the United States
brieﬂy. During Tanner’s stay in France, the
country was reevaluating its colonist (and
racist) attitude toward Africa, yet the artist
appeared unaffected by this process.
Tanner’s art reﬂects his transatlantic ex-
periences and the inﬂuence of both Eakins
and the French painters, Jean Joseph
Benjamin-Constant and Jean Paul Laurens.
In 1893–1894, Tanner painted black genre
scenes including The Banjo Lesson and The
Thankful Poor,which was his attempt to re-
store dignity to his race that previous genre
pieces neglected. His works reﬂect the real-
ist style of Eakins and the popular genre of
France that depicted peasants, and these
paintings became a symbol of African
American potential and a vehicle for racial
uplift. After 1894, Tanner never painted
black ﬁguration again; he began the grand
religious paintings that compose the major-
ity of his work. These religious paintings
are biblical narratives that encapsulate
themes of struggle, hope, liberation, and re-
demption, and they contain the bold colors
of French academic painting and Eakins’s
reliance on light. In 1895, Daniel and the
Lion’s Den won an honorable mention at
the French Salon. In 1897, the French gov-
ernment purchased The Resurrection of
Lazarus for the Luxembourg Gallery, which
was a rare honor to be bestowed on an
American artist. In 1923, Tanner was hon-
ored with the Chevalier Legion of Honor,
the highest honor France awarded to for-
eigners. His religious works were his most
famous, and he continued to paint religious
scenes until his death in 1937. His art and
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1130 ---
1042 T ANZANIA
his religious beliefs provided him solace
from the racism that he confronted. Tanner
was a crucial, transatlantic ﬁgure because
he represented the artistic styles of both
America and France, and he was a forbearer
of the canon of “Negro” art that would de-
velop in the 1920s.
Kelly J. Baker

TANZANIA
Located in East Africa, the United Republic
of Tanzania has a population of approxi-
mately 36,400,000. Formerly a part of the
German colonial empire, Tanzania became
a British colony after the defeat of Germany
in World War I. Tanzania was formed
in 1964 through the consolidation of
Tanganyika, a British protectorate that
gained independence in 1961, and the island
of Zanzibar into a single political entity.
Tanzania’s history of relations with the
Americas after colonialism is tied to the
broader history of the Cold War and its
aftermath.
Important cultural changes were insti-
tuted soon after independence. While
English is a major language as a consequence
of colonialism, Tanzania adopted Kiswahili
as a national language in the 1960s. In part
this was a shedding of a colonial legacy,
while also a seeking to create national unity
through a common language. More
broadly, Tanzania’s public education system
has sought to adopt Western educational
materials and methods to the postcolonial
cultural, economic, and political reality.
In contrast to its northern neighbor,
Kenya, Tanzanian, independence was gained
relatively peacefully. Under the leadership of
Julius Nyerere, Tanzania engaged in a
process of nation-building that attempted
to blend both Western concepts of national
unity and economics with what Nyerere re-
garded as the unique dimensions of African
history, politics, and culture. Nyerere was
one of the architects of the Non-Aligned
Movement that sought to create a coalition
outside of the conﬂict between the United
States and the Soviet Union. Developing
nations in Africa and Latin America were
the backbone of the Non-Aligned Move-
ment. Even though Cuban leader Fidel
Castro would visit Tanzania in 1977, seeing
the nation as an ideological ally, Tanzania’s
balancing act during the Cold War made
it possible for Tanzania to maintain rela-
tively friendly relations with the United
States despite its strong socialist national
policies.
In 1967, Nyerere announced the
Arusha Declaration, which made the search
for self-reliance a national policy. In the
context of the Cold War, and the conﬂict
between U.S.-style capitalism and Soviet-
style communism, Nyerere sought a third
path, seeking to blend socialism with the
speciﬁc dimensions of Africa’s history and
Tanzania’s cultural circumstances. Central
to Tanzania’s development, Nyerere be-
lieved, was organizing the nation’s extensive
but fragmented rural economy. Tanzania’s
policies of socialist rural development
under Nyerere were termed ujamaa (“family-
hood”) socialism. It is a model of social-
ism that did not follow the models of either
the Soviet Union or Maoist China. Rural
areas were collectivized in an attempt to
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1131 ---
TAYLOR,C HARLES 1043
economically and socially consolidate far-
ﬂung villages. At the same time, Tanzania
sought to decentralize power by giving
authority to councils at the district and vil-
lage levels.
Tanzania is a regional power. In 1979,
Tanzanian troops toppled the violent Idi
Amin regime in Uganda. Nyerere himself
reached international prominence as a
strong supporter of Pan-Africanism. In
1984–1985, Nyerere served as chairman of
the Organization of African Unity (OAU),
an organization promoting cooperation
among African nations later renamed the
African Union (AU).
Despite a history of political stability,
Tanzania endured a substantial economic
crisis in the 1980s and 1990s as the econ-
omy worsened under socialist policies and
with the collapse of the Soviet Union. In
1985, Nyerere retired as president. Subse-
quently, pushed by global economic forces
and the rising tide of neoliberal economic
policies promoted by the United States and
international institutions such as the Inter-
national Monetary Fund and the World
Bank, the nation began to revise its eco-
nomic policies to favor international in-
vestment and capitalism.
Environmental issues have created sig-
niﬁcant ties between the United States and
Tanzania, particularly around wildlife con-
servation. With Mount Kilimanjaro, the
highest point on the African continent, the
Serengeti National Park, and many other
complex ecological regions, Tanzania is an
important site for wildlife and biodiversity
conservation efforts. Mount Kilimanjaro
and the Serengeti National Park are both
World Heritage Sites of the United Nations
Educational, Scientiﬁc and Cultural Orga-
nization (UNESCO) and popular tourist
destinations. The environmental issues that
arise from extensive tourism have resulted
in an important dialogue in Tanzania
about creating environmentally sustainable
tourism industries. This dialogue is part of
a broader transatlantic and international
concern about balancing environmental
preservation and economic development.
In June 2006, the U.S. Agency for Interna-
tional Development (USAID) allocated
$1.5 million and initiated the Community
Conservation Project for the Urambo Dis-
trict, a ﬁve-year-long biodiversity conserva-
tion effort intended to consolidate ongoing
environmental preservation and economic
development efforts in the Ugalla ecologi-
cal region.
Tanzania became embroiled in U.S.
geopolitics on August 7, 1998, when the
U.S. embassy in Tanzania’s capital, Dar es
Salaam, along with the U.S. embassy in
Kenya, were bombed by Al Qaeda linked
terrorists.
Richard Juang

Miguel, Edward. “T ribe or Nation?: Nation-

TAYLOR,C HARLES (1948–)
Charles Taylor, a Liberian of American
descent, has been a controversial political
leader in Liberia and internationally. Born on
January 28, 1948, to an Americo-Liberian
father and a native Gola tribeswoman,
Taylor was interested in the connections
between the United States and Liberia,
which was colonized by freed slaves in

--- PAGE 1132 ---
1044 T CHICAYAU TAM’SI
1847. On a student visa, Taylor went to
study in Massachusetts in 1972 and stayed
there until 1980. During this period, Taylor
rose through the ranks of the Union of
Liberian Associations and eventually be-
came its national chairman. Upon return-
ing home in 1980, Taylor was involved in a
violent coup originating from the socioeco-
nomic disparity between descendants of
Americans and the native people of Liberia,
a rebellion that brought Taylor into a key
position as the director of purchases within
the new dictator Samuel Doe’s government.
He was expelled from this role in 1983
when he was accused of embezzling govern-
ment funds. He ﬂed to the United States
but was arrested and jailed there in 1984; he
escaped, however, before he could be extra-
dited. He hid for four years, making a violent
reemergence in Liberia on December 24,
1989, at the head of an anti-Doe guerrilla
force called the National Patriotic Front of
Liberia (NPFL). The NPFL split into two
competing fractions, one led by Taylor, the
other by Prince Johnson (the latter faction
executed Doe). This rupture within the
NPFL incited a bloody ﬁve-year civil war,
which ended in Taylor’s election as presi-
dent in July 1997. As president, he became
actively involved in the deadly civil war in
Sierra Leone. Taylor was indicted by an in-
ternational court for war crimes in 2003.
T rapped between two insurrectionary rebel
forces, Taylor accepted asylum from Nigeria
in that same year.

TCHICAYAU TAM’SI
(1931–1988)
Tchicaya U Tam’si is the pen name of
Gerald-Félix Tchicaya. Tchicaya was born
in Mpili in the French Congo, the son of
Jean-Félix, a member of parliament who
represented the colony in Paris. His mother,
from whom he was separated at the age of
three, was from the Belgian Congo. Tchicaya
represents a second generation of African
Charles T aylor was a guerilla leader during Liberia’s
long civil war. Known for staggering brutality, he was
made president of Liberia in 1997, in strong part out of
Liberian fears of the war’s continuation. Subsequently
deposed, he has been put on trial for war crimes in the
Hague. (AFP/Getty Images)
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1133 ---
TCHICAYAU TAM’SI 1045
writers and poets who sought to depict
African experiences in both Africa and the
New World in complex, often surrealist, po-
etic forms.
Tchicaya was a rebellious spirit,
prompt to revolt against any form of
power. He stopped his schooling very early.
At 20, he started working in factories, and
also held a position in a printing works.
Later he became a journalist, and in 1960
he served as editor of the journal Congo of
the MNC (Congolese National Movement)
in Leopoldville. He witnessed Patrice Lu-
mumba’s rise and fall. After the imprison-
ment of Lumumba in 1960, he went back to
France to work for 20 years at UNESCO.
He retired in 1980 to dedicate the rest of his
lifetime to writing and literature. He died in
1988 in Bazancourt.
Tchicaya started writing under the
shade of a circle of French writers and intel-
lectuals like Supervielle, Luc Estaing,
Fombeure, and Bosquet. His father once
submitted his son’s poems to his colleague,
Aimé Césaire, who prophetically stated:
“He will be a great poet.” His works have
been translated into many languages, in-
cluding English and German. Three main
periods form his literary career.
The ﬁrst period (1955–1978) is essen-
tially poetic. Under the name of Tchicaya
U Tam’si, which means in Vili language
“the leaf that tells its country’s story,” he
published collections of poems: Le Mauvais
Sang (The Bad Blood, 1955), Feu de brousse
et A Triche-cœur (1957), Epitomé (1962),
Le Ventre (1964), Arc musical (1970), La
Veste d’intérieuret Notes de veille (1977),
and Le Pain ou la Cendre(1978). Reviewers
generally deemed Tchicaya’s poetry as her-
metic, suggesting that “keys” are needed to
interpret it. Although Rimbaud, Mallarmé
and Lautréamont were his models, his work
was enriched with the mythical image of
the Congo River. T o many critics, Tchicaya
is the best poet of the second generation of
African writers.
The second period is theatrical and
covers the years 1976 to 1980. Works from
this period include Le Zulu and Vuène le
fondateur (both 1978), Le Destin glorieux
du Maréchal Nnikon Nniku prince qu’on
sort (1979), and Le Bal de Ndinga (1987).
Originally a novella, Le Bal de Ndinga was
dramatized by G. Garan and performed
over two hundred times on European stages
in the 1990s.
The third period, from 1980 to his
death, is mainly dedicated to novels and
short stories. Tchicaya’s four novels are Les
Cancrelats (The Cockroaches) and The
Madman and the Medusa (both 1980), Les
Phalènes (1984), and Ces fruits si doux de
l’arbre à pain(1987). The ﬁrst novel could
have been published in 1958 if he had
found a publisher. Some of Tchicaya’s
novellas were published in a collection, La
main sèche (1980); others appeared in
newspapers or in journals. Tchicaya also
published an anthology—Légendes africaines
(1966).
The Americas were part of Tchicaya’s
life and literary work. He dedicated poems
or statements to Harlem, Cuba, the
Caribbean, and Latin America. His per-
sonal mythology of black blood included
all blacks. His “surrealistic poetry” was as
sophisticated as Césaire’s cosmology, with
which it was constantly compared. The two
men also shared common mythical topics,
such as the ﬁgure of Lumumba or the con-
ception of blackness.
In Epitomé, Tchicaya evokes Cuban
poet Nicolas Guillen, pointing out the des-
tiny of Amerindians and the exploitation of
the Americas by the conquistadores. He
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1134 ---
1046 T ECHNOLOGY TRANSFERS
identiﬁes himself with all exploited peoples
of the world. In his imagery the sea sym-
bolizes death since it emptied Africa and
helped slave merchants to commit their
crime. The sea therefore is a source of be-
trayal, frustration, and suffering for black
Africans deported to the Americas.
He visited, at the end of his life,
Cartagena de Indias in Colombia. His
encounter with Colombian writer Manuel
Zapata Olivella clearly shows his interest in
discovering three centuries later the rem-
nants of African values, rites, words, and
habits in people who have experienced the
existential trauma of deportation and slav-
ery. Zapata Olivella and Tchicaya agreed to
organize a joint colloquium of black writers
from Africa and Colombia, which would
take place in August 1988. Unfortunately
the Congolese poet died in April of that year.

TECHNOLOGY TRANSFERS
The transfer of African technologies and
knowledge affected agriculture, building,
and manufacturing in the Americas from
the time of European conquests. Each colo-
nizing nation—Portugal, Spain, Holland,
Denmark, France, England—began the
economic exploitation of the Americas with
the labor and manufacturing experience of
enslaved Africans. This African labor force
was knowledgeable and skilled in the
mining and forging of iron, in gold, copper,
and silver metallurgy, in planting crops of
rice, cotton, sugar, indigo, and tobacco, in
spinning and weaving textiles, and in many
methods of construction and transportation.
T echnologies that moved with enslaved
populations were numerous and interre-
lated. Iron making and forging techniques
produced steel and other metal tools for
agriculture, hunting, and construction.
Africans prepared the forests, swamps, and
jungles for cultivation and irrigation from
Brazil to the Hudson River. They dug the
mines and then processed the ores. Africans
ﬁshed the bays in dugout canoes called pet-
tiaugers, built with African methods of
boatbuilding. Those canoes also transported
raw materials, products, and people on
coastlines and rivers until the nineteenth
century. T echniques for woodworking were
further applied to Caribbean hardwoods to
create ﬁne furniture. African techniques for
strong knitted nets used in skein ﬁshing
were readily transferred for the ﬁshing in-
dustry and for their own consumption
(ﬁsh, locally caught, was frequently the
only protein that the enslaved people had
to supplement meager rations). Brick mak-
ing, regularly done from Morocco to the
Congo, was a source of construction mate-
rials in the New World. Culturally, cooper-
ative marketing and methods of working in
unison were practices that readily crossed
the Atlantic. Craft and trading networks
organized by women, as they were in
Yoruba societies, ﬂourished in the margins
of the New World colonies.
The evidence of African technologies
in the Americas varies depending on how
technology is deﬁned through different his-
torical periods. In general, however, it is
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1135 ---
TECHNOLOGY TRANSFERS 1047
not coincidental that both the European
scientiﬁc and industrial revolutions oc-
curred during the period of the transat-
lantic slave trade. Also, slaves were often
taken from the regions in which they might
have worked with the same raw materials
that they would work on in the Americas,
with the notable exception of sugarcane.
The historical recognition of the role of
African technologies and knowledge has
been blocked by the assumption that tech-
nologies were created solely by Europeans
and Euro-Americans and could not be in-
vented or even imagined by Africans, a prej-
udice that took hold in the nineteenth cen-
tury. In general, the African technologies
and knowledge transferred to the Americas
may be deﬁned as methods of production
often leading to further manufacture.
In fact, African technologies had sub-
stantial effects on the political and industrial
revolutions of North America and Europe.
While gold was the initial motive for early
European conquests in the New World, the
largest deposits, in California, would not be
discovered until 1848. Iron and ironworking
has an overlooked importance in the indus-
trial revolution. Brazil holds 25 percent of
the world’s iron ore, which became increas-
ingly more important when put into use by
African technology. Iron production in the
British colonies of the United States was
founded on using enslaved African labor.
At the time of the American Revolution,
Pennsylvania iron makers had the largest
number of slaves in the North. Additionally,
proﬁts from the manufactures of enslaved
Africans and their descendants paid for the
subsequent Industrial Revolution in England
in the mid-1700s.
As iron-producers, West and Central
African societies had the tools to cultivate
many crops since the ﬁrst millennium.
African understanding of cotton cultiva-
tion was important to the development of
the American South. Well before European
arrival in the Americas, cotton was pro-
duced on plantations in Upper Guinea in
Africa that often used domestic slave labor
as well as mechanical means of separating
seeds. The cotton was spun into yarn by
women and made into textiles by weavers
who were primarily men, whose craft guild’s
identity and visual language could be read
in the colors and threads.
Evidence of African architecture and
construction techniques abound in the
Americas. Houses, whether round or rec-
tangular, with thatched roofs in com-
pound, communal living styles, are regu-
larly noted in historical narratives. The
construction practices from diverse home-
lands guided the African craftsmen and la-
borers in the New World. For example, the
Mande architecture traditions of cylindrical
buildings and thatched roofs were diffused
throughout the West; round-house archi-
tecture on the west coast of Mexico was in-
troduced to the decimated Native Ameri-
can population by enslaved Mande. The
mayor of Guatulco wrote to the viceroy of
New Spain in 1591 that “I have been in-
formed that in a hilly place called Coyula,
two leagues from said town...there are
black runaway slaves. And to the present
time they are there, with their houses,
maize cultivation, cotton-growing, and
other things, as if they were in Guinea”
(Thompson, 1983, pp. 197–199). African
construction could often be sturdier than
European techniques. When a major earth-
quake shook the Caribbean in 1692, level-
ing Port Royal in Jamaica with such force
most of the structures, especially houses of
brick, were reduced to rubble, “Only the
humble slave huts...escaped destruction
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1136 ---
1048 T ECHNOLOGY TRANSFERS
because of their resilient stick and thatch
construction. Symbolically, the distraught
English survivors ejected the Negroes from
these quarters and moved into the slave
huts themselves” (Dunn, 1986, p. 186).
In early New York City, previously
New Amsterdam, Africans cleared the road
now named Broadway and the African
Burial Ground bears testimony to the skills
of the (mostly) enslaved people who were
an estimated 20 percent of the English
colonial population in the eighteenth cen-
tury. The Africans also built a wall now
known as Wall Street. In the upper New
York countryside, the Dutch brought a
group of experienced Africans to ﬁrst clear
the swampy land for agriculture.
The transatlantic slave trade moved
people with knowledge in all directions.
Both the goober peanut and tobacco, and
knowledge of their cultivation, were
brought from South America to the Canary
and Cape Verde Islands, then to West
Africa and back again by the enslaved farm-
ers in North America. As early as 1607, be-
fore the British brought enslaved Africans
into Jamestown, Virginia, tobacco, which is
indigenous to the Americas, was routinely
planted, traded, and smoked in Senegambia
and Sierra Leone. The descendants of rice
cultivators brought enslaved to North
America returned the original African tech-
nological process to the homelands. The
African American ship owner Paul Cuffe
(known as a mulatto because his mother
was a Massachusetts Indian) organized the
ﬁrst back-to-Africa movement in North
America with his own ships seeking to
establish viable farms in Sierra Leone.
In the era of the American Civil War,
Dr. Martin R. Delany planned to reestablish
cotton production in Africa and rebuild
infrastructure by a railroad linking the
West African Atlantic coast with the Red
Sea. Free people in Brazil, who had pur-
chased manumission for themselves in co-
operative brotherhoods known as cofradias,
returned as merchants and then became
part of a larger trading network of mixed
African and European people on both sides
of the Atlantic.
Knowledge was often carefully passed
from one generation to the next. There are
many occupational examples of sons fol-
lowing fathers as apprentices on aristocratic
plantations and in the industrial shops of
Southern cities. The occupational clan tra-
dition continued even in the choosing of
names following manumission and emanci-
pation: the name Woodland was estab-
lished in freedom by a Maryland kinship
group that was assigned to woods tasks in
slavery; after emancipation they lived as a
group in Baltimore, the family elder with a
sawing business.
The evidence of technological transfer
is complicated by biases in historical re-
search and by the immediate resistance to
production by the newly enslaved, who was
not interested in cooperating with the
slaveholder or overseer who was oppressing
him. For example, nails with cores of steel
from the caskets of ﬁrst-generation Africans
in the slave burial ground of Catoctin Fur-
nace, Maryland, were overlooked for many
years by archeologists.
The evidence is structured on three
African regional ethnic streams to the
Americas in the Atlantic slave trade: Wolof,
Mande, and Mandingo from Upper Guinea
(Mali, Senegal, Sierra Leone); Yoruba, Ibo,
Mina, and Akan from Lower Guinea
(Benin, Ghana, Nigeria); and N’Gola,
Makongo, and Bakongo from Central
Africa (Cameroon, Angola, Congo). The
sources of existing African technology for
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1137 ---
TELEVISION IN AFRICA,A MERICAN INFLUENCE ON 1049
mining and the growing of sugar, rice, and
cotton in the Americas are established by
early Muslim and European traders and
travelers in Africa whose narratives suggest
the industrial nature of African cities in the
savanna, the forest, and the interior deserts.
The Mali kingdom of the fourteenth to sev-
enteenth centuries, formed by Mende and
Mandinga who converted to Islam, is fre-
quently noted as the source of enslaved
African people in the Americas who were lit-
erate in Arabic, and who had great mathe-
matical and technical knowledge. The trav-
els of Mungo Park, a Scotsman who made
two journeys in Upper Guinea in 1798 and
1801, offer descriptions of agriculture, iron
smelting, and other technologies.
Scholarly research on technological
transfers between Africa and the Americas
is currently in rapid growth at many
archeological sites. In Cuba, historians,
architects, and archaeologists have begun
to study coffee plantations. In Benin,
caves of iron-rich soil that are hundreds of
years old are being examined by a cooper-
ative venture of Denmark and Benin. The
African Burial Ground in New York City
was declared a national monument in
2006.

TELEVISION IN AFRICA,
AMERICAN INFLUENCE ON
T elevision, a major source of entertainment
and enjoyment, has become a vehicle
through which the United States has
opened up African cultures to its language,
consumer products, political beliefs, and
economic system. Many researchers assert
these TV programs are used to entice view-
ers to watch content that has foreign cul-
tural values imbedded within them, with
the objective of eroding the local values and
traditions and replacing them. As a result,
what Africans believe, what they aspire to,
and what moves them to act or not has
been subjected to external inﬂuence and
control.
Culture is deﬁned as the total pattern
of human behavior; its products are em-
bodied in speech, action, and artifacts and
dependent upon humanity’s capacity for
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1138 ---
1050 T ELEVISION IN AFRICA,A MERICAN INFLUENCE ON
learning and transmitting knowledge to
succeeding generations. Critical for a soci-
ety’s chances of survival are the internal ca-
pacity and external freedom to develop its
cultural system autonomously. However,
current trends under the broad deﬁnitional
umbrella of “globalization” are bringing to-
gether all societies and promoting Western
values and culture at the detriment of other
cultures. The unfettered global market
erodes national boundaries in terms of the
ﬂow of goods and at the same time con-
fronts national sensibilities and values. In
the postindustrial marketplace, the major-
ity of goods exchanged in the marketplace
are of essentially cultural nature, such as
television programs, games, videos, toys,
and music.
Though modern communications
technology is offered to the world with the
suggestion that the expression of cultural
diversity is guaranteed, centrally controlled
technology has become the instrument
through which diversity is being destroyed
and replaced by a single global culture. A
critical assessment of the history of rela-
tionships between the industrial nations
and African countries since the colonial era
indicates that such interactions have tech-
nological, economic, and cultural dimen-
sions. African countries are markets for the
manufactured goods and cultural products
with accompanying beliefs, values, and
ideologies of dominant nations, especially
the United States. With the creation of a
single world market, all societies yield in
some measure to Western values, which
have supplanted all aspects of cultures in
developing countries. In the area of con-
sumption, the capitalist culture has imposed
a Western consumption pattern—a pen-
chant for Western-made products like
food, cars, electronic gadgets, and movies.
This desire for Western products plays a
major role in dissociating people from their
cultural roots and traditions of solidarity,
replacing them with media-created “needs”
and producing common behaviors result-
ing in a new breed of men, women, and
youth for whom religion, culture, and
nationality can seem only marginal elements
in a working identity.
According to Rob Kroes, the United
States dominates the global trafﬁc in infor-
mation and ideas, and American music,
movies, television, are software are so dom-
inant, so sought after, and so visible that
they are now available literally everywhere
on the Earth. American products, from cars
to movies, from clothing styles to kitchen
apparel, are agents of American cultural
diplomacy. T elevision has become a major
source of information and entertainment
all over the world, and audience percep-
tions of social realities closely correspond to
the “realities” portrayed on television, and
audiences adopt values and behaviors em-
phasized in television programs. Informa-
tion presented on television is readily avail-
able; little effort is needed to process
it—realities are presented in summary
forms, with simple solutions. Some re-
searchers believe that television presents a
distorted but uniform picture of reality that
is internalized and accepted by heavy view-
ers, primarily because of the pervasiveness
of its images.
It is believed that Western powers,
mainly the United States, export mass
media, especially television programs, to
developing countries as a device to broaden
their domestic commercial activities and
with a deliberate intention of corroding the
traditional cultures of these countries.
Many researchers further assert that after
inﬂuencing the local inhabitants with their
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1139 ---
TELEVISION IN AFRICA,A MERICAN INFLUENCE ON 1051
television programs and convincing them
to adopt the American ways of life, the
United States then sends its transnational
corporations to take their country’s natural
resources, convinces them to provide cheap
labor for manufacturing U.S. goods, sells
these same products back to them, and
takes the proﬁts back to the United States.
African cultures have entertainment
traditions that favor the reception of Amer-
ican programs whose cross-cultural appeal
makes them universal products. In large
part, the dominance of American-style en-
tertainment, information, and educa-
tional programs during primetime repre-
sents the attempts to reach out to the elite
class who are cultural hybrids, as well as to
the masses, which are being steadily incor-
porated into a pro-American reality. In the
process, they re-contextualize and re-
semanticize American culture to make it
function within expressive settings entirely
of their own making.
Exploring the signiﬁcance and impact
of the Americanization of Nigerian televi-
sion, Nosa Owens-Ibie concluded that be-
cause the production of television programs
is expensive and because most African
nations lack the technological base for
hardware and software production, they
rely on foreign suppliers and experts for
their regular program schedules, which ac-
count for about one-third of total transmis-
sion time, and mostly on programs from
the United States since it offers cheaper and
ready alternatives. 
American shows have the clear advan-
tage over local programs in terms of stan-
dard programming requirements, owing to
their technical quality, set, style of presenta-
tion, and sequence. Drawing on America’s
unique advantage as a cultural “melting
pot” and its ability to fashion products with
an appeal to peoples all over the world, tele-
vision program producers create quality
movies, soaps, sitcoms, sports, musicals,
and cartoons. These shows are considered
dynamic, and they successfully project and
capture the global cultural imagination,
and consequently have a heavy impact on
the popular culture.
According to G. K. Kieh, Jr., Africans
are taught from early childhood to accept
capitalism as the only correct and realistic
route to development. They learn to be
docile and passive and to accept their sub-
servience to all that is Western, and so
when they grow up, they are open to the
further colonizing of their minds by the
Western movies and television programs
imported into these countries. Young chil-
dren spend a signiﬁcant amount of time
with media and experience pleasure from
and identify with media texts, but because
they lack cognitive skills and the life expe-
riences necessary to evaluate media mes-
sages as adequately as might an adult, they
are likely to learn and be inﬂuenced by TV
content. They turn to media texts to con-
struct and make sense of their emerging
identities, and to develop strategies for act-
ing on their own dreams and coping with
social dilemmas.
Jeremy Seabrook conﬁrms the popular-
ity of the internationally acclaimed Ameri-
can children’s television programs all over
the world, which have children in 130 coun-
tries as devoted viewers of what producers
call “universal values,” such as racial har-
mony, peaceful dispute resolution, respect
for the environment, and equal rights for
women, regardless of the culture of the re-
ceiving countries. The programs serve to de-
mobilize the poor in the places where they
live: hope becomes increasingly concen-
trated in the distant and exotic; delight is

found not in celebrating their own lives and

a result, the model of society handed down
by ancestors is smashed and replaced by an-
other. Despite the attempt to regulate the
content of television in African countries,
very little success has been achieved in re-
ducing the proliferation of American pro-
grams. The inﬂuence is evident in the con-
cept, context, presentation styles, costumes,
set, and informality of some parts of other-
wise serious local programs. Compounding
the problem is the lack of sufﬁcient local
alternatives to challenge African dependence
on foreign products.
There is clearly a need for media liter-
acy to be included in national and regional
educational policies toward developing a
critical media consciousness of Africans.
Media education would teach people to
critically engage popular media materials,
including the most familiar ﬁlms, televi-
sion, music, and other forms of media cul-
ture. Though resistance to the effects of
Western cultural products in general, and
American television speciﬁcally, has devel-
oped as the condition intensiﬁes, and dif-
ferent African nations are formulating na-
tional cultural policies to curb the trend,
economic development of these nations re-
mains the solution to the invasion and sub-
ordination of their culture to the commu-
nication output and perspectives of a few
powerful, market-dominated economies of
their cultures.
Esther F . Ojo
