TERRORISM
T errorism is an attempt to, through the
threat or use of violence, create fear to co-
erce people to comply with the terrorists’
demands. T errorist attacks have occurred
throughout the Americas and Africa in the
United States, Colombia, Peru, Mexico,
Algeria, Egypt, Kenya, Namibia, South
Africa, and Tanzania, among other coun-
tries. T errorist groups run the gamut from
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1141 ---
TERRORISM 1053
the single-issue driven Animal Liberation
Front and Environmental Liberation Front
in the United States and Canada to groups
with broader political and economic agen-
das, such as Revolutionary Armed Forces of
Colombia (FARC), National Liberation
Army (ELN), and United Self-Defense
Forces of Colombia (UAC) in Colombia;
T upac Amaru and Sendero Luminoso in
Peru; the Lord’s Resistance Army in
Uganda; National Liberation Front (FLN)
in colonial Algeria; South-West Africa Peo-
ple’s Organization (SWAPO) in formerly
South African-held Namibia; and Al Qaeda,
the Armed Islamic Group, the Egyptian
Islamic Group, and the Salaﬁst Group for
Preaching and Combat (GSPC) through-
out much of northern Africa.
Historically, terrorist demands have
been political, economic, or social, includ-
ing independence from colonial rule, with-
drawal of foreign troops, the freeing of
prisoners, the end of racial and ethnic dis-
crimination, and redistribution of wealth.
T errorism has traditionally been aimed at
garnering widespread attention and creat-
ing fear that would force governments to
reverse existing or adopt new policies. Such
groups as FARC in Colombia and the
African National Congress in South Africa
sought to minimize the number of casual-
ties but maximize the publicity and effect
such attacks would have. T o this end, these
groups have engaged most commonly in
assassinations, hostage-taking, and limited
bombings. Targets typically have included
government and military personnel and
installations, foreign citizens, and corporate
facilities. Such groups often take credit for
their attacks, stating demands that must
be met to achieve the release of hostages
or prevent future attacks. T errorism is
used largely to discredit the government,
demonstrating its inability to protect the
citizenry from attacks and therefore its lack
of legitimacy. These motivescontinue to be
prevalent in Latin America, where key
organizations like FARC, ELN, and the
UAC in Colombia, Sendero Luminoso and
T upac Amaru in Peru, and the Popular
Revolutionary Army in Mexico continue to
seek economic redistribution and political
power.
In recent years, terrorist groups seeking
goals based on religious beliefs have be-
come increasingly prevalent. This shift has
been most prevalent in Africa. Whereas his-
torically groups in Africa, such as the FLN
in Algeria, SWAPO in Namibia, and the
ANC in South Africa, sought indepen-
dence from colonial rulers or the end of
apartheid government, many terrorist orga-
nizations in twenty-ﬁrst century Africa are
seeking the religious purity of their respec-
tive countries. These groups, including 
Al Qaeda, the Armed Islamic Group in
Algeria, the Egyptian Islamic Group, and the
Lord’s Resistance Army in Uganda, advo-
cate the total restructuring of societies to
correspond with their religious tenets.
While such organizations also seek to
delegitimize and replace the government,
their goal is broader: it is to create a vacuum
into which the terrorist groups may enter
and reorder the society. Whereas traditional
terrorists seek to gain allies among the pop-
ulation, these new terrorists do not. Their
goal is the destruction of those who are un-
believers. T o accomplish this, they engage
in far more destructive attacks, such as the
1998 destruction of the U.S. embassies in
Kenya and Tanzania. It is these groups who
are most likely to seek and use weapons of
mass destruction.
In addition to goals and tactics, terrorist
organizations increasingly are not organized
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1142 ---
1054 T ERRORISM
along hierarchical, centralized lines as was
Sendero Luminoso, but along a networked,
or hub, structure. These are decentralized
structures with autonomous cells, most of
which have no knowledge of other cells.
While there is typically an acknowledged
center, as with Al Qaeda’s Osama bin Laden,
it may provide little more than ideological
guidance, training, and support. The
U.S./Canada-based Animal Liberation
Front (ALF) and Earth Liberation Front
(ELF), formed in 1992 and 1976 respec-
tively, are extreme examples of this form of
group. Anyone espousing similar ideas to
these two issues (animal rights and environ-
mentalism) may consider themselves mem-
bers, and cells undertake actions with no
guidance from the center. These groups have
a number of advantages. They are ﬂexible,
able to adapt rapidly to changes in technol-
ogy or to the tactics of counterterrorist orga-
nizations. They are also difﬁcult to stop; de-
struction of individual cells has little effect
on the whole and even the capture, isolation,
or incapacitation of a leader does little to
stop the terrorist threat. This removes from
governments a traditional tactic: capturing
or killing and delegitimizing terrorist lead-
ers, as Peru did with Sendero Luminoso’s
Abimael Guzman in 1992.
There is no internationally accepted
deﬁnition of terrorism. The United Nations
has long debated deﬁnitions; while its
members condemned all terrorist actions
at its World Summit in 2005, they failed
to specify what terrorism was. The Organi-
zation of American States has similarly
proscribed terrorism but failed to clearly
deﬁne it. Debates about deﬁnition often
revolve around the motivation behind the
acts of terror. The terms “terrorist” and
“terrorism” have negative connotations
in contrast to other terms, including
“guerrilla,” “insurgent,” and “revolutionary.”
T errorism is a tactic used by organizations
to combat forces too strong to combat
using conventional or guerrilla tactics. In-
deed, terrorism is often used to augment
these military forms, particularly guerrilla
warfare. Groups such as Sendero Luminoso
in Peru and the Armed Islamic Group in
Algeria have supplemented guerrilla war
with terrorist attacks. Whether an attack
qualiﬁes as a military action or a terrorist
attack is often unclear. The most common
differentiation is target. When civilians,
government ofﬁcials, or off-duty military
personnel are targeted, the action is con-
sidered terrorist; when on-duty military
personnel are targeted, it is most com-
monly considered a guerrilla or insurgent
action. Countries supporting groups
whose ﬁghts for self-rule have included ter-
rorist actions often oppose labeling those
movements as terrorism.
The African Union is among the few
international organizations to deﬁne terror-
ism. In 1999, the organization’s members,
excluding Zambia and Zimbabwe, signed
and/or ratiﬁed the Convention on the Pre-
vention and Combating of T errorism, also
known as the Algiers Convention. While it
includes a clause explicitly excluding efforts
to achieve “liberation or self-determination”
(Part 1, Article 3), this convention deﬁnes
terrorism as “any act...which may en-
danger the life, physical integrity or free-
dom of, or cause serious injury or death to,
any person, any number or group of per-
sons or causes or may cause damage to pub-
lic or private property, natural resources,
environmental or cultural heritage and is
calculated or intended to...intimidate,
put in fear, force, coerce or induce any gov-
ernment, body, institution, the general
public . . . to do or abstain from doing any
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1143 ---
TERRORISM 1055
act or to adopt or abandon a particular
standpoint” (Part 1, Article 1).
T errorism is not new in the Americas
or Africa. In both regions, terrorism was an
integral part of the anticolonial revolution-
ary movements. Prior to the American Rev-
olution, tarring and feathering was used to
intimidate those collecting taxes for the
British. In the 1950s through the 1970s,
independence movements throughout
Africa utilized terrorism in order to expel
the colonial powers, most notably in Algeria
where the National Liberation Front (FLN)
attacked French facilities and personnel.
Elsewhere, the failed Mau Mau rebellion in
Kenya utilized terrorist actions to try to
force Kenyans to support the rebellion and
the British to leave the country. In 1966,
the South-West Africa People’s Organiza-
tion (SWAPO) launched attacks to free
Namibia from South African rule.
In the 1960s, terrorism in both re-
gions was based heavily on left-wing ideol-
ogy. Throughout the Americas, the Cuban
revolution was an inspiration to groups.
In Brazil, the Popular Revolutionary
Vanguard was formed following a 1964
military coup and conducted kidnappings
and raids until 1970. Beyond providing
inspiration, Cuba actively aided a number
of groups in Bolivia, Venezuela, Peru,
Colombia, and Guatemala. In Bolivia, the
communist National Liberation Army was
formed in 1966 and conducted a limited
number of operations until 1988. Except-
ing Colombia, where terrorist groups
formed in the 1960s operate with signiﬁ-
cant success in the twenty-ﬁrst century,
these revolutionary movements failed. In
the late 1960s, terrorism spread throughout
Latin America; even traditional guerrilla
groups began relying more heavily on ter-
rorist methods.
In the United States, the communist
antiwar group the Weathermen emerged in
1969 and engaged in several bombings of
public property. In 1966, the Black Pan-
thers was formed; it and its militant off-
shoot, the Black Liberation Army, engaged
in criminal activities, facing off with police
several times into the early 1970s.
In the 1970s and 1980s, terror contin-
ued throughout the Americas and Africa,
often playing out the Cold War in coun-
tries across the continents. As in the 1960s,
much of the terrorism was employed by
left-wing organizations, typically espousing
forms of Marxism. These groups included
the Movement of April 19 (M-19), which
was formed in 1970 in Colombia, and the
pro-Moscow T upac Amaru and Maoist
Sendero Luminoso in Peru. At the same
time, there was a rise of anticommunist
groups, including the Contras in Nicaragua
and smaller groups in Honduras and Costa
Rica. While the communist groups often
received assistance from Cuba and the Soviet
Union, the anticommunist groups received
similar logistical, intelligence, and weapons
support from the United States.
In South Africa, the African National
Congress, formed in 1912, adopted terror-
ist tactics in the early 1960s, seeking racial
equality and an end to apartheid rule. In
the 1970s and 1980s, it continued its at-
tacks, bombing facilities of international
corporations doing business in South
Africa. SWAPO, ﬁghting for the indepen-
dence of what is now Namibia, continued
attacks against South African-supported
businesses into the late 1980s. T errorism
occurred elsewhere on the continent, in-
cluding the assassination of Anwar Sadat in
Egypt in 1981 by al-Jihad al-Islami.
During this period, state terrorism
and state-sponsored terrorism were also

1056 T ERRORISM
prevalent in both the Americas and Africa.
State terrorism refers to acts of terror con-
ducted by a state against its own citizens
or other governments. Within Chile,
Augusto Pinochet’s government arrested,
killed, and “disappeared” thousands of its
citizens. South Africa was widely con-
demned as conducting state terror
throughout the 1970s and 1980s, both for
its attacks on its own citizens and for
sponsoring attacks on sub-Saharan states
such as Zimbabwe. State-sponsored ter-
rorism refers to the assistance given by a
country to terrorist organizations, most
commonly in the form of sanctuary, train-
ing facilities, weapons, and funds. In the
1980s, Libya was particularly active, re-
sponsible for at least four attacks, includ-
ing the 1988 bombing of Pan Am ﬂight
103 over Lockerbie, Scotland, the 1986
bombing of a West Berlin discotheque fre-
quented by U.S. soldiers, and the 1989
bombing of a French airliner over Niger.
Cuba was also considered an active spon-
sor of terrorist organizations across Latin
America and in Africa.
The end of the Cold War did not
mean the end of terrorism in either the
Americas or Africa. While terrorism did
decline in Central America in the 1980s,
left-wing militants launched sporadic at-
tacks against U.S. targets. In Mexico, the
Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR)
emerged and a number of bombings oc-
curred following the 1994 Zapatista upris-
ing. In Colombia, too, right-wing groups
emerged, including the umbrella organiza-
tion United Self-Defense Forces/Groups of
Colombia (AUC), which grew from sev-
eral paramilitary groups in the 1980s to
combat FARC and the ELN. In the United
States, there was a rise in right-wing “pa-
triot” groups, espousing antigovernment
sentiments, and anti-Semitic and racist
Christian “identity” and neo-Nazi groups.
Among their followers was Timothy
McVeigh, who in April 1995 detonated a
truck bomb at the Alfred P . Murrah Federal
Building in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma,
killing 168 people.
In both Chile and Peru, terrorist attacks
declined after the ﬁrst two years of the
1990s. Successful crackdowns in Peru by
President Alberto Fujimori’s government
led to a decline in activities by Sendero
Luminoso, the largest terrorist (and guer-
rilla) group in Peru; its leader, Abimael
Guzman, was arrested in 1992. T upac
Amaru, another Peruvian Marxist organiza-
tion, continued its activities in the 1990s,
culminating in the 1997 attack on the
Japanese ambassador’s residence, leading to
a four-month standoff as the terrorists held
72 hostages. Elsewhere in Latin America,
following the U.S. invasion of Panama, the
December 20 Movement (M-20) was
formed, carrying out attacks throughout
the 1990s in an attempt to destabilize the
government. In Argentina, the Lebanese-
based organization Hezbollah bombed
Jewish sites: the Israeli embassy in 1992
and a Jewish community center in 1994; the
two attacks killed more than one hundred
people.
By the mid-1990s, “narco-terrorism”
became a common term, reﬂecting an in-
creasing link between illegal narcotics pro-
duction and terrorist activities, most no-
tably in Colombia. T errorist organizations,
such as the left-wing FARC and ELN and
the nationalist AUC have all utilized the
drug trade, as well as other criminal activi-
ties, especially kidnapping and extortion,
to fund their organizations. Such funding
has allowed these groups signiﬁcantly in-
creased sustainability.

One organization that has an impres-
sive ability to fund itself and to garner
widespread support is Al Qaeda. Al Qaeda
(also Al Qaida), meaning “the base,” was
founded in the late 1980s by Osama bin
Laden. Bin Laden had, in the 1980s, joined
the mujahideen in their war against the
Soviets in Afghanistan and had been drawn
to the teachings of Abdullah Azzam, a leader
of the Egyptian Muslim Brotherhood. In
Afghanistan, bin Laden would also meet
Ayman al-Zawahiri, who had spent time in
an Egyptian prison suspected of having
conspired to assassinate Anwar Sadat.
While bin Laden provided funding, the
other two men provided spiritual guidance,
calling for a strict version of Sunni Islam
and condemning those governments
deemed insufﬁciently Islamist, including
those of Egypt and Saudi Arabia. In 1989,
bin Laden returned to his native Saudi
Arabia. His voicing of disapproval with the
Saudi government and opposition to its
willingness to allow U.S. troops on its soil
for the Gulf War led to a revocation of bin
Laden’s citizenship.
In 1991, bin Laden went to Sudan
where he and Al Qaeda bought land and
engaged in the training of Al Qaeda mem-
bers for attacks on U.S. interests as well as
against Middle Eastern governments. Be-
ginning in 1992, Al Qaeda began to launch
periodic attacks against Western interests.
It takes credit for arming Somali forces that
battled American soldiers, leading to the
deaths of 18 Americans in Mogadishu in
October 1993. In 1995, four Al Qaeda
members aided the Egyptian Islamic Group
in an attempted assassination of Egyptian
president Hosni Mubarak. In 1996, Al
Qaeda would be expelled from Sudan and
move to Afghanistan. However, its involve-
ment in Africa and relations with African
terrorist organizations became closer. In
1998, Al Qaeda allegedly orchestrated the
bombing of U.S. embassies in Kenya and
Tanzania. That same year, Al Qaeda also
created an umbrella organization called the
Islamic World Front for the Struggle
against the Jews and the Crusaders (Al-
Jabhah al-Islamiyyah al-’Alamiyyah li-Qital
al-Yahud wal-Salibiyyin), including many
African Islamist terrorist organizations.
Mostly in northern Africa, these organiza-
tions, encouraged by the emergence of
Wahhabism in the 1960s Middle East,
grew out of the increasing disenchantment
with the West and pro-Western govern-
ments and the worsening economic situa-
tions in many of the countries.
The September 11, 2001, attacks by
Al Qaeda on the World T rade Center and
Pentagon were the most costly attacks on
U.S. soil since Pearl Harbor. Four planes
were hijacked by members of Al Qaeda;
two were ﬂown into the World T rade
Center in New York City and one into the
Pentagon in Washington, D.C.; the fourth
plane crashed in Pennsylvania as passengers
sought to retake control. Nearly 3,000 peo-
ple were killed.
Africa has become one of the key
regions in the resulting U.S. War on
T error. Al Qaeda has been particularly
active in Kenya: bombing a hotel in 2002,
attacking an Israeli airliner with SA-7
surface-to-air missiles in 2002, and, in
2003, attempting to attack the U.S. em-
bassy in Nairobi with light aircraft. Al
Qaeda has also received funding through
the diamond trade in Sierra Leone and
Liberia; however, cells in these countries
do not appear to have been active in terror-
ism. Other groups have been linked to
Al Qaeda, including the Libyan Islamic
Fighting Group, al-Ittihad al-Islamiyyaa in

Somalia, al-Jihad in Egypt, and the Salaﬁst

Al Qaeda is not the only terrorist orga-

Of the 80 terrorist groups listed by the U.S.

the other hand, the AUC agreed to disarm

THIONG’O,N GUGI WA
(1938–)
Ngugi wa Thiong’o is a Kenyan novelist,
dramatist, essayist, and teacher whose
works are frequently taught in African and
postcolonial literary surveys. He was born
in British-ruled Kenya on January 5, 1938.
As part of his re-formation of identity, he
ofﬁcially changed his name from (James)
Ngugi to Ngugi wa Thiong’o in 1977.
Ngugi’s works memorably depict the pro-
longed liberation struggle of Kenya. His
early novels, Weep Not, Child (1964), The
River Between (1965), and A Grain of
Wheat (1967), portray oppressive life under
colonial rule and revolve around the Mau
Mau rebellion, the militant anticolonial
movement during the 1950s that led to
Kenya’s independence from colonial rule.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1147 ---
TITANIC 1059
After regaining independence in 1963, the
Kenyan authoritarian government associ-
ated with the comprador bourgeois line
used not only the inherited colonial state
machinery but also relied on Western capi-
tal. In Petals of Blood (1977), Ngugi de-
scribes the neocolonial exploitation of a
ruling minority on behalf of U.S.-led impe-
rialism and the political struggle of the
marginalized masses of peasants and work-
ers in postindependence Kenya. In contrast
to Chinua Achebe’s argument for the adop-
tion of the English language by African
writers, Ngugi claims that writing in an
African language is a necessity, that it is
part of the anti-imperialist struggle of
African peoples. By emphasizing the politi-
cal power and responsibility of a writer, he
insists that African writers use African lan-
guages. Also, Ngugi denounces the mind-
control of colonial education that imposes
negative qualities of backwardness and un-
derdevelopment upon African peoples, cul-
tural values, and languages. He advocates
the necessity of teaching African languages
and literatures as an essential part of the
process of decolonizing the mind. Thus,
with his novel Devil on the Cross, and con-
tinuing to his later novels, including
Wizard of the Crow (2006), Ngugi began
authoring his works in his mother-tongue,
Kikuyu, which then are translated into the
English language. Having been actively in-
volved in the promotion of African litera-
ture and ongoing engagement with political
social issues, Ngugi has made tremendous
impact on Africans and the African Dias-
poras with his outspoken critique of power,
state and social injustice, and the African
political experience in a global context.
Since 1982, Ngugi has lived in exile in
Europe and the United States. As of 2007
he serves as Distinguished Professor of
Comparative Literature and Director of the
International Center for Writing and
T ranslation at the University of California,
Irvine.
Heejung Cha

TITANIC
The ill-fated voyage of the RMS Titanic,
which sank on April 14, 1912, has occa-
sioned various cultural responses, from car-
toons and advertisements to poems, songs,
and ﬁlms. From soon after the sinking,
African Americans have taken a leading
role in this outpouring, despite the fact that
there were reputedly no blacks on board at
all. Probably the ﬁrst African American sec-
ular song about the voyage was Butler
“String Beans” May’s Titanic Blues of 1913,
which inaugurated the humorous boast
that the singer himself was aboard and sur-
vived due to his great athleticism. During
the next 15 years such an extravagant lie
was less common than moralistic ballads
that used the disaster to indict Anglo-
American bourgeois culture for its hubris
and lack of concern for the poor. An espe-
cially moving example wasGod Moves on the
Water, recorded by Blind Willie Johnstone
in 1929. According to an undying rumor,
world heavyweight champion Jack Johnson
was denied passage on the ship because of
his color. Huddie Ledbetter (“Leadbelly”)
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1148 ---
1060 T OGO
composed his blues Titanic with this “fact”
as central to the disaster. When Johnson
wants to get on board, the captain refuses
with the racist retort, “I ain’ haulin’ no
coal”; however, he and his passengers are
punished for this racism by the disaster
itself that the song revels in:
Black man oughta shout for joy,
Never lost a girl or either a boy
Cryin’, “Fare thee, Titanic, fare thee well!”
In a similar vein, the Titanictoasts that
came into their own after World War II
took issue with a tragic reading of the dis-
aster and emphasized the humorous. Ex-
tremely lewd and bawdy, they were long
oral narratives that had as their hero a sup-
posed black stoker on the ship, Shine. He
warns the captain that the ship will sink,
but the captain refuses to listen and initiate
the disembarkation of his passengers until
it is too late. Meanwhile, Shine is already
swimming to safety and refusing the bland-
ishments of the rich white men and women
aboard.
Big man from Wall Street came on the
second deck.
In his hand he held a book of checks.
He said, “Shine, Shine, if you save 
poor me,
“Say I’ll make you as rich as any black man
can be.”
Shine said, “You don’t like my color and you
down on my race,
get your ass overboard and give these sharks
a chase.” (Jackson, 2004, p. 190)
The reversal of traditional power rela-
tions in these poems made them very pop-
ular among African Americans and they are
still told today. Latest revelations about the
passenger list on the Titanic, however, have
exploded one of the myths that created
them. There was in fact one black man
aboard, a Joseph Larouche, a Haitian with
a white wife who boarded in France and
traveled second class. He died in the disas-
ter, but his wife and children survived. 
The Titanic disaster continues to be
the subject of narrative interpretations, not
the least of which is the epic James
Cameron ﬁlm Titanic (1997). A twenty-
ﬁrst century African American take on the
disaster was shown by an extended joke on
the subject in Spike Lee’s ﬁlm Original
Kings of Comedy (2000). Here again, black
agency is emphasized as the black band
members refuse to go down with their ship,
but make improvisatory boats out of tables,
with tablecloths for sails, and survive the
disaster. RMS Titanic might have been a
virtually lily-white ship, but this has not
stopped African American artists from ex-
ploring its multiple valences for discussing
black Atlantic realities.
Alan Rice

TOGO
Located in West Africa, the Republic of
T ogo, with a narrow coastline, and stretch-
ing inland to Burkina Faso, has a popula-
tion of approximately 5,557,000, many of
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1149 ---
TOOMER,J EAN 1061
whom live along the coast in the south of
the country. It was originally a German
colony after German commercial agents
signed “treaties of protection” in 1884. The
German government then took over con-
trol of T ogoland and governors were
appointed from 1898. James Nathan
Calloway, an American agriculturalist
from T uskegee Institute (now T uskegee
University), Alabama, moved to German
T ogoland, where he was involved in an
experimental station growing cotton until
at least 1930. T ogo’s economy is heavily tied
to phosphate, some of which is exported to
the Americas, and the rest to France.
At the outbreak of World War I, the
British and the French invaded and cap-
tured the colony, with most of it continu-
ing under French rule, and the western sec-
tion being placed under British control and
being absorbed into the Gold Coast (now
Ghana). The French administered their sec-
tion, T ogo, under the mandate of the
League of Nations, independent of their
other colonies, and in 1946 it was trans-
ferred to a United Nations trusteeship.
From the 1930s some U.S. missionaries
with the United Presbyterian Church of
North America went to T ogo.
In 1956 T ogo was granted internal
autonomy; it became independent on
April 27, 1960. The ﬁrst U.S. ambassador
to T ogo was Leland Judd Barrows, who
was succeeded in 1961 by Leon B aqueiro
Poullada. The U.S. Peace Corps started
working in T ogo from 1962. In the follow-
ing year there was a coup d’état against the
president, Sylvanus Olympio, who had for
many years championed T ogo indepen-
dence, but who had become unpopular with
many army ofﬁcers. On January 13, 1963,
he was ambushed and pursued to the gates
of the U.S. embassy, where he was intending
to seek asylum. Soldiers shot him dead out-
side the gates, and Nicolas Grunitzky, a
longtime rival, came to power until he him-
self was deposed in a coup four years later.
Gnassingé (Étienne) Eyadéma was president
from 1967 until his death in 2005, although
the position was largely ceremonial for much
of that time. 
There has been signiﬁcant intellectual
exchange between T ogo and the Americas.
In the late 1970s and early 1980s, a few
students from T ogo started studying at
Harvard, and Mensah Kpognon of the
ministry of planning in Lomé attended the
Massachusetts Institute of T echnology.
Now most of the theses on T ogo are written
by people from T ogo. Indeed, as of 2006,
of the 16 recent Canadian master’s and
doctoral theses on T ogo, all but one are
authored by people from T ogo.
Music from T ogo has long been popu-
lar in France and has traveled to French
colonies in the Americas. King Mensah,
one of the best-known musicians from
T ogo, moved to French Guiana during the
mid-1990s before settling in Paris, where
he leads his own group, Favaneva.
Justin Corﬁeld

TOOMER,J EAN (1894–1967)
Early twentieth-century philosopher and
writer Jean T oomer was born Nathan
Pinchback T oomer in Washington, D.C.,
on December 26, 1894. His best known
work, Cane, was claimed by both the
American modernist movement and the
Harlem Renaissance. He was the only child
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1150 ---
1062 T RADE,FAIR
of North Carolina planter Nathan T oomer
and Nina Pinchback, daughter of biracial
politician P . B. S. Pinchback who was elected
to the U.S. House of Representatives and
U.S. Senate during Reconstruction. Al-
though Pinchback could pass as a white
man, he ran for ofﬁce on the Negro ticket
and was denied entrance to both the House
and Senate as a result. Like his maternal
grandfather, T oomer’s physical appearance
did not betray his race, so he moved easily
through white society, even identifying his
race as white on ofﬁcial documents such as
college applications and marriage licenses.
The theme of race occupies much of
T oomer’s writing and philosophy. Inspired
by his 1921 trip to Sparta, Georgia, where
he served as principal at an industrial and
agricultural school for blacks, T oomer’s
breakthrough work Cane (1923) depicts
Southern black folk culture in the interim
between slavery and civil rights. The book’s
compelling and authentic treatment of
rural Southern blacks and its innovative
structure—a montage of poetry, ﬁction,
and drama—represented a modernist ad-
vance for African American literature, and
today Cane is widely recognized as the sem-
inal literary masterpiece of the Harlem
Renaissance.
In spite of the black community’s over-
whelmingly positive response to the book,
Jean T oomer was disheartened by the luke-
warm response of white critics and moder-
ate sales marketwide because his goal had
been to achieve universal praise without re-
gard to race. Abandoning ﬁction writing
for more philosophical pursuits, T oomer
immediately began to search for a means
of transcending racial divisions. He found
it in the Russian philosopher Georges
Gurdjieff in early 1924. Gurdjieff’s Unitism
philosophy promised a higher consciousness
and paralleled some of T oomer’s own ideas,
so T oomer devoted himself almost wholly
to Gurdjieff, becoming his disciple and
using his writer’s skills to spread Gurdjieff’s
message.
Though T oomer experimented with
other means of enlightenment, such as Sci-
entology, spiritual travels in India, and
Quakerism, his life and work after 1924
and until his death in a nursing home on
March 30, 1967, were devoted to Gurdjieff.
Dana Nicholas

Renaissance

TRADE,FAIR
Fair trade is a component of international
trade within the complex system of devel-
opment. Declining prices of primary prod-
ucts such as coffee, abhorrent labor condi-
tions in garment sweatshops, the worldwide
increase in human trafﬁcking, and unsus-
tainable agriculture practices have all con-
tributed to the groundswell of support by
producers and consumers for fair trade mea-
sures to address these global problems. Fair
trade measures to address these problems in
Latin America and Africa have focused on
product pricing and working conditions. In
particular, products such as coffee, tea,
cocoa, and garments have all been affected
to some degree by fair trade measures.
Governments in Latin America and
Africa have similar objectives for economic
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1151 ---
TRADE,FAIR 1063
growth, increased employment, price sta-
bility, and improved equity in income dis-
tribution. Increasing international trade
through trade liberalization (removal of
trade restrictions) is often mentioned as a
primary component of any country’s at-
tempts to accomplish these objectives. Yet
the speciﬁc prescription for achieving these
objectives is different for every country, and
must take into account the actions of both
developing and industrial countries. Many
argue that industrial countries have a re-
sponsibility to construct a global trade sys-
tem that enhances the participation of de-
veloping countries and ensures that they
access a fair share of the potential gains that
arise from international trade.
Latin American and African nations
have used international trade and/or the
liberalization of trade agreements to in-
crease employment, economic growth, and
stability; to improve foreign relations; and
to increase political and economic status
within the world community. International
trade agreements and various types of in-
dustrial and protectionist policies enacted
within a country also affect income distri-
bution and the overall welfare of a nation’s
citizens. The results of these efforts have
often been mixed. T en years after the North
American Free T rade Agreement (NAFTA)
was signed between Mexico, the United
States, and Canada, Mexican exports had
grown approximately 10 percent per year
but mean real wages of Mexican workers
were lower in 2000 than in 1990. Both
poverty and inequality increased for Mexican
workers since NAFTA was adopted as the
agriculture sector lost jobs due to cheap
food imports from the United States.
There have always been frequent de-
bates among policymakers and producers
and consumers regarding the relative merits
of unrestricted (free) international trade.
While international trade is a necessary in-
gredient in economic growth, the argu-
ment is often made that international trade
without a fair trade component will not re-
sult in sustainable development. Interna-
tional trade is often portrayed as having
positive macroeconomic effects (e.g., increase
in overall economic growth and invest-
ment), but mixed microeconomic effects
(e.g., individual workers and ﬁrms can
experience gains or losses in the demand for
their skills/products). Thus the net effect of
international trade on employment and
ﬁrm expansion often varies between sectors
and products. The negative distributional
effects of international trade on speciﬁc
employment sectors (e.g., farming), speciﬁc
geographic regions (e.g., coffee or tea pro-
ducing regions), or speciﬁc classes (e.g.,
low-income vs. middle or upper-income
classes) often result in winners and losers.
Theoretically the winners compensate the
losers through government transfer pro-
grams or the provision of social safety nets.
In reality, this type of compensation rarely
occurs—especially in low-tech industries.
T rade liberalization can result in cheap im-
ports ﬂooding the domestic markets of
both developing countries (e.g., U.S. grain
into Mexican markets) and industrial coun-
tries (e.g., Chinese apparel into U.S. mar-
kets), resulting in domestic unemployment
and business bankruptcies. 
T rade liberalization may also lead to
the removal of government subsidies and
government protection from the world
market for products such as cotton and
sugar. This removal would have adverse
effects on some producers: for example,
U.S. cotton and sugar beet producers. But
it would have positive effects on others: for
example, West African cotton producers
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1152 ---
1064 T RADE,FAIR
would be released from a controlled pricing
system imposed by the DAGRIS corpora-
tion. In contrast, producers of coffee and
other beverage products are competing to
sell their products in liberalized world mar-
kets dominated by a few large multina-
tional corporations (MNCs). In the coffee
market, Nestle, Sara Lee, Kraft, and
Proctor and Gamble purchase 50 percent
of the world’s beans.
The fair trade component within in-
ternational trade focuses on product prices
and working conditions. Fair trade is often
presented as a socioeconomic contract be-
tween producers and consumers that guar-
antees the producers a fair price for their
labor. The fair trade price has historically
been higher than the market price for com-
modities such as coffee, tea, and cacao
(used in the production of chocolate). Fair
trade pricing is often described as a ﬂoor
price or minimum price that will be paid
for a product. Advocates of fair trade
maintain that when consumers pay a fair
trade price they are contributing to sus-
tainable development for producers and
their families in Latin America, Asia, and
Africa.
Fair trade is also concerned with im-
proving the conditions under which prod-
ucts are produced. Working conditions in
developing countries often violate basic
worker standards. Many workplaces force
employees to work long hours without
breaks, employ children, pay workers in
company script rather than wages, and do
not observe basic safety requirements. Ad-
ditionally, environmental degradation from
soil erosion, misuse of chemicals, and fac-
tory pollution occur when products (e.g.,
cacao and garments) are grown or manu-
factured in areas with few health and envi-
ronmental regulations.
The implementation of fair trade pric-
ing and improved working conditions
requires challenging international trade
agreements, national laws, business pur-
chasing policies, and consumer attitudes.
Fair trade policies encourage the education
and organization of consumers and pro-
ducers in order to negotiate a socioeco-
nomic contract that provides the required
leverage to implement fair trade pricing
and improved working conditions. Since
the mid-1990s, fair trade education and or-
ganization have occurred using a variety of
vehicles: rallies, grassroots campaigns, Web
sites, and shareholder resolutions. Product
markets do not demand changes in pricing
or working conditions, but activists utiliz-
ing the above vehicles in their “name and
shame” campaigns have successfully chal-
lenged corporations to change the way they
do produce and market their products.
Companies such as Nike, Proctor and
Gamble, and The Gap have been success-
fully pressured to adopt corporate codes of
conduct with their suppliers, implement
production site monitoring, and offer
higher-priced fair trade products.
Organizations that provide certiﬁca-
tion and information to consumers and
businesses on fair trade practices include
T ransFair, Fair T rade Certiﬁed, Fair T rade
Federation, and Rainforest Alliance. T rans-
Fair, a certifying fair trade labeling organi-
zation, was established to increase con-
sumer awareness and provide information
on purchasing fair trade commodities.
Begun in Europe in the 1980s, T ransFair
was ﬁrst organized in the United States in
1999. Since its debut in the United States,
it has resulted in $55 million additional in-
come to more than 800,000 farmers and
their families in 50 countries. Increasing
numbers of businesses in the United States
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1153 ---
TRADE ZONES,A FRICAN 1065
have begun offering a line of retail products
to consumers with fair trade labels. These
products include wood (Home Depot),
coffee (Proctor and Gamble, Dunkin’
Donuts), bananas (Wild Oats Markets),
handicrafts (T en Thousand Villages), and
cocoa and tea (Equal Exchange, which sells
fair trade products to 19,000 churches).
Fair trade pricing can be illustrated
using the example of coffee. Historically,
producer prices per pound of coffee have
ranged from $2.30 in 1965 to $4.30 in
1985 to $0.90 in 1997 and $0.55 on aver-
age since 2003. Due to the sharp decline in
coffee prices since 1997, 600,000 Central
Americans lost employment opportunities
and 5 million were living below the poverty
line. As of 2006, returns to coffee producers
from a pound of roasted coffee vary from
$0.55 for coffee marketed by MNCs such as
Proctor and Gamble and sold in grocery
stores (e.g., Folgers) to $1.26 for fair trade
blends to $3.77 for fair trade coffee sold di-
rectly to the consumer by a producer coop-
erative under the T ransFair label.
A discussion of the principles of fair
trade is often broader than the economic
language of prices and working conditions.
Fair trade can also include providing eco-
nomic opportunities for the poor, increas-
ing transparency and accountability in
relations between the poor and other indi-
viduals and institutions, building capacity
of the poor and their enterprises, gender
equity, and advocating sustainable environ-
mental practices. The complexity of devel-
opment is exempliﬁed when utilizing this
broader view of fair trade with regard to
sweatshops. While sweatshops often exhibit
characteristics of unfair pricing structures
and horriﬁc working conditions, they also
provide socioeconomic opportunities for
poor women that were nonexistent in the
countryside. In the “race to the bottom” of
low wages and minimal working condi-
tions, the application of fair trade princi-
ples can raise the level of this bottom.
Gayle A. Morris

TRADE ZONES,A FRICAN
T rade zones in Africa, of which several have
emerged recently, are designed primarily to
liberalize trade and harmonize markets
among regionally aligned countries as well
as, signiﬁcantly, to inﬂuence government
policy along neoliberal lines. Major trade
zones on the continent include the Com-
mon Market for Eastern and Southern
Africa (COMESA), the Southern African
Development Community (SADC), the
Economic Community of West African
States (ECOWAS), the Communaute
Financiere Africaine (CFA) Franc Zone, and
the Arab Maghreb Union (UMA). The trade
zones are viewed as crucial to the further
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1154 ---
1066 T RANSCULTURATION
expansion of neoliberal socioeconomic
regimes across the continent through the
New Economic Partnership for African
Development (NEPAD).
The largest trading bloc in Africa is
COMESA, with 27 member-states span-
ning the continent from Egypt in the north
to Namibia in the south. With almost 385
million people, the member-states of
COMESA encompass almost half of Africa’s
population. ECOWAS includes 16 member-
states covering 220 million people, while
SADC involves 14 member-states and
almost 190 million people.
There is some overlap among Africa’s
trade zones. Eight SADC members (Angola,
Malawi, Mauritius, Namibia, Seychelles,
Swaziland, Tanzania, and Zimbabwe) are also
members of COMESA. The Francophone
countries of Benin, Burkina Faso, Cote
d’Ivoire, Mali, Niger, Senegal, and T ogo are
also part of the CFA Franc Zone.
Critics contend that trade zone empha-
sis on competitive markets, enhanced re-
source exploitation, and industrial prof-
itability have only exacerbated extreme
levels of poverty and low social and health
indicators. T rade areas such as COMESA,
ECOWAS, and SADC are further troubled
by, and as some critics suggest, contribute
to, inequalities in regional economies. Each
zone shows a mix of larger and more dy-
namic economies alongside some of the
world’s poorest countries. These unequal
relations have given rise to concerns about
the domination of weaker economies by
the regional powerhouses.
Jeff Shantz

TRANSCULTURATION
Fernando Ortiz, the Cuban omnivorous
scholar who wrote extensively on Afro-
Cuban culture, was the ﬁrst to coin the
term “transculturation” in analyzing the
historical, cultural, and economic counter-
point between tobacco and sugar, which he
claimed could be the organizing image for
understanding the island’s rich sociocul-
tural brew. Ortiz analyzed transculturation
as occurring in a subjugated culture under
colonialism and slavery that is able to in-
corporate, transform, and subtly subvert el-
ements of the dominant culture in order to
fashion meanings that ensure not only the
survival of a culture and its people but also
the ability of such subjugated people to
thrive and create a new culture. For exam-
ple, Regla de Ocha (also known as Santeria)
is a religion that is neither purely Yoruba
nor purely Spanish, but owes much to both
and is uniquely Cuban, even if its African
roots are primary. T ransculturation is a hy-
brid emblem of cultural creativity, a mate-
rial practice that both reinscribes the past
and transforms the present, a performative
philosophical reasoning, and an act of so-
cial resistance.
In a Caribbean context, transcultura-
tion has understandably focused on the in-
teraction and transmutation of European
and African cultures, but often ignored is
that the ﬁrst transculturations were among
different African peoples themselves, say,
between Yoruba and Kongo, between
Mandingo and Fon, between Wolof and
Ashanti. Also signiﬁcant in some instances
are Amerindian-African transculturations,
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1155 ---
TRANSCULTURATION 1067
as with the Garífuna peoples, and in the
histories of Guyana, French Guiana, and
Suriname.
Examples of transculturation can be
musical (danzón, zouk, reggae), religious
(Regla de Ocha, Voodoo, Shango), culinary
(callaloo, ajiaco), and linguistic (Papiamento,
Sranan-T ongo, the English and French
Creoles spoken in different islands).
T ransculturation (in the Anglophone
Caribbean the term creolization is pre-
ferred; creolitéis used in the Francophone
countries) is by no means a smooth trans-
action, but instead a long, often painful
historical process ﬁrst marked by decultur-
ation and forced assimilation, as when
slaves were stripped of their humanity and
culture (clothing; changing of names; reli-
gious prohibition; physical, sexual, and
psychic violence). But over centuries, as
power relationships changed both during
and after slavery, the Caribbean began to
evolve Euro-African cultural realities that
became uniquely Jamaican, Cuban, or
Martinican.
T ransculturation is often seen as having
a racial meaning, and in this sense, a syn-
onym of mestizaje, or racial mixing, is used.
Some intellectuals, including Ortiz, have
used the term to describe their countries as
racial democracies, and also as a way to
deny the existence of racism, indirectly im-
plying that whiteness is still the norm.
T ransculturation’s racial dimension does
not mean that racial mixing denies the ex-
istence of racism (“intimacy does not mean
equality”) nor “shadism”—the obsession
with a person’s degree of whiteness or
blackness—but it does mean that both race
and identity, as deﬁnitions and lived rela-
tions, change over time and are embedded
within historically speciﬁc power relation-
ships. T ransculturation requires using the
past as a means to envision how we will
shape the future, as Stuart Hall has sug-
gested. That all individuals bear a responsi-
bility in deﬁning how racial and cultural
identities operate is especially important
when considering how being black, mixed-
race, or white is shaped so differently in
Puerto Rico, T rinidad, Martinique, Haiti,
or the United States.
In analyzing Afro-Caribbean culture,
scholars and artists have come up with a
wealth of metaphors trying to capture the
racial, social, and cultural complexity of the
region: culinary (callaloo, ajiaco, stew),
metallurgical (crucible, melting pot, forge),
spatial or architectural (crossroads, four-
storied house, limbo, repeating island,
open Gnostic space), natural-ecological
(trees, roots, rhizomes, mangrove, manigua),
literary (cross-cultural poetics), as well as
the above mentioned references to racial
and cultural mixing (Creolization, mesti-
zaje, hybridity). None of these metaphors
alone are sufﬁcient, but they help us under-
stand that being African in the Caribbean,
as a transculturated being, is a matter of
roots that have been (and are) routes that
extend to and from all corners of the
planet.
Alan West-Durán

TRAVEL WRITING
A term coined by the cultural studies critic
Raymond Williams, travel writing encom-
passes literary journeys across a range of
genres that address or illustrate cultural
contact, conﬂict, and interchange. There is
wide-ranging travel literature on Africa and
the Caribbean. Though the black Atlantic
was formed—and continues to evolve—
through the movement of people, their
journeys are rarely represented by conven-
tional travel books. Typically written by
professional authors as the result of a spe-
cially undertaken expedition or assign-
ment, such works are poorly equipped to
describe the enforced journeys of slaves or
those ﬂeeing oppression or in search of ed-
ucation or employment. But accounts of
these journeys, though neglected, do exist,
if scattered across a range of genres—
autobiographies, diaries, letters, speeches,
journalism—sometimes ghost-written, fre-
quently unpublished, often out of print.
Recent attempts to draw attention to
the richness of this material have helped to
force a reconsideration of the rather narrow
deﬁnition of travel writing employed by the
Western publishing industry (often uncrit-
ically assimilated by critics and theorists).
Since the 1980s, a considerable body of this
work has been reprinted, and a new gener-
ation of authors has emerged, conscious of
this heritage which they seek to continue.
Most of the ﬁrst-person accounts of
enslavement in Africa and the Middle
Passage appear in eighteenth-century
slave narratives, such those of Olaudah
Equiano, Ottobah Cuguano, and Ukawsaw
Gronniosaw. The stories of American-born
slaves tell of enforced marches and ﬂights
to freedom across the United States. A sig-
niﬁcant number offer accounts of journeys
to Europe and farther aﬁeld as fugitives, as
public speakers, as domestic servants, or—
in the case of David Dorr, author of A
Colored Man Round the World(1858)—as a
slave accompanying his master. Dorr went
on a tour that took him as far as Egypt,
Palestine, and Syria.
Some former slaves went on to play a
leading role in public life in the United
States following the Civil War. The Life
and Times of Frederick Douglass (1881,
1892) consolidated Frederick Douglass’s
reputation as a man of the world with his
accounts of crossing oceans and continents,
inaugurating a tradition that would include
future political leaders such as Kwame
N’krumah, Malcolm X, and Nelson
Mandela. W riters such as Claude McKay
and Langston Hughes traveled so exten-
sively that their autobiographies are effec-
tively travel narratives. Predictably too,
perhaps, the careers of prominent musicians
and sportsmen and women have provided a
rich source of travel anecdotes: for instance,
the memoirs of concert pianist Philippa
Duke Schuyler (Adventures in Black and
White, 1960) and of soccer star Pele (My
Life and the Beautiful Game, 1977).
The life stories of lesser-known ﬁgures
may ﬁnd their way into print with small
publishers, and often repay the effort of
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1157 ---
TRAVEL WRITING 1069
tracking them down. More fragmentary bi-
ographies are found in diaries and letters,
usually published posthumously. Other ex-
periences may be captured by oral histori-
ans, typically appearing in themed collec-
tions that address immigration or military
service. But many travelers have left only
the barest record of their experiences, their
words recorded by writers who met them,
often brieﬂy, incorporating their stories
within their own.
Journalism offers much of interest.
One ﬁnds a wide range of accounts of visits
abroad in The Crisis(whose editor, W . E. B.
Du Bois, contributed many notable
pieces), London-based The Keys, Barbadian
magazine Bim, and Essence (selections from
which have recently been anthologized in
Go Girl! ). C. L. R. James’s memorable ﬁrst
impressions of London were ﬁrst published
in the Port of Spain Gazette (1932); Nicolás
Guillén’s reports from the Spanish Civil
War and the Eastern Bloc appeared in
Cuban periodicals; and Nat Nakasa and
Lewis Nkosi offered black South African
perspectives on New York City and Paris in
the 1960s and 1970s. T ravel also inspired
some of the best essays of June Jordan: for
instance, “Beyond Apocalypse Now”
(1980) presents reﬂections on race and
identity prompted by a winter visit to St
Paul, Minnesota, in a manner reminiscent
of James Baldwin’s “A Stranger in the
Village” (1953).
Perhaps one of the ﬁrst conventional
book-length travel narratives by a black
author was The Wonderful Adventures of
Mary Seacole in Many Lands (1857). John
Ocansey’s account of his attempt to recover
money owed by a Liverpool merchant ( An
African Trading, 1881) and Ham Mukasa’s
record of a Bugandan chief’s journey to at-
tend Edward VI’s coronation (Uganda’s
Katakiro in England, 1904) are classic
books that have been reprinted. Booker T .
Washington’s The Man Furthest Down(1912)
is an unjustly neglected study of poverty in
Europe. Zora Neale Hurston and Katherine
Dunham brought their anthropological
training to bear on their reﬂections on
Jamaica and Haiti, which they visited in
the 1930s and 1940s.
After World War II, major travelogues
by Richard Wright (on Spain, Gold Coast,
and Indonesia), Bernard Dadié (Paris, New
York, Rome), Andrew Salkey (Guyana,
Cuba), and An African in Greenland
(1981) by Tété-Michel Kpomassie ap-
peared. Caryl Phillips’s The European Tribe
(1987) and The Atlantic Sound (1999),
Colleen McElroy’s A Long Way from St
Louie (1997), and Gary Younge’s No Place
Like Home (1999) mark the emergence of
a tradition-conscious body of black travel
writing.
Probably the richest evocations of
travel are to be found in imaginative works
of ﬁction, poetry, and drama, which often
recreate experiences otherwise poorly rep-
resented in print. These may include more
or less autobiographical novels, which cap-
ture the experience of migration, such as
George Lamming’s The Emigrants (1954)
or Jamaica Kincaid’s Lucy (1991). The
plays of August Wilson and the poems of
Grace Nichols suggest how other literary
forms can address questions of displace-
ment and belonging. Finally, the diasporic
scope of novels such as Sandra Jackson-
Opoku’s The River Where Blood Is Born
(1997), or extended verse sequences such
as Edward Brathwaite’s The Arrivants
(1967), have the freedom to range across
continents and generations to provide
memorable syntheses of black Atlantic his-
tories and memories.

Several themes may be identiﬁed in
this body of work. Predictably enough,
their authors often tell of travel under
duress, from the enforced voyage of the
slave ship to the rushed ﬂight of fugitives
and refugees, or the dull compulsion of
“economic” migration. But the obstacles
preventing travel are almost as common:
the difﬁculties in obtaining passports, the
segregation of public transport, the sheer
lack of access to transport at all. Journeys
across national borders frequently prompt
reﬂections on the change of social status—
even of “color”—occasioned by the transi-
tion from one racial regime to another.
If the dominant tradition in travel lit-
erature tells of journeys from the metropol-
itan center to a (neocolonial) periphery
that is assumed to be unfamiliar to the au-
thor and his or her readers, black Atlantic
travelers frequently recount journeys in the
opposite direction. But with personal and
family ties to more than one continent, the
question of “home” is often a vexed one.
Alasdair Pettinger

TRINIDAD ANDTOBAGO
The Caribbean islands of T rinidad and
T obago have evolved into a multiracial so-
ciety comprised mostly of East Indian and
African descendants. In 1498, Christopher
Columbus charted the islands during his
exploration of the southern Caribbean, and
the Spanish established a more permanent
outpost in T rinidad after 1514. Hundreds
of Spanish missionaries and planters mi-
grated to T rinidad and T obago, but the
islands’ population remained stagnant until
the late eighteenth century when French
and British colonizers and their African
slaves settled the islands in larger numbers.
As the competition for colonies among
European powers intensiﬁed, the British
Crown, in particular, saw T rinidad and
T obago as a lucrative sugar-growing colony
and as a strategic outpost to challenge
Dutch, Spanish, and Portuguese hegemony
in the southern Caribbean. The British
gained control over French-occupied
T obago by 1763 and took T rinidad from
Spain in 1797. Merchants and planters
quickly established large plantations that
produced sugar to be exported to Great
Britain, Europe, and its North American
colonies. This led to the importation of
more African slaves (which outnumbered
Europeans and Amerindians combined)
until the British declared in 1807 that it
would end its participation in the Atlantic
slave trade.
In 1833, the colonial government
adopted a plan to abolish slavery gradually,
declaring that slaves would be required by
law to remain on plantations for a term of
six years. Nonviolent slave resistance has-
tened the death of this scheme, and by
1838, T rinidad became the ﬁrst British
colony to end chattel slavery. Still, British
administrators did not want abolition and
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1159 ---
TRINIDAD ANDTOBAGO 1071
the rise of a free Afro-T rinidadian laboring
class to threaten the ﬂow of sugar exports,
and they immediately turned to the impor-
tation of indentured laborers from other
parts of the Empire. Between 1838 and
1917, the colonial government authorized
the importation of more than 145,000
Chinese laborers; yet, East Indians (mainly
Hindus) constituted the largest contin-
gency of these migrants. By 1900, East
Indians constituted one-third of T rinidad’s
population.
Building on their success in preventing
the rise of an Afro-T rinidadian laboring
class through the creation of a class of in-
dentured laborers, the British continued to
enforce labor control policies as sugar culti-
vation gradually gave way to cacao produc-
tion, a more proﬁtable commodity. Admin-
istrators viewed African and East Indian
aspirations and rituals as challenges to colo-
nial rule. Carnival celebrations in T rinidad
were closely monitored. In 1884, the
Muharram Massacre chilled relations be-
tween the growing East Indian community
and the British Crown. As Hindus and
Muslims and many Afro-T rinidadians joined
together to commemorate Muharram, the
ﬁrst month of the Islamic calendar, colonial
forces opened ﬁre on a crowd and killed
almost two dozen East Indians.
In the 1920s and 1930s, labor unrest
continued with the decline in prices for the
colony’s agricultural commodities. Afro- and
Indo-T rinidadian labor unions organized for
better wages and working conditions in key
sectors of the economy, including the bur-
geoning oil industry. These efforts later
helped bolster the aspirations of many
Afro-T rinidadian politicians, including
T ubal Uriah “Buzz” Butler, leader of the
British Empire Citizens’ and Workers’
Home Rule Party, and Eric Williams, head
of the People’s National Movement (PNM),
the most successful party.
The variety of ethnic and racial groups
resulted in signiﬁcant overlap in the popu-
lation’s cultural, religious, and social tradi-
tions. Inﬂuenced by the Afro-T rinidadian
population, drum music emerged in the
early nineteenth century and continued to
develop into steel drum music by the
1940s. The Orisha (Shango) religion has its
origins in African, Roman Catholic, Hindu,
Protestant, and Kabbalah traditions. Food
in T rinidad and T obago, such as curried
goat and roti,clearly has East Indian origins.
The national musical style, calypso, origi-
nated in the late nineteenth century, and in
the twentieth century, calypso performers
such as the Lord Melody, Lord Invader,
Mighty Sparrow, and Lord Kitchener had
perfected the craft of inserting political cri-
tique into their entertaining lyrics and
spreading news under the guise of song.
By the early 1940s, support for politi-
cal independence from the British gained
momentum. The British were clearly de-
clining as a world power as the United
States looked to expand its markets in the
hemisphere. When World War II ended,
nationalist movements in T rinidad and
T obago mirrored those of the Caribbean,
Africa, and Asia. In 1956, the British al-
lowed T rinidad and T obago to join the West
Indian Federation. This effort collapsed
partly because T rinidad wanted to develop
its petroleum industry, and T rinidad and
T obago ultimately decided together to de-
clare independence in 1962.
Eric Williams, author of the seminal
work Capitalism and Slavery(1944), became
the country’s ﬁrst prime minister, and he
had to cope with deep racial and ethnic divi-
sions. He was a skilled politician who ably
brought together disparate Afro-T rinidadian
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1160 ---
1072 T RUTH AND RECONCILIATION COMMISSIONS
groups into the PNM; however, East
Indian politicians and writers, such as Hari
Prasad Singh, criticized Williams and
other black leaders for excluding their in-
terests. East Indian cultural retention re-
mained high as the development of the
communities of Banara, Chapra, Ballia,
Gorakhpur, and Patna attests. Williams
was also challenged by a Black Power
movement, which had developed in the
context of other movements in North
America and the Caribbean. In 1970,
Geddes Granger (now Makandal Daaga)
and others led mass demonstrations
sparked by the arrest of T rinidadian stu-
dents in Canada. These demonstrations
led to riots and looting, paralyzing the
country until the Williams government de-
clared a state of emergency. From the
1980s onward, racial divisions continued
to affect the development of T rinidad and
T obago. Some Afro-T rinidadians have
gravitated toward Muslim organizations,
such as the Jamaat al Muslimeen. One of
its leaders, Imam Yasin Abu Bakr, led a
failed coup attempt in 1990.

TRUTH AND RECONCILIATION
COMMISSIONS
Since 1974, more than 20 ofﬁcially sanc-
tioned truth and reconciliation commis-
sions have been established in various parts
of the Americas and Africa in the aftermath
of ethnic cleansings and conﬂicts, state terror,
genocides, and widespread abductions, dis-
appearances, tortures, and detentions. These
commissions tend to be ad hoc tribunals
that are granted a variety of extrajudicial re-
sponsibilities and functions, which include
the investigation of past human rights viola-
tions or atrocities within a particular setting
and historical time period. Yet, within these
broad parameters, truth commissions may
also investigate groups or individuals that
have engaged in state-sponsored acts of
widespread violence.
In the last several decades, truth and
reconciliation commissions have been initi-
ated by several types of groups and organi-
zations. They have emerged as a result of in-
ternational pressure from nongovernmental
organizations (NGOs), as in the case of
Rwanda and Paraguay in the 1990s. Inter-
national bodies, such as the United Nations,
have also mandated the creation of commis-
sions to investigate human rights abuses and
atrocities (e.g., El Salvador in 1992). T ruth
and reconciliation commissions have also
emerged as part of peace agreements be-
tween political groups in the ﬁnal stages of
long-lasting political conﬂicts. For example,
South Africa’s T ruth and Reconciliation
Commission was charged with investigating
abuses committed by the apartheid govern-
ment. In 1995, this commission was ofﬁ-
cially sanctioned by the majority party, the
African National Congress, when it gained
control of the government.
The leaders and members of these
commissions are a diverse lot. They are
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1161 ---
TRUTH AND RECONCILIATION COMMISSIONS 1073
usually prominent ex-politicians, academi-
cians, grassroots leaders, lawyers, judges,
human rights and peace activists, and lead-
ers of international organizations. In some
cases, religious leaders, such as Archbishop
Desmond T utu in South Africa and
Cardinal Paulo Evaristo Arns of Brazil,
have accepted prominent roles as heads of
commissions of inquiries in their respective
countries.
Typically, truth and reconciliation
commissions issue ﬁnal reports that re-
count speciﬁc past episodes of violence
committed against civilian populations,
but the outcomes of these reports are just as
diverse as the purposes of these commis-
sions. Final reports usually include bio-
graphical information about perpetrators
and victims and their testimony; statistical
and demographic information about the
dead, wounded, tortured, and raped; and
an assessment on the political, psychologi-
cal, and social impact that these events had
on society. Yet, there is no requirement for
what type of information is released to the
public. Commissions in Argentina and
Chile did not publicly issue the names of
perpetrators, while South Africa’s commis-
sion did. Thus, truth and reconciliation
commissions largely act as vehicles for ofﬁ-
cially recognizing past human rights abuses
and atrocities and for disseminating this
past to the public. The emphasis is usually
on commemorating and remembering
those who were victimized rather than
seeking retributive justice against those sus-
pected of committing human rights abuses
and violations. In fact, truth and reconcili-
ation commissions are rarely given full legal
authority to subpoena, convict, punish, or
jail suspects of human rights violations, al-
though South Africa’s commission was
given the power to grant immunity.
Because they vary in purpose and
powers, truth and reconciliation commis-
sions are difﬁcult to assess and remain con-
troversial. They usually are created within
the context of dramatic political shifts,
such as transitions from authoritarian to
democratic regimes. T ruth commissions
often create high expectations that perpe-
trators of human rights abuses will be
caught and punished for their crimes.
However, these commissions are almost al-
ways plagued by pressures and limitations,
such as the inexperience of commissioners,
the capacity of processing hundreds or
thousands of complaints, staff corruption,
poor budgets, and military or police intim-
idation. In addition, testimony is very dif-
ﬁcult to elicit from both perpetrators and
victims. Eliciting cooperation is especially
challenging when democratically elected
leaders pardon those who participated in
atrocities and human rights abuses. Perpe-
trators may escape judgment or decide not
to testify without some agreement in place
to provide blanket amnesty or immunity
from future prosecution. If some type of
immunity is granted, then victims and
their supporters may feel betrayed by this
and lose faith in the new regime and per-
haps in democracy itself if the new regime
is democratically elected. Perpetrators may
also feel the need to justify what they did in
the name of security, safety, anticommu-
nism, nationalism, and war. Various mili-
tary ofﬁcials who appeared before the com-
missions in disparate places like South
Africa and Argentina have justiﬁed their
acts by claiming that they were ﬁghting to
save their countries from subversive ele-
ments and that they were vested with emer-
gency powers to protect national security.
The ﬁrst truth commissions that ap-
peared in Latin America were established in
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1162 ---
1074 T RUTH AND RECONCILIATION COMMISSIONS
Bolivia and Argentina in the early 1980s.
The most widely publicized truth and
reconciliation commission occurred in
Argentina after Raúl Alfonsín, the ﬁrst civil-
ian president elected after the military ruled
between 1976 and 1982, appointed the
National Commission of the Disappeared
in 1983. What emerged was a seminal doc-
ument titled Nunca Más (translated as
Never Again), which recounted testimony
of those who were tortured. A growing
number of commissions in Brazil, Chile,
Ecuador, Guatemala, Haiti, Panama, and
Peru during the 1990s have also investi-
gated past abuses. In most cases, the results
of these investigations show that members
of the government and the military
committed most of the atrocities. In El
Salvador, for example, the United Nations-
sponsored truth commission found that
85 percent of the 900,000 human rights
violations and 95 percent of the thousands
of deaths occurred at the hands of govern-
ment-sponsored death squads. In addition,
as with the cases of Argentina and Peru,
most of the victims had little to do with the
political conﬂicts of the time.
In Africa since the 1990s, truth and
reconciliation commissions have been set
up in Chad, Ghana, Nigeria, Sierra Leone,
Uganda, and Zimbabwe. However, South
Africa’s T ruth and Reconciliation Commis-
sion is the most widely recognized. It was
headed by Archbishop Desmond T utu and
focused primarily on gathering testimony
from victims and perpetrators alike on
human rights abuses during the years of
apartheid in the country. In a controversial
move, Archbishop T utu granted full immu-
nity to those who committed human rights
abuses in exchange for their testimony. This
appeal to the Christian idea of forgiveness
and reconciliation clashed with the local,
alternative African value of ubuntu, which
called for punishment. Still, the procedures
of South Africa’s commission have been
modeled in other parts of Africa and
elsewhere.
A variety of groups and individuals
have called for new truth and reconciliation
or similar types of commissions of inquiry
to be established in a variety of Latin
American and African countries including
Angola, Cambodia, Colombia, Jamaica,
Kenya, Mexico, Morocco, Sudan, Uganda,
Venezuela, and Zimbabwe. Recently, in the
United States, leaders of grassroots organi-
zations have asked the government for an
ofﬁcial apology for past atrocities commit-
ted against American Indians or African
Americans. However, since the end of
World War II, the U.S. government has
consistently decided to grant reparations
rather than establish ofﬁcially sponsored
truth commissions as a means of making
amends for past injustices. For example,
millions of dollars have been given to
Japanese Americans who were interned dur-
ing World War II. The state of Maryland
has given more than $16 million to histor-
ically black colleges in order to correct past
inequities in funding them. Still, many
truth and reconciliation commissions have
been founded as result of grassroots move-
ments. While these efforts are not usually
officially sanctioned, they have raised
awareness about past injustices. In
Oklahoma, for example, the T ulsa Race
Riot Commission recommended that repa-
rations be paid to the family members of
those who were lynched during the T ulsa
riots of 1921. In Greensboro, North
Carolina, a truth and reconciliation commis-
sion, modeled after similar efforts in Peru
and South Africa, met to hear testimony
from perpetrators and victims in the 1979

TRUTH,S OJOURNER
(1797–1883)
Sojourner T ruth (Isabella Braumfree) was
an African American escaped slave, aboli-
tionist speaker, and preacher. She was the
second youngest child born to slave parents
in Ulster County, New York, a Dutch set-
tlement. She spoke only Dutch until she
was sold at age 11 in 1806. She quickly
learned to speak English, but never learned
to read or write. She was sold numerous
times, and many of her owners treated her
poorly. When she reached adulthood she
stood 5 feet and 11 inches tall. She was
forced to marry Thomas, and bore him ﬁve
children on the Durmont farm. When
New York ended slavery in 1828, she feared
her owner had no intention of following
the freedom granted by the law. She ﬂed
A poster celebrating Sojourner Truth’s ﬁght for suffrage,
and commemorating her famous “Ain’t I a Woman?”
speech at the 1851 Women's Rights Convention in
Akron, Ohio. It would not be until 1920 that women
of all races received the right to vote through the
Nineteenth Amendment. (Library of Congress)
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

with only her infant son to New York City,
where she found domestic work. During
the next two years, she sued to regain her
son who had been sold into slavery, found
refuge from a couple who bought her and
gave her freedom, and had a religious expe-
rience that she explained allowed her to talk
directly to God. In 1843 she changed her
name to Sojourner T ruth and walked from
Long Island to Connecticut preaching on
antislavery and women’s suffrage. In 1851
she gave her most notable speech, “Ain’t I a
Woman?” After the Civil War, T ruth
worked with freed slaves. She died in
November 1883 in Battle Creek, Michigan.

TUBMAN,H ARRIET
(CA. 1820–1913)
Harriet T ubman (Araminta Ross) was an
abolitionist leader and conductor on the
Underground Railroad. She was born into
slavery in Dorchester County, Maryland. As
a child she worked as a house servant and
ﬁeld hand. At the age of 13 she suffered a
vicious assault, which caused her to have
fainting spells throughout the rest of her life.
She married John T ubman, a free man, in
1844, who later died. Fearing she would be
sold South, she made her escape to Canada
in 1849 on the Underground Railroad, a
system of safe holdings that allowed free per-
sons and slaves to escape from the South to
the North. Working with leaders of the anti-
slavery movement, she successfully assisted
members of her family in their relocation to
St. Catharine’s, Canada. During her 19 re-
turns to Maryland over a 10-year period as a
conductor on the Underground Railroad,
she helped free an estimated 300 individuals.
During the Civil War, in 1861, she served as
spy, cook, nurse, and soldier. After the war,
she moved to Auburn, New York, and mar-
ried Nelson Davis in 1869. From the Civil
War period on, she spoke for the antislavery
cause and the women’s movement. She died
in poverty on March 10, 1913, and was
buried in Fort Hill Cemetery in Auburn.
Laura Madeline Wiseman

TUNISIA 1077
TUNISIA
T unisia, in North Africa, is bordered by
Algeria to the west and Libya to the east,
and has a population of about 9,975,000.
Most of the population lives in the northern
region around the capital T unis and in the
east along the Mediterranean coast. Most
of the south is part of the Sahara Desert.
T unisia’s ties to the United States are histor-
ically distinctive as part of naval and diplo-
matic history.
T unisia has long ties to Mediterranean
culture. In classical times, T unisia was the
center of the Carthaginian Empire, later
conquered and occupied by the Romans.
After the conquest of Rome by the Vandals
in the seventh century, T unisia became part
of the Arabic world, and eventually the
Ottoman Empire.
In the 1780s, corsairs (considered pi-
rates by Europeans and Americans) started
seizing U.S. ships off the T unisian coast. In
1790, the U.S. government signed a treaty
with the T unisian leader Hamuda Bey, pay-
ing $100,000 to prevent future attacks on
their shipping. From 1801 to 1805, the
United States was involved in the T ripolitan-
American War, ﬁghting pirates operating
from ports in North Africa. On August 1,
1805, Commodore John Rodgers in the
USS Constitutionsailed into T unis and forced
Bey to make peace.
In 1881, the French occupied and col-
onized T unisia. During World War II, after
the fall of France to Germany in 1940,
T unisia was run by a Vichy French admin-
istration. British and American forces in-
vaded in 1943. In Operation T orch, U.S.,
Canadian, and British soldiers attacked
from the west, with British, Indian, and
New Zealand soldiers from the east. Many
U.S. soldiers were killed in the campaign,
especially at the Kasseine Pass. A number of
the dead remain buried in the North Africa
Cemetery at Carthage. Run by the Ameri-
can Battle Monuments Commission, it
contains the graves of 2,841 U.S. service-
men. In a notable advance in the history of
ﬁlm-making, Allied soldiers in T unisia dur-
ing the war were ﬁlmed by the U.S. ﬁlm
producer Darryl Zanuck.
After the end of World War II, T unisia
sought independence. It was granted on
March 20, 1956, with Habib Bourguiba
becoming the nation’s ﬁrst president. Prior
to independence, Bourguiba had visited the
United States to get support for T unisian
independence, but the U.S. government
was committed to supporting France.
However, Bourguiba, after independence,
received in total some $1 billion in U.S.
aid. Bourguiba remained head of state for
30 years. He was deposed in a bloodless
coup in November 1987.
The prime minister, Zine Al-Abidine
Ben Ali, became the new president. A for-
mer student of electronic engineering at the
School of Intelligence and Security in the
United States, he created close relations
with the Reagan and Bush administrations.
T unisia has maintained good relations with
the United States in spite of tensions that
arose from the U.S. bombing of Libya in
1986. In recent years there have been some
anti-U.S. demonstrations by Muslim radi-
cals. Nonetheless, T unisia has remained po-
litically stable and continued to have strong
diplomatic and cultural ties to the ties to
the United States and Canada.
Justin Corﬁeld

T errorism; World War II

TURNER,N AT (1800–1831)
In 1831, Nat T urner led one of the most fa-
mous and bloody slave rebellions in North
American history. T urner had been born a
slave in Southampton, Virginia, in 1800.
He learned how to read as a child, and as an
adult became a preacher among the local
slaves. As he began to develop plans for an
organized slave rebellion, his leadership
role among the slaves was instrumental.
T urner experienced a number of spiri-
tual revelations he took as signs for a slave
rebellion. Around midnight on August 22,
1831, his revolt went into action as a hand-
ful of slaves crept into the home of T urner’s
owner, Samuel T ravis, and killed the white
family in their beds. From there, the group
moved from farm to farm, attacking whites
and gathering weapons and more rebels.
Over the next two days, T urner’s force skir-
mished with armed whites and local militia
units. By August 31, most of the rebels had
been captured, except for T urner who
eluded pursuers until October 31 by hiding
in the surrounding swamps. Once appre-
hended, he was executed less than two
weeks later.
Around 70 slaves had joined the revolt,
and around 60 whites, many of them
women and children, had been killed. seven-
teen rebels, including T urner, were executed,
and 12 more were sent out of Virginia.
T urner’s revolt caused a white backlash
against blacks. White vigilantes rounded up
hundreds of blacks for questioning and tor-
ture, killing many of them. Fear of further
slave revolts swept across the South and led
to increased tension. It also temporarily led
some Virginians to openly question the
future of slavery in their state, and a politi-
cal debate ensued in 1832. However,
Virginians voted to maintain slavery and
enacted laws to further repress slaves and
free blacks.
Ian M. Spurgeon
