TUSKEGEE AIRMEN
The T uskegee Airmen were African
American ofﬁ cers who established distin-
guished ﬂying records in the U.S. Army Air
Corps. These men formed the ﬁrst all-black
ﬂying units in the U.S. Armed Forces. In
1941–1946, more than 2,000 African
Americans trained as military personnel at
T uskegee Institute in Alabama. Three-
quarters were pilots (T uskegee Airmen), and
the rest were navigators, bombardiers, gun-
ners, radiomen, and mechanics (airmen).
These brave men countered the racist
stereotype that blacks lacked the mental and
physical acumen to ﬂy combat missions. At
a time when Jim Crow laws separated blacks
from whites in the military, black civic
leaders and organizations pressured the U.S.
War Department to implement training for
black pilots and personnel.
On January 19, 1941, 13 African
American men formed the ﬁrst class of
trainees. Fifteen grueling weeks later, only
ﬁve men graduated at the T uskegee Army
Air Field. Among the new pilots was
Benjamin O. Davis Jr., who later became
commander of the 99th Fighter Squadron.
In the ﬁve-year existence of the rigorous
training program at T uskegee, 992 black
ﬁghter pilots successfully graduated.
Negro Air Corps cadets, the Tuskegee Airmen undergo training in Tuskegee, Alabama, 1942. (National Archives)
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1168 ---
1080 T USKEGEE INSTITUTE
Once engaged in combat during World
War II, these men garnered many awards,
citations, and honors. Collectively, the
T uskegee Airmen, aided by their crews,
ﬂew 1,578 missions, 15,333 sorties, de-
stroyed 261 enemy aircraft, and won over
850 medals, including 150 Distinguished
Flying Crosses. The 332nd Fighter Group
holds the distinction of never losing an es-
corted bomber to enemy ﬁre.

TUSKEGEE INSTITUTE
On July 4, 1881, the T uskegee Normal and
Industrial Institute opened on the grounds
of the Butler Chapel AME Zion Church.
Lewis Adams, a former slave, made a deal
with state senator W . F . Foster to secure the
vote of Macon County African Americans
in return for a permanent coeducational
school. Foster and fellow representative
Arthur Brooks then drafted and passed
Alabama House Bill 165, creating the insti-
tution and appropriating money for teach-
ers’ salaries. That appropriation brought
Booker T . W ashington to the school.
Washington soon purchased a nearby
abandoned plantation to serve as the cam-
pus of the institute, an area that still serves
as the nucleus of the school. Washington’s
tenure lasted until his death in 1915, and
during that time the institute’s principal
expanded the faculty, student body, and
campus. Washington helped develop
African American education throughout
the South, emphasizing the need for black
self-sufﬁciency through the development
of black business. He stressed the need for
practicality in education, a philosophy ex-
emplified by the institute’s botanist,
George Washington Carver. Carver taught
botany and agriculture, encouraging his
students to replace cotton crops with
protein-rich soybeans and peanuts. Along
with agriculture, the institute had a pilot
training program, which brought a con-
tract from the U.S. Army to train African
American aviators for military service. The
program produced the T uskegee Airmen,
who were members of the 332nd Fighter
Group that fought with distinction in the
European theater of World War II. The in-
stitute became a National Historic Site in
1974 and changed its name to T uskegee
University in 1985.
Thomas Aiello

TUSKEGEE SYPHILIS
EXPERIMENT
The “T uskegee Syphilis Study” was a non-
therapeutic study to examine the progres-
sion of untreated late-stage syphilis in
African American men. It was conducted
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1169 ---
TUTSI 1081
from 1932 to 1972 in Macon County,
Alabama, by the U.S. Public Health Service
in conjunction with T uskegee Institute. Six
hundred men were enrolled in the study;
399 suffered from late-stage syphilis and
201 were uninfected. The infected men
were not informed that they had syphilis—
they were simply told they had “bad
blood”—nor were they offered any treat-
ment for the fatal disease. They may also
have been actively discouraged from receiv-
ing treatment from other physicians.
When news of the study broke in
1972, the American public was outraged to
ﬁnd that therapeutic treatment, which had
been readily available since at least the
1940s, had been withheld from partici-
pants, many of whom were poor and illiter-
ate. For African Americans already wary of
the medical community, the revelation of
the Public Health Service’s apparent indif-
ference to the health of these men inspired
further distrust.
The study did have one positive effect.
Public concern about lax protocols and po-
tential harm motivated the U.S. govern-
ment to reevaluate standards for federally
supported studies involving human sub-
jects. The changes made included requiring
proof of informed consent by subjects and
mandatory review of all proposed studies
by groups called independent review
boards (IRBs). These new standards en-
courage ethical treatment of subjects, and
help to make certain that people are aware
of the potential beneﬁts and risks of partic-
ipation in research.
Katherine Bobo

TUTSI
Although a minority population in both
nations, the T utsi have largely dominated
the central African nations of Burundi and
Rwanda. In Rwanda, they constitute less
than 10 percent of the population, and in
Burundi, just over 10 percent. There has
been considerable controversy about the
origins of the T utsi. Early scholars believed
that the T utsi had Hamitic origins, migrat-
ing into central Africa from an ancestral
homeland in the Sudan or Ethiopia. But
more recent researchers have discovered
that there are few physical and cultural dif-
ferences between the T utsi and the Hutu,
who are the majority population in both
Burundi and Rwanda. They have largely
discounted the superﬁcial physical differ-
ences between the two peoples. The T utsi
do tend to be somewhat taller and leaner,
but this difference in the body types has
now been attributed largely to differences
in diet.
It is widely agreed that the T utsi en-
tered central Africa in the sixteenth cen-
tury and fairly quickly dominated the
much more numerous, loosely unified
Hutu. The T utsi placed a higher value on
warrior skills. Whereas the Hutu were pre-
dominantly farmers, the T utsi were herders.
Indeed, under T utsi rule, the Hutu also
adopted T utsi emphasis on cattle as a mea-
sure of wealth. The T utsi dominated the
central African hill country up until the
Germans, and then the Belgians, asserted
colonial control over the region. Favored
by the colonizers with whom they made
accommodations, the T utsi maintained
their privileged position after Burundi and
Rwanda became independent in the early
1960s.
In the late 1950s, the early 1970s, and
the mid-1990s, the Hutu revolted violently
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1170 ---
1082 T UTU,D ESMOND
against T utsi rule, but in each case were
crushed by the T utsi ability to marshal
superior military force. In fact, while in-
ternational sympathy may have been
largely with the majority Hutu, the car-
nage of the mid-1990s reached the level of
a genocide, and sympathies shifted largely
to the victims, both the T utsi and Hutus
whose loyalties to their respective ethnici-
ties had been brought into question. With
a total death toll in the hundreds of thou-
sands, the conﬂict between the T utsi and
the Hutu stands as one of the bloodiest
ethnic conﬂicts of the post–World War II
period.
Martin Kich

TUTU,D ESMOND (1931–)
Desmond Mpilo T utu is a South African
priest who became the ﬁrst African arch-
bishop of Cape T own. He was a vocal op-
ponent of apartheid as well as the chair of
South Africa’s T ruth and Reconciliation
Commission following the end of the
apartheid regime. A charismatic speaker, he
received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1984 for
his leading role in the struggle against
apartheid.
T utu was born in Klerksdorp, in the
province of T ransvaal. T utu’s father was a
teacher, and his mother was a domestic
worker for white families. The family
eventually moved to Krugersdorp, near
Johannesburg, and T utu attended Western
Native T ownship High School, the only
public high school for Africans in the area.
During a lengthy convalescence from
tuberculosis, T utu was befriended by the
Anglican priest T revor Huddleston, who be-
came a major ﬁgure in the struggle against
apartheid, ﬁrst in South Africa and then in
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1171 ---
TUTU,D ESMOND 1083
his native Britain. Huddleston was one of
T utu’s role models, and they maintained a
lifelong friendship.
When T utu graduated from high
school, he became one of 0.5 percent of
Africans to qualify for admission to univer-
sity that year. He originally enrolled in
medical school at the University of the
Witwatersrand but was unable to afford the
tuition. Instead, he pursued a teaching
diploma from Bantu Normal College near
Pretoria, enrolling there in 1951. This was
around the time that the formal apartheid
system was being implemented through
such measures as the Prohibition of Mixed
Marriages Act (1949), the Population
Registration Act (1950), the Group Areas
Act (1950), the Bantu Education Act
(1951), and the Reservation of Separate
Amenities Act (1953), all of which sepa-
rated the races geographically and socially
and insured the inferiority of public ser-
vices provided to Africans.
T utu was not politically active as a stu-
dent at Bantu Normal College, though he
and his colleagues were concerned about
the deepening divide in South Africa. He
taught English and Afrikaans at his old
high school upon ﬁnishing his diploma,
but he continued his education via corre-
spondence courses, earning his BA from
the University of South Africa in 1954. The
following year, he married Leah Nomalizo
Shenxane, also a teacher. Both, however, re-
signed their teaching posts in 1958 in re-
sponse to the implementation of the Bantu
Education Act, which guaranteed inferior
education for Africans.
Following his resignation, T utu de-
cided to become a priest. He entered the
Anglican St. Peter’s Theological College in
Johannesburg. Shortly after being or-
dained, he received scholarships to attend
King’s College at the University of London
to pursue a degree in theology. He attended
King’s College from 1962 to 1966, and also
served as a curate at St. Alban’s Church,
ministering to a predominantly white con-
gregation for the ﬁrst time. He credited his
time in London with developing his conﬁ-
dence in interacting with whites on an
equal basis. He also made an effort to edu-
cate his parishioners about the situation in
South Africa. He left London with a mas-
ter’s degree that focused on Islam, having
set himself the objective to become more
familiar with this important African and
global religion.
Head of the Anglican Church in southern Africa and
archbishop of Cape T own until mid-1996, Desmond
Tutu received the 1984 Nobel Prize for peace for his
nonviolent opposition to apartheid and was one of the
major ﬁgures in the struggle for black liberation.
(AFP/Getty Images)
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1172 ---
1084 T UTU,D ESMOND
While T utu was in London, the situa-
tion in South Africa had deteriorated. The
African National Congress (ANC) and the
Pan Africanist Congress (PAC) had both
been banned, and many antiapartheid
activists were either in jail or exile, or had
been killed. T utu’s ﬁrst position on his re-
turn was teaching at the Federal Theological
Seminary in Alice, in the Eastern Cape. He
also became the Anglican chaplain at Fort
Hare, the only university in South Africa
open to Africans. Fort Hare was becoming a
major center for the black consciousness
movement, which held that blacks needed
to develop their own ideas and take their
own initiative in the antiapartheid struggle.
Steven Biko, whom T utu came to greatly
admire, was the movement’s most famous
leader. T utu earned the respect of move-
ment leaders by speaking against apartheid
in his sermons and by supporting the
students in a strike against the university
administration. He also began thinking
more deeply about the role of Christian
churches in the struggle against apartheid,
feeling that it was the responsibility of
Christians to oppose the oppressive system
of rule.
In 1970, T utu was invited to become
a lecturer at an institution that became
known as the University of Botswana,
Lesotho, and Swaziland, which was located
in Roma, Lesotho, a former British protec-
torate entirely surrounded by South Africa.
During this time, T utu began making con-
tributions to black theology, which was de-
veloping in southern Africa as a way of
addressing the needs of oppressed black
populations. T utu saw black theology as a
means to restore the dignity and hope that
many black South Africans had lost under
apartheid rule. He developed a theological
model based on Ubuntu, a word from the
Zulu and Xhosa languages that refers to hu-
mans in community with each other, rather
than the individualistic approach to salva-
tion of Western theology.
T utu left Lesotho in 1972, when he
was offered a position as associate director
of the World Council of Churches’ Theo-
logical Education Fund in London. This
move began a long association with the
World Council of Churches (WCC), an or-
ganization that openly opposed apartheid
and supported the ANC and PAC after
they had been banned.
T utu remained in London until he was
offered the position of Anglican dean of
Johannesburg in 1975; he became the ﬁrst
African to serve in that position. He and
his wife settled in Soweto, a black township
near Johannesburg, rather than live in the
dean’s residence in the wealthy white sub-
urb of Houghton. T utu used his new pub-
lic position to become more politically out-
spoken, openly expressing his idea that
white freedom depended on black freedom.
Sensing growing unrest among Africans in
Soweto and other townships, he wrote a
letter to Prime Minister B. J. Vorster urging
him to take steps toward making South
Africa a more just society, but his sugges-
tions were ignored. Shortly after this, in
June 1976, the Soweto riots broke out and
more than 170 people were killed, mostly
young students.
Just before the riots, T utu had been
elected bishop of Lesotho. He moved to
Lesotho in July 1976, but returned to
South Africa in 1978 when he was asked
to become the secretary general of the
South African Council of Churches
(SACC), the country’s chapter of the
World Council of Churches, a position
he held until 1984. As secretary general,
he traveled widely, although his passport
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1173 ---
TUTU,D ESMOND 1085
was confiscated several times by the
South African government. He advocated an
international response to apartheid in the
form of economic pressure and sanctions,
particularly during his trips to Europe
and the United States. Within South
Africa, the SACC openly criticized apartheid
and the speciﬁc government policies that
supported it. T utu’s proﬁle rose dramatically
during this time, both internationally and
among black South Africans. His speeches
emphasized racial reconciliation, rather
than conﬂict or revenge, and the need for
both blacks and whites to build a just
society.
T utu took several trips to the United
States in the early 1980s, educating
Americans about the situation in South
Africa. This was during the era of P . W .
Botha’s “reform apartheid” and President
Ronald Reagan’s policy of “constructive
engagement,” under which the U.S. gov-
ernment supported the South African gov-
ernment economically and militarily. In his
public speeches and meetings with American
ofﬁcials, T utu emphasized that oppression
of Africans in South Africa continued
unchecked and that international pressure
in the form of economic sanctions and pri-
vate divestment was the best way to bring
apartheid to an end.
During a sabbatical at General Theo-
logical Seminary in New York City in
1984, T utu received the news that he had
been awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in
recognition of his work against apartheid.
This award gave him much more interna-
tional clout; he was even invited to meet
with President Reagan, though the latter
did not change his mind about the U.S.
relationship with South Africa. Reagan con-
tinued to oppose sanctions against South
Africa, though he was eventually overruled
when Congress passed the Comprehensive
Anti-Apartheid Act in October 1986. T utu
continued to speak out about apartheid,
despite the South African government’s
efforts to discredit him, and he continued
to press for stronger economic sanctions. In
the meanwhile, he rose through the ranks
of the Anglican Church, becoming bishop
of Johannesburg in 1985 and archbishop of
Cape T own in 1986.
In 1990, President de Klerk began the
process of dismantling the apartheid sys-
tem, paving the way for negotiations with
the ANC, led by Nelson Mandela, for a
new constitution and government. Dur-
ing the transition period, T utu continued
to speak in favor of racial reconciliation
and against the government, whose sincer-
ity he questioned. He retired as arch-
bishop of Cape T own in 1996, and was
appointed chair of the T ruth and Recon-
ciliation Commission (TRC) by President
Mandela. The purpose of the TRC was to
bring about a process of reconciliation and
forgiveness by granting amnesty to perpe-
trators of racial crimes under apartheid if
they made a full disclosure. The TRC also
offered reparations to victims of these
crimes. T utu led the commission until it
submitted its final report in October
1998. While polls indicated that South
Africans believed the TRC had worsened
race relations in South Africa, T utu main-
tained that reconciliation is a slow process
that cannot occur without exposing the
truth.
Following his retirement, T utu contin-
ued to travel the world and speak about
South Africa as a model for conﬂict resolu-
tion. He was visiting professor of theology
at Emory University in Atlanta, Georgia,
from 1998 to 2000, and visiting professor
in postconﬂict societies at King’s College

UGANDA
Located in East Africa and landlocked, the
Republic of Uganda has a population of
about 26,405,000, most of whom are
farmers or involved in the production of
coffee and cotton. The British originally
took over the region in search of the source
of the White Nile, one of the two main
rivers ﬂowing into the Nile, under the lead-
ership of General Charles Gordon (“Gordon
of Khartoum”). The British in the region
were also involved in suppressing the slave
trade. General Gordon had, as his chief of
staff, Charles Chaillé-Long from Somerset
County, Maryland. Chaillé-Long had
fought in the American Civil War and was
the ﬁrst American to reach Buganda. His
accounts of the Upper Nile were published
in a number of books, most important of
which was Central Africa: Naked Truths of
Naked People; An Account of an Expedition to
the Lake Victoria Nyanza(1876).
When the kingdom of Buganda was
involved in dynastic disputes in the 1880s,
the British East Africa Company started to
exert its control over the region. In 1894,
Buganda was declared a protectorate and
had a privileged status in the colony of
Uganda. Some people, including several
Americans, came to Uganda for safaris.
One, William Fitzhugh Whitehouse, wrote
about his time there in Scribner’s Magazine
in 1902. The Africa Inland Mission sent
missionaries from 1918; missionaries to
Uganda have included Ellsworth Faris and
Vincent J. McCauley, who worked with the
Holy Cross Foreign Mission Society in
Uganda 1958–1972.
During World War I, because of the
transatlantic span of the British Empire, a
large number of Britons were posted to
Uganda and Kenya from the Americas, in-
cluding from Argentina. A number of British
administrators in Uganda also had served, or
later served, in the West Indies or South
Atlantic. James Hayes Sadler, commissioner
of Uganda from 1902 to 1905, later was
governor of the Windward Islands; his suc-
cessor, Henry H. J. Bell, the ﬁrst governor of
Uganda, came straight from being governor
of Dominica and went on to be governor of
the Leeward Islands. Bell’s successor, Henry
E. S. Cordeaux went on to be governor of
St. Helena, and then the Bahamas. Uganda’s
wartime governor, Charles C. F . Dundas pre-
viously served as governor of the Bahamas,
where he was replaced by the Duke of
Windsor. Uganda’s last governor, Walter
Fleming Coutts, had also served in the West
Indies as governor of St. Vincent.
On October 9, 1962, Uganda gained
its independence from the British, and in
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1176 ---
1088 U GANDA
the following year became the Republic of
Uganda. Olcott Hawthorne Deming be-
came the ﬁrst U.S. ambassador to Uganda
in the following year, and the U.S. Peace
Corps started work in Uganda from 1964.
Uganda’s ﬁrst president, Sir Edward Mutesa,
was deposed in 1966 and replaced by
Dr. Milton Obote, who ran the country
until he, in turn, was deposed in 1971 by
Idi Amin Dada Oumee (most commonly
known as Idi Amin), an army ofﬁcer.
Soon after coming to power, Amin began
his campaign against the Indians living
in Uganda, who made up the “merchant
class.” Amin expelled them all from the
country, and in 1973, expelled most British
citizens. The work of the Peace Corps
ended as well. Thomas Melady, who was
U.S. ambassador to Uganda in 1972–1973,
spent the ﬁrst part of his posting writing
about his previous ambassadorship in
Burundi; he later coauthored with his wife
Idi Amin: Hitler in Africa (1977).
By 1977 Amin was notorious around
the world for his tyranny, which included
the forced expulsion of Israelis and Asians
from Uganda in 1972. In July 1976, an Air
France plane was hijacked to Entebbe, with
U.S. citizens onboard. Eventually all but
the Israeli passengers were released. On July
4, 1976, the plane was stormed by Israeli
commandos.
Amin, humiliated by world opinion,
stepped up his murders and human rights
abuses. He was denounced by U.S. presi-
dent Jimmy Carter after the Anglican arch-
bishop in Uganda was assassinated. Amin
replied by rounding up all U.S. citizens in
the country. He relented when the United
States sent a naval force to Mombasa and
released them all unharmed. Amin was
overthrown in 1979 when Tanzanian sol-
diers invaded.
Amin’s successor was Yusufu Lule who
was ousted from power two months later
by Godfrey Binaisa. Binaisa had spent
many years in exile from Idi Amin’s regime,
some of that period working for a law ﬁrm
in New York. He himself was overthrown
in May 1980, and went into exile, replaced
by Paulo Muwanga, who set the scene for
Milton Obote returning to power. Eventu-
ally a rebel force invaded Uganda and
Yoweri Museveni came to power in 1986,
stabilizing the country. During the turmoil,
many Ugandans ﬂed overseas. In 1980,
3,804 Ugandans were documented living in
the United States; by 1990, the ﬁgure had
risen to 6,684. Sizable numbers of people
from Uganda, including many Ugandan
Indians, have also settled in Canada.
Since the mid-1990s, Uganda has also
become highly visible internationally for
successes in preventing the spread of
human immunodeﬁciency virus (HIV), one
of the leading public health issues in Africa.
In 1990, Uganda had an infection rate of
approximately 15 percent of its population.
By 2001, this rate had declined to roughly
5 percent. Uganda’s success was due to a
strong government and community-based
education campaign, including sex educa-
tion. In 2005, Uganda became the focus
of signiﬁcant controversy when the United
States began promoting and funding
abstinence-only education programs, forc-
ing substantial changes in Uganda’s HIV
prevention efforts. In the United States and
internationally, researchers and activists
have raised concerns that such a U.S. policy
will undermine Uganda’s success at combat-
ing the spread of HIV .
Justin Corﬁeld

UNITED NATIONS
Founded in San Francisco, California,
through an effort led by the United States
after World War II, the United Nations
(UN) is a multipurpose international orga-
nization with nearly universal membership
among the world’s countries. Established
on October 24, 1945, the original 51 
UN countries committed to preserving
peace through international cooperation
and collective security. It has since grown to
191 participants. Emerging from World
War II’s global devastation, the United
Nations established three primary objec-
tives: protect international peace, promote
prosperity among nations, and publicize
human rights. The United Nations is di-
vided into six major organs: the General
Assembly, the Security Council, the Eco-
nomic and Social Council, the T rusteeship
Council, the International Court of Justice,
and the Secretariat. It also has numerous
subdivisions dedicated to economic devel-
opment, humanitarian issues, women’s is-
sues, arms control, and educational and
cultural development and preservation.
Both Latin America and Africa have
been signiﬁcantly involved in and inﬂu-
enced by the United Nations, but the na-
ture of their interactions has diverged as a
consequence of the history of colonialism.
While many Latin American countries
(notably Argentina, Brazil, Chile, and Cuba)
were among the original UN members,
almost all present-day African states re-
mained under colonial rule in 1945. Latin
American states have frequently used the
United Nations to expand their own inde-
pendent voice by criticizing actions of more
dominant countries such as the United
States. African states have primarily viewed
the United Nations as a source of ﬁnancial
and resource support, and to a lesser extent
almost as a surrogate, but usually pater-
nalistic, colonial power. In some cases, for-
mer European colonial powers have used
their UN roles to perpetuate their political
and commercial inﬂuence on their for-
mer colonies. In contrast to Latin America,
which experienced far less direct UN
political involvement, the United Nations
actively supervised, encouraged, and imple-
mented African decolonization. Justiﬁably,
African states often view the United
Nations’s existence as a contributing fac-
tor for successfully obtaining political
independence.
Another key difference between Latin
American and African-UN relations in-
volves direct diplomatic intervention.
When plagued by military conﬂict, Latin
American states have been less likely to rely
on the United Nations to negotiate or set-
tle the situation, whereas African countries
will either ask or obtain UN assistance.
These differences may be explained by sev-
eral mitigating factors: the youthful state
of African nations, African dependence
on European and U.S. assistance to de-
velop, and Latin America’s different colo-
nial past: Spain primarily had the most
power over the South America continent;
Africa had been divided among many im-
perial nations.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1178 ---
1090 U NITED NATIONS
Since the Berlin West Conference in
1884–1885 that formalized European
claims, Africa has dealt with many colo-
nial masters. Though Latin America dur-
ing that same period of time experienced
substantial internal strife, it had relatively
few foreign or colonial entanglements.
While Latin American states had mixed
emotions regarding U.S. dominance in
the Western Hemisphere, they beneﬁted
from the Monroe Doctrine because it
minimized European imperial ambitions.
The Monroe Doctrine was a U.S. foreign
policy that warned European and other
foreign powers to keep away from the
Western Hemisphere. The U.S. victory in
the 1898 Spanish-American War solidiﬁed
the United States as a colonial power and
effectively drove off any future foreign
incursions into the Western Hemisphere.
Keeping Latin America clear from European
inﬂuence in the twentieth century allowed
it to gradually develop more indepen-
dently, which later contributed to less UN
dependency.
Though African states have beneﬁted
from UN support programs, critics of UN
efforts, such as President Robert Mugabe of
Zimbabwe and President Thabo Mbeki of
South Africa, have sometimes claimed that
UN involvement with their domestic issues
threatens their sovereignty and represents a
new form of colonialism. However, though
foreign assistance is sometimes resented,
can be treated with suspicion, and is por-
trayed as imperialism, most African states
view the United Nations as a reliable source
of much needed assistance. The United
Nations is often more popular with the
people it most directly supports—those
languishing in extreme poverty.
Both African and Latin American
states beneﬁt from UN consultation efforts,
which include actions to help build
economies and stabilize markets. The
United Nations also protects vulnerable
groups such as children, women, refugees,
minorities, the illiterate, and the disabled.
For less developed countries in Latin
America and Africa, these protection mea-
sures are much needed. Over the years, as
an organization, the United Nations has
received eight Nobel prizes for its humani-
tarian efforts, including one in 1974 that
was involved with work in Namibia. In
2001, Ghana-born UN secretary general
Koﬁ Annan shared his Nobel Prize for
Peace with the United Nations. For Africa
and the Americas, the United Nations is
necessary also because it provides the ma-
chinery to establish international technical
and legal standards. The United Nations is
a catalyst for acting upon major global is-
sues such as the environment.
At the same time, the United Nations
remains an instrument of its members,
meaning that the United Nations serves
but does not control its member states. The
UN charter’s strong safeguards for sover-
eignty have unintentionally hindered some
African democratic and political reform
possibilities because it strongly discourages
changes in political borders. The inclina-
tion to not more freely adjust political
boundaries and to maintain the inherited
status quo geographic structure has dis-
couraged African political restructuring,
which could have prevented and mini-
mized ongoing ethnic conﬂict and violent
tribalism. Instead, UN sovereignty safe-
guards effectively reinforce the European-
imposed political boundaries.
Within the UN’s structure, African and
Latin American states can freely participate
and present their views on global policies
and issues. The UN’s General Assembly (GA)
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1179 ---
UNITED NATIONS 1091
is a unique world forum that represents all
member states. Sometimes referred to as a
“parliament of nations,” the world’s most
pressing problems, such as civil wars and
global epidemics, are regularly addressed by
the GA. Because all member states hold
only one vote, the votes often accurately
reﬂect world opinion. If the GA makes
major decisions, such as the budget and
admitting new members, it requires a two-
thirds majority. Minor decisions need only a
simple majority. In recent years, administra-
tive leaders have made special efforts to
reach decisions through consensus rather
than through a formal vote. Though the GA
can meet for emergency sessions anytime,
its regular sessions run from September to
December.
The Security Council’s primary role is
to maintain international peace and secu-
rity. It convenes whenever peace is threat-
ened. Under the UN charter, all member
states are obligated to carry out its decisions.
The SC has ﬁve permanent members: the
United States, the United Kingdom,
France, Russia, and China. Every two years,
the GA elects its ten rotating members.
African nations that have served as rotating
members include the Republic of the
Congo, Tanzania, and Ghana. Argentina
and Peru have served as Latin American
rotating members. The SC’s procedural
matters decisions require an afﬁrmative
vote of at least nine of the 15 members.
Decisions on substantive matters need nine
votes, including the concurring votes of all
ﬁve permanent members. This need for
concurrence is the rule of “Great Power
unanimity,” often referred to as the “veto”
power of a single permanent member.
Therefore, Security Council decisions
cannot be made if any permanent member
vetoes a vote.
If the SC perceives a threat to peace, it
may suggest forms of settlement or under-
take acceptable remedies. During wars, the
SC may attempt to secure a ceaseﬁre, or
it may deploy UN soldiers called peace-
keepers. Some measures to enforce deci-
sions include imposing economic sanc-
tions, arms embargoes, or use of collective
military action. A current African example
is the United Nations Integrated Ofﬁce in
Sierra Leone (UNIOSIL), established on
January 1, 2006, by Security Council reso-
lution 1620 to effectively coordinate the
UN system in Sierra Leone to help consol-
idate peace; to assist the government of
Sierra Leone in strengthening state institu-
tions, rule of law, human rights, and secu-
rity; and to help hold “free and fair elec-
tions” in 2007. UNIOSIL succeeded a
large Sierra Leone UN peacekeeping opera-
tion, UNAMSIL, which was deployed
from October 1999 to December 2005.
Prior to Sierra Leone, the United Nations
has maintained African peacekeeping oper-
ations in the following countries: Angola,
Central African Republic, Chad, Congo,
Liberia, Libya, Mozambique, Namibia,
Rwanda, Uganda, and Somalia. For Latin
America, past UN peacekeeping operations
have been in the following countries:
Dominican Republic, El Salvador,
Guatemala, Haiti, and Nicaragua.
The Economic and Social Council
(ECOSOC) coordinates the UN’s eco-
nomic and social work system. The
ECOSOC strives to foster international
cooperation for development. It cooperates
and consults with nongovernmental orga-
nizations (NGOs) to maintain vital links
between the United Nations and civil
society. Its subordinate bodies focus on a
variety of socioeconomic issues. An exam-
ple of ECOSOC’s most recent signiﬁcant
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1180 ---
1092 U NITED NATIONS
effort is the UN Millennium Development
Goals. By 2015, all UN member states
have pledged to meet eight common de-
velopment goals: (1) eradicate extreme
poverty and hunger; (2) achieve universal
primary education; (3) eliminate gender
disparity in education; (4) reduce child
mortality; (5) improve maternal health;
(6) combat HIV/AIDS, malaria, and other
diseases; (7) ensure environmental sustain-
ability; and (8) develop a global partnership
for economic development. These efforts
address many Latin American and African
developmental problems.
In years past, the T rusteeship Council
provided international supervision for
T rust T erritories administrated by its seven
members to ensure the territories’ prepara-
tion for self-government and independence.
African countries that fell under T rustee
Council supervision included T ogo, Ghana,
Somalia, Cameroon, northern Nigeria,
Tanzania, Rwanda, and Burundi. By 1994,
when all the territories had gained self-
rule, the T rusteeship Council amended its
rules to meet only when the occasion
may require. If future African and Latin
American states experience severe auton-
omy issues, the T rusteeship Council may be
reactivated.
The UN’s main judicial organ is the
International Court of Justice, otherwise
known as the World Court. With 15 judges,
the World Court decides international
disputes. States voluntarily take part in pro-
ceedings, but if a state agrees to participate
it is then obligated to comply with the
World Court’s decisions. The World Court
also writes advisory opinions to the United
Nations.
The Secretariat supervises the UN’s
administrative work as directed by the
GA, SC, and others. The secretary-general
manages its administrative mission. Drawn
from 170 states, the Secretariat consists of
ofﬁces with a total staff of about 7,500
under regular budget, and a nearly equal
number under special funding. UN stafﬁng
guidelines encourage hiring people from
African and Latin American countries.
People from all parts of the world,
regardless of their country of origin’s
wealth, work for the UN Secretariat.
A signiﬁcant accomplishment of the
United Nations is its formulated historic
Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
This document provides the foundation for
all modern human rights efforts. Most
African nations included parts of the
Universal Declaration of Human Rights
in their ofﬁcial constitutions. The strong
inﬂuence of the UN’s human rights policies
are also witnessed in the recent constitu-
tional revisions throughout Latin America.
T o defend the ethics and values of the
United Nations, peacekeeping operations
are vital tools.
Other UN activities include numerous
social and development programs. UN
environmental conventions resulted in
reduced acid rain in Europe and America,
lowered global marine pollution, and
protected the ozone layer. UN agencies
continue to implement numerous develop-
ment projects in a variety of African and
Latin American states. In addition to its
constitutional inﬂuence on developing na-
tions, the UN’s legal successes include more
substantial development of international
law than in all previous history. Regarding
health issues, each year the UN’s immu-
nization program saves three million
children and its food program provides
about a third of global food aid. Also, the
UN’s International Civil Aviation Organi-
zation ensures greater safety for global air
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1181 ---
UNITED NATIONS EDUCATIONAL,S CIENTIFIC, AND CULTURAL ORGANIZATION 1093
travel. Finally, the United Nations provides
a voice for Latin America and Africa’s
smallest, most impoverished states to com-
municate their pressing needs. For the
Americas, Haiti is an ongoing case.
Despite its achievements, the United
Nations still faces various future challenges.
The UN constantly learns from its past
difﬁculties and responds by improving its
rules, methods, organization, and opera-
tions. These adjustments often address the
changing dynamics of an increasingly inter-
dependent world. Though the United
States is not always pleased with all UN de-
cisions, it needs UN support to succeed
with many foreign policy goals. Some
political analysts estimate that the U.S.’s
and UN’s major objectives are roughly
75 percent compatible.
The United Nations may be seen as
Africa and Latin America’s great security
net, benefactor, and promoter. In times of
trouble and crisis, the most dependent
African and Latin American states can call
upon UN assistance without fearing an-
other round of imperialism or nightmarish
exploitation. This world governmental
organization operates with a mixture of
idealism and pragmatism. Africa and Latin
America by most any measurement are net
beneﬁciaries.
Josiah Baker

UNITED NATIONS
EDUCATIONAL,S CIENTIFIC,
AND CULTURAL
ORGANIZATION
The United Nations Educational, Scientiﬁc,
and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) was
ﬁrst discussed on November 16, 1945, and
implemented on December 14, 1946.
UNESCO was a direct response to the
destruction of World War II. The mission
of this new organization, part of the newly
created United Nations, was to restore
educational and cultural structures that
were disrupted by war and neglect.
UNESCO is divided into three
branches: the General Conference, which is
the decision-making body of UNESCO;
the Executive Board, consisting of 58 mem-
ber states; and the Secretariat, elected by
the Executive Board to act as the face of
UNESCO to the world. As UNESCO has
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1182 ---
1094 U NITED STATESCOLORED TROOPS
evolved, it has become the only UN orga-
nization with National Commissions. These
commissions function to communicate
between the organization and the people of
UNESCO member states.
Within the ﬁrst year of UNESCO’s
existence, the organization sent missions
to Austria, Czechoslovakia, Greece, Italy,
Poland, and Yugoslavia. UNESCO sup-
ported reforms in education that included
revised curriculum and textbooks to end
the glamorization of war, the free circula-
tion of books, and the creation of the
Center for Information Service. In 1948,
UNESCO encouraged all of its member
states to provide free compulsory education
to every child. In 1980, UNESCO Publish-
ing started a series of continental histories
by publishing The General History of Africa.
Though its immediate purpose was to
help rebuild war-torn Europe, UNESCO
drew the membership of countries from
around the world. Central and South
American nations have also engaged the
assistance of UNESCO in tackling their
educational and social needs. The similar
political situations of Latin American and
African nations have made these member
states work in unison toward the substan-
tial goals of the organization.
Several scientiﬁc groups within
UNESCO have helped improve scientiﬁc
study and application to everyday life. In
1968, UNESCO held a conference on man
and the environment, which led to the cre-
ation of the Man and the Biosphere program.
This program consists of several hundred nat-
ural areas that attempt to ﬁnd the best possi-
ble approach to sustainable development.
UNESCO works to preserve cultural
values and traditions throughout the world
by protecting language and improving the
dialogue of cultural diversity. The cultural
branch of UNESCO has attempted to
protect dying languages with the Atlas of
Endangered Languages . Cultural diversity
has also been promoted throughout the
organization’s history and has taken form in
the UNESCO Global Alliance for Cultural
Diversity.
Over the last 20 years, questions of
bureaucratic indiscretions and inefﬁcient
management have been raised by some
member states. In 1984, the United States,
along with the United Kingdom and
Singapore, pulled support from UNESCO
claiming that their funds were not being
used properly. Though these organizations
would return as members, their protests
have opened the organization to more
scrutiny about its priorities and money
management.
Nicholas Katers

UNITED STATES
COLORED TROOPS
The United States Colored T roops (USCT)
was a group of black soldiers who served in
the Civil War and struggled for ofﬁcial
recognition. By the end of the American
Civil War, around 180,000 black men had
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1183 ---
UNIVERSAL NEGRO IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION,THE 1095
served in the Union Army. Ofﬁcial recogni-
tion and organization of black troops, how-
ever, had not begun until the second year of
the war. The ﬁrst black units raised for the
Union cause were individual and unautho-
rized attempts by federal ofﬁcials in South
Carolina and Kansas.
During the summer of 1862, Congress
began paving the way for ofﬁcial black mili-
tary service. The ﬁrst recognized black unit
was the First Regiment of the Louisiana
Native Guards, a free black militia unit,
which was sworn into Union service in
September 1862. Still, black military service
was minimal, as no large effort to place the
thousands of willing black men into uni-
form had yet gone into effect. This changed
with enforcement of Abraham Lincoln’s
Emancipation Proclamation in January
1863, which included a special provision
for black soldiers.
T ens of thousands of black volunteers
were placed in all-black units with white
commissioned ofﬁcers. Black soldiers faced
particular hardships and circumstances
unlike those of white soldiers. They were
originally paid less and confronted other
discrimination from white Union soldiers.
They were primarily used for laboring
duties. And, if captured, black soldiers
faced possible execution or enslavement as
the Confederacy originally refused to rec-
ognize black soldiers as legitimate combat-
ants. Still, thousands of black men served
the Union faithfully, taking part in as
many as 449 separate battles and demon-
strating bravery that often won praise from
fellow white soldiers. Approximately
38,000 black soldiers died during the
war—over 2,800 from combat, most others
from disease.
Ian M. Spurgeon

UNIVERSAL NEGRO
IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION,
THE
On August 1, 1914, Marcus Garvey
founded the Universal Negro Improvement
Association (UNIA) in Jamaica. Armed
with the slogan “Africa for Africans,” the
organization aimed at freeing Africa from
European colonization and arranging the
return of all blacks to Africa. Beyond its
idealism, the UNIA had concrete goals
such as improving the social and economic
life of all black people through self-reliance
and nationhood. In North America, the
UNIA had successes in both its labor and
economic struggles. However, due to
strategic problems in and outside the orga-
nization, its success in the United States
was short-lived.
The UNIA came to the United States
during the turbulent decade of the 1910s
when racial violence against African
Americans in northern cities was rampant.
Garvey established a branch of the UNIA
in New York at some point between the
summer of 1917 and early 1918. From the
late 1910s to the early 1920s, the UNIA
developed social and economic projects
that had positive impact on the African
American community. In 1919, the organi-
zation created businesses in trucking and
owned buildings located in New York and
in other cities in the United States, South
America, and the Caribbean. By the end
of the 1920s, UNIA corporations in the
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1184 ---
1096 U RUGUAY
United States employed more than 1,000
African Americans.
In addition, the UNIA helped train
black professionals. The coalition formed
nurses and veterans who supported their
local community through charity and
entertainment projects in social clubs and
churches. In Boston, the association focused
on education of the masses. It created a
Literary and Publicity Club to educate its
members in literary and oratory skills and in
the standard history of the world. The aim
of this education was to give blacks a way to
social success and political awareness.
Furthermore, the UNIA sponsored
programs that sought to improve the work-
ing skills of local black communities. In
New York and other larger cities, the asso-
ciation taught young and adult black
females how to practice military drills and
driving. These women handled cars, taxis,
and ambulances operated by the associa-
tion. In the South, the UNIA had a special
Committee on Social Conditions that ex-
horted adult blacks to build secure homes
where the young could be taught courtesy,
clean speech, correct manners, and good
character, which are elements that Garvey
perceived as the hallmarks of true leaders
and gentlemen.
The success of the UNIA in the United
States was jeopardized by various circum-
stances. First, due to internal mismanage-
ment of funds, the UNIA was bankrupt by
the mid-1920s “with liabilities of over
$200,000.” Second, because of his success
among black people to whom he told that
“Africa is for Africans” and that “being
black is beautiful” Garvey was soon tar-
geted as a troublemaker in America and
abroad. In January 1922, he and three of
his aides had been arrested and convicted
on accusations of mail fraud. These events
precipitated the downfall of the UNIA in
the United States.
Babacar M’Baye

URUGUAY
Since the sixteenth century, African-
descended peoples have profoundly shaped
the historical development of the Banda
Oriental region, today known as Uruguay.
The ﬁrst Africans arrived as acculturated
servants in 1534 with Pedro de Mendoza,
one of the most well-known Spanish ex-
plorers of the River Plate. A century later,
Spanish colonial administrators relied
heavily on African slave labor in establish-
ing settlements. In fact, the very survival of
these colonies depended on slaves as sol-
diers who fought with Spaniards against
hostile indigenous groups. The colony’s
growing demands for workers in the ﬁelds,
mines, and households of the Banda Orien-
tal forced settlers to turn to African-born
slave labor even more. This need for labor
encouraged smuggling, which is the princi-
pal reason why it is so difﬁcult to count
with any precision the number of slaves im-
ported into the region. Locating the place
in Africa where Uruguay’s slaves originated
is difﬁcult at best. Records of slave ship-
ments reveal that they hailed from all parts
of West, Central, and East Africa. Until
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1185 ---
URUGUAY 1097
1810, the port city of Buenos Aires at-
tempted to monopolize the supply of slaves
to inland Spanish settlements, including
the one at Montevideo, now Uruguay’s
main port city and capital. However,
Portuguese slave traders based in Colônia
do Sacramento, a colony situated directly
west of Montevideo, provided an available
yet expensive supply of African slaves to the
region in spite of the Spanish Crown’s best
efforts to stop this practice. Colonial
administrative records show that between
1606 and 1628, only 288 out of 12,778
African slaves were licensed to be sold
within the River Plate. Contraband slave
trade continued well into the seventeenth
and eighteenth centuries as the Dutch and
the British established a greater commercial
presence. Spain eventually adopted a free
trade policy in the late eighteenth century.
As a result, Montevideo evolved as a key
center for the slave trade, and between
1751 and 1810, more than 20,000 slaves
were sold legally in the port city. While
slaves were transported to other regions,
many remained in the area, altering the
country’s demographic situation. Historian
John H. Williams calculated that African-
descended peoples remaining in Montevideo
only numbered 817 by 1800 but grew to
over 2,500 within just a decade later.
Afro-Uruguayans worked in a wide
array of occupations. Most were employed
as domestic slaves and day laborers in
Montevideo’s meat-salting plants, slaugh-
terhouses, workshops, bakeries, and general
stores. Female slaves tended to work as
seamstresses, cooks, laundresses, wet nurses,
and duennas, while males often engaged in
artisan work, tailoring, shoemaking, pest
control, and various jobs at the docks of
Montevideo. Some urban slave owners
allowed their slaves to contract themselves
out and earn a free wage, which allowed
many to buy their freedom. This is why the
urban slavery of Montevideo is often
described as relatively benign compared to
other regions of the Americas. In the hin-
terlands, the Society of Jesus, or the Jesuits,
bought African slaves to work in their
missions and sugar plantations throughout
the River Plate. Consequently, the Jesuits
eventually became the largest slave owners
in the region. Slaves not owned by the
missionary groups on the frontier were
employed as peons and gauchos on large
ranches. The most well-known is Patricio
de Belén, who, in the early nineteenth cen-
tury, achieved the status of foreman and
eventually became the administrator of a
lucrative cattle ranch.
Although a few African slaves achieved
some upward social mobility, this does not
mean that slaves were content with their
condition. Various forms of resistance were
practiced. Enslaved and freed blacks, for
example, stole cattle in order to earn income
and subsistence. African slaves resisted cul-
turally as they preserved their own mixed
forms of ancestral rites, music, and dance.
More violent expressions of resistance, such
as those in the size and scope of Haiti,
Brazil, or the southern United States, were
uncommon in the River Plate. A notable
exception is a slave rebellion that occurred
in Montevideo in 1803 when almost two
dozen enslaved and freed blacks conspired
to leave the port city and settle on a small
island in the River Yi. The Spanish gover-
nor responded by attacking the settlement,
which was ultimately defeated.
Slavery ended gradually in Uruguay
with the establishment of so-called “free
womb” laws in the early 1810s. These de-
crees guaranteed that subsequent genera-
tions of slaves in Uruguay would be born
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1186 ---
1098 U RUGUAY
free; however, slavery and slave trading per-
sisted into the 1840s and 1850s despite
lawmakers passing laws against these prac-
tices. Loopholes in these laws existed be-
cause the period of servitude for slaves born
under free-womb legislation was often
extended. The loopholes allowed for abuse
to occur as slave owners extended this
time as they saw ﬁt. Final emancipation for
Uruguayan slaves did not happen until
1853 when abolitionist principles were in-
corporated within the national constitution.
Following independence and the aboli-
tion of slavery in the ﬁrst half of the nine-
teenth century, African-descended peoples
gradually assimilated into Uruguayan soci-
ety. Afro-Uruguayans joined the ranks of
the colonial and national militaries. Military
service provided a viable yet risky path to
freedom, especially since the region was
constantly embroiled in a variety of civil
wars and foreign invasions during the early
nineteenth century. Black ﬁghters typically
sided with José Gervasio Artigas, one of the
founders of the Uruguayan nation, against
the Spanish during the independence
struggles between 1816 and 1820. They
also helped Uruguayans regain their inde-
pendence after Brazil’s occupation of the
Banda Oriental region in 1821. By 1825,
Uruguayan insurgent leaders, or the so-
called “Immortal 33,” accomplished a key
victory against the Brazilian invaders, and
among this group were several Afro-
Uruguayan slaves. Other lower-ranked
Afro-Uruguayan soldiers fought heroically
with General Artigas. Considering these
sacriﬁces, their socioeconomic conditions
did not improve greatly. Although legal re-
strictions of the colonial period and slavery
had been dismantled by the mid-nineteenth
century, Afro-Uruguayans continued to
face various degrees of alienation and
discrimination. If they lived in Montevideo,
they tended to live in conventillos, or poor
tenement houses, such as Medio Mundo,
Palermo, Reus, and Sur. The arrival of
European immigrants also added to their
socioeconomic marginalization.
Despite this marginalization, Afro-
Uruguayan leaders began to form their own
institutions. Founded in 1917, the journal
Nuestra Raza was published widely and
continued in print until the middle of the
twentieth century. The political party
Partido Autóctono Negro (PAN) was
formed in 1937 by Ventura Barrios, Elemo
Cabral, and Salvador Betervide. Consid-
ered more a movement than a political
party, PAN never developed a speciﬁc
political program nor was able to mobilize
its Afro-Uruguayan base. As a result,
Afro-Uruguayans never voted for the party
as a bloc and chose from the traditional
Colorado or Blanco parties. By 1944,
PAN disbanded amid divisions over the
direction of the party. Another notable
Afro-Uruguayan cultural institution was
the T eatro Negro Independiente, founded
by playwright Andrés Castillo in the 1950s
and enduring until 1982. The theater
company sought to celebrate black cultural
contributions to Uruguay.
Even though Afro-Uruguayans consti-
tute only about 6 percent of the total pop-
ulation of Uruguay, they have profoundly
inﬂuenced Uruguay’s language and culture.
Linguists have noted African inﬂuences in
the nation’s speech patterns. Words such
as cacunda, mandinga, and quilombo have
been incorporated within the everyday
Spanish language of the country. In music,
African inﬂuences are also evident in the
payada, or a “chant and response” type of
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1187 ---
URUGUAY 1099
singing similar to contrapuntal and satiric
African songs known as makawas or
ibiririmbo on the African continent and
common among black communities
throughout the Americas. Prominent Afro-
Uruguayan artists of the twentieth century
include Ildefonso Pereda Valdés, Juan Julio
Arrascaeta, Carlos Cardoso Ferreira, Cristina
Rodríguez Cabral, José Emilio Cardoso,
and Julio Guadalupe. Black Uruguayans
either created or helped shape Platine
music and dance, especially the candombe,
the milonga, and the tango. Music and
popular religion intersect in Montevideo
during particular holidays, especially dur-
ing carnival and the festival of San Baltasar.
Furthermore, folklore also reﬂects uniquely
African elements. The legend of Mandinga
is common to the River Plate’s folklore.
Mandinga is a devil, usually represented as
a black cowboy or gaucho, who roams the
Platine frontier in search of souls to steal.
Black writers have written on the African
experience. Pilar Barrios wrote a powerful
drama of racism in Piel morena (1947).
Virginia Brindis de Salas stressed black
pride, liberation, and accomplishment in
Pregón de Marimorena (1974). Visual artists
have long been fascinated with African
themes in their works. The nineteenth-
century Impressionist Pedro Figari, a white
painter, was enamored with the culture of
the conventillo and the candomble. Further-
more, Afro-Uruguayan entertainers, such
as Rey Charol and Rubén Rada, and ath-
letes, especially soccer players, have proudly
represented the Uruguayan nation on the
world stage.
On a general level, blacks throughout
Uruguay have assimilated into the general
population, and the slow but steady inﬂux
of Afro-Brazilians into the country means
the constant presence of African-descended
peoples. Popular histories are slow to recog-
nize the far-reaching impact of Afro-
Uruguayans, but this is changing.
Jesse Hingson

URBANIZATION
Urbanization, the movement of people into
cities in North America, Latin America,
and Africa, as in other regions of the globe,
is related to a range of economic activities
involving the concentration of people
being affected by processes such as industri-
alization, whereby large numbers of people
gather in cities in order to engage in manu-
facturing jobs and services. In the African
and Latin American experience, cities were
often tools for colonialism since they oper-
ated as links for international economic
networks as well as serving as local centers
of political dominance. For instance, cities
in western Sudan were founded in connec-
tion to trans-Saharan trade in the ninth
century, and the Guinea coastal cities in
response to the transatlantic slave trade
and later in relation to the colonial rule.
T enochtitlan in Mexico was a regional
center for trade in the same manner that
Chan Chan and Cuzco were in Peru. More
broadly, cities played a major role in both
capital accumulation and the generation
of dependence, structural inequality, and
poverty, which are part of a broader history
of asymmetric relations existing within and
between societies. Cities in Africa and Latin
America share a common history in which
land use structures have been strongly inﬂu-
enced by colonial planning practices. In
North America, urbanization and the growth
of cities is closely related to the growth of
capitalism through industrial development,
technological changes such as the growth of
mass transit, and demographic changes, in-
cluding immigration.
During the precolonial period, ancient
cities in Africa were, on the one hand, in-
extricably related to international long-
distance trade, especially through the Sahara
Desert or the Indian Ocean. Some early
kingdoms developed into major empires in
the twelfth century until the early eigh-
teenth century, where cities served as trade
and administrative centers, such as in the
Songhay Empire in Sudan, Mali, and
Benin. Ancient Ghana is credited for hav-
ing drawn its wealth and power from trans-
Saharan trade of gold, salt, and slaves.
However, in the thirteenth century it was
conquered and incorporated into the Mali
kingdom, which would be later eclipsed by
the Songhay Empire, but nevertheless re-
maining as an autonomous kingdom.
The lasting inﬂuence of the Arabs in
Africa started with their initial conquest
around the seventh century that spread
Islam; however, it was not until the twelfth
century that most North African cities were
converted. The conquest extended across
the northern part of the continent and into
the sub-Saharan region of the medieval
kingdoms of Sudan, later southward along
the Nile Valley and into the eastern coast of
the continent. Arabs normally established
their settlements outside existing ancient
cities along the fringes of the Sahara Desert
(like Timbuktu), at the intersection of water
and land routes (in the Niger and Nile
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1189 ---
URBANIZATION 1101
Valleys), or at the seafronts where trade
would ﬂourish. Important trade centers
and state capitals were laid out around
mosques and markets, including Kano,
Katsina, and Maiduguri in the Hausa
region of Nigeria as well as Lamu, Zanzibar,
and Mombasa on the eastern African
coastline.
European domination of Africa started
with Portuguese attempts to ﬁnd a safe
route to India in order to attract the lucra-
tive Sudanese trade of gold, slaves, and
ivory controlled by Arabs and Swahili for
centuries. Later, maritime powers like
England, France, and Holland established
coastal trading stations under which slave
trade rapidly expanded. During Portuguese
rule, urbanization expanded during the
seventeenth century, and, in Ghana, it was
a result of the process of land privatization.
Moreover, slave trading and merchant
capitalism had a considerable imprint on
Portuguese colonies such as in the cities of
Mozambique, Salvador de Bahia in Brazil,
and Goa in the Indian Ocean, speeding
even further their urbanization.
Precolonial cities in North Africa were
densely populated, reaching their peak in
the fourteenth century when Cairo had
more than half a million inhabitants, whereas
Fez and Marrakech counted 150,000 and
200,000 people, respectively. These urban
concentrations favored European trade ex-
pansion in the ﬁfteenth century com-
manded by the Portuguese and carried on
by a class of merchants who traded gold
and later slaves. The slave trade has been
credited for having had a devastating effect
on the economies and political structures of
the coastal kingdoms, since an estimated
12 million slaves were taken from Africa to
America. Further on, the Portuguese ex-
tended their trading networks down the
west coast and eventually to eastern Africa,
where in the sixteenth century they
founded Bissau in Guinea; Luanda,
Benguela, and Sao Salvador in Angola;
various towns in Mozambique; and even
struggled to take over Zanzibar and
Mombasa from the Arab traders. In the
meantime, the French and the British
established a number of city ports in West
Africa like Accra, Conakry, and Cape Coast,
while the Dutch founded Cape T own.
In America, the Spanish conquista-
dores seized the Aztec’s capital city of
T enochtitlan in 1521 and founded the
colonial center under the same layout that
the capital of the Aztec Empire had. The
conquest was violent and complex, and
later Nueva España became the regional
center for conquering and establishing new
domains. In 1534, Pizarro reached Cuzco
in Peru, but its inaccessibility made him
decide to establish the viceroyalty’s capital
in Lima, which had a coastline suitable as
the operations center for the conquest
of the rest of South America. Around 1540,
the Portuguese established an urban net-
work along the west coast of Brazil, estab-
lishing Bahia as its ﬁrst capital and later
founding Rio de Janeiro and Paraiba as
secondary cities.
The colonial period in the Americas
extended from the sixteenth to the early
nineteenth century and brought different
development stages. It is arguable whether
to credit the Spaniards for introducing
urbanization to America since the Aztec,
Maya, and Inca settlements already featured
monumental architecture, advanced in-
frastructure networks, highly specialized
manufacturing workers, and sophisticated
administrative urban structures. However,
it has been acknowledged that a European
city planning framework was implemented
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1190 ---
1102 U RBANIZATION
following Spanish regulations and build-
ing codes (Leyes de las Indias and the
Ordenanzas), which dictated a basic land
use zoning, street orientation and width, as
well as forms of land tenure. In Brazil, as
the Portuguese did not ﬁnd such an ad-
vanced and large indigenous population as
the Spanish did, they brought slaves from
Africa to work in agriculture, and it was
only at the beginning of the eighteenth
century that they were able to develop a
mining economy comparable to the Spanish
colonies that demanded larger urban
centers. Therefore, in 1762 Rio de Janeiro
replaced Bahia as the capital and became
the center of the ﬂourishing mining region
of Minas Gerais, as well as the focal point
for the Crown in its expansionism and
colonization. 
The colonial period in Africa extended
from 1880 to 1912 and, apart from the
exceptions of Liberia and Ethiopia, the
entire continent fell under the control of
European powers. The colonial powers in
Africa restructured and reorganized labor,
introducing new administrative systems
and transforming the patterns of urbaniza-
tion in urban centers. As a general policy,
colonial cities were established on existing
settlements already engaged in interna-
tional trade. However, rather than stressing
the role of cities as instruments for local
development, they were used instead as ad-
ministrative control centers for the extrac-
tion of commodities and unprocessed
materials for industrial use in European
cities while preventing local development.
T ransportation infrastructures followed the
same principle, favoring accessible and
productive urban centers over existing
settlements, therefore concentrating jobs,
services, economic activities, amenities,
and commercial districts in a limited
number of cities, and polarizing and exac-
erbating regional differences.
After the 1920s, industries in Africa re-
quired workers to live in urban areas for the
duration of their extended working life.
However, having a stable working force en-
tailed a considerable impact on urban poli-
cies, such as the need to secure land for
urban development, setting an effective tax
system, and providing basic infrastructures
and services. Therefore, land tenure and
urban legislation were put in place in order
to consolidate city control and administra-
tion of the urban economy and the built
environment. Nevertheless, when com-
modity prices collapsed in the 1930s, living
conditions deteriorated in cities to the ex-
tent that citizens were forced to go back
into their former rural communities. By
the 1950s only 15 percent of the popula-
tion lived in urban areas, even when a
number of cities held large concentrations
of people such as Cairo (2.41 million),
Johannesburg (915,000), as well as middle-
size cities such as Cape T own, Durban,
T unis, Casablanca, and Ibadan, which each
accounted for slightly under half a million
inhabitants.
During the colonial period of both
Africa and the Americas, colonizers had to
create the infrastructure (markets, housing,
railways, etc.) for the occupation forces,
which provided the occasion for developing
urban centers. In Latin America, previous
settlements were used to establish the colo-
nial cities since their locations already had a
symbolic signiﬁcance, which facilitated the
transfer for the new powers (for example,
Mexico City, Antigua, and Cuzco). How-
ever, in many cases dual cities were created
in which sharp divisions between classes
(Spaniards, Creoles, Mestizos, Indians),
hierarchy, and condition (colonizers or
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1191 ---
URBANIZATION 1103
colonized), or economic activity marked
the spatial segregation of the cities. In this
sense, colonizers in Africa and the Americas
used and adapted existing networks and
hierarchies to serve the interests of the elites
controlling the political and economic cen-
ters of trade. In Africa a dual urban scheme
consistently opposed the traditional built
environment to an urbanized modernization,
creating the ancient-modern dichotomy for
years to come; the novel areas of the city
were largely built as places to organize the
ﬂow of resources and constructing the
mechanisms through which broader terri-
tories could be administered.
Several emerging urban models were
experimented in colonial cities, such as “the
garden city” scheme, which, from Dakar to
Lubumbashi, was implemented on grounds
by prominent European architects and
planners. In Latin America, the garden city
was also envisioned as a solution to the
contradictory opposition between growing
industrial cities, unhealthy conditions, and
the countryside. However, during the sec-
ond phase of colonization, urban planning
schemes admitted some adaptations in
order to soften the colonial rule, such as
considering the historical context for urban
interventions as well as their role for social-
izing urban colonialism.
An interesting cross-fertilization be-
tween Africa and the Americas was the
Brazilian house known as a sobrado, which
accounts today for 90 percent of the actual
Yorubaland housing in Nigeria. Former
slaves trained in Brazil as skilled construc-
tion workers went back to Nigeria and
started a rapid diffusion of the Brazilian
housing method. Furthermore, these peo-
ple asserted their authority, status, and
prestige by replicating their former masters’
scheme of occupying the ﬁrst ﬂoor while
letting the ground ﬂoor be for servants (in
Brazil it would be the place for slaves).
Another parallel between cities in Africa
and the Americas is that modern urbanism
maintained and even accentuated the so-
cioeconomic and spatial contrast between
the formal or institutionalized part of the
city and the segregated, marginal, and un-
controlled territories, which were, however,
generated on a structural basis. This dual
view of the city could only be sustained
through a class-related approach, for which
only the settlements governed by some sort
of ofﬁcial power (being colonial, regional,
or municipal) were to be recognized as
legitimate. Even when this dual scheme
already existed in precolonial times, colo-
nial urban policies portrayed this historical
trend as inherent to development in order
to maintain social control within the struc-
tural inequality.
T raditionally, South African cities have
been considered as particular cases, even if
segregation was used as a tool of domina-
tion just as in other African colonial cities.
In any case, planning was clearly used as a
weapon for apartheid, since it justiﬁed seg-
regation as the only way to prevent race
frictions, which were said to produce con-
ﬂict itself. Some scholars claim that South
African and Latin American cities have
similar levels of social and economic devel-
opment and inequality, and that market
forces are increasingly the dominant forces
behind urban processes.
Latin American countries gained their
independence in the 1800s, when cities
were already consolidated as the socioeco-
nomic and political centers of the conti-
nent. However, Mexico City and Salvador
were the only cities with more than
100,000 inhabitants at the time, which
showed the limited economic development
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

1104 U RBANIZATION
and diversity they had achieved when min-
ing became no longer proﬁtable. At the end
of the nineteenth century, French urbanism
was very inﬂuential all over the continent,
especially after Baron Haussmann’s inter-
ventions by 1860 in Paris to transform that
city’s infrastructure, plans which were con-
sidered compelling high-proﬁle urban op-
erations to transform cities such as Buenos
Aires, Rio de Janeiro, and Caracas into
world-class cities. In the twentieth century,
the continent experienced considerable
economic expansion, the modernization of
infrastructure, and a process of urbaniza-
tion without precedent. In the 1930s, the
industrialization of Mexico, Venezuela,
Colombia, Panama, Peru, and Brazil took
place and increased right after World War
II, when national policies to substitute im-
ports fostered development. The economic
centralization of power was to overtly favor
national capitals as engines of growth. In-
dustrialization policies in Latin American
cities followed the North American urban
model of introducing industrialized con-
struction technology as well as automobile-
oriented urban schemes, which epitomized
the ultimate instruments of modernity.
Urbanization in North America fol-
lowed the pattern of industrial development
and expanded when electric mass transit
systems were developed and implemented
at the end of the nineteenth century. Mass
transit permitted the expansion of suburbs
within 10 miles of the urban core. The mo-
bility created by cars further fostered urban
decentralization and created a new form of
metropolitan sprawl. Moreover, in the
United States, the Federal Highway Act of
1956 allocated $105 billion to create
42,500 miles of freeways, boosting road
construction industries, car-making, oil,
and tire industries. After World War II, the
Federal Housing Authority in the United
States released home loans that are credited
for having fostered the construction of
an estimated 2 million houses per year, a
production scale that made buying more
convenient than renting a dwelling. Con-
currently, large housing developments were
built to house the post–World War II baby
boom generation; Levittown, Long Island,
became home to more than 70,000 white
residents in a new suburban compound.
Urbanization did not benefit all
equally. Even after the passage of civil rights
legislation, segregation persisted due to
housing policies in which Afro-Americans,
Hispanics, and Native Americans were ex-
cluded from the minimal bank guarantees
for loans and mortgages. T o a limited ex-
tent, the racial segregation of U.S. cities in
post–World War II America might be said
to have resembled some forms of colonial
segregation.
In the United States, use of automo-
biles over collective transportation such as
trolleys, subways, and urban buses suited
suburban rather than urban growth. Job
structures also reﬂected the drive from the
urban core to the suburbs: while 37 percent
of all jobs were located outside the central
city in the 1960s, by the end of the 1980s
nearly 70 percent had already been trans-
ferred to the outskirts. This trend is cred-
ited for driving downtown depopulation
and economic decline, concentrating
poverty, and reinforcing segregation pat-
terns in the central city. In the 1960s,
urban renewal operations were credited for
bulldozing “blighted” areas and displacing
Italian, Hispanic, and African American
communities elsewhere. Since the mid-
1990s, urban policies for rehabilitating, re-
vitalizing, and preserving the urban fabric
have capitalized on the culture and historic
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1193 ---
UNITED STATES AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT 1105
architecture of the central city for the gen-
triﬁcation of traditional neighborhoods.
Socioeconomic segregation is not a
new phenomenon in African and American
cities. In fact, zoning and urban planning
itself emerged as an instrument designed to
maintain privileges for a certain segment of
the population through the regulation of
land uses and construction densities. In the
United States, the segregated structure of
cities—and subsequent segregation of
resources, political power, property values,
and educational access—has been an im-
portant focus of civil rights activism up to
the present day.
Even though colonial rule ended for
the large majority of African countries
during the 1960s, cities remain centers for
the consolidation of political power and the
centralized management of economic re-
sources. This concentration of power has
often led to autocratic governments, cor-
ruption, inequality, and social repression.
Since the mid-1990s, cities in Africa
and Latin America have experienced sub-
stantial economic restructuring measures
under the International Monetary Fund
schemes, emphasizing the decentralization
of formal political authority and responsi-
bilities, if not necessarily actual decision-
making powers.
