UNITED STATESAGENCY
FOR INTERNATIONAL
DEVELOPMENT
Congress passed the Foreign Assistance Act
on September 4, 1961, creating the U.S.
Agency for International Development
(USAID), and President John F . Kennedy
organized the agency on November 3,
1961, as part of the State Department. Like
the Marshall Plan before it, USAID was to
be sensitive to the realities of the Cold War,
targeting aid to nations that might other-
wise capitulate to communism. Unlike the
Marshall Plan, USAID was to make foreign
aid a permanent feature of U.S. policy.
Moreover USAID consolidated in a single
agency the relief efforts that had been part
of disparate federal agencies.
At least since the Monroe Doctrine,
the United States had singled out Latin
America as something akin to an American
protectorate. Africa had been part of Europe’s
colonial empire, but after World War II the
United States sought to guard African
nations in their ﬂedgling independence
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1194 ---
1106 U NITED STATES AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT
against communism. In both continents
the United States proposed to use foreign
assistance to align these regions with itself.
The United States did not propose
through USAID to revolutionize the
economies of Latin America and Africa but
rather to reinforce traditional patterns.
Agriculture remained the foundation of the
economy in both Latin America and Africa.
In ﬁscal year 2004, USAID spent $134
million of its $1 billion budget for Africa
on the development of agriculture. More-
over the commitment to cash crops re-
mained adamantine. In ﬁscal years 2001
and 2002, USAID granted more than
$57 million to coffee growers in 18 coun-
tries in Latin America and Africa. In ﬁscal
year 2003, USAID extended $5.7 million
in trade credits to farmers’ cooperatives that
grew coffee in Latin America. USAID ex-
tended aid to 230 coffee growers in El
Salvador, Mexico, Nicaragua, Costa Rica,
and Guatemala, and in Ethiopia, Rwanda,
Tanzania, Uganda, and Zambia. Where
plantations once dominated production,
USAID has targeted aid to small farmers in
hopes of replicating the Jeffersonian model
of a polity of yeomen. USAID has sought
to buoy small farmers by diversifying
agriculture. The agency funds the growing
of broccoli in Ecuador, sweet potatoes in
Honduras, bamboo in Haiti, oregano in
Bolivia, and plantains in Nicaragua.
In addition to funding the development
of agriculture, USAID has through ﬁscal year
2004 spent $118 million in the Caribbean to
rebuild institutions and infrastructure after
T ropical Storm Jeanne and $1 million for
similar efforts in Guyana. USAID apportions
money to protect forests and fauna in
Bolivia, Haiti, Panama, and Guatemala. In
ﬁscal year 2004, USAID spent $125.6 mil-
lion on education in twenty African nations,
$82.2 million on the restoration of the
environment in Cameroon, Central African
Republic, Democratic Republic of the
Congo, Equatorial Guinea, Gabon, and the
Republic of Congo, and $67.8 million on
political reform throughout Africa.

VESEY,D ENMARK
(1767?–1822)
Denmark Vesey was the author of an intri-
cate, but failed, 1822 slave rebellion in
Charleston, South Carolina. The abolition-
ist later known as Denmark Vesey was most
likely born on the Danish sugar island of
St. Thomas. In the fall of 1781, at approxi-
mately the age of 14, the boy was purchased
as part of a cargo of 390 slaves by Joseph
Vesey, a Bermuda-born slave trader. The
child’s “beauty, alertness and intelligence”
caught the captain’s eye, and during the
voyage to Saint Domingue, the crew
adopted him as a “ship’s pet and plaything.”
In 1782 Vesey rechristened the young slave
with the name of T elemaque and employed
him as a cabin boy. Shortly thereafter, when
the British evacuated South Carolina, Vesey
relocated to Charleston in 1783 to work as
a ship chandler.
For the next 17 years, T elemaque—
whose name was ﬁrst corrupted into T elmak,
and then Denmark—served Vesey in a num-
ber of capacities. Fluent in both English
and French, Denmark was evidently a
manservant, yet on occasion he traveled to
the docks to sign in the captain’s consign-
ments, which on occasion included slaves.
At some point during these years he mar-
ried Beck, later a bondwoman of grocer
John Paul’s, who bore him at least three sons:
Polydore, Robert, and Sandy, the last of
whom would be the only one of his children
to be implicated in his 1822 conspiracy.
On November 9, 1799, in an amazing
stroke of luck, Denmark won $1,500 in the
city’s East Bay lottery. Mary Clodner, the
captain’s common-law wife, agreed to
manumit Denmark for $600. Joseph
Vesey witnessed the deed on December 31,
so Denmark Vesey began the ﬁrst day of the
nineteenth century as a free man worth
$900. Beck’s owner, however, would not sell
at any price, and his ﬁrst wife and children
remained slaves. After his marriage to Beck
ended, Vesey married a much younger slave
named Susan, who later became free and
took his adopted surname of Vesey. She
lived in Charleston after his death until at
least 1830.
After Vesey established himself as a car-
penter, he rented a home at 20 Bull Street
from attorney George Cross. Despite later re-
ports that he died a rich man worth $8,000,
there is no evidence that Vesey ever owned a
single piece of property. Susan Vesey took in
laundry, and Denmark persisted in playing
the city’s lottery in hopes of winning again.
Despite this, Vesey stubbornly refused to
defer to white privilege. Upon seeing a
companion bow to a white man in the street,
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1196 ---
1108 V ESEY,D ENMARK
the physically imposing carpenter observed
that “all men were born equal, and that he
was surprised that anyone would degrade
themselves by such conduct.”
Although brieﬂy a member of the
Second Presbyterian Church, around 1818
Vesey joined the city’s new African Methodist
Episcopal congregation. Sandy Vesey also
joined, as did three of Vesey’s closest friends,
Monday Gell, Peter Poyas, and Jack Pritchard.
As a lay preacher in the church, Vesey turned
his back on the New T estament and what he
regarded as its false promise of universal
brotherhood. As former Charleston slave
Archibald Grimke put it, Vesey found “in
the stern and Nemesis-like God of the Old
T estament” a suitable vision “for a day of
vengeance and retribution.” The temporary
closure of the church by city authorities in
June 1818, and the arrest of 140 congre-
gants, one of them presumably Vesey him-
self, only reinforced the determination of
black Carolinians to maintain a place of in-
dependent worship.
At the age of ﬁfty-one, Vesey brieﬂy
considered emigrating to the English
colony of Sierra Leone. But as Beck’s chil-
dren remained slaves, Vesey resolved in-
stead to orchestrate a rebellion followed by
a mass exodus from Charleston to Haiti.
President Jean-Pierre Boyer had recently
encouraged black Americans to bring their
skills and capital to his beleaguered repub-
lic. Vesey planned the escape for nearly four
years. His chief lieutenants included Poyas,
a literate and highly skilled ship carpenter,
Gell, an African-born Ibo who labored as a
harness maker, and Rolla Bennett, the
manservant of Governor Thomas Bennett.
Vesey’s inner circle also included “Gullah”
Jack Pritchard, an East African priest pur-
chased in Zinguebar in 1806. Although
there are no reliable ﬁgures for the number
of recruits, Charleston alone was home to
12,652 slaves. Pritchard, probably with
some exaggeration, boasted that he had
6,600 recruits on the plantations across the
Cooper and Ashley Rivers. The plan called
for Vesey’s followers to rise on the night
of Sunday, July 14—Bastille Day, and the
day blacks in Boston celebrated their
freedom—slay their masters, and sail for
Haiti and freedom. As one southern editor
later conceded, “The plot seems to have
been well devised, [and] its operation was
extensive.”
The plot unraveled in June 1822 when
two slaves, including Bennett’s friend
George Wilson, a fellow class leader in the
African Church, revealed the plan to their
owners. Mayor James Hamilton called up
the city militia and convened a special
court to try the captured insurgents. Vesey
was captured at the home of Beck, his ﬁrst
wife, on June 21 and hanged on the morning
of T uesday, July 2, together with Bennett,
Poyas, and three other rebels. According to
Hamilton, the six men collectively “met
their fate with the heroic fortitude of
Martyrs.” In all, 35 slaves were executed.
Forty-two others, including Sandy Vesey,
were sold outside the United States; some,
if not all, became slaves in Spanish Cuba.
Charleston authorities also demolished the
African Church and banished its leaders.
The state assembly subsequently passed laws
prohibiting the reentry of free blacks into
the state, and city ofﬁcials enforced ordi-
nances against teaching African Americans
to read. Robert Vesey lived to rebuild the
African Church in the fall of 1865.
Douglas R. Egerton

VOICE OF AMERICA
Voice of America (VOA) began broadcast-
ing on the radio in 1942 as part of the U.S.
war effort against the Axis powers in World
War II. VOA is funded by the U.S. govern-
ment; the ﬁscal year 2005 budget was $158
million. VOA transmits more than 1,000
hours of news and programming every
week in 44 languages, distributed by radio,
television, and the Internet, but only to for-
eign countries: the Smith-Mundt Act of
1948 prohibits VOA from broadcasting to
the United States. Besides news broadcasts,
VOA programming includes shows about
sports, music, and other cultural topics.
Since 1959 some VOA programs have been
broadcast in “Special English” which aims
to communicate with people whose ﬁrst
language is not English through use of a
limited vocabulary and short sentences.
Although VOA believes itself to be an
accurate, reliable, and unbiased source of
news, some foreign governments have con-
sidered it to be an instrument of American
propaganda and have responded by jam-
ming the VOA signal (broadcasting noise at
the same frequencies used by VOA so that
the VOA signal cannot be heard). VOA
shortwave radio signals were commonly
jammed by the Soviet Union during the
Cold War, and the Cuban government reg-
ularly jams the VOA television signal today.
Sarah Boslaugh

VOODOO
Voodoo is a form of magic and witchcraft
derived from syncretic African and
Catholic beliefs and practiced in African
American and Caribbean communities.
The religion flowered in Haiti, being
formed in the eighteenth and nineteenth
centuries through blending elements of cer-
tain West and Central African beliefs and
practices with those of Catholicism. A
variant of Voodoo also ﬂourished in New
Orleans in the nineteenth century. From
the 1880s, the term came to be used more
generally—often interchangeably with
“hoodoo”—to refer to (often unrelated)
forms of magic and witchcraft practiced in
African American communities in the
United States. For a long time the subject
of inaccurate and sensationalist reportage,
Voodoo is now more widely understood by
outsiders as a result of the studies of
anthropologists and its reappraisal by cre-
ative artists.
Slaves in the French Caribbean colony
of Saint-Domingue came from many areas
of Africa, from Senegambia to Mozambique.
But the majority came from two regions:
the Slave Coast (roughly corresponding to
present-day T ogo and Benin) and Kongo in
Central Africa. During the colonial period,
the religious beliefs from each area may
have existed side by side, for even today
the ethnic provenance of the main deities
(or loa) worshipped in Haiti are reﬂ ected
in their twofold classification: Petro
(of Kongo origin) and Rada (a name
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1198 ---
1110 V OODOO
derived from Allada, a major kingdom on
the Slave Coast before the rise of Dahomey
in the early eighteenth century).
Although Kongo slaves outnumbered
those from the Slave Coast by three to one,
the Rada gods seem to have been predomi-
nant. Already, in his classic Description
topographique de la partie Française de l’isle
Saint-Domingue (1797), M. L. E. Moreau
de Saint-Méry’s attention was drawn to the
cult of vaudoux, an all-powerful god repre-
sented by a snake, and whose name clearly
derives from vodun, the generic word for
deity or spirit in Fon and related languages
spoken on the Slave Coast. Vaudoux was
used in English-language accounts to refer
to both the religion and its adherents until
it was domesticated as “Voodoo” in the
1880s.
T radition has it that the slave revolt that
began on the night of August 22–23, 1791,
was inaugurated with an African—possibly
Dahomean—religious ceremony involving
the slaughter of a pig and the drinking of its
blood. But if Voodoo played some role in
mobilizing the insurrection and the military
forces that eventually expelled the British,
French, and Spanish, the independent
republic—Haiti—that emerged in 1804 de-
clared Catholicism the ofﬁcial religion, and
apart from a brief period during the reign of
Emperor Soulouque, Voodoo was sup-
pressed. However, this probably only inten-
siﬁed the cross-fertilization between the two
religions as Voodoo ceremonies appropri-
ated Catholic ritual and many of the loa
became identiﬁed with Christian saints.
Voodoo ceremonies are presided over
by a houngan (priest) or mambo (priestess).
They may be private family affairs con-
vened on priestly advice, or regular public
dances. In each case, spirit possession
may take place, participants adopting the
behavior characteristic of a loa, to whom
offerings (including animal sacriﬁces) are
made. There is no evidence that human
sacriﬁce and cannibalism were ever a part
of religious practice in Haiti, despite the
sensational claims made in travelers’ ac-
counts. But the much-discussed zombie—a
person poisoned so as to appear dead, and
later disinterred, revived, and put to
work—is a ﬁgure of symbolic importance
in Haitian folklore.
Waves of refugees from Saint-
Domingue from the 1790s left their mark
on the Afro-Creole culture of New Orleans.
Dances in Congo Square and other gather-
ings on the shores of Lake Pontchartrain or
at the private residences of “Voodoo
Queens,” such as Marie Laveau, attracted
much prurient interest in the press at the
time and left a rich legacy of Voodoo tales
of often dubious authenticity. Some dances
and songs address spirits that have unmis-
takable counterparts in Haiti, but the
evidence suggests that if Voodoo was an
organized r eligion in Louisiana, it quickly
mutated into a number of separate cults as-
sociated with charismatic (and often un-
scrupulous) individuals.
By the end of the nineteenth century,
in the United States “Voodoo” would refer
exclusively to the business of competing
“root doctors” or “conjure men and
women” offering advice and paraphernalia
to clients seeking to inﬂuence or harm
others—or protect themselves from such in-
ﬂuence or harm. Also known as “hoodoo,”
this informal and somewhat clandestine
practice (which overlaps with fortune-
telling, spiritualism, and herbal medicine) is
found across the rural South and any large
cities where there are signiﬁcant African
American populations, although it attracts a
substantial white clientele too.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

VOODOO 1111
Opponents of the abolition of slavery
in the West Indies and the southern United
States often invoked lurid misrepresenta-
tions of Haitian Voodoo in attempts to
demonstrate the unsuitedness of blacks to
self-government. Apologists of U.S. impe-
rialist ventures in the Caribbean, including
the occupation of Haiti, recycled many
such stereotypes. The tradition continues
in travelogues, Hollywood ﬁlm, and the use
of the word as a metaphor for anything sin-
ister, inexplicable, unlucky, or simply wrong-
headed, with “voodoo economics” being a
fairly recent prominent example. Unfortu-
nately such a usage may have found some re-
newed justiﬁcation with the appropriation of
Voodoo by the dictatorship of Francois and
Jean-Claude Duvalier (Papa and Baby Doc),
who recruited many houngans to the much-
feared civilian militia known as the tontons
macoutes.
For that reason, there are those who
recommend the adoption of non-English
spellings that render more closely Haitian
and Louisiana Creole pronunciations:
vodun, vodoun, voudou, and vodou (in the
absence of ofﬁcial orthography, there are
plenty of options). But at least since the
1920s, there has existed an alternative tra-
dition that has sought to represent Voodoo
in a more positive light. During the U.S.
occupation, Haitian intellectuals such as
Jean Price-Mars sought to challenge the re-
luctance of the country’s Francophile elite
to recognize the value of Creole folklore.
Meanwhile, African American
authors—from Z ora Neale Hurston to
Ishmael Reed—have woven traditional
hoodoo themes into their ﬁction, drama,
and poetry. In music, such themes, already
present in blues and jazz, were self-
consciously reworked in the 1960s by New
Orleans singer-songwriter Mac Rebennack,
known as “Dr John” (named for an associ-
ate of Marie Laveau). Voodoo is now
widely invoked across many popular cul-
tural forms from acid house to cyberpunk
science ﬁction.
Alasdair Pettinger

WALCOTT,D EREK (1930–)
Derek Walcott is one of the most well-
known and important Caribbean writers
of the twentieth and twentieth-ﬁrst cen-
turies and a recipient of the Nobel Prize for
Literature. He has been as wide-ranging in
his work as he has been proliﬁc. Perhaps
most famous for his poetry, Walcott is also
an essayist, painter, critic, and playwright,
founding the T rinidad Theater Workshop.
He was born in 1930 in the former British
colony of Saint Lucia. After he studied
there at St. Mary’s College and in Jamaica
at the University of the West Indies, he
moved to T rinidad in 1953. Committed to
his Caribbean roots but compelled by
Western literary conventions, Walcott’s
work investigates the conﬂicts between
and complexities within West Indian and
European cultures. Propelling the theme of
exile in this manner, his poetry frames
characters like Robison Crusoe and
Ulysses in Caribbean contexts. Perhaps the
most famous example of this is his epic
Omeros; however, practically all of his verse
references Homer. For Walcott, Ulysses
represents the Caribbean subject, spliced
between constant migration and a desire
for home. Walcott’s emphasis on the rest-
less searches and journeys and the resulting
hybrid identities have, at times, placed him
at odds with Black Nationalism. His essay
“What the T wilight Says,” for example, re-
jects a singular liberation on the basis of
race. An unabashed look at the anxieties
and advantages of pluralism has remained
consistent throughout his work. His ﬁrst
collection of poetry, 25 Poems,was published
when he was 18; however, he became known
only after the poems in In a Green Night
came out in 1962. The recipient of many
honors and awards, including the Royal
Society of Literature Award and the 1988
Queen’s Medal for Poetry, Walcott won the
Nobel Prize in Literature in 1992. Still a
journeyer, Walcott divides his time between
T rinidad and the United States, where he
teaches at Boston University.
Merinda Simmons Dickens

1114 W ALKER,A LICE
WALKER,A LICE (1944–)
Alice Walker is an African American novel-
ist, womanist, and activist best known as
the author of the novel The Color Purple.
She was born in Eatonton, Georgia, in
1944. At a young age she was blinded in
one eye accidentally. However, the injury
did not impede her success as a writer. She
attended Spellman College and Sarah
Lawrence College where she completed a
collection of poetry, Once: Poems (1968).
This collection begins many themes that
Walker continues in her later work, such as
Africa, the South, and love. Shortly after,
Walker gave birth to her only daughter as
she continued to write her ﬁrst novel, The
Third Life of Grange Copeland (1970). This
text explores racism, economic oppression,
the civil rights movement, and African
American folk culture. Walker continued
to write, publishing collections of short
stories, poetry, nonﬁction essays, and chil-
dren’s books until the acclaimed Book
Award, T ownsend Prize, and Pulitzer Prize–
winning novel The Color Purple (1982)
launched her literary career. The Color Pur-
ple, which was made into a Steven Spielberg
ﬁlm in 1985, tells the story of Celie, an
abused woman living in the South. Entirely
composed of letters written in black folk
English (also referred to as vernacular), the
book explores women’s relationships with
men, sexual assault, domestic abuse, and
women’s sexuality. 
In 1984, Walker published In Search of
Our Mothers’ Gardens: Womanist Prose, a
collection of essays, interviews, and
speeches. In this text she deﬁnes “woman-
ist” as her term for black feminism. In
many of Walker’s works, a transatlantic
context is achieved as Walker’s characters
make connections between Africa and the
United States. For example, in Possessing the
Secret of Joy (1992), Tashi chooses to have
female genital mutilation performed on her
before moving from Africa to the United
States. The novel focuses on the aftermath
of this ritual and how it ultimately affects
Tashi and her ties to both countries. Walker
currently writes and lives in northern
California.
Laura Madeline Wiseman

WARNER-VIEYRA,M YRIAM
(1939–)
Born at Pointe à Pitre in Guadeloupe in
1939, Myriam Warner-Vieyra is a leading
writer of the Francophone transatlantic ex-
perience, writing about Guadeloupe, Senegal,
and France. She lived on the Caribbean
island, which was a French overseas depart-
ment, for only about 12 years. Leaving her
home, she moved to France where she spent
her teenage years and met her future husband
Paulin Vieyra. By age 22, she had married
Vieyra, and they settled in Senegal, West
Africa. Warner-Vieyra’s relocations from her
native Caribbean to France, and ﬁnally
Senegal, account in part for the transatlantic
inﬂuence and popularity of her literary
achievements. In an interview conducted by
James Gaasch, the author recalls her time in
France as a “transition très impor tante qui
a laissé une empreinte profonde: l’éducation,

la vie parisienne, ma rencontre avec des

selves, between book instruction and the

Washington was author of several books
and speeches. His Atlanta Convocation Ad-

audience that blacks and whites would re-

be as separate as the ﬁngers, yet one as the

progress.” In Up from Slavery Washington
described his successful life story and his
approach to “the Negro problem,” or the
question of black advancement, uplift, and
assimilation in America. This text, com-
bined with Washington’s public persona,
exerted an enormous inﬂuence on black
Americans and consolidated his image as a
black leader.

WEDDERBURN,R OBERT
(1762–1834?)
Robert Wedderburn was a Jamaican-born
radical campaigner who raised awareness
of the plight of black African American
slaves among lower-class citizens of early
nineteenth-century London and created
empathy for the slaves by comparing their
plight to that of the exploited poor in
England. Wedderburn was born in 1762 in
Kingston, Jamaica. He was the result of
nonmarital miscegenation between a Scottish
sugar planter, James Wedderburn, and
Rosanna, a slave. Rosanna was sold by
Robert’s father when pregnant, but Robert
was born free and was baptized as an
Anglican.
After some education, and after serving
as an enlisted person in the Royal Navy,
Wedderburn arrived in England in 1778.
He scraped a living through legal and ille-
gal means, sometimes working as a tailor.
In the early years of the nineteenth century,
Wedderburn embraced Unitarian preach-
ers’ encouragement of nonconformist, indi-
vidualistic qualities. Wedderburn became a
preacher, earning renown for ﬁery, politi-
cally charged sermons and speeches. He
met the agrarian reformer, Thomas Spence,
just before Spence’s 1814 death. By 1815,
Wedderburn was a leading ﬁgure of the di-
verse group of loosely afﬁliated radicals—
the Spenceans—who commemorated and
sought to bring to fruition the reforming
intent of Spence. He associated closely with
the Spencean leader Thomas Evans, re-
maining loyal to him when Evans was im-
prisoned in 1817, but falling out with him
subsequently. Wedderburn continued to
preach and pursue political agitation, cam-
paigning for actual revolution rather than
mere reform.
In 1819, Wedderburn opened a Unitar-
ian church in Hopkins Street, Soho.
Spurred by enthusiastic, change-seeking au-
diences, he became a perceived threat to the
status quo. Government spies (John Castle
was the most signiﬁcant) often reported on
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1206 ---
1118 W EIMAR REPUBLIC,B LACK ENTERTAINERS IN THE
his antiestablishment tirades. He was
charged with blasphemy and libel on a
number of occasions, spending several short
spells in prisons. One supportive associate,
William Dugdale—who was notorious as
a seller of pornographic materials—
published Wedderburn’s seminal work, the
unambiguously titled autobiographical
polemic The Horrors of Slavery. Wedderburn
claimed to have seen his mother and grand-
mother being whipped by slave owners. He
insisted that this dehumanizing maltreat-
ment of African Americans differed little
from the Industrial Age exploitation of
Britain’s laboring poor in the late eighteenth
and early nineteenth centuries. (A revolution
led by radicals from the lower orders would
crush the twin brutalities of American slav-
ery and British class-based exploitation.)
Wedderburn’s ultraradicalism became less
and less palatable to even previously sym-
pathetic reformers in the 1820s, causing a
reduction in his inﬂuence, if not his noto-
riety. An isolated ﬁgure at the end of his
life, he died sometime between 1834 and
1836. Latter-day scholars maintain that
Wedderburn was not only an energetic rad-
ical, a dedicated abolitionist, and a serious
religious thinker but also a determined
advocate for democracy, general emancipa-
tion, and free speech.

WEIMAR REPUBLIC,B LACK
ENTERTAINERS IN THE
African, African American, and German
cultural and artistic exchanges in the early
twentieth-century period preceding the
Nazi takeover took advantage of new forms
of mass communication, including radio
and recordings. Entertainers of African de-
scent were a common sight by the end of
the nineteenth century in Europe. African
Americans in particular enjoyed an envi-
ronment which, although not free from
racial discrimination, was much preferable
to even the somewhat more liberal North
of the United States. The several hundred
African American entertainers who toured
Germany, as well as England, France,
Russia, and other countries, year after year,
were neither socially nor economically felt
to be a threat; exotic as they were in appear-
ance, they could lead a normal professional
life.
World War I was to bring about a sud-
den and lasting change. Black entertainers
left Germany, Germany lost its African
colonies, and the never clearly deﬁned legal
status of Afro-Germans led to social segre-
gation and exodus. Black colonial troops
and Afro-Americans not only served in uni-
form in the French, British, and American
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1207 ---
WEIMAR REPUBLIC,B LACK ENTERTAINERS IN THE 1119
armies but were part of the forces that oc-
cupied the Rhineland after the war. Black
people were now considered the “black
threat” and the “black shame” in Germany.
A defeated Germany was plagued by
poverty, political chaos, and inﬂation. The
war was over, but peace had not yet arrived.
After the unprecedented atrocities of the
Great War, there was an almost licentious
and decadent longing for amusement and
stupefaction. But at entertainment venues
there was no opportunity for foreigners: it
was not until 1924, after monetary reform
and introduction of the Rentenmark that
entertainers could be paid in currency that
could be taken out of Germany.
Then, all of a sudden, cultural life virtu-
ally exploded in Berlin, Germany’s capital
city. By 1927 some 270 movies were ﬁlmed
annually—more than in all the other coun-
tries of Europe combined. Broadcasting was
introduced in 1923, and in 1930 there were
3 million subscribers—more than in any
other country in continental Europe. In a
period of just over eight years, 1925–1933,
Berlin became the focal point of the modern
world, the center of industrial culture and
mass media. Music, theater, sport, commerce,
painting, ﬁlm, and poetry all made the
Golden T wenties happen in Berlin. Seventeen
airlines connected Berlin and its more than
40 theaters with distant provinces of the
republic and other parts of the world, and
the daily newspapers produced up to four
issues a day. In this environment there was
acceptance for black entertainers again. The
production of three black revues— Chocolate
Kiddies, Revue Nègre,and Black People—were
important events in the Weimar Republic, as
they exposed audiences all over Germany to
black, and especially African American, arts
and artists and caused a long discussion of
their merits.
On May 25, 1925, the Berlin
Admiralspalast theater treated invited guest
to a gala premiere of the Chocolate Kiddies
revue, the ﬁrst authentic black production
to perform in Germany since the war
ended. The music was provided by 
Neger-Jazz-Orchester, an 11-piece orchestra
under the direction of Sam Wooding. The
music was a shock. The inﬂuential music
critic Hans Stuckenschmidt referred to it as
“orgies of hot style”—in other words, jazz.
In autumn 1924, impresario Ivan
Leonidow (Russian born but operating
from Berlin) visited New York. While there
he was exposed to black revues, heard Sam
Wooding, and contracted Duke Ellington,
Joe T rent, and Arthur James Johnston to
write the music for a new revue to be titled
Chocolate Kiddies. By 1925 interest in black
performers was less enthusiastic in London
and Paris, where black musicians had
worked through and after the war years.
But for Berlin, Leonidow’s scheme worked.
The opening enjoyed an enthusiastic re-
sponse, and for the next ﬁve years right up
to the worldwide economic depression, jazz
was truly en vogue in Germany. The liter-
ary magazine Das blaue Heft noted the
rhythm in the performance’s song, dance,
comedy, and movement. 
The black artists were adored. Their
dances—Shimmy, Black Bottom, Charleston,
and Foxtrot—become fashionable and
were being promoted widely by innumer-
able instruction books. Their music inﬂu-
enced not only entertainment circles but
also serious composers. Jazz in Weimar in-
spired the now-legendary composers Paul
Hindemith as well as Ernst Kˇ renek and
Kurt Weill. Yet in spite of their readiness to
accept Americanisms, the Germans lacked
any experience and any understanding of
the sociocultural environment that gave
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1208 ---
1120 W EIMAR REPUBLIC,B LACK ENTERTAINERS IN THE
birth to blues as a rural, and jazz as an
urban, black music. Rhythm, harmony,
melody, or intonation of black musicians
were difﬁcult to comprehend. The tones,
approach, and informality were far outside
the experience of critics for social reasons,
and in the Weimar era, jazz was being arti-
ﬁcially transposed to the level of art and
Gebrauchsmusik, or utility music intended
for performance by an amateur musician
rather than a virtuoso. At best, the result
was only a quasi-symphonic pseudo-jazz.
Apart from a few months in Argentina
and New York, Sam Wooding continued
his musical activities in Europe. Under the
inﬂuence of European music and musicians,
including Paul Whiteman’s saccharine and
popular “symphonic jazz,” Wooding denied
his African American roots and reoriented
his group from a hot jazz band to a concert
orchestra, trading in his signature instru-
ment, the muted trumpet, for the violin.
In 1926 Caroline Dudley Reagan went
to New York, saw the black revue Shufﬂe
Along, and employed orchestra leader
Claude Hopkins and composer Spencer
Williams to assemble a revue that was to
open in Paris as Revue Nègre. The revue
went to Brussels and 10 weeks later arrived
at the Nelson Theater in Berlin where, at
last, it created a sensation. The star attrac-
tion was a young, unknown girl who had
been engaged for the show because she
could not demand a top salary in New
York City. Josephine Baker could dance a
little, was not a good comedienne, but she
had a perfect body. Her spectacular stage
appearance—clad in little more than a
skirt of bananas—her electrifying pres-
ence, and her suggestion of sexual avail-
ability made her an irresistible attraction in
a prudish German environment. Baker
became an enduring favorite as a performer,
appearing on stage as well as in ﬁlm, and
obtaining an especially popular reputation
in France, which granted her citizenship
in 1937. 
On stage and on posters, the racial
stereotypes of the late nineteenth-century
minstrel shows were still employed in
1920s Europe: blacked-up Negro clowns in
Chocolate Kiddies, banana skirts in the
Revue Nègre, plantation overalls in Black
People. Therefore, Baker’s performances,
which emphasized song and dance and di-
minished supporting jazz structures, were
used by her German audience to translate
fears of black culture into a more palatable
image of a primitive stereotype.
In spite of modern mass communica-
tion technologies, the stage remained the
most important medium. German record
companies issued extremely little authentic
jazz music, and no blues, although all of
them had excellent business connections
with American partner companies. The
Sam Wooding orchestra recorded disc
records for the Vox Company in Berlin, but
sales dwindled after a few weeks or months
when the band moved on; all of the record-
ings are extremely rare today. Thus, the re-
ception of jazz in Germany was not so
much inﬂuenced by recordings by black
jazz bands, but rather by white American
dance orchestras, which sold recordings in
great numbers.
Apart from disc records, another po-
tential medium for the dissemination of
jazz music was radio broadcasting. Between
1926 and 1930 the number of jazz broad-
casts in Germany steadily increased. On
close examination it becomes evident, how-
ever, that those broadcasts rarely offered
hot jazz but rather modern Foxtrots in
“jazz” or “symphonic jazz” instrumentation
performed by normal dance bands, often
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1209 ---
WEST INDIES FEDERATION 1121
with string sections. Only occasionally
were there live broadcasts featuring visiting
black orchestras. Wooding’s orchestra was
transmitted in July 1928 and in June 1930.
There were several live broadcasts by the
Mississippi Jazzers, the orchestra of the
Louis Douglas revue Black People. In 1931
German radio even exposed its listeners to
a short-wave live radio transmission
straight from the Harlem Cotton Club,
featuring blues and Cab Calloway’s jazz or-
chestra (disc recordings of this event have
been discovered, with a reporter’s comments
in the German language).
Less problematic than hot jazz to the
German ear were folk songs and spirituals,
which had been present in German con-
cert halls since the 1870s. German radio
stations repeatedly devoted programs to
concerts and lectures about song and po-
etry, folk songs and spirituals, by black
Americans. Classically trained American
singer Marian Anderson recorded both
arias and spirituals while studying in
Berlin in 1930. Anderson was not alone, as
traditionally many other black artists,
singers, and instrumentalists came to
Germany for further training. Among those
was Roland Nathaniels, a representative of
the Anlo-Ewe people of the Gold Coast,
whose family moved there from the former
German colony T ogo. After the 1933 as-
sumption to power by the Nazis, appear-
ances by black ensembles ceased even
though they were not formally forbidden.
Individual black entertainers, musicians,
artists, acrobats, and actors continued to
work in Germany. Herb Flemming, ex-
trombonist in the Wooding orchestra, had
engagements up to 1937. Adelaide Hall
was at the Etablissement Rex at the time of
the Olympic Games in 1936. Una Mae
Carlisle appeared at the Berlin Scala
revue theater until war was declared in
September 1939.

WEST INDIES FEDERATION
The West Indies Federation was a united
system of island states of the West Indies
that was established as a form of regional
self-government. The West Indies Federation
lasted from January 3, 1958, to May 31,
1962. The short-lived federation was the
result of an important desire by many West
Indian people to have a united system of
island states. Some West Indians still argue
for a renewed ofﬁcial federation. Even
though the federation of 1958 was still part
of the British Empire, it did initiate even-
tual West Indian independence from
British rule. The terms “West Indian” and
“Caribbean” are often used as synonyms,
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1210 ---
1122 W EST INDIES FEDERATION
except in the context of discussing speciﬁc
political histories within the region; in this
context, “West Indian” is used to desig-
nate the British colonial islands, while
“Caribbean” is holistically inclusive of the
region.
After World War II, island nations
colonized by the British were asking for
independence. By 1947, at a conference at
Montego Bay, Jamaica, British representa-
tives agreed to think further about these
ideas. The British liked the idea of some
changes; the idea they liked most consisted
of a centralized system of government for
the islands that would manage itself, instead
of the British having to do business with
the numerous individual Crown Colonies.
Eventually, British Parliament passed the
British Caribbean Federation Act of 1956.
The West Indies Federation became ofﬁcial in
1958 as a form of regional self-government.
The federation consisted of the majority of
the British West Indies coming together in
a uniﬁed government system within the
British colonial system. The island nations
that were part of this federation were Jamaica
(which at the time included the T urks and
Caicos Islands and the Cayman Islands
as dependencies), T rinidad and T obago,
Dominica, Grenada, Barbados, Montserrat,
St. Kitts-Nevis-Anguilla, St. Lucia, Antigua
and Barbuda, and St. Vincent and the
Grenadines. After some debate between
Jamaica and T rinidad, the capital of the
federation was proclaimed as Chaguaramas,
T rinidad, just outside of T rinidad’s own
capital, Port of Spain. Its national anthem
was “God Save the Queen.” Grantley Adams
from Barbados became prime minister.
In hindsight, it is easier to under-
stand that this mixture of colonialism
and democracy were incompatible, and a
federation existing within these limits
could not last. The federation did not
last mainly because of Jamaicans’ and
T rinidadians’ problems with a couple of
central tenets of federation. The first
problem was the establishment of a cus-
toms union, which would create univer-
sal tariffs for all exports and imports of
goods between the federation member
nations. The second problem was that
Jamaicans (especially) felt that they would
be shouldering the burden of the federa-
tion on behalf of much smaller states;
Anguilla and Montserrat were relatively
small with 10,000 inhabitants compared
to Jamaica’s more than 2 million popula-
tion. In 1961 Jamaica passed a referen-
dum to withdraw from the federation.
Furthermore, Jamaica desired full inde-
pendence from Britain. Within a year,
T rinidad also withdrew from the federa-
tion and requested independence. Thus,
the two major West Indian players in the
federation had abandoned the project.
The federation collapsed.
British Parliament’s West Indies Act of
1962 formally reverted the remaining feder-
ation members back to colony status. Thus
the British ofﬁcially created and ended the
West Indies Federation, but it was the West
Indians’ federation to lose or keep.
In the wake of the federation, the
Caribbean holds numerous regionally inte-
grative organizations. In 1962 the West In-
dies Associated States administered to the
British islands’ reestablished colonial rela-
tionship with the United Kingdom.
In the years following the breakup
of the federation (1960s–1970s), islands
throughout the Caribbean gained indepen-
dence, beginning with Jamaica and T rinidad
and T obago in 1962. Through political
independence, the region recommenced its
integrative ideology. It created for itself the
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1211 ---
WEST,C ORNEL 1123
Caribbean Free T rade Area (CARIFTA),
which lasted from 1965 to 1972. CARIFTA
was replaced in 1973 by the Caribbean
Community and Common Market, or
CARICOM. CARICOM oversees, among
other things, the regional import and export
customs regulations initiated by the West
Indies Federation so many years ago.
CARICOM is a more regionally integrative
system than the federation was because it is
more inclusive of the nations in the
Caribbean region; for instance, it includes
island nations that were not part of the
modern British colonial system, such as
Haiti and Surinam. Through the power of
regional integration, Caribbean nations
have become more signiﬁcant players in the
wider world. Caribbean nations joined the
group of African, Caribbean, and Paciﬁc
Countries (ACP), which has negotiated
commerce with the European Community
since the 1975 Lome Convention. During
the 1970s, Jamaica became a leading repre-
sentative of the ACP group.
Besides opening the door to indepen-
dence, one of the major beneﬁts of the
West Indies Federation was that it validated
the pressing need for West Indians to con-
cern themselves with the politics of regional
integration. Cooperative r egional integra-
tion still plays a signiﬁcant role in each of
the local island economies.
David W . Hart

WEST,C ORNEL (1953–)
Cornel West is noted for his interest in
areas of academic study as diverse as religion,
history, economics, politics, philosophy,
and sociology. He has penned over a dozen
books that engage his singular concern
for rendering visible an African American
ontology. One of America’s most charismatic
academics, his best-known work, Race
Matters (1993), has been credited by some
with changing America’s dialogue on race,
justice, and democracy.
Born in T ulsa, Oklahoma, in 1953,
West’s academic potential was realized
when he graduated magna cum laude
from Harvard University in Near Eastern
Languages and Literatures (1973). He
went on to earn his MA (1975) and PhD
(1980) degrees at Princeton while simulta-
neously beginning his teaching career at
the Union Theological Seminary in New
York City. In 1984 he took up an appoint-
ment at Yale Divinity School only to re-
turn to the Union Theological Seminary
three years later. In 1988 West accepted
the positions of professor of religion and
director of the African-American Studies
program at Princeton, positions he held
until his departure to Harvard University
and the W . E. B. Du Bois Institute for
African and African-American Research in
1993. However, after a public quarrel with
Harvard’s then new university president,
Lawrence Summers, West decided to re-
turn to Princeton and former positions
in 2002.
West is best known to those outside of
academia for his direct involvement with
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1212 ---
1124 W HEATLEY,P HILLIS
community-based black empowerment
events such as the Million Man March, his
defense of hip-hop music, and his attempts
to broker national summits to end gang vi-
olence. Yet, while many applaud his efforts
to improve social harmony and mutual
civility, and recognize the value of his at-
tempts to make learning accessible to those
on the streets through innovative schemes
like his rap CD Sketches of My Culture,
which narrates the history of some great
African American leaders of the past, his
unorthodox approach to social issues and
his continued association with dissident
ﬁgures of America’s contemporary civil
rights struggle have led some to question
whether West’s strong political convictions
compromise the integrity of his academic
work.
However, such criticism fails to ac-
knowledge that West’s entire academic
career has been built in tandem with his
involvement with antiracism organizations
and civil rights activism. In an interview for
National Public Radio, West recalled how
he met the captivating ﬁgure of Randall
Robinson at a Pan-African Liberation
Committee meeting at Harvard in 1970.
Robinson, a fellow student at Harvard, was
an active antiracism campaigner who, at
that time, was targeting the apartheid
system in South Africa. For many African
Americans, South Africa was indelibly
linked to America because of its familiar
history of racial and cultural oppression.
Moreover, the operation of the apartheid
system seemed to be the overt expression
of the same kind of racism that simmered
beneath the surface of American society. As
such, any attempt to problematize South
Africa’s apartheid system was also an attempt
to further the liberation of the African
American community.
So it was that West, among others,
pointed toward the Reagan administration’s
policy of “constructive engagement” with
the South African apartheid regime. For
West, this policy amounted to a tacit ap-
proval of the apartheid system, an approval
that consequently exposed the American
government’s apathy toward all black suf-
fering. Since such apathy betrayed the low
priority that the American government
gave to black suffering, West argued that
the Reagan administration’s working rela-
tionship with the South African govern-
ment stood as a thinly coded expression of
racism. Indeed, West later argued that the
American government’s ability to ignore
the multitude of abuses perpetrated on
blacks under the apartheid system in order
to enjoy access to cheap labor markets and
cheap resources was nothing less than a na-
tional disgrace and moral shame.
Grant Hamilton

WHEATLEY,P HILLIS
(1753–1784)
Phillis Wheatley was an African American
poet and founding ﬁgure of an African
American literary tradition. On July 11,
1761, the slave ship Phillis docked in
Boston, after stops in Senegal, Sierra
Leone, and the Isles de Los. From its cargo
Boston tailor John Wheatley purchased a
young girl, naming her after the vessel.
While he did not record her origins, Phillis
later assumed herself to be from Gambia.
Later scholars have posited she was Wolof
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1213 ---
WHEATLEY,P HILLIS 1125
or Fula and from a Muslim community;
certainly her only recorded memory of
Africa was of her mother’s morning libation
to the sun.
Finding her precocious, the Wheatleys
educated her in subjects as diverse as gram-
mar, history, geography, mathematics,
Greek, and Latin, and she soon began to
compose poetic works. In 1770 Wheatley’s
poem on the death of Reverend George
Whitﬁeld brought her fame throughout the
colonies. However, it also produced cynics
who believed a black woman incapable
of producing art. And so, in 1772, 18
prominent Bostonians examined her, later
signing a letter which asserted she was a ca-
pable author. Still thwarted by American
publishers, in 1773 Wheatley, with her
master’s son, visited England to oversee the
publication of Poems on Various Subjects,
Religious and Moral. The Countess of
Huntingdon facilitated Wheatley’s intro-
duction to society and endorsed her volume;
famed abolitionist Granville Sharp served as
her escort.
Wheatley’s volume was prefaced by the
Boston letter, which afﬁrmed Wheatley as
the author of the poems and identiﬁed her
as a “Negro servant,” indicating her en-
slavement. But her success in England drew
attention to her status, and she was freed.
Though the Revolutionary War diminished
her career prospects, it did enable her meet-
ing with George Washington.
While Wheatley’s poetry advocates
black social, intellectual, and artistic equal-
ity, her social reality prevented her from ex-
plicitly condemning slavery, though she did
so in private correspondence. Historically,
some critics have condemned her reticence;
others have celebrated her as a “shrewd ac-
commodationist under Puritan petticoats”
(Hull, cited in Flanzbaum, 74). T ellingly,
her black contemporaries endorsed her:
Jupiter Hammon and “Horatio” celebrated
her in verse; Scipio Moorhead and the
Briton Ignatius Sancho were admirers.
Wheatley acknowledged her heritage,
calling Africa “my country” and expressing
concern about its spiritual state. In this she
was a product of her Puritan upbringing,
wishing to see Africa Christianized and
thus saved not from sin but from “spiritual
famine.” Yet she refused an invitation to
return as the wife of a black missionary.
Setting aside her health, her mistress’s, and
that Wheatley did not know either of the
men proposed as her suitors, she observed,
“Upon my arrival how like a Barbarian
shou’d I look to the natives; I can promise
that my tongue shall be quiet, for a strong
reason indeed, being an utter stranger to
the Language of Anamaboe.” Even as she
Poet Phillis Wheatley was born in Africa and brought
to America as a slave. Gifted with extraordinary
language abilities, she learned multiple languages, and,
by the eve of the American Revolution, was famous in
both the American colonies and England for her poetry.
(Library of Congress)

wholeheatedly endorsed the missionary en-

In 1778 Wheatley married a free black,

WIDEMAN,JOHN EDGAR
(1941–)
Essayist, novelist, nonﬁction writer, poet,
college professor, and sports analyst John
Edgar Wideman is a masterful storyteller in
the tradition of African griots. An activist
African American writer and social critic,
he was born in 1941 in Washington, D.C.
Wideman’s family moved prior to his ﬁrst
birthday to Homewood, Pennsylvania,
an African American community of
Pittsburgh—itself famous as a blue-collar
steel town. Growing up, Wideman ignored
the pitfalls of drugs or crime derailing other
black youth and kept his eyes on scholarly
and athletic achievements, as indicated by
his Ivy League educational path: graduate
of Peabody High School, Pittsburgh;
Benjamin Franklin scholar, Phi Beta Kappa
member, accomplished athlete, and graduate
of the University of Pennsylvania (BA.
English, 1963); Rhodes Scholar and graduate
of Oxford University, England (B. Philosophy,
1966); and ﬁnally, Kent Fellow and graduate
of the University of Iowa Writer’s Workshop
(1967). Up to the Iowa experience, Wideman
seemed destined to follow the traditional
Eurocentric academic route. But, to para-
phrase one of his heroes, Wideman recog-
nized at Iowa that he had to “move forward
in order to go backwards” to see the enrich-
ing resources of his own African American
culture awaiting creative expression. The
author’s reversed, self-reﬂective Afrocentric
perspective materialized in Wideman’s
1967 ﬁrst novel, A Glance Away, about the
hazards of drug addiction for inner-city
youth.
Building upon the 1930s ideas of
Richard Wright and the 1960s platform
of the Black Arts Movement, Wideman
continued over the next 30 years to script
the ideological map deﬁning the contours
of Afrocentric writing. His reprisal and
modiﬁcations of black nationalistic core
themes of ancestry, home, and community
attendant to the genocidal and schizophrenic
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1215 ---
WILBERFORCE,WILLIAM 1127
slave experiences of African Americans he
connects to the nihilistic experiences of the
Black Atlantic Diaspora to expose the trans-
historicity of racism. The artist is a master-
ful storyteller recalling African traditions
while ingeniously connecting the deleterious
effects of slavery to African American expe-
rience by utilizing his real-life Homewood
community as a collective symbol for black
culture’s metanarratives of dissolution, sur-
vival, and achievement. This technique has
netted Wideman accolades of an American
Book Award and two PEN/Faulkner
Awards for his ﬁction. However, his convo-
luted, postmodern style of narration has
often eluded his readers and delayed
Wideman’s full public reception until the
resurgence of black masculine studies in the
1990s.
Wideman’s other novels include Hurry
Home (1970), The Lynchers (1973), Hiding

Sent for You Yesterday (1985), Reuben

WILBERFORCE,WILLIAM
(1759–1833)
William Wilberforce was a British Member
of Parliament, an evangelical leader, and an
antislavery campaigner. Wilberforce, the
son of a prosperous merchant, inherited
considerable wealth in his teenage years.
He studied at Cambridge, where he
William Wilberforce, a leader of British abolitionism,
ca. 1884. (Library of Congress)

1128 W ILBERFORCE,WILLIAM
acquired influential friends, in cluding
William Pitt the Younger, a future prime
minister. In 1780 Wilberforce was elected
T ory MP for his hometown of Hull; from
1784 to 1812 he represented Yorkshire
in Parliament. During 1784–1785,
Wilberforce experienced a spiritual conver-
sion in which he abandoned what he called
formal religion for real faith, evangelical
Christianity. He determined to seek God’s
will for his life and with the encouragement
of the Reverend John Newton, the former
slave trader, he came to believe that he was
divinely called to undertake “two great ob-
jects: the suppression of the slave trade and
the reformation of manners.” He devoted
his life to achieve both aims.
Wilberforce found support among
Quakers and also Anglican evangelicals of
the Clapham Sect for both his causes. His
attempts to control and direct the religion
and morals of people through the Society
for the Suppression of Vice, formed in
1802, not surprisingly failed to be an effec-
tive means of changing the social and moral
problems of society. His other passion, to
abolish Britain’s brutal transatlantic trade
in slaves from Africa to the West Indies in-
volved a long struggle. In 1787 Wilberforce
joined with the Anti-Slavery Committee
recently created by Thomas Clarkson and
Sir Charles Middleton. The extraparlia-
mentary committee was one of the earliest
and most inﬂuential popular lobbies in
Britain, its campaign in the country greatly
helped by the support of Wilberforce’s per-
sistent voice in the House of Commons.
West Indian economic interests vigorously
opposed abolition, and Wilberforce’s initial
attempts to secure legislation to ameliorate
or end it failed. In the 1790s the antislavery
cause was hindered by the threats posed by
the French Revolution, the long war with
France, the slave rebellion in St. Domingo,
and Wilberforce’s often ill health. Eventu-
ally, in 1807, after Pitt’s death, and helped
by the declining economic signiﬁcance of
the West Indies, a bill to abolish the slave
trade passed through Parliament. In order
to get the act passed, Wilberforce did not
press for the emancipation of slaves in the
British Empire, although that remained his
ambition. The act, making it illegal for
British subjects and ships to be involved in
the slave trade, became law in 1808.
Wilberforce’s opposition to slavery
gave him an interest in Africa. This interest
was marked by his support for various
causes: the Church Missionary Society,
formed in 1799, and in particular, the
African Institution, created in the year of
abolition in order to promote “the Civiliza-
tion and Improvement of Africa.” The
institution urged that abolition be pressed
on other European countries, and also
advocated for the establishment of a pro-
tectorate based on the colony of Sierra
Leone that would introduce “industry and
the arts of peace” to the interior of West
Africa. In Parliament, Wilberforce argued
that diplomatic and military pressure
should be used to impose abolition on
European states and also Brazil, the major
slaving state in South America, as well as on
African rulers who continued the trade.
With the end of the Napoleonic Wars
in 1815, antislavery sentiment grew. In
1823, Wilberforce, along with Clarkson
and others, formed the Anti-Slavery Soci-
ety for “the Gradual Abolition of Slavery,”
a cause that became popular with local
groups formed throughout Britain intent
on lobbying Parliament for an end to slav-
ery. Wilberforce’s views were laid out in An
Appeal to the Religion, Justice and Humanity
of the Inhabitants of the British Empire on
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

WILLIAMS,F RANCIS 1129
Behalf of the Negro Slaves in the West Indies,
published in 1823. Opposition came from
not only slaveholders and the West Indian
lobby but also from William Cobbett, the
radical journalist, who harshly and unfairly
denounced Wilberforce in particular as ig-
norant of the condition of black slaves and
indifferent to the harsh lives of working
men in Britain. Wilberforce was conserva-
tive on many domestic political issues,
supporting repressiv e legislation in the
1790s, but he was radical in his concerns
and actions for the relief of suffering
among the poor. In 1825 ill health forced
Wilberforce to retire from Parliament.
However, he continued to give his political
and moral support to the antislavery cause.
He died in 1833 with the knowledge that a
bill to abolish slavery was passing through
Parliament.

WILLIAMS,F RANCIS
(1697?–1762)
Francis Williams was a Jamaican-born poet,
legal manipulator, and symbol of black
intellect. He was born sometime before
December 26, 1697, when he was chris-
tened in Spanish T own, St. Catherine’s
Parish, Jamaica. He was probably the
youngest of the three sons of their free black
parents, John and Dorothy Williams. His
father was a prosper ous merchant, planter,
and exporter, with signiﬁcant economic
and political inﬂuence in both Jamaica and
Britain. By an act of Parliament in London
in 1711, John Williams gained for himself
and his family the right to be witnesses in
civil cases and to be exempt from evidence
against them by slaves in any part of the
plantations. In November 1716, the Jamaica
Assembly also approved “an act to prevent
negroes being evidence against” any member
of the Williams family. No doubt to enhance
the family’s social status, John Williams sent
Francis to enter Lincoln’s Inn in London,
where he was admitted on Au gust 8, 1721,
though no record has been found of his
having actually attained a law degree.
Before the end of 1724, Francis
Williams was back in Jamaica, where he
inherited the family’s property, slaves, and
debts owed them, together worth approxi-
mately £12,000 sterling. During the 1720s
Williams had inherited and amassed so
much land and power in Jamaica that he
clearly posed a serious threat to the social,
political, and economic status quo in
Jamaica. On November 19, 1724, William
Brodrick, a white gentleman, petitioned
the Jamaica Assembly to reduce Williams’s
legal status to that of other free blacks
because Williams had insulted and struck
him. Consequently, Williams was a particular
target of “An Act for the better regulating
Slaves, and rendering free Negroes and
Mulattoes more useful” passed by the
Jamaica Assembly on March 28, 1730.
Williams showed his own power and inﬂu-
ence by petitioning the Colonial Ofﬁce in
London to overturn the Jamaican vote.
Williams spoke for all the free blacks and
Indians affected by the new act. As the
only free black in Jamaica who had the
legal right to bear arms and wear a sword,
a right the act would remove, he empha-
sized that his opposition was also personal.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1218 ---
1130 W ILLIAMS,H ENRY SYLVESTER
His petition further reveals that Williams
had a history of relying on the law to pro-
tect his interests in Jamaica. Williams won
his case, getting the Jamaica act repealed in
November 1731.
For reasons unknown, Francis
Williams lost most of the wealth and prop-
erty he had inherited. The register of
St. Catherine’s Parish, Jamaica, records the
burial of “Francis Williams a Negroe” on
July 19, 1762. His will, proved on
September 9, 1762, indicates that he died
worth slightly less than £700, including
the value of “a parcel of old books and
furniture” and 15 slaves.
During his lifetime, Francis Williams
was a transatlantic celebrity because of his
economic and social status in Jamaica, his
learning, and his practice of greeting each
new governor of Jamaica with a panegyrical
poem in Latin. After his death, Williams’s
fame led the philosophers David Hume and
James Beattie to cite him as evidence in
arguments, respectively, against and for the
educability of Africans. In 1774, Edward
Long included a brief biography of Williams
and one of his Latin panegyrics in his three-
volume History of Jamaica, published in
London. Although Long intended to under-
mine any claims made for Williams’s literary
merit, and his account of Williams is racist
in tone and almost completely unreliable in
content, Long made Williams more widely
known than ever. Consequently, when orga-
nized opposition to the transatlantic slave
trade developed at the end of the eighteenth
century, Williams, often along with Phillis
Wheatley and Ignatius Sancho, was fre-
quently mentioned as an example of the
intellectual abilities and literary achievements
of people of African descent.
Vincent Carretta

WILLIAMS,H ENRY SYLVESTER
(1869–1911)
By organizing the ﬁrst Pan-African Confer-
ence in London in 1900, the T rinidadian
lawyer Henry Sylvester Williams laid the
foundations for the Pan-African move-
ment. He was born in Arouca in 1869 as
the eldest child of Bishop and Elizabeth
Williams, Barbadian immigrants of African
descent. Through stories about black
Barbadians who had risen to important
positions, his parents instilled in him the
goal of black freedom, dignity, and integrity,
which became the motivating forces in his
life. When he was ﬁfteen, Williams enrolled
at the Normal School in Port of Spain to
train as an elementary teacher. In 1887, he
became headmaster of a government school
in San Fernando. In 1889, while in charge
of the San Juan government school,
Williams helped to found the T rinidad
Elementary T eachers’ Union. In search of a
profession that paid higher wages and
accrued more status, he went to New York
in 1891. Because of racial barriers and a
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1219 ---
WILLIAMS,H ENRY SYLVESTER 1131
lack of congenial work, Williams moved to
Canada. In 1893, he entered Dalhousie
University in Halifax, where he registered
as a general student in the faculty of law.
In 1896, Williams moved to England
and enrolled at King’s College to ﬁnish his
law degree. He earned a living as an ofﬁcial
lecturer for the Church of England
T emperance Society. In September 1897,
he gave the term Pan-Africanism an organi-
zational form when he founded the African
Association. The association, which was
dominated by West Indians and limited its
scope to British subjects, aimed “to encour-
age a feeling of unity and to facilitate
friendly intercourse among Africans in gen-
eral; to promote and protect the interests of
all subjects claiming African descent”
through the dissemination of information
and lobbying. In December 1897, he was
admitted to Gray’s Inn to read for the bar.
Not long thereafter, he married Agnes
Powell, daughter of Captain Francis Powell
of Gillingham, Kent, despite the captain’s
refusal to give consent because of his skin
color. Their first child, Henry Francis
Sylvester, was born in 1899.
In 1898, Williams gave a lecture on
T rinidad in which he called for an elected
legislative council. He reiterated this de-
mand in his pamphlet The People’s Case
(1899) and also in a meeting with liberal
Members of Parliament (MPs) in April
1899. Gradually Williams turned his atten-
tion from T rinidad to Africa. On behalf of
the African Association, he lobbied MPs to
ask questions about conditions in South
Africa; wrote to the colonial secretary about
the welfare of Africans in Rhodesia; and
wrote letters to newspapers highlighting
the colonial policies that caused the suffer-
ing of millions of Africans. He soon real-
ized that these measures were insufﬁcient to
win sympathy for the cause of the associa-
tion and suggested holding a world confer-
ence of black people. The ﬁrst Pan-African
Conference was held in London in July
1900. For three days leading race thinkers
from Africa, the United States, the West
Indies, and Europe, including W . E. B. Du
Bois, discussed how to secure the freedom
and justice of Africans in Africa and the
Diaspora. On the last day, the conference
adopted Williams’s proposal to issue a for-
mal protest against the treatment of colored
people in South Africa. It furthermore
decided to turn itself into a permanent 
Pan-African Association (PAA) with head-
quarters in London and branches overseas.
Williams was elected general secretary.
Finally, the conference wrote “An Address
to the Nations of the World,” which de-
manded an end to color and race prejudice
and called on Britain to grant its colonies
representative government and the United
States to end the oppression of the American
Negro. It contained the famous phrase
“The problem of the twentieth century is
the problem of the color line,” which later
appeared in Du Bois’s The Soul of Black
Folk (1903).
In the spring of 1901, Williams went
to Jamaica and T rinidad to arouse interest
in the PAA. He held public meetings,
which drew large crowds that included rep-
resentatives of the colonial government. In
both islands, hundreds of people joined the
PAA and various branches were formed. He
visited American PAA ofﬁcers and execu-
tive members on his way back to London.
On arrival home in September, he immedi-
ately restarted his lobbying on West Indian
issues. He wrote a memorandum to the
colonial secretary in which he raised the
question of the franchise and the plight of
the peasant proprietor and called for a
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1220 ---
1132 W ILLIAMS,J AMES
federation of the West Indies. In October,
he launched The Pan-African. This
monthly journal, which was not the organ
of the PAA but a private venture, survived
for only six issues. The short life of the
journal reﬂected that of the PAA, which
was last heard of in 1902.
In June 1902, Williams was eventually
called to the bar. A year later he migrated to
South Africa, where he became the coun-
try’s ﬁrst African lawyer. He soon got in-
volved in local politics. He was elected to
the board of a school, which catered to the
children of Cape T own’s colored elite. This
school board served partly as a means to ad-
vance the status of South Africa’s colored
population. In February 1904, Williams
led a deputation of the board to put to the
Cape T own attorney general the grievances
that nonwhites had on trial by jury. A
month later, he attended a mass meeting in
protest against the treatment of colored
people in the T ransvaal. As a follow-up, the
South African Citizens’ Defence Commit-
tee was established, with Williams as presi-
dent. Probably because of his boycott by
the Cape Law Society, which affected his
earning power, Williams moved back to
England in 1905.
On his return, Williams lobbied ac-
tively on behalf of African issues. In 1907,
for instance, he fought the case for two
branches of the Basuto nation deprived of
their lands in the Orange River colony. He
furthermore tried to realize the idea, ﬁrst
mounted by the African Association, that
there should be an African spokesman in
Parliament. T o increase his chances of
becoming an MP , he joined the Fabian
Society and the National Liberal Club, but
failed to get a nomination. In 1906, how-
ever, he was elected to the Marylebone
Council, which made him probably the
ﬁrst black man to be elected to public ofﬁce
in Britain. In January 1908, he visited
Liberia upon the invitation of President
Barclay, whom he had interviewed for the
Jamaican in 1907. For reasons unknown, in
August 1908 he moved to T rinidad with his
wife and four children, where he set up a
successful law practice. He continued to
speak out on political issues until late 1910,
when he was struck down with a kidney ail-
ment from which he died on March 26,
1911.
Williams’s legacy is manifold. The con-
ference he organized became the model for
the later Pan-African conferences, ﬁrst or-
ganized by W . E. B. Du Bois and later by
George Padmore and Kwame N’krumah,
while his racial thinking inspired other
black leaders, such as Marcus Garvey, who
not only modeled his Universal Negro Im-
provement Association on the PAA but also
espoused Williams’ theme of Africa for the
Africans.
Henrice Altink

WILLIAMS,J AMES (1818–?)
James Williams was a Jamaican former slave
and coproducer of A Narrative of Events,
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1221 ---
WILLIAMS,J AMES 1133
Since the First of August 1834, by James
Williams, an Apprenticed Labourer in Jamaica
(1837). He was born on a Jamaican pimento
plantation to an African enslaved woman
and an unknown black, and probably en-
slaved, father. Williams’s autobiographical
narrative made him well known to British
antislavery audiences. The Narrative de-
scribes the inequity and cruelty of the ap-
prenticeship system, the four-year transi-
tional system between slavery and
emancipation, which slaves in most British
colonies experienced prior to “full” emanci-
pation in 1838. It recounts Williams’s suffer-
ings at the hands of his vindictive owners, as
a result of the corruption of the Jamaican
stipendiary magistracy, and because of the
unfairness of apprenticeship law. Williams
was ﬂogged and imprisoned on multiple
occasions, and witnessed many abusive and
violent incidents in the house of correction,
which he recounts in the Narrative.
A Narrative of Eventswas produced as a
result of the Quaker abolitionists Joseph
Sturge and Thomas Harvey’s investigative
visit to the West Indies in 1837. They de-
scribed their visit in The West Indies in
1837 (1838). Perhaps with the example of
the earlier slave narrative The History of
Mary Prince in mind, Sturge used his con-
tacts with missionaries in Jamaica to ﬁnd
an apprentice with experiences that would
be useful for anti-apprenticeship propa-
ganda, who had the necessary narrative and
memory skills to produce a worthwhile
account, and who was willing to travel to
England. Sturge located Williams with the
help of Baptist missionary John Clark and
black Baptist leader James Finlayson. Fur-
thermore, he provided the money with which
Williams purchased his freedom, and then
brought him to England. There, Williams
worked on the Narrative in collaboration
with an amanuensis, Dr Archibald Leighton
Palmer, a former stipendiary magistrate in
Jamaica.
The Narrative is one of a tiny handful
of ﬁrst-person accounts of the lives of slaves
and former slaves from the Anglophone
Caribbean. It is written in a version of
Jamaican Creole, and is probably the only
slave narrative to use Creole as the main
narrative voice. In other ways it is more
conventional, using traditional authenticat-
ing framing devices, in this case the words
of Baptist minister Thomas Price. The
Narrative’s publication was an important
development in the campaign to end ap-
prenticeship. It led to a governmental en-
quiry in Jamaica in which more than 100
apprentices gave evidence, and it formed
part of a series of events prompting in-
creased concern about prisons in the
Caribbean colonies. Abolitionist publicity
about poor conditions in West Indian pris-
ons contributed to the ending of appren-
ticeship, two years earlier than planned, in
1838.
James Williams stayed in England for
only a few months. Letters from Joseph
Sturge, ironically echoing the language of
slaveholders, describe the older man’s belief
that Williams was in danger of becoming
“indolent” and needed to be “compelled to
labour for his bread.” Williams returned to
Jamaica in late 1837 with the promise that
he would be apprenticed to a trade in
Kingston. Almost nothing is known about
what happened to him after his return, ex-
cept that he was alive in early 1838 and in
close contact with the apprentices living on
his former plantation in the parish of
St. Ann, Jamaica.
Diana Paton

WILLIAMS,J OHN A. (1925–)
Author of 12 novels, eight nonfiction
books, one volume of poetry, two plays,
43 articles and essays, 10 edited/coedited
volumes, and librettist for an opera, the
American Book Award winner John A.
Williams, in his various positions of Navy
hospital corpsman, journalist, professional
writer, and university professor, has trav-
eled globally in the 40 years of his writing
career to illuminate the conditions of racial
disparity and struggles for freedom experi-
enced by African Americans at home and
abroad. As a politically conscious black
intellectual whose nascent writing career
started in the 1950s and progressed to
coincide with the 1960s Civil Rights
Movement in the United States, Williams
has worked diligently to expose and to
ameliorate the transcendent effects of racial
injustices to people of African descent. Like
his freedom-ﬁghter predecessors Frederick
Douglass and Richard Wright, Williams
believes that the struggle for black libera-
tion is a lifelong commitment of the black
intellectual.
Born on December 5, 1925, in Jackson,
Mississippi, John A. Williams found him-
self moved shortly after birth to Syracuse,
New York, where his parents placed him
and his four siblings in a seemingly racist-free
environment. Quitting high school during
World War II to join the Navy in 1943,
Williams learned the contrary ﬁrsthand
while playing the role of patriot in a racially
charged military system. He returned to
Syracuse after an honorable discharge in
1946 not only to complete high school and
pursue his undergraduate degree at Syracuse
University in 1950 but also to enter graduate
school in 1951. He worked alternately as a
manual laborer and social worker before he
landed more lucrative stints with CBS and
NBC as a journalist during the mid-1950s.
During the latter part of this decade,
Williams completed the two drafts of his
ﬁrst novel, One for New York (later retitled
The Angry Ones ), which was published in
1960.
The 1960s was the angry period of
black militancy, and Williams was angry
but prideful, too. From 1960 to 1964, he
traveled globally and domestically through-
out Africa, Europe, the Mideast, and the
United States as a broadcast journalist for
CBS and NBC and a print journalist for
Holiday, Ebony, and Jet magazines. The
post–World War II era brought varied
global crises—African and Asian peoples
clamoring for decolonization, the race for
power between the United States and the
Soviet Union, and incipient civil turbu-
lences from blacks in the United States;
Williams wrote articles on the state of af-
fairs of blacks scattered throughout the
African Diaspora. Not accepting rising
1960s black nationalist platforms that ex-
cluded white scholars, critics, or writers
from engaging in black cultural critiques,
Williams, nonetheless, stood ﬁrm in re-
sisting gross misrepresentations of black
culture. In 1962, he began writing
counter responses to negative images and
distorted histories of blacks created by
white historians through shifting the lens
of representation to the perspective of a
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1223 ---
WILLIAMS,J OHN A. 1135
well-educated, well-traveled black intellec-
tual. His style marked the trend of other
black writers of the 1960s onward.
Williams also began producing book-
length works; he wrote Africa: Her History,
Lands and People (1963) and edited the
Angry Black (1962), later nominated for the
Prix de Rome but then rejected by the
American Academy in Rome.
Not bitter by such outward American
racism, Williams simply responded by be-
coming more vocal. He published three
more nonfiction books, The Protectors
(1964), This Is My Country T oo(1965), and
Omowale, The Child Returns Home (1965),
reﬂecting black pride and cultural con-
sciousness springing from his travels and
emerging militancy. The acclaim of his sec-
ond, third, and fourth novels earned
Williams entry into academia around this
time as a lecturer in writing at City College
of New York. With the publication of
Night Son (1961), a nihilistic novel loosely
based on the life of Charlie Parker, and
Sissie (1963), a counter-discourse novel ex-
alting black culture traditionalism within
cohesive black American families, Williams
followed the trend of sociological writing
established by Richard Wright, his prede-
cessor. However, with The Man Who Cried
I Am (1967), often viewed as the third
novel in a trilogy, Williams not only estab-
lished himself as a realist writer but also as
a politicized writer critiquing the plight
and dangers of the black intellectual
through his character Max Reddick, a hero
clearly parodic of Richard Wright and his
electrifying rise and tragic fall as a man and
writer.
From the mid-1960s to the present,
Williams has produced a book or work of
art each year, whether ﬁction, nonﬁction
(both adult and juvenile), editions of
books, a volume of poetry, or coauthorship
of an opera. His ﬁction includes Sons of
Darkness, Sons of Light (1969), Captain
Blackman (1972), Mothersill and Foxes
(1975), The Junior Bachelor Society (1976),
Click Song (1981), The Berhama Account
(1985), Jacob’s Ladder(1999), and Clifford’s
Blues (1999). Critics note Williams’s style
synthesizes fact and ﬁction, denoting post-
modernist writing, and illuminates the his-
torical consciousnesses of his main male
characters, sometimes allegorical ﬁgures, as
in The Man Who Cried I Am, Captain
Blackman, and Clifford’s Blues . Further,
Williams writing recalls tradition, and
namely the stylistics of slave narrator, play-
wright, and travel writer William Wells
Brown. Following Brown’s lead, Williams
challenges how truth is authenticated
and/or legitimated as illustrated by his pub-
lic outcry, along with nine other black writ-
ers, against white Southern writer William
Styron’s gross distortion of slave hero Nat
T urner’s militant character captured in
Thomas Gray’s jailhouse transcript The
Confessions of Nat Turner (1831). With
Williams’s focus on the arbitrariness of fact
and ﬁction as explored in the triptych of his
historical novels, he ensures that his readers
relive history with his characters by way of
their interlocking past and present experi-
ences. In Captain Blackman, the characters
were black soldiers in the American Revo-
lution through the Vietnam War, while in
Clifford’s Blues,the exemplary character was
a black civilian concentration camp victim
at Dachau in World War II during the
Nazis’ ﬁnal solution to exterminate all ves-
tiges of racial impurity.
Williams has also written biographies
for adult and children audiences, including
The Most Native of Sons: Richard Wright
(1970), The King God Didn’t Save (1970),

Reﬂected in Malcolm: Living in The Time of

tentatively titled Over My Shoulder. Williams’s
