WOLOF
Wolof, an African language, is spoken pri-
marily in Senegal and the Gambia but can
also be heard in France, Guinea-Bissau,
Mali, and Mauritania. The total number of
Wolof speakers in Senegal is 3,568,060,
while the total number of Wolof speakers
throughout the world is 3,612,560. Wolof
is one of six national languages in Senegal,
which means that it can be the language of
instruction in schools where the majority of
students’ ﬁrst language is Wolof.
The Wolof people themselves make up
about 43 percent of Senegal’s population.
Wolof has become a lingua franca in Senegal,
thus other ethnic groups have adopted Wolof
as their native language, and more than one-
half of the remaining population also speaks
Wolof in addition to their ﬁrst language.
Because Wolof is used as a commercial
language in Senegal, individuals in trading
centers, who may be Lebanese or Moroccan,
also speak it.
Wolof is the language of the Wolof
people as well as the Lébou. The language
was ﬁrst written using the Arabic alphabet
with the addition of some letters that do
not exist in Arabic. The language was ﬁrst
written with the Roman alphabet during
the time of colonization. T oday, Wolof
written in the Arabic alphabet is seen in re-
ligious texts and is used by authors who
have had a Koranic education.
Because Dakar was the center of
French West Africa during the colonial era,
individuals from surrounding areas fre-
quently migrated there; this contributed to
the Woloﬁzation of other languages. Addi-
tionally, Wolof borrows from French the
names of goods manufactured in Europe,
while the language uses Arabic words to
discuss Islamic practices and traditions.
Wolof is considered part of the West
Atlantic language unit. It is characterized
by a system of noun classes. There are also
root words that remain the same while aux-
iliary words and adjacent pronouns indi-
cate the speciﬁcs of that word; furthermore,
a distinction is made between root words
that involve actions and those that involve
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1225 ---
WORLD ANTISLAVERY CONVENTIONS 1137
states of being. Relatively few dialectical dif-
ferences can be found across regions where
Wolof is spoken. However, the Wolof spoken
in Dakar has more borrowed vocabulary
from French than does the Wolof spoken in
rural areas.
Mahriana Rofheart

WORLD ANTISLAVERY
CONVENTIONS, 1840, 1843
On March 21, 1840, an American aboli-
tionist, Joshua Leavitt, editorialized in the
New York Emancipator: “We venture to sug-
gest to our British fellow laborers the expe-
diency of calling together, from all civilized
nations, a general anti-slavery conference to
be held in London in the months of May or
June, 1840.” This initiative, intended to
foster international cooperation in the
struggle against slavery, culminated in the
two World Antislavery Conventions that
were held in London from June 12 until
June 23, 1840, and from June 13 until June
23, 1843. Both conventions were organized
under the rubric of the British and Foreign
Anti-Slavery Society.
After circulating preconvention ques-
tionnaires, the London Committee of the
society sent out invitations to 35 different
countries. These countries included the
United States, France, Spain, Switzerland,
Haiti, Jamaica, T rinidad, Demerara, Berbice,
the Bahamas, Antigua, British Guinea,
Mauritius, Sierra Leone, and Canada. The
largest response came from the United
States: 53 delegates excluding the women
delegates whom the London Committee
declined to seat. The next largest delegation,
with six members, was from France. When
the sittings commenced, in Freemasons’
Hall, Great Queen Street, the American
women delegates were exiled to the gallery.
The London Committee insisted, as it had
indicated in a second summons to the
convention issued in February 1840, only
gentlemen delegates would be given seats
on the convention ﬂoor as active partici-
pants. Voices of dissent to this decision
came largely from the Garrisonian wing of
the American delegation, with William
Lloyd Garrison himself deciding to take his
seat in the gallery with the women.
The ﬁrst day’s proceedings were taken
up with controversy over this issue. Al-
though British delegates highly praised
women’s contributions within auxiliary fe-
male antislavery societies, they insisted that
to allow the women’s participation in the
convention as speakers would be contrary
to custom. They had not anticipated the
degree to which “the woman question”
had divided the antislavery movement in
America, and were concerned that the
convention not become a platform for the
debate of the controversial issue of women’s
rights. Although never explicitly stated, the
delegates implied that to allow the American
women an active part in proceedings may
expose the convention to ridicule and
detract from its serious purpose. When
invitations to the second convention were
sent out with the same condition attached,
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1226 ---
1138 W ORLD ANTISLAVERY CONVENTIONS
Garrisonian abolitionists declined to at-
tend. The American delegation to the 1843
convention was subsequently represented
by members of the “new organization,” the
American and Foreign Anti-Slavery Soci-
ety, which had split from the Garrisonian-
dominated American Anti-Slavery Society
over this issue in 1840.
The opening address to the ﬁrst con-
vention, on June 12, 1840, was delivered
by British abolitionist Thomas Clarkson,
author of The History of the Rise, Progress,
and Accomplishment of the Abolition of the
African Slave Trade by the British Parliament
(1808, 1839). Other delegates, shown in
the painting by Benjamin Robert Haydon
that hangs in the National Portrait Gallery,
London, included Daniel O’Connell,
James G. Birney, Joseph Sturge, Henry 
B. Stanton, Wendell Phillips, and Thomas
Fowell Buxton, all British or American
abolitionists. Among those exiled to the
gallery were Quaker abolitionist Lucretia
Mott, attending the convention with her
husband James Mott, and feminist-
abolitionist-in-the-making E lizabeth Cady
Stanton, attending with her husband
Henry B. Stanton, president of the American
Anti-Slavery Society. While in London,
Lucretia Mott and Elizabeth Cady Stanton
conceived the idea for another convention,
this time to debate the issue on the basis of
which they had been excluded from the
ﬂoor of Freemasons’ Hall. The idea came to
fruition when eight years later the two
women met again in a small town near
New York for the 1848 Seneca Falls
Women’s Rights Convention. The 1840
World Anti-Slavery Convention is cele-
brated as the birthplace of this landmark
event in nineteenth-century feminism.
Papers presented at the Antislavery
Conventions were followed by a general
discussion, after which each matter was re-
ferred to a subcommittee for resolution.
The resolutions of the subcommittees were
then returned to the ﬂoor for approval by
the convention as a whole. The topics of
papers included the attitude of the
churches to slavery, the boycott of products
that involved the use of slave labor, eman-
cipation in the British West Indies, sugar
production in the colonies, slavery in Cuba
and Brazil, the Atlantic slave trade, and also
less debated topics such as Red Indian slav-
ery in Canada and Egyptian slave hunts.
Delegates from abroad emphasized the im-
portance of links with the British antislav-
ery movement. The American Garrisonian
Wendell Phillips, for example, stressed the
potential inﬂuence that British abolitionists
may exert on American public opinion
regarding the possibility of peaceful
abolition.
After 1840 Anglo-American relations
became increasingly strained as British
societies took up opposing allegiances in
relation to the schisms that had developed
within the American abolitionist move-
ment. One subject on which there was
general agreement, however, was the im-
practicability of the colonization scheme,
which proposed to repatriate emancipated
African Americans to Africa, and the need,
therefore, to ﬁnd other ways to achieve the
transition from a slave to a free labor econ-
omy. The proceedings of the 1840 Conven-
tion, running to 600 pages and published
by the British and Foreign Anti-Slavery
Society in 1841, constitute a detailed
record of the issues and debates that ani-
mated the antislavery movement in the
early 1840s. The proceedings of the second
convention, which focused more narrowly
on American slavery, were published by the
same organization in 1843, supplementing
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1227 ---
WORLD BANK 1139
this emerging proﬁle of an international
antislavery vanguard.
The two World Antislavery Conven-
tions of 1840 and 1843 may be regarded as
watershed events in the history of the abo-
litionist movement. With these events abo-
litionism moved onto a world stage, albeit
one dominated by British and American
abolitionists, and became recognizably
global in its reach.

WORLD BANK
In July 1944, representatives from 44 coun-
tries meeting in Bretton Woods, New
Hampshire, created the International Bank
for Reconstruction and Development
(World Bank) to rebuild the economies of
Europe. The Cold War led the United
States to believe that this task exceeded the
capabilities of the World Bank; in a massive
effort to revive Europe, it embarked on
the Marshall Plan. Bereft of its original
purpose, the World Bank turned to shoring
up the economies of Latin America and
Africa against the encr oachment of com-
munism. In its early days, the World Bank
differentiated itself from the International
Monetary Fund (IMF). Whereas the IMF
provided short-term loans, the World Bank
ﬁnanced projects that enhanced the pro-
ductivity of agriculture and industry. In
pursuit of this aim, Mexico on April 29,
1947, applied for $208.9 million from the
World Bank to build a hydroelectric plant,
railroads, highways, a pipeline, and an irri-
gation system. On March 25, 1948, the
World Bank offered its ﬁrst loan to a country
in Latin America, funding the construction
of an electric power plant and an irrigation
system and the production of trucks, tractors,
harvesters, and threshers for use on farms
in Chile. The World Bank approved a loan
for Mexico, the second to a Latin American
country, on January 7, 1949, but for only
$24.1 million.
In March 1949, the World Bank
toured Egypt in the ﬁrst mission to Africa;
in March and April 1950, World Bank vice
president Robert L. Garner visited South
Africa and Zimbabwe; and on March 23,
1950, the World Bank dispatched advisors
to Ethiopia. On September 13, 1950, the
World Bank offered its ﬁrst loan to an
African nation: $7 million to Ethiopia for
the construction of roads and the ﬁnanc-
ing of banks. On January 23, 1951, in
the ﬁrst cooperative venture between the
World Bank and private ﬁnanciers, the
World Bank and eight private U.S. banks
loaned South Africa $80 million to in-
crease its capacity to generate electricity.
This loan marked the evolution of the
World Bank toward the position that
countries, so far as possible, should fund
development with capital from private
banks. The World Bank and IMF were to
be lenders of last resort. In September 1962,
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1228 ---
1140 W ORLD BANK
the World Bank, in its ﬁrst loan to educa-
tion, funded the development of vocational
training in T unisia. In October 1962, the
World Bank announced its commitment
to funding education as a precondition to
economic growth and in July 1963 pub-
lished a study on public schools in T unisia.
In 1971, the World Bank joined the
United Nations Food and Agriculture Or-
ganization, the United Nations Develop-
ment Programme, and the Ford, Rocke-
feller, and Kellogg Foundations in creating
the Consultive Group for International
Agricultural Research (CGIAR) to spread
the Green Revolution throughout the third
world. In pursuit of this aim, the World
Bank began to fund science in addition to
the economy and education. In December
1971, the CGIAR pledged $15 million for
research and on February 3, 1972, the
World Bank granted $1.3 million to the
International Center for Wheat and Maize
Improvement in Mexico, the International
Potato Center in Peru, and the International
Crop Research Institute for the Semi-Arid
T ropics in Nigeria. On October 28, 1975,
the World Bank published a study on
farming in Cameroon, Ethiopia, Kenya,
Malawi, Mali, Nigeria, and Tanzania.
In August 1982, Mexico suspended
repayment of its debt; over the next two
years, nearly every other debtor in Latin
America and Africa defaulted also. In
January 1983, the World Bank created a
type of loan similar to the short-term credit
of the IMF to alleviate the debt crisis. This
action drew the policies of the World Bank
closer to those of the IMF . Between January
1983 and April 1984, the World Bank ap-
proved more than $4 billion in short-term
loans but only four of the 16 recipients
were in Latin America: Bolivia, Guyana,
Colombia, and Panama. The IMF had
loaned money to Bolivia, Guyana, and
Panama as a precondition to their receiving
a loan from the World Bank. In December
1987, the World Bank approved loans to
the poorest countries in Africa to help them
pay down debt and by 1990 had loaned
money to 21 African countries.
Famine in Africa led the World Bank
in 1992 to grant $20 million to Somalia,
Djibouti, Ethiopia, and Kenya and on
November 29, 1993, to convene in
Washington, D.C., the Conference on
Agenda to Reduce World Hunger. T o aid
its efforts in Africa, the World Bank joined
the United Nations in creating on March
15, 1996, the United Nations Special
Initiative for Africa. Under this program
the World Bank targeted loans to agricul-
ture, water treatment, and information
technology. T o underscore the importance
of knowledge in economic development,
the World Bank convened with Morocco
on May 12, 1997, the Mediterranean
Development Forum and joined with the
Institute de la Mediterranee on September
11, 2002, in a conference on the Middle
East and North Africa. Subsequent initia-
tives include loans for debt reduction in
Latin America and for AIDS education in
Africa.

WORLD HEALTH ORGANIZATION 1141
WORLD HEALTH
ORGANIZATION
World Health Organization (WHO) is the
United Nations specialized agency for
health, established in 1948. It is governed
by member states through the World
Health Assembly and has the mandate to
promote the attainment of “the highest pos-
sible level of health” by all peoples. WHO is
ﬁnanced primarily from annual contribu-
tions made by member governments.
WHO keeps member countries in-
formed of the latest developments in vaccines,
cancer research, nutritional discoveries, con-
trol of drug addiction, and health hazards of
nuclear radiation. It also sponsors measures
for the control of epidemic and endemic dis-
eases and instruction in the use of antibiotics
and insecticides. WHO encourages efforts to
strengthen and expand public health services
by providing technical advice in the prepara-
tion of long-term national health plans and
offering aid in the development of national
training institutions for medical and nursing
personnel.
The African continent and the Americas
are faced with many severe health challenges
and millions have died from malnutrition,
malaria, and diarrhea diseases, and most re-
cently from HIV infections. T o curb this
trend, WHO’s activities have focused on ef-
forts to bring about improvements in health
care to confront the epidemic of AIDS and
other diseases. WHO, in collaboration with
the United States, has contributed funds to
ﬁght AIDS and other health problems in
ways that develop and support indigenous
primary health care systems.
The Pan American Health Organization
(PAHO) and World Health Organization
Regional Ofﬁce for Africa (WHO/AFRO),
which are the regional offices for the
Americas and A frica, respectively, have
been successful to a large extent in eradi-
cating polio, measles, leprosy, smallpox,
yellow fever, and cholera epidemics in
these regions by promoting mass cam-
paigns involving nationwide vaccination
programs. Recognizing that HIV/AIDS is
the leading cause of death in adults and
children, WHO, in collaboration with the
U.S. Agency for International Develop-
ment (USAID), is working to confront the
frightening epidemic of AIDS, especially
in Africa, by working in cooperation with
the governments to study the causes and
prevention of AIDS and HIV-related
diseases.
With the aim of reducing maternal and
child mortality, WHO provides quality re-
productive health services, including family
planning, community-based maternity ser-
vices, and accessible ﬁrst-level referral services.
T o help people learn and practice improved
health and disease prevention, WHO pro-
vides health education for people living in
rural communities and also organizes effec-
tive advocacy, social mobilization, health
campaigns, and other communication strate-
gies to publicize its health programs. These
campaigns have had signiﬁcant success in
eradicating tuberculosis, malaria, venereal
disease, cholera, trachoma, and yellow fever
in Africa and the Americas.
WHO has also been instrumental in in-
volving the support of leaders in Africa and
the Americas to providing equitable access
to basic health care, quality drugs, and vac-
cines; strengthening health information and
surveillance systems; improving access to
water and sanitation; and using technology
to support health care. WHO has also
played a leading role in coordinating health
issues in these regions by ensuring that the
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

leaders make commitments to health-sector
reform, women’s health, and environmental
issues so as to provide better health care for
their citizens.

WORLD TRADE
ORGANIZATION
In 1947 the United Nations enacted the
General Agreement on Tariffs and T rade
(GATT) to promote free trade. In 1994 the
signatories of GATT formed the World
T rade Organization (WTO). The WTO re-
quires unanimity among its members to
act. Rather than attempt to forge consensus
among all 142 members, the WTO con-
ducts business in small committees. Several
African nations charge that wealthy coun-
tries comprise a disproportionate share of
the committees. These critics assert that the
appearance of consensus masks the reality
that a cabal of wealthy nations overrides the
interests of the majority of developing
countries. T o increase their leverage, several
developing nations have allied among
themselves and with afﬂuent countries to
inﬂuence policy. Nearly half the more than
20 developing nations in the International
T extile and Clothing Bureau, a group of
clothing exporters that advises the WTO,
are in Latin America. The same is true of
nine of the 15 members of the Cairns Group,
a confederation of developing and afﬂuent
countries that seeks to shape agricultural
policy.
The Cairns Group aims to reduce gov-
ernment intervention in the economy.
Such a policy would in principle eliminate
tariffs and subsidies. Proponents of trade
liberalism hope to use the WTO to coax
the United States to end its subsidies to
agriculture, thereby driving up prices to a
level at which Cairns Group countries can
compete in the U.S. market. Caribbean na-
tions oppose the Cairns Group in the belief
that the elimination of tariffs would allow
the United States to dump food in Latin
America, lowering prices. Underlying this
view is the premise that U.S. agribusiness
benefits from economies of scale that
would enable it to drive inefﬁcient small
farmers from the market. Accordingly,
Caribbean nations wish to revise the
Uruguay Round’s Agreement on Agriculture
to permit developing nations to retain
subsidies and a tariff on imports.
The issue of trade liberalization pits the
developing world against the WTO’s Intel-
lectual Property Rights Agreement, which
allows U.S. pharmaceutical companies to
protect themselves against competition
from generic drugs. In 1997 South Africa
ﬂouted the agreement by permitting its
medical providers to shop worldwide for
the cheapest drugs. Pharmaceutical compa-
nies challenged South Africa at the WTO’s
Dispute Panel before withdrawing their
complaint in April 2001. In an attempt at
compromise, the WTO proposed to permit
the poorest counties to suspend the agree-
ment until 2016 but to require middle-
income nations—Brazil, Cote d’Ivoire,
Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria, and South
Africa—to comply with it. The nations of
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1231 ---
WORLD WAR I 1143
Africa and Latin America are also wary of
biotechnology ﬁrms using the agreement to
patent plant varieties and thereby deprive
farmers from growing a cultivar without
paying a fee. These reservations have led
one scholar, writing about the effects of
WTO regulations on Kenya, to recommend
that the WTO study the consequences of
current policies on the nations of Africa
before beginning a new round of talks.

WORLD WAR I
Although centered in Europe, World War I
(1914–1918), or the “Great War,” pro-
foundly affected Latin America and Africa
as well as the United States. World War I is
commonly seen as a conﬂict of the Entente
Powers of Great Britain, France, and
Russia, also known as the Entente Alliance
(or “Allies”) against Germany and Austria-
Hungary, the two great powers of Central
Europe, or the Central Powers. Beyond
Europe, however, the war increased the U.S.
presence in Latin America and placed
Africa on a road toward decolonization and
autonomy.
Beginning in the early nineteenth cen-
tury, the United States exercised a semi-
proprietary interest in Latin America. The
Monroe Doctrine (1823), which sought to
contain and minimize European colonial
inﬂuence in the Western Hemisphere, is
the most recognized, though not ﬁrst, ex-
pression of this caretaker view. Sixteen years
before the start of the war, the United
States had freed Cuba and the Philippines
from the Spanish on the long-standing be-
lief that freedom should be had by all; with
the outbreak of the war, the United States
felt it essential to reemphasize its hegemony
in the Americas.
Increased emphasis on the Monroe
Doctrine was not well received in Latin
America. Only Nicaragua immediately
sided with the United States during World
War I. Other countries feared that the
United States might draw them into the
war. Finally, Guatemala, out of economic
necessity because its markets in Germany
collapsed, supported the United States. As
the war was ending, Honduras entered the
war on the side of the Allies. El Salvador
alone proclaimed neutrality. Costa Rica,
under Federico Tinoco, sided with the United
States hoping to gain recognition; Tinoco
came to power through a 1917 coup that the
United States never recognized. T o further
pressure the United States, Tinoco claimed
that the Germans threatened the Panama
Canal. However, two months after Tinoco
gained power, he resigned at the arrival of
U.S. ships at Limon. Costa Rica remained
uncommitted to the Allies.
By war’s end, many Latin American
states were on the brink of war among
themselves over issues unrelated to the
Great War. U.S. intervention stayed the
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1232 ---
1144 W ORLD WAR I
conﬂict, and the 1923 Latin American
Peace Conference formalized the end of
hostilities. The Latin American states were,
for the most part, thoroughly frustrated
with U.S. policies, interventions, and arbi-
trary control, but they nevertheless wel-
comed the peace they could not secure on
their own.
Africa witnessed military action in
three main theaters: Cameroon and part of
Nigeria (then T ogoland and Kamerun),
Tanzania and Zambia (German East
Africa), and Namibia (German Southwest
Africa). In addition, Allied forces were also
based in Mozambique, South Africa,
Rhodesia (now Zimbabwe), and the Belgian
Congo (now the Democratic Republic of
the Congo). There was no conﬂict in these
areas, but troop mobilization affected the
local population.
Britain’s ﬁrst action in Africa began on
July 31, 1914, against German T ogoland,
in advance of the declaration of war against
Germany on August 4, 1914. French forces
from French West Africa combined with
the British to overrun T ogoland in 27 days.
Kamerun also fell quickly to British,
French, and Belgian troops. The German
defense was miniscule, and the Allies were
heavily mechanized and able to blockade
the region from resupply.
The conﬂict in German East Africa was
longer and more a running gun battle than
a war. Both the German colony and British
East Africa (Kenya and Uganda) declared
neutrality, so no war was expected. However,
a German colonel, Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck,
effectively declared war on behalf of the
German government by raiding British East
Africa. He had 200 Ge rman ofﬁcers and

2,500 African soldiers and cr eated a tiny
navy on Lake Victoria. The British sent two
brigades from India and some gunboats via
railway. They landed at Tanga Beach on
November 2, 1914, but were repelled. The
supplies abandoned by the British loss
sustained the Germans through 1915.
In 1916, the Allies sent General Jan
Smuts from South Africa to crush the
German presence. General Smuts had
20,000 troops: 13,000 Boer, English, and
Rhodesians, and 7,000 Indians and South
Africans. In addition, he had reserve Belgian
and Portuguese troops. Colonel von Lettow-
Vorbeck, meanwhile, had increased his
army to 15,500 troops: 3,500 Germans and
12,000 Africans.
Smuts failed to achieve the expected
decisive victory, and his troops suffered
miserably from disease and the adverse ter-
rain. One unit, the Ninth South African
Infantry, dropped from 1,135 men to 116
in one year (averaging three per day) de-
spite minimal ﬁghting. Smuts was recalled
to England in January 1917 to join the War
Cabinet. He was succeeded by General
Hoskins and then by South African General
van Deventer. Van Deventer was the only
one to show any success. He forced the sur-
render of 5,000 of von Lettow-V orbeck’s
men. Von Lettow-Vorbeck nonetheless con-
tinued to evade the Allies and even celebrated
victories two days after the Armistice was
signed on November 11, 1918. He ﬁnally
surrendered, undefeated, on November 23.
The third African theater was German
Southwest Africa. The South African gov-
ernment prepared vigorously for campaigns
against the Germans. However, Lt. Colonel
Manie M aritz, a Boer in the South
African army, took exception to attacking
the Germans, and many South Africans
agreed. Germany had assisted the Boers only
eleven years earlier, providing arms to the
Boers against British forces in the Boer War,
and was considered an ally of a kind.
Colonel Maritz urged whites of all na-
tionalities to rise up and form an indepen-
dent South Africa. T welve thousand troops
quickly materialized, but were just as
quickly crushed. Martial law was imposed
on October 14, 1914, and Maritz was ex-
iled ten days later. Order was reestablished
and a successful campaign against German
Southwest Africa began in March 1915.
Sixty-seven thousand South African sol-
diers completely occupied the German ter-
ritory, taking the capital by May 12, 1915.
All remaining German forces surrendered
by July 9, 1915.
The social ramiﬁcations of the Great
War in Africa were far more important than
the military operations. African involve-
ment in the war caused the strengthening
of regional colonial authority, the advance-
ment of regional economies, and the ram-
pant exploitation of black people through
impressed service and in other ways. Fur-
thermore, oppressed peoples were exposed
to radically different social possibilities,
while the British engaged in a systematic ef-
fort to prevent such inﬂuences. Finally,
Africa saw the growth of the number of
black Africans with European-style educa-
tions and knowledge.
African colonial governments rushed
legislation granting greater local control.
Colonial governments geared up to meet
the dramatically increased demand for
minerals, rubber, petroleum, and nonedible
crops such as cotton. The surge in exports
greatly improved the colonies’ economic
strength. In the Gold Coast (Ghana), the
intense need for mineral resources resulted
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1234 ---
1146 W ORLD WAR II
in a comprehensive survey of the country.
New assets were discovered. These resources
further added to the economic strength of
the colonial administration of Gold Coast.
In South Africa, the demand for labor on
white-owned farms became so great that
blacks who considered joining the military
were told that their homes would be
burned if they left.
Conscription was considerable. The
French brutally conscripted Africans to
support the Third Republic during its
seventy years of stumbling existence. Con-
scription intensiﬁed during the Great War,
and thousands ﬂed to Liberia and British
colonies, with over 15,000 refugees to the
Gold Coast alone. While the British were
not brutal, salaries were poor or nonexis-
tent, food and living conditions were not
as promised, and black Africans were
forced into subordinate roles. The British
would not tolerate the possibility of blacks
giving orders to whites. Black resistance to
conscription was strong. This resistance
strengthened tribes because the tribal
groups became the means of hiding and
protecting those who evaded service.
Africans who had been recruited as
soldiers and support staff were, at the end
of the war, better equipped for indepen-
dence. They had new language skills and
educations. They observed new leadership
techniques. In some areas, the war exposed
them to a new religion, Islam, which could
serve as a basis of uniﬁcation against colo-
nialism. As a result, the Great War
strengthened Africa while weakening the
grip of colonial powers. The stage was set
for decolonization and independence in
the subsequent decades of the twentieth
century.

WORLD WAR II
Lasting from 1939 to 1945, World War II
(WWII) transformed diplomatic relations,
economies, and social structures through-
out the globe. Latin America and Africa
were affected both indirectly and directly.
Indirectly, regional politics and economies
were shaped by their contributions to the
war machines of the Allied and Axis powers
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1235 ---
WORLD WAR II 1147
and by their strategic locations. Latin
America saw increased regional stability, at
the price of the crushing of political dissent
in certain cases, as a consequence of the
war. Africa was put on the road to decolo-
nization and independence. Africa alter-
nately enriched its infrastructure and lost
much capital, resources, and labor to distant
powers. Directly, Africa saw considerable
combat over strategic resources and geo-
graphic advantages. African soldiers were
conscripted or recruited to both Axis and
Allied forces. While the epicenters of WWII
were in Europe, the Paciﬁc, and East Asia,
Latin America and Africa were inﬂuential in
determining the war’s outcome.
Latin America offered logistical sup-
port and a primary deployment point.
Latin America’s internal matters during
WWII were far more complicated than its
general external relations. After World War
I, the United States dominated trade and
intergovernmental political relations. For-
mal recognition from the United States be-
came important; without it countries could
suffer from lack of aid, the inability to nego-
tiate trade, and the absence of international
representation. At the 1936 Inter-U.S. Peace
Conference on War and Peace in Buenos
Aires, Latin American nations felt that the
war was too remote to be a concern and
asked for the United States to abide by its
nonintervention pledge. However, the
strategic importance of the Panama Canal
drew considerable attention and Ger-
many’s invasion of Poland in 1939 led to
Latin American leaders suppor ting Allied
forces.
The United States initiated two sets of
measures to protect its Panamanian invest-
ment and shipping artery. It created high
value land-lease agreements to provide
naval yards, to defend against German
submarines (U-boats), and to create long-
range aerial operations for both Atlantic
and Paciﬁc theaters. Second, the United
States provided an infusion of capital. U.S.
military forces in Latin American nations
modernized their hosts’ armies. Many for-
mally unrecognized dictators showered
U.S. troops with support, hoping that the
show of solidarity would result in U.S. ap-
proval for their regimes.
The foreign military presence in Latin
America, coupled with prior unresolved
diplomatic issues and the desire to reduce
political conﬂict, led many Latin American
leaders to portray dissidents as “commu-
nists.” Often, the United States was not
concerned enough to notice the difference
between political dissent and communist
insurgency. As a result, the United States
often gave approval to the eradication of
such dissidents or provided the means of
removal. The fear of market disruption
combined with the search for stability dur-
ing WWII promoted the modernization of
local military forces and reinforced the
power structures that existed in Latin
America for some time. Attempts to change
social and political structures and to im-
prove the livelihoods of people through re-
distributions of wealth or power were
viewed as threats. These trends continued
throughout the war and afterward, during
the Cold War.
In Africa, combat took place over the
control of supply routes and the control of
war resources and commodities produced
in Africa. Military strategies for African
campaigns were tied to the production of
war material, strategic points of transship-
ment, and the recruitment of ofﬁcers. Many
forces were drawn into Africa. The most
well-known conﬂict occurred on the south-
ern shores of the Mediterranean between
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1236 ---
1148 W ORLD WAR II
British and German forces, the latter led by
Irwin Rommel. North African battles were
intense. Italian forces stationed in Libya
raided Egypt in order to obtain oil, suffered
great losses, and were reinforced by the
Deutsches Afrikakorps (Germany), the
corps-level command group for the opera-
tion of Panzer and light infantry divisions.
British forces also sustained great losses
repelling them. A costly and exhausting
back-and-forth desert conﬂict took place
between Allied and Axis forces, coming to
a conclusion when U.S. military forces
eventually landed in T unisia to cut Italian
supply lines to German forces. British
Commonwealth forces and the arriving
American troops proceeded to work in
tandem on both sides, resulting in the sur-
render of the German forces in the region.
Rommel led a remarkable defense. Early
on, Rommel had come within a hair-
breadth of capturing Alexandria, which
would have brought Egypt under Axis
control and provided fuel for Hitler’s
armies in Europe. Had Rommel suc-
ceeded, Hitler would have had less moti-
vation to attack Russia for her petroleum
and the course of the war would have been
quite different.
The war in West Africa included
armed conﬂicts in Gabon and the Battle of
Dakar. Allied forces also attempted to gain
control of Gabon, French Equatorial
Africa, and French West Africa, initially
freeing all but the last. Blurring the lines
between West and North African cam-
paigns, attacks were launched from Free
French Chad against Italian-controlled
Libya, which was the principal supply route
for the Deutsches Afrikakorps.
General Erwin Rommel with his troops in the desert at El Alamein, Egypt. The Allied forces under Bernard

WORLD WAR II 1149
In Italian East Africa, a large military
force of about 250,000 African recruits was
present. This army threatened the supply
routes through the Suez Canal and outlying
areas. British Commonwealth forces based
in Egypt, Sudan, and British Somaliland
were too few to combat this threat. By rec-
ognizing the authority of Haile Selassie, the
local leader and representative of the indige-
nous Ethiopian forces, the Allied Forces har-
nessed enough manpower to advance against
the Axis. Italian forces saw an initial success
in capturing British Somaliland. However,
their naval forces became irrelevant because
of fuel shortages. After a failed attempt to at-
tack an Allied convoy, Italian naval forces in
the region were all but neutralized.
With the threat of shipping interfer-
ence resolved, conventional ground warfare
resumed by British Commonwealth forces,
including troops from Australia, India,
South Africa, Nigeria, and Gold Coast ter-
ritories. Indian and Australian forces at-
tacked from northern fortiﬁcations and
supply lines in Egypt. South African,
Nigerian, and Gold Coast forces rolled in
from the south. Finally, Indo-Free French
forces made amphibious assaults on Italian
East Africa. These battles eliminated Italy’s
threat to the surrounding areas.
In an important political change, the
Allied victory also established Ethiopian
sovereignty. Though not claimed by colo-
nial powers in the Berlin Conference, many
European powers had previously refused to
accept Ethiopia as a self-ruling African state.
The success of the Allied alliance with Haile
Selassie helped recognize Ethiopia as an in-
dependently sovereign nation. Ethiopia of-
fers a case of WWII furthering the process
of African political independence.
Africa’s location was of strategic impor-
tance also to the war of Allied forces against
Japan. Japanese inﬂuence dominated much
of Asia and the Paciﬁc theater, and the fall
of south Asian nations to imperial rule
would have granted the Japanese greater ac-
cess to the Indian Ocean. This led to the
fortification of Madagascar by Vichy
French forces, in an attempt to create a for-
ward base of operations so that Japanese
long-range submarines could travel into
Atlantic waters.
During and after the war, colonial
economies in Africa experienced a variety
of changes. African economies saw devel-
opment and diversiﬁcation, the recognition
of their global role as exporters of exotic,
conventional, and strategic mineral re-
sources, and further class stratiﬁcation.
Portuguese Africa (Cape Verde, Angola,
and Mozambique) offers an important case
of such changes. During the war from 1939
through 1943, German U-boats intercepted
shipments from North America to the
United Kingdom. The battle between 
U-boats and shipping is often called the
“Second Battle of the Atlantic.” British trade
with the United States, Africa, Spain, and
Portugal was severely affected. Prior to the
war, Portugal had restricted industrial
growth in its colonies to maintain their de-
pendence on Portugal. Now, a lack of British
transports meant that Portugal could not
transport raw materials from its African
colonies. Manufacturing was consequently
encouraged inside its colonies, with rubber
and steel as the main products. Roads, train-
ing, and processing plants were built to sup-
port the new industries. Management skills
were developed and created a new type of
labor force. Laborers prospered, including
native peoples despite the biases they faced.
This industrial prosperity in the Portuguese
colonies set the stage for independence and
economic growth following the war.
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1238 ---
1150 W RIGHT,R ICHARD
The resulting growth in smelting opera-
tions, steel manufacturing, rubber produc-
tion and processing, and other industrial
ﬁelds expanded resources and markets and
allowed for infrastructure development. The
latter included the construction of shipment
conduits, ports, and the creation of a clerical
infrastructure for quality control, customs,
and the enforcement of quotas. A skilled
workforce was created to operate advanced
industries. Increases in capital and com-
modity reserves resulted in an infrastructure
that could operate after wartime.
In general, colonial powers across
Africa could not remotely manage such op-
erations and regional authority was deemed
crucial during the war. Consequently, colo-
nial territories experienced a greater, if still
limited, degree of self-rule. Labor shortages
brought better terms for potential workers,
including local peoples. While Africans re-
mained subjected to classist and racist colo-
nial policies, opportunities arose for a few
to make substantial personal advances.
Overall, WWII increased the stability
of many regimes in Latin America through
U.S. support of dictatorships that opposed
political dissidence. This would set the stage
for anticommunist politics in the Western
Hemisphere during the Cold War. For
Africa, more steps toward political indepen-
dence were created; however, the disparity
between rich and poor continued. The bat-
tles in Africa set the stage for subsequent
battles for independence and between con-
ﬂicting African groups in the postcolonial
era. While Latin America’s remoteness from
the war reinforced its stability, Africa’s prox-
imity created an increasingly unstable polit-
ical environment that would unravel in the
decades of decolonization after the war.
Josiah Baker, Matthew 
Shannon, and Robert A. Baker

WRIGHT,R ICHARD
(1908–1960)
Richard Wright was an African American
novelist, essayist, and social critic of mod-
ern America, and is best known for his
novel Native Son (1940). The early life of
Richard Wright did not portend his destiny
to emerge in the twentieth century as the
foremost black writer in America during
the 1940s, and the leading global humanist
in the ﬁght to relieve worldwide oppression
of people of color in the 1950s. Author of
six novels, two collections of short stories,
seven nonﬁction works, a collection of es-
says, and a host of unpublished works now
housed at the Beinecke Library at Yale
University, the poet, ﬁction and nonﬁction
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1239 ---
WRIGHT,R ICHARD 1151
writer, playwright, essayist, journalist,
bluesman, and social critic Richard Wright
gave to the world a deluge of words during
the 52 years of his short life. Born on
September 4, 1908, on a plantation in
Roxie, Mississippi, located 15 miles from
Natchez—the Deep South city boasting
dual reputations as the locale containing
the largest number of antebellum million-
aires and the second largest slave auction
site during the 1850s—Wright stayed
brieﬂy in the backwoods until his parents
moved into town with Wright’s maternal
grandparents. When Richard was four,
Nathaniel Wright, an illiterate sharecropper
unable to ﬁnd work, moved his family to
Memphis, T ennessee, in an effort to ﬁnd
employment. It was here that Wright’s life
fragmented and deteriorated between 1914
and 1920, starting with Nathaniel Wright’s
desertion of his family and Ella Wright’s
immediate struggles as a single parent earn-
ing low wages from domestic work that re-
sulted in young Wright’s experience of years
of transient housing and disruptive moves
between Memphis; Elaine, Arkansas; and
Jackson, Mississippi, where his maternal
grandparents now resided.
Despite the Deep South’s social, politi-
cal, and religious edicts supporting race
codes that insisted upon Negro inferiority
and staunch Jim Crow separatism in every
aspect of life, young Wright thrived, but his
food was knowledge. The fables of litera-
ture were Wright’s salvation, despite disap-
proval from his family. Literature gave the
young self-taught writer reason to live and
to hope. At age 16, Wright wrote his ﬁrst
short story entitled “The Voodoo of Hell’s
Half Acre,” which was published in a
Negro newspaper. The story garnered the
wrath of his zealous grandmother for its
sacrilegious language.
Graduating as class valedictorian from
ninth grade at 17 in 1925, Wright, with
little hope of a better future, cast his eyes
North. From the distance of the South, it
appeared a promised land. However, his
arrival in Chicago, Illinois, in 1927 after a
two-year stint of manual labor in Memphis,
dissolved his optimism. He worked many
manual positions as a cook, janitor, and
hospital worker after he brought his
mother and brother North, while stealing
moments to continue his voracious reading
habit begun in Memphis and to embark
upon efforts to teach himself the craft of
writing. His efforts were rewarded when his
short story “Superstition” won a writing
contest sponsored by Abbott’s Monthly
Novelist Richard Wright, photographed in 1939.
Wright introduced a new realism to literary treatments
of race and racism in American literature. (Library of
Congress)
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868

1152 W RIGHT,R ICHARD
magazine, literary journal of the Chicago
Defender, and was published in 1931. Still
craving for the ﬁner arts, not pulp ﬁction or
romance writing, Wright got a major break
while working as a postal worker in 1933
that opened the door to his writing career.
A coworker took him to a meeting of the
John Reed Club of the Chicago Communist
Party, at which Wright met the great white
intellectuals and leftist writers of New Masses
and other party organs who changed his
philosophies of life and writing into a
Marxist perspective. It was after that meeting
that Wright, like other Marxists, saw the
solution to racial inequities through a class
war against capitalism. The young recruit
went home and wrote his ﬁrst poem, “I
Have Seen Black Hands,” reﬂecting his
new proletarian ideology. Starting out as a
respected poet, Wright plunged enthusias-
tically into his writing apprenticeship with
party intellectuals.
Wright, by 1934, was gaining popular-
ity as a poet, publishing his works in party
organs such as New Masses, Left Front, In-
ternational Literature, and The Anvil maga-
zines. At night, however, he worked
steadily on his ﬁrst love, writing ﬁction. In
two years he had completed a novel and a
series of short stories, all but one of which
met with rejections: “Big Boy Leaves
Home.” This story earned him the Story
prize in 1936 along with a contract with
Harper and Row. At this juncture, not only
had Wright become independent of the
Communist Party by working for pay as a
writer for the Federal Writers Project, but
he openly broke with the Communists be-
cause they insisted upon controlling his in-
tellectuality and dictating the politicization
of his art, which Wright dismissed as rote
dogma. Thus, Wright moved to New York
in 1937 to not only remove himself from
the tensions and attacks of the Chicago
Communist Party and to take on writing
for the Communist Daily Worker but also
to fulﬁll his contract with Harper and Row
and to hire a literary agent. The conse-
quence of these decisions proved to be wise;
through his literary agent, Wright earned a
Guggenheim Fellowship to complete the
ﬁrst draft of his novel Native Son, which
would be published in 1940. Native Son
garnered Wright both national and interna-
tional acclaim that earned him the mantle
of foremost black writer in America since
W . E. B. Du Bois, Booker T . Washington,
and Frederick Douglass.
The Book-of-the-Month Club selec-
tion of Native Son in March 1940 was the
beginning of multiple accolades accorded
to Wright, as well as public speaking en-
gagements and travels beyond America’s
boundaries. While turning out his novel-
turned-short-story “Almos’ A Man” (1940),
his novella The Man Who Lived Under-
ground (1941), and his photographic text
12 Million Black Voices: A Folk History in
the United States (1941)—which still holds
its position as a “classic” in the genre—
Wright worked with Paul Green to adapt
Native Son for the stage and began writing
his autobiography American Hunger.
Dorothy Canﬁeld Fisher of the Book-of-
the-Month Club insisted that Wright alter
the title of his autobiography, which ap-
peared as Black Boy (1945) and remains in
print to the current year of 2007.
Yet the United States, with its en-
trenched racism and Jim Crow policies and
growing surveillance and intimidation of
Communists, remained unrelenting in its
reach. So Wright bid farewell to America in
1946 and moved with his Jewish wife Ellen
and daughter Julia to Paris, France, where
he remained until his death in 1960. And
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1241 ---
WRIGHT,R ICHARD 1153
while American critics deemed Wright’s ex-
odus to distant shores as the end of his
skillfulness at critiquing America’s race
problems, he, on the other hand, was gain-
ing broader intellectual grounding in
French existentialism. Moreover, at this
juncture in history with the end of World
War II, the emergence of the Soviet bloc,
the Cold War and race for world dominion
with the United States, and the clamoring
for independence of African and Asian
countries, Wright was taking on global
concerns as a Pan-Africanist humanist afﬁl-
iated with African nationalist Kwame
N’krumah and West Indian nationalists C.
L. R. James and George Padmore. All these
leaders were at the Manchester Conference
of 1946 in England to spearhead initiatives
for decolonizing Africa.
Europe and Africa were Wright’s global
playgrounds in the 1950s, and here he
developed his existentialist, sometimes
Freudian-grounded, Pan-Africanist philo-
sophical critiques. He wrote three novels
with American settings of The Outsider
(1953), Savage Holiday (1954), and The
Long Dream (1957). He also wrote three
travel books Black Power: Record of a Land
of Pathos (1954), about N’krumah’s reforms
in Ghana; The Color Curtain: Report on the
Bandung Conference (1955), about African
and Asian race leaders meeting in Indone-
sia and voting not to align themselves
against the West; and Pagan Spain: A Re-
port of a Journey into the Past (1957), about
Franco’s fascist policies and persecutions of
Protestants whom Wright labeled as “white
Negroes.” A collection of essays entitled
White Man, Listen! (1957) provided
Wright’s assessment of the criteria required
of black literature, echoing “A Blueprint for
Negro Writing,” an essay he had published
in 1937. The collection has additional
commentary about the political affairs of
Africa and Asia not published in his travel
books. A fourth travel book entitled French
West Africa that was circumvented by
Wright’s untimely death of a heart attack in
a Paris clinic on November 28, 1960,
would have illuminated the expansion of
the author’s mind in terms of his Pan-
Africanist visions for West Africa from his
position as a rootless, self-appointed global
humanist ﬁghting white imperialism and
oppression for people of color worldwide.
Since Wright’s death, his works have
continued to remain popular, especially
since black masculine studies and gender
studies gained new footing in the 1990s,
but most importantly, because, as Wright
forecasted in The Color Curtain, postcolo-
nial studies have emerged and prevailed as
well. Moreover, his estate has released
posthumously his novels Lawd T oday
(1963) and Rite of Passage (1994), and the
second half of his autobiography, retitled
American Hunger (1977), that enable more
ways for scholars and students to study
Wright since only a select number of the
author’s private letters have been released.
Virginia Whatley Smith

YORUBA
Yoruba people mainly live in southwest
Nigeria: Lagos, Ogun, Oyo, Osun, Ondo,
Kwara, and part of Bendel states. They speak
Yoruba language and are linked together by
culture, language, and history. The Yoruba
consist of many kingdoms: Oyo, Ijebu,
Egado, Ekiti, Ijesha, and Egba. Yoruba
people originated from Ile-Ife, today’s capi-
tal of Ondo State. According to the Yoruba
creation myth, Oduduwa, the founder of
the Yoruba, landed at Ile-Ife after his descent
from heaven. Ile-Ife remained the ﬁrst
capital city of the Yoruba until Oyo became
the capital city in the nineteenth century.
Major cities in Yorubaland include Lagos,
Abeokuta, Ibadan, Ijebu-Ode, Oyo,
Oshogbo, O gbomoso, Ile-Ife, Ilesha, and
Ondo. Hausa people used the name Yoruba
for the people of Oyo kingdom. Yoruba are
people of great culture, unique traditions,
and the most social group in West Africa, as
evident in their arts, music, and religions.
They earn their social status through hard
work and service to their community. Their
population is 25 million.
The Yoruba are extremely religious.
Religion is the core governing principle of
their lives. They believe in one Supreme
God (Olorun/Olodumare) and many lesser
gods (orishas), including Sango (the god of
thunder and lightning), Ifa or Orunmila
(the god of divination and knowledge),
Ogun (the god of war and iron), and Oya
(the goddess of the sea). The lesser gods
function as intermediaries to the Supreme
God. Orishas’ powers are sought after for
protection and blessings. The Yoruba are
tolerant and accommodative of other reli-
gions and live peacefully with them. Many
Yoruba have converted to Islam or Chris-
tianity; yet they often fall back onto their
orishas in difﬁcult times.
The Yoruba political structure is based
on democracy. They select and appoint
their traditional rulers and kings through
electoral committees of chiefs. They unseat
or exile their leaders when they fail to serve
them. Women also play essential roles in
the political, religious, economic, and so-
cial lives of the Yoruba, especially on trade
and market issues.
Yoruba interaction with the outside
world began with the Portuguese in the six-
teenth century, with the British in the nine-
teenth century, and with the Muslim traders
in the nineteenth century. During the eigh-
teenth and nineteenth centuries, the Yoruba
engaged in transatlantic slave trade and sold
their own people to Europeans who shipped
them to the New World. They found them-
selves in slavery in Brazil, Cuba, Jamaica,
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1244 ---
1156 Y ORUBA
and South and North America. Their expe-
riences in slavery were tragic. However, be-
fore their emancipation and the return of
some of them to Liberia, they left behind
aspects of their culture: music, religions,
arts, storytelling, and tribal medicine. They
created their own feasts, drama, painting,
dance and entertainments, which still dom-
inate the daily life of people in the countries
where the Yoruba were slaves.
The main occupations of the Yoruba are
farming and trading. They produce cocoa
and kola nut for exportation, and yams,
maize, plantains, beans, and peanuts for
local consumption. They engage in black-
smithing, textile manufacturing, and wood-
working, and invest heavily in education.
The missionaries introduced Western educa-
tion into Yorubaland in the 1860s the
through the ex-slaves. Before Western educa-
tion, there were local Islamic schools in
Yorubaland. The Yoruba’s value of education
is evident today in the many universities,
colleges, schools, and technical institutions
in Yorubaland. Due to their advancement in
Western and Middle East educations, The
Yoruba work and serve in all disciplines in
Nigeria, West Africa, Arabia, Europe, and
America. Finally, they exhibit a very strong
sense of right and wrong. Good character
and high moral standards are of paramount
importance to them. Yoruba are proud of
their culture, history, and arts, which have
won international recognition.
Yushau Sodiq

ZAMBIA
With a population of about 10,462,000,
Zambia, in southern Africa, is dominated
by the copper industry and farming. Orig-
inally under the control of the British
South African Company, the area that is
now Zambia was administered as North-
Eastern Rhodesia and North-Western
Rhodesia from 1895 until 1911, when the
two regions were brought together to form
Northern Rhodesia.
The most important factor in the
colony’s economy was copper. Its discovery
is partly owed to an American, Frederick
Russell Burnham. In the United States, he
had worked copper mines and saw many
similarities when he was near the Kafue
River in Northern Rhodesia. In 1895, ﬁ-
nanced by British and South Africa busi-
nessmen, he began a massive exploration
project that found rich deposits of copper.
Railways were established to take the copper
through Mozambique to the coast where it
could be shipped overseas.
In 1924, the ﬁrst governor of Northern
Rhodesia was appointed. The fourth gover-
nor, from 1934 to 1938, was Hubert
Winthrop Young, who, after his term ended,
was appointed governor of T rinidad. He was
succeeded by John Maybin; Maybin’s
successor, Eubule John Waddington, had
previously been governor of Barbados. By
this time plans had been drawn up for a
proposed merger of Northern Rhodesia
with Southern Rhodesia and Nyasaland.
This plan followed from the meeting of
the 1938 Rhodesia-Nyasaland Royal Com-
mission that included in its members
Patrick Ashley Cooper, who later moved to
Argentina where he became a prominent
businessman and chairman and managing
director of the Buenos Aires Waterworks
Company Ltd. The merger ﬁnally came
about in 1953 with the creation of the
Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland.
When the federation was dissolved in 1963,
Northern Rhodesia gained its indepen-
dence as Zambia on October 24, 1964, and
remains a republic within the British
Commonwealth.
The ﬁrst president of Zambia was
Kenneth Kaunda, who had been chief min-
ister for nine months until independence.
He remained president until 1991. During
that time he became a major ﬁgure in the
British Commonwealth, establishing strong
links with Canada. Kebby Musokotwane,
who was prime minister from 1985 until
1989, later served as high commissioner to
Canada.
There has been a steady migration of
people from Zambia to the United States.

ZIMBABWE
Geography
The Republic of Zimbabwe is a landlocked
nation located in southern Africa. Formerly
known as Southern Rhodesia and then
Rhodesia, its name, Zimbabwe, means
“great house of stone” in Shona and refers
to the country’s many monumental stone
structures. Harare is the capital. Zimbabwe
is bordered by South Africa to the south,
Mozambique to the east, Zambia to the
north, and Botswana to the west. The total
area of the country is 242 square miles
(390,580 square kilometers), which makes
it slightly larger in area than the state of
Montana. The terrain is mostly high
plateau with the majority of the country at
altitudes between 984 feet (300 meters)
and 4,101 feet (1,250 meters). There are
three major elevation levels: an elevated
ridge called the high veldt which runs from
the southwest to the northeast, a middle
veldt which slopes down from either side
of the high veldt, and a low veldt that
reaches as low as 531 feet (162 meters) in the
southeast of the country, and includes
the Zambezi River valley in the northwest.
The eastern highlands form the border
with Mozambique to the east, and the
highest point in this range is Mount
Inyangani, at an elevation of 8,503 feet
(2,592 meters). Other important geo-
graphical landmarks are the Victoria Falls,
bordering Zambia, which are considered
the world’s largest curtain of falling water at
a width of 1 mile (1.7 kilometers), and Lake
Kariba, the world’s second largest man-
made dam, also on the Zambezi, which was
opened in 1960 after a four-year building
process that cost 87 workers’ lives and dis-
placed hundreds of inhabitants.
Due to its high elevation Zimbabwe
has a modiﬁed tropical climate. The rainy
season runs from November to March,
although rainfall can be unpredictable and
droughts are common. Average tempera-
tures range from 60.8°F (16°C) in July to
69.8°F (21°C) in January, although average
temperatures in the months before the
rains start can run higher, and the low veldt
often sees temperatures above 95°F (35°C)
toward the end of the rainy season.
The most widespread ecosystem in
Zimbabwe is savanna grassland, although
indigenous woodlands are also prevalent.
Mineral resources include coal, chromium,
iron, asbestos, gold, nickel, lithium, tin,
and platinum. Large outcroppings of
dolomite and granite led to a distinctive
landscape, particularly where erosion has
led to the formation of balancing rock for-
mations, such as the Matobo Hills in the
southwest.
People
According to July 2005 census estimates,
Zimbabwe’s population is 12,746,990 and
the population growth rate is 0.51 percent.
Youth make up a signiﬁcant portion of the
population: 39.2 percent are under the age
of 15 years. The vast majority of the popu-
lation is comprised of Bantu-speaking
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1247 ---
ZIMBABWE 1159
black Africans. Shona make up 82 percent
of the population, Ndebele 14 percent, other
African ethnic groups 2 percent, mixed race
and Asians 1 percent, and whites less than
1 percent. Zimbabwe’s ofﬁcial language is
English.
The most prevalent religions in
Zimbabwe are indigenous beliefs and
Christianity. Fifty percent of the popula-
tion practices a syncretic mixture of indige-
nous traditional belief and Christianity, 25
percent are Christian (with Roman
Catholicism, Anglicanism, and various
Protestant denominations represented), 24
percent practice indigenous traditional reli-
gion, and another 1 percent are Muslim,
Hindu, Jewish, or other. The 2003 estimates
place the Zimbabwean literacy rate in
English at 90.7 percent for the total popu-
lation, with a rate of 94.2 percent for males
and 87.2 percent for females. Education is
free and compulsory for children between
the ages of 7 and 15.
History and Politics
The earliest inhabitants were the San
(Bushmen), whose rock paintings can still
be seen. From the ﬁrst century BCE Bantu-
speaking immigrants, likely from East
Africa or the Congo, began to arrive and
peacefully coexisted with the small, dis-
persed San population. They brought inno-
vations in iron working and pottery, and
introduced crop cultivation and animal do-
mestication. By the end of the fourth cen-
tury CE there were two geographical clus-
ters, the Ziwa culture centered at Nyanga
and the Gokomere, which covered the
southern area. This latter group may have
migrated, or a third group arrived to form
another cluster at Leopard’s Kopje, which
introduced mining, particularly for gold.
By 900 CE there were important trade
links with East Africa: ivory, gold, and cop-
per were exchanged for cloth, beads, china,
and seashells. From about 1075 CE the
Karanga civilization became dominant.
They introduced important innovations:
building in stone without mortar, organiz-
ing a centralized state, and a monotheistic
state religion, the Mwari cult (which coex-
isted with ancestral worship). The Karanga
kingdom expanded rapidly in the ﬁfteenth
century under the rule of King Mutota,
who became known as Mwene Mutapa
(the one who pillages), which the Por-
tuguese corrupted to Monomutapa. He
established an empire that eventually in-
cluded all of modern-day Zimbabwe and
parts of Mozambique. The Monomutapa
empire began to shrink with the arrival of
better-armed Portuguese and the rise of the
Rozvi dynasty under its first leader,
Changa. The Rozvi remained a political
hegemony until 1831.
From the 1830s a series of invasions,
ﬁrst by the Ngoni people from the south,
and then by the forces of Mzilikazi (who
had founded the Ndebele state in 1821),
brought the Shona under domination.
When Mzilikazi died in 1868, his son
Lobengula was installed as king. In 1888
Lobengula granted the Brit Cecil Rhodes
the Rudd Concession. The document ap-
peared in two versions, and the translation
given to Lobengula misrepresented the
rights sought as limited mining access for
a small number of European prospectors.
Efforts to repudiate the concession failed.
The first collective resistance to
European invasion was the Ndebele and
Shona uprisings known as the first
Chimurenga in 1896–1897. The uprisings
began in March 1896 in Matebeleland, and
by June, the Shona had also started a war of
resistance, inspired by the leadership of two
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1248 ---
1160 Z IMBABWE
spirit mediums, Sekuru Kaguvi and Mbuya
Nehanda, and Chief Makoni. All three
were eventually executed. After the Shona
uprising was suppressed, settlers began to
arrive (although in limited numbers, due to
the limited mineral wealth). The 1930
Land Apportionment Act formalized the
dispossession of indigenous Zimbabweans
by granting 50 percent of the country’s
land to white settlers (and the most fertile
land at that) and 30 percent to Africans.
When European settlers began to arrive in
greater numbers after World War II,
Africans were forcibly removed to the
Special Native Areas and reserves.
In 1953 the Federation of Rhodesia
and Nyasaland was formed to include the
territories of modern-day Zambia, Malawi,
and Zimbabwe. Frustration with discrimi-
natory colonial policies fostered several
underground resistance groups and by the
mid-1950s it was felt that a common front
was needed. In 1957 the Southern Rhodesia
African National Congress was formed but
was banned within two years. Other parties
would follow. Meanwhile, in 1963, the
federation dissolved and Malawi and
Zambia gained independence. However, in
Southern Rhodesia, the new prime minis-
ter, Ian Douglas Smith, of the Rhodesian
Front, made a unilateral declaration of in-
dependence (UDI). This brought interna-
tional condemnation and further fueled the
resistance.
By 1964 the leading resistance groups
were the Zimbabwe African People’s Union
(ZAPU) and the Zimbabwe African
National Union (ZANU). These groups
began armed struggle against white rule,
gathering momentum in the 1970s. By
1976 it was clear that majority rule was
simply a matter of time, and the patriotic
front, which opposed the more reformist
approach of the African National Council
under Bishop Abel Muzorewa, was formed.
In 1979 Muzorewa became prime minister
of the transitional state Zimbabwe-
Rhodesia. The Lancaster House Conference
paved the way for the ﬁrst elections with
universal suffrage in 1980. On April 18,
1980, Zimbabwe became independent,
with Robert Mugabe as its ﬁrst prime min-
ister and Canaan Banana as its ﬁrst presi-
dent. Mugabe has remained the country’s
only ruler, as executive president since
1987.
In the early 1980s relations between
ZANU and ZAPU deteriorated rapidly.
ZAPU was portrayed as supporting dissi-
dents in the western provinces and
Matebeleland, and its activities were sup-
pressed. Between 1982 and 1988, a low
intensity war was conducted by the govern-
ment in Matebeleland, which was brought
to an end by the unity accord of 1988,
which absorbed ZAPU into ZANU, and
made Joshua Nkomo a vice president of
Zimbabwe. Drought and economic struc-
tural adjustment policies of the 1990s
slowed the pace of improvement in the
postindependence standard of living, and
between 1994 and 1999 women’s and
worker’s groups held strikes. In 1997
Mugabe announced plans for a land redis-
tribution program to resettle black
Zimbabweans on land owned by white
commercial farmers. In spite of the rejec-
tion of a referendum to change the consti-
tution and enable the conﬁscation of this
land from farmers without compensation,
the government proceeded on a fast track
plan for land redistribution. Meanwhile, a
new political party, the Movement for
Democratic Change, led by trade-unionist
Morgan Tsvangirai, posed a new threat to
ZANU’s monopoly of political power,
www.abc-clio.com                              ABC-CLIO                              1-800-368-6868


--- PAGE 1249 ---
ZIMBABWE 1161
winning 57 of 120 elected seats in parlia-
mentary elections in 2000. An increasing
climate of political repression, acute eco-
nomic problems (due in large part to the
collapse of commercial agriculture), and
the undisclosed extent of Zimbabwe in-
volvement in the war in the Democratic
Republic of the Congo have made the
nation a subject of international contro-
versy since then.

ABOUT THE
EDITORS
Noelle Morrissette is assistant professor of English at the University of North Carolina at
Greensboro. She received her Ph.D. in African American studies and English literature
from Yale University in 2002. Her publications include an introduction to James Weldon
Johnson’s novel, The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man, and essays on black perfor-
mance and black feminism. Forthcoming works include a book on James Weldon
Johnson’s life and works and a study of feminism in post-soul black culture.
Richard M. Juang, Ph.D., is an independent scholar living in Boston, Massachusetts, who
has taught at Susquehanna University, Oberlin College, and Cornell University. A special-
ist in the transatlantic literature of eighteenth-century Britain and the Caribbean, he is a
contributor to the Encyclopedia of Britain and the Americas (ABC-CLIO). His writing
also appears in the Greenwood Encyclopedia of African American Literature, Contemporary
Justice Review, Symbiosis, and New Perspectives in Transatlantic Studies.
